# What Movers Actually Cost in St. Louis (and the Question That Makes Quotes Comparable)

Revised July 28, 2026

How much do movers actually cost?

**Most local moves land between $500 and $2,500**, driven by volume and access. But two things make quotes incomparable: **hourly rates are quoted two different ways** — some per mover, some per crew, so “$50/hr” and “$100/hr” can be identical — and **travel time is usually billed and rarely mentioned**. ⚠️ Page one for this search is other cities’ template pages: Oregon, Indianapolis, Houston, Los Angeles. 💡 Ask four things before comparing anything: **is that per mover or per crew** · **when does the clock start — when you leave your shop or when you arrive at my house** · **are there separate charges for the truck, equipment, blankets, boxes or tape** · **is the estimate binding**. An all-in hourly rate covering truck and materials is a completely different number from the same rate plus supplies.

You have a closing date, a lease that ends on the 31st, and a vague sense that movers cost either four hundred dollars or four thousand.

So you search it, and the top results tell you what movers cost in Oregon. Then Indianapolis. Then Houston, then Los Angeles. Which is a strange way to answer a question nobody asked.

## How much do movers actually cost?

For a local move, most households land somewhere between **$500 and $2,500**, driven almost entirely by how much stuff you have and how hard it is to carry.

But before you compare a single quote, know the two things that make quotes incomparable:

- **Hourly rates are quoted two different ways.**Some companies quote- *per mover*, some quote- *per crew*. A “$50 an hour” quote and a “$100 an hour” quote can be the identical price.
- **Travel time is usually billed and rarely mentioned.**Many companies charge for driving from their yard to you and back again, which can add an hour or two to a job you thought was three.

Ask these four before comparing a single price:

- **Is that rate per mover, or for the whole crew?**
- **When does the clock start — when you leave your shop, or when you arrive at my house?**And when does it stop?
- **Are there separate charges for the truck, equipment, blankets, boxes or tape?**
- **Is the estimate binding, non-binding, or binding not-to-exceed?**

That third one matters more than it sounds, because the hourly figure is often *labor only*. A three-person crew quoted at $175 an hour can arrive and bill the truck, the blankets, the boxes and the tape as separate line items on top of it. Nothing about “$175 an hour” tells you which arrangement you are in, and the difference across a full day is substantial. Ask what the rate covers and what it does not, item by item, and get the answer before the truck is loaded rather than when the invoice appears.

## Why the published numbers are useless

Line up what the top results actually say and the problem is obvious — they are not measuring the same thing.

- A storage company: **$25 to $50 an hour per mover**, roughly $200 to $600 for two, with totals from $550 to $12,000.
- A consumer review site: **$80 to $100 an hour for a team of two**.
- An Indianapolis page: **$95 to $110 an hour per mover**.
- A Los Angeles page: **$100 to $170 an hour for two movers and a truck**.
- A moving-quote site: **local average $1,400**, long distance $5,450 at a thousand miles.

Read those again and notice the unit switching underneath. $25–$50 per mover is the same money as $80–$100 for a team of two. They look like wildly different markets and they are describing the same job.

The other problem is geography. Those pages are city templates — the same article with the city name changed. Rates genuinely differ between Los Angeles and the Midwest, so a number calculated for LA tells you nothing useful about moving from Affton to St. Peters.

## What actually determines your bill

Four things, roughly in order of impact.

**Volume.** How much you own is the whole game. Crews and trucks are sized to it, and hours follow from it. This is also the one variable you can genuinely change — every item you get rid of beforehand is money you do not spend moving it.

**Access.** Stairs, elevators, long carries from the truck to the door, and narrow streets where the truck cannot park close. A second-floor walk-up on both ends can add hours to an otherwise ordinary move. Say this up front; it is the most common reason a quote gets revised on the day.

**Packing.** Full-service packing is a separate line and often a large one, because it is labor plus materials. Partial packing — where they do the kitchen and the fragile things and you do the rest — is frequently the sensible middle.

**Specialty items.** Pianos, gun safes, treadmills, pool tables, oversized appliances and anything requiring disassembly get priced separately. Mention them when you book, not when the crew arrives.

## The travel-time charge nobody warns you about

This is the single most resented line on a moving invoice, and it is worth understanding before you see it rather than after.

The specific thing to pin down is **when the clock starts and stops**. Some companies start billing the moment the truck leaves their yard and stop when it returns — which means you are paying for their commute at both ends. Others bill door to door. The difference on a metro this spread out can be an hour or two of crew time on an otherwise ordinary job.

Many companies bill for getting the truck to you and back to their yard. Some charge a flat trip fee. Some add a fixed amount of time to the clock. Some bill actual drive time at both ends, which on a metro this spread out — a crew based in one county working a job in another — can be a genuinely significant chunk of the bill.

None of that is a scam. The truck and crew really are on the clock, and they cannot take other work. What makes people angry is discovering it at the end. Ask exactly how travel is billed, get the answer in writing, and factor it in when comparing two quotes — because a lower hourly rate with heavy travel billing frequently loses to a higher rate without it.

## Binding, non-binding, and why it matters

Ask which kind of estimate you are being given. It is the most important sentence in the whole transaction.

A **non-binding estimate** is a guess. The final price is what the job actually takes, which means it can go up. Most local hourly moves work this way, and that is normal — but it means your quote is a forecast, not a price.

A **binding estimate** is a fixed price for the agreed inventory. If the crew works slower than expected, that is their problem. If you add three rooms of furniture on the day, the binding estimate is void.

A **binding not-to-exceed** estimate is the best of both: you pay the actual cost if it comes in lower, and never more than the quoted ceiling. If it is offered, take it.

For any move crossing into Illinois, the company must be registered with the federal regulator and carry a USDOT number. That number is public and checkable, and a company that will not give you one is telling you something.

## Getting a real quote without the phone call

A common and entirely reasonable complaint about this industry: every site demands a phone call before it will say a number.

You can usually get around it. Most companies will now do a video survey — you walk through the house on a video call, they see the actual inventory, and you get a real quote instead of a range. It takes fifteen minutes and it is dramatically more accurate than describing it over the phone.

Whatever the format, get every quote to include the same things so they are actually comparable: hourly rate *and whether it is per mover or per crew*, how travel is billed, minimum hours, what packing materials cost, fees for stairs or long carries, and the estimate type. Two quotes that do not cover the same list are not two quotes.

## When to move, if you have any choice

Timing moves the price more than most people realize, because the industry has severe peaks.

Summer is peak season, and it is not close — leases and school calendars concentrate demand into a few months. The end of the month is peak within that, because leases end then. Weekends are peak within that.

Which means the cheapest slot is broadly the opposite: **a weekday, mid-month, outside summer**. A Tuesday in the middle of October is a different market from the last Saturday in July, with better crews available because they are not stretched.

If you cannot choose the date, book early anyway. Late bookings in peak season get whoever is left.

## What movers will not take

Every company refuses a similar list, and finding out on the morning of is a genuine problem because these things do not fit in the car with the plants and the cat.

- **Anything flammable or pressurized**— propane tanks, gasoline, kerosene, lighter fluid, aerosols, paint thinner. Drain the mower and the grill tank in advance.
- **Paint and chemicals**, including most cleaning products and pool chemicals.
- **Ammunition**, and often firearms depending on the company.
- **Perishable food**, and anything from the freezer.
- **Plants**, frequently — they do not survive a hot truck, and some companies simply will not carry them.
- **Irreplaceable items**— documents, jewelry, medication, hard drives. Not because they are banned, but because you should carry them yourself.

Paint and chemicals go to household hazardous waste, which every county in the region runs, not into the truck and not into the trash.

## The cheapest ways to move

Full service is one option on a spectrum, not the only one.

**Labor-only** — you rent the truck, they load and unload it — is the biggest single saving for most people, because loading is the skilled part and driving is not.

**Portable containers** get dropped at your house, you fill them on your own schedule, and they are collected and delivered. Useful when the two dates do not line up.

**Truck rental with friends** is genuinely cheapest and genuinely worst, and the calculation people forget is the risk: your furniture, your walls, your backs, and no insurance on any of it.

And the free one that beats all of them: move less. Sell, donate or dispose of things before the estimate, not after — and check whether your city will haul the bulky items for free before paying anyone to take them.

## Insurance, and what “covered” means

The word insurance gets used loosely here, and the default coverage is far thinner than people assume.

Basic liability, which is included at no charge on interstate moves, pays by *weight* rather than value. That means a heavy, cheap item and a light, expensive one are compensated the same way — and for anything genuinely valuable, the payout will not come close to replacing it. Full value protection costs extra and obligates the company to repair, replace or pay the actual value.

Two things worth doing regardless of which you choose: photograph anything valuable before it goes on the truck, and check whether your homeowner’s or renter’s policy covers goods in transit, because some do and it changes what you need to buy.

And note what voids coverage: boxes you packed yourself are generally not covered for internal damage, since nobody but you saw what went in or how. If a box holds something you would be upset to lose, let them pack it.

## Finding movers here

Get three quotes, insist they cover the same list, and ask every one of them the per-mover-or-per-crew question. Browse local movers on the home services coverage map, which covers both sides of the river.

If the move is into an older home, it is worth knowing what you are moving into — what an inspection does and does not cover is a useful read before closing day.

## Frequently asked questions

### How much should you budget for a move?

For a local move, budgeting $500 to $2,500 covers most households, with volume and access driving where you land. Add packing if you want it done for you, and add a buffer for travel time, which is billed more often than people expect. Long-distance moves are a different market and run several thousand.

### What day is the cheapest to hire movers?

A weekday, mid-month, outside summer. Demand concentrates at month-end because leases turn over, on weekends because people are off work, and in summer because of school calendars. A Tuesday in mid-October is genuinely a different price from the last Saturday in July.

### What is the cheapest day to hire movers?

Mid-week, and the further from the first and last few days of the month the better. If your dates are fixed, book as far ahead as you can — in peak season the late bookings get whatever crew is left, which affects quality as much as price.

### What’s the cheapest way to move your stuff?

Labor-only: you rent the truck, professionals load and unload it. That captures most of the value, because loading a truck properly is the skilled part. Portable containers are next. Doing it entirely yourself is cheapest on paper and carries all the risk — your furniture, your walls, and no coverage if something goes wrong.

### What do movers not take?

Flammables and pressurized containers (propane, gasoline, aerosols), paint and chemicals, ammunition, perishable food, and often plants. Drain the mower and grill tank in advance. Carry documents, jewelry, medication and hard drives yourself — not because they are prohibited, but because you do not want them on a truck.

### Is the moving quote per mover or for the whole crew?

Ask, every time. Some companies quote per mover and some per crew, and the published guides use both units without flagging it — which is exactly why $25 an hour and $100 an hour can be the same price. Two quotes are only comparable once you have normalized this.

**Ready to get quotes?** Ask all three companies the same two questions first — per mover or per crew, and how travel time is billed. Browse movers across the metro on the home services coverage map or on St Louis Near Me Directory.

Moving less is the cheapest move there is: see what it costs to clear the rest and whether that old appliance is worth taking with you. Run a moving company? Listing it is how these jobs find you.

## Boosting Your Business's Online Presence Revised July 23, 2026 What are local citations and why do they matter? A local citation is any online mention of your business name, address, and phone number — directory profiles, chamber rosters, blog mentions, news stories. They matter because customers lose trust in businesses with incorrect details, and because search engines and AI assistants cross-check your information across sources before recommending you: consistent citations build that confidence, conflicting ones quietly hold you back. That scattered trail of mentions has a name — local citations — and tidying it up is one of the cheapest ways to win back trust you did not know you were losing. A citation is any place online that lists your business name, address, and phone number. The industry shorthand for those three is NAP. A profile on St Louis Near Me Directory is a citation. So is a mention in a neighborhood blog, a chamber of commerce roster, or a local news story. This guide covers what they are, why consistency beats volume, and how to get yours in order — whether you do it by hand or let a directory carry the load. ## Why do local citations actually matter? Because wrong information does not just look careless — it loses the sale outright. A striking 62% said they would avoid a business altogether if they found incorrect information about it online (BrightLocal, 2023). Both count. The structured ones you build on purpose; the unstructured ones you earn. ## Which citations matter most? A simple hierarchy Not all mentions pull the same weight. If you’re starting from scratch, work down this list in order: - **Tier one — the majors:**your Google Business Profile, Bing Places, and Apple Maps listing. These feed the maps and the AI assistants directly. Get them claimed, complete, and identical before anything else. - **Tier two — quality local and industry directories:**a maintained metro directory like St Louis Near Me Directory, your chamber of commerce roster, and the one or two directories specific to your trade (contractors, restaurants, and medical practices each have their own). These add local relevance the national sites can’t — and a signal that you’re a real, present part of this metro rather than a name in a database. - **Tier three — earned mentions:**the neighborhood blog that covers your opening, the league you sponsor, the local news story. You can’t fill these out in an afternoon, but they’re the ones competitors can’t copy, because they were earned rather than filled out. What to skip: bulk “submit your site to 500 directories” services. Most of those 500 are ghost towns that exist to sell links, and a pile of low-quality, slightly-mismatched listings creates exactly the inconsistency this whole exercise is meant to fix. ## The new reason consistency matters: AI is reading your listings Something big shifted in the last year. People no longer only Google a business — they ask an AI assistant. ## How to Find a Trustworthy Immigration Lawyer in St. Louis Revised July 24, 2026 How do you find a trustworthy immigration lawyer in St. Louis? Confirm the person is authorized to give immigration advice: a licensed attorney (verify free on the Missouri Bar directory at mobar.org) or a DOJ/EOIR-accredited representative at a recognized nonprofit. In St. Louis, trusted low-cost options include Legal Services of Eastern Missouri’s Immigration Law Program, the MICA Project, the International Institute of St. Louis, and Interfaith Legal Services for Immigrants. Avoid “notarios” and unlicensed “consultants” — they cannot legally give immigration advice — get all fees in writing, and never trust anyone who guarantees an outcome. Keep reading ↓Imagine you’ve got a letter with a deadline on it — a court date, a status question, a form that has to be right the first time — and your family’s future is riding on it. Maybe you’re helping a parent, a coworker, or a neighbor in Affton, Bevo, or south city navigate a system that feels designed to be confusing. The single most important decision you’ll make is *who you trust to help*, and it’s a decision people get pressured into every day. Here’s an honest, plain-English guide to finding a trustworthy immigration lawyer in St. Louis — how to tell a real attorney from someone who just claims to be one, the local nonprofits that offer low-cost help, and the questions that separate a good fit from an expensive mistake. ## Where to start Start by confirming the person is actually authorized to give immigration legal advice: either a **licensed attorney** (verify them free on the Missouri Bar’s directory at mobar.org) or a **DOJ/EOIR-accredited representative** working at a recognized nonprofit. In St. Louis, trusted low-cost options include **Legal Services of Eastern Missouri’s Immigration Law Program**, the **MICA Project**, the **International Institute of St. Louis**, and **Interfaith Legal Services for Immigrants**. Avoid “notarios” and immigration “consultants” who are not either of those — get all fees in writing, and never trust anyone who guarantees an outcome. ## The most important warning: “notario” fraud This is the one thing to understand before anything else. In many Latin American countries, a *notario público* is a highly trained legal professional. In the United States, a “notary public” is **not a lawyer** and is **not allowed to give legal advice** — they can only witness signatures. Dishonest “notarios” and unlicensed “immigration consultants” prey on that confusion, charging real money to fill out forms they don’t understand. A botched or fraudulent filing can wreck a case that a real attorney could have won — sometimes triggering a denial or even removal. The rule that protects you: **only two kinds of people can legally give you immigration advice** — a licensed attorney, or a representative accredited by the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) working at a DOJ-“recognized” nonprofit organization. Anyone else — a notario, a “consultant,” a tax preparer moonlighting on the side — is not qualified, no matter how confident or well-reviewed they seem. When in doubt, walk out. ## How to verify a real immigration attorney Verifying credentials takes about five minutes and costs nothing: - **Check the Missouri Bar.**Every licensed Missouri attorney is listed in the free directory at mobar.org, which also shows whether they’re in good standing and any public discipline history. If someone claims to be a lawyer and isn’t listed, that’s a full stop. - **Or confirm DOJ accreditation.**Nonprofit legal reps who aren’t attorneys should be DOJ/EOIR-accredited at a recognized organization — the kind of low-cost help the St. Louis nonprofits below provide. That accreditation is a real, checkable credential. - **Ask about their bar membership directly.**A trustworthy attorney will happily tell you which state bar(s) they belong to. ## Car Detailing in St. Louis: What It Is, and What It’s Worth Revised July 24, 2026 Is car detailing worth it in St. Louis? For most St. Louis drivers, yes — at least once a year, ideally twice. Our winters coat a car in road salt that drives rust and corrosion, and our summers bake interiors and clear coat under strong sun. A proper detail (especially a spring one that strips out the salt) is genuinely protective, not just cosmetic, and it pays off again at resale, where a clean, well-kept car earns a better, faster offer. Keep up simple washes yourself and hire out the skilled work — paint correction, ceramic coating, deep interior extraction. Keep reading ↓You slide into the car on the first warm day of spring and really *see* it for the first time in months: the chalky film of road salt down the doors, the grit ground into the floor mats, a windshield haze no wiper will touch, and a dull grey cast where the paint used to shine. Winter did this. Whether you park in Affton, Florissant, or out in St. Charles, a St. Louis winter is hard on a car — and this is the moment a lot of people start wondering whether a real detail is worth it. Here’s the honest answer, plus how detailing actually differs from a car wash, what the different service tiers include, when to DIY, roughly what it costs, and how to choose a detailer who’ll protect your investment rather than just make it shiny for a week. ## The honest case for a real detail For most St. Louis drivers, yes — at least once a year, and ideally twice. The reason is local: our winters coat a car in road salt that drives rust and corrosion, and our summers bake interiors and clear coat under strong sun. A proper detail (especially a spring one that strips out the season’s salt) is genuinely protective, not just cosmetic, and it pays off again at resale, where a clean, well-kept car reliably earns a better, faster offer. If you plan to keep a car for years or sell it well, detailing is one of the higher-return things you can do for it. ## Detailing vs. a car wash A car wash cleans the surface. **Detailing** is a deep, meticulous restoration inside and out: thorough interior cleaning (vacuum, shampoo, conditioning), exterior paint decontamination and polishing, and a protective finish — wax, a longer-lasting sealant, or a **ceramic coating** that shields the paint for years. It’s the difference between “clean for now” and “protected and preserved.” Think of it as a spectrum. An automatic car wash is maintenance — good for knocking salt off between details, though the brush-style tunnels can add fine swirl marks over time. A hand wash is gentler. A full detail is a different category of work entirely: hours of labor, specialized products, and a finish designed to last months, not days. Knowing which one you actually need for the job in front of you is the first step to not overpaying — or underdoing it. ## What the service tiers usually include “Detailing” means wildly different things at different shops, so it helps to know the rough ladder before you call. Most detailers offer some version of these: - **Basic / maintenance detail.**A thorough wash, interior vacuum and wipe-down, windows, and a spray wax or quick sealant. Great upkeep between bigger services; the least expensive tier. - **Full interior detail.**Deep extraction of carpets and upholstery, shampooing, leather cleaning and conditioning, vents and crevices, and odor treatment. This is the one to book after a winter of salt and slush tracked inside, or before selling. - **Full exterior detail.**A careful hand wash, clay-bar decontamination to pull embedded grime out of the paint, and a wax or sealant. Some add a light polish to knock back haze. - **Paint correction.**Machine polishing that actually removes swirl marks, light scratches, and oxidation to restore real depth and gloss. Skilled, time-intensive work — the biggest visual transformation, and priced accordingly. - **Ceramic coating.**A semi-permanent protective layer applied over corrected paint that repels water, salt, and UV and can last years. The premium tier, and the one where a detailer’s skill matters most. The single most useful habit when comparing shops: ask exactly what each named package includes, in writing. Two detailers can both sell a “full detail” that differ by hours of labor and a hundred dollars — you want to compare the same thing, not the same word. Looking for mechanical work rather than a detail? See our guide to finding top-rated auto repair in St. Louis. Ready to hire instead of DIY? See our roundup of the best independent auto detailers in St. Louis. The easiest way to find a well-reviewed detailer near you is to compare a few at once. If you run a detailing business, being on that directory — with your before-and-afters and reviews on display — is how a car owner staring at a salt-caked door finds you. ## The Best Tacos in St. Louis: A Verified Local Guide
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/best-tacos-in-st-louis
Somebody asks where to get the best tacos in St. Louis, you Google it, and you get a list somebody wrote in 2021. You drive to the address. It’s a different restaurant now.
That’s not hypothetical. The article currently ranking near the top for this exact search is from May 2021, and at least four of its sixteen recommendations are closed or have moved. One of them shut its doors six months after that piece was published.
So we did the boring part. Everything below was verified open in July 2026, and there’s a list at the bottom of the ones that aren’t — because knowing where not to drive is worth something too.
### What are the best tacos in St. Louis?
It depends what you’re after. For traditional taqueria tacos, the Cherokee Street corridor is the metro’s anchor and always will be — Taqueria El Bronco, La Vallesana, La Manganita and the taco counter inside El Torito grocery are all within a few blocks. For birria, Taco Drip STL is the metro’s only true specialist. For al pastor cut from an actual vertical spit, Mestiza on Hampton. For vegan, Terror Tacos on South Grand, and it isn’t a consolation prize.
### Cherokee Street: the anchor
If you only make one trip, make it here. Four genuinely good taco options sit within a short walk of each other, and the street’s Mexican food scene has roots going back more than thirty years — Latino-owned businesses began opening on what was then a largely empty commercial strip around 1990, and the corridor grew from there. Its Cinco de Mayo celebration now draws tens of thousands of people.
Taqueria El Bronco, 2817 Cherokee St. A past winner of the local “Taco de Oro” competition. Classics, executed straight, no reinvention.
La Vallesana, 2801 Cherokee St. Street tacos and margaritas served in a hollowed pineapple. It started in 2002 as an ice cream shop — it’s still a nevería, so leave room.
La Manganita, 2812 Cherokee St. Michoacán-style, and the tortillas are pressed to order. That difference is obvious from the first bite.
El Torito Taqueria & Supermercado, 2753 Cherokee St. A taco counter inside a grocery store — barbacoa, tripa, al pastor. If the idea of eating tacos next to the produce aisle appeals to you, this is the one.
### Birria, and who actually does it
Birria went from unknown to unavoidable in about four years, and now every Mexican restaurant in the metro lists it. Three places are doing something distinct.
Taco Drip STL, 1920 Carr St. The metro’s only true birria specialist. Owner Steph Boyd is a former pastry chef who started out of her home kitchen in 2021 and drew forty-person lines before opening a brick-and-mortar. Dipped birria tacos with fried-crisp shells.
Lucha, 522 N. Grand Blvd. Oaxacan lamb birria wrapped in agave leaves — not the standard beef version, and worth ordering specifically because almost nobody else here is doing it.
Terror Tacos, 3191 S. Grand Blvd. Vegan seitan birria with consommé for dipping, everything scratch-made. It’s a fully vegan, horror-themed taco restaurant, and it has that lane essentially to itself in this market.
### Al pastor and the trompo question
Real al pastor is cooked on a trompo — a vertical spit, marinated pork stacked in a cone, shaved off as it cooks, usually with pineapple on top. It’s the same principle as shawarma, which is not a coincidence; Lebanese immigrants brought the technique to Mexico.
Plenty of places here sell “al pastor” that was cooked on a flat-top instead. That’s not a scandal — it can still taste good — but it is a different thing, and the spit is a quality marker worth knowing about.
The one place we could confirm is running a genuine trompo is Mestiza, 3279 Hampton Ave in Lindenwood Park, which has a “Del Trompo” section on its menu and serves the al pastor with cut pineapple. They also do a Birria Fundida, and they bring you a complimentary potato taco when you sit down. We are not naming other trompo spots because we could not verify them, and guessing about this would defeat the point.
### South City and the Grove
Cuatro Tacos, 3173 Morgan Ford Rd. Michoacán-rooted, sold four to an order, run by chefs Manny and Dorian. Tower Grove South’s reliable answer.
Chico Bueno, 4156 Manchester Ave in the Grove. Chef-driven and smoker-forward — carnitas, lamb belly barbacoa, baja fish. This is the one to take somebody who thinks they don’t care about tacos.
Taco Buddha, 1634 Tower Grove Ave in Botanical Heights, plus University City and Kirkwood. Global-fusion rather than traditional, and they do breakfast tacos from 8:30 a.m. on weekends.
Session Taco, 908 Lafayette Ave in Soulard. Mexi-Cali, bar-forward, crunchy tacos and baja tuna ceviche. More on this one below — the chain has changed a lot.
### North, South and West County
La Tejana Taqueria, N. Lindbergh Blvd near St. Ann and Bridgeton. A taqueria attached to a meat market. Order the barbacoa and the consomé de borrego — lamb broth, and the reason to make the drive.
Taqueria Durango, 10238 Page Ave in Overland. Straightforward street tacos, no ceremony.
La Oaxaqueña, 2925 Lemay Ferry Rd in Mehlville. Oaxacan specialties from an operation that grew out of pop-ups and still runs a truck alongside the restaurant.
El Jarocho, Stonegate Center in Valley Park, with a second location in Maryland Heights. A tienda with a taqueria in it — street tacos and breakfast burritos.
Locoz Tacoz, 7374 Manchester Rd in Maplewood. Birria tacos and street corn.
Random, but: Creve Coeur owners — here’s how locals find you.
### What happened to Mission Taco
If you’ve been looking for Mission Taco Joint and not finding it, the name was retired in September 2024 after a trademark dispute with the company behind Mission Foods. The restaurants became Session Taco.
The chain has also contracted sharply, which most current lists haven’t caught up with. Town & Country closed in November 2025. The Central West End location at 398 N. Euclid closed and became LaPez Mod Mex in December 2025. Kirkwood closed in January 2026, and St. Charles closed in February 2026 and is set to reopen under a different name. As of now the official Session Taco site lists Soulard, the Delmar Loop, and Kansas City.
Reporting has suggested the Maplewood location survived, but the company’s own location page doesn’t list it — so if that’s the one you want, call first.
### Closed, moved, or not what the internet thinks
These still appear as open in currently-circulating St. Louis taco guides. They are not.
Taco Circus on Southwest Ave closed in November 2021; that address is now El Milagro Azteca. Nixta left Tower Grove at the end of 2023 and reopened on Delmar in January 2025 — and it’s a chef-driven restaurant now, not a taco stop. The Taco & Ice Cream Joint on Cherokee closed in June 2024. Taqueria Morita closed in January 2025, El Burro Loco in July 2025, Mezcaleria las Chupacabras in November 2025, and Tacos La Jefa on Meramec in January 2026 — though La Jefa still caters and does pop-ups, which is worth knowing.
Even Cherokee Street’s own food guide is out of date on this — it still lists the Taco & Ice Cream Joint and its Taco Tuesday deal, two years after the place closed.
### A note on Taco Tuesday
We looked hard and could verify exactly one current deal from a first-party source: Sports & Social at Ballpark Village, 651 Clark Ave, running $2 tacos and $5 margaritas — though not on Cardinals home game days, which is a meaningful exception downtown.
Most Taco Tuesday roundups you’ll find are recycling deals that ended. Beef prices climbed sharply through 2026 and taco specials have been squeezed accordingly. Assume any deal you read about needs a phone call.
### How to order like you know what you're doing
A traditional taqueria taco is small, served on two stacked corn tortillas, and dressed with nothing but onion, cilantro and a squeeze of lime. The double tortilla isn’t a mistake or a gimmick — it’s structural, because the fillings are juicy and one tortilla gives out.
The common fillings, plainly: asada is grilled beef. Carnitas is pork, simmered then crisped. Al pastor is marinated pork, ideally off a spit. Barbacoa is slow-cooked, usually beef here, sometimes lamb or goat. Lengua is beef tongue and is far better than the name makes it sound — it’s the most tender thing on most menus. Tripa is intestine, crisped, and it’s an acquired texture. Suadero is a cut from between the belly and the leg, and when a place offers it, that’s a sign somebody in the kitchen is serious.
Order three or four to start, in different fillings. They’re meant to be eaten in a few bites, and ordering one of each is how you find out what a kitchen is actually good at.
### Where this fits
This guide is about tacos specifically. For the wider picture — full-service restaurants, regional cooking, where to take a group — see our guide to the best Mexican food in St. Louis. For a deeper walk through the corridor that anchors all of it, we have a dedicated guide to authentic Mexican on Cherokee Street.
Everything here was verified open in July 2026. Small taquerias change hours fast and trucks move — call ahead if you’re driving across the metro for one specific place.
Two questions come up every time this list gets shared: how much is the average cost of a taco once you order enough to be full, and where can I get good tacos right now without driving across the county. Both are answered by format rather than by ranking.
### Frequently asked questions about tacos in St. Louis
### Q. What happened to Mission Taco Joint?
A.  The name was retired in September 2024 following a trademark dispute with the company behind Mission Foods, and the restaurants were rebranded as Session Taco. The chain has also closed several locations since — Town & Country, the Central West End, Kirkwood and St. Charles — and its official site currently lists Soulard, the Delmar Loop and Kansas City.
### Q. Who has the best birria tacos in St. Louis?
A.  Taco Drip STL on Carr St is the metro’s only true birria specialist, run by former pastry chef Steph Boyd, who started from her home kitchen in 2021. Lucha on N. Grand serves Oaxacan lamb birria in agave leaves, and Terror Tacos on South Grand makes a vegan seitan birria with consommé.
### Q. What is al pastor cooked on a trompo?
A.  A trompo is a vertical spit — marinated pork stacked in a cone and shaved off as it cooks, usually with pineapple on top. The technique came to Mexico with Lebanese immigrants and is the same principle as shawarma. Many places cook al pastor on a flat-top instead; in St. Louis, Mestiza is the spot we could confirm runs an actual trompo.
### Q. Are there vegan tacos in St. Louis?
A.  Terror Tacos at 3191 S. Grand Blvd is a fully vegan, horror-themed taco restaurant making everything from scratch, including a seitan birria with dipping consommé. It’s the only dedicated vegan taco restaurant in the metro.
### Q. Which St. Louis taco places have closed recently?
A.  Taco Circus closed in 2021, The Taco & Ice Cream Joint in June 2024, Taqueria Morita in January 2025, El Burro Loco in July 2025, Mezcaleria las Chupacabras in November 2025, and Tacos La Jefa in January 2026 (though it still caters and does pop-ups). Nixta moved from Tower Grove to Delmar. Several of these still appear as open in circulating guides.
### Q. Where can I get tacos in St. Charles County?
A.  St. Charles County is the thinnest area for verified taco recommendations right now — several spots come up repeatedly but we could not confirm current operation to the standard used for the rest of this guide, so we have left them out rather than send you on a drive.
### Q. How much is the average cost of a taco?
A.  It depends almost entirely on format. A street-style taco on a small corn tortilla is priced per taco and you order three or four; a plated or specialty taco at a sit-down spot costs several times that and comes with sides. Compare per-order, not per-taco, or the cheap-looking menu wins unfairly.
### Q. Why are tacos so expensive now?
A.  The same pressures behind every menu: beef and produce costs, labor, and rent. Slow-cooked fillings like birria carry a real time cost too. Where prices have held is at the places doing high volume on a short menu — fewer items, faster turns, less waste.
### Q. What is a must eat in St. Louis?
A.  Locally the answers people give are toasted ravioli, gooey butter cake, St. Louis-style pizza and a slab of ribs. Tacos have earned a place on that list in the last decade, which is the reason this guide exists rather than a single paragraph in a general food roundup.
### Q. Where can I get good tacos right now?

## How to Choose a Mortgage Lender in St. Louis (First-Time Buyer’s Guide) Revised July 24, 2026 How do you choose a mortgage lender in St. Louis? Get written quotes from at least three lenders of different types — a bank, a local credit union, and a mortgage broker — then compare them on the APR and total fees, not just the headline interest rate. Get pre-approved (not just pre-qualified) so your offer is taken seriously. Before you commit, check Missouri Housing Development Commission (MHDC) first-time-buyer programs, which pair below-market rates with down-payment assistance. The best lender gives you a clear, competitive Loan Estimate and answers your questions without pressure. Keep reading ↓Picture yourself finally ready to buy your first place — a brick two-bedroom in Affton, a bungalow in south city, a starter home out in St. Charles County. You’ve got a little saved, a decent credit score, and a browser with fourteen tabs open, each one shouting a slightly different interest rate at you. Somewhere in that noise is a real question that will shape your budget for the next thirty years: *which lender do you actually go with?* Here’s a plain-English guide to choosing a mortgage lender in St. Louis — the kinds of lenders out there, how to compare offers without getting fooled by a low headline rate, the local first-time-buyer programs worth knowing, and the questions that tell you whether you’re in good hands. None of it requires a finance degree — just a little structure and the willingness to make lenders compete for your business, which is exactly what they expect a smart buyer to do. ## The short version Get **written quotes from at least three lenders** of different types — a bank, a local credit union, and a mortgage broker — then compare them on the **APR and total fees**, not just the headline interest rate. Get **pre-approved** (not just pre-qualified) so your offer is taken seriously. And before you commit, look into **Missouri Housing Development Commission (MHDC)** first-time-buyer programs, which pair below-market rates with down-payment assistance. The best lender is the one who gives you a clear, competitive Loan Estimate and answers your questions without pressure. ## The types of mortgage lenders “Lender” covers a few different animals, and it’s worth knowing the difference: - **Banks.**Big national and regional banks offer one-stop convenience, especially if you already bank there. Rates and service vary, and their products can be less flexible for tricky situations. - **Local credit unions.**Member-owned, not-for-profit, and often very competitive on rates and fees for St. Louis buyers — frequently the friendliest option for first-timers, with a more personal touch. You typically have to be (or become) a member, which in St. Louis is usually as simple as opening a small savings account. - **Mortgage brokers.**A broker isn’t a single lender — they shop your loan across many lenders to find a fit, which is handy if your situation is less than textbook. They’re paid through the loan, so ask exactly how. - **Online / direct lenders.**Fast, tech-driven, sometimes sharp on rate — but you trade the local relationship for a call center, which can matter when a closing gets complicated. There’s no single “best” type — the right answer is whichever one gives you the best total deal and treats you well. That’s exactly why you get quotes from more than one. Need legal help too? It lays out the rate, monthly payment, closing costs, and fees in the same format for every lender — so you can lay three of them side by side and compare line for line. - **Watch the “points.”**Paying “discount points” buys down your rate for an upfront fee. Sometimes it’s worth it, sometimes it just makes a rate look better than it is — make sure you’re comparing offers with and without points fairly. ## Nail Salons in St. Louis: Where to Go, What It Costs, and What to Check
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/nail-salons-in-st-louis
Most guides to nail salons are a list of names and a star rating. That tells you where people liked the polish. It doesn’t tell you whether the tools touching your skin were disinfected properly, or that there’s a flyer Missouri legally requires every salon to post that almost nobody knows to look for.
This covers both. Where to go across the metro, what things cost, and — the part that actually matters — what you can check in the first thirty seconds of walking in.
### What are the best nail salons in St. Louis?
It depends what you want. For nail art, Polish Room Nail Bar in Richmond Heights does bespoke work and Nails By MIMI in Ballwin prices designs per nail. For Gel-X and soft gel, Jonails in Breckenridge Hills and Nails By Sofia in O’Fallon. For the cleanest setup in the metro, Sonder Lush downtown runs waterless manicures and jetless ceramic pedicure basins, and Frenchies in O’Fallon refuses acrylic, dip powder, drills and jetted tubs entirely. For all-inclusive pricing with no tipping, Tints Polish in Frontenac.
### By area
City. Sonder Lush Nail Studio, 2704 Locust St — a solo, appointment-only studio doing waterless manicures and jetless pedicures in ceramic basins. 314 Nails and Spa, 2329 N. Union Blvd, which also runs as a training academy and is one of the more affordable options in the city. Kary Beauty Salon, 5633 S. Kings Highway in St. Louis Hills, with a Spanish-language service menu.
Mid-county. Tints Polish, 10281 Clayton Rd — all-inclusive pricing, no tipping accepted, five-free polishes and LED lamps only. Frontenac Nail Lounge, 9838 Clayton Rd, for spa pedicures and rhinestone work. Polish Room Nail Bar at 18 The Boulevard in Richmond Heights for bespoke art. Olivia & Oliver, 8472 Eager Rd in Brentwood. Nail Doctor Unblemished, 7403 Manchester Ave in Maplewood, which does corrective and therapeutic pedicure work in long appointment slots, booked more like the metro’s top-rated Asian massage and bodywork spas than a walk-in polish change.
West County. Sweet Mia Nail Spa, 13275 Manchester Rd in Des Peres. The Pedicure Plus in Ellisville, a pedicure-only specialist. Nails By MIMI, 13949 Manchester Rd in Ballwin, pricing chrome and French tip and per-nail designs individually. Color Nails in Ellisville for acrylic. Lisa Amor Nails N Spa, 12528 Olive Blvd in Creve Coeur, with tiered spa pedicures.
North and northwest county. Janae Nail Co, 2055 Craigshire Rd in Maryland Heights. Lavish Lab Nails, 2278 McKelvey Rd. V Nail Lounge, 13933 New Halls Ferry Rd in Florissant, open until 8 most nights. Jonails, 9456 St. Charles Rock Rd in Breckenridge Hills, the best-verified Gel-X option out this way — and one of the few that offers Gel-X refills rather than a full new set every time.
South County. Gentle Nails, 9949 Lin Ferry Dr in Green Park, appointment-only and inexpensive. TD Nail & Bar, 9800 Watson Rd in Crestwood.
St. Charles County. Frenchies Modern Nail Care, 3027 Hwy K in O’Fallon. Nails By Sofia, 33 Coach Line Dr in O’Fallon, with the cheapest verified Gel-X in the metro. Sa’Chas Nailz & More in St. Charles for a long-format luxury combo.
Metro East. EXO Nail Bar in Edwardsville, inside a large med-spa complex of the kind covered in our guide to massage, medical spas and wellness retreats, and open until 10 p.m. Tuesday through Saturday. Nail Pro’s, 5800 W. Main St in Belleville — appointment only, explicitly no walk-ins. Mi Nail, 5725 Belleville Crossing St, which publishes its prices, and Kreative to the T on W. Main for colored acrylic.
### What things cost here
These are published prices from live booking pages, not estimates.
Manicure: $25 at Mi Nail in Belleville and Kary Beauty, up to $65 for a signature luxury manicure in St. Charles. Gel manicure: around $35 at Lavish Lab and Mi Nail, $45 and up at EXO. Pedicure: $25 at 314 Nails, $40 for a classic at Lisa Amor or a wellness pedi at The Pedicure Plus, $50 for tiered spa versions, and $85 and up at Nail Doctor Unblemished for corrective work in an 80-minute to two-hour slot. Acrylic full set: $55 at Color Nails, $60 at Kreative to the T, $65 for colored acrylic. Gel-X: $30 for a short set at Nails By Sofia, $75 to $82 at Jonails — where a refill runs $60, which is worth asking about since many technicians only do full new sets.
One pricing model worth knowing about: Tints Polish charges all-inclusive and does not accept tips, and sells a monthly membership for unlimited polish changes. Whether that suits you depends on how often you go, but it removes the arithmetic at the end.
### What Missouri actually requires
Missouri regulates nail work as its own license class. A manicurist is anyone doing this work for compensation, and they need a full manicurist license — not a lighter registration. This is a genuine difference from hair braiding, which Missouri moved to a simpler registration track in 2018. That change applied only to braiding. Nail technicians were never part of it.
Three specific rules in Missouri’s cosmetology sanitation regulations are worth knowing as a customer.
Tools must be immersed, not wiped. Implements that touch your skin must be completely immersed in an EPA-registered disinfectant — one labeled as bactericidal, virucidal and fungicidal — for at least five minutes. Afterward they’re either kept in the solution or stored in a covered container or drawer. A quick spray and wipe between clients does not meet that standard.
MMA is banned in Missouri, by name. The rule prohibits any liquid product containing methyl methacrylate, and puts the responsibility on the licensee to ensure their products don’t contain it. Ethyl and butyl methacrylate are permitted. Worth being precise here, because most articles get it wrong: there is no federal regulation specifically prohibiting MMA in nail products. The FDA considers it harmful in fingernail preparations and removed products from the market decades ago through court action rather than rulemaking. So MMA isn’t banned by the FDA — it’s banned in Missouri.
Callus razors are illegal to use or even possess. Missouri bars licensees from using or keeping a credo blade or any razor-type callus shaver on the premises — possession alone counts as rendering services in an unsafe and unsanitary manner. And every establishment is required to post a flyer about it in plain view of the public. That flyer is the single easiest compliance signal to check, and virtually no customer knows to look for it.
### The thing nobody tells you about inspections
You cannot look up a Missouri nail salon’s inspection results. The state doesn’t publish them and doesn’t require salons to post them, and complaint files are closed to the public.
Kansas City television station KSHB reported on this gap, noting that Kansas requires inspection results be posted publicly and makes complaint investigations public, and that Kansas inspects twice a year to Missouri’s annual schedule. A bill to open Missouri’s cosmetology investigations to the public was filed and never referred to committee.
What you can check is licensing. The Missouri Division of Professional Registration runs a public licensee search where you can verify an individual or establishment’s license status, number, expiration and any disciplinary action, at pr.mo.gov. It won’t show you inspection findings, but it will tell you whether the person doing your nails is licensed and in good standing.
### Pedicure tubs: the risk that's actually documented
This is the best-evidenced hygiene issue in the whole category, and it’s about plumbing.
In 2000, more than a hundred pedicure customers at a northern California salon developed persistent boils on their lower legs caused by Mycobacterium fortuitum, a bacterium that had colonized the footspas. Investigators found it behind the recirculation screens of all ten tubs, and matched the strains from the tubs to the strains from patients.
A follow-up study published by the CDC in 2005 sampled thirty whirlpool footbaths across eighteen salons. Twenty-nine of the thirty grew mycobacteria. Nearly half carried M. fortuitum specifically. Twenty-five of thirty had visible debris or slime behind the recirculation screen, and half of the operators said they had never cleaned behind that screen at all. The organisms turned up whether or not disinfectants were reportedly used.
The researchers were careful to add that while the bacteria are widespread in footspas, the actual risk of infection remains unclear — so this isn’t a reason to panic. But one detail is directly actionable: customers who had shaved their legs before the pedicure were at higher risk. Tiny nicks are the entry point.
The mechanism explains the fix. Bacteria colonize the internal piping and the debris trap behind the screen. Pipeless and jetless tubs have no internal plumbing to colonize. That’s why Sonder Lush’s ceramic basins and Frenchies’ refusal to use jetted tubs are substantive choices rather than marketing.
Wildly off-topic: polish dries in ten minutes, so go eat in Bunker Hill.
Worth noting plainly: Missouri’s sanitation rule for cosmetology establishments does not address pedicure footbaths at all. California adopted specific footspa cleaning regulations after the outbreak. Missouri’s rule, last amended in 2013, is silent on them — which means how a salon cleans its tubs is largely a matter of that salon’s own standards.
### Eleven things you can check yourself
All of these are observable in the first few minutes, and each maps to a rule or a documented risk rather than a hunch — the same walk-in read that separates the best tattoo studios in St. Louis from the rest.
1. Look for the posted callus-blade flyer. Missouri requires it in plain view. Its absence is a real signal. 2. Look for posted licenses, then verify the names at pr.mo.gov. 3. Ask what kind of pedicure tub it is — pipeless, jetless or ceramic basin, or a jetted whirlpool. If it’s jetted, ask whether they scrub behind the screen nightly. 4. Watch how tools are handled. Five minutes fully immersed in disinfectant is the standard; a wipe-down is not. 5. Tools should come out of a covered container or a sealed pouch, not a drawer of loose metal. 6. A UV box is storage, not disinfection. If that’s all they show you, ask what the tools were immersed in first. 7. Ask whether they use MMA. It’s banned here. A harsh sweet smell and a product that won’t soak off in acetone are the classic tells. 8. Notice the air. Heavy fumes mean poor ventilation, which is worse for the technician than for you. 9. Don’t shave your legs in the twenty-four hours before a pedicure. 10. Don’t let anyone cut your cuticles — push them back instead. 11. If you go often, consider bringing your own tools.
Points nine through eleven come from the American Academy of Dermatology.
### Gel, acrylic and your actual nails
A systematic review published in late 2025 looked at fifty-eight studies on nail cosmetics, and the pattern is consistent: acrylates are the main culprit in reactions. Allergic contact dermatitis showed up in roughly half the gel-manicure literature and around sixty percent of the acrylic literature.
One ingredient does most of the work — HEMA, found in about sixty percent of the nearly four hundred products reviewed. Nail technicians bear the heaviest burden: they made up eighty percent of occupational cases in one multi-year study, which is the strongest practical argument for choosing a well-ventilated salon.
On UV lamps, the same review found documented cases of skin reactions and, in one long-term immunosuppressed patient, skin cancers — but judged the overall carcinogenic potential low while advising caution. That’s the honest framing. If it concerns you, LED-only salons exist; Tints Polish is one.
The most encouraging finding: among patients with acrylate dermatitis, simply avoiding contact cleared it completely in eighty percent of cases.
### A note on what we couldn't verify
Every salon above was confirmed through its own website or a live booking calendar in July 2026. Several others that come up in local roundups were left out because we couldn’t confirm them — one salon’s domain now redirects to a parking page, another’s website has an expired security certificate.
Also worth flagging: Sonder Lush appears at an old Washington Avenue address on at least one major review site. Its own website gives 2704 Locust St. When a business’s own site and an aggregator disagree, trust the business.
And one genuine gap: we couldn’t verify a single St. Louis salon offering a Russian manicure from a source we’d stand behind, so we’re not naming one. If you find a good one, we’d like to know.
Two things are worth knowing before you sit down: how to tell if a nail salon is good from across the room, and what type of salon nails are least damaging to the nail you have to live with afterwards. Both are checkable in the first two minutes.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Can you look up nail salon inspection results in Missouri?
A.  No. Missouri does not publish nail salon inspection results and does not require salons to post them, and complaint files are closed to the public. You can verify license status, expiration and disciplinary history for individuals and establishments through the Missouri Division of Professional Registration licensee search at pr.mo.gov — but not inspection findings.
### Q. Is MMA banned in nail salons?
A.  In Missouri, yes — state cosmetology rules prohibit any liquid product containing methyl methacrylate by name, and permit ethyl or butyl methacrylate instead. There is no federal regulation specifically prohibiting MMA; the FDA considers it harmful in nail products and acted through the courts rather than rulemaking. Telltale signs are a harsh sweet odor and a product that won’t soak off in acetone.
### Q. Are pedicure foot spas safe?
A.  Jetted whirlpool tubs carry a documented risk. A CDC study of thirty salon footbaths found mycobacteria in twenty-nine of them, with visible debris behind the recirculation screen in twenty-five and half of operators reporting they had never cleaned behind it. Researchers noted the actual infection risk remains unclear, but customers who shaved their legs beforehand were at higher risk. Pipeless and jetless tubs have no internal plumbing for bacteria to colonize.
### Q. Should you shave your legs before a pedicure?
A.  No — shave afterward, or at least twenty-four hours before. The American Academy of Dermatology advises against pre-pedicure shaving, and the CDC footbath outbreak investigation found that customers who had shaved beforehand were at higher risk of infection, because small nicks provide an entry point.
### Q. Is a UV sterilizer box enough to clean nail tools?
A.  Not on its own under Missouri’s rule. Implements must be completely immersed in an EPA-registered disinfectant for at least five minutes; the regulation describes cabinets only as storage for tools already disinfected. If a salon shows you a UV box, ask what the tools were immersed in first.
### Q. Do nail technicians need a license in Missouri?
A.  Yes, a full manicurist license — Missouri defines manicuring as its own regulated practice covering nail care, artificial nails, and hand and arm work for compensation. This differs from hair braiding, which Missouri moved to a lighter registration track in 2018; that change did not apply to nail technicians.
### Q. How much does a manicure cost in St. Louis?
A.  Published prices run from about $25 for a classic manicure at budget-friendly salons up to $65 for a signature luxury service. Gel manicures generally start around $35. Pedicures range from $25 to $85 or more for corrective and therapeutic work. Gel-X sets span $30 to $82 depending on length and salon.
### Q. How to tell if a nail salon is good?
A.  Watch the things that do not depend on taste: a current license posted where you can read it, tools that come out of sealed pouches, pedicure basins with disposable liners, and staff wearing masks when they file. A salon that is relaxed about being watched on those points is usually the one to book.
### Q. What type of salon nails are least damaging?
A.  A plain manicure on your own nail with regular polish does the least. Gel is gentler than acrylic on the nail plate, but only if it is soaked off rather than scraped or peeled — removal causes most of the damage people blame on the product. Give bare nails a break between sets.
### Q. How much do you tip for a $40.00 pedicure?
A.  The usual range people work from is eighteen to twenty percent, and more if the technician fixed something or ran long. Cash reaches the technician directly in a way a card line sometimes does not, and it matters most in salons where technicians rent their station.
### Q. How much does it cost to get nails done in Missouri?
A.  Price tracks service and time: a basic manicure, a gel set, and a full acrylic set with art are three different numbers, and removal is often billed separately. Ask what the quote covers before you sit down — a set that arrives cheap and leaves expensive is almost always about add-ons.
Own a nail salon in St. Louis? Customers are searching for exactly what you do — and increasingly comparing on hygiene, not just price. If your salon isn’t showing up, that search goes somewhere else. Listing your business takes a few minutes.
Looking for other personal care services? Browse the metro on St Louis Near Me Directory.
If it is a cut rather than nails you are after, the best barbershops in south city covers the chairs worth booking.

## Jiu-Jitsu in St. Louis: Every Academy, What It Costs, and What to Check Revised July 27, 2026 Where can I train jiu-jitsu in St. Louis? The metro has ~18 verifiable academies. Deepest credentials: **Vaghi BJJ** (15739 Manchester Rd, Ellisville) — Rodrigo Vaghi is a 6th-degree black belt under Rickson Gracie, highest-ranked in the region, and taught most of the metro’s next generation of black belts. Strongest competition room: **BJJ Lifestyle Academy** (4274 Telegraph Rd) under Mike Rethmeyer, Pan-American champion. Structured beginner curricula: **Gracie Jiu-Jitsu St. Louis** (Ravensridge Dr), **Gracie Humaitá** (Weldon Spring), **Gracie Barra** (Lake St. Louis, Collinsville IL). Cheapest: **Nomad Jiu Jitsu** (3139 S. Grand) at $50/mo or $10/class, no contract. ⚠️ Published STL rates run $50–$160/mo — the $150–250 figure repeated online is unsupported. Missouri does NOT license or inspect martial arts gyms, so vetting is on you. No verifiable academy exists in North County. Almost every article about jiu-jitsu in St. Louis tells you it costs $150 to $250 a month. We checked every academy in the metro that actually publishes its rates. They charge **$50, $120 and $160**. That number appears to be a national guess that got repeated until it sounded local. It’s a decent illustration of why this guide exists: the useful information about training here — what it costs, who’s actually qualified, and what to look at before you put your bare feet on a mat — mostly isn’t written down anywhere. ## Where can I train jiu-jitsu in St. Louis? The metro has around eighteen verifiable academies. The deepest credentials are at **Vaghi BJJ** in Ellisville — Rodrigo Vaghi is a sixth-degree black belt under Rickson Gracie and the highest-ranked black belt in the region. **BJJ Lifestyle Academy** in South County is the strongest competition room, run by Mike Rethmeyer, a Pan-American champion. For structured beginner curricula, the **Gracie** and **Gracie Barra** schools run defined fundamentals programs. For cheap, no-contract, no-gi training, **Nomad Jiu Jitsu** on South Grand is $50 a month. ## What it actually costs here Only three academies in the metro publish their prices. Here they are. **Nomad Jiu Jitsu** — $50 a month, or $10 a class, no contract. **Arnold BJJ** — $120 a month for one person, $216 for two, $324 for three; wrestling-only $100; six months $648; a year $1,224. They advertise no long-term contracts. **Gracie Jiu-Jitsu St. Louis** — $160 a month unlimited for the Combatives program, with 25% off for military, first responders and law enforcement, and family discounts. So the honest range for published St. Louis rates is roughly **$50 to $160** — not $150 to $250. Most academies here don’t publish anything and want you to call. That’s not sinister, but it does mean you should ask three specific questions on the phone: is there an enrollment or registration fee, how long is the contract, and what does cancellation require. A gym that won’t answer those plainly is telling you something. ## The part nobody mentions: nobody is checking Missouri does not license, register or inspect martial arts gyms. There is no state credential to teach jiu-jitsu here. Anyone can lease a space, buy mats, and call themselves an instructor. The state does regulate professional combat sports — the Office of Athletics licenses promoters, fighters, referees, judges and physicians for boxing, kickboxing and MMA *contests* held in Missouri. But that authority covers events, not schools. It licenses the people running a fight card. It has nothing to do with the gym where your kid takes class on Tuesday. Which means credential-checking and hygiene assessment are entirely on you. # Jiu-Jitsu in St. Louis: Every Academy, What It Costs, and What to Check Revised July 27, 2026 Where can I train jiu-jitsu in St. Louis? The metro has ~18 verifiable academies. Cheapest: **Nomad Jiu Jitsu** (3139 S. Grand) at $50/mo or $10/class, no contract. ⚠️ Published STL rates run $50–$160/mo — the $150–250 figure repeated online is unsupported. Missouri does NOT license or inspect martial arts gyms, so vetting is on you. No verifiable academy exists in North County. Almost every article about jiu-jitsu in St. Louis tells you it costs $150 to $250 a month. We checked every academy in the metro that actually publishes its rates. They charge **$50, $120 and $160**. That number appears to be a national guess that got repeated until it sounded local. It’s a decent illustration of why this guide exists: the useful information about training here — what it costs, who’s actually qualified, and what to look at before you put your bare feet on a mat — mostly isn’t written down anywhere. ## Where can I train jiu-jitsu in St. Louis? The metro has around eighteen verifiable academies. The deepest credentials are at **Vaghi BJJ** in Ellisville — Rodrigo Vaghi is a sixth-degree black belt under Rickson Gracie and the highest-ranked black belt in the region. **BJJ Lifestyle Academy** in South County is the strongest competition room, run by Mike Rethmeyer, a Pan-American champion. For structured beginner curricula, the **Gracie** and **Gracie Barra** schools run defined fundamentals programs. For cheap, no-contract, no-gi training, **Nomad Jiu Jitsu** on South Grand is $50 a month. ## What it actually costs here Only three academies in the metro publish their prices. Here they are. **Nomad Jiu Jitsu** — $50 a month, or $10 a class, no contract. **Arnold BJJ** — $120 a month for one person, $216 for two, $324 for three; wrestling-only $100; six months $648; a year $1,224. They advertise no long-term contracts. **Gracie Jiu-Jitsu St. Louis** — $160 a month unlimited for the Combatives program, with 25% off for military, first responders and law enforcement, and family discounts. So the honest range for published St. Louis rates is roughly **$50 to $160** — not $150 to $250. Most academies here don’t publish anything and want you to call. That’s not sinister, but it does mean you should ask three specific questions on the phone: is there an enrollment or registration fee, how long is the contract, and what does cancellation require. There is no state credential to teach jiu-jitsu here. Anyone can lease a space, buy mats, and call themselves an instructor. The state does regulate professional combat sports — the Office of Athletics licenses promoters, fighters, referees, judges and physicians for boxing, kickboxing and MMA *contests* held in Missouri. But that authority covers events, not schools. It licenses the people running a fight card. It has nothing to do with the gym where your kid takes class on Tuesday. ## Eco-Friendly Cleaning Services: How to Tell Who Actually Means It Revised July 28, 2026 What does eco-friendly cleaning actually mean? **By itself, almost nothing — “green” and “eco-friendly” are marketing words, not regulated terms.** Two things are verifiable: **EPA Safer Choice** certifies the *products*, and **Green Seal GS-37** certifies the *service company*. ⚠️ Every page-one result for this search is a cleaning company applying the label to itself — none explains how to check. 💡 Safer Choice screens every ingredient **including fragrance**, which is normally exempt from disclosure, on a green/yellow/red scale where no red-rated ingredient is allowed. Fragrance is usually what people actually react to. You come home to a spotless house, and the first thing that hits you is not how clean it looks. It is the smell — that sharp chemical bite that makes your eyes water a little and hangs in the air for hours. Then the baby crawls across the just-mopped floor. Or the dog stretches out on it and rolls. And a small thought nags at you: what exactly did they wipe all of this down with? Whether your place is a bungalow in Affton, a rental in Belleville, a farmhouse outside Wentzville or a shared office suite in Maryland Heights, it is a fair question — and a surprisingly hard one to get a straight answer to. ## What does eco-friendly cleaning actually mean? By itself, almost nothing. **“Eco-friendly” and “green” are marketing words, not regulated terms** — anybody can print them on a van. What separates a real green cleaner from a claim is verifiable, and it comes down to two things: - **EPA Safer Choice**— certifies the- *products*. Every ingredient is screened, including fragrance. - **Green Seal GS-37**— certifies the- *service company*, not just what is in the bottle. Ask which of those a company can point to. That single question does more than an hour of reading reviews, because it is the one thing a business cannot answer with adjectives. ## Why the label alone tells you nothing Search for a green cleaner and look at what comes back: cleaning companies. All of them. A map pack of three, then a page of firms with “eco” or “green” in the business name, then two booking aggregators. Every result is a company applying the label to itself. Not one of them explains how you would check. That is not a conspiracy — it is just what happens when a term has commercial value and no definition behind it. The practical consequence shows up in an unexpected place. Look at what people actually do when they need one of these services, and you find neighborhood groups full of posts like this, from the last few weeks alone: *“I have searched and haven’t seen anyone advertising green, non-toxic products, and it’s very important to me.”* *“I searched the group with no luck.”* *“Looking for a house cleaner — need eco-friendly products.”* People who want this cannot find it by searching, so they fall back on asking a neighbor. That is a failure on both sides of the transaction: the customer cannot find the cleaner, and the cleaner — who may well be doing everything right — is invisible to the exact person looking for them. ## The two certifications that mean something ### EPA Safer Choice (the products) This is the one worth knowing about, and it is stricter than most people assume. To carry the Safer Choice label, every single ingredient in a product is evaluated against the EPA’s Safer Chemical Ingredients List and rated on a traffic-light system — green for preferred, yellow for use with caution, red for not allowed. **A product containing any red-rated ingredient cannot be certified.** Nearly 2,000 products currently qualify. Here is the detail that matters most in a house with a kid or an asthmatic in it: **the screening includes fragrance components**. Fragrance is normally exempt from ingredient disclosure — a manufacturer can list “fragrance” and stop there, covering dozens of compounds. Safer Choice does not permit that shortcut. Given that scent is what most people actually react to, this is the difference between a real standard and a nice-sounding one. It is also not a boutique label. Under the fiscal year 2025 National Defense Authorization Act, the Department of Defense is required to purchase Safer Choice-certified products to the maximum extent possible — a procurement standard, not a marketing badge. You can look products up yourself on the EPA’s searchable list, which is the fastest way to check whether the products your cleaner named are actually certified. ### Green Seal GS-37 (the company) The distinction people miss: Safer Choice certifies bottles. **Green Seal GS-37 certifies the cleaning service itself** — how the company works, not only what it buys. That matters because a crew can carry excellent products and still undo the benefit: over-applying, cross-contaminating cloths between the bathroom and the kitchen, running a vacuum that pushes fine dust straight back into the room. Products are the easy half. Practice is the half that shows up in your air. ## The questions to ask before you book Five minutes on the phone settles it. Ask these in this order: - **“What products do you actually use?”**You want brand names, not categories. A company doing this properly answers immediately, because they chose those products on purpose. - **“Are any of them Safer Choice certified?”**Then ...

## DIY Interior Painting in St. Louis: Lead, Plaster, and What It Really Costs Revised July 28, 2026 Do I need to be certified to paint my own house? ⭐ EPA’s lead rule (RRP) **does NOT apply to a homeowner painting their own home** — it governs anyone PAID to disturb paint in pre-1978 housing. Exceptions that pull you back in: you rent out part of the home, run a childcare center in it, or flip houses. ⚠️ But **~87% of City of St. Louis housing was built 1979 or earlier** (median 1938), and St. Louis County’s median is 1970 with ~67% pre-1980 — so assume lead. 🎁 The City offers **FREE lead inspections** where a child under 6 or a pregnant woman lives: **622-4800**. Test kits work in ONE direction — EPA says no kit meets both criteria, so a NEGATIVE is fairly reliable and a POSITIVE is not validated. Never dry-sand or dry-scrape; no heat gun above 1,100°F; HEPA vac then wet-wipe. Plaster holds via “keys” behind lath — plaster pulled loose from the lath is STRUCTURAL, not a patching job. 🔑 Missouri doesn’t license painters, but any firm you PAY must be **EPA Lead-Safe certified**. Federal lead-paint rules do not apply to you painting your own house. That is the actual text of the EPA rule, and almost nobody says it plainly — the guidance you find is written for contractors, so homeowners come away thinking they need certification to paint a bedroom. But before you reach for the sander: **87% of houses in the City of St. Louis were built in 1979 or earlier** — before the 1978 lead-paint ban. The rule doesn’t bind you. The dust doesn’t care. ## Do I need to be certified to paint my own house? No. EPA states that the Renovation, Repair and Painting Rule “does not apply to homeowners doing RRP projects in their own home.” The rule governs **anyone paid** to disturb painted surfaces in pre-1978 housing. There are three exceptions that pull you back in: it *does* apply if you **rent out all or part of your home, operate a childcare center in it, or buy and renovate homes to sell for profit.** If any of those describe you, you are inside the rule and need a certified firm. ## The square-footage numbers are not your permission slip You’ll see thresholds quoted everywhere: more than **6 square feet** of paint disturbed inside a room, or more than **20 square feet** outside, makes a job a regulated renovation. Below that it’s “minor repair and maintenance.” Those numbers decide whether a *paid contractor’s* job is regulated. They are not a homeowner safety line. A homeowner painting their own primary residence is outside the rule at 6 square feet and at 600. Two details worth knowing anyway, because they catch people hiring out small jobs: **window replacement and demolition of painted surfaces are always covered** regardless of square footage, and multiple jobs in the same room within 30 days count as one job for the threshold. ## Why 1978 matters so much here Lead in consumer paint was banned effective February 1978. The ban stopped new sales; it did not require anyone to remove what was already on the walls. Which is why the date lands so hard in this market. **About 87% of St. Louis city housing units were built in 1979 or earlier**, and the median city home dates to **1938** — forty years before the ban. The Missouri Department of Health and Senior Services designates **the entire city** a high-risk area for lead poisoning. And this is not only a city story, which is where most coverage gets it wrong. **St. Louis County’s median home was built in 1970 — also pre-1978 — and about 67% of county housing predates 1980.** Florissant, Webster Groves, Kirkwood, Maplewood, Overland, Ferguson: all inside the frame. ## Before you sand anything, check this Here is the most useful thing in this article, and it is buried on a page almost nobody reads. **The City of St. Louis offers free lead inspections** on residential property where a child under six or a pregnant woman lives. Call the Building Division’s lead program at **622-4800**. There is also remediation assistance, income- and occupancy-based. If that describes your household and you are about to disturb paint in a pre-1978 house, make the call first. It costs nothing and it changes what you should do next. ## Test kits work in one direction only EPA recognizes exactly three lead test kits: **LeadCheck**, **D-Lead**, and a Massachusetts state kit that works on drywall and plaster only. The first two work on wood, ferrous metal, drywall and plaster. Now the part that changes how you should read your result. EPA says plainly that **“to date no lead test kit has met both of the performance criteria outlined in the RRP rule.”** The recognized kits satisfy only the *negative*-response criterion — a demonstrated false-negative rate of no more than 5% at 95% confidence. In plain terms: **a negative result is reasonably trustworthy. A positive result is not independently validated.** A swab turning red is a signal to stop and get real testing — not a confirmed measurement. Real testing means one of two things a homeowner can’t do at the kitchen table: **XRF analysis**, which reads lead concentration through multiple layers without damaging anything, or **paint chips sent to ...
