### 😀 Frequently Asked Questions 😀
### Q. Where can employers post job openings for local St. Louis positions?
A.  Imagine you're a business owner who can practically hear the buzz of eager job seekers looking for local opportunities. Employers can post jobs on St Louis Near Me Directory by purchasing a business listing membership. This connects local businesses directly with job seekers in Missouri and Illinois who are specifically looking for nearby employment opportunities.
Boost your credibility with a local presence
### Q. What government resources are available for job seekers in St. Louis?
A.  Think of these resources as your safety net - reliable, solid support you can feel confident leaning on. Key government resources include SLATE Missouri Job Center, Jobs.mo.gov, and various city employment programs. These offer free services like career counseling, job training programs, and assistance with resume writing and interview preparation.
### Q. What industries are hiring the most for st louis jobs near me?
A.  You can almost feel the energy in the air as these growing sectors are actively seeking new talent. Growing sectors include green energy and environmental services, creative and entertainment industries, community and social services, education and training support, and hospitality and customer experience roles. Many of these offer entry-level opportunities and career growth potential.
### Q. What training programs are available for St. Louis job seekers?
A.  Imagine walking into a classroom where you can smell the fresh possibilities and hear the excitement of others starting new careers alongside you. Training options include community college programs, workforce development initiatives, online certification courses, apprenticeships, and veteran-specific training programs. Many are available at low cost or free, with flexible schedules for working adults.
### Q. How can I transition from military service to civilian jobs in St. Louis?
A.  Picture translating that familiar military discipline and structure into a thriving civilian career where you can taste success in a new environment. Veterans can leverage their leadership skills, discipline, and specialized training by working with veteran employment services, translating military experience to civilian terms, and exploring industries that value military backgrounds like logistics, security, and project management.
### Q. Are there remote or hybrid jobs available in the St. Louis area?
A.  Yes, and across more fields than most people expect. Customer service roles are often fully remote, event planners tend to work remotely through the planning stages and travel only for the events themselves, and compliance specialists review reports from home with occasional site visits. Many of the growing industries covered above offer a hybrid option even when the listing does not advertise it — ask.
### Q. What are the most in-demand jobs in St. Louis?
A.  Healthcare, the skilled trades, logistics and warehousing, and customer-facing service roles have been the steady answers here, with technology and compliance work growing alongside them. The Job Center keeps the current local list, which matters more than any national ranking — demand is regional, and it shifts.
### Q. Why is it so hard to get a job right now in 2026?
A.  Mostly volume and filtering. Online postings collect hundreds of applications, and automated screening cuts most of them before a person reads one. That is why the networking and government-resource sections above matter: a referral or a Job Center counselor puts your name in front of a human, which the application queue rarely does.
### Q. What is the most demanded job in 2025?
A.  Nationally the demand has sat in healthcare and skilled trades, and St. Louis reflects that. Rather than chase a single job title, look at which sectors here are hiring continuously — a sector that always has openings is a safer bet than a role that topped one year's list.
### Q. What is the 3 month rule for jobs?
A.  There is no official rule. The phrase usually refers to the first ninety days — the window where you learn whether the role matches what was described, and where employers form their view of you. Treat it as a two-way trial: keep notes on what the job actually is, not what the posting said.
### Q. What companies are currently hiring in St. Louis?
A.  The list turns over constantly, so a named roster on a page goes stale within weeks. The Job Center keeps the current one and its counselors know which employers are actively interviewing rather than just collecting applications — that distinction is worth more than any published list.

### Essential Job Search Skills: Resumes and Interviews
Let's talk about two aspects of job searching that make many people feel anxious - creating resumes and handling interviews. Both of these become much less intimidating when you understand what employers are really looking for and how to present yourself authentically and confidently.
St Louis Jobs Near Me Resumes and Interviews
### What to Expect in Your First Interview
If you've never been through a job interview before, or if it's been so long that you can barely remember the experience, let me walk you through what to expect so you can feel prepared rather than nervous.
Picture yourself walking into a clean, professional office where you can smell fresh coffee and hear the quiet hum of productive work happening. The interviewer will likely greet you with a warm handshake and a smile, trying to put you at ease because they want you to succeed. They're not looking for reasons to reject you - they're hoping you'll be the perfect fit for their team.
Most interviews follow a predictable pattern. You'll start with small talk to help everyone relax, then move into questions about your background, experience, and interest in the position. The interviewer wants to understand not just what you've done, but how you think, solve problems, and work with others.
Common questions include variations of "Tell me about yourself," "Why are you interested in this position," and "Describe a challenge you've faced and how you handled it." These aren't trick questions - they're opportunities for you to share your story and help the interviewer understand what you'd bring to their team.
You'll also have the chance to ask questions, which is actually one of the most important parts of the interview. This is when you can demonstrate your genuine interest in the role and the company. Ask about training opportunities, team dynamics, or what success looks like in the position.
### What to Expect in Your Next Resume
If you haven't written a resume in several years - or maybe decades - the process might feel completely different from what you remember. Modern resumes focus more on accomplishments and results rather than just listing job duties and responsibilities.
Today's employers want to see what you've achieved, not just what you were supposed to do. Instead of saying "Responsible for customer service," you might write "Resolved customer issues with 95% satisfaction rate, resulting in increased repeat business and positive reviews."
The format might feel unfamiliar too. Many modern resumes include a professional summary at the top that gives hiring managers a quick snapshot of your qualifications. You might see skills sections that highlight technical competencies, or achievement sections that showcase quantifiable results from your work experience.
If this feels overwhelming, remember that professional resume services exist specifically to help people navigate these changes. They can help you translate your experience - whether it's from decades ago or from non-traditional work like volunteering, parenting, or military service - into a document that makes hiring managers excited to meet you.
### Building Confidence Through Preparation
The key to feeling confident in interviews and about your resume is preparation. Practice describing your experience and accomplishments in ways that sound natural and conversational. If you can tell your professional story to a friend over coffee, you can tell it to a hiring manager in an interview.
Remember that employers are looking for people who can do the job and fit well with their team. You don't need to be perfect - you just need to be genuine, prepared, and enthusiastic about the opportunity to contribute to their organization.
### Practical Job Search Strategies That Actually Work
Let's get into the nitty-gritty of conducting an effective job search which amplify your professional skills. These aren't theoretical strategies - they're practical approaches that real people use to land jobs they love in communities across Missouri and Illinois.
### The Multi-Channel Approach
Successful job seekers don't rely on just one method to find opportunities. Picture your job search like fishing in multiple spots rather than just sitting by one pond hoping something bites. You want to cast your net wide while still being strategic about where you focus your energy.
Start with st louis jobs near me searches on local platforms like St Louis Near Me Directory, where you can find opportunities specifically posted by employers in your area. Combine this with broader searches on national job boards, but filter for local positions to avoid wasting time on opportunities that would require relocation.
Don't overlook the power of networking, which is really just a fancy word for talking to people about your career goals. You might mention to the person behind you in line at the grocery store that you're looking for work, and discover they know someone who's hiring. These casual conversations often lead to opportunities that never get advertised publicly.
### Timing Your Search Effectively
Job searching has rhythms, just like farming or any other seasonal activity. Many companies do their hiring in cycles, often at the beginning of fiscal years, after budget approvals, or when specific projects launch.
In Missouri and Illinois communities, you might notice increased hiring in late spring as businesses prepare for summer activities, or in early fall as organizations gear up for end-of-year initiatives. Pay attention to these patterns in your target industries and communities.
However, don't let timing discourage you from applying when you see the right opportunity. The perfect job might be posted at any time, and being the early applicant for a newly posted position can give you a significant advantage.
### Following Up Without Being Annoying
Following up on job applications feels like walking a tightrope - you want to show continued interest without appearing desperate or pushy. The key is to be professional, concise, and genuinely helpful.
A week after submitting an application, you might send a brief email reiterating your interest and mentioning something specific about why you're excited about the opportunity. This shows you're paying attention and genuinely interested, not just sending mass applications.
If you had an interview, following up is even more important. Send a thank-you note within 24 hours, mentioning specific points from your conversation and reaffirming your interest. This small gesture helps you stay top-of-mind as they make their decision.
### Managing Rejection and Staying Motivated
Let's be honest - job searching can feel like an emotional rollercoaster. Some days you'll feel optimistic and energized, and other days you might feel discouraged and question your worth. This is completely normal, and experienced job seekers know how to manage these ups and downs.
When you receive a rejection - or worse, when you never hear back at all - try to reframe it as information rather than a personal judgment. That position wasn't the right fit, but the right fit is still out there waiting for you to find it.
Keep a record of your applications, interviews, and any feedback you receive. This helps you see your progress over time and identify patterns that might help you improve your approach. Sometimes you'll notice that certain types of positions generate more interest, or that particular ways of describing your experience resonate better with employers.

## What Replaced the Yellow Pages? Free Business Listing Sites
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/7-essential-free-business-listing-yellow-pages-for-2025-success
There was a time when getting your business “in the book” was the whole marketing plan. A listing in the Yellow Pages — maybe a bold-print upgrade if you were feeling ambitious — was how customers found a plumber, a florist, or a lawyer. For a St. Louis business owner who remembers that era, a fair question lingers: does any of that still matter, and if the phone book is gone, what took its place?
The short version is that the Yellow Pages didn’t so much disappear as scatter and digitize — the function it served is bigger than ever, just spread across new platforms. This is a straight answer to what replaced the Yellow Pages, whether the physical book still exists, and — most usefully — the free business listing sites a St. Louis business should actually claim in 2026 to get found.
### What Has Replaced the Yellow Pages?
The Yellow Pages was replaced not by a single thing but by the whole ecosystem of online local search: Google (especially the Google Business Profile and the map pack), review platforms, online directories, and now AI assistants like ChatGPT and Google’s AI Overviews. Where you once flipped to a category in a paper book, customers now type a service and “near me” into Google or simply ask an AI for a recommendation. The job the Yellow Pages did — connecting a local customer who’s ready to buy with a nearby business that does the thing — is exactly what these tools do, at far greater scale and with much better targeting.
The most important single replacement is your Google Business Profile. It’s free, it’s what surfaces in the map pack for local searches, and it is, in effect, the modern Yellow Pages listing — except it also carries your reviews, photos, hours, and a direct line to call or get directions. If the old goal was to be “in the book,” the new goal is to be complete and consistent across this handful of digital platforms.
### Do Physical Yellow Pages Still Exist?
Technically, yes — but their role has collapsed. Printed directories are still produced and distributed in some areas, and a small segment of the population, skewing older, still occasionally reaches for one. But for the overwhelming majority of customers, the search has moved to their phone and their browser, and paying for a prominent print Yellow Pages ad is, for most businesses, no longer money well spent. YP.com, the digital descendant, still exists as an online directory, and a free, accurate listing there is a minor consistency signal worth claiming — but the print book is a legacy channel, not a growth strategy. If your marketing budget is going into a big print directory ad out of habit, that money almost certainly works harder on the free and low-cost digital foundations below.
### Where Can I List My Business for Free Online?
This is the practical heart of it, and the encouraging news is that the most valuable listings cost nothing. For a St. Louis business, the free listings worth claiming, in rough order of importance, are: your Google Business Profile (non-negotiable, the single most important one); the major review platforms customers check; Apple Maps and Bing Places, which increasingly feed Apple’s and Microsoft’s AI-powered results; Facebook, which still functions as a de facto directory for many; a strong local directory built for the St. Louis metro; and the two or three niche directories that specifically matter in your industry. Claim each of those, fill them in completely, and keep the details identical, and you’ve covered where the vast majority of local customers — and the AI tools they increasingly ask — actually look.
### What Is the Best Free Business Listing Site?
If there’s a single winner, it’s your Google Business Profile, hands down. Nothing else comes close for local visibility: it powers the map pack, shows your reviews and photos, and is the first thing most people see when they search for a business like yours. It’s free, and a complete, active profile routinely outperforms a half-finished one from a bigger competitor. After that, “best” depends on your business — a restaurant leans on review platforms, a contractor on the listing sites built for their industry, and every local business benefits from a strong metro directory. The honest answer to “what’s the best free listing site?” is: start with Google Business Profile, then add the specific handful that fit your industry and your area. Don’t chase a long list; win the important few.
### Quality and Consistency Beat a Long List
Here’s the mistake that wastes the most effort: believing more listings automatically means more visibility. It doesn’t. What matters is that your business name, address, and phone number are identical everywhere they appear, across a focused set of quality platforms. Search engines and AI assistants cross-reference these citations to decide whether your business is real and trustworthy; when they match, you earn trust and visibility, and when they conflict — an old address on one site, a wrong number on another — you can actually suppress your own rankings. This is why the old “get listed on 500 sites” pitch backfires: it multiplies inconsistency across junk directories. A tight, perfectly consistent set of listings is far more powerful than a sprawling, sloppy one. Before you add a new listing, make sure the ones you already have all agree.
### A St. Louis Business Listing Starter Set
If you want a concrete place to begin, here’s a sensible starter set for a St. Louis-area business, all free. Lock in your Google Business Profile first — claim it, verify it, and complete every field. Add Bing Places and Apple Maps next, since they’re quick and increasingly feed AI and phone-based map results. Set up or update your Facebook business page, which many locals still use to check hours and legitimacy. Claim your spot in a strong St. Louis metro directory to anchor your local relevance. Then add the major review site and the one or two industry directories that matter most in your field. That’s six to eight high-quality listings — not a hundred — and together they cover the platforms where nearly all of your local customers, and the AI tools they ask, actually search. Do those well before you even think about anything else.
### Should You Ever Pay for the Print Yellow Pages?
For the vast majority of St. Louis businesses in 2026, the honest answer is no. The audience still reaching for a printed phone book is small and shrinking, and a prominent print ad is expensive relative to the handful of calls it’s likely to generate. There are narrow exceptions — a business whose customer base skews significantly older, in a specific area where the book still circulates, might see modest returns — but even then, it should come after the free digital foundation, never instead of it. If you’re currently spending real money on a print directory ad out of long habit, it’s worth honestly asking how many customers actually mention it, and redirecting that budget toward the digital pieces that reach far more people for far less.
Unrelated, and we know it — where to book a St. Louis spa day.
### How Do You Actually Claim a Listing?
The process is more approachable than it looks. For most platforms, you search for your business to see if a listing already exists (many are auto-generated), then click to “claim” or “manage” it and verify that you’re the owner — usually by phone, email, or a postcard code. Once verified, you fill in every field completely and consistently: the same business name, address, phone, hours, categories, description, and photos across all of them. Set aside an afternoon, work through your starter set one platform at a time, and keep a simple document with your exact business details so every listing matches. It’s a few hours of focused, mostly clerical work — and it’s some of the highest-value, lowest-cost marketing a local business will ever do.
### Why This Matters More in the AI Era
The reason to get this right in 2026 isn’t nostalgia for the Yellow Pages — it’s AI. Customers increasingly skip searching entirely and ask an assistant: BrightLocal’s 2026 research found about 45% of consumers now use AI tools like ChatGPT for local recommendations, up from just 6% a year earlier. When an AI answers “who’s a good option near me?”, it builds that answer from the consistent, trustworthy local data it can find — exactly the data your listings provide. So the humble business listing has quietly become one of the most important marketing assets you have: it’s how you stay visible not just in Google, but in the AI answers that a growing share of your customers now trust. The Yellow Pages is gone, but being findable has never mattered more.
Looking for the strong local directory to add to your free listings? The St Louis Near Me Directory is a focused, hyper-local directory built to connect nearby customers — and the AI tools they now ask — with businesses across the whole St. Louis metro, Missouri and Illinois alike.
Claim your spot. Listing your business adds a consistent, trusted citation that feeds both local search and AI discovery — one of the highest-return, lowest-cost moves you can make.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. Do physical Yellow Pages still exist?
A.  Technically yes — printed directories are still produced in some areas, and a small, older-skewing segment occasionally uses them — but their role has collapsed. Nearly all customers now search on their phones. YP.com survives as an online directory, and a free accurate listing there is a minor consistency signal, but paying for a big print ad is, for most businesses, no longer money well spent.
### Q. Where can I list my business for free online?
A.  The most valuable listings are free: your Google Business Profile (the most important), the major review platforms, Apple Maps, Bing Places, Facebook, a strong local directory for your metro, and the two or three niche directories that matter in your industry. Claim each, fill it in completely, and keep every detail identical — that covers where local customers and AI tools actually look.
### Q. What is the best free business listing site?
A.  Your Google Business Profile, without question — it’s free, powers the local map pack, carries your reviews and photos, and is the first thing most people see when searching for a business like yours. After that, the “best” depends on your industry: restaurants lean on review sites, contractors on trade directories, and every local business benefits from a strong metro directory. Start with Google, then add the few that fit you.
### Q. How many free listing sites should my business use?
A.  The right handful, not hundreds. Cover your Google Business Profile, the major review sites, Apple Maps and Bing Places, Facebook, a strong local directory, and the couple of niche sites in your industry — keeping every detail identical. Consistency across a focused set beats volume every time; anyone selling “500 free submissions” is offering noise that can hurt you by scattering inconsistent information.
### Q. Are free business listings actually worth it?
A.  Yes — they’re among the highest-return, lowest-cost moves a local business can make. Consistent listings help you rank in Google’s map pack, bring referral traffic, and feed the trustworthy data AI assistants use to recommend businesses. With about 45% of consumers now using AI for local recommendations, complete and matching free listings are how you stay visible in both search results and AI answers.
### Q. What sites can I list my business for free?
A.  Google Business Profile, Apple Business Connect, Bing Places, Facebook, Yelp and your local Chamber — all free. A St. Louis directory on top of those is about local relevance, not volume. The one principle that matters more than the list: identical name, address and phone everywhere.
### Q. What are some alternatives to Yellow Pages?
A.  The maps platforms took the demand, so the practical alternatives are Google, Apple and Bing, plus a category directory where your industry genuinely has one. What is not an alternative is a service submitting you to hundreds of junk sites — that multiplies inconsistency rather than reach.
### Q. Why are there no Yellow Pages anymore?
A.  Search moved the demand, and the advertising revenue followed it. Print directories still exist in some markets, but nobody reaches for one to find a plumber at nine at night. The behavior changed first and the book simply caught up.
### Q. Do they still make phone books in 2026?
A.  A few are still printed in some markets, and you can generally opt out of delivery. Circulation and use have fallen far enough that no St. Louis business should count on one for calls. If you inherited a listing, leave it be — just do not pay to renew it.

## Local SEO Citations & Google Business Profile: An Honest Guide Revised July 23, 2026 What are local SEO citations and do they still matter? Local SEO citations are online mentions of your business’s name, address, and phone number (NAP) on directories, review sites, and other websites. They help confirm your business is real and located where you say, supporting the ‘prominence’ signal Google uses to rank local results. They still matter — and have grown more important for AI search — but your Google Business Profile carries the most weight, so build that first, then keep your NAP consistent everywhere. Keep reading ↓Picture a customer three blocks from your St. Louis shop, phone in hand, searching for exactly what you sell. Whether your business shows up in that little map pack — or your competitor does — comes down to a handful of signals you can actually influence. Two of the biggest are your Google Business Profile and your **citations**: the mentions of your business name, address, and phone number scattered across the web. This is a plain-English guide to how citations and Google Business Profile optimization actually move the needle for local search — what matters, what’s overhyped, and a workflow you can run yourself. No inflated promises, no invented multipliers; just how local ranking really works and what to do about it. You’ll see plenty of guides throwing around dramatic numbers — “rank X times higher!” — that trace back to no real source. We’re skipping those. The honest picture is less flashy and far more useful, because it tells you where to actually spend your limited time. A quick reassurance if you’re a busy owner: you do not need to become an SEO professional to get this right. The highest-value moves are a small, learnable set, and most of them are things only you can do because only you know your real business details. An afternoon of focused work on the fundamentals beats months of scattered effort on the fringes. ## How Google actually ranks local businesses Start with the source. Google publicly states that local results are ranked on three factors: **relevance, distance, and prominence.** Relevance is how well your profile matches what someone searched. Distance is how close you are to the searcher. Prominence is how well-known and established your business is — and that’s where citations, reviews, and links do their work. You can’t change how far away a searcher is standing. But you have real control over relevance (through an accurate, complete profile) and prominence (through consistent citations, genuine reviews, and local links). That’s the whole game, and every tactic below serves one of those two levers. Notice what’s *not* on Google’s list: gimmicks, keyword stuffing, or paying for a hundred junk directory links. Google is telling you plainly what it rewards — being genuinely relevant, genuinely close, and genuinely established — so the winning strategy is to actually be those things and make them easy to verify. ## What a citation is, and why NAP consistency matters A local citation is any online mention of your business’s Name, Address, and Phone number — on directories like Yelp and Bing Places, on your Google Business Profile, in a local news article, or in a chamber-of-commerce listing. Search engines cross-reference these mentions to confirm your business is real, located where you say, and reachable how you say. The key word is **consistency**. When your NAP is identical everywhere — same suite number, same phone format, same spelling of “Ave” versus “Avenue” — the signals reinforce each other. When they conflict (an old address here, a disconnected number there), you fragment your own trust and make it harder for Google to confidently show you. In the current local ranking-factor research, whether your website’s NAP matches your Google Business Profile is a top-tier local-pack signal. It’s not glamorous, but it’s foundational. ## How much do citations actually matter? An honest answer Citations matter — but keep them in proportion. In the most-cited local ranking-factor research, your Google Business Profile signals carry the most weight (roughly a third of local-pack ranking), while citation signals account for a smaller but real share (in the neighborhood of 6–7%). Reviews and links fill in much of the rest, which is why a great profile with strong reviews will usually out-rank a mediocre one padded with directory listings. Two honest takeaways follow. First: nail your Google Business Profile before you spend hours chasing obscure directory listings — it’s where the leverage is. Second: don’t dismiss citations either, because research shows they’ve actually grown more important for how AI assistants and large-language-model search decide who to cite. Consistent citations are increasingly how you get recommended by tools like ChatGPT and Google’s AI answers, not just the classic map pack. Build the foundation; skip the obsession. Here’s the practical version for a St. Louis business: a complete, accurate listing in a local directory *is* a citation. Every consistent NAP entry — name, address, phone — adds one more trust signal that Google and AI assistants cross-reference when they decide whether to recommend you. A profile in the St Louis Near Me Directory gives you exactly that: a consistent, local citation with your real details, reviews, and service area, working alongside your Google Business Profile rather than competing with it. It’s one of the simplest citation-building moves you can make in an afternoon. ...

Keep reading ↓You searched “Bing Places for Business” because you know Google isn’t the only place people (and now AI assistants) look — and you’re right. So let’s do this in order. Otherwise, verify by phone or email (usually instant), by confirming your website in Bing Webmaster Tools, or by postcard (one to two weeks). - **Publish and note your login.**Save, and keep the account details so you can update the listing later. ## Essential Local Business Listing Sites by Industry (St. Louis Edition) Revised July 27, 2026 Which business directory is best? There’s no single best business directory — it depends on your industry. Every business needs the universal core first (Google Business Profile above all, then Bing Places, Apple Business Connect, Yelp, Facebook, and a strong local directory). Beyond that, the directories that matter are the niche ones your customers actually use: Angi and the BBB for home services, Healthgrades and Zocdoc for medical, Avvo for legal, Tripadvisor for restaurants. The best directory is the one your specific customers check. Keep reading ↓You searched for the listing sites your business needs — and most guides hand you the same generic list every time. Here’s the part they skip: beyond a universal core that every business needs, *which* directories actually matter depends on your industry. A roofer and a dentist do not belong on the same niche sites. So let’s do this in order. First, the universal core in one minute. Then the real value: the directories that matter for *your* trade. Then the honest part — how few of them you actually need, and where all of it fits in a real St. Louis growth plan. **Short version: every business needs the same six-or-so universal listings first. After that, the “best” directory isn’t universal — it’s the one or two niche sites your specific customers use to choose a business. Claim the core, add the two that matter for your industry, keep every listing identical, and stop there. Chasing the rest is busywork.** Here’s the map. ## Start With the Universal Core (Every Business, First) No matter your industry, the same handful of listings does the heavy lifting: your **Google Business Profile** (the single most important, by a wide margin), **Bing Places**, **Apple Business Connect**, **Yelp**, **Facebook**, and a **strong local directory**. These are the platforms that feed Google’s map pack, Apple and Bing maps, and the AI assistants people increasingly ask for recommendations. If you haven’t locked those down yet, start there — we cover the full rundown in our guide to the best free local business listing sites. Everything below is what you add *on top* of that core, not instead of it. ## The Directories That Matter for Your Industry So where else can you list your business beyond the big six? That depends entirely on your trade — because niche directories only help when your customers actually use them to decide. Here are the ones that matter, by industry: **Home services & contractors** (roofers, plumbers, HVAC, remodelers): **Angi** (formerly Angie’s List) and **Thumbtack** for lead generation, the **Better Business Bureau (BBB)** for trust, **Houzz** for remodeling and design portfolios, **Porch**, and **Nextdoor** for neighborhood word-of-mouth. For most trades, Angi, the BBB, and Nextdoor are the three that earn their keep. **Restaurants & food**: **Yelp** (already in your core, but critical here), **Tripadvisor**, **OpenTable** or **Resy** for reservations, and the delivery platforms (**DoorDash**, **Grubhub**) that double as discovery. Reviews and photos carry more weight in food than almost anywhere else. **Medical & health** (doctors, dentists, clinics): **Healthgrades**, **Zocdoc**, **WebMD**, and **Vitals**. Patients research providers on these before they ever call, so accurate profiles and reviews here directly shape who books. **Legal**: **Avvo**, **FindLaw**, **Justia**, and **Martindale-Hubbell**. Legal directories with peer ratings and verified credentials are where prospective clients vet an attorney’s reputation. **Beauty & wellness** (salons, spas, barbers): **Vagaro**, **Booksy**, and **StyleSeat** — booking-first platforms where clients discover, review, and schedule in one place. **Automotive**: **Cars.com**, **CarGurus**, and **RepairPal** for repair shops. Buyers and drivers comparison-shop here before choosing. **Weddings & events**: **The Knot** and **WeddingWire** — the two directories couples live in while planning. **Real estate & home**: **Zillow** and **Realtor.com** for agents; **Houzz** for designers and remodelers. Notice the pattern: two or three sites per industry, not twenty. Find the ones your customers actually open when they’re ready to buy, claim those, and skip the rest. ## How to Find the Right Directories for Your Trade Not sure which niche sites matter for you? Three quick tests answer it. **Search the way a customer would** — type your service plus “near me” or “best [service] in St. Louis” into Google and see which directories keep showing up on page one; those are the ones with real authority in your field. **Ask your own customers** where they found you or how they usually pick a provider like you — their answer is your shortlist. And **check a few successful competitors**: the directories where your best-reviewed rivals appear are almost certainly the ones worth claiming. If a site fails all three tests — it doesn’t rank, no customer names it, and your competitors ignore it — it isn’t worth your ten minutes. ## Are Business Directories Still Useful in 2026? Yes — but not the way they were a decade ago. Directories didn’t disappear; their job changed. They no longer drive much direct browsing traffic, and citation *volume* barely moves rankings anymore (Near Media). What they still do is two things that matter: feed **consistent, verifiable business data** to the search engines and AI assistants that decide who to recommend, and give **your customers a trusted place to vet you** in the moment they’re choosing. A complete Healthgrades profile or a strong Angi rating isn’t traffic — it’s a trust signal exactly where a decision gets made. So ...

## Yahoo Business Listing: How to Add Your Business (and Is It Worth It?) Revised July 27, 2026 Does Yahoo have business listings? Yes — Yahoo has free business listings, but they’re no longer run by Yahoo itself. Yahoo Local now partners with The Real Yellow Pages (YP), so you claim or add a free listing at local.yahoo.com/claim-business.html (or through Yext) — look for the free ‘Basic Listing’ link and skip the paid upsells. Yahoo Search results are also powered by Bing, so claiming a free Bing Places listing strengthens how you appear on Yahoo too. Keep reading ↓You searched “how to add my business to Yahoo” expecting a signup form like Google’s or Bing’s. Here’s the good news and the twist: you *can* still get a free Yahoo business listing — but Yahoo doesn’t run it itself anymore. So let’s do this in order. First, the practical part you came for: how Yahoo listings actually work now and how to claim yours in about ten minutes. Then the honest part: whether it’s worth your time, and where it fits in a real St. Louis growth plan. **Short version: Yahoo still has free business listings, but they’re now powered by a partnership with The Real Yellow Pages (YP) — you claim yours at local.yahoo.com, or through Yext, and you look for the free “Basic Listing” option instead of the paid upsell. On top of that, Yahoo Search results run on Bing, so claiming a free Bing Places listing quietly strengthens your Yahoo presence too. It’s a legitimate free citation to check off — just a minor one, not a growth strategy.** Here’s how it really works. ## How Yahoo Business Listings Work Now For years, Yahoo ran its own local listings. That changed. Today, Yahoo Local’s business listings are managed through a **collaboration with The Real Yellow Pages (YP)** — the same brand behind the old Yellow Pages, now a digital listings company. When you go to claim a Yahoo listing, you’re really working through that YP-powered system. There are two practical doorways: **Yahoo Local’s own claim page** (local.yahoo.com/claim-business.html) and **Yext**, a listings-management platform that counts Yahoo among its publisher network. Either way, a basic listing is free — the trick is finding the free option, because both paths will happily show you paid plans first. There’s a second thing worth knowing: **Yahoo Search is powered by Bing.** How your business shows up in Yahoo’s *search* results is shaped by Bing’s index and local data, not by anything Yahoo maintains separately. So the full picture is two moves: claim the free Yahoo/YP listing, and claim a free Bing Places listing — together they cover how you appear across Yahoo. ## How to Add or Claim Your Yahoo Listing (Step by Step) This is the part you came for. It’s free, and it takes about ten minutes. - **Go to the Yahoo Local claim page**at local.yahoo.com/claim-business.html (or use the Yext Yahoo listing tool). Enter your business name and phone number to see whether a listing already exists. - **Claim or create.**If your business already appears, claim it so you control the information. If not, add a new listing. - **Find the free option.**You’ll likely be shown paid pricing plans first. Look for the small link to- **“claim your Basic Listing”**— the free tier — unless you have a specific reason to pay. - **Copy your NAP, don’t retype it.**Open your Google Business Profile alongside the form and move the- **name, address, and phone**across exactly as they read there — same abbreviations, same suite formatting, same area code style. Because Yahoo, Bing, and Google all get read together, a difference you’d never notice is a difference the systems will. This consistency is the whole point; a mismatch does more harm than a missing listing. - **Complete the profile and publish.**Add hours, categories, a description, and photos, then follow the email verification to confirm the listing. Through YP’s system it’s often as simple as: log in, update your profile, publish. - **Keep the login.**Note your account details so you can update the listing later — a stale listing (old address, dead phone) is worse than none. One caveat worth knowing: some large citation services have quietly dropped Yahoo from their databases, so a “set it everywhere” tool may skip it — but the Yahoo Local claim page and Yext both remain reliable ways to manage your Yahoo footprint directly. ## Don’t Forget: Yahoo Search Runs on Bing Because Yahoo Search is powered by Bing, the single best thing you can do for your Yahoo *search* visibility isn’t even on Yahoo — it’s claiming a free **Bing Places for Business** listing. Bing lets you import your details straight from your Google Business Profile in about two clicks, and that clean data then informs how you appear across Bing-powered surfaces, Yahoo included. So the complete, free Yahoo play is really two listings: the Yahoo/YP business listing for Yahoo’s directory, and Bing Places for Yahoo’s search. Do both once and you’ve covered the platform coming and going. ## Why the “7 Yahoo Directories” Advice Is Outdated A lot of older guides — including the one this article replaces — talk about a list of “essential Yahoo directories” to submit to. ## Local SEO for Restaurants in St. Louis: What Actually Works
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/local-seo-for-restaurants-in-st-louis
There are roughly 5,700 food service establishments in the St. Louis metro. About 2,100 in St. Louis County, about 900 in the city itself.
That is who you are competing with for a search that takes four seconds and ends in a decision.
Most advice on this subject is written by companies selling you software. What follows is mostly Google's own documentation, Missouri's own tax rulings, and the delivery platforms' own published rates — including one number Uber puts on its own pricing page that is worth the read by itself.
### How do I do SEO for my restaurant?
Start with the free things Google actually documents. Claim and complete your Business Profile — hours, menu link, photos, attributes. Add your menu through the built-in menu editor, which takes 24 to 48 hours to appear. Set your own ordering links and choose your preferred provider so a delivery app isn’t the default path to your food. Ask for honest reviews and reply to them. And know the limit up front: Google states plainly that “there’s no way to request or pay for a better local ranking.”
### The menu rich result you cannot get
You will be told that adding menu structured data to your website earns you a rich result in Google — a carousel of your dishes, prices, the works.
In the United States, that is not available.
Google’s own developer documentation for the restaurant carousel says the feature “is also only available in European Economic Area (EEA) countries, Turkey, and South Africa.” It is a beta, and the US is not in it. A restaurant in Maplewood cannot earn that result no matter how perfect its markup is.
There is no dedicated menu rich result page in Google’s documentation at all. The menu property lives inside Local Business structured data, and Google lists it as recommended, not required.
Same story for taking orders or reservations directly inside search results. That isn’t something you achieve with markup — Google routes it through a partner program, the Maps Booking API. It is not a do-it-yourself feature.
So is menu markup worthless? No. It helps search engines and AI assistants understand what you serve and confirms your hours and cuisine. Just do it for accuracy, not because someone promised you a carousel that isn’t available on this continent.
### The delivery math, from the platforms themselves
This is the part with real money in it, and every number here comes from the platforms’ own published pricing pages.
DoorDash lists three marketplace tiers: 15%, 25%, and 30% on delivery orders, with pickup at 6% across all three. No monthly fee, no signup fee, no contract.
Uber Eats lists 20%, 25%, and 30% on delivery, with pickup at 7% — though that 7% requires validated in-store pricing, and it’s 10% without. Self-delivery, where you use your own drivers, is 15%.
Now the line on Uber’s own page that deserves your attention. Their Webshop product — ordering through your own website — is 2.5% plus 29 cents per order, with pickup commission-free.
Same company. Same page. Between 2.5% and 30%, depending entirely on whose front door the customer walks through.
We’re not going to tell you to drop the marketplaces — they bring genuine discovery you don’t otherwise get, and for a new restaurant that matters. But the difference between a customer who finds you on an app and one who finds you and orders direct is roughly a quarter of the ticket. Every dollar you spend making yourself findable on your own is defending that margin.
### You control the ordering buttons on your own profile
Most owners don’t know this, and it is free.
Google’s Business Profile lets you add custom ordering links that “direct customers to other web pages where they can place orders” — including your own site. You can set a preferred provider, separately for pickup and for delivery, so that your chosen link is the one shown first. And if a third-party link is on your profile that you want gone, Google states that “providers must remove third-party links from a profile within 5 business days.”
One warning, because it’s an easy mistake with a real cost: turning off “Accept orders on your profile” hides all ordering options — including yours. If your intent is to steer people to direct ordering, set a preferred provider. Do not switch ordering off.
Also worth knowing: Google itself no longer processes food orders. Its own help documentation says that to place an order “you’ll be redirected to the provider’s website.” Whoever holds that link holds the customer.
### The Missouri tax rule that surprises operators
If you sell through a delivery app, you may assume the app handles your sales tax. In Missouri, for a Missouri restaurant selling to Missouri diners, that assumption is wrong.
The Missouri Department of Revenue addressed this directly in a 2024 letter ruling. Its conclusion was that the delivery platform is not required to collect and remit Missouri sales tax as a marketplace facilitator in that scenario — because the restaurants “are the sellers with primary reporting and remittance obligations.”
Translation: the app showing tax on the receipt does not transfer the liability to them. It stays with you.
This is not a marketing question, it is a bookkeeping one, and it is the kind of thing that surfaces during an audit rather than during a good month. Confirm your treatment with your accountant or with the Department directly.
While we’re here: Missouri has a reduced sales tax rate of 1.225% on food, against the full state rate of 4.225% — but restaurants are generally excluded where prepared food for immediate consumption is more than 80% of gross receipts. Most restaurants do not qualify. Worth knowing why, so you don’t assume you’re owed a rate you aren’t.
### Your inspection scores are public, and searchable
The City of St. Louis publishes restaurant inspection reports online. The searchable system covers reports issued after May 2012, and it includes restaurants, taverns, carry-outs, grocery stores, caterers and day cares.
Which means a diner deciding between you and the place across the street can look you both up in about a minute.
There is nothing to do about this except the obvious. But it belongs in a conversation about online visibility, because it is part of your online presence whether you manage it or not — and it is one of the few parts a competitor cannot outspend you on.
Wildly off-topic — even restaurant owners get a night off, and Dardenne Prairie eats well.
### What Google actually says about reviews
Google’s published position on reviews and ranking is a single sentence: “More reviews and positive ratings can help your business’s local ranking.”
And here is a distinction that restaurant-marketing content routinely gets wrong. On replying to reviews, Google says only that helpful and positive replies “can show that you’re responsive to your customers.” Google makes no ranking claim about replies at all. Reply because it’s good practice and because the next reader sees it — not because someone told you it moves you up the map.
Third-party research does exist and is worth reading with the right label attached. A 2026 consumer survey of just over a thousand US adults reported that 74% prioritize reviews from the last three months, 47% say they won’t use a business with fewer than 20 reviews, and 80% favor businesses that respond to every review.
Two honest caveats on those numbers. They are self-reported stated preferences, not observed behavior — what people say they do and what they do diverge. And that survey is not restaurant-specific. Useful directionally. Not a law of physics.
You will also encounter a widely-quoted study assigning percentage weights to ranking factors. It is a survey of 47 practitioners scoring factors from their experience, and the study says outright that “none of the experts have special access to the internal workings of Google’s local search algorithm.” Informed opinion. Not measurement.
### The AI question, without the hype
Pew Research surveyed 5,119 US adults in February 2026: 49% now use AI chatbots, up from 33% in 2024 and 23% in 2023. Of chatbot users, 42% use them to search for information.
That trend is real and it is steep.
What Pew did not measure is restaurant recommendations specifically, and we could not find any credible research that does. So anyone telling you a specific percentage of diners are picking restaurants through AI is making it up.
What we’ll say instead, labeled as reasoning rather than data: these assistants are drawing on structured information about your restaurant — hours, cuisine, menu, location, reviews. The work that makes that accurate is the same work that helps a human find you. You don’t need a separate AI strategy. You need your hours to be right.
### What’s actually worth doing
Free, documented, and in rough order of return:
Fix your hours, and keep special hours current. Google supports temporary hours changes for exactly this. A closed door at a listed open time is the most expensive small error in this business.
Use the menu editor. Items with descriptions and prices, grouped into sections. Allow 24 to 48 hours to appear on Search and Maps. You can also add a menu URL, photo, or PDF.
Set your ordering links and preferred provider. This is the single highest-value free setting on this page, and it’s the difference between a 2.5% order and a 30% one.
Check your popular dishes. Google generates them and lets you edit — and they’re frequently wrong on the item you most want to sell.
Ask for honest reviews and reply to them all. Never buy reviews and never trade a discount for one; both are explicitly prohibited and the documented penalty is losing reviews you already have.
Add menu structured data for accuracy — while knowing the carousel is not available here.
None of that costs anything but an afternoon. And in a metro with 5,700 places to eat, the restaurants that get found are disproportionately the ones whose information is simply correct.
Two questions owners ask before spending anything: what is the 80/20 rule for SEO when you have a kitchen to run, and can a beginner do SEO for a single restaurant without hiring an agency. The honest answers are that a small share of the work carries most of the result, and yes.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How much do local SEO services cost?
A.  Pricing varies enormously and there is no published benchmark we can source. What we can tell you is what the free tier covers: profile completion, menu, ordering links, hours, photos and review responses are all no-cost and account for most of what Google documents as influenceable. Establish what you can do yourself before you evaluate any quote.
### Q. Is doing local SEO worth it?
A.  The free portion, yes — there are roughly 5,700 food service establishments in the St. Louis metro, and accurate hours, menu and ordering links are what separate you from the ones that get skipped. Whether paid services are worth it depends on what they do beyond the free work, which is a fair question to ask any vendor directly.
### Q. Can ChatGPT do SEO?
A.  It can help draft descriptions and organize a menu, but it cannot verify your hours, claim your profile, or change your ranking — and it does not have access to your local data. Note also that Pew found 49% of US adults now use AI chatbots, so a more useful question is whether your restaurant information is accurate enough for one to describe you correctly.
### Q. What is the 30/30/30 rule for restaurants?
A.  It is an informal budgeting rule of thumb — typically splitting revenue roughly into food cost, labor, and overhead, with the remainder as profit. Versions of it differ and no authoritative body defines it, so treat it as a rough planning heuristic rather than a standard. It is unrelated to search visibility.
### Q. Can I get a menu rich result in Google search?
A.  Not in the United States. Google’s documentation states the restaurant carousel feature is only available in European Economic Area countries, Turkey and South Africa. There is no dedicated menu rich result in the US, and the menu property is listed as recommended rather than required. Add it for accuracy, not for a carousel.
### Q. Does the delivery app handle my Missouri sales tax?
A.  Not necessarily. A 2024 Missouri Department of Revenue letter ruling concluded that a delivery platform is not the marketplace facilitator for a Missouri restaurant selling to Missouri diners, because the restaurants are the sellers with primary reporting and remittance obligations. Confirm your own treatment with your accountant or the Department.
### Q. Are St. Louis restaurant inspection scores public?
A.  Yes. The City of St. Louis publishes restaurant inspection reports online through a searchable system covering reports issued after May 2012, including restaurants, taverns, carry-outs, grocery stores, caterers and day cares. Anyone comparing you to a competitor can look up both in about a minute.
### Q. What is the 80/20 rule for SEO?
A.  The idea that a small share of the work produces most of the result. For a restaurant that share is unglamorous: an accurate Google Business Profile, correct hours, a real menu on your own site, and reviews you actually respond to. Do those four before anything anyone sells you as advanced.
### Q. Can a beginner do SEO?
A.  For a single restaurant, yes — most of what moves the needle is data entry and consistency rather than technical work. Claim the profile, fix the hours, put the menu in readable text instead of a photo, and keep the ordering buttons pointed where you want them. Hire out only what stays hard after that.
### Q. Is SEO still worth it in 2026?
A.  For restaurants, yes, and arguably more than before. AI answers and map results both read the same underlying facts about you — hours, menu, location, reviews. Getting those right feeds every surface at once, which is a better return than chasing any single ranking.
### Q. What are the 3 C's of SEO?
A.  Content, code and credibility, in most tellings. For a restaurant that translates to a menu and pages that answer real questions, a site a phone can load and a crawler can read, and the reviews and citations that make you look real to both people and search engines.
Our interest, stated plainly: we run a St. Louis directory, so a listing is one more accurate, structured record of your restaurant — hours, cuisine, location — in a place people and AI assistants look. It is not a ranking shortcut and we won’t pretend it is. Listing your restaurant takes a few minutes.
Also useful: optimizing your Business Profile and responding to reviews.

## Black-Owned Restaurants in St. Louis: What's Actually Open
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/black-owned-restaurants-in-st-louis
In September 2025, Lee Enterprises shut down Feast Magazine.
Feast maintained the guide — the one everybody linked to, the one that got updated when a place moved or closed. When it went dark, the maintenance stopped, and every list that had been quietly copying from it stopped being true at the same time.
That’s why the first page of results right now will send you to a restaurant that closed in 2022, one that closed this past May, one whose owners retired in 2024, and at least one that isn’t Black-owned at all. We checked every name against a source. Here’s what’s actually open.
### What are the best Black-owned restaurants in St. Louis?
For barbecue, C&K Barbecue (4390 Jennings Station Rd) has been serving snoots and rib tips since 1963. For West African, FUFU n’ Sauce (8100 Page Ave) is run by a winner of PBS’s The Great American Recipe. For Senegalese, Chez Ali at City Foundry. For soul food, Gourmet Soul (1620 Delmar Blvd), whose chef won Good Morning America’s Soul Food Showdown. For pastry, La Pâtisserie Chouquette (1626 Tower Grove Ave). For coffee, Northwest Coffee Roasting (4251 Laclede Ave). And in Ferguson, Cathy’s Kitchen (250 S Florissant Rd), which stayed open through 2014 and never left.
### The sixty-year-old one
C&K Barbecue, 4390 Jennings Station Rd, is the deepest story on this list and the one most worth your afternoon.
It was founded in 1963 by Forris and Lucille King, who came to St. Louis from Mississippi during the Second World War — part of the same migration that built much of north city and north county. Daryle Brantley came into the business as a partner in 1982 and opened the Jennings Station Road location in 1983. It has been family-operated the whole time.
Order the snoots if you have never had them. They are pig snouts, fried crisp, and they are a genuinely St. Louis thing that barely exists anywhere else in America — a dish that came up out of making the whole animal worth eating and stayed on the menu because people love it. Rib tips are the other order.
### Where to eat, by what you’re after
Cathy’s Kitchen, 250 S Florissant Rd, Ferguson. Cathy and Jerome Jenkins opened it in 2013, which means it was one year old when Ferguson became a word the whole country knew. It stayed open. It is still there, and a second counter — Cathy’s Kitchen ToGo, 10198 W Florissant Ave in Dellwood — opened on Juneteenth 2024. Diner food, soul food and seafood. Their food later reached Schnucks shelves.
FUFU n’ Sauce, 8100 Page Ave, University City. Adjo Honsou started it as a food truck in May 2022 and opened her first storefront in August 2025. The food is Togolese — West African, built around fufu and the sauces that go with it. She won season three of PBS’s The Great American Recipe. If you have never eaten West African food, this is the easiest possible place to start.
Chez Ali, in the food hall at City Foundry. Alioun Thiam came to the United States in 1999 and to St. Louis in 2013 by way of New York. The food is Senegalese and Afro-Caribbean — yassa chicken, thieboudienne, which is essentially Senegal’s national dish. Sauce named it one of the year’s best new restaurants in 2021.
Gourmet Soul, 1620 Delmar Blvd, Downtown West. Chef Lavinia McCoy won Good Morning America’s Soul Food Showdown, which is a national credential almost nobody in this market has. Elevated soul food — lamb chops, an Old Bay bowl. Their published hours are unusual, running Friday through Sunday, so check before you go.
Jerk Unlimited, 3108 Cherokee St. Jamaican, chef-owned by Trevoy Woods. This address previously held Jerk Soul, whose founder relocated to Ghana; Jerk Unlimited is the rebrand that continued in the space.
### Coffee, pastry and dessert
The most interesting part of this list isn’t restaurants at all.
Northwest Coffee Roasting Co., 4251 Laclede Ave in the Central West End, has been roasting since 2003. Jason Wilson acquired the company around 2012 and runs it now — a Black-owned roaster, not just a cafe, which is rare anywhere in the country. Open 7am to 6pm daily, with a second counter inside the Schnucks at 8650 Big Bend in Webster Groves that opened, pointedly, on the last day of Black History Month.
La Pâtisserie Chouquette, 1626 Tower Grove Ave, Botanical Heights. Simone Faure is a New Orleans native who trained in Ritz-Carlton kitchens and opened her own patisserie here in 2013. Macarons, cakes, French pastry done properly. Tuesday to Friday 9 to 2, Saturday 9 to 3.
SweetArt, 3701 Lindell Blvd. Chef Reine Keis has been at this since 2008, and the food is entirely plant-based — vegan soul food and baking, which is a harder trick than it sounds. There’s also a SweetArt stall at City Foundry, though the Lindell location is the one we could confirm operating.
### What closed, and what’s still being recommended anyway
This section exists so you don’t drive somewhere that isn’t there. Every one of these still appears on live pages as a going concern.
Sweetie Pie’s is the big one. The last location closed in 2022. A revival called Sweetie Pie’s 2nd Act has been announced for north city with a $1.5 million city grant and a banner on the building — but it is not open, and no opening date has been given. Do not plan a meal around it.
Turn, in Midtown, closed at the end of May; the chef and his wife relocated to Little Rock. Ms. Piggies’ Smokehouse on Page closed when the Matthews family retired around Thanksgiving 2024. Brother’s Diner on Whittier is permanently closed. Jerk Soul on Cherokee is gone, though its address lives on as Jerk Unlimited. Prime 55 shows one location closed and another permanently closed.
And the instructive one: Deli Divine on Delmar appears on Black-owned roundups constantly. It is not Black-owned. Its owner is Ben Poremba, an Israeli-born restaurateur. It ends up on those lists because it sits inside the Delmar DivINe building. Nobody did that maliciously — one list guessed from the address, and everyone downstream copied it. That is exactly how these lists decay.
### Two we won’t claim either way
If you search this term right now, Google’s own local results put Blazin Kitchen (3636 Page Blvd) and 4 Hens Creole Kitchen (City Foundry) at the top. Both are open — we verified that — and both look genuinely good.
We could not find a published source naming their ownership. Google’s ranking is an inference from how people search and tag, not a statement of fact. So we’re telling you they exist, that they’re open, and that we couldn’t confirm the one thing this list is about. That’s more useful to you than a confident guess, and it’s the same standard that kept Deli Divine off the list above.
### Where the map is thin
Honest geography, because padding this would be easy and useless.
The verified list concentrates in the city (Gourmet Soul, SweetArt, Chouquette, Northwest Coffee, Chez Ali, Jerk Unlimited) and north county (Cathy’s Kitchen and ToGo, C&K, plus FUFU n’ Sauce just over in University City). North county also holds the oldest and deepest roots on the list.
Hard left turn — Highland, Illinois is a short drive east and worth a Saturday.
South county, west county and the Metro East are effectively uncovered. We found no Black-owned restaurant in west county or Illinois that we could source ownership for — not because none exist, but because nobody has documented them. Several candidates appear on old lists with no owner named and no independent confirmation anywhere.
If you run one of those places, that gap is the whole point of the box at the bottom of this page.
### About the numbers you’ll see quoted
One more thing worth being straight about, because it gets repeated locally as though it were local.
The encouraging figures — Black-owned employer businesses up roughly 57 percent between 2017 and 2022, revenue up about two thirds — come from U.S. Census Bureau data and are national. They are real, and they are not a St. Louis statistic. We looked for a trustworthy metro-level number and could not confirm one we’d be willing to print, so we’re not printing one.
What we can tell you is what we found doing this: a short list of operators, several of them decades deep, working in a market where the publication that used to keep track of them no longer exists. Whether that’s a boom or a squeeze, the practical response is the same — go eat at them.
Two searches bring most people to this page: what are some black-owned businesses in St. Louis beyond the obvious, and what are some good black soul food restaurants in St. Louis, Missouri specifically. This guide answers the first through food and points the second at the dedicated soul food list.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is Sweetie Pie's still open in St. Louis?
A.  No. The last Sweetie Pie’s location closed in 2022. A revival called Sweetie Pie’s 2nd Act has been announced for north St. Louis with a $1.5 million city grant and signage on the building, but it has not opened and no opening date has been announced.
### Q. What is the oldest Black-owned restaurant in St. Louis?
A.  C&K Barbecue, founded in 1963 by Forris and Lucille King, who moved to St. Louis from Mississippi during World War II. Daryle Brantley joined as a partner in 1982 and opened the Jennings Station Road location in 1983. It has been family-operated for more than sixty years.
### Q. Is there a Black-owned coffee roaster in St. Louis?
A.  Yes. Northwest Coffee Roasting Co. at 4251 Laclede Ave in the Central West End has roasted since 2003 and has been owned by Jason Wilson since roughly 2012. There is a second location inside the Schnucks at 8650 Big Bend in Webster Groves. A roaster rather than just a cafe, which is uncommon.
### Q. Where can I find Black-owned West African or Caribbean food in St. Louis?
A.  FUFU n’ Sauce at 8100 Page Ave in University City serves Togolese food; owner Adjo Honsou won season three of PBS’s The Great American Recipe. Chez Ali at City Foundry serves Senegalese and Afro-Caribbean dishes including yassa chicken and thieboudienne. Jerk Unlimited at 3108 Cherokee St serves Jamaican.
### Q. Why are so many Black-owned restaurant lists for St. Louis out of date?
A.  Feast Magazine maintained the definitive local guide, and Lee Enterprises shut Feast down in September 2025. Most other lists were copying from it, so when updates stopped, every downstream list froze. Several now recommend restaurants that closed between 2022 and 2026.
### Q. Are there Black-owned restaurants in west county or the Metro East?
A.  We could not verify any. The businesses we could source ownership for are concentrated in the city, north county and University City. That does not mean none exist in south county, west county or Illinois — it means no published source documents them, which is a gap in the record rather than in the market.
### Q. Is Deli Divine a Black-owned restaurant?
A.  No. Deli Divine on Delmar is owned by Ben Poremba, an Israeli-born restaurateur. It appears on Black-owned roundups because it operates inside the Delmar DivINe building, and one list’s assumption was copied by others. It is a good illustration of why these lists need checking.
### Q. What are some black-owned businesses in St. Louis?
A.  They run well past restaurants — salons, coffee and pastry counters, contractors, and professional services. This guide covers the food side because that is what it can verify. Search the directory by category to find the rest, and judge them the way you would any local business.
### Q. What are some good black soul food restaurants in St. Louis, Missouri?
A.  The soul food kitchens sit mostly in the city and north county, and they are organized above by what you are after rather than ranked. If soul food specifically is the goal rather than Black-owned restaurants broadly, the dedicated soul food guide goes deeper on the neighborhoods and the menus.
### Q. Is there a Black-owned Chinese restaurant in St. Louis?
A.  This guide does not claim one either way. Ownership claims circulate online and get repeated without anyone confirming them, which is exactly the trap the section above flags. Where we could not verify ownership, we left the restaurant off rather than guess.
### Q. What are some Black neighborhoods in St. Louis, Mo.?
A.  Historically north city and north county, with a long presence in the central corridor, and that history is why the restaurants in this guide cluster where they do. It also explains where the map is thin: decades of disinvestment show up as gaps in a restaurant list.
Own a Black-owned business in the St. Louis metro? The publication that used to keep track closed in 2025, and we found almost nothing documented in south county, west county or the Metro East. That means searches are turning up stale lists instead of you. Being listed somewhere current is how that gets fixed — adding your business takes a few minutes.

That’s the kind of link that ages well. Say you’re a wedding photographer. Your website might rank for “St. Louis wedding photographer,” but searches like “affordable wedding photography St. Louis” or “event photographer near me” are separate contests — and a complete, well-written profile page can show up for long-tail searches your website misses. More lines in the water, each one honestly baited with real information about what you do. ## Part 4: More of the first page that’s about you Search your business name and look at what comes up. Every result you own is one a customer can trust and one a competitor’s ad isn’t occupying. A complete directory profile reliably becomes one of those owned results for your name searches — which matters most at the exact moment a referred customer is checking you out before calling. Referrals don’t convert on the recommendation alone; they convert after the quick search that confirms it. ## Part 5: The referral traffic — fewer visitors, better ones Directories will never out-traffic Google, and anyone claiming otherwise is fibbing. But consider who visits a local directory: someone who came specifically to find a local business to hire. That’s as high-intent as traffic gets. A profile that answers their questions — services, photos, reviews, hours — converts that intent instead of bouncing it. Quality of visitor beats quantity of visitor for a business that needs customers, not pageviews — ten people actively hiring beat a thousand people idly scrolling. ## Part 6: Location and category reach — claimed honestly A Gold profile can carry up to 40 location tags and 10 business categories, surfacing your business in searches across every community and service you cover — the full mechanics, with a worked example, live in the Up to 400 Keywords section of the Gold Plan page. The rule that makes this work: **claim what you genuinely serve.** Most businesses under-claim — they tag three towns and stay invisible in the ten others they’d happily drive to. A metro-wide service company or a destination restaurant legitimately claims dozens of communities, because that’s the truth of its footprint. But padding your tags with towns you’d decline a job in just generates wrong-fit calls and clutter.
