## Explore the Cosmos at the McDonnell Planetarium in St. Louis Revised July 23, 2026 What is the planetarium at the Saint Louis Science Center? The James S. McDonnell Planetarium is the iconic, hyperboloid-shaped planetarium at the Saint Louis Science Center in Forest Park (5050 Oakland Ave). Opened in 1963 and designed by architect Gyo Obata, it reopened in July 2026 after a major renovation with a new GOTO star projector and a Cosm Digistar full-dome system. The Science Center itself is free to enter; the immersive star shows in the StarBay Theater are ticketed. It’s regularly ranked among the best planetariums in the country. Keep reading ↓Look up almost anywhere in Forest Park and you’ll spot it: a great white hourglass of a building, curving up against the sky like something that landed rather than was built. That’s the James S. McDonnell Planetarium, one of St. Louis’s most beloved landmarks — and after a major upgrade, it’s better than ever. This is your honest guide to exploring the cosmos right here in St. Louis: what it is, what you’ll see, and how to plan a visit. The timing couldn’t be better. The planetarium reopened in July 2026 after a nearly six-month renovation, emerging with cutting-edge technology that has it billed as one of the most advanced hybrid planetariums in the country. If you haven’t been in a while — or ever — now is the moment. The upgrade was significant enough to make national news, and locals who grew up with the old star projector are discovering a genuinely transformed experience under the same iconic roof. ## A St. Louis icon, reborn The McDonnell Planetarium is part of the **Saint Louis Science Center** in Forest Park, and it’s been the city’s home for all things space for more than 60 years. It first beamed a star show on April 16, 1963, and its unmistakable shape — a thin-shell concrete hyperboloid designed by celebrated St. Louis architect Gyo Obata of HOK — has been a landmark on the Forest Park skyline ever since. It’s named for aviation pioneer James Smith McDonnell, whose aerospace legacy is woven through the whole building and, in a real sense, through the whole city. For generations of St. Louisans, a trip here was a childhood rite of passage — the school field trip where space suddenly felt close enough to touch. The reopening gives a whole new generation that same first moment of looking up in the dark and feeling small in the best possible way. What makes the reopening a genuine event is what’s now inside. The renovation installed a first-of-its-kind-in-the-U.S. hybrid star projector paired with a state-of-the-art full-dome digital system, letting the theater fly you through more than 100 million stars in immersive, 360-degree detail under what the Science Center calls the largest artificial sky in the Western Hemisphere. It’s a serious leap, and it earned national recognition even before the upgrade — the McDonnell Planetarium was named the best planetarium in the country in a recent USA TODAY 10Best Readers’ Choice poll. Planning a St. Louis day around the planetarium? Pair it with the rest of Forest Park — the free Zoo, Art Museum, and History Museum are all a short walk away. Our guide to exploring St. Louis maps a full day out. Run a St. Louis business families would love to find? A directory listing puts you in front of people searching “things to do near me” and planning their next outing. ## Six decades of looking up The planetarium’s history is a real part of its charm. When it opened in 1963, its space-age silhouette felt like a promise about the future — fitting, in a city that built the Mercury and Gemini capsules that carried the first Americans into orbit. That aerospace heritage isn’t decoration here; it’s local history. James McDonnell’s company put St. Louis at the center of the space race, and the planetarium that bears his name has spent generations turning that legacy into wonder for kids and adults alike. Gyo Obata’s hyperboloid design — that graceful, curving concrete shell — has aged into one of the most recognizable pieces of mid-century architecture in the region. It’s the kind of building that makes an impression before you ever walk inside, and it’s been a fixture in the memories of St. Louisans who came here on childhood field trips and now bring their own kids. Few attractions manage to be both a genuine scientific institution and a nostalgic landmark; this one has been both for over 60 years. ## What you’ll experience The heart of a visit is a live or immersive show in the **Bill and Laura Orthwein StarBay Theater**, under the big dome. Current programs cover a real range: - **The Sky Tonight**— a live, educator-guided tour of the current night sky, so you’ll actually know what you’re looking at when you step outside. - **The Earth Today: A Changing Planet**— a striking look at our own world using real-time geospatial data. - **The Little Star That Could 360**— a gentle, immersive show made for younger kids and families, and a great first planetarium experience for the smallest visitors. Because programming rotates and new shows debut over time, it’s worth checking the current lineup before you visit — there’s usually something for both the serious space enthusiast and the kid who just wants to see ...

## Hiring a Personal Injury Lawyer in St. Louis: Deadlines, Fees and the State Line Revised July 27, 2026 How long do I have to file an injury claim in St. Louis? **Which side of the river decides your case.** Missouri: **5 years** for personal injury, 3 for wrongful death (from death), 2 for med-mal. Illinois: **2 years** for injury and wrongful death, and only **1 year** against a local public entity. Shorter deadlines override: **30 days** written notice to your employer for a work injury, **90 days** written notice to the mayor for a City of St. Louis street/sidewalk defect. ⚖️ **Fault works oppositely:** Missouri is PURE comparative fault, Illinois bars recovery above 50%. At 60% at fault on $100,000 — **Missouri pays $40,000, Illinois pays $0**. 💰 Missouri’s rules require your contingency agreement to state whether expenses come off BEFORE or AFTER the fee — on a $100K settlement that one sentence is worth $3,333. Provider liens are capped at 50% of NET (after fees and costs). 🚫 A lawyer phoning or approaching you after a crash is prohibited outright; written solicitation is barred for 30 days. Two cars crash the same way on the same afternoon. One wreck happens on Kingshighway, the other on a street in Belleville, twenty minutes east. The Missouri driver has **five years** to file. The Illinois driver has **two**. And if a jury later decides each driver was 60% at fault, the Missouri driver still collects a substantial check while the Illinois driver collects **nothing at all.** St. Louis straddles a state line, which means the single most important fact about an injury claim here is one almost nobody explains: *which side of the river it happened on.* ## How long do I have to file an injury claim in St. Louis? In **Missouri**, generally **five years** for personal injury, **three years** for wrongful death from the date of death, and **two years** for medical malpractice. In **Illinois**, it’s **two years** for personal injury and wrongful death, and only **one year** for a claim against a local public entity. If your claim is against the City of St. Louis for a street or sidewalk defect, written notice must reach the mayor within **90 days**. And a work injury must be reported to your employer in writing within **30 days**. Which deadline applies is a legal question — don’t self-diagnose it. ## Missouri’s five years is a trap Missouri’s general five-year window is unusually generous, and that generosity is exactly what hurts people. Someone hears “five years,” relaxes, and blows through every shorter deadline that actually governs their case. Because the five years is the *exception* in this list, not the rule: **Wrongful death: three years** from the date of death, not from the injury. **Medical malpractice: two years** from the act, with a ten-year outer limit. **A work injury: 30 days** to notify your employer in writing. **Street or sidewalk defect in the City of St. Louis: 90 days** written notice to the mayor. **Anything that happened in Illinois: two years** — or one year against a municipality. One more that surprises people: for a minor, the Missouri clock is paused until the disability is removed — and the statute sets that at age **twenty-one**, not eighteen. Medical malpractice has its own separate rule for minors. ## The 90-day rule almost nobody knows If you were hurt by a defect in a street, sidewalk, bridge, boulevard or thoroughfare in a Missouri city of 100,000 or more — which in this metro essentially means the City of St. Louis — you must give **written notice to the mayor within 90 days** of the occurrence. The notice has to state the place, the time, the character and circumstances of the injury, and that you will claim damages. Two limits worth being precise about, because they get blurred constantly. It applies only to **cities** over 100,000 — St. Louis County is a county, not a city, so this particular provision doesn’t reach it. And it applies only to **those specific kinds of defects**, not to every claim against a city. Suing a public entity is harder in another way, too. Missouri governments are generally immune, with narrow exceptions — principally the negligent operation of a motor vehicle by a public employee on the job, and injuries caused by a dangerous condition of public property. Outside those windows the claim often does not exist at all. Where immunity is waived, damages are capped, and the cap is adjusted for inflation every year. For **2026** the Department of Commerce and Insurance publishes it at **$532,148** for any one person and **$3,547,658** for all claims from a single occurrence. Those numbers change every January 1 — if you see them quoted without a year attached, they’re probably stale. ## Partly your fault? It depends which state This is the single biggest practical difference across the river, and it’s the reason people who assume they have no case sometimes do. **Missouri uses pure comparative fault.** There is no cutoff. Your recovery is reduced by your share of the blame, and that’s all. (Worth noting for accuracy: for ordinary negligence this comes from a 1983 Missouri Supreme Court decision rather than a statute, so anyone citing “the Missouri comparative fault statute” for a car wreck is misinformed.) **Illinois uses modified comparative negligence with a bar.** If you are found *more ...

## The Best Dance Clubs in St. Louis: Where to Go Out Revised July 23, 2026 What are the best places to go dancing in St. Louis? St. Louis nightlife clusters in a few walkable districts: Washington Avenue downtown for big clubs, The Grove for LGBTQ+-friendly and eclectic spots, Soulard for bars and live music, and the Delmar Loop for a mixed crowd. Whether you want a DJ-driven dance floor, Latin night, or a live band, these entertainment districts are where the scene lives — check each venue’s nights and age policy before you head out. Keep reading ↓You know the itch. It’s Friday, the group chat is lighting up, and somebody finally says it out loud: *let’s go dancing.* Not a quiet wine bar. Not a booth where you have to lean in and shout. You want the real thing — a floor, a good DJ, bass you feel in your chest, and a couple of hours where the only decision is whether to stay for one more song. Whether you’re getting ready in Florissant, pre-gaming in Soulard, or piling into a rideshare from St. Charles, the night starts with the same question: *where do we actually go?* Here’s the honest truth about dancing in St. Louis — the scene is genuinely good, but it’s scattered across a half-dozen neighborhoods, and it changes fast. Clubs open, close, and rebrand; the hot spot from three years ago might be a food hall now. So this is the current, on-the-ground guide: where to dance right now, sorted by vibe and neighborhood, plus the one local quirk that quietly decides how your whole night ends. **The best places to go dancing in St. Louis span a few districts: Washington Avenue downtown (EDM and hip-hop at Europe, dressy dancing at Pepper Lounge), The Grove (the heart of LGBTQ+ nightlife and Latin nights), Soulard’s DJ bars, Latin dancing at Club Viva, country line-dancing at PBR in Ballpark Village, and true after-hours clubs across the river in Sauget, Illinois. Most are 21+.** ## The Local Quirk That Shapes Your Whole Night: Last Call by Zone Before you pick a spot, know this — it’s the single most useful thing about St. Louis nightlife. **When the music stops depends entirely on which side of which line you’re standing on.** Across most of the Missouri metro, last call is 1:30am. But qualifying high-volume venues in the City of St. Louis and St. Louis County can serve until 3am, which is why the downtown and Grove spots keep going after the suburbs have gone dark. And if you’re still not ready to quit? Cross the Mississippi into Sauget, Illinois, where the clubs run until 5 or 6am — and one legendary spot never closes at all. So the shape of your night is really a choice: a normal-hours neighborhood bar, a 3am downtown club, or a dawn-patrol run across the river. It inherited the crowds from the downtown clubs that have closed around it, which is exactly why it still feels alive on a Saturday at midnight. ## Local SEO for Contractors in St. Louis: What Google Actually Says Revised July 27, 2026 How does local search ranking actually work? ⭐ Google’s own words: **“There’s no way to request or pay for a better local ranking on Google.”** Ranking is relevance + distance + prominence — and you cannot influence distance. **Service-area rules:** up to 20 service areas (cities/ZIPs, NOT a radius), ~2 hours max driving time, remove your address if customers don’t visit, and **never create a separate listing per suburb** — Google prohibits it and it’s the top cause of suspension. Virtual offices and PO boxes are ineligible. ⚠️ **Missouri does NOT license HVAC/mechanical, plumbing or general contractors statewide** — despite what several sites claim. That bill has FAILED in six sessions. Electrical contractors are the only construction trade licensed by the state, it’s optional, and municipalities must recognize it in lieu of a local license. 🚫 Reviews: Google publishes NO threshold; incentivized reviews (even a discount) are explicitly prohibited and can get existing reviews unpublished. Google publishes a sentence that most of the marketing industry would rather you didn’t read: **“There’s no way to request or pay for a better local ranking on Google.”** That is Google’s own help documentation, not our opinion. And it is worth starting there, because if you search the question this article answers, *every single result on the first page is written by someone selling the service.* Including a block of ads for SEO agencies. We sell directory listings, so we have our own interest — and we’ll be upfront about where it shows up. But most of what follows is Google telling you how this works, and Missouri law telling you something about your license that a lot of websites are getting flatly wrong. ## How does local search ranking actually work? Google says local results are ranked on three things. **Relevance** is “how well a Business Profile matches what someone is searching for.” **Distance** is “how far each business is from the customer who’s searching.” **Prominence** is “how well-known a business is.” You can influence relevance and prominence. You cannot influence distance, and you cannot buy position — Google states plainly there is no way to request or pay for better local ranking. ## The thing about being a service-area business Most trades don’t have a shop customers walk into. You drive to them. Google calls that a service-area business, and the rules are specific, published, and routinely violated by people trying to game them. You can list **up to 20 service areas**, defined by city, postal code, or similar. You **cannot set a radius** — “thirty miles around Kirkwood” is not an option; you name places. Google says your service area should not exceed **about two hours of driving time** from your base, which in this metro means the whole thing, Illinois included, is fair game. If customers don’t come to you, Google says to **remove your address from your profile**. If you have a showroom and also go out, you can run as a hybrid and keep the address visible. Now the rules that get businesses penalized, all in Google’s own words: **“Do not create more than one page for each location of your business.”** That kills the scheme somebody will eventually pitch you — a separate listing for Ballwin, one for Florissant, one for O’Fallon. It is against the rules, in writing, and it is the most common reason a trade business gets its profile suspended. A rented mailing address you don’t operate from — a virtual office — **“isn’t eligible for a Business Profile.”** Neither are P.O. boxes or remote mailboxes. And your business name has to be your actual business name, “as used consistently on your storefront, website, stationery, and as known to customers.” Not *Smith Plumbing — Emergency Plumber St. Louis Ballwin Kirkwood*. ## The uncomfortable math nobody selling you services will explain Put those three facts together and you get a conclusion worth sitting with. Distance from the searcher is a confirmed ranking factor. A service-area business has to hide its address. And you are allowed exactly one listing. Which means **you cannot rank equally across the whole St. Louis metro, and no amount of money changes that.** A plumber based in Affton will have a harder time surfacing for someone searching in St. Peters than a plumber based in St. Peters will — not because of effort or budget, but because of geometry. That is not a reason to do nothing. It is a reason to be skeptical of anyone promising metro-wide dominance, and a reason to think hard about which twenty areas you actually name. ## The Missouri license thing that half the internet gets wrong If you have searched for what license you need in Missouri, you may have read that the state has a statewide HVAC or mechanical contractor license, and possibly that it took effect in early 2026. **That is not true.** The Missouri Statewide Mechanical Contractors Licensing Act has been introduced *and has failed* in at least six sessions — 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2025, and the current one, where it sits in committee. Bills carry conditional effective dates, and websites keep mistaking those for law. ## How to Choose a Real Estate Agent in St. Louis (After the 2024 Rule Change) Revised July 27, 2026 How do you choose a real estate agent in St. Louis? Verify the license first — Missouri’s free lookup is at **mopro.mo.gov/license/s/license-search**, and disciplinary actions since 2011 are posted separately at **pr.mo.gov/realestate-disciplines.asp**. Since **August 17, 2024** (the *Burnett v. NAR* settlement, decided in a Missouri federal court), buyer-agent compensation no longer appears on the MLS and buyers must sign a written agreement BEFORE touring a home — and that agreement’s compensation must be “objectively ascertainable” and “not open-ended,” so a blank or “standard rate” does not qualify. ⚠️ Commissions did NOT fall: Redfin tracked 2.36% (Q3 2024) → 2.42% (Q3 2025), and homes under $500K average **2.52%** — the highest tier, where nearly all St. Louis sales sit. Only 27.2% of buyers negotiate. Watch the geography on any median quoted: City ~$261K vs County ~$325K vs MSA list price ~$290K (June 2026). The rules for hiring a real estate agent changed in August 2024, and the lawsuit that changed them was decided in a Missouri federal courtroom — the Western District, in Kansas City. If you are buying a house in St. Louis right now, you will be asked to sign something before you are allowed to walk through your first front door. Most people sign it without reading it. Here is what actually changed, what didn’t, and the specific things worth checking before you pick anyone. ## How do you choose a real estate agent in St. Louis? Start by verifying the license. Missouri’s public lookup is at **mopro.mo.gov**, and disciplinary actions since 2011 are posted separately at **pr.mo.gov/realestate-disciplines.asp** — both free, both take a minute. Then interview at least three, and before signing anything, get the compensation figure written as an actual number. Since August 2024 a buyer must sign a written agreement before touring a home, and that agreement’s compensation term must be, in the National Association of Realtors’ own words, “objectively ascertainable” and “not open-ended.” A blank, or “standard rate,” or “whatever the seller offers” does not meet that standard. ## What actually changed in 2024 The case was *Burnett v. National Association of Realtors*. NAR agreed to pay $418 million, and a judge granted final approval in November 2024. The practice changes took effect on August 17, 2024. Two of them matter to you. **One: offers of buyer-agent compensation came off the MLS.** This is the change that gets described wrong more than any other. Compensation was *not* banned. Sellers can still offer to pay a buyer’s agent — it just can’t be advertised through the multiple listing service anymore. Seller concessions toward your closing costs can still appear there. **Two: you sign before you tour.** An agent working with you must have a signed written agreement in place before showing you a home. There are exceptions — an open house hosted by the seller’s agent doesn’t require one, and neither does a showing where you’re unrepresented. What did **not** change: commissions were always negotiable. The settlement didn’t create that, cap anything, or set a rate. NAR now requires agents to conspicuously disclose that compensation “is not set by law and is fully negotiable” — which was true before, and is now something they have to say out loud. ## Commissions did not go down You will read that the settlement drove commissions down. The data doesn’t support it, and you should know that before you sit across from anyone. Redfin’s research tracked the average buyer’s-agent commission at **2.38% in the second quarter of 2024**, dipping to **2.36% in the third quarter** as the rules took effect — and back to **2.42% by the third quarter of 2025**. Slightly higher than before the change. A separate analysis by AccountTECH, covering more than 224,000 closed transactions across roughly 1,300 offices, found the same shape: a real dip in late 2024 that round-tripped within about five months. Two independent datasets, same conclusion. Anyone telling you the market has settled this for you is wrong. And there’s a detail in that data that lands directly on St. Louis. Broken out by price, the average buyer-agent commission in the third quarter of 2025 ran **2.52% on homes under $500,000**, 2.32% between $500,000 and $999,000, and 2.22% above a million. The cheaper the house, the higher the percentage. Nearly every St. Louis transaction sits in that first tier — so buyers and sellers here are in the segment paying the *most*, proportionally, and have the most to gain from asking. Which almost nobody does. A survey conducted by Ipsos for Redfin in spring 2025 found **37.4% of sellers** negotiated or tried to negotiate commission — against just **27.2% of buyers.** Buyers are leaving the most on the table, in the tier where the percentage is highest. ## Verify the license in about a minute Two free public tools, and almost nobody uses either. **License status:** the Missouri Division of Professional Registration portal at **mopro.mo.gov/license/s/license-search**. You can confirm the license is real, active, and whether the person is a salesperson or a broker. (If you find an older link floating around, note that Missouri migrated portals — the legacy address redirects here.) **Disciplinary history:** a separate page, **pr.mo.gov/realestate-disciplines.asp**, which posts actions taken since June 30, 2011 as downloadable PDFs you can search by name. Know the limits of what you’re seeing. ...

## Old-House Wiring in St. Louis: Knob-and-Tube, Aluminum, and Your Panel Revised July 28, 2026 What is knob-and-tube wiring, and is it dangerous? The median home in the **City of St. Louis was built in 1938** and 57.9% predate 1940 (Census ACS 2020–2024); **St. Louis County’s median is 1969** with ~34% built 1960–1979. That means two different problems: the city is **knob-and-tube** country, the county is **aluminum branch wiring** (1965–73) and questionable-panel country. Existing knob-and-tube is legal and grandfathered — the real hazard is **insulation covering it**, which the electrical code prohibits, because it was designed to shed heat into open air. CPSC: pre-1972 aluminum-wired homes are **55× more likely** to reach “Fire Hazard Conditions” (cover-plate screws at 300°F). ⚠️ CPSC closed its Federal Pacific investigation in 1983 *without* a conclusion either way. 100 amps is the code MINIMUM, not a deficiency — a load calculation decides. In the City you may NOT pull your own permit for a rewire or service change. The median house in the City of St. Louis was built in **1938**. Nearly **58%** of the city’s housing went up in 1939 or earlier, per the Census Bureau’s five-year American Community Survey estimates. In St. Louis County the median is **1969**, and about a third of the housing stock was built between 1960 and 1979. Those two numbers, both from the Census Bureau, mean the city and the county have *completely different* electrical problems hiding in their walls. City houses are knob-and-tube country. County houses are aluminum-wiring and questionable-panel country. Here’s how to tell what you have, what actually matters, and what you can ignore. ## What is knob-and-tube wiring, and is it dangerous? Knob-and-tube was the standard wiring method from roughly the 1880s through the 1940s — two separate conductors run several inches apart, supported by white porcelain knobs and passing through porcelain tubes where they cross framing. It has no ground wire, and its cloth-and-rubber insulation gets brittle with age. But the single biggest hazard isn’t age at all: **it was engineered to shed heat into open air, so burying it in insulation is what makes it dangerous.** The National Electrical Code prohibits concealed knob-and-tube in spaces filled with loose, rolled or foamed-in insulation for exactly that reason. ## The city problem: knob-and-tube A 1938 median puts the typical city house dead in the middle of the knob-and-tube era. If you own a brick house in south city, Tower Grove, Dutchtown, Baden or the north side, there is a genuine chance some original wiring is still in service somewhere in it. **Go look, and don’t touch anything.** In an unfinished basement or attic you’re looking for white porcelain spools nailed to the joists with a single wire running through each, porcelain tubes where wire passes through wood, and — the giveaway — two separate wires running parallel several inches apart instead of one modern cable. The sheathing is cloth or rubber, often cracked. The thing you are actually hunting for is **knob-and-tube buried under or inside blown-in insulation.** That is the combination the Code specifically bans, and it is the realistic fire scenario. It usually happens innocently: somebody insulated the attic decades after the wiring went in and had no idea it mattered. Two more clues that you’re on an ungrounded system: two-prong outlets throughout the house, and no third slot anywhere. ## So is it legal? Yes. Existing knob-and-tube is generally grandfathered — the electrical code is not retroactive, and neither Missouri nor the federal government bans living with it. You are not breaking a law by owning it. Where it bites is the moment you *touch* it. The Code permits knob-and-tube only as an extension of an existing installation, typically with the local inspector’s approval, and new installation isn’t allowed at all. Insulating over it is prohibited outright. The City of St. Louis enforces the 2017 edition of the National Electrical Code; St. Louis County runs on its own adopted edition, so confirm with the County before planning work out there. ## The county problem: aluminum branch wiring If your house went up in the late sixties or early seventies — which describes about a third of St. Louis County — your risk is different and better documented. And the CPSC finding is blunt: homes built before 1972 wired with aluminum are **55 times more likely** to have one or more connections at outlets reach what the agency calls “Fire Hazard Conditions.” That phrase has an actual definition, which almost nobody quoting the statistic bothers to include. It means the cover plate screws on a receptacle reaching **300°F**, or sparks coming out of the receptacle, or the material around it charring. # Old-House Wiring in St. Louis: Knob-and-Tube, Aluminum, and Your Panel Revised July 28, 2026 What is knob-and-tube wiring, and is it dangerous? The median home in the **City of St. Louis was built in 1938** and 57.9% predate 1940 (Census ACS 2020–2024); **St. Louis County’s median is 1969** with ~34% built 1960–1979. That means two different problems: the city is **knob-and-tube** country, the county is **aluminum branch wiring** (1965–73) and questionable-panel country. Existing knob-and-tube is legal and grandfathered — the real hazard is **insulation covering it**, which the electrical code prohibits, because it was designed to shed heat into open air. CPSC: pre-1972 aluminum-wired homes are **55× more likely** to reach “Fire Hazard Conditions” (cover-plate screws at 300°F). ⚠️ CPSC closed its Federal Pacific investigation in 1983 *without* a conclusion either way. 100 amps is the code MINIMUM, not a deficiency — a load calculation decides. In the City you may NOT pull your own permit for a rewire or service change. The median house in the City of St. Louis was built in **1938**. Nearly **58%** of the city’s housing went up in 1939 or earlier, per the Census Bureau’s five-year American Community Survey estimates. In St. Louis County the median is **1969**, and about a third of the housing stock was built between 1960 and 1979. Those two numbers, both from the Census Bureau, mean the city and the county have *completely different* electrical problems hiding in their walls. City houses are knob-and-tube country. County houses are aluminum-wiring and questionable-panel country. Here’s how to tell what you have, what actually matters, and what you can ignore. ## What is knob-and-tube wiring, and is it dangerous? Knob-and-tube was the standard wiring method from roughly the 1880s through the 1940s — two separate conductors run several inches apart, supported by white porcelain knobs and passing through porcelain tubes where they cross framing. It has no ground wire, and its cloth-and-rubber insulation gets brittle with age. But the single biggest hazard isn’t age at all: **it was engineered to shed heat into open air, so burying it in insulation is what makes it dangerous.** The National Electrical Code prohibits concealed knob-and-tube in spaces filled with loose, rolled or foamed-in insulation for exactly that reason. ## The city problem: knob-and-tube A 1938 median puts the typical city house dead in the middle of the knob-and-tube era. If you own a brick house in south city, Tower Grove, Dutchtown, Baden or the north side, there is a genuine chance some original wiring is still in service somewhere in it. **Go look, and don’t touch anything.** In an unfinished basement or attic you’re looking for white porcelain spools nailed to the joists with a single wire running through each, porcelain tubes where wire passes through wood, and — the giveaway — two separate wires running parallel several inches apart instead of one modern cable. The sheathing is cloth or rubber, often cracked. The thing you are actually hunting for is **knob-and-tube buried under or inside blown-in insulation.** That is the combination the Code specifically bans, and it is the realistic fire scenario. It usually happens innocently: somebody insulated the attic decades after the wiring went in and had no idea it mattered. Two more clues that you’re on an ungrounded system: two-prong outlets throughout the house, and no third slot anywhere. ## So is it legal? Yes. Existing knob-and-tube is generally grandfathered — the electrical code is not retroactive, and neither Missouri nor the federal government bans living with it. You are not breaking a law by owning it. Where it bites is the moment you *touch* it. The Code permits knob-and-tube only as an extension of an existing installation, typically with the local inspector’s approval, and new installation isn’t allowed at all. Insulating over it is prohibited outright. The City of St. Louis enforces the 2017 edition of the National Electrical Code; St. Louis County runs on its own adopted edition, so confirm with the County before planning work out there. ## The county problem: aluminum branch wiring If your house went up in the late sixties or early seventies — which describes about a third of St. Louis County — your risk is different and better documented. Between roughly **1965 and 1973**, a copper shortage pushed builders to aluminum branch circuit wiring. The Consumer Product Safety Commission estimates about **two million homes** got it. And the CPSC finding is blunt: homes built before 1972 wired with aluminum are **55 times more likely** to have one or more connections at outlets reach what the agency calls “Fire Hazard Conditions.” That phrase has an actual definition, which almost nobody quoting the statistic bothers to include. It means the cover plate screws on a receptacle reaching **300°F**, or sparks coming out of the receptacle, or the material around it charring. The important nuance: **the danger is at the connections, not in the wire itself.** Aluminum expands, contracts and oxidizes where it terminates at a switch or outlet, and those spots turn into high-resistance hot spots over decades. ## Kaslik Mediterranean Cuisine: A Hazelwood Middle Eastern Favorite Revised July 23, 2026 What kind of food does Kaslik Mediterranean Cuisine serve? Kaslik Mediterranean Cuisine (7847 North Lindbergh Blvd, Hazelwood, MO 63042; (314) 972-8282) is a family-owned Middle Eastern and Mediterranean restaurant in north St. Louis County. It serves Levantine classics — chicken and beef shawarma, lamb shish kebab, kefta, and a mixed grill, plus mezze like hummus, baba ganoush, fattoush, falafel, and stuffed grape leaves, with baklava for dessert. In north St. Louis County, Kaslik Mediterranean Cuisine is exactly that spot. This is an honest look at what it is, what to order, and why it’s spent more than a decade earning a loyal Hazelwood following. If you’ve driven North Lindbergh and never stopped, you’ve been missing some of the best Middle Eastern food on the north side — shawarma, kebabs, hummus, and mezze made from scratch by a family that’s been doing it right for years. It’s the sort of place that doesn’t advertise much because it doesn’t have to; word of mouth and a loyal regular base keep it going, which is usually the best possible sign about a restaurant. ## What Kaslik is Kaslik Mediterranean Cuisine sits at **7847 North Lindbergh Boulevard in Hazelwood, MO 63042**, phone **(314) 972-8282**. It’s a family-owned Mediterranean and Middle Eastern restaurant serving Levantine classics — the shawarma, kebabs, and mezze of the eastern Mediterranean. It first opened in Florissant around 2013 and moved to its Hazelwood home a couple of years later, and it’s been a north-county fixture ever since. A note on the name and the food, because it’s a nice story: “Kaslik” is a town in Lebanon, and the menu draws on that whole Levantine tradition — but the family behind the restaurant is Palestinian, having come to St. Louis from the West Bank. The result is honest, home-style Middle Eastern cooking rooted in real heritage rather than a corporate concept, which is exactly why it tastes the way it does. ## What to order The menu covers the Levantine greatest hits, and a few dishes anchor any good order: - **Shawarma**— chicken or beef, sliced from the spit, wrapped or over rice. The gateway dish and a reliable favorite. - **Kebabs and grilled meats**— lamb shish kebab, chicken kabob, kefta, and a mixed grill platter for the table that wants a bit of everything off the fire. - **The mezze**— hummus, baba ganoush, fattoush, and stuffed grape leaves. Order a few to share; they turn a sandwich run into a proper spread. - **Falafel and vegetarian options**— crisp, herby falafel and a genuinely good veggie platter make this an easy call for meatless eaters. - **Baklava**— the classic sweet, flaky finish. If you’re new to the cuisine, a mixed grill with a couple of mezze and warm pita is the perfect introduction. It’s the kind of food that tends to surprise skeptics: fresh, satisfying, and far more interesting than the fast-casual chain versions of “Mediterranean bowls” that have popped up everywhere. The Levantine tradition — the cooking of the eastern Mediterranean, from Lebanon and Syria through Palestine and Jordan — is built on fresh, bright, generous flavors: grilled meats seasoned simply and well, fresh herbs, lemon and garlic, olive oil, and a whole family of dips and salads meant for sharing with warm bread. It’s food that feels both healthy and deeply comforting, which is a rare combination — you can eat well here without the heavy, over-full feeling a lot of restaurant meals leave you with, and still walk out satisfied. ## Candicci’s: A 40-Year St. Louis Italian Favorite, Reinvented Revised July 23, 2026 Is Candicci’s still open, and what does it serve now? Yes, but in a new form. The full-service Candicci’s restaurant closed in 2024 and reopened as Candicci’s Catering & Express at 14870 Clayton Road on the Chesterfield/Ballwin border, (636) 220-8989. It focuses on takeout, delivery, and catering — St. Louis-style thin-crust pizza, toasted ravioli, pastas, Italian-American entrees, family specials, and catering trays — rather than sit-down dining. Keep reading ↓If you’ve been ordering from Candicci’s for years — a family pizza night, a toasted-ravioli fix, a catered office lunch — here’s the news that matters: the beloved St. Louis Italian institution is still very much alive, but it has changed shape. This is an honest, up-to-date look at what Candicci’s is *now*, so you know exactly what to expect before you call. The short version: after more than 40 years as a full-service restaurant, Candicci’s closed its longtime Ballwin dining room in 2024 and reopened as **Candicci’s Catering & Express** — a takeout-and-catering operation built around the pizzas, pastas, and family favorites that made its name. If you’re picturing the old white-tablecloth veal-and-seafood dining room with its patio and sit-down service, gently update that picture; the format is different now, but the pizzas, pastas, and toasted ravioli you love are still here, just served a new way. ## What Candicci’s is today Candicci’s Catering & Express operates from **14870 Clayton Road**, on the Chesterfield/Ballwin border in west St. Louis County (ZIP 63017), phone **(636) 220-8989**. It moved here in 2024 into the former Chirco’s Pizza space at Clayton and Baxter — not in Old Town Chesterfield or the Valley, but along the Clayton Road corridor between the two communities. The concept shifted from sit-down dining to **takeout, delivery, and catering**. Owner Bob Candice has been candid in local coverage about why: staff shortages, rising lease costs, and food-cost pressure made the full-service model untenable, so the family reinvented the business around what it does best rather than closing the doors for good. It’s a genuinely admirable pivot — keeping a 40-year name alive by changing the format instead of giving up, and a reminder that the restaurants worth rooting for are often the ones that find a way to keep going when the easy choice would be to walk away. ## The food: St. Louis Italian, built for takeout The menu centers on the crowd-pleasers that travel well: - **St. Louis-style thin-crust pizza**— the local classic, cut into squares — alongside a New York hand-tossed option for a different mood. - **Toasted ravioli**— the quintessential St. Louis appetizer, and a Candicci’s staple. - **Pastas and Italian-American entrees**— think pasta con broccoli, pasta primavera, spaghetti and meatballs, lasagna, eggplant Parmesan, and chicken Marsala. - **Starters and salads**— spinach-artichoke dip, mozzarella sticks, house salad. - **Family specials and a kids’ menu**— built to feed a household without a big-night-out bill. - **Catering trays**— the same favorites scaled up for a crowd, from pastas to pizzas to sliced-meat spreads. It’s an Italian-American menu in the truest, most comforting sense — not chasing trends, just doing the classics well. That’s exactly what you want from a takeout order on a busy night: food you already know you like, made by a kitchen that has been making it for decades. A quick honesty note for longtime fans: the express menu focuses on pizzas, pastas, and select items, so some of the old full-service specialties — the veal and seafood entrees the sit-down restaurant was known for — may not be available in the new format. If you have a specific dish in mind, the safest move is a quick call to confirm it’s on the current menu before you order. Looking for more St. Louis Italian? Our guide to the best Italian food in St. Louis covers the metro’s classics, from The Hill to the suburbs — real places, real reviews. Run a restaurant or catering business? When plans change — a new location, a new model — a current, accurate directory profile makes sure customers find the *real* you, not an outdated listing. It’s how loyal regulars follow you when you move. ## A quick word on St. Louis-style pizza If you’re new to the metro, Candicci’s pizza is a good introduction to a genuinely local style that divides visitors and delights natives. St. Louis-style thin-crust is cracker-thin, unleavened, and cut into squares (“tavern cut”) rather than wedges — a format built for sharing a corner while you talk. Order it once and you understand the city’s fierce, slightly baffling-to-outsiders pizza loyalty a little better. Candicci’s serving both the local thin-crust and a New York hand-tossed means you can settle a house debate with a single order, which is exactly the kind of practical flexibility a family takeout spot needs. Pair a pizza with an order of toasted ravioli — another St. Louis original, breaded and fried, meant for dunking in marinara — and you’ve basically ordered the city on a plate. These aren’t trendy dishes; they’re comfort food with local roots, and a 40-year Italian kitchen makes them the way they’re supposed to taste. That’s the quiet argument for ordering from a place like this instead of a national chain: the recipes have decades behind them, and it shows in the details a corporate kitchen tends to sand off. ## 9 St. Louis Restaurants Locals Actually Love (Not the Chains)
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/discover-the-top-fast-food-spots-in-st-louis-a-2025-guide
Picture a Friday night when nobody at the table wants a drive-thru. Maybe you’re showing an out-of-town friend around, or you’re just tired of the same three chains off the highway in Chesterfield, Kirkwood, or Florissant. You want somewhere that actually tastes like St. Louis — a place a local would send you, not a logo you could find in any city in America.
This is that list. A quick honesty note first: despite how it sometimes gets labeled, none of these are “fast food” in the drive-thru sense. They run the range from order-at-the-counter barbecue to sit-down, special-occasion kitchens — the common thread is that they’re independent, they’re beloved, and they’re the opposite of an interchangeable chain. Here are nine St. Louis spots worth going out of your way for.
### Nine St. Louis restaurants worth the drive
St. Louis’s most beloved local restaurants span every price point and craving: Pappy’s Smokehouse for Memphis-style barbecue, Hi-Pointe Drive-In and Stacked STL for standout burgers, The Frisco Barroom in Webster Groves for elevated tavern food, Havana’s Cuisine in the Central West End for a real Cuban sandwich, Menya Rui for Tokyo-style shoyu ramen, The Golden Hoosier for sandwiches with a side of taxidermy, and, when you want something more refined, Acero in Maplewood and Peppe’s Apt. 2 in Kirkwood. Below is what to order at each.
### 1. Pappy’s Smokehouse
If you only eat at one place on this list, make it Pappy’s. This is the St. Louis barbecue institution — old-school, Memphis-style, and worth every minute of the line that regularly forms out the door. The dry-rubbed ribs are the headliner: smoked low and slow, tender without turning to mush, with that deep bark that tells you someone who cares was tending the pit.
Don’t stop at ribs, though. The brisket comes off moist and thinly sliced, the pulled pork is smoky and piled high, and the sides pull their weight — rich baked beans, sweet potato fries, and applesauce that tastes homemade. Go early; the most popular cuts sell out, and when the meat’s gone for the day, they close. It’s casual, family-friendly, and about as St. Louis as a plate of food gets.
### 2. Hi-Pointe Drive-In
Part burger joint, part retro movie set, Hi-Pointe Drive-In leans into a fun, nostalgic vibe — pop-culture touches everywhere and a menu built around genuinely excellent burgers. You can build your own or order one of the signature creations, and the staff are happy to walk a first-timer through it.
A few crowd favorites to point you in the right direction: the Frisco Melt, a rich, melty burger on sourdough; the Arch D-Lux, a stacked, bold-flavored classic; the Taco Burger for something crunchy and a little different; and the Cowboy Burger loaded with fixings. Add a thick shake — the flavors get creative — and you’ve got the whole experience. It’s a burger a step above the usual, in a room that makes you smile.
### 3. Stacked STL
Stacked STL is for the person who wants their burger built exactly their way. You pick the patty — beef, pork, turkey, or a beef-pork blend — then the bun (brioche, pretzel, gluten-free, or a lettuce wrap), the cheese, the sauces, and a genuinely long list of toppings. If decision fatigue sets in, there’s a lineup of a dozen signature burgers ready to go.
People rave about the juicy patties and the crispy fries, and the vibe is laid-back and friendly, with customer artwork on the walls. It gets busy at peak hours and parking can take a lap or two, but for a burger made precisely to your spec, that’s a small price. Not in the mood to go out? It’s an easy one to get delivered.
### 4. The Frisco Barroom
Over in Webster Groves, on Big Bend Boulevard near Webster University, The Frisco Barroom does elevated tavern food in a warm, rustic room — and its upstairs patio is one of the better places in the area to lose an afternoon. There are heaters up there, so it works well past the first cold snap, too.
The kitchen keeps it fresh and consistent: the burgers get real praise (the double cheeseburger with horseradish cheese has a following), the salads are surprisingly good, and they turn out solid pierogies and kielbasa when you want something heartier. There’s a deep whiskey list with generous pours, and live music turns up now and then. It’s the kind of place you settle into for a few hours.
Hungry for more? Our guide to exploring St. Louis and our neighborhood dining guides — from the Delmar Loop to the Grove — map out where locals actually eat, neighborhood by neighborhood.
Run a restaurant in the St. Louis area? This is exactly how diners find you when they search “best local restaurants near me” or ask an AI assistant where to eat tonight. Listing your restaurant keeps your menu, hours, and reviews in front of hungry locals instead of the chains.
### 5. Havana’s Cuisine
For a genuine Cuban sandwich — no trendy reinvention, just the classic done right — Havana’s Cuisine, now in the Central West End, is the answer. The sandwich is built the traditional way: quality ham, slow-roasted pork, Swiss, pickles, and yellow mustard, all pressed between bread imported from Tampa’s legendary La Segunda Bakery. They’ll even do the Tampa version with salami if that’s your style.
Beyond the sandwich, the menu sticks to satisfying Cuban classics rather than chasing food trends, and that focus is exactly the point. Sometimes you just want food that tastes the way it’s supposed to, made by people who care about getting the tradition right — and Havana’s delivers that in every bite.
### 6. Menya Rui
Menya Rui has earned a serious reputation for one thing done exceptionally well: Tokyo-style shoyu ramen. Rather than chase every ramen style at once, the kitchen focuses on a clear, soy-based broth built on real technique — savory, layered, and balanced — the kind of bowl that rewards a place that takes its time.
The details are where it shines: a perfectly cooked egg, tender meat, noodles with the right chew, and toppings arranged with obvious care. Add a starter or two and you’ve got a meal that feels considered rather than thrown together. It’s a standout example of St. Louis’s independent food scene — a specialist doing specialist work, and doing it right.
### 7. The Golden Hoosier
Sometimes you want a place that’s a little weird in the best way. The Golden Hoosier is a grill and cocktail bar whose walls are lined with taxidermy — equal parts charming and delightfully odd, and a fun way to show a visitor that St. Louis has more character than the tourist checklist suggests.
Random, but — ever actually looked at the Gate District?
The real draw is the food. The sandwiches are done right — a standout BLT dressed up with pesto aioli is a good place to start — and the cocktails hold their own. It doesn’t take itself too seriously, which is refreshing, and it lands as a reliable, memorable pick for a casual meal with a personality all its own.
### 8. Acero
When you want a meal that feels like an occasion, Acero in Maplewood is worth the reservation. This is upscale Italian, not fast food — a chef-driven kitchen that plates food as beautifully as it tastes, with bright colors and careful composition that make you want a photo before the first bite.
A dish like the Chicken Milanese shows the approach: a lightly floured chicken breast cooked so it stays juicy, served with Yukon potatoes and leeks in a caper sauce with just the right tang. The care shows in every element, main course to sides. It’s the kind of place that reminds you what a genuinely thoughtful, ingredient-first restaurant can do — a special-night spot rather than a quick bite.
### 9. Peppe’s Apt. 2
Rounding out the list, Peppe’s Apt. 2 in Kirkwood offers something a little different — a curated, course-based dining experience that lets you choose your way through a multi-course meal. It’s a smart middle ground for anyone who likes a structured menu but still wants some say in what lands on the table.
The result is a chance to taste a variety of dishes in one sitting without the stiffness of a formal tasting menu. It leans more refined than a quick counter meal, and that’s the appeal: a memorable, slightly special evening in one of the metro’s most walkable downtowns. Pair it with a stroll around downtown Kirkwood and you’ve got a full night out.
### How to use this list
Notice how much ground these nine places cover: smoky barbecue and build-your-own burgers on one end, chef-driven Italian and a course-based Kirkwood dinner on the other, with Cuban sandwiches, ramen, and taxidermy-lined cocktails in between. That range is the point. St. Louis’s best eating isn’t concentrated in one neighborhood or one price bracket — it’s spread across the whole metro, from Webster Groves to Maplewood to the Central West End, waiting for anyone willing to look past the chains.
If you’re building your own rotation, mix it up: a casual counter night at Pappy’s or Hi-Pointe one week, a special-occasion dinner at Acero or Peppe’s the next, a ramen or Cuban-sandwich run when you want something specific and done well. And when you find your own favorite — the little independent spot that becomes your regular — that’s the real win. Those are the places that give a city its flavor, and the ones most worth supporting.
### Why local spots beat the chains
There’s a reason a list like this skips the drive-thrus. Independent restaurants are cooked by people making the food they know and love, for a community they’re part of — and that shows up on the plate in a way a corporate spec sheet never can. Every dollar you spend at one of them stays closer to home and keeps a real local business, and a real local family, going.
It’s also just better eating. The chains are engineered to be the same everywhere; these places are memorable precisely because they’re not. So the next time the easy move is the familiar logo off the highway, take the small detour instead. Your taste buds — and your neighbors running these kitchens — will thank you for it. And if you have a go-to that isn’t on this list, that’s the whole idea: St. Louis has far more great independent restaurants than any nine-spot roundup could hold, and the fun is in finding your own.
### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What is a must eat in St. Louis?
A.  A few things are close to mandatory: Memphis-style barbecue ribs at Pappy’s Smokehouse, a St. Louis-style burger at Hi-Pointe Drive-In or Stacked STL, and a genuine Cuban sandwich at Havana’s Cuisine on Tampa-imported La Segunda bread. Round it out with Tokyo-style shoyu ramen at Menya Rui. Between them you’ll taste why locals are so loyal to their independent spots.
### Q. Where do famous people eat in St. Louis?
A.  There’s no single celebrity hangout, but well-regarded, chef-driven rooms like Acero in Maplewood and Peppe’s Apt. 2 in Kirkwood draw the special-occasion crowd, while institutions like Pappy’s Smokehouse pull everyone from families to visiting musicians — its walls are covered in photos of the bands who’ve stopped in. In St. Louis, the best tables are democratic; anyone can grab one.
### Q. What is Saint Louis famous for food?
A.  St. Louis is known for a distinctive local canon: thin-crust St. Louis-style pizza with Provel cheese, toasted ravioli, gooey butter cake, and a strong barbecue tradition. But the everyday reality is a deep bench of independent restaurants — barbecue, burgers, ramen, Cuban, Italian, and more — spread across neighborhoods from the Central West End to Maplewood, Webster Groves, and Kirkwood.
### Q. What food is unique to St. Louis, Missouri?
A.  Toasted ravioli, gooey butter cake, the St. Paul sandwich, frozen custard concretes, pork steaks, and cracker-crust pizza with Provel. Most of it came out of working neighborhoods rather than restaurant kitchens, which is why it is still best at corner places.
### Q. Where do locals eat in St. Louis?
A.  Neighborhood streets rather than destination districts — South Grand, Cherokee, The Hill, Delmar in the Loop. The pattern is that locals eat where parking is annoying and the room is small, which is usually a good sign about the kitchen.
### Q. What restaurants is St. Louis famous for?
A.  The city is better known for its dishes than for any single restaurant — toasted ravioli, Provel pizza, gooey butter cake, the St. Paul sandwich. Ask which place does one of those well and you will get a real answer; ask for the famous restaurant and you will get an argument.

## Discover Unique Finds: Your Guide to St. Louis Union Station Shopping Revised July 23, 2026 What shopping is at St. Louis Union Station? St. Louis Union Station is more experience than traditional mall now — the old shops gave way to attractions like the aquarium, the St. Louis Wheel, and mini-golf, alongside gift shops, candy and sweets stores, and boutiques inside the historic 1894 train shed. Expect souvenirs and local treats rather than a full retail mall, plus restaurants, hotels, and the nightly fire-and-light show. Keep reading ↓If you grew up around St. Louis in the ‘80s or ‘90s, “Union Station” probably means one thing: the mall. The Disney Store, the Fudgery pulling taffy in the window, the food court, that whole festival-marketplace buzz under the old train shed. So it’s a fair question when you’re planning a visit today — *can I still go shopping at Union Station?* The honest answer is that Union Station isn’t the shopping mall it used to be. But it turned into something arguably better: one of St. Louis’s top family destinations, where the “shopping” is now charming gift shops and sweet treats woven through a whole complex of attractions, restaurants, and a landmark hotel. Here’s the straight story on what happened to the mall, what shopping and gifts you’ll actually find at Union Station today, and how to make a great visit out of it — verified against Union Station’s current information for 2026. **Bookmark this before you go — and set your expectations right: Union Station is a play-and-dine destination now, not a mall.** ## Is there still a mall at Union Station in St. Louis? **No — the traditional shopping mall at Union Station is gone.** The 1980s festival marketplace, with its dozens of stores, declined through the 2000s and eventually closed. In a fitting twist, the **St. Louis Aquarium literally took over the old interior mall space** when Union Station was redeveloped into an entertainment destination. So if you’re picturing a day of retail browsing, that’s not what Union Station offers anymore. What replaced it is, for most visitors, a lot more fun: an aquarium, a 200-foot observation wheel, a ropes course, mini golf, a mirror maze, nightly light and fire shows, a slate of restaurants, and a beautifully restored historic hotel. The “shopping” today is the gift-shop-and-treats kind — a nice add-on to a day of attractions rather than the main event. ## What shopping and gifts you’ll find at Union Station today Set your expectations for **specialty gift shops and sweets**, not department stores, and you’ll have a great time. Here’s what’s actually there: - **The St. Louis Aquarium gift shop**— the biggest “store” at Union Station, packed with plush sharks and otters, toys, apparel, and souvenirs. You don’t always need an aquarium ticket to browse it, and it’s the go-to for a kid’s keepsake. - **Cookies and Cupcakes**— a bakery for a sweet grab-and-go treat. - **The Soda Fountain**— part restaurant, part candy-and-sweets shop, famous for over-the-top “Freak Shakes” and old-fashioned confections. - **Attraction shops and kiosks**— small gift and photo stands tied to the Wheel and the other attractions, good for souvenirs and mementos. It’s the perfect setup for grabbing a gift or a sweet on your way through — just don’t arrive expecting a mall directory. Looking for a keepsake? The best Union Station souvenirs skew local and kid-friendly: a plush shark or otter from the aquarium shop, a St. Louis Wheel photo, gooey-butter-flavored treats, or classic candy from the Soda Fountain. It’s enough to satisfy the “can we get something?” request without a full shopping trip — and the aquarium store in particular is roomy and genuinely fun to browse. ## What happened to the Union Station mall? The story is a St. Louis landmark’s reinvention. **Union Station opened in 1894** as the largest and busiest railroad terminal in the world, serving 22 railroads beneath its jaw-dropping Grand Hall. As passenger rail faded, the last train pulled out in 1978, and the station sat looking for a purpose. In 1985 it reopened as a **festival marketplace mall** — the era most St. Louisans remember, full of shops and restaurants. That format thrived for a while, then slowly declined as retail changed, until the stores emptied out. Rather than let a National Historic Landmark fade, developers reimagined it: beginning around 2018–2019, Union Station was **redeveloped into a family entertainment and hospitality destination**, anchored by the new St. Louis Aquarium (opened Christmas Day 2019) and the St. Louis Wheel. The Grand Hall became the centerpiece for a spectacular free 3D light show. The building was saved — just with a new job. It’s a history worth appreciating while you’re there. At its opening, Union Station was the largest and busiest passenger terminal in the world, and generations of travelers — soldiers heading off to war, families heading West, dignitaries and everyday St. Louisans — passed beneath that Grand Hall ceiling. Standing in the same room today, now full of families on their way to see sharks, is its own kind of only-in-St.-Louis moment. ## What Union Station is now — the real reason to visit Come for a full day, not a shopping trip, and Union Station shines. ## Cate Zone Chinese Cafe: The University City Spot for Real Northeastern Chinese Revised July 23, 2026 What’s the best Chinese restaurant in St. Louis? Cate Zone Chinese Cafe, at 8148 Olive Blvd in University City, is one of St. Louis’s most-loved authentic Chinese restaurants — a Northeastern (Dongbei) kitchen, not Sichuan. Order the hot crispy fish, the sweet and sour pork, and the housemade dumplings. Closed Mondays; an Ian Froeb STL 100 honoree. Keep reading ↓You know the difference. There’s the Chinese takeout you order on autopilot — the same crab rangoon, the same neon sweet-and-sour — and then there’s the real thing, the food someone’s grandmother would actually recognize. If you’ve been craving the second kind, and you’re willing to point the car toward Olive Boulevard, there’s a small storefront in University City that has built a devoted following doing exactly that. Cate Zone Chinese Cafe isn’t trying to be everything to everyone. It’s rooted in Northeastern Chinese cooking — hearty, homestyle food from the Dongbei region up near the Russian and Korean borders — and it does it well enough to keep landing on the city’s best-restaurant lists. Here’s what it is, what to order, and what to know before you go. ## At a Glance: What to Order ## What Cate Zone Actually Is This is Northeastern Chinese food — a point of confusion worth clearing up, because plenty of listings mislabel it as Sichuan. It isn’t. Dongbei cooking is heartier and homier than the mouth-numbing spice most Americans associate with Sichuan, and the menu here first attracted notice for that Northeastern focus, even if it also reaches into other regions with dishes like Yangzhou fried rice and spicy Chengdu chicken. The restaurant is owned by Daniel Ma and Quincy Lin, and it has quietly become one of St. Louis’s most respected authentic Chinese kitchens — a longtime pick on Ian Froeb’s STL 100 list of the region’s best restaurants (named in 2018, 2019, 2020, and 2023), and the subject of a glowing Riverfront Times review that singled out its hot crisp fish as the dish it’s best known for. It’s the kind of unassuming strip-mall spot that food-obsessed St. Louisans send their out-of-town friends to. Don’t let the modest storefront fool you — some of the best food in any American city hides in exactly these rooms. Cate Zone isn’t chasing trends or plating for photos; it’s cooking the food of a specific place and doing it with care. That focus is the whole appeal. When a menu commits to one regional tradition instead of trying to please everyone, you get dishes with real point of view, and Cate Zone has built its reputation on precisely that. ## A quick primer on Northeastern (Dongbei) Chinese food If “Dongbei” is new to you, here’s the short version. Dongbei means China’s northeast — the provinces of Heilongjiang, Jilin, and Liaoning, up against the Russian and North Korean borders. It’s a cold-winter region with a short growing season, so the cooking leans on preserved and pickled vegetables, wheat as much as rice, and pork as the favorite meat. The result is hearty, savory, generous food built on a few bold flavors rather than delicate ones. The region’s history shows up on the plate: Dongbei cooking carries influences from neighboring Russian, Mongolian, and Korean kitchens, and it grew out of the older Shandong and Manchu traditions. Cold-weather staples — wheat-flour breads and dumplings, crocks of fermented cabbage, big braises — make sense the moment you picture the winters they were built for. A few dishes tell the whole story. **Guo bao rou** — crispy fried pork in a bright sweet-and-sour sauce — is the Northeastern original that the gloopy American-Chinese “sweet and sour pork” was loosely descended from; tasting the real one is a small revelation. **Suan cai**, fermented sour cabbage, gets stewed with fatty pork belly into something deeply comforting. **Di san xian** braises potato, eggplant, and green pepper into a savory, glossy classic. And dumplings — thick-skinned, pan-fried or boiled — are the heart of the table, often served with chilled noodles alongside. Compared with fiery Sichuan or light, seafood-forward Cantonese cooking, Dongbei food is the rustic, warming, pickle-and-pork cousin — less about shock-and-awe spice, more about deep, satisfying, cold-night flavor. ## What to Order at Cate Zone Start with the **hot crisp fish** — the dish Cate Zone is best known for, lightly battered and fried with a Sichuan-pepper kick that sneaks up on you. The **guo bao rou** (sweet and sour pork) is the Northeastern version done right: crisp pork cutlets in a light, ginger-snapped sauce, nothing like the neon takeout goo you’re picturing. The **housemade dumplings** are a must — hand-folded in-house, thick-skinned and satisfying, and a specialty the second location leaned into even harder. From there, don’t skip the **sour cabbage with pork belly**, a true Dongbei signature where fermented cabbage and fatty pork stew into something warming and a little tangy, and the **cumin lamb**, fragrant with toasted cumin, a little heat, and fresh cilantro. If your table is adventurous, ask what’s good that day — the kitchen’s homestyle Northeastern dishes are where it shines. Everything is meant to be shared family-style, so bring people and order across the menu; portions are generous and half the fun is passing plates around. ## Before You Go: Hours & Tips Cate Zone Chinese Cafe ...
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/cate-zone-stl-your-guide-to-authentic-chinese-cuisine-in-st-louis

## The Best Coffee Shops in Wentzville, MO: A Local’s Guide
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/discover-the-best-coffee-shops-in-wentzville-mo-your-local-guide
Wentzville runs on coffee — it just about has to. This is one of the fastest-growing cities in Missouri, a place where half the town seems to be commuting east on I-70 or wrangling kids to a Saturday soccer game, and everyone needs a good cup somewhere along the way. Whether you want a two-minute drive-thru fix, a laptop-friendly table, or a genuinely only-in-Wentzville spot worth the detour, the town delivers.
Here’s a local’s guide to the best coffee shops in and around Wentzville — the quirky independents, the reliable drive-thrus, and one lavender-farm café just up the road that’s worth the short drive.
### What coffee shops does Wentzville have?
Put plainly, people search this as What are some good coffee places in Wentzville, MO? — and the useful answer sorts them by what you need that morning rather than by star rating.
### Which independent shops stand out?
Start with the one you’ll tell people about. Flower Coffee Collective serves espresso out of a lovingly restored 1960s Nomad camper trailer — you can drive up or park and sit at the outdoor tables. It was started by a young local, Faith McDonald, who opened it at nineteen, and it pours locally roasted coffee (the beans come from a small Missouri roaster) with homemade cold foam and salted-caramel lattes that have a real following. It’s the kind of place that gives a growing suburb some soul, and it’s the single best “only in Wentzville” coffee stop.
Heading into the city instead? Our metro guide covers how to pick a St. Louis coffee shop by neighborhood and errand.
Downtown on Main Street, Ellbee’s General Store is the sit-down-and-linger pick. Part old-fashioned general store, part café, it does espresso drinks, frappes, milkshakes, and ice cream alongside candy and sandwiches — a nostalgic, charming spot to actually stay a while rather than grab and run. Between the two, Wentzville’s independent scene punches above its weight.
What makes both worth seeking out is the thing the chains can’t bottle: a sense of place. Flower Coffee Collective feels like a Wentzville story — a young local betting on her hometown, roasting-partner beans from just up the river, a camper that people now plan their morning around. Ellbee’s leans the other direction, into old-fashioned Americana, the kind of counter where you might actually strike up a conversation. In a town that’s adding rooftops and strip malls by the month, these are the spots that still feel like Wentzville, not Anywhere, USA. If you only have time for one independent stop, make it the camper — but locals rotate through both.
### Where are the reliable drive-thrus?
Sometimes you just need caffeine, fast. 7 Brew Coffee on Wentzville Parkway is the speed champion — a drive-thru-only stand known for fast, customizable orders, infused energy drinks, Italian sodas, and shakes, open early morning to late at night, which matters in a metro where only a handful of coffee shops stay open late. The newest option, Ziggi’s Coffee (which opened off I-70 in early 2026), splits the difference: it’s a full cafe and a drive-thru with WiFi, handcrafted espresso, and the trendy “dirty soda” drinks, so you can grab and go or come in and sit. And there’s the dependable Starbucks on Wentzville Parkway (drive-thru plus seating), with a second grab-and-go kiosk inside the Target. None of these will surprise you — that’s exactly the point on a rushed morning.
A quick word on the drive-thru boom, because it says something about Wentzville. Fast, made-to-order coffee stands like 7 Brew and Ziggi’s have exploded across the fast-growing western suburbs precisely because so much of life here happens in the car — the commute to the GM plant or east toward the city, the school runs, the ballfields. These spots compete on speed, friendliness, and a menu of energy drinks, dirty sodas, and blended treats that goes well beyond a plain latte. If you’ve got a carful of kids or a meeting in twenty minutes, they’re a genuine convenience, not a compromise — and the regulars have strong opinions about which line moves fastest.
### Do you want a drive-thru or a sit-and-work room?
Pure drive-thru speed: 7 Brew. Drive-thru or a table with WiFi: Ziggi’s or the Wentzville Parkway Starbucks. Grab-and-go kiosk: the Starbucks inside Target. The quirky, sit-outside camper: Flower Coffee Collective. Sit down and stay a while: Ellbee’s General Store downtown. Match the spot to your morning and you’ll never be stuck, whether you’ve got two minutes or a whole lazy Saturday.
### Is Long Row Lavender worth the short drive?
Just up the road in Wright City — near Wentzville, not in it — Long Row Lavender is a destination lavender farm with a real café and coffee bar. The signature draw is the lavender latte, and the farm serves coffee, desserts, and a light lunch on a pretty patio, generally Wednesday through Saturday. It’s less a quick-coffee run than a little outing — a lovely way to turn a morning coffee into a half-day escape when the weather’s nice. Wander the lavender rows, grab a latte and a dessert on the patio, and you’ve got the makings of a genuinely pleasant Saturday that just happens to start with coffee. Just check the days and hours before you go, since the farm keeps a limited, seasonal schedule rather than café hours.
### How did a fast-growing town end up running on coffee?
It’s no accident Wentzville’s coffee scene keeps expanding. The city has been one of the fastest-growing in Missouri for two decades — its population has ballooned to roughly 48,000, a jump of several hundred percent since 2000 — and all those new neighbors mean new cafes keep opening to serve them, alongside the other shops and services in our Wentzville city guide. What was once a small crossroads town now has everything from a vintage coffee camper to a brand-new franchise cafe, and the options only keep improving. For a suburb its size, that’s a genuinely good coffee map.
It also reflects a broader shift in how a fast-growing town builds its identity. Coffee shops are often the first “third places” a booming suburb gets — somewhere that isn’t home or work where neighbors actually run into each other. As Wentzville has filled in, the independents like Flower Coffee Collective and Ellbee’s have quietly become community anchors, the kind of small businesses that give a growing place its character. Supporting them is part of how a suburb keeps a little soul as it scales, and it’s a big reason a “best coffee in Wentzville” list is worth keeping current.
Nothing to do with coffee — but Clifton Heights is worth a Saturday.
### Which One Should You Try First?
If you’re new to Wentzville coffee, here’s the short version. Want the story and the best local cup? Start at Flower Coffee Collective. Want to sit, sip, and soak up some downtown charm? Ellbee’s General Store. Running late and just need great coffee fast? 7 Brew or the Wentzville Parkway Starbucks. Curious about the newest spot with room to work? Ziggi’s. And when you’ve got a free morning and nice weather? Point the car toward Long Row Lavender in Wright City for a lavender latte on the farm. Work your way through all five and you’ll have tasted the full range of what the area does well — from vintage-camper charm to lightning-fast drive-thru.
### How do you make a morning of it?
Coffee in Wentzville pairs naturally with the rest of a laid-back suburban morning. Grab a cup from the camper and walk it over to one of the parks — Rotary Park and the Quail Ridge area give you trails and green space to sip and stroll. Downtown around Main Street, an Ellbee’s coffee goes hand-in-hand with browsing the little shops, and if the morning stretches toward lunch, our guide to where to eat in Wentzville picks up right where the coffee leaves off. And if you’re headed out to the wine country or the Katy Trail for the day, a drive-thru on Wentzville Parkway is the logical fuel stop on the way out of town. The point is that good coffee here isn’t just a transaction — it’s the start of a good Saturday.
One more practical tip: hours vary a lot between the fast drive-thrus (open early to late) and the sit-down spots (which keep more limited, daytime hours, and the lavender farm is only open a few days a week). A quick check before you drive out saves a disappointing locked door, especially for the destination spots.

Exploring Wentzville and the western suburbs? Local coffee shops, bakeries, and cafes are exactly what a good directory helps you find. Search St Louis Near Me Directory for spots across Wentzville, St. Charles County, and the whole metro before you head out.
