### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. Is there a coffee shop in a camper in Wentzville?
A.  Yes — Flower Coffee Collective serves espresso and specialty drinks out of a restored 1960s Nomad camper trailer, with outdoor tables where you can sit. It uses locally roasted beans and is known for homemade cold foam and salted-caramel lattes. It’s the most distinctive, only-in-Wentzville coffee stop in town.
### Q. Where can I get coffee and work in Wentzville?
A.  For a table, WiFi, and space to work, the new Ziggi’s Coffee off I-70 and the Starbucks on Wentzville Parkway are your best bets — both have indoor seating alongside a drive-thru. Ellbee’s General Store downtown is a cozier sit-down option if you want charm over a corporate cafe feel.
### Q. Does Wentzville have a drive-thru coffee shop?
A.  Several. 7 Brew on Wentzville Parkway is a drive-thru-only stand famous for fast, customizable drinks and long hours. Ziggi’s Coffee and the Wentzville Parkway Starbucks also have drive-thrus (plus indoor seating). On a rushed morning, any of the three gets you caffeinated without leaving the car.
### Q. Is Long Row Lavender in Wentzville?
A.  Not quite — Long Row Lavender is in nearby Wright City, a short drive west of Wentzville. It’s a lavender farm with a café and coffee bar, best known for its lavender latte, plus desserts and a light lunch on the patio (generally Wednesday through Saturday). Treat it as a fun day-trip add-on rather than a quick local coffee run.
### Q. What is the most unique coffee shop in Wentzville?
A.  Flower Coffee Collective, hands down — it operates out of a restored 1960s Nomad camper trailer, serves locally roasted coffee, and was opened by a local who started the business at nineteen. Between the vintage camper, the outdoor tables, and the homemade cold foam and salted-caramel lattes, it’s the most distinctive, photogenic, and genuinely local coffee stop in town.
### Q. Where can I get coffee near the Katy Trail or wine country from Wentzville?
A.  Wentzville sits at the eastern edge of Missouri’s wine-country day trips, so a drive-thru on Wentzville Parkway — 7 Brew, Ziggi’s, or Starbucks — makes an easy fuel stop before heading west. For a more scenic coffee outing, Long Row Lavender’s café in nearby Wright City combines a lavender latte with a pretty farm setting, a natural pairing with a Katy Trail or Augusta wine-country afternoon.
### Q. Where can I find the best coffee in St. Charles County?
A.  Wentzville, St. Charles, O’Fallon and St. Peters each have independents worth a stop, and the county is spread out enough that drive time usually decides it for you. Rather than chase one county-wide winner, work out whether you want a fast window, a table for an hour, or a weekend destination, then pick the closest shop that does that one thing well.
### Q. Which coffee shop has the best WiFi?
A.  The shops that mean it advertise it — outlets along the wall, tables sized for one, and staff who do not mind a second refill. The tell for the opposite is a room of tall stools and a queue at nine. If working is the point of the trip, call ahead and ask whether laptops are welcome at the hour you plan to arrive; most places will tell you plainly.
### Q. Do coffee shops have secure WiFi?
A.  Treat every shop network as open, because most are. That is fine for ordinary browsing and a bad idea for banking or anything you would not want read over your shoulder. Use your phone’s hotspot or a VPN for anything sensitive, avoid saving the network, and log out of accounts when you pack up.
### Q. Why are coffee shops closing early?
A.  Afternoon trade in a commuter town is thin and staffing it is expensive, so a lot of independents now run a strong morning and shut mid-afternoon rather than pay for quiet hours. Hours also move with the season and with staffing, which is why any list of times goes stale fast. Check the shop’s own page the morning you go.
### Q. Why does Wentzville have so many coffee shops?
A.  Because it’s booming. Wentzville has been one of Missouri’s fastest-growing cities for two decades, with its population climbing to around 48,000 and a big commuter base along I-70. All those new residents keep drawing new cafes — from independent spots to national franchises — so the coffee options have grown right along with the town. For a suburb its size, the range of genuinely good, locally owned coffee is a pleasant surprise, and it keeps getting better every year.

The appeal is real: total customization (great for picky eaters, big appetites, and dietary needs alike), consistent cooking every time, and a bit of novelty that makes it a fun stop with kids or friends. Nobody has to send a dish back or pick around ingredients — you simply didn’t add them in the first place. The robotic cooking adds a second, quieter benefit: consistency. A human wok cook has good nights and rushed nights; an automated barrel cooks your bowl the same way every time, at the right heat, without the guesswork. For a fast, fresh, made-to-order meal, that reliability is genuinely useful — you know what you’re getting, and you built it yourself. It also tends to be quick, which makes Tasty Bowl a solid option for a weeknight dinner when you want something fresher than fast food but faster than a sit-down. ## Beyond the bowls: sushi, ramen, and bubble tea The stir-fry gets the attention, but Tasty Bowl is a full Asian-fusion menu: - **Sushi and sashimi**— hand-rolled to order, a proper sit-down-and-share option rather than a grab-and-go afterthought. - **Ramen**— warming, brothy bowls loaded with toppings for when the stir-fry mood isn’t calling and you want something to curl up with. - **Build-your-own stir-fry**— the robot-cooked signature, endlessly customizable from base to sauce. - **Appetizers and bubble tea**— starters to share and the sweet, chewy-pearled tea in a range of flavors that rounds out the meal or stands in for dessert. - **A bar**— drinks to go with dinner, which not every Asian-fusion ...

You can wander through their beautiful grounds, which are absolutely covered in over two million twinkling lights. They often have projections and immersive experiences that make the whole place feel magical. It’s a more serene way to enjoy the lights, and they sometimes offer festive drinks and s’mores. ## St. Louis Annual Events: A Season-by-Season Guide to the City's Best Festivals Revised July 24, 2026 What are the best annual events and festivals in St. Louis? St. Louis marks its seasons with mostly-free annual festivals: Soulard Mardi Gras (late winter); the Downtown and Dogtown St. Patrick’s Day parades (March); Shakespeare in the Park and PrideFest (late spring/June); the Fourth of July on the Gateway Arch grounds; Festival of Nations, the Japanese Festival, and Big Muddy Blues (late summer); the Saint Louis Art Fair and Great Forest Park Balloon Race (September); Soulard Oktoberfest (October); and the Ameren Thanks-For-Giving Parade (late November), which bridges into the winter holidays. Confirm each year’s exact date before you go. Keep reading ↓Have you ever moved to a new city and felt like everyone else already knew the rhythm of the year — when the parades roll, when the balloons go up, when the whole town seems to spill outdoors at once? St. Louis runs on exactly that kind of calendar. From the first beads of a late-winter Mardi Gras to the smell of bratwurst at an October Oktoberfest, the city marks its seasons with festivals that are, more often than not, free and open to anyone who shows up. Here is a season-by-season guide to the annual events St. Louis throws every single year — the traditions worth building a weekend around, whether you’ve lived here for decades or just unpacked the last box. Dates shift a little year to year, so treat this as the shape of the calendar and confirm the exact weekend before you go. ## Late winter: Mardi Gras season St. Louis takes Mardi Gras seriously — fittingly, for a city with French roots. The heart of it is **Soulard Mardi Gras**, one of the largest Mardi Gras celebrations in the country, unfolding over several weeks in the historic Soulard neighborhood and peaking with a massive Grand Parade the Saturday before Fat Tuesday. There are family-friendly events earlier in the season and a rowdier street party on parade day; either way, it’s the city’s first big outdoor gathering of the year and a genuine only-in-St.-Louis experience. Bundle up, get there early for parking, and let the beads fly. ## Spring: parades and green rivers of people March belongs to St. Patrick. St. Louis runs **two** beloved St. Patrick’s Day parades, and locals have strong opinions about them. The **Downtown St. Patrick’s Day Parade** is the big, decades-old civic one along Market Street, with floats, bands, and a run to match. Out in **Dogtown** — the historically Irish neighborhood near Forest Park — the **Ancient Order of Hibernians parade on March 17** is the neighborhood-party version, a wall-to-wall street celebration that’s as much block party as parade. Pick your style, wear green, and plan your ride: both draw enormous crowds. ## Late spring and early summer: culture in the park As the weather turns, St. Louis heads to Forest Park and downtown. The **St. Louis Shakespeare Festival’s “Shakespeare in the Park”** stages a free, professional production in Forest Park’s Shakespeare Glen across late May and June — bring a blanket, a picnic, and a bottle of wine. In late June, **PrideFest**, the region’s largest Pride celebration, fills downtown with a parade and festival. It’s a stretch of the calendar defined by long evenings, free entertainment, and the city rediscovering its outdoor self. ## Summer: fireworks over the Arch The Fourth of July is a marquee event here. The annual **Fourth of July celebration on the Gateway Arch grounds** (the long-running successor to Fair Saint Louis) packs the riverfront and downtown with live music, an air show, and one of the biggest fireworks displays in the Midwest, framed by the Arch itself. It’s hot, it’s crowded, and it’s worth it — stake out a spot early, hydrate, and enjoy a genuinely spectacular backdrop. Smaller municipal fireworks light up communities all across the metro the same week if downtown feels like too much. ## Late summer: the world comes to St. Louis Late August and early September are the city’s most gloriously international stretch. The **Festival of Nations** in Tower Grove Park — a free, decades-old celebration put on by the International Institute — gathers dozens of cultures for food stalls, music, and dance, and it is a food-lover’s dream. Over Labor Day weekend, the **Japanese Festival** at the Missouri Botanical Garden (running since the 1970s) turns the world-class Japanese Garden into a showcase of taiko drumming, tea ceremonies, and lantern-lit evenings, while the **Big Muddy Blues Festival** brings free live blues to Laclede’s Landing. Between them, you could eat and listen your way around the globe without leaving town. ## Early fall: art, balloons, and beer September and October are arguably peak festival season. The **Saint Louis Art Fair** transforms downtown Clayton into one of the top-ranked juried art fairs in the country, free to browse. Nearby, the **Great Forest Park Balloon Race** — and its can’t-miss Friday-night **Balloon Glow**, when the balloons light up after dark — is a free, decades-old St. Louis tradition that draws a hundred thousand people to Forest Park. Then the season turns to beer: **Soulard Oktoberfest** brings German food, music, and steins to Soulard Market Park, one of several Oktoberfests across the metro. Cooler air, big crowds, and a lot to do outdoors before winter. ## Late fall: the bridge to the holidays As the ...
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/st-louis-annual-events-a-season-by-season-guide-to-the-citys-best-festivals

Smaller municipal fireworks light up communities all across the metro the same week if downtown feels like too much. ## Late summer: the world comes to St. Louis Late August and early September are the city’s most gloriously international stretch. The **Festival of Nations** in Tower Grove Park — a free, decades-old celebration put on by the International Institute — gathers dozens of cultures for food stalls, music, and dance, and it is a food-lover’s dream. Over Labor Day weekend, the **Japanese Festival** at the Missouri Botanical Garden (running since the 1970s) turns the world-class Japanese Garden into a showcase of taiko drumming, tea ceremonies, and lantern-lit evenings, while the **Big Muddy Blues Festival** brings free live blues to Laclede’s Landing. Between them, you could eat and listen your way around the globe without leaving town. ## Early fall: art, balloons, and beer September and October are arguably peak festival season. The **Saint Louis Art Fair** transforms downtown Clayton into one of the top-ranked juried art fairs in the country, free to browse. Nearby, the **Great Forest Park Balloon Race** — and its can’t-miss Friday-night **Balloon Glow**, when the balloons light up after dark — is a free, decades-old St. Louis tradition that draws a hundred thousand people to Forest Park. Then the season turns to beer: **Soulard Oktoberfest** brings German food, music, and steins to Soulard Market Park, one of several Oktoberfests across the metro. Cooler air, big crowds, and a lot to do outdoors before winter. ## Late fall: the bridge to the holidays As the ...

## Golden Chicken: A Beloved St. Peters Mediterranean Eatery Revised July 23, 2026 What kind of food does Golden Chicken in St. Peters serve? Golden Chicken at 632 Jungermann Rd in St. Peters serves Mediterranean and Middle Eastern halal food — rotisserie chicken, shawarma, kebabs, gyros, falafel, and wings, plus mezze like hummus, baba ghanoush, tabbouleh, and fattoush. Despite the name it is not a Southern or fried-chicken spot; the ‘golden’ refers to its rotisserie chicken. It holds 4.7 stars across 1,000+ Google reviews, is closed Thursdays, and offers dine-in, takeout, catering, and delivery. Keep reading ↓Picture a Friday evening in St. Peters — Friday, because on Thursdays this particular kitchen goes dark, and more than one hopeful diner has learned that the hard way. The light is going amber over Jungermann Road, everyone in the car is tired of the same three dinners on rotation, and someone votes for “something different, but not a whole production.” A few minutes later you’re unwrapping a warm shawarma, the garlic sauce doing exactly what garlic sauce is supposed to do, and the car has gone quiet in that good way. Maybe you’ve driven past the little storefront in the Spencer Creek Shopping Center a hundred times on your way through St. Charles County and never stopped. Maybe a coworker in O’Fallon swears by the falafel, or a neighbor in Cottleville keeps bringing it to gatherings. However you get there, Golden Chicken has a way of turning first-timers into regulars — which is roughly what a thousand-plus reviews will tell you before you ever taste a bite. The word-of-mouth in this corner of the metro does a lot of the restaurant’s advertising for it, and once you’ve been, you understand why people bother to tell their neighbors. This is an honest look at what the place actually is, what to order, and why a small, family-owned spot on Jungermann Road has quietly become one of the St. Peters area’s most beloved kitchens. ## What Golden Chicken actually is (and isn’t) Let’s clear up the name first, because it fools people. Golden Chicken is not a fried-chicken chain and not a Southern-food joint. It’s an independent, family-owned **Mediterranean and Middle Eastern** restaurant serving **halal** food — shawarma, kebabs, gyros, falafel, and the from-scratch **rotisserie chicken** that gives the place its name. Feast Magazine described it simply as a spot cooking “classic Middle Eastern fare,” and the St. Louis Post-Dispatch summed up the signature dish as chicken that “spins delight from the rotisserie.” That’s the truest picture you’ll find. It sits at 632 Jungermann Rd, St. Peters, MO 63376, a modest storefront that TripAdvisor reviewers lovingly call “small, unassuming… with world-class food.” That gap — humble room, serious kitchen — is a big part of the charm. Open since around 2021 and family-run the whole way, it’s the kind of independent spot a chain-heavy stretch of suburbia badly needs more of. You are not paying for chandeliers here. You are paying for the food. ## What to order the first time If you’re new, a few dishes do the introducing better than others: - **Rotisserie chicken**— the “golden” in the name. Whole or half, juicy under a burnished skin, with garlic sauce and warm pita that disappears fast. - **Shawarma**— chicken or beef, sliced from the vertical spit, wrapped or served over rice. The gateway dish, and for good reason. - **Kebabs**— grilled, generous, and the move when you want a proper plate rather than a handheld. - **Falafel**— the reliable test of any Mediterranean kitchen: crisp outside, green and herby inside. Regulars order it on repeat. - **The mezze and salads**— hummus, baba ghanoush, tabbouleh, fattoush, tahini. Order a couple to share; they turn a sandwich run into an actual spread. Save room for baklava. The wings deserve a mention too — done in a few styles for the table that can’t agree. One honest note on the menu: it evolves, and the kitchen leans on doing things fresh rather than pinning down a hundred fixed items. If you have a specific craving, the safest move is to glance at the current menu at goldenchicken-stpeters.com or simply ask when you order — and yes, there is no such thing as too much garlic sauce. Hungry now? Golden Chicken is at 632 Jungermann Rd in St. Peters. ## Your Ultimate Guide: How to Plan a Trip to St. Louis, Missouri Revised July 28, 2026 How should I plan a trip to St. Louis? To plan a St. Louis trip, base yourself downtown or in a walkable neighborhood like the Central West End and give yourself two to three days for the highlights: the Gateway Arch, the free museums and Saint Louis Zoo in Forest Park, the Missouri Botanical Garden, and City Museum. Spring and fall bring the best weather. Get around by car or MetroLink, and stretch your budget with the city’s many free attractions and off-peak hotel rates. Keep reading ↓Thinking about your next getaway? St. Louis, Missouri, is a fantastic choice, offering a mix of history, culture, and fun. Whether you're drawn to the iconic Gateway Arch, the vibrant blues music scene, or delicious barbecue, this city has a lot to offer. Planning a trip to St. Louis, Missouri, can seem like a lot, but don't worry, we've got you covered with tips to make your adventure smooth and enjoyable. Let's get started on planning your ultimate St. Louis experience! ### Key Takeaways - When you plan a trip to St. Louis, consider visiting during the spring or fall for pleasant weather, though summer offers lively festivals and off-season travel can save you money. - Getting around St. Louis is manageable; while renting a car offers flexibility, the public MetroLink and MetroBus system, along with rideshares and scooters, provide good alternatives. - St. Louis offers a range of lodging, from downtown hotels and charming neighborhood stays to family-friendly options, so you can pick what fits your style and budget. - Don't miss the iconic Gateway Arch, explore world-class museums like the City Museum, and enjoy the city's beautiful green spaces like Forest Park. - Immerse yourself in St. Louis's culture by trying its unique cuisine, experiencing live blues music, and exploring historic neighborhoods like The Hill or Laclede's Landing. ## Planning Your St. Louis Adventure Thinking about a trip to St. Louis? It's a fantastic choice! This guide is here to help you get organized so you can focus on enjoying the Gateway City. We'll cover the best times to visit, how the city is laid out, and some smart ways to save money. ### Best Times To Visit St. Louis When you decide to visit St. Louis can really shape your experience. The weather is generally pleasant in the spring and fall, making these popular times for a reason. Spring brings blooming flowers and comfortable temperatures, perfect for exploring parks and outdoor attractions. Fall offers crisp air and a vibrant foliage display, plus it's festival season! Think food fairs, art shows, and the famous Great Forest Park Balloon Race. Summer can be quite warm and humid, but it's also when many outdoor events and activities are in full swing. If you're looking to save a bit, consider visiting during the shoulder seasons or even the winter. While it can be cold, you'll often find fewer crowds and lower prices on accommodations. Here's a quick look at what weather to expect: - **Spring (April-May):**Mild temperatures, blooming gardens, and outdoor activities begin. Great for sightseeing. - **Summer (June-August):**Hot and humid, but lots of festivals and events. Ideal for riverfront activities. - **Fall (September-October):**Cooler, pleasant weather, beautiful foliage, and peak festival season. - **Winter (November-March):**Cold, but fewer crowds and potentially lower prices. Good for indoor attractions. ### Understanding St. Louis's Layout St. Louis is pretty spread out, but understanding its general layout can make getting around much easier. The city is bisected by the Mississippi River, with downtown on the west bank. Many of the major attractions, like the Gateway Arch, are located downtown or nearby in Forest Park. The neighborhoods radiate outwards from the city center. Knowing this helps you group activities by area, saving you travel time. For instance, if you're visiting the Arch, you might want to explore the nearby riverfront and downtown attractions on the same day. If you plan to visit the Missouri Botanical Garden, you can group that with other attractions in the southern part of the city. It's helpful to think of the city in terms of these general zones. Planning your itinerary around these key areas will help you make the most of your time and minimize unnecessary travel. ### Budget-Friendly Travel Tips St. Louis can be surprisingly affordable if you plan smart. One of the easiest ways to save is by visiting during the off-season when hotel rates tend to drop. Look for deals and packages, especially if you're a member of travel clubs. Eating like a local can also cut costs; instead of always opting for sit-down restaurants, try grabbing a bite from a food truck or a casual eatery. Many of the city's best attractions are free, like exploring Forest Park or visiting the grounds of the Gateway Arch. Consider purchasing a city pass if you plan on visiting multiple paid attractions, as this can offer significant savings. Also, keep an eye out for local events and festivals, which often provide free entertainment and a chance to experience the city's culture without breaking the bank. You might even find some great local businesses listed on a local directory if you're looking for specific services or shops. ## Game Day After Heritage: The Best Sports Bars in the Metro East
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/experience-the-best-game-day-at-heritage-sports-bar-grill
Imagine it’s a Saturday in Collinsville and your group text is already going: kickoff’s at noon, who’s got a table? Somebody suggests Heritage on Main Street — and somebody else has to break the news. Heritage Sports Bar & Grill closed its doors in July 2026, without public notice or explanation. No farewell post, no final send-off — one week it was hosting watch parties and fundraisers, the next the lights were off.
This page used to be our guide to game day at Heritage, and we’re not going to pretend otherwise. The bar had only opened in mid-2025, built a real following for live games and community events, and its sudden closing left regulars — and employees — without answers. We don’t know why it closed, so we won’t speculate. What we can do is answer the question the group text actually needs answered: where does the Metro East watch the game now? From Collinsville’s own Main Street to Edwardsville’s bar row, from Troy to Belleville to Granite City, the Illinois side of the metro still has plenty of rooms where the sound is up, the wings are hot, and somebody at the bar will argue the call with you. Here’s the town-by-town tour, verified and current.
Every spot below was verified open as of this writing — recent reviews, active kitchens, current listings. (One local bar we considered including turned out to have gone quiet since 2023; it didn’t make the list. That’s the whole point of checking.) One honest note before you go: hours shift, especially on holidays and during slow seasons, so give any of these a quick call before you load up the car.
### What Game Day Actually Means in the Metro East
Part of what made Heritage work — and what makes every bar on this list work — is that the Metro East’s sports calendar never really stops. Summer belongs to the Cardinals, and a bar with the radio call on the patio is its own kind of church. Fall splits the room: this is Illini country on paper, but Mizzou flags fly on half the blocks, and the SEC-versus-Big-Ten needling is a local sport in itself. Winter brings the Blues, spring brings the Battlehawks packing the Dome across the river, and Friday nights year-round belong to high school football and basketball — several of these bars are where the postgame crowds land, win or lose.
That calendar is why a good sports bar here is never just about the TVs. It’s the fundraiser for the booster club, the trivia night in the off-season, the watch party that turns strangers into regulars. Heritage had started to become that in barely a year — which is exactly why its silent closing stung, and why the bars that remain deserve the business.
### Collinsville: You Don’t Even Have to Leave Main Street
Sloan’s Pub House (119 W. Main St.) sits on the very same downtown strip as the old Heritage spot — a short walk west, historic brick and all. It’s more pub than warehouse-of-TVs, and that’s its charm: a mushroom Swiss burger with a real reputation, a ribeye that surprises people, and a weekend brunch crowd that rolls straight into the afternoon games. Late hours on weekends make it a natural landing spot when the night game runs long. If losing Heritage stung, Collinsville’s Main Street still has your back.
### Edwardsville: Three Options in Two Blocks (Plus One More)
Downtown Edwardsville has quietly become the deepest game-day bench on the Illinois side — a college town (SIUE is minutes away) with a walkable Main Street where you can scout three bars in two blocks and pick your atmosphere on the spot. Park once, walk the strip, and let the crowd noise decide for you.
Big Daddy’s (132 N. Main St.) has anchored the corner since 2008 with a beer garden and outside bar, HD TVs inside and out, and DJs later in the evening Thursday through Saturday. On a warm Saturday with a full slate of games, the patio is the place to be.
Foundry Public House (126 N. Main St.) is literally next door — a gastropub take on game day with a weekday lunch buffet, weekend brunch, fried Brussels sprouts that convert skeptics, and live music nights. If half your table cares about the food as much as the score, Foundry settles the argument.
Hotshots Sports Bar & Grill (2511 Illinois 157) is the pure sports-bar option — the regional chain has been doing the wall-of-TVs, every-game-at-once formula since 1990, with garlic cheese curds and a kitchen that stays open late. When you genuinely need to watch three games simultaneously, this is the machine built for it.
### Glen Carbon and the Troy–Maryville Corridor
The Wooden Nickel Pub & Grill (171 S. Main St., Glen Carbon) does the rustic old-town-pub thing on Glen Carbon’s historic Main Street — a handful of flat screens, a daily kitchen, outdoor seating when the weather cooperates, and the kind of bar where the regulars learn your name by the second visit.
Time Out Sports Bar & Grill (111 W. Market St., Troy) covers the Troy–Maryville corridor — a chamber-of-commerce local staple that runs late every night of the week, handles catering, and fills up fast when the Cardinals or a big SEC matchup is on. For everyone east of the interchange, this is the default answer.
### O’Fallon and Fairview Heights
Hotshots — O’Fallon (1319 Central Park Dr.) sits across from the cinema and pulls the Fairview Heights crowd too — pool tables, wings, the Hotshots Supreme pizza, and the same every-screen-a-different-game setup as its Edwardsville sibling.
Shooters (113 E. 1st St., downtown O’Fallon) is the sleeper pick: a BBQ joint and sports bar in one, with a big tap list, ten-plus TVs, and a cheap-beer reputation it has earned honestly. Smoked meat plus the early window of games is a combination the chains can’t touch.
### Belleville and Granite City
Demo’s Sports Bar (3829 N. Belt W., Belleville) is a neighborhood bar in the best sense — welcoming bartenders, a crowd that actually watches the game, and hours that run late every day. It won’t win design awards; it wins repeat customers.
In Granite City, KG’s Sportsbar & Banquet Center (5050 Nameoki Rd.) doubles as an event space — but heads up: its bar hours are limited to later in the week, so this one especially deserves a call before you go.
### Picking Your Spot: A Quick Decision Guide
Big group, multiple games at once: either Hotshots — Route 157 in Edwardsville or Central Park Drive in O’Fallon. Screens everywhere, kitchen built for volume.
Half the table cares more about the food: Foundry Public House in Edwardsville — gastropub menu, game still on.
Perfect-weather Saturday: Big Daddy’s beer garden in Edwardsville, or the Wooden Nickel’s outdoor seats in Glen Carbon.
BBQ craving plus the noon window: Shooters in downtown O’Fallon — smoked meat and a deep tap list.
Quiet neighborhood watch, no scene: Demo’s in Belleville or the Wooden Nickel — bars where the regulars actually watch.
Late game, later night: Time Out in Troy or Sloan’s in Collinsville — both run late, and both are used to overtime.
Closest to the old Heritage spot: Sloan’s Pub House, a short walk west on the same Main Street.
### Adopting a New Bar: A Word From the Regulars
Losing a home bar is a small grief, and the fix isn’t complicated — but it does take more than one visit. Show up for a non-marquee game, not just the playoff crowd, and you’ll see what the place is actually like. Learn the bartender’s name; they’ll learn your order faster than you expect. Tip like you want the place to still exist next season — Heritage’s quiet exit is a reminder that no bar is guaranteed. And when the chalkboard says trivia night or booster-club fundraiser, come to one. That’s the difference between a bar you go to and a bar that’s yours.
If the bar’s packed — or the group is all toddlers and dogs — flip the script and host: Time Out in Troy handles catering, Shooters’ BBQ travels well, and a couple of to-go racks of ribs plus your own couch beats a forty-five-minute wait for a table on a playoff Sunday.
Unrelated, but Mark Twain I-70 Industrial might be the metro’s best neighborhood name.
### How We Picked These (and What We Left Out)
Every bar above showed current, verifiable signs of life — recent reviews, active listings, working websites — because recommending a closed bar is exactly the mistake this rewrite exists to fix. We skipped the national wing chains (you know where they are), left out one Belleville spot whose trail went cold in 2023, and favored places with their own personality over interchangeable big-box sports bars. The Metro East’s bar scene is overwhelmingly independent and local — which means every game-day tab you run keeps a neighbor’s lights on. We’ll keep re-checking the spots we feature; if you beat us to news of a closure or a great new opening, we genuinely want to hear about it.
Making a full evening of it on the Illinois side? Our Belleville dining guide covers the Main Street scene beyond the barstools, and if you’re crossing the river afterward, the late-night eats guide knows what’s still open when the overtime thriller ends at midnight.
### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What’s the closest sports bar to downtown Collinsville now?
A.  Sloan’s Pub House at 119 W. Main Street — on the same downtown Collinsville strip Heritage occupied, a short walk west. It leans pub rather than mega-sports-bar, with a well-loved mushroom Swiss burger, weekend brunch, and late weekend hours. For the full wall-of-TVs experience, the nearest Hotshots is about ten minutes up Route 157 in Edwardsville.
### Q. Which Metro East sports bar is best for watching multiple games at once?
A.  The two Hotshots locations — Route 157 in Edwardsville and Central Park Drive in O’Fallon — are built exactly for that, with screens on every wall showing different games simultaneously. Among the independents, Big Daddy’s in Edwardsville runs nine HD TVs inside and out, including its beer garden.
### Q. Do I need to check hours before going?
A.  Yes — always call ahead. Bar and kitchen hours across the Metro East shift with seasons, holidays, and staffing, and at least one spot on this list keeps limited late-week-only hours. A thirty-second call beats a wasted drive, especially for an early kickoff or a weeknight game. Most of these bars answer quickly, and asking “are you showing the game tonight?” doubles as a reservation of sorts — a busy bar will tell you honestly whether there’s room for your group.
### Q. Are there sports bars on the Granite City side?
A.  KG’s Sportsbar & Banquet Center on Nameoki Road is Granite City’s main dedicated option, doubling as an event space — but its bar hours are limited to the back half of the week, so call before you go. Otherwise, Granite City crowds often drift toward Edwardsville’s Main Street, about fifteen minutes up the road.
### Q. What about Fairview Heights?
A.  Fairview Heights doesn’t have a standalone independent sports bar on this list, but the Hotshots on Central Park Drive in O’Fallon sits right on the border and openly courts the Fairview Heights crowd — it’s a few minutes from the Route 159 shopping corridor. Belleville’s Demo’s is the nearest neighborhood-bar alternative in the other direction.
Hunting more spots on either side of the river? Browse bars, restaurants, and local favorites across Missouri and Illinois on St Louis Near Me Directory — photos, reviews, and hours in one place.
If you run a bar or restaurant, listing it is how the game-day crowd finds you — especially the week their old spot closes.
### Q. What's the difference between a sports bar and a bar?
A.  A sports bar is built around the broadcast. Screens are positioned for viewing rather than decoration, the sound system can carry a game, and the schedule drives the staffing. A regular bar may have a television; a sports bar arranges the room around it.
### Q. What is sports bar etiquette?
A.  Ask before you claim a table on a big game day, and ask early if you want your game on sound — not at kickoff. Do not stand in someone’s sightline. Keep the rivalry good natured. And if you are camping on a table for three hours, keep ordering.
### Q. How much should you tip at a sports bar?
A.  The usual restaurant standard applies, and tip on the pre-discount total when a special or happy-hour price is involved — the work is the same. A long occupancy on a busy game day is worth more, because you are holding a table the server would otherwise turn.
### Q. What is the most ordered item at a sports bar?
A.  Wings, near-universally, with nachos and a shareable fried platter close behind — food built for a table watching a screen rather than each other. If you are ordering for a group during a rush, expect the kitchen to run long and order before the half.
### Q. What makes a great sports bar?
A.  Sightlines and sound, mostly. Enough screens that you are not craning your neck, the game you came for actually on with audio rather than captions, and a kitchen still running in the fourth quarter. Parking and a room that stays loud without being unbearable do the rest. Booths beat high-tops over three hours.

## The Best Outdoor Activities in St. Louis: Parks, Trails & Day Trips Revised July 22, 2026 What are the best outdoor things to do in St. Louis? The best outdoor activities in St. Louis range from easy strolls to real hikes: Forest Park, the Gateway Arch grounds, the Missouri Botanical Garden, and Tower Grove Park for an easy day; the free Saint Louis Zoo and Grant’s Farm for families; and Castlewood State Park, Cliff Cave Park, and the Katy Trail when you want a real hike or bike ride. Many are free. Keep reading ↓Picture a bright St. Louis Saturday with nothing on the calendar. Maybe you’re a family looking to wear the kids out, a couple after a cheap and pretty date, or a transplant who keeps hearing the metro has more green space than you’d expect. The good news: St. Louis is quietly one of the best outdoor cities in the Midwest, and a huge amount of it is free. From a park bigger than Central Park to a 240-mile bike trail to genuine bluff hikes twenty minutes from downtown, here’s a local’s guide to the best outdoor activities in St. Louis — sorted by the kind of day you’re after, with what’s free, what’s worth the drive, and what to know before you go. ## St. Louis Outdoors at a Glance ## Easy Does It: Strolls, Gardens, and Icons Start with the crown jewel. **Forest Park** is about 1,300 acres — larger than New York’s Central Park — and it’s the beating heart of outdoor St. Louis, with paved paths for walking and biking, boating on the Grand Basin, and four free attractions (the Zoo, the Saint Louis Art Museum, the Saint Louis Science Center, and the Missouri History Museum) scattered across it. You could spend a dozen weekends here and not repeat yourself. Downtown, the grounds of **Gateway Arch National Park** are free to roam, with riverside paths beneath the country’s tallest monument (the tram to the top is ticketed, the walk around is not). And in the city’s south side, **Tower Grove Park** — a 289-acre Victorian gem next to the Missouri Botanical Garden — is a favorite for a farmers-market morning or a shady picnic. For manicured beauty, the **Missouri Botanical Garden** (paid admission) is one of the oldest botanical gardens in the country, and **Laumeier Sculpture Park** pairs 105 free acres with more than 60 large outdoor sculptures — it’s celebrating its 50th year in 2026. *Tower Grove Park’s West Gatehouse at the Kingshighway entrance — look for the “TGP” worked into the slate roof. (Photo: Lane Forman)* ## Bring the Kids: Animals and Wide-Open Space Few cities make family days this affordable. The **Saint Louis Zoo** is consistently ranked among the country’s best — and general admission is **free**. **Grant’s Farm**, the Busch family’s historic animal preserve, is also free to enter (you just pay for parking), with a tram ride past roaming deer and bison, a goat corral, and the famous Clydesdales. For a quieter outing, **Suson Park** in south county has a small working farm with animals kids can meet, and **Creve Coeur Lake Memorial Park** — the largest lake in St. Louis County — offers flat trails, sailing and rowing, and plenty of room to run. ## Real Adventure: Bluffs, Trails, and a River Think St. Louis is all flat? The bluffs will fix that. **Castlewood State Park**, about twenty minutes west, is the local hiker’s favorite, with switchback trails up to dramatic overlooks above the Meramec River. **Cliff Cave Park** in south county offers rugged riverbluff trails (the cave itself is usually closed, and trails occasionally close after flooding, so check the county’s status first). For a woodsy, wildflower-filled ramble, **Shaw Nature Reserve** in Gray Summit protects 2,400+ acres of Ozark-border landscape with miles of trails. ## On Two Wheels: The Trails St. Louis is a genuinely great trail city. The **Katy Trail** is the longest developed rails-to-trails path in the country — about 240 crushed-limestone miles running from near Kansas City to the St. Louis suburbs — and the stretch through the Missouri River wine country near Augusta is a bucket-list ride. Closer in, the **Great Rivers Greenway** network links more than 140 miles of paved greenways across the region, and the **Old Chain of Rocks Bridge** carries walkers and cyclists across the Mississippi on a historic Route 66 span with skyline views. Rent a bike or lace up your shoes; the mileage is there. And you don’t have to be a serious cyclist to enjoy it — the crushed-limestone Katy Trail and the paved greenways are flat, shaded, and beginner-friendly, so a casual family ride is just as doable as a long training day. Several outfitters near the trails rent bikes by the hour if you don’t have your own. ## Want to Get Out of Town? Easy Day Trips When you’ve got a full day, a few destinations are worth the drive. Just across the river in Illinois, **Cahokia Mounds** is a UNESCO World Heritage Site — the largest pre-Columbian settlement north of Mexico, where you can climb **Monks Mound**, the biggest prehistoric earthwork in the Americas. (Note: the site’s Interpretive Center is currently closed for renovation, but the grounds, mounds, and trails remain open.) South of the city, **Elephant Rocks State Park** lets you scramble over billion-year-old granite boulders the size of small ...

It’s an easy way to add something light and bright to a meal. ### Steaks and Chops Beyond pasta and seafood, Roberto’s serves up steaks and chops chosen for quality and cooked exactly how you order them — a nod to the classic chophouse style with an Italian touch. It’s the place to go for a hearty, satisfying plate. You can browse recent diner photos and reviews of the steak and chop side at Roberto’s Trattoria & Chophouse. ### A Few Menu Highlights The kitchen keeps one foot in the trattoria and one in the chophouse, so the menu reaches across both. On the Italian side, you’ll find pasta done the classic way — think chicken fettuccine and a veal piccata — alongside seafood like salmon, scallops, sea bass, and shrimp. On the chophouse side, hand-cut steaks such as a strip and a filet share the page with lamb chops. Nothing here is trying to reinvent Italian-American cooking; it’s doing the familiar things carefully. Menus change with the season and the market, so it’s always worth asking your server what’s fresh that night. The menu is built around classic tastes and good ingredients — food that feels both familiar and special, without any fuss. ## Enhance Your Meal With Fine Wines ### Affordable Wine Choices A great meal shouldn’t break the bank, and the wine list reflects that. There’s a solid selection of American and European wines that pair well with the food without costing a fortune — the right glass to go with your pasta or steak, whatever your budget. ### Premium Italian Reserve Wines For special occasions, there’s a curated collection of premium Italian reserves — top-tier selections meant to be savored. ## The Best Christmas Lights in St. Louis: A Local’s Guide
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/discover-the-best-christmas-lights-in-st-louis-this-holiday-season
There’s a particular kind of magic to a St. Louis December evening: the car warm, cocoa in the cupholders, someone in the back seat gasping as a whole hillside or historic building suddenly blazes to life in color. Whether you like to cruise slowly through a dazzling drive-thru or bundle up and walk beneath a canopy of a million bulbs, the metro goes genuinely all out for the holidays, from grand institutions to entire neighborhoods that band together to light up a street.
This is a local’s guide to the best Christmas light displays across St. Louis and the surrounding communities — the long-running traditions, the huge drive-thru spectacles, and a free neighborhood gem or two. We’ve split them into walk-through and drive-through so you can pick based on the weather, the kids, and how much you feel like leaving the car. Since dates and hours shift a little each year, treat this as your map and check each display’s official page or call ahead for this season’s exact schedule before you head out — a thirty-second check saves a disappointed carload.
### The big walk-through spectacles
### Garden Glow at the Missouri Botanical Garden
A St. Louis holiday centerpiece. The Missouri Botanical Garden transforms after dark into a wonderland of more than two million lights strung along a roughly mile-long path, with the bulbs shimmering off the water features and illuminating the Rose Garden, the Japanese Garden, and other iconic spots you know by day but have never seen glowing after dark. Expect immersive themed areas, plenty of photo-worthy moments, and festive refreshments like hot cocoa and s’mores along the way. It’s self-paced, so give yourself a relaxed hour or more, and buy tickets online ahead of time — this one genuinely sells out on the busiest nights. It’s the walk-through most locals name first when someone asks where to take out-of-town guests, and the garden setting makes it feel a cut above a parking-lot light show.
### Brewery Lights at the Anheuser-Busch Brewery
You can’t talk St. Louis holiday lights without the Anheuser-Busch Brewery, a 40-plus-year tradition. Stroll Pestalozzi Street beneath over a million lights that make the historic Germanic-Romanesque buildings glow, catch the nightly parade with vintage trucks, floats, and the famous Budweiser Clydesdales, and — for guests 21 and up — enjoy a complimentary beer. You can gather around a private fire pit with friends and there’s festive food and drink throughout the grounds. It’s equal parts holiday cheer and local history, and it’s free to walk the grounds — a genuinely generous tradition in a season that can get expensive fast. Arrive a little before the nightly parade if you want a good spot, and give yourself time to wander; the historic buildings under a million lights are worth lingering over.
### Wild Lights at the Saint Louis Zoo
The Zoo lights up after hours with Wild Lights, a walk-through of glowing, themed areas — think Frosted Forest, Butterfly Grove, Toy Town, Arctic Alley, and a towering 40-foot lighted tree — perfect for photos and little ones. The animals are mostly tucked in for the night; the dazzling light installations are the star. It runs select nights, often with a sensory-friendly evening for families who need a calmer experience, so grab tickets in advance and check the schedule. Being in the heart of Forest Park, it pairs naturally with the free museums nearby if you’re building a whole day out of it, and the walk itself is stroller- and grandparent-friendly.
Want to stay in the warmth of the car? We have a dedicated guide to the metro’s best drive-through Christmas light displays, plus more seasonal ideas in the St Louis Near Me Directory events listings.
Run a St. Louis business with a holiday event, popup, or seasonal special? Listing it in the directory puts it in front of families out looking for exactly that — the same neighbors driving around hunting for lights.
### The great drive-through shows
### Winter Wonderland at Tilles Park (Ladue)
A cherished St. Louis tradition since the 1980s, Winter Wonderland at Tilles Park — the larger park in Ladue, in St. Louis County — strings up over a million lights across roughly 75 acres, with more than a hundred festive scenes and a glittering canopy overhead. You can drive through (the classic, cozy option), walk it, or splurge on a horse-drawn carriage ride for something romantic. It’s a beloved local ritual generations of families return to year after year, and for many St. Louisans it simply is the start of the holiday season — the night you finally feel it’s December. Note it’s the larger Tilles Park in Ladue you want, not the smaller city park of the same name in St. Louis Hills.
### Santa’s Magical Kingdom (Eureka)
Out at Jellystone Park in Eureka, near Six Flags, Santa’s Magical Kingdom sprawls over 35 acres with more than four million lights, animated scenes, and special effects — reindeer overhead, elves in the trees, the works. Drive through in your own car or hop an open-air wagon ride for a 360-degree view. Kids can drop letters in the North Pole mailbox, and the Kringle General Store handles treats and souvenirs. It’s open nightly across the season, including holidays, so there’s plenty of time to fit it in even when the calendar gets busy. The sheer scale — those four million lights over 35 acres — makes it one of the most immersive drive-throughs in the region, and the wagon-ride option is worth it if you want an unobstructed view without craning around the car windows.
### WonderLight’s Christmas at World Wide Technology Raceway
One of the biggest drive-thru shows around, WonderLight’s Christmas turns World Wide Technology Raceway in the Metro East (the Illinois side, near Madison/Fairmont City) into miles of synchronized light. Over a million LED lights pulse to holiday music you tune in on your car radio — shooting stars, falling snowflakes, glowing tunnels you drive right through, dancing candy canes, and animated figures at every turn. Pack the family in, cue the music, and let it wash over you from the warmth of the car. It’s a particularly good pick for the coldest nights, when nobody in the group is enthusiastic about walking, and for families with very young kids who do better staying buckled in. Check the nightly hours for this year’s run, since it’s popular enough that weekend lines can build.
### Holiday Lights at Grant’s Farm
Grant’s Farm offers both a drive-through and a walk-through option. The drive winds past the historic Busch family home and the German-inspired Bauernhof courtyard, decked out and synced to holiday music on your radio, with a giant 50-foot LED tree and appearances from Santa and Mrs. Claus. Prefer to stretch your legs? A tram takes you to the Bauernhof for a stroll at your own pace, with seasonal food and drinks along the way. Some evenings add a ‘Breakfast with Santa’ event in the Carriage House. Reservations are smart for the popular nights and add-ons, which tend to book up fast closer to Christmas.
### Celebration of Lights in O’Fallon, MO
For a straightforward, classic drive-through, the Celebration of Lights at Fort Zumwalt Park in O’Fallon, MO, has been a St. Charles County favorite since the early 1990s. You cruise through the park past festive displays with holiday music — simple, cozy, and easy to fold into an evening. It typically runs from late November through the holidays; check the city’s page for this year’s dates. For families out in St. Charles County, it’s the closest of the big drive-throughs and an easy weeknight tradition — no long trek across the metro required, which makes it a favorite for a quick dose of holiday spirit after dinner.
Wildly off-topic — if you’re house-hunting, start with our Holly Hills guide.
### A free neighborhood gem: Candy Cane Lane
Not every great display charges admission. In the St. Louis Hills neighborhood, residents around the 6500 block of Murdoch Avenue (and now several nearby streets) transform their homes into a dazzling, grassroots winter wonderland known as Candy Cane Lane. It’s a labor of love by the homeowners, free to drive or walk through, with many residents collecting donations for local charities — the display has raised well into the hundreds of thousands of dollars for good causes over the years — so bring a few dollars if you can. It’s a residential street, not a formal attraction, so go slow, keep the noise down, and be respectful of the neighbors who pour weeks of work into making it happen for everyone else’s enjoyment. Conveniently, it’s right by Francis Park and Ted Drewes, so you can turn it into a full frozen-custard-and-lights evening.
### Making a whole evening of it
Half the fun is stringing stops together. A few combinations locals love: pair Garden Glow with dinner in nearby Tower Grove or on The Hill, since the Botanical Garden sits right between them. Fold Candy Cane Lane into a St. Louis Hills evening with a Ted Drewes concrete just up the road. Out in St. Charles County, the Celebration of Lights makes an easy add-on to a night around O’Fallon. And for a pure drive-thru marathon, Winter Wonderland in Ladue and the bigger county displays can be chained in a single loop if you plan the route before you leave.
If you’re hosting out-of-town family for the holidays, the lights are an easy crowd-pleaser that works for every age — toddlers and grandparents alike — and much of it costs little or nothing. One walk-through and one drive-through in an evening gives you variety without wearing anyone out. Just remember the region spreads across Missouri and Illinois, so a little planning around drive times keeps the night merry instead of cramped in the car. Group nearby stops together rather than crisscrossing the metro, and you’ll spend the evening looking at lights instead of staring at the highway.
### Tips for a smooth lights night
Check this year’s schedule. Dates, hours, and ticket prices shift annually — confirm on each display’s official page before you drive out, especially around holidays.
Buy walk-through tickets in advance. Popular events like Garden Glow and Wild Lights sell out; online tickets save you a line and sometimes money.
Go on a weeknight if you can. Weekends and the nights closest to Christmas draw the biggest crowds; earlier in the season and midweek are calmer.
Prep the car for drive-thrus. Full tank, working radio for the synced-music shows, and cocoa for the cupholders.
Dress warm for walk-throughs. Layers, comfortable shoes, and a thermos make a mile of lights a joy instead of a shiver.
### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. Are there free Christmas light displays in St. Louis?
A.  Yes. The best-known free display is Candy Cane Lane around the 6500 block of Murdoch Avenue in the St. Louis Hills neighborhood, where residents decorate their homes elaborately — many collect donations for local charities, so bring a little cash. You can also spot free neighborhood displays throughout the metro during the season.
### Q. Which St. Louis light displays can you drive through?
A.  Winter Wonderland at Tilles Park (Ladue), Santa’s Magical Kingdom (Eureka), WonderLight’s Christmas at World Wide Technology Raceway, the Celebration of Lights at Fort Zumwalt Park in O’Fallon, and Grant’s Farm all offer drive-through experiences. For a full rundown, see our drive-through Christmas lights guide.
### Q. Do I need to buy tickets in advance for St. Louis light shows?
A.  For popular walk-through events like Garden Glow and Wild Lights, buy online ahead of time — they sell out and advance tickets save you a wait. Many drive-through displays let you pay at the entrance, but checking the official page first is always wise, since hours and pricing change each season.
### Q. Where is the biggest display of Christmas lights?
A.  The Anheuser-Busch Brewery display is the long-running large one, a 40-plus-year tradition. For sheer density on a walkable street, Pestalozzi Street sits beneath over a million lights against the historic Germanic-Romanesque buildings — a very different experience from a drive-through.
### Q. Is Candy Cane Lane St. Louis free?
A.  Neighborhood light displays are generally free to drive or walk through — residents decorate their own homes. Ticketed events are usually the park and venue installations. Go on a weeknight if you want to actually move; weekend queues can be substantial.
### Q. Where can I buy discounted Christmas lights?
A.  The reliable window is the week after Christmas, when retailers clear stock at deep discounts for the following year. Hardware stores tend to carry better-quality commercial-grade sets than seasonal pop-ups, which matters if you want them to survive more than two winters.
### Q. What are the current trends for Christmas lights?
A.  Warm-white LED has largely displaced incandescent on cost and heat, and app-controlled permanent roofline systems have moved from commercial into residential. The practical trend for renters and older homes is battery and clip systems that need no fixings.

## The Best Arcades in St. Louis: Barcades, Pinball & Family Fun
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/discover-the-best-arcades-in-st-louis-mo-from-classic-games-to-modern-fun
There’s something universal about the pull of an arcade — the beep and clatter, the glow of a hundred screens, the muscle memory of a game you haven’t touched since you were twelve. Maybe you want a date night with a drink in one hand and a joystick in the other, a rainy afternoon that wears the kids out, or a serious pinball session with people who take flippers as seriously as you do.
Whatever your speed, St. Louis has become a genuinely great arcade town. Here’s a local’s guide to the best arcades in St. Louis and across the metro — sorted by the two questions that actually matter: are you bringing kids or a cocktail, and how deep is your pinball obsession?
### The Two Kinds of Arcade Night
St. Louis arcades really split into two camps. There are the 21+ barcades — grown-up bars stuffed with retro cabinets and pinball, where the games are cheap and the drinks are the point — and the all-ages family entertainment centers, the big rooms with redemption games, laser tag, and prize counters for a kid’s birthday. Then there’s a passionate third lane running through both: pinball, which has a devoted St. Louis scene all its own. Know which one you want, and the choice gets easy. The good news is you’re rarely far from one: the metro has barcades in its trendy neighborhoods, family centers in the suburbs, pinball bars tucked into corners you’d never expect, and a whole second cluster across the river in the Metro East. Whatever mood and age group you’re working with, there’s a room full of games nearby.
### The Barcades: Beer, Nostalgia, and 25-Cent Classics
For adults, the barcade is the perfect low-stakes night out. Up-Down STL in the Central West End is the flagship — more than 60 retro arcade games, pinball, skee-ball, console classics, and a rooftop bar. It’s 21+ in the evenings (with daytime family hours), and it nails the nostalgia-plus-cocktails formula. Over in The Grove, Purple Quarters is a newer cocktail-and-arcade bar from a beloved local team, mixing games with comedy and karaoke nights. And out in St. Charles, Two Plumbers Brewery + Arcade pairs house-brewed beer with free-play cabinets — a genuinely fun combination. A couple of newer St. Charles spots, including Rec Hall and the recently opened Rec Haus, round out a growing west-of-the-river barcade scene.
What makes barcades such an easy win is the low pressure. You don’t need a reservation, you don’t need to be good at anything, and you don’t need to commit to a whole evening — you can drop in for one drink and a round of Mario Kart or stay till close working the pinball. They’re also a rare night-out option that’s genuinely fun sober or not: the games carry the evening either way. For a first date, a small group, or a “we don’t know what we want to do” night, a barcade almost never misses.
### The St. Louis Pinball Trail
If pinball is your thing, St. Louis over-delivers. The legendary Silver Ballroom in the Bevo neighborhood — a punk-rock bar in a former bowling alley — keeps dozens of machines and a fierce local following. Murphy’s On 21 in south county and the Benton Parkade in Benton Park are favorites for league players, and Red Fish Blue Fish in St. Charles keeps a solid bank of tables. For an all-ages pinball fix, the Lazarus Pinball Museum in Fenton is a dedicated collection you can play, and there’s even a pinball-and-arcade room tucked inside the City Museum. St. Louis runs real pinball leagues, so if you catch the bug, there’s a whole community waiting. The scene stretches into the Metro East too, where Atomic Pinball Arcade and the Pump House in Wood River keep dozens of machines for Illinois-side players.
What’s great about the pinball trail is how welcoming it is to newcomers. You don’t need to be good — most of these spots keep older, easier tables alongside the brutal modern ones, and the regulars are usually happy to show a first-timer the ropes. Drop a few dollars in, learn to nudge without tilting, and you’ll understand why pinball, of all things, became one of the city’s most durable nightlife hobbies.
### Family Game Centers: Bring the Kids
When the point is to wear kids out (and win a plastic prize), the big all-ages centers deliver. Dave & Buster’s in Maryland Heights is the reliable classic — a wall of games, sports on the screens, and a full menu. Main Event in Chesterfield stacks bowling, multi-story laser tag, and 100-plus arcade games under one roof, and Swing-A-Round Fun Town in Fenton adds go-karts and mini golf to its 80-game arcade. For the youngest kids, Chuck E. Cheese has several metro locations with the tokens-and-tickets formula that never dies. And on the Delmar Loop, Joe Edwards’ Magic Mini Golf mixes indoor mini golf with pinball, a basketball arcade, and a mini Ferris wheel — a fun, all-ages Loop stop.
### Don’t Forget the Metro East
Cross the river into Illinois and the arcade options keep coming. Edison’s Entertainment Complex in Edwardsville is a big all-ages spot with a 65-plus-game arcade, bowling, and laser tag; Game Over in Alton packs 200-plus games across three levels; and the pinball crowd has Atomic Pinball Arcade and the Pump House, both in Wood River. If you’re on the Illinois side of the metro, you don’t have to drive back across the river for a great arcade night. Edison’s in particular works well for a mixed-age group or a birthday, since it combines the arcade with bowling and other attractions in one place — the Metro East answer to a Dave & Buster’s night.
### Why St. Louis Is Quietly a Great Arcade Town
It wasn’t always like this. Like a lot of cities, St. Louis watched its old mall arcades fade — and then the barcade boom brought the games back for grown-ups, and a passionate pinball community rebuilt the scene from the machines up. Today the metro spans the whole spectrum: slick national chains, indie neighborhood barcades, dedicated pinball museums, and a bunch of bars that keep a few tables in the corner for the regulars. The result is a city where “let’s go play some games” can mean almost anything, at almost any budget, on almost any night of the week.
Part of the fun is how the arcades reflect their neighborhoods. A barcade in the Central West End feels different from a pinball bar in Bevo, which feels different from a brewery-arcade in St. Charles or a big family center out in Chesterfield. Chasing them down is a low-key way to see parts of the metro you might otherwise skip — and to end up somewhere new with a controller in your hand.
### St. Louis Arcades at a Glance
### Which St. Louis Arcade Is Right for You?
Date night: Up-Down STL or Purple Quarters — games and cocktails. Pinball die-hards: the Silver Ballroom or Lazarus Pinball Museum. Little kids: Chuck E. Cheese or Swing-A-Round Fun Town. Teens and big groups: Dave & Buster’s or Main Event. Retro purists: a barcade with a pocket full of quarters. Metro East: Edison’s or Game Over. There’s a version of the arcade night out for everyone here. The scene also keeps evolving — new barcades open, machines rotate, and pop-up tournaments come and go — so it’s worth checking a venue’s socials for special nights. Half the fun of a good arcade town is that there’s always a new high score to chase or a spot you haven’t tried yet.
Wildly off-topic: The Grove sits inside a neighborhood called Forest Park Southeast.
### Know Before You Go
A couple of quick tips. Check the age policy — barcades like Up-Down and Purple Quarters are 21+ in the evenings, so bring an ID (and plan around it if you’ve got kids). Ask how games are priced; some spots are free-play with a cover or per-game, others still run on cards or quarters. Weeknights are calmer than weekend evenings if you want elbow room at the machines. And for the smaller independent spots, a quick check of hours or Facebook before you go is smart, since game bars sometimes host private events or league nights.
### Make a Day (or Date) of It
Arcades pair perfectly with the neighborhoods around them. Hit Up-Down in the Central West End and grab dinner nearby; make a night of The Grove around Purple Quarters; or turn a St. Charles trip into barcade-hopping down historic Main Street. On the Delmar Loop, Magic Mini Golf sits steps from Blueberry Hill and the Walk of Fame. The games are the anchor, but the neighborhood makes it an outing — dinner, drinks, a little friendly competition, and a walk somewhere you don’t usually go.
### Find great local spots (and a note for the owners)
An arcade night is better with the right dinner or drinks nearby — and that’s what a local directory is for. You can search St Louis Near Me Directory to find spots near any of these arcades before you go.
And if you run a bar, arcade, or restaurant anywhere in the St. Louis area, getting found by people looking for a night out is the whole game. Listing your business is how locals searching “arcade near me” end up at your door.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. Which St. Louis arcade has the best reviews?
A.  There’s no single winner, but a few St. Louis spots earn the most devotion. Up-Down STL is the flagship barcade, and the Silver Ballroom in Bevo keeps a fierce local following. For families, Dave & Buster’s in Maryland Heights and Main Event in Chesterfield are the reliably popular picks. The best fit depends on whether you want cocktails, pinball, or kids.
### Q. What is the most popular arcade?
A.  Up-Down STL in the Central West End is the metro’s flagship arcade, with more than 60 retro games, pinball, skee-ball, and a rooftop bar. Among pinball fans, the legendary Silver Ballroom in Bevo draws the most devoted crowd, while Dave & Buster’s in Maryland Heights is the go-to family pick. Popularity really depends on your crowd.
### Q. What is the best barcade in St. Louis?
A.  Up-Down STL in the Central West End is the flagship barcade, with 60-plus retro games, pinball, skee-ball, and a rooftop bar. It’s 21+ in the evenings, with daytime family hours. Purple Quarters in The Grove and Two Plumbers Brewery + Arcade in St. Charles are excellent alternatives that pair games with a full bar.
### Q. Where can you play pinball in St. Louis?
A.  St. Louis has a deep pinball scene. The Silver Ballroom in Bevo is the iconic pinball bar, the Lazarus Pinball Museum in Fenton is an all-ages collection you can play, and Murphy’s On 21, Benton Parkade, and Red Fish Blue Fish keep strong lineups. There’s even a pinball room inside the City Museum, plus more machines across the Metro East.
### Q. Are there arcades in St. Louis for kids?
A.  Yes. Dave & Buster’s (Maryland Heights), Main Event (Chesterfield), Swing-A-Round Fun Town (Fenton), and Chuck E. Cheese are all-ages family centers with redemption games, laser tag, and prizes. Magic Mini Golf on the Delmar Loop mixes mini golf with arcade games, and Edison’s in Edwardsville is a big family option on the Illinois side.
### Q. Are there arcades on the Illinois side of St. Louis?
A.  Yes, the Metro East has several. Edison’s Entertainment Complex in Edwardsville offers an arcade, bowling, and laser tag; Game Over in Alton packs 200-plus games across three levels; and pinball fans have Atomic Pinball Arcade and the Pump House, both in Wood River. They’re easy options if you’re on the Illinois side of the metro.
### Q. How much does an average arcade game cost?
A.  Classic cabinets on quarter or token play are the cheapest entertainment in the building, while modern ticket-redemption and motion games cost several times as much per play. Card systems make this harder to feel, so decide your spend before you load the card, not after.
### Q. Why are arcade games so expensive now?
A.  Newer cabinets cost operators far more to buy and maintain than an eighties machine did, and redemption games are priced around the prizes they pay out. That is why the barcades leaning on restored classics can still run cheap play — the machines are paid for and the beer covers the rent.
### Q. What are some tips for choosing an arcade bar?
A.  Check whether the machines are on free play or coin, whether food is served or you can bring it, and how loud the room gets after nine. If pinball is the draw, ask whether the tables are maintained in-house — a well-kept table plays completely differently from a neglected one.
### Q. What are some fun adult things to do in St. Louis?
A.  Barcades and pinball are the obvious ones on this page, and they pair well with the rest of a night out because they are clustered near bars and food rather than stranded in a strip mall. Weeknights are the move if you want to actually get on a machine.

## How Much Does a Bookkeeper Cost? (And Why Missouri Licenses None of Them) Revised July 28, 2026 How much does a bookkeeper cost? Roughly **$200–$400 a month** for straightforward monthly bookkeeping, rising toward **$1,500+** as scope grows. Hourly, the reported median is about **$24**; freelancers commonly quote **$25–$50**. ⚠️ Treat those loosely — almost every page publishing bookkeeping rates is published by an outsourced bookkeeping company. Price tracks **transaction volume and number of accounts**, not your revenue. 💡 And the part nobody mentions: **Missouri doesn’t license bookkeepers at all** — no exam, no registry, no board. Anyone may use the title. **“CPA” is protected**; bookkeeper isn’t, so look for AIPB or NACPB certification and professional liability insurance instead. ## How much does a bookkeeper cost? For most small businesses, somewhere between **$200 and $400 a month** for straightforward monthly bookkeeping, rising toward **$1,500 or more** as the work gets more involved. Hourly, the reported median sits around **$24**, with freelancers commonly quoting **$25 to $50**. A word on those numbers before you rely on them. Almost every page publishing bookkeeping rates is published *by an outsourced bookkeeping company*, and their in-house-versus-outsourced comparisons are marketing. The ranges above appear consistently enough across sources to be useful as a sanity check. Treat any single figure — including a quote you are given — as a starting point rather than a market rate. What actually drives your price is not your revenue. It is **transaction volume, number of accounts, and how bad the shoebox is.** A consultant billing four invoices a month is cheap to keep straight. A restaurant with daily deposits, tips, vendor accounts and a payroll run is not, at any revenue level. ## The thing nobody tells you: anyone can call themselves a bookkeeper This is the part worth knowing before you hand someone your bank logins. **Missouri does not license bookkeepers.** There is no state exam, no registry, no board, and no complaint process. The title is unregulated, and a person who took a weekend course and a person with twenty years in the trade may describe themselves identically. **“CPA” is different.** Certified Public Accountant is a protected title in Missouri — only licensees may use it, or any designation implying it. That protection is what makes the letters meaningful, and it is why the distinction matters when you are comparing quotes. Worth being precise about what that protection does and does not do, because the internet gets this wrong in both directions: a non-licensee may still perform a great deal of legitimate accounting work, including preparing tax returns, advisory work, and preparing non-attest financial statements. The restriction is on *calling yourself a CPA*, not on doing bookkeeping. If this pattern feels familiar, it should — it is the same structure as the trades here. Missouri does not license contractors either, which is why verifying a contractor works differently in this state. In both cases the vetting is yours to do. ### What to look for instead of a license Since there is no state credential, these carry the weight: - **Voluntary certification.**The AIPB Certified Bookkeeper and NACPB Certified Public Bookkeeper credentials are the recognized ones. Neither is required, which is rather the point — someone who obtained one chose to be tested. - **Professional liability insurance.**Ask directly. Someone touching your financial records without it is asking you to carry the risk. - **References from businesses like yours.**Restaurant books and contractor books are different animals; experience in one does not transfer cleanly. - **A named CPA they work with.**Good bookkeepers usually have one, and are quick to say where their scope ends. ## Bookkeeper, accountant, CPA — what you are actually buying These get used interchangeably and they are not the same purchase. **A bookkeeper** handles the ongoing record: categorizing transactions, reconciling accounts, chasing invoices, producing monthly statements. This is the recurring work, and it is what most small businesses are actually short of. **An accountant** works on what the records mean — financial statements, tax planning, structure. Often seasonal or periodic rather than monthly. **A CPA** is a licensed accountant, and the license matters most where independence and attestation are required — audits, reviewed statements, representation before tax authorities. Most small businesses need the first regularly and the second occasionally. Paying CPA rates for monthly transaction categorization is a common and expensive mistake; so is having nobody look at the year until March. ## In-house, freelance, or a service **A service or a freelancer** is where nearly every small business should start. You pay for the hours the work takes, not for a person’s day, and you can leave. **A full-time in-house bookkeeper** reportedly runs roughly $45,000 to $60,000 in salary before benefits and overhead, which is commonly estimated to add another 25% to 40%. That is a real employer decision — and if you are contemplating it, note that the obligations attach the moment you hire anyone. We covered them in hiring your first employee in Missouri. The honest test is not cost, it is volume. If the work genuinely fills a week, hire. If it fills two afternoons a month, hiring for it is expensive in a way the salary figure understates. ## How do you know when it is time? Most owners do their own books at the start, and that is usually correct. The question is not whether you *can* keep doing it ...
