### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What is the difference between an HOA and an association?
A.  A homeowners association (HOA) is mandatory — membership and dues are a binding condition of owning the property, and it can enforce rules and fees. A neighborhood association is voluntary; it advocates and organizes but can’t force you to join or fine you. Most of the City of St. Louis has voluntary neighborhood associations, while mandatory HOAs are more common in newer county subdivisions.
### Q. Is a neighborhood association a nonprofit?
A.  Many are. Neighborhood associations often incorporate as nonprofit organizations so they can hold a bank account, accept donations and grants, and operate formally — but not all do, and it isn’t required to function. Smaller or newer groups may operate informally with volunteer leaders and optional dues before ever filing for nonprofit status.
### Q. How do I find my neighborhood association in St. Louis?
A.  Enter your address on the City of St. Louis neighborhood lookup at stlouis-mo.gov to find your neighborhood, ward, and contacts, then check the city’s Neighborhood Organization Registry and its list of association websites and social media. SLACO (slaco-mo.org) and Nextdoor help too. If the info is outdated, email NAM@stlouis-mo.gov to update it.
### Q. What ward am I in in St. Louis?
A.  The easiest way to find your ward is the address lookup on stlouis-mo.gov — entering your address returns your neighborhood, your ward, and your local officials in one place. Knowing your ward matters because your alderperson is a key ally for neighborhood issues, from vacant buildings to traffic calming to city-service requests.
### Q. Can you legally refuse to join an HOA?
A.  Generally no — if a property is already governed by a mandatory HOA, membership and dues run with the deed and you accept them when you buy. You can avoid HOA obligations by buying a property that isn’t in one, which describes most homes in the City of St. Louis, where neighborhood associations are voluntary rather than binding.
### Q. What is the difference between an HOA and a neighborhood association?
A.  Membership and power. An HOA is tied to your deed, membership is mandatory, dues are enforceable and it can place a lien. A neighborhood association is voluntary, has no legal authority over your property, and works by organizing rather than by rule.
### Q. What is the purpose of a neighborhood association?
A.  To give a block collective voice — on zoning cases, city services, traffic and safety — and to organize the things nobody owns individually, like clean-ups and events. Its power is attention and turnout, not enforcement.
### Q. Can you refuse to join an HOA?
A.  Generally not, if the covenants run with the land; buying the property means accepting them. That is the key difference from a neighborhood association, which you can join or ignore freely. Read the covenants before closing, not after.
### Q. What are the pros and cons of a homeowners association?
A.  Pros: maintained common areas, consistent standards, and a mechanism for dealing with a genuinely bad neighbor. Cons: dues that can rise, rules on what you may do with your own property, and enforcement that varies enormously with whoever is on the board that year.

## Where to Eat in Maplewood, MO: A Local's Guide to St. Louis's Tastiest Small Town Revised July 24, 2026 Where should I eat in Maplewood, MO? Maplewood, MO packs an outsized number of independent restaurants into a walkable stretch of Manchester Road and Sutton Boulevard. Highlights: Robin (2026 James Beard Best New Restaurant finalist), Acero and Robata for dinner, Sabroso and Thai Table for global flavors, Side Project and Schlafly Bottleworks for beer, The Blue Duck and Bolyard’s for sandwiches, plus La Cosecha, Mauhaus cat café, Prioritized Pastries, Gus’s fried chicken, and more. Park once and graze on foot; reserve ahead only for the marquee dinner rooms. Keep reading ↓Picture a Friday evening when you want more than another strip-mall dinner. You want to park once, wander a few blocks, and let the night unfold — a craft beer here, a plate of fresh pasta there, maybe a slice of allergy-friendly cake on the walk back to the car. Whether you’re coming from Kirkwood, Webster Groves, the city, or just down Manchester Road, there’s one walkable little town that delivers exactly that — and it punches so far above its weight that the national food press has started to notice. That town is **Maplewood**. ## Why Maplewood is St. Louis's tastiest few blocks Tucked just inside the city’s southwest edge, Maplewood packs an outsized number of independent restaurants, bakeries, and breweries into a compact, walkable stretch of **Manchester Road and Sutton Boulevard**. Almost everything here is locally owned — no endless chains, just chefs and owners who live nearby. Park once and you can eat your way around the world (and back to comfort food) on foot. Here’s how to do it. ## Start with coffee and something sweet Fuel up at **La Cosecha Coffee Roasters**, where the beans are roasted on-site, or do something delightfully different at **Mauhaus Cat Café & Lounge** — St. Louis’s original cat café, where your latte comes with adoptable cats padding around the lounge. Got dietary limits? **Prioritized Pastries** is an entirely allergy-friendly bakery whose rainbow cake and “cosmic” brownies don’t taste like compromises. ## Brunch and easygoing bites For a sandwich you’ll think about later, **The Blue Duck** is famous for its DLT — smoked duck ham and a fried egg on house sourdough — plus daily brunch. In the same spirit, **Bolyard’s Meat & Provisions** is a whole-animal butcher shop with a sandwich counter and tallow fries the locals swear by. Craving something lighter or quicker? **BLK MKT Eats** rolls burrito-sized sushi and build-your-own poke bowls, and **Revel Kitchen** handles the gluten-free bowls and cold-pressed juice. ## Dinner and date night Here’s where Maplewood gets serious. **Robin**, chef Alec Schingel’s tiny modern-Midwestern room of about nine tables, landed on the *New York Times*’ list of America’s best restaurants and is a **2026 James Beard finalist for Best New Restaurant** — reserve well ahead. A few doors away, **Acero** turns out house-made pasta and a thoughtful wine list, **Robata** serves rich tonkotsu ramen and robata-grilled skewers, and **Michael’s Bar & Grill** has been the neighborhood’s go-to for Greek classics like moussaka and braised lamb shank for years. ## Around the world, Maplewood-style For Mexican, **Sabroso Cocina Mexicana** brings chef Miguel Pintor’s Yucatán-style cochinita pibil and birria, full bar included. **Thai Table** covers the khao soi and curries, and **Gus’s World Famous Fried Chicken** delivers the Memphis-born, spicy-crisp kind worth the extra napkins. ## Beer lovers, this is your town Maplewood is a genuine craft-beer destination. **Side Project** — both the Brewing tasting room and the **Side Project Cellar** — pours nationally acclaimed saisons and barrel-aged ales, with a James Beard–recognized bar program. **Schlafly Bottleworks** is the brewpub home of St. Louis’s original craft brewery, with pizza, beer-cheese soup, and weekend brunch. Catch a game with loaded tots at **The Post Sports Bar & Grill**, or settle in with comfort food and cheese curds at **The Crow’s Nest**. ## A few more stops worth knowing Maplewood keeps rewarding the wanderer, so leave room for these. **Living Room Coffee & Kitchen** on Sutton is a family-owned café roasting its own beans with a full breakfast-and-lunch menu — a calmer alternative when La Cosecha is packed. For dessert on the stroll, **Boardwalk Waffles & Ice Cream** presses waffle ice-cream sandwiches that are exactly as fun as they sound. **Foundation Grounds** (now also branded the Maplewood Deli & Coffeehouse) pairs organic coffee with a deli counter and breakfast burritos. Tea people have a home base at **Traveling Tea**, a loose-leaf shop with dozens of varieties plus matcha and hojicha lattes. And between courses, **Vom Fass** lets you taste and fill your own bottles of imported olive oils, aged balsamics, and small-batch spirits — a browse-worthy stop that makes an easy gift. ## How to plan your Maplewood crawl The trick to a great Maplewood day is treating it as one long, unhurried grazing session rather than a single sit-down meal. **Start with coffee** at La Cosecha, Living Room, or Foundation Grounds. **Graze mid-day** — a Blue Duck sandwich, a Bolyard’s counter plate, a sushi burrito from BLK MKT — so you leave room to keep going. **Break up the eating with browsing** at The Book House or Vom Fass, which is half the charm of a walkable district. ## The Best Dog Parks in St. Louis: A Local Guide for Every Corner of the Metro Revised July 24, 2026 What are the best dog parks in St. Louis? St. Louis has dog parks in every quadrant. Free: the St. Charles County parks (Quail Ridge/Wentzville, Veterans Tribute/St. Charles, Broemmelsiek/Defiance) plus Rock Springs (O’Fallon IL), Brent Leh (Edwardsville IL), and the SLU Dog Park (Midtown). Free with registration: Florissant/Duchesne (North County). Paid membership: Tails & Trails at Queeny (Manchester, day pass available), Southwest City at Willmore Park, Frenchtown (Soulard area), Lucas (downtown), and Treecourt (South County). Bring current vaccinations, use the small-dog side for a shy pup, and confirm each park’s policy first — a fenced dog park is the only place off-leash is legal. Keep reading ↓Imagine a Saturday morning, leash in hand, your dog already spinning circles by the door because they know. They don’t care about your inbox or the weather app — they just want grass, room to run, and the chance to meet a few four-legged friends. Whether you’re in the city, out in St. Charles, or across the river in the Metro East, St. Louis has more places to give them exactly that than most owners realize. Here’s your guide to the best dog parks across the metro — plus a few spots where your pup is welcome to tag along for a beer or a little shopping. ## Big, fenced, and built for zoomies: the county parks **Tails & Trails Dog Park at Queeny Park** (Manchester) is the gold standard for many local owners — five fenced acres with separate areas for large and small dogs, walking trails, agility equipment, and water stations. It’s a St. Louis County Parks facility, so you’ll need proof of vaccination and a membership (a day pass is available too). **Creve Coeur Dog Park** at Conway Park — a City of Creve Coeur park open to registered members — offers 2.5 fenced acres, also split into a big-dog area and a small-dog area for pups under 30 pounds. ## City dog parks In the city, the **Southwest City Dog Park** at Willmore Park in St. Louis Hills is one of the oldest and largest membership parks, with two play areas — one for active dogs and a quieter one for smaller, older, or shy pups. **Frenchtown Dog Park** in the near-south-side Frenchtown neighborhoods (the Soulard/Benton Park area) is a community-run, members-only park with a gated entry, and the downtown **Lucas Dog Park** brings fenced space, artificial turf, water bowls, and kiddie pools to the heart of the city (it’s membership-based, run by the Lucas Park Dog Park group, rather than open drop-in). ## St. Charles County The St. Charles County Parks system runs three standouts: **Quail Ridge Park** in Wentzville (about 2.5 fenced acres with separate large and small areas and a covered shelter), **Veterans Tribute Park** in St. Charles (roughly three acres, also split by size), and **Broemmelsiek Park** in Defiance (nearly five fenced acres with a shaded grove, a shelter, and an on-site pond for swimming). ## Metro East (Illinois) Across the river, **the dog park at Rock Springs Park** in O’Fallon offers about 1.5 fenced acres with separate large- and small-dog enclosures, shaded benches, and climbing structures, while **Brent Leh Dog Park** in Edwardsville features an easy-clean astroturf surface, agility equipment, and seasonal water stations. ## Where your dog can tag along (beer and browsing) St. Louis loves a dog-friendly patio. Leashed pups are welcome in the beer gardens at **Urban Chestnut Brewing Co.** in The Grove and **Schlafly Tap Room** downtown, and **Earthbound Beer** on Cherokee Street keeps water bowls (and often treats) on the patio. For a stroll-and-shop afternoon, the **Delmar Loop** is dotted with dog-welcoming sidewalk patios — look for the green paw-print decals — and a few stores roll out the welcome mat indoors, including the **Alpine Shop** in Kirkwood and **Rolling Ridge Nursery** in Webster Groves. (Pet policies do change, so it never hurts to call ahead.) ## South and North County (and a city option) The parks above lean west, city, and Illinois — so here’s the rest of the compass. In **North County**, the **Florissant Dog Park at Duchesne Park** is free to use but requires a quick, free City of Florissant registration (bring your dog’s vaccination records to a community center), and it splits large and small dogs. In **South County**, **Treecourt Unleashed Dog Adventure Park** near Oakville is a private, membership-based “adventure” park — a large, multi-acre spread with trails, shaded spots, and water features that’s a step beyond a standard fenced lot (registration required, and it has some breed restrictions). Out in far **West County**, the **Chesterfield Dog Park** on Lydia Hill Drive adds a couple of fenced acres with a separate small-dog area, a pavilion, and paved paths next to a full community park (confirm its current use policy on the city’s page). And right in the **city core**, the free, fenced **SLU Dog Park & Sculpture Garden** in Midtown is a handy, no-membership option for downtown and university-area dogs. Between these and the parks above, every quadrant of the metro is covered. ## Membership or free? ## St. Louis's Best Independent Bookstores: A Guide for Book Lovers Revised July 28, 2026 What are the best independent bookstores in St. Louis? St. Louis has a deep independent-bookstore scene: Left Bank Books (Central West End, since 1969, the oldest and largest), Subterranean (Delmar Loop), The Novel Neighbor and its Open Door Romance and Betty’s Books (Webster Groves), EyeSeeMe (University City, African American children’s books), Anchovy (Cherokee St, cookbooks), The Book House (Maplewood, 350,000+ used/rare), Dunaway and Leviathan (South Grand), Read A Book STL (Dutchtown), Main Street Books (St. Charles), Spine (Benton Park), plus Afterwords (Edwardsville) and Belleville Books in the Metro East. Most will special-order nearly any title, often at the same price as online. Keep reading ↓Imagine a slow Sunday with nowhere you have to be. You push open a shop door, a little bell rings, and you’re hit with that unmistakable smell of paper and possibility. An hour later you walk out with two books you didn’t know you needed and a recommendation scribbled on a receipt by someone who actually read it. In a world of one-click ordering, that experience is getting rare — but in St. Louis, it’s alive and well. From the city to St. Charles to the Metro East, the metro is full of independent bookstores worth a special trip. Here are the ones to know. ## The anchors: beloved new-book shops **Left Bank Books** in the Central West End is the grande dame — St. Louis’s oldest and largest independent bookstore, open since 1969 and famous for its author-event series. Out on the Delmar Loop, **Subterranean Books** has been championing indie bestsellers and small presses since 2000. In Webster Groves, **The Novel Neighbor** doubles as a community hub with events and classes — and recently spun off **Open Door Romance**, a sister shop devoted entirely to the genre. ## Bookstores with a mission Some of the metro’s most special shops are built around a purpose. **EyeSeeMe** in University City bills itself as the country’s largest African American children’s bookstore, Black-owned and dedicated to positive representation. **Betty’s Books** in Webster Groves is the place for comics, graphic novels, and manga (now in a bigger space with a café), and **Anchovy Book Co.** on Cherokee Street is a cookbook lover’s dream (it’s expanding to a larger Cherokee Street storefront, so check the current address before you go). ## For used, rare, and out-of-print treasures Bibliophiles, this is your section. In Maplewood, **The Book House** stocks a staggering 350,000-plus new, used, and rare titles — an easy place to lose an afternoon (and a perfect stop on our Maplewood food crawl). On South Grand, **Dunaway Books** has built a deep used and antiquarian collection of some 80,000 volumes, while the newer **Leviathan Bookstore** brings a sharply curated literary selection to the same stretch — both easy add-ons to a South Grand dining day. For affordable secondhand finds, **Read A Book STL** in Dutchtown is worth a browse. ## Across the river: Metro East Illinois readers aren’t left out. **Afterwords Books** in Edwardsville is a family-owned shop of new and used titles known for its children’s story times, and **Belleville Books** brought a new-and-used independent to downtown Belleville in 2024. ## More indie shops worth the trip The metro keeps growing new independents, and a couple are worth going out of your way for. In historic St. Charles, **Main Street Books** has been the go-to indie since 1993, recently moving just a few doors down its cobblestone stretch of South Main Street — a general new-book shop with a steady events calendar and the kind of walkable, coffee-and-antiques district that makes an afternoon of it. In Benton Park, **Spine Indie Bookstore & Café** does something genuinely different: its shelves are stocked exclusively with independent authors and small presses on consignment, paired with a café and a busy calendar of poetry readings, author showcases, and even comedy. Between them they round out the map — St. Charles County to the west, the near-south side in the city — so wherever you are, a real bookstore is closer than the nearest big-box. ## How to get the most out of an indie bookstore A good independent gives you things an app never will, if you know to ask. **Staff picks** are the whole point — those little handwritten shelf-talkers are a curated recommendation engine run by people who actually read the book, so start there instead of the bestseller table. Most shops will **special-order** nearly anything and have it in a few days, often for the same price as ordering online, which quietly makes the “but they didn’t have it” excuse disappear. Get on the **events calendar**: Left Bank alone runs hundreds of author signings a year, and The Novel Neighbor, Craft Alliance-adjacent readings, and Spine keep the literary community humming with launches and book clubs. # St. Louis's Best Independent Bookstores: A Guide for Book Lovers Revised July 28, 2026 What are the best independent bookstores in St. Louis? St. Louis has a deep independent-bookstore scene: Left Bank Books (Central West End, since 1969, the oldest and largest), Subterranean (Delmar Loop), The Novel Neighbor and its Open Door Romance and Betty’s Books (Webster Groves), EyeSeeMe (University City, African American children’s books), Anchovy (Cherokee St, cookbooks), The Book House (Maplewood, 350,000+ used/rare), Dunaway and Leviathan (South Grand), Read A Book STL (Dutchtown), Main Street Books (St. Charles), Spine (Benton Park), plus Afterwords (Edwardsville) and Belleville Books in the Metro East. Most will special-order nearly any title, often at the same price as online. Keep reading ↓Imagine a slow Sunday with nowhere you have to be. You push open a shop door, a little bell rings, and you’re hit with that unmistakable smell of paper and possibility. An hour later you walk out with two books you didn’t know you needed and a recommendation scribbled on a receipt by someone who actually read it. In a world of one-click ordering, that experience is getting rare — but in St. Louis, it’s alive and well. From the city to St. Charles to the Metro East, the metro is full of independent bookstores worth a special trip. Here are the ones to know. ## The anchors: beloved new-book shops **Left Bank Books** in the Central West End is the grande dame — St. Louis’s oldest and largest independent bookstore, open since 1969 and famous for its author-event series. Out on the Delmar Loop, **Subterranean Books** has been championing indie bestsellers and small presses since 2000. In Webster Groves, **The Novel Neighbor** doubles as a community hub with events and classes — and recently spun off **Open Door Romance**, a sister shop devoted entirely to the genre. ## Bookstores with a mission Some of the metro’s most special shops are built around a purpose. **EyeSeeMe** in University City bills itself as the country’s largest African American children’s bookstore, Black-owned and dedicated to positive representation. **Betty’s Books** in Webster Groves is the place for comics, graphic novels, and manga (now in a bigger space with a café), and **Anchovy Book Co.** on Cherokee Street is a cookbook lover’s dream (it’s expanding to a larger Cherokee Street storefront, so check the current address before you go). ## For used, rare, and out-of-print treasures Bibliophiles, this is your section. In Maplewood, **The Book House** stocks a staggering 350,000-plus new, used, and rare titles — an easy place to lose an afternoon (and a perfect stop on our Maplewood food crawl). On South Grand, **Dunaway Books** has built a deep used and antiquarian collection of some 80,000 volumes, while the newer **Leviathan Bookstore** brings a sharply curated literary selection to the same stretch — both easy add-ons to a South Grand dining day. For affordable secondhand finds, **Read A Book STL** in Dutchtown is worth a browse. ## Across the river: Metro East Illinois readers aren’t left out. **Afterwords Books** in Edwardsville is a family-owned shop of new and used titles known for its children’s story times, and **Belleville Books** brought a new-and-used independent to downtown Belleville in 2024. ## More indie shops worth the trip The metro keeps growing new independents, and a couple are worth going out of your way for. In historic St. Charles, **Main Street Books** has been the go-to indie since 1993, recently moving just a few doors down its cobblestone stretch of South Main Street — a general new-book shop with a steady events calendar and the kind of walkable, coffee-and-antiques district that makes an afternoon of it. In Benton Park, **Spine Indie Bookstore & Café** does something genuinely different: its shelves are stocked exclusively with independent authors and small presses on consignment, paired with a café and a busy calendar of poetry readings, author showcases, and even comedy. Between them they round out the map — St. Charles County to the west, the near-south side in the city — so wherever you are, a real bookstore is closer than the nearest big-box. ## How to get the most out of an indie bookstore A good independent gives you things an app never will, if you know to ask. **Staff picks** are the whole point — those little handwritten shelf-talkers are a curated recommendation engine run by people who actually read the book, so start there instead of the bestseller table. Most shops will **special-order** nearly anything and have it in a few days, often for the same price as ordering online, which quietly makes the “but they didn’t have it” excuse disappear. Get on the **events calendar**: Left Bank alone runs hundreds of author signings a year, and The Novel Neighbor, Craft Alliance-adjacent readings, and Spine keep the literary community humming with launches and book clubs. ## The Best Indoor Play Places for Kids in St. Louis: Rainy-Day and Winter Lifesavers
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/the-best-indoor-play-places-for-kids-in-st-louis-2026-rainy-day-and-winter-lifesavers
Picture a gray February Saturday, rain (or worse) tapping the windows, and two kids who have already asked “what are we doing today?” four times before 9 a.m. Cabin fever is real — and in St. Louis, it has a cure.
Whether you’re in the city, the county, or across in the Metro East, the metro is loaded with indoor places built to burn off energy and spark imaginations, no matter the weather. Here are the best ones to keep in your back pocket, sorted by the kind of day you’re trying to rescue.
### Hands-on museums and discovery
The crown jewel is the City Museum downtown — a wild, multi-story playscape of caves, tunnels, slides, and a rooftop that thrills toddlers and teenagers alike. It’s built from salvaged materials, so every corner is a surprise; wear closed-toe shoes, bring knee-friendly clothes, and plan on a few hours because nobody leaves quickly.
In Kirkwood, The Magic House (St. Louis Children’s Museum) packs tens of thousands of square feet of hands-on exhibits for the younger set — a three-story slide, a make-believe grocery, a pretend construction site, and rooms that change with the seasons. Its maker-focused offshoot, The Magic House @ MADE for Kids on Delmar, is geared to a slightly older crowd, roughly ages six to thirteen, and lets kids actually build, sew, print, and tinker with real tools.
The Saint Louis Science Center in Forest Park offers galleries of hands-on science with free general admission — a genuinely great deal on a cold day — and its recently upgraded planetarium is worth the ticketed add-on. (Note: another local favorite, Myseum in Town and Country, has been temporarily closed while it relocates, so check its status before you drive out.)
### Animals and wonder, indoors
The St. Louis Aquarium at Union Station brings touch tide pools, sharks, and river-to-ocean galleries under one roof, with a train-station theme kids love. For something gentler, the Sophia M. Sachs Butterfly House at Faust Park in Chesterfield is a warm tropical conservatory with more than a thousand free-flying butterflies — a guaranteed mood-lifter when it’s freezing outside — and right next door, the historic indoor St. Louis Carousel gives little ones a cheap, joyful spin (closed Mondays).
### For the high-energy crowd
When the kids need to move, St. Louis delivers. Trampoline parks lead the way: Sky Zone in Fenton and Urban Air Adventure Park — with locations in Sunset Hills, Cottleville, and Fairview Heights on the Illinois side — pack in trampolines, foam pits, obstacle courses, and climbing walls, with dedicated toddler times at slower hours.
A newer category has arrived, too: Slick City Action Park is an all-indoor slide park — think a dozen giant slides plus air-jump courts — with metro locations in Chesterfield and St. Peters, and it’s a blast for kids who’ve outgrown the ball pit. For climbers, Climb So iLL (downtown St. Louis and St. Charles) has walls and auto-belays sized for families, a great way to wear out an energetic kid safely. Older kids and tweens gravitate to Amp Up Action Park in Town and Country (indoor go-karts, laser tag, a ninja course) and Puttshack at City Foundry, which reinvents mini-golf with tech-enabled scoring and a full menu, which makes it a rare spot that entertains a squirrelly nine-year-old and a couple of adults at the same table. If your kids fall somewhere between “still wants the ball pit” and “too cool for it,” this action-park tier is where a rainy afternoon really gets rescued — there’s enough novelty to hold attention and enough physical activity to guarantee an easy bedtime. A tip worth knowing: most of these action parks charge per attraction or by the hour rather than a flat gate fee, so you can keep a visit short and cheap when you only have a little time or a little patience to spare.
### Little ones and play cafés
Got toddlers? Go Play! in Chesterfield (with a second spot in Lake St. Louis) offers a three-story play structure, slides, and ball pits with coffee for the grown-ups. TotSpot Social in Clayton’s DeMun neighborhood is a play-space-and-café built for newborns through age six, with sessions timed so it never gets overwhelming. And We Rock the Spectrum in Fenton is a wonderful sensory-inclusive gym designed so kids of all abilities — including those with autism or sensory needs — can play side by side. These smaller spots are the sanity-savers when you have a napper and a runner in the same stroller.
Nothing to do with kids — but Soulard is worth a wander.
### Union Station: a rainy day in one building
It’s worth calling out that St. Louis Union Station is more than the aquarium. Under the same historic roof you’ll find a mirror maze, a ropes course, mini-golf, a carousel, a Build-A-Bear Workshop, and the giant Ferris wheel just outside — enough to build a whole rainy day around without ever going back to the car. Buying a combo ticket usually beats paying for attractions one at a time, so check the packages first.
### A few planning tips
Two things save every indoor-play outing. First, check hours and tickets before you load the car — many of these spots shift with the seasons and the school calendar, sell timed-entry tickets, or book up for parties on weekends. Second, pack the right gear: grippy socks are required at every trampoline and slide park (buy them there or bring your own), closed-toe shoes make City Museum far more fun, and a change of clothes is never a bad idea. Midweek and the first hour after opening are the calmest times; rainy Saturdays are when everyone else has the same idea, so go early.
### Making a rainy day actually work
The difference between a great indoor outing and a meltdown usually comes down to a little strategy. Go early. Almost every spot on this list is calmest in the first hour after opening; by mid-afternoon on a rainy Saturday, the parking lot at the popular trampoline parks and the Magic House can be a scene. Have a backup. Timed-entry venues occasionally sell out on the exact days you need them most, so keep a second option in your pocket — if the Aquarium is booked, the Science Center down the road rarely is. Pack a bag. Water bottles, a snack, grippy socks, and a change of clothes cover most disasters, and they keep you from paying concession prices for a forgotten juice box.
It also helps to match the venue to your window of time. If you’ve got ninety minutes before a nap, a play café or the Carousel is perfect; if you’ve got a whole miserable-weather afternoon to fill, City Museum or Union Station will happily eat all of it. And don’t underestimate the smaller neighborhood spots — a quiet play café on a Tuesday morning can save your sanity just as well as a big-ticket attraction on a Saturday.
### By age: what actually works when
The right indoor spot depends a lot on who’s in the back seat. For babies and young toddlers, the winners are the calm, contained spaces: TotSpot Social, the soft-play areas at Go Play!, the Carousel at Faust Park, and the toddler hours at the trampoline parks, where the big kids aren’t bouncing them off the mats. For preschoolers and early grade-schoolers, The Magic House is almost unbeatable, and the Aquarium, Butterfly House, and City Museum’s lower levels hit the sweet spot of “amazing but not overwhelming.”
Once you’re into the grade-school years, the whole map opens up: City Museum top to bottom, Science Center experiments, Slick City’s slides, Climb So iLL’s walls, and the trampoline parks all land. And for tweens and teens — the age that’s hardest to impress — lean on Amp Up’s go-karts and laser tag, Puttshack’s tech mini-golf, Climb So iLL, and the Union Station attractions, which feel less “little-kid” and more like an outing they’d actually choose. Mixed-age group? City Museum and Union Station are the two spots where a three-year-old and a thirteen-year-old can both have a genuinely good time.
### The Illinois side counts, too
Metro-East families don’t have to cross the river for every rainy day. Urban Air in Fairview Heights covers the trampoline-and-climbing itch, and larger all-in-one entertainment centers in Belleville and Edwardsville add bowling, laser tag, and arcades under one roof. If you live on the Illinois side, it’s worth keeping one close-to-home option and one “worth the drive” option (like City Museum) on your list.
### Budgets, memberships, and keeping it cheap
Indoor play can add up fast with a couple of kids, so a few money moves help. The Science Center is free, which makes it the go-to when the budget is tight. If you find yourselves at The Magic House, the Aquarium, or the Science Center more than two or three times a year, a membership usually pays for itself and often includes reciprocal admission to museums in other cities — handy for road trips. For the pay-to-play spots, look for weekday or off-peak pricing, buy grippy socks once and reuse them, and check each venue’s site for combo deals and homeschool or toddler mornings, which are both cheaper and calmer. Birthday packages, as at the fun centers, are frequently the best value if you were going to visit anyway.
### Find more (and a note for owners)
Looking for more local family fun — classes, camps, parties, and activity centers? Browse the Activities listings in the St Louis Near Me Directory to find kid-friendly spots across the metro.
Want bowling, karts, and laser tag too? See our guide to the best family fun centers across the St. Louis suburbs.
When the weather turns genuinely cold, the ice is the other indoor option — here is what a family of four really pays to get on the ice around St. Louis.
Ready for something more structured than open play? See our guide to the best kids’ music, art, and dance classes in St. Louis.
Chasing a rainy-day plan? Browse the St Louis Near Me directory to find indoor play, museums, and activities across the metro.
If you run a kids’ activity business, listing it is how a frazzled parent searching “indoor play near me” finds you first.
On a grey Saturday the search is always the same: what are some fun indoor activities to do in Saint Louis on a rainy day, and is there an indoor playground for kids in St. Louis that suits the age you are actually dealing with. Both answers are yes, and the sections below sort them by energy level.
### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What are the best indoor activities for kids in St. Louis on a rainy day?
A.  Top picks include the City Museum, The Magic House in Kirkwood, the Saint Louis Science Center, and the St. Louis Aquarium at Union Station — all fully indoors and open year-round. For high energy, add a trampoline or slide park like Sky Zone, Urban Air, or Slick City.
### Q. Where can toddlers play indoors in St. Louis?
A.  Try Go Play! in Chesterfield, TotSpot Social in DeMun, the Butterfly House and Carousel at Faust Park, or The Magic House — all geared toward younger children, with calmer spaces and toddler-friendly hours.
### Q. Are there sensory-friendly indoor play options?
A.  Yes — We Rock the Spectrum in Fenton is a sensory-inclusive gym designed for children of all abilities, including those with autism or sensory processing needs. Many trampoline parks and museums also offer quieter sensory hours; check each venue’s calendar.
### Q. What’s the best free or low-cost indoor option?
A.  The Saint Louis Science Center in Forest Park has free general admission and hours of hands-on exhibits, making it the best value on a cold day. The St. Louis Carousel at Faust Park is also just a dollar or two per ride.
### Q. Do indoor play places require special socks or shoes?
A.  Trampoline and slide parks (Sky Zone, Urban Air, Slick City) require grippy socks, sold on-site or bring your own. Closed-toe shoes make City Museum easier, and a change of clothes is smart for water- or paint-heavy exhibits.
### Q. Can I build a whole day around one indoor spot?
A.  Yes — St. Louis Union Station bundles an aquarium, mirror maze, ropes course, mini-golf, carousel, and more under one roof, and City Museum can easily fill an afternoon on its own. Combo tickets usually cost less than paying per attraction.
### Q. Which indoor spots are best for a kid’s birthday party?
A.  The Magic House, City Museum, the trampoline and slide parks (Sky Zone, Urban Air, Slick City), and Amp Up all run birthday packages that bundle admission, a room, and a host. If you were going to visit anyway, the party package is usually the best value — and it saves you from setting up and cleaning up yourself. Book ahead, since weekend slots fill fast in winter.
### Q. What are some fun indoor activities to do in Saint Louis on a rainy day?
A.  The options split by energy level: hands-on museums and discovery spaces for curious kids, climbing and trampoline places for the ones who need to burn it off, and play cafes for toddlers. Union Station puts several under one roof, which is the easy answer when the forecast collapses your plans.
### Q. Is there an indoor playground for kids in St. Louis?
A.  Yes — more than one, and they are not interchangeable. Some are open-play spaces with padded structures, some are membership play cafes with a coffee counter for adults, and some are large climbing and trampoline venues aimed at older kids. Match the venue to the age, not to the drive time.
### Q. How much does it cost for an indoor playground?
A.  Almost all charge per child rather than per family, usually with a lower rate for walkers and toddlers and a free or reduced adult admission. Check three things before you go: whether grip socks are required and sold there, whether re-entry is allowed, and whether the price changes on weekends.
### Q. What are some fun winter games for kids to play indoors?
A.  The ones that work are the ones with a physical outlet: obstacle courses down a hallway, indoor bowling with soft balls, scavenger hunts with written clues for readers. Save screens for the recovery hour. If the walls are closing in, the venues above exist for exactly that afternoon.

## The Best Barbershops in South City St. Louis Revised July 24, 2026 What are the best barbershops in South City St. Louis? The best South City St. Louis barbershops span old-school institutions and modern shops: Wyoming Barber Shop (South Grand), St. Louis Barber & Beauty (Bevo Mill, walk-ins), Union Barbershop (Soulard/Benton Park, straight-razor shaves), Yasser’s (Tower Grove South, cash only), SOHA (Southampton, by appointment), Idle Hands (Shaw), Nisus and Latin (Cherokee St, walk-in), Legacy (Dutchtown), and Angelo’s Barber Collective (Southampton). Bring a reference photo, be specific about the sides, ask walk-in vs. appointment, tip 15–20%, and rebook before you leave. Keep reading ↓Imagine you’ve let it go a few weeks too long. The sides are creeping over your ears, the beard has gone from “rugged” to “forgot,” and you want to walk out feeling like the sharpest version of yourself. You don’t want a rushed chain-store buzz — you want a real barber who knows what they’re doing. Good news: the south side of St. Louis is loaded with them. From old-school institutions to modern shops with a proper hot-towel straight-razor shave, here are the South City barbershops worth the chair. ## The old-school institutions On South Grand, **Wyoming Barber Shop** has been a neighborhood fixture for well over a decade, known for meticulous classic cuts, clean skin fades, and traditional straight-razor shaves — the dependable, no-nonsense barbering that earns a loyal following. (It’s an easy add to a stroll through the South Grand International District.) Over in Bevo Mill, **St. Louis Barber & Beauty Salon** mixes traditional barber culture with a modern twist and welcomes walk-ins seven days a week. ## For the perfect shave If it’s the full hot-towel ritual you’re after, a few South City shops do it right. **Union Barbershop** in the Soulard/Benton Park area is known for its traditional two-pass straight-razor shave, beard trim and skin products included, alongside sharp fades. **Yasser’s Barbershop** in Tower Grove South offers full-service grooming — cuts, shampoo, facials, and hot-towel shaves — from a barber with one of the better reputations on the south side (note: it’s cash only, so plan accordingly). ## Modern shops and full-service grooming **SOHA Barbershop** in Southampton was opened by two longtime barbers who honed their craft for years before going out on their own; expect a clean, friendly, fairly-priced cut — it’s appointment-based, so book ahead rather than dropping in. In historic Shaw, **Idle Hands Grooming Company** is a co-owned shop blending barbering with high-end styling in a laid-back, design-forward space. On Cherokee Street, **Nisus Barbershop** keeps famously long, walk-in-friendly hours for fades and everyday cuts, and in Dutchtown, **Legacy Barber & Beauty** is a community-minded neighborhood shop known for clean cuts, shaves, and razor lining. ## A few more South City chairs worth knowing The south side runs deep, and a couple more shops round out the map. Out toward Macklind and the St. Louis Hills edge of Southampton, **Angelo’s Barber Collective** is a modern men’s shop that literally brands itself “south city barbers” — sharp fades and clean cuts in a different pocket than the Grand and Cherokee crowd, handy if you’re on the west side of the south side. And on Cherokee Street, **Latin Barber Shop** is a long-tenured, old-school institution — open seven days, walk-in friendly, with the kind of loyal following a shop only earns over many years. Between them you’ve got the two ends of the spectrum covered: the modern appointment shop and the neighborhood mainstay where you can just show up. ## Walk-in or appointment? Know before you go South City shops split fairly cleanly into two camps, and knowing which is which saves you a wasted trip. The **walk-in mainstays** — St. Louis Barber & Beauty in Bevo Mill (open seven days), Nisus and Latin on Cherokee Street (long daily hours) — are built for “I need a cut today.” The **appointment shops** — SOHA in Southampton and Idle Hands in Shaw — run on a booked schedule and are worth planning around, especially for a first visit or a more involved cut-and-style. A few, like Wyoming and Yasser’s, take walk-ins but book up fast, so a quick call ahead is the move. When in doubt, check the shop’s Instagram or booking page; most post their current hours and their booking link right there. ## What a real barbershop cut costs — and how to tip South City barbering is still a bargain compared with a salon. A standard men’s cut at these shops generally runs in the range of a chain price to modestly above it, a beard trim or lineup adds a little, and a full hot-towel straight-razor shave — the real ritual, hot lather and all — is priced as the small luxury it is. The unwritten rule: **tip like you would at a good restaurant**, around fifteen to twenty percent, more if your barber squeezed you in or nailed a tricky cut. Cash is always appreciated and, at a cash-only shop like Yasser’s, required — so hit the ATM first. And the single best money-saving habit is also the best-grooming habit: rebook on a regular cadence (every two to four weeks depending on your style) so you’re never walking in shaggy and hoping for a miracle. ## Why South City is a barber town There’s a reason the south side has this many good shops. ## How to Find a Trustworthy Auto Repair Shop in St. Louis Revised July 24, 2026 How do I find a trustworthy auto repair shop in St. Louis? To find a trustworthy mechanic in St. Louis, look for ASE-certified technicians and AAA-Approved shops, insist on a written estimate before any work, confirm a parts-and-labor warranty, and read recent reviews on Google, CARFAX, and the BBB. Watch for red flags like pressure to fix everything at once or a refusal to itemize the bill, ask whether a repair is safety-critical or can wait, and get a second opinion on big jobs. Using an independent shop won’t void your factory warranty under the federal Magnuson-Moss Warranty Act. Keep reading ↓Imagine the dashboard light flickers on during your commute, or there’s a new noise you really hope is nothing. Right behind that worry comes the second one: *who do I take it to without getting taken for a ride?* Whether you’re in the city, the county, or out in St. Charles, finding a mechanic you trust is one of the most valuable things a car owner can do. Here’s how to vet a shop like a pro — plus a few well-regarded St. Louis-area independents to get you started. ## How to spot a trustworthy shop Before you hand over your keys, run through this quick checklist: - **Look for ASE certification.**Technicians certified by the National Institute for Automotive Service Excellence (ASE) have passed national exams and must re-test every five years. ## The Best Yoga Studios in St. Louis: A Guide for Every Style and Budget Revised July 24, 2026 What are the best yoga studios in St. Louis? St. Louis has yoga for every style and budget: donation-based community studios (The Collective STL, Brick City), the volunteer-run Solar Yoga Center (Hatha since the 1960s), hot and power studios (Namaste, Pure Hot Yoga, FLY in Midtown), specialty practice (Joy of Yoga, Urban Breath prenatal, Shanti restorative), Iyengar at Yoga St. Louis, aerial at Studio Aire, YogaSix in West County, Marbles on Cherokee St, and Metro East options (Vive, Go Yoga Express, Yoga on West Main). Most offer a free first class — try a few on intro deals before committing. Keep reading ↓Maybe you’ve been meaning to start. Maybe your back has been begging you to. Or maybe you’ve practiced for years and just moved to a new corner of the metro and need to find your people again. Whatever brought you here, the question is the same: *which studio is right for me?* St. Louis has an unusually rich yoga scene — donation-based community spaces, sweaty power studios, and decades-old institutions among them. Here’s a guide to some of the best, by what you’re looking for. ## Community-first and donation-based If cost or intimidation has kept you off the mat, start here. **Brick City Yoga** in Benton Park West keeps classes accessible with a flat low price and donates monthly revenue to local nonprofits. **The Collective STL** in Old North is a donation-based, Black-owned nonprofit studio — pay what you can — with welcoming community classes. And the **Solar Yoga Center**, teaching traditional Hatha since the late 1960s, is the oldest yoga center in the city, run by volunteer instructors. ## Bring the heat: hot and power yoga Like to sweat? **Namaste Yoga Studio** in Kirkwood offers approachable hot, warm, and non-heated classes and a respected teacher-training program. **Pure Hot Yoga** on Clayton Road (at the Clayton/Richmond Heights edge) is a long-running hot-yoga mainstay, and **FLY Yoga Studio** in Midtown runs alignment-based classes in a modern, infrared-heated space. ## Specialty practices and deeper study For something specific: **Joy of Yoga** in Brentwood blends yoga with Ayurveda, meditation, and energy work, plus teacher training and retreats. **Urban Breath Yoga** in Maplewood is known for its prenatal offerings and a scholarship program that keeps the practice within reach — an easy pairing with a wander through Maplewood’s food scene. And **Shanti Yoga + Wellness** (Tower Grove and Maplewood) focuses on restorative, nervous-system-calming practice for life’s transitions. ## Metro East options Illinois practitioners have good choices too: **Vive Yoga Studio** in Edwardsville offers Vinyasa, Power, Sculpt, and Yin in a welcoming all-levels space, **Go Yoga Express** (Belleville/Swansea and Edwardsville) adds hot yoga, hot Pilates, and an infrared sauna, and **Yoga on West Main** in Belleville is a boutique studio with small-group power, barre fusion, and restorative classes. ## More studios worth knowing (and a few more styles) The list above leans south-city, community, and Metro East — so here are a few that widen the map and the menu of styles. In West County and St. Charles County, **YogaSix** (Town & Country and the Streets of St. Charles) offers six clearly-labeled class types — hot, power, sculpt-and-flow, restorative, slow, and TRX-style — which makes it easy to know exactly what you’re walking into, and it fills the western-suburb gap the rest of this list leaves open. Out in Lake Saint Louis, **Studio Aire** specializes in **aerial yoga** (plus aerial hoop and pole) — a genuinely different practice using suspended silks, great for anyone bored of the mat. On the south side, **Yoga St. Louis** in Lindenwood Park has taught **Iyengar** yoga — a precise, prop-supported, alignment-first method — since 1984, which makes it one of the best choices in the metro for beginners, older students, or anyone working around an injury. And on Cherokee Street, **Marbles Yoga Studio** runs traditional, progressive **Hatha** classes (Levels I through IV) in a walkable arts-district setting. ## Which style is right for you? “Yoga” covers a lot of very different rooms, so it helps to know the vocabulary before you book. **Hatha** is slower and foundational — great for beginners. **Vinyasa** (or “flow”) links movement to breath at a steadier pace. **Power yoga** is the athletic, strength-building end. **Hot yoga** (including the fixed Bikram sequence) runs the room to 95–105°F for a deep sweat and looser muscles — energizing for some, too much for others, so hydrate and go in rested. **Iyengar** is precise and prop-supported, ideal for alignment and injuries. **Restorative and yin** are slow, deeply relaxing, and nervous-system-calming. And **aerial** uses a hammock to take pressure off the joints while you build strength. If you’re not sure, start with a Hatha, gentle, or explicitly “all-levels” class — you can always chase the heat or the challenge once you know the basics. ## Yoga on any budget: from free to premium One of the best things about St. Louis’s scene is that cost is rarely a real barrier. At the **free-to-low end**, The Collective STL in Old North is fully donation-based (pay what you can), Brick City Yoga keeps a low flat rate and gives back to nonprofits, and the volunteer-run Solar Yoga Center charges only minimal fees. In the **middle**, most independent studios sell class packs or monthly memberships, and nearly all offer an **intro ...

## St. Louis's Best Craft Cocktail Bars and Speakeasies Revised July 28, 2026 What are the best craft cocktail bars and speakeasies in St. Louis? St. Louis’s best craft cocktail bars and speakeasies include award-winners Planter’s House (Lafayette Square), Blood & Sand (downtown), and The Gin Room (South Grand); hidden spots None of the Above (City Foundry), Bemiston (Clayton), Lazy Tiger (CWE), Thaxton Speakeasy (downtown, password on Instagram), and Mother May I (South Grand, behind a bookcase); plus Yellowbelly and Retreat (CWE), Monstera Mezcaleria (South Grand, agave), Wright’s Tavern (Clayton), and Pat Connolly Tavern (Dogtown). Tell the bartender two flavors you like, reserve the small rooms, and plan a safe ride home. Keep reading ↓Picture a night out that’s actually about the drink in your hand — a cocktail built with intention, in a room with a little mystery to it. Maybe there’s an unmarked door, a single red light, or a bartender who asks what you’re in the mood for and then surprises you. St. Louis has quietly become a serious cocktail town, with award-winning bars and hidden speakeasies scattered across the metro. Here are the ones worth dressing up for. ## The award-winners **Planter’s House** in Lafayette Square has anchored St. Louis’s craft-cocktail scene since 2013 with one of the city’s most decorated bar programs and seasonal, handcrafted drinks. Downtown, **Blood & Sand** — once a members-only club, now open to all — pairs a globally inspired cocktail list with nationally recognized food. And on South Grand, **The Gin Room** is the domain of Natasha Bahrami, the “Gin Girl of St. Louis,” whose gin program has earned national and James Beard recognition (and sits right along our South Grand dining stretch). ## Hidden doors and speakeasies Half the fun is finding the entrance. **None of the Above**, the modern speakeasy from James Beard winner Gerard Craft’s team at City Foundry, hides behind original factory tunnels marked only by a single red light. In Clayton, **Bemiston Cocktail & Social Club** tucks a 60-seat lounge down a long hallway behind a marked door. And in the Central West End, **Lazy Tiger** is the intimate, hard-to-find “hidden gem” sibling to Yellowbelly, serving its own sharply focused cocktail list. For a true password-protected experience, **Thaxton Speakeasy** downtown hides a 1920s Art Deco lounge behind a marked-only door and posts its weekly hours and password on Instagram — about as close to the real Prohibition-era ritual as the metro gets. ## Tropical, agave, and the classics For something with a passport: **Yellowbelly** in the Central West End leans into rum-forward, island-inspired drinks and coastal fare, while **Monstera Mezcaleria** on South Grand is all about small-batch mezcal, tequila, and agave spirits — and in its basement, the newer **Mother May I** hides a “cocktail dive” behind a bookcase door, pairing a serious drink program with dive-bar prices (think twelve-dollar martinis) on a walk-in-only basis. Prefer a perfectly built classic? **Wright’s Tavern** in Clayton runs a tight, classics-driven list (its negroni and Chartreuse julep are local favorites), and the historic **Pat Connolly Tavern** in Dogtown backs its deep Irish-whiskey selection with well-made standards. ## The people behind the bars St. Louis’s cocktail scene is smaller and more interconnected than it looks, and knowing the family trees helps you find your next favorite. In the Central West End, **Retreat Gastropub** is the parent concept that spun off both **Yellowbelly** and **Lazy Tiger** — a seasonal, spirit-forward program built on house-made juices, syrups, and shrubs, and the thread that ties the whole CWE cluster together. Over at City Foundry, **None of the Above** comes from James Beard winner Gerard Craft’s Niche Food Group, which is why the drinks and the food both punch well above “hidden bar” expectations. And on South Grand, the Bahrami family’s **Gin Room** has a new wrinkle as of 2026: it reunited with the returning Café Natasha Persian kitchen, so you can now pair one of the country’s deepest gin lists with genuine Persian cooking under one roof. The takeaway: once you love one of these bars, its siblings and its team’s other projects are a reliable map to the next great night out. ## How to actually order at a craft cocktail bar The best way to drink at a place like this is to trust the bar. If nothing on the menu jumps out, don’t default to a vodka soda — tell the bartender **two things you like** (a spirit and a flavor profile: “something with mezcal, on the smoky-and-citrusy side,” or “bourbon, but not too sweet”) and let them build to it. A good bartender at any of these rooms would rather make you something you’ll love than pour a rote order. A few habits make you a welcome regular: **read the room on pace** (a carefully built cocktail takes a few minutes — this isn’t a shot bar), **tip well** because craft bartending is a craft, and if you’re not sure what to try, ask what the bar is **known for** — Wright’s negroni, Yellowbelly’s rum drinks, the Gin Room’s gin flights all exist for a reason. Order the house signature first, then explore. ## Finding the door: a speakeasy primer Half the appeal of St. Louis’s hidden bars is the small thrill of getting in, but a little prep saves the fumbling. **Thaxton Speakeasy** literally posts its hours and a rotating password on Instagram — check before you ...

Order the house signature first, then explore. ## Finding the door: a speakeasy primer Half the appeal of St. Louis’s hidden bars is the small thrill of getting in, but a little prep saves the fumbling. **Thaxton Speakeasy** literally posts its hours and a rotating password on Instagram — check before you ...

## The Best Day Trips from St. Louis: 15 Escapes Within Two Hours Revised July 24, 2026 What are the best day trips from St. Louis within two hours? When the city starts to feel small, the Ozark foothills, the wine country, and a string of historic river towns are all close enough for a spontaneous Saturday — no hotel required. Gas up the car. Here are fifteen of the best day trips from St. Louis, by what you’re in the mood for. ## Wine country **Augusta** (about an hour west) sits in America’s very first official wine region, with a cluster of walkable hilltop wineries and patios made for an afternoon. Push a little farther to **Hermann**, a German heritage river town on its own wine trail of family-owned wineries and distilleries, or stop in **Washington, MO**, a historic brick river town with downtown tasting bars and a lively festival calendar. ## State parks and natural wonders For scenery you won’t believe is so close: **Elephant Rocks State Park** (about 90 minutes south) lets you walk among 1.5-billion-year-old granite boulders the size of small houses, and nearby **Johnson’s Shut-Ins** turns the Black River into natural water chutes perfect for summer wading (a record 2026 flood forced a temporary closure, so check its current status before you go). Closer in, **Meramec State Park** pairs river floating with a tour of the famous **Meramec Caverns**, while **Onondaga Cave State Park** offers ranger-guided show-cave tours (seasonally, April through October). And just 30 minutes west, **Castlewood State Park** delivers bluff-top Meramec overlooks and miles of trails when you only have a half day. ## Historic and charming towns **Ste. Genevieve** (about an hour south) is Missouri’s oldest town and home to the largest collection of French colonial buildings in North America, now a National Historical Park. For something smaller and sweeter, **Kimmswick** is a restored 1859 river village of boutique shops anchored by the Blue Owl Restaurant and its towering apple pie — just 30 minutes from the city. ## River towns along the Great River Road Cross into Illinois for the bluffs. **Grafton** (about an hour north), where the Illinois meets the Mississippi, offers a scenic SkyTour chairlift to the bluff tops, plus wineries and ferries (the SkyTour runs seasonally). Nearby **Alton** brings a historic riverfront, an antiques district, and the famous Piasa Bird bluff mural. The two anchor the “Meeting of the Great Rivers” scenic byway — and in January and February, the area becomes one of the region’s best spots to watch bald eagles. ## History and the unexpected Just across the river in Collinsville, **Cahokia Mounds** is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and the largest pre-Columbian earthworks in the Americas — climb Monks Mound and walk the trails (the grounds are open year-round; the interpretive center partially reopened in June 2026 with its gift shop and several exhibits, Wednesday through Sunday, with the main gallery due to reopen later in the year). South of the city, **Mastodon State Historic Site** preserves an Ice Age fossil bed and pairs naturally with Kimmswick. And if you don’t mind a longer haul, **Springfield, Illinois** (about 90 minutes northeast) is Lincoln country, with his home, tomb, and the living-history village of New Salem. ## Three more worth the drive A few standouts sit a little farther out (or a little off the usual river-town loop) and reward the extra miles. **Hannibal, Missouri** (about two hours north) is Mark Twain’s boyhood home — a cluster of preserved historic properties on a single ticket, plus the Mark Twain Cave, the oldest operating show cave in the state. **Cuba, Missouri** (about 75 minutes southwest on I-44) is the self-styled “Route 66 Mural City,” with roughly fifteen outdoor history murals downtown and, just outside town at the Fanning 66 Outpost, a 42-foot-tall rocking chair that’s exactly the kind of roadside Americana a good day trip is made of. And for something quieter, **Maramec Spring Park** near St. James (about 90 minutes southwest) surrounds one of Missouri’s largest springs — roughly a hundred million gallons a day — with trout fishing, easy trails, and the ruins of a 19th-century ironworks. Together they add a literary landmark, a slice of Route 66, and a natural wonder to the mix. ## How to build the perfect day trip A little planning turns a good drive into a great one. First, **match the trip to the season**: wine country and the river bluffs are golden in fall, the caves are a cool escape in the July heat, the Shut-Ins and river floats are summer-only, and the Alton–Grafton stretch peaks in January and February for bald eagles. ## St. Louis Live Music: The Neighborhood Venues Locals Actually Love Revised July 24, 2026 Where can I see live music in St. Louis? St. Louis is full of neighborhood live-music spots locals love. For free shows, try dive bars like CBGB in South Grand, Hammerstone’s and the 1860 Saloon in Soulard, or Atomic by Jamo’s lounge in the Grove. For intimate listening, the Focal Point in Maplewood and Grand Center’s jazz clubs (Jazz St. Louis, the Dark Room, the Sheldon) stand out. Blues and Irish music run seven nights a week in Soulard, and big touring acts play the Pageant, Delmar Hall, and Stifel Theatre. Keep reading ↓Everyone knows the big rooms — the marquee names where the touring acts roll through. They’re great, and we’ll get to them. But the real soul of St. Louis live music is smaller and closer to home: a corner bar where a local band plays for free, a 100-seat listening room where you could hear a pin drop, a blues joint that’s been swinging seven nights a week for decades. Whether you’re in Tower Grove, Soulard, the Grove, or out in Maplewood, here are the St. Louis music spots worth seeking out — the ones locals love and tourists never find. We’ve grouped them by the kind of night you’re after: free neighborhood bars, quiet listening rooms, the blues-and-jazz joints that swing seven nights a week, the eclectic rooms of the Grove and Cherokee Street, the arts-district clubs of Grand Center, and, yes, the big touring stages. Wherever you land, the through-line is the same — real music, close up, at a price that won’t scare you off. ## Neighborhood bars where local bands play (often free) **The Heavy Anchor** in Bevo Mill was built by two music-loving locals to showcase St. Louis bands — drink free at the bar, pay a small cover only for the back-room show. **CBGB** on South Grand is a cash-only, sticker-covered dive where the live bands are *always free* and the drinks are famously cheap. **Pop’s Blue Moon**, a tiny corner bar near the Hill built from lumber salvaged from the 1904 World’s Fair, hosts live music up to six nights a week. And **Tick Tock Tavern** in Tower Grove East — connected to Steve’s Hot Dogs — brings singer-songwriters to a cozy neighborhood room. Up in the Crown District, **The Attic Music Bar** tucks an intimate stage into the second floor of a 1929 building. Two more South City institutions belong on any list: **Off Broadway**, a 30-plus-year, roughly 400-capacity all-ages room down on Lemp near the river bluffs that regularly books touring indie and roots acts, and the **Venice Café** in Benton Park — a cash-only, mosaic-covered art bar with a magical patio and local bands most nights. ## Listening rooms for the music lovers If you want to actually *hear* the music, St. Louis has some gems. **The Focal Point** in Maplewood is a volunteer-run, 100-seat all-acoustic listening room now in its sixth decade — folk, roots, and fingerstyle guitar to a pin-drop-silent crowd, and a perfect cap to a night out on our Maplewood food crawl. **Joe’s Café**, a quirky BYOB art-environment venue in Skinker-DeBaliviere built by a City Museum co-creator, puts jazz and singer-songwriters on a tiny stage amid welded sculptures. The **Blue Strawberry Showroom & Lounge** in the Central West End is a 90-seat supper-club-style room for cabaret, folk, and jazz, and nearby **Evangeline’s** serves hot jazz and swing alongside its Creole brunch. These smaller rooms are where St. Louis music feels most personal — the artist is a few feet away, the crowd is there to listen, and you often walk out having discovered someone you’ll follow for years. If you only ever visit the big touring rooms, this is the whole side of the scene you’d miss. ## Blues, jazz, and trad: the seven-nights-a-week joints For live music almost any night you wander in: **Hammerstone’s** in Soulard runs blues about a dozen times a week, most of it free. Down the street, the **1860 Saloon** has live music 365 days a year, and **John D. McGurk’s Irish Pub** — named one of America’s most authentic Irish pubs by National Geographic — brings traditional Irish music seven nights a week, often with touring musicians straight from Ireland. Downtown, the **Broadway Oyster Bar** pairs Cajun food with blues and zydeco in one of the oldest buildings in daily use in the city. Good news for blues fans: the beloved **BB’s Jazz, Blues & Soups**, closed since 2023, is being revived on South Broadway by the Broadway Oyster Bar team — check for its reopening if you’re downtown. ## The Grove and Cherokee: where it gets eclectic For something a little different: **Atomic by Jamo** in the Grove offers free live music in its lounge Thursday through Sunday (the happy-hour and late-night sets are the local secret), while next-door **Platypus** hides a stage in the back room of a shotgun-style bar known for cocktails and popcorn chicken. On Cherokee Street, **The Golden Record** carries the DIY torch with everything from indie to experimental, and **Yaqui’s** doubles as a wood-fired pizza spot and a cozy jazz room — both anchors of the Cherokee Street Jazz Crawl. Cherokee Street in general rewards wandering — the block mixes vintage shops, taquerias, and DIY spaces, so a show there usually comes with a whole evening ...

## The Best Coworking Spaces in St. Louis Revised July 24, 2026 What are the best coworking spaces in St. Louis? St. Louis coworking spans startup hubs (T-REX and CIC in Cortex, OPO Startups in St. Charles), creative/boutique spots (TechArtista, Nebula on Cherokee Street), premium flex offices (Serendipity Labs, Spark, ThriveCo, Office Evolution, Spaces, Regus, and STL Fusion downtown), and specialized labs (Helix Center). NexCore has moved to a new South County campus on Tesson Ferry Road. Expect roughly low-hundreds a month for a hot desk up to a private office, with day passes often $20–30. Match the space to whether you’re a solo founder, a remote employee, or a small team, and take the free day pass before you commit. Keep reading ↓Working from your kitchen table loses its charm fast. The dog barks, the coffee runs out, and you start craving something most home offices can’t give you: other people, a real meeting room, and a reason to put on real pants. Whether you’re a solo founder, a remote employee, or a small team that’s outgrown the living room, St. Louis has a coworking space for the way you actually work. Here’s a guide to the metro’s best, by what you’re looking for. ## Startup hubs and incubators If you’re building something, plug into the energy. **T-REX** downtown is a roughly 100,000-square-foot nonprofit startup incubator tied to Arch Grants, with events, mentorship, and complimentary food and drink, home to 400-plus founders in the historic Railway Exchange building. **CIC St. Louis** (the Cambridge Innovation Center) anchors the Cortex innovation district with roughly 160,000 square feet across multiple buildings for entrepreneurs and life-science teams — including wet labs, a podcast studio, and 24/7 access. ## Creative and boutique spaces For something with more personality, **TechArtista** rotates art exhibits through its locations in the Central West End, the Grove, downtown, and the Loop — one membership unlocks them all. **Nebula** on Cherokee Street is the city’s oldest coworking space (since 2010), a boutique, art-gallery-lined home for contractors, nonprofits, and filmmakers, and **NexCore**, which recently relocated to a larger campus in South County on Tesson Ferry Road, brings a neighborhood-investment ethos with podcast and photography studios. ## Premium and professional Need polish and quiet? **Serendipity Labs** in Clayton offers a premium national-brand experience with private and day offices, while **Spark St. Louis** downtown is a women-led space with skyline and stadium views. **ThriveCo** (Clayton and Chesterfield) leans concierge-style with free private parking, and the established **Office Evolution** (Creve Coeur and Clayton), **Spaces** (Central West End), and **Regus** (locations across the metro) round out the professional flex-office options. Downtown also gained **STL Fusion** at 555 Washington Avenue, which took over a full floor of the former Industrious space and leans into amenities — a rooftop deck, a golf simulator, and event space alongside private offices and open desks. ## Specialized spaces For science and biotech founders, the **Helix Center** in Creve Coeur is a dedicated life-science incubator with wet and dry labs near the Danforth Plant Science Center — a reminder that “coworking” in St. Louis spans everything from a laptop-and-latte desk to a fully equipped laboratory. ## Coworking in St. Charles and the suburbs The list above leans city and inner-ring, but the metro’s edges have real options too. In St. Charles, **OPO Startups** spreads a startup campus across several historic buildings on and around South Main Street — a genuine coworking-plus-incubator community with day passes, private offices, and access to mentors and investors, and by far the strongest pick if your work or your customers sit in St. Charles County. West County and Chesterfield are covered by the professional-flex brands (ThriveCo, Office Evolution, Regus), and South County now has NexCore’s new Tesson Ferry campus. The upshot: you rarely have to drive downtown just to escape the kitchen table — there’s usually a desk within fifteen minutes, whichever quadrant you live in. ## What coworking actually costs in St. Louis Pricing tiers up with how much privacy and access you need. A **flexible hot desk** — sit anywhere, first-come — often runs in the low-to-mid hundreds per month, and a **dedicated desk** that’s always yours sits a step above that. A **private office** for one to a few people is the biggest jump, scaling with headcount and location. Most spaces also sell a **day pass** (frequently in the twenty-to-thirty-dollar range) and punch-card or part-time memberships for people who only need a few days a month. Watch the extras: some rates include conference-room hours, printing, and coffee, while others meter them. St. Louis generally runs cheaper than the coasts for the same setup, which is part of why the scene has held up — but always confirm what’s bundled before you compare two prices head-to-head. It’s also worth asking about discounts: many spaces knock money off for paying a few months up front, for nonprofits or students, or simply because you asked during a slow stretch. And read the exit terms as carefully as the price — a cheap rate locked into a twelve-month commitment can cost more in the end than a slightly higher month-to-month plan you can leave the day your situation changes. ## Coworking vs. the coffee shop, the home office, and a private lease If you’re weighing options, think in trade-offs. A **coffee shop** is free-ish and social but unreliable — no guaranteed seat, spotty calls, and no real ...

Watch the extras: some rates include conference-room hours, printing, and coffee, while others meter them. St. Louis generally runs cheaper than the coasts for the same setup, which is part of why the scene has held up — but always confirm what’s bundled before you compare two prices head-to-head. It’s also worth asking about discounts: many spaces knock money off for paying a few months up front, for nonprofits or students, or simply because you asked during a slow stretch. And read the exit terms as carefully as the price — a cheap rate locked into a twelve-month commitment can cost more in the end than a slightly higher month-to-month plan you can leave the day your situation changes. ## Coworking vs. the coffee shop, the home office, and a private lease If you’re weighing options, think in trade-offs. A **coffee shop** is free-ish and social but unreliable — no guaranteed seat, spotty calls, and no real ...

## How to Choose a Financial Advisor in St. Louis: What to Ask Before You Trust Anyone With Your Money Revised July 24, 2026 How do I choose a financial advisor in St. Louis? To choose a financial advisor in St. Louis: hire a fiduciary (legally bound to your best interest at all times — stronger than a broker’s point-of-sale Reg BI standard), prefer fee-only pay (no commissions) over fee-based or commission, and look for a CFP or ChFC for planning or a CFA for investing. Here’s how to choose a financial advisor in St. Louis you can actually trust — and the questions that separate the real ones from the salespeople. ## First, understand who you’re hiring “Financial advisor” isn’t a protected title — it can mean a fee-only fiduciary planner or a commissioned product salesperson. Two terms matter most: - **Fiduciary.**A fiduciary is- *legally required*to act in your best interest at all times — an ongoing duty of loyalty. Brokers who aren’t fiduciaries are held to the SEC’s- **Regulation Best Interest (Reg BI)**, in force since 2020: they must act in your “best interest”- *when they make a recommendation*, but that’s a lighter, point-of-sale standard than a fiduciary’s constant duty. Ask, “Are you a fiduciary, 100% of the time?” — and get the answer in writing. - **How they’re paid.**There are three models, and they’re easy to mix up. A- **fee-only**advisor is paid only by you — a flat fee, hourly rate, or a percentage of assets — and earns no product commissions. A- **fee-based**advisor charges you a fee- *and*can also collect commissions, a dual model with a built-in conflict. A- **commission**advisor is paid by the products they sell you. Fee-only is the cleanest of the three; with the other two, always ask exactly how a recommendation makes them money. ## Check the credentials (it takes five minutes) Look for real designations: a **CFP** (Certified Financial Planner) has met rigorous education, exam, and ethics requirements, and a **CFA** is the gold standard for investment analysis and portfolio management (note: that’s a different job than comprehensive financial *planning*). A **ChFC** (Chartered Financial Consultant), issued by The American College of Financial Services, is a planning-focused credential similar in scope to the CFP. The credential names the specialty; a CFP or ChFC signals planning, a CFA signals investing. ## Verify anyone in ten minutes (three free tools) Before a second meeting, run any advisor through the free public databases — it takes minutes and it’s the single best fraud check you can do: - **FINRA BrokerCheck**(brokercheck.finra.org) — brokers and brokerage firms: licenses, employment history, and any disclosures or complaints. - **SEC Investment Adviser Public Disclosure / IAPD**(adviserinfo.sec.gov) — investment advisers and their Form ADV, which spells out fees, conflicts, and disciplinary history in plain sight. - **CFP Board “Verify a CFP Professional”**(cfp.net) and the consumer site LetsMakeAPlan.org — confirms a planner’s current CFP status and any disciplinary or bankruptcy history. For a Missouri-specific check, the **Missouri Secretary of State’s Securities Division** registers and regulates investment advisers who operate in the state (generally those managing under $100 million; larger firms register with the SEC). You can confirm an adviser’s registration status and file a complaint through the Division — a real, local layer of protection worth knowing about. ## Do you even need a human advisor? Not everyone does, and it’s worth being honest about that before you pay for one. A **robo-advisor** — an automated service that builds and rebalances a portfolio for a low fee, often around a quarter percent of assets — is a perfectly good fit for someone with a straightforward situation who mainly needs disciplined, low-cost investing. Where a **human advisor (ideally a CFP)** earns their fee is complexity and life transitions: an inheritance, selling a business, navigating retirement drawdown, a divorce, equity compensation, or a tangled tax and estate picture. If your finances are simple, a robo-advisor or a one-time hourly planning session may be all you need; if your life has gotten complicated, that’s exactly when a good local advisor is worth the cost. Paying an ongoing 1%-of-assets fee for a situation a robo-advisor could handle is one of the quieter ways people overpay. ## The questions to ask in the first meeting A good advisor welcomes these; a bad one dodges them: - Are you a fiduciary 100% of the time? - How exactly do you get paid — and what will I pay in total, including fund fees? - What are your credentials, and can I verify them? - Who is your typical client, and do you work with people in my situation? - How and how often will we communicate? - Who is the custodian actually holding my money? ## What ...
