## Dog-Friendly Patios & Breweries in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/dog-friendly-patios-and-breweries-in-st-louis
There are few better ways to spend a mild St. Louis afternoon than on a shady brewery patio with a cold beer in your hand and your dog stretched out at your feet. Your pup gets a change of scenery and a hundred new smells; you get a pint and a place to actually relax. And St. Louis, as it happens, is a genuinely dog-loving beer town — a lot of the region’s best breweries roll out the welcome mat (and a water bowl) for four-legged regulars.
Here’s a local’s guide to the best dog-friendly patios and breweries in St. Louis: the beer gardens built for a lazy afternoon with your dog, a few that even let pups inside, the etiquette that keeps everyone welcome, and the new dog-park-plus-bar that takes the whole idea to its logical conclusion.
### Why St. Louis Is a Dog-Beer Town
It’s no accident that so many St. Louis breweries welcome dogs. The city’s craft-beer boom grew up alongside its walkable, dog-heavy neighborhoods — Tower Grove, the Grove, Maplewood, Soulard — where a brewery patio doubles as a de facto community backyard. Add St. Louis’s long stretches of patio-friendly weather in spring and fall, and you get a culture where “let’s grab a beer” and “let’s walk the dog” became the same plan. For a lot of locals, the neighborhood brewery is where they know the bartender, the regulars, and each other’s dogs by name.
The upshot for you: whether you want a big beer garden with room to run, a quiet corner patio, or a cold-weather enclosed space, there’s a dog-welcoming option that fits. Below, the standouts — starting with the beer gardens that have earned their reputation.
### The Classic Dog-Friendly Beer Gardens
A handful of spots have earned reputations as the go-to dog patios, and they’re the ones to start with.
Civil Life Brewing Company in Tower Grove South is the gold standard — a spacious, shady, leash-friendly patio with multiple water bowls, an English-pub sensibility, and a crowd that’s equal parts families, regulars, and dogs. Locals consistently name it their favorite neighborhood spot to bring a pup, and it’s an easy first recommendation. Rockwell Beer Garden, tucked into Francis Park in St. Louis Hills, is the true beer-garden experience: a big outdoor space where dogs are welcome on the grounds, with fire pits, on-site pizza, and posted dog rules (keep them off the tables, bring a cup for water). It sits right by the park, so a walk and a beer go hand in hand.
Urban Chestnut’s Grove Bierhall and Midtown Biergarten both welcome dogs in their outdoor German-style biergartens (note: after a 2023 dust-up, dogs are patio-only, not indoors). Urban Chestnut is also known for its summer “Dog Day Fridays” on the Grove lawn — food, live music, and a share of sales going to a rotating animal charity. It’s a genuine event, not just a tolerated policy.
### More Great Patios for Your Pup
The list runs deep from there. 4 Hands Brewing near LaSalle Park welcomes leashed dogs across its outdoor areas (with pup cups), and 2nd Shift Brewing on the Hill is famously dog-devoted — dogs are welcome on the patio and inside, with water bowls and treats on hand. Alpha Brewing in south city keeps a leash-friendly patio with bowls and treats too. For cooler weather, Bluewood Brewing has an enclosed, heated patio where your dog can join you even when it’s chilly, and Side Project in Maplewood offers dog-friendly patios (its Cellar and enclosed Patio locations).
Add to that Rockwell’s Grove/Midtown taproom, Wellspent Brewing (dogs inside and out), Perennial Artisan Ales, Square One Brewery & Distillery in Lafayette Square, The Modern Brewery, Heavy Riff, and Blue Jay Brewing in the Grove — all with dog-welcoming patios and water bowls. Even the big names play along: the Schlafly Tap Room downtown welcomes dogs on its patio. And if you like a cocktail over a craft beer, Narwhal’s Crafted keeps a dog-friendly patio with pup cups. In short, wherever you are in the city, there’s a good dog patio within a few minutes.
### Out in the Suburbs and Metro East
The love extends well beyond the city. In St. Charles County, Third Wheel Brewing in St. Peters welcomes dogs on its patio and inside, with leash hooks on the tables and treats, and Friendship Brewing in Wentzville has a large patio with a grassy area, water bowls, and treats. Good News Brewing welcomes dogs at its several locations (Defiance, O’Fallon, Augusta), Six Mile Bridge in Maryland Heights has a front patio, and Ferguson Brewing keeps a covered patio. Across the river in Illinois, Old Bakery Beer in Alton and Old Herald in Collinsville both roll out dog-friendly patios. No matter which corner of the metro you’re in, there’s a pup-friendly pint nearby.
### The Ultimate Dog Bar: K9 Garden
If a patio isn’t enough and you want your dog fully off-leash, St. Louis now has the answer. K9 Garden, which opened in early 2026 in the former Bar K space on McRee Avenue, combines a full off-leash dog park with a bar and restaurant — Urban Chestnut runs an indoor bar and 4 Hands took over an outdoor bar, so you can grab a beer while your dog runs free with the pack. It’s membership-based with day options, and it’s a genuinely different experience from a patio: less “dog under the table,” more “dog park with drinks.” For social dogs, it’s a blast — and a genuinely novel St. Louis addition worth knowing about.
It’s worth being honest about the tradeoff, though. A patio hang works for almost any dog, including the shy or senior ones who’d rather nap under the table. An off-leash park like K9 Garden is best for social, well-adjusted dogs who enjoy a pack; if yours gets overwhelmed by a crowd of strange dogs, a quiet brewery patio is the better call. Know your dog, pick the setting that suits them, and everyone has a better afternoon.
### Dog-Patio Etiquette (So Everyone Stays Welcome)
These policies exist because owners follow a few simple rules — and they can disappear when people don’t. Keep it easy for everyone:
Keep your dog leashed and close to your table, not roaming the patio.
Bring your own collapsible water bowl. Many patios offer communal bowls, but a shared bowl can pass along germs, so fresh water from home is the safer bet.
Dogs stay on the ground — not on tables, chairs, or laps at the table (an explicit rule at places like Rockwell).
Clean up promptly and carry waste bags.
Only well-behaved dogs. No nonstop barking or lunging, and always ask before letting your dog greet another dog or guest.
Outdoor only, usually. Most breweries allow dogs on the patio but not indoors (Urban Chestnut is the well-known example) — confirm patio vs. inside before you walk in, and mind “no outside food” and no-glass rules near dogs.
Follow those and you’re the kind of dog owner that keeps these patios dog-friendly for the next person.
Nothing to do with beer — but Fountain Park is worth a look.
### One Quick Heads-Up
Dog policies and even whole breweries change, so it’s worth a quick check before a special trip. A couple of once-popular dog spots have closed — Earthbound Beer on Cherokee Street shut its doors in late 2024, and the Bar K dog-bar chain closed before K9 Garden took over its St. Louis location. When in doubt, a glance at a brewery’s website or a recent review confirms both that it’s open and that dogs are still welcome on the patio.

Planning a patio day with your pup? Dog-friendly breweries, bars, and patios are exactly what a good local directory helps you find. Search St Louis Near Me Directory for spots across the city, the suburbs, and the Metro East before you head out.
Run a brewery, bar, or patio in the metro? The dog owners looking for their next hangout are searching for you right now. Listing your business is how St. Louis and Illinois locals — and their dogs — find your door.

### A Few Things to Pack Before You Go
A little prep turns a good brewery afternoon into an easy one. Toss a collapsible water bowl and a bottle of fresh water in the car — even patios with communal bowls are cleaner and safer when your dog drinks from their own. Bring a couple of poop bags (more than you think you’ll need), a short leash rather than a retractable one so your dog stays close to your table, and a chew or favorite toy to keep them settled while you linger over a pint. A towel is smart if rain is in the forecast or the patio’s a little muddy.
Timing matters too. Weekend afternoons at the popular gardens — Rockwell, Urban Chestnut, Civil Life — get crowded and loud, which is great for a social dog and overwhelming for a nervous one. If your pup is on the shy side, aim for a weekday or an early hour when the patio is calm. And do a quick gut-check on the weather: St. Louis summer pavement gets brutally hot, so stick to shaded patios in July and August, and save the sun-drenched beer gardens for a mild spring or fall day when everyone — two legs and four — is more comfortable.
Two questions decide the afternoon: are there any dog friendly breweries in St. Louis that mean it rather than tolerate it, and what if my dog barks at a brewery once you are three tables deep. The patio rule and a willingness to leave early handle both.
### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. Where can I take my dog in St. Louis?
A.  Plenty of St. Louis brewery patios welcome dogs. Start with Civil Life in Tower Grove South, Rockwell Beer Garden in Francis Park, and Urban Chestnut’s biergartens. 4 Hands, 2nd Shift on the Hill, the Schlafly Tap Room patio, and the off-leash K9 Garden dog bar are all great pup-friendly options across the city.
### Q. Can dogs go inside breweries in St. Louis, or just the patio?
A.  Most St. Louis breweries allow dogs on the patio but not indoors — Urban Chestnut, for example, moved to patio-only after 2023. A few are more generous: 2nd Shift and Wellspent welcome dogs inside as well. Always confirm patio-versus-indoor before you walk in, since policies vary and can change.
### Q. What's the etiquette for dogs at breweries?
A.  Keep your dog leashed and close to your table, bring your own water bowl, keep them off tables and chairs, clean up promptly, and make sure they’re well-behaved around other dogs and guests. Most breweries are patio-only for dogs, so confirm before going inside and mind any no-outside-food or no-glass rules.
### Q. Why are some breweries not dog-friendly?
A.  Health-code and food-safety rules keep many breweries from allowing dogs indoors where food is served, so they limit dogs to the patio. A single bad incident can tighten a policy too — Urban Chestnut moved to patio-only after a 2023 dust-up. Allergies, glass hazards, and poorly behaved dogs are other reasons.
### Q. Is there a dog park bar in St. Louis?
A.  Yes — K9 Garden, which opened in early 2026 on McRee Avenue in the former Bar K space, pairs a full off-leash dog park with a bar and restaurant (Urban Chestnut and 4 Hands run the bars). Your dog runs off-leash with the pack while you grab a beer. It’s membership-based with day options.
### Q. Are there dog-friendly breweries in the St. Louis suburbs?
A.  Plenty. Third Wheel Brewing in St. Peters and Friendship Brewing in Wentzville have dog-welcoming patios with water bowls and treats, Good News Brewing welcomes dogs at its several locations, and Six Mile Bridge and Ferguson Brewing have patios too. Across the river, Old Bakery Beer in Alton and Old Herald in Collinsville are dog-friendly Metro East options.
### Q. Are there any dog friendly breweries in St. Louis?
A.  Plenty — the beer garden format suits it, and several taprooms treat dogs as expected rather than tolerated. Policies still differ between the patio and inside, and between the taproom and its kitchen partner, so check the patio rule rather than the brewery rule.
### Q. What if my dog barks at a brewery?
A.  Take the walk. A short lap around the block resets most dogs, and leaving early once is far better than becoming the table nobody wants near them. If barking is reliable rather than occasional, a quieter patio on a weekday is the honest choice over a packed Saturday garden.
### Q. Are there any dog friendly coffee shops in Saint Louis, Missouri?
A.  On patios, commonly yes; inside, much less often, because food service rules are stricter than they are for a taproom. Assume the patio is the offer, bring water, and ask rather than walking a dog through the door of a place that serves pastry.
### Q. Are there any dog friendly places in Saint Louis?
A.  Beyond patios and breweries, the metro has off-leash parks, several walkable districts, and at least one bar built around a dog yard. The pattern is outdoor-first: if there is a patio, a fence or a yard, the answer is usually yes with a leash and a little judgment.

## St. Louis Vintage, Thrift, and Antique Shops Worth the Trip
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/st-louis-vintage-thrift-and-antique-shops-worth-the-trip
Picture a slow Saturday. You’ve got a coffee, no particular plan, and the itch to find something with a little history to it — a leather jacket that’s already been broken in by someone else’s decade, a mid-century lamp, a stack of pulpy paperbacks, a ring nobody else will be wearing. Maybe you’re furnishing a first apartment on a budget. Maybe you just can’t stomach one more identical thing off a big-box shelf. Either way, St. Louis is quietly one of the best thrifting and antiquing towns in the Midwest — if you know where to point the car.
This is the local’s guide to the shops worth the trip: the antique row that anchors it all, the vintage-clothing boutiques with real curation, the weekend markets, and the deep-discount thrifts — plus how to shop them without wasting a Saturday.
### Cherokee Antique Row: the heart of it
If you only have time for one stop, make it Cherokee Antique Row. It’s the largest antique shopping district in St. Louis — roughly six blocks of Cherokee Street packed with more than thirty independently owned antique shops, galleries, and specialty stores, all within an easy walk of each other. You don’t plan a single store here; you plan an afternoon, and you let the block pull you along.
A few anchors are worth knowing before you go. Riverside Architectural Antiques (1947 Cherokee Street) has been in the district since 1979 and is the place for architecturals, salvaged hardware, and genuine oddities — the kind of doorknobs, mantels, and one-off curiosities you can’t reproduce. Hammond’s Antiques, tucked into a building that dates to 1896, is a treasure chest of old books, vintage costume jewelry, historical paper, and posters. And Remember When Antiques is the cozy, family-run stop for vintage toys, collectibles, furniture, and sterling — the kind of place where you go in for nothing and leave with a childhood memory in a shopping bag.
Cherokee Street isn’t just antiques, either. The same walk is lined with taquerias, coffee shops, and murals, so it’s easy to turn a hunting trip into a full day — browse, eat, browse again.
### Where to shop for true vintage clothing
If your hunt is for clothes with a past — real vintage denim, a ’70s coat, a party dress with a story — St. Louis has a genuinely good bench of curated shops, not just picked-over racks.
Avalon Exchange in the Delmar Loop leans vintage and runs bigger than most, with real variety because it buys clothing directly from the St. Louis community — so the racks are, in their words, a reflection of the local community. It’s also home to a beloved ritual: twice a year, Avalon holds a Dollar Sale, where hundreds of items go for a single dollar apiece. Time your visit right and it’s the best deal in the city.
Found Vintage takes the opposite tack — an upscale, artfully curated boutique of trendy-and-timeless true vintage and modern retro. The detail that sets it apart is the in-store repair station, where staff rescue torn or damaged pieces with patches, new fabric, and creative fixes, so what you buy is ready to wear. Mesa Home is the spot for impeccably curated ’70s, ’80s, and ’90s finds, with some pieces reworked and upcycled through the owner’s slow-fashion label — a great stop if you want vintage with a modern edit.
### The markets: many dealers, one roof
For maximum finds per minute, hit a vintage market. St. Louis hosts weekend markets that gather 36 to 50 rotating sellers under one roof — racks that swing from two-dollar t-shirts to over-the-top ballgowns, plus shoes, jewelry, and housewares. The best of them lean into the experience: food trucks, a full bar, music, and even an on-site seamstress to tailor your find before you leave. It’s the fastest way to see a huge range of vintage in one trip, and the vendor mix changes constantly, so it rewards repeat visits.
### Records, books & the specialty hunt
Not every treasure is furniture or a jacket. St. Louis has a deep bench for the specialty collector, and knowing where to point yourself saves a lot of wandering. Vinyl is having a moment, and the metro’s independent record shops — concentrated around the Delmar Loop, Cherokee Street, and South Grand — keep well-stocked used bins where a patient flip through the crates turns up the album you gave up finding online. Used and rare books are a Cherokee Street specialty (Hammond’s alone is a rabbit hole of old paper), and the neighborhood’s shops carry everything from dime-store paperbacks to genuinely collectible first editions.
For the bigger-ticket hunt — mid-century furniture, sterling, art, real antiques — the move is to watch for estate sales alongside the shops. Weekend estate sales across the county are where dealers themselves shop, and getting there early on the first day is how you beat them to the good stuff. Pair a Saturday estate sale with a Cherokee Street or Maplewood browse and you’ve covered both the curated and the raw ends of the St. Louis vintage world in one trip.
### Why secondhand is booming
There’s a reason the racks are busier than they were a decade ago. Buying secondhand is simply the most sustainable way to shop — every jacket or table that gets a second life is one that stays out of a landfill — and in a stretch of rising prices, a $6 flannel or a $40 solid-wood dresser is a genuinely smart money move, not a compromise. Add the thrill of the hunt and the plain fact that vintage gives you a look nobody else at the party will be wearing, and you have a scene that spans every age in St. Louis, from teenagers chasing Y2K fits to retirees furnishing a den in real oak. It’s budget-friendly, it’s greener, and it’s a small act of keeping the city’s stuff — and its stories — in circulation.
### Thrift for the deepest deals
When the goal is volume and the lowest possible price — furnishing a place, building a wardrobe from scratch, or just digging for the thrill of it — the big nonprofit thrifts are where St. Louis shoppers go. Goodwill, The Salvation Army, and St. Vincent de Paul run large stores across the metro with constantly-rotating racks, and your dollars support their programs. The trade-off is curation: you do the digging yourself. But that’s exactly the appeal for a lot of thrifters — the score you find is the one nobody else spotted.
The deepest deals reward the digger — the big nonprofit thrifts turn a slow Saturday into a treasure hunt.
### When the season opens up
The hunt has a calendar, too. Once the weather warms, estate sales, garage sales, and outdoor flea markets multiply across the metro — spring through early fall is prime time, with weekends bringing the widest spread of sales in a single day. Cooler months push the action indoors to the antique malls and thrift stores, which stay open and often quieter, so you dig with less competition. If you’re after a specific piece, warm-season Saturdays give you the most ground to cover; if you just love the browse, a slow winter afternoon in a Cherokee Street shop is its own reward.
### Neighborhoods worth a browse
Half the fun is pairing the shop with the neighborhood, so you can make a day of it:
Cherokee Street — the antique heart of the city, plus great food and murals.
The Delmar Loop — Avalon Exchange, restaurants, music venues, and the Walk of Fame.
Maplewood — a walkable stretch of antique malls, resale shops, and indie storefronts just west of the city.
The Hill & South Grand — mom-and-pop shops mixed with some of the metro’s best Italian and international food.
Clayton & University City — more upscale consignment and antique-adjacent finds.
Nothing to do with thrifting — every St. Louis exterminator, mapped.
### How to shop it like a local
A few habits separate a great haul from a wasted afternoon:
Bring cash. Plenty of small dealers and market vendors prefer it, and cash gives you leverage to politely ask, “Is this your best price?”
Go early. The best racks and the rare pieces are gone by afternoon — especially at markets and on Dollar-Sale days.
Inspect before you buy. Check clothing for stains, moth holes, broken zippers, and true fit (vintage sizing runs small and inconsistent), and test that lamps, radios, and drawers actually work.
Call or check hours first. Independent shops keep independent hours, and some antique dealers are weekend-only.
Pair the shop with the neighborhood. Build the trip around a block, not a single store, and leave room for lunch.
Thrifting and crafting run on the same instinct, and the metro has a whole category of shop built for the second one — see where to buy craft supplies in St. Louis, including the places that sell materials by the pound.
One more local nicety: haggle, but kindly. At antique shops, estate sales, and markets, a polite “Is there any flexibility on this?” is expected and often works — especially on higher-priced pieces, on multiple items bought together, or late in an estate sale when sellers would rather move it than box it. What doesn’t fly is lowballing a small maker or nonprofit thrift where prices are already rock-bottom; those tags fund real programs and support independent dealers. Read the room, be friendly, and you’ll not only save a few dollars but become the kind of regular a dealer tips off when the good stuff comes in.
The best finds go to the patient hunter. Pick a block, go early, bring cash, and leave room for lunch — St. Louis’s vintage and antique scene rewards the people who wander it. Pair your trip with more local guides on St Louis Near Me Directory.
Run a vintage, thrift, or antique shop in the metro? The hunters in this guide are actively looking for you. Listing it on St Louis Near Me Directory puts your shop in front of shoppers across Missouri and Illinois who want exactly what you sell.

### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What is the largest antique store in St Louis?
A.  The largest concentration of antiques in St. Louis is Cherokee Antique Row — not a single store but roughly six blocks of Cherokee Street with more than thirty independent antique shops, galleries, and specialty stores. It’s the biggest antique shopping district in the city, so it’s the best single place to go when you want selection and a full afternoon of browsing.
### Q. Where are the best vintage stores?
A.  For true vintage clothing in St. Louis, start with Avalon Exchange in the Delmar Loop (big selection, twice-yearly Dollar Sale), Found Vintage (upscale, curated, with an in-store repair station), and Mesa Home (curated ’70s–’90s with upcycled pieces). For breadth in one trip, hit a weekend vintage market, where dozens of dealers set up under one roof.
### Q. What are the best thrift stores in St. Louis?
A.  For deep-discount digging, the big nonprofit thrifts — Goodwill, The Salvation Army, and St. Vincent de Paul — run large, constantly-restocked stores across the metro. For curated secondhand, resale and consignment shops in the Delmar Loop, Cherokee Street, and Maplewood do the digging for you. The best thrift store is really the one whose racks match how much sorting you enjoy.
### Q. What to be careful of when thrifting?
A.  Inspect everything: check clothes for stains, moth holes, broken zippers, and missing buttons, and test that electronics, lamps, and drawers work before you buy. Vintage sizing runs small and inconsistent, so try things on or measure rather than trusting the tag. Wash secondhand clothing and clean furniture before use, and know that most thrift sales are final.
### Q. Why is Gen Z obsessed with thrifting?
A.  Thrifting hits three things Gen Z cares about at once: it’s affordable, it’s more sustainable than fast fashion (keeping clothes out of landfills), and it delivers genuinely unique style you can’t buy at the mall. Add the treasure-hunt thrill and the Y2K and vintage trends driving demand, and secondhand shopping has become both a budget move and a form of self-expression.
### Q. Are vintage thrift stores expensive?
A.  Curated vintage costs more than a charity shop and less than new retail — you are paying for someone having done the sorting. The value argument holds either way: every jacket or table that gets a second life is one that did not need making.
### Q. What are some hidden gems in St. Louis that are off the beaten path?
A.  The antique and vintage corridors themselves qualify — Cherokee Street in particular rewards a slow afternoon rather than a targeted trip. Go on a weekday if you want to talk to owners, who are usually the ones who know what just came in.
### Q. What is a good souvenir from St. Louis, Missouri?
A.  Something secondhand and specific beats an airport shelf every time — old advertising, brewery memorabilia, a piece of local pottery. It comes with a story and it is genuinely from here, which is the whole point of bringing something home.
### Q. What is the largest thrift store in St. Louis?
A.  Size is a poor guide to what you will actually find. The big-box charity stores turn over the most volume, but the estate and consignment shops are where the older, better pieces surface — smaller floor, higher hit rate.

## Easy, Family-Friendly Hiking Trails Around St. Louis Revised July 24, 2026 What are the easiest family-friendly hiking trails near St. Louis? Some of the easiest family hikes near St. Louis are paved and stroller-friendly: Powder Valley in Kirkwood, Forest Park’s loop, Creve Coeur Lake, Grant’s Trail, and the Mississippi Trail at Cliff Cave. For bluff views with a little more effort, try Castlewood, Shaw Nature Reserve, Klondike Park, or Pere Marquette in Illinois. Most are free (Shaw and Klondike charge a small fee), and all allow leashed dogs. Go early in summer, and check conditions after rain on the river trails. Keep reading ↓There is a particular kind of St. Louis Saturday where the kids are bouncing off the walls, the weather is finally cooperating, and you just need everyone outside before noon. The good news: you do not have to drive to the Ozarks to find a real trail. Some of the best easy hikes in the region are 20 minutes from wherever you are right now, with paved paths for strollers, shade for the dog, and just enough adventure to wear out a seven-year-old. Here are the family-friendly trails locals actually come back to — with the practical stuff: how long, how hard, where to park, whether it is paved, and whether the kids and the dog will actually make it to the end without a meltdown. ## Powder Valley Conservation Nature Center (Kirkwood) If you are easing little ones into hiking, start here. Powder Valley sits on 112 acres of oak-hickory forest, and all three of its trails are paved, totaling a bit over two miles. The **Tanglevine Trail** is short, fully accessible, and lined with signs that explain what you are looking at — great for curious kids and grandparents alike. Want a little more? The **Hickory Ridge** and **Broken Ridge** trails roll through more varied terrain. **Good to know:** Trails are open daily 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. in summer. The free visitor center is open Tuesday through Saturday and has hands-on exhibits, a nice rainy-day backup. Admission is free. ## Forest Park (St. Louis City) You already know Forest Park, but it is genuinely one of the best walking spots in the country. The signed loop that circles the park runs roughly 5.6 miles on asphalt with a parallel gravel path, so walkers and bikers stay out of each other's way. You do not have to do the whole thing — pick a chunk near the Zoo, the Art Museum, or the Jewel Box and turn around whenever the kids tap out. It is flat, paved, and stroller-perfect, with bathrooms and water along the way. **Good to know:** Free, open year-round. Parking lots ring the park, so start wherever you like. ## Creve Coeur Lake Memorial Park (Maryland Heights) St. Louis County's oldest and largest park wraps a paved path around a big lake, and it is hard to beat for a flat, scenic family walk. The **Lakeview Loop** is about 3.8 miles of fully paved trail around the water — do the full loop or start on the shorter **Mallard Lake Loop** (about 1.7 miles) if little legs are involved. There is even a small waterfall to hunt for. Bikes, joggers, and leashed dogs all share the path happily. **Good to know:** Free, open daily. Multiple lots and trailheads, plus playgrounds nearby for a post-hike reward. ## Castlewood State Park (Ballwin area) Castlewood is the crowd favorite for a reason — bluff views over the Meramec River that feel a world away from the suburbs. The famous **River Scene Trail** is a 3.1-mile loop rated moderate, with a stretch of stairs up to the bluff overlook (worth it). If you want flat and easy instead, the **Castlewood Trail** is a gentle 1.5-mile option. Heads up: parts of the River Scene Trail have been closed at times due to flood damage along the river, so check current conditions before you go. **Good to know:** Free, open daily. Popular with mountain bikers too, so stay alert on shared sections. ## Shaw Nature Reserve (Gray Summit) About 40 minutes southwest on I-44, Shaw Nature Reserve is an extension of the Missouri Botanical Garden spread across 2,400 acres. There are 18 miles of trails total, but you can absolutely keep it short and sweet — wander the prairie, the wetland, or the native plant areas on flat grassy and gravel paths. The **Rus Goddard River Trail** is a 2.5-mile loop that drops down to a gravel bar on the Meramec, a fun turnaround spot for kids. **Good to know:** Open daily from 8 a.m., typically to 5 p.m. but with extended hours (to 8 p.m.) in summer — check current hours before you go, since last entry is 30 minutes before close. Admission is $5, $3 for seniors, free for Missouri Botanical Garden members. This is the one paid stop on the list, and worth it. ## Cliff Cave Park (Oakville) Down in south county, Cliff Cave Park is named for a real limestone cave that is home to a colony of bats (the cave itself is gated and closed to protect them, but the setting is dramatic). The **Mississippi Trail** here is a flat, paved loop of roughly six and a half miles (walk as much or as little of it as you like) through bottomland woods and wetlands — easy walking with a river-bluff ...

## The Best Tattoo Studios in St. Louis Revised July 24, 2026 What are the best tattoo studios in St. Louis? St. Louis has strong tattoo studios across the metro: longtime shops like Iron Age in the Loop, Trader Bob’s on South Jefferson, and All Star in Maplewood; custom-focused studios like Self Inflicted downtown and Alchemy Tattoo Collective in the CWE and South City; plus well-reviewed spots like TRX and Tower Classic in Tower Grove and Steel & Ink in South County. Before you book, check the artist’s Missouri license, watch their sterilization, study healed portfolios, and have a consultation. Keep reading ↓Walk down Cherokee Street on a First Friday and you will pass at least three people comparing fresh ink under the streetlights, sleeves still wrapped in plastic. St. Louis takes its tattoos seriously, and it has for decades. This is a city with shops that have been buzzing since before some of their newest clients were born, sitting right next to newer studios reinventing what a tattoo parlor can feel like. The hard part is not finding a place to get tattooed here. It is knowing which shops have earned their reputations and which ones just have a good sign out front. Below are six St. Louis tattoo studios that have built genuine trust over the years — clean, licensed, professional, and staffed by artists who take the craft seriously. After the list, you will find a practical guide to vetting any shop yourself, because a tattoo is permanent and the studio you choose matters more than almost any other decision in the process. ## Studios Worth Knowing ### Iron Age Studios — The Delmar Loop Open since 1994 on Delmar Boulevard in the Loop, Iron Age is one of the cornerstones of the local scene. It is a full-service body art studio handling everything from a tiny first tattoo to a full back piece, plus a dedicated piercer on staff seven days a week. They take both walk-ins and appointments, and the long history at one address tells you something on its own — shops that cut corners do not last thirty years in the same neighborhood. ### Trader Bob's Tattoo — South Jefferson Trader Bob's, on South Jefferson Avenue near the edge of Soulard and Benton Park, calls itself St. Louis's oldest and finest, and the claim holds up. It is one of the older shops in the entire country, a walk-in-friendly spot open every day, and a piece of local tattoo history that still does steady, dependable work. If you want a place with roots, this is it. ### All Star Tattoo — Maplewood The sister shop to Trader Bob's, All Star sits on South Big Bend Road in Maplewood and has been at it since 2002. The artists here are known for traditional, illustrative, and neotraditional styles — bold lines and work built to age well. They welcome both appointments and walk-ins, and the shared lineage with Trader Bob's means a similar standard of professionalism. ### Self Inflicted Studios — Downtown on Washington Avenue On Washington Avenue downtown, Self Inflicted has built a name as a destination for people who want next-level custom work. It has built a strong reputation for custom work across the greater St. Louis area, runs a second location in St. Peters for north and west county clients, and keeps generous hours most of the week. A strong pick if you are planning a larger, more ambitious piece. ### Alchemy Tattoo Collective — Central West End and South City Alchemy is a woman-owned, LGBTQ-friendly studio with a location on Olive Street in the Central West End, steps from SLU, and a second shop on Chippewa in South City. They specialize in fine line and custom work, and also offer walk-ins, apprentice tattoos, and permanent makeup. The welcoming, no-pressure atmosphere comes up again and again in how clients describe the place. ### Steel & Ink Studio — South County Steel & Ink, in South County (3565 Ritz Center, near Mehlville), is a tattoo and piercing studio staffed by licensed artists with decades of combined experience drawn from around the world. The shop's owners have picked up first-place awards for their tattooing, and the studio leans into a clean, professional, custom-focused approach. Worth a consultation if you are after technical precision. ### TRX Tattoos — South Grand On South Grand Boulevard in Tower Grove South, TRX Tattoos is one of the most consistently well-reviewed shops in the city, with hundreds of positive reviews and a crew tattooing on that stretch since the early 2000s. It fits the South Grand vibe — walk-in friendly, unpretentious, and dependable across a wide range of styles — and it’s a natural stop if you’re already exploring the neighborhood’s restaurants and shops. ### Tower Classic Tattooing — Tower Grove Also in the Tower Grove area, Tower Classic Tattooing is a premier custom parlor that has spent more than a decade earning a spot on local “best of” lists. It leans custom and appointment-driven, so it’s the kind of shop you book ahead for a planned piece rather than a spur-of-the-moment walk-in — a good fit when you want a specific artist and a considered design. ## How to Vet a Tattoo Shop Before You Commit The ink lasts forever, so the homework is worth it. ## The Best Independent Auto Detailers in St. Louis Revised July 24, 2026 Who are the best independent auto detailers in St. Louis? St. Louis’s best independent auto detailers span shops and mobile pros across the metro: Detail To The Max (Richmond Heights), A&G Auto Spa (Maryland Heights, IDA-certified since 2002), The Detailing Pros (Ellisville), Reflective Touch (mobile, South County), Xtreme Detail (Arnold), Soap Stars (St. Charles), CAMO (Lake Saint Louis, since 2006), Metro East Auto Spa (mobile, Edwardsville IL), and David’s Auto Spa (mobile, central corridor). A wash cleans; a detail restores. For big paint-correction or ceramic-coating jobs favor a fixed shop; for upkeep, a mobile pro. Confirm paint-correction prep is included in any coating quote. Keep reading ↓If you have driven a St. Louis winter, you know what it does to a car. The MoDOT trucks salt I-44 and I-270 the second the forecast hints at ice, and that brine spray cakes into your wheel wells, eats at exposed metal, and leaves a chalky gray film that no quick rinse fully removes. Then spring arrives, the Bradford pears and oaks dump a yellow-green sheet of pollen over every windshield in the metro, and by July the sun is baking it all into the clear coat. A car here takes a beating that a car in San Diego never will. That is exactly why a good detailer is worth knowing. Below are independent St. Louis detailers and hand car-wash shops that are open and working in 2026, plus a plain-English guide to what these services actually do, so you can spend smart instead of guessing. ## Detail versus car wash: what you are actually paying for A car wash cleans the surface. A detail restores it. That is the whole difference in one sentence, but the gap between the two is big. A hand car wash means a person, not a tunnel of spinning brushes, touches your paint with soap and a mitt. It is gentler and reaches spots automatic washes miss, like door jambs and the lower rocker panels where road salt collects. A full detail goes much further: clay-barring the paint to pull out embedded grit, vacuuming and shampooing carpets and seats, cleaning vents and crevices, dressing the trim, and often a paint correction step to buff out light swirls and scratches. A wash is maintenance. A detail is a reset. ## Ceramic coating, explained without the sales pitch Ceramic coating is a liquid that bonds to your clear coat and hardens into a thin, glassy layer. It is not magic and it is not a force field, but it does three useful things: it makes water bead and sheet off (so dirt and that winter salt-brine rinse away easier), it adds real gloss, and it gives the paint a sacrificial layer that takes the hit from sun, bird droppings, and tree sap instead of your factory finish. A few honest points most shops will confirm if you ask. A quality professional coating lasts anywhere from a couple of years to five or more, depending on the product and how you maintain it. It is not scratch-proof — it resists fine swirls, not curb rash or a shopping cart. And it works best on paint that has been corrected first, because the coating locks in whatever is underneath. Coat over swirls and you have just preserved the swirls. Good detailers will not skip the prep, which is part of why a real coating costs what it does. ## Independent St. Louis shops worth knowing ### Detail To The Max — Richmond Heights Sitting on South Big Bend Blvd in Richmond Heights, Detail To The Max bills itself as a hand car wash, detailing, and ceramic coating center, and it offers convenient pickup and drop-off, which is handy if you are working in Clayton or the Central West End. It is a central-corridor option for folks who do not want to drive out to the suburbs for a proper hand wash. ### A&G Auto Spa — Maryland Heights Open since 2002, A&G Auto Spa runs out of Centerline Industrial Dr in Maryland Heights and carries certifications from the International Detailing Association and the Organization of Certified Professional Detailers — credentials that actually mean something in a trade with no licensing requirement. They handle ceramic coating, paint correction, paint protection film, and window tint, and they serve the western county and St. Charles side. ### The Detailing Pros — Ellisville Out in the Westwoods Business Park in Ellisville, The Detailing Pros lean hard into paint correction and paint protection, which makes them a fit if you care about getting the swirls out before a coating goes on. A good pick for West County drivers. ### Reflective Touch Auto Wash — South County Reflective Touch is a mobile operation serving the Sappington and South County area, run by an owner who has been detailing since the late 1990s. They will come to you for a hand wash, ceramic coating, polishing, and steam cleaning — useful if your schedule does not allow dropping a car off for a day. ### Xtreme Detail — Arnold Despite the “STL” branding, Xtreme Detail is actually in **Arnold** (Jefferson County, the south metro), not the city proper. It’s a full independent shop — a Feynlab ceramic-coating installer that also does paint correction, window tint, clear bra (paint protection film), and vinyl wraps — and a ...
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/the-best-independent-auto-detailers-in-st-louis

## The Best Independent Gyms and Studios in St. Louis Revised July 24, 2026 What are the best independent gyms in St. Louis? St. Louis has a deep bench of independent, locally owned gyms and studios: Climb So iLL and Upper Limits for climbing; CrossFit boxes like Gambit, Two Six, and Blues City Athletics; StrongHer Everyday for women’s strength; yoga at Urban Breath and Southtown; The Boxing Gym STL for boxing; and TruFusion for mixed boutique classes. Keep reading ↓Every January the parking lots at the big-box chains overflow with resolution crowds. By March, half those cars are gone. ## St. Louis Dive Bars Worth Pulling Up a Stool For
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/st-louis-dive-bars-worth-pulling-up-a-stool-for
Picture a Thursday night when you don’t want a $16 cocktail or a bar with a name you can’t pronounce. You want a cold beer, a worn-in stool, a bartender who calls you “hon,” and a jukebox that hasn’t been updated since the Clinton administration. Maybe you’re coming off a long week in Dogtown, maybe you’re showing an out-of-town friend the St. Louis that doesn’t make the tourism brochures. Either way, what you’re after is a dive.
The good news: St. Louis is a dive-bar town down to its bones. This is a place built by brewery workers and factory shifts, and a lot of the corner taverns that served them are still pouring, still cheap, and still gloriously unbothered by whatever’s trending. Some are grimy in the best way; some are just old and honest; one or two are secretly works of art. All of them are the kind of place where you can walk in a stranger and leave with a story.
Here’s a local’s guide to the St. Louis dive bars worth pulling up a stool for — where to find them, what makes each one worth the trip, and how to be the kind of regular these places are built for.
### What Makes a St. Louis Dive a Dive
A real dive isn’t about being dirty — it’s about being unpretentious. The drinks are cheap and poured strong. The decor is accidental, accumulated over decades rather than chosen by a designer. There’s usually cash-only or a suspiciously old card reader, a bartender who’s seen everything, and a crowd that mixes neighborhood regulars with whoever wandered in. You come for the beer and the price, but you stay for the characters.
St. Louis has its own flavor of dive. Many of these bars sit in the old working-class neighborhoods — Benton Park, Bevo, Dutchtown, Dogtown, Tower Grove — where corner taverns once served the brewery and factory crews within walking distance. That history is baked into the buildings and, often, into the regulars whose families have been drinking there for generations. Here are the ones locals send you to.
### The St. Louis Legends
The Venice Cafe (1903 Pestalozzi, Benton Park) is the one that breaks the rules — it’s a dive in spirit and price but a jaw-dropping outsider-art wonderland in practice. Every inch of the place, inside and out onto one of the best patios in the city, is covered in mosaic, found objects, and decades of accumulated weirdness. Cheap drinks, live music, and an atmosphere you simply cannot get anywhere else. If you take one out-of-towner to one bar, make it this one.
Tick Tock Tavern (3459 Magnolia, Tower Grove East) is the platonic ideal of a neighborhood dive done right: stiff drinks, a great jukebox, a photo booth, pinball, and a crowd that’s equal parts old-timers and Tower Grove twenty-somethings. It’s dark, it’s friendly, and it does the impossible trick of feeling like a genuine dive while actually being well-run. A perfect first stop on a Tower Grove crawl.
### South City Corner Bars
CBGB (3163 South Grand, Tower Grove South) — not the New York punk club, but a beloved little South Grand dive with a punk heart, cheap cans, a patio, and a genuinely welcoming vibe. It’s the kind of place that anchors a neighborhood: unpretentious, friendly to newcomers, and a reliable landing spot on the South Grand strip after dinner up the block.
The Silver Ballroom (4701 Morgan Ford, Bevo) is a pinball-lover’s dive — a wall of machines, horror-movie decor, cheap drinks, and a punk-and-metal soul. It’s one of the best places in the city to sink quarters into pinball while you drink, and it draws a loyal, friendly crew. Come for the games, stay for the beer, and don’t be surprised if you close the place out.
The Heavy Anchor (5226 Gravois, Dutchtown) splits the difference between dive bar and music venue: a comfortable, unfussy front bar with cheap drinks and a back room that hosts live bands, comedy, and trivia. It’s the kind of spot where you can have a quiet pint on a slow night or catch a sweaty local show on a busy one — a true neighborhood workhorse on Gravois.
### Dogtown’s Old Guard
Nick’s Pub (6001 Manchester, Dogtown) is a Dogtown institution — an old-school Irish neighborhood bar with cheap drinks, live music, and a fierce local loyalty, especially around St. Patrick’s Day when Dogtown becomes the center of the St. Louis Irish universe. It’s not fancy and doesn’t want to be. It’s where the neighborhood actually drinks.
Pat Connolly Tavern (6400 Oakland, Dogtown) is a half-step up from a pure dive — a historic, family-run Irish tavern that’s been serving Dogtown for generations. It’s known as much for its food (that toasted ravioli and a serious burger) as its beer, but it keeps the warm, worn-in, everybody-knows-everybody feel that makes the old Dogtown taverns special. A great pairing with Nick’s on a neighborhood crawl.
Riley’s Pub (3458 Arsenal, Tower Grove) rounds out the old-guard neighborhood taverns — a low-key Irish-leaning corner bar with cheap drinks, occasional live music, and a mellow regulars-first feel. It’s the kind of place that doesn’t try to be a destination and is all the better for it.
### The Deep Cuts
Pop’s Blue Moon (5249 Pattison, The Hill/Southwest Garden) is one of the oldest bars in the city, reportedly built with lumber salvaged from the 1904 World’s Fair. It’s a cozy, history-soaked neighborhood bar with cheap drinks, live music, patio space, and a friendly, unpretentious crowd — the sort of place that feels like it’s always been there because it very nearly has.
Iowa Buffet (2727 South 12th Street, Benton Park West/Soulard edge) is the platonic cash-only dive — a no-frills, no-nonsense corner tavern famous among regulars for its cheap pours and its legendary “Hank” burger. Bring cash, don’t expect a menu of craft anything, and settle in. It’s the kind of unvarnished neighborhood bar that reminds you what a dive is supposed to be.
### Build Your Own Dive-Bar Crawl
The beauty of St. Louis dives is that they cluster by neighborhood, so you can string several together on foot or with a short rideshare hop. In Tower Grove, start at Tick Tock on Magnolia, walk over to Riley’s on Arsenal, and cap the night at CBGB on South Grand — three distinct dives inside a mile, with plenty of late-night food on Grand in between. It’s the easiest crawl in the city and the one most likely to end in a new favorite.
For a Dogtown night, pair Nick’s Pub and Pat Connolly Tavern — a block apart on the neighborhood’s Irish spine, and unbeatable around St. Patrick’s Day. Down in south city, the Silver Ballroom in Bevo and the Heavy Anchor in Dutchtown make a great pinball-and-live-music pairing, while Iowa Buffet and the Venice Cafe anchor a grittier, more soulful Benton Park loop. Wherever you start, the rule is the same: go slow, tip well, and let the bartender point you to the next stop — even if that next stop is one of the late-night dance clubs across St. Louis. Half the fun of a dive crawl is the local intel you pick up along the way.
One practical note: these are neighborhood bars, and their hours can be looser than a chain’s. Some don’t open until late afternoon or evening, a few are closed early in the week, and holiday hours vary. A quick call or a look at the bar’s social page before you head out saves you from finding a dark window and a locked door.
Wildly off-topic, but nobody drinks well on an empty stomach — eat something first.
### How to Be a Good Dive Regular
Dives run on unwritten rules, and the fastest way to belong is to respect them. Bring cash — plenty of these places are cash-only or heavily prefer it, and there may not be an ATM. Tip well and tip every round; bartenders remember, and a good tipper becomes a regular fast. Don’t show up expecting a cocktail menu or table service — order a beer or a well drink, keep it simple, and you’ll fit right in.
Beyond that, it’s just basic barroom decency: be friendly to the regulars without crowding them, respect the bartender’s pace on a busy night, take the jukebox seriously (read the room before you queue up ten songs), and don’t be the loudest person in a quiet bar. Do that, and any of these places will feel like yours by the second visit. That’s the whole point of a dive — it’s a living room that happens to serve beer.
Hunting for your new favorite bar, neighborhood by neighborhood? The St Louis Near Me Directory is a great place to find and compare local bars, taverns, and restaurants across the whole metro — from Benton Park to Dogtown to the Metro East — so you can spend less time searching and more time on a stool.
Run a bar, pub, or corner tavern yourself? Listing it on the directory is how new regulars find you when they search for a spot near them. Add your business here and get on the map.

Where to eat on South Grand
Beyond the Arch: unique things to do for adults
Two things settle whether a place is the real thing: what should I order at a dive bar without slowing the room down, and whether the dive bars making a comeback on every list are the ones that were here all along. A short list and a cheap pour answer both, and the comeback is mostly people noticing again.
### Frequently Asked Questions
### Q. What is the difference between a regular bar and a dive bar?
A.  A dive bar is defined by being unpretentious rather than dirty. Compared with a regular bar, a dive keeps drinks cheap and poured strong, decor that is accidental and accumulated over decades, and a mix of neighborhood regulars. You come for the price and stay for the characters.
### Q. Are dive bars usually cash only?
A.  Often, yes. Many St. Louis dives are cash-only or strongly prefer cash, and some have unreliable card readers with no ATM nearby. Iowa Buffet is famously cash-only. Bringing cash is always smart: you’ll tip more easily and won’t get caught out if the machine is “down” for the night.
### Q. What not to order at a dive bar?
A.  Skip the cocktail menu and table service, because most dives don’t offer either. Order a beer or a simple well drink, keep it uncomplicated, and you’ll fit right in. Don’t expect a list of craft anything; these are neighborhood bars built for cheap, strong pours, not mixology.
### Q. What is the oldest bar in St. Louis MO?
A.  Pop’s Blue Moon (5249 Pattison, near the Hill) is the one locals most often name among the oldest bars in the city. It’s reportedly built partly from lumber salvaged from the 1904 World’s Fair. Several old corner taverns go back generations, but Pop’s wins for sheer history and cheap drinks.
### Q. Which St. Louis dive bar has the best pinball?
A.  The Silver Ballroom (4701 Morgan Ford, Bevo) is the pinball dive: a full wall of well-maintained machines, horror-movie decor, and a punk-and-metal atmosphere. Tick Tock Tavern in Tower Grove also has pinball and a photo booth. For a night built around games and cheap drinks, the Silver Ballroom is the pick.
### Q. What’s the best dive bar in St. Louis for live music?
A.  The Heavy Anchor (5226 Gravois, Dutchtown) pairs a comfortable dive bar with a back-room music venue hosting local bands, comedy, and trivia. Nick’s Pub in Dogtown and Pop’s Blue Moon also feature live music regularly. For a genuine dive-bar-plus-stage experience, the Heavy Anchor is the most reliable bet on any given night.
### Q. Is The Venice Cafe really a dive bar?
A.  Sort of: it has dive prices and an unpretentious, come-as-you-are crowd, but it’s wrapped in one of the most extraordinary settings in St. Louis, a mosaic-and-found-object outsider-art wonderland with a legendary patio. Think of it as a dive with a soul and an art budget. It’s a must-visit either way.
### Q. What should I order at a dive bar?
A.  Whatever is on tap and cheap, or a simple pour with one mixer. Dive bars are built around a short list done fast, and a complicated cocktail order slows a one-bartender room down. If there is a kitchen and it has been there for decades, order from it.
### Q. Are dive bars expensive?
A.  That is close to the definition — if the drinks are priced like a cocktail lounge, it is a themed bar wearing the look. Expect to pay noticeably less than downtown, expect cash to be welcome or required, and expect the tip to matter more than the tab.
### Q. What is a dirty dive bar?
A.  Usually a compliment about wear rather than an actual hygiene complaint: scuffed floors, taped stools, decades of stickers. Worn is character; sticky is a warning. The bars that last are the ones where the room looks its age and the glassware does not.
### Q. Are dive bars making a comeback?
A.  They never left here, which is why this list exists. What has changed is attention — rising prices elsewhere sent people looking for a cheap stool and a jukebox, and the corner bars that survived the last twenty years were waiting. The risk now is imitation rather than extinction.

## Great River Road: Best Stops from Alton to Grafton Revised July 24, 2026 What are the best stops on the Great River Road from Alton to Grafton? The Great River Road from Alton to Grafton, Illinois is one of the best day trips near St. Louis. Start in Alton with Fast Eddie’s, the free National Great Rivers Museum, and winter bald-eagle watching, then see the Piasa Bird and the historic village of Elsah. In Grafton, ride the SkyTour to Aerie’s, hit the wineries and The Loading Dock, take the free Brussels Ferry, and finish at Pere Marquette State Park. Most stops are free, and you can do it in a day. Keep reading ↓There is a stretch of road about a half hour northeast of St. Louis where the city falls away and limestone bluffs rise straight up out of the Mississippi. The Great River Road from Alton to Grafton, Illinois hugs the water the whole way, with the bluffs on one side and the river on the other. In winter, bald eagles hang in the bare trees overhead. In summer, the wineries fill their terraces and the river towns hum. It is one of the easiest big-payoff day trips in the region, and you can do the whole thing on a tank of gas and a free afternoon. Here is how to drive it, stop by stop, heading upriver from Alton to Grafton with a worthwhile detour into the bluffs at the end. ## Start in Alton Alton is the gateway. It is a river town with a long history, antique shops, and one bar that has become a regional institution: **Fast Eddie's Bon Air**. Open since the 1930s, Fast Eddie's is cash-friendly, loud, and famous for cheap food and a packed calendar of live music. It is not fancy, and that is the point. Get there early on a weekend if you want a seat. Before you leave the Alton area, swing by the **National Great Rivers Museum** at the Melvin Price Locks and Dam in East Alton. Admission is free, the museum is open daily, and the interactive exhibits walk you through how the Mississippi shapes everything around here. They also run free guided tours of the working locks and dam most days, where you can watch barges actually lock through. It is a genuinely good stop for kids and adults alike, and the price is right. A mile or so up the road, keep an eye on the bluff face for the **Piasa Bird** — a huge, brightly painted recreation of a Native American legend that stares out over the river from the rock. There’s a small pull-off where you can stop for a photo; it’s free, always visible, and one of the most striking sights on the whole drive. ## Watch for eagles (especially in winter) If you are driving this route between December and February, slow down and look up. The Alton-to-Grafton corridor hosts one of the largest wintering bald eagle populations in North America. Eagles gather near the open water below the dams to fish, and you can spot them perched in trees right along the byway. Across the river in West Alton, the **Audubon Center at Riverlands Migratory Bird Sanctuary** is a prime viewing spot and hosts an annual Eagle Days event in early February with spotting scopes and live raptor programs. Bring binoculars and a thermos. ## Detour into Elsah Between Alton and Grafton, watch for the small turnoff into **Elsah**. This tiny village tucked into a gap in the bluffs was one of the first places in the country added to the National Register of Historic Places in its entirety. Walk the quiet streets past preserved 19th-century stone cottages, poke into a shop or two, and enjoy the fact that almost nothing here has changed in over a century. It takes maybe twenty minutes to stroll, and it is the kind of place that makes you want to move slower. ## Spend the afternoon in Grafton Grafton sits where the Illinois River meets the Mississippi, and it is the heart of the trip. The town has reinvented itself around the water, with wineries up on the bluffs and patios down on the riverfront. For the best view, ride the **Grafton SkyTour** up to **Aerie's Resort**. The SkyTour is an open chairlift (with enclosed gondola cars available) that carries you 300 feet up the bluff to a winery terrace overlooking the river confluence. Aerie's has an award-winning winery, a restaurant, lodging, a zipline, and an alpine coaster if you are bringing thrill-seekers. The view from the top alone is worth the ticket. Down in town, the **Grafton Winery** pours local wines, and its riverside Brewhaus on West Main is an easy place to land. If you want your drink with your toes practically in the river, head to **The Loading Dock** on Front Street — an open-air bar and grill built on the old Grafton Boatworks site, with weekend live music, casual food, and tropical drinks served right at the water's edge. Traveling with kids in summer? Just outside Grafton, **Raging Rivers WaterPark** is a seasonal water park (open roughly Memorial Day through Labor Day) with slides, a wave pool, and a lazy river tucked against the bluffs — an easy way to turn the drive into a full family day when it’s hot. ## Cross on the free ferry ...
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/great-river-road-best-stops-from-alton-to-grafton

Down in town, the **Grafton Winery** pours local wines, and its riverside Brewhaus on West Main is an easy place to land. If you want your drink with your toes practically in the river, head to **The Loading Dock** on Front Street — an open-air bar and grill built on the old Grafton Boatworks site, with weekend live music, casual food, and tropical drinks served right at the water's edge. Traveling with kids in summer? Just outside Grafton, **Raging Rivers WaterPark** is a seasonal water park (open roughly Memorial Day through Labor Day) with slides, a wave pool, and a lazy river tucked against the bluffs — an easy way to turn the drive into a full family day when it’s hot. ## Cross on the free ferry ...

## Best Family Fun Centers Across the St. Louis Suburbs Revised July 24, 2026 What are the best family fun centers near St. Louis? The best family fun centers around St. Louis are spread across the suburbs and Metro-East: Kokomo Joe’s in St. Peters and The Edge in Belleville do a bit of everything; Amp Up in Town and Country and Swing-A-Round in Fenton cover go-karts; Tropicana Lanes is the big bowling pick; Urban Air handles trampolines; and Main Event, Dave & Buster’s, Topgolf, and Edison’s round out the list. Keep reading ↓It is 2 p.m. on a gray Saturday, the kids have already asked “what are we doing today” four times, and nobody wants another afternoon staring at a screen. Anyone raising a family around St. Louis knows the feeling. The good news: you do not have to drive downtown or wait for summer at Six Flags to wear everybody out. Some of the best family fun centers in the metro are tucked into the suburbs and across the river in the Metro-East — bowling, trampolines, go-karts, laser tag, mini golf, and arcades, often all under one roof. Here are real spots worth the drive, spread from St. Charles County to the Illinois side, with a little about what makes each one click for families. A quick note on how to read this list: it is organized by area, from St. Charles County through West and South County and over to the Illinois Metro-East, so you can start with whatever is closest and work outward. Most of these places are indoors or have a solid indoor core, which makes them just as useful on a rainy spring Saturday as on a blazing July afternoon. And because they range from a quiet weekday bowling outing to a full-blown, everything-under-one-roof extravaganza, there is a right answer here for a low-key two hours and for a marathon birthday party alike. ## St. Charles County: where the big indoor centers live ### Kokomo Joe's — St. Peters If you want one place that does almost everything, Kokomo Joe's on N. Cloverleaf Drive is hard to beat. The locally owned center packs 12 full-size bowling lanes, laser tag and a laser maze, bumper cars, escape rooms, and a big arcade into one building. It runs on a pay-as-you-play game card, so you are not forced into an all-day pass if you only have a couple of hours. ### Urban Air Adventure Park — Cottleville For families with kids who simply need to *jump*, the Urban Air on Mid Rivers Mall Drive in Cottleville (just outside O'Fallon, Missouri) is built for it. Trampolines, climbing walls, obstacle courses, and indoor adventure zones give younger and older kids different ways to burn energy. It is a chain, but it is a verified suburban location and a reliable rainy-day release valve for St. Charles County parents. ## West County: racing and bowling traditions ### Amp Up Action Park — Town and Country This one is for the speed crowd. Amp Up on Manchester Road runs European-style electric go-karts on an indoor track where drivers can hit 40 to 45 miles per hour on the straightaway. There is no admission charge — you pay only for what you do — and beyond karting they offer axe throwing, laser tag, a high-ropes ninja course, and patio games. Junior karts keep the younger drivers (ages 7 to 11) in the action, so it is not just a teenagers-and-up spot. ### Tropicana Lanes — Richmond Heights Sometimes you just want to bowl. Tropicana Lanes on Clayton Road has been a St. Louis bowling tradition since 1960 and is the largest bowling center in Missouri, with 52 lanes plus arcade games, billiards, and party rooms. Bumpers and assist ramps are available, which makes it genuinely workable with little kids who would otherwise gutter every ball. It is an easy, no-fuss outing close to the center of the county. ## South County and Jefferson County: the classic fun-town feel ### Swing-A-Round Fun Town — Fenton Swing-A-Round on Skinker Lane in Fenton has been entertaining St. Louis families for more than 30 years, and it leans into the old-school outdoor fun center vibe. The Fenton location has go-karts with Honda engines, three nine-hole mini golf courses laid out around ponds and waterfalls, batting cages (they bill theirs as St. Louis' largest), bumper boats, bumper cars, an indoor playground, and an 80-game arcade. Fun passes come in one-hour, two-hour, and all-day flavors, so you can match the visit to your kids' stamina. ## Illinois Metro-East: two heavyweight centers across the river ### The Edge — Belleville Do not skip the Illinois side. The Edge on S. Belt West in Belleville is an 82,000-square-foot complex that genuinely has it all: go-karts, six lanes of black-light bowling, bumper cars, virtual reality attractions, multiple video arcades, and what they call the world's largest laser tag arena — a 14,000-plus-square-foot space that can run up to 60 players at once across five different game modes. For a group of mixed ages or a big birthday crowd, it is tough to outgrow. ### Edison's Entertainment Complex — Edwardsville A little north in Edwardsville, Edison's on S. State Route 157 brings a more polished, boutique feel. Think 12 lanes of upscale bowling with blacklight at night, a 4,000-square-foot laser tag ...

## Best Tutoring and Learning Centers Across the St. Louis Metro Revised July 24, 2026 Where are the best tutoring and learning centers in the St. Louis metro? St. Louis has strong tutoring across the metro: math-focused Mathnasium (St. Charles, St. Peters, Des Peres) and worksheet-based Kumon (Chesterfield, Wildwood, Ballwin, Clayton); multi-subject Sylvan (Ballwin, Chesterfield, O’Fallon IL); local independent Mackler Associates in Frontenac and the Huntington chain for diagnostic test prep; and Brain Balance for focus and attention. Match the program to the actual problem, take the free assessment, mind the drive, and check free options first — library homework help, National Honor Society peer tutoring, and Khan Academy. Keep reading ↓Report cards come home, and suddenly the kitchen table turns into a battleground. Maybe it is fractions in third grade, or chemistry that stopped making sense in October, or the looming ACT that decides which scholarships your high schooler qualifies for. If you have ever Googled “math help near me” at 9 p.m. on a Sunday, you are in very good company across the St. Louis metro. The good news: the region is loaded with quality tutoring and learning centers, and they are spread out from St. Charles County to the Illinois Metro-East. You do not have to drive downtown or settle for whoever a neighbor happened to mention. Here is a practical look at where to find help, how to choose, and what it actually costs. ## When it is time to get a tutor A rough patch on one quiz is normal. The signs that point toward outside help are more persistent: grades sliding two quarters in a row, homework that triggers tears or shutdowns, a kid who says “I am just bad at math” (a confidence problem, not an ability one), or a standardized test on the calendar with real stakes attached. Tutoring is not a punishment or an admission of failure. It is the same logic as hiring a swim coach. Some skills are easier to build with a trained outside eye. The other common trigger is timing. Reading and math gaps compound. A second grader who never locked in place value will struggle with long division in fourth grade and algebra in eighth. Catching it early is almost always cheaper and faster than catching it late. ## The national learning centers, town by town The familiar chains run on proven systems, and the St. Louis suburbs have plenty of them. What matters is finding the specific location near you, because quality and hours vary by franchise owner. **Mathnasium** focuses purely on math, K-12 through pre-calculus, with a free assessment that maps a student's exact gaps before any lessons begin. You will find centers in **St. Charles**, **St. Peters** (the St. Peters North location on Mexico Road), and **Kirkwood** (technically on Manchester Road in Des Peres, serving Kirkwood and Webster Groves families). Across the river, **Mathnasium of O'Fallon, Illinois** serves the Metro-East including Belleville families. **Kumon** takes a different angle: a worksheet-based, self-paced method in both math and reading that builds independent study habits over the long haul. Metro centers include **Chesterfield** (on Olive Boulevard), **Wildwood**, **Manchester** (located in Ballwin on Manchester Road), and **Clayton** (on Ladue Road). Kumon tends to reward consistency. It is a marathon, not a quick fix. **Sylvan Learning** covers the widest subject range: math, reading, writing, science, and ACT/SAT prep, with personalized plans tied to local school curriculum. The **Ballwin** center serves Ballwin, Chesterfield, and Kirkwood, there is a dedicated **Chesterfield** location, and **Sylvan of O'Fallon, Illinois** serves the Metro-East. Sylvan is a strong pick when a student needs help across several subjects rather than just one. ## Local independents and specialized programs The national chains aren’t the whole picture. St. Louis has homegrown independents and specialty programs that fill gaps the big brands don’t. **Mackler Associates** in Frontenac is a longtime local name in academic tutoring and ACT/SAT prep, the kind of established, one-location practice families pass along by word of mouth. **Huntington Learning Center**, another established brand with metro locations, runs K-12 tutoring and intensive, diagnostic-driven test prep, and is often a fit when a student needs a structured, results-focused plan rather than casual help. A different category worth knowing: **Brain Balance**, which has a presence in the metro, is not subject tutoring at all — it’s a drug-free program aimed at focus, attention, and behavior for kids who struggle to sit still and absorb material in the first place. If the real obstacle is attention rather than the algebra itself, a focus-and-executive-function program can matter more than another hour of math. Beyond any brand, plenty of independent one-on-one tutors — retired teachers, graduate students, and subject specialists — work across the metro, and they often cost less and flex around your schedule. ## Match the help to the subject The best choice depends on what’s actually hard. For **reading struggles or dyslexia**, look specifically for a tutor or center trained in a structured, multisensory method like Orton-Gillingham — it’s the researched approach for stubborn reading gaps, and not every general tutor offers it. For **math**, a diagnostic center that pinpoints the exact missing building block usually beats generic homework help. For **writing**, you want someone who’ll coach the process, not just fix a paper the night before it’s due. And for **ACT and SAT prep**, ask about real practice tests, score tracking, and whether the tutor knows ...

## The Best Local Credit Unions in the St. Louis Metro Revised July 13, 2026 What are the best credit unions in the St. Louis area? The St. Louis metro has strong member-owned credit unions on both sides of the river. St. Louis–headquartered options include First Community (the largest, about $4.78 billion in assets), Together (formerly the Anheuser-Busch Employees’ Credit Union), Vantage, Neighbors, Alliance, West Community, Alltru, and the community-focused St. Louis Community Credit Union; Scott and 1st MidAmerica anchor the Illinois Metro East. Most now let anyone who lives or works in the area join, and members typically get better loan and savings rates than at a bank. Keep reading ↓Imagine it’s a Saturday morning and you’re finally staring down the bank statement you’ve been avoiding — a $12 “maintenance” fee here, an ATM charge there, a savings rate that rounds to nothing. Maybe a neighbor in Florissant just financed a car and mentioned the rate she got through her credit union, and it was a full point lower than what your big bank quoted. You start to wonder if you’ve been leaving money on the table for years. If that sounds familiar, you’re in one of the best metros in the country to do something about it. St. Louis — on both sides of the river — is thick with strong, member-owned credit unions, several of them founded right here for local workers and neighborhoods. This guide walks through the best local credit unions across the metro, who’s allowed to join each one, and why so many St. Louisans quietly bank this way. ## What Makes a Credit Union Different From a Bank The short version: a credit union is a not-for-profit financial cooperative that’s owned by its members, not by outside shareholders. When you open an account, you become a part-owner with a vote. Because there are no stockholders to pay, the money a credit union earns flows back to members as lower loan rates, higher savings rates, and fewer fees. A bank, by contrast, answers to investors who expect a profit. That difference shows up in real numbers. According to the National Credit Union Administration (NCUA), the federal regulator, credit unions nationally averaged a 6.27% rate on a 60-month new-car loan versus 7.50% at banks, and paid 3.26% on a one-year $10,000 CD versus 2.41% at banks (NCUA, 2025). On a car loan or a mortgage, a point or more adds up to real money over the life of the loan. And your money is just as safe. Deposits at federally insured credit unions are protected up to $250,000 by the NCUA — the credit-union equivalent of FDIC insurance, backed by the full faith and credit of the U.S. government. The coverage amount is identical to a bank’s; only the insuring agency’s name changes. ## The St. Louis–Headquartered Credit Unions These are the home-grown institutions — founded and headquartered in the St. Louis area, most now open to anyone who lives or works in the metro. **First Community Credit Union** (Chesterfield) is the largest credit union headquartered in St. Louis — roughly $4.78 billion in assets, more than 408,000 members, and about 42 branches. It celebrated its 90th anniversary in 2024, and its community charter covers St. Louis City plus a wide sweep of Missouri and Illinois counties, so most metro residents can join. **Together Credit Union** (St. Louis) began in 1939 as the Anheuser-Busch Employees’ Credit Union — a beer-industry credit union that grew into a roughly $2.64-billion institution with about 145,000 members and 26 branches. It rebranded to Together in 2020 and is now a founding and official banking partner of St. Louis CITY SC. Membership is open to people who live or work across the core metro counties, plus employees of partners like Anheuser-Busch, Nestlé Purina, and BJC, and their families. **Vantage Credit Union** (Bridgeton) runs about 14 metro branches and has one of the friendliest community charters around: you can join if you live, work, *worship, or attend school* in St. Louis, St. Charles, Jefferson, or Franklin counties in Missouri, or St. Clair or Madison counties in Illinois. **Neighbors Credit Union** (St. Louis), with about 8 branches, leans on a “once a member, always a member” promise and serves the core Missouri and Illinois metro counties, plus select employer groups like Costco and Bi-State/Metro. **Alliance Credit Union** (Fenton) was founded in 1948 and carries deep labor-union and skilled-trades roots — its field of membership includes dozens of employer groups and several labor organizations alongside the usual live-or-work-here counties on both sides of the river. ## A Metro That Keeps Growing: Recent Mergers The St. Louis credit-union map has shifted recently, and it’s worth knowing so you don’t go looking for a branch that’s changed its sign. **West Community Credit Union** (O’Fallon, MO) completed a legal merger with Gateway Metro Federal Credit Union on April 7, 2026, creating a roughly $670-million credit union with 43,000-plus members and about 16 branches under the West Community name. **Alltru Credit Union** (Wentzville) is another rebrand to know: it was 1st Financial Federal Credit Union until late 2020, and it started life in 1968 as the McDonnell Douglas Credit Union — a nod to St. Louis’s aerospace heritage. Alltru is a certified Community Development Financial Institution (CDFI) serving St. Louis City, St. Louis County, and St. Charles County. And there’s a big new entrant: **CommunityAmerica Credit Union**, ...
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/the-best-local-credit-unions-in-the-st-louis-metro

Membership is open to people who live or work across the core metro counties, plus employees of partners like Anheuser-Busch, Nestlé Purina, and BJC, and their families. **Vantage Credit Union** (Bridgeton) runs about 14 metro branches and has one of the friendliest community charters around: you can join if you live, work, *worship, or attend school* in St. Louis, St. Charles, Jefferson, or Franklin counties in Missouri, or St. Clair or Madison counties in Illinois. **Neighbors Credit Union** (St. Louis), with about 8 branches, leans on a “once a member, always a member” promise and serves the core Missouri and Illinois metro counties, plus select employer groups like Costco and Bi-State/Metro. **Alliance Credit Union** (Fenton) was founded in 1948 and carries deep labor-union and skilled-trades roots — its field of membership includes dozens of employer groups and several labor organizations alongside the usual live-or-work-here counties on both sides of the river. ## A Metro That Keeps Growing: Recent Mergers The St. Louis credit-union map has shifted recently, and it’s worth knowing so you don’t go looking for a branch that’s changed its sign. **West Community Credit Union** (O’Fallon, MO) completed a legal merger with Gateway Metro Federal Credit Union on April 7, 2026, creating a roughly $670-million credit union with 43,000-plus members and about 16 branches under the West Community name. **Alltru Credit Union** (Wentzville) is another rebrand to know: it was 1st Financial Federal Credit Union until late 2020, and it started life in 1968 as the McDonnell Douglas Credit Union — a nod to St. Louis’s aerospace heritage. Alltru is a certified Community Development Financial Institution (CDFI) serving St. Louis City, St. Louis County, and St. Charles County.
