## Benton Park Businesses & Neighborhood Guide | St Louis Near Me Directory

 Benton Park, St. Louis

Benton Park serves as one of South St. Louis’s most historically dense and architecturally distinctive neighborhoods — built around the city’s second-oldest park (dedicated 1866 over a former cholera-era cemetery), anchored by the Lemp Brewery Complex, the Lemp Mansion, Cherokee Street Antique Row, the Chatillon-DeMenil Mansion, and the National Register-listed Benton Park Historic District (1985) — offering fine dining, craft breweries, historic event venues, live music, custom woodworking, and Cherokee corridor businesses across the heart of South City.

Benton Park is one of St. Louis’s 79 official neighborhoods, located in South St. Louis at **38.5980° N, 90.2238° W**. Its official boundaries run north along **Gravois Avenue**, south along **Cherokee Street**, east along **Interstate 55**, and west along **Jefferson Avenue**. The neighborhood is bordered by **McKinley Heights** and **Fox Park** to the north, **Soulard** to the east, **Marine Villa** to the southeast across I-55, **Gravois Park** and **Benton Park West** to the south across Cherokee Street, and the rest of **Benton Park West** to the west across Jefferson Avenue. The 2020 census recorded the neighborhood’s racial composition as 68.1% White, 22.3% Black, 6.8% Two or More Races, 1.3% Asian, 1.1% Some Other Race, and 0.4% Native American. Important internal streets include **Utah, Arsenal, Pestalozzi, Sidney, Lemp, Wisconsin, Salena, and DeMenil Place**. Benton Park (the neighborhood) is unrelated to **Benton Place**, a private street in Lafayette Square.

The land that became Benton Park traces back to the **St. Louis Commons**, originally set aside by French settlers **Pierre Laclede and Auguste Chouteau**. Sale of the Commons was authorized in 1836, but active platting did not begin until the early 1850s. The 17-acre site at the heart of the neighborhood was first designated as the **City Cemetery in 1842** — far from the urban core, which at the time barely reached Soulard. It was heavily used during the **1849 cholera epidemic** that killed approximately 7,000 St. Louisans (bodies were often buried fully clothed because people feared touching the infected dead). Beginning in the late 1850s and early 1860s, **German immigrants** began settling the area due to the cheap undeveloped land and proximity to the breweries. By 1865, the population had grown enough that the city ordered the bodies exhumed and reinterred at **Bellefontaine Cemetery** and the Quarantine burial grounds on Arsenal Island.

On **June 25, 1866**, the 17-acre site was dedicated by city ordinance as **City Park**. Two acres of the perimeter were carved out to form Jefferson Avenue, Arsenal Street, Illinois Avenue, and Wyoming Street. Park superintendent and noted horticulturist **Edward F. Krausnick** landscaped the rolling terrain with a greenhouse, footbridge, circular fountain, rustic stone bridges, and two lakes (the reconfigured lake perches over a subterranean cave system and is still stocked with fish today). In **1882**, City Park was renamed **Benton Park** in honor of **Thomas Hart Benton**, the five-term U.S. Senator from Missouri (1821–1851) and proponent of Manifest Destiny. A granite monument was later erected in the park to commemorate **Friedrich Franz Karl Hecker**, a German revolutionist and renowned Civil War colonel. Benton Park is St. Louis’s second-oldest park and one of the oldest west of the Mississippi River.

The neighborhood’s most consequential industry was beer. Benton Park sits atop a system of **natural limestone caves** that maintain a constant 55°F — ideal for the German *lagering* process — and attracted multiple breweries to the area. The most famous was the **Lemp Brewery Complex**, founded in 1864 by **William J. Lemp**, who expanded his father **Adam Lemp’s** 1838 brewing operation (Adam Lemp was the first in the United States to produce lager-style beer and is considered the father of modern brewing in St. Louis). The Lemps selected the site for its underground limestone caves and proximity to the Mississippi River, building what became the **largest brewery in St. Louis — larger even than neighbor Anheuser-Busch** — and one of the largest in the United States, with national brands **Falstaff, Lemp Standard Lager, and Culmbacher**. The Lemps operated their own refrigerated railroad (the Western Cable Railway Company), were first in the nation to establish coast-to-coast beer distribution, shipped globally by the 1890s, and in 1912 were first in the world to deliver beer by airplane.

The Lemp Brewery Complex, designed in the **Italian Renaissance style** by **Widmann, Walsh and Boisselier** architects, eventually covered five city blocks with 29 buildings (the Barnett and Record Construction Company designed the granary stacks in 1905). The **Lemp Mansion** at 3322 DeMenil Place was built in 1868 and purchased by William J. Lemp in 1876 as the Lemp family home and brewery offices. National Prohibition forced all brewing operations to shut down in 1919, and on **June 28, 1922**, the Lemps sold the complex at public auction to the **International Shoe Company**, which operated it as a shoe manufacturing center until 1992. The complex was designated a St. Louis City Landmark in 1975 and is part of the **Lemp Brewery-Cherokee City Historic District**. Famously, the Lemp family’s history includes the suicides of three family members in the mansion, contributing to its widely-told status as one of America’s most haunted buildings. The mansion today operates as a restaurant, inn, and event space hosting ghost tours, mystery dinners, and brunches.

Benton Park’s other landmark caves and brewing heritage include the **McHose & English Cave**, said to run underneath Benton Park to the Lemp Brewery, which housed **Ezra English’s** underground beer garden and bowling alley before the 1849 cholera epidemic. In the 1880s and 1890s, a mushroom farm and a winery operated in the cave; the city sealed the entrances in the early 1900s. The cave was rediscovered through hi-tech imagery in 2020 by St. Louis Magazine historian Chris Naffziger. Other notable historic structures include the **Chatillon-DeMenil Mansion** at 3352 DeMenil Place (built in 1848 by Henri Chatillon as a two-room brick farmhouse, expanded in 1861 by Nicolas N. DeMenil, now a period museum), the **Schollmeyer Building** at the corner of Arsenal and Illinois (Queen Anne-style brick commercial building, 1889, NRHP-listed), and three distinctive structures on **Wisconsin Avenue** north of Arsenal built by **Icarians** — the French socialist utopian community who followed founder Etienne Cabet to St. Louis in 1856. The **Benton Park Historic District** was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1985, became a City Historic District in 2006, and was governed by the Benton Park Historic District Ordinance published November 10, 2010.

Beyond Benton Park itself, the neighborhood contains three additional city parks: **Cherokee Park** (nearly 9 acres with the Cherokee Community Center built in 1967, indoor swimming pool, gymnasium, baseball/softball/soccer fields), **Carnegie Park** (2 acres with playground), and **Fremont Park** (2 acres with playground and ball field). The southern boundary, **Cherokee Street**, anchors the renowned **Cherokee-Lemp Historic District** — called a “Street Museum,” covering Cherokee and DeMenil Place for roughly a mile and located less than 2 miles from the Gateway Arch. Cherokee Street Antique Row remains one of the city’s premier independent shopping districts. The active **Benton Park Neighborhood Association** hosts the **Benton Park Classic Criterium** (the closing day of the Labor Day weekend **Gateway Cup Bike Race**), the annual 5K Run/Walk/Stroll with family festival, summer concerts, National Night Out, and the fall **Benton Park Art and Harvest Festival** (with VW Bus Show and Chalk Art Festival). St. Louis Public Schools serves the area, though no SLPS schools sit within the neighborhood boundaries themselves.

Image: Historic German-immigrant red-brick architecture in the Benton Park neighborhood — part of the National Register-listed Benton Park Historic District (1985), one of South St. Louis’s most architecturally distinctive corridors anchored by the 1866 Benton Park, the Lemp Brewery Complex, and Cherokee Street Antique Row — Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0 by Onegentlemanofverona

Benton Park sits on the rolling South City terrain at 38.5980° N, honeycombed beneath the surface by the limestone cave system that made it a 19th-century brewing capital and still maintains a constant 55°F underground. The neighborhood experiences St. Louis’s full humid continental climate: hot, humid summers with frequent 90°F days, cold winters with regular freezing temperatures, and a notably active spring severe weather season including real tornado corridor exposure. Peak outdoor activity falls during spring and fall, when Benton Park’s stocked fishing lake, the Cherokee Street Antique Row, the Lemp Mansion ghost tours, the Benton Park Classic Criterium (Gateway Cup bike race), the Benton Park Art and Harvest Festival (with VW Bus and Chalk Art shows), and the Venice Café outdoor patio draw the heaviest visitor use. Cool seasons drive intense indoor activity at Frazer’s Restaurant & Lounge, Sidney Street Cafe, Bluewood Brewing’s historic Lemp stable house, Shameless Grounds, the Lemp’s Grand Hall event venue, the Cherokee Community Center’s indoor pool, and Lemp Mansion’s restaurant and inn. Winter shifts commerce indoors to the Cherokee Street independent antique shops, the Benton Parkade, and the neighborhood’s long-standing restaurants. The neighborhood’s 1860s–1890s red-brick German-immigrant housing stock, the Italian Renaissance-style Lemp Brewery Complex (1864–1922), the Lemp Mansion (1868), the Chatillon-DeMenil Mansion (1848), and the Schollmeyer Building (1889) have weathered more than 130 years of Missouri climate with the durability typical of South City’s working-class German-immigrant building tradition.

### Benton Park West Businesses & Neighborhood Guide | St Louis Near Me Directory
Benton Park West, St. Louis
Benton Park West serves as the cultural and commercial heart of South St. Louis — positioned along the historic Cherokee Street corridor between Jefferson and Gravois — offering specialized PR, custom gift design, craft brewing, fine dining, event venues, and century-old millwork services for residents, creatives, and small business owners across the metro.
Benton Park West sits in South St. Louis City at 38.5990° N, 90.2377° W , occupying a compact 0.40-square-mile triangle that the 2020 Census recorded as home to 4,238 residents at a density of roughly 11,000 per square mile. The neighborhood’s official boundaries are Jefferson Avenue on the east, Gravois Avenue (Missouri Route 30) on the north and west, and an irregular southern edge that follows Cherokee Street , South Compton Avenue, and Potomac Street. The 63118 zip code makes Benton Park West a direct neighbor to Benton Park (across Jefferson), Gravois Park (to the south), Tower Grove East and Shaw (to the west), and Fox Park / McKinley Heights (to the north).
The neighborhood’s modern form is the conglomeration of two 1970s neighborhoods — Compton Hill and Marquette-Cherokee — whose boundaries the City of St. Louis redrew during that era’s neighborhood-mapping effort. The original Marquette-Cherokee neighborhood ran from Arsenal Street on the north to Bates Street on the south, with Grand Boulevard as its western edge and the Mississippi River as its eastern edge. Today, Benton Park West holds the highest percentage of Latino residents of any St. Louis neighborhood, and in 2005 it was added to the National Register of Historic Places as part of the Gravois-Jefferson Streetcar Suburb National Historic District.
Benton Park West was already a working community by the mid-1880s — an immigrant German neighborhood with carpenters, builders, stone masons, dairymen, gardeners, market owners, grocers, saddle and harness makers, a blacksmith, a midwife, and two saloons serving roughly 50 city blocks. The earliest buildings cluster near the late-nineteenth-century horse-drawn and electric streetcar lines that ran along Gravois Avenue , Arsenal Street , and South Jefferson Avenue , and the blocks between Juniata, Arsenal, and Pestalozzi Streets are noticeably smaller than the surrounding grid because of the skewed intersection of Gravois and Jefferson — roads that themselves date to the original 1830s sale of the St. Louis Commons. South of Juniata Street toward Potomac, the residential and commercial buildings of the 1880s reflect the early horse-drawn streetcar lines that ran along Jefferson Avenue and Cherokee Street.
The defining commercial spine is Cherokee Street , the east-west corridor that runs from Grand Boulevard to Broadway and serves as the southern boundary of Benton Park West before continuing through Benton Park to the Mississippi. Cherokee Street is the largest Hispanic-owned business corridor in St. Louis and the site of two of the city’s most beloved annual festivals: the Cinco de Mayo Cherokee Street Festival (with its three music stages and the coincident People’s Joy Parade organized by C.A.M.P.) and Fiestas Patrias STL , held in September to celebrate Mexican Independence Day. The street’s Antique Row east of Jefferson, the Latino business district west of Jefferson, and the Cherokee Street Jazz Crawl, Print Bazaar, and Brewed Arts Festival keep the corridor active year-round.
Benton Park West’s historic anchors are unusually well preserved. The Ferdinand Herold Mansion , built in 1888 by the owner of the Cherokee Brewery, still stands on South Jefferson. The Casa Loma Ballroom , built in 1926 as the “Cinderella Dance Academy,” continues to host Friday-night dining and big-band dance events more than a century later. Our Redeemer Lutheran Church , founded in 1892, was the first English-speaking Lutheran congregation in South St. Louis. The neighborhood is also where Fred Wehrenberg — a Cherokee Street blacksmith, saloon-keeper, grocer, and butcher — was inspired by a 1904 World’s Fair film exhibit to open the Cherokee Theatre in 1906, founding what became the oldest family-owned theater chain in the nation.
No discussion of Benton Park West is complete without the Lemp Brewery complex . Founded in 1840 by German immigrant Johann Adam Lemp and dramatically expanded by his son William J. Lemp beginning in 1864, the Western Brewery (later the William J. Lemp Brewing Company) grew into one of the largest breweries in the country — larger than its neighbor Anheuser-Busch at its peak — built atop a network of natural limestone caves that provided pre-refrigeration lagering temperatures. The 13.7-acre, 27-building complex spans the southeastern edge of Benton Park into Marine Villa; its Lemp Brewery stables on Cherokee Street (now home to Bluewood Brewing) directly anchor Benton Park West, and the family’s celebrated — and famously haunted — Lemp Mansion sits just east of the neighborhood. The brewery shut its doors in 1919 with Prohibition; the buildings have housed everything from International Shoe Company to artist studios since.
Public green space is anchored by Benton Park itself — just across Jefferson Avenue at Wyoming, the city’s second-oldest park, originally laid out in 1842 as City Cemetery and converted to a park in 1866 — and Gravois Park , bounded by Potomac, Miami, Compton, and Louisiana Avenues just south of the neighborhood. Between them they offer more than 22 acres of fishing lake, picnic facilities, tennis courts, and playgrounds. The neighborhood is also home to St. Frances Cabrini Academy , a Catholic K-8 private school.
Today Benton Park West is one of the most architecturally intact and culturally vibrant neighborhoods in St. Louis — a working creative district where senior-led PR agencies operate on Wyoming Street, century-old millworks still cut custom cabinetry on Juniata, breweries occupy the original Lemp stables, and the Cherokee Street corridor hosts art galleries, taquerias, vintage shops, antique row, and live music venues alongside the everyday rhythm of a working-class South City neighborhood.
Image: The Lemp Brewery complex on Cherokee Street — Wikimedia Commons / Paul Sableman, CC BY 2.0

Benton Park West runs on a four-season Midwest climate — humid summers that fill Cherokee Street’s Cinco de Mayo crowds and brewery patios, crisp falls built for Antique Row strolls and the Jazz Crawl, and winters that push business indoors to the corridor’s cafes, breweries, and historic dining rooms.

### Frequently Asked Questions 
Q. What defines the Benton Park West neighborhood? 
A. Benton Park West is the Cherokee Street corridor neighborhood of South St. Louis — a compact 0.4-square-mile triangle between Jefferson, Gravois, and Cherokee, built by German immigrant tradesmen in the 1880s. Formed from the 1970s merger of Compton Hill and Marquette-Cherokee, it now holds the city’s highest share of Latino residents and sits on the National Register as part of the Gravois-Jefferson Streetcar Suburb district.

Q. How does St Louis Near Me Directory help Benton Park West businesses? 
A. St Louis Near Me Directory strengthens neighborhood-focused visibility for businesses serving Benton Park West by pairing local content with curated listings. Q. What types of businesses are most common in Benton Park West? 
A. Benton Park West mixes senior-led PR and creative agencies, independent gift and apparel shops, craft breweries, fine dining, century-old custom millwork, and historic event venues. Most operate out of restored 1880s brick storefronts along Cherokee Street, South Jefferson Avenue, or the former Lemp stables — anchored by the largest Hispanic-owned business corridor in St. Louis.

Q. What kinds of dining, retail, and recreation options are available in Benton Park West? 
A. Residents and visitors can find Chemistry PR & Multimedia on Wyoming Street, Baskets by Stephanie on South Jefferson, STL Style House and La Vallesana on Cherokee, Shameless Grounds on Withnell, Venice Café and Frazer’s on Pestalozzi, Bluewood Brewing in the Lemp stables, the 131-year-old Gravois Planing Mill on Juniata, and Lemp’s Grand Hall — a working mix of dining, retail, and creative services.

Q. Are there neighborhood landmarks, parks, and historic sites in Benton Park West? 
A. Yes — the Lemp Brewery complex (founded 1840), the 1888 Ferdinand Herold Mansion, the 1926 Casa Loma Ballroom, Our Redeemer Lutheran Church (1892), and the site of Fred Wehrenberg’s 1906 Cherokee Theatre, birthplace of the oldest family-owned theater chain in America. Benton Park and Gravois Park together add more than 22 acres of green space along the neighborhood’s edges.

Q. What is it like to live in Benton Park West? 
A. Benton Park West is a dense, walkable South City neighborhood of restored 1880s brick rowhouses and storefronts, home to roughly 4,200 residents and the city’s highest concentration of Latino households. Cherokee Street’s festivals, antique shops, and taquerías sit blocks from quiet residential streets, giving it a working-class, immigrant-rooted character that is increasingly drawing artists and small business owners.

Q. How do residents and visitors get around Benton Park West? 
A. Benton Park West’s triangular footprint between Jefferson, Gravois, and Cherokee keeps most daily errands within walking distance, and street parking serves the Cherokee Street corridor’s shops and restaurants. The neighborhood connects quickly to I-44 and I-55, and to neighboring Tower Grove East, Shaw, Soulard, and Lafayette Square for anyone driving across South City.

### Bevo Mill Businesses & Neighborhood Guide | St Louis Near Me Directory
Bevo Mill, St. Louis
Bevo Mill serves as one of South St. Louis’s most architecturally iconic and immigrant-shaped neighborhoods — named for August A. Busch Sr.’s 1917 Dutch-style windmill at Gravois and Morgan Ford, anchored by the St. Louis City Landmark Bevo Mill (now Das Bevo), the Bevo Community Improvement District, Long Middle School (1924), and Oak Hill Elementary (1908) — offering biergartens, restaurants, contractors, event venues, wholesale suppliers, and Bosnian-heritage food businesses across the Gravois corridor.
Bevo Mill is one of St. Louis’s 79 official neighborhoods, located in South St. Louis at 38.5816° N, 90.2672° W . Its boundaries run north along Chippewa Street , south along Holly Hills Boulevard , west along Christy Boulevard and South Kingshighway Boulevard , and east along Leona Street and the Missouri Pacific Railroad tracks . The neighborhood is bordered by Tower Grove South and Southampton to the north, Dutchtown to the east, Mount Pleasant and Boulevard Heights to the southeast, Princeton Heights and Holly Hills to the south, and North Hampton to the west. The 2020 census recorded the neighborhood’s population at 11,941, with a racial composition of 58.3% White, 20.6% Black, 4.8% Asian, 9.9% Two or More Races, 5.7% Some Other Race, 0.6% Native American, and 11.6% of Hispanic or Latino origin. The heart of the neighborhood is the three-way intersection of Gravois Avenue, Morgan Ford Road, and Delor Street — widely considered one of the most architecturally distinctive intersections in the entire city.
The land that became Bevo Mill remained largely rural until the discovery of clay deposits in the 1830s spurred industrial development. The largest pre-1830s landowner was the Christy family , whose mansion still stands as a nursing home at Alfred and Taft. Gravois Avenue — the neighborhood’s main artery — originated as a Native American trail to a salt spring and later served as the public road to Fenton and its ferry; by 1914, the state-maintained portion outside the city limits became the first concrete highway in Missouri . The arrival of clay furnaces, brick plants, and the Oak Hill rail line (which connected Missouri Pacific’s mainline in Mill Creek Valley with its Iron Mountain Railroad along the Mississippi in Old Carondelet) drew waves of German immigrant clay mine and factory workers who built the neighborhood’s characteristic single-family homes and apartment buildings in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.
The defining act in Bevo Mill’s history occurred in 1916–1917 , when August A. Busch Sr. , head of Anheuser-Busch, commissioned architects Klipstein and Rathmann (the same firm that designed the Busch family stables — today’s “Bauernhof” at Grant’s Farm) to design a Tudor Revival / Flemish-style restaurant and beer garden at the strategic halfway point between the Soulard Anheuser-Busch brewery and the Busch family home at what is now Grant’s Farm . Busch personally toured Holland for a year in advance of construction, studying authentic Dutch windmills. The structure was completed by Grone Construction (owned by Louis Henry Grone, whose cousins ran H. Grone Brewery) at the then-incredible cost of $250,000 . The 60-foot windmill originally had wooden blades propelled by wind, which were replaced with aluminum blades after wind damage in 1954 and are now electronically operated. The exterior is finished in stones — of all colors, shapes, and textures — personally gathered by Busch from his Grant’s Farm property and set in stucco. The mill was named for “Bevo,” Anheuser-Busch’s non-alcoholic malt beverage introduced ahead of Prohibition (the name derives from pivo , the Bohemian/Slavic word for beer). The Bevo Mill is one of three Busch family “prohibition houses,” the others being the Stork Inn on Virginia Avenue and the Feasting Fox at Grand and Meramec.
Inside, the mill houses a famous collection of porcelain tile murals of idyllic pastoral scenes (children, peacocks, country landscapes) manufactured in Germany around 1890 and purchased by Busch from Tony Faust — reportedly for $50,000 — after Faust’s downtown restaurant closed in 1916. The grand dining room features wooden ceiling beams, vaulted archways ending in stone-carved gnomes, and a triple stone fireplace. The octagonal Mill Room was used as Busch’s private dining room. Following German and Dutch tradition, a pair of storks were mounted on top of the chimney to ensure good luck. The lower level operated famously as a speakeasy during Prohibition . The Bevo Mill was designated a St. Louis City Landmark in 1971 , operated under its original name until its closure in 2009, and reopened in 2017 as Das Bevo after a $1.5 million-plus renovation by Pat and Carol Schuchard , who restored the windmill to operation and reactivated the building as a biergarten, event venue, and historic destination.
Bevo Mill’s most consequential modern chapter began in the early 1990s , when waves of Bosnian and Croatian immigrants fleeing the Bosnian War settled along the Gravois corridor — transforming a neighborhood once known for crime into one of the most demographically dynamic pockets in the city. The St. Louis metro area is now home to an estimated 70,000 Bosnians , the largest Bosnian population in the United States. The community established bakeries (including Sana Bakery for fresh-daily Bosnian bread, or kruh ), cafes, taverns, nightclubs, restaurants, neighborhood grocers, and butcher shops. The 1990–2000 census reflected this transformation with a rare 5% population gain (to 13,319) — one of the only St. Louis neighborhoods to grow during that decade. The Sebilj fountain in front of the Mill, a gift from Sarajevo, anchors the neighborhood’s Bosnian identity. The Bevo Community Improvement District and Better Bevo Now Neighborhood Association work alongside the City of St. Louis on the Bevo Great Streets project for traffic calming, streetscape enhancements, and placemaking along Gravois. In the years since, Vietnamese-owned restaurants and Latino-owned markets and taquerias have opened alongside the Bosnian and Croatian storefronts, so Gravois today reads less like a single-immigrant-group corridor than a genuinely international one — a different story from neighboring Dutchtown’s immigrant history a few blocks east.
The neighborhood is served by St. Louis Public Schools. Long Middle School (6th–8th grade), opened in 1924 and designed by district architect Rockwell M. Milligan , also operates as one of the district’s “Community Education Full Service Schools” offering adult classes in foreign languages, computers, fitness, and GED completion. Oak Hill Elementary School (Preschool–5th grade), designed by famed St. Louis school architect William B. Ittner , opened in 1908. Woerner Elementary School (Kindergarten–5th grade) also serves neighborhood families. Two large cemeteries occupy significant portions of the neighborhood, and large industrial parcels along the eastern edge remain in operation today. The Bevo Bazaaro community yard sale , the Bevo Farmer’s Market at Gravois and Morgan Ford, and the annual Bevo Mill Oktoberfest remain key community gatherings. South of Gravois, Joseph R. Leisure Park and Christy Park (bisected by Christy Boulevard) provide green space and access to the River des Peres Greenway’s 9 miles of paved trails .
Image: The Bevo Mill at 4749 Gravois Avenue — the Tudor Revival / Flemish-style restaurant and 60-foot windmill commissioned by August A. Busch Sr. in 1916, designed by architects Klipstein and Rathmann, completed in 1917 for $250,000, and designated a St. Louis City Landmark in 1971 — Wikimedia Commons , CC BY-SA

Bevo Mill gets the standard South St. Louis climate — humid summers, cold winters, and an active spring storm season — and the Das Bevo Biergarten and the Bevo Farmer’s Market draw the heaviest outdoor crowds from spring through fall.

## Bevo Mill Businesses & Neighborhood Guide | St Louis Near Me Directory

 Bevo Mill, St. Louis

Bevo Mill serves as one of South St. Louis’s most architecturally iconic and immigrant-shaped neighborhoods — named for August A. Busch Sr.’s 1917 Dutch-style windmill at Gravois and Morgan Ford, anchored by the St. Louis City Landmark Bevo Mill (now Das Bevo), the Bevo Community Improvement District, Long Middle School (1924), and Oak Hill Elementary (1908) — offering biergartens, restaurants, contractors, event venues, wholesale suppliers, and Bosnian-heritage food businesses across the Gravois corridor.

Bevo Mill is one of St. Louis’s 79 official neighborhoods, located in South St. Louis at **38.5816° N, 90.2672° W**. Its boundaries run north along **Chippewa Street**, south along **Holly Hills Boulevard**, west along **Christy Boulevard and South Kingshighway Boulevard**, and east along **Leona Street and the Missouri Pacific Railroad tracks**. The neighborhood is bordered by **Tower Grove South** and **Southampton** to the north, **Dutchtown** to the east, **Mount Pleasant** and **Boulevard Heights** to the southeast, **Princeton Heights** and **Holly Hills** to the south, and **North Hampton** to the west. The 2020 census recorded the neighborhood’s population at 11,941, with a racial composition of 58.3% White, 20.6% Black, 4.8% Asian, 9.9% Two or More Races, 5.7% Some Other Race, 0.6% Native American, and 11.6% of Hispanic or Latino origin. The heart of the neighborhood is the three-way intersection of **Gravois Avenue, Morgan Ford Road, and Delor Street** — widely considered one of the most architecturally distinctive intersections in the entire city.

The land that became Bevo Mill remained largely rural until the **discovery of clay deposits in the 1830s** spurred industrial development. The largest pre-1830s landowner was the **Christy family**, whose mansion still stands as a nursing home at Alfred and Taft. **Gravois Avenue** — the neighborhood’s main artery — originated as a **Native American trail to a salt spring** and later served as the public road to Fenton and its ferry; by 1914, the state-maintained portion outside the city limits became the **first concrete highway in Missouri**. The arrival of clay furnaces, brick plants, and the **Oak Hill rail line** (which connected Missouri Pacific’s mainline in Mill Creek Valley with its Iron Mountain Railroad along the Mississippi in Old Carondelet) drew waves of **German immigrant clay mine and factory workers** who built the neighborhood’s characteristic single-family homes and apartment buildings in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.

The defining act in Bevo Mill’s history occurred in **1916–1917**, when **August A. Busch Sr.**, head of Anheuser-Busch, commissioned architects **Klipstein and Rathmann** (the same firm that designed the Busch family stables — today’s “Bauernhof” at Grant’s Farm) to design a Tudor Revival / Flemish-style restaurant and beer garden at the strategic halfway point between the **Soulard Anheuser-Busch brewery and the Busch family home at what is now Grant’s Farm**. Busch personally toured Holland for a year in advance of construction, studying authentic Dutch windmills. The structure was completed by **Grone Construction** (owned by Louis Henry Grone, whose cousins ran H. Grone Brewery) at the then-incredible cost of **$250,000**. The **60-foot windmill** originally had wooden blades propelled by wind, which were replaced with aluminum blades after wind damage in **1954** and are now electronically operated. The exterior is finished in stones — of all colors, shapes, and textures — personally gathered by Busch from his Grant’s Farm property and set in stucco. The mill was named for **“Bevo,”** Anheuser-Busch’s non-alcoholic malt beverage introduced ahead of Prohibition (the name derives from *pivo*, the Bohemian/Slavic word for beer). The Bevo Mill is one of **three Busch family “prohibition houses,”** the others being the Stork Inn on Virginia Avenue and the Feasting Fox at Grand and Meramec.

Inside, the mill houses a famous collection of **porcelain tile murals** of idyllic pastoral scenes (children, peacocks, country landscapes) manufactured in Germany around 1890 and purchased by Busch from Tony Faust — reportedly for $50,000 — after Faust’s downtown restaurant closed in 1916. The grand dining room features wooden ceiling beams, vaulted archways ending in stone-carved gnomes, and a triple stone fireplace. The octagonal Mill Room was used as Busch’s private dining room. Following German and Dutch tradition, a pair of **storks were mounted on top of the chimney** to ensure good luck. The lower level operated famously as a **speakeasy during Prohibition**. The Bevo Mill was designated a **St. Louis City Landmark in 1971**, operated under its original name until its closure in 2009, and reopened in 2017 as **Das Bevo** after a $1.5 million-plus renovation by **Pat and Carol Schuchard**, who restored the windmill to operation and reactivated the building as a biergarten, event venue, and historic destination.

Bevo Mill’s most consequential modern chapter began in the **early 1990s**, when waves of **Bosnian and Croatian immigrants fleeing the Bosnian War** settled along the Gravois corridor — transforming a neighborhood once known for crime into one of the most demographically dynamic pockets in the city. The St. Louis metro area is now home to an estimated **70,000 Bosnians**, the largest Bosnian population in the United States. The community established bakeries (including **Sana Bakery** for fresh-daily Bosnian bread, or *kruh*), cafes, taverns, nightclubs, restaurants, neighborhood grocers, and butcher shops. The 1990–2000 census reflected this transformation with a **rare 5% population gain** (to 13,319) — one of the only St. Louis neighborhoods to grow during that decade. The **Sebilj fountain** in front of the Mill, a gift from Sarajevo, anchors the neighborhood’s Bosnian identity. The **Bevo Community Improvement District** and **Better Bevo Now Neighborhood Association** work alongside the City of St. Louis on the Bevo Great Streets project for traffic calming, streetscape enhancements, and placemaking along Gravois.

The neighborhood is served by St. Louis Public Schools. **Long Middle School** (6th–8th grade), opened in 1924 and designed by district architect **Rockwell M. Milligan**, also operates as one of the district’s “Community Education Full Service Schools” offering adult classes in foreign languages, computers, fitness, and GED completion. **Oak Hill Elementary School** (Preschool–5th grade), designed by famed St. Louis school architect **William B. Ittner**, opened in 1908. **Woerner Elementary School** (Kindergarten–5th grade) also serves neighborhood families. Two large cemeteries occupy significant portions of the neighborhood, and large industrial parcels along the eastern edge remain in operation today. The **Bevo Bazaaro community yard sale**, the **Bevo Farmer’s Market** at Gravois and Morgan Ford, and the annual **Bevo Mill Oktoberfest** remain key community gatherings. South of Gravois, **Joseph R. Leisure Park** and **Christy Park** (bisected by Christy Boulevard) provide green space and access to the **River des Peres Greenway’s 9 miles of paved trails**.

Image: The Bevo Mill at 4749 Gravois Avenue — the Tudor Revival / Flemish-style restaurant and 60-foot windmill commissioned by August A. Busch Sr. in 1916, designed by architects Klipstein and Rathmann, completed in 1917 for $250,000, and designated a St. Louis City Landmark in 1971 — Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA

Bevo Mill sits on the gently rolling South City terrain at 38.5816° N, with the Gravois Avenue corridor — the original Native American salt-spring trail and Missouri’s first concrete highway — running diagonally through its center. The neighborhood experiences St. Louis’s full humid continental climate: hot, humid summers with frequent 90°F days, cold winters with regular freezing temperatures, and a notably active spring severe weather season including real tornado corridor exposure. Peak outdoor activity falls during spring and fall, when the Das Bevo Biergarten, the Bevo Farmer’s Market at Gravois and Morgan Ford, Joseph R. Leisure Park, Christy Park, the River des Peres Greenway, the Bevo Bazaaro community yard sale, and the Bevo Mill Oktoberfest draw the heaviest neighborhood and visitor use. Cool seasons drive intense indoor activity at Das Bevo’s Historic Bierhall and Underground speakeasy, The Little Bevo on Morgan Ford, Bevo Caffe Lounge, Vegan Deli and Butcher, Himalayan Yeti just west, Sana Bakery, and the Bosnian and Croatian cafes lining Gravois. 

Winter shifts commerce indoors to the Long Middle School community education programs, the Carondelet branch library systems to the south, and the suburban retail centers along Gravois and South Kingshighway. The neighborhood’s 1880s–1930s brick housing stock, the Bevo Mill itself, and the surrounding Long Middle School (1924) and Oak Hill Elementary (1908) buildings have weathered more than a century of Missouri climate with the durability typical of South City’s working-class German-immigrant building tradition.

### Botanical Heights Businesses & Neighborhood Guide | St Louis Near Me Directory
Botanical Heights, St. Louis
Botanical Heights is a revitalized near-south St. Louis neighborhood — once known as McRee Town — that sits just north of the Missouri Botanical Garden, with Tower Grove Avenue running through it as a busy commercial spine of bakeries, fitness studios, and home-services companies.
Tucked into the near-south side of the City of St. Louis, Botanical Heights is a small but busy neighborhood of roughly four-tenths of a square mile. It is bounded by Chouteau Avenue to the north, Interstate 44 to the south, 39th Street to the east, and Vandeventer Avenue to the west. Tower Grove Avenue threads north to south through the heart of the neighborhood and carries much of its commercial life, while interior and edge streets such as McRee Avenue, Park Avenue, Blaine Avenue, and Central Industrial Drive fill in the rest.
For most of the twentieth century this place was called McRee Town . Built in the early 1900s, it began as a mixed-use district where small manufacturing and distribution businesses stood alongside rows of housing. The neighborhood thrived until the late 1960s, when the construction of Interstate 44 carved through the area and physically split it from the Shaw neighborhood to the south. That highway is still the southern edge of Botanical Heights today.
Through the later decades of the century, McRee Town slid into decline. Rising vacancy, absentee landlords, and crime took hold, and by 2000 roughly 56 percent of the area’s structures were vacant or deteriorated. The City of St. Louis described the neighborhood at its low point in stark terms, and many of its original residents — a community that by the 2000 Census was largely Black and heavily renter-occupied — were living amid serious disinvestment.
The turning point came through the Garden District Commission . In 1998, Jonathan Kleinbard founded this independent nonprofit, whose board drew from residents and institutions near the Missouri Botanical Garden, to steer a planned renovation. In 2000 the City adopted a redevelopment plan, and in 2004 and 2005 one of the most extensive land-clearance efforts seen in St. Louis in decades cleared six blocks of McRee Town. It was during this period that the neighborhood was rebranded Botanical Heights , taking its new name from the world-famous garden just to the south.
On the cleared blocks, McBride & Sons built roughly 143 to 150 new single-family homes and townhomes, priced from about $155,000 to $400,000 and all sold by 2007. Beginning around 2010, the developer UIC added contemporary modern infill housing west of Thurman Avenue, and adaptive-reuse projects followed — among them Rockwell Beer Co. , which opened in a former electrical-supply building on Vandeventer, and the MaTovu Jewish Neighborhood Center , which reopened in a rehabbed 1920s building in 2018. City Garden Montessori School also put down roots here, moving to Tower Grove Avenue in 2012.
The transformation has not been without debate. The Garden’s role in clearing the original housing stock has been criticized as gentrification, and that history is part of an honest picture of the neighborhood. What stands today is a centrally located, largely rebuilt community whose population has grown modestly since 2010 and whose corridors now host an eclectic mix of bakeries, a brewery, fitness and recording studios, home-services companies, and small makers. The blocks of the former McRee Town redevelopment, anchored by Tower Grove Avenue and shadowed by the Missouri Botanical Garden, are the setting for the businesses featured in this guide.
Like the rest of St. Louis, Botanical Heights sees hot, humid summers, a spring severe-weather season, and cold but rarely extreme winters — typical of the region’s humid subtropical climate.
Botanical Heights is small — about four-tenths of a square mile — and mostly residential, but its Tower Grove Avenue corridor is real: a landmark bakery, a boutique fitness studio, and the headquarters of one of the city’s largest home-services companies all sit within a few blocks of each other, alongside a dispensary, a recording studio, a hair-braiding salon, and a members’ dog park on the side streets. Only one of the businesses on this page, Mediplex Healthcare Professionals, is a member of St Louis Near Me Directory — the rest are simply the neighborhood’s own, verified against live Google data. Where the list runs short on variety, this guide adds one of the best options in Forest Park Southeast (The Grove), clearly labeled by its real neighborhood and distance, because a two-minute walk to The Grove is a fact worth knowing, not something to hide.
A street scene in Botanical Heights. Photo: “Botanical Heights (6)” by Paul Sableman, licensed under CC BY 2.0 via Wikimedia Commons.

### Frequently Asked Questions 
Q. Is the Missouri Botanical Garden worth it? 
A. Yes — it’s one of the oldest botanical gardens in the country and home to the landmark Climatron conservatory, sitting immediately south of Botanical Heights. The neighborhood itself was renamed in the Garden’s honor during its 2000s redevelopment. This guide focuses on Botanical Heights’ own businesses rather than Garden ticketing, but the shared border alone makes a visit convenient for anyone in the area.

Q. What day is the Missouri Botanical Garden free? 
A. Free-admission days are set directly by the Missouri Botanical Garden and can change, so check the Garden’s own site for the current schedule rather than relying on a neighborhood guide. What’s certain here: the Garden sits immediately on Botanical Heights’ southern border, close enough that residents can walk over, and the neighborhood was renamed in its honor.

Q. What is the Missouri Botanical Garden in St. Louis most famous for? 
A. The Missouri Botanical Garden is best known as one of the oldest botanical gardens in the country and as home to the Climatron, its landmark geodesic-domed conservatory. It sits directly south of Botanical Heights, and the neighborhood — rebuilt in the 2000s from the former McRee Town — was renamed in the Garden’s honor because of that shared border.

Q. How much does it cost to visit the Missouri Botanical Garden? 
A. Admission pricing is set by the Missouri Botanical Garden itself and changes over time, so this neighborhood guide won’t guess at a dollar figure — check the Garden’s site for current rates. What this guide can confirm is that the Garden sits directly on Botanical Heights’ southern border, close enough that many residents can walk to the entrance.

Q. What defines the Botanical Heights neighborhood? 
A. Botanical Heights is a small, revitalized near-south St. Louis neighborhood — formerly McRee Town — bounded by Chouteau Avenue, Interstate 44, 39th Street, and Vandeventer Avenue, with Tower Grove Avenue as its commercial spine. Rebuilt after a major 2004-2005 redevelopment led by the Garden District Commission, it sits just north of the Missouri Botanical Garden, which inspired its current name.

### Boulevard Heights Businesses & Neighborhood Guide | St Louis Near Me Directory
Boulevard Heights, St. Louis
Boulevard Heights is one of the southernmost neighborhoods in the City of St. Louis — a quiet, residential pocket of brick homes near the city limits, bordered by Carondelet Park to the north and threaded by the Gravois, Loughborough, and Morganford corridors that hold its shops, restaurants, and local services.
Boulevard Heights sits at the far-south end of St. Louis, hard against the southern city limits. It is bounded by Gravois Avenue on the west, Holly Hills Boulevard and Carondelet Park on the north, South Grand Avenue and I-55 on the east, and the city limits on the south. Covering roughly 1.5 square miles, it is a compact, almost entirely residential neighborhood whose commercial life clusters along its edges rather than its interior streets.
The land here carries an old name: Morganford . The portion east of Morganford Road was once part of the Carondelet Commons — the shared common-field lands of the village of Carondelet, which the City of St. Louis annexed in 1870. The broad, parkway-style streets along the north edge, including Holly Hills Boulevard, echo the “Heights and Boulevard” naming style that ran through many early-twentieth-century south-side subdivisions.
Americans and German immigrants began subdividing the area into residential lots in the early 1870s. That German heritage — shared across much of the south side — shows up in the neighborhood’s church history. St. Lucas Evangelical Lutheran Church , founded in 1905 at 7100 Morganford Road, was described as the first Slovak Lutheran church west of the Mississippi, anchoring a German and Slovak story that still threads through the area.
Though some building went up along Grand Avenue before 1910, most of Boulevard Heights was built out after World War II . That timing gave the neighborhood its defining look: a dense, steady fabric of mid-century St. Louis brick homes on quiet residential blocks. As one of the city’s southernmost neighborhoods, it meets the city limits and the River Des Peres corridor at the edge of St. Louis.
Parks frame the neighborhood on nearly every side. Carondelet Park — the city’s third-largest park, purchased in 1875, with its lakes and historic boathouse — borders Boulevard Heights to the north. Willmore Park , donated in 1947 and sitting just west across the River Des Peres, adds lakes, a paved loop, and an accessible playground. Christy Park brings recreational fields inside the area, and the regional River Des Peres Greenway follows the channel along the city’s southern edge.
Day-to-day commerce gathers on the corridors. Gravois Avenue runs the west edge, the Loughborough and Morganford pockets hold restaurants, dental and real-estate offices, and neighborhood shops, while interior and south-side streets such as Robert, Blow, Tennessee, and Eugene host trades and small studios. Just to the north sits the historic Bevo Mill landmark in the adjacent Bevo Mill neighborhood.
Today Boulevard Heights remains what its post-war buildout made it: a settled, family-oriented neighborhood of brick homes and tidy blocks, close to big parks and easy interstate access, with a working main-street life spread along its bordering avenues. The ten businesses below — ranked by Google rating — represent some of the most established and best-reviewed local options in and around the neighborhood.
The boathouse at Carondelet Park, which borders Boulevard Heights to the north. Photo: “Boathouse at Carondelet Park” by DiamondRemley39, licensed under CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons.

Boulevard Heights runs the full range of St. Louis’s humid subtropical climate — hot, sticky summers, cold winters with real snow, and the spring storms that come with sitting inside Tornado Alley — and its sturdy post-war brick homes have shrugged off that swing of seasons for eighty years running.
Walk any block here and the pattern repeats itself: a story-and-a-half brick bungalow or a boxy brick four-square, one after another, house after house — the unmistakable fingerprint of a neighborhood built out fast in the years right after World War II rather than assembled piecemeal over a century like the older parts of the city.

### Frequently Asked Questions 
Q. What is Boulevard Heights known for? 
A. Boulevard Heights is known for its dense fabric of post-WWII St. Louis brick homes on quiet residential blocks, its position against the city’s southern limits, and Carondelet Park — the city’s third-largest park, with lakes and a historic boathouse — bordering it to the north. Its commercial life runs along the Gravois, Loughborough, and Morganford corridors rather than the interior streets.

Q. Where is the Boulevard Heights neighborhood in St. Louis? 
A. Boulevard Heights sits at the far-south end of the City of St. Louis, hard against the southern city limits. It is bounded by Gravois Avenue on the west, Holly Hills Boulevard and Carondelet Park on the north, South Grand Avenue and I-55 on the east, and the city limits on the south, covering roughly 1.5 square miles.

Q. How does St Louis Near Me Directory help Boulevard Heights businesses? 
A. St Louis Near Me Directory is a hyper-local, SEO-optimized directory that helps Boulevard Heights businesses get found by nearby customers. We use plain-English search marketing to expand a Google Business Profile rather than replace it, with no competitor ads and no long-term contracts, plus a 7-day free trial. Businesses can get started by joining the directory.

Q. What types of businesses are most common in Boulevard Heights? 
A. The businesses on this page reflect the neighborhood’s corridor-based commercial pattern: dental and medical offices, restaurants, pet care, and home-service trades cluster along Gravois, Loughborough, and Morganford, while interior streets like Robert, Blow, Tennessee, and Eugene host smaller studios and garages — interior design, cleaning services, martial arts instruction, and auto repair among them.

Q. What kinds of dining, retail, and recreation options are available in Boulevard Heights? 
A. For dining, The Gyro Company on Gravois Avenue is a busy favorite for gyros and Greek plates, The Haven Bistro on Morganford serves casual American fare, and 1 Stop Sushi X offers dine-in, takeout, and delivery. Retail is limited since Boulevard Heights is mostly residential. For recreation, Carondelet Park borders the neighborhood to the north and Willmore Park adds a paved loop and playground to the west.

Q. Are there neighborhood landmarks, parks, and historic sites in Boulevard Heights? 
A. Yes. Carondelet Park, the city’s third-largest park with lakes and a historic boathouse, borders the neighborhood to the north, and Willmore Park, donated in 1947, sits just west with a paved loop and accessible playground. Historically, St. Lucas Evangelical Lutheran Church, founded in 1905 at 7100 Morganford Road, is described as the first Slovak Lutheran church west of the Mississippi.

Q. What is it like to live in Boulevard Heights? 
A. Boulevard Heights is a settled, family-oriented neighborhood of dense post-WWII brick homes on quiet blocks at the far-south edge of the city, with big parks nearby and easy interstate access. That residential character supports steady neighborhood-serving businesses — dentists, restaurants, pet care, and home-service trades — along its Loughborough, Morganford, and Gravois corridors.

Q. How do residents and visitors get around Boulevard Heights? 
A. The neighborhood is easy to reach by car, with Gravois Avenue running its west edge and I-55 bordering it to the east for quick interstate access. Loughborough and Morganford Road carry local traffic to the neighborhood’s restaurants, dental offices, and shops, and the regional River Des Peres Greenway offers a walking and biking route along the city’s southern edge.

Q. What defines the Boulevard Heights neighborhood? 
A. Boulevard Heights is one of the southernmost neighborhoods in the City of St. Louis, sitting against the southern city limits. It is a quiet, almost entirely residential area defined by its dense fabric of post-WWII St. Louis brick homes, bordered by Carondelet Park on the north and bounded by Gravois Avenue, Holly Hills Boulevard, South Grand Avenue, and I-55. Most of its commercial life runs along the Gravois, Loughborough, and Morganford corridors at its edges.

### Carondelet Businesses & Neighborhood Guide | St Louis Near Me Directory
Carondelet, St. Louis 
Carondelet is a historic river neighborhood on the far south side of St. Louis, founded as a French village in 1767 by Clément Delor de Treget — just three years after St. Louis itself. Long an independent town, it was annexed to the city in 1870 and remains one of St. Louis's oldest and most distinct neighborhoods, with a walkable business stretch along South Broadway.
The village carried several names before this one — Delor's Village, then Catalan's Prairie, then Louisbourg — before settling on Carondelet, chosen to flatter Baron de Carondelet, the Spanish colonial governor, in exchange for a land commission. French and then German immigrants built it up through the 1800s as a riverfront, industrial town.
Carondelet earned a permanent place in American history in 1873, when Susan Blow opened the first continuous, publicly-funded kindergarten in the United States at the neighborhood's Des Peres School — a civic milestone the neighborhood still celebrates.
Carondelet exists because of the river. During the Civil War, shipyards along its riverfront — most famously James Eads’s ironworks — built Union ironclad gunboats, part of the fleet that helped secure the Mississippi. One of those City-class ironclads, the USS Carondelet, was named for the neighborhood that built it, a piece of the neighborhood’s industrial founding that still explains why its oldest blocks sit close to the water.
Carondelet is bounded by Eichelberger Street to the northeast, the River Des Peres to the southwest, the Mississippi River to the southeast, and Grand Boulevard and Interstate 55 to the northwest (ZIP 63111). Its southern edge wraps around Carondelet Park, one of the largest and oldest parks in the city.
Today's business life clusters along South Broadway, Ivory Avenue, and the blocks near Michigan Avenue — a burger joint ranked among the city's best, a nationally-known brewery, a soul-food diner, authentic Mexican, and neighborhood coffee shops. Those local spots are featured below.
Carondelet today is mostly what it has been for generations — a working, family-rooted neighborhood, not a rebranded one. Its narrow lots and close-set housing trace back to the French and German riverfront town it was built as, and that history still shapes who lives here: longtime residents, younger families drawn to affordable historic housing near a genuine city park, and a slowly growing run of independent restaurants and shops filling in South Broadway.
The Carondelet neighborhood, St. Louis. 
Carondelet shares St. Louis’s humid subtropical climate — warm, sometimes stormy summers and cold but rarely brutal winters.

### Frequently Asked Questions
Q. What does carondelet mean in English? 
A. Carondelet isn’t an English word — it’s a surname. St. Louis’s Carondelet neighborhood was renamed in the 1790s to honor Baron de Carondelet, the Spanish colonial governor of Louisiana, after being called Delor’s Village, then Catalan’s Prairie, then Louisbourg. Founder Clément Delor de Treget made the change to help secure an official land commission.

Q. What defines the Carondelet neighborhood? 
A. Carondelet is a historic river neighborhood on St. Louis’s far south side (ZIP 63111), founded as an independent French village in 1767 and annexed to the city in 1870 — older than the city it eventually joined. It’s bounded by Eichelberger Street, the River Des Peres, the Mississippi River, and Grand Boulevard/Interstate 55, and wraps around Carondelet Park.

Q. How does St Louis Near Me Directory help Carondelet businesses? 
A. St Louis Near Me Directory builds hyper-local, SEO-optimized pages like this Carondelet guide so nearby customers can find neighborhood businesses when they search. Simple Gold, Platinum, and Diamond plans come with a 7-day free trial, no long-term contracts, and no competitor ads running on your listing — the goal is expanding your existing Google Business Profile, not replacing it.

Q. What types of businesses are most common in Carondelet? 
A. Carondelet’s business mix leans toward food and drink — sandwich shops, a Mexican restaurant, a soul-food diner, coffeehouses, a neighborhood bar, and Perennial Artisan Ales, one of St. Louis’s best-known craft breweries. The corridor also includes creative and service businesses like a recording studio and a retirement community, reflecting the neighborhood’s working, riverfront roots.

Q. What kinds of dining, retail, and recreation options are available in Carondelet? 
A. Dining runs from Stacked STL’s build-your-own burgers and Big Mouth Sandwich Co.’s sandwiches to Doña Gloria’s homestyle Mexican food and Your Place Diner’s soul food, plus coffee at Speakeasy Café and Piper’s Tea & Coffee. For recreation, Carondelet Park anchors the neighborhood’s southern edge with lakes, trails, and the historic Boathouse.

Q. Are there neighborhood landmarks, parks, and historic sites in Carondelet? 
A. Yes. Carondelet Park, one of St. Louis’s largest and oldest public parks, has lakes, trails, the Boathouse, and the historic Lyle House. The neighborhood’s Des Peres School is where Susan Blow opened the first continuous, publicly-funded kindergarten in the United States in 1873, and its riverfront once held the Civil War-era shipyards that built Union ironclad gunboats.

Q. What is it like to live in Carondelet? 
A. Carondelet is a walkable, working-class-rooted neighborhood built around a South Broadway business stretch of restaurants, a brewery, and coffee shops, with a retirement community nearby for seniors. Its housing and street grid date to its 19th-century French and German settlement, and Carondelet Park gives residents lakes and trails within walking distance of home.

Q. How do residents and visitors get around Carondelet? 
A. Interstate 55 and Grand Boulevard form Carondelet’s northwest edge, giving quick access to and from downtown St. Louis and the rest of the metro. Locally, the neighborhood is walkable along South Broadway, Ivory Avenue, and Michigan Avenue, where its restaurants, brewery, and cafés cluster within a few blocks of each other.

### Carr Square Businesses & Neighborhood Guide | St Louis Near Me Directory
Carr Square, St. Louis
Carr Square serves as a redevelopment-driven Near North Side neighborhood positioned between the new NGA West campus and the Washington Avenue / Locust Street creative office corridor — offering data center consulting, creative coworking, legal process serving, digital marketing, and historic mixed-use office space for residents, professionals, and growing tech and marketing firms across the metro.
Carr Square sits on the Near North Side of St. Louis at 38.6373° N, 90.2021° W , occupying the zip code 63106 just north of downtown. The 2020 Census recorded a 94.9% Black population with 2.1% White, 2.0% two-or-more races, and a small Hispanic/Latino presence. The neighborhood’s official boundaries are Cass Avenue on the north, Carr Street on the south, North Tucker Boulevard / North 13th Street on the east, and North Jefferson Avenue on the west. Its immediate neighbors are St. Louis Place to the north, Columbus Square to the east, Downtown West to the south, and JeffVanderLou to the west — placing Carr Square within a 10-minute walk of the Gateway Arch grounds, the Edward Jones Dome, and the new National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency (NGA) West campus just north on Cass.
Carr Square’s history is one of successive immigrant waves and 20th-century housing experiments. German Protestants first inhabited the area in the early 19th century, settling around the original Carr Square itself. Around 1842, a group of Irish immigrants from County Kerry settled to the northeast near 18th Street and O’Fallon, creating the legendary “ Kerry Patch ” — a tight cluster of one-room shacks built under squatter’s rights on land owned by the sympathetic Irish-American Mullanphy family , who refused to displace their countrymen. The Kerry Patch Irish quickly became St. Louis’s police, firemen, lawyers, doctors, editors, and political fixtures, leaving a cultural mark on the city that long outlasted the shacks. After 1870, Polish immigrants supplanted the Irish in Kerry Patch, founding St. Stanislaus Kostka Parish in 1878 — the church building completed in 1880 still stands on the National Register of Historic Places and as a St. Louis City Landmark.
By the 1880s, German Protestants began migrating outward and Orthodox Jews succeeded them in Carr Square. By 1920, the neighborhood had taken on a polyglot character of Russian and Balkan immigrants. The Depression and World War II then brought a major wave of African-American migration from the rural South into the central city — arrivals who often found themselves living in 19th-century tenement buildings subdivided into smaller and smaller units, in conditions so dense that an official 1947 city survey found that 33,000 homes in St. Louis still had communal toilets, and Carr Square earned the grim nickname “ the lung block ” for its tuberculosis rates.
It was against this backdrop that Carr Square and adjacent Columbus Square became the most consequential testing grounds for public housing in American history. Carr Square Village , completed in 1942 under the New Deal’s Housing Act of 1937, was the first generation of St. Louis public housing — a low-rise development for African-American families that opened as a sibling project to the racially segregated Clinton-Peabody for white families on the South Side. In 1954, just south of Cass Avenue and bounded by Jefferson, 20th Street, and Carr Street, the federal government opened Pruitt-Igoe — 33 eleven-story modernist towers designed by Minoru Yamasaki (later the architect of the original World Trade Center) on a 57-acre site, originally intended to be segregated as the Wendell O. Pruitt Homes (for African-Americans) and the William Igoe Apartments (for whites). When the Supreme Court’s Brown v. Board ruling forced integration, the project opened to nearly all Black tenants. Vaughn Family Apartments went up just to the east during the same era. By the 1970s, Pruitt-Igoe’s televised demolition (beginning March 16, 1972) became internationally known as “the day Modern architecture died,” and Carr Square Village pivoted to become one of the first public housing projects in the country to convert to tenant management .
Today, the 57-acre Pruitt-Igoe site is largely a wooded fenced lot whose future is being shaped by the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency (NGA) West campus rising just north on Cass Avenue. The NGA project — a federal intelligence facility expected to bring thousands of jobs and billions of dollars in investment to Carr Square and the surrounding Near North Side — is the single largest economic catalyst the neighborhood has seen in over a century, and Ponce Health Sciences University has announced plans for an $80 million medical school facility on the former Pruitt-Igoe ground. Around the site today, Preservation Square Apartments and Townhomes provides nearly 700 new rental units, while the older Murphy Park, O’Fallon Place, and Vaughn redevelopments continue to stabilize the residential base.
Carr Square’s civic infrastructure includes three city parks — De Soto Park (the largest, 17.38 acres at the south end of the former Pruitt-Igoe site, with a paved walking trail and soccer field), Murphy Park , and Loretta Hall Park — totaling more than 30 acres of green space with soccer fields, softball and baseball diamonds, full-court basketball, picnic facilities, and an asphalt walking trail. St. Stanislaus Kostka Church continues to anchor the neighborhood’s eastern edge as the last Polish parish in St. Louis, an independent lay-board-run congregation with a Polish Heritage Center on site. The neighborhood’s schools include the Gateway Schools complex (Gateway Elementary, Gateway Michael, and Gateway Middle on 20 acres of the former Pruitt-Igoe site, which opened in September 1995), Carr Lane Visual and Performing Arts Middle School , Jefferson Elementary , and the private Catholic Central Catholic St. Nicholas School .
Because Carr Square sits at the geographic hinge between downtown St. Louis, the NGA campus, and the redeveloping Washington Avenue / Locust Street office corridor, many of the businesses that serve its residents and professionals are located along these adjacent corridors — particularly the historic mixed-use buildings of Washington Avenue south of Cole Street and the Locust Central Business District just south of the neighborhood. The listings on this page reflect that practical reality, drawing from the broader service area that Carr Square residents and professionals actually use.
Image: Pruitt-Igoe housing complex, Carr Square, St. Louis — USGS aerial photograph, March 3, 1968 — Wikimedia Commons / U.S. Geological Survey, Public Domain

Carr Square sits in the dense Near North Side urban core, where the four-season Midwest climate shapes the rhythm of the neighborhood’s redeveloping commercial and residential blocks. Hot, humid summers with highs in the upper 80s°F drive the use of De Soto Park’s soccer fields and the outdoor programming at adjacent Columbus Square; cool springs and falls are the high seasons for NGA-area construction milestones and Washington Avenue office leasing; cold winters with periodic snow shift commerce indoors to the creative office spaces, coworking studios, and historic mixed-use buildings that line Washington Avenue and Locust Street just south of the neighborhood. The area’s flat topography between the Mississippi bluffs and the city’s street grid means it remains highly walkable and transit-accessible year-round, with multiple MetroBus connections and a quick MetroLink ride to downtown.

### Frequently Asked Questions 
Q. What defines the Carr Square neighborhood? 
A. Carr Square is a Near North Side St. Louis neighborhood bounded by Cass Avenue, Carr Street, Tucker Boulevard, and North Jefferson Avenue. Its defining story is 20th-century public housing — Carr Square Village opened in 1942 and the nearby Pruitt-Igoe towers rose in 1954 — and today it sits at the hinge between downtown, the new NGA West federal campus, and the Washington Avenue creative office corridor.

Q. How does St Louis Near Me Directory help Carr Square businesses? 
A. St Louis Near Me Directory builds a neighborhood-focused page tying a Carr Square business to local search signals around the NGA West campus, the Washington Avenue creative corridor, and the Near North Side redevelopment zone. Plans expand a business’s existing Google Business Profile rather than replace it, with plain-English service, no competitor ads, and no long-term contracts.

Q. What types of businesses are most common in Carr Square? 
A. A mix of creative coworking and event studios, legal process serving, digital marketing, and historic mixed-use office buildings along Washington Avenue and Locust Street, plus a small run of neighborhood retail — a corner grocery, an early-learning preschool, and a nearby nail studio. The neighborhood’s identity is shaped by proximity to the new NGA West campus and the Locust Central Business District just to the south.

Q. What kinds of dining, retail, and recreation options are available in Carr Square? 
A. Carr Square has no restaurants of its own — Carr Mini Mart on Carr Street covers daily grocery needs, and the closest sit-down option, Imo’s Pizza, sits just over the line in Downtown West on Delmar Boulevard. For recreation, three in-boundary city parks — De Soto Park, Murphy Park, and Loretta Hall Park — provide more than 30 acres of soccer fields, ball diamonds, and walking trails.

Q. Are there neighborhood landmarks, parks, and historic sites in Carr Square? 
A. Yes — St. Stanislaus Kostka Church, founded 1878 and on the National Register of Historic Places, anchors the neighborhood’s Polish immigrant history near the old “Kerry Patch.” The 57-acre former Pruitt-Igoe site, once the country’s most infamous public-housing project, is now partly the Gateway Schools complex, and De Soto Park, Murphy Park, and Loretta Hall Park together provide more than 30 acres of green space.

Q. What is it like to live in Carr Square? 
A. Carr Square is a neighborhood in transition: its 20th-century story was public housing, from 1942’s Carr Square Village to the demolished Pruitt-Igoe towers, and today redevelopments like Preservation Square provide nearly 700 rental units alongside Murphy Park, O’Fallon Place, and Vaughn. The arriving NGA West federal campus is the largest economic catalyst the neighborhood has seen in over a century.

Q. How do residents and visitors get around Carr Square? 
A. Carr Square’s flat, walkable Near North Side street grid gives immediate access to Interstates 44, 64, and 70, plus MetroLink and multiple MetroBus routes. The neighborhood is within a 10-minute walk of the Gateway Arch grounds, and Washington Avenue and Locust Street just to the south connect directly to downtown’s creative office corridor.

Q. How can residents and visitors explore more services around Carr Square? 
A. ### Central West End Businesses & Neighborhood Guide | St Louis Near Me Directory
Central West End, St. Louis
The Central West End serves as one of St. Louis’s premier mixed-use neighborhoods — anchored by the Cortex Innovation Community, the Washington University Medical Center, the Cathedral Basilica, and the historic gated mansions of Westmoreland and Portland Places — offering coworking and lab space, upscale grocery and fine dining, live music, specialty coffee, ice cream, salons and boutique retail, and contemporary art and design for residents, scientists, students, and professionals across the metro.
The Central West End sits at 38.6395° N, 90.2547° W across the 63108 and 63110 zip codes, just east of Forest Park. The neighborhood’s boundaries are Delmar Boulevard on the north, I-64 / US 40 on the south, North Vandeventer Avenue on the east, and Union Boulevard with the eastern edge of Forest Park on the west. Recognized by the American Planning Association as one of America’s Great Neighborhoods , the Central West End is consistently rated the most walkable neighborhood in St. Louis and one of the most architecturally distinguished urban districts in the Midwest.
The Central West End’s development is inseparable from Forest Park , established west of the city in 1876 as a 1,300-acre civic park. When St. Louis extended its western boundary past Forest Park in the 1880s, the area immediately north of the park became the preferred address for the city’s industrialists, brewers, and merchants — especially as St. Louis raced to become the host city for the 1904 Louisiana Purchase Exposition (World’s Fair). In 1887, civil engineer Julius Pitzman — the master planner of Forest Park itself — was retained by the Forest Park Improvement Association to plat what would become the neighborhood’s defining feature: the gated private streets of Westmoreland Place and Portland Place , modeled on Pitzman’s earlier work at Benton Place, Vandeventer Place, Kingsbury Place, and Washington Terrace.
By 1888, the two sister streets were laid out on the former Cabanne Dairy Farm, landscaped by Forest Park designer Maximillian G. Kern , and gated with sentinel gatehouses designed by some of St. Louis’s most prominent architects. Listed together on the National Register of Historic Places in 1974 as the Portland and Westmoreland Places Historic District , the two streets hold 94 mansions in Italian palazzo, French chateau, English country estate, Georgian Revival, Renaissance Revival, and Italianate styles. Residents over the decades included Charles Stix (founder of Stix, Baer & Fuller), Edward Faust (vice president of Anheuser-Busch), shoe magnate George Warren Brown, and contributors to the financing of Charles Lindbergh’s 1927 transatlantic flight. The two streets remain privately owned, gated, and governed by resident boards of trustees to this day — some of the very few World’s Fair-era private streets still operating in America.
The Central West End is equally defined by its literary and cultural legacy. The poet T. S. Eliot ’s family home stands on Locust Street; playwright Tennessee Williams grew up in the neighborhood; Beat writer William S. Burroughs ’s childhood home sits on Pershing Avenue (formerly Berlin Avenue); and novelist Kate Chopin wrote here. A.G. Edwards and Ralston Purina were both founded or led from Central West End addresses, and the neighborhood’s mansions hosted some of the planners of the 1904 World’s Fair itself. The 1959 St. Louis tornado damaged parts of the district, and insurance proceeds helped fund the gas-lit reinvention of the commercial blocks — giving rise to the Gaslight Square art-and-nightlife district that established the Central West End’s national reputation as an artistic incubator.
Dominating the neighborhood’s skyline is the Cathedral Basilica of Saint Louis (the “New Cathedral”), completed in 1914 at Lindell Boulevard and Newstead Avenue. Designed by the firm of Barnett, Haynes & Barnett in a striking Neo-Byzantine / Romanesque Revival style, the cathedral houses one of the largest mosaic installations in the Western Hemisphere — a 41.5 million-tessera interior completed over 76 years (1912 to 1988). Designated a basilica by Pope John Paul II in 1997, the Cathedral Basilica was honored with a papal visit in January 1999. Other neighborhood institutions include Saint Nicholas Greek Orthodox Church with its popular Labor Day festival, Rosati-Kain High School (the Archdiocesan girls’ preparatory school founded in 1911), and the historic Chase Park Plaza Hotel .
The modern Central West End is also defined by the Cortex Innovation Community , the 200-acre tech and bioscience district that has reshaped the southern portion of the neighborhood. Anchored by the 4220 Duncan and 4240 Duncan Cambridge Innovation Center (CIC) campuses, Cortex provides specialized lab space, coworking suites, and a global innovation network for biotech startups and tech firms. Just south, the Washington University School of Medicine and Barnes-Jewish Hospital form one of the largest academic medical campuses in the country — including the Siteman Cancer Center , ranked among the top cancer centers in the United States by U.S. News & World Report. The World Chess Hall of Fame on North Maryland Avenue completes the cultural roster, housing the largest publicly accessible chess piece on Earth (the 14-foot, 6-inch World’s Largest Chess Piece ) and rotating exhibitions on the game’s history and art.
None of this — Cortex, the mansions, the Cathedral — is what actually employs the Central West End today. That is Barnes-Jewish Hospital, the Washington University School of Medicine, St. Louis Children’s Hospital, and the rest of the BJC HealthCare campus immediately south of Forest Park Avenue, which together make up one of the largest employers in the St. Louis region and are the reason lunch crowds, parking demand, and apartment turnover in the neighborhood look nothing like they did a generation ago. That economic reality splits the Central West End into two neighborhoods that share one name: a genuinely walkable commercial core along Euclid and Laclede Avenues, dense enough to run errands, eat, and get a haircut without a car, and a quieter residential edge — the private streets, the blocks toward Kingshighway and Vandeventer — where the pace slows and the business mix thins out fast. A guide that only describes the Euclid strip is describing maybe a third of the neighborhood.
The neighborhood’s commercial heart runs along Euclid Avenue , where more than 75 independent businesses — including the 125-year-old Straub’s Market (founded 1901), Clementine’s Naughty & Nice Ice Cream , Left Bank Books (the largest independently owned full-line bookstore in St. Louis), and Northwest Coffee Roasting — share the corridor with cafes, art galleries, and patios. The geography of the Central West End is uniquely advantageous: positioned on level ground above the formerly flood-prone River des Peres (now culverted under Forest Park), the neighborhood is eminently walkable, MetroLink-accessible via the Central West End and Cortex stations, and within minutes of downtown, Clayton, the Delmar Loop, and the Cathedral Basilica complex.
Image: Cathedral Basilica of Saint Louis, Central West End, St. Louis — completed 1914, designated a basilica 1997 — Wikimedia Commons , CC BY-SA 2.5

Summers push the crowds onto the Euclid and Laclede Avenue patios and winters move them indoors to the Cathedral Basilica’s concerts and the Cortex coworking floors, but the neighborhood’s level, walkable grid keeps it one of the more weather-resilient commercial strips in the city.
