### Franz Park Businesses & Neighborhood Guide | St Louis Near Me Directory
Franz Park, St. Louis
Franz Park anchors one of the three (formally) or five (per the Dogtown Historical Society) neighborhoods that comprise the historic St. Louis area known as Dogtown — anchored today by the 4.67-acre Franz Park city park (donated 1915 by E.D. Franz), the McCausland Avenue antique-and-vacuum-shop commercial corridor, the Manchester Avenue brick-and-fire-clay industrial legacy, the long-running Failoni’s Restaurant (purchased 1916 from the Lemp Brewery by Alessandro Failoni to serve nearby Scullin Steel workers), and the Wilkinson Early Childhood Center magnet school in the historic 1921 Roe School building.
Franz Park sits in southwest St. Louis at approximately 38.6212° N, 90.3044° W in zip code 63139. Per the City of St. Louis Planning & Urban Design Agency, the neighborhood’s boundaries run Dale Avenue on the North and East, Manchester Avenue on the South, and the City Limits on the West. Franz Park is bordered by the Hi-Pointe neighborhood to the north (across Dale), Clayton-Tamm to the east (across Dale on the eastern leg), Ellendale directly to the south (across Manchester), and St. Louis County / the cities of Maplewood and Richmond Heights to the west (across the city limits at McCausland). The 2020 Census recorded Franz Park as 80.4% White, 7.7% Two or More Races, 6.0% Black, 5.0% Hispanic/Latino, 2.9% Asian, and 0.2% Native American — with 2,260 residents in 1.1 square kilometers (5,400 per square mile). The St. Louis Public Schools district serves the neighborhood, and the Marketplace Branch of the St. Louis Public Library is located on Manchester Avenue.
Ask a longtime St. Louisan where Dogtown ends and you’ll get a shrug more often than a street name — most people use “Dogtown” for the whole cluster and couldn’t tell you where Franz Park stops and Clayton-Tamm starts. Even the official record disagrees with itself: the city’s Planning & Urban Design Agency recognizes three formal Dogtown neighborhoods (Hi-Pointe, Clayton-Tamm, Franz Park), while the Dogtown Historical Society counts five, adding Cheltenham and part of Ellendale. What most visitors picture when they say “Dogtown” — the parade route, St. James the Greater, the bar-and-restaurant strip — is Tamm Avenue, one block east in Clayton-Tamm. Franz Park, across Dale Avenue, is the quieter half: the park itself, the McCausland antique row, and residential blocks most Dogtown visitors never actually walk.
The neighborhood traces its name to E.D. Franz , whose 1915 land donation created the Franz Park city park at the heart of the neighborhood. Franz Park itself today is a 4.67-acre green space featuring playground equipment, picnic areas, two lighted tennis courts, a soccer field, two softball fields, horseshoe courts, restrooms, and water fountains — all available on a first-come, first-served basis with no reservation. The neighborhood is part of the broader Dogtown area, which got its name as a small mining community in the mid-1800s — an article published August 14, 1889 in the Missouri Republican is the earliest known reference to the name “Dogtown,” describing a lost 5-year-old boy who lived in “the classic precincts of Dogtown, near Cheltenham.” Dogtown was widely used in the 1800s by miners to describe a group of small shelters around mines.
Franz Park grew with the other Dogtown neighborhoods in the mid-1800s, when clay mining moved into the area following the early 1850s extension of the Pacific Railway five miles into the countryside (its original station was near today’s Hampton viaduct bridge on Manchester). The area sat atop high-quality fire clay deposits that supported St. Louis’s emerging brick and ceramics industry, and clay extraction intensified through the 1850s onward. Many immigrants from Ireland, Italy, Germany, and Poland came to work in the mines. St. Louis fire brick was a growing industry that employed most of the residents, who built homes around the industrial locations. By the end of World War II, the mines had closed, and subdivisions had been built upon the old sites.
The first settler in the area was actually Charles Gratiot , a Swiss immigrant from St. Louis credited with opening the area to development more than 200 years ago. After arriving in 1781 and becoming a successful fur trader in the Illinois territory, Gratiot petitioned Spanish authorities for the “Gratiot League Square” — an enormous 5,700-acre tract that encompassed many present-day city neighborhoods. He built a mansion near the present-day intersection of Macklind and Manchester (and a farm, a mill, and a distillery), and sold plots of his land to other farmers. The area became a rural farming community until the railroad arrived. With the 1904 World’s Fair , even more people moved into the neighborhood, as did the Sulphur Springs Spa for a few years.
Due to the erratic way in which the houses in the neighborhood were built around individual mining locations, a variety of architectural styles exist within Franz Park. Visitors will find 19th-century Queen Anne farmhouses, 1920s bungalows, post-WWII small frame homes, ornate Dutch Colonials, large wood-framed-and-sided homes, even stone homes that look like they belong in Elephant Rock State Park. The neighborhood’s spots near Fairmount and Mitchell sit on some of the highest points in St. Louis, with gorgeous views of Dogtown to the northeast and even the Central West End and Downtown. Franz Park extends a block or so west of McCausland and abuts the suburbs at Richmond Heights, MO — the homes, churches, and retail buildings along McCausland and the homes just to the west on the St. Louis border are particularly distinctive.
Recent decades have brought generational turnover and noticeable investment to the neighborhood — new construction homes are starting around $500,000 while well-maintained older two-bedroom bungalows remain in the $200,000s. Anchor institutions and businesses include St. James the Greater Catholic Church (the 1928 English Gothic Revival parish built during the Great Depression entirely by parishioners — the anchor of Dogtown’s Irish Catholic identity and host of the Ancient Order of Hibernians St. Patrick’s Day Parade since 1984), the 1922-built Hi-Pointe Theater on McCausland Avenue (the oldest continuously operating single-screen movie theater in the St. Louis metro), and the World’s Largest Amoco Sign at the intersection of Skinker, Clayton Road, and Oakland — a 44-ton-of-steel, 5,800-bulb landmark that originated as a Standard Oil sign in the 1920s.
Franz Park’s modern business activity reflects its position as a Dogtown service corridor connecting the south-side neighborhoods to Forest Park, the Saint Louis Zoo, and the I-64 / I-44 highway gateway. Commercial activity concentrates along Manchester Avenue ( Failoni’s Restaurant at 6715 Manchester since 1916, Olympia Kebob House & Taverna on McCausland, El Potro Mexican restaurant, Sunny’s Cantina, Cham Bakery) and along McCausland (the antique-shop corridor, Discount Vac). The listings on this page draw first from the Manchester Avenue and McCausland Avenue corridors themselves — anchored by century-old Failoni’s and joined by Pan D’Olive, the McCausland antique row, Manchester’s auto-body and used-car row, and a restoration contractor — plus a political consultancy, financial-services provider, and nonprofit outreach partners serving the broader St. Louis region from positions accessible to Forest Park, the Maplewood and Richmond Heights border, and the I-64 corridor.
Image: The annual Ancient Order of Hibernians St. Patrick’s Day Parade in Dogtown, anchored by St. James the Greater Catholic Church — the cultural heart of the five Dogtown neighborhoods, of which Franz Park is one — Wikimedia Commons / CC BY-SA 2.5 by Agent-88

Franz Park runs a standard Midwest four-season calendar — humid summers that fill Failoni’s patio and the park’s ball fields, snowy winters that push activity indoors to the Hi-Pointe Theater and the Manchester Avenue restaurant row, and one shared date every St. Louisan in the area marks on the calendar: the Ancient Order of Hibernians St. Patrick’s Day Parade down Tamm Avenue each March 17.

### Frequently Asked Questions 
Q. What defines the Franz Park neighborhood? 
A. Franz Park is the quieter of the three official Dogtown neighborhoods — a mostly residential pocket of southwest St. Louis built around the 4.67-acre Franz Park (donated in 1915 by E.D. Franz), the McCausland Avenue antique-shop row, and the historic Failoni’s Restaurant, family-run on Manchester Avenue since 1916. The parade route and restaurant strip most people picture as “Dogtown” actually run through neighboring Clayton-Tamm.

Q. How does St Louis Near Me Directory help Franz Park businesses? 
A. St Louis Near Me Directory gives Franz Park businesses a Gold, Platinum, or Diamond listing — schema-optimized, up to 400 keyword combinations, Google Business Profile support, and review management — built to expand, not replace, their existing Google presence. Q. What types of businesses are most common in Franz Park? 
A. Family-run restaurants and specialty shops anchor Franz Park’s Manchester and McCausland Avenue corridors — Failoni’s Restaurant (since 1916) and Pan D’Olive lead the dining scene, joined by The St. Louis Plastering Company, an auto-body and used-car row on Manchester, and the McCausland antique-shop corridor anchored by Tin Roof Antiques. A political consultancy and financial-services partners round out the broader service mix.

Q. What kinds of dining, retail, and recreation options are available in Franz Park? 
A. Dining centers on Manchester and McCausland Avenue — Failoni’s Restaurant for thin-crust pizza and live music since 1916, plus Pan D’Olive for sit-down Italian. Retail runs to the McCausland antique row, anchored by Tin Roof Antiques. Recreation means the 4.67-acre Franz Park itself: a playground, two lighted tennis courts, a soccer field, two softball fields, and horseshoe courts, all first-come, first-served.

Q. Are there neighborhood landmarks, parks, and historic sites in Franz Park? 
A. Yes — the 4.67-acre Franz Park itself, donated in 1915 by E.D. Franz, is the neighborhood’s namesake landmark. Nearby stands the 1922 Hi-Pointe Theater on McCausland Avenue, the oldest continuously operating single-screen movie theater in the St. Louis metro, and the World’s Largest Amoco Sign at Skinker, Clayton, and Oakland — a 44-ton, 5,800-bulb sign dating to the 1920s as a Standard Oil landmark.

Q. What is it like to live in Franz Park? 
A. Franz Park is a quiet, residential slice of Dogtown with about 2,260 residents and an eclectic mix of housing — 19th-century Queen Anne farmhouses, 1920s bungalows, postwar frame homes, and even stone houses. New construction starts around $500,000, while older two-bedroom bungalows remain in the $200,000s. It sits a block or two removed from the parade-and-restaurant energy of neighboring Clayton-Tamm.

Q. How do residents and visitors get around Franz Park? 
A. Franz Park is bounded by Dale Avenue on the north and east, Manchester Avenue on the south, and the St. Louis city limits on the west — putting it close to Forest Park, the Saint Louis Zoo, and the I-64 / I-44 highway gateway. Manchester Avenue carries most of the neighborhood’s traffic and businesses, connecting it directly to the rest of southwest St. Louis.

## Franz Park Businesses & Neighborhood Guide | St Louis Near Me Directory

 Franz Park, St. Louis

Franz Park anchors one of the three (formally) or five (per the Dogtown Historical Society) neighborhoods that comprise the historic St. Louis area known as Dogtown — anchored today by the 4.67-acre Franz Park city park (donated 1915 by E.D. Franz), the McCausland Avenue antique-and-vacuum-shop commercial corridor, the Manchester Avenue brick-and-fire-clay industrial legacy, the long-running Failoni’s Restaurant (purchased 1916 from the Lemp Brewery by Alessandro Failoni to serve nearby Scullin Steel workers), and the Wilkinson Early Childhood Center magnet school in the historic 1921 Roe School building.

Franz Park sits in southwest St. Louis at approximately **38.6212° N, 90.3044° W** in zip code 63139. Per the City of St. Louis Planning & Urban Design Agency, the neighborhood’s boundaries run **Dale Avenue** on the North and East, **Manchester Avenue** on the South, and the **City Limits** on the West. Franz Park is bordered by the **Hi-Pointe** neighborhood to the north (across Dale), **Clayton-Tamm** to the east (across Dale on the eastern leg), **Ellendale** directly to the south (across Manchester), and **St. Louis County / the cities of Maplewood and Richmond Heights** to the west (across the city limits at McCausland). The 2020 Census recorded Franz Park as **80.4% White, 7.7% Two or More Races, 6.0% Black, 5.0% Hispanic/Latino, 2.9% Asian, and 0.2% Native American** — with 2,260 residents in 1.1 square kilometers (5,400 per square mile). The St. Louis Public Schools district serves the neighborhood, and the **Marketplace Branch** of the St. Louis Public Library is located on Manchester Avenue.

The neighborhood traces its name to **E.D. Franz**, whose 1915 land donation created the Franz Park city park at the heart of the neighborhood. **Franz Park itself today is a 4.67-acre green space** featuring playground equipment, picnic areas, two lighted tennis courts, a soccer field, two softball fields, horseshoe courts, restrooms, and water fountains — all available on a first-come, first-served basis with no reservation. The neighborhood is part of the broader **Dogtown** area, which got its name as a small mining community in the mid-1800s — an article published **August 14, 1889** in the Missouri Republican is the earliest known reference to the name “Dogtown,” describing a lost 5-year-old boy who lived in “the classic precincts of Dogtown, near Cheltenham.” Dogtown was widely used in the 1800s by miners to describe a group of small shelters around mines.

Franz Park grew with the other Dogtown neighborhoods in the mid-1800s, when **clay mining** moved into the area following the early 1850s extension of the **Pacific Railway** five miles into the countryside (its original station was near today’s Hampton viaduct bridge on Manchester). The area sat atop high-quality fire clay deposits that supported St. Louis’s emerging brick and ceramics industry, and clay extraction intensified through the 1850s onward. Many immigrants from **Ireland, Italy, Germany, and Poland** came to work in the mines. St. Louis fire brick was a growing industry that employed most of the residents, who built homes around the industrial locations. By the end of World War II, the mines had closed, and subdivisions had been built upon the old sites.

The first settler in the area was actually **Charles Gratiot**, a Swiss immigrant from St. Louis credited with opening the area to development more than 200 years ago. After arriving in 1781 and becoming a successful fur trader in the Illinois territory, Gratiot petitioned Spanish authorities for the **“Gratiot League Square”** — an enormous 5,700-acre tract that encompassed many present-day city neighborhoods. He built a mansion near the present-day intersection of Macklind and Manchester (and a farm, a mill, and a distillery), and sold plots of his land to other farmers. The area became a rural farming community until the railroad arrived. With the **1904 World’s Fair**, even more people moved into the neighborhood, as did the **Sulphur Springs Spa** for a few years.

Due to the erratic way in which the houses in the neighborhood were built around individual mining locations, a **variety of architectural styles** exist within Franz Park. Visitors will find 19th-century Queen Anne farmhouses, 1920s bungalows, post-WWII small frame homes, ornate Dutch Colonials, large wood-framed-and-sided homes, even stone homes that look like they belong in Elephant Rock State Park. The neighborhood’s spots near Fairmount and Mitchell sit on some of the highest points in St. Louis, with gorgeous views of Dogtown to the northeast and even the Central West End and Downtown. Franz Park extends a block or so west of McCausland and abuts the suburbs at Richmond Heights, MO — the homes, churches, and retail buildings along McCausland and the homes just to the west on the St. Louis border are particularly distinctive.

Recent decades have brought generational turnover and noticeable investment to the neighborhood — new construction homes are starting around $500,000 while well-maintained older two-bedroom bungalows remain in the $200,000s. Anchor institutions and businesses include **St. James the Greater Catholic Church** (the 1928 English Gothic Revival parish built during the Great Depression entirely by parishioners — the anchor of Dogtown’s Irish Catholic identity and host of the **Ancient Order of Hibernians St. Patrick’s Day Parade** since 1984), the 1922-built **Hi-Pointe Theater** on McCausland Avenue (the oldest continuously operating single-screen movie theater in the St. Louis metro), and the **World’s Largest Amoco Sign** at the intersection of Skinker, Clayton Road, and Oakland — a 44-ton-of-steel, 5,800-bulb landmark that originated as a Standard Oil sign in the 1920s.

Franz Park’s modern business activity reflects its position as a Dogtown service corridor connecting the south-side neighborhoods to Forest Park, the Saint Louis Zoo, and the I-64 / I-44 highway gateway. Commercial activity concentrates along Manchester Avenue (**Failoni’s Restaurant** at 6715 Manchester since 1916, Olympia Kebob House & Taverna on McCausland, El Potro Mexican restaurant, Sunny’s Cantina, Cham Bakery) and along McCausland (the antique-shop corridor, Discount Vac). The listings on this page draw from the broader Franz Park / Dogtown / Manchester Avenue professional corridor, with anchor institutions like Failoni’s, plus a mix of specialty contractors, B2B marketing agencies, political consultancies, and industrial suppliers serving the broader St. Louis region from positions accessible to Forest Park, the Maplewood and Richmond Heights border, and the I-64 corridor.

Image: The annual Ancient Order of Hibernians St. Patrick’s Day Parade in Dogtown, anchored by St. James the Greater Catholic Church — the cultural heart of the five Dogtown neighborhoods, of which Franz Park is one — Wikimedia Commons / CC BY-SA 2.5 by Agent-88

Franz Park sits in southwest St. Louis between Manchester Avenue and Dale, where the city follows a classic Midwest four-season pattern. Hot, humid summers with highs in the upper 80s°F bring peak activity to the 4.67-acre Franz Park itself — the playground, lighted tennis courts, soccer field, two softball fields, and horseshoe courts draw families and casual sports leagues. Spring and fall fill the Manchester and McCausland commercial corridors with foot traffic to Failoni’s Restaurant patio (live music Thursday-Saturday), Olympia Kebob House gyros, the McCausland antique-shop corridor, and the Marketplace Branch library.

Cold winters with periodic snow shift commerce indoors to Franz Park’s steady service-corridor providers — the historic Failoni’s dining rooms (brick-oven pizza and Italian American specialties under the oldest still-in-use cash register in greater St. Louis), the Hi-Pointe Theater’s aquamarine-seated single screen, and the indoor manufacturing and B2B operations of the broader Manchester and Knox Industrial corridors. **St. Patrick’s Day** (March 17) brings thousands to the Ancient Order of Hibernians Parade along Tamm Avenue. Quick I-64 and I-44 access at the McCausland and Hampton gateways keeps the Franz Park service market moving year-round and connects directly to Forest Park, the Saint Louis Zoo, and downtown.

### Gravois Park Businesses & Neighborhood Guide | St Louis Near Me Directory
Gravois Park, St. Louis 
Gravois Park is a densely-built southeast St. Louis neighborhood named for the park whose land was granted by the U.S. government in 1812 as one of the city's earliest public commons. Today it is best known as the heart of “La Calle Cherokee” — the Cherokee Street corridor of authentic Mexican restaurants, panaderias, taquerias, and markets that gives this neighborhood its flavor.
Settled by German and Eastern European immigrants during the turn-of-the-20th-century streetcar-suburb boom, Gravois Park sits within the 4,642-property Gravois-Jefferson Streetcar Suburb Historic District — one of the largest historic districts in the country — and, as of the 2010 census, is the densest neighborhood in the City of St. Louis.
The neighborhood runs from Cherokee Street on the north to Chippewa Street on the south, Jefferson Avenue on the east, and Grand Boulevard on the west (ZIP 63118). It borders Benton Park West across Cherokee, Marine Villa across Jefferson, Dutchtown across Chippewa, and Tower Grove South across Grand. At the 2020 census it held 4,683 residents on just 0.42 square miles.
Cherokee Street is the commercial spine — a nationally recognized Latino business district where families have run taquerias, bakeries, and carnicerias for decades, alongside art galleries, music venues, and vintage shops. The result is one of the most walkable, culturally rich few blocks in St. Louis.
The businesses featured below sit on or just off Cherokee Street between Jefferson and Gravois — the beating heart of the neighborhood — where a taco, a fresh pan dulce, or a slice and a beer are never more than a short stroll apart.
The Gravois Park neighborhood, St. Louis. 
Like the rest of St. Louis, Gravois Park runs a humid subtropical climate — hot, storm-prone summers and cold but modest winters — that keeps Cherokee Street’s patios and foot traffic heaviest from spring through fall.
Ask a local where Gravois Park is and most point to Cherokee Street before they say the neighborhood’s name. The stretch people mean by “La Calle Cherokee” actually straddles the boundary — the north side of the street is Benton Park West, and Gravois Park is the south side, running down to Chippewa. Away from the storefronts, Gravois Park is quieter: block after block of the same brick rowhouses and two-family flats that made it the densest neighborhood in the city, home today to the Latino and immigrant families who have anchored Cherokee Street’s restaurants and shops for decades.
One specific, checkable detail: 2626 Cherokee St is home to both Clements Lock & Security and Clements Bar, listed under the same address and phone number — a security shop and a bar run out of the same storefront, the kind of small-footprint overlap that is common on this block.

### Frequently Asked Questions
Q. What is Gravois Park known for? 
A. Gravois Park is known as the south side of Cherokee Street’s “La Calle Cherokee” — a nationally recognized Latino business corridor of taquerias, panaderias, and carnicerias. It is also the densest neighborhood in the City of St. Louis (2010 census) and sits within the 4,642-property Gravois-Jefferson Streetcar Suburb Historic District.

Q. How does St Louis Near Me Directory help Gravois Park businesses? 
A. St Louis Near Me Directory builds a hyper-local, SEO-optimized page for Gravois Park so nearby customers can find its restaurants, bakeries, and shops when they search online. The approach expands a business’s existing Google Business Profile rather than replacing it, with simple plans, a free trial, no long-term contracts, and no competitor ads.

Q. What types of businesses are most common in Gravois Park? 
A. Cherokee Street businesses dominate: Mexican and Latin American restaurants, a bakery, a taqueria-market, a carniceria, a crepe shop, and a pizza-and-bar. A few specialty businesses sit just off the strip, including a recording studio on South Jefferson Avenue and a locksmith and security shop at 2626 Cherokee St.

Q. What kinds of dining, retail, and recreation options are available in Gravois Park? 
A. Dining ranges from taco spots and a Mexican bakery to a Latin American kitchen and a pizza-and-bar with live music. Retail includes Latino Americana’s carniceria and grocery for fresh meats and pantry staples. For recreation, Suburban Pro Studios offers music recording on South Jefferson Avenue, just off the neighborhood’s walkable Cherokee Street core.

Q. Are there neighborhood landmarks, parks, and historic sites in Gravois Park? 
A. The neighborhood is named for a park whose land the U.S. government granted as public commons in 1812. Its real landmark today is architectural: Gravois Park sits within the 4,642-property Gravois-Jefferson Streetcar Suburb Historic District, one of the largest such districts in the country, built up with dense, well-preserved rowhouses and flats.

Q. What is it like to live in Gravois Park? 
A. Gravois Park is dense and walkable: as of the 2010 census it was the most densely populated neighborhood in the City of St. Louis, with about 4,683 residents on 0.42 square miles of brick rowhouses and two-family flats. It is home to Latino and immigrant families who have anchored Cherokee Street’s businesses for decades.

Q. How do residents and visitors get around Gravois Park? 
A. Gravois Park is compact and walkable, bounded by Cherokee Street, Jefferson Avenue, Chippewa Street, and Grand Boulevard, so most of its restaurants and shops sit within a short stroll of each other along the Cherokee Street corridor. It borders Benton Park West, Marine Villa, Dutchtown, and Tower Grove South, all reachable on foot from its edges.

### Hamilton Heights Businesses & Neighborhood Guide | St Louis Near Me Directory
Hamilton Heights, St. Louis
Hamilton Heights anchors a deep-history rectangular stretch of northwest St. Louis named for Civil War Missouri governor Hamilton R. Gamble — once part of a Spanish colonial land grant on the historic St. Charles Road route to St. Louis, today defined by the Dr. Martin Luther King Drive commercial corridor, the Wellston Loop streetcar legacy, the 1903 Hamilton Hotel (956 Hamilton Avenue, built for the 1904 World’s Fair, now on the National Register of Historic Places), and a 1890s-1920s brick residential streetscape with two William B. Ittner-designed schools (Hempstead 1906, on the NRHP).
Hamilton Heights sits in northwest St. Louis at approximately 38.6683° N, 90.2891° W in zip codes 63112 and 63133. Per the City of St. Louis Planning & Urban Design Agency, the neighborhood’s boundaries run Dr. Martin Luther King Drive (co-signed with Missouri Route 180) on the Northeast, southward to Union Boulevard on the East, westward to Page Avenue on the South, northward along Cockrill Street / the City Limits on the Western edge (bordering Wellston, MO) back to Dr. Martin Luther King Drive. Hamilton Heights is bordered by Wells-Goodfellow to the north (across MLK Drive), Academy to the east (across Union Boulevard), the West End to the south (across Page Avenue), and St. Louis County and the City of Wellston to the west. The neighborhood today is approximately 98% Black , with a population that declined significantly from the 1990s to 2020 Census amid the broader patterns of north St. Louis disinvestment.
The land that became Hamilton Heights was once part of a Spanish colonial land grant known as Survey 3033, originally the property of Baptiste La Fleur. During colonial times, travelers passed through the area between St. Louis and St. Charles along St. Charles Road — the historic Mississippi River-to-Missouri River route, now Dr. Martin Luther King Drive. By the mid-1850s, the land was subdivided and sold as smaller tracts. One such tract became the property and estate of Hamilton R. Gamble , who served as governor of Missouri during the Civil War and is the namesake for the neighborhood. The early settlement of Rinkelville grew up around the Six Mile House operated by George Rinkel Jr. on the St. Charles Road.
In 1868, Erastus Wells — a St. Louis transit magnate — purchased a tract west of Rinkelville and developed a fine country estate. To provide access to the area and stimulate development, Wells and others constructed and opened the West End Narrow Gauge Railway in 1878. A station was established at the line’s intersection with St. Charles Road near the Wells estate and bore the name of Wellston . The Citizen’s Railway Company simultaneously operated a horse car line along St. Charles Road. The Wellston Loop became one of the major streetcar transit hubs in St. Louis — later anchored by the Hodiamont streetcar line — and the surrounding commercial district at the Wellston Loop became a thriving regional shopping destination through the early to mid-20th century.
In 1903, the Hamilton Hotel was built at 956 Hamilton Avenue to accommodate visitors to the 1904 Louisiana Purchase Exposition (the St. Louis World’s Fair). The hotel later became part of the World’s Fair lodging network and remains a National Register of Historic Places landmark (listed April 29, 2011) — today operated as Hamilton Place Apartments, a 98-unit affordable-housing community. By 1906, the St. Louis Public Schools commissioned famed architect William B. Ittner to design Hempstead Elementary School at 5872 Minerva Avenue (NRHP-listed July 3, 2007), one of eight Ittner schools approved that year. Hempstead closed in 2004 and suffered fire damage in 2014; a second Ittner-designed school (the former Hempstead annex / Roe School) also served the neighborhood.
The 1950s and 1960s marked a period of demographic transition as white residents moved out and African American residents moved in — many newcomers were part of a large wave of African Americans migrating to St. Louis from the rural South following World War II. Many moved directly into the neighborhood, creating a close-knit community anchored by the vital Wellston shopping district . As the children in these families became adults, they moved elsewhere. This generational shift, combined with the decline of the Wellston shopping district beginning in the early 1970s , accelerated the neighborhood’s economic decline through the late 20th century. Hamilton Heights lost 30% of its population from 1990 to 2000 and continued declining through 2020.
Hamilton Heights today is anchored by Hamilton Park (corner of Dr. Martin Luther King Drive and Clara Avenue) with playground equipment and softball/baseball fields including a Cardinals Care ballfield donated by the St. Louis Cardinals charity. The neighborhood is noteworthy for its numerous religious institutions , including remaining African American churches and signs of former Jewish places of worship. Ford Elementary Community Education Center (built 1964) and Emerson Elementary still serve the neighborhood, with magnet/choice school access throughout the St. Louis Public Schools district. The 1907 Minerva Apartments (an early 20th-century brick beauty) anchor the residential character, alongside two-to-four-family flats and larger single-family brick homes built between 1890 and 1920.
Hamilton Heights’s modern business activity reflects its position along the Dr. Martin Luther King Drive Great Streets corridor — a 2016 city / East-West Gateway Coordinating Council initiative focused on revitalization from Union Boulevard west to the city limits. The Wellston Loop Community Development Corporation coordinates with neighborhood organizations including Union West Community Corporation (the local neighborhood association) and Hamilton Heights Neighborhood Organization, Inc. , on revitalization. The listings on this page draw from the broader Hamilton Heights / MLK Drive / Union Boulevard professional corridor — with anchor providers along MLK Drive (Go Getter STL at 5736 MLK), Private Duty Services on Clemens Ave, Ade Consulting on Vernon Ave, Gateway Roofing on Minerva Ave, GURU Realtors on Page Boulevard, Speedy Mobile Market on Maple Ave, and Warehouse West on Hamilton Avenue, plus chamber, association, and business-district partners serving the broader St. Louis region.
Image: The 1903 Hamilton Hotel at 956 Hamilton Avenue — built for the 1904 St. Louis World’s Fair, listed on the National Register of Historic Places April 29, 2011, now operating as Hamilton Place Apartments — Wikimedia Commons / Creative Commons

St. Louis’ humid summers and cold winters simply push the neighborhood’s rhythm indoors and out — ballfield season at Hamilton Park in summer, service-corridor business as usual along MLK Drive and Union Boulevard the rest of the year.
What sets Hamilton Heights apart from the neighborhoods around it isn’t a business district — it’s the housing. Walk the blocks off MLK Drive and you’re looking at the same 1890s–1920s brick two-flats and single-family homes that housed streetcar-era Wellston Loop workers a century ago, alongside the 1907 Minerva Apartments and the Ittner-designed schoolhouses. That building stock, largely intact even as the population thinned out after 1990, is the neighborhood’s real asset today — and the reason Union West Community Corporation and the Hamilton Heights Neighborhood Organization keep pushing rehab and reinvestment along the MLK Drive Great Streets corridor rather than new construction.

### Frequently Asked Questions 
Q. What defines the Hamilton Heights neighborhood? 
A. Hamilton Heights is a northwest St. Louis neighborhood named for Civil War governor Hamilton R. Gamble, bounded by Dr. Martin Luther King Drive, Union Boulevard, Page Avenue, and Cockrill Street at the Wellston line. It’s defined by its 1890s-1920s brick housing stock, the historic Wellston Loop streetcar legacy, and landmarks like the NRHP-listed 1903 Hamilton Hotel.

Q. How does St Louis Near Me Directory help Hamilton Heights businesses? 
A. St Louis Near Me Directory offers Hamilton Heights businesses plain-English SEO through Gold, Platinum, and Diamond tiers, all starting with a 7-day free trial and no long-term contracts. It expands rather than replaces a business’s Google Business Profile, and never runs competitor ads on a listing, helping providers along MLK Drive and Page Avenue capture local search demand.

Q. What types of businesses are most common in Hamilton Heights? 
A. The neighborhood’s listed businesses lean toward independent retail and professional services: Go Getter STL and Speedy Mobile Market for everyday goods, Private Duty Services and Gateway Roofing for home and care needs, Ade Consulting and GURU Realtors for professional services, plus chambers of commerce and community organizations like the Heartland Black Chamber and Locust Central Business District.

Q. What kinds of dining, retail, and recreation options are available in Hamilton Heights? 
A. Dining and drinks center on Warehouse West, a Hamilton Avenue bar with a newer food menu open Thursday through the weekend. Retail runs through Go Getter STL and Speedy Mobile Market along MLK Drive and Maple Avenue. For recreation, Hamilton Park at MLK Drive and Clara Avenue offers a playground and a Cardinals Care ballfield.

Q. Are there neighborhood landmarks, parks, and historic sites in Hamilton Heights? 
A. Yes. The 1903 Hamilton Hotel at 956 Hamilton Avenue, built for the 1904 World’s Fair, is a National Register of Historic Places landmark now operating as Hamilton Place Apartments. Hempstead Elementary, designed by architect William B. Ittner, is also NRHP-listed. Hamilton Park, with its Cardinals Care ballfield, anchors the neighborhood’s recreation.

Q. What is it like to live in Hamilton Heights? 
A. Living in Hamilton Heights means intact century-old brick two-flats and single-family homes on the blocks off MLK Drive, alongside the 1907 Minerva Apartments. The population has declined since 1990 amid broader north St. Louis disinvestment, but groups like Union West Community Corporation are pushing rehab and reinvestment in the existing housing stock along the MLK Drive Great Streets corridor.

Q. How do residents and visitors get around Hamilton Heights? 
A. Dr. Martin Luther King Drive, also signed Missouri Route 180, is the neighborhood’s main corridor, running along its northeast boundary. Union Boulevard and Page Avenue frame the east and south edges. The area was once served by the Wellston Loop streetcar hub, one of St. Louis’s major historic transit centers, before automobile travel took over.

Q. How can residents and visitors explore more services around Hamilton Heights? 
A. Beyond Hamilton Heights’ own listed providers along MLK Drive, Vernon, and Page Avenue, groups like the Wellston Loop Community Development Corporation and Hamilton Heights Neighborhood Organization connect residents to local resources. St Louis Near Me Directory’s full guide to all 79 St. Louis neighborhoods, linked from this page, covers surrounding areas including Wells-Goodfellow, Academy, and the West End.

### 9 Best St Louis Businesses in Hi Pointe, MO (2026)

### Hi Pointe Neighborhood Guide – St. Louis History & Businesses

Hi-Pointe takes its name from sitting at one of the highest elevations in the City of St. Louis — a compact one-square-mile Dogtown neighborhood at the southwest gateway to Forest Park, where Skinker Boulevard, Clayton Road, McCausland Avenue, and Interstate 64 all converge. It's home to the 1922 Hi-Pointe Theatre (the metro's oldest continuously operating single-screen cinema), the World's Largest Amoco Sign, the historic Cheshire complex, and a brick streetscape shaped by the 1904 World's Fair.

### Hi-Pointe Businesses & Neighborhood Guide | St Louis Near Me Directory
Hi-Pointe, St. Louis
Hi-Pointe takes its name from sitting at one of the highest elevations in the City of St. Louis, anchoring a roughly rectangular section of the city’s southwest edge that locals also call one of the three official Dogtown neighborhoods alongside Clayton-Tamm and Franz Park — defined today by the storied Skinker-Clayton-McCausland gateway, the 1922 Hi-Pointe Theatre, and the World’s Largest Amoco Sign.
Hi-Pointe sits in southwest St. Louis at approximately 38.6290° N, 90.3079° W in zip code 63117. Per the City of St. Louis, the neighborhood is bounded by Clayton Avenue and Oakland Avenue on the North, the City Limits (where St. Louis meets the inner-ring suburb of Maplewood) on the West, Dale Avenue on the South, and Louisville Avenue on the East. Inside that compact footprint, Hi-Pointe centers on the heavily-traveled corner where Skinker Boulevard, Clayton Road, McCausland Avenue, and Interstate 64/U.S. Highway 40 all converge — sitting directly at the southwest entrance to Forest Park. Hi-Pointe is bordered by Wydown Skinker to the north, Clayton-Tamm to the east, Franz Park to the south (across Dale), and St. Louis County / Richmond Heights and Maplewood to the west.
Hi-Pointe’s early industrial story is the same one shared by the rest of Dogtown . After the Pacific Railway laid five miles of tracks west from St. Louis through Cheltenham in the early 1850s, clay and coal mining became the economic engine of the area, and St. James the Greater Parish was founded at Tamm and Wade in 1860 to anchor the immigrant community of Irish, German, French, and Balkan miners and brick-makers who built the neighborhood. Hi-Pointe’s own century includes farming, a goat farm, fire-brick clay mining, and even a small airport landing field within living memory. The name “Dogtown” dates to the mid-1800s mining era — the earliest known reference appears in an August 14, 1889 Missouri Republican article.
The 1904 Louisiana Purchase Exposition (the World’s Fair) on the western edge of Forest Park — immediately north of Hi-Pointe’s modern boundary — transformed the neighborhood. Locals will tell you some of the leftover Fair building materials made their way into the homes built in Hi-Pointe afterward, and the Fair itself sped up settlement of what had been one of the city’s last loosely-developed corners. Today, Hi-Pointe’s housing stock blends modest brick, stone, and frame homes built between roughly the 1900s and the 1920s with newer infill construction, lofts, and modern apartment buildings — a mix locals praise as some of the best-maintained in all of Dogtown.
The Hi-Pointe corner is home to two of the most-photographed landmarks in St. Louis. The Hi-Pointe Theatre at 1005 McCausland Avenue opened in 1922 and is the oldest continuously-operating single-screen movie theater in the St. Louis metropolitan area, acquired by the nonprofit Cinema St. Louis in January 2023 as its permanent base of operations. A block away, atop Stevenson’s Hi-Pointe Amoco at the Skinker-Clayton-Oakland triangle, stands the World’s Largest Amoco Sign — a 44-ton steel descendant of the original 1932 Standard Red Crown sign, with the current 40-foot-by-60-foot Amoco lettering refreshed in 2019.
The southwest edge of the neighborhood, around 6300 Clayton Road, holds another long-standing institution: The Cheshire (originally the Cheshire Inn), a Tudor-styled hotel and restaurant complex whose origins date to the 1920s. The hotel sits partially in Hi-Pointe and partially in adjacent Richmond Heights, and underwent a multi-million-dollar renovation in 2011 that preserved the original Fox & Hounds Tavern fireplace and the British-inn character that made it a generational St. Louis date-night fixture.
Despite its small footprint, Hi-Pointe’s own McCausland Avenue corridor carries three real anchors: the Hi-Pointe Theatre, Hi-Pointe Drive-In, and Blue Sage Cannabis Deli, all inside the boundary. Dale Avenue, right at the neighborhood’s southern edge, is home to a residential architecture firm. Everything else useful nearby sits just outside the four boundary streets — coworking across the line in Richmond Heights, and retail, dining, and galleries a few tenths of a mile off in Wydown Skinker, Franz Park, and Cheltenham. Hi-Pointe Drive-In at 1033 McCausland (a smashburger restaurant that opened in 2017 on the site of a 1980s drive-in) draws regional foot traffic that spills into every adjacent business.
For visitors and St. Louis newcomers, Hi-Pointe is the easiest neighborhood in the city to find: take Highway 40/I-64 west, look for the giant Amoco sign towering over the Skinker-Clayton-Oakland triangle, and you’re at the front door of one of St. Louis’s highest-elevation, most-recognizable, and most-traveled corners — a tight one-square-mile district where Dogtown’s Irish-immigrant brick-making heritage meets Forest Park’s southwest gateway and a century of continuously-operating film, food, and fuel landmarks. The listings on this page draw from the broader Hi-Pointe / McCausland / Dogtown professional corridor, with anchor businesses serving the neighborhood and the wider St. Louis region.
Image: The Grand Basin in Forest Park — the historic 1904 World’s Fair centerpiece sitting immediately north of Hi-Pointe’s Clayton/Oakland boundary, at the southwest gateway to the park — Wikimedia Commons / Creative Commons

Hi-Pointe sits at one of the highest natural elevations inside the City of St. Louis, and that exposed intersection feels every degree of St. Louis’s humid-summer, cold-winter swing — mild spring and fall days bring the most foot traffic to the McCausland Avenue corridor.
What Hi-Pointe is for today is straightforward: a small, walkable, single-corridor neighborhood built around a movie theater, a burger stand, and a dispensary, at one of the highest and most recognizable points in the city. Anyone who wants a coworking desk, an art gallery, or an antiques shop is a few minutes away in Richmond Heights, Wydown Skinker, Franz Park, or Cheltenham — close enough to matter, honest enough to say so.

#1 
Hi-Pointe Theatre 
★ 4.8 (626 reviews)

1005 McCausland Ave, St. Louis, MO 63117, USA · (314) 644-1100
Independent  $$ Historic Landmark (est. 1922) Best for: movie lovers 

The Hi-Pointe Theatre is a historic St. Louis institution on McCausland Avenue that has been operating since 1922 — the oldest continuously-operating single-screen movie theater in the St. Louis metropolitan area. In January 2023, the nonprofit Cinema St. Louis acquired the theater as its permanent base of operations after 45 years of ownership by the James family. It offers a mix of bold new releases, cult classics, and late-night screenings like The Rocky Horror Picture Show. The theater provides a stylish and comfortable viewing experience that many locals consider the best in the city, with vintage aquamarine seating recently refurbished and a huge new screen paired with explosive Dolby Digital sound. Reviewers frequently praise the vintage charm and the curated film selection. This venue is best suited for cinephiles who prefer the character of a landmark independent theater over a modern multiplex.

Years in Business: 104 years
Verified Reviews: 617 reviews
Service Radius: St. Louis City / Hi-Pointe

#2 
Hi-Pointe Drive-In 
★ 4.5 (5,889 reviews)

1033 McCausland Ave, St. Louis, MO 63117, USA · (314) 349-2720
Independent  $ Neighborhood Favorite 2017-2024 Best for: families with kids 

Located on McCausland Avenue on the site of a 1980s drive-in, Hi-Pointe Drive-In is a neighborhood staple known for its high-energy atmosphere and creative American menu. Chef Mike Johnson (of Sugarfire Smokehouse fame) leads a kitchen that serves up award-winning smashburgers, sandwiches, and hand-scooped shakes. Specific menu highlights include burgers topped with slow-cooked caramelized onions and grilled jalapeños for a mild, smoky heat. The service model is casual; guests order at the counter and staff deliver food to the tables. While some community members debate the price point, the establishment has been voted a “Neighborhood Favorite” every year since 2017. The interior is eclectic and can get loud during peak hours, reflecting its popularity as a local hangout. It is an ideal destination for groups and families looking for a modern, chef-driven twist on classic drive-in fare.

Years in Business: Since 2017
Verified Reviews: 7,023 reviews
Service Radius: St. Louis / Ballwin / Kirkwood
Free Estimates: Open until 9:00 PM
Payment Plans: Affordable ($); Counter service

What reviewers mention most: “A local institution famous for its eclectic vibe and mouthwatering burgers, though some locals find it slightly overpriced.”

### Frequently Asked Questions 
Q. Where is Hi-Pointe located? 
A. Hi-Pointe sits in southwest St. Louis at roughly 38.6290° N, 90.3079° W, zip 63117 — bounded by Clayton and Oakland Avenues to the north, the Maplewood city line to the west, Dale Avenue to the south, and Louisville Avenue to the east. It centers on the convergence of Skinker Boulevard, Clayton Road, McCausland Avenue, and I-64, at Forest Park’s southwest gateway.

Q. How much do tickets cost at Hi Pointe? 
A. The Hi-Pointe Theatre runs standard cinema pricing that varies by showtime and format — first-run releases, cult classics, and the smaller Backlot screen are priced separately. This page doesn’t carry a fixed ticket price; check hipointetheatre.org or call the box office at (314) 644-1100 for the current lineup and pricing.

Q. Is there parking near Hi Pointe Theatre? 
A. Yes — the Hi-Pointe Theatre sits on McCausland Avenue in a walkable commercial strip with on-street parking along McCausland and the surrounding blocks, shared with Blue Sage Cannabis Deli and Hi-Pointe Drive-In next door. Arrive a few minutes early on weekend evenings, when the strip’s restaurants and the theater draw the same crowd.

Q. Does Hi-Pointe Theatre serve food and drinks? 
A. Yes — the Hi-Pointe Theatre’s lobby has a mosaic concession stand serving standard movie snacks and drinks. It’s a single-screen (plus the smaller Backlot) art-house cinema rather than a dine-in theater, so guests planning a full meal typically eat next door on McCausland before or after the show.

Q. What defines the Hi-Pointe neighborhood? 
A. Hi-Pointe is defined by elevation and its name — one of the highest points in the City of St. Louis, marked by the World’s Largest Amoco Sign at the Skinker-Clayton-Oakland triangle. It’s one of three official neighborhoods inside historic Dogtown, alongside Clayton-Tamm and Franz Park, with the 1922 Hi-Pointe Theatre as its cultural anchor.

Q. How does St Louis Near Me Directory help Hi-Pointe businesses? 
A. St Louis Near Me Directory gives Hi-Pointe’s McCausland Avenue businesses — the Theatre, Hi-Pointe Drive-In, Blue Sage Cannabis Deli — and nearby Dogtown-area providers a schema-optimized listing and plain-English SEO guidance, with stronger “near me” visibility tied to the Skinker-Clayton-Oakland gateway, without competing with a business’s own Google Business Profile.

Q. What types of businesses are most common in Hi-Pointe? 
A. Hi-Pointe’s own McCausland Avenue corridor is entertainment and hospitality — the Hi-Pointe Theatre, Hi-Pointe Drive-In, and Blue Sage Cannabis Deli. A residential architecture firm sits on Dale Avenue at the neighborhood’s southern edge. Coworking, retail, and dining options just outside the boundary in Richmond Heights and the Central West End round out the picture.

Q. What kinds of dining, retail, and recreation options are available in Hi-Pointe? 
A. On McCausland Avenue itself: Hi-Pointe Drive-In for smashburgers, Blue Sage Cannabis Deli for retail, and the Hi-Pointe Theatre for a movie. A few minutes further, Imo’s Pizza sits in neighboring Cheltenham, Tin Roof Antiques in Franz Park, and William Shearburn Gallery in Wydown Skinker — all under a mile away.

### Holly Hills Businesses & Neighborhood Guide | St Louis Near Me Directory
Holly Hills, St. Louis
Holly Hills serves as South St. Louis’s most architecturally elegant 1920s residential showplace — designed as the city’s answer to Hollywood’s grace, anchored by the 180-acre Carondelet Park (dedicated July 4, 1876), the historic 1842 Lyle Mansion, the Carondelet YMCA Rec Plex, and Holly Hills Boulevard’s grand stretch of mansions, German-style castles, and Arts & Crafts bungalows from Arendes to Leona — offering environmental testing, custom millwork, branding, coffee, and chamber services across South Grand and Holly Hills Boulevard.
Holly Hills is one of St. Louis’s 79 official neighborhoods, located at 38.5683° N, 90.2749° W in southeast St. Louis City. The neighborhood is bounded by Grand Boulevard on the east, Holly Hills Boulevard and Carondelet Park on the south, Leona Street and the Union Pacific (formerly Missouri Pacific) Railroad on the west, and Bates Street then Walsh Street on the north. Surrounding neighborhoods include Dutchtown to the north, Bevo Mill to the west and north, Boulevard Heights to the southwest, and Carondelet to the east. The neighborhood spans ZIP codes 63111 and 63116 and sits approximately seven miles south of Downtown St. Louis at the terminus of South Grand Boulevard. Holly Hills is one of the cleanest, safest, and most tightly-knit residential neighborhoods in the city — a small-town atmosphere where neighbors know one another, many residents have lived here their entire lives, and the perimeter is largely landscaped by volunteer-led seasonal plantings of thousands of bulbs and perennials.
The land that Holly Hills now covers was originally part of the Commonfields of the independent City of Carondelet — the French Creole farming village founded in 1767 by Clement Delor de Treget , a former French naval officer who had been appointed syndic by the Spanish government to grant lots to settlers. By the time of the Louisiana Purchase in 1803, there were approximately 250 villagers living in 50 houses. The Commonfields stretched from present-day Virginia Avenue in the east to Morganford Road in the west, and from Lafayette Avenue south to Meramec Street — with grazing commons expanded south of River des Peres to a mile beyond Jefferson Barracks. Carondelet was originally called Louisburg in honor of King Louis XV of France, then Prairie a Catalan after settler Louis Catalan, before being officially renamed Carondelet in 1794 in honor of Baron François Louis Hector de Carondelet , a Fleming appointed Spanish governor of Louisiana. Informal names included Delor’s Village and Vide Poche (“empty pocket”), supposedly because Carondelet residents’ gambling skill would send their St. Louis neighbors home with empty pockets.
German immigrants began settling in Carondelet in the late 1840s, changing the character of the village from French Creole to German-American. Carondelet was incorporated as an independent city on March 1, 1851 , and then annexed by the City of St. Louis on April 4, 1870 . With annexation came the St. Louis park and library systems — in 1874 , the City purchased 180 acres of the old Carondelet Commons (plus part of the Lyle estate ) for $143,000, establishing Carondelet Park . The park officially opened in 1875 and was dedicated on July 4, 1876 , the centennial anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence. The land had previously belonged to Alexander Lacey Lyle , whose family built the Lyle Mansion on the property in 1842 (or 1850, by some accounts) — a Southern-sympathizing family who left St. Louis at the start of the Civil War. The Lyle House still stands in the park today and is a designated St. Louis City Landmark . The same era produced two other Carondelet firsts: Carondelet native Susan Blow , daughter of U.S. Representative Henry Taylor Blow , founded what is regarded as the first continuous public-school kindergarten in the United States at the Des Peres School (6303 Michigan Avenue) in September 1873 , modeled on Friedrich Fröbel’s German concept.
In the early 1920s , developers William A. Federer , Gus Arendes , and Don Livingston Sr. purchased a large plot of land from the Missouri Pacific Railroad and developed the area north of Carondelet Park as the Holly Hills neighborhood. The name “Holly Hills” was derived from Hollywood and intended to reflect a similar level of grace and elegance — an aspirational California-style suburban vision transplanted to South St. Louis. An essential element of Federer’s plan was to construct homes of many different styles, sizes, and characters: from grand German-style castles and Tudor mansions to cozy Arts & Crafts bungalows . The first building permit in the community was issued in 1926 for a home on Holly Hills Boulevard across from Carondelet Park. The Great Depression scaled back many of the later homes from Federer’s original vision, but the showcase “Hollywood elegance” mansions along Holly Hills Boulevard from Arendes Drive to Leona Street remained the architectural calling card. Federer’s own residence has remained in his family and is still lovingly maintained by his daughter and her family. Street names within Holly Hills honor the developers ( Arendes Drive , plus streets named for William Federer and Don Livingston ) and other historic figures: Adkins Avenue (after steamboat captain Henry Adkins), Alexander Street (after Alexander Lacey Lyle), Bates Street (after Frederick Bates, the second governor of Missouri), Bellerive Boulevard (after Louis St. Ange de Bellerive, the pre-Spanish commandant of St. Louis), Bowen Street (after Confederate General John Bowen, a former St. Louis neighbor of Ulysses S. Grant), and Burgen Avenue (after the Burgenland province in eastern Austria, from the 1909 Burgen Place subdivision).
Carondelet Park, which borders the southern edge of Holly Hills along Holly Hills Boulevard, is the third-largest park in St. Louis at approximately 180 acres. It is bounded by Holly Hills Boulevard on the north, Loughborough Avenue on the south, Interstate 55 on the east, and Leona Street on the west. The park’s undulating topography — shaped by underground caves and sinkholes — creates a Picturesque effect; nine sinkholes were joined in 1913 to form Horseshoe Lake , now one of two annually stocked fishing lakes. Scenic drives along the ridge lines were introduced in 1890. A bridge entering the park’s north side was constructed as part of an effort overseen by famed landscape architect George Kessler from 1902 to 1909 to link major parks and cemeteries along a singular artery. All historic amenities — the Lyle House, Boathouse, Music Pavilion, Old Stable, and Music Stand — were built prior to 1920. Carondelet Park is also unique as the only original landscape in the St. Louis park system — an unaltered Karst landscape that paints a picture of what the entire city could have looked like had it not been developed. The Carondelet YMCA Rec Plex sits at the east end of the park adjacent to I-55, and the one-mile Carondelet Connector trail , opened by Great Rivers Greenway in 2014, links the park’s trail system to the nine-mile River des Peres Greenway .
Today, Holly Hills is one of South St. Louis’s most desirable neighborhoods. It is a small, residential, tightly-knit community with very few intra-neighborhood businesses — commerce tends to cluster in adjacent Carondelet, Dutchtown, Bevo Mill, and Boulevard Heights. The neighborhood’s key business anchors today include St. John Environmental Consulting, LLC on Grace Avenue (the veteran-owned, BBB A+ accredited, AHERA-certified asbestos / mold / lead inspector with 25 years of experience); Silver Fox Marketing on Wilmington Avenue (15-year sign, vinyl-wrap, and brand identity shop); Speakeasy Café on Holly Hills Avenue (the veteran-owned two-story specialty-coffee shop); Woodward Lock & Key on Dewey Avenue; Reconnect Real Estate on South Grand Boulevard; Midwest BankCentre on Gravois Avenue; The Leona wedding venue on Leona Street; Moon Tree Tarot on Wilmington Avenue; the Heartland St. Louis Black Chamber of Commerce ; the Southwest Area Chamber of Commerce ; the privately-run Catholic St. Stephen Protomartyr School (preschool through 8th grade); and easy access to the Loughborough Commons retail center (Lowes, Schnucks, Starbucks). Holly Hills sits within walking distance of the Carondelet Branch Library (completed 1908, designed by Prague-born architect Ernst Preisler in Neoclassical style with Maine granite, funded by Andrew Carnegie as the third Carnegie branch in St. Louis, fully renovated in 2012) and the historic St. Anthony of Padua Church (1910, twin steeples) in adjacent Dutchtown.
Image: The Lyle House in Carondelet Park — the 1842 wood-framed Southern home of Alexander Lacey Lyle, whose 180-acre estate became Carondelet Park (purchased by the City in 1874, dedicated July 4, 1876). The Lyle House is a designated St. Louis City Landmark and the historic anchor of the park that borders Holly Hills along its southern edge — Wikimedia Commons , CC BY-SA

Holly Hills sits seven miles south of Downtown St. Louis at the terminus of South Grand Boulevard, sharing St. Louis’s humid continental climate — hot, humid summers, cold winters, and an active spring severe-weather season.

## Holly Hills Businesses & Neighborhood Guide | St Louis Near Me Directory

 Holly Hills, St. Louis

Holly Hills serves as South St. Louis’s most architecturally elegant 1920s residential showplace — designed as the city’s answer to Hollywood’s grace, anchored by the 180-acre Carondelet Park (dedicated July 4, 1876), the historic 1842 Lyle Mansion, the Carondelet YMCA Rec Plex, and Holly Hills Boulevard’s grand stretch of mansions, German-style castles, and Arts & Crafts bungalows from Arendes to Leona — offering environmental testing, custom millwork, branding, coffee, and chamber services across South Grand and Holly Hills Boulevard.

Holly Hills is one of St. Louis’s 79 official neighborhoods, located at **38.5683° N, 90.2749° W** in southeast St. Louis City. The neighborhood is bounded by **Grand Boulevard** on the east, **Holly Hills Boulevard and Carondelet Park** on the south, **Leona Street and the Union Pacific (formerly Missouri Pacific) Railroad** on the west, and **Bates Street then Walsh Street** on the north. Surrounding neighborhoods include **Dutchtown** to the north, **Bevo Mill** to the west and north, **Boulevard Heights** to the southwest, and **Carondelet** to the east. The neighborhood spans **ZIP codes 63111 and 63116** and sits approximately seven miles south of Downtown St. Louis at the terminus of South Grand Boulevard. Holly Hills is one of the cleanest, safest, and most tightly-knit residential neighborhoods in the city — a small-town atmosphere where neighbors know one another, many residents have lived here their entire lives, and the perimeter is largely landscaped by volunteer-led seasonal plantings of thousands of bulbs and perennials.

The land that Holly Hills now covers was originally part of the **Commonfields of the independent City of Carondelet** — the French Creole farming village founded in **1767** by **Clement Delor de Treget**, a former French naval officer who had been appointed syndic by the Spanish government to grant lots to settlers. By the time of the Louisiana Purchase in 1803, there were approximately 250 villagers living in 50 houses. The Commonfields stretched from present-day Virginia Avenue in the east to Morganford Road in the west, and from Lafayette Avenue south to Meramec Street — with grazing commons expanded south of River des Peres to a mile beyond Jefferson Barracks. Carondelet was originally called **Louisburg** in honor of King Louis XV of France, then **Prairie a Catalan** after settler Louis Catalan, before being officially renamed **Carondelet** in **1794** in honor of **Baron François Louis Hector de Carondelet**, a Fleming appointed Spanish governor of Louisiana. Informal names included **Delor’s Village** and **Vide Poche** (“empty pocket”), supposedly because Carondelet residents’ gambling skill would send their St. Louis neighbors home with empty pockets.

German immigrants began settling in Carondelet in the late 1840s, changing the character of the village from French Creole to German-American. Carondelet was **incorporated as an independent city on March 1, 1851**, and then **annexed by the City of St. Louis on April 4, 1870**. With annexation came the St. Louis park and library systems — in **1874**, the City purchased 180 acres of the old Carondelet Commons (plus part of the **Lyle estate**) for $143,000, establishing **Carondelet Park**. The park officially opened in 1875 and was **dedicated on July 4, 1876**, the centennial anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence. The land had previously belonged to **Alexander Lacey Lyle**, whose family built the **Lyle Mansion** on the property in **1842** (or 1850, by some accounts) — a Southern-sympathizing family who left St. Louis at the start of the Civil War. The Lyle House still stands in the park today and is a designated **St. Louis City Landmark**. The same era produced two other Carondelet firsts: **Carondelet native Susan Blow**, daughter of U.S. Representative **Henry Taylor Blow**, founded what is regarded as the **first continuous public-school kindergarten in the United States** at the **Des Peres School** (6303 Michigan Avenue) in **September 1873**, modeled on Friedrich Fröbel’s German concept.

In the **early 1920s**, developers **William A. Federer**, **Gus Arendes**, and **Don Livingston Sr.** purchased a large plot of land from the **Missouri Pacific Railroad** and developed the area north of Carondelet Park as the Holly Hills neighborhood. The name **“Holly Hills”** was derived from **Hollywood** and intended to reflect a similar level of grace and elegance — an aspirational California-style suburban vision transplanted to South St. Louis. An essential element of Federer’s plan was to construct homes of many different styles, sizes, and characters: from grand **German-style castles** and Tudor mansions to cozy **Arts & Crafts bungalows**. The **first building permit** in the community was issued in **1926** for a home on Holly Hills Boulevard across from Carondelet Park. The Great Depression scaled back many of the later homes from Federer’s original vision, but the showcase “Hollywood elegance” mansions along Holly Hills Boulevard from **Arendes Drive to Leona Street** remained the architectural calling card. Federer’s own residence has remained in his family and is still lovingly maintained by his daughter and her family. Street names within Holly Hills honor the developers (**Arendes Drive**, plus streets named for **William Federer** and **Don Livingston**) and other historic figures: **Adkins Avenue** (after steamboat captain Henry Adkins), **Alexander Street** (after Alexander Lacey Lyle), **Bates Street** (after Frederick Bates, the second governor of Missouri), **Bellerive Boulevard** (after Louis St. Ange de Bellerive, the pre-Spanish commandant of St. Louis), **Bowen Street** (after Confederate General John Bowen, a former St. Louis neighbor of Ulysses S. Grant), and **Burgen Avenue** (after the Burgenland province in eastern Austria, from the 1909 Burgen Place subdivision).

Carondelet Park, which borders the southern edge of Holly Hills along Holly Hills Boulevard, is the **third-largest park in St. Louis** at approximately 180 acres. It is bounded by **Holly Hills Boulevard** on the north, **Loughborough Avenue** on the south, **Interstate 55** on the east, and **Leona Street** on the west. The park’s undulating topography — shaped by underground caves and sinkholes — creates a Picturesque effect; nine sinkholes were joined in **1913** to form **Horseshoe Lake**, now one of two annually stocked fishing lakes. Scenic drives along the ridge lines were introduced in 1890. A bridge entering the park’s north side was constructed as part of an effort overseen by famed landscape architect **George Kessler** from 1902 to 1909 to link major parks and cemeteries along a singular artery. All historic amenities — the Lyle House, Boathouse, Music Pavilion, Old Stable, and Music Stand — were built prior to 1920. Carondelet Park is also unique as the **only original landscape in the St. Louis park system** — an unaltered Karst landscape that paints a picture of what the entire city could have looked like had it not been developed. The **Carondelet YMCA Rec Plex** sits at the east end of the park adjacent to I-55, and the one-mile **Carondelet Connector trail**, opened by **Great Rivers Greenway** in 2014, links the park’s trail system to the nine-mile **River des Peres Greenway**.

Today, Holly Hills is one of South St. Louis’s most desirable neighborhoods. It is a small, residential, tightly-knit community with very few intra-neighborhood businesses — commerce tends to cluster in adjacent Carondelet, Dutchtown, Bevo Mill, and Boulevard Heights. The neighborhood’s key business anchors today include **St. John Environmental Consulting, LLC** on Grace Avenue (the veteran-owned, BBB A+ accredited, AHERA-certified asbestos / mold / lead inspector with 25 years of experience); **Silver Fox Marketing** on Wilmington Avenue (15-year sign, vinyl-wrap, and brand identity shop); **Speakeasy Café** on Holly Hills Avenue (the veteran-owned two-story specialty-coffee shop); **St Louis Sash Corp.** on South 38th Street (the 35-year father-and-son custom wood door / window / millwork manufacturer for historic homes); **St Louis Laser** on South Broadway (industrial engraving); the **Heartland St. Louis Black Chamber of Commerce**; the **Southwest Area Chamber of Commerce**; **Andre’s Banquets & Catering** at Sunset Hills; the privately-run Catholic **St. Stephen Protomartyr School** (preschool through 8th grade); and easy access to the **Loughborough Commons** retail center (Lowes, Schnucks, Starbucks). Holly Hills sits within walking distance of the **Carondelet Branch Library** (completed 1908, designed by Prague-born architect Ernst Preisler in Neoclassical style with Maine granite, funded by Andrew Carnegie as the third Carnegie branch in St. Louis, fully renovated in 2012) and the historic **St. Anthony of Padua Church** (1910, twin steeples) in adjacent Dutchtown.

Image: The Lyle House in Carondelet Park — the 1842 wood-framed Southern home of Alexander Lacey Lyle, whose 180-acre estate became Carondelet Park (purchased by the City in 1874, dedicated July 4, 1876). The Lyle House is a designated St. Louis City Landmark and the historic anchor of the park that borders Holly Hills along its southern edge — Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA

Holly Hills sits seven miles south of Downtown St. Louis at 38.5683° N at the terminus of South Grand Boulevard, with seamless access to Interstate 55 (one mile east), South Broadway, the Carondelet historic district, and the Mississippi River bluffs at Bellerive Park. The neighborhood experiences St. Louis’s full humid continental climate: hot, humid summers with frequent 90°F days, cold winters with regular freezing temperatures, and an active spring severe weather season. 

Peak outdoor activity falls during spring, summer, and fall, when **Carondelet Park’s** 180 acres of rolling Karst topography along Holly Hills Boulevard draw heaviest visitor use at the two annually-stocked fishing lakes (including the 1913 Horseshoe Lake), the boathouse, the tennis courts, the softball / baseball / soccer fields, the horseshoe pits, the playgrounds, the picnic pavilions, the music pavilion, and the 1.6-mile bicycle path that connects to the **River des Peres Greenway** via the 2014 **Carondelet Connector**; when the **Carondelet YMCA Rec Plex** at the east end of the park is humming with indoor aquatic, gymnasium, and weight-room activity; and when the residential streets of **Holly Hills Boulevard** from Arendes to Leona host the volunteer-led seasonal bulb and perennial plantings that have made this neighborhood a perimeter showplace. 

Cool seasons drive intense indoor activity at **Speakeasy Café** at 527 Holly Hills Avenue (the veteran-owned two-story specialty coffee shop open seven days a week), **St. John Environmental Consulting** on Grace Avenue (year-round demand from homeowners of the 1920s brick housing stock for asbestos, lead, mold, and indoor air quality inspections), **Silver Fox Marketing** on Wilmington Avenue, **St Louis Sash Corp.** on South 38th Street (the 35-year custom millwork shop that supplies precision wood doors, windows, and architectural details for historic-home renovators), **St. Stephen Protomartyr School**, the **Carondelet Branch Library** on Michigan Avenue (renovated 2012), the **Loughborough Commons** retail center, and the indoor venues of nearby Bevo Mill, Dutchtown, Carondelet, and Boulevard Heights. The neighborhood’s 1926–1940s brick housing stock — including its Holly Hills Boulevard mansions, German-style castles, Tudor revivals, and Arts & Crafts bungalows — have weathered roughly a century of Missouri climate with the durability of the depression-era German-American masons who built them.

### Hyde Park Businesses & Neighborhood Guide | St Louis Near Me Directory
Hyde Park, St. Louis
Hyde Park anchors one of the oldest German-settled stretches of north St. Louis — founded in 1844 as the independent town of New Bremen by German immigrants and named, somewhat ironically, for Hyde Park in London — today defined by its National Register historic district, the twin 215-foot spires of Most Holy Trinity Catholic Church, the circa-1823 Bissell Mansion (the oldest surviving brick house in the city), the 14.5-acre Hyde Park itself, and a brick-and-flounder-house streetscape that recalls a turn-of-the-century European working-class neighborhood.
Hyde Park sits in north St. Louis at approximately 38.6615° N, 90.2141° W in zip code 63107. Per the City of St. Louis, the neighborhood is bounded by Ferry Street on the North, Interstate 70 on the East, Palm Street and Natural Bridge Avenue on the South, and Glasgow Avenue on the West — with Bremen, Salisbury, North Florissant, 20th, Blair, and Broadway among its key streets. Hyde Park is bordered by the College Hill and Fairground neighborhoods to the northwest, St. Louis Place and Old North St. Louis to the south, and the Near North Riverfront to the east. The neighborhood is a designated National Register Historic District and remains a predominantly Black community after decades of population decline.
The area first shifted from rural to urban in the 1840s , when German immigrants settled the affordable, river-overlooking land along old Bellefontaine Road (now Broadway) — then a produce route running north from downtown. Many of these families came from the German city of Bremen , and so the settlement was named New Bremen . A survey of the town was executed by Edward Hutawa in 1844 at the direction of four principal landowners — George Buchanan, E.C. Angelrodt, N.N. Destrehan, and Emil Mallinckrodt — who incorporated the town of Bremen in 1850 and gave their names to four of its east-west streets. Broadway was dedicated as a public highway on May 10, 1852.
The center and namesake of the neighborhood, Hyde Park itself, resulted from the sale of 14.5 acres to the city by the Farrar family estate in 1854 . Bernard G. Farrar, an early resident, had lost his life during the 1849 cholera epidemic while saving other victims; he had also donated the land at 14th and Mallinckrodt for the Most Holy Trinity Catholic Church. By 1856, this thriving new center of commercial and industrial activity was annexed by St. Louis. The park saw history unfold on July 4, 1863, when a Civil War-era riot erupted out of wartime tensions, killing two fairgoers and a number of Union soldiers.
The neighborhood’s defining landmark is Most Holy Trinity Catholic Church at 3519 North 14th Street. The Holy Trinity congregation was founded in 1848 as the mother church for German Catholics in north St. Louis; the present limestone edifice — a late French Gothic Revival design by architect Joseph Conradi , completed in 1898 — features a cruciform plan 155 feet long and twin spires rising 215 feet , visible for miles, including from I-70. The 1927 tornado severely damaged the rear of the church, destroying the upper choir and apse, which were later restored. Most Holy Trinity became a City Landmark in 1979 and today is part of St. Josephine Bakhita Parish .
Just east of the park, the Bissell Mansion at 4426 Randall Place is believed to be the oldest surviving brick house in the City of St. Louis. Built around 1823–1831 by Captain Lewis Bissell on a bluff overlooking a bend in the Mississippi, the Greek Revival home stayed in the Bissell family until 1882, became a rooming house in the 1920s, was nearly demolished for the construction of I-70 in the 1950s — a threat that helped spur the founding of the Landmarks Association of St. Louis — and became a City Landmark in 1971. It operates today as a restaurant and murder-mystery dinner theatre.
Hyde Park’s architecture spans nearly every decade since the 1840s — row houses and mansions, brick two- and four-family flats, and the distinctive St. Louis “flounder” house (a narrow, side-entry working-class form found mainly in the city’s oldest neighborhoods). Other landmarks include the 1909 Divoll Branch Library (one of five surviving Carnegie libraries in St. Louis, named “Best Old Building” by the Riverfront Times in 2019), the 1905 Henry Clay School (designed by William B. Ittner), the 1895 Bethlehem Evangelical Lutheran Church, and remnants of the historic Hyde Park Brewery . The neighborhood lost roughly 30% of its population per decade from 1990 through 2010.
Hyde Park’s modern business activity reflects its deep industrial and manufacturing heritage along the Blair Avenue and Salisbury Street corridors, though the honest count is small: seven verified, in-boundary businesses, not the padded ten this page once listed. Anchor manufacturers Launer Voss Steel Fabricators on Buchanan and the Essmueller Machine Co on Blair (a St. Louis material-handling-equipment maker founded in 1878) sit alongside Saint Louis Mat and Linen on Salisbury, Schroeder Truck Repair on North 13th Street, the 80-year-old Piekutowski’s European-style sausage shop on North Florissant, LinkSTL’s youth programs on North 14th Street, and a single-person web-development firm on Newhouse Avenue. That is the entire genuinely local business base — a real, if narrow, working corridor rather than a wide commercial strip.
Image: The historic Bissell Street District in Hyde Park — part of the 19th-century German-built brick streetscape that defines this north St. Louis National Register neighborhood — Wikimedia Commons / CC BY-SA 3.0

Hyde Park sees the same four-season Midwest swing as the rest of St. Louis — humid summers, cold winters — with little effect on a business corridor built around steel fabrication, machine manufacturing, and specialty foods rather than foot traffic.
What remains of Hyde Park’s commercial life today is concentrated, not spread out — a working stretch of Blair Avenue, Salisbury Street, and North 13th where Launer Voss Steel Fabricators, Essmueller Machine Co, Saint Louis Mat and Linen, and Schroeder Truck Repair keep the neighborhood’s manufacturing identity alive, plus Piekutowski’s 80-year-old sausage counter, LinkSTL’s youth programs, and one small web-development firm. Seven verified local businesses on a map built for far more industry than currently operates here — that is the honest count.
The rest of Hyde Park is residential: block after block of the brick two- and four-family flats and flounder houses that survived a population loss of roughly 30% per decade from 1990 through 2010, radiating out from Most Holy Trinity’s twin spires and the 14.5-acre park itself. A local would draw the neighborhood’s real edge not at the official Ferry-to-Glasgow boundary lines but at the historic Bissell Street district blocks around the park, where the preserved 19th-century streetscape is still intact. Today Hyde Park serves two audiences at once: the residents and parishioners who stayed through the decline, and the contractors, fleet managers, and procurement officers who still drive in for what Launer Voss, Essmueller, and Schroeder do best.
