### Frequently Asked Questions 
Q. What defines the Hyde Park neighborhood? 
A. Hyde Park is a National Register Historic District in north St. Louis, founded in 1844 as the German immigrant town of New Bremen and renamed for London’s Hyde Park after the city bought its namesake 14.5-acre park in 1854. Its boundary runs Ferry Street, Interstate 70, Palm Street/Natural Bridge Avenue, and Glasgow Avenue, in zip code 63107.

Q. How does St Louis Near Me Directory help Hyde Park businesses? 
A. St Louis Near Me Directory gives Hyde Park businesses a dedicated, schema-optimized local listing built around the Blair Avenue and Salisbury Street corridor, Most Holy Trinity Church, and the historic district — helping local manufacturers, food makers, and service providers capture “near me” searches a national profile alone would miss. Join St Louis Near Me Directory to get listed.

Q. What types of businesses are most common in Hyde Park? 
A. Hyde Park’s business base is small and industrial: Launer Voss Steel Fabricators and the 1878-founded Essmueller Machine Co anchor the Blair Avenue manufacturing corridor, joined by Saint Louis Mat and Linen, Schroeder Truck Repair, the 80-year-old Piekutowski’s sausage shop, LinkSTL’s youth programs, and a small local web-development firm — seven verified businesses, not ten.

Q. What kinds of dining, retail, and recreation options are available in Hyde Park? 
A. Dining and retail are limited to what is already on this list — Piekutowski’s 80-year-old Polish sausage shop on North Florissant is the neighborhood’s best-known food stop. Recreation centers on the 14.5-acre Hyde Park itself and neighboring Windsor Park, with a fishing lake, picnic pavilions, playgrounds, tennis and basketball courts, horseshoe pits, and softball fields.

Q. Are there neighborhood landmarks, parks, and historic sites in Hyde Park? 
A. Yes — Hyde Park is a National Register Historic District. Landmarks include Most Holy Trinity Catholic Church (1898, twin 215-foot spires), the circa-1823 Bissell Mansion (the city’s oldest surviving brick house, now a dinner theatre), the 1909 Divoll Branch Carnegie Library, the 1905 Henry Clay School, and the 14.5-acre Hyde Park itself, all within the historic Bissell Street brick streetscape.

Q. What is it like to live in Hyde Park? 
A. Hyde Park is a quiet, predominantly residential, historically Black neighborhood of brick flats and flounder houses that lost roughly 30% of its population per decade between 1990 and 2010. Commercial activity is thin — seven verified local businesses — concentrated on the Blair Avenue and Salisbury Street corridor, with most of the neighborhood given over to housing, the historic district, and the park itself.

Q. How do residents and visitors get around Hyde Park? 
A. Interstate 70 runs along Hyde Park’s eastern edge, giving quick access to downtown St. Louis and the riverfront. Inside the neighborhood, the historic street grid of Bremen, Salisbury, North Florissant, 20th, Blair, and Broadway carries local traffic past the park, Most Holy Trinity Church, and the Blair Avenue business corridor.

Q. How can residents and visitors explore more services around Hyde Park?

### 10 Best St Louis Businesses in Jeff-Vander-Lou, MO (2026)

### Jeff-Vander-Lou Neighborhood Guide – St. Louis History & Businesses

Jeff-Vander-Lou — known across the city as "JVL" — is a north St. Louis neighborhood whose name was coined in 1966 by housing activist Macler Shepard, drawn from the Jefferson, Vandeventer, and St. Louis Avenue thoroughfares. Historically the Yeatman district, it was one of the first areas where African Americans could own property, home to the former Sportsman's Park and the landmark St. Alphonsus "Rock" Church, with a deep legacy of grassroots community development.

### Jeff-Vander-Lou Businesses & Neighborhood Guide | St Louis Near Me Directory
Jeff-Vander-Lou, St. Louis
Jeff-Vander-Lou — known throughout the city simply as “JVL” — is a north St. Louis neighborhood whose name was coined in 1966 by housing activist Macler C. Shepard, drawn from the three major thoroughfares that frame it: Jefferson, Vandeventer, and St. Louis Avenue. Historically the Yeatman district, it was one of the first areas in St. Louis where African Americans were allowed to own real estate, and it remains anchored today by Grand Avenue, the historic Sportsman’s Park site, and a deep legacy of grassroots community development.
Jeff-Vander-Lou sits in north St. Louis at approximately 38.6504° N, 90.2280° W , spanning zip codes 63106, 63107, 63108, and 63113. Per the City of St. Louis, the neighborhood is situated between North Vandeventer Avenue on the northwest, Natural Bridge Avenue on the northeast, North Jefferson Avenue on the east, Delmar Boulevard on the south, and North Compton Avenue and Dr. Martin Luther King Drive on the southwest. Grand Avenue serves as the central commercial corridor, giving residents and visitors easy access to Interstates 70 and 64. JVL borders Covenant Blu-Grand Center, the Ville, St. Louis Place, and Old North St. Louis.
Historically, most of JVL was part of the Yeatman area , named for James E. Yeatman , a prominent Tennessee native who relocated to St. Louis in 1842, co-founded the Mercantile Library Association, served as president of the Merchants Bank, and directed the Western Sanitary Commission during the Civil War. Yeatman’s historic boundaries ran Grand on the west, Delmar on the south, Jefferson on the east, and St. Louis Avenue on the north. The neighborhood’s two national historic districts — Yeatman Square and the Lindell Park Subdivision — testify to its historic significance, and a sub-neighborhood called Lindell Park (just east of Grand and Dodier) still features beautiful homes.
In a time of racial segregation following the end of slavery, JVL was originally designated as the city’s “Negro District” under a controversial 1915 segregation ordinance — and was one of the only places where African Americans were permitted to own land. It grew into a vibrant African American community whose contributions are still felt across St. Louis. By the second half of the 20th century, however, housing conditions had declined sharply, and federal “urban renewal” programs threatened to demolish large sections of the neighborhood.
The neighborhood’s defining story is the work of Macler C. Shepard (1917–2005) , an Arkansas-born upholsterer and housing activist who had twice been displaced by downtown clearance — including the construction of the infamous Pruitt-Igoe complex. When the city proposed a 1966 bond issue to carve a highway through the near-north side, Shepard and his neighbors fought back, and that year he founded Jeff-Vander-Lou, Inc. Between 1968 and 1978, the organization acquired and rehabilitated dozens of buildings, building or renovating more than 600 units of housing and attracting a shoe factory and millions in private investment — work that earned Shepard a Rockefeller Public Service Award in 1979.
JVL’s most famous lost landmark is Sportsman’s Park at Grand and Dodier — built in 1881 and, for decades, home to both the St. Louis Browns and the St. Louis Cardinals. More Major League games were played there than at any other ballpark, and it hosted ten World Series, three All-Star Games, and hometown greats like Stan Musial, Bob Gibson, and Lou Brock before baseball moved downtown in 1966. The site is now home to the Herbert Hoover Boys & Girls Club . Towering over the neighborhood’s western edge is the St. Alphonsus Liguori “Rock” Church (1118 N. Grand), a Gothic Revival landmark built of rough-cut stone in 1872 with a 237-foot steeple, and one of the city’s most historic Black Catholic parishes.
Architecturally, JVL preserves some of the largest concentrations of Second Empire and limestone-faced row housing in St. Louis outside Lafayette Square, particularly south of Cass Avenue. Anchor institutions today include St. Louis Community College , the St. Louis Housing Authority , Vashon High School, Columbia Community School, and the only U.S. branch of the worldwide corporation Sensient Colors. The neighborhood is roughly 97% African American and, after decades of population loss, is the focus of intensive place-based redevelopment.
JVL’s modern business activity reflects its position as a hub for economic-empowerment and professional services along the Grand Avenue and North Jefferson Avenue corridors, fueled by place-based investment and redevelopment initiatives that aim to transform vacant lots into viable commercial and residential space. The listings on this page draw from the broader Jeff-Vander-Lou / Yeatman / Grand Avenue corridor — with anchor providers including the Northside Economic Empowerment Center on Cass Avenue, the Heartland St. Louis Black Chamber of Commerce, the St. Louis Record Center on Glasgow, Liberty Tax on Page, the third-generation Clark’s Barbershop on St. Louis Avenue, Doorways’ Jefferson Campus, and the Jeff-Vander-Lou Neighborhood Association, plus chamber and directory partners serving the broader St. Louis region.
Image: The St. Alphonsus Liguori “Rock” Church (1872) on North Grand Boulevard — the Gothic Revival stone landmark and historic Black Catholic parish that anchors Jeff-Vander-Lou’s western edge — Wikimedia Commons / CC BY-SA by Farragutful

Jeff-Vander-Lou runs on St. Louis’s ordinary four-season calendar, with summer bringing the most foot traffic to Grand Avenue and the Herbert Hoover Boys & Girls Club at the old Sportsman’s Park site, and winter pushing business indoors to the tax office, the record center, and Doorways’ year-round housing services.
What a visitor notices first in Jeff-Vander-Lou is not subtle: block after block carries vacant lots and boarded storefronts where the row houses and small industry Macler Shepard’s organization fought to save once stood, and the population has kept shrinking for decades. What is easy to miss driving through is the amount of real work aimed at reversing that — the Northside Economic Empowerment Center training small-business owners out of the old Sumner High School annex, the Jeff-Vander-Lou Neighborhood Association still doing the resident advocacy Shepard’s organization started in 1966, and Doorways’ Jefferson Campus running supportive housing a few blocks from where Sportsman’s Park once stood. Neither picture is the whole story by itself, and a fair account of JVL has to hold both at once.

A. Jeff-Vander-Lou — known locally as “JVL” — takes its name from the three streets that frame it: Jefferson, Vandeventer, and St. Louis Avenue, coined in 1966 by housing activist Macler C. Shepard. Historically the Yeatman district, it was one of the first St. Louis neighborhoods where African Americans were allowed to own real estate, and it remains anchored by Grand Avenue and the old Sportsman’s Park site.

Q. What kinds of dining, retail, and recreation options are available in Jeff Vanderlou? 
A. Jeff-Vander-Lou has no commercial strip of its own left — most dining and retail followed the city’s population south of Delmar decades ago. For recreation, the Herbert Hoover Boys & Girls Club now occupies the former Sportsman’s Park site at Grand and Dodier.

Q. Are there neighborhood landmarks, parks, and historic sites in Jeff Vanderlou? 
A. Yes — the neighborhood’s most famous lost landmark is Sportsman’s Park at Grand and Dodier, former home of the Cardinals and Browns, now the site of the Herbert Hoover Boys & Girls Club. Q. What is it like to live in Jeff Vanderlou? 
A. Living in Jeff-Vander-Lou today means holding two realities at once: block after block of vacant lots and boarded storefronts where row houses once stood, alongside real, active redevelopment work. 2801 Dr Martin Luther King Dr, St. Louis, MO 63106, USA · (314) 535-8976

Association $

Neighborhood Association

Best for: local residents and seniors



The Jeff-Vander-Lou Neighborhood Association is the modern continuation of Jeff-Vander-Lou, Inc., the community development organization founded in October 1966 by housing activist Macler C. Shepard (1917–2005). The organization took its name — and gave the neighborhood its name — from the three major thoroughfares of Jefferson, Vandeventer, and St. Louis Avenue, the routes by which downtown commuter traffic once flowed through the area. For more than a decade, Shepard and the JVL organization worked to acquire and rehabilitate hundreds of homes and improve living conditions for homeowners and renters at a time when federal urban-renewal programs threatened the neighborhood with demolition. Today the association continues that legacy through resident advocacy, affordable and senior housing support, an opportunity house serving those experiencing homelessness, and neighborhood resource coordination. Best suited for Jeff-Vander-Lou residents, seniors, and homeowners seeking community resources, housing assistance, and a voice in the neighborhood’s ongoing revitalization.

### Kings Oak Businesses & Neighborhood Guide | St Louis Near Me Directory
Kings Oak, St. Louis
Kings Oak is one of the smallest neighborhoods in St. Louis — a compact, highly visible enclave just south of Forest Park and Interstate 64, named for two of the streets that frame it: Kingshighway Boulevard and Oakland Avenue. With fewer than 80 homes tucked among major institutions like Saint Louis University High School and the Saint Louis Science Center, it’s a quiet, walkable pocket of early-1900s homes anchored by an industrial-and-hospitality corridor that has increasingly turned former garages and warehouses into breweries, coworking spaces, and event venues.
Kings Oak sits in the central-south part of St. Louis at approximately 38.6268° N, 90.2726° W in zip code 63110. Per the City of St. Louis, the neighborhood is bounded by Oakland Avenue on the North, Manchester Avenue on the South, Kingshighway Boulevard on the East, and Macklind Avenue on the West. The neighborhood’s name comes from the first syllables of two of those boundary streets — “Kings” from Kingshighway and “Oak” from Oakland. It is highly visible from I-64, sitting directly across from Forest Park’s baseball fields and horse stables.
The houses in Kings Oak were nearly all built in the early 1900s , around the time of the 1904 St. Louis World’s Fair held in adjacent Forest Park. With fewer than 80 homes — most clustered along the neighborhood’s eastern edge near Kingshighway, on streets like Lawn Place, Berthold, and Wise — Kings Oak is one of the smallest and least-populous neighborhoods in the city. Rows of densely arranged, well-kept centennial homes line tree-shaded sidewalks, giving the residential core a quiet, peaceful character despite its position between several heavily trafficked corridors.
Several recognizable institutions anchor the small neighborhood and account for much of its land. The Saint Louis Science Center at 5050 Oakland — with its James S. McDonnell Planetarium, OMNIMAX theater, and 700-plus interactive exhibits — occupies the former Falstaff Brewing Corporation headquarters site (earlier the location of St. Louis University’s Walsh Stadium). Saint Louis University High School (SLUH) and the Compton-Drew Investigative Learning Center middle school (built where the St. Louis Merchants Exchange once stood) round out the institutional anchors.
Kings Oak’s history traces to the broader Oakland area within the old Gratiot League Square. The Manchester Avenue corridor along the southern edge developed as a light-industrial district, spurred by the arrival of the Pacific Railroad in the 1850s and the excellent clay deposits that brought fire-brick works to the vicinity. A notable surviving landmark is the Swedish National Society building (erected 1913) along Kingshighway just north of Manchester — one of several historic structures reflecting the area’s layered industrial and immigrant past.
Today the neighborhood is best known for the adaptive reuse of its industrial spaces. Former garages and warehouses along Oakland, Macklind, and Manchester have become modern coworking and co-warehousing facilities, microbreweries, and event venues — with Modern Brewery on Oakland a standout, occupying a transformed café space. The neighborhood also hosts the Carol Gates Throop pet memorial park along Macklind, across from the Humane Society, and is connected to Forest Park via a pedestrian tunnel under I-64.
Kings Oak’s position is its defining business asset: it sits at the convergence of Forest Park, the Cortex Innovation Community, The Grove entertainment district, and the Central West End, with Barnes-Jewish Hospital just across I-64 and downtown St. Louis a five-minute drive east. That central, high-visibility location draws a steady mix of professionals, students, museum visitors, and diners from across the metro into its small footprint.
Kings Oak’s modern business activity reflects this blend of light industry, professional services, and destination hospitality along the South Kingshighway, Oakland, Manchester, and Macklind corridors. The listings on this page draw from the broader Kings Oak / Oakland-Kingshighway corridor, with anchor providers including ISC Contracting and Essential Audio Visual on South Kingshighway, Modern Brewery & The Kings Oak on Oakland, and the Ten by Three nonprofit gift shop — plus the neighborhood’s two biggest destinations by far, the Saint Louis Science Center and its OMNIMAX Theater, both also on Oakland Avenue.
Image: A residential streetscape in Kings Oak — one of St. Louis’s smallest neighborhoods, with early-1900s homes near Forest Park and the Saint Louis Science Center — Wikimedia Commons / CC BY-SA 2.0 by Paul Sableman

Kings Oak follows St. Louis’s typical four-season pattern — hot, humid summers and cold winters — the same as the rest of the city, with the Saint Louis Science Center and Modern Brewery’s patio drawing the neighborhood’s heaviest foot traffic in the warmer months.
What actually makes Kings Oak unusual isn’t the weather — it’s the math. At roughly 0.17 square miles with fewer than 80 houses, this is one of the smallest of St. Louis’s 79 official neighborhoods, and a large share of even that small footprint belongs to institutions rather than houses or shops: the Science Center’s campus, SLUH’s grounds, the Compton-Drew middle school. There isn’t a real commercial “main street” here the way a bigger neighborhood has one — there’s a short run of former light-industrial buildings along South Kingshighway and Macklind that has turned into a general contractor, an AV company, and a landscaper; a handful of residential blocks tucked against the eastern edge; and two of the region’s most-visited attractions sitting on land that used to be a brewery headquarters and a college ballpark. A business with a Kings Oak address isn’t really serving a self-contained neighborhood the way a business in a bigger, denser part of the city is — it’s serving the tens of thousands of people who pass through for the Science Center, a SLUH event, or a drive down Kingshighway, alongside barely 80 houses’ worth of actual neighbors.

### Frequently Asked Questions 
Q. What defines the Kings Oak neighborhood? 
A. Kings Oak is one of St. Louis’s smallest neighborhoods — a compact 0.17-square-mile enclave just south of Forest Park and I-64, with fewer than 80 homes. Its name comes from the two streets that frame it, Kingshighway Boulevard and Oakland Avenue, and much of its footprint belongs to major institutions like Saint Louis University High School and the Saint Louis Science Center rather than houses.

Q. How does St Louis Near Me Directory help Kings Oak businesses? 
A. St Louis Near Me Directory builds a neighborhood-focused page tying a Kings Oak business to local search signals around the Saint Louis Science Center, Modern Brewery, and the South Kingshighway, Oakland, Manchester, and Macklind corridors. Plans expand a business’s existing Google Business Profile rather than replace it, with plain-English service, no competitor ads, and no long-term contracts.

Q. What types of businesses are most common in Kings Oak? 
A. A mix of light industry, professional services, and destination hospitality along the South Kingshighway, Oakland, Manchester, and Macklind corridors — a general contractor, an AV company, a landscaper, two chambers of commerce, a fair-trade gift shop, and a craft brewery. Two regional destinations, the Saint Louis Science Center and its OMNIMAX Theater, dwarf everything else by visitor volume.

Q. What kinds of dining, retail, and recreation options are available in Kings Oak? 
A. Modern Brewery & The Kings Oak on Oakland Avenue anchors dining, with communal seating, a patio, and its signature Citrapolis IPA. Ten by Three, a fair-trade gift shop, and Glorious Gardens, a residential landscaper, cover retail and outdoor design. For recreation, the Saint Louis Science Center and OMNIMAX Theater sit right in the neighborhood, with Forest Park a short walk through the I-64 pedestrian tunnel.

Q. Are there neighborhood landmarks, parks, and historic sites in Kings Oak? 
A. The Saint Louis Science Center at 5050 Oakland Avenue is the defining landmark, built in 1991 on the former Falstaff Brewing Corporation headquarters site — once Saint Louis University’s Walsh Stadium. Saint Louis University High School and the Swedish National Society building (1913) round out the neighborhood’s institutional and historic anchors, alongside the Carol Gates Throop pet memorial park on Macklind.

Q. What is it like to live in Kings Oak? 
A. Quiet and unusually small: fewer than 80 houses, most clustered along the eastern edge near Kingshighway, on tree-shaded streets of well-kept early-1900s homes. A resident here isn’t really part of a self-contained neighborhood the way a bigger district is — it’s a tiny residential pocket surrounded by tens of thousands of daily visitors to the Science Center, SLUH, and Forest Park.

Q. How do residents and visitors get around Kings Oak? 
A. Kings Oak is bounded by Oakland Avenue to the north, Manchester Avenue to the south, Kingshighway Boulevard to the east, and Macklind Avenue to the west — all heavily trafficked corridors highly visible from Interstate 64. A pedestrian tunnel under I-64 connects the neighborhood directly to Forest Park, and downtown St. Louis is about a five-minute drive east.

### Kingsway East Businesses & Neighborhood Guide | St Louis Near Me Directory
Kingsway East, St. Louis
Kingsway East is a compact north St. Louis neighborhood within the historic Arlington section, bounded by the Natural Bridge Avenue commercial corridor and anchored by W.C. Handy Park — named for the “Father of the Blues,” composer of the “St. Louis Blues.” Defined by brick bungalows, frame cottages, and multi-unit flats built largely between 1900 and 1920, and ringed by some of the most beautifully landscaped stretches of North Kingshighway in the city, Kingsway East is a close-knit, predominantly Black community holding tightly to its history.
Kingsway East sits in north St. Louis at approximately 38.6683° N, 90.2526° W , spanning parts of zip codes 63113 and 63115 across roughly 0.49 square miles. Per the City of St. Louis, the neighborhood is defined by Natural Bridge Avenue on the North, Dr. Martin Luther King Drive on the South, Marcus Avenue on the East, and Kingshighway Boulevard on the West. It is bordered by The Greater Ville, Penrose, Kingsway West, and Fountain Park , and falls within the city’s 12th Ward. The 2020 census counted 2,502 residents — roughly 93% Black — reflecting a steady population decline over recent decades.
The neighborhood lies within an historic section known as Arlington , which takes its name from John W. Burd’s Arlington Grove subdivision of 1868 . A memorable disaster in the area’s history occurred in October 1916 , when the Christian Brothers College building was destroyed by fire — one of the worst in the city’s history, taking ten lives. Industrial activity in the area owes its development to the construction of the Terminal Railroad belt line around 1900 , and the housing stock that followed gave Kingsway East its enduring character of early-20th-century brick residences.
The neighborhood’s signature green space is W.C. Handy Park , an 11.96-acre park established in 1941 at Euclid and Ashland. It is named for William Christopher Handy (1873–1958) , widely known as the “Father of the Blues,” who spent time in St. Louis around 1893 — an experience that inspired one of his best-known works, the “St. Louis Blues” (published 1914), one of the first blues songs to succeed as a pop standard and the inspiration for the foxtrot dance step. The park offers four baseball fields, a playground, a three-quarter-mile asphalt walking trail, four horseshoe pits, a full basketball court, and multi-purpose athletic fields.
Historically, Natural Bridge Avenue was a major St. Louis commercial corridor, lined with notable buildings constructed in the late 1920s and early 1930s — many of which still stand and frame the neighborhood’s northern edge today. The housing stock throughout Kingsway East is varied, blending shotgun houses, four-squares, and bungalows, with several beautifully maintained streets including Wabada Place, Northland Place, and Maffitt Avenue , plus a distinctive stretch of mid-century homes unlike any elsewhere in the city.
Community institutions remain central to the neighborhood. Hickey Elementary School is the sole school within Kingsway East’s boundaries, with Sumner High School, Ashland Elementary, and others nearby. The Kingsway Housing Corporation works alongside residents to preserve and continue the neighborhood’s revitalization, while ECHO (Emergency Children’s Home) provides social, emotional, and residential services to area youth. Neighboring churches — especially Immanuel Lutheran and Cote Brilliante Presbyterian — offer a range of activity programs for the community.
The stretch of North Kingshighway bordering the neighborhood is among the most thoughtfully designed in the city, with landscaped gardens, mature trees, and narrowed lanes that create an attractive, calming gateway between Kingsway East and the rest of St. Louis. Quick connections to Interstates 70 and 64 via the Kingshighway and Natural Bridge corridors keep the neighborhood linked to downtown, the Cortex Innovation Community, and the broader metro.
Kingsway East’s modern business activity is anchored by the Natural Bridge Avenue and Kingshighway Boulevard corridors , with a notable concentration of beauty and personal-care retailers alongside established general contractors who handle the seasonal demands of Missouri weather. The listings on this page draw from the broader Kingsway East / Natural Bridge / Arlington corridor — with anchor providers including the high-volume Hollywood Beauty Supply on Kingshighway, the artisan oils of The Prince Collection on Natural Bridge, Global Bundles on Dr. Martin Luther King Drive, the 25-year, BBB A+ / MBE-certified Tough Enough Construction, World Electronics, Hunt Brothers Pizza on North Euclid Avenue, plus the civic and directory partners serving the broader St. Louis region.
Image: A residential streetscape along Wabada Avenue in Kingsway East — one of the neighborhood’s well-maintained streets of early-20th-century brick homes — Wikimedia Commons / CC BY 2.0 by Paul Sableman

Like the rest of north St. Louis, Kingsway East runs a classic Midwest four-season cycle — humid summers that fill W.C. Handy Park’s ballfields and walking trail, and snowy winters that keep Tough Enough Construction’s emergency roofers busy on the neighborhood’s century-old brick homes.
Kingshighway Boulevard is the literal line the two Kingsways split on. East of it — here — you get the Blues history and the beauty-retail corridor: W.C. Handy Park, Hollywood Beauty Supply, The Prince Collection, Global Bundles, all inside a residential grid of century-old brick bungalows. Cross Kingshighway west and the character changes fast: Kingsway West trades the beauty-retail storefronts for logistics and rigging firms working the I-70 gateway, anchored by Sherman Park and the Wohl Recreation Center instead of W.C. Handy Park. Same Arlington-era brick, same railroad-driven history on both sides — but a different corridor and a different set of businesses.
Kingsway East today is overwhelmingly residential — a close-knit, predominantly Black community with far more homes than storefronts. The businesses anchoring its corridor lean toward everyday, walk-to needs: beauty supply, hair extensions, a general contractor for the century-old housing stock, an electronics shop, and now a convenience-store pizza counter on North Euclid. It is not a retail destination like Central West End, a mile or so away; it is a neighborhood serving itself.

### Frequently Asked Questions 
Q. What defines the Kingsway East neighborhood? 
A. Kingsway East is a compact north St. Louis neighborhood within the historic Arlington section, bounded by Natural Bridge Avenue, Dr. Martin Luther King Drive, Marcus Avenue, and Kingshighway Boulevard. It is anchored by W.C. Handy Park and defined by brick bungalows, frame cottages, and multi-unit flats built largely between 1900 and 1920, home to a close-knit, predominantly Black community.

Q. How does St Louis Near Me Directory help Kingsway East businesses? 
A. St Louis Near Me Directory strengthens neighborhood-focused visibility for businesses serving Kingsway East by combining local content with curated listings. Joining gives a Kingsway East business stronger local search signals tied to the Natural Bridge and Kingshighway corridors, Dr. Martin Luther King Drive, and W.C. Handy Park, helping it stand out to nearby residents and shoppers.

Q. What types of businesses are most common in Kingsway East? 
A. Kingsway East’s business activity is anchored by the Natural Bridge Avenue and Kingshighway Boulevard corridors, with a strong concentration of beauty and personal-care retailers alongside established contractors — Hollywood Beauty Supply, The Prince Collection’s botanical oils, and Global Bundles, joined by the 25-year Tough Enough Construction, World Electronics, and a Hunt Brothers Pizza counter serving everyday, walk-to needs.

Q. What kinds of dining, retail, and recreation options are available in Kingsway East? 
A. Dining is limited to a Hunt Brothers Pizza counter on North Euclid Avenue for a quick, cheap slice. Retail centers on beauty and personal care: Hollywood Beauty Supply on Kingshighway, The Prince Collection’s hand-crafted botanical oils on Natural Bridge, and Global Bundles’ hair extensions. For recreation, W.C. Handy Park offers four baseball fields, a walking trail, horseshoe pits, and a basketball court.

Q. Are there neighborhood landmarks, parks, and historic sites in Kingsway East? 
A. Yes — W.C. Handy Park, 11.96 acres established in 1941, honors the “Father of the Blues,” who wrote the “St. Louis Blues” after time spent in the city around 1893. The neighborhood sits in the historic Arlington section, named for an 1868 subdivision, and the Natural Bridge Avenue corridor still carries notable commercial buildings from the late 1920s and early 1930s.

Q. What is it like to live in Kingsway East? 
A. Kingsway East today is overwhelmingly residential — a close-knit, predominantly Black community with far more homes than storefronts. The businesses anchoring its corridor lean toward everyday, walk-to needs: beauty supply, hair extensions, a general contractor for the century-old housing stock, an electronics shop, and a convenience-store pizza counter. It is not a retail destination like Central West End; it is a neighborhood serving itself.

Q. How do residents and visitors get around Kingsway East? 
A. Kingsway East is framed by the Natural Bridge Avenue and Kingshighway Boulevard corridors, with quick connections to Interstates 70 and 64 that keep the neighborhood linked to downtown, the Cortex Innovation Community, and the broader metro. The stretch of North Kingshighway bordering the neighborhood is landscaped with mature trees and narrowed lanes, forming a calming gateway between Kingsway East and the rest of the city.

### Kingsway West Businesses & Neighborhood Guide | St Louis Near Me Directory
Kingsway West, St. Louis
Kingsway West is a north St. Louis neighborhood within the historic Arlington section, framed by the Natural Bridge Avenue commercial corridor and a tight residential grid of early-1900s brick homes. Bordered by Union Boulevard, Dr. Martin Luther King Drive, Natural Bridge Avenue, and North Kingshighway, it sits at a geographically central, well-connected point in the city — close to Interstate 70, anchored by Sherman Park and the Wohl Recreation Center, and home to a mix of long-standing community institutions, logistics and industrial firms, and neighbor-led organizations working on revitalization.
Kingsway West sits in northwest St. Louis at approximately 38.6712° N, 90.2701° W , spanning parts of zip codes 63113 and 63115. Per the City of St. Louis, the neighborhood is defined by Union Boulevard on the Northwest, Dr. Martin Luther King Drive on the Southwest, Natural Bridge Avenue on the Northeast, and North Kingshighway on the Southeast. It is bordered by the Kingsway East, Academy, Wells/Goodfellow, and Mark Twain/I-70 Industrial neighborhoods, and falls within the city’s 12th Ward. The compact, roughly 0.42-square-mile neighborhood is home to about 2,600 residents.
The neighborhood lies within an historic section known as Arlington , which takes its name from John W. Burd’s Arlington Grove subdivision of 1868 . A memorable disaster in the area’s history occurred in October 1916 , when the Christian Brothers College building was destroyed by a fire — one of the worst in the city’s history, taking ten lives. Like neighboring Kingsway East, the area shares the layered residential-and-industrial story of the broader Arlington district along the Kingshighway corridor.
Industrial activity in Kingsway West owes its development to the construction of the Terminal Railroad belt line around 1900 . The convenience of rail access, combined with plenty of adjacent land, brought numerous industrial plants and logistics operations to the area — a legacy still visible today in the warehousing, distribution, and rigging firms clustered near the I-70 corridor and along Union Boulevard. A stretch of businesses and commercial uses runs along Natural Bridge Avenue through the neighborhood.
The neighborhood’s housing reflects its early-1900s origins, with a tight grid of brick residences alongside newer development. The Academy -adjacent edges feature large single-family homes and two- and four-family structures, while Kings Heights is a newer development of condominiums and attached townhomes in a private setting, and new residential construction has appeared on Norwood Square . Several historic churches anchor the community, including Cote Brilliante Presbyterian, Immanuel Lutheran, Most Blessed Sacrament Catholic, and Memorial Boulevard Christian Church.
Civic life in Kingsway West is anchored by Sherman Park and the Wohl Recreation Center on Kingshighway, which offers an indoor swimming pool, fitness and dance classes, cooking courses, and homework help for students. Lexington Elementary School (built 1995) serves the neighborhood’s youngest students, and the nearby Julia Davis and Cabanne branch libraries provide additional resources. ### Frequently Asked Questions 
Q. What defines the Kingsway West neighborhood? 
A. Kingsway West is defined by its place in the historic Arlington section of north St. Louis, bounded by Union Boulevard, Dr. Martin Luther King Drive, Natural Bridge Avenue, and North Kingshighway. It’s a tight grid of early-1900s brick homes anchored by Sherman Park and the Wohl Recreation Center, with a legacy of logistics and industrial firms drawn by the Terminal Railroad belt line built around 1900.

Q. What types of businesses are most common in Kingsway West?

Listed providers include the neighbor-led Kingsway West Neighborhood Association, WIN Warehouse, Clark Logistic Services and HWP Rigging in distribution and industrial moving, business and answering-service firms, and the Wohl Recreation Center.

Q. What kinds of dining, retail, and recreation options are available in Kingsway West? 
A. Kingsway West has little dining or retail of its own beyond the general commercial stretch along Natural Bridge Avenue — no restaurants are named among its listed businesses. Recreation is the strength: Sherman Park and the Wohl Recreation Center offer an indoor pool, tennis courts, ball fields, dance and cooking classes, and homework help, making it the neighborhood’s true community hub.

Q. Are there neighborhood landmarks, parks, and historic sites in Kingsway West? 
A. Yes — Sherman Park and the Wohl Recreation Center anchor civic life, and several historic churches remain, including Cote Brilliante Presbyterian, Immanuel Lutheran, and Most Blessed Sacrament Catholic. The neighborhood sits within the historic Arlington section, named for John W. Burd’s 1868 Arlington Grove subdivision, and was the site of a deadly 1916 fire that destroyed the Christian Brothers College building.

Q. What is it like to live in Kingsway West? 
A. Kingsway West is a compact, 0.42-square-mile neighborhood of about 2,600 residents living in a tight grid of early-1900s brick homes, newer Kings Heights condos and townhomes, and new construction on Norwood Square. Observers describe it as “holding on” and steadily stabilizing, with proud long-time residents, well-kept properties, active churches, and the resident-led Kingsway West Neighborhood Association working on revitalization since 2018.

Q. How do residents and visitors get around Kingsway West? 
A. Kingsway West sits at a geographically central point in the city, bounded by Union Boulevard, Dr. Martin Luther King Drive, Natural Bridge Avenue, and North Kingshighway, with quick access to Interstate 70. Natural Bridge Avenue carries most of the commercial traffic through the neighborhood, connecting residents to downtown St. Louis, the airport, and distribution routes across the Midwest.

### Kosciusko Businesses & Neighborhood Guide | St Louis Near Me Directory
Kosciusko, St. Louis
Kosciusko is a riverfront industrial neighborhood on the near-south side of St. Louis, tucked between downtown, Soulard, and the Mississippi River just south of the Gateway Arch. Once a dense neighborhood of 19th-century rowhouses, it was largely cleared during mid-20th-century urban renewal and rebuilt as an industrial-and-logistics district. Today it’s defined by heavy manufacturing, distribution, and engineering firms — alongside two enduring landmarks: the Anheuser-Busch brewery and the 1.9-mile Mississippi River Floodwall, the “Mural Mile” that hosts the annual Paint Louis event.
Kosciusko sits in the near-south part of St. Louis at approximately 38.6023° N, 90.2212° W , within zip code 63104 (with the brewery edge in 63118). The neighborhood is named in honor of Tadeusz Kościuszko , the Polish-born general of the American Revolutionary War. Locals typically pronounce it kozz-ee-OSS-co . Its rough borders are Interstate 55 on the north, the Mississippi River on the east, Seventh Street on the west, and St. George and Dorcas Streets on the south. The northern edge of the neighborhood includes an area historically known as “Chouteau’s Landing.” 
Industrial activity here dates to the mid-1850s, when the St. Louis and Iron Mountain Railroad (later the Missouri Pacific) was built along the riverfront, bringing plants that produced cotton, matches, tobacco products, and stoneware. The riverfront location offered shipping by steamboat and rail, and the surrounding immigrant population — Eastern European Jews, Croats, Germans, and others — furnished a ready labor source. Before its clearance, Kosciusko was part of the greater Soulard area, with red-brick rowhouses, a lively South Broadway commercial wall, and churches serving its diverse community.
The neighborhood’s modern form was shaped by the Kosciusko Urban Renewal Area of the late 1950s and 1960s. Following the city’s 1947 Comprehensive Plan, the Land Clearance for Redevelopment Authority finalized a plan in 1958 to clear 221 acres across roughly 70 blocks for industrial expansion. The 19th-century rowhouses and businesses — including the John J. Roe & Co. pork-packing plant (built 1859) that supplied Union soldiers — were demolished. The result is the heavily industrial district seen today, though the change came at the cost of a once-vibrant residential community.
A handful of significant buildings survived the clearance. Chief among them is the historic St. Mary of Victories Church (1843), the second Catholic church built in the city and now a St. Louis Landmark and National Register property, long known as the “Hungarian Church.” The C. Hager & Sons Hinge Company Building on Victor Street is also National Register–listed. These landmarks anchor the neighborhood’s connection to its pre-urban-renewal past along the riverfront.
Kosciusko’s best-known modern feature is the Mississippi River Floodwall — the “Mural Mile,” the longest continuous graffiti wall, running roughly 1.9 miles between Victor and Chouteau Avenues. Started in 1997 and organized by the nonprofit Paint Louis, the wall draws hundreds of graffiti artists from across the country every Labor Day weekend. A trailhead at the north end connects to the Riverfront Trail, which runs all the way to the Chain of Rocks Bridge at the northern tip of the city.
The neighborhood’s anchor employer is the Anheuser-Busch brewery , a cornerstone of the Soulard and Kosciusko area since the 1850s and home to the Budweiser brand and the famous Clydesdales. Heavy industry remains the defining economic activity, led by firms like the long-standing Nooter industrial-construction operation. Kosciusko is also home to Lift for Life Academy, the first charter school in St. Louis, housed in a former Mercantile Bank building.
Kosciusko’s modern business activity still centers on heavy industry and the businesses that keep an industrial corridor running — general contracting, interior design for commercial and industrial buildouts, commercial tire and truck-rental service, heavy industrial construction, and the historic Anheuser-Busch brewery. The listings on this page draw from the Kosciusko / South Broadway corridor itself and the surrounding region, rounded out by the chamber and directory partners that serve businesses across the metro.
Image: St. Mary of Victories Church (1843) in Kosciusko — the second Catholic church built in St. Louis and a surviving landmark of the neighborhood’s pre-urban-renewal past — Wikimedia Commons / CC BY-SA 4.0 by Nheyob

Kosciusko follows St. Louis’s ordinary four-season pattern, but because the neighborhood is almost entirely industrial the weather barely touches the workday — the loading docks, the brewery, and the floodwall keep running through the summer humidity and the winter freeze alike, and the one real exception is Labor Day weekend, when Paint Louis draws a crowd to the Mural Mile no matter the forecast.
Kosciusko has almost no one living inside its own boundary today — the urban renewal that cleared its rowhouses in the late 1950s and 1960s never brought housing back, and the district that replaced them is built for trucks and plant floors, not front porches. What brings people here now falls into three groups: the industrial and logistics workforce that staffs the brewery and the surviving plants each shift; the contractors, haulers, and property owners who lean on the general contractor’s office, the interior-design studio, the tire shop, and the truck-rental yard along South 7th, South 3rd, and South Broadway to keep other job sites running; and the once-a-year crowd that shows up over Labor Day weekend, when the Mural Mile becomes the reason to visit rather than the brewery tour. This is a neighborhood to work in, or to walk the floodwall in for an afternoon — not one to move into.

### Frequently Asked Questions 
Q. What defines the Kosciusko neighborhood? 
A. Kosciusko is defined by its transformation from a dense 19th-century immigrant rowhouse district into a nearly all-industrial corridor. The 1958 Kosciusko Urban Renewal Area cleared roughly 221 acres for manufacturing and logistics, and today the neighborhood is anchored by the Anheuser-Busch brewery, the Mississippi River Floodwall’s 1.9-mile Mural Mile, and the trades that keep an industrial corridor running — with almost no residents left.

Q. How does St Louis Near Me Directory help Kosciusko businesses? 
A. St Louis Near Me Directory gives Kosciusko businesses a schema-optimized Gold listing (up to 10 categories, 40 locations), with Platinum adding Google Business Profile cleanup and AI-powered posts, and Diamond adding reputation management and 60+ citation sync. All plans come with a 7-day free trial, no long-term contracts, and no competitor ads on your listing — helping industrial and logistics businesses along South Broadway get found.

Q. What types of businesses are most common in Kosciusko? 
A. Kosciusko’s business mix is overwhelmingly industrial: general contracting, commercial interior design, commercial tire and truck-rental service, and heavy industrial construction, anchored by the historic Anheuser-Busch brewery. Listed providers include Superior Building Group, VERVE Design Studio, Best-One Tire & Service, City Rent A Truck, and NOOTER St. Louis, rounded out by regional chamber and directory partners serving the wider St. Louis metro.

Q. What kinds of dining, retail, and recreation options are available in Kosciusko? 
A. Kosciusko has almost no dining or retail of its own — the neighborhood is nearly all industrial, with businesses built around loading docks and plant floors rather than storefronts. Recreation is the exception: the 1.9-mile Mural Mile floodwall gallery, the Riverfront Trail connecting north to the Chain of Rocks Bridge, and the Anheuser-Busch brewery’s tours and Biergarten, busiest during the annual Labor Day Paint Louis event.

Q. Are there neighborhood landmarks, parks, and historic sites in Kosciusko? 
A. Yes — despite decades of industrial clearance, Kosciusko keeps several landmarks: St. Mary of Victories Church (1843), the second Catholic church built in St. Louis and a National Register property; the National Register–listed C. Hager & Sons Hinge Company Building on Victor Street; the historic Chouteau’s Landing area at the neighborhood’s north end; and the Anheuser-Busch brewery, itself on the National Register of Historic Places.

Q. What is it like to live in Kosciusko? 
A. Almost no one lives in Kosciusko today — the urban renewal that cleared its rowhouses in the late 1950s and 1960s never brought housing back. It’s a neighborhood built for trucks and plant floors, populated by an industrial and logistics workforce during the day, contractors and haulers keeping job sites running, and a once-a-year crowd for the Labor Day Paint Louis event. It’s a place to work, not to live.

Q. How do residents and visitors get around Kosciusko? 
A. Kosciusko is built for trucks, not transit — it sits against the I-44, I-55, I-64, and I-70 interchange, with South Broadway and South 7th and 3rd Streets carrying freight to the brewery, tire shop, and truck-rental yard. The Riverfront Trail runs along the floodwall for cyclists and walkers, connecting north to the Chain of Rocks Bridge, but there is little foot traffic otherwise.

A. ### Lafayette Square Businesses & Neighborhood Guide | St Louis Near Me Directory
Lafayette Square, St. Louis
Lafayette Square serves as St. Louis’s first historic district and most architecturally celebrated Victorian neighborhood — dedicated November 12, 1851 by City Ordinance 2741, anchored by the 30-acre Lafayette Park (the oldest urban park west of the Mississippi River), Benton Place (Montgomery Blair’s 1866 private street designed by Julius Pitzman), and the Second Empire “Painted Ladies” mansions — offering historic restoration, fine dining, wine bars, wellness, coworking, and artisanal markets across the South Jefferson and Park Avenue corridors.
Lafayette Square is one of St. Louis’s 79 official neighborhoods, located at 38.6173° N, 90.2200° W approximately one mile south of Downtown St. Louis. The neighborhood is bounded by Chouteau Avenue to the north, Interstate 44 to the south, Truman Parkway to the east, and South Jefferson Avenue to the west. Surrounding neighborhoods include Downtown West to the north, LaSalle Park and Peabody-Darst-Webbe to the east, Soulard to the southeast, and Gate District / Tiffany to the west. The neighborhood lies within ZIP code 63104 and surrounds the 30-acre Lafayette Park , the oldest public park in the City of St. Louis and the oldest urban park west of the Mississippi River. Today Lafayette Square is one of the most architecturally and historically significant neighborhoods in St. Louis — a meticulously preserved district of Second Empire Victorian town houses, Italianate mansions, and Romanesque Revival homes that earned the title of St. Louis’s first historic district by City Ordinance in 1972 and was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1973 (with additional NRHP listings in 1986).
The story of Lafayette Square begins with the founding of the French village of St. Louis in 1764 . The land that became the neighborhood was originally part of the St. Louis Commons — a European-style common field system in which land was held in common by village settlers for agricultural use and pasture for livestock. Lafayette Park, at the center of the neighborhood, has the distinction of being the only land in the city which has never been privately owned . In 1835 , under American rule, Mayor John Darby gained permission from the state legislature to begin selling the Commons to drive out the bands of criminals who had been using the unfenced commons as encampments to attack travelers. When the city began to sell the common pasture, the Board of Aldermen set aside approximately 30 acres for community recreation — making it the first such preserve within the area of the Louisiana Purchase . The site was officially designated a public square in 1836 , and the surrounding streets were laid out with the southern street named Lafayette Avenue in honor of Marquis de Lafayette (Marie-Joseph-Paul-Roch-Yves-Gilbert du Motier), the French statesman and Revolutionary War general who had volunteered under George Washington and who had visited St. Louis during his famous 1824–1825 tour of the United States .
In 1837 , a real estate panic forced many who had bought land surrounding the Square to cease their payments, causing the land to revert to the City. In the early 1850s, after courts had adjudicated the ownership of these properties, several prominent St. Louisans bought most of the land bordering the southern end of the park, built expensive homes along Lafayette Avenue , and secured state legislation preventing “any nuisance within a distance of 600 feet from the Park.” The 30-acre tract was separated from the Commons in 1844 . On November 12, 1851 , the park was formally dedicated as “Lafayette Square” by City Ordinance 2741 — the name that became associated with the neighborhood that grew up around the park. With the dedication ordinance, funds were raised to build a wood fence around the park and to plant trees and shrubs. The park was renamed Lafayette Park in 1854 . By 1856 , real estate developers had begun to sell lots on the western edge of the park along Missouri Avenue , and by 1858 lots on the east side along Mississippi Avenue were being sold. The athletic field at the park’s northwest corner was used in 1858 as a training site for local militias who referred to it as the “parade grounds.” On the north side of the park, Benton Place was platted by Montgomery Blair in 1866 and designed by Julius Pitzman — one of the earliest private streets in the nation. The lots on Park Avenue along the north edge of the Square were developed by the 1870s.
The 1870s through early 1890s were Lafayette Square’s heyday. Lafayette Park became one of the most popular gathering places in St. Louis — the park was tended by thirteen gardeners, and free concerts at the music stand on Thursdays and Sundays routinely drew crowds in the thousands (sometimes more than 10,000). Victorian visitors strolled the curvilinear paths designed by superintendent Maximilian Kern , picnicked under canopy trees, cruised the main lake in swan boats , admired the decorative stone grotto , and enjoyed the flower gardens . The original iron and stone fence was erected in 1869 and still encircles the park today. A bronze statue of Senator Thomas Hart Benton (1868) and a bronze statue of George Washington (1869) — cast from the Houdon original by French sculptor Jean-Antoine Houdon — were erected within the park. The Benton statue is inscribed with his famous phrase “ There is the East. There is India ,” reflecting his belief that the Western United States contained all the fabled riches of India and more. A police substation (Park House) was constructed in 1867 to maintain order during the park’s busiest gatherings. By 1890 , Lafayette Square had reached the zenith of its development as the most exclusive residential district in St. Louis — home to several mayors , congressmen , cabinet members (including Montgomery Blair , U.S. Postmaster General under President Abraham Lincoln, and co-counsel for Dred Scott in Dred Scott v. Sandford ), a Supreme Court Justice ( Louis Brandeis ), the president of the American Bar Association , and famous steamboat pilots Horace Bixby and Joseph LaBarge .
Everything changed on May 27, 1896 . The Great St. Louis Tornado tore through the near south side of the city, devastating Lafayette Square in the worst urban tornado disaster in American history. The tornado uprooted nearly all of the trees in the Park as well as the trees on Benton Place, damaged the iron fence, destroyed the bandstand , destroyed the Union Club and the Methodist church at Jefferson and Lafayette Avenues, crippled the Presbyterian and Methodist churches , tore the roof off the Unitarian church , and crippled or destroyed many homes on the Square. The tornado did millions of dollars of damage and killed many. Rebuilding began immediately and the area improved enough by 1904 to earn special commendation from foreign landscape architects visiting the World’s Fair in Forest Park. But Lafayette Square never recovered its former grandeur. Improved transportation and the rise of the much larger Forest Park caused many wealthy residents to move west rather than rebuild. The original 1876 Music Stand was demolished in 1951 . The cannons in the park today are from the British warship HMS Acteon , which sank attacking Fort Moultrie at the Battle of Sullivan’s Island in June 1776 ; they were raised from Charleston Harbor in the late 19th century and donated to Lafayette Park by St. Louis veterans in 1897 .
The City’s first zoning ordinance in 1918 classified the park’s perimeter as residential, briefly protecting the neighborhood from commercial encroachment. But when the Missouri Supreme Court declared the zoning law unconstitutional in 1923 (in City of St. Louis v. Evraiff ), commercial interests began to impinge on the park’s surroundings, speeding the exodus of the remaining Victorian families. Beginning in the Depression, many of the large old homes were converted into rooming houses . The post-war decades brought further decline: the west pond (today’s Rock Garden) was filled in during the 1950s; Interstate 44 was cut through the southern edge of the neighborhood, destroying many homes; and by the late 1960s the Park House had fallen into disrepair and was boarded up. By 1970 the neighborhood was nearly leveled for urban renewal, with crime, dilapidated homes, squatters, and abandoned mansions throughout. The turning point came that year when Ruth Kamphoefner visited Lafayette Square on a house tour, purchased one of the old Victorian homes, and began renovating it herself. She bought several more homes and renovated those as well — sparking a renaissance.
A group of like-minded preservationists formed the Lafayette Square Restoration Committee , and in 1972 their efforts resulted in Lafayette Square becoming St. Louis’s first historic district by City Ordinance . In 1973 , the U.S. Congress placed Lafayette Square on the National Register of Historic Places (with additional NRHP listings in 1986 ). In 1976 , as part of the U.S. Bicentennial, the park received a gift from the people of France: a Jean-Antoine Houdon bust of the Marquis de Lafayette, now displayed in the restored Park House. The majority of the houses in the district were built before 1900 — some dating before the Civil War — with the period of greatest construction activity (the two decades after 1865) producing the Square’s signature Second Empire Victorian town houses : two full stories topped by a third-floor mansard roof with dormer windows, arched doorways and windows, bay windows, and ornate cornices, with limestone or sandstone facades and brick side and rear walls. The largest examples are on Benton Place and Park Avenue north of the park. In 2001 , the Lafayette Park Conservancy (LPC) was formed on the 150th anniversary of the park’s dedication. A 2004 Master Plan developed by H3 Studio with the LPC and the City of St. Louis guided park restoration; the grotto and bridge were rehabilitated in 2012 , and the Mediterranean boathouse (built 1908) was restored in 2014 as the Kern Lakeside Pavilion . A Tree Master Plan for Lafayette Park was prepared in 2016 by SWT Design.
Today, Lafayette Square is one of St. Louis’s most desirable and architecturally celebrated neighborhoods — a walkable, vibrant Victorian district of restored “Painted Ladies” mansions doused in vibrant hues of yellow, salmon, green, blue, and purple. The neighborhood’s key anchor businesses today include the Lafayette Square Restoration Committee on Lafayette Avenue (the non-profit that started the 1970s renaissance); Lafayette Construction on South Jefferson (the 24-year licensed-and-bonded general contractor specializing in Victorian historic restorations under Ree Winston); The Dreamer’s Loft at 2710 Lafayette (St. Louis’s first creative coworking space); Lafayette Square Chiropractic Centre at 1013 South 18th Street (Dr. Crystal B. Peairs’s 15-year family-oriented practice); Vicini Pastaria Cafe & Market at 1916 Park Avenue (artisanal handmade pasta); Winnie’s Wine Bar at 2101 Chouteau (opened 2022 by Paul and Wendy Hamilton); Polite Society Restaurant and Bar at 1923 Park Avenue; McAvoy Realty and Modern Dollar Planning on Park Avenue; Pastel Devil Studio on Chouteau Avenue; the Lafayette Park Conservancy housed in the 1867 Park House; Sqwires Restaurant in the former Western Wire Factory; Square One Brewery at Park and 18th; and the annual Lafayette Square Holiday Parlour Tour & Winter Fair , the summer free concert series (June–September), the summer movie screenings , the St. Louis Perfectos vintage baseball club , and the Lafayette Park Conservancy events at the Park House, Betsy Cook Pavilion, and Kern Lakeside Pavilion.
Image: Lafayette Park — the 30-acre urban green space at the center of the Lafayette Square neighborhood, set aside from the St. Louis Commons in 1836 and dedicated by City Ordinance 2741 on November 12, 1851. The oldest public park in St. Louis and the oldest urban park west of the Mississippi River — Wikimedia Commons , CC BY-SA 3.0 by Onegentlemanofverona

Like the rest of St. Louis, Lafayette Square runs hot and humid in summer and cold in winter, with an active spring storm season that has hit the neighborhood hard before — the Great St. Louis Tornado of May 27, 1896 uprooted nearly every tree in the park and damaged buildings on Benton Place.
What the street grid tells you: Park Avenue and Benton Place carry the neighborhood’s largest, best-preserved Second Empire town houses because they were among the last blocks platted, through the 1870s, after the 1837 real estate panic and the 1850s court fights over ownership had already sorted out who could actually afford to build. Benton Place itself has been a private street — owned and maintained by its own residents rather than the city — since Montgomery Blair platted it in 1866.
Locals draw the neighborhood a little tighter than the official map: most of the walkable business district sits on Park Avenue and Chouteau Avenue within two blocks of the park, while the blocks toward Truman Parkway and Interstate 44 read as quieter and mostly residential. It is a neighborhood for people who want a five-minute walk to a 30-acre historic park and do not mind Victorian-restoration prices for the privilege of living behind a Second Empire façade.

### Frequently Asked Questions 
Q. What are some things to do near Lafayette Square in St. Louis? 
A. Walk the 30-acre Lafayette Park within its original 1869 iron-and-stone fence, past the 1868 Thomas Hart Benton statue and the 1869 George Washington bronze by Jean-Antoine Houdon. Catch the free summer concert series (June–September) or a St. Louis Perfectos vintage baseball game, then eat at Vicini Pastaria or Polite Society and drink at Winnie’s Wine Bar.

Q. Who is Lafayette Square in St. Louis named after? 
A. The neighborhood and its park are named for the Marquis de Lafayette, the French Revolutionary War general who volunteered under George Washington and toured the United States in 1824–1825, including a stop in St. Louis. The park was formally dedicated as “Lafayette Square” by City Ordinance 2741 on November 12, 1851, and renamed Lafayette Park in 1854.

Q. What defines the Lafayette Square neighborhood? 
A. Lafayette Square is St. Louis’s first historic district, designated by City Ordinance in 1972 and added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1973. It is defined by its ring of restored Second Empire “Painted Ladies” mansions around the 30-acre Lafayette Park, bounded by Chouteau Avenue, Interstate 44, Truman Parkway, and South Jefferson Avenue.

Q. How does St Louis Near Me Directory help Lafayette Square businesses? 
A. St Louis Near Me Directory builds a neighborhood-specific page for Lafayette Square, like this guide, so local businesses on Park Avenue, Chouteau Avenue, and around the park show up when nearby customers search. Plans start with a 7-day free trial, carry no long-term contract, and never run a competitor’s ad on a member’s listing.

Q. What types of businesses are most common in Lafayette Square? 
A. Historic restoration and general contracting, fine dining and wine bars, real estate and financial services, and wellness practices dominate the Lafayette Square business mix — most concentrated on Park Avenue and Chouteau Avenue. The neighborhood is also anchored by preservation advocacy: the nonprofit Lafayette Square Restoration Committee, active since the late 1960s.

Q. What kinds of dining, retail, and recreation options are available in Lafayette Square? 
A. Park Avenue carries the neighborhood’s dining row — Vicini Pastaria’s handmade pasta, Polite Society’s American menu, and Winnie’s Wine Bar a block over on Chouteau. Recreation centers on the 30-acre Lafayette Park: walking paths, a playground, a lake with the restored 1908 Kern Lakeside Pavilion boathouse, and the annual Holiday Parlour Tour & Winter Fair.

Q. Are there neighborhood landmarks, parks, and historic sites in Lafayette Square? 
A. Yes — Lafayette Park itself is the centerpiece: the oldest public park in St. Louis and the oldest urban park west of the Mississippi River, set aside from the St. Louis Commons in 1836. Benton Place, platted in 1866 by Montgomery Blair, and the entire Second Empire Victorian historic district (NRHP 1973, 1986) surround it.

Q. What is it like to live in Lafayette Square? 
A. Living in Lafayette Square means a Victorian town house or a converted rowhouse a short walk from a 30-acre park, with a genuinely walkable stretch of restaurants and wine bars on Park Avenue and Chouteau Avenue. It also means historic-district rules on renovation and a housing stock built mostly before 1900, so restoration work is a way of life here.

- Where to Eat in Lafayette Square: A Local's Guide to St Louis's Most Romantic Neighborhood
## Lafayette Square Businesses & Neighborhood Guide | St Louis Near Me Directory

 Lafayette Square, St. Louis

Lafayette Square serves as St. Louis’s first historic district and most architecturally celebrated Victorian neighborhood — dedicated November 12, 1851 by City Ordinance 2741, anchored by the 30-acre Lafayette Park (the oldest urban park west of the Mississippi River), Benton Place (Montgomery Blair’s 1866 private street designed by Julius Pitzman), and the Second Empire “Painted Ladies” mansions — offering historic restoration, fine dining, wine bars, wellness, coworking, and artisanal markets across the South Jefferson and Park Avenue corridors.

Lafayette Square is one of St. Louis’s 79 official neighborhoods, located at **38.6173° N, 90.2200° W** approximately one mile south of Downtown St. Louis. The neighborhood is bounded by **Chouteau Avenue** to the north, **Interstate 44** to the south, **Truman Parkway** to the east, and **South Jefferson Avenue** to the west. Surrounding neighborhoods include **Downtown West** to the north, **LaSalle Park** and **Peabody-Darst-Webbe** to the east, **Soulard** to the southeast, and **Gate District** / **Tiffany** to the west. The neighborhood lies within **ZIP code 63104** and surrounds the 30-acre **Lafayette Park**, the oldest public park in the City of St. Louis and the oldest urban park west of the Mississippi River. Today Lafayette Square is one of the most architecturally and historically significant neighborhoods in St. Louis — a meticulously preserved district of Second Empire Victorian town houses, Italianate mansions, and Romanesque Revival homes that earned the title of **St. Louis’s first historic district by City Ordinance in 1972** and was added to the **National Register of Historic Places in 1973** (with additional NRHP listings in 1986).

The story of Lafayette Square begins with the founding of the French village of St. Louis in **1764**. The land that became the neighborhood was originally part of the **St. Louis Commons** — a European-style common field system in which land was held in common by village settlers for agricultural use and pasture for livestock. Lafayette Park, at the center of the neighborhood, has the distinction of being the **only land in the city which has never been privately owned**. In **1835**, under American rule, Mayor John Darby gained permission from the state legislature to begin selling the Commons to drive out the bands of criminals who had been using the unfenced commons as encampments to attack travelers. When the city began to sell the common pasture, the **Board of Aldermen set aside approximately 30 acres for community recreation** — making it the **first such preserve within the area of the Louisiana Purchase**. The site was officially designated a public square in **1836**, and the surrounding streets were laid out with the southern street named **Lafayette Avenue** in honor of **Marquis de Lafayette** (Marie-Joseph-Paul-Roch-Yves-Gilbert du Motier), the French statesman and Revolutionary War general who had volunteered under George Washington and who had visited St. Louis during his famous **1824–1825 tour of the United States**.

In **1837**, a real estate panic forced many who had bought land surrounding the Square to cease their payments, causing the land to revert to the City. In the early 1850s, after courts had adjudicated the ownership of these properties, several prominent St. Louisans bought most of the land bordering the southern end of the park, built expensive homes along **Lafayette Avenue**, and secured state legislation preventing “any nuisance within a distance of 600 feet from the Park.” The 30-acre tract was separated from the Commons in **1844**. On **November 12, 1851**, the park was formally dedicated as **“Lafayette Square”** by **City Ordinance 2741** — the name that became associated with the neighborhood that grew up around the park. With the dedication ordinance, funds were raised to build a wood fence around the park and to plant trees and shrubs. The park was renamed **Lafayette Park** in **1854**. By **1856**, real estate developers had begun to sell lots on the western edge of the park along **Missouri Avenue**, and by **1858** lots on the east side along **Mississippi Avenue** were being sold. The athletic field at the park’s northwest corner was used in **1858** as a training site for local militias who referred to it as the “parade grounds.” On the north side of the park, **Benton Place** was platted by **Montgomery Blair** in **1866** and designed by **Julius Pitzman** — one of the earliest **private streets** in the nation. The lots on Park Avenue along the north edge of the Square were developed by the 1870s.

The **1870s through early 1890s** were Lafayette Square’s heyday. Lafayette Park became one of the most popular gathering places in St. Louis — the park was tended by thirteen gardeners, and free concerts at the music stand on Thursdays and Sundays routinely drew crowds in the **thousands** (sometimes more than 10,000). Victorian visitors strolled the curvilinear paths designed by superintendent **Maximilian Kern**, picnicked under canopy trees, cruised the main lake in **swan boats**, admired the **decorative stone grotto**, and enjoyed the **flower gardens**. The original **iron and stone fence** was erected in **1869** and still encircles the park today. A bronze statue of **Senator Thomas Hart Benton** (1868) and a bronze statue of **George Washington** (1869) — cast from the Houdon original by French sculptor **Jean-Antoine Houdon** — were erected within the park. The Benton statue is inscribed with his famous phrase “*There is the East. There is India*,” reflecting his belief that the Western United States contained all the fabled riches of India and more. A **police substation (Park House)** was constructed in **1867** to maintain order during the park’s busiest gatherings. By **1890**, Lafayette Square had reached the zenith of its development as the most exclusive residential district in St. Louis — home to several **mayors**, **congressmen**, **cabinet members** (including **Montgomery Blair**, U.S. Postmaster General under President Abraham Lincoln, and co-counsel for Dred Scott in *Dred Scott v. Sandford*), a **Supreme Court Justice** (**Louis Brandeis**), the **president of the American Bar Association**, and famous steamboat pilots **Horace Bixby** and **Joseph LaBarge**.

Everything changed on **May 27, 1896**. The **Great St. Louis Tornado** tore through the near south side of the city, devastating Lafayette Square in the worst urban tornado disaster in American history. The tornado **uprooted nearly all of the trees in the Park** as well as the trees on Benton Place, damaged the iron fence, destroyed the **bandstand**, destroyed the **Union Club** and the Methodist church at Jefferson and Lafayette Avenues, crippled the **Presbyterian** and **Methodist churches**, tore the roof off the **Unitarian church**, and crippled or destroyed many homes on the Square. The tornado did millions of dollars of damage and killed many. Rebuilding began immediately and the area improved enough by **1904** to earn special commendation from foreign landscape architects visiting the World’s Fair in Forest Park. But Lafayette Square never recovered its former grandeur. Improved transportation and the rise of the much larger Forest Park caused many wealthy residents to move west rather than rebuild. The original **1876 Music Stand** was demolished in **1951**. The cannons in the park today are from the **British warship HMS Acteon**, which sank attacking Fort Moultrie at the **Battle of Sullivan’s Island in June 1776**; they were raised from Charleston Harbor in the late 19th century and donated to Lafayette Park by St. Louis veterans in **1897**.

The City’s **first zoning ordinance in 1918** classified the park’s perimeter as residential, briefly protecting the neighborhood from commercial encroachment. But when the **Missouri Supreme Court declared the zoning law unconstitutional in 1923** (in *City of St. Louis v. Evraiff*), commercial interests began to impinge on the park’s surroundings, speeding the exodus of the remaining Victorian families. Beginning in the Depression, many of the large old homes were converted into **rooming houses**. The post-war decades brought further decline: the **west pond** (today’s Rock Garden) was filled in during the 1950s; **Interstate 44** was cut through the southern edge of the neighborhood, destroying many homes; and by the late 1960s the Park House had fallen into disrepair and was boarded up. By 1970 the neighborhood was nearly leveled for urban renewal, with crime, dilapidated homes, squatters, and abandoned mansions throughout. The turning point came that year when **Ruth Kamphoefner** visited Lafayette Square on a house tour, purchased one of the old Victorian homes, and began renovating it herself. She bought several more homes and renovated those as well — sparking a renaissance.

A group of like-minded preservationists formed the **Lafayette Square Restoration Committee**, and in **1972** their efforts resulted in Lafayette Square becoming **St. Louis’s first historic district by City Ordinance**. In **1973**, the U.S. Congress placed Lafayette Square on the **National Register of Historic Places** (with additional NRHP listings in **1986**). In **1976**, as part of the U.S. Bicentennial, the park received a gift from the people of France: a Jean-Antoine Houdon bust of the Marquis de Lafayette, now displayed in the restored Park House. The majority of the houses in the district were built before 1900 — some dating before the Civil War — with the period of greatest construction activity (the two decades after 1865) producing the Square’s signature **Second Empire Victorian town houses**: two full stories topped by a third-floor mansard roof with dormer windows, arched doorways and windows, bay windows, and ornate cornices, with limestone or sandstone facades and brick side and rear walls. The largest examples are on **Benton Place** and **Park Avenue** north of the park. In **2001**, the **Lafayette Park Conservancy (LPC)** was formed on the 150th anniversary of the park’s dedication. A **2004 Master Plan** developed by H3 Studio with the LPC and the City of St. Louis guided park restoration; the **grotto and bridge** were rehabilitated in **2012**, and the **Mediterranean boathouse** (built 1908) was restored in **2014** as the **Kern Lakeside Pavilion**. A **Tree Master Plan** for Lafayette Park was prepared in 2016 by SWT Design.

Today, Lafayette Square is one of St. Louis’s most desirable and architecturally celebrated neighborhoods — a walkable, vibrant Victorian district of restored **“Painted Ladies”** mansions doused in vibrant hues of yellow, salmon, green, blue, and purple. The neighborhood’s key anchor businesses today include the **Lafayette Square Restoration Committee** on Lafayette Avenue (the non-profit that started the 1970s renaissance); **Lafayette Construction** on South Jefferson (the 24-year licensed-and-bonded general contractor specializing in Victorian historic restorations under Ree Winston); **The Dreamer’s Loft** at 2710 Lafayette (St. Louis’s first creative coworking space); **Lafayette Square Chiropractic Centre** at 1013 South 18th Street (Dr. Crystal B. Peairs’s 15-year family-oriented practice); **Vicini Pastaria Cafe & Market** at 1916 Park Avenue (artisanal handmade pasta); **Winnie’s Wine Bar** at 2101 Chouteau (opened 2022 by Paul and Wendy Hamilton); **CBD Kratom Lafayette Square** at 1917 Park Avenue; **HITS** on Chouteau Avenue (the 25-year document scanning and digital record transformation firm with 2+ billion documents scanned); the **Lafayette Park Conservancy** housed in the 1867 Park House; **Sqwires Restaurant** in the former Western Wire Factory; **Square One Brewery** at Park and 18th; and the annual **Lafayette Square Holiday Parlour Tour & Winter Fair**, the **summer free concert series** (June–September), the **summer movie screenings**, the **St. Louis Perfectos vintage baseball club**, and the **Lafayette Park Conservancy events** at the Park House, Betsy Cook Pavilion, and Kern Lakeside Pavilion.

Image: Lafayette Park — the 30-acre urban green space at the center of the Lafayette Square neighborhood, set aside from the St. Louis Commons in 1836 and dedicated by City Ordinance 2741 on November 12, 1851. The oldest public park in St. Louis and the oldest urban park west of the Mississippi River — Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0 by Onegentlemanofverona

Lafayette Square sits one mile south of Downtown St. Louis at 38.6173° N, with seamless access to Interstate 44 along its southern boundary, Truman Parkway to the east, South Jefferson Avenue to the west, and Chouteau Avenue to the north. The neighborhood experiences St. Louis’s full humid continental climate: hot, humid summers, cold winters, and an active spring severe weather season — punctuated historically by the **Great St. Louis Tornado of May 27, 1896**, which destroyed virtually every tree and structure in the park. 

Peak outdoor activity falls during spring, summer, and fall, when **Lafayette Park’s** 30 acres draw heaviest neighborhood and citywide use at the **summer free concert series** on select Saturdays from **June through September**, the **summer movie screenings**, the **St. Louis Perfectos vintage baseball club** on the parade-grounds athletic field, the wedding-photo sessions at the **Betsy Cook Pavilion** and the historic **Rockery** (1866), the **Kern Lakeside Pavilion** (the restored 1908 Mediterranean boathouse), the kids climbing the **three Revolutionary War cannons** from HMS Acteon, and the dawn-to-dusk strolling within the original **1869 iron-and-stone fence**. 

The annual **Holiday Parlour Tour & Winter Fair** draws weekend foot traffic during the holiday season.
