### LaSalle Park Businesses & Neighborhood Guide | St Louis Near Me Directory
LaSalle Park, St. Louis
Tucked just south of downtown St. Louis, LaSalle Park is one of the city’s smallest and most quietly remarkable neighborhoods — a tight grid of restored red-brick rowhouses that survived because a hometown company refused to let it disappear. Today it pairs Civil War–era architecture with the world headquarters of a Fortune 500 pet-food giant, all within walking distance of the Arch.
LaSalle Park sits along the southern edge of downtown St. Louis, in ZIP code 63104 . Its boundaries run roughly from Chouteau Avenue on the north to Interstate 55 on the southeast and Tucker (12th Street) on the west, packing a remarkable amount of history into about 0.21 square mile . The neighborhood is part of the older “Old Frenchtown” area that also includes Lafayette Square and Soulard, and it shares Ward 8 representation in city government.
The land was first settled by French families — the Soulards and Chouteaus among them — whose names still mark the surrounding streets and districts. After the Civil War and the California gold rush, waves of German, Lebanese, Czech, and African-American immigrants moved in, and within a few decades the French presence had largely faded; by the early 20th century, the City’s own history notes, only four residents in a hundred were French. That immigrant story is written into the neighborhood’s historic churches, including St. John Nepomuk , noted as the first Czech Catholic church in America, and the Romanesque St. Vincent de Paul , completed in 1843.
Like much of the near-south side, LaSalle Park declined badly after 1950s highway construction sliced through the old street grid. What saved it was an unusual partnership. Ralston Purina — in the neighborhood since 1894 and today known as the Nestlé Purina PetCare Company — chose to invest in the streets around its own factory rather than flee them. In March 1969, 137 acres were declared blighted, and the St. Louis Land Clearance for Redevelopment Authority sought a federal planning grant.
Ralston Purina formed a subsidiary, the LaSalle Park Redevelopment Corporation , to carry out the work. Federal redevelopment funds were approved in 1971 , and in early 1976 property across the neighborhood was sold to individuals and developers willing to restore the historic homes and businesses or build sympathetic in-fill houses on the gaps. Through that effort LaSalle Park was, in effect, re-founded as a “new” neighborhood, legally distinct from the larger Soulard district from which it was carved.
The payoff is visible on nearly every block. Historic-district plans filed in 1977 and revised through 1982 placed the area on the National Register of Historic Places , and a mixture of Victorian and Federalist rowhouses — many dating to the 1860s — was carefully rehabbed. The standout is the 10th Street pedestrian way , a restored stretch of red-brick rowhouses that has become the neighborhood’s signature image. Anchoring it all, Nestlé Purina still keeps its world headquarters here at Checkerboard Square , a reminder that this restoration was as much a corporate-civic experiment as a preservation project.
LaSalle Park remains intimate — the 2020 census counted just 1,088 residents — but its central position is hard to beat. Soulard and the historic Soulard Farmers Market sit immediately to the south and east, downtown and Busch Stadium are minutes north, and the Gateway Arch, the Mississippi riverfront, and the Anheuser-Busch Brewery are all close by. The businesses below — distilleries, breweries, a celebrated live-music venue, trade schools, and more — make the most of that near-downtown setting.
The 10th Street pedestrian streetscape of restored rowhouses in LaSalle Park. Photo: Dan7a7davis, licensed under CC BY-SA 3.0 via Wikimedia Commons.

LaSalle Park shares St. Louis’s four-season climate — hot, muggy summers, cold winters, and the occasional severe spring storm — weather the neighborhood’s solid 19th-century brick rowhouses have shrugged off for more than 150 years.
There is no grocery store or commercial strip here — what LaSalle Park has instead is concentrated: a live-music venue, a nationally known brewery, a craft distillery, and a bed-and-breakfast, all within a five-minute walk of Nestlé Purina’s headquarters gates. For a neighborhood of roughly 1,088 residents, that makes it less a bedroom district than a compact night-out pocket at the edge of downtown — the kind of place people drive in for a show or a pour, then head home to somewhere else.

### Lewis Place Businesses & Neighborhood Guide | St Louis Near Me Directory
Lewis Place, St. Louis
Lewis Place is a historic north-central St. Louis neighborhood named for the oldest African-American private street in the city — a parkway-lined boulevard whose residents played a pivotal role in the national fight against racially restrictive housing covenants. Laid out in 1890 and listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1980, the street and its surrounding neighborhood sit just north of the Central West End and the Cortex Innovation Community, blending deep civil-rights heritage with an active, resident-led revitalization effort.
Lewis Place sits in north-central St. Louis at approximately 38.6551° N, 90.2564° W , spanning parts of zip codes 63108 and 63113. Per the City of St. Louis, the neighborhood is defined by Dr. Martin Luther King Drive on the North, Delmar Boulevard on the South, Newstead Avenue on the East, and Walton Avenue on the West. It is bordered by Fountain Park, the Central West End, The Greater Ville, The Ville, Kingsway East, and Vandeventer, falling within the city’s 10th and 12th Wards. The roughly 0.33-square-mile neighborhood is home to about 1,360 residents.
The neighborhood takes its name from Lewis Place , the oldest African-American private street in St. Louis. It was laid out beginning in 1890 by the family of real-estate developer William J. Lewis — a three-block street with a landscaped center parkway, lined on both sides with homes built between 1890 and 1928 . A monumental ornamental gate, designed in 1895 by the celebrated architectural firm Barnett, Haynes & Barnett , marks the Taylor Avenue entrance and remains the street’s signature landmark.
Lewis Place holds a singular place in American civil-rights history. In the 1940s, its residents fought back against the racially restrictive covenants used to bar Black families from buying homes — a struggle led locally by figures such as Robert Witherspoon. That fight helped propel the landmark Shelley v. Kraemer case, which originated in St. Louis and in 1948 reached the U.S. Supreme Court, where restrictive covenants were struck down across the entire nation, opening the door to modern fair-housing law.
The Lewis Place Historic District — 78 homes along the private street — was placed on the National Register of Historic Places on September 15, 1980 , and is also a designated City Historic District. The housing stock reflects the turn-of-the-century elegance of the nearby Euclid–Central West End area, with refined Victorian and revival-style residences. Several were designed by prominent St. Louis architects, including work tied to the Barnett architectural dynasty, whose name is among the most illustrious in the city’s building history.
By the 1950s, Lewis Place had become a desirable neighborhood for Black professionals, and it remained strong even as surrounding areas declined — residents modernized street lighting, repaved streets through a special levy, and kept the neighborhood association active. After decades of disinvestment in the late 20th century, residents led by Pamela Talley formed Lewis Place Historic Preservation, Inc. in 2000, a nonprofit dedicated to preserving the street’s historic homes and improving the surrounding community.
Today Lewis Place sits at the heart of a revitalizing community, within a three-mile radius of Saint Louis University, Washington University, and Ranken Technical College, and immediately adjacent to the booming Central West End and Cortex Innovation Community. Anchors like the Lewis Place Historical Preservation Garden — a community garden launched in 2000 that also serves as an educational space — reflect the neighborhood’s ongoing, resident-driven beautification and food-access efforts.
Lewis Place has no commercial strip of its own. Its one true institution is the Lewis Place Historical Preservation Garden , on the historic street itself. Everything else useful to residents — coworking, dining, retail, art — is a half-mile walk or short drive south into the Central West End : TechArtista CWE, Alchemy Tattoo Collective, Studio Escargot, Evangeline’s Bistro and Music House, and Duane Reed Gallery all sit within seven-tenths of a mile. None of them are inside Lewis Place, but they’re the closest real options, and this page says so plainly rather than pretending otherwise.
Image: The Lewis Place Historic District — the oldest African-American private street in St. Louis, listed on the National Register of Historic Places — Wikimedia Commons / CC BY-SA 4.0 by LittleT889

Lewis Place sees the same humid summers and cold winters as the rest of the city; hot months bring the most activity to the Historical Preservation Garden and the tree-lined center parkway, while winter pushes the neighborhood’s residents south to the Central West End for everything else.
What Lewis Place is for today is its own history: a single, tightly preserved private street with a gated entrance and a civil-rights legacy that reaches the U.S. Supreme Court. It is not a shopping or dining destination, and this guide won’t pretend otherwise — it’s a quiet residential block worth knowing for what it is, a half-mile from the Central West End for everything else.

A. Lewis Place is defined by its namesake street — the oldest African-American private street in St. Louis, laid out in 1890 with a landscaped center parkway and a monumental 1895 gate at Taylor Avenue. Its civil-rights history, anchored by the 1948 Shelley v. Kraemer case, matters more here than any commercial strip; the neighborhood is almost entirely residential.

### Lindenwood Park Businesses & Neighborhood Guide | St Louis Near Me Directory
Lindenwood Park, St. Louis
Lindenwood Park is one of far-southwest St. Louis’s quietest, most settled residential neighborhoods — a tidy grid of brick bungalows and single-family homes wrapped around its namesake city park, bounded by the busy Hampton Avenue and Watson Road (Historic Route 66) corridors.
Tucked into the far southwest corner of the City of St. Louis, Lindenwood Park is a roughly 1.5-square-mile residential neighborhood defined by Arsenal Street and Interstate 44 to the north, Watson and Chippewa Street to the south, Hampton Avenue on the east, and the city limits to the west . That western edge runs close to the River Des Peres, and just across Chippewa to the south sits the St. Louis Hills neighborhood. With around 9,400 residents counted in the 2020 census, it ranks among the larger neighborhoods in south city.
The land here has a long history. It was part of a vast Spanish colonial land grant in 1798, then carved into large tracts by about 1850. For decades the area stayed mostly agricultural and undeveloped. Real building only began pushing in along and north of Fyler Avenue, east of the River Des Peres, in the 1880s, as the growing city slowly reached this far southwest corner.
Lindenwood Park took the residential shape you see today during a rapid building boom in the 1920s and 1930s , with most of its housing finished by 1950. The defining look is brick — rows of sturdy brick bungalows and single-family homes from the 1920s through the 1950s, mixed in with a handful of older 19th-century farmhouses, some 1950s “prestige” houses, and a few art-deco apartment buildings. Because so little open land was left once the boom ended, newer construction has been limited, and the neighborhood keeps its early-20th-century feel. As of the early 2000s, about 83% of its homes were single-family detached and largely brick.
The neighborhood is named for its namesake city park, Lindenwood Park , which actually came along after most of the surrounding houses were already built. The roughly 12-acre park tract was secured through a settlement with Darst Realty — a firm owned by then-Mayor Joseph Darst — that would otherwise have placed multi-family housing on the land. The park did not take its real shape until after a 1955 bond issue; before that it was a four-block-by-one-block stretch of woods dotted with sinkholes. Today the city park offers walking trails, a soccer field, two softball fields, tennis courts, a picnic pavilion, a playground, and a skating rink.
The neighborhood’s edges do most of its commercial work. Hampton Avenue , the eastern boundary, is a major south-city artery lined with shops and services, while the southern boundary along Chippewa Street and Watson Road carries Historic Route 66 (Missouri Route 366). That Route 66 frontage gives the area a real slice of Americana — the beloved Donut Drive In has served classic donuts on Chippewa for generations, and just across Chippewa in neighboring St. Louis Hills you’ll find the famous Ted Drewes Frozen Custard , a Route 66 landmark that sits adjacent to (not within) Lindenwood Park.
Historically a white, middle-class neighborhood — more than 99% white as recently as 1990 — Lindenwood Park has grown somewhat more mixed, with the 2020 census recording about 83% White, 6% Black, and smaller Asian and multiracial shares. What hasn’t changed is the appeal: solid brick homes, a central park, easy I-44 access, and a wall of small businesses along Hampton, Watson, and the interior streets of Ivanhoe and Lansdowne. The local shops, bakeries, auto shops, and restaurants profiled below are the everyday backbone of the neighborhood.
Brick homes in Lindenwood Park. Photo: “Lindenwood Park Homes” by Paul Sableman, licensed under CC BY 2.0 via Wikimedia Commons.

Like the rest of St. Louis, Lindenwood Park sees a humid subtropical climate of hot, muggy summers and cold winters — the kind of seasonal swing its sturdy 1920s-to-1950s brick housing stock has always shrugged off with ease.
A couple of the interior streets carry their own history: Hancock Avenue , where Off The Press Tees sits today, honors Civil War general and 1880 presidential candidate Winfield Scott Hancock, while Ivanhoe Avenue takes its name from the Ivanhoe Park subdivision platted in 1927 — one of several tracts, alongside Southwest Park, Watson Terrace, Somerset Park, and Wenzlick Park, that filled the neighborhood in block by block during the building boom described above.

### Frequently Asked Questions 
Q. What are the main attractions in Lindenwood Park? 
A. The neighborhood’s centerpiece is its namesake Lindenwood Park, a roughly 14-acre city park with walking trails, a soccer field, two softball fields, tennis courts, a picnic pavilion, a playground, and a skating rink. Just off its Route 66 edge, Donut Drive In draws visitors from across St. Louis, and Farmhaus Restaurant on Ivanhoe Avenue is a destination for special-occasion dining.

Q. What is Lindenwood Park known for? 
A. Lindenwood Park is known for its sturdy brick bungalows built during the 1920s-to-1950s building boom, its namesake 14-acre city park at the neighborhood’s center, and its stretch of Historic Route 66 along Chippewa Street and Watson Road — home to the beloved Donut Drive In, a longtime Route 66 donut institution.

Q. Is Lindenwood Park a good neighborhood in St. Louis? 
A. Yes. Lindenwood Park is a stable, largely residential neighborhood prized for its durable brick housing stock, a central city park, and easy I-44 access in far-southwest St. Louis. Its commercial corridors along Hampton Avenue and Watson Road, plus interior streets like Ivanhoe and Lansdowne, support a steady mix of shops, restaurants, and service businesses for residents.

Q. Is Lindenwood Park a good area? 
A. For location, yes — Lindenwood Park sits in the far southwest corner of the city, bounded by Arsenal Street and I-44 to the north and the city limits to the west near the River Des Peres, with Hampton Avenue and the Historic Route 66 corridor along Chippewa and Watson giving quick access to shopping, dining, and the neighboring St. Louis Hills.

Q. What are the demographics of Lindenwood Park, St. Louis? 
A. The 2020 census counted about 9,400 residents in Lindenwood Park, making it one of the larger neighborhoods in south city. The population was roughly 83% White, 6% Black, with smaller Asian and multiracial shares. That marks a shift from decades past — as recently as 1990, the neighborhood was more than 99% White.

Q. What types of businesses are most common in Lindenwood Park? 
A. The businesses profiled on this page reflect the neighborhood’s edges and interior streets: a recording studio and dental practice on Hampton and Chippewa, a bakery and garden center along Watson and Hampton, a custom-apparel shop and barbershop on the interior streets, plus an upscale restaurant and an auto dealer & repair shop — a practical mix of retail, food, and personal services.

Q. What kinds of dining, retail, and recreation options are available in Lindenwood Park? 
A. For dining, Farmhaus Restaurant on Ivanhoe Avenue serves farm-to-table fare, Pint Size Bakery & Coffee on Watson Road is known for its salted-caramel croissants, and Donut Drive In on Chippewa is a Route 66 classic. For retail, The Garden Shop and Off The Press Tees cover plants and custom apparel. For recreation, the namesake Lindenwood Park offers trails, ballfields, and a playground.

Q. What defines the Lindenwood Park neighborhood? 
A. Lindenwood Park is a residential neighborhood in far-southwest St. Louis defined by its brick bungalows and single-family homes, most built during the 1920s-to-1950s building boom. It is named for its namesake city park, Lindenwood Park, which sits at the center of the community. The neighborhood is bounded by Arsenal Street and I-44 to the north, Watson and Chippewa to the south, Hampton Avenue to the east, and the city limits to the west.

### Marine Villa Businesses & Neighborhood Guide | St Louis Near Me Directory
Marine Villa, St. Louis
Marine Villa is a historic working-class neighborhood on the south St. Louis riverfront, set along the bluffs of the Mississippi River just south of the Anheuser-Busch Brewery. Named in 1968 for the rivermen who once made their community here, it pairs a German streetcar-suburb heritage of brick flounder houses and rowhomes with the vibrant retail energy of Cherokee Street’s Antique Row along its northern edge — a blend of riverfront industry, neighborhood revitalization, and an eclectic arts-and-vintage commercial scene.
Marine Villa sits in south St. Louis at approximately 38.5866° N, 90.2293° W , within zip code 63118. Per the City of St. Louis, the neighborhood lies just south of the Anheuser-Busch Brewery along the Mississippi River bluffs, and is defined by Cherokee Street’s Antique Row on the North, Gasconade Street on the South, South Broadway and Jefferson Avenue on the West, and the Mississippi River on the East. The roughly 0.65-square-mile neighborhood is home to about 2,530 residents and falls within the city’s 8th Ward.
The neighborhood’s name and boundaries came into existence in 1968 , chosen as a tribute to the large number of rivermen who once had their own community in the area. The old Marine Hospital — one of several hospitals authorized by an act of Congress in 1837 for the treatment of sick and disabled rivermen — was located at Marine and Winnebago Streets. The riverfront location, just a few miles south of downtown, made the area a natural home for those who lived and worked on the Mississippi.
Originally part of the St. Louis Commons , the area was subdivided and gridded in 1855 , with early development consisting of small farms and brickyards. Some of the oldest surviving buildings are small frame and brick farmhouses from the 1860s, many in the form of the distinctive flounder house — a simple one-and-a-half-story vernacular home with a slanted roof unique to St. Louis. The Lemp Brewery relocated from downtown to the northern edge of Marine Villa in the 1860s, drawing an influx of German immigrants to the area.
When a streetcar line opened on South Broadway in 1890 , the district developed rapidly into one of St. Louis’s many working- and middle-class streetcar suburbs , populated largely by German immigrant families. That heritage is preserved in the Marine Villa Neighborhood Historic District , listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 2009, which encompasses ten blocks and 356 buildings — 187 of them contributing to the district’s historic character. The German Cultural Society building on South Jefferson reflects this lasting immigrant legacy.
Today Marine Villa is a neighborhood transforming its industrial bones. The northern half has benefited from the reinvestment along Cherokee Street , whose Antique Row and arts district anchor an eclectic mix of vintage shops, galleries, and source-direct retail. Adaptive reuse of historic buildings into coworking spaces, art studios, and professional offices has accelerated, supported by neighborhood developers and an active neighborhood association. Brick townhouses, Second Empire designs, and flounder homes draw buyers and renovators to one of the city’s more affordable historic markets.
Marine Villa’s business landscape reflects this blend of riverfront industry, specialty retail, and creative revitalization along the Cherokee Street and South Broadway corridors. The listings on this page draw from the broader Marine Villa / Cherokee Antique Row area and the surrounding St. Louis region — with providers spanning riverfront industrial terminals, fine-art and vintage retail, crystal and jewelry shops, historic-building redevelopment, business chambers and districts, B2B marketing, and the regional directory partner that serves businesses across the metro.
Image: Looking south on Indiana Avenue at Potomac Street in Marine Villa — a historic brick streetscape in this south St. Louis riverfront neighborhood — Wikimedia Commons / CC BY 2.0 by Paul Sableman

Marine Villa runs on a four-season Midwest climate — summer and fall bring peak foot traffic to Cherokee Street’s Antique Row shops and galleries, while winter pushes activity indoors and the riverfront grain terminal keeps working through every season.

### Frequently Asked Questions 
Q. What defines the Marine Villa neighborhood? 
A. Marine Villa is a riverside, working-class neighborhood on the Mississippi bluffs just south of the old Anheuser-Busch Brewery, named in 1968 for the rivermen once treated at the Marine Hospital nearby. Its brick flounder houses and German streetcar-suburb rowhomes sit between the industrial river edge and Cherokee Street’s Antique Row, which forms its lively northern boundary.

Q. How does St Louis Near Me Directory help Marine Villa businesses? 
A. St Louis Near Me Directory strengthens neighborhood-focused visibility for businesses serving Marine Villa by pairing local content with curated listings. Joining gives a Marine Villa business improved local SEO, GEO, and AEO performance and stronger “near me” signals tied to Cherokee Street’s Antique Row, South Broadway, and the riverfront corridor.

Q. What types of businesses are most common in Marine Villa? 
A. Marine Villa blends riverfront industry with the specialty retail and arts scene of Cherokee Street’s Antique Row. Providers on this page include the ADM North Terminal river facility, the LA Marler fine-art gallery, the STL Rocks crystal shop, Retro 101/Cherry Bomb Vintage, Sump Coffee, the South Side Spaces historic-redevelopment agency, and area business chambers — a mix of industrial, creative, and professional commerce.

Q. What kinds of dining, retail, and recreation options are available in Marine Villa? 
A. Cherokee Street’s Antique Row anchors most of Marine Villa’s retail and dining — STL Rocks for crystals and jewelry, the LA Marler gallery for fine art, Retro 101/Cherry Bomb Vintage for mid-century apparel, and Sump Coffee on South Jefferson for specialty coffee. Reinvestment keeps turning historic buildings into studios, workshops, and coworking space along the corridor.

Q. Are there neighborhood landmarks, parks, and historic sites in Marine Villa? 
A. Yes — the Marine Villa Neighborhood Historic District, listed on the National Register in 2009, covers ten blocks and 356 buildings, including 1860s flounder houses with their single-sloped roofs and later Second Empire townhomes. The old Marine Hospital site, the German Cultural Society building, and the ADM North Terminal on the riverfront round out the neighborhood’s historic and working landmarks.

Q. What is it like to live in Marine Villa? 
A. Marine Villa is a quiet, affordable pocket of about 2,530 residents living in century-old brick flounder houses and rowhomes a few blocks from Cherokee Street’s shops and galleries. It is a neighborhood in transition — historic housing stock drawing renovators, adaptive reuse turning old buildings into studios, and the Mississippi riverfront and ADM grain terminal as a constant industrial backdrop.

Q. How do residents and visitors get around Marine Villa? 
A. Marine Villa sits a few miles south of downtown with quick access to Interstate 55 and South Broadway, keeping it connected to the riverfront, Cherokee Street, and the wider metro. Most day-to-day errands cluster along Cherokee Street’s Antique Row, making the northern edge of the neighborhood walkable even though the riverfront and industrial edge are best reached by car.

### Mark Twain Businesses & Neighborhood Guide | St Louis Near Me Directory
Mark Twain, St. Louis
Mark Twain is a small, quiet residential neighborhood on St. Louis’s far north side, tucked between Interstate 70 and the historic Bellefontaine and Calvary Cemeteries — named not for any personal connection between Samuel Clemens and this stretch of the city, but for the elementary school that once anchored it. It’s one of the smallest and most overlooked of St. Louis’s 79 neighborhoods, with a handful of businesses of its own and a short list of honest, clearly-marked options just beyond its borders.
Mark Twain sits in far north St. Louis at approximately 38.6899° N, 90.2417° W , within zip code 63115 with some addresses in 63120. The neighborhood’s official boundaries are West Florissant Avenue (fronting Bellefontaine and Calvary Cemeteries) to the northeast, Interstate 70 to the south and southwest, and Emerson Avenue to the northwest — a compact 0.65 square miles split across the city’s 12th and 13th Wards. Named streets inside the neighborhood include Union Boulevard (formerly Bernays Avenue), Geraldine, Claxton, Arlington, North Kingshighway, Lilian, Shreve, and Ruskin . As of the 2020 Census, Mark Twain had 3,257 residents — 95.1% Black, 2.4% White, 1.4% two or more races — down from 6,902 residents in 1990, a decline that has tracked much of St. Louis’s north side over the past three decades.
The neighborhood’s name is often assumed to mark some personal connection between the author and this part of St. Louis. It doesn’t — the real story runs through a school. In 1911 the city built a new school at 5316 Ruskin Avenue, designed by noted St. Louis architect William B. Ittner in his Jacobethan style, with an innovative “open” floor plan that put classrooms on only one side of each corridor to maximize natural light. It opened in September 1912 under the name of the neighborhood it served, Harney Heights School . In 1918 — eight years after Samuel Clemens’s death — the St. Louis Board of Education renamed it Mark Twain School , honoring, as the Post-Dispatch reported at the time, “the great literary son of Missouri.” The neighborhood around it gradually took the school’s new name instead of the other way around. Mark Twain School closed after the 2009–2010 school year and has sat vacant since, though its exterior remains in good condition. One more coincidence, told carefully because Twain scholars dispute the exact timeline: riverboat captain Isaiah Sellers (1802–1864), whom Samuel Clemens credited in Life on the Mississippi as the source of his pen name, is buried at Bellefontaine Cemetery — the same cemetery that borders this neighborhood today.
Mark Twain’s ground was still farmland and undeveloped lots when the city annexed the area in 1876. Development followed the streetcar: the Bellefontaine line reached the area from downtown in 1893, running out to serve the cemeteries, and the neighborhood’s first residential subdivisions were platted around Bernays Avenue — today’s Union Boulevard — starting in 1898. Early residents were largely of German stock, part of the same wave of German settlement that shaped much of north St. Louis in this period, later joined by other working-class European immigrant families. Interstate 70’s construction in 1961 cut through the neighborhood, displacing homes and businesses along its new path. From the mid-1960s through the early 1970s, Mark Twain transitioned to a predominantly African-American neighborhood — part of the same broader demographic shift that reshaped St. Louis’s north side, including nearby Penrose, in those same decades.
St. Louis, as it happens, has two different neighborhoods with “Mark Twain” in the name, and it’s an easy mix-up to make. Just south of this residential Mark Twain, across I-70, sits the separately-named Mark Twain/I-70 Industrial neighborhood — bounded by I-70, North Kingshighway, and Natural Bridge Road — home to the chemical plants, warehouses, and logistics operations that run along that stretch. It’s a real and distinct place with its own identity, not this one. The Mark Twain covered on this page is the small residential neighborhood between I-70 and the cemeteries.
Population here has fallen by more than half since 1990 — from 6,902 residents to 3,257 as of the 2020 Census — and the city’s own neighborhood profile describes commercial activity today as minimal, with numerous vacant storefronts along its edges. That’s the honest picture: Mark Twain today is mostly quiet residential blocks bordered by two of the largest, oldest cemeteries in the city, not a shopping or dining destination. For the households who live there, that isn’t necessarily a downside — it’s a small, settled corner of north St. Louis a short walk from West Florissant Avenue and a short drive from just about everywhere else.
Image: New and old buildings standing side-by-side in the Mark Twain neighborhood, north St. Louis — Wikimedia Commons / CC BY 2.0 by Paul Sableman

Mark Twain sees the same four-season Midwest weather as the rest of St. Louis, with hot, humid summers and cold, occasionally snowy winters that mostly just mean a quieter block on a bad-weather day in a neighborhood that’s already quiet most days.

### Frequently Asked Questions 
Q. Did Mark Twain live in St. Louis? 
A. That’s a common assumption, but it doesn’t hold here — the Mark Twain neighborhood carries no personal connection to Samuel Clemens. It’s named for Mark Twain School, built in 1912 as Harney Heights School and renamed in Clemens’s honor in 1918, eight years after his death. One genuine link survives nearby: riverboat captain Isaiah Sellers, credited as the source of Clemens’s pen name, is buried at bordering Bellefontaine Cemetery.

Q. What defines the Mark Twain neighborhood? 
A. Mark Twain is a small, quiet residential neighborhood on St. Louis’s far north side, wedged between Interstate 70 and the historic Bellefontaine and Calvary Cemeteries, spanning about 0.65 square miles. It’s named for Mark Twain School, not for any personal Clemens connection, and it’s one of the smallest, most overlooked of the city’s 79 neighborhoods, with only a handful of businesses of its own.

Q. How does St Louis Near Me Directory help Mark Twain businesses? 
A. St Louis Near Me Directory strengthens neighborhood-focused visibility for businesses serving Mark Twain by combining local content with curated listings, tied to search signals around West Florissant Avenue, Union Boulevard, and the Bellefontaine and Calvary Cemetery area. Plans expand a business’s existing Google Business Profile rather than replace it, with no long-term contracts and no competitor ads.

Q. What types of businesses are most common in Mark Twain? 
A. Very few — Mark Twain is small and overwhelmingly residential, with only a preschool (Radiant Faith Academy) and a gas station (bp) carrying genuine Mark Twain addresses. A downtown business-district association and a highly-rated barbershop about two miles south in Jeff Vanderlou round out this guide, clearly labeled as outside the neighborhood. Most everyday needs send residents just beyond Mark Twain’s small footprint.

Q. Are there neighborhood landmarks, parks, and historic sites in Mark Twain? 
A. The defining landmark is Mark Twain School itself — a 1912 William B. Ittner design renamed for the author in 1918, closed since the 2009–2010 school year but still standing on Ruskin Avenue. The neighborhood also borders the historic Bellefontaine and Calvary Cemeteries along West Florissant Avenue, where riverboat captain Isaiah Sellers, source of Clemens’s pen name, is buried.

Q. What is it like to live in Mark Twain? 
A. Mostly quiet: Mark Twain’s population has fallen by more than half since 1990, from 6,902 residents to 3,257 as of the 2020 Census, and the city’s own profile describes commercial activity as minimal with vacant storefronts along its edges. For the households who stay, that means a small, settled residential corner — not a shopping or dining destination — a short walk from West Florissant Avenue.

Q. How do residents and visitors get around Mark Twain? 
A. Interstate 70 forms the neighborhood’s south and southwest edge, and West Florissant Avenue runs along its northeast side past the cemeteries — both easy connections to the rest of north St. Louis. Inside the neighborhood, named streets like Union Boulevard, Ruskin Avenue, and Shreve Avenue carry local traffic; it’s described as a short walk to West Florissant and a short drive from just about everywhere else.

Local St. Louis neighborhood guides, researched and maintained ## Mark Twain I-70 Industrial Businesses & Neighborhood Guide | St Louis Near Me Directory

 Mark Twain I-70 Industrial, St. Louis

Mark Twain / I-70 Industrial is a critical logistics-and-freight corridor in north St. Louis, defined by its strategic position between Interstate 70 and Natural Bridge Road. Anchored by the Union 70 Center industrial hub, the corridor is currently in the middle of a major revitalization that is expanding its identity from heavy industry alone into a mixed-use district where warehouses, urban farms, nonprofits, greenway-trail networks, and independent retail share the same I-70 freight gateway.

Mark Twain I-70 Industrial sits in north St. Louis at approximately **38.6875° N, 90.2714° W**, within zip code 63120. The corridor is framed by **Interstate 70** on the north and **Natural Bridge Road** on the south, with **North Kingshighway** and **West Florissant Avenue** forming the primary east-west arteries. The district shares its name and freight-corridor identity with the adjacent Mark Twain residential neighborhood, and serves as the industrial-and-logistics backbone connecting north St. Louis to downtown, Lambert Airport, and the Illinois side via the I-70 / I-44 / I-64 gateway.

The corridor’s cornerstone is the **Union 70 Center**, a major industrial hub bounded by Interstate 70 and Natural Bridge Road. As the central component of the area’s commercial infrastructure, the center provides extensive warehouse and distribution space designed for large-scale logistics and manufacturing tenants, with immediate access to I-70 for regional freight movement. Union 70 is a key piece of the city’s strategic plan to revitalize the corridor into one of the region’s leading mixed-use industrial-and-innovation districts.

Beyond the warehouses and distribution facilities, Mark Twain I-70 Industrial is currently being reshaped by a growing layer of **neighborhood-based providers** supporting the surrounding residential pockets and workforce. **Good Life Growing** brings urban-agriculture and sustainable food systems to the corridor. The **American Red Cross of Missouri** anchors community service with blood drives, disaster relief, and CPR/first-aid training. **Great Rivers Greenway** connects north St. Louis neighborhoods to the broader regional trail network. **Garden District STL** and **Maypop Coffee & Garden Shop** bring botanical retail and cafe culture to the district. And the local **Imo’s Pizza** franchise on Natural Bridge serves classic St. Louis-style pizza to residents and workers alike.

Consumers navigating the Mark Twain I-70 Industrial market will find a landscape undergoing significant revitalization aimed at diversifying the local economy. While the area is traditionally dominated by large-scale industrial operations, the growing network of neighborhood-based providers reflects the broader strategic shift toward modernizing existing facilities to attract innovation-focused enterprises. Current market dynamics show a steady demand for warehouse and distribution space alongside increasing investment in urban-agriculture, community-service, retail, and hospitality businesses that round out the corridor’s evolving identity.

Mark Twain I-70 Industrial’s modern business activity reflects this blend of **heavy industry, logistics, and emerging mixed-use commerce** along the I-70 freight corridor and the Natural Bridge / North Kingshighway / West Florissant arteries. The listings on this page draw from the broader I-70 Industrial district and the surrounding north St. Louis region — with providers spanning industrial real estate, urban farming, regional nonprofit services, greenway-trail development, independent botanical and cafe retail, and classic St. Louis-style pizza.

Image: The Mark Twain / I-70 Industrial corridor — north St. Louis’s logistics-and-freight backbone along Interstate 70 and Natural Bridge Road

The Mark Twain I-70 Industrial corridor sits on high ground along the I-70 freight gateway in north St. Louis, where the city follows a classic four-season Midwest pattern. Hot, humid summers with highs in the upper 80s°F bring peak activity to the Union 70 Center distribution operations, the Good Life Growing urban-agriculture work, the outdoor trail-network projects of Great Rivers Greenway, and the patio seating at Maypop Coffee & Garden Shop. Spring and fall draw steady traffic to the corridor’s independent retail and the neighborhood Imo’s Pizza franchise.

Because the corridor is dominated by warehousing and freight logistics, its core operations run year-round regardless of weather. Cold, snowy St. Louis winters keep the Union 70 Center industrial tenants, the American Red Cross of Missouri’s blood-drive and disaster-relief services, and the indoor retail at Garden District STL fully active. The I-70 corridor’s expressway access keeps freight moving through every season, while neighborhood-based providers maintain steady year-round service to residents and workers along the Natural Bridge / North Kingshighway / West Florissant arteries.

### McKinley Heights Businesses & Neighborhood Guide | St Louis Near Me Directory
McKinley Heights, St. Louis
McKinley Heights is one of the smallest and most tightly knit neighborhoods on the near South Side of the City of St. Louis — a compact, half-square-mile pocket of historic brick homes and townhouses tucked between Lafayette Square, Soulard, and Benton Park. It is one of the 79 official City neighborhoods, and almost the entire neighborhood sits inside a protected historic district.
The neighborhood is easy to place on a map. It is bounded by Interstate 44 on the north , Jefferson Avenue on the west , and Gravois Avenue and Interstate 55 on the east and south . That puts McKinley Heights within walking distance of Lafayette Square and Lafayette Park to the northwest, the Soulard Farmers Market just east, and Benton Park and Fox Park to the south. Despite covering only about 0.22 square miles, it sits at a genuine crossroads of the near South Side, with the Jefferson Avenue and Gravois Avenue corridors carrying most of its small-business activity.
McKinley Heights grew up as a working-class neighborhood in the second half of the 19th century. The land was originally part of the old Petit Prairie Common Field and was first platted in the 1850s. By 1875 it was filling in with small- to medium-sized single-family brick dwellings that closely resembled the homes going up in neighboring Soulard. Early streetcar service from the Gravois Railway Company ran along Jefferson Avenue, and the first corner stores appeared around 1875 before larger commercial strips took shape along Jefferson and Gravois.
Like much of south St. Louis, McKinley Heights was built by immigrants. German immigrants settled here first , followed in later decades by Serbian and Russian families . You can read that history directly in the buildings: Second Empire Victorian townhouses from the 1860s through the 1880s, Italianate homes from the late 1880s, and houses of clear Germanic influence after 1890. Most of the surviving brick housing stock was built between roughly 1900 and 1915, though buildings in the historic district date as far back as 1865.
The neighborhood’s churches still carry that immigrant story. The Russian Orthodox Church of St. Michael (1927) stands near Ann and Gravois, St. Marcus U.C.C. (1914) sits at Russell and McNair, and the Holy Trinity Serbian Eastern Orthodox Church anchors the corner of Geyer and McNair. Together they trace the German, Serbian, and Russian families who built and worshiped here, and they remain some of the most recognizable landmarks in a neighborhood made mostly of houses.
McKinley Heights takes its name from President William McKinley , a connection echoed in the nearby McKinley School on Russell Avenue and the McKinley Classical Leadership Academy on Ann Avenue. The neighborhood’s historic character earned it formal protection: it was listed as the McKinley-Fox National Register Historic District in 1984 and became a local historic district in 2008. That status now guides how the area’s brick homes are repaired and restored.
The neighborhood has not always had it easy. The mid-20th-century construction of Interstates 44 and 55 boxed McKinley Heights in on two sides, cutting it off from its surroundings and contributing to a long stretch of population loss and building deterioration. Today the story is one of repair. Owners and rehabbers are steadily bringing the historic brick housing stock back to life, and the small businesses along Jefferson and Gravois — a veterinarian, a contractor, photographers, a screen printer, a piano bar, and a couple of well-loved kitchens — make up the working fabric of the neighborhood profiled in this guide.
A historic brick streetscape in McKinley Heights. Photo: “McKinley Heights” by Paul Sableman, licensed under CC BY 2.0 via Wikimedia Commons.

Like the rest of St. Louis, McKinley Heights runs through hot, humid summers and cold winters — the kind of swing that makes solid brick and steady upkeep matter for a neighborhood built almost entirely out of it.
Ask someone who actually lives here instead of reading a map, and they will draw the edges differently: McKinley Heights functions less like a neighborhood with borders and more like an island, since I-44 and I-55 leave only Jefferson, Gravois, and a few underpasses as the way in or out. Those are the same chokepoints that cut the area off from Lafayette Square and Soulard once the interstates went in, and they are still why the handful of blocks along those two avenues carry essentially all of the neighborhood’s commercial life today.

### Midtown Businesses & Neighborhood Guide | St Louis Near Me Directory
Midtown, St. Louis
Sitting at the geographic center of the city around the Saint Louis University campus at Grand and Lindell, Midtown blends one of America’s oldest universities with City Foundry STL’s food hall and shops — and opens onto the adjacent Grand Center arts district just north, home to the Fox, Powell Hall and the Pulitzer.
Midtown is one of the City of St. Louis’s 79 official neighborhoods, covering roughly 1.35 square miles at the heart of the city. Its boundaries run along Chouteau Avenue on the south, Jefferson Avenue on the east, Vandeventer Avenue on the west, and Delmar Boulevard and Olive Street on the north . The neighborhood falls within ZIP codes 63103, 63108 and 63110 and sits in Ward 11, about three miles west of the Mississippi riverfront.
Midtown’s story begins with the Camp Jackson Affair of May 10, 1861 — the only Civil War clash fought in St. Louis — which took place on land that is now part of the Saint Louis University campus. As the city pushed west from the riverfront, the district filled in through the 1870s and became one of the city’s defining western neighborhoods.
Saint Louis University has anchored Midtown for more than a century. Founded in 1818, SLU is the oldest university west of the Mississippi River and the second-oldest Jesuit university in the country. The university bought land at Grand and Lindell in 1867 and opened DuBourg Hall on its Midtown campus in 1888, with St. Francis Xavier (College) Church rising at the same intersection between 1884 and 1914. In the 1970s, Father Paul C. Reinert led the urban-renewal work that helped steady the district during a period of decline.
By the 1920s the stretch around Grand Boulevard had become a bustling entertainment district often compared to New York’s Times Square, lined with grand movie palaces and theaters. Much of that legacy lives on just north of SLU in the adjacent Grand Center arts district — officially the separate Covenant Blu Grand Center neighborhood — which today is home to the Fox Theatre, the St. Louis Symphony at Powell Hall, the Sheldon, the Grandel, the Pulitzer Arts Foundation and the Contemporary Art Museum St. Louis. The Midtown Historic District was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1979.
Today Midtown is once again on the rise. The 2020 Census counted 6,862 residents, up more than 21 percent from 2010, and the neighborhood’s biggest recent landmark is City Foundry STL — a $220 million, 15-acre adaptive reuse of the former Century Electric factory whose food hall opened in August 2021, bringing a movie theater, the Museum of Illusions and dozens of restaurants and shops to the center of the city.
The businesses below sit in Midtown proper or just steps away in the adjacent Grand Center arts district, and each one is labeled honestly so you know exactly where it is. From a Tadao Ando-designed museum to a dine-in cinema at City Foundry, here are the highest-rated places anchoring this central St. Louis neighborhood.
The Fabulous Fox Theatre in the Grand Center arts district just north of Midtown. Photo: “Fabulous Fox Theatre” by Matthew (m shipp22), licensed under CC BY 2.0 via Wikimedia Commons.

St. Louis has a humid subtropical climate — July highs near 89.6°F, January highs near 40.4°F, about 41.7 inches of rain and 16.6 inches of snow a year, and a spot within the broader Tornado Alley risk zone.
What makes Midtown pop is a kind of density most St. Louis neighborhoods don’t have: within a few blocks you can watch SLU Billikens basketball at Chaifetz Arena, catch a touring act up Grand at the Fox, and grab barbecue on Olive Street, all on foot. It’s also home to two of the city’s universities within a short walk of each other — Saint Louis University and Harris-Stowe State University, one of Missouri’s historically Black institutions — a pairing nobody else writes up. That institutional density isn’t an accident of geography: much of Midtown’s mid-century footprint was reshaped by the Mill Creek Valley urban renewal project, which cleared blocks of an existing residential community to make way for the campus, civic and highway expansion that still defines the area today. It’s part of why Midtown reads more like a campus-and-arts district than a street of front porches — built for people passing through as much as living there: students, concertgoers, hospital and university staff. That’s what makes it worth visiting, not just driving past.

### Frequently Asked Questions 
Q. What is Midtown St. Louis like? 
A. Midtown feels like a campus-and-arts district built for people passing through as much as living there — students, concertgoers, and university staff moving between Saint Louis University, City Foundry STL’s food hall, and the Grand Center arts district just north. Two universities, SLU and Harris-Stowe State, sit within a short walk of each other, and dense city blocks put dining, museums, and live entertainment within walking distance of campus.

Q. What is Midtown St. Louis? 
A. Midtown is one of the City of St. Louis’s 79 official neighborhoods, sitting at the geographic center of the city around Saint Louis University at Grand and Lindell. It covers roughly 1.35 square miles across ZIP codes 63103, 63108, and 63110, bounded by Chouteau Avenue, Jefferson Avenue, Vandeventer Avenue, and Delmar Boulevard/Olive Street, and opens directly onto the Grand Center arts district just north.

Q. What are some things to do in Midtown St. Louis? 
A. The biggest draw is City Foundry STL, a 15-acre food hall and entertainment complex with an Alamo Drafthouse dine-in cinema and the Museum of Illusions. From there, Midtown offers the Pulitzer Arts Foundation and Moto Museum for art and vehicle lovers, the historic Samuel Cupples House on the SLU campus, Chaifetz Arena for Billikens basketball, and Grand Center’s Fox Theatre just steps north.

Q. What defines the Midtown neighborhood? 
A. Midtown is defined by Saint Louis University, founded in 1818 and the oldest university west of the Mississippi, which has anchored the district since buying land at Grand and Lindell in 1867. Its footprint was reshaped by the mid-century Mill Creek Valley urban renewal project, and today it pairs SLU and Harris-Stowe State University with City Foundry STL and the neighboring Grand Center arts district.

Q. What kinds of dining, retail, and recreation options are available in Midtown? 
A. Dining ranges from Pappy’s Smokehouse’s St. Louis-style barbecue on Olive Street to Vito’s Sicilian Pizzeria near campus and the dozens of stalls inside City Foundry STL’s food hall. Recreation centers on Chaifetz Arena for SLU basketball and concerts and the Alamo Drafthouse for dine-in movies, while retail leans toward Grand Center’s museum shops just north rather than standalone stores.

A. Yes — the Samuel Cupples House, a late-19th-century Richardsonian Romanesque mansion of pink and gray sandstone on the SLU campus, and the Midtown Historic District, added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1979, anchor the area’s history. Camp Jackson, site of the only Civil War clash fought in St. Louis, sits on what is now SLU’s campus.

### Mount Pleasant Businesses & Neighborhood Guide | St Louis Near Me Directory
Mount Pleasant, St. Louis
Mount Pleasant serves as one of the city’s most historically layered Near Southside river-bluff neighborhoods — anchored by Sugarloaf Mound (the only surviving Mississippian platform mound in St. Louis, now fully reacquired by the Osage Nation in September 2025), the 1863 St. Anthony of Padua Catholic Church with its twin 175-foot towers, the 1895 Mount Pleasant School on the National Register, and the Neighborhood Innovation Center microbusiness incubator at 3207 Meramec Street — offering Black and Hispanic chamber advocacy, event venues, microbusiness incubation, and the apartment communities and rental-property management that serve a neighborhood where renters have long outnumbered owners, for residents and businesses across the Greater Dutchtown corridor.
Mount Pleasant sits along the South Side river bluff at 38.5723° N, 90.2436° W in zip code 63111. The neighborhood’s official boundaries run from Meramec Street on the north, south to Eichelberger Street , east to the Mississippi River , and west to South Compton Avenue . The neighborhood’s primary corridors are South Broadway — the commercial and industrial spine running along the river bluff — Meramec Street (the main east-west commercial corridor), Virginia Avenue , Mount Pleasant Street , and the interior grid of Minnesota Avenue , Nebraska Avenue , Ohio Avenue , and Delor Street . The street grid follows the distinctive South Side convention: east-west streets are named for Native American nations (Meramec, Osceola, Iowa, Itaska), and north-south streets are named for U.S. states (Compton, Virginia, Minnesota, Pennsylvania, Ohio, Indiana). Mount Pleasant is bordered by Marine Villa and Benton Park West to the north, Dutchtown to the west, Carondelet to the south, and the Mississippi River to the east. Despite a widely held local belief that Mount Pleasant is part of Dutchtown, the two are distinct neighborhoods — Mount Pleasant occupies the southeastern sector of the broader Greater Dutchtown cultural area, a regional identity that derives from Deutsch , a colloquial reference to the German Catholic immigrants who settled this part of south St. Louis beginning in the 1840s and 1850s.
The neighborhood’s land has a remarkably deep history. A portion of Mount Pleasant was originally part of the old St. Louis Commons , the colonial-era public land tract that the City of St. Louis purchased in 1836 and gradually sold off through the 1860s, retaining only what eventually became Gravois Park, Laclede Park, and Mount Pleasant Park . Residential development took place east to west, with most of the area built up by 1910. The 1849 fire destroyed most of the wooden buildings along the riverfront. Single-family brick structures filled in along South Compton north of Delor between 1900 and 1930. The neighborhood’s primary green space is Mount Pleasant Park at Michigan and Dakota — a 3-acre city park established by ordinance in 1812, making it among the oldest park reservations within the city limits — featuring a roller hockey rink in some of the best condition in St. Louis and open neighborhood grounds. The Minnie Wood Memorial Playground at Broadway and Meramec was acquired as a gift in 1925. Riverfront properties along South Broadway include both 19th-century industrial parcels and a handful of remaining large stately homes converted to elder-care facilities like Edgewater.
Mount Pleasant’s most extraordinary landmark predates European settlement entirely. Sugarloaf Mound at 4420 Ohio Avenue is the only surviving Native American mound within the City of St. Louis — constructed between 600 and 1200 AD by the Mississippian culture, the same civilization that built Cahokia Mounds across the river. St. Louis was once known as “Mound City” for the approximately 40 to 100 earthen structures that European settlers found in the area at the city’s 1764 French founding; by 1875, nearly all had been leveled for railroads, residences, beer gardens, and the 1904 World’s Fair preparation. Sugarloaf alone survived. The mound was named for its conical shape that resembled the sugar loaves transported in the 18th century. Listed on the National Register of Historic Places on February 17, 1984 , the mound’s sole-ownership reacquisition by its ancestral stewards is one of the most significant Native land repatriation events in Missouri history. After 17 years of advocacy beginning in 2008, the Osage Nation Historic Preservation Office announced on September 22, 2025 the complete reacquisition of the three-tier mound, in partnership with the St. Louis arts and civic-impact organization Counterpublic . On September 19, 2025 , St. Louis Mayor Cara Spencer declared the day “Sugarloaf Mound Preservation Plan Day” at a public City Hall event — the city’s first public acknowledgment of the sovereignty of the Osage Nation’s rights to the sacred site. The 1928 home at the summit (the Adams House, 4420 Ohio Street mailing address) was razed in September 2017; remaining structures will be carefully demolished and the mound stabilized, with a future interpretive center under development.
The neighborhood’s most visible architectural legacy from the German immigrant era is St. Anthony of Padua Catholic Church at 3140 Meramec Street , whose twin 175-foot Romanesque towers are visible for miles across the South Side. Founded in 1863 specifically for the German Catholic immigrants who were filling Mount Pleasant and the surrounding neighborhoods, the present 1910 Romanesque sanctuary features Emil Frei art glass windows of exceptional quality, an organ regularly cited as one of the finest in the city, and ornate paintings and statuary that local guidebooks rank among the most magnificent Catholic interiors in St. Louis. The parish has been served by the Order of Friars Minor (Franciscans) for more than 160 years. The parish food pantry at 3130 Meramec Street, run by lay volunteer Outreach Ministries, remains one of the most important social-service operations on the South Side. The St. Anthony parish school on Meramec was recently sold and is being adapted for new neighborhood use. Nearby, St. Hedwig Catholic Church at Compton and Pulaski — founded in 1904 for Polish immigrant families and now operating as Diverse City Church — is having its former school building converted into a campus for Gene Slay’s Girls & Boys Club of St. Louis , one of the most successful adaptive-reuse projects in the neighborhood. The Mount Pleasant School on Nebraska Avenue, a three-story brick structure built in 1895 by the St. Louis Public Schools architectural office, is on the National Register of Historic Places and has been converted to apartments.
Mount Pleasant’s 20th-century history was disrupted, like much of south-city St. Louis, by the construction of Interstate 55 in the mid-20th century, which bisected the neighborhood and cleared blocks of historic housing stock. The mid-century homes built in the wake of the interstate construction now form a distinctive pocket of post-war architecture amid the predominantly Victorian and early-20th-century brick fabric. The Maryville Academy , a long-established Catholic girls’ school, moved to the suburbs in 1961, leaving behind a fenced post-office site and the Maryville Gardens apartments (1978) with their massive surface parking lot on what was once the academy’s sports field. White flight and suburbanization through the 1960s and 1970s changed the neighborhood’s demographic balance dramatically. The 2000 Census recorded 4,302 residents (59% White, 32% Black, 4% Asian, 2% Hispanic/Latino) in 2,281 housing units, with 85% occupied and a 31%/69% owner-to-renter split — a low owner-occupancy rate for a South Side neighborhood, reflecting Mount Pleasant’s position as a transitional corridor connecting Dutchtown, Marine Villa, Carondelet, and the river-bluff industrial parcels.
The neighborhood’s commercial corridors have followed the city’s usual North-South pattern of disinvestment followed by selective revitalization. Meramec Street , with its many former storefronts (the Schaeffer Hobby Store moved to the suburbs years ago) and Virginia Avenue have both seen extended periods of vacancy. The current wave of revitalization is centered on three major institutional efforts: the Neighborhood Innovation Center (NIC) at 3207 Meramec Street is a nonprofit microbusiness incubator providing coworking space, digital upskilling programs, community-market and farmers’-market hosting, and high-speed infrastructure access to entrepreneurs who might otherwise lack it. The center also functions as a local polling place. The Marquette Homes affordable housing project (182 units, expected completion in 2026) and the St. Joseph Housing Initiative home sales program are working to rebuild the residential housing stock, while the Dutchtown Main Streets façade grant program is restoring commercial storefronts along Meramec and Virginia. Mount Pleasant is actively engaged in the PlanSTL Area 7 planning process (2026–2027), which will set the strategic framework for the broader Greater Dutchtown corridor.
South Broadway’s industrial fabric — 19th-century warehouses and rail-adjacent parcels along the river bluff — still carries specialty operations today, including St. Louis Laser , just over the Eichelberger Street line in Carondelet. The neighborhood’s own commercial footprint leans residential instead: Mount Pleasant’s high renter-occupancy rate (69% at last full Census count) shows up today in apartment communities like the 120-unit Chapel View Apartments on Michigan Avenue and property managers like Meramec Valley Properties , headquartered right on Mt Pleasant Street, who handle much of the neighborhood’s rental housing stock. The combination of pre-European Native heritage, German Catholic religious institutions, river-bluff industrial fabric, mid-century interstate disruption, and 21st-century microbusiness incubation makes Mount Pleasant one of the most layered and culturally distinctive neighborhoods on the South Side. As Mayor Spencer wrote on September 19, 2025: “St. Louis came much too close to losing all of the more than 100 mounds that were here before European settlers arrived and ultimately tore down all but one” — a sentiment that captures both the fragility and the resilience of Mount Pleasant’s extraordinary heritage.
Image: Sugarloaf Mound at 4420 Ohio Avenue in Mount Pleasant — the last Native American mound in St. Louis (constructed 600–1200 AD), reacquired in full by the Osage Nation in September 2025 after a 17-year preservation effort — Wikimedia Commons , CC BY-SA 3.0 by Parker Botanical

Mount Pleasant’s river-bluff position keeps summers a touch cooler and winters a touch milder than neighborhoods further from the water, and the neighborhood’s century-old brick housing stock has held up to all of it without much trouble.

### Frequently Asked Questions 
Q. What defines the Mount Pleasant neighborhood? 
A. Mount Pleasant is a Near Southside river-bluff neighborhood bounded by Meramec Street, Eichelberger Street, the Mississippi River, and South Compton Avenue, part of the broader Greater Dutchtown cultural area. It’s defined by deep history layered atop each other: Sugarloaf Mound, the 1863 St. Anthony of Padua Catholic Church, and 21st-century microbusiness incubation at the Neighborhood Innovation Center.

Q. What types of businesses are most common in Mount Pleasant? 
A. Mount Pleasant’s listed businesses lean toward chambers of commerce and community organizations, like the Heartland Black Chamber, Hispanic Chamber, and Southwest Area Chamber, alongside event venues such as Celebrate Event Venue and A Royal Event Party Planning, plus property managers like Chapel View Apartments and Meramec Valley Properties serving the neighborhood’s largely renter population.

Q. What kinds of dining, retail, and recreation options are available in Mount Pleasant? 
A. This page doesn’t list dining or retail storefronts in Mount Pleasant itself, though St Louis Laser offers specialty engraving just over the Eichelberger line. For recreation, Mount Pleasant Park at Michigan and Dakota has a roller hockey rink in some of the best condition in the city, and the Neighborhood Innovation Center hosts community and farmers’ markets.

Q. Are there neighborhood landmarks, parks, and historic sites in Mount Pleasant? 
A. Yes. Sugarloaf Mound at 4420 Ohio Avenue is the only surviving Native American mound in St. Louis, built 600-1200 AD and reacquired by the Osage Nation in September 2025. St. Anthony of Padua Catholic Church, with its twin 175-foot towers, and the NRHP-listed 1895 Mount Pleasant School are also neighborhood landmarks, along with Mount Pleasant Park.

Q. What is it like to live in Mount Pleasant? 
A. Living in Mount Pleasant means a river-bluff setting with century-old brick housing stock and a renter-majority population, at a 31%/69% owner-to-renter split as of the last full Census count. Apartment communities like Chapel View and property managers like Meramec Valley Properties handle much of the rental housing, while the Neighborhood Innovation Center supports local microbusinesses.

Q. How do residents and visitors get around Mount Pleasant? 
A. Meramec Street runs east-west as the neighborhood’s main commercial corridor, while South Broadway serves as the industrial spine along the river bluff. Interstate 55 bisected the neighborhood in the mid-20th century, and today Mount Pleasant Street, Virginia Avenue, and the interior grid of state-named streets connect residents to Dutchtown, Marine Villa, and Carondelet nearby.

### Near North Riverfront Businesses & Neighborhood Guide | St Louis Near Me Directory
Near North Riverfront, St. Louis
Near North Riverfront is one of the most unusual neighborhoods in St. Louis: a large, overwhelmingly industrial stretch of the Mississippi River just north of downtown, where rail yards, freight tracks, cold-storage warehouses, vacant land, and barge traffic vastly outnumber the roughly 395 people who actually live here. It is not a residential neighborhood in the ordinary sense — it is a working riverfront corridor with deep history, anchored by the McKinley Bridge and threaded by the St. Louis Riverfront Trail.
The neighborhood is the City of St. Louis neighborhood #64 , sitting in north St. Louis along the riverfront north of Laclede’s Landing . Its rough boundaries run along Tucker Boulevard, West Florissant Avenue, and N. Broadway , with the Mississippi River forming the eastern edge. It spans Wards 8 and 14 and covers about 2.17 square miles — a big footprint for such a small population, which is exactly what you would expect from a district built for industry rather than houses. (Note that it is a separate neighborhood from the City’s North Riverfront district, #79, farther upriver.)
In the 19th century this stretch of riverfront was an emblematic cross-section of the Gateway City, a place where the Mississippi, heavy industry, commerce, and (then) dense residential blocks all collided. Early land here traced to former mayor Bryan Mullanphy and prominent owner Peter Lindell , who ran a stone quarry near the river. The Wiggins Ferry , a critical crossing to the Illinois side, departed from near here — and that river-crossing role drew the extensive rail connections that would come to define, and ultimately demolish much of, the historic fabric of the district.
Industry flourished on the riverbank. Luther Kennett’s Shot Tower used gravity to make lead shot, and the area hosted what was described as one of the grandest sugar refineries in America. The skyline of smokestacks, grain elevators, riverboats, and rocky bluffs was distinctive enough that Compton & Dry chose the district for their 1876 Pictorial St. Louis . Into the 20th century, large refrigerated cold-storage warehouses — several designed by architect Isaac Taylor and his competitors — rose north of the Martin Luther King (MLK) Bridge, and a number of those warehouse buildings still stand today.
Over the 20th century the once-populous neighborhood emptied out. What remains is a landscape of vacant lots, surviving historic industrial buildings, active freight rail, barge and tugboat traffic, and open Mississippi River frontage. Population has never been high here — it rose to 648 in 2000, then fell to 553 in 2010 and 395 in 2020 — and the City counts only about 95 housing units in the whole neighborhood. We want to be honest with readers: this is a sparsely populated working industrial and riverfront corridor, not a place with a traditional residential main street.
For visitors and cyclists, the river edge is the draw. The St. Louis Riverfront Trail (Mississippi Greenway) runs along this stretch, offering river-meets-industry views — tugboats pushing barges, freight trains on the commodity tracks, and the wide brown sweep of the Mississippi. At Branch Street the trail meets the McKinley Bridge Bikeway , where the historic “Iron Horse” Trestle project has been converting an abandoned steel rail trestle into an elevated park reaching toward Old North St. Louis.
The McKinley Bridge itself is the neighborhood’s signature landmark: a historic early-1900s span over the Mississippi to Venice, Illinois, now carrying road traffic plus the bikeway that links to trails on the Illinois side. Inland, the neighborhood abuts the historic Mullanphy area and Old North St. Louis on its western edge, while the I-70 Stan Musial Veterans Memorial Bridge sits just to the south near downtown and Laclede’s Landing. Together these crossings, trails, and surviving warehouses make Near North Riverfront a fascinating place to explore on two wheels, even if few people call it home.
The McKinley Bridge over the Mississippi at the Near North Riverfront. Photo: “McKinley Bridge 2025” by Antony-22, licensed under CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons.

St. Louis sits in a humid subtropical climate, and out on the open river the Near North Riverfront feels all of it — warm, humid summers with July highs near 89.6°F , cold winters with January highs near 40.4°F and about 16.6 inches of snow , roughly 41.7 inches of rain a year, and a low-lying riverbank exposed to flooding and the occasional spring tornado warning that comes with sitting near Tornado Alley.
None of that industry actually left — it just changed hands. The rail lines that once fed sugar refineries and cold-storage warehouses still carry active freight along N. Broadway, and the district’s real business today is what riverfront rail access has always been good for: moving material in bulk. SA Recycling runs scrap yards on N. Broadway and Hall Street, Z & L Wrecking Company and Subsurface Constructors work out of rail-served lots off N. Broadway and Angelica Street, and St. Louis Composting operates a commercial depackaging facility that turns spoiled grocery and food waste into compost at industrial scale. Even the newest arrival plays by the same logic: a 10,000-square-foot warehouse near the McKinley Bridge is now Mississippi Underground Hall, an electronic-music venue with two event spaces and a club-grade sound system, proof the district’s oversized industrial buildings still have a second act. That is who the Near North Riverfront is for now — heavy users of rail and river access, plus a handful of real destinations along N. Broadway — and the honest pitch to a visitor is the trail and the bridge, not a shopping day.

Q. What defines the Near North Riverfront neighborhood? 
A. Near North Riverfront is defined by heavy industry, not housing — a 2.17-square-mile stretch of the Mississippi riverfront just north of downtown where rail yards, freight tracks, cold-storage warehouses, and barge traffic vastly outnumber the roughly 395 people who live here. It’s anchored by the historic McKinley Bridge and the St. Louis Riverfront Trail, a working district with deep 19th-century roots in quarrying, milling, and rail.

### North Hampton Businesses & Neighborhood Guide | St Louis Near Me Directory
North Hampton, St. Louis 
North Hampton is a quiet residential neighborhood on the near-southwest side of St. Louis (ZIP 63109), a tidy grid of brick bungalows and gabled homes on tree-lined streets. It is bounded by Scanlan and Connecticut Avenues on the north, South Kingshighway Boulevard on the east, Chippewa Street on the south, and Hampton Avenue on the west, and is made up of two smaller areas — Tilles Park from Hampton to Macklind, and Kingshighway Hills from Macklind to Kingshighway.
North Hampton holds a curious distinction: much of it was the City of St. Louis's last large tract of open land. While neighborhoods around it filled in during the streetcar era, this ground sat over the working coal and clay mines of the Oak Hill railroad, and serious home-building had to wait until those deposits were played out. The blocks west of Macklind did not fully develop until after World War II — late by St. Louis standards.
The result is a settled, family-friendly enclave anchored by the city's Tilles Park, near Hampton and Fyler — a green pocket of ballfields and shade trees that gives the neighborhood its northwestern character. It is the kind of place people put down roots and stay for decades.
Because North Hampton is first and foremost residential, its shopping and dining sit in the ring of business districts that surround it on three sides: restaurants and a supper club along South Kingshighway to the east, the Hampton Village center and Hampton Avenue shops to the south and west, and the beloved Macklind Business District just to the southwest.
The locally owned spots featured below sit in that ring, at the neighborhood's edges — a farm-to-table cafe and bakery, a retro supper club, wood-fired pizza, a globe-spanning newcomer, and St. Louis barbecue among them — all within an easy hop of any North Hampton front porch.
North Hampton is not entirely without businesses of its own, either. A bakery and a real estate office sit on its interior streets rather than its business-district edges — a small but genuine exception to a neighborhood that is otherwise built, block for block, for people to live in rather than shop in.
The North Hampton neighborhood, St. Louis. 
North Hampton shares St. Louis’s humid subtropical climate — warm, sometimes stormy summers and cold but rarely brutal winters.

### Frequently Asked Questions
Q. What defines the North Hampton neighborhood? 
A. North Hampton is a quiet residential neighborhood on St. Louis’s near-southwest side (ZIP 63109), bounded by Scanlan and Connecticut Avenues, South Kingshighway Boulevard, Chippewa Street, and Hampton Avenue. It’s made up of two areas — Tilles Park, from Hampton to Macklind, and Kingshighway Hills, from Macklind to Kingshighway — and was one of the city’s last large tracts to be built out.

Q. How does St Louis Near Me Directory help North Hampton businesses? 
A. St Louis Near Me Directory builds hyper-local, SEO-optimized pages like this North Hampton guide so nearby customers can find neighborhood businesses when they search. Simple Gold, Platinum, and Diamond plans come with a 7-day free trial, no long-term contracts, and no competitor ads running on your listing — the goal is expanding your existing Google Business Profile, not replacing it.

Q. What types of businesses are most common in North Hampton? 
A. North Hampton is overwhelmingly residential, so its businesses cluster along its edges — wood-fired pizza, a Pakistani and Vietnamese kitchen, and a barbecue joint sit near its Macklind and Hampton Avenue borders, alongside a supper club and a farm-to-table cafe on South Kingshighway. A bakery and a real estate office also sit on its own interior streets.

Q. What kinds of dining, retail, and recreation options are available in North Hampton? 
A. Dining is North Hampton’s strength: Russell’s on Macklind for brunch and baked goods, The Golden Hoosier for burgers and cocktails, Onesto Pizza & Trattoria and Mortar & Pestle in the Macklind Business District, Himalayan Yeti for Indian food, and Salt + Smoke and JJ Twig’s along Hampton Avenue. For recreation, the neighborhood leans on the city’s nearby Tilles Park.

Q. Are there neighborhood landmarks, parks, and historic sites in North Hampton? 
A. Tilles Park, near Hampton and Fyler, is North Hampton’s green anchor — ballfields and shade trees that give the neighborhood’s Tilles Park section its name. The neighborhood’s real landmark is what’s underneath parts of it: the old Oak Hill railroad coal and clay mines, which delayed home-building west of Macklind until after World War II.

Q. What is it like to live in North Hampton? 
A. North Hampton is a settled, family-friendly enclave of brick bungalows and gabled homes on tree-lined streets — the kind of place people put down roots and stay for decades. It’s residential by design, but a ring of business districts on three sides means restaurants, a bakery, a chiropractor, and a real estate office are all within an easy walk or short drive.

Q. How do residents and visitors get around North Hampton? 
A. North Hampton sits inside a ring formed by Hampton Avenue, South Kingshighway Boulevard, and Chippewa Street — all major St. Louis corridors that connect the neighborhood to the rest of the metro. Its interior tree-lined streets are quiet and walkable, with the Macklind, Hampton, and Kingshighway business districts each reachable on foot from most North Hampton blocks.

Q. How can residents and visitors explore more services around North Hampton? 
A. St Louis Near Me Directory’s North Hampton guide lists the neighborhood’s top-rated local businesses, from Russell’s on Macklind to Dan Brassil Real Estate, each linked to more detail.
