For dining and retail, the closest real options are Epic Pizza & Subs in Soulard, Frenchtown Records, Antiques & More in LaSalle Park, and Polite Society Restaurant and Bar in Lafayette Square — all under half a mile away.

Q. Are there neighborhood landmarks, parks, and historic sites in Peabody Darst Webbe? 
A. Yes. The City Hospital Historic District (NRHP 2001), now The Georgian Condominiums, anchors the east side; Clinton Peabody, the oldest public housing project in St. Louis, anchors the west. Mestres Park, the Al Chappelle Community Center, and Ray Leisure Park serve residents, with Lafayette Park — the city’s first public park — just to the west.

Q. What is it like to live in Peabody Darst Webbe? 
A. Living in Peabody Darst Webbe today means a small, transitional neighborhood mid-redevelopment: Clinton Peabody’s $150 million rebuild is reshaping the western half through the early 2030s, while The Georgian Condominiums offer loft living in a restored 1912 hospital building. It’s quiet and mostly residential, with Soulard and Lafayette Square a short walk away for everything else.

Q. How do residents and visitors get around Peabody Darst Webbe? 
A. Peabody Darst Webbe sits at one of St. Louis’s most connected transit points, ringed by I-44, I-55, and I-64, two miles from SSM Health Saint Louis University Hospital. It’s a walkable few blocks to Soulard, LaSalle Park, and Lafayette Square, and 16 miles from Lambert St. Louis International Airport.

## Peabody Darst Webbe Businesses & Neighborhood Guide | St Louis Near Me Directory

 Peabody Darst Webbe, St. Louis

Peabody Darst Webbe serves as a compact “Near Southside” neighborhood of St. Louis — anchored by The Georgian Condominiums at the historic City Hospital site, the A.T. Still University Missouri School of Dentistry & Oral Health, and the 350-unit Clinton-Peabody mixed-income redevelopment — offering B2B marketing, beverage distribution, historic condominium living, affordable housing, and professional services for residents and businesses across the south St. Louis corridor.

Peabody Darst Webbe sits just south of downtown St. Louis at **38.6065° N, 90.2073° W** in zip code 63104. The neighborhood’s official boundaries are **Chouteau Avenue** on the north, **South Tucker Boulevard / 12th Street** on the east, the **I-55 / I-44 interchange** on the south, and **Dolman Street** on the west. Also known historically as the **Near Southside**, the neighborhood is hemmed in by Lafayette Square to the west, LaSalle Park to the east, Downtown West to the north, and Soulard and McKinley Heights to the south. As of the 2020 Census, the neighborhood’s racial makeup was 79.7% Black, 15.3% White, 3.6% two or more races, 0.8% Asian, and 1.6% Hispanic or Latino — reflecting a 65-resident gain and a substantial 52-unit drop in vacancy since 2010, when the population had already grown 61 percent from the 2000 count.

The neighborhood’s identity is inseparable from three mid-20th-century public housing projects whose names it still bears. **Clinton-Peabody**, built in 1942 under the New Deal Housing Act of 1937, was the first generation of St. Louis public housing — a low-rise development that opened as the segregated white-tenant sibling to **Carr Square Village** on the Near North Side, which was built for Black families. The **Joseph M. Darst Apartments** followed in 1956 (four nine-story towers, 645 units), named for Mayor Joseph Darst (1949–1953), the same St. Louis mayor whose urban-renewal vision also produced the infamous Pruitt-Igoe. The **Anthony M. Webbe Apartments** opened in 1961 (two nine-story towers, one twelve-story, one eight-story, 578 units). Designed by the famed firm of **Leinweber, Yamasaki & Hellmuth** — led by architect Minoru Yamasaki, who would later design Pruitt-Igoe and the original World Trade Center — the Darst-Webbe complex was built on the grounds of a 1940s-cleared near-south neighborhood between Soulard and Lafayette Square.

Like Pruitt-Igoe, Darst-Webbe declined quickly under chronic underfunding by the St. Louis Housing Authority — elevators failed, sanitation lapsed, and by the 1990s the high-rises were widely regarded as failures of mid-century housing policy. **The Darst-Webbe apartments were demolished in 1999**, and the site was replaced with the current two-story, mixed-income brick properties — designed to echo the older brick rowhomes of Soulard and Lafayette Square — that define the neighborhood’s residential streets today. The neighborhood also contains a small number of Italianate-style rowhomes (some dating to the turn of the 20th century, others recent infill) plus a corridor along Park Avenue that has seen new construction in the years since the demolitions.

The redevelopment story continues today with the **Clinton-Peabody Apartments** — St. Louis City’s oldest public housing development, built in 1942. In 2023, residents voted overwhelmingly to demolish the existing buildings and replace them with a **$150 million POAH-led redevelopment** creating 350 new mixed-income apartments and affordable homes, centered around a reconfigured street grid, a renovated community center, and a new central park. Demolition began in 2025; current residents were relocated to refreshed on-site units in 2023 and 2024; and the first wave of new units broke ground in early 2026. The 10-year project is expected to fundamentally reshape the western half of the neighborhood through the early 2030s.

Anchoring the eastern side of the neighborhood is the **City Hospital Historic District**, listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 2001. The site has served continuously as a public-health landmark since the city built its first hospital here in 1846, in response to a cholera outbreak. The original wooden complex was destroyed by fire in 1856; rebuilt the next year; then leveled by the “Great Cyclone” tornado of 1896 — the third-deadliest tornado in U.S. history. The current **Georgian Revival complex**, designed by famed St. Louis architect **Albert B. Groves** of Grable, Weber & Groves, was completed in 1912 on the same 10-acre site at 1515 Lafayette Avenue. Under Dr. Max C. Starkloff — the St. Louis City Health Commissioner whose 1918–19 Spanish flu protocols are still studied today — the hospital became a state-of-the-art institution and was renamed the Max Starkloff Memorial Hospital after his death. The complex grew to 18 buildings, included a power plant and laundry building, and operated continuously until it closed in 1985.

After two decades of abandonment, the City Hospital site was successfully redeveloped. In 2006, the 1912 Administration Building reopened as **The Georgian Condominiums** — 102 loft-style residences with high ceilings, hardwood floors, gas fireplaces, walk-in closets, and 360-degree views of downtown St. Louis. The old **Power Plant** became Climb So iLL, an indoor climbing gym; the **Laundry Building** (a 1940 Public Works Administration project) became Palladium St. Louis, a private event space. In 2014, **A.T. Still University’s Missouri School of Dentistry & Oral Health** broke ground on the former Malcolm Bliss Psychopathological Institute site — a 79,000-square-foot dental school that opened in 2013 and now serves as ATSU’s third campus after Kirksville, Missouri, and Mesa, Arizona. By 2018, redevelopment had moved on to the remaining vacant buildings — the Commissioner’s Building (1907), Commissary (1940), Ambulance Garage (1921), and Clinic Building (1921) — under Pearl Companies of Indianapolis with design by Trivers Associates.

The neighborhood’s civic infrastructure includes **Peabody Academy** (built 1957 on 14th Street, the St. Louis Public Schools system’s only school in the neighborhood, serving Kindergarten through 8th grade), the **Al Chappelle Community Center** (a St. Louis Housing Authority operation with public meeting rooms), **Mestres Park** (a 3-acre linear park parallel to the neighborhood), and the adjacent **Ray Leisure Park** with its **12th & Park Recreation Center** (gymnasium, multipurpose courts, and indoor pool). The neighborhood’s most visible amenity remains the proximity to **Lafayette Park** — established in 1851 as the city’s first public park — just to the west, with its biweekly summer concert series, fall festival, and historic Victorian-era surroundings.

Today Peabody Darst Webbe sits at one of the most strategic transit positions in St. Louis: surrounded by I-44, I-55, and I-64, two miles east of SSM Health Saint Louis University Hospital, and 16 miles south of Lambert St. Louis International Airport. The neighborhood’s mix of historic condominium living, ongoing affordable-housing redevelopment, brick infill homes, and B2B professional services makes it a uniquely transitional district — one whose blocks reflect every major chapter of 20th- and 21st-century St. Louis housing policy, from the New Deal’s first public housing experiments to today’s mixed-income reinvestment.

Image: City Hospital Historic District (now The Georgian Condominiums), 1515 Lafayette Avenue, Peabody Darst Webbe, St. Louis — designed by Albert B. Groves, completed 1912 — Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0

### Penrose Businesses & Neighborhood Guide | St Louis Near Me Directory
Penrose, St. Louis
Penrose serves as a stable residential and small-business neighborhood on the Near North Side of St. Louis — anchored by the 51.22-acre Penrose Park, the historic Penrose Park Velodrome (one of only 27 in the United States), and the Heartland St. Louis Black Chamber of Commerce at the North Spring Empowerment Center — offering chamber advocacy, telecom infrastructure, general contracting, mold remediation, screen printing manufacturing, industrial packaging, chemical distribution, and wholesale tire supply for residents, contractors, and Near North Side businesses across the metro.
Penrose sits on the north side of St. Louis at 38.6815° N, 90.2578° W in zip code 63115, just south of I-70 and west of O’Fallon Park. The neighborhood’s official boundaries are Florissant Avenue and I-70 on the north, Natural Bridge Avenue on the south, North Newstead and Pope Avenues on the east, and Kingshighway Boulevard on the west. The neighborhood is split between the city’s 21st Ward and 1st Ward, and as of the 2020 Census, Penrose had 5,243 residents — 95.3% Black, 0.9% White, 2.8% two or more races, with 0.8% Hispanic or Latino origin. Familiar residential streets like Penrose, Euclid, Shreve, Lee, Margaretta, and Steinlage Drive tie the area together, with Natural Bridge, West Florissant, and Kingshighway carrying most of the commercial activity.
Penrose’s name comes not from a settler but from a speculator: in the early 19th century, the area was characterized more by land speculation than actual settlement. The neighborhood takes its name from Clement B. Penrose , whom Thomas Jefferson appointed land commissioner in 1805 to settle disputed Louisiana Purchase land claims. Penrose lived on a nearby estate and was one of the region’s prime land investors. Another early landowner was the Kentucky statesman Henry Clay , a shaper of the Missouri Compromise of 1820 — making the Penrose ground one of the few St. Louis neighborhoods to claim a direct connection to two major figures of the early American republic.
Penrose did not take on the contours of a community until the late 1880s, when farmers and dairymen, most of German heritage , moved their families into the area. By 1900, the community — though still rural — was sufficiently settled to boast two German churches: St. Engelbert’s Catholic Church and Salem German Evangelical Church . The 1920s brought commercial development and transit lines, raising land values around the northern edges of the city, and most of Penrose’s subdivisions date from that era when single-family brick homes sprang up along Euclid, Shreve, and Lee Avenues. Some subdivisions were the work of outside investors; others were developed by long-time residents — a prime example being the area around Steinlage Drive , a street named for a local German family in the dairy business whose properties were subdivided for housing.
The early 1960s were years of transition for Penrose. As older residents moved out, middle- and upper-income African-American families moved in. The well-constructed brick houses were ideal for moderate-sized families, offering many their first opportunity for home ownership. Teachers, nurses, and city and government employees made Penrose their new home — a significant number coming from The Ville , located to the southeast and long the city’s premier African-American neighborhood. As Penrose’s African-American population grew from 33 percent in 1960 to 95 percent in 1970, African-American institutions helped solidify the neighborhood: St. Peter’s A.M.E. Church , a historic African Methodist Episcopal congregation, relocated to the corner of Shreve and Margaretta in 1962, and in 1974 the Julia Davis Branch Library — named to honor the well-known St. Louis educator — opened on Natural Bridge Avenue. Penrose developed into a stable African-American middle-class neighborhood, though residents were long subjected to redlining by financial institutions because of the neighborhood’s location north of Delmar.
One of the standout features of Penrose is the 51.22-acre Penrose Park , proposed in the city’s landmark 1907 comprehensive plan by the “Inner and Outer Parks Committee” — whose members included George Kessler and Julius Pitzman, the same Forest Park master planner who would later plat the Central West End’s Westmoreland and Portland Places. Established in 1910, the park is bisected by North Bircher and Kingshighway Boulevards and east-west oriented train tracks. Its amenities include ball fields, basketball and handball courts, a softball field, tennis court, playground, pavilions with BBQ grills, a jogging path with fitness stations — and the centerpiece, the Penrose Park Velodrome : a banked outdoor cycling track measuring 1/5 of a mile long with a 28-degree bank, one of only 27 velodromes in the United States and the only one in Missouri.
The Penrose Park Velodrome has a remarkable origin story. When highway officials announced in 1958 that they would expand U.S. Highway 40 along the southern edge of Forest Park — razing the city’s 1930s-built Forest Park bicycle track in the process — the City of St. Louis donated land adjacent to Penrose Park for a replacement velodrome. Built in 1962 and designed by Olympic cyclist and Schwinn Bicycle Company designer Frank Burlando , the new Penrose Park Velodrome hosted the prestigious U.S. National Track Cycling Championships in its inaugural year. A sewer collapse in the 1970s left the track with the affectionate nickname “ Mr. Bumpy Face ”; resurfacings in 1984 and 2005 followed, and in 2019 the track was rebuilt with a brand-new concrete surface that restored it to championship caliber. Open dawn to dusk, 365 days a year, the velodrome remains a regional cycling destination and a defining feature of Penrose.
Beyond Penrose Park, the neighborhood’s civic infrastructure includes the St. Elizabeth Mother of John the Baptist Catholic Church on Shreve Avenue (operated by the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of St. Louis), the historic St. Peter’s A.M.E. Church on Margaretta Avenue, the Julia Davis Branch Library on Natural Bridge, and the small neighborhood park Eugene “Tink” Bradley Park (3.18 acres, established 1958). The neighborhood’s housing stock remains predominantly classic North St. Louis brick — many homes built during the 1920s boom on Euclid, Shreve, Lee, and surrounding side streets — with deep front yards, front porches, and mature street trees that give Penrose a traditional St. Louis feel. Economically, Penrose is largely residential but closely tied to the broader north-city business network along I-70, Natural Bridge, and West Florissant, giving many residents short commutes to industrial, logistics, health care, and public sector jobs.
Image: Residential Modern Infill, North Newstead Avenue, St. Louis — photo by Paul Sableman — Wikimedia Commons , CC BY 2.0

Penrose runs on a typical four-season Midwest calendar, with the velodrome’s Thursday-night racing series livening up Penrose Park from May through August and winter shifting the neighborhood’s rhythm indoors to its churches, chambers, and the storefronts along Natural Bridge and West Florissant.
What sets Penrose apart from a lot of north-side St. Louis is what’s still standing. The 1920s building boom left Euclid, Shreve, Lee, and the side streets around them lined with the classic North Side mix — single-family brick bungalows and brick two-family flats, deep-set on their lots with covered front porches and mature street trees — and a 2021 survey of the neighborhood by the local urbanist site NextSTL described the housing stock as “overall quite solid and stable,” with abandoned properties carefully boarded rather than left open and new infill going up on some of the vacant lots. That’s not the case on every block north of Natural Bridge, where entire streets have thinned out to a handful of occupied homes. Penrose still reads as a neighborhood, block by block, porch by porch — which is a big part of why the 1920s owners who built it and the families who bought in from The Ville in the 1960s both saw the same thing: solid brick housing worth staying in.

### Frequently Asked Questions 
Q. What defines the Penrose neighborhood? 
A. Penrose is defined by its 51.22-acre namesake park and the Penrose Park Velodrome — one of only 27 in the country — and by its history as a German-dairy-farm district that became a stable African-American middle-class neighborhood starting in the 1960s, when teachers, nurses, and city workers, many from The Ville, bought into its classic North St. Louis brick housing stock.

Q. How does St Louis Near Me Directory help Penrose businesses? 
A. Q. What types of businesses are most common in Penrose? 
A. Penrose’s business mix centers on chamber advocacy, telecom and residential contracting, mold remediation, screen printing and digital printing manufacturing, industrial packaging, chemical distribution, wholesale tire supply, and everyday retail like the corner store on Margaretta Avenue. Some providers, like Lawson Screen & Digital Products (1949) and Harcros Chemicals (100 years), have anchored the Near North Side for generations.

Q. What kinds of dining, retail, and recreation options are available in Penrose? 
A. Penrose’s own retail is thin — Kingz Korner Store on Margaretta Avenue is one of the few storefronts inside the residential core, offering everyday essentials and Grubhub delivery. Recreation is the strength: 51.22-acre Penrose Park has ball fields, basketball and handball courts, a jogging path, and the Penrose Park Velodrome, whose Thursday-night races run May through August.

Q. Are there neighborhood landmarks, parks, and historic sites in Penrose? 
A. Yes — chief among them 51.22-acre Penrose Park (established 1910) and its Penrose Park Velodrome, built in 1962 by Olympic cyclist and Schwinn designer Frank Burlando, one of only 27 velodromes in the country. Also notable: the historic St. Peter’s A.M.E. Church, St. Elizabeth Mother of John the Baptist Catholic Church, the Julia Davis Branch Library (1974), and the small Eugene “Tink” Bradley Park.

Q. What is it like to live in Penrose? 
A. Penrose is a stable, working- and middle-class residential neighborhood of classic North St. Louis brick homes, home to about 5,243 residents, 95% Black, as of the 2020 Census. A 2021 survey by the urbanist site NextSTL called the housing stock “overall quite solid and stable,” with vacant properties boarded rather than abandoned and new infill on some empty lots — though blocks north of Natural Bridge have thinned out more.

Q. How do residents and visitors get around Penrose? 
A. Penrose sits just south of I-70, bounded by Florissant Avenue to the north, Natural Bridge Avenue to the south, North Newstead and Pope Avenues to the east, and Kingshighway Boulevard to the west. Natural Bridge, West Florissant, and Kingshighway carry most through-traffic and commercial activity, while residential streets like Penrose, Euclid, Shreve, Lee, and Margaretta connect the neighborhood’s brick-home blocks.

### Princeton Heights Businesses & Neighborhood Guide | St Louis Near Me Directory
Princeton Heights, St. Louis
Princeton Heights is a quiet, walkable south St. Louis neighborhood of early-1900s brick bungalows, anchored by the lively Macklind Avenue Business District and bordered by Hampton, Eichelberger, Christy, and Gravois.
Princeton Heights sits in south St. Louis, bounded by Hampton Avenue on the west, Eichelberger Street on the north, Christy Boulevard on the east, and Gravois Avenue on the south. It covers roughly 0.83 square miles and falls within the city’s Wards 2 and 5.
Long before the brick streets arrived, this was rural farmland known as Gardenville , and one 1860s Moellenhoff-family farmhouse still stands on Loughborough as a reminder of those days. The neighborhood name has two roots: the historic Princeton Creamery that once operated on Kingshighway near Gravois, and the “Princeton Place” subdivision platted in 1906 — the “Heights” nodding to the gentle rise up from the River Des Peres.
Gravois Road was the first road paved by the State of Missouri , and streetcar lines soon followed it south. By around 1920, nearly all of the old farms had been developed, with the main buildout coming in the 1920s and 1930s . Many of the earliest homeowners were German families, and a number of street names were later Anglicized after the World Wars.
The housing stock is the defining feature of Princeton Heights. Block after block is lined with 1920s and 1930s brick Craftsman bungalows, “storybook” gingerbread houses, and American Foursquares — the kind of sturdy, gabled brick homes that give south city its character. The resident-run Princeton Heights Neighborhood Association (PHNA) , a 501(c)(3) incorporated in 1976 , helps look after those streets, organizes the neighborhood, and keeps residents connected.
Daily life centers on the Macklind Avenue Business District , a compact, walkable strip of locally owned restaurants, cafés, and shops that promotes the Southampton and Princeton Heights area together. Just off the southeast edge sits Christy Park , a roughly 16-acre city park founded in 1910 and named for brick-industry businessman William Tandy Christy; its Christy Greenway connects toward Carondelet Park. Along the south and southwest edge, the River Des Peres Greenway and Christy Greenway (part of Great Rivers Greenway) offer adjacent trails for walking and biking.
The Laundry Basket, a neighborhood laundromat on Macklind Avenue — the kind of locally owned, everyday business that gives the Macklind corridor its character. Photo by Lane Forman, July 2026.

A few landmarks border the neighborhood without sitting squarely inside it. Our Lady of Sorrows parish, at the Kingshighway edge, was founded in 1907 with a school that opened in 1908 — a longtime heritage anchor, though the parish closed in 2023 . Just northwest, across Hampton Avenue, lie St. Louis Hills and Francis Park , popular adjacent destinations that many Princeton Heights residents treat as part of their extended backyard.
Princeton Heights is known for its early-1900s brick ‘gabled’ bungalows on quiet, tree-lined streets. Photo: “Princeton Heights” by Paul Sableman, licensed under CC BY 2.0 via Wikimedia Commons.

Fine Art Deco stonework crowns the windows of an unassuming brick building on January Avenue in Princeton Heights — one of the small architectural surprises tucked into this 1920s–30s south-city neighborhood. Photo by Lane Forman, July 2026.

Like the rest of St. Louis, Princeton Heights gets hot, sticky summers and cold winters, and the neighborhood’s mature street trees do most of the work of making both bearable.
What makes Princeton Heights work today is the same thing that built it: a walkable grid of small, well-kept brick homes within a few blocks of everything you need. It runs quieter than its flashier neighbor, St. Louis Hills, next door — which is exactly the appeal for the young families and downsizing empty-nesters who keep choosing a starter bungalow here over a bigger, pricier block a half-mile north.
Macklind Avenue backs that up with real, everyday businesses instead of boutiques built for Instagram — a screen-printer, two pizzerias, a florist, a women’s fitness studio, a family-run auto shop a few blocks over on Kingshighway. It is the unglamorous mix that keeps a neighborhood functioning long after the trend pieces move on to somewhere else.

### Frequently Asked Questions 
Q. What defines the Princeton Heights neighborhood? 
A. Princeton Heights is defined by its brick-bungalow housing stock, platted as Princeton Place in 1906 and mostly built out in the 1920s and 1930s as a classic streetcar suburb. The Macklind Avenue Business District anchors its commercial life, and the resident-run Princeton Heights Neighborhood Association, incorporated in 1976, keeps the community organized around safety and tree care.

Q. How does St Louis Near Me Directory help Princeton Heights businesses? 
A. St Louis Near Me Directory gives Princeton Heights businesses a curated, schema-optimized listing built to show up in ‘near me’ and AI-powered searches, plus done-for-you marketing support explained in plain English. We expand your Google Business Profile rather than replace it, never run competitor ads on your listing, and offer a 7-day free trial with no long-term contracts.

Q. What types of businesses are most common in Princeton Heights? 
A. The neighborhood’s ten listed businesses lean toward everyday services and food: a NAPA AutoCare auto shop, a licensed CPA, a women’s fitness and day spa, and a floral design studio, alongside pizza spots like Onesto Pizza & Trattoria and Imo’s Pizza. Many cluster on or near the Macklind Avenue Business District, the neighborhood’s small commercial core.

Q. What kinds of dining, retail, and recreation options are available in Princeton Heights? 
A. Dining centers on the Macklind Avenue Business District’s independent restaurants and cafes, plus brick-oven pizza at Onesto Pizza & Trattoria and classic St. Louis-style pies at Imo’s Pizza. Retail includes custom apparel at Onetime Supply Co. and floral design at Snapdragon Studio, while This Way Ladies Fitness & Wellness Center covers recreation and wellness.

Q. Are there neighborhood landmarks, parks, and historic sites in Princeton Heights? 
A. Princeton Heights’ defining landmark is its housing itself — streets of brick Craftsman bungalows and ‘storybook’ gingerbread houses built during the streetcar era after Gravois became the first state-paved road in Missouri. The River Des Peres and Christy Greenways run nearby, giving residents walking and biking access to green space beyond the neighborhood’s tree-lined residential grid.

Q. What is it like to live in Princeton Heights? 
A. Princeton Heights is a safe, walkable south-city neighborhood of historic brick homes and mature tree-lined streets, with an active neighborhood association that gives residents a direct voice in local priorities. Its central location near Hampton, Gravois, and the River Des Peres Greenway keeps both residents and Macklind Avenue business owners connected to the rest of the city.

Q. How do residents and visitors get around Princeton Heights? 
A. Princeton Heights is a classic streetcar-era neighborhood, so its grid of brick-lined streets is genuinely walkable, especially around the Macklind Avenue Business District. Most homes and shops rely on free on-street parking, and major routes like Hampton, Gravois, and Kingshighway make it easy to drive in and out.

Q. How can residents and visitors explore more services around Princeton Heights? 
A. Residents and visitors can browse St Louis Near Me Directory’s Princeton Heights guide to compare ratings and service details for businesses like Onetime Supply Co., Fairway Automotive, and Onesto Pizza & Trattoria, all clustered around the Macklind Avenue Business District. The directory highlights verified local providers so newcomers and visitors can find trusted options near Hampton, Gravois, and Kingshighway.

Q. How were the businesses on this page ranked? 
A. Businesses are ranked primarily by their Google star rating, with review count used as the tie-breaker when ratings are equal. We focus on active, established businesses and community organizations with confirmed physical locations and genuine ties to the Princeton Heights area. Rankings are merit-based and are never influenced by paid placements or advertising.

### Riverview Businesses & Neighborhood Guide | St Louis Near Me Directory
Riverview, St. Louis
Riverview is a far-north St. Louis riverfront area strung along Riverview Drive at the Chain of Rocks, where the Mississippi bends past historic water-intake towers and the Old Chain of Rocks Bridge — a stretch of the city defined by its river, its 19th-century waterworks, and the small, quiet residential blocks that line Riverview Drive itself.
This guide covers primarily the City of St. Louis “Riverview” neighborhood, which sits at the far-northern edge of the city along Riverview Drive near the Chain of Rocks. For accuracy, note that there is also a separately incorporated Village of Riverview just to the north in St. Louis County — a distinct community of roughly 2,397 residents that was incorporated in 1950 and voted in November 2023 to become a fourth-class city. This is not the same as Riverview Gardens, a different area nearby. The city neighborhood itself is small, with about 242 residents recorded in the 2020 census and a population that is roughly 70 percent Black.
The story of the area begins with Riverview Drive itself. Around 1830 it took shape as the “Columbia Bottoms road,” a farm-to-market route that ran through north St. Louis County and down through Baden to the city market. Residential building along its southern end began in the early 1870s and picked up again in the early 1890s, a wave that coincided with construction of the new Chain of Rocks waterworks. That road, now lined with shops, distributors, and small industrial firms, is still the spine of the neighborhood today.
Water shaped Riverview as much as the road did. The Chain of Rocks site was chosen for the St. Louis waterworks in 1865; construction began in 1887, and the plant went into service in 1894. A 1915 filter-plant addition was, at the time, the largest in the world, and the facility is still operational today — recognized as a historic civil-engineering landmark by the American Society of Civil Engineers. Out in the Mississippi, the castle-like Chain of Rocks water intake towers still stand; Tower #1, built in 1894 in a Romanesque Revival style, remains in use by the St. Louis Water Works. The connected Chain of Rocks Water Treatment Plant , established in 1894, is known for award-winning tap water drawn from the river.
The neighborhood’s most famous landmark is the Old Chain of Rocks Bridge . Opened in 1929 and stretching about 5,353 feet across the Mississippi, it once carried Bypass Route 66 and is known for the dramatic 22-degree bend at its middle, where the span turns mid-river. It closed to car traffic on February 25, 1970, and reopened in 1998 as a pedestrian and bicycle bridge. Today it serves as the northern point of the Mississippi Greenway / Riverfront Trail , a riverside path that runs about 12 miles toward downtown St. Louis.
The riverfront has seen new investment as well. Chain of Rocks Park , a 16-acre park at roughly 10840 Riverview Drive, reopened in April 2024 through Great Rivers Greenway. It offers a river overlook with access to the bridge, a pavilion, and a restored prairie, giving residents and visitors a place to take in the Mississippi up close. The area also carries a lighter slice of local history: the former Chain of Rocks Amusement Park operated nearby from 1927 to 1978 and, though long gone, is still remembered as part of the neighborhood’s recreational past.
Taken together, these landmarks — the 1830s farm-to-market road, the historic bridge, the river intake towers, the working treatment plant, the new riverfront park, the long greenway trail, and the memory of the old amusement park — give Riverview a character rooted firmly in the Mississippi. Riverview itself has no standalone businesses of its own — the verified businesses listed below sit a mile or two away in neighboring Baden and the Bellefontaine Neighbors area, and each is labeled with its real location and distance.
The historic Old Chain of Rocks Bridge spans the Mississippi at the northern edge of St. Louis, beside Riverview. Photo: “Chain of Rocks Bridge” by Marcin Wichary, licensed under CC BY 2.0 via Wikimedia Commons.

St. Louis sits in a humid climate zone (Köppen Cfa) with hot, sticky summers and cold winters, and because Riverview sits directly on the Mississippi, that humidity is amplified near the water while the low riverfront ground stays prone to periodic flooding, with the Great Flood of 1993 as the local benchmark.
What Riverview actually is today is easy to miss on a map: a narrow strip of houses wedged between Riverview Drive’s working, industrial frontage and the Mississippi bluff, bounded on the north by the St. Louis County line and the separate Village of Riverview. With only a couple hundred residents and no storefronts of its own, it functions now as a quiet, almost entirely residential pocket at the city’s edge — the kind of place suited to people who want river access, Chain of Rocks Park, and the Riverfront Trail close by, and who are fine driving a mile or two for groceries, dining, or a mechanic rather than walking to a commercial strip. Those everyday errands mean a short trip south into Baden or a similar distance north across the county line into the Bellefontaine Neighbors area, both covered in the verified list below.

### Frequently Asked Questions 
Q. Where is Riverview in St. Louis? 
A. Riverview sits at the far-northern edge of the City of St. Louis along Riverview Drive, near the Chain of Rocks bend in the Mississippi River, bounded on the north by the St. Louis County line. It is a separate place from the incorporated Village of Riverview just across that line in North County, near Bellefontaine Neighbors.

Q. What defines the Riverview neighborhood? 
A. Riverview is a small, far-north St. Louis riverfront neighborhood strung along Riverview Drive at the Chain of Rocks bend of the Mississippi. It’s defined by 19th-century waterworks landmarks, the Old Chain of Rocks Bridge, and a quiet residential population of about 242 people, bounded north by the St. Louis County line.

Q. How does St Louis Near Me Directory help Riverview businesses?

Q. What types of businesses are most common in Riverview? 
A. Riverview itself has no standalone businesses within its boundary. The closest verified providers sit a mile or two away in Baden and the Bellefontaine Neighbors area: a liquor store, an auto repair shop, a fast-food counter, a child care provider, and a pizza chain location, all serving Riverview households willing to make the short drive.

Q. What kinds of dining, retail, and recreation options are available in Riverview? 
A. Dining and retail options sit just outside Riverview’s boundary: Imo’s Pizza and St.Louis Fish & Chicken Grill for food, Randall’s Wines & Spirits for retail, all within a couple of miles in Baden or Bellefontaine Neighbors. For recreation, Chain of Rocks Park and the Riverfront Trail sit right along Riverview Drive.

Q. Are there neighborhood landmarks, parks, and historic sites in Riverview? 
A. Yes. The Old Chain of Rocks Bridge, opened in 1929 with its dramatic 22-degree bend, is the neighborhood’s most famous landmark, now a pedestrian and bike crossing. The historic Chain of Rocks waterworks and 1894 water intake towers still operate nearby, and the 16-acre Chain of Rocks Park reopened in April 2024.

Q. What is it like to live in Riverview? 
A. Living in Riverview means a small, quiet residential strip of about 242 people wedged between Riverview Drive’s industrial frontage and the Mississippi bluff, with no storefronts of its own. Residents get river access, Chain of Rocks Park, and the Riverfront Trail close by, but drive a mile or two into Baden or Bellefontaine Neighbors for groceries and everyday errands.

Q. How do residents and visitors get around Riverview? 
A. Riverview Drive, which began around 1830 as the Columbia Bottoms farm-to-market road, is the neighborhood’s spine, running south into Baden toward the city market. The Old Chain of Rocks Bridge now carries pedestrians and cyclists across the Mississippi, and the Riverfront Trail runs about 12 miles south toward downtown St. Louis.

### Shaw Businesses & Neighborhood Guide | St Louis Near Me Directory
Shaw, St. Louis 
Shaw is a near–South Side St. Louis neighborhood named for Henry Shaw, whose 1840 land purchase gave the city both the Missouri Botanical Garden and Tower Grove Park. A Certified Local Historic District since 1985, it is one of St. Louis's most architecturally intact neighborhoods — and its walkable pocket of cafés, wine shops, and ice cream along Shaw Boulevard and 39th Street keeps it lively today.
The land began as the French colonial Prairie des Noyers (“Meadows of the Walnut Trees,” 1769), narrow farm strips running west from Grand Boulevard. By the mid-1800s Henry Shaw and Mary L. Tyler dominated the area, and in 1857 the two agreed by deed to open Shaw, Flora, and Tower Grove Avenues with restrictions against “offensive factories” — conditions that produced one of the most consistent streetscapes in the city.
Henry Shaw arrived from England in 1819 as a young hardware merchant. By 1840 he had bought a 2,000-acre prairie tract, and in 1850 he built his Italianate villa, Tower Grove House, the first building of what became the Missouri Botanical Garden (1859, the oldest in the country). In 1868 he gave the city Tower Grove Park — 276 acres on the neighborhood's southern edge.
Designated a Certified Local Historic District in 1985, Shaw is prized for its Flora Place private boulevard (1897–1901), the 1878–1883 Shaw Place subdivision, and an 1890–1924 mix of Victorian, Queen Anne, Colonial Revival, American Foursquare, and Art Deco homes.
Shaw runs from Interstate 44 on the north to Magnolia Avenue and Tower Grove Park on the south, South Grand Boulevard on the east, and Tower Grove Avenue and the Botanical Garden on the west (ZIP 63110). It borders Botanical Heights and Tiffany to the north, Compton Heights to the east, Tower Grove South to the south, and Southwest Garden to the west; Shaw Boulevard and Flora Place are its main east–west spines.
Most of the neighborhood's businesses cluster on Shaw Boulevard and the walkable 39th Street node near Tower Grove Park — a patio-and-wine-bar row, a liquid-nitrogen ice cream shop, a wine-and-cheese provisioner, a Thai kitchen, and a vegetarian café — alongside a restored 1915 theatre now hosting weddings and a #1-ranked bed & breakfast across from the park.
A street in the Shaw neighborhood, St. Louis. Photo via Wikimedia Commons (CC). 
Shaw sees the same humid subtropical swing as the rest of St. Louis — hot, storm-prone summers and cold but manageable winters — the kind of climate the neighborhood's deep porches and steep-pitched brick roofs were built for a century ago.
Shaw exists as a coherent neighborhood, rather than a mixed industrial patchwork, because of a single 1857 deed: when Henry Shaw and Mary L. Tyler opened Shaw, Flora, and Tower Grove avenues, they wrote in a restriction against “offensive factories.” That clause is why the blocks between the Botanical Garden and Tower Grove Park still read as one unbroken run of 1890–1924 brick flats and foursquares today, instead of housing stitched between warehouses the way many near-south neighborhoods are.
Longtime residents draw Shaw's center a little tighter than the official map does — the real gravity is the four blocks where Shaw Boulevard meets 39th Street, by the northwest corner of Tower Grove Park, where nearly every business on this page sits within an easy walk of the next. The quieter blocks toward Interstate 44 are almost entirely residential. It is, in practice, a neighborhood for people who want a short walk to the Garden and the park and do not mind a few tour buses on a Saturday.

### Frequently Asked Questions
Q. Is the Missouri Botanical Garden worth it? 
A. Yes — it's the oldest botanical garden in continuous operation in the United States, founded in 1859 by Henry Shaw, the neighborhood's namesake. It anchors Shaw's western edge, so a visit pairs naturally with a walk through the neighborhood's historic streets, Shaw Boulevard's cafés, and the 39th Street restaurant row just blocks away.

Q. What day is the Missouri Botanical Garden free? 
A. The Garden has long offered free general admission to Missouri residents on Wednesdays, and free entry before noon on Saturdays for St. Louis city and county residents — though hours and current admission policies are always worth confirming directly with the Garden before a visit. Either way, it's an easy walk from Shaw's western edge.

Q. What is the Missouri Botanical Garden in St. Louis most famous for? 
A. The Garden is best known for the Climatron, one of the first geodesic-dome greenhouses in the world, and for Seiwa-en, its large Japanese garden built around a koi-filled lake. Founded in 1859 by Henry Shaw on land that also became Tower Grove Park, it remains one of the oldest botanical gardens in the country.

Q. How much does it cost to visit the Missouri Botanical Garden? 
A. Admission is charged per visitor, with free-entry windows for Missouri and St. Louis residents built into the schedule (see above). Current adult, child, and member pricing changes periodically, so the most accurate number is always the Garden's own ticketing page rather than a fixed figure repeated elsewhere — but it remains one of the region's most affordable major attractions.

Q. What is the history of the Shaw neighborhood in St. Louis? 
A. Shaw grew from the French colonial Prairie des Noyers farm strips, then from Henry Shaw's 1840 purchase of a 2,000-acre prairie tract. An 1857 deed with neighbor Mary Tyler opened Shaw, Flora, and Tower Grove avenues under restrictions against “offensive factories,” and the neighborhood became a Certified Local Historic District in 1985.

Q. What defines the Shaw neighborhood? 
A. Shaw is a compact, near-south St. Louis neighborhood bounded by Interstate 44, Magnolia Avenue and Tower Grove Park, South Grand Boulevard, and Tower Grove Avenue and the Missouri Botanical Garden. What defines it is consistency: a Certified Local Historic District since 1985, built almost entirely between 1890 and 1924, with little of the industrial mix common nearby.

Q. How does St Louis Near Me Directory help Shaw businesses? 
A. St Louis Near Me Directory builds a neighborhood-specific page for Shaw, like this guide, so local businesses on Shaw Boulevard, 39th Street, and the surrounding blocks show up when nearby customers search. Plans start with a 7-day free trial, carry no long-term contract, and never run a competitor's ad on a member's listing.

Q. What types of businesses are most common in Shaw? 
A. Food and drink dominate: cafés, a coffee roaster, a wine bar, a Thai kitchen, and a nitro ice cream shop cluster along Shaw Boulevard and 39th Street. The rest of the mix is small and personal — a stylist, a landscape lighting installer, a preschool, an event venue, and a wellness studio, almost all independently owned.

Skinker-DeBaliviere, St. Louis
Tucked into west-central St. Louis between Forest Park and the Delmar Loop, Skinker-DeBaliviere is a compact, leafy neighborhood of early-1900s homes that is best known for the deliberate way its neighbors kept it diverse and stable through decades when many nearby areas came apart.
The neighborhood takes its name from the two streets that bookend it: Skinker Boulevard on the west edge, near the City limits, and DeBaliviere Avenue on the east. Delmar Boulevard forms the northern edge, while Forsyth and Lindell Boulevards mark the south, where the neighborhood meets Forest Park. It is officially City Neighborhood #46, covers about 0.52 square miles, and sits within ZIP code 63112.
For most of the 1800s this was farmland. The land began as an eighteenth-century French colonial grant to Marie Louise Chouteau Papin and stayed largely in the Chouteau-Papin family into the late 19th century, kept rural in part because the unruly River Des Peres ran across it. That changed at the turn of the 20th century, when the 1904 World’s Fair in adjacent Forest Park set off a streetcar-era building boom across the city’s west end.
The neighborhood is generally dated to 1908, and its private subdivisions went up in quick succession: Parkview platted in 1905 , Washington Heights in 1907, and the Catlin Tract developed in 1909. Hamilton Elementary School opened in 1914, and three churches built in the 1910s — Grace Methodist, New Cote Brilliante Baptist, and St. Roch Catholic — still anchor the area today. The Parkview Historic District and the Catlin Tract preserve street after street of architecturally significant early-1900s houses, and Parkview is listed on the National Register of Historic Places.
What put Skinker-DeBaliviere on the national map is its mid-1960s integration story. The neighborhood became racially integrated in 1964 , and in 1966 residents formed the Skinker-DeBaliviere Community Council to manage that transition on their own terms and resist the blockbusting and white flight that destabilized so many other St. Louis neighborhoods. The Council’s work is widely credited with keeping the area diverse and steady; the 2020 census still recorded a notably mixed community of about 3,899 residents. In 1978 the City designated the area a Local Historic District .
The neighborhood’s edges are its biggest draw. Forest Park — the roughly 1,300-acre park that hosted the 1904 World’s Fair and is home to the St. Louis Zoo and the Art Museum — runs along the southern boundary, and Washington University in St. Louis and its Danforth Campus sit just southwest across the park. Along the northern Delmar Boulevard edge runs the Delmar Loop , one of the region’s liveliest dining, shopping, and live-music districts, which straddles the city and University City line.
Getting around is easy by St. Louis standards. Two MetroLink light-rail stations serve the area — the Forest Park–DeBaliviere station on the eastern side and the Skinker station on the west — putting downtown, the airport, and Washington University a short train ride away, while the Loop and the park are walkable from most blocks. The businesses below reflect that geography: a mix of long-running Loop venues and shops on Delmar, a few spots tucked strictly inside the neighborhood, and trusted service providers that serve residents here.
The Delmar Loop along the northern edge of Skinker-DeBaliviere. Photo: “Delmar Loop - Parkview Gardens Historic District” by Liezl Moss, licensed under CC BY-SA 3.0 via Wikimedia Commons.

Skinker-DeBaliviere shares the St. Louis region’s humid subtropical climate — July highs near 89.6°F , January highs near 40.4°F , and about 16.6 inches of snow a year — softened here by a mature tree canopy and Forest Park’s green edge next door.
Walk a few blocks in any direction and the housing stock tells the rest of the story: mansions along Lindell built for the 1904 fair crowd, brick craftsman homes and classic foursquares on the Pitzman-platted Parkview and Catlin Tract blocks, two-family flats, and newer townhomes at Kingsbury Square, all mixed with apartment buildings that keep rents within reach of Washington University students and young families. That range — not just the integration history, though that is the headline — is what keeps Skinker-DeBaliviere genuinely mixed today: longtime homeowners, WashU faculty and students, and renters drawn by a walk to Forest Park or the Loop, all on the same blocks.

### Frequently Asked Questions 
Q. What is the history of the Skinker-DeBaliviere neighborhood? 
A. The neighborhood takes its name from Skinker Boulevard and DeBaliviere Avenue, its west and east edges, on land that stayed rural French-colonial farmland into the late 1800s. The 1904 World’s Fair in adjacent Forest Park triggered a streetcar-era building boom, and Skinker-DeBaliviere is generally dated to 1908. It became nationally known for its 1964 integration and the 1966 Community Council that kept it diverse and stable.

Q. What defines the Skinker DeBaliviere neighborhood? 
A. Skinker-DeBaliviere is defined by its edges: Forest Park and Washington University to the south and southwest, and the Delmar Loop entertainment strip along its northern border. Officially City Neighborhood #46, it covers about 0.52 square mile in ZIP 63112, and its early-1900s Parkview and Catlin Tract subdivisions — Parkview individually listed on the National Register — still shape its architecture today.

Q. What types of businesses are most common in Skinker DeBaliviere? 
A. The dozen listed businesses lean toward personal services and dining: hair and beauty salons like V Vegaz and Locs Of Glory, a family dental practice, and restaurants spanning barbecue, Thai, and Asian cuisine. The Pageant concert hall and Pin-Up Bowl add entertainment, while Sunshine Daydream and Avalon Exchange round out a small but eclectic retail mix along Delmar.

Q. What kinds of dining, retail, and recreation options are available in Skinker DeBaliviere? 
A. Dining runs from Salt + Smoke’s barbecue and whiskey to Fork & Stix’s Thai cooking and Kimchi Guys’ quick Asian eats near Washington University. Retail includes Sunshine Daydream’s eclectic gifts and Avalon Exchange’s vintage resale, plus STL GRILLZZ for custom jewelry. For recreation, Pin-Up Bowl pairs bowling with cocktails, and The Pageant hosts national touring concerts.

Q. Are there neighborhood landmarks, parks, and historic sites in Skinker DeBaliviere? 
A. Yes — the Parkview Historic District is individually listed on the National Register of Historic Places, and the wider neighborhood earned Local Historic District status in 1978 for its early-1900s Parkview, Washington Heights, and Catlin Tract subdivisions. Forest Park, host of the 1904 World’s Fair and home to the St. Louis Zoo and Art Museum, forms the entire southern edge.

Q. What is it like to live in Skinker DeBaliviere? 
A. Many residents find it a rewarding place to live — a pairing of historic, well-built early-1900s homes with a diverse, engaged community shaped by the neighborhood’s 1964 integration and its Community Council. Its location between Forest Park, Washington University, and the Delmar Loop gives residents an unbeatable mix of green space, culture, and walkable dining.

Q. How do residents and visitors get around Skinker DeBaliviere? 
A. The neighborhood is unusually transit-friendly for St. Louis. Two MetroLink light-rail stops — Forest Park–DeBaliviere on the east and Skinker on the west — connect it to downtown, the airport, and Washington University, while the Loop and Forest Park are walkable from most blocks. Many residents handle daily errands on foot.

### Soulard Businesses & Neighborhood Guide | St Louis Near Me Directory
Soulard, St. Louis
Soulard serves as St. Louis’s oldest neighborhood — founded in 1779 around the city’s third public marketplace, anchored by the Soulard Farmers Market (oldest west of the Mississippi, donated by Julia Cerré Soulard in 1841), the Anheuser-Busch Brewery (a National Historic Landmark since 1966), St. Vincent de Paul and St. John Nepomuk churches, and the Second Empire and Italianate “flounder house” row homes of the NRHP-listed Soulard Historic District — offering breweries, restaurants, blues bars, wedding venues, coffee, board games, and brewery tours across the Russell, 12th, and 9th Street corridors.
Soulard is one of St. Louis’s 79 official neighborhoods and one of eight certified local historic districts in the City of St. Louis, located at 38.6028° N, 90.2103° W on the near south side of the city, just south of Downtown. The neighborhood’s triangular boundaries are defined by Interstate 55 on the west and north, 7th Street and South Broadway to the southeast, and the Anheuser-Busch Brewery complex extending south to Arsenal Street. Surrounding neighborhoods include LaSalle Park and Lafayette Square to the north (across I-55), Benton Park West to the west, and Benton Park and the Mississippi River to the south. The neighborhood sits within ZIP code 63104 . Soulard is divided roughly by Lynch Street — north of which is mostly 19th-century brick row homes, Second Empire Victorians, Italianate town houses, Federal-style buildings, and the unique “flounder houses” (narrow homes built with only one slope to the roof) — while south of Lynch Street is largely the campus of Anheuser-Busch (the North American headquarters and St. Louis Brewery) and its surviving 19th-century brewery buildings.
The story of Soulard begins with the founding of the Soulard Farmers Market in 1779 — a flat meadow where farmers from the surrounding French Creole village of St. Louis (founded 1764) came to sell fresh fruit, vegetables, dairy, and livestock. This was the third public marketplace in St. Louis , and the meadow lay on land that had been granted by the Spanish government to French merchant Jean-Gabriel Cerré . The neighborhood takes its name from Cerré’s son-in-law, Antoine Pierre Soulard — born in 1766 in Rochefort, France, a French aristocrat and former French naval officer who escaped the French Revolution and arrived in St. Louis around 1794. In 1795 , Antoine Soulard married Julia Cerré , and the couple received a 122-acre plot of land that included the market grounds; additional land was given to Antoine by the Spanish colonial government as a gift for his service as Surveyor of Upper Louisiana under Governor Carlos de Hault de Lassus.
The 1803 Louisiana Purchase threw the land grant into legal limbo, and following Antoine’s death in 1825 , his widow Julia Cerré Soulard fought a thirty-year courtroom battle to confirm the deed. She prevailed in 1836 , then began subdividing the land and selling lots — becoming the first female real estate developer west of the Mississippi River . Her most enduring gift came in 1841–1842 , when she donated two city blocks to the City of St. Louis with the stipulation that the land remain a public marketplace in perpetuity. Julia Soulard died in 1845 ; the City formally acquired title in 1850. The first market building was constructed in 1843 , a one-story red brick structure; a second-story meeting hall was added in 1865. The original Soulard Market and many surrounding buildings were heavily damaged by the Great St. Louis Tornado of May 27, 1896 . For more than three decades, vendors operated from temporary sheds and wagons until the current Italian Renaissance Grand Hall opened in 1929 , designed by City Architect Albert E. Osburg and modeled on Filippo Brunelleschi’s Ospedale degli Innocenti (Florentine Foundling Hospital, 1419).
During the mid-19th century, Soulard transformed from French Creole farmland into one of the most densely settled immigrant neighborhoods in St. Louis. The first wave was French ; the much larger wave was German — particularly during the political upheavals of 1848 — followed by Syrian, Hungarian, Croatian, Italian, Serbian, Irish, Slovak, and Czech immigrants. The Eastern European population earned the area the nickname “Bohemian Hill.” The principal industry was beer brewing : Soulard hosted at least half a dozen breweries , including the Green Tree Brewery on Sidney Street, the Excelsior Brewery on Seventh Street, Anthony & Kuhn’s Brewery on Sidney Street, the Lemp Brewery , and Eberhard Anheuser’s brewery — which his son-in-law Adolphus Busch transformed into Anheuser-Busch . Most of these breweries sat atop a rumored cave system that runs along Sidney Street. By Prohibition , only Anheuser-Busch and Falstaff (formerly Lemp) survived. Notable 19th-century residents included Max J. Feuerbacher , Dr. Franz Artzt , Thomas Allen , Adam Lemp , and Eberhard Anheuser .
The Anheuser-Busch Brewery on Lynch Street, founded in the 1850s as Eberhard Anheuser’s Bavarian Brewery, transformed under Adolphus Busch from a small neighborhood brewery into a global icon. The campus — with its elaborate red-brick German Romanesque buildings , the original 1885 Brew House , the Clydesdale Stables , and the historic 19th-century buildings — was designated a National Historic Landmark in 1966 . Today the brewery offers the Budweiser Brewery Experience with the Clydesdale VIP Experience, the Finisher Tour, and a 7-step brewing process tour. The famous Clydesdale horses — trademark of Anheuser-Busch since they were used to pull wagons of beer for Prohibition-repeal deliveries in 1933 — are regularly rotated in from the company’s farms near Grant’s Farm and Boonville. Beyond the brewery, the neighborhood is home to several nineteenth-century church buildings : Saints Peter and Paul Catholic Church , St. Vincent de Paul Catholic Church (built on land donated by Julia Soulard to Bishop Joseph Rosati), St. John Nepomuk Czech Catholic Church (the first Czech national church in the United States, founded 1854), and Trinity Lutheran Church .
In 1972 , the Soulard Historic District was placed on the National Register of Historic Places and became one of eight certified local historic districts in the City of St. Louis. The neighborhood is preserved by the Soulard Restoration Group and the Soulard Business Association , which publishes the neighborhood newspaper The Soulard Renaissance . The district is renowned for its surviving examples of Greek Revival farmhouses , Federal Transitional , Federal , Italianate , Second Empire Victorian (with characteristic mansard roofs inspired by 17th-century French architect François Mansart), and the uniquely St. Louis flounder houses — narrow brick homes with only one slope to the roof, built by working-class immigrants on long, narrow lots. The neighborhood is also known for its Mardi Gras celebration , the second-largest in the United States (behind New Orleans), the world’s largest parade of costumed pets (the Beggin’ Pet Parade), the annual Oktoberfest , and the blues / jazz scene that hosted barrelhouse blues piano player James Crutchfield from 1984 until his death in 2001.
Today, Soulard remains one of St. Louis’s most vibrant, walkable, and architecturally intact historic neighborhoods. The neighborhood’s key business anchors include the Soulard Farmers Market at 730 Carroll Street (140+ vendors, City Landmark 1971, open Wednesday through Saturday year-round), the Budweiser Brewery Experience at 1200 Lynch Street, the Soulard Spice Shop inside the market (Neighborhood Favorite 2023, 600–800 pounds of spices moved weekly), Pieces Board Game Bar & Restaurant at 2727 South 12th Street (1,200+ games), Goshen Coffee Roasters at 910 Geyer Avenue (Good Food Award winner), The Franklin of Soulard at 816 Allen Avenue (the 1905 wedding venue under Daniel and Christina Walsh), Soulard Art Gallery at 2028 South 12th Street (co-op under curator Earl Miller), International Tap House (iTap) at 1711 South 9th Street (40 beers on tap, 480+ bottles), Soulard Market Lofts at 1531 South 8th Street (managed by Sansone Group), Molly’s In Soulard at 816 Geyer Avenue (rooftop patio and brunch), the Pontiac Square Park (1.50 acres, 1908), the Soulard Market Park (1.94 acres, 1908), and dozens of independent restaurants, blues bars, microbreweries, and boutiques.
Image: Soulard Farmers Market — the oldest farmers’ market west of the Mississippi River, founded 1779, donated to the City of St. Louis by Julia Cerré Soulard in 1841. The 1929 Italian Renaissance Grand Hall by City Architect Albert E. Osburg was modeled on Brunelleschi’s 1419 Ospedale degli Innocenti in Florence and designated a St. Louis City Landmark in 1971 — Wikimedia Commons , CC BY-SA

Soulard sits one mile south of Downtown St. Louis at 38.6028° N along the Mississippi River, with seamless access to Interstate 55 (the western boundary), South Broadway (the eastern boundary along the river), the Anheuser-Busch Brewery complex (the southern boundary), Lafayette Square and LaSalle Park to the north, and Benton Park and Cherokee Street to the south. 
Soulard runs St. Louis’s full swing of seasons — hot, humid summers and cold winters — with the outdoor market, Mardi Gras, and patio scene busiest from spring through fall and the neighborhood’s bars, restaurants, and the Grand Hall carrying the winter months.

### Soulard Today
Soulard runs on two different clocks now. By day it is the market crowd and dog walkers on the brick sidewalks around Lynch and Russell, browsing the same stalls families have used for generations; by night — especially Friday and Saturday — South 9th Street and the blocks around International Tap House and Molly’s In Soulard turn into one of the city’s busiest bar corridors, loud enough that longtime residents joke the neighborhood earns its Mardi Gras reputation year-round. The Farmers Market itself still functions as a genuine grocery stop, not just a tourist draw. Housing here means a 19th-century row home or flounder house with real upkeep demands, not a renovated loft — buyers who want move-in-ready typically look elsewhere in south city, while buyers who want the oldest, most walkable blocks in St. Louis accept the trade-off.

### Frequently Asked Questions 
Q. What is Soulard in St. Louis known for? 
A. Soulard is St. Louis’s oldest neighborhood, founded in 1779 around the Soulard Farmers Market — still open Wednesday through Saturday with 140+ vendors inside its 1929 Grand Hall. It is equally known for the National Historic Landmark Anheuser-Busch Brewery, the NRHP-listed historic district of flounder houses and Second Empire row homes, the second-largest Mardi Gras celebration in the country, and a dense blues-bar nightlife scene along South 9th Street.

Q. Is Soulard Market still open? 
A. Yes. The Soulard Farmers Market at 730 Carroll Street has operated continuously since 1779 and remains open Wednesday through Saturday year-round, with 140+ vendors selling produce, meats, spices, and baked goods inside the 1929 Italian Renaissance Grand Hall. Saturday mornings draw the heaviest crowds. It is the oldest farmers’ market west of the Mississippi River and still functions as a working grocery stop, not just a tourist attraction.

Q. Is Soulard a good neighborhood? 
A. It depends what you want. Soulard offers genuine walkability, one of the city’s densest concentrations of historic 19th-century row homes and flounder houses, and the Farmers Market as a daily anchor — real draws for residents who want an urban, historic feel close to Downtown. It also carries a loud, bar-crawl-heavy nightlife identity on weekends around South 9th Street, which suits some residents and not others.

Q. What is Molly’s Soulard known for? 
A. Molly’s In Soulard, on Geyer Avenue, is known for its rooftop patio and weekend brunch, plus a steady late-night trade as part of Soulard’s year-round blues and jazz bar scene. With 13,057 Google reviews, it is one of the most-reviewed businesses in the neighborhood — a sign of how central it is to a typical Soulard night out.

Q. What is there to do in Soulard? 
A. Shop the 1779 Soulard Farmers Market, take the Budweiser Brewery Experience and meet the Clydesdales, play one of 1,200+ games at Pieces Board Game Bar, browse the co-op Soulard Art Gallery, or drink along the South 9th Street blues corridor at spots like International Tap House and Molly’s. February and March bring the second-largest Mardi Gras celebration in the country, plus the Beggin’ Pet Parade.

## Soulard Businesses & Neighborhood Guide | St Louis Near Me Directory

Soulard, St. Louis

Soulard serves as St. Louis’s oldest neighborhood — founded in 1779 around the city’s third public marketplace, anchored by the Soulard Farmers Market (oldest west of the Mississippi, donated by Julia Cerré Soulard in 1841), the Anheuser-Busch Brewery (a National Historic Landmark since 1966), St. Vincent de Paul and St. John Nepomuk churches, and the Second Empire and Italianate “flounder house” row homes of the NRHP-listed Soulard Historic District — offering breweries, restaurants, blues bars, wedding venues, coffee, board games, and reputation management across the Russell, 12th, and 9th Street corridors.

Soulard is one of St. Louis’s 79 official neighborhoods and one of **eight certified local historic districts** in the City of St. Louis, located at **38.6028° N, 90.2103° W** on the near south side of the city, just south of Downtown. The neighborhood’s triangular boundaries are defined by **Interstate 55** on the west and north, **7th Street** and **South Broadway** to the southeast, and the **Anheuser-Busch Brewery** complex extending south to Arsenal Street. Surrounding neighborhoods include **LaSalle Park** and **Lafayette Square** to the north (across I-55), **Benton Park West** to the west, and **Benton Park** and the Mississippi River to the south. The neighborhood sits within **ZIP code 63104**. Soulard is divided roughly by Lynch Street — north of which is mostly 19th-century brick row homes, Second Empire Victorians, Italianate town houses, Federal-style buildings, and the unique **“flounder houses”** (narrow homes built with only one slope to the roof) — while south of Lynch Street is largely the campus of **Anheuser-Busch** (the North American headquarters and St. Louis Brewery) and its surviving 19th-century brewery buildings.

The story of Soulard begins with the **founding of the Soulard Farmers Market in 1779** — a flat meadow where farmers from the surrounding French Creole village of St. Louis (founded 1764) came to sell fresh fruit, vegetables, dairy, and livestock. This was the **third public marketplace in St. Louis**, and the meadow lay on land that had been granted by the Spanish government to French merchant **Jean-Gabriel Cerré**. The neighborhood takes its name from Cerré’s son-in-law, **Antoine Pierre Soulard** — born in 1766 in Rochefort, France, a French aristocrat and former French naval officer who escaped the French Revolution and arrived in St. Louis around 1794. In **1795**, Antoine Soulard married **Julia Cerré**, and the couple received a **122-acre plot** of land that included the market grounds; additional land was given to Antoine by the Spanish colonial government as a gift for his service as **Surveyor of Upper Louisiana** under Governor Carlos de Hault de Lassus.

The **1803 Louisiana Purchase** threw the land grant into legal limbo, and following Antoine’s death in **1825**, his widow **Julia Cerré Soulard** fought a **thirty-year courtroom battle** to confirm the deed. She prevailed in **1836**, then began subdividing the land and selling lots — becoming the **first female real estate developer west of the Mississippi River**. Her most enduring gift came in **1841–1842**, when she donated **two city blocks** to the City of St. Louis with the stipulation that the land remain a public marketplace in perpetuity. Julia Soulard died in **1845**; the City formally acquired title in 1850. The first market building was constructed in **1843**, a one-story red brick structure; a second-story meeting hall was added in 1865. The original Soulard Market and many surrounding buildings were heavily damaged by the **Great St. Louis Tornado of May 27, 1896**. For more than three decades, vendors operated from temporary sheds and wagons until the **current Italian Renaissance Grand Hall** opened in **1929**, designed by City Architect **Albert E. Osburg** and modeled on Filippo Brunelleschi’s **Ospedale degli Innocenti** (Florentine Foundling Hospital, 1419).

During the mid-19th century, Soulard transformed from French Creole farmland into one of the most densely settled immigrant neighborhoods in St. Louis. The first wave was **French**; the much larger wave was **German** — particularly during the political upheavals of **1848** — followed by **Syrian, Hungarian, Croatian, Italian, Serbian, Irish, Slovak, and Czech** immigrants. The Eastern European population earned the area the nickname **“Bohemian Hill.”** The principal industry was **beer brewing**: Soulard hosted at least **half a dozen breweries**, including the **Green Tree Brewery** on Sidney Street, the **Excelsior Brewery** on Seventh Street, **Anthony & Kuhn’s Brewery** on Sidney Street, the **Lemp Brewery**, and **Eberhard Anheuser’s brewery** — which his son-in-law **Adolphus Busch** transformed into **Anheuser-Busch**. Most of these breweries sat atop a rumored cave system that runs along Sidney Street. By **Prohibition**, only Anheuser-Busch and Falstaff (formerly Lemp) survived. Notable 19th-century residents included **Max J. Feuerbacher**, **Dr. Franz Artzt**, **Thomas Allen**, **Adam Lemp**, and **Eberhard Anheuser**.

The **Anheuser-Busch Brewery** on Lynch Street, founded in the 1850s as Eberhard Anheuser’s Bavarian Brewery, transformed under **Adolphus Busch** from a small neighborhood brewery into a global icon. The campus — with its elaborate **red-brick German Romanesque buildings**, the original 1885 **Brew House**, the **Clydesdale Stables**, and the historic 19th-century buildings — was designated a **National Historic Landmark in 1966**. Today the brewery offers the **Budweiser Brewery Experience** with the Clydesdale VIP Experience, the Finisher Tour, and a 7-step brewing process tour. The famous **Clydesdale horses** — trademark of Anheuser-Busch since they were used to pull wagons of beer for Prohibition-repeal deliveries in 1933 — are regularly rotated in from the company’s farms near Grant’s Farm and Boonville. Beyond the brewery, the neighborhood is home to several **nineteenth-century church buildings**: **Saints Peter and Paul Catholic Church**, **St. Vincent de Paul Catholic Church** (built on land donated by Julia Soulard to Bishop Joseph Rosati), **St. John Nepomuk Czech Catholic Church** (the first Czech national church in the United States, founded 1854), and **Trinity Lutheran Church**.

In **1972**, the **Soulard Historic District** was placed on the **National Register of Historic Places** and became one of **eight certified local historic districts** in the City of St. Louis. The neighborhood is preserved by the **Soulard Restoration Group** and the **Soulard Business Association**, which publishes the neighborhood newspaper *The Soulard Renaissance*. The district is renowned for its surviving examples of **Greek Revival farmhouses**, **Federal Transitional**, **Federal**, **Italianate**, **Second Empire Victorian** (with characteristic **mansard roofs** inspired by 17th-century French architect François Mansart), and the uniquely St. Louis **flounder houses** — narrow brick homes with only one slope to the roof, built by working-class immigrants on long, narrow lots. The neighborhood is also known for its **Mardi Gras celebration**, the second-largest in the United States (behind New Orleans), the **world’s largest parade of costumed pets** (the Beggin’ Pet Parade), the annual **Oktoberfest**, and the blues / jazz scene that hosted barrelhouse blues piano player **James Crutchfield** from 1984 until his death in 2001.

Today, Soulard remains one of St. Louis’s most vibrant, walkable, and architecturally intact historic neighborhoods. The neighborhood’s key business anchors include the **Soulard Farmers Market** at 730 Carroll Street (140+ vendors, City Landmark 1971, open Wednesday through Saturday year-round), the **Budweiser Brewery Experience** at 1200 Lynch Street, the **Soulard Spice Shop** inside the market (Neighborhood Favorite 2023, 600–800 pounds of spices moved weekly), **Pieces Board Game Bar & Restaurant** at 2727 South 12th Street (1,200+ games), **Goshen Coffee Roasters** at 910 Geyer Avenue (Good Food Award winner), **The Franklin of Soulard** at 816 Allen Avenue (the 1905 wedding venue under Daniel and Christina Walsh), **Soulard Art Gallery** at 2028 South 12th Street (co-op under curator Earl Miller), **International Tap House** (iTap) at 1711 South 9th Street (40 beers on tap, 480+ bottles), **Soulard Market Lofts** at 1531 South 8th Street (managed by Sansone Group), **Unreview** at 1400 Russell Boulevard (reputation management SaaS), the **Pontiac Square Park** (1.50 acres, 1908), the **Soulard Market Park** (1.94 acres, 1908), and dozens of independent restaurants, blues bars, microbreweries, and boutiques.

Image: Soulard Farmers Market — the oldest farmers’ market west of the Mississippi River, founded 1779, donated to the City of St. Louis by Julia Cerré Soulard in 1841. The 1929 Italian Renaissance Grand Hall by City Architect Albert E. Osburg was modeled on Brunelleschi’s 1419 Ospedale degli Innocenti in Florence and designated a St. Louis City Landmark in 1971 — Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA

Soulard sits one mile south of Downtown St. Louis at 38.6028° N along the Mississippi River, with seamless access to Interstate 55 (the western boundary), South Broadway (the eastern boundary along the river), the **Anheuser-Busch Brewery** complex (the southern boundary), Lafayette Square and LaSalle Park to the north, and Benton Park and Cherokee Street to the south. 

The neighborhood experiences St. Louis’s full humid continental climate: hot, humid summers, cold winters, and an active spring severe weather season — punctuated historically by the **Great St. Louis Tornado of May 27, 1896**. Peak outdoor activity falls during late winter, spring, summer, and fall, when the **Soulard Farmers Market** (open Wednesday through Saturday year-round, with Saturday morning crowds of 10,000+) draws shoppers from across the bi-state region; when the **Budweiser Brewery Experience** and **Clydesdale Stables** host daily tours; when **Pontiac Square Park** (1.50 acres, 1908), **Soulard Market Park** (1.94 acres, 1908), and the two neighborhood **dog parks** draw residents; when the annual **Mardi Gras** celebration (the second-largest in the United States with the Beggin’ Pet Parade) takes over the streets each February or March; when **Oktoberfest** arrives in autumn; and when the year-round blues / jazz scene fills the patios of **1860 Saloon**, **Molly’s in Soulard**, **The Shanti**, **Hammerstone’s**, and **McGurk’s**. 

Cool seasons drive intense indoor activity at **International Tap House** on South 9th, **Goshen Coffee Roasters** on Geyer, **Pieces Board Game Bar & Restaurant** on South 12th, **The Franklin of Soulard** on Allen, **Soulard Spice Shop**, **Soulard Art Gallery**, **Soulard Market Lofts**, **Unreview**, and the indoor venues of the 1929 Soulard Market Grand Hall, the Anheuser-Busch Brewery’s 19th-century buildings (including the 1885 Brew House), and the historic 19th-century churches (Saints Peter and Paul, St. Vincent de Paul, St. John Nepomuk, Trinity Lutheran). The neighborhood’s 1830s–1890s housing stock — Federal-style row homes, Greek Revival farmhouses, Italianate town houses, Second Empire Victorians with mansard roofs, and unique flounder houses — has weathered more than 180 years of Missouri climate with the durability of the French Creole, German, and Bohemian masons who built them.
