### The Greater Ville Businesses & Neighborhood Guide | St Louis Near Me Directory
The Greater Ville, St. Louis
The Greater Ville is the upside-down-U-shaped north St. Louis neighborhood wrapping The Ville on three sides — home to the 1945 Shelley House at 4600 Labadie Avenue (National Historic Landmark and site of the 1948 Supreme Court case Shelley v. Kraemer that ended racially restrictive covenants) and to Chuck Berry’s 3137 Whittier Street home (NRHP-listed December 2008) where he wrote “Maybellene,” “Johnny B. Goode,” and “Roll Over Beethoven.” The corridor offers chamber advocacy, business publishing, sustainability consulting, federal contract coaching, managed IT, enterprise consulting, technology integration, regional chamber networking, experiential marketing, and women’s business support services across the broader north St. Louis area.
The Greater Ville is a north St. Louis neighborhood centered at 38.6621° N, 90.2483° W in zip codes 63107, 63113, and 63115, forming an upside-down-U shape that wraps around the smaller inner neighborhood of The Ville on three sides. Its official boundaries run north to Natural Bridge Avenue , south to Dr. Martin Luther King Drive and St. Louis Avenue , east to N. Vandeventer Avenue , and west to Marcus Avenue . Interior streets including Labadie Avenue , Whittier Street , Dick Gregory Place (renamed to honor the comedian and activist born at 1803 N. Taylor Avenue just across the boundary in The Ville), and the broad Natural Bridge Avenue commercial corridor anchor the neighborhood’s daily life. The 131-acre Fairground Park lies along the neighborhood’s northern edge, offering a swimming pool, roller rink, 9-acre stocked fishing lake, walking trails, and athletic fields that have served north St. Louis families since 1908. The 2020 Census recorded nearly 8,000 residents across the neighborhood’s historic brick housing stock.
The Greater Ville is surrounded by seven neighborhoods: Penrose and O’Fallon to the north, JeffVanderLou to the east, Covenant Blu-Grand Center to the southeast, Vandeventer and Lewis Place to the south, and Kingsway East to the west. As St. Louis Magazine described it, the neighborhood is “an oddly shaped neighborhood, more of an upside-down U, wrapping itself around the Ville ‘Proper.’” That shape itself encodes the history: before 1948, The Ville (the inner neighborhood) was African American and largely middle class, while The Greater Ville (the outer ring) was white middle class — protected from Black ownership by 1900-1910-era racially restrictive covenants embedded in property deeds. The two names get used interchangeably — even in some city records and press coverage — but they are two separate, officially mapped St. Louis neighborhoods that happen to share a name. The Ville is the smaller, original neighborhood inside the U, home to Sumner High School, Homer G. Phillips Hospital, and Annie Malone’s Poro College; St Louis Near Me Directory covers that history in a separate guide to The Ville . This guide covers The Greater Ville specifically — the larger ring neighborhood that grew up around it once those restrictions were struck down.
The case that changed that for the entire country arose from one house in this neighborhood: 4600 Labadie Avenue . The J.D. Shelley family had moved from Starkville, Mississippi in 1930 , fleeing racially-motivated violence. After renting for a time, in 1945 J.D. and Ethel Lee Shelley purchased the home through prominent Black realtor James Bush via a sympathetic white intermediary, unaware that the block carried a 1911 covenant prohibiting sale to anyone of the “Negro or Mongolian race” for 50 years. They moved in on September 11, 1945 . White neighbors Louis and Fern Kraemer sued to void the sale. While the trial court held for the Shelleys, the Missouri Supreme Court reversed in 1946; the Shelleys appealed to the U.S. Supreme Court in 1947 with NAACP representation. The U.S. Office of the Solicitor General filed an amicus curiae brief in support of the Shelleys — the first time in a civil rights case. The Court ruled unanimously in Shelley v. Kraemer (1948) that courts could not enforce racially restrictive covenants under the Fourteenth Amendment’s Equal Protection Clause.
The Shelley House at 4600 Labadie was declared a National Historic Landmark in 1990 and is now part of the National Park Service’s African American Civil Rights Network. It remains one of the most consequential private residences in American constitutional history. Twenty years later, the Fair Housing Act of 1968 — passed six days after the slaying of Martin Luther King Jr. — outlawed racial, religious, and sex discrimination in real estate transactions outright, completing what the Shelley decision had begun.
The opening of The Greater Ville to Black ownership after 1948 brought some of the city’s most significant cultural figures to the neighborhood. Chuck Berry — the father of rock and roll — and his wife Themetta “Toddy” Suggs purchased the 1910-built, three-bedroom, one-bathroom red-brick bungalow at 3137 Whittier Street in 1950 for $4,500, shortly after the Shelley decision invalidated the area’s covenants. They lived there from 1950 to 1958, raising daughters Ingrid and Melody, and Chuck Berry composed and rehearsed his landmark songs in this small house — “Maybellene” (1955), “Roll Over Beethoven” (1956), “Too Much Monkey Business” (1956), “Rock and Roll Music” (1957), “School Day” (1957), “Sweet Little Sixteen” (1958), and “Johnny B. Goode” (1958) — recordings that defined a genre. During those years he worked at a Chrysler assembly plant and as a photographer for the St. Louis Argus. The Chuck Berry House was added to the National Register of Historic Places on December 12, 2008, retains features including the original awning with a letter “B” for Berry on the front porch, and has been vacant since the early 2000s.
The St. Louis Argus , founded in 1912 by brothers J. E. and William Mitchell, is the oldest continuously operating Black business in St. Louis and has been a voice for The Greater Ville across more than a century of change. Holy Ghost Catholic School , integrated by Archbishop Joseph Ritter in 1947 — a year ahead of the Supreme Court’s Shelley decision and seven years before Brown v. Board of Education — demonstrated what moral courage looked like at the parish level. The Julia Davis Branch Library on Natural Bridge Avenue has served The Greater Ville residents through the full arc of the neighborhood’s transformation. The neighborhood is served by St. Louis Public Schools including Cote Brilliante Elementary School and Hickey Elementary School (both on Cora Avenue), Farragut Elementary School on Sullivan Avenue, and the private De La Salle Middle School on Kennerly Avenue (a Catholic school).
Today, Natural Bridge Avenue is the neighborhood’s primary commercial and institutional corridor. The Urban League of Metropolitan St. Louis Entrepreneurship and Women’s Business Center , which opened in July 2024 at 4401 Natural Bridge Avenue in a beautifully restored 1920-era former Commerce Bank building, is the anchor of a new chapter in The Greater Ville’s commercial life — providing startup counseling, the SBA-backed “Ready!” graduation series, and workshops specifically designed for women founders and minority entrepreneurs. Beloved community staples include Firehouse 282 (a proud Black-owned business in the former 1900s firehouse on Vandeventer Avenue), Jaden’s Diner , St. Louis Fatburger , and Midtown Bar & Grill . Bus routes 19, 4, and 70 connect The Greater Ville to downtown St. Louis just under 4 miles to the east and to the broader regional transit network.
The housing stock is what makes The Greater Ville immediately readable on a drive through: block after block of early-20th-century brick two- and three-family flats and modest single-family homes, built mostly between 1900 and 1930 for the white working- and middle-class families the restrictive covenants were written to protect, then passed to the Black families the Shelley decision let in after 1948. That brick has held up — much of it is still standing more than a century later — but the neighborhood carries the same story as most of north St. Louis: decades of population loss as St. Louis’s Black middle class gained the same access to the county that white families already had, leaving solid brick buildings next to boarded and vacant lots on side streets off the Natural Bridge corridor. That is the honest present-day picture, not a story of neglect alone. Today The Greater Ville is home mostly to longtime residents with roots here going back generations, alongside a smaller number of newcomers drawn by affordable brick housing and post-tornado rehab activity — a neighborhood that is still overwhelmingly residential, with Natural Bridge Avenue carrying what commercial activity exists rather than a dense retail corridor of its own.
Like its inner neighbor The Ville, The Greater Ville sustained significant damage in the EF3 tornado on May 16, 2025 and is part of the “A Stronger Northside” neighborhood plan adopted in December 2025, which includes the MLK Cultural Boulevard project and a modular housing pilot now underway. Community organization 4theVille — co-founded by neighborhood advocate Ms. Ranson and others — gives tours of the neighborhood and advocates for recognition of the Shelley House, the Chuck Berry House, and the full arc of the neighborhood’s civil rights and cultural significance.
Image: The Shelley House at 4600 Labadie Avenue — National Historic Landmark (1990) and site of the 1948 Supreme Court case Shelley v. Kraemer , where J.D. and Ethel Lee Shelley’s 1945 home purchase produced the constitutional ruling that ended court enforcement of racially restrictive covenants — Wikimedia Commons , CC BY 3.0 by FrancisNancy

The Greater Ville sits on the flat Grand Prairie upland about four miles northwest of downtown St. Louis, sharing the region’s hot, humid summers, cold winters, and spring tornado risk — a risk the neighborhood now knows firsthand after the EF3 storm of May 16, 2025.

### Frequently Asked Questions 
Q. Where is the Greater Ville neighborhood in St. Louis? 
A. The Greater Ville sits in north St. Louis, an upside-down-U-shaped neighborhood centered near 38.6621° N, 90.2483° W in zip codes 63107, 63113, and 63115 that wraps around the smaller inner neighborhood of The Ville on three sides. Its boundaries run north to Natural Bridge Avenue, south to Dr. Martin Luther King Drive and St. Louis Avenue, east to N. Vandeventer Avenue, and west to Marcus Avenue.

Q. What defines the Greater Ville neighborhood? 
A. The Greater Ville is defined by its upside-down-U shape wrapping The Ville, the 1945 Shelley House, site of the landmark Supreme Court case Shelley v. Kraemer, and Chuck Berry’s boyhood home on Whittier Street. Natural Bridge Avenue is its primary commercial corridor, anchored today by the Urban League’s Entrepreneurship and Women’s Business Center in a restored 1920s bank building.

Q. How does St Louis Near Me Directory help Greater Ville businesses? 
A. St Louis Near Me Directory gives Greater Ville businesses a hyperlocal listing tied to the neighborhood’s own landmarks — the Shelley House, the Chuck Berry House, Fairground Park, and the Urban League Entrepreneurship and Women’s Business Center — helping providers along Natural Bridge Avenue stand out to residents, history visitors, and the community partners rebuilding after 2025’s tornado.

Q. What types of businesses are most common in Greater Ville? 
A. The Greater Ville mixes chamber advocacy, business publishing, and women’s business support with a couple of everyday neighborhood shops just across its boundary. On-page options include the Heartland St. Louis Black Chamber of Commerce, St. Louis Small Business Monthly, the St. Louis Regional Chamber, Momentum Worldwide, and the neighborhood’s own Urban League Women’s Business Center on Natural Bridge Avenue.

Q. What kinds of dining, retail, and recreation options are available in Greater Ville? 
A. The Greater Ville leans residential, with Natural Bridge Avenue carrying its commercial activity rather than a dense retail strip. For recreation, 131-acre Fairground Park anchors the neighborhood’s northern edge with a swimming pool, roller rink, a 9-acre stocked fishing lake, walking trails, and athletic fields that have served north St. Louis families since 1908.

Q. Are there neighborhood landmarks, parks, and historic sites in Greater Ville? 
A. Yes — the Greater Ville holds the 1945 Shelley House at 4600 Labadie Avenue, a National Historic Landmark and site of the 1948 Supreme Court case Shelley v. Kraemer, and the Chuck Berry House at 3137 Whittier Street, NRHP-listed in 2008, where Berry composed “Maybellene” and “Johnny B. Goode.” Fairground Park and the Julia Davis Branch Library round out the neighborhood’s landmarks.

Q. What is it like to live in Greater Ville? 
A. Living in the Greater Ville today means block after block of early-20th-century brick two- and three-family flats, home mostly to longtime residents alongside newcomers drawn by affordable housing. The neighborhood sustained real damage in the May 2025 EF3 tornado and is now part of the “A Stronger Northside” revitalization plan adopted in December 2025.

Q. How do residents and visitors get around Greater Ville? 
A. Natural Bridge Avenue is the Greater Ville’s primary corridor, connecting residents to Dr. Martin Luther King Drive, St. Louis Avenue, N. Vandeventer Avenue, and Marcus Avenue at the neighborhood’s boundaries. Bus routes 19, 4, and 70 link the Greater Ville to downtown St. Louis, just under 4 miles to the east, and the broader regional transit network.

### The Hill Businesses & Neighborhood Guide | St Louis Near Me Directory
The Hill, St. Louis
The Hill serves as the largest and most intact Italian-American neighborhood in the United States — a 52-block Little Italy in south-central St. Louis built on the fire-clay deposits that drew German, Irish, and African-American immigrants in the 1830s and Northern Italian and Sicilian immigrants from the 1880s onward — anchored by St. Ambrose Catholic Church (1903, current Lombard Romanesque Revival building 1926, modeled after the Basilica of Sant’Ambrogio in Milan), the Hill 2000 Neighborhood Association, Yogi Berra and Joe Garagiola’s adjacent boyhood homes on Elizabeth Avenue, Berra Park, the Italian Heritage Parade & Festa, and the green-white-and-red fire hydrants painted in Italian flag colors — offering Italian bakeries and confectioners, family-owned restaurants and taverns, plant-based soap manufacturers and artisanal goods, design-build construction firms, antique markets, craft breweries, professional services, and community-led cultural commerce across the Marconi, Macklind, Shaw, and Sublette Avenue corridors.
The Hill is one of St. Louis’s 79 official neighborhoods, located at 38.6184° N, 90.2870° W in south-central St. Louis City. The neighborhood’s official boundaries are Manchester Avenue (Route 100) on the north, South Kingshighway Boulevard on the east, Columbia and Southwest Avenues on the south, and Hampton Avenue on the west. Total area is 0.97 square miles , with a 2020 census population of 2,487 residents and a density of approximately 2,600 per square mile . ZIP code is part of 63110 , and the neighborhood sits in the 5th Ward of the City of St. Louis under Alderman Matt Devoti. Surrounding neighborhoods include Kings Oak and Cheltenham to the north, Forest Park Southeast and Southwest Garden to the east, Southwest Garden and North Hampton to the south, and Ellendale and Clifton Heights to the west. The neighborhood’s defining streets are Marconi Avenue (the cultural and commercial spine), Macklind Avenue , Shaw Avenue , Daggett Avenue , Wilson Avenue , Edwards Street , and Sublette Avenue .
The neighborhood’s name comes from its proximity to the highest point in the City of St. Louis — about an eighth of a mile south of the official boundaries at the intersection of Arsenal Street and Sublette Avenue , near the former St. Louis State Hospital (today the St. Louis Psychiatric Rehabilitation Center, opened 1869). The area was originally called Cheltenham , a rugged stretch of land on the city’s western edge five miles from the Mississippi River. The pivotal event came in 1849 , when a massive fire destroyed 15 blocks of downtown St. Louis and new city building codes required brick construction — triggering an explosive demand for fire brick. After the Evens and Howard Fire Brick Company and its clay mines opened in 1854–1855 , more than a dozen brick and tile factories sprang up along the banks of the River Des Peres, drawing waves of German, Irish, and African-American workers. Italians from Northern Italy (especially Lombardy) and later Sicily began arriving in the 1880s to work in the clay mines, initially living in boarding houses before bringing families and building permanent homes. By 1910, six foundries were fully operational.
By the 1920s , The Hill had become a self-sustaining Italian-American community where residents could find everything within walking distance — grocers, bakeries, butchers, tailors, barbers, and doctors. St. Ambrose Catholic Parish , founded in 1903 by members of St. Aloysius Gonzaga Parish to serve the area’s growing Lombard immigrant population, became the spiritual and cultural heart of the neighborhood. After the first wooden church burned in 1921 , a brick-and-terracotta replacement designed by architect Angelo Corrubia in the Lombard Romanesque Revival style was completed in 1926 , modeled after the Basilica of Sant’Ambrogio in Milan . Parishioners bought individual bricks and pews to fund construction. The parish school opened in 1906 and helped bridge the divide between northern and southern Italian families. The Italian Immigrants sculpture by Rudolph Edward Torrini, installed in front of the church, commemorates the 100-year history of both Northern and Southern Italians settling here. Across the street is Piazza Imo , the neighborhood’s informal central square.
The Hill’s most celebrated native sons are baseball Hall of Famer Yogi Berra (1925–2015), an 18-time All-Star and 10-time World Series champion with the New York Yankees, and his lifelong friend Joe Garagiola (1926–2016), a Major League catcher turned broadcaster — their boyhood homes face each other on Elizabeth Avenue . The neighborhood also produced four of the five St. Louisans on the U.S. soccer team that famously defeated England in the 1950 FIFA World Cup — Frank Borghi , Charlie Colombo , Gino Pariani , and Frank “Pee Wee” Wallace — a story told in the book and 2005 film The Game of Their Lives . Other notable residents include MLB player Frank Crespi (the first Hill resident on a World Series championship team, the 1942 Cardinals), NFL player Ben Pucci , and singer Toni Carroll . The neighborhood was historically known by the disparaging nickname “Dago Hill” — the Mississippi blues singer Luella Miller recorded “Dago Hill Blues” in 1926, Charlie Patton referenced the area in his 1934 single “Love My Stuff,” and Tampa Red and Georgia Tom Dorsey sang of The Hill’s Prohibition-era bootlegging in their 1932 “You Can’t Get That Stuff No More.”
The Hill thrived through the 1950s and 1960s. More than 1,020 men from The Hill served in World War II ; 23 did not return, and their names are inscribed on a bronze plaque in the back of St. Ambrose Church and on a column in Piazza Imo. Manufacturing companies including Magic Chef , Marlo Coil , and Style Craft employed hundreds. Politics shifted from Republican to Democratic in the 1930s, and leaders like Midge Berra used political connections to improve the neighborhood. By the mid-1970s , however, two threats emerged: in 1971 , the USDOT began construction on a section of Interstate 44 that cut through nearly a third of The Hill, demolishing 109 homes . Under the leadership of Father Salvatore Polizzi , residents raised $50,000 to build a car bridge on Edwards Street crossing over the highway to reconnect the community. The collective action gave rise to the Hill 2000 Neighborhood Association in 1970 with the motto “Don’t Move, Improve” — the campaign that ensured The Hill survived while other Little Italys across America disappeared.
Today The Hill remains a tightly knit, multi-generational community where homes are often sold privately rather than listed on the open market and where Italian-American families pass houses down across four or five generations. The 2020 census recorded a racial makeup of 90.4% White, 2.5% Black, 1.1% Asian, 4.5% Two or More Races, and 1.2% Some Other Race (3.3% Hispanic or Latino origin). The neighborhood is famous for the fire hydrants painted green, white, and red in the colors of the Italian flag, the Italian-flag crosswalks at Shaw and Marconi (completed 2022), the Italian Heritage Parade & Festa , Carnevale (February), Ferragosto (August), the Hill Wine Walk , the Soap Box Derby , the Christmas on the Hill festivities, and the annual Giro della Montagna cycling race (part of the Gateway Cup over Labor Day weekend). The St. Louis Italian Language Program is housed at Gateway Science Academy on Fyler Avenue. St. Louis’s Italian sister city is Bologna . Berra Park , the neighborhood’s only green space, covers nearly five acres with soccer and softball fields, a playground, and seasonal events.
The Hill’s commercial life is concentrated along Marconi Avenue, Macklind Avenue, Shaw Avenue, and Daggett Avenue, where the businesses listed on this page operate. The neighborhood’s defining anchors include the Hill 2000 Neighborhood Association at 1935 Marconi (volunteer-led since 1970), Herbaria at 2016 Marconi (24 years of plant-based, vegan, chemical-free handcrafted soaps), Missouri Baking Co at 2027 Edwards (the 1924 Italian bakery famous for cassata cake, cannoli, gooey butter cake, and chocolate drops), Anthonino’s Taverna at 2225 Macklind (the Greek-Italian taverna with 13,918+ Google reviews famous for its toasted ravioli), The Hill Antique Market at 4923 Daggett (75+ vendors in a renovated brick warehouse), 2nd Shift Brewing at 1601 Sublette (the craft brewery and tasting room founded by Steve Crider), Gioia’s Deli at 1934 Macklind (an Italian deli on the same corner since 1918), Charlie Gitto’s On the Hill at 5226 Shaw, Joe Fassi Sausage and Sandwich Factory at 2323 Sublette, Randall’s Wines & Spirits at 4925 Southwest, the Hill Neighborhood Center at Daggett and Marconi, the 1929 Big Club building at Shaw and Marconi (today a photography studio), and dozens of family-run grocers, butchers, bakeries, salons, and bocce gardens that have made The Hill an internationally recognized Little Italy destination.
Image: St. Ambrose Catholic Church on The Hill — the 1926 Lombard Romanesque Revival church modeled after the Basilica of Sant’Ambrogio in Milan and the cultural heart of St. Louis’s Italian-American community — Wikimedia Commons / CC BY-SA

The Hill sits on the city’s highest ridge just south of Forest Park, which gives it slightly better drainage than the neighborhoods below it — otherwise it runs the same hot, humid summers and cold, snowy winters as the rest of St. Louis, with festival season (the Italian Heritage Parade & Festa, Carnevale, Ferragosto, the Hill Wine Walk) timed for spring through fall and the bakeries, delis, and taverns carrying the neighborhood through winter.
What The Hill is today isn’t really a walkable retail strip in the usual sense — it’s a place people drive to from across the metro for a specific table or a specific loaf of bread, then leave. The line for a table at Charlie Gitto’s or a number at Gioia’s Deli on a Saturday afternoon regularly outnumbers the neighborhood’s own population of 2,487, and most of those residents didn’t buy their house on the open market — they inherited it or bought it directly from a neighbor before a for-sale sign ever went up. That turnover pattern is the honest answer to why national chains have never gotten a foothold here: there’s no real estate cycling through to buy into, and the customers keeping Missouri Baking Co’s ovens and Gioia’s slicers running aren’t shopping for a Little Italy experience — they’re St. Louisans eating where their grandparents ate.

Gioia’s Deli has operated on Macklind Avenue since 1918, making it one of the oldest continuously run businesses on The Hill. The deli is best known for the Original Hot Salami sandwich — a St. Louis-specific style of cured, smoked salami sliced thin and piled onto crusty bread — along with house-made Italian sausage, provolone, and a full case of cured meats and cheeses. Lines regularly stretch toward the door around lunchtime, especially on weekends, and the counter runs on a deli-ticket system rather than table service. Regulars order by the pound for parties and holiday gatherings as much as for a single sandwich. It’s a working deli, not a sit-down restaurant — expect a line, a ticket number, and a to-go bag. This is the stop for anyone who wants to taste what made The Hill a food destination, still run out of the same storefront it opened in over a century ago.

### Frequently Asked Questions 
Q. Is the hill in St. Louis worth visiting? 
A. Yes — The Hill is a rare, still-thriving 52-block Little Italy that people drive across the metro to visit rather than a preserved museum piece. Visitors can eat where St. Louisans’ grandparents ate at Gioia’s Deli (since 1918) or Missouri Baking Co (since 1924), tour St. Ambrose Catholic Church’s 1926 Lombard Romanesque Revival building, and walk streets marked by green-white-and-red fire hydrants and Italian-flag crosswalks.

Q. What is the hill in St. Louis known for? 
A. The Hill is known as America’s largest and most intact Italian-American neighborhood — a 52-block Little Italy built by immigrants who came to work its 19th-century clay mines and brick foundries. It’s home to St. Ambrose Catholic Church, Yogi Berra and Joe Garagiola’s boyhood homes on Elizabeth Avenue, green-white-and-red fire hydrants, and family-run institutions like Gioia’s Deli and Missouri Baking Co that have operated for a century.

Q. Is the Hill a good neighborhood in St. Louis? 
A. By most measures, yes — the Hill 2000 Neighborhood Association’s “Don’t Move, Improve” campaign is credited with keeping The Hill intact while other American Little Italys disappeared, and it remains a tightly knit, multi-generational community where homes are often passed down rather than sold on the open market. Its businesses, from Gioia’s Deli to Anthonino’s Taverna, draw diners from across the metro rather than relying on foot traffic alone.

Q. Is the Hill in St. Louis still Italian? 
A. Culturally and commercially, yes. St. Ambrose Catholic Church still anchors the neighborhood, the Italian Heritage Parade & Festa and Ferragosto still run every year, and Gioia’s Deli (since 1918) and Missouri Baking Co (since 1924) are still run by the families that started them. The 2020 Census recorded the neighborhood as 90.4% White overall — but homes still pass down within Italian-American families across generations rather than selling openly.

Q. What famous people are from the Hill in St. Louis? 
A. The Hill’s best-known native sons are Yogi Berra and Joe Garagiola, whose boyhood homes face each other on Elizabeth Avenue. The neighborhood also produced four of the five St. Louisans on the U.S. soccer team that upset England at the 1950 FIFA World Cup — Frank Borghi, Charlie Colombo, Gino Pariani, and Frank “Pee Wee” Wallace — plus MLB infielder Frank Crespi, NFL player Ben Pucci, and singer Toni Carroll.

Q. How does St Louis Near Me Directory help The Hill businesses? 
A. St Louis Near Me Directory strengthens neighborhood-focused visibility for businesses that serve The Hill by combining local content with curated listings. Joining connects a Hill business to stronger “near me” signals tied to St. Ambrose Catholic Church, the Italian Heritage Parade & Festa, Berra Park, and the Marconi, Macklind, Shaw, and Sublette Avenue corridors — helping it stand out to multigenerational Italian-American families and festival visitors.

Q. What types of businesses are most common in The Hill? 
A. The Hill’s business mix is dominated by Italian institutions: bakeries like Missouri Baking Co, delis like Gioia’s Deli, and restaurants like Charlie Gitto’s and Anthonino’s Taverna, alongside a craft brewery (2nd Shift), a wine and spirits shop (Randall’s), an antique market, and specialty manufacturers like Herbaria’s plant-based soaps. Most are family-run and multi-generational rather than chains, clustered along Marconi, Macklind, Shaw, and Sublette Avenues.

Q. What kinds of dining, retail, and recreation options are available in The Hill? 
A. Dining runs from Gioia’s Deli’s Original Hot Salami sandwiches and Missouri Baking Co’s cassata cake to sit-down Italian at Charlie Gitto’s and Anthonino’s Taverna’s toasted ravioli. Retail includes Randall’s Wines & Spirits, Herbaria’s handcrafted soaps, and The Hill Antique Market’s 75+ vendors. For recreation, Berra Park offers soccer and softball fields, and 2nd Shift Brewing’s tasting room rounds out the corridor.

### The Ville Businesses & Neighborhood Guide | St Louis Near Me Directory
The Ville, St. Louis
The Ville is the historic 42-square-block north St. Louis neighborhood that served from 1911 to 1950 as the cultural center of Black St. Louis — home to Sumner High School (the oldest Black high school west of the Mississippi), Homer G. Phillips Hospital (which trained more Black doctors than any institution in the world), and Annie Malone’s Poro College. Notable alumni include Chuck Berry, Tina Turner, Arthur Ashe, Dick Gregory, Grace Bumbry, and Robert Guillaume. The corridor today is almost entirely residential, with commercial activity limited to the chamber-advocacy and business-district organizations tied to the neighborhood’s legacy, plus a handful of small businesses — a barbershop, a corner store — in the immediately surrounding blocks.
The Ville is one of the most historically significant neighborhoods in American urban history — a compact 42-square-block rectangle centered at 38.6591° N, 90.2446° W in zip codes 63113 and 63107 on the city’s north-central plateau, bounded north by St. Louis Avenue , south by Dr. Martin Luther King Drive , east by Sarah Street , and west by Taylor Avenue . Interior streets including Whittier Street (formerly Wash), Annie Malone Drive (formerly Goode Avenue, renamed to honor the neighborhood’s greatest entrepreneur), Cottage Avenue , W. Kennerly Avenue , Aldine Avenue , Maffitt Avenue , and St. Ferdinand Avenue form a tight residential grid that, at its peak in the 1930s and 1940s, was among the most prosperous Black communities in America. The name itself is a shortening of “Elleardsville,” the old settlement named for horticulturist Charles M. Elleard who arrived from San Francisco in the 1860s; the area was annexed by St. Louis in 1876, and Black residents coined “The Ville” in the late 1880s as the neighborhood became one of the few parts of St. Louis free of racially restrictive covenants.
The transformation was rapid and well-documented. In 1873, St. Louis built Elleardsville Colored School No. 8 (later renamed Simmons School) — the neighborhood’s first Black institution and the earliest African American institution in the community. After Missouri’s 1911 introduction of racially restrictive housing covenants concentrated Black residents in the few open neighborhoods, The Ville’s African American population went from 8% in 1920 to 86% by 1930 and reached 95% by 1950 — the Ville of proud Black St. Louis folklore. James Kennerly had owned a large Cote Placquemine (Persimmon Hill) plantation near present-day Kennerly and Taylor avenues, which was destroyed by fire in 1863. Original street names like Kennerly, Wash (now Whittier), Goode (now Annie Malone Drive), and Taylor preserve traces of those early landowners.
The institutions that defined The Ville’s golden era are without parallel in the story of Black St. Louis. Sumner High School (4248 West Cottage Avenue) was founded in 1875, named for abolitionist U.S. Senator Charles H. Sumner, and relocated to The Ville in 1910 (current building constructed 1908). It is the oldest Black high school west of the Mississippi River , and was added to the National Register of Historic Places in December 2025. Sumner alumni include Chuck Berry , who was born and raised in The Ville before recording the songs that shaped rock and roll; comedian and activist Dick Gregory , born at 1803 N. Taylor Avenue; actress and singer Tina Turner (born Anna Mae Bullock), who moved to The Ville at 16 and graduated from Sumner in 1958; opera diva Grace Bumbry ; tennis champion Arthur Ashe , who completed his senior year at Sumner; Emmy-winning actor Robert Guillaume ; civil rights attorney Frankie Freeman ; activist Julia Davis; African Methodist Episcopal pioneer Charleton Tandy; and operatic baritone Robert McFerrin. Lloyd Lionel Gaines — plaintiff in the 1938 Gaines v. Canada Supreme Court case — was also tied to the neighborhood.
Across St. Ferdinand Avenue from Sumner stood Poro College , founded in 1917 by Annie Turnbo Pope Malone — one of America’s first Black female millionaires, whose hair-care and cosmetics empire (the “Poro System”) employed nearly 200 African Americans in St. Louis alone and reached 75,000 worldwide. Annie Malone arrived in St. Louis from Illinois in 1902; one of her early salespeople was Sarah Breedlove, who later became Madam C. J. Walker . The Poro Building — a million-dollar complex housing her Poro College of Beauty Culture, manufacturing plant, and numerous community organizations — became the symbol of African American enterprise in St. Louis. Malone was a generous philanthropist to the St. Louis Colored Orphans’ Home (which moved to The Ville in 1922 thanks to her gift and was later renamed the Annie Malone Children’s Home , now the Annie Malone Children and Family Service Center at 2612 Annie Malone Drive, NRHP-listed), St. James A.M.E. Church, and successfully pushed the city to pave streets in The Ville.
Homer G. Phillips Hospital (2601 North Whittier Street, NRHP-listed) opened in 1937 after a 15-year campaign led by attorney Homer G. Phillips — who was assassinated in 1931 , four years before he could see the hospital built in his name. By 1961, Homer G. Phillips had trained more Black doctors and nurses than any other institution in the world, employing more than 800 people at peak as a fully Black-staffed teaching hospital at a time when racial segregation barred Black physicians from white St. Louis hospitals. It closed in 1979 amid community protests and is now a 220-unit senior living facility; its red brick towers remain the visual anchor of the neighborhood, with the Homer G. Phillips Ambulatory Care Center continuing health services in the building. The Ville was designated a local historic district in 1987 .
Tandy Park (5.6 acres, established 1918, at Kennerly and Billups) is the neighborhood’s central green space, featuring the Arthur Ashe Tennis Courts , the Tuskegee Airman Football Field , basketball courts, a skating rink, and a playground. The adjacent Tandy Community Center (4206 West Kennerly Avenue, built 1938 as Public Works Administration Project No. 8483 by the same architect who designed Homer G. Phillips Hospital) is an Art Deco recreation facility on the National Register of Historic Places (NRHP since 1999), remaining in active use. St. James African Methodist Episcopal Church (organized 1885) and Antioch Baptist Church (organized 1884) anchor the neighborhood’s spiritual and civic life. Other landmarks include the Marshall School (4342 Aldine Avenue, built 1918, NRHP-listed), Turner Middle School (4235 Kennerly, originally the Charles Henry Turner Open Air School for Crippled Children, opened 1925 and named for the distinguished entomologist who taught at Sumner from 1908-1922), and the former Lincoln University Law School (1939-1955, later absorbed into the University of Missouri Law School).
The Ville today faces real challenges alongside real momentum. An EF3 tornado struck the neighborhood on May 16, 2025 , causing significant damage including the temporary displacement of Sumner High School students. A “Stronger Northside” neighborhood revitalization plan was formally adopted in December 2025, a $3.2 million ARPA-funded modular housing pilot is underway on Aldine Avenue, and community organization 4theVille is developing an MLK Cultural Boulevard project to anchor the southern corridor. The 2000 census recorded 97% Black residency among 2,695 residents; that number kept falling, to 1,868 residents by the 2010 census and 1,427 by the 2020 census — a neighborhood that once anchored a thriving Black business and cultural district now counts under 1,500 residents. The Ville today continues working to rebuild and reinvest at a fraction of its mid-century population. The Annie Malone Children and Family Service Center continues its century-long mission, and the work of rebuilding is ongoing.
Image: Homer G. Phillips Hospital, the 1937 NRHP-listed landmark at 2601 North Whittier Street that trained more Black doctors than any institution in the world and is now a 220-unit senior living facility — Wikimedia Commons , CC BY 3.0 by Onegentlemanofverona

North St. Louis runs the region’s full humid continental range — hot, humid summers and cold winters — but for The Ville that exposure hasn’t been abstract: the EF3 tornado of May 16, 2025 tore directly through the flat, open plateau the neighborhood sits on, and the rebuilding is still underway.

### Frequently Asked Questions 
Q. What is “The Ville” known for? 
A. The Ville is known as the historic cultural center of Black St. Louis, the 42-square-block neighborhood that from 1911 to 1950 produced an unmatched roster of institutions and residents — Sumner High School, Homer G. Phillips Hospital, and Annie Malone’s Poro College, plus alumni Chuck Berry, Tina Turner, Arthur Ashe, Dick Gregory, and Grace Bumbry.

Q. Where is The Ville neighborhood in St. Louis? 
A. The Ville sits in north-central St. Louis, a compact 42-square-block neighborhood in zip codes 63113 and 63107 centered near 38.6591° N, 90.2446° W. Its four boundary streets are St. Louis Avenue to the north, Dr. Martin Luther King Drive to the south, Sarah Street to the east, and Taylor Avenue to the west.

Q. How does St Louis Near Me Directory help The Ville businesses? 
A. St Louis Near Me Directory gives Ville-area businesses a hyperlocal listing tied to the neighborhood’s own landmarks — Sumner High School, Homer G. Phillips Hospital, the Annie Malone Children and Family Service Center, and Tandy Park — so providers show up in searches from residents, history visitors, and the community partners rebuilding the corridor after 2025’s tornado.

Q. What types of businesses are most common in The Ville? 
A. The Ville today is almost entirely residential — a local historic district of homes, churches, schools, and NRHP-listed institutions rather than a commercial strip. The closest verified options are the Heartland St. Louis Black Chamber of Commerce, the Locust Central Business District, Clark’s Barbershop in neighboring JeffVanderLou, and Kingz Korner Store in neighboring Penrose.

Q. What kinds of dining, retail, and recreation options are available in The Ville? 
A. The Ville itself has no dining or retail corridor of its own — the closest options are Clark’s Barbershop and Kingz Korner Store just outside its boundary. For recreation, Tandy Park anchors the neighborhood with the Arthur Ashe Tennis Courts, the Tuskegee Airman Football Field, basketball courts, a skating rink, and a playground.

Q. Are there neighborhood landmarks, parks, and historic sites in The Ville? 
A. Yes — The Ville holds an extraordinary concentration of landmarks: Sumner High School (NRHP-listed December 2025), the former Homer G. Phillips Hospital, the Annie Malone Children and Family Service Center, Tandy Park with its Arthur Ashe Tennis Courts, the Art Deco Tandy Community Center, and the neighborhood’s anchor congregations, St. James A.M.E. Church and Antioch Baptist Church.

Q. What is it like to live in The Ville? 
A. Living in The Ville today means a quiet, historic residential street grid still rebuilding after an EF3 tornado struck the neighborhood in May 2025. The “Stronger Northside” revitalization plan and a $3.2 million ARPA-funded modular housing pilot on Aldine Avenue are underway, while population has fallen to under 1,500 residents from its mid-century peak.

Q. How do residents and visitors get around The Ville? 
A. The Ville is built on a tight residential grid — Whittier Street, Annie Malone Drive, Cottage Avenue, W. Kennerly Avenue, Aldine Avenue, Maffitt Avenue, and St. Ferdinand Avenue — framed by its four boundary streets, which connect directly to St. Louis Avenue and Dr. Martin Luther King Drive, the main routes linking the neighborhood to downtown and the rest of north St. Louis.

### Tiffany Businesses & Neighborhood Guide | St Louis Near Me Directory
Tiffany, St. Louis
Tiffany is the south-central St. Louis neighborhood named for the 1890 Tiffany streetcar line that ran along the former Tiffany Street (now 39th Street) and transformed Mary McRee’s 1888-sold farmland into a middle-class commuter suburb. The neighborhood’s 215-structure Tiffany Neighborhood Historic District (NRHP-listed December 1978) is anchored by the $550 million SSM Health Saint Louis University Hospital that opened in 2020 on Grand Boulevard. Tiffany’s own commercial footprint is small — a city park, a veterinary clinic, and a gym on its own boundary streets — while the wider SLU Medical Center corridor around it supplies everything else.
Tiffany is one of St. Louis’s 79 official neighborhoods, centered at 38.6218° N, 90.2459° W in zip code 63110 on the city’s south-central section. Its boundaries run north to Chouteau Avenue , south to Interstate 44 , east to Grand Boulevard , and west to 39th Street — the same corridor once called Tiffany Street, from which the neighborhood takes its name. That western boundary, 39th Street, was home to the massive United Railways Company car shop complex, the hub of St. Louis’s entire streetcar network, and the Tiffany streetcar line that gave the area its identity long before the neighborhood was formally named. The eastern spine, Grand Boulevard , carries the region’s most-used bus route and anchors the SLU/SSM Health medical campus that now defines the neighborhood’s eastern face. Interior streets — McRee Avenue, Lafayette Avenue, Blaine Avenue, and Folsom Avenue — weave through a residential fabric that has been on the National Register of Historic Places since December 1978 . Adjacent neighborhoods include Forest Park Southeast to the north, Shaw to the south across I-44, the medical district to the east, and Botanical Heights (the rebranded former McRee Town) to the west.
The name Tiffany has nothing to do with jewelry. It derives from Louis and P. D. Tiffany , a family of landowners whose tract ran along what is now 39th Street. That street was called Tiffany Street until 1926; the Tiffany streetcar line took the same name. Before any of this, the land was part of the French colonial Prairie des Noyers , laid out in 1769 as communal agricultural strips west of the early St. Louis settlement. After the Louisiana Purchase, the tract passed through various hands before William McRee — a retired Army officer and Surveyor General of the Missouri and Illinois District — assembled most of it between 1825 and 1832. His widow Mary Urquhart McRee developed a subdivision called McRee City in 1869 (Mary married Samuel McRee at age 14, lived in New Orleans during the Mexican-American War, and inherited the land when Samuel died of cholera). Mary sold her remaining land in 1888, just before her death at 83. The purchaser was the Dundee Land and Investment Company , run by Thomas A. Scott , a young Canadian real estate developer described by contemporaries as “one of the most daring real estate operators St. Louis has ever known.”
Scott platted the land as Dundee Place in June 1889 (covering the area between McRee and Park Avenues, westward from Grand to Old Manchester Road, now Vandeventer) and held a grand auction in June 1891, naming two new streets in a deliberate bipartisan gesture: Folsom (for Frances Folsom Cleveland, wife of President Grover Cleveland) and Blaine (for James G. Blaine, the Republican nominee Cleveland had just defeated). With the completion of the Grand Avenue Viaduct in 1890 and electrified streetcar lines by the turn of the century, Tiffany developed rapidly as a middle-class commuter suburb. Nearly all of the 215 contributing structures in the Tiffany Neighborhood Historic District were built between 1891 and 1928 — a catalogue of late-Victorian and early-20th-century brick construction, from the celebrated rows of blonde brick homes on Blaine Avenue to Dutch colonial houses on Rutger Street to classical ornament reflecting the post-1904 World’s Fair confidence in the city’s future.
Architectural landmarks within Tiffany include the Bell Telephone Exchange Building (1902, architect F.C. Bonsack) at McRee and Grand and the Marquette Apartments (1912, Lafayette and Spring) which anchor the historic commercial and residential character of the neighborhood’s core. Parallel to all of this, the medical corridor on Grand Boulevard was taking shape: the Josephine Heikamp Hospital opened in 1900, Saint Louis University acquired its medical school in 1903, and the landmark Firmin Desloge Hospital — a 15-story green-roofed tower — opened in 1933. The $550 million SSM Health Saint Louis University Hospital that replaced Desloge opened September 1, 2020 , and a new $300 million Cardinal Glennon Children’s Hospital is planned for the former Pevely Dairy site at Grand and Chouteau with a projected 2027 completion. As one local urbanist put it, “residential Tiffany is in reality a different neighborhood than ‘Tiffany’” — the neighborhood is more than half owned by SSM Health and Saint Louis University, with the residential core compressed into the six square blocks south of the medical campus.
The neighborhood’s single park, Tiffany Park (3801 McRee Ave, 1.1 acres, established 1980), was created by the Midtown Medical Center Redevelopment Corporation as part of a late-1970s stabilization effort. Its western boundary was deliberately designed to block through-traffic on Blaine Avenue — a practical crime-reduction measure that also gave the park an unusual triangular presence on the residential block. The park features a tiered concrete semi-circle, a pavilion, a playground, and a basketball court, and remains the neighborhood’s primary outdoor gathering point. The Tiffany Community Association , formed in the early 1990s when the MMCRC program stalled, developed the long-range plan that helped stabilize reinvestment through the 2000s and into the present. In 2017, the Association partnered with Park Central Development on a new neighborhood plan addressing the residential core’s future.
Today Tiffany is anchored on its eastern edge by the SLU/SSM Health medical campus — a Level 1 trauma center that draws patients from across the region — while the residential core continues to fill in with renovations and adaptive reuse along McRee, Folsom, and Blaine Avenues. About 75% of Tiffany residents rent their properties , with many being SLU medical residents who buy homes during residency and either sell upon graduation or stay as permanent neighborhood residents. Downtown St. Louis sits just over 3 miles to the east; Forest Park is approximately 2 miles to the west; the Missouri Botanical Garden is just across I-44 in adjacent Shaw.
Image: Skyline of the Tiffany Neighborhood showing the SLU/SSM Health medical campus along Grand Boulevard and the surrounding 215-structure NRHP-listed historic district — Wikimedia Commons , CC BY 3.0 by Onegentlemanofverona

Tiffany sees St. Louis’s full humid continental swing — hot summers, a real spring tornado season, cold winters — with Interstate 44’s southern edge and the elevation drop toward 39th Street doing more to shape daily life here than any one season does.
The honest count for Tiffany is four verified connections, not eight: Tiffany Park itself, St Louis Veterinary Center and The L.A.B. Gym on the neighborhood’s own Chouteau and Grand boundary streets, and Park Central Development, the nonprofit that partnered with the Tiffany Community Association on the 2017 neighborhood plan. That is genuinely all of it — more than half of Tiffany’s land belongs to SSM Health and Saint Louis University, and the residential core is compressed into roughly six square blocks with almost no retail of its own.
What fills the gap sits just outside the boundary, and is worth naming honestly rather than pretending it’s Tiffany’s own: Fresh Gatherings Cafe + Farm is about half a mile northeast in The Gate District , and Fiddlehead Fern Cafe is about 0.7 miles south in Shaw . Both are real, well-reviewed options a short walk or drive from Tiffany’s residential core — not Tiffany businesses, but close enough that residents use them routinely.

### Tower Grove East Businesses & Neighborhood Guide | St Louis Near Me Directory
Tower Grove East, St. Louis
Tower Grove East serves as one of south St. Louis’s most architecturally splendid Victorian-era neighborhoods — a 0.51-square-mile residential and commercial corridor settled by 1850s German Catholic dairy farmers and built up by the relatives of the prominent German immigrants who founded Compton Heights and Flora Place — anchored by Tower Grove Park (the 289-acre 1868 Henry Shaw gift just across South Grand Boulevard), the South Grand Business District’s internationally renowned restaurant row, Roosevelt High School, the Carpenter Branch Library, Stray Dog Theatre at the Tower Grove Abbey, and the four-square Victorian and Italianate flats with carved fretwork, stained-glass windows, and elaborate staircases — offering community and immigrant-service organizations, custom floral design, live theatre, scratch-kitchen restaurants and cocktail bars, and neighborhood corner taverns across the South Grand, Shenandoah, Arsenal, and Gravois Avenue corridors.
Tower Grove East is one of St. Louis’s 79 official neighborhoods, located at 38.6029° N, 90.2364° W in south-central St. Louis City. The neighborhood’s official boundaries are Shenandoah Avenue on the north, Nebraska Avenue on the east, Gravois Avenue (MO Route 30) on the south, and South Grand Boulevard on the west. Total area is 0.51 square miles , with a 2020 census population of 5,708 residents and a density of approximately 11,000 per square mile . ZIP codes are parts of 63104 and 63118 , and the neighborhood sits in the 7th Ward of the City of St. Louis under Alderwoman Alisha Sonnier. Surrounding neighborhoods include Compton Heights to the north across Shenandoah, Fox Park and Benton Park West to the east, Gravois Park and Dutchtown to the south across Gravois, and Shaw and Tower Grove South to the west across South Grand. The neighborhood is approximately six miles south of downtown St. Louis.
Tower Grove Park itself belongs to neither neighborhood — it’s an independently governed 289-acre place, run by its own Board of Commissioners under the terms of Henry Shaw’s 1868 gift, not a piece of Tower Grove East’s own 0.51-square-mile footprint. Tower Grove East runs along the park’s eastern flank, its South Grand Boulevard boundary facing the park’s Grand Avenue entrance directly across the street. Tower Grove South, on the park’s opposite side, borders its southern edge along Arsenal Street — and shares a border with Tower Grove East of its own, along Grand Boulevard south of the park.
Tower Grove East was originally part of La Petite Prairie , settled by the French in the early 1700s. Grazing land was held in common, and farming land was divided into long narrow tracts. The commons system was abandoned around 1800, and the land began to be sold into private hands. By the 1850s , much of the property was owned by German Catholics — recent immigrants fleeing the aftermath of Germany’s 1848 civil war — who found the area ideal as pasture land for their dairy farming operations. The neighborhood takes its name from its position bordering the east entrance of Tower Grove Park across South Grand Boulevard. The park was deeded to the City of St. Louis in 1868 as a gift from Henry Shaw (1800–1889), the 19th-century English-born businessman and botanist who owned much of the surrounding land and also founded the adjacent Missouri Botanical Garden .
As the German immigrants prospered, the wealthiest began building mansions in the adjacent Compton Heights and along Flora Place — the city’s exclusive private streets just north of Shenandoah. Their siblings, cousins, and extended family members later settled the pastures of what is now Tower Grove East and built beautiful homes and flats of their own, using similar architectural detail to what is found in the wealthier Compton Heights and Flora Place. The typical Tower Grove East house was built on the four-square plan — a pyramid or hipped roof on a two-story cube, often with a pressed-brick or limestone course separating the stories. Buyers chose architectural elements from pattern books that illustrated multiple styles of windows, doors, stairways, and fireplace mantels. The often austere exterior facades typically hide a wealth of richly designed entries with carved fretwork , built-in hall benches, mirrors, and bookcases, wood paneling, stained-glass windows , and elaborate staircases.
The neighborhood’s civic and educational anchors include Roosevelt High School on Hartford Street (opened 1925, designed by Rockwell M. Milligan in an impressive Collegiate Gothic style), Shenandoah Elementary School on Shenandoah Avenue, and the Carpenter Branch Library on South Grand Boulevard (one of 15 branches in the St. Louis Public Library system). The neighborhood is also home to the Stray Dog Theatre at the Tower Grove Abbey on Tennessee Avenue. A monument in nearby Reservoir Park commemorates The Westliche Post , the German-language newspaper that Joseph Pulitzer later acquired and merged to form the St. Louis Post-Dispatch . Houses of worship include St. Wenceslaus Church on Oregon Avenue, St. Pius V Catholic Church and Messiah Lutheran Church on South Grand Boulevard, Holy Trinity Baptist Church on Minnesota Avenue, and the Body of Christ Temple on Louisiana Avenue.
The neighborhood’s commercial heartbeat is the South Grand Business District (also known simply as South Grand ) — a six-block stretch of South Grand Boulevard that has been branded and improved through the South Grand Community Improvement District. The district anchors one of the most internationally diverse restaurant rows in the Midwest, with Vietnamese, Thai, Ethiopian, Italian, Chinese, Middle Eastern, Japanese, Lebanese, Afghan, and Mexican restaurants alongside specialty grocers, rare bookstores, jewelry boutiques, natural food stores, and international gift shops. Many storefronts retain their original late-19th-century commercial architecture, and most restaurants offer outdoor dining that animates the streetscape year-round.
Tower Grove East’s history through the second half of the 20th century followed the trajectory of many south-side St. Louis neighborhoods. The 2000 census recorded 7,211 residents across 3,485 housing units (79% occupied, 39% owner-occupied, 61% renter-occupied). Like much of south St. Louis, the neighborhood lost 8% of its population between 1990 and 2000. By 2020, the population had stabilized at 5,708 residents with a racial makeup of 55.6% White, 28.9% Black, 5.0% Asian, 5.3% Hispanic/Latino , and other backgrounds. The neighborhood’s late-20th-century recovery accelerated in the 2010s and 2020s, with extensive historic restoration along Shenandoah, Arsenal, Humphrey, and the smaller cross streets, and with the South Grand business district’s emergence as a regional destination for international dining and independent retail.
Today, Tower Grove East’s active redevelopment is driven by neighborhood and immigrant-service organizations, floral and hospitality businesses, live theatre, and the steady pull of Tower Grove Park’s programming next door. The businesses listed on this page include the Tower Grove East Neighborhood Association (TGENA) , the St Louis Near Me Directory , Stray Dog Theatre at the Tower Grove Abbey on Tennessee Avenue, the International Institute of St. Louis on Arsenal Street (the 1919-founded immigrant and refugee service hub and host of the Festival of Nations), Botanicals Design Studio on South Grand (the custom florist founded by Keith McDonnell and Dean Riebeling), Riley’s Pub on Arsenal Street, Tick Tock Tavern and its next-door neighbor Buzz’s Hawaiian Grill on Magnolia Avenue, and Crafted. and Sheesh , two of the newer additions to South Grand’s international restaurant row. Tower Grove Park itself, just across South Grand, adds 2,185+ Google reviews of its own, 13 restored early-20th-century picnic pavilions, the Piper Palm House, the Tower Grove Farmers’ Market, “sip and stroll” events, and Food Truck Friday to the neighborhood’s doorstep.
Roosevelt High School — the 1925 Collegiate Gothic landmark on Hartford Street, designed by district architect Rockwell M. Milligan, in the Tower Grove East neighborhood of St. Louis, Missouri. Photo: St Louis Near Me Directory.

Tower Grove East follows the same four-season Midwest climate as the rest of St. Louis — humid summers that fill Tower Grove Park and the South Grand patios, and cold winters that push commerce indoors to South Grand’s restaurants, Riley’s Pub, Tick Tock Tavern, and Stray Dog Theatre at the Abbey.
Tower Grove East is Tower Grove South’s opposite in almost every way that matters to a resident. It’s a third the size — 0.51 square miles against 1.49 — and its German Catholic settlers were the relatives and employees of the families building mansions in neighboring Compton Heights and along Flora Place, not the mine and brickyard workers who built up Tower Grove South. There’s no equivalent to South Grand’s restaurant row or Morganford’s retail strip inside its own boundary; instead, Tower Grove East’s commercial life is a handful of long-running institutions — a neighborhood theatre in a converted church, a florist, two corner bars — clustered a short walk from the park and from South Grand next door. It suits residents who want that South Grand access without living inside the commercial corridor itself.

The Tower Grove East Neighborhood Association (TGENA), founded in 1965, is a nonprofit, volunteer-run organization serving the residents of the Tower Grove East neighborhood. Its mission is to engage all TGE residents in fostering a community that is warm and welcoming, where people thrive and local businesses, schools, and faith centers serve as anchors — working toward an outstanding urban neighborhood characterized by a diverse population unified in an atmosphere of trust, respect, and friendship. TGENA hosts regular monthly general meetings with updates from its president and committee chairs, an SLMPD neighborhood liaison, and city, business, and legislative leaders, along with neighborhood happy hours and community events. As a steward of one of south St. Louis’s most historic and architecturally rich neighborhoods, the association is the central civic resource for residents, new neighbors, and businesses looking to connect with the Tower Grove East community.

The International Institute of St. Louis (IISTL) is the region’s immigrant and refugee service and information hub, located on Arsenal Street in Tower Grove East. A 501(c)(3) United Way agency established in 1919, the Institute serves roughly 7,500–8,000 new Americans from about 75 countries each year, with locally and nationally acclaimed programs spanning English and citizenship classes, refugee resettlement, employment and training, immigration assistance, and services for vulnerable populations including elderly refugees and trafficking survivors. The Institute anchors the city’s thriving International District and hosts the celebrated annual Festival of Nations and the Race for Refugees in Tower Grove Park, reaching tens of thousands of area residents through its outreach. It is an essential resource for newcomers building independence in St. Louis and for community members seeking to connect across cultures.

### Frequently Asked Questions 
Q. What defines the Tower Grove East neighborhood? 
A. Size and lineage. At just 0.51 square miles — a third the size of Tower Grove South next door — Tower Grove East was settled in the 1850s by German Catholic dairy farmers related to the wealthier families who built Compton Heights and Flora Place. It’s defined today by its four-square Victorian flats, Tower Grove Park across South Grand, and a tight cluster of civic and community institutions.

Q. What types of businesses are most common in Tower Grove East? 
A. Community and immigrant-service organizations, live theatre, custom floral design, and a handful of corner bars and restaurants define Tower Grove East, alongside the South Grand corridor’s international dining. The neighborhood is too small for a shopping strip of its own — its commercial identity comes from a few tightly clustered, long-running institutions rather than a continuous retail row.

Q. What kinds of dining, retail, and recreation options are available in Tower Grove East? 
A. Dining ranges from Turkish (Sheesh) and Hawaiian (Buzz’s Hawaiian Grill) to a cocktail-and-kitchen spot (Crafted.) and two classic corner bars, Riley’s Pub and Tick Tock Tavern. Botanicals Design Studio covers custom floral work. For recreation, Tower Grove Park sits just across South Grand with its Farmers’ Market, Food Truck Friday, and 13 restored Victorian picnic pavilions.

Q. Are there neighborhood landmarks, parks, and historic sites in Tower Grove East? 
A. Yes. Stray Dog Theatre performs inside the Tower Grove Abbey, a former 1912 German Evangelical church on Tennessee Avenue. Roosevelt High School’s 1925 Collegiate Gothic building and the Carpenter Branch Library anchor the neighborhood’s civic core. Tower Grove Park, across South Grand Boulevard, isn’t technically inside Tower Grove East’s boundary but borders it directly along the park’s east side.

Q. What is it like to live in Tower Grove East? 
A. Quiet and tightly knit. At 5,708 residents packed into 0.51 square miles, it’s one of the denser pockets of south St. Louis, but its scale keeps it feeling like a small town rather than a commercial strip. Residents live in four-square Victorian flats with carved fretwork and stained glass, walk to South Grand for dinner, and lean on TGENA, active since 1965, for neighborhood life.

Q. How do residents and visitors get around Tower Grove East? 
A. Tower Grove East is entirely walkable at 0.51 square miles, with South Grand Boulevard as its commercial spine and fast access to Interstates 44 and 55 for the rest of the metro. Most residents walk or bike to South Grand’s restaurants and Tower Grove Park across the street; the neighborhood’s compact grid makes a car unnecessary for daily errands within its own boundary.

## Tower Grove East Businesses & Neighborhood Guide | St Louis Near Me Directory

 Tower Grove East, St. Louis

Tower Grove East serves as one of south St. Louis’s most architecturally splendid Victorian-era neighborhoods — a 0.51-square-mile residential and commercial corridor settled by 1850s German Catholic dairy farmers and built up by the relatives of the prominent German immigrants who founded Compton Heights and Flora Place — anchored by Tower Grove Park (the 289-acre 1868 Henry Shaw gift just across South Grand Boulevard), the South Grand Business District’s internationally renowned restaurant row, Roosevelt High School, the Carpenter Branch Library, Stray Dog Theatre at the Tower Grove Abbey, and the four-square Victorian and Italianate flats with carved fretwork, stained-glass windows, and elaborate staircases — offering historic-restoration general contractors, eco-friendly retail and zero-waste marketplaces, biotechnology and lab services, boutique real estate, handyman services, scratch-kitchen restaurants, and community-led cultural organizations across the South Grand, Shenandoah, Arsenal, and Gravois Avenue corridors.

Tower Grove East is one of St. Louis’s 79 official neighborhoods, located at **38.6029° N, 90.2364° W** in south-central St. Louis City. The neighborhood’s official boundaries are **Shenandoah Avenue** on the north, **Nebraska Avenue** on the east, **Gravois Avenue (MO Route 30)** on the south, and **South Grand Boulevard** on the west. Total area is **0.51 square miles**, with a 2020 census population of **5,708 residents** and a density of approximately **11,000 per square mile**. ZIP codes are parts of **63104** and **63118**, and the neighborhood sits in the **7th Ward** of the City of St. Louis under Alderwoman Alisha Sonnier. Surrounding neighborhoods include **Compton Heights** to the north across Shenandoah, **Fox Park** and **Benton Park West** to the east, **Gravois Park** and **Dutchtown** to the south across Gravois, and **Shaw** and **Tower Grove South** to the west across South Grand. The neighborhood is approximately six miles south of downtown St. Louis.

Tower Grove East was originally part of **La Petite Prairie**, settled by the **French** in the early 1700s. Grazing land was held in common, and farming land was divided into long narrow tracts. The commons system was abandoned around 1800, and the land began to be sold into private hands. By the **1850s**, much of the property was owned by **German Catholics** — recent immigrants fleeing the aftermath of Germany’s 1848 civil war — who found the area ideal as pasture land for their dairy farming operations. The neighborhood takes its name from its position bordering the east entrance of **Tower Grove Park** across South Grand Boulevard. The park was deeded to the City of St. Louis in **1868** as a gift from **Henry Shaw** (1800–1889), the 19th-century English-born businessman and botanist who owned much of the surrounding land and also founded the adjacent **Missouri Botanical Garden**.

As the German immigrants prospered, the wealthiest began building mansions in the adjacent **Compton Heights** and along **Flora Place** — the city’s exclusive private streets just north of Shenandoah. Their siblings, cousins, and extended family members later settled the pastures of what is now Tower Grove East and built beautiful homes and flats of their own, using similar architectural detail to what is found in the wealthier Compton Heights and Flora Place. The typical Tower Grove East house was built on the **four-square plan** — a pyramid or hipped roof on a two-story cube, often with a pressed-brick or limestone course separating the stories. Buyers chose architectural elements from **pattern books** that illustrated multiple styles of windows, doors, stairways, and fireplace mantels. The often austere exterior facades typically hide a wealth of richly designed entries with **carved fretwork**, built-in hall benches, mirrors, and bookcases, wood paneling, **stained-glass windows**, and elaborate staircases.

The neighborhood’s civic and educational anchors include **Roosevelt High School** on Hartford Street (opened 1925, designed by Rockwell M. Milligan in an impressive Collegiate Gothic style), **Shenandoah Elementary School** on Shenandoah Avenue, and the **Carpenter Branch Library** on South Grand Boulevard (one of 15 branches in the St. Louis Public Library system). The neighborhood is also home to the **Stray Dog Theatre** at the **Tower Grove Abbey** on Tennessee Avenue. A monument in nearby Reservoir Park commemorates **The Westliche Post**, the German-language newspaper that Joseph Pulitzer later acquired and merged to form the **St. Louis Post-Dispatch**. Houses of worship include **St. Wenceslaus Church** on Oregon Avenue, **St. Pius V Catholic Church** and **Messiah Lutheran Church** on South Grand Boulevard, **Holy Trinity Baptist Church** on Minnesota Avenue, and the **Body of Christ Temple** on Louisiana Avenue.

The neighborhood’s commercial heartbeat is the **South Grand Business District** (also known simply as **South Grand**) — a six-block stretch of South Grand Boulevard that has been branded and improved through the South Grand Community Improvement District. The district anchors one of the most internationally diverse restaurant rows in the Midwest, with **Vietnamese, Thai, Ethiopian, Italian, Chinese, Middle Eastern, Japanese, Lebanese, Afghan, and Mexican** restaurants alongside specialty grocers, rare bookstores, jewelry boutiques, natural food stores, and international gift shops. Many storefronts retain their original late-19th-century commercial architecture, and most restaurants offer outdoor dining that animates the streetscape year-round.

Tower Grove East’s history through the second half of the 20th century followed the trajectory of many south-side St. Louis neighborhoods. The 2000 census recorded **7,211 residents** across **3,485 housing units** (79% occupied, 39% owner-occupied, 61% renter-occupied). Like much of south St. Louis, the neighborhood lost 8% of its population between 1990 and 2000. By 2020, the population had stabilized at **5,708 residents** with a racial makeup of **55.6% White, 28.9% Black, 5.0% Asian, 5.3% Hispanic/Latino**, and other backgrounds. The neighborhood’s late-20th-century recovery accelerated in the 2010s and 2020s, with extensive historic restoration along Shenandoah, Arsenal, Humphrey, and the smaller cross streets, and with the South Grand business district’s emergence as a regional destination for international dining and independent retail.

Today, Tower Grove East’s active redevelopment is driven by neighborhood and immigrant-service organizations, historic-restoration and property-management firms, eco-friendly landscaping, floral design, scratch-kitchen pubs, live theatre, and the steady pull of Tower Grove Park’s programming. The businesses listed on this page include the **Tower Grove East Neighborhood Association (TGENA)**, the **St Louis Near Me Directory**, **Stray Dog Theatre** at the Tower Grove Abbey on Tennessee Avenue, **Seasons Cycle** landscaping on Louisiana Avenue, **Heritage Properties** on Shenandoah Avenue (the historic-home rehab and property-management firm founded by Warren Popp and Tristan Mackenzie), the **International Institute of St. Louis** on Arsenal Street (the 1919-founded immigrant and refugee service hub and host of the Festival of Nations), **Botanicals Design Studio** on South Grand (the custom florist founded by Keith McDonnell and Dean Riebeling), **Riley’s Pub** on Arsenal Street, **Tick Tock Tavern** on Magnolia Avenue, and the irreplaceable **Tower Grove Park** itself with 7,868+ Google reviews, 13 restored early-20th-century picnic pavilions, the Piper Palm House, the Tower Grove Farmers’ Market, “sip and stroll” events, and Food Truck Friday.

Roosevelt High School — the 1925 Collegiate Gothic landmark on Hartford Street, designed by district architect Rockwell M. Milligan, in the Tower Grove East neighborhood of St. Louis, Missouri. Photo: St Louis Near Me Directory.

Tower Grove East sits roughly six miles south of downtown St. Louis between South Grand Boulevard and Nebraska Avenue, where the climate follows a classic Midwest four-season pattern. Hot, humid summers with highs regularly reaching the upper 80s°F bring peak outdoor activity to Tower Grove Park’s 289 acres, the Tower Grove Farmers’ Market, Food Truck Friday, the “sip and stroll” events, the Piper Palm House, the 13 restored Victorian picnic pavilions, and the South Grand restaurant patios. Cool springs and falls are the busiest seasons for the historic four-square architectural walking tours along Shenandoah, Arsenal, and Humphrey, Carpenter Branch Library programming, the International Institute’s outdoor events, and Stray Dog Theatre productions at the Tower Grove Abbey. 

Cold winters with periodic snow and ice shift commerce indoors to the South Grand restaurant row’s Vietnamese, Thai, Ethiopian, Italian, Chinese, Middle Eastern, Japanese, Afghan, Lebanese, and Mexican restaurants, the neighborhood pubs like Riley’s Pub and Tick Tock Tavern, Botanicals Design Studio’s floral work, and the Stray Dog Theatre seasonal program. The neighborhood’s position at one of the higher residential elevations in south St. Louis gives it good drainage and slightly drier conditions than the lower corridors along Mississippi-side neighborhoods to the east. The late-19th-century pressed-brick and limestone four-square Victorian housing stock — with stained-glass windows, carved fretwork, and elaborate staircases — has weathered nearly 150 years of Missouri climate with remarkable durability, sustaining the work of historic-restoration and property-management firms like Heritage Properties.
