### Common questions

### How do I know what watch is right for me?
Think about how and when you will wear it, such as daily, for work, or special occasions, and choose a size and style that fits your wrist and wardrobe. Try several styles on in person, since comfort and proportion matter more than any single feature.

### What style of watch is most popular?

### What should I know before buying a watch?

### Neighborhoods & Zip Codes 

- Old Webster (63119): One of the city's oldest and most historic areas, featuring a charming “Main Street” vibe with local businesses, restaurants, and shops. Known for exceptional walkability and community events like the Old Webster Jazz and Blues Festival. The district originated from the 1853 Webster Stop on the Pacific Railroad and maintains its quaint character with Victorian-era architecture and tree-lined streets. 
- Old Orchard (63119): Popular business district along Big Bend Boulevard with a vibrant mix of shopping, dining, and entertainment. Features tree-lined streets, parks, and walking paths that make it highly family-friendly. Known for its “Main Street” feel with boutiques, cafes , and modern amenities blended with historic charm. 
- Webster Park (63119): Originally promoted in the 1890s as the “Queen of the Suburbs,” this affluent residential neighborhood features expansive homes on large lots with Colonial Revival and Tudor architectural styles. Home to the historic Algonquin Golf Club and close to Webster University. Known for its tree-lined streets and upscale character. 
- Tuxedo Park (63119): Historic residential district developed along the railroad with preserved architecture including the original Tuxedo Park Station (now repurposed). Features early 20th-century homes with diverse architectural styles and maintains its residential charm through historic preservation efforts. 
- Central Webster Historic District (63119): Designated historic area encompassing streets like Gore and Plant, featuring homes built from the 1860s to the 1920s. Includes architectural gems like the Helfenstein House in Italianate style, with ongoing preservation efforts ensuring new developments blend with existing historic structures.

### FAQ – Webster Groves, MO City Guide 

### Q. Is Webster Groves wealthy?

### Q. Is Webster Groves walkable? 
A.  Yes, parts of Webster Groves, Missouri are quite walkable, especially Old Webster, the historic district that grew up around an 1853 railroad stop and carries a walk score of 81. Its Main Street-style strip of shops and restaurants makes it easy to park once and explore on foot, though outlying residential areas are more car-dependent.

### Q. Where is Webster Groves, MO located? 
A.  Webster Groves, Missouri sits in St. Louis County, roughly 2 miles from Forest Park and about 5.91 square miles in size. It's a close-in suburb southwest of the city of St. Louis, known for historic districts like Old Webster, Webster Park, and Tuxedo Park, with easy access to the city's major attractions.

### Q. What is there to do in Webster Groves?

### Q. Is Webster Groves part of St. Louis city? 
A.  No, Webster Groves, Missouri is its own independent municipality in St. Louis County, separate from the city of St. Louis. ### Q. What cities are located near Webster Groves, Missouri?

### Parks & Recreation 

- Quail Ridge Park : Located just south of Wentzville, this 250-acre park features more than seven miles of natural and paved trails, a dog park, disc golf, fishing, camping, playgrounds, and a lodge that can be rented for weddings and events. It’s a favorite destination for hiking, biking, and family gatherings amid rolling hills and scenic views. 
- Progress Park & Recreation Center: A community hub offering indoor and outdoor recreation amenities, including sports fields, fitness facilities, and the Progress Park Pool, which hosts summer swim activities and events. The center supports youth programs, leagues, and community gatherings throughout the year. 
- Splash Station Aquatic Center: A seasonal water park with slides, a lazy river, and interactive water features that provide summer fun for children and families. Its variety of depths and attractions make it accessible to a wide range of ages 
- Peruque Valley Park & Fireman’s Park: Local parks offering ball fields, playgrounds, trails, and picnic areas for everyday recreation, team sports, and community events. Residents rely on these parks for youth sports, walking, and outdoor relaxation close to home. 
- Regional Access to Katy Trail & Nature Areas: While the Katy Trail does not run directly through Wentzville, nearby trailheads and conservation areas in St. Charles County offer easy access to extended biking and hiking routes along the Missouri River and through surrounding countryside. This regional connectivity appeals to outdoor enthusiasts and active families.

### FAQ – Wentzville, MO City Guide 

### Q. What is Wentzville, MO known for? 
A.  Wentzville, Missouri is known as the Crossroads of the Nation, sitting at the intersection of Interstates 70 and 64, and as home to the General Motors Wentzville Assembly Center, which employs more than 4,000 workers. It's also recognized as one of Missouri's fastest-growing cities, with new subdivisions and retail expanding along the Wentzville Parkway corridor.

### Q. Is Wentzville a good place to live? 
A.  Yes, Wentzville, Missouri is widely considered a good place to live, with a median household income around $111,000 to $112,000, a poverty rate below 5 percent, and a young, family-oriented population with a median age in the mid-30s. Strong job growth tied to General Motors and steady population growth add to its appeal.

### Q. Where is Wentzville, Missouri located? 
A.  Wentzville, Missouri sits in western St. Charles County, at the point where Interstate 70 meets Interstate 64 and US 40. That junction earned the city its Crossroads of the Nation nickname. Wentzville covers roughly 22 to 23 square miles under the 63385 zip code and marks the western edge of the St. Louis metropolitan area, west of downtown St. Louis.

### Q. How diverse is Wentzville School District? 
A.  The Wentzville R-IV School District, which serves Wentzville, Missouri, enrolls roughly 17,500 to 18,000 students and is about 77 percent White. Black students make up close to 8 percent, Hispanic or Latino students about 6 percent, students of two or more races about 6 percent, and Asian students roughly 3 percent. That makes the district somewhat more diverse than Wentzville overall.

### Q. What is there to do in Wentzville, Missouri? 
A.  Wentzville, Missouri offers Quail Ridge Park's 250 acres and seven-plus miles of trails, the seasonal Splash Station Aquatic Center, and Progress Park's sports fields and recreation center. Families can visit Big Joel's Safari for animal encounters, browse the Wentzville Flea Market, or catch live music at the Quarry Wine Garden on a weekend evening.

### Q. Is Wentzville considered St. Charles County? 
A.  Yes, Wentzville, Missouri is in St. Charles County, sitting at its western end along Interstate 70. The city shares the county with O'Fallon, St. Peters, and St. Charles itself, and it falls inside the St. Louis metropolitan area. Wentzville is not in St. Louis County or St. Louis City, which are across the Missouri River to the southeast.

### Q. Where did Chuck Berry live in Wentzville, MO? 
A.  Rock and roll pioneer Chuck Berry lived for decades at his Berry Park estate on the edge of Wentzville, Missouri, until his death in 2017. The property became closely tied to his legacy in the area, and Wentzville remains proud of the connection as part of its local history alongside its growth as a St. Charles County suburb.

### Q. What restaurants are in Wentzville, Missouri? 
A.  Wentzville, Missouri has a mix of national chains and locally owned spots covering family dining, fast-casual, pubs, pizza, and breakfast, plus destinations like the Quarry Wine Garden for food paired with live music and Playtime Arcade & Bar for food alongside arcade games and axe throwing. See the Wentzville dining guide for specific recommendations.

### Q. What are some good restaurants in Wentzville, MO? 
A.  In Wentzville, Missouri, the Quarry Wine Garden stands out for scenic outdoor seating paired with live music and food and wine pairings, while Playtime Arcade & Bar combines dining with arcade games and axe throwing for something different. Beyond those, the city's Wentzville Parkway corridor carries a steady mix of family dining, pizza, and breakfast spots.

### Q. What are the demographics of Wentzville, Missouri? 
A.  Wentzville, Missouri counted 45,282 residents in the 2020 Census and is projected past 50,000 by 2026. The population is roughly 86 percent White, 5 to 6 percent Black or African American, and about 3 percent two or more races. Median age runs 35 to 36 years, median household income sits near 111,000 dollars, and the poverty rate stays below 5 percent.

### Q. Is Wentzville the fastest growing city in Missouri? 
A.  Wentzville, Missouri is consistently ranked among the fastest-growing cities in the state, with its population climbing from about 45,282 at the 2020 Census to an estimated 50,000-plus today, an annual growth rate near 1.7 percent. Whether it holds the single fastest spot varies by year and source, but it's firmly in the state's top tier.

### Q. What are the most unique restaurants in Wentzville? 
A.  For something different in Wentzville, Missouri, the Quarry Wine Garden offers scenic outdoor seating with live music and wine and food pairings, while Playtime Arcade & Bar blends food and drinks with arcade games and axe throwing. Both stand out from the city's more typical family dining, pizza, and fast-casual chain options along Wentzville Parkway.

By Lane Forman , Founder of St Louis Near Me Directory Local restaurant guides, researched and maintained · Updated June 2026 
Part of South County — explore the whole region in our South County restaurant guide .
Affton is old-school St. Louis to the bone — Provel cheese, cracker-thin tavern-cut pizza, toasted ravioli, and gooey butter cake, mostly strung along one road. Gravois Road is the town's main course: a near-mile stretch where a 1966 bakery, a cruise-ship-trained diner cook, a barbecue joint next to a gun range, and the region's first food-truck garden all sit within a short drive of each other. This is South County food culture, unbothered by trends.
From a 60-year gooey-butter-cake institution to ribs beside a shooting range, here's where to eat in Affton.
Nearly everything lines up along Gravois Road (63123), which makes Affton a genuine walk-the-strip food crawl. Most spots run budget-friendly ($–$$), several are breakfast-and-lunch only, and a couple keep limited or seasonal hours (9 Mile Garden especially). Affton is unincorporated South County — some addresses read "St. Louis, MO 63123."

### Affton Diner
Affton Diner is the cozy 34-seat greasy-spoon run by Jonathan Aka — Turkish-born, ten years cooking on Royal Caribbean ships, now greeting customers himself. Get the Cochon (French toast layered with ham steak and Swiss) or the chopped steak with brown-mushroom gravy. Breakfast and lunch only.
📍 10020 Gravois Rd, Affton, MO 63123

### Sharpshooter Pit and Grill
Sharpshooter smokes slow brisket and pulled pork — "Bang Good BBQ" — with baby-back ribs and four house-made sauces, and yes, it sits right next to the Sharp Shooter indoor range, so you can eat ribs next door to the gun range. All sides scratch-made.
📍 8135 Gravois Rd, Affton, MO 63123

### Concord Grill
Concord Grill built its name on roughly 40 half-pound burger variations — from hot sauce and Provel to port-wine cheddar and bacon — plus daily specials. A true sit-down-with-the-regulars South County burger room that bills itself "Home of the BEST Burgers in Town."
📍 11427 Concord Village Ave, St. Louis (Affton), MO 63123

### Bar Roma
Bar Roma is the cozy family-run American grill that quietly works Greek classics into a standard breakfast menu — the namesake "Affton Special" omelet is gyro-inspired, named for the neighborhood itself, alongside biscuits and gravy.
📍 9416 Gravois Rd, Affton, MO 63123

### Affton Pizza Co.
Affton Pizza Co. does the real St. Louis thing — crispy, buttery cracker-thin crust loaded with creamy Provel, cut into the tavern squares — not a chain pretending to. Plus wings. Closed Mondays.
📍 9163 Reavis Barracks Rd, St. Louis (Affton), MO 63123

### Federhofer's Bakery
Federhofer's is the neighborhood institution — a family-run bakery at Gravois and Mathilda since 1966, turning out roughly fifteen dozen gooey butter cakes a week in five flavors. Their version uses no cream cheese and skips the powdered-sugar dusting unless you ask. The old-guard anchor.
📍 9005 Gravois Rd, Affton, MO 63123

### 9 Mile Garden
9 Mile Garden is billed as St. Louis's first food-truck garden — an open-air park where the menu literally changes by the night depending on which local trucks roll in, plus craft beer, wine, and cocktails from the on-site Canteen, live music, and a big communal patio. Something different every visit.
📍 9375 Gravois Rd, Affton, MO 63123

### Why this town matters
Affton is one of the last strongholds of classic St. Louis flavor — Provel, tavern-cut pizza, toasted rav, and gooey butter cake within a few blocks, most of it budget-friendly and family-first. The chain apps don't get the culture; they just see Gravois Road. We map the 1966 bakery and the ship-cook's diner.

### FAQ
What's the most iconic place to eat in Affton, MO?
Federhofer's Bakery — a family-run gooey-butter-cake landmark at Gravois and Mathilda since 1966 (their recipe skips the cream cheese, which locals argue makes it the real one).
Is Affton good for classic St. Louis food?
Very — within a few Gravois Road blocks you'll find Provel-topped tavern-cut pizza (Affton Pizza Co.), toasted ravioli, gooey butter cake (Federhofer's), and barbecue (Sharpshooter). It leans classic South County, not trend-chasing.
Is Affton budget-friendly and family-friendly?
Yes — most independents run $–$$, and spots like 9 Mile Garden (rotating food trucks, live music, kid- and dog-friendly) and Concord Grill (40 burgers) are built for families.
What's the food-truck garden in Affton?
9 Mile Garden on Gravois — St. Louis's first food-truck park, where the lineup of trucks rotates nightly. Hours are seasonal/limited, so check before you go.

By Lane Forman , Founder of St Louis Near Me Directory Local restaurant guides, researched and maintained · Updated June 2026 
Alton is a Mississippi River town on the Great River Road, ~20 minutes upriver from St. Louis, where limestone bluffs (painted with the legendary Piasa Bird) meet a historic downtown. It's the hometown of Robert Wadlow, the “world's tallest man,” and of abolitionist printer Elijah Lovejoy — a place thick with history, antiques, river views, and a genuinely strong independent food-and-drink scene.
From a legendary dive bar to an organic brewery in an old bakery, here's where to eat in Alton.
The independents cluster in historic downtown / Broadway , near the river and the Clark Bridge, with a couple up in Upper Alton (Fosterburg/9th St). A few are dinner-only or have shifting hours, so check first. Pair a meal with the Robert Wadlow statue , the riverfront, the bluffs, or the Thursday-evening Alton Night Market .

### Fast Eddie's Bon Air
Start at the icon. Fast Eddie's is a 1921 Prohibition-era Anheuser-Busch roadhouse turned legendary dive — absurdly cheap grilled food (shrimp, the “Big Elwood on a Stick,” burgers) funded by the volume, a huge outdoor stage, and live music. A regional destination; come for the experience as much as the food.
📍 1530 E 4th St, Alton, IL 62002

### Old Bakery Beer Company
Old Bakery Beer is a certified-organic craft brewery and scratch kitchen in a restored former bakery downtown — rotating seasonal beers, sandwiches, soups, salads, and pizza. One of only a handful of organic breweries in the country, and a Riverbend favorite.
📍 400 Landmarks Blvd, Alton, IL 62002

### My Just Desserts
My Just Desserts has been the downtown pie-and-lunch institution since 1986 — homestyle lunch, half-pound chicken-salad sandwiches, and famous homemade pies (Mrs. Ledbetter's Chocolate Pie is the one). Save room.
📍 31 E Broadway, Alton, IL 62002

### Gentelin's on Broadway
Gentelin's is Alton's premier fine-dining room (since 2006) — contemporary New American with bridge-and-river views downtown. The special-occasion pick.
📍 122 E Broadway, Alton, IL 62002

### Bluff City Grill
Bluff City Grill is the downtown American casual-dining and sports-lounge spot on Broadway near the Clark Bridge and the Alton Amphitheater — a dependable, do-it-all room.
📍 424 E Broadway, Alton, IL 62002

### Tony's Restaurant
Tony's has served steaks and Italian since 1954 — home of the “World Famous Pepperloin Steak,” 20 house pastas, and a deep wine list. A genuine Alton classic (now at its 9th Street location).
📍 102 W 9th St, Alton, IL 62002

### Castelli's Restaurant at 255
Up in Upper Alton, Castelli's has been serving Italian-American since 1937 — homemade tortellini and fettuccine, fried ravioli, and the trademarked “Talk-N-Chic.” A few miles off the riverfront, and worth it.
📍 3400 Fosterburg Rd, Alton, IL 62002

### Morrison's Irish Pub
Morrison's is the family-owned Irish-American pub at State and Broadway — comfort plates and specialty cocktails in a friendly downtown room.
📍 200 State St, Alton, IL 62002

### Germania Brew Haus
For coffee, Germania Brew Haus is the independent coffeehouse — espresso, tea, smoothies, pastries, and breakfast. (Heads-up: it recently moved to Ridge Street and is currently drive-thru-focused during construction, so check before planning to sit down.)
📍 211 Ridge St, Alton, IL 62002

### Why this little town matters
Alton is a Great River Road town where the history and the food are equally deep — a 1921 dive-bar legend, an organic brewery in an old bakery, a 1937 Italian spot, a 1954 steakhouse, and a 1986 pie shop, all under the bluffs and the Clark Bridge. The national apps reduce it to a few names; we map the riverfront that makes it worth the drive.

### FAQ
What's the most famous place to eat in Alton, IL?
Fast Eddie's Bon Air — a 1921 Prohibition-era roadhouse turned legendary dive bar with absurdly cheap grilled food, a big stage, and live music. A regional destination.

By Lane Forman , Founder of St Louis Near Me Directory Local restaurant guides, researched and maintained · Updated June 2026 
Arnold is the big front door to Jefferson County — a city of 20,000-plus stitched together in 1972 from old communities with names like Beck, Flamm City, and Maxville, near where the Meramec spills into the Mississippi. Long before the strip malls, a French-Canadian ran a Meramec River ferry here on the old St. Louis–to–Ste. Genevieve trail. Today the action runs down Jeffco Boulevard , and it's a surprisingly deep bench of locally owned spots.
From a BBQ joint run by the Imo's pizza family to a diner with a Filipino twist, here's where to eat in Arnold.
Most of the independents line Jeffco Boulevard , so you can practically eat your way down it. A couple of the newest spots opened in the last year (so confirm hours), and the coffee shop closes Sunday–Monday. Time a summer trip for Arnold Days , the city's festival since 1973, with a parade, car show, and fireworks at the city park.

### Smokee Mo's Arnold BBQ
Start with the best story in town. Smokee Mo's was founded by Frank Imo — eldest son of the Imo's Pizza founders — who trained with a four-time BBQ world champ and smokes his meats overnight. Burnt ends, pork steaks, ribs, and desserts from the Blue Owl Bakery in Kimmswick. Consistently the #1-rated restaurant in Arnold, and family-owned (not the pizza chain).
📍 606 Jeffco Blvd, Arnold, MO 63010

### Nowhere Food & Drink Co.
Nowhere is the independent bar-and-grill with award-winning wings, St. Louis-style pizza, and the "Nowhere Burger" — comfort food and late-night hours. The everybody-ends-up-here spot on Jeffco.
📍 3946 Jeffco Blvd, Arnold, MO 63010

### The Local House Restaurant & Bar
The hometown newcomer: The Local House opened in late 2024 in the former Cafe Arnold space, cooking about 85% from scratch — dressings included. Two local guys built it to be "YOUR hometown restaurant," and Arnold's embraced it.
📍 2236 Michigan Ave, Arnold, MO 63010

### Rowena's Diner
Here's the curveball — Rowena's is the family diner doing American comfort food with a Filipino twist . All-day breakfast next to genuine Filipino dishes, a distinctive combination you won't find at any chain. Small, beloved, and worth seeking out.
📍 7 Village Plz, Arnold, MO 63010

### Pink Margaritas Modern Mexican Cuisine
The newest arrival, Pink Margaritas opened in late 2025 from a husband-and-wife team — modern Mexican and the signature sparkling pink glitter margaritas . Fresh energy on Jeffco Boulevard.
📍 1424 Jeffco Blvd, Arnold, MO 63010

### Coco's Coffeehouse & Cafe
For coffee, Coco's is the independent neighborhood café (tucked inside a local salon) pulling Kaldi's espresso, plus sandwiches, bagels, smoothies, and baked goods with local honey. The genuine local coffee stop in a town where most "Arnold" coffee results are actually in the next town over. Closed Sunday–Monday.
📍 170 Richardson Xing, Arnold, MO 63010

### Twisted Tavern
Twisted Tavern does upscale-casual smash burgers and a deep bourbon list, with desserts from a local Arnold cake shop. It's part of the St. Louis Syberg's restaurant family (a sister to Twisted Tree Steakhouse) — a regional local group rather than a one-off independent, but genuinely local and a popular night out.
📍 3606 W Outer Rd, Arnold, MO 63010

### Why this little town matters
Arnold is easy to mistake for just another I-55 suburb — but down Jeffco Boulevard you'll find a world-class-trained pitmaster from the Imo's family, a diner blending American and Filipino cooking, a from-scratch hometown restaurant, and a Mexican spot pouring glitter margaritas. That's a real, growing independent scene, and the national apps bury it under chain logos.

What's the best restaurant in Arnold, MO?

Each summer at the city park — a festival running since 1973 with a parade, car show, fishing derby, and fireworks.

Restaurants near me in Augusta, MO ? Here’s where to eat in Augusta right now: Mount Pleasant Estates, Augusta Winery, and Noboleis Vineyards.
Searching Augusta food near me ? These are real, locally owned Augusta restaurants worth knowing — updated June 2026 .

By Lane Forman , Founder of St Louis Near Me Directory Local restaurant guides, researched and maintained · Updated June 2026 
Here's a fact that surprises even St. Louisans: Augusta was America's first wine region. Not Napa — Augusta. The federal government drew the very first American Viticultural Area right here in 1980, eight months before Napa got its line on the map. The German immigrants who settled these Missouri River bluffs in the 1800s knew what the rest of the country took a century to figure out: this dirt grows wine.
Today Augusta is in the middle of a big, well-funded reinvention — a Florida family has bought up most of the famous wineries and a chunk of downtown, betting on a "Midwest Napa." That's worth knowing before you go, because the marquee names you'll see are mostly under that new ownership now. But the bones are real, the views are unreal, and a couple of genuinely independent spots — a family winery, a farm-to-table restaurant, a brewery — keep the place honest. Here's where to eat and drink in Augusta.
Augusta runs on wine-country hours : most spots open late morning and close by 5 (a few push to 8 on weekends), some restaurants are weekends-only , and any of them can close for a private event — so call ahead, especially for dinner. The town sits on the Katy Trail , so it's a favorite cyclist refuel; time your trip for the Augusta Harvest Festival in September if you want the place at full tilt.

### Mount Pleasant Estates
Start where it all started. Mount Pleasant is Augusta's oldest winery, established in 1859 by the German Muench brothers, and it's billed as the historic site where America's first AVA was signed into being. The tasting room and estate sit on some of the prettiest ground in the region. (Now part of the Hoffmann family of wineries, but the 1859 history is all its own.)
📍 5634 High St, Augusta, MO 63332

### Augusta Winery
Right downtown, Augusta Winery is a boutique tasting room with a grapevine arbor and a covered terrace, pouring estate-bottled, award-winning wines with live music on weekends from spring through fall. Founded in 1988 by Tony Kooyumjian — the same vintner who founded Montelle — it's the easy, walkable heart-of-town pour.
📍 5601 High St, Augusta, MO 63332

### Noboleis Vineyards
If you want the genuinely family-owned pour, this is it. Noboleis describes itself as the only family-owned-and-operated winery in Augusta — Bob and Lou Ann Nolan bought the land in 2005 and built the whole 84-acre estate themselves. Panoramic hill views, family-friendly, and a real local story in a town full of new ownership.
📍 100 Hemsath Rd, Augusta, MO 63332

### Montelle Winery (with Klondike Café)
For the "most scenic" claim, Montelle sits up on the bluff with a view that does half the work — and its on-site Klondike Café means you can actually eat here: wood-fired pizzas, sandwiches, salads, and fresh-baked bread, plus reservation-only Sunset Dinners on summer Saturdays. Wine and a real plate, both with the valley falling away below you.
📍 201 Montelle Dr, Augusta, MO 63332

### Balducci Vineyards
Balducci pairs estate wines with vineyard-view dining — hand-tossed pizza, salads, and Italian-inspired plates carrying the original Balducci family's tradition forward. An easy spot to slow down with a bottle and a meal among the vines.
📍 6601 S Hwy 94, Augusta, MO 63332

### Root Food + Wine
Here's the destination dinner. Root Food + Wine is a boutique, hyper-seasonal restaurant in a restored 1905 home near the Katy Trail — a prix-fixe (or à la carte) menu from Chef Philip Day built around what's growing, including the on-site herb garden. A regional magazine named it the #1 best new restaurant . Weekends only, reservations strongly recommended.
📍 5525 Walnut St, Augusta, MO 63332

### Good News Brewing
Not everything here is wine. Good News Brewing pours house-brewed craft beer alongside wood-fired pizza — the brewery's main facility, with a beer-instead-of-grapes option for the group member who's had enough Norton. Limited hours (largely weekends) and occasional private events, so call before you count on it.
📍 5521 Water St, Augusta, MO 63332

### The Augusta Emporium
For the coffee-and-browse stop, The Augusta Emporium is a restored 1800s general store with a coffee shop inside — coffee, light food, wine, sundries, and gifts in a building as old as the town's wine roots. The relaxed in-between-tastings stop right downtown.
📍 5595 Walnut St, Augusta, MO 63332

### Why this little town matters
Augusta is a paradox worth understanding: the place that invented American wine country is being reinvented in real time, with big outside money behind the famous old names. The history is genuine — first AVA in the nation, 1859 winery, German bluff-country roots — and so are the holdouts, like the Nolan family at Noboleis and the chef at Root. Knowing which is which is exactly the kind of honest, on-the-ground intel the glossy travel sites won't give you.
We will. Search St Louis Near Me Directory for Augusta and St. Charles County before you go — and string it together with our New Haven guide and Warrenton guide for a full Missouri wine-country weekend.
And if you run an Augusta place — a tasting room, a café, a Katy Trail stop — a listing is how the next cyclist or carful of day-trippers finds you among the big names.

### FAQ
Is Augusta, MO really older than Napa as a wine region?
Yes — the Augusta AVA was the first American Viticultural Area ever established, designated on June 20, 1980, about eight months before Napa Valley.
Which Augusta winery is actually family-owned?
Noboleis Vineyards bills itself as the only family-owned-and-operated winery in Augusta — built by the Nolan family, who bought the land in 2005. Several of the bigger-name wineries (Mount Pleasant, Montelle, Augusta Winery, Balducci) are now under the Hoffmann family of companies.
Where can I actually eat (not just drink) in Augusta?
Root Food + Wine for a destination dinner (weekends, reservations), Montelle's Klondike Café and Balducci for winery-view pizza and plates, Good News Brewing for wood-fired pizza and craft beer, and the Augusta Emporium coffee shop for a casual bite.
What are the hours like in Augusta?
Wine-country hours — most spots open late morning and close around 5 (some to 8 on weekends), several restaurants are weekend-only, and venues sometimes close for private events. Always call ahead, especially for dinner.

### Plan your Augusta day
Taste the history at Mount Pleasant, find the family pour at Noboleis, eat wood-fired with a view at Montelle, and book ahead for dinner at Root. For more local spots across St. Charles County and the St. Louis metro, explore St Louis Near Me Directory .

Ballwin is West County suburbia — and the Manchester Road corridor that runs through it is quietly one of the most international suburban food strips in the metro. On one short drive you can eat Zacatecas-style Mexican, from-scratch Thai, Afghan-Persian-Pakistani, and Sicilian Italian. The chain apps see strip malls; locals see a mother-and-son taqueria that just doubled in size and a family Italian room named “my sister.”
From a 1994 Mexican institution to a ranch grill where you pour your own beer, here's where to eat in Ballwin.
Ballwin's independents cluster on Clayton Road and the Manchester Rd corridor (63011) — and because Manchester Rd is a city line, the same block can show as “Ballwin” or “Manchester” depending on the app (see our Manchester guide for that side). A few spots are family local groups rather than one-offs; we label those honestly.

### Mi Lupita Mexican Restaurant
The marquee. Mi Lupita is a Ballwin institution since 1994, run by mother-and-son team Lety and David Sanchez — Zacatecas-style Mexican, with tamales made fresh every Thursday. In January 2025 they finally outgrew their cramped original space and moved into the old Candicci's building, more than doubling their size and adding a patio. Get Lety's Tacos.
📍 100 Holloway Rd, Ballwin, MO 63011

### Marcella's Mia Sorella
Marcella's Mia Sorella is the casual Italian spot brothers Jamie and Steve Komorek opened in 2012 as the more relaxed sibling to their original restaurant — hence “my sister.” In-house toasted ravioli, pappardelle with chicken and prosciutto, and truffle fries the regulars rave about.
📍 14426 Clayton Rd, Ballwin, MO 63011

### 6 North Cafe
6 North Cafe is the independent, family-owned breakfast-and-lunch café with a rare sit-down-indie drive-thru — all-day breakfast, the 6 North Turkey Club, homemade chicken salad, and house-baked cookies and oatmeal bars. The easy morning stop.
📍 14438 Clayton Rd, Ballwin, MO 63011

### Circle 7 Ranch
Circle 7 Ranch is the locally owned modern bar and grill (Ballwin and Des Peres) that was the first place in Missouri to put personal table taps in — pour your own ice-cold draft right at the table. Slow-smoked brisket, burgers, and craft beer. The fun group night.
📍 14412 Clayton Rd, Ballwin, MO 63011

### Massa's
Massa's is the family-owned local Italian room (also in Ellisville) known for its toasted artichoke hearts — quartered, tempura-battered, fried, and served with house poppy-seed dressing — plus pizza, pasta, and a banquet room locals book for showers and celebrations.
📍 15310 Manchester Rd, Ballwin, MO 63011

### Lal Qila
Lal Qila is one of the rare West County spots serving Pakistani, Afghan-Persian, and Mediterranean food under one roof — goat biryani, joojeh chicken kabob, Kabuli palau, and a midday halal buffet locals rate among the best in the area.
📍 15222 Manchester Rd, Ballwin, MO 63011

### Why this town matters
Ballwin proves a West County suburb can eat like a world tour — Zacatecas Mexican, Thai, Afghan-Persian, Sicilian — most of it tucked into strip-center plazas the chain apps flatten into logos. The corridor even crosses into Manchester, so the real story is the whole Manchester Rd stretch. We map the people behind the storefronts.

Along Clayton Road and the Manchester Rd corridor — Mi Lupita, Marcella's, 6 North Cafe, Circle 7 Ranch, Massa's, and Lal Qila. Note many corridor addresses straddle the Ballwin/Manchester line.

It fields a genuinely strong cluster of locally owned independents along Highway 61/67 and Metropolitan Blvd, no national chains among the standouts: a 40-year burger-and-custard drive-in, a since-1999 breakfast-through-dinner pub, a remodeled sports-bar with a known wing sauce, a burger-and-pool-hall, and an early-bird diner. People in Barnhart eat well — these are the real spots.
From a 40-year custard window to the "Bombman Burger," here's where to eat in Barnhart.

### Ginny's Kitchen & Custards
The Barnhart institution. A 40-plus-year old-school burger-and-custard drive-in — fresh-ground-chuck burgers cooked to order, custard concretes, shakes, and homemade chili. The dining room closes at 8:30 but the walk-up custard window stays open till 9: the classic small-town summer-night move.
📍 7022 Hwy 61/67, Barnhart, MO 63012

### Holties Restaurant & Pub
The local hub, family-owned and "Serving Friends Like Family Since 1999" — the Bombman Burger is the calling card, alongside a Frisco melt, Philly cheesesteak, and BBQ wings. One of the few spots out here that opens at 7 a.m. for a real breakfast.
📍 1374 Old State Rd M, Barnhart, MO 63012

### Case & Bucks Grub & Pub
The sports-bar standout — the house Case & Bucks wing sauce is locally known, plus the Kodiak Slider and pizza. Locally owned by Jeff Fitter (the Imperial restaurateur behind Super Smokers BBQ), who remodeled it in 2022: a big interior, 12 drafts, and the latest hours in town (Fri to 1:30 a.m.).
📍 7095 Metropolitan Blvd, Barnhart, MO 63012

### Kenny's Bar & Grill
"Best Burgers in Barnhart" — and a late-night pool hall with well-kept tables, weekend live music, and a smoke-free room (kids welcome on the pool side until ~9). Comfort pub food and burgers till 1:30 a.m. most nights.
📍 7045 Hwy 61/67, Barnhart, MO 63012

### Sherwood's Classic Eats
The early-bird option — a classic American diner opening at 6 a.m. with breakfast and home-style comfort plates, a small local outfit with a sister spot in De Soto.
📍 1725 Catlin Dr, Barnhart, MO 63012

From a Beard-pedigree pitmaster to a corner brewery, here's where to eat in Belleville.

### BEAST Craft BBQ Co.
Start here. BEAST is the work of independent pitmaster David Sandusky, who came out of fine dining and now smokes brisket over white oak in the building that was Belleville's Hy-Ho Restaurant for 48 years. The barbecue — fall-apart brisket, St. Louis-style pork steak — has been compared favorably to Texas standards, and the cleaver in the logo is the one he inherited from his grandfather.
📍 20 S Belt W, Belleville, IL 62220

### The Abbey Espresso Bar & Café
The Abbey is a West End institution that's been open since 2000 — it started as a coffee shop and now roasts its own beans and runs a gourmet shared-plate dinner menu. Homemade breakfasts, soups, sandwiches, and coffee that smells like the morning it was roasted.
📍 5801 W Main St, Belleville, IL 62226

### Fletcher's Kitchen & Tap
Fletcher's has been family-owned since 2004, cooking American scratch food over a hickory-fired grill. The move is the "Fat Sam," a half-pound burger kissed by the hickory, alongside hand-cut steaks and hand-rolled pizza. They make their own dressings and sauces — you can taste the difference.
📍 6101 W Main St, Belleville, IL 62223

### Tavern on Main
Tavern on Main is the brick-lined downtown room right on historic Main Street — casual American and Italian, pizza and pasta and sandwiches, with a welcoming patio when the weather turns. The easy downtown sit-down.
📍 301 E Main St, Belleville, IL 62220

### Casa Maria Mexican Grill
Casa Maria is the family Mexican spot where the owner tends to greet you at the door and the portions are generous — puffy tacos, chorizo cheese dip, the kind of plate that fills a table. The neighborhood Mexican standby.
📍 1926 W Main St, Belleville, IL 62226

### Shoehorn Brewing
Shoehorn Brewing is the downtown microbrewery on East Main — a small Main Street taproom pouring its own beer, with food coming from a partnership with a neighboring bistro so you can eat with your pint. The local-craft corner.
📍 225 E Main St, Belleville, IL 62220

By Lane Forman , Founder of St Louis Near Me Directory Local restaurant guides, researched and maintained · Updated June 2026 
Benld is a coal town of about 1,500 with a secret: it's deeply, authentically Italian. Founded around 1903 coal mining, it was built by northern Italian, Croatian, and Lithuanian immigrants — into the 1950s you'd hear Italian dialects on the street, and the legacy survives in street signs (Saracco Drive), the Bertetti Library, and an Italian pavilion in the park. That's exactly why a town this small has a genuine Italian deli making basement-recipe salami and a #1-rated Italian restaurant. People here eat well — here are the real spots.
From fried chicken and tortellini at a 1977 deli to risotto balls at the town's pride, here's where to eat in Benld.
The independents are scattered around 2nd Street, Central Avenue, and Staunton Road (62009). A few keep small-town hours (the deli is daytime; the Italian spot runs Wed–Sun evenings), so call ahead. The only chain presence is a Casey's gas-station pizza counter. For more, Gillespie is ~2 miles south and Staunton a short drive — both with their own deep Italian roots.

### Fema Catering
Living coal-town history. "FEMA" isn't the agency — it's Fe rrari + Ma nalia, two families who started making salami in a basement in the 1970s and opened this Italian deli in 1977. Fried chicken and tortellini are the most-named plates, alongside house-made fresh salami, "saltisa," dry salami, and antipasto. Three generations deep, daily lunch specials. (Deli-and-counter, not full sit-down.)
📍 103 N 2nd St, Benld, IL 62009

### JoDanni's Amore
The town's pride — ranked Benld's #1 restaurant and a local Business of the Year, the "Amore" name itself a nod to all those Italian surnames. Risotto balls (arancini) are the standout starter, with pasta, chicken Italian entrées, and well-reviewed pizza. Carryout, delivery, and catering, too.
📍 2422 Staunton Rd, Benld, IL 62009

### Dud's Bar and Grill
The genuine small-town tavern — burgers, white cheddar cheese curds, a basket of tots, and fried Brussels sprouts, with slots, sports on the TVs, occasional live music, and a patio. A 4.8-star regulars' room (closed Mondays).
📍 413 E Central Ave, Benld, IL 62009

### Why this town matters
Benld punches way above 1,500 people because of its coal-mining Italian roots — a basement-salami deli named for two founding families, a #1 Italian restaurant, a beloved tavern. That heritage is the whole story, and it's exactly the kind of overlooked, genuinely-distinct local food nobody writes about. We do.

Why does a coal town this small have authentic Italian food?
Benld was built around 1903 coal mining by northern Italian (and Croatian and Lithuanian) immigrants — Italian dialects were spoken on the street into the 1950s, and the legacy lives on in street signs, the Bertetti Library, and an Italian pavilion. ### Geno's 140 Club
Geno's 140 Club is the oldest restaurant in town — a classic American supper club and bar-and-grill since 1942, same family gathering place for over 80 years. The Stromboli has been on the menu for 70-plus years, and the Geno's 140 Burger was voted Best Burger in Madison County. Closed Tuesdays.
📍 120 W Bethalto Blvd, Bethalto, IL 62010

### Roma's Pizza
Roma's is the family pizzeria the Pizzo family (originally from Sicily) opened February 20, 1973 — now third generation, on original recipes, and it survived an armed robbery, a burglary, and a fire that destroyed the original building. Get the pizza and the famously cheesy lasagna. Closed Mondays.
📍 121 E Bethalto Dr, Bethalto, IL 62010

### El Mezcal Mexican Restaurant
El Mezcal is the locally run sit-down Mexican spot — homemade-style tacos and burritos, margaritas, and a from-scratch sangria, with weekday lunch specials Monday through Saturday. The neighborhood go-to.

### Eagles Nest Family Restaurant
Eagles Nest is the locally owned family diner since 1999 — from-scratch breakfast (biscuits and gravy, omelets, pancakes) from 6 a.m. and home-style lunch plates. The kind of place where the morning regulars have a usual booth.
📍 117 E Bethalto Dr, Bethalto, IL 62010

### B Town Restaurant
B Town is the newer locally run home-style diner that leans hard into hometown pride — big-plate breakfast (biscuits and gravy, omelets, waffles) and rotating weekly specials, branded around "Eagle Nation" for the town's school colors.
📍 312 W Bethalto Dr, Bethalto, IL 62010

### Laux Brickhouse Grille
Laux Brickhouse Grille is the family-friendly neighborhood bar and grill — the Brickhouse Burger, wings with 13-plus sauces, hand-battered onion rings, and pizza — with a patio, a wall of game-day TVs, and a golf-simulator room for quieter dining.

Add a 1951 drive-in, a 1953 inn famous for fried chicken, and a 1988 pizza joint, and Breese turns out to be a real little food town under the Gothic spire of St. Dominic Church.
Here's where to eat (and drink a Ski) in Breese.
The independents cluster downtown around 4th Street and 2nd Street , with a couple of spots out on the edges. Excel runs weekday tours of the bottling-and-brewing operation — call ahead. A few kitchens close Mondays. Time it for the Clinton County Fair in July, or just come hungry any week.

### Excel Bottling & Brewing Co.
Start with the icon. Excel has bottled soda since 1936 — its citrus Ski in returnable glass is the local legend — and added a craft brewery in 2012 (West Coast hoppy beers and German lagers). It's a bottler-and-brewery with retail and tours, not a sit-down restaurant, so grab your Ski and your beer here, then go eat at the spots below. The most uniquely Breese stop there is.
📍 488 S Broadway, Breese, IL 62230

### Wally's Drive-In
A 1951 classic. Wally's is the old-school drive-in — the smashed-patty Wally Burger , beer-battered onion rings, fried fish sandwiches, toasted ravioli, and shakes. Cash and checks only , just like it's always been. Pure small-town nostalgia, done right.
📍 711 N 4th St, Breese, IL 62230

### Knotty Pine Inn & Motel
Knotty Pine has been a family-owned bar and restaurant since 1953 , local-famous for its pizza and fried chicken (and it rents motel rooms too). Seventy years of feeding Breese — the kind of staying power you can taste.
📍 215 N 4th St, Breese, IL 62230

### Little Augie's Pizza & Pasta
Little Augie's has been the independent pizza-and-pasta spot since 1988 — pizza, pasta, sandwiches, salads, and a full bar. The dependable Friday-night pick downtown.
📍 620 N 2nd St, Breese, IL 62230

### Olde City Cafe & Bar
Olde City Cafe & Bar is the downtown café-and-bar combo — a breakfast-and-lunch café by day, a bar with later hours into the weekend. The casual coffee-and-a-bite anchor.
📍 292 N Clinton St, Breese, IL 62230

### El Arado
For Mexican, El Arado holds down the heart of downtown — chimichangas, fajitas, margaritas, and the chips-and-salsa start, with a big local following. The reliable taco-night spot.
📍 50 N 4th St, Breese, IL 62230

### China Pearl & a steakhouse on the edge
Rounding it out: China Pearl (6 N 4th St) is the downtown independent Chinese buffet, and Popeye's Chop House (17910 St Rose Rd) is a rustic country-western steakhouse — it carries a Breese address but sits a few miles out toward St. Rose, so plan the short drive.
📍 6 N 4th St, Breese, IL 62230

### Why this little town matters
Breese is a German-Catholic farm town most St. Louisans have never visited — yet it's the home of Ski soda, the last returnable bottling line in Illinois, a 1951 drive-in, and a 1953 inn still frying chicken. That's a town that kept its own institutions alive, generation after generation, under the spire of an 1867 church. The national apps will show you a gas-station logo and miss every bit of it.

### FAQ
What is Breese, IL famous for?
Ski soda — the cult citrus soft drink bottled in returnable glass by Excel Bottling Co. since the 1960s. Excel has been a family bottler since 1936 and added a craft brewery in 2012; it offers weekday tours.
What's the oldest restaurant in Breese?
Wally's Drive-In (1951, cash only, home of the Wally Burger) and the Knotty Pine Inn (1953, known for pizza and fried chicken) are the two longtime institutions.
Where do locals get pizza in Breese?
Little Augie's (since 1988) and the Knotty Pine Inn are the go-tos.
Can you tour Excel Bottling?
Yes — Excel offers tours of its soda-bottling and brewing operation on weekdays; call ahead to confirm times.

Brentwood calls itself the "Hub of St. Louis County," and it sits right where I-64 meets Brentwood and Hanley — so it's easy to blow past on your way to a chain. Don't. Behind the Promenade big-boxes is a 1959 drive-in still making its own root beer, a 1978 hockey bar, a 30-year family Italian room, and a wave of new locally owned spots taking over old chain boxes. One heads-up: a lot of "Brentwood" restaurants on the map are actually next door in Rock Hill — these are the real 63144 ones.

### Carl's Drive-In
Carl's has been a Manchester Road institution since 1959 — a genuine surviving '50s drive-in, a row of counter stools inside, famous for griddle burgers and a house-recipe root beer made on-site from a formula acquired in 1975. The original building survived a tornado that same first year. A true St. Louis landmark.
📍 9033 Manchester Rd, Brentwood, MO 63144

### O.B. Clark's
O.B. Clark's has been family-owned since 1978 — one of the best Blues hockey bars in St. Louis, with 27 TVs, a wall of Stanley Cup history, and a legendary house pizza. The neighborhood watering hole, open late.
📍 1921 S Brentwood Blvd, Brentwood, MO 63144

### Frank Papa's Ristorante
Frank Papa's is the husband-and-wife white-tablecloth Italian room Frank and Diana Papa have run since 1994 — veal, house pastas and risotto, mussels diavolo, and a deep wine list. Thirty years in the family. Reservations by phone.
📍 2241 S Brentwood Blvd, Brentwood, MO 63144

### Maize & Wheat Colombian Café
Maize & Wheat is the family Colombian café that started selling at local festivals before opening a storefront in 2017 — arepas, corn-and-flour empanadas, caldo de costilla, fresh guanábana juice, and murals of the Colombian flag. Homestyle and unpretentious.
📍 1912 S Brentwood Blvd, Brentwood, MO 63144

### Tona's Margarita Bar
Tona's is the newest arrival — a locally owned sit-down Mexican spot and margarita bar that opened in late 2025 on the Strassner corridor, with house-made tortillas, oversized margaritas, and a big patio. The fresh face in town.
📍 1221 Strassner Dr, Brentwood, MO 63144

### Sal y Limón Mexican Grille
Sal y Limón is the local operator who filled the long-empty Houlihan's box on Strassner in late 2024 — tacos and classic Mexican grille plates, open seven days and late on weekends. Quick, fresh, and homegrown.
📍 1221 Strassner Dr, Brentwood, MO 63144

### Revel Kitchen
Revel Kitchen is the St. Louis-grown healthy spot (locally founded, a few metro locations) — build-your-own grain bowls, plant-based sauces, smoothies, and fresh-pressed juices, with staff who actually know the dietary ropes. The feel-good option.
📍 8388 Musick Memorial Dr, Brentwood, MO 63144

### El Morelia Supermercado
The hidden gem. El Morelia is a Mexican grocery whose in-house taquería gets ranked the best Mexican in the St. Louis area — over the famous Cherokee Street markets. Tacos al pastor, quesabirria, chilaquiles, fresh tortillas, horchata. It started as a weekend taco stand at the front door and grew into a daily taquería with a big seating area.
📍 11982 Paul Mayer Ave, Bridgeton, MO 63044

### Esther's Persian Cafe
Esther's is owner Reza Toghiyany's flame-grilled Persian kabob house — beef koobideh, filet soltani, fesenjan (chicken in walnut and pomegranate) — all cooked fresh. As Reza puts it: "It's not fast food. I'm cooking it fresh." Named for his daughter.
📍 12466 St Charles Rock Rd, Bridgeton, MO 63044

### Massa's (The Old Place)
Massa's at 4120 N Lindbergh is what the family calls "The Old Place" — the original anchor of their small St. Louis group. St. Louis-style thin-crust pizza with the provolone blend, toasted ravioli, the Filet Pepe, Cajun pasta. A true St. Louis Italian-American room.
📍 4120 N Lindbergh Blvd, Bridgeton, MO 63044

### China House
China House is the neighborhood Chinese carryout where the portions are huge and a four-piece wing order means four full-size wings — orders out the door in 10 to 15 minutes. The reliable value pick.
📍 11247 Saint Charles Rock Rd, Bridgeton, MO 63044

### El Maguey (Bridgeton)
El Maguey is a St. Louis regional Mexican chain — not a one-off independent, but locally grown — with chimichangas and combo plates served on piping-hot plates, open daily till 10. A dependable sit-down option in the corridor when you want a sure thing.
📍 12460 Natural Bridge Rd, Bridgeton, MO 63044

Brooklyn, Illinois — also called Lovejoy — is a village of about 600 people, and it carries something no chain directory will tell you: it's the oldest town in America incorporated by African Americans. Founded by free and freed families who crossed the Mississippi to build a "Freedom Village" around 1830, incorporated in 1873, its streets sit atop genuine Underground Railroad history. ### Bottoms Up
The safest genuine pick — a neighborhood corner sports bar with a real working kitchen: chicken, fried fish, hot dogs, soup, at friendly prices. A genuinely good late-night Cajun-and-Creole spot — crab-leg feasts a reviewer rated "top tier," seafood boils, and a famous jerk "rasta" pasta. Hours run Wed–Sun into the early morning, so it operates within Brooklyn's late-night scene; come for the seafood, and call to confirm.
📍 213 Madison St, Brooklyn, IL 62059

### Mill's Place
A real-deal soul-food kitchen on Illinois Route 3 — big plate-lunches "with a side of love" and twice-monthly Soul Food Sundays. (Exact street number isn't published publicly, so call before you go.)
📍 Illinois Route 3, Brooklyn, IL 62059

### Why this town matters
Brooklyn's dining is thin, but its story is towering — the first town in the country incorporated by African Americans, named Lovejoy for the abolitionist martyred in nearby Alton, with Underground Railroad roots literally beneath its streets. Why is Brooklyn, IL historically important?
It's the oldest town in the United States incorporated by African Americans — founded by free and freed families (by tradition led by "Mother" Priscilla Baltimore) who crossed the Mississippi around 1830 to build a Freedom Village, and incorporated in 1873. ### Gokul Indian Restaurant (Delmar Loop)
A one-of-a-kind — 100% vegetarian North Indian and the only fully kosher restaurant in St. Louis, with an all-you-can-eat buffet (and a 100% vegan buffet every Monday night). Closed Tuesdays.

### Africana (Delmar Loop)
West and East African fusion with a cultural lounge — the jollof rice arrives as a sculpted, smoky mound (tomato, peppers, Scotch bonnet, ginger, thyme) with chicken, goat, catfish, and more. A 2026 St. Louis Magazine review praised its "smoky redolence." Closed Mon–Tue.
📍 5860 Delmar Blvd, St. Louis, MO 63112

### Mom's Soul Food Kitchen (The Ville)
Classic Southern soul food east of Cabanne Place — fried chicken, oxtails, and the standard sides done right.
📍 2601 Whittier St, St. Louis, MO 63113

Caseyville started life as "Casey's Station" — a coal-and-railroad town built in 1849 to move coal out of the Metro East bluffs, named for a state politician named Zadok Casey. The mines are long gone, the village settled into about 4,400 people at the foot of the Mississippi bluffs, fifteen minutes from downtown St. Louis. It's a small town, and it eats like one — in the best way: taverns, a great family taqueria, a weekend donut window.
Nobody's going to call Caseyville a dining destination, and we won't pretend otherwise. But the mom-and-pop spots that are here are the real thing. Here's where to eat in Caseyville.
Caseyville's scene is tavern-and-bar-grill heavy — that's the honest shape of the town — with one standout sit-down restaurant and a weekend-only donut shop. ### Tres Caminos Mexican Restaurant

### Bob & Carol's Bridge Inn

Chesterfield is West County money — and a flat floodplain called Chesterfield Valley that went from cornfields to one of the densest restaurant rows in the metro. Yes, the chains are everywhere out here. But behind the strip-mall facades hides some of the most serious independent Italian in St. Louis, run by Sicilian families cooking from memory, plus a country-fine-dining legend next to a 1937 butcher shop.
From a Beard-name destination to a Sicilian mother-and-son kitchen, here's where to eat in Chesterfield.
The dining engine is Chesterfield Valley (Chesterfield Airport Rd and Long Rd, 63005), with more along Olive and Woods Mill in 63017. Several of the best are dinner-only and closed Mondays, so check first. And don't let the strip-mall storefronts fool you — the Italian back here is the real thing.

### Annie Gunn's
The marquee. Annie Gunn's is upscale country-American fine dining beside the Smoke House Market — a working butcher and gourmet shop that's held the same ground since 1937, back when it stood alone in the cornfields. Chef Lou Rook III has run the kitchen for decades; get the smoked shrimp and the famous house chili.
📍 16806 Chesterfield Airport Rd, Chesterfield, MO 63005

### Paul Manno's Cafe
Paul Manno's is the neighborhood institution locals call Chesterfield's best-kept secret — upscale traditional Italian, dinner only, tucked into a strip-mall storefront. The rack of lamb is the celebrated plate; finish with the homemade tiramisu.
📍 75 Forum Shopping Center, Chesterfield, MO 63017

### GIO Modern Italian
GIO is the husband-and-wife modern Sicilian spot from Gio and Jess LaFata — house-made pastas, arancini, whiskey shrimp, and real Sicilian-style pizza. Voted Best Italian in West County in 2025, with a weekend brunch.
📍 138 Chesterfield Towne Center, Chesterfield, MO 63005

### Buzzetta's Italian Cafe
Buzzetta's is the mother-and-son team — Lia and Tony Buzzetta — cooking the fresh-daily, never-frozen style of Palermo. The Sicilian Chicken is a perennial 10/10, and the lemon tiramisu is made with real limoncello. Authentic Italian, no shortcuts.
📍 120 Chesterfield Valley Drive, Chesterfield, MO 63005

### EdgeWild Restaurant & Winery
EdgeWild is a locally owned restaurant and winery under one roof — pair a wood-fired pizza with a flight of their own house wines and seasonal, regionally sourced plates. The easy-going date spot.
📍 550 Chesterfield Center, Chesterfield, MO 63017

### Firefly Grill
Firefly Grill is owned and run by Christy Hall — a true single-location, owner-operated American spot. The Firefly Smash Burger with caramelized shallots and the creamy Cajun pasta keep the regulars coming. Casual and dependable.
📍 101 Chesterfield Towne Center, Chesterfield, MO 63005

### Spiro's Restaurant
Spiro's has served Greek and Mediterranean classics since 1975 — the kind of family place where the owner still walks the room table to table. Get the fall-off-the-bone lamb shank and a Greek salad with the house dressing.
📍 1054 N Woods Mill Rd, Chesterfield, MO 63017

### YaYa's Euro Bistro
YaYa's is a small St. Louis-based independent (not a national chain) known for oak-fired pizzas, beef tenderloin, and a chocolate soufflé — with a patio that draws a weekend crowd and full daily hours. The dressy-but-easy Mediterranean option.
📍 15601 Olive Blvd, Chesterfield, MO 63017

Clayton is the St. Louis County seat — a square mile of office towers and tree-lined blocks that runs on power lunches by day and turns into the metro's best date-night cluster after five. Two of these kitchens carry James Beard and Michelin pedigrees, and they're a short walk from each other. This is fine dining and serious Italian, mostly independent, mostly within a few blocks of Forsyth and Maryland.
From a Beard winner's pasta counter to a French bistro with three-star roots, here's where to eat in Clayton.
Everything below sits in walkable downtown Clayton (63105), clustered on Forsyth, Maryland, and Wydown. Several of the best are dinner-only or closed Sundays/Mondays — check first. Good news on parking: Shaw Park and the Center of Clayton are free, street meters run only weekdays 8–5, so evenings and weekends much of downtown parks free.

### Pastaria
Pastaria is the casual flagship of James Beard Award-winning chef Gerard Craft — handmade pastas, wood-fired Neapolitan pizzas, and daily gelato. There's even a retail counter selling fresh pasta and gelato to take home. The accessible side of greatness.
📍 7734 Forsyth Blvd, Clayton, MO 63105

### Bistro La Floraison
Bistro La Floraison is the French bistro from a team that trained in Michelin-starred rooms — including three-star Quince in San Francisco. Cassoulet, olive-oil-poached salmon, house bread to start and Basque cheesecake to finish. The most awarded room in the district.
📍 7637 Wydown Blvd, Clayton, MO 63105

### The Crossing
The Crossing is chef Jim Fiala's farm-to-table fine-dining anchor, open since 1998 — a four-course tasting menu, house-made pasta, and a warm chocolate torte on every menu. The elder statesman of Clayton dining.
📍 7823 Forsyth Blvd, Clayton, MO 63105

### Café Napoli
Café Napoli has held the same Forsyth corner since 1989, where owner Tony Pietoso still works the room and remembers regulars by name. Regional Italian, dinner only, with a bread-and-tapenade service that's a calling card. Old-school hospitality.
📍 7754 Forsyth Blvd, Clayton, MO 63105

### Dominic's Trattoria
Dominic's Trattoria has been family-owned since 1997, tucked into the ground floor of a Clayton condo building — an unassuming address hiding one of the city's most beloved chicken parmesans. The comfortable Italian standby.
📍 200 S Brentwood Blvd, Clayton, MO 63105

### Herbie's
Herbie's is the modern reincarnation of the legendary Herbie's Vintage '72 — New American cooking with French-bistro technique, handsome rooms and patios that flip from power-lunch to candlelight. Open seven days, which is rare here.
📍 8100 Maryland Ave, Clayton, MO 63105

### Ivy
Ivy is the café and small-plates spot built on house-baked sourdough — nearly every tartine starts on bread pulled from the oven that morning, alongside seasonal plates and specialty cocktails. The bright daytime-into-evening pick.
📍 14 N Meramec Ave, Clayton, MO 63105

### Half & Half
Half & Half is chef Mike Randolph's chef-driven brunch spot paired with a serious coffee program — the Clara Cakes pancakes with raspberry jam and mascarpone are the line-out-the-door order on Saturdays. Daytime only.
📍 8135 Maryland Ave, Clayton, MO 63105

Clayton packs Beard- and Michelin-pedigree kitchens into one walkable square mile — power lunches that become date nights, French bistros next to family Italian rooms open since the '80s. Bistro La Floraison, The Crossing, and Café Napoli — all dinner-focused, all within a short walk downtown.

Clifton Heights is one of St. Louis's quiet charmers — a tiny half-square-mile neighborhood of curving, hilly streets and early-1900s homes wrapped around a little lake-and-park, bounded by I-44, Hampton Avenue, and Arsenal Street. There's no restaurant strip inside it; the magic is that you barely have to leave the lines to eat well. Step across Hampton or up toward the Hill and Southwest Garden and you're in great hands. People here get hungry too — here are the closest spots.
From a Best-Gyro-in-STL to toasted ravioli that wins awards, here's where to eat near Clifton Heights.
Clifton Heights itself (4th Ward, ~63139) is residential — homes and Clifton Heights Park (a 4.4-acre green space with a lake). The eating is a short walk or drive across Hampton Avenue or up into the Hill and Southwest Garden . A couple of spots are at the very edge of the neighborhood line (noted below); call ahead for hours.

### Ari's Restaurant & Bar (Hampton edge)
Right across Hampton on the neighborhood's eastern edge — Greek-American with a gyro named Best Gyro by the Riverfront Times (fresh pita, big tomato, house tzatziki), plus a rare Sunday-morning Greek breakfast from 8 a.m.

### Southwest Diner (Southwest Garden)
A beloved Southwestern breakfast-and-lunch spot since 2012 — buttermilk-cornmeal pancakes, scratch biscuits and gravy, and New Mexican red-and-green-chile huevos rancheros. Closed Tuesdays.

### Joey B's on the Hill (Hampton / Hill edge)
The everyday family option on Hampton — locally owned, with pastas, steaks, late-night weekend pizza, and lunch and happy-hour specials.
📍 2524 Hampton Ave, St. Louis, MO 63139

By Lane Forman , Founder of St Louis Near Me Directory Local restaurant guides, researched and maintained · Updated June 2026 
Collinsville is the Metro East town that grows about 60% of the world's horseradish — yes, really, it's the self-declared Horseradish Capital of the World — with an Italian-immigrant heritage to match (the Italian Fest has run since 1983). It's also home to two landmarks you've definitely seen: the world's largest catsup bottle (a 170-foot Route 66 water tower) and Cahokia Mounds , the UNESCO World Heritage site that was the largest city in pre-Columbian North America.
A town with that much character eats well. Here's where to go in Collinsville.
The independents cluster in Uptown / downtown along Main Street , with a couple out near the I-55/70 plaza. A few close a day midweek (Mungo's is dinner-only, closed Mondays; Carisilo's closed Wednesdays), so check first. Time it for the International Horseradish Festival in early June or Italian Fest in September — both genuine Collinsville institutions.

### Old Herald Brewery & Distillery
Start with the showpiece. Old Herald is a brewery and craft distillery and restaurant inside the former Collinsville Herald newspaper building — exposed-brick adaptive reuse, a pet-friendly patio, and a “Cold Herald” ice creamery. The anchor of the Uptown drinks scene.
📍 115 E Clay St, Collinsville, IL 62234

### Kruta Bakery
A century-old institution: Kruta Bakery was founded in 1919 , moved to Collinsville in 1974, and is now run by the third and fourth generations — gooey butter, peanut cake, stollen, and rye breads. A genuine living landmark.
📍 300 St Louis Rd, Collinsville, IL 62234

### Mungo's Italian Eatery
Mungo's is the Italian spot with a heart — owner Tony Mazzola named it for his late friend and mentor, Charlie “Mungo” Mugavero. Dinner-only, closed Mondays, and a real reflection of the town's Italian roots.
📍 100 E Main St, Collinsville, IL 62234

### Ravanelli's Italian Steakhouse & Wine Bar
Ravanelli's has been “comfort food since 1964” — family-owned Italian and steakhouse with huge portions and famous broasted chicken. The big-occasion, leave-full classic.
📍 26 Collinsport Dr, Collinsville, IL 62234

### Bert's Chuckwagon
Don't let the name fool you — Bert's Chuckwagon is a beloved Tex-Mex institution, a Collinsville fixture since 1963 , known for its tacos, chimichangas, and hand-breaded onion rings. (It's Tex-Mex, not BBQ.) Pure local nostalgia.
📍 101 E Main St, Collinsville, IL 62234

### Porter's Steakhouse
For the upscale night, Porter's is the independent steakhouse near the I-55/70 plaza — hand-cut steaks and chops, seafood flown in daily, and a 200-plus-bottle wine list. The dress-it-up option.
📍 1000 Eastport Plaza Dr, Collinsville, IL 62234

### Verona Coffee Company
Verona Coffee is the independent downtown coffee house (since 2017) — espresso, hand-brews, pastries, and a little brunch, giving Uptown its own morning anchor.
📍 101 E Main St, Collinsville, IL 62234

### Carisilo's Mexican Restaurant
Carisilo's is the family-owned authentic Mexican spot with the longest track record of the local taquerias — the dependable fajitas-and-margaritas pick. Closed Wednesdays.
📍 1978 Vandalia St, Collinsville, IL 62234

### Heritage Sports Bar & Grill
The newcomer: Heritage opened in 2025 in a restored historic Main Street building (exposed brick) — kabobs, brats, a covered patio, and a game-day room. Fresh energy in Uptown.
📍 118 E Main St, Collinsville, IL 62234

### Why this little town matters
Collinsville is a town with genuine identity — horseradish capital, Italian-fest heritage, the world's biggest catsup bottle, and an ancient UNESCO city in its backyard — and the food lives up to it: a brewery-distillery in an old newspaper building, a 1919 bakery, a 1964 Italian steakhouse, a 1963 Tex-Mex landmark, and a new sports bar in a restored brick storefront. The national apps can't capture any of that; they just list logos by the interstate.

### FAQ
What's Collinsville, IL famous for?
It's the “Horseradish Capital of the World” (about 60% of the global supply grows here, celebrated at the June Horseradish Festival), home of the world's largest catsup bottle water tower, and next to Cahokia Mounds, a UNESCO World Heritage site.
What's the oldest restaurant in Collinsville?
Bert's Chuckwagon (Tex-Mex, since 1963) and Ravanelli's (Italian steakhouse, since 1964) are the longtime institutions, and Kruta Bakery dates to 1919.
Does Collinsville have a brewery?
Yes — Old Herald Brewery & Distillery, a combined brewery, craft distillery, and restaurant inside the former Collinsville Herald newspaper building Uptown.
Is Bert's Chuckwagon a BBQ place?
No — despite the name, Bert's is a beloved Tex-Mex spot (tacos, chimichangas, hand-breaded onion rings), a Collinsville fixture since 1963.

By Lane Forman , Founder of St Louis Near Me Directory Local restaurant guides, researched and maintained · Updated June 2026 
Columbia is a growing Metro East town on the Illinois bluffs, about twelve minutes south of downtown St. Louis — platted in 1820, settled hard by German immigrants in the mid-1800s, and still wearing that heritage on its menus. It sits on a plateau between the Mississippi bottoms and bluffs rising to 700 feet, which is exactly why the area's best sunset-and-a-glass spot is here.
From a German pub to a farm-to-bottle distillery to a café in a former church, here's where to eat in Columbia.
The independents cluster downtown on Main Street , with the distillery and the bluff-top bar a short drive out. A few spots close a day or two midweek, so check first. Time a fall trip for FestiFall at Metter Park — German potato pancakes and all.

### Tiny's Pub & Grill
Start with the heritage pick. Tiny's has been a Columbia bar-and-grill since 1975 , and it's leaned hard into the town's German roots — Sauerbraten, Jägerschnitzel, sausages, Currywurst, ten biers on tap, plus American fare and a Main Street patio. A multi-generation community staple.
📍 602 N Main St, Columbia, IL 62236

### Stumpy's Spirits Distillery
The signature landmark. Stumpy's is a true farm-to-bottle craft distillery on an eighth-generation family farm — award-winning bourbon, vodka, and whiskey made from grain grown on-site and limestone-well water, with guided tours and a tasting room. One of the few genuine farm-distilleries in the country.
📍 1727 Centerville Rd, Columbia, IL 62236

### Sunset Overlook
Sunset Overlook is the wine, craft-beer, and cocktail bar in an 1850s farmhouse on Bluff Road — small plates (flatbreads, warm pretzels, charcuterie, gourmet grilled cheese), live music, and the best sunset view in the area, just minutes from the city. Kid- and dog-friendly outdoors.
📍 11604 Bluff Rd, Columbia, IL 62236

### Cafe on the Abbey
The most distinctive room in town: Cafe on the Abbey serves coffee and all-day breakfast and lunch inside a former Catholic church and convent — specialty drinks, from-scratch desserts, and Keto options under the old bones of the building. Worth it for the setting alone.
📍 322 S Main St, Columbia, IL 62236

### Washy's Pub
Washy's is the hometown bar-and-grill (since 2019) — handmade, charbroiled-to-order burgers, fried chicken, wings, and grilled cod, breakfast through dinner daily. The friendly everyday spot on Main.
📍 210 S Main St, Columbia, IL 62236

### Miller's on Main
Miller's on Main is the American restaurant with a genuine Columbia lineage — formerly Reifschneider's, rebranded with the same menu — doing burgers, pizza, pasta, steaks, hand-cut filet, and Cajun shrimp pasta. The reliable sit-down dinner.
📍 608 N Main St, Columbia, IL 62236

### Marie's Ice Cream Shoppe
For the sweet finish, Marie's is the local ice cream shop — the classic small-town scoop to cap a Columbia visit.
📍 1220 Columbia Centre, Columbia, IL 62236

### A local pizza name to know
For pizza, Joe Boccardi's (117 S Main St) has anchored downtown since 1992 — hand-rolled St. Louis-style pizza and toasted ravioli. It's part of a small, family-owned St. Louis-area group (four locations), so a local favorite rather than a one-off independent.

### Why this little town matters
Columbia is a German-rooted bluff town the apps treat as a commuter exit — but it keeps a 1975 German pub, a farm-to-bottle distillery, a bluff-top sunset bar in an 1850s farmhouse, and a café in a former church. That's a real, distinctive food scene built on genuine local history, and it deserves more than a list of chain logos.

Sunset Overlook on Bluff Road — a wine, beer, and cocktail bar in an 1850s farmhouse with small plates, live music, and the best sunset view in the area, minutes from St. Louis.

Yes — Stumpy's Spirits, a farm-to-bottle craft distillery on an eighth-generation family farm, with award-winning bourbon and guided tours (reserve ahead).

By Lane Forman , Founder of St Louis Near Me Directory Local restaurant guides, researched and maintained · Updated June 2026 
Cottleville is the rare St. Charles County town that kept its old bones. Back when Boone's Lick Road — the trail Daniel Boone's sons cut west — crossed Dardenne Creek right here, travelers kept getting stranded in the mud and ending up in town for the night. Two hundred years later, people still come to Cottleville to linger, except now it's for a walkable little strip of Highway N where nearly every door is an independent restaurant, brewery, coffee roaster, or wine garden.
This is one of the best pure food-and-drink strolls in the metro — and the local-ownership stories run deep, right down to a BBQ joint named for the year Captain Cottle got his land grant. Here's where to eat in Old Town Cottleville.
Most of these sit shoulder-to-shoulder on Highway N in Old Town, so park once and wander. A few keep their own rhythm (the coffee roaster is mornings; some kitchens close Mondays), so glance at hours first. Come on a Twilight Tuesday in summer and the amphitheater concerts plus food trucks turn the whole town into a block party.

### Plank Road Pizza
Start with the cornerstone. Plank Road Pizza does from-scratch craft pies and gets called the best pizza in St. Charles for a reason. It's owned by local operator Andrew Brewer — who also runs the cookie shop and the BBQ joint next door — making this stretch of Old Town a genuine one-family labor of love.
📍 5212 Highway N, Cottleville, MO 63304

### 1798 BBQ
Right next door, 1798 BBQ slow-smokes pulled pork, ribs, and brisket — and the name is pure Cottleville: 1798 is the year Captain Warren Cottle received his Spanish land grant on this ground. History you can eat, from the same owner as Plank Road.
📍 5210 Highway N, Cottleville, MO 63304

### Exit 6 Pub & Brewery
Exit 6 was St. Charles County's first nano-brewery — five house beers, a couple dozen taps, no kitchen (bring or order your own food), and a cheeky streak that once made it briefly internet-famous. A true beer-first neighborhood taproom.
📍 5055 Highway N, Ste 113, Cottleville, MO 63304

### The Rack House Kitchen Wine Whiskey
For the upscale night, The Rack House does from-scratch modern American plus weekend brunch — and a wine-and-whiskey list so deep it's been named one of America's Top Whisky Bars by Whisky Advocate. The dress-it-up option without leaving Old Town.
📍 5065 State Hwy N, Cottleville, MO 63304

### Bemo's Grill
Bemo's Grill is the locally owned, all-things-to-everyone neighborhood favorite — burgers, sandwiches, steaks, pasta, seafood — with a near-perfect local reputation across thousands of reviews. The reliable family pick on the strip.
📍 5373 Highway N, Cottleville, MO 63304

### Upshot Coffee
Upshot Coffee is the independent specialty roaster and café — espresso, cold brew, matcha, baked goods, even bone broth, plus a mural by a local artist on the wall. The morning anchor of Old Town, and the S'mores Croffle is the indulgence to split.
📍 5326 Highway N, Cottleville, MO 63304

### Cottleville Wine Seller
Cottleville Wine Seller is the Old Town wine shop, wine garden, and live-music spot rolled into one — 200-plus labels, an outdoor garden, and bands on weekends. The easy, lingering middle of a Cottleville afternoon.
📍 Old Town Cottleville (Highway N), Cottleville, MO 63304

### Cottle Village Farmstead + Distillery
On the eastern edge of town, Cottle Village is the ambitious new destination — a restaurant (The Tavern), a distillery, and an outdoor venue across a few acres, built by a St. Louis hospitality couple who moved to Cottleville and made it an homage to the area's farmstead past. Kentucky-bourbon-country energy, twenty minutes from the airport.
📍 6470 Highway N, Cottleville, MO 63304

### Why this little town matters
Cottleville proves a small town doesn't have to trade its history for a strip mall. The same Boone's Lick crossing that stranded travelers two centuries ago now anchors a walkable Old Town where a single local family runs the pizza-cookies-BBQ corner, the county's first nano-brewery pours next to a top-rated whisky bar, and a returning hometown couple just built a distillery as a love letter to the place. The national apps will sell you the nearest chain; they'll never tell you that story.
We will. Search St Louis Near Me Directory for Cottleville and St. Charles County before you go — and our Augusta guide is the natural next stop deeper into Missouri wine country.
And if you run a Cottleville spot — a café, a tasting room, a food truck — a listing is how the next carful wandering Old Town finds you .

### FAQ
What's the best area to eat in Cottleville?
Old Town Cottleville along Highway N — a walkable strip with pizza, BBQ, a brewery, a top whisky bar, a coffee roaster, and a wine garden, mostly within a couple of blocks.
What's the story behind 1798 BBQ's name?
1798 is the year Captain Warren Cottle received his Spanish land grant on the land that became Cottleville — the BBQ joint (same owner as next-door Plank Road Pizza) named itself after the town's founding year.
Does Cottleville have a brewery or distillery?
Both — Exit 6 Pub & Brewery (St. Charles County's first nano-brewery) in Old Town, and Cottle Village Farmstead + Distillery on the town's eastern edge.
When is the best time to visit Cottleville?
Summer Twilight Tuesdays bring amphitheater concerts and food trucks to Legacy Park — a great night to pair with an Old Town dinner.

### Plan your Cottleville day
Coffee at Upshot, BBQ at 1798, a flight at Exit 6, and live music in the Wine Seller garden. For more local spots across St. Charles County and the St. Louis metro, explore St Louis Near Me Directory .
