By Lane Forman , Founder of St Louis Near Me Directory Local restaurant guides, researched and maintained · Updated June 2026 
Granite City was built on purpose — German-immigrant brothers Frederick and William Niedringhaus founded it in 1896 as a planned steel company town, named for the speckled "granite ware" kitchenware William patented and stamped out here. The mill still defines the place, and the food matches: honest, working-class, and proud, strung mostly along the Nameoki Strip with the 74-acre Wilson Park (and the region's second-biggest Fourth of July fireworks) at its heart.
This is genuine steel-town eating — a Route 66 diner, a 1951 bakery, a saloon since Prohibition, and a Southern kitchen. Here's where to eat in Granite City.
Most of these sit along Nameoki Road and the nearby downtown grid. (Heads-up: Granite City shares ZIP 62040 with Pontoon Beach and Mitchell, so map apps blur them — these are Granite City spots; for the Pontoon Beach side, see that guide.) A couple keep limited hours, so check first. Pair a visit with Wilson Park or the historic Old Chain of Rocks Bridge nearby.

### Teri's Route 66 Diner
Start with the classic. Teri's Route 66 Diner is the retro, jukebox-and-chrome diner doing all-day breakfast, a bourbon burger, homemade tacos, pork tenderloin, and Philly cheesesteaks. A genuine local favorite and a great Route 66-themed stop downtown.
📍 1416 20th St, Granite City, IL 62040

### Duke Bakery
A true institution: Duke Bakery has been family-owned since 1951 — daily donuts, custom cakes, breads, and the signature "Yum Yum," a Duke original. It's celebrating its 75th anniversary, and it's the sweet heart of the Nameoki Strip.
📍 3202 Nameoki Rd, Granite City, IL 62040

### Jacobsmeyer's Tavern
Jacobsmeyer's is the historic Granite City saloon — established 1933 , the year Prohibition ended — revitalized with a smokehouse menu (the Meat Eater pizza, a Steak House burger, blackened salmon). The genuine old steel-town bar, still going strong.
📍 2401 Edwards St, Granite City, IL 62040

### Buoy's Southern Kitchen & More
Buoy's is the family-owned Southern comfort-and-seafood spot near Wilson Park — catfish nuggets, honey-glazed wings, and homestyle plates. Soul-warming cooking from a genuine local kitchen.
📍 3361 Fehling Rd, Granite City, IL 62040

### Big Meechie's
Big Meechie's is the Black-owned kitchen, caterer, and food-truck operation on the Nameoki Strip — wings, burgers, house sauces, and soul-food leanings. Hours vary, so check the Facebook, but the food's worth the timing.
📍 2918 Nameoki Rd, Granite City, IL 62040

### Meme's Coffee Shop
For coffee, Meme's is the local independent pouring Blueprint Coffee (a respected St. Louis roaster) from a drive-thru with indoor seating, plus breakfast items. The homegrown alternative to the chains.
📍 1529 Johnson Rd, Granite City, IL 62040

### Why this little town matters
Granite City is a planned steel town with a working-class soul, and its food tells that story straight — a 1951 bakery, a saloon from the year Prohibition ended, a Route 66 diner, a Black-owned soul kitchen, an independent coffee shop pouring local beans. ### FAQ
What's the oldest place to eat in Granite City, IL?
Duke Bakery, family-owned since 1951 (celebrating its 75th anniversary, home of the "Yum Yum"), and Jacobsmeyer's Tavern, a saloon established in 1933.
Where's a good Route 66 diner in Granite City?
Teri's Route 66 Diner on 20th Street — a retro, jukebox diner with all-day breakfast and a bourbon burger.
Is Granite City the same as Pontoon Beach?
No — they're separate towns that share ZIP 62040, so listings blur them. This guide covers Granite City spots; Pontoon Beach has its own where-to-eat guide.
What's the name "Granite City" about?
The town was founded in 1896 around a steel works that stamped out speckled "granite ware" kitchen utensils — the cookware gave the company town its name.

By Lane Forman , Founder of St Louis Near Me Directory Local restaurant guides, researched and maintained · Updated June 2026 
Let's be honest about Hamel: it's tiny. About 900 people, a crossroads village north of Edwardsville where Historic Route 66 crosses Illinois 140. You will not find a dozen restaurants here. What you'll find is something better — a couple of genuine Route 66 survivors with real history in their walls, the kind of unglamorous, decades-deep roadside cooking that the Mother Road was actually made of.
This isn't a long list, and we won't pad it with spots that are really in Edwardsville. It's three honest stops and one of the most moving little Route 66 landmarks in Illinois. If you're driving the old road — or just want a burger with a backstory — here's where to eat in Hamel.
Hamel sits right where Old Route 66 meets I-55 and IL-140, so it's an easy pull-off from the interstate. The two main spots keep roadside hours (the ice cream stand can run shorter in winter), so a quick check before a cold-weather trip is wise. And whatever you do, drive past St. Paul Lutheran Church just north of town to see the landmark below — it's the real reason road-trippers slow down here.

### Weezy's (Route 66 Bar & Grill)
This is the anchor. The building opened in 1937 as "Tourist Haven" and over the decades wore other names — Village Inn, Earnie's Roadhouse, Scotty's — and you can still see those old signs and black-and-white photos on the walls. Today it's Weezy's , a checkered-floor, red-vinyl-booth roadhouse doing charbroiled burgers, fried chicken with real mashed potatoes and gravy, hearty breakfasts (the biscuits and gravy use fresh sausage from locally raised hogs), and homemade pie. A designated Route 66 Scenic Byway stop, and a genuine one.
📍 108 S Old US Route 66, Hamel, IL 62046

### Route 66 Creamery
A few doors down, Route 66 Creamery lives inside Hamel's former train depot, built in 1906 — now a burger-and-ice-cream stand on the Mother Road. Smash steak burgers, chili, cheese dogs, onion rings, and loaded nachos on the savory side; soft-serve, hard-dip, concretes, malts, and floats on the sweet. There's a covered patio with hanging porch swings to watch the cars roll by, and the owner says international road-trippers — England to California, Chicago to Santa Monica — call ahead to make sure they catch it. Dog-friendly.
📍 11 S Old US Route 66, Hamel, IL 62046

### DK's Market
Not a restaurant, but worth knowing: DK's Market is Hamel's locally owned hometown grocery and meat market, run by four local couples since 2007 — a real fresh-cut meat department, a full deli and bakery, "DK's fried chicken," and BBQ Thursdays . It's the spot to grab fried chicken or a deli lunch to take down the road. Frame it for what it is: a great local market with a serious deli, not a sit-down meal.
📍 225 W State St, Hamel, IL 62046

### The landmark: the Route 66 "Neon Cross"
Just north of town stands St. Paul Lutheran Church — a congregation founded in 1856 by German Lutheran settlers — and its blue neon cross , visible to travelers on Route 66 (and later I-55) for generations. The cross was donated by the Brunnworth family in memory of their son Oscar , killed at the Battle of Anzio in World War II. It's a small thing on a small stretch of road, and it'll stick with you longer than most billboards. That's Hamel: tiny, honest, and quietly worth the stop.

### Why this little town matters
Hamel is the kind of place a national app can't help you with at all — too small to register, too easy to flatten into a couple of misfiled listings or, worse, padded out with restaurants that are actually in the next town over. But the truth of a Route 66 village is exactly this: a 1937 roadhouse, a 1906 depot turned ice cream stand, a four-couple grocery, and a neon cross with a war story. The Mother Road was always made of small, real places like these.
That's the whole reason we built a hyper-local directory — to give the little places their due. Search St Louis Near Me Directory for Hamel and Madison County before your Route 66 run — and if you're working the Illinois side, our Lebanon guide and Jerseyville guide are an easy drive away.
And if you run a place along the old road — a diner, a stand, a market — a listing is how the next Route 66 traveler, foreign or local, knows to pull over for you .

### FAQ
Is Hamel, IL worth stopping in on a Route 66 trip?
Yes — it's a genuine, small Route 66 village with real history: Weezy's roadhouse (1937), Route 66 Creamery in the 1906 depot, and the St. Paul Lutheran neon cross. Small, but authentic in a way the big stops aren't.
What's the most famous restaurant in Hamel?
Weezy's Route 66 Bar & Grill — a charbroiled-burger roadhouse in a 1937 building that's been a roadside stop under several names for nearly 90 years.
What's the story behind the neon cross near Hamel?
The blue neon cross at St. Paul Lutheran Church was donated by the Brunnworth family in memory of their son Oscar, killed at the Battle of Anzio in WWII. It's been a Route 66 landmark for generations.
Are there a lot of restaurants in Hamel?
No — Hamel is a small crossroads village of about 900 people, so the honest list is short: Weezy's and Route 66 Creamery for meals, DK's Market for deli and fried chicken to go. For more options, nearby Edwardsville and the Metro East towns have fuller scenes.

### Kaslik Mediterranean Cuisine
Kaslik is the Lebanese standout — from-scratch chicken and beef-lamb shawarma, a mixed-grill platter, falafel and hummus, with a near-perfect county health score and a hidden-gem reputation. The most reliable good meal on the strip.

### WorldWide International Food Market & Restaurant
WorldWide is a halal Middle Eastern grocery, bakery, and restaurant under one roof — they bake fresh pita and Lebanese bread nearly every day, and the shawarma, falafel, and foul draw a steady crowd. The most distinctive eat in town (the Riverfront Times called it a hidden gem).

### Kasabi Hibachi, Sushi & Ramen
Kasabi is the rare North County sit-down sushi-and-ramen spot — hibachi, the Volcano Roll with its showy plating, ramen bowls and boba. A genuine alternative to the chain restaurants up and down Lindbergh.

La Norteña is the no-frills taqueria with a perfect 100/100 health score — authentic corn street tacos, quesabirria, gorditas, and lengua tacos. Come for the tacos, not the frills.

📍 6162 Howdershell Rd, Hazelwood, MO 63042

By Lane Forman , Founder of St Louis Near Me Directory Local restaurant guides, researched and maintained · Updated June 2026 
Herculaneum is a small Mississippi River town with an outsized history — laid out in 1808 by Moses Austin as a lead-shipping port, with shot towers built into the bluffs that dropped molten lead to make ammunition (some of it fired in the War of 1812). It was Jefferson County's first county seat. It is not , however, a big restaurant town — and we won't pretend otherwise.
But people in Herculaneum get hungry too, and when you need a bite right now, there are a couple of genuinely good local spots right off the highway — plus two more in the twin town of Pevely, a minute south. Here's where to eat in the Herculaneum–Pevely area.
Herculaneum and Pevely sit shoulder to shoulder along I-55 and share one little dining scene, so we've grouped them honestly — each spot below is clearly marked by town. The two Herculaneum spots are in the Scenic Plaza off exit 178; the two Pevely spots are off exit 180. Pair a meal with the Mississippi River overlook at Dunklin-Fletcher Memorial Park while you're here.

### Joe's Pizza (Herculaneum)
The local pizza pick. Joe's Pizza in Scenic Plaza is a three-generation family business tracing a secret recipe back to Sicily and a small Illinois town in 1972 — Chicago and Sicilian-style pies, carryout and delivery. The signature is the "Joe-Boli," a stuffed pizza roll with their house sauce. Closed Mondays.
📍 1185 Scenic Dr, Ste 101, Herculaneum, MO 63048

### La Pachanga Mexican Restaurant (Herculaneum)
Right next door in the same plaza, La Pachanga is the town's sit-down Mexican spot — dine-in, patio, and curbside, open late. The most-praised plate is the quesabirria tacos , crisped and served with consommé for dipping. The reliable Herculaneum craving-killer.
📍 1185 Scenic Dr, Ste 105, Herculaneum, MO 63048

### TJ's Bar & Grill (Pevely)
A minute south in Pevely , TJ's Bar & Grill is the family-owned neighborhood bar and grill that's been at it since 1993 — known for its homemade sauces (the wing sauce especially), burgers, wings, and a weekly Tuesday jam night. Family- and biker-friendly, and a genuine local institution just over the Herculaneum line.
📍 8641 Commercial Blvd, Pevely, MO 63070

### Las Brisas Authentic Mexican (Pevely)
Also in Pevely , Las Brisas rounds out the area's Mexican options with generous, consistent plates — nachos, burritos, fajitas, enchiladas — and a loyal local following. The second sit-down Mexican spot in the twin towns, if La Pachanga's busy.
📍 8620 Daniel Dunklin Blvd, Pevely, MO 63070

### Just need something quick or a glass of wine?
When you only want something fast, the Scenic Drive exit has the familiar highway lineup. And if you're up for a short drive, Jefferson County's winery-and-brewery scene — including Main & Mill Brewing in nearby Festus — is close enough to turn a Herculaneum lunch into a fuller afternoon.

### Why this little town matters
Herculaneum is a true river town with a wild history — lead, shot towers, the county's first courthouse — that the national apps reduce to a row of gas-station logos at the I-55 exit. The honest truth is it's small, and its dining scene is shared with twin-town Pevely. Is there much to eat in Herculaneum, MO?
Honestly, it's a small river town — the two main local spots are Joe's Pizza and La Pachanga, both in the Scenic Plaza off I-55. The twin town of Pevely, just south, adds TJ's Bar & Grill and Las Brisas.
What's the best pizza in Herculaneum?
Joe's Pizza — a three-generation family shop with a Sicilian recipe dating to 1972, known for the stuffed "Joe-Boli."
Where's the best Mexican near Herculaneum?
La Pachanga in Herculaneum (quesabirria tacos) and Las Brisas a minute south in Pevely.
What's Herculaneum known for?
Its history — founded in 1808 by Moses Austin as a Mississippi River lead-shipping town with bluff-side shot towers, and Jefferson County's first county seat. There's a river overlook at Dunklin-Fletcher Memorial Park.

High Ridge got its name honestly — it sits on the second-highest point in Jefferson County , up where old Gravois Road climbs out of the river hills southwest of St. Louis. It's not a town with a downtown square; it's a long ribbon of a community strung along Route 30, the kind of place you'd assume is all gas stations and drive-thrus. Assume wrong. Some of the best honest cooking in the county is hiding right here on the Boulevard.
This is diner country — 24-hour fried chicken, scratch breakfasts, Provel pizza done the St. Louis way — plus a Cajun-and-BBQ joint that took over a legendary local room and a hometown brewery two brothers started in a bathtub. Here's where to eat in High Ridge.
Most of these line up along High Ridge Boulevard and Gravois Road (Route 30), so you can hit several without much driving. A couple close Mondays, but at least one diner here never closes at all. And if you've got the afternoon, High Ridge is the on-ramp to the Jefferson County winery and brewery trail — LaChance, Wild Sun, Villa Antonio — all a short drive south.

### Pupillo's Wicked Chicken Cafe
Start your morning here. Pupillo's Wicked Chicken Cafe is the owner-run breakfast-and-brunch spot on the Boulevard, cooking from scratch with the chicken front and center — the signature Pupillo Chicken Dinner stacks a big grilled breast with sautéed mushrooms and melted St. Louis cheese. Family-run, no corners cut.
📍 3021 High Ridge Blvd, High Ridge, MO 63049

### Dave's Diner
Some towns have a 24-hour diner. High Ridge is one. Dave's Diner runs around the clock, locals will tell you it's "the best fried chicken around," and the all-day breakfast and catfish keep the booths full at hours when nothing else out here is awake. A genuine round-the-clock anchor in a rural stretch of road.
📍 2823 High Ridge Blvd, High Ridge, MO 63049

### La Casona Mexican Restaurant
For the Mexican plate, La Casona has been the family-run go-to for twenty-plus years — the kind of longevity that only happens when a town genuinely adopts a place. Sit-down, generous, and the local default when somebody says "let's get Mexican."
📍 5660 Missouri PP, High Ridge, MO 63049

### Peggs Restaurant On the Boulevard
Peggs is the family-owned comfort spot with the most St. Louis menu in town — thin-crust Provel pizza with house sauce, scratch pasta made daily, toasted ravioli, boom-boom shrimp. The tagline is "Eat. Laugh. Belong," and after twenty-some years on the Boulevard, it's earned it.
📍 1001 Crossroads Pl, High Ridge, MO 63049

### Saucy's Pizzeria
When it's a pizza night, Saucy's holds down the Gravois Road corner — made-to-order pies (the BBQ builds get ordered on repeat), wings, and the rest. It's a small Jefferson County operation, not a national chain, so the pizza tastes like somebody local actually owns it. Because they do.
📍 1630 Gravois Rd, High Ridge, MO 63049

### High Ridge Family Diner
High Ridge Family Diner is exactly what the name promises — biscuits and gravy, omelets, classic plates, and a "feels like home" room that locals rate highly across hundreds of reviews. The honest small-town breakfast counter, doing the basics right.
📍 4560 Gravois Rd, High Ridge, MO 63049

### Johnny's Hideout (featuring Smokey D's BBQ)
Here's the spot with a story. For years this room was Iron Barley , a beloved local restaurant — until its chef-owner passed and it closed. Now it's Johnny's Hideout , run by a 40-year St. Louis restaurant hand alongside the owner of Smokey D's BBQ : Cajun plates like shrimp voodoo and gumbo on one side, 26-ounce pork steaks and pulled pork on the other. A new soul in a famous old room, and it cooks.
📍 3367 High Ridge Blvd, High Ridge, MO 63049

### Make it a day: Bastard Brothers Brewing & the Jeffco trail
For a drink with a hometown backstory, Bastard Brothers Brewing Co. (2114 Penta Dr) was started by two brothers who began homebrewing from a magazine kit in a bathtub back in 1986 and finally opened their own taproom here in 2016. Call ahead for current hours. From High Ridge, the wider Jefferson County winery and brewery trail — LaChance, Wild Sun, Villa Antonio — is an easy southward drive.

### Why this little town matters
High Ridge doesn't have a postcard square, and that's exactly why people underestimate it. But strung along the Boulevard and Gravois Road is a 24-hour diner, an owner-run chicken café, a 20-year family Mexican spot, Provel pizza done right, and a Cajun-BBQ joint carrying a legendary local room forward. (It's also the hometown of UFC champ Michael Chandler and an Olympic triathlete, if you need bragging rights.) The chain-logo highway maps will never tell you any of it.

Iron Barley closed after its chef-owner passed away. The space at 3367 High Ridge Blvd is now Johnny's Hideout, featuring Smokey D's BBQ — Cajun food plus smoked pork steaks and pulled pork.

By Lane Forman , Founder of St Louis Near Me Directory Local restaurant guides, researched and maintained · Updated June 2026 
Highland was founded in 1831 by Swiss pioneers who named it “New Switzerland” — and that heritage still runs through the town, from the courthouse-square plaza to the annual Schweizerfest. It's also a place with an outsized footnote in food history: Highland is the birthplace of evaporated milk (the Helvetia/PET Milk company started here). Today the Square anchors a genuinely good small-town food scene known across the region for one thing in particular — sky-high meringue pies.
From a trackside brewery to a Food Network-famous pie café, here's where to eat in Highland.
Most spots are on or near the Square and downtown; a couple sit just out (Blue Springs is on George Street, a little out from the core). A few are dinner-only or closed Mondays, so check first. Time a June trip for Schweizerfest , Highland's Swiss-heritage homecoming at the Square.

### Railshake
Start with the town brewery. Railshake pours 18 rotating craft taps in an 1856 historic building overlooking the train tracks , with a Cajun-Creole and American menu and a three-season patio. The trackside building and the name nod to Highland's railroad past.
📍 504 Walnut St, Highland, IL 62249

### Blue Springs Cafe
The famous one. Blue Springs Cafe is the home-cooking institution known across the region for its foot-high meringue pies (banana, chocolate, coconut crème, lemon) — plus chicken and dumplings and family-style dinners. Featured by Food Network; save serious room for pie.
📍 3505 George St, Highland, IL 62249

### Urban Farmhouse Eatery & Pie Company
Urban Farmhouse is the comfort-food spot with its own pie-and-cake counter — fried chicken, meatloaf, burgers, tacos, and to-die-for homemade pies. Hearty, home-style, and right downtown.
📍 15 Central Blvd, Highland, IL 62249

### Sam's Pizza & Pub
Sam's is the long-running neighborhood pizza pub — St. Louis-style thin crust with Provel from a brick oven, draft beer, and casual games. Five decades of local pizza tradition.
📍 1017 Broadway, Highland, IL 62249

### Michael's Restaurant
Michael's is the white-tablecloth supper-club-style room — steaks, seafood, fried chicken, and a fireside cocktail lounge. Founded in 1941 and run by the Michael family for 85 years; it recently passed to new ownership but remains open as a Highland institution.
📍 415 Broadway, Highland, IL 62249

### Broadway Bar & Grill
Broadway Bar & Grill is the casual downtown American bar-and-grill — the dependable everyday spot for a burger and a beer near the Square.
📍 1013 Broadway, Highland, IL 62249

### E.L. Flanagan's
E.L. Flanagan's is the bar-and-grill with the big outdoor scene — a large covered patio, volleyball, horseshoes, washers, and live bands. More party-and-patio than fine dining, and a fun warm-weather hang.
📍 2635 Plaza Dr, Highland, IL 62249

### Why this little town matters
Highland is a Swiss-founded “New Switzerland” that quietly gave the world evaporated milk — and today it keeps a trackside brewery, a Food Network-famous pie café, and a 1941 supper club, all near a genuine town Square. The national apps reduce it to highway logos; we point you to the Square and the pie.

What's Highland, IL famous for (besides food)?
It was founded by Swiss immigrants as “New Switzerland” in 1831, and it's the birthplace of evaporated milk — the Helvetia/PET Milk company started here. Its Swiss heritage is celebrated at the June Schweizerfest.
Where are the famous pies in Highland?
Blue Springs Cafe (foot-high meringue pies, Food Network-featured) and Urban Farmhouse Eatery & Pie Company (homemade pies and a pie/cake counter).

Yes — Railshake, with 18 craft taps and a Cajun-Creole menu, in an 1856 building overlooking the train tracks.

Michael's Restaurant, a fine-dining institution founded in 1941 and run by the Michael family for 85 years (recently under new ownership, still open).

You've got a free afternoon and you point the car south on Highway 21, the suburbs loosening into Jefferson County hills until you roll into Hillsboro — courthouse on the square, a community college on the edge of town, and a covered bridge from 1872 just up the road. You weren't sure there'd be anywhere good to eat out here. There is. More than you'd guess.
Hillsboro is the Jefferson County seat , and county-seat towns keep their food where the town gathers — near the courthouse, along Business 21, and out toward the fairgrounds. What you won't find much of is the interchangeable highway stuff. What you will find is a Cordon Bleu chef cooking catfish, a coffee bar locals built their mornings around, and two winery-breweries close enough to make a whole day of it. Here's where to eat in Hillsboro.
This is a small town with a courthouse rhythm — several spots are weekday-focused or close early , and a couple of the best (the cafés especially) shut down on weekends or Mondays. Check hours before you drive. And if you've got the time, the Jefferson County Fair in July, the oldest in the county, is the food-and-crowds event of the Hillsboro year.

### Cool Beans Cafe
Start your morning where downtown does. Cool Beans Cafe is the coffee house by the courthouse — Kaldi's-brewed coffee, smoothies, baked goods, and a short, honest lunch of sandwiches, soups, and salads (the Hawaiian on ciabatta has a following). It opens at 6 a.m. for the early crowd and closes on weekends, so it's a weekday ritual, not a Sunday stop.
📍 316 Locust St, Hillsboro, MO 63050

### Lala's Roast & Bistro
The newest face in town, Lala's Roast & Bistro opened in spring 2024 to local TV and newspaper coverage — a cozy coffee-and-bistro spot doing flavored coffees, sandwiches, soups, and salads for breakfast and lunch. It's the kind of fresh independent that signals a small downtown still has fight in it.
📍 10632 Business 21, Hillsboro, MO 63050

### Fountain City Grille
Here's the surprise plate. Fountain City Grille is a locally owned American grill whose menu was built by a Le Cordon Bleu-trained chef — which is why the catfish and the chicken Modego punch well above small-town expectations. Family vibe, real cooking, no pretense.
📍 4660 Yeager Rd, Hillsboro, MO 63050

### Saucy's Pizzeria
Saucy's is the family pizzeria locals default to — Tom and Shannon opened it in 2013 with 40-plus combined years in the pizza business, and it shows in made-to-order pies, wings, burgers, and pasta. This is Friday-night-with-the-kids food, done by people who actually know the craft.
📍 10859 Business 21, Hillsboro, MO 63050

### Los Portales
For the Mexican plate-and-margarita night, Los Portales holds down Main Street downtown — a long-running independent where the shrimp fajitas and the margaritas get the repeat orders. It's the dependable, been-here-forever option right in the heart of town.
📍 201 Main St, Hillsboro, MO 63050

### Taco Tequila Bar
Want a second, newer Mexican option with more of a cantina lean? Taco Tequila Bar on Business 21 brings the tacos, the tequila, and a full-bar margarita focus — proof a town this size can support two distinct independent Mexican spots, each with its own crowd.
📍 10814 Business 21, Hillsboro, MO 63050

### Four Lakes Restaurant & Event Center
Here's the comeback story. When the owners of the old Boro downtown closed up, they reopened in early 2024 at the former Raintree clubhouse — a restaurant-and-event space that had sat dark since 2015 — as Four Lakes . It's American-and-Italian bar food in a setting most small towns don't get, and it's open to the public, not members only.
📍 5925 Plantation Dr, Hillsboro, MO 63050

### Make a day of it: two winery-breweries
Hillsboro quietly has two places that brew and pour their own. Wild Sun Winery & Brewery (4830 Pioneer Rd) does local-grape wines, house beer, and Friday live music in season. Villa Antonio Winery (3660 Linhorst Rd), with Sandy Valley Brewery, leans Italian — wood-fired pizza , artisan beer, and live music. Either one turns a Hillsboro lunch into a Hillsboro afternoon.

### Why this little town matters
Hillsboro is easy to underestimate — a courthouse, a college, a fair. But the streets around the square hold a Cordon Bleu chef, a 2013 family pizzeria, two independent Mexican spots, and a downtown café that opens at six, plus two winery-breweries on the edge of town. That's a real food economy, and it's exactly the kind the national apps reduce to a row of franchise logos off the highway.

What's the best restaurant in Hillsboro, MO?
It depends on the craving, but Fountain City Grille stands out — its menu was built by a Le Cordon Bleu-trained chef, with the catfish and chicken Modego as local favorites. For pizza, Saucy's; for coffee, Cool Beans.
Where do locals get coffee in Hillsboro?
Cool Beans Cafe by the courthouse (Kaldi's coffee, opens 6 a.m., closed weekends) and the newer Lala's Roast & Bistro on Business 21.

When is the Jefferson County Fair?
It runs in July at the Jefferson County Fairgrounds in Hillsboro — the oldest fair in the county, with concerts, 4-H exhibits, and plenty of fair food.

House Springs doesn't have a downtown square or a welcome arch — it's a stretch of Jefferson County strung along Gravois Road where the Big River winds through the hills southwest of St. Louis. People floated and fished this river before they built much of anything here; a German immigrant named Adam House bought the land and its spring back around 1795, and the name stuck. What you'd never guess driving through is how well the place eats.
This is honest, unpretentious Gravois Road food: a retro diner with a burger the size of your forearm, a BBQ joint that started as a trailer, a coffee drive-thru locals built their mornings around, even sushi with a roll named after the town. Here's where to eat in House Springs.
Most of these line up along Gravois Road and Gravois Station Road , so you can hit several without much driving. A couple close Mondays. And if the weather's right, build a float or fishing trip around it — Rockford Beach and the Big River are the local draw, and a riverside lunch is the whole point.

### Slingers
Start at the diner that owns the name. Slingers is the family-owned retro diner where the colossal "Slinger" burger and a big classic breakfast keep the booths full. It's the comfort-food anchor of the whole strip, and exactly the kind of place a chain can only photograph, never replicate.
📍 4662 Gravois Rd, House Springs, MO 63051

### Slo Odie's
Slo Odie's is the local pizza-wings-and-beer joint — house pizzas, burgers, and a neighborhood-bar feel, the spot you end up at on a Friday without really planning to. Independent and proud of it.
📍 28 Gravois Station Rd, House Springs, MO 63051

### Smokey D's
Great BBQ usually starts humble, and Smokey D's started as a mobile rig before planting a permanent stand here in 2021 — pulled pork, pork steaks, and burnt ends from a local pitmaster who earned the storefront the hard way.
📍 4561 Gravois Rd, House Springs, MO 63051

### Grind Coffee Company
Skip the gas-station cup. Grind Coffee Company is the independent drive-thru that opened in 2023 — cold coffee, lotus energy drinks, house syrups, and baked goods, the kind of locally owned caffeine stop that signals a community is growing up around it.
📍 4561 Gravois Rd, House Springs, MO 63051

### Happy Wok
Happy Wok is the long-running independent Chinese spot locals lean on for big portions and dependable flavor — takeout or dine-in, the reliable weeknight answer when nobody wants to cook.
📍 17 Walters Dr, House Springs, MO 63051

### Osaka Sushi & Grill
Sushi in a river town this size? Yes. Osaka Sushi & Grill does Japanese and rolls with a hometown sense of humor — including a house-named "House Springs Roll" alongside the Meltdown and King Kong. Independent, and a nice change of pace from the BBQ-and-burgers default.
📍 38 Gravois Station Rd, House Springs, MO 63051

### Salty Myke's Saloon
Salty Myke's is the neighborhood saloon with karaoke and a real kitchen — bar food, cold drinks, and the where-everybody-knows-you energy that makes a small town feel like one.
📍 4551 Gravois Rd, House Springs, MO 63051

### Shenanigan's Pub & Grill
Rounding it out, Shenanigan's is the little Irish-style pub punching above its weight with gyros and chicken souvlaki with tzatziki alongside the nachos and the party-night vibe. An unexpected Mediterranean streak in a Jefferson County pub — go figure, and go hungry.
📍 5642 Gravois Rd, House Springs, MO 63051

### Make it a day: ice cream and a short drive for BBQ
For dessert, Silver Spoon Ice Cream & Sweets (22 Gravois Station Rd) scoops up the sweet finish. And if you want more smoke, Company B BBQ is a quick hop just over the line in Byrnes Mill — close enough to count as a House Springs-area run.

### Why this little town matters
House Springs is the kind of place the national apps can't make sense of — unincorporated, spread along a country highway, easy to write off as gas stations and dollar stores. But the Big River runs through it, the spring that named it has been here since the 1790s, and the food along Gravois is almost all locally owned: a retro diner, a trailer-turned-smokehouse, a coffee drive-thru, a sushi bar with a sense of humor. That's a real community, and it deserves to be found.

What's House Springs, MO known for?
The Big River and outdoor recreation — floating and fishing at spots like Rockford Beach — plus an unexpectedly deep lineup of locally owned eateries along Gravois Road. It's an unincorporated Jefferson County community named for 1790s settler Adam House and his spring.
What's the must-try spot in House Springs?
Slingers for the namesake colossal burger and all-day breakfast; Smokey D's for BBQ that started as a food trailer; Osaka for the house "House Springs Roll."

Imperial is a Jefferson County town on I-55 with a genuinely wild claim to fame: the Mastodon State Historic Site here preserves the Kimmswick Bone Bed, where a Clovis-culture spear point was found alongside mastodon bones — the first solid proof that humans and mastodons coexisted in eastern North America. People come for the Ice Age bones and the covered bridge nearby. They stay, if they're smart, for the food.
For a town its size, Imperial eats well — an owner-run Italian destination, a couple of family kitchens that have been at it for years, and a handful of taquerias worth hunting down. Here's where to eat in Imperial.
Most of the independents sit along Imperial Main Street and Old Highway 21 / US-61 , just off I-55. A few of the Mexican spots keep food-truck or shorter hours — worth a quick check before you drive. Pair a meal with Mastodon State Historic Site or the Sandy Creek Covered Bridge (one of only four left in Missouri, just southwest) for a real half-day.

### Trattoria Giuseppe
Start with the destination. Trattoria Giuseppe is the owner-run Italian spot — Joe and Grace Prezzavento's place, where Joe works the room and the strip steak Paulo (brandy mushroom cream) and seared tuna Siciliano are the orders. Reservations recommended a few days out; this is Imperial's special-occasion table.
📍 5442 Old State Rte 21, Imperial, MO 63052

### Frankie Gianino's
Frankie Gianino's has served Jefferson County since 2007 — a family-owned Italian-and-comfort kitchen doing chicken modiga, scratch pasta, toasted ravioli, and Provel bites in big from-scratch portions. The reliable family dinner, with a private room for a crowd.
📍 1209 Imperial Main St, Imperial, MO 63052

### At Sunrise
For the morning, At Sunrise is Imperial's breakfast-and-brunch spot — scratch pancakes, loaded omelettes, and brunch with a twist, open daily till early afternoon. A genuinely good independent breakfast in a town that mostly had to drive for one.
📍 1277 Imperial Main St, Imperial, MO 63052

### Detour Grill and Bar
Detour bills itself "best burgers in Jefferson County" — burgers, St. Louis-style pizza, prime rib, and all-you-can-eat fried chicken, with a patio, a full bar, and weekend karaoke. The casual everybody's-welcome hang on Seckman Road.
📍 2855 Seckman Rd, Imperial, MO 63052

### Marcos Tacos & the Imperial taquerias
For tacos, Imperial quietly has a few independent options: Marcos Tacos (a husband-and-wife taqueria on Imperial Main), Adelita's Mexican Cuisine (a sit-down spot on Main), and Stop N Go Taqueria (a US-61 hidden gem). Hours can vary, so check ahead — but these are the local, made-fresh alternatives to the highway chains.
📍 1006 Imperial Main St, Imperial, MO 63052

### Why this little town matters
Imperial is the kind of place the apps reduce to a row of I-55 logos — but it's got an owner-run Italian destination, a since-2007 family kitchen, a real breakfast spot, and a clutch of independent taquerias, all wrapped around an Ice Age fossil site and a covered bridge. That's a genuine town, and it deserves better than a list of exits.

What's the best restaurant in Imperial, MO?
Trattoria Giuseppe — an owner-run Italian spot (the Prezzavento family) that's the town's special-occasion destination; reservations recommended.
Where do locals go for breakfast in Imperial?
At Sunrise on Imperial Main Street — scratch pancakes, loaded omelettes, and brunch, open daily into the early afternoon.
Is there good Mexican food in Imperial?
Several independent options — Marcos Tacos, Adelita's, and Stop N Go Taqueria — all local and made fresh. Check hours before you go, as a couple keep food-truck schedules.
What's there to do in Imperial besides eat?
Mastodon State Historic Site (the Ice Age Kimmswick Bone Bed and a mastodon skeleton replica) is in Imperial, and the historic Sandy Creek Covered Bridge is a short drive southwest.

Jennings is a working-class North County suburb, and its food is exactly what that means: soul food, wings, fish-and-chicken, and BBQ, mostly along West Florissant Avenue and Jennings Station Road. This isn't white-tablecloth territory — it's counters and carryout windows and generous, flavor-first plates. But the real thing is here, led by a soul-food spot serving old-school cuts you can't find at a chain. People in Jennings get hungry too, and these are the genuinely local spots.
From catfish and mac at a beloved soul-food counter to a 12-hour-smoked rib, here's where to eat in Jennings.
Jennings dining runs along West Florissant Ave and Jennings Station Rd (63136) — counters and pickup windows, not reservations. The 63136 ZIP also covers Dellwood and bits of St. Louis City, so a couple of spots sit right on the line (flagged below). For a bigger sit-down meal, Ferguson and Florissant are minutes away.

### Sonja's Soul Food
The standout. Sonja's is the family-run soul-food counter where the line moves fast and the staff will walk a first-timer through the menu — catfish and mac & cheese draw the loudest praise, and the old-school deep cuts (BBQ snoots, a tripe sandwich) are genuinely local. Smothered pork chops, candied yams, collard greens. Closed Mon–Tue.
📍 9841 West Florissant Ave, Jennings, MO 63136

### Roadkilldriveup & King's Kitchen
Roadkilldriveup is the gas-station kitchen with a cult following for its sweet-n-tangy wing sauce — double cheeseburgers, chicken Philly party packs, loaded fries. The kind of unassuming North County spot locals send you to that out-of-towners would never find. Weekdays only.
📍 8319 Jennings Station Rd, Jennings, MO 63136

### China King
China King is the neighborhood Chinese takeout window — pick-up only, no delivery, no dine-in. You call, grab, and go. A true local standby. Closed Sundays.
📍 8021 W. Florissant Ave, Suite B, Jennings, MO 63136

### Ice Paradise
Ice Paradise is the afternoons-and-evenings shaved-ice and sweet-treat stop (opens 3 p.m.) — the warm-weather destination for North County kids and families after school. Closed Sundays.
📍 8980 Jennings Station Rd, Jennings, MO 63136

### Roper's Ribs
Roper's is a family-owned BBQ pitmaster operation going since 1976 — St. Louis-style ribs and rib tips hand-rubbed and smoked 12 hours over hickory, once named a Hillshire Farm "Best Barbecue Place." It sits at the south end of West Florissant, right on the Jennings/St. Louis edge.
📍 6929 W Florissant Ave (Jennings/St. Louis edge), 63136

By Lane Forman , Founder of St Louis Near Me Directory Local restaurant guides, researched and maintained · Updated June 2026 
Maybe you know the feeling: you're up in the Riverbend for the day — antiquing, or out on the Great River Road, or visiting family — and that mid-afternoon question hits. Where's actually good around here? Not the gas-station sandwich. Not the highway chain. Somewhere a local would send you.
In Jerseyville, the answer usually starts at the courthouse square and works outward. This Jersey County seat, about forty-five minutes north of St. Louis along the scenic-byway corridor, has a downtown anchored by a gorgeous 1893 Romanesque courthouse and a food scene that's far deeper than its size suggests — barbecue, all-day breakfast, real Mexican, a friendly downtown pub, and ice cream people will argue beats Ted Drewes. Here's where to eat in Jerseyville.

### Steve's Old Cabin BBQ
Just outside town on Cabin Lane, Steve's Old Cabin BBQ is the family-run smokehouse locals send you to first — and the thing to order is the pulled-pork egg rolls , an only-here mashup that ruins you for regular barbecue sides. The cheesy corn and hashbrown casserole don't hurt either.
📍 29150 Cabin Ln, Jerseyville, IL 62052

### Nick's Pancake House
When Jerseyville wants breakfast — at any hour — it goes to Nick's . Breakfast is served all day, the portions are big, the prices are kind, and the home-style spread runs from pancakes and crepes to a proper beef Manhattan. It's the comfortable, fill-you-up corner every good town has.
📍 891 S State St, Jerseyville, IL 62052

### George's Pub & Grill
For a casual burger-and-a-beer downtown, George's Pub & Grill is the local favorite — solid pub fare and a friendly room to land in after a day on the river road, right on the main S State Street strip near the courthouse.
📍 205 S State St, Jerseyville, IL 62052

### McCarry's Dairyland
Seasonal and beloved, McCarry's Dairyland is the walk-up-and-drive-thru ice cream stop with a patio, homemade soft serve, malts, and a signature "ooey gooey glacier" that has locals making the better-than-Ted-Drewes claim out loud. When the window's open, the line tells you everything.
📍 400B W Carpenter St, Jerseyville, IL 62052

### Los Tres Amigos
For a sit-down Mexican night, Los Tres Amigos has been the casual local go-to for margaritas and carne asada. Easygoing, accessible, and the kind of reliable that keeps a town coming back.
📍 929 S State St, Jerseyville, IL 62052

### A real town, not a thin one
What makes Jerseyville click is how much genuine food sits in a few walkable blocks of S State Street , with the 1893 courthouse keeping watch. The town's been a crossroads forever — the c.1827 "Little Red House" was the area's first stagecoach stop, and Jerseyville was even a minor Underground Railroad waypoint before the Civil War. Come fall, the Jersey County Apple Festival loads downtown with fried fish, ham-and-beans with cornbread, and homemade pie; the Jersey County Fair (running since 1869) brings the funnel cakes every July.
This is the stuff a national app flattens into nothing — and the reason a hyper-local directory wins. ### FAQ
What food is Jerseyville, IL known for?
A surprisingly deep independent scene for its size — standouts include Steve's Old Cabin BBQ (those pulled-pork egg rolls) and McCarry's homemade ice cream, with all-day breakfast at Nick's and real Mexican at Los Tres Amigos rounding it out.
Where's the best ice cream in Jerseyville?
McCarry's Dairyland on W Carpenter St — a seasonal homemade-soft-serve stand that locals will tell you rivals Ted Drewes. Check that the window's open before you go.
Is downtown Jerseyville walkable for food?
Largely yes — most of the picks cluster along S State Street near the 1893 Jersey County Courthouse, making for an easy stroll-and-eat afternoon.
When are Jerseyville's food festivals?
The Jersey County Fair runs in mid-July, and the Jersey County Apple Festival lands in early October — both heavy on classic local fair and festival food.

By Lane Forman , Founder of St Louis Near Me Directory Local restaurant guides, researched and maintained · Updated June 2026 
Picture a Saturday in late October. You've driven twenty-some minutes south of the city, the Mississippi flat and brown on your left, and you roll into a town that's barely a few blocks wide — gravel lanes, 1800s log cabins, the smell of apple butter bubbling in copper kettles somewhere just out of sight. You weren't even that hungry when you parked. Now your stomach has other ideas.
Maybe you've lived this exact day. Maybe a friend dragged you out to Kimmswick once and you've been meaning to go back ever since. Either way, here's the thing locals already know: for a town this small, Kimmswick punches absurdly far above its weight when it comes to food. This isn't a place you grab a bite because you're stuck here. It's a place people drive to , on purpose, for one pie or one pretzel-bread pizza.
So before your next trip down 2nd Street, here's where to eat — all of it real, independent, and worth the parking spot.
Kimmswick keeps small-town hours. **Most places here close Mondays (some Monday and Tuesday) , and the whole town swells to bursting during its festivals. If you're coming for the Apple Butter Festival** — the last full weekend of October, and the biggest event in all of Jefferson County — come hungry, come early, and wear shoes you don't mind walking in.

### The Blue Owl Restaurant & Bakery
If Kimmswick has a beating heart, it's here. Founded in 1985 by Mary Hostetter, The Blue Owl turned a tiny river town into a dessert pilgrimage with one outrageous creation: the Levee High Apple Pie , stacked with around eighteen hand-peeled apples into a dome so tall it looks photoshopped. It's been on Oprah's Favorite Things and half the food shows on cable, but the part that matters is that it's still family-run and still made by hand.
Come for the pie, but the from-scratch breakfast and lunch hold their own.
📍 6116 2nd St, Kimmswick, MO 63053

### The Dough Depot Café
A few doors down on Market Street, The Dough Depot built its name on handmade soft pretzels and pretzel-bread everything. Regulars come for the Mandarin Orange Salad and the pretzel-bread pizza — but the conversation-starter is the St. Louis-style pickle pizza : cracker crust, Provel, dill pickle slices, exactly as unhinged and delicious as it sounds.
📍 216 Market St, Kimmswick, MO 63053

### Sodie Specialty Drinks
Every walkable little town needs a fun place to cool off between shops, and on Market Street that's Sodie Specialty Drinks — a specialty soda and flavored-drink shop turning out colorful, hand-crafted sodas and refreshers. It's the no-alcohol, all-ages stop that gives the kids (and you) a reason to keep strolling. A bright, easy pause in the middle of a Kimmswick afternoon.
📍 113 Market St, Kimmswick, MO 63053

### LaChance Vineyards / Old House Steakhouse
For something slower, LaChance runs a restaurant in a restored log cabin that dates to roughly 1770 — older than the country it sits in. Expect filets, kabobs, Cajun pasta, and weekend dinners with live local music drifting out the open windows. The family's main vineyard estate is just up the road in De Soto, which makes for an easy two-stop afternoon.
📍 6035 2nd St, Kimmswick, MO 63053

### Frenchy's Café & Creperie
Brand new for 2026, Frenchy's revived a family name — owner Gina Otto's parents ran a "Frenchy's Carryout" in Herculaneum back in the '80s. Now it's sweet and savory crêpes, good coffee, and mimosas on Market Street. The savory Monte Cristo crêpe (ham, turkey, Swiss, Gruyère) is the move; finish with a Chantilly-cream sweet one.
📍 119 Market St, Kimmswick, MO 63053

### Behold Coffee
Also new in 2026, Behold Coffee took over the old Pothos Coffee corner and turned it into a proper roastery-café, pulling in beans from Conductor Coffee out of nearby De Soto. Espresso, matcha, house-made syrups, free wifi, and a community-table vibe — the place to land between antique shops.
📍 105 Market St, Kimmswick, MO 63053

### Why this little town matters
Kimmswick is the kind of place the big review sites barely bother with — too small, too easy to overlook. But the streets between Market and 2nd hold more genuinely good, genuinely independent food than towns ten times its size. Throw in the Anheuser Estate overlooking the Mississippi, the 1874 wrought-iron pedestrian bridge, and Mastodon State Historic Site minutes away, and a meal here turns into a whole afternoon.
That's exactly the kind of hyper-local find our directory exists for. ### FAQ
Is Kimmswick worth the drive just for food?
For most St. Louisans, yes — it's only about 25 minutes south, and the Levee High Apple Pie alone has been pulling people down here for decades. Pair it with the antique shops and it's an easy half-day.
When is the Apple Butter Festival?
The last full weekend of October. It's the largest event in Jefferson County, drawing huge crowds and hundreds of food and craft vendors — plan for traffic and arrive early.
What days are restaurants open in Kimmswick?
Most close Mondays, and several close Monday and Tuesday both. Weekends are your safest bet, but always check the individual spot's hours before driving down.
Are there chain restaurants in Kimmswick?
Practically none in the historic core — that's the whole appeal. Everything above is locally owned and independent.

Part of St. Louis County — explore the whole region in our St. Louis County restaurant guide .
Kirkwood was the first planned suburb west of the Mississippi — founded in 1853 around the railroad and nicknamed the "Queen of the Suburbs." It still has the bones to back it up: a beautiful 1893 train station (an active Amtrak stop run by volunteers), the oldest farmers market in the area, and a walkable downtown packed with independent restaurants that range from a 1947 griddle diner to a James Beard winner's lobster joint.
For a deep, genuinely local food town, here's where to eat in Kirkwood.
Everything below is in downtown Kirkwood (Kirkwood Road, Argonne, Jefferson, Adams, Clinton), walkable from the train station. A couple are dinner-only — check first. Time a visit for the Kirkwood Farmers Market (founded 1976) or the Greentree Festival each September in Kirkwood Park, and the Magic House children's museum is right in town.

### Spencer's Grill
Start at the icon. Spencer's Grill has run at this spot since 1947 — a classic American griddle diner, a Route 66-era landmark that once stayed open 24 hours to catch travelers. Breakfast and lunch, every day, the way it's always been. A genuine Kirkwood institution.
📍 223 S Kirkwood Rd, Kirkwood, MO 63122

### Citizen Kane's Steak House
Citizen Kane's has been family-owned since 1993 , serving hand-cut steaks in a turn-of-the-century Victorian home — tenderloin medallions, Delmonico ribeye, NY strip. The special-occasion classic.
📍 133 W Clinton Pl, Kirkwood, MO 63122

### Café Provencal
For something romantic, Café Provencal is the authentic French/Provençal bistro — bistro classics, crème brûlée, and thoughtful wine pairings in an intimate downtown room. A little corner of Provence in the suburbs.
📍 427 S Kirkwood Rd, Kirkwood, MO 63122

### Sunset 44 Bistro
Sunset 44 is the upscale-casual American bistro the Menendez family has run since 1986 — a 250-plus-bottle wine list and a long-standing downtown fine-dining reputation. The grown-up night out.
📍 118 W Adams Ave, Kirkwood, MO 63122

### Honey Bee's Biscuits + Good Eats
For brunch, Honey Bee's is the all-day biscuits-and-breakfast spot — honey-glazed buttermilk biscuits the signature, run by Mike and Meredith Shadwick. The cheerful morning anchor of downtown.
📍 200 N Kirkwood Rd, Kirkwood, MO 63122

### Billy G's Kirkwood
Billy G's on Argonne is the family-owned Italian-and-American spot — St. Louis-style pizza, chef daily specials, a lively room. It's part of the locally owned Gianino family of restaurants (a St. Louis family operator, not a national chain) and a downtown Kirkwood staple.
📍 131 W Argonne Dr, Kirkwood, MO 63122

### Peacemaker Lobster & Crab (at 4 Hands Kirkwood)
The newest big arrival: Peacemaker Lobster & Crab — James Beard winner Kevin Nashan's New England-style seafood (lobster rolls, crab, oysters) — opened inside the new 4 Hands Brewing Kirkwood taproom in 2025. Two beloved St. Louis names, one room.
📍 150 W Argonne Dr, Kirkwood, MO 63122

### Mike Duffy's Pub & Grill
Mike Duffy's has been the downtown family pub since 1986 — hand-crafted burgers and pizza, a friendly neighborhood room. The dependable, everybody's-welcome hang to round out the Kirkwood lineup.
📍 124 W Jefferson Ave, Kirkwood, MO 63122

### Why this little town matters
Kirkwood earns "Queen of the Suburbs" at the table — a 1947 griddle diner, a 1986 fine-dining bistro, a French café, a 1993 steakhouse in a Victorian house, and a James Beard winner's lobster joint, all walkable from a 130-year-old train station. That's a downtown the national apps reduce to a few logos; we walk you through the real one.

### Truffles
The local anchor. Truffles has done French and Modern American fine dining since 1999, with its own retail Butchery Market next door selling the same prime meats and seafood the kitchen cooks with — so the chef builds rotating entrees around the day's best cuts. An award-winning wine list. Dinner Tue–Sat.
📍 9202 Clayton Rd, Ladue, MO 63124

### Companion Café (Ladue)
Companion is the café built on St. Louis's own Companion artisan-bread bakery — sandwiches and soups on award-winning house bread, plus gooey butter cake and cookies. Locals treat the sprawling patio as a daytime living room. Open daily, ~7 a.m.–3 p.m.

### Lester's Restaurant & Sports Bar
Lester's is the original — a chef's show kitchen behind an upscale sports-bar room, doing overstuffed New York-style deli sandwiches (meats prepped in-house daily) and baby-back ribs smoked about four and a half hours before they hit the plate. Locally owned.

Neon Banana is the locally founded wellness café tucked beside the Ladue Schnucks — the Neon Banana smoothie, fresh-pressed turmeric juice, berry-and-goat-cheese toast — scoring a near-perfect 99/100 health rating. The spot health-minded Ladue parents hit after the gym.
📍 10283 Clayton Rd, Ladue, MO 63124

### The Original Pancake House — Ladue
The Original Pancake House is a breakfast franchise (labeled honestly), but the Ladue location is a genuine weekend-line institution — the oven-baked Apple Pancake and griddle-thick bacon many locals call the best in town. Open ~7 a.m.–2 p.m., closed Mondays.

### BC's Kitchen
The standout. BC's Kitchen is the chef-driven New American room most consistently named the area's best sit-down independent — seasonal, local-ingredient cooking like an andouille-chicken-shrimp gumbo with cornbread, in a wine-list-and-craft-cocktail setting rather than a sports bar.

### Burnt Barrel Brewery, Distillery & Meadery
Burnt Barrel is a Missouri craft spot making beer, honey-wine (mead), and spirits under one roof — taste a mead flight next to a bourbon they distilled themselves, with crispy fried mushrooms, a signature soft pretzel, and toasted ravioli. Order food at the bar. Thu–Sun.

Fuego ("fire") is the 2026 newcomer that took over the former Prados suite — fire-grilled Tex-Mex with chicken mole enchiladas, quesabirria tacos, and house-made salsas from an independent operator. Fresh and new; hours may still be settling.

Hygge — named for the Danish idea of cozy contentment — is the healthy café and juice bar sourcing from local farmers: açaí bowls, pressed juices and immunity boosters, smoothies, and coffee. The "cozy, healthy, happy place" of the district.

By Lane Forman , Founder of St Louis Near Me Directory Local restaurant guides, researched and maintained · Updated June 2026 
Here's a thing most St. Louisans don't know, even ones who've lived here their whole lives: about twenty-five minutes east, in a little Illinois college town called Lebanon, there's a red-brick main street so well-preserved that Charles Dickens stayed the night there in 1842 and wrote it up afterward, praising the local inn for cleanliness and comfort that would shame any village alehouse back in England.
That inn — the Mermaid House, built in 1830 by a retired sea captain who swore he'd seen mermaids — still stands on St. Louis Street. And the brick street around it, anchored by McKendree University (the oldest college in Illinois), has quietly become one of the more charming places to eat in the whole Metro East. It's a small scene, and an honest guide has to admit a few good spots have closed recently — but the survivors are worth the drive. Here's where to eat in Lebanon.

### The Gasthaus
Lebanon's German bones show at The Gasthaus , a German-American bar and grill on the brick street where schnitzel, bratwurst, and proper potato salad share a menu with burgers, steaks, and seafood. Locals point to the seafood chowder and the shrimp and grits with Andouille — and there's a roomy, dog-friendly patio for when the weather cooperates.
📍 115 W St. Louis St, Lebanon, IL 62254

### The Lantern BLE
For breakfast and lunch, The Lantern is the home-cooked heart of downtown — biscuits and gravy, peaches-and-cream French toast, and "famous" meatball subs, with a rotating seasonal menu that keeps regulars checking back. It's the kind of place that fills up with students and locals both.
📍 222 W St. Louis St, Lebanon, IL 62254

### St. Louis Coffee World
One of Lebanon's best surprises: St. Louis Coffee World moved to the brick street in late 2024 and brought something you won't find at any chain — espresso and signature lattes plus a full Filipino menu. Think ube cheese pandesal, crispy lumpia, and leche flan alongside a Peanut Butter Tiramisu latte, all inside a historic exposed-brick storefront.
📍 125 W St. Louis St, Lebanon, IL 62254

### Smitty's Pizzeria
Newer to the downtown strip, Smitty's hand-tosses its pizzas and earns its reviews on the crust and the fresh parmesan. Heads up on the hours — it runs Thursday through Sunday only — so plan your pizza night accordingly.
📍 122 E St. Louis St, Suite B, Lebanon, IL 62254

### Mexico Tipico
Just off the brick street on the Madison corridor, Mexico Tipico is the full-service Mexican spot — burritos, enchiladas, Caldo del Mar, Pollo Jalisco, Steak Ranchero — with dine-in, takeout, curbside, and delivery all on the table. The dependable, sit-down south-of-the-border option in town.
📍 501 S Madison St, Lebanon, IL 62254

### Creekside Bar and Grill
Over on the west side, Creekside Bar and Grill is the neighborhood sports-bar play — burgers, wings, pizzas, and a full bar with craft beer and cocktails. When you want a game on and a basket of wings, this is the room.
📍 800 W McAllister St, Lebanon, IL 62254

### A town that earns the trip
Lebanon is small, and it's honest to say its food scene runs tight — a few longtime spots have closed in the last year, which is exactly why supporting the survivors matters. But few towns this size offer this much atmosphere : the preserved brick of St. Louis Street , the 1830 Mermaid House with its Dickens connection, and McKendree University keeping the place young. Come the first Saturday in October, the Lebanon Fall Festival fills the brick street with 100-plus vendors and food stands — kettle corn, caramel apples, funnel cakes, homemade bread — for a 50-year-running tradition.
That kind of place is precisely what gets lost on the big national apps, and precisely what a hyper-local directory is built to surface. Search St Louis Near Me Directory for Lebanon and the Metro East before you head over. Exploring more of the Illinois side? The Riverbend county seat of Jerseyville up in Jersey County is another genuine find.
And if you run a spot on the brick street — or want to — getting listed is how the next carful of visitors (or the next hungry McKendree student) finds you.

### FAQ
Is Lebanon, IL worth visiting for food?
For the combination, yes — a handful of genuinely good independents (German fare, Filipino-fusion coffee, hand-tossed pizza, real Mexican) set against one of the best-preserved historic brick main streets in the Metro East.
What's the story with Charles Dickens and Lebanon?
Dickens stayed at the Mermaid House Hotel on St. Louis Street in 1842 and praised it in his travel book American Notes . The 1830 building still stands and is on the National Register of Historic Places.
Are Lebanon's restaurants open every day?
Not all — Smitty's Pizzeria runs Thursday through Sunday only, and a few spots close one weekday. The town has seen some turnover recently, so it's worth a quick call before driving over.
When is the Lebanon Fall Festival?
The first Saturday in October, on the downtown brick street — a 50-plus-year tradition with 100+ vendors and plenty of festival food.

No — Madison Station is a small named locality (a former rail-station spot) inside the city of Madison, IL, with no business district of its own. For a meal, residents drive a few minutes into Madison proper or the neighboring Tri-Cities.
What is Madison Station?
A federally recorded populated place in Madison County, Illinois, inside the city of Madison — a residential rail-corridor pocket, not a separate town, sharing ZIP 62060.

Mostly on Madison Avenue in Madison, IL — the cook-to-order Delectable Eatery and the iconic, nearly century-old Marko's Fish House — or a few minutes out in Granite City and Pontoon Beach. See our guides.

Manchester runs right along its namesake road, and that corridor hides a deeper food bench than a West County drive-through would suggest — a 1982 steakhouse, a pancake house that opens at 6 a.m., a fish-and-game grill with walleye, and a tucked-away row of Thai, sushi, and Indian. From a 40-year steakhouse to a walleye-and-frog-legs grill, here's where to eat in Manchester.
Most of Manchester's independents sit along Manchester Road and Big Bend (63011/63021), several tucked into plazas like Lafayette Center and Nationalway. Because the road is a city line, don't be thrown when an app says "Ballwin" — the spots below are confirmed Manchester. A couple are local family groups, labeled honestly.

### Tucker's Place
Tucker's Place has been grilling hand-cut steaks here since 1982 — a dim-lit, no-frills neighborhood steakhouse (part of a small local St. Louis group) where the porterhouse, not the decor, is the point. Closed Sundays, which tells you it's run like a neighborhood place.
📍 14282 Manchester Rd, Manchester, MO 63011

### Uncle Bill's Pancake & Dinner House
Uncle Bill's is the West County outpost of the longtime St. Louis pancake original — open at 6 a.m. seven days a week, Belgian waffles and omelets and corned beef hash, coffee that keeps coming, breakfast served all day. The old-school morning anchor.
📍 14196 Manchester Rd, Manchester, MO 63011

### Lazy River Grill
Lazy River Grill is the independent American grill where the walls are a working outdoor museum of fishing, hunting, and camping gear — and the dish regulars drive in for is the in-house-breaded walleye, with frog legs on the side. A genuine West County original.
📍 631 Big Bend Rd, Manchester, MO 63021

### Manee Thai
Manee Thai has been family-owned in West County since 2009 — from-scratch curries (Panang, Masaman, pineapple), sauces made daily, and a patio when the weather turns. An award-winning neighborhood Thai kitchen, not a franchise.
📍 481 Lafayette Center, Manchester, MO 63011

### Sushi Ai
Sushi Ai is the small, locally owned sushi and hibachi bar tucked into the Lafayette Center plaza — one location, recently renovated, no chain behind it. Rolls, hibachi entrees, and udon done right.
📍 471 Lafayette Center, Manchester, MO 63011

### Joey B's Food & Drink
Joey B's (part of the St. Louis Gianino family group) has one of the biggest outdoor bars and patios in West County — award-nominated wings, Fried Chicken Tuesday, burgers, and a bottomless weekend brunch. The warm-weather corridor gathering spot.
📍 14445 Manchester Rd, Manchester, MO 63011

### Cheers Bar & Grill
Cheers Bar & Grill is the genuine neighborhood watering hole — breakfast plates and biscuits-and-gravy in the morning, bar-and-grill fare until 1 a.m., pool and a regulars' crowd. Recently reopened in a new Manchester location.
📍 61 Nationalway Shopping Center, Manchester, MO 63011

By Lane Forman , Founder of St Louis Near Me Directory Local restaurant guides, researched and maintained · Updated June 2026 
Part of St. Louis County — explore the whole region in our St. Louis County restaurant guide .
Maplewood is the little inner-ring town that turned two streets into one of the best independent food-and-drink strips in St. Louis. Park once on Manchester or Sutton and you can walk from a whole-animal butcher's lunch counter to a nationally famous brewery to a 30-seat chef's tasting room. Almost none of it is a chain — which is exactly why people drive in from across the region.
From a barrel-aged beer legend to a duck-fat-fries butcher shop, here's where to eat in Maplewood.
Nearly everything clusters along Manchester Road and Sutton Boulevard (63143), so it's a true park-once-and-walk strip — and a designated Green Dining District, with a lot of local sourcing. A couple of spots are daytime-only or closed Mondays/Tuesdays. One honest note: the old Boardwalk ice cream shop has closed, so don't come chasing it.

### Side Project Brewing
Side Project is one of the most award-decorated breweries in the entire country, sitting on a quiet Maplewood corner — barrel-aged and farmhouse ales that beer fans drive in from across the Midwest to chase, with food from their on-site mobile kitchen. (Sister spots nearby: Side Project Cellar and Side Project Pizza.)
📍 7458 Manchester Rd, Maplewood, MO 63143

### Schlafly Bottleworks
Schlafly Bottleworks is the brewpub arm of St. Louis's original craft brewery — house beers on tap plus a full kitchen of beer-cheese soup, wings, and tacos, served at long communal tables. Maplewood's de facto town square for a pint. Open daily.
📍 7260 Southwest Ave, Maplewood, MO 63143

### Bolyard's Meat & Provisions
Bolyard's is billed as St. Louis's only whole-animal butcher — and you can eat a sandwich and a cone of beef-tallow fries on the patio while they break down pasture-raised hogs in the open cutting room. House sausages, broths, weekend breakfast sandwiches.
📍 2733 Sutton Blvd, Maplewood, MO 63143

### Robin Restaurant
Robin is the tiny 30-seat room where chef Alec Schingel plates a seasonal "fine comfort" tasting menu — elevated Midwestern dinner-party food (think hot dish and pork schnitzel) that reads indulgent but eats like home. Reservations recommended.
📍 7268 Manchester Rd, Maplewood, MO 63143

### The Blue Duck
The Blue Duck is the New American smokehouse where they cure, smoke, and pickle in-house — BBQ burnt ends with pickled red onion, bacon-fat hand-cut fries, and a smoked-meat brunch. They even wash a rye whiskey in duck fat for a house cocktail.
📍 2661 Sutton Blvd, Maplewood, MO 63143

### Sabroso Cocina Mexicana
Sabroso is chef Miguel Pintor's traditional Mexican kitchen — the move is the cochinita pibil, Yucatán pork slow-roasted four to five hours until it falls apart, with pickled habanero onions that bite back. The real-deal Mexican on Sutton.
📍 2726 Sutton Blvd, Maplewood, MO 63143

### The Crow's Nest
The Crow's Nest is the dim, horror-movie-decorated gastropub with a metal soundtrack — pork poutine, cheese curds, a heavy-metal "Metal Brunch," and a kitchen that runs late into the night. The fun, loud one.
📍 7336 Manchester Rd, Maplewood, MO 63143

### Living Room Coffee & Kitchen
Living Room is the family-owned café and in-house coffee roaster — fresh-roasted coffee, scratch breakfast and lunch, a bakery case, wooden tables, and a patio. The neighborhood morning anchor.
📍 2810 Sutton Blvd, Maplewood, MO 63143

### Why this town matters
Maplewood proves what an independent strip can be — a butcher, a tasting-menu room, a national-name brewery, and a Mexican kitchen, all walkable on two streets, all locally owned. It's regularly named one of St. Louis's best indie food neighborhoods, and the chain apps barely register it. We map the whole strip.

### FAQ
What's the best restaurant in Maplewood, MO?
Depends on the night: Robin for a chef's tasting menu, The Blue Duck for smokehouse New American, Sabroso for traditional Mexican. For the marquee name, Side Project Brewing is a nationally awarded destination.
Is Maplewood walkable for food and drink?
Very — almost everything sits along Manchester Road and Sutton Boulevard, so you can park once and walk between a butcher-shop lunch, a brewery, and a scratch-kitchen dinner.
Does Maplewood have a distillery?
No — that's a common mix-up. Maplewood's craft-spirits identity is its breweries (Side Project, Schlafly); StilL 630 is a downtown St. Louis distillery, and a similarly named "Maplewood" distillery is actually in Chicago.
Where's the best coffee in Maplewood?
Living Room Coffee & Kitchen on Sutton roasts its own beans and does a scratch breakfast and lunch — the neighborhood morning spot.

Coffee at Living Room, a butcher-counter lunch at Bolyard's, a pint at Side Project, and a smokehouse dinner at The Blue Duck — all on foot. For more local spots across the metro, explore St Louis Near Me Directory .

Marine is a tiny Madison County village of about 900 people, and its food scene is exactly that size — and that's part of the small-town charm. There's no pretending it's a dining destination, but people in Marine get hungry too, and when you want a bite right here, there are three genuinely local spots, all within a couple of blocks of each other in the village center: a flat-top diner with an ice cream window, a 60-year family tavern, and a scratch-cooking restaurant in the old café building.

### The Marine Diner
The Marine Diner is the locally owned flat-top diner and burger joint that took over the old Millie's Diner building — fresh-griddled cheeseburgers (including the Frisco Burger), corn dogs, rotating daily specials (Wednesday taco salads, Thursday pork steaks, Friday fish), and an ice cream window for after. Closed Sun/Mon.
📍 302 W Division St, Marine, IL 62061

### Phyl's Chet & Rose's Tavern
Phyl's is a 60-plus-year family tavern — grilled cheeseburgers, wings, wraps, a Friday fried-fish special, and tacos on the last Sunday of the month. A known stop for bikers and Harley riders, with karaoke nights. The small-town bar where everyone seems to know each other.
📍 204 N Duncan St, Marine, IL 62061

### The Food Dude Restaurant & Catering
The Food Dude moved into the old Parkview Café building and turned the village's longtime breakfast corner into a scratch-cooking comfort-food spot — chicken Parmesan with skin-on mashed potatoes, house chicken salad, creamy pastas, made-from-scratch desserts. Primarily catering and food-truck, with limited evening dine-in (Wed–Sun) — confirm before you go.
📍 330 N Duncan St, Marine, IL 62061

By Lane Forman , Founder of St Louis Near Me Directory Local restaurant guides, researched and maintained · Updated June 2026 
Marthasville is a tiny Warren County town — barely a thousand people — but it sits in a sweet spot: right on the Katy Trail at mile marker 77, in the heart of Missouri wine country, a short ride from where Daniel Boone was first buried. It's not a town with a long restaurant row. It's a town where cyclists roll in hungry, day-trippers wander through, and locals know the handful of spots that are genuinely worth a stop.
When you're out here and ready to eat, here's what's close — in town and just up the road in wine country.
Marthasville is small, so plan a little: a couple of these keep limited or weekend hours, and one trailside café's status can flip seasonally (call ahead). The town sits on the Katy Trail , minutes from the Daniel Boone Monument and original burial site and a short drive from the Augusta/Dutzow wineries — so it's easy to build a half-day around a single meal here.

### Philly's Pizza
The in-town anchor. Philly's Pizza is the locally owned pizzeria right on the Katy Trail — pizza, pasta, salads, and wings, with a Chicago-style deep dish as the signature (first topping's free). Delivery, takeout, and outdoor seating make it the easy refuel after a ride.
📍 207 Depot St, Marthasville, MO 63357

### Cori's Twin Gables Bar & Grill
Cori's Twin Gables is the family-owned, home-cooking bar and grill a few minutes' walk from the trail — burgers, a praised steak sandwich, calamari, daily specials, and a full bar, with live music every weekend . The community hangout where the town actually gathers.
📍 101 MO-47, Marthasville, MO 63357

### KT Caboose
The most charming stop in town — if it's open. KT Caboose is a healthy, plant-leaning café set inside a vintage 1960s train car right on the Katy Trail: avocado toast, veggie burgers, parfaits, and ice cream, plus $10 tent camping for trail riders (shower and ice cream included). It's a seasonal, weekend-ish operation whose hours can change, so call before you count on it — but when it's running, it's pure Katy Trail magic.
📍 600 Depot St, Marthasville, MO 63357

### Lake Creek Winery
For a sit-down meal with a view, Lake Creek Winery has a full-service restaurant in a restored 1860s farmhouse on the Missouri River bluffs — German-leaning plates, a chef's charcuterie board, Missouri wines, and live music, with a deck, patio, and pavilion over a 24-acre lake. It's just outside the town center and worth the few-minute drive.
📍 15088 Boone Monument Rd, Marthasville, MO 63357

### Make a day of it: Blumenhof in nearby Dutzow
Three or four miles west in the historic German village of Dutzow , Blumenhof Winery is one of Missouri's most-awarded family wineries — a tasting room with a big patio, free weekend live music, and a Brat Haus grill on weekends. It's a different town, but it's the natural "extend your wine-country afternoon" stop from Marthasville.
📍 13699 S Hwy 94, Dutzow, MO 63342

### Why this little town matters
Marthasville is exactly the kind of place the big sites skip — too small to register — but it's a genuine Katy Trail and wine-country gem, sitting where Daniel Boone spent his last years and was first laid to rest. The honest truth is it's a handful of spots, not a dozen: a deep-dish pizzeria, a family bar with weekend bands, a café in a train car, and a bluff-top winery restaurant. Is there food right on the Katy Trail in Marthasville?

Where can I eat with a wine-country view near Marthasville?

Maryland Heights has two food worlds. There's Westport Plaza — a genuine walkable dining-and-entertainment hub off I-270 with hibachi, the original Drunken Fish sushi, and a brand-new wood-fired Italian room. And there's the Dorsett Road corridor, where the workaday locals live: a 20-year family taqueria, a deep-menu Thai kitchen, a char-grill counter, and a Gioia's hot-salami walk-up window. Plus a lakeside bar and grill right on the Creve Coeur Park trail.
From a tableside hibachi show to a century-old hot salami, here's where to eat in Maryland Heights.
Two zones: Westport Plaza (63146, date-night and groups) and the Dorsett Road corridor (63043, everyday and carryout). A few spots are dinner-only or closed early in the week. Some park-area addresses read “St. Louis 63146” but are inside Maryland Heights city limits.

### Basso on the Plaza
Basso is Westport's newest dining anchor (opened 2025) — the second location of the local Basso, doing wood-fired steaks and pizzas. Get the marrow-butter Wood-Fire Burger or the hot-honey pepperoni pizza, and finish with the Spumoni Sundae. Date-night caliber. Closed Sunday and Monday.
📍 545 West Port Plaza Dr, Maryland Heights, MO 63146

### Drunken Fish — Westport Plaza
Drunken Fish is the very first one — the Westport location that launched a St. Louis sushi brand in 2003 — with happy hour three times a day and weekend DJ nights. Rolls and sake on the plaza's second level.
📍 639 Westport Plaza Dr, Maryland Heights, MO 63146

### Kobe Steak House of Japan
Kobe has done tableside teppanyaki since 1985 — your dinner cooked and performed by your own chef, onion volcano and flying-rice tricks included. Built-in dinner-and-a-show, great for groups and celebrations.
📍 645 Westport Plaza Dr, Maryland Heights, MO 63146

### Gioia's Deli (Maryland Heights window)
Gioia's is a century-old St. Louis legend, and this is its to-go walk-up window — order the Original Hot Salami, house-ground and served hot on a crusty Italian loaf with pepperoncini and spicy mustard. A true only-in-St.-Louis bite. Weekday lunch only, carryout.
📍 11855 Adie Rd, Maryland Heights, MO 63043

### Casa Juárez Mexican Town
Casa Juárez is the 20-plus-year family Mexican fixture on Dorsett — street tacos come four to a plate instead of three, with a full bar and margaritas. The weekly-regular neighborhood spot.
📍 12710 Dorsett Rd, Maryland Heights, MO 63043

### Thai Kitchen
Thai Kitchen is the owner-run Thai spot with a no-shortcuts menu — well over 100 items, including some 30 curries and 47 noodle and rice dishes. The kind of from-scratch range you only get when the owner's in the kitchen. Closed Mondays.
📍 2031 Dorsett Village, Maryland Heights, MO 63043

### Off The Grill
Off The Grill is the independent char-broil counter built for the Dorsett lunch crowd — char-broiled burgers and steakhouse-quality sirloin tips without the steakhouse bill. Closed Sundays.
📍 11640 Dorsett Rd, Maryland Heights, MO 63043

### Creve Coeur Lakehouse Bar & Grill
Creve Coeur Lakehouse sits right on the trail at Creve Coeur Park with lake views and a dog-friendly patio — pull off a bike ride and eat lakeside, burger and fried tilapia in hand. Family-owned since 2006. Closed Mon–Tue.
📍 2160 Creve Coeur Mill Rd, Maryland Heights, MO 63146

### Trainwreck Saloon — Westport
Trainwreck is an Old-West rustic saloon (a St. Louis-area tavern group, not a national chain) — Wreck Wings, a pub-cheddar burger, fried pickles, toasted ravioli, live music, and a kitchen open late. The plaza's go-to game-day and late-night spot.
📍 314 West Port Plaza Dr, Maryland Heights, MO 63146
