Mascoutah is a small German-founded town near Scott Air Force Base, and it's got something a lot of Metro East suburbs don't: a genuine, walkable Main Street with real locally-owned spots a few blocks apart. Two family Mexican restaurants, a cocktail lounge inside a restored 1890 bank, a veteran-and-woman-owned coffee shop, and a hometown bar-and-grill — all downtown. The old German restaurant has closed, so that heritage is history now, but the Main Street is very much alive.
From a cocktail bar inside an 1890 bank vault to parmesan-crusted tacos, here's where to eat in Mascoutah.
Mascoutah's independents pack into a few blocks of Main Street (62258), genuinely walkable for a small town. It serves a steady mix of locals and Scott AFB families. For more variety, O'Fallon and Belleville are a short drive west. (The old German spot, Roemertopf, has closed — heritage only.)

### The Vault
The town landmark. The Vault is a craft-cocktail and burger lounge set inside the restored 1890 First National Bank of Mascoutah building — you sip a bourbon where townsfolk once cashed checks, in a downtown landmark renovated by local owners. The in-house “Hawkins Burger Bar” handles the food.
📍 28 E. Main St., Mascoutah, IL 62258

### Camino Real Authentic Mexican Restaurant
Camino Real is the Main Street Mexican standby — authentic plates with a tortilla soup reviewers call “the most refreshing and relaxing,” local enough that the Mascoutah Heritage Museum has a history page on the building. Open seven days.
📍 9 W. Main St., Mascoutah, IL 62258

### El Sombrero Mexican Restaurant
El Sombrero is the second locally-owned Mexican kitchen a few doors down — chimichangas, quesadillas, and classic plates. That tiny Main Street supports two independent Mexican spots is a real point of local pride. Closed Mondays.
📍 215 W. Main St., Mascoutah, IL 62258

### Skootr's Restaurant & Bar
Skootr's is the family-owned hometown bar and grill — pulled pork, pork steak, ribeye, a bacon cheeseburger, and a Friday fish plate, with late-night hours and karaoke Thursdays. The kind of place where the kitchen closes but the bar keeps going till 2 a.m.
📍 323 E. Main St., Mascoutah, IL 62258

### The Juicy Peanut Bar & Grill
The Juicy Peanut is the bar and grill whose tacos come on freshly fried, parmesan-cheese-crusted shells with a house “Valentine” hot sauce — a small-town twist locals come back for, plus wings and a pork tenderloin sandwich, and $1.75 Taco Mondays.
📍 724 W. Main St., Mascoutah, IL 62258

### St. Louis Coffee World
St. Louis Coffee World is the woman-, veteran-, and minority-owned Main Street coffee shop — specialty espresso, breakfast and lunch, boba, and ice cream. Owner “Richie” gets named in the reviews; the opposite of a faceless drive-thru.
📍 200 E. Main St. #100, Mascoutah, IL 62258

Part of South County — explore the whole region in our South County restaurant guide .
Mehlville is the heart of South County — Lemay Ferry Road running straight through it — and the food is classic, unpretentious St. Louis: toasted ravioli, Provel-square pizza, brain sandwiches, affordable steakhouses, and a nationally famous donut. This is neighborhood-tavern and family-kitchen territory, value-priced and proud of it, with addresses that bleed across Mehlville, Lemay, and Tesson Ferry.
From a nationally ranked "Cinnamon Glob" to an old-school brain sandwich, here's where to eat in Mehlville.
The independents string along Lemay Ferry Rd and the Tesson Ferry corridor (63125/63128). Because Mehlville is an unincorporated area, addresses often read St. Louis, Lemay, or Oakville — all the same South County dining spine. A few keep early or odd hours (the donut shop sells out by midday).

### The Donut Stop
The Donut Stop has made donuts on Lemay Ferry since 1953 — and earned national fame for the Cinnamon Glob , a dense, hole-less ball of fried dough that Saveur and The Daily Meal both honored (it ranked #19 among America's best donuts). Open 4:30 a.m.; the best globs sell out early. Closed Mon–Tue.
📍 1101 Lemay Ferry Rd, St. Louis, MO 63125

### Fergie's Bar & Restaurant
Fergie's is a Lemay institution since 1990 — and one of the last places in St. Louis where you can still order an old-school fried brain sandwich on rye. The fried chicken is the house specialty; regulars call it the best in town. Two longtime employees bought it from the founder in 2020.
📍 1699 Lemay Ferry Rd, St. Louis, MO 63125

### Tucker's Place South County
Tucker's Place South County is the family-run South County fixture for ~40 years — hand-cut steaks at a fair price, house-made toasted ravioli, breaded mushrooms with homemade marinara, and a house salad dressing with a following. Closed Sunday.
📍 3939 Union Rd, St. Louis, MO 63125

### Liliana's Italian Kitchen
Liliana's is the family kitchen Tim and Kathy named for their daughter — house-made toasted ravioli, fried calamari, and a celebrated St. Louis-style square ("quadrangle") pizza. The old-school red-sauce-and-Provel-square Italian South County grew up on. Closed Monday.
📍 11836 Tesson Ferry Rd, St. Louis, MO 63128

### Thai Orchid
Thai Orchid is the unassuming strip-center storefront South County locals quietly guard as their go-to for real Thai — authentic curries and noodle dishes on the Lemay Ferry strip. Closed Monday.
📍 3027 Lemay Ferry Rd, St. Louis, MO 63125

### La Fiesta Mexican Restaurant
La Fiesta is the family-run Mexican spot tucked into the Home Depot plaza off S. Lindbergh — fresh-made traditional plates and margaritas, the neighborhood's weeknight fajitas-and-margaritas stop for over a decade.
📍 7439 S Lindbergh Blvd, Mehlville, MO 63125

### Lemay Wok
Lemay Wok is the strip-mall Chinese hidden gem where a regular will argue with anyone that the General Tso's chicken and crab rangoon are the best in town. Opens at 2:30 p.m. (no lunch); closed Sunday.
📍 4530 Lemay Ferry Rd, St. Louis, MO 63129

By Lane Forman , Founder of St Louis Near Me Directory Local restaurant guides, researched and maintained · Updated June 2026 
Cross the river and climb the bluffs about twenty-five minutes from downtown St. Louis and you reach Millstadt — a German farming village so thoroughly settled by immigrants from the Rhineland-Pfalz that an 1881 county history claimed only seven English families were left in town. They came in 1834, named it Centreville, got overruled by the post office, and ended up Millstadt. Nearly two centuries later, the German bones still show — in the church names, the festival in Liederkranz Park, and the tavern-and-fish-fry food culture.
This is a walkable little Main Street town where nearly every good spot sits within a few blocks on Washington Street — a cash-only corner tavern with a famous fish stand, a gas-station-turned-brewery, an ice cream shop pulling Kaldi's espresso, and a Cajun gastropub that has no business being this far from New Orleans. Here's where to eat in Millstadt.
Most of these line up on Washington Street , so you can park once and graze. A heads-up: Ott's is cash only (ATM on site), and a couple of the breakfast spots close Mondays. If you want the town at full volume, come for Millstadt Homecoming over Labor Day weekend at Liederkranz Park — parades, food, and the kind of small-town turnout that tells you the place still has a heartbeat.

### Ott's Tavern & Millstadt Fish Stand
Start at the institution. Ott's is the classic Metro-East corner tavern — burgers, wings, pizza — with an attached fish stand turning out the famous fried cod, house slaw, and jalapeño hush puppies. There's a beer garden out back, daily lunch specials at the bar, and a strict cash-only policy that somehow makes it taste better. Pure small-town tavern culture.
📍 20 E Washington St, Millstadt, IL 62260

### Millpond Brewing
The newest reason to drive out: Millpond Brewing turned a former Shell gas station into the town's hometown craft brewery — lagers, hazy IPAs, barrel-aged beers, rotating food trucks on weekends, and a homebrewer "incubator" where local brewers scale up their recipes on Millpond's system. Community-sourced beer in a town that's all community. You can even bring in food from the other Main Street spots.
📍 308 E Washington St, Millstadt, IL 62260

### Reinhardt's Restaurant & Lounge
Reinhardt's is the old-school family restaurant-and-lounge — crispy fried chicken, country-fried steak, sausage gravy, and fish, served in a neighborhood-gathering room with a pool table. The German surname fits the town, and so does the stick-to-your-ribs cooking.
📍 201 W Madison St, Millstadt, IL 62260

### Good Morning Cafe
For breakfast and brunch, Good Morning Cafe partners with local coffee roasters, bakes its own goods, and runs a Tex-Mex streak through the morning menu — the "GM Slam," huevos rancheros, banana pancakes. There's even a rear drive-thru window for the running-late crowd. Closed Mondays.
📍 725 W Washington St, Millstadt, IL 62260

### Sunrise Pancake House
The other morning option, Sunrise is the family-owned-and-operated breakfast-and-lunch diner doing old-fashioned pancakes, French toast, crepes, and cheese omelets — generous, affordable, homestyle. It's been name-checked in "biscuits and gravy worth a road trip" roundups, which is exactly the energy you want from a small-town diner.
📍 548 E Washington St, Ste 8, Millstadt, IL 62260

### Happy Days Ice Cream & Coffee Shop
A Main Street fixture for 25-plus years , Happy Days scoops up to 30 flavors, milkshakes, sundaes, and concretes (a proper St. Louis-region nod) — and runs a full espresso bar on Kaldi's Coffee , the beloved local roaster. The all-ages, year-round, walk-and-cool-off stop in the middle of town.
📍 119 W Washington St, Millstadt, IL 62260

### Spike's Public House
Here's the curveball — a Cajun/Creole gastropub in a German village. Spike's does muffulettas, fried crawfish tails, a crawfish po'boy, plus calzones and tacos, right in the Washington Street core. Unexpected, a little rowdy, and a fun break from the fish-fry-and-fried-chicken default.
📍 4 E Washington St, Millstadt, IL 62260

### Mariachi's Mexican Restaurant & Cantina
Rounding out the town, Mariachi's fills the full-service Mexican niche — a locally run, sit-down cantina on the west end of Washington Street, the place for fajitas and a margarita after a Main Street stroll.
📍 717 W Washington St, Millstadt, IL 62260

### Why this little town matters
Millstadt is a 190-year-old German village on the bluffs that most St. Louisans have never once driven through — and it quietly fields a cash-only tavern with a legendary fish stand, a brewery in an old gas station, a 25-year ice cream shop pulling Kaldi's espresso, and a Cajun gastropub, nearly all of it walkable on one street. That's a real Main Street, the kind the national apps reduce to a couple of misfiled listings.

And if you run a Millstadt spot — a tavern, a food truck, a bakery — a listing is how the next carful coming over the bluffs finds you on Washington Street.

### FAQ
What's the most famous place to eat in Millstadt, IL?
Ott's Tavern & Millstadt Fish Stand — a cash-only corner tavern with a beer garden and a fish stand known for fried cod and jalapeño hush puppies.
Does Millstadt have a brewery?
Yes — Millpond Brewing, built inside a former gas station, pours craft beer with weekend food trucks and runs a homebrewer incubator program.
Where do locals get breakfast in Millstadt?
Good Morning Cafe (local-roaster coffee, Tex-Mex breakfast, closed Mondays) and Sunrise Pancake House (family-owned homestyle diner). For coffee and ice cream, Happy Days has been on Main Street 25-plus years.
Is there a German restaurant in Millstadt?
Despite the deep German heritage, there's no standalone German restaurant or bakery in town today — the heritage lives on in the festivals, the church and family names, and the tavern-and-fish-fry food culture rather than a dedicated German menu.

The old-school diner where the waitresses know the regulars by name — the "chubby burger" and fries, breakfast from 6 a.m. (hand-smoked bacon, chicken-fried steak), and a Friday all-you-can-eat buffet with fried chicken, fish, shrimp, and frog legs. The brand-new Mexican room (opened late 2025/2026) from the team behind Five Finger Wings — tacos and a full Mexican menu, greeted by locals with a genuine "we're so excited to have this option." A sign of the town's growth pulling in fresh sit-down choices.

By Lane Forman , Founder of St Louis Near Me Directory Local restaurant guides, researched and maintained · Updated June 2026 
Mt Olive is a small town of about 2,000 on a historic alignment of Route 66 — and notably home to the Union Miners Cemetery and the Mother Jones Monument, the only union-owned cemetery in the country. The food scene is small but entirely local: there are no sit-down chains here, just four genuine independents and a small-batch coffee roaster. People in Mt Olive get hungry too, and this is horseshoe country — the central-Illinois open-face specialty shows up on the menus.
From an 1982 tavern's horseshoes to scratch coconut cream pie, here's where to eat in Mt Olive.
The independents sit downtown around East/West Main Street and out on Route 138 (62069). It's a tiny scene — no national franchises with a dining room — so for more variety, neighbors up and down I-55 (Staunton, Gillespie, Litchfield) are short drives. A diner stop pairs naturally with a Route 66 / Mother Jones day trip.

### Tilley's Tavern
The standout. Tilley's has been Mt Olive's premier bar and grill since 1982 — known across the area for its horseshoe platters (the open-face Illinois specialty: meat on Texas toast, piled with fries, smothered in cheese sauce) and signature burgers, with pool, darts, and gaming. Open daily till 2 a.m.
📍 303 E. Main St., Mt Olive, IL 62069

### Route 138 Cafe
Route 138 Cafe is the home-style diner just off the highway (formerly Sunset Restaurant, renamed under new ownership) where the pies are scratch-made — coconut cream is the one locals call "amazing" — alongside french toast, catfish nuggets, and chicken and dumplings. Closed Mondays.
📍 21224 Rt 138, Mt Olive, IL 62069

### Little Italy's Pizza
Little Italy's is the small-town pizzeria that also scoops ice cream — hand-tossed and thin-crust pizza, plus pasta, subs, wings, and salads, with later weekend hours for the after-the-game crowd.
📍 110 W. Main St., Mt Olive, IL 62069

### Mel's Place
Mel's Place is the remodeled neighborhood tavern — the after-work gathering spot for "friendly faces, good music, and cold drinks," with karaoke every Friday night. The local watering hole.
📍 208 E. Main St., Mt Olive, IL 62069

### Why this town matters
Mt Olive is a 2,000-person Route 66 town with zero sit-down chains — just an 1982 horseshoe tavern, a scratch-pie diner, a pizzeria, and a corner bar, plus a coffee roaster. Pair it with the Mother Jones Monument and you've got a genuine small-town stop. Nobody writes about Mt Olive's food. We do.

What's the standout place to eat in Mt Olive, IL?
Tilley's Tavern (since 1982) — the local institution known for its horseshoe platters. For breakfast and scratch pie, Route 138 Cafe; for pizza, Little Italy's.
What's a horseshoe?
A central-Illinois open-face sandwich: meat on Texas toast, piled with fries, smothered in cheese sauce. Mt Olive is horseshoe country, and Tilley's is the place to try one.
Why is Mt Olive worth a stop?
It's on a historic Route 66 alignment and home to the Union Miners Cemetery and Mother Jones Monument — the only union-owned cemetery in the U.S. A diner breakfast pairs perfectly with the history. (Note: the old Crossroads Route 66 Diner has closed.)

Neighbors up and down I-55 — Staunton (~8 mi), Gillespie (~10 mi), and Litchfield (~12 mi, the bigger Route 66 food hub) — are short drives.

By Lane Forman , Founder of St Louis Near Me Directory Local restaurant guides, researched and maintained · Updated June 2026 
New Baden was built by German immigrants in 1855 and named, plainly enough, after Baden, Germany — and the town never let go of that thread. The main drag is Hanover Street (a German place-name itself), St. George Catholic Church anchors the skyline, and after an 1896 tornado leveled the place, the neighboring German villages helped rebuild it bigger than before. Today it's a tidy town of about 3,400 that eats far better than its size suggests.
This is genuine small-town German heartland: a homestyle diner famous for fried chicken, a bakery some call the best donuts in Illinois, a nonprofit café with a real mission, and a couple of authentic Mexican spots for good measure. Here's where to eat in New Baden.
Most of the good stuff is on Hanover Street , so it's an easy crawl. The bakery keeps early hours and closes Mondays; the nonprofit café is daytime-only — check before you go. And one honest note: this is a homestyle-diner-and-bakery town, not a fine-dining one, which is precisely its charm. Want to make a day of it? Hidden Lake Winery (Aviston) and Excel Brewing (Breese) are a short drive.

### Good Ol' Days Family Restaurant
Start at the anchor. Good Ol' Days is the American homestyle diner — breakfast served all day, classic comfort cooking, and a fried chicken that's the town's pride. Family-owned and ranked #1 in town for a reason; this is New Baden's living room.
📍 5 E Hanover St, New Baden, IL 62265

### Berkemann's Baker's Dozen
The local star. Berkemann's Baker's Dozen is the old-school German bakery — donuts, cakes, and breads — that's been called the best donuts in Illinois . Early hours, closed Mondays, and worth getting up for. A genuine small-town institution.
📍 115 W Hanover St, New Baden, IL 62265

### The Red Porch Cafe
Here's the one that'll stick with you. The Red Porch Cafe — coffee, soups, sandwiches, and health-conscious plates — is run by the nonprofit Community Link under the motto "Brew Good. Do Good." It employs people with disabilities, so every cup you buy does a little extra. Warm food, warmer mission.
📍 301 E Hanover St, New Baden, IL 62265

### Margarita's Mexican Restaurant
Margarita's is the independent sit-down Mexican cantina on Hanover Street — authentic plates, a full bar, and the dependable taco-and-margarita night for the east end of town.
📍 807 E Hanover St, New Baden, IL 62265

### El Indio Authentic Mexican
A second, distinct Mexican option, El Indio cooks fresh daily using traditional methods — out on the IL-160 strip but firmly New Baden, and locals call it excellent. Two genuine independent Mexican spots in a town of 3,400 is its own kind of small-town flex.
📍 7551 State Route 160, Ste F, New Baden, IL 62265

### China King
Rounding out the lineup, China King is the independent Chinese spot — good food at a fair price, the reliable carryout-or-dine-in answer on Hanover Street.
📍 450 W Hanover St, Ste 5, New Baden, IL 62265

### Why this little town matters
New Baden is a German village that got knocked flat by a tornado in 1896 and rebuilt itself bigger — and that stubborn, neighborly spirit still shows up at the table. A diner everyone votes #1, a bakery people drive in for, a café that hires folks the rest of the world overlooks: that's a community feeding itself with real care, and it's exactly what the national apps miss when they only show you the chains out on the highway.

What's the best place to eat in New Baden, IL?
Good Ol' Days Family Restaurant — a family-owned homestyle diner ranked #1 in town, famous for its fried chicken and all-day breakfast.
Where can I get the best donuts in New Baden?
Berkemann's Baker's Dozen, an old-school German bakery on Hanover Street that's been named the best donuts in Illinois. Early hours, closed Mondays.

By Lane Forman , Founder of St Louis Near Me Directory Local restaurant guides, researched and maintained · Updated June 2026 
For a town of about 2,400 people, New Haven has no business being this good. It sits on a bluff above the Missouri River out in Franklin County wine country, a tidy historic main street facing a riverwalk — the kind of place a man named John Colter, the Lewis and Clark expedition's "first mountain man," chose to settle down after he'd seen the whole frontier. He's honored on a bluff just outside town. You'll understand the choice about an hour into your visit.
Here's the part that surprises people: this little river town fields an estate winery older than most of us, a craft distillery, a riverfront brewery, an 1880s Old-West resort restaurant, and a downtown coffee-and-artisan shop — all within a short stroll of the water. It's a genuine wine-country day trip masquerading as a dot on the map. Here's where to eat and drink in New Haven.
Wine-country hours are real hours — several of the best spots here run limited days (weekends, or afternoons only), and the brewery and resort restaurant keep especially tight schedules. Check before you drive. New Haven is roughly 11 miles from Washington and 13 from Hermann, so it slots neatly into a Hermann Wine Trail day — New Haven is the trail's eastern anchor.

### Röbller Vineyard & Winery
Start with the flagship. Röbller is a family estate winery founded in 1988 by Bob and Lois Mueller on an 85-acre farm — and their Norton (Missouri's state grape) won Best in Show and the very first Governor's Cup at the 1994 state fair. Run today by their son Jerry, it pours complimentary tastings on a covered deck over the vines, with cheese-and-sausage picnic plates to go with the view.
📍 275 Röbller Vineyard Rd, New Haven, MO 63068

### Pinckney Bend Distillery
A river town with its own craft distillery — that's New Haven punching above its weight again. Pinckney Bend makes an award-recognized American Dry Gin plus vodka and whiskey, and the tasting room runs distillery tours and even "blend your own" gin and whiskey classes. The kind of hands-on stop you can't get at a chain anything.
📍 1101 Miller St, New Haven, MO 63068

### Paddle Stop Brewery
Right on the historic riverfront, Paddle Stop Brewery pours lagers, IPAs, and stouts with live music indoors and out, and a calendar full of the stuff small towns do best — a Stoutfest, a chili cook-off. It's the riverfront hang, the one with the river-and-adventure spirit baked right into the name.
📍 204 Front St, New Haven, MO 63068

### Town Hall Tap Room at Cedar Creek
This one's pure character. Out at Cedar Creek, Town Hall Tap Room sits on a recreated 1880s Old-West town street — a saloon-and-restaurant with wood interiors, a pool table, local beers and spirits, live music, and wine-country views. It runs weekend-only hours (Friday evening and Saturday), so plan around it, but it's worth the planning.
📍 Cedar Creek, New Haven, MO 63068

### New Day Mercantile
Downtown's morning stop, New Day Mercantile is a coffee shop and local-artisan store run by sisters Rachel and Wilhelmina Bartels — good coffee alongside a curated collection of locally made pottery, jewelry, woodwork, and signs. Caffeine and a souvenir from the same counter, on the historic Front Street block.
📍 123 Front St, New Haven, MO 63068

### Lang-A-Tang Deli, Catering & Charcuterie
For lunch downtown, Lang-A-Tang does coffee, pastries, soups, salads, paninis, and proper charcuterie boards — the kind of from-scratch deli a riverwalk town deserves, with sandwiches locals rave about. A great grab before or after a winery run.
📍 125 Front St, New Haven, MO 63068

### Paddle Stop, Pinckney Bend, and the riverwalk
(For Mexican and pub options, Dos Bros on Front Street and T & T Hilltop Lounge on Highway 100 round out the town — confirm the current name/hours before you go, as the Front Street spot has changed hands recently.) However you fill the afternoon, end it on the restored Front Street riverwalk above the Missouri River, where the John Colter memorial marks the bluff. It's the kind of view that explains why a mountain man stopped wandering.

### Why this little town matters
New Haven is the proof of Lane's whole thesis: a town of 2,400 with a 35-year estate winery, a craft distillery, a riverfront brewery, an 1880s saloon restaurant, and a downtown coffee-and-artisan shop — every one of them independent, every one of them invisible on the national maps that only know chains. A place like this doesn't survive on drive-by traffic. It survives because people find it.

### FAQ
Is New Haven, MO worth the drive from St. Louis?
For wine-country fans, absolutely — it's about an hour out and packs an estate winery, a craft distillery, a riverfront brewery, and a historic riverwalk into one small town. Pair it with Washington or Hermann for a full day.
What's the oldest winery in New Haven?
Röbller Vineyard & Winery, a family estate founded in 1988 and known for its award-winning Norton — Missouri's state grape.
Does New Haven have a distillery?
Yes — Pinckney Bend Distillery, known for its American Dry Gin, with a tasting room, distillery tours, and "blend your own" classes.
Is New Haven on the Katy Trail?
The Katy Trail runs along the north bank of the Missouri River across from town, not directly through downtown — but New Haven is the eastern anchor of the Hermann Wine Trail and an easy add to a Katy Trail or wine-country trip.

By Lane Forman , Founder of St Louis Near Me Directory Local restaurant guides, researched and maintained · Updated June 2026 
New Melle is tiny — about 540 people — a German village in western St. Charles County, founded in 1839 by immigrants from Melle, Germany, who named their new home after the one they'd left. It sits at the quiet edge of Missouri wine country, just north of the Defiance corridor and the Daniel Boone Home. You don't come here for a big restaurant row. You come for a couple of genuinely good local spots, a glass of something, and the kind of small-town welcome that's getting harder to find.
When you're out this way and hungry, here's where to eat in New Melle.
New Melle is small, so plan a little: the spots below keep their own hours (a couple are evening-focused), and a newer one or two are worth a quick call first. The town sits minutes from the Defiance / Femme Osage wine corridor and the Historic Daniel Boone Home , so it's easy to build a wine-country afternoon around a meal here.

### Liz's Bar & Grill
Start at the heart of town — and the best story in it. Liz's Bar & Grill is home of "Liz's Famous Half-Pound Burger," plus fried chicken, steak, and Taco Tuesday. Original owner Liz Holloway ran it for nearly 30 years until she passed in early 2025; her friend Zach King, who'd worked for her and talked with her about taking it over, reopened it that October to carry her name forward. Recent regulars say he's done her proud.
📍 3585 Mill St, New Melle, MO 63365

### The Quarry
The destination spot. The Quarry (Quarry Wine Garden & Resort) is a restaurant, wine bar, and live-music venue set in a former quarry — patios, fire pits, sand volleyball, even a floating golf green and indoor golf bays. New owners (one of them a Meier, an old New Melle family name) took over in late 2025, added full table service and a new menu, with a beer garden coming. Wine, bites, music, and golf in one scenic stop.
📍 3960 Highway Z, New Melle, MO 63365

### Die Wasserstelle
The name says it all — Die Wasserstelle is German for "the watering hole," a fitting nod to the village's heritage. It's a pub-style bar and grill doing burgers, chili dogs, wings, and fish tacos — simple, high-quality, with a pet-friendly patio (family-friendly early, adults-only after 9). A good local hang to round out the town.
📍 30 W Hwy D, New Melle, MO 63365

### Make a day of it: the Defiance wine corridor
New Melle's real superpower is where it sits . A short drive south drops you into the Defiance / Femme Osage wine corridor — Defiance Ridge Vineyards, Good News Brewing's Defiance café, and the gateway to the Augusta and Dutzow wineries — with the Historic Daniel Boone Home as the anchor. Eat in New Melle, then chase the afternoon into wine country.

### Why this little town matters
New Melle is a 540-person German village that most maps treat as a dot — but it keeps a beloved bar-and-grill (now lovingly carried on in its founder's name), a genuine quarry-side destination, and a German-named watering hole, all minutes from one of Missouri's best wine corridors. That's a real community, and the honest, human stories behind these places are exactly what a national app will never show you.

What's the story behind Liz's Bar & Grill?
Original owner Liz Holloway ran it for nearly 30 years until her passing in early 2025; her friend Zach King reopened it in October 2025 to carry on her name. (Ignore any old "closed" listings — it's back and well-reviewed.)

By Lane Forman , Founder of St Louis Near Me Directory Local restaurant guides, researched and maintained · Updated June 2026 
Part of South County — explore the whole region in our South County restaurant guide .
Oakville is far South County — Telegraph Road running down toward Jefferson Barracks and the Mississippi — and like a lot of the suburbs out here, the highway frontage is chain-heavy. But Telegraph hides a genuine core of long-running, family-owned rooms: a 50-year Italian institution, the family next door that claims to have invented the trashed wing, and a barbecue-and-pizza spot doing crab rangoon pizza and German dumplings in the same kitchen.
From a half-century Gianino family room to brisket egg rolls, here's where to eat in Oakville.
The independents cluster on Telegraph Road (63129) — or one block off it at the Gianino family plaza (Telegraph and Yaeger). It's a compact local scene surrounded by chains, so for broader range, Oakville blends into Mehlville and greater South County just north and west. Several spots run cheap daily specials.

### Bill Gianino's Restaurant
Bill Gianino's has anchored Oakville Italian since 1975 — home-cooked pastas, St. Louis-style pizza, steaks, and toasted ravioli. Founder Bill passed in 2020, but his sons still run it: over 50 years in the same family. The town's longest-running name.
📍 4571 Chestnut Park Plaza, Oakville, MO 63129

### Frankie G's Grill & Bar
Frankie G's is the Gianino family's grill-and-bar right next to the flagship — open since 1991, and it claims to be the inventor of the "trashed wing." Two family concepts side by side in one plaza.
📍 4565 Chestnut Park Plaza, Oakville, MO 63129

### Crusoe's Restaurant & Croc's Sports Bar
Crusoe's is the family-owned casual American spot and sports bar tucked in the Oakville Shopping Center — breaded wings, the Crusoe's Party Sub, chicken fettuccine, and toasted ravioli. The neighborhood living-room kind of place.
📍 5591 Oakville Shopping Center, St. Louis (Oakville), MO 63129

### Garvey's Grill
Garvey's is the true corner neighborhood joint that's been pouring and grilling 25-plus years — wings (voted among the best in St. Louis), St. Louis-style Chicken Modiga pizza, and "Super Dave's Smokers" house barbecue, with a $4.95 burger-and-fries Monday special.
📍 5647 Telegraph Rd, St. Louis (Oakville), MO 63129

### Las Fuentes Mexican Restaurant
Las Fuentes has served the area since 1996 — Northern Mexican, with tacos al pastor, sizzling fajitas, and house-made margaritas. The vibrant, family-friendly go-to Mexican on Telegraph for nearly 30 years.
📍 6025 Telegraph Rd, Oakville, MO 63129

### Nubby's Telegraph
Nubby's is the locally owned barbecue-and-pizza spot owner Matt Hines opened in 2021 in a long-vacant space — smoked ribs and burnt ends, but also the talked-about crab rangoon pizza and brisket egg rolls, plus down-home German plates like dumplings with sauerkraut. The wild-card menu of the strip.
📍 6039 Telegraph Rd, St. Louis (Oakville), MO 63129

### Oakville Sports Pub
Oakville Sports Pub is the neighborhood's game-day living room — a wall of HDTVs for Cardinals, Blues, and Mizzou, the Billy Burger, ravioli pizza, and classic St. Louis thin-crust with the Provel-and-Monterey-Jack blend. Open late on weekends.
📍 6348 Telegraph Rd, St. Louis (Oakville), MO 63129

### Why this town matters
Oakville's a compact local scene hemmed in by chains — but the Telegraph Road independents are the real thing: a 50-year family Italian room, a trashed-wing inventor, and a barbecue kitchen sneaking German dumplings onto the menu. The apps bury them under franchise logos; we map Telegraph.

### FAQ
What's the best restaurant in Oakville, MO?
The longest-running local name is Bill Gianino's (since 1975), still family-run, paired with sister spot Frankie G's next door. For wings, Garvey's; for a wild menu, Nubby's.
Where's the independent food in Oakville?
Almost all of it is on Telegraph Road (Garvey's, Las Fuentes, Nubby's, Oakville Sports Pub) or one block off at the Gianino plaza (Telegraph and Yaeger). Telegraph is the main artery.
Is Oakville family-friendly for eating out?
Yes — Crusoe's and Las Fuentes are explicitly family-owned, family-friendly rooms, and several spots run cheap daily specials (Garvey's $4.95 Monday burger).
Where's more variety near Oakville?
Oakville borders Mehlville and Lemay, with Jefferson Barracks Park at its southern edge — a few minutes north or west on Telegraph or Lemay Ferry opens up the wider South County scene.

A family Italian dinner at Bill Gianino's, wings at Garvey's, and a crab-rangoon-pizza curveball at Nubby's. For more local spots across South County, explore St Louis Near Me Directory .

By Lane Forman , Founder of St Louis Near Me Directory Local restaurant guides, researched and maintained · Updated June 2026 
O'Fallon, Illinois is one of the fastest-growing communities in the Metro East — a railroad-and-coal town platted in 1854, named for a wealthy St. Louisan, and shaped for over a century by nearby Scott Air Force Base. (Quick note: this is O'Fallon Illinois , not its Missouri namesake.) All that growth brings chains, but the genuine independents are here — anchored by a downtown wood-fired pizzeria with its own brewery and a beloved mother-daughter bakery café.
From craft-beer pizza to a charcuterie wine bar, here's where to eat in O'Fallon.
The best independents sit in the historic downtown district (Cherry, First, and State Streets), with a few out on the Green Mount / Regency commercial corridor. A couple are weekday-focused, so check first. Time it for the O'Fallon Fall Festival , the town's signature event.

### Peel Wood Fired Pizza & Brewery
Start downtown. Peel does award-winning wood-fired Neapolitan-style pizza alongside its own Peel Brewing Company craft beer — blistered pies and house brews in a lively downtown room. The flagship of O'Fallon's independent scene.
📍 104 S Cherry St, O'Fallon, IL 62269

### Sweet Katie Bee's Bakery Café
Sweet Katie Bee's is the mother-daughter-owned bakery café — French and American pastries, all-day breakfast, lunch, espresso, and plenty of vegan, allergy-friendly, and keto options. Eleven-plus years downtown and deeply community-minded.
📍 131 E First St, Ste B, O'Fallon, IL 62269

### Shooter's Bar & BBQ
Shooter's is the family-owned downtown sports bar and BBQ — slow-smoked meats, Southern sides, fried chicken and catfish, and 30-plus local brews. The casual game-day hang.
📍 113 E First St, O'Fallon, IL 62269

### Boarding House Bistro
Boarding House Bistro is the vintage-charm bistro and wine bar — elevated charcuterie boards , classic cocktails, wine, bourbon, and American small plates. A more grown-up downtown evening.
📍 212 E State St, O'Fallon, IL 62269

### Wahaka Margarita Bar & Grill
Wahaka is the independent Mexican bar-and-grill — crafted margaritas (the blueberry-rosemary gets named), tacos, and wings. Newer, highly rated, and a fun night out.
📍 1405 N Green Mount Rd, Ste 100, O'Fallon, IL 62269

### La Casa Mexicana
La Casa Mexicana is the dependable everyday sit-down Mexican spot — a full menu and a loyal local following. The reliable taco-and-fajita option.
📍 1222 Central Park Dr, Ste 101, O'Fallon, IL 62269

### Andria's Restaurant
Andria's is the award-winning independent steakhouse that's anchored O'Fallon since 1978 — hand-cut steaks with its signature steak sauce, a genuine local institution and a great special-occasion pick.
📍 O'Fallon, IL 62269

### Why this little town matters
O'Fallon grew fast enough that the chains crowd the corridors — which is exactly why the downtown independents matter: a wood-fired pizzeria with its own brewery, a mother-daughter bakery café, a family BBQ sports bar, a charcuterie wine bar, and a 1978 steakhouse. That's the real O'Fallon, and the national apps fly right over it.

By Lane Forman , Founder of St Louis Near Me Directory Local restaurant guides, researched and maintained · Updated June 2026 
O'Fallon is one of the metro's biggest suburbs — and no, not the Illinois one. This is O'Fallon, Missouri , in St. Charles County, where the food runs from a Highway K Italian room named for the chef's father in Aversa to a historic Main Street brewpub pouring barrel-aged beer. Between the breweries downtown and the independents along Highway K, there's a lot more here than the strip-mall surface suggests.
From a family Italian tribute to a Peruvian ceviche worth the drive, here's where to eat in O'Fallon, MO.
Two pockets: the Highway K / WingHaven corridor (63368) and historic downtown on South Main Street (63366), which anchors the brewery scene. A few of the best are dinner-only or closed Mondays. And yes — this is O'Fallon Missouri ; there's a separate O'Fallon, Illinois 40+ miles east, so always check the ZIP.

### Osteria Forto
Osteria Forto is O'Fallon's top-rated independent Italian — chef-owner Dominic Pietoso named it for his father, Chef Fortunato “Forto,” who grew up in Aversa, Italy, and runs it with his wife Elizabeth as a family tribute. Rigatoni Cardinale with shrimp and lobster is the order. Dinner only, closed Sunday and Monday.
📍 2509 Highway K, O'Fallon, MO 63368

### Los Incas Peruvian Restaurant
Los Incas is the family-owned Peruvian spot from a kitchen team with 20 years of experience in Peru — bright ceviche with toasted cancha corn and choclo, and a lomo saltado that co-owner Luis Moreno says he could eat every single day.
📍 4279 Keaton Crossing Blvd, O'Fallon, MO 63368

### The Brass Rail Steakhouse
The Brass Rail is the locally owned steakhouse-and-tavern that's been an O'Fallon staple for years — hand-cut steaks and classic American bar fare, where regulars come for the bar as much as the ribeye.
📍 4601 Highway K, O'Fallon, MO 63368

### Goodwood Brewing & Spirits
Goodwood anchors downtown O'Fallon's Main Street in a historic building (the former McGurk's Public House) — barrel-aged beers, chicken and waffles, and a flower-and-water-feature patio with live music. It's a Kentucky-rooted brewery brand, but this is O'Fallon's Main Street brewpub.
📍 108 S Main St, O'Fallon, MO 63366

### Crossroads Brewery
Crossroads is the locally owned WingHaven brewery running about 30 taps — house beer, cider, mead, even house-made seltzer and margaritas — plus a deep bourbon shelf and standouts like the Dragon Ass Oatmeal Stout. The local craft-beer hub.
📍 9995 Winghaven Blvd, O'Fallon, MO 63368

### CJ's Restaurant & Bar
CJ's is the genuine small family-run neighborhood spot on Highway K — American-Italian plates that read like someone's home kitchen, with a full bar. Closed Mondays. The unfussy local pick.
📍 2974 Highway K, O'Fallon, MO 63368

### The Irish Gypsy
The Irish Gypsy is the independent Irish pub and sports-bar-and-grill open 11 a.m. to 1:30 a.m. daily — making it O'Fallon's go-to late-night kitchen when most of Highway K has gone dark.
📍 1250 Bryan Road, O'Fallon, MO 63366

Old Monroe is genuinely tiny — a couple hundred people on the Hwy 61 / Hwy C stretch of Lincoln County between Moscow Mills and Winfield — and its food scene is exactly two spots. Both are locally owned bar and grills, no chain in sight, and that's the charm of a small river town, not a knock. People in Old Monroe get hungry too, and when you want a burger and a cold one close by, these are it — plus the closest spots a short drive away.
From an oversized pork tenderloin to a Saturday-night live-music dive, here's where to eat in (and near) Old Monroe.
Old Monroe (63369) has two genuine in-town restaurants, both bar and grills. Kitchen hours run shorter than the bar hours, so call ahead for a late bite. For more variety, Moscow Mills (~5 min southwest) and Winfield (~10 min northeast) are the nearest hubs, with Troy a bit farther. Name trap: "Monroe City, MO" is a different town ~140 miles away near Hannibal — this is Old Monroe in Lincoln County.

### Main Street Bar & Grill
The downtown anchor. Main Street Bar & Grill is the classic small-town hangout — burgers, a pork tenderloin sandwich locals say could feed two, a crappie (fish) dinner, and a Sunday breakfast — with lotto and keno going and servers the regulars know by name. Budget-friendly; bar runs late Fri–Sat, kitchen closes earlier.
📍 145 Main St, Old Monroe, MO 63369

### Chain Bar and Grill
Chain Bar and Grill (out on Highway OO) leans roadhouse, not family diner — a loaded onion-ring cheeseburger, jumbo fried shrimp, and weekend omelets with notably good gravy, plus live music every Saturday, outdoor seating, and biker parking. A true small-town dive with a stage.
📍 584 State Highway OO, Old Monroe, MO 63369

### Closest spots a short drive away
Old Monroe is small, so for more options the neighbors are close — and these are fresh picks you won't find on our other guides:
- Trax Pizza Company — Winfield (316 E Main St) — locally owned St. Louis-style pizza with a flaky thin crust and good specials.
- Don Julio's — Winfield — the nearest real Mexican option (there's none in Old Monroe itself).
For a full sit-down dinner, Moscow Mills (Harry J's Steakhouse, Chubby's diner) and Troy (Taormina's Italian, Woods Fort) have the most variety — see their guides below.

Old Monroe is a two-restaurant town, and we say so plainly — two locally owned bar and grills, no chains, on a quiet Lincoln County highway. Are there restaurants in Old Monroe, MO?

Where do I go near Old Monroe for more options?

Overland is a working mid-county suburb with a better independent scene than its strip-mall surface suggests. Woodson Road is the spine — a hand-cut-fries diner that's held the same corner for 50-plus years, a Black-owned coffee café, a Taiwanese kitchen run by the cook herself — and the Page Avenue corridor is the Mexican-food destination, anchored by a taqueria that survived a fire and a pandemic to reopen. No fine dining here; just genuine, generous, locally owned food.
From hand-cut diner fries to fire-tested birria tacos, here's where to eat in Overland.
Overland's independents cluster on Woodson Road and the Page Avenue corridor (63114). It shares the 63114 ZIP with St. John and Breckenridge Hills, so a couple of nearby landmarks (Chuck-A-Burger, Nick & Elena's pizza) sit just over the line — we've flagged those as "right next door." Most spots are budget-friendly ($–$$); a few are breakfast-and-lunch only.

### George's Diner
The old-St.-Louis standout. George's is a hand-cut-fries greasy spoon where you can watch the owner cutting fresh potatoes — chicken-fried steak with white gravy, the Slinger Plate, breakfast and lunch only. The diner's held this Woodson Road corner under a few names for over 50 years.
📍 2539 Woodson Rd, Overland, MO 63114

### LaJoy's Coffee Cafe
LaJoy's is the Black-owned, woman-owned coffee café owner LaJoy Dabney opened because nothing was within walking distance of her own Overland home — a dirty chai and a house gooey-butter Danish her daughter bakes, bright yellow walls, made-to-order everything.
📍 8909 Lackland Rd, Overland, MO 63114

### Taqueria Durango
Taqueria Durango on Page is a comeback story — a March fire gutted it, then the pandemic hit, and it fought all the way back to reopen in Overland. Birria tacos, gorditas, free unlimited chips with three salsas, and most people eat for under $10.
📍 10238 Page Ave, Overland, MO 63114

### Chimi's Fresh-Mex
Chimi's is the neighborhood Fresh-Mex favorite — the sizzling Molcajete, steak tacos, chimichangas — pulling 1,800-plus reviews at a single small-suburb storefront, regulars naming their servers by name.
📍 2435 Woodson Rd, Overland, MO 63114

### Kitchen 95
Kitchen 95 is the Taiwanese and pan-Asian spot two restaurant veterans opened in 2021, where the proprietress is also the chef — a small, fresh-ingredient kitchen where the cook owns the place. Closed Wednesdays; call ahead on hours.
📍 2336 Woodson Rd, Overland, MO 63114

Overland's Woodson Road and Page Avenue hide a genuine local scene — a 50-year hand-cut-fries diner, a homegrown coffee café, a fire-tested taqueria, a chef-owned Taiwanese kitchen. Pacific calls itself "Train Town, USA," and it earns it — the rails and old Route 66 run right through the middle of this Franklin County town, past sandstone bluffs pocked with the silica-sand caves that once supplied glassmakers. The historic Red Cedar Inn, a 1934 cedar-post roadhouse, still stands as a Route 66 museum. People pass through on the Mother Road and the interstate; the smart ones stop to eat.
For a town this size, Pacific's food scene is genuinely independent — a 1963 custard drive-in, grass-fed burgers, BBQ with live blues, and a coffee shop that doubles as an open-mic stage. Here's where to eat in Pacific.
The good stuff clusters in downtown along St. Louis Street and 1st Street , just off Route 66, plus a couple of spots out by Lamar Parkway. A few keep limited days (the burger bar closes Wednesdays; the BBQ joint Monday–Tuesday), so check first. Pair a meal with Jensen's Point (the CCC-built bluff overlook over the Meramec) or the Pacific Palisades for a real afternoon.

### Hoffman's Drive-In
Start at the institution. Hoffman's Drive-In has scooped frozen custard and ice cream in Pacific since 1963 — burgers and lunch specials too, but the vintage drive-in and the custard window are the point. A genuine multi-generation local landmark.
📍 306 S 1st St, Pacific, MO 63069

### Off The Rails Burger Bar
Downtown on Main, Off The Rails does gourmet grass-fed burgers — they source beef from Crooked Creek Farm — plus rotating specials in the heart of Train Town. Closed Wednesdays; worth planning around.
📍 100 E St Louis St, Pacific, MO 63069

### Brown Jerry's Blues, Brews and Barbecue
The one with a stage. Brown Jerry's is the slow-smoked BBQ spot founded in 2017 by Jerry Holloway — Southern sides, wood-fired pizza, a full bar, and live blues. Locally voted among the best BBQ around. Closed Monday–Tuesday.
📍 147 W St Louis St, Pacific, MO 63069

### Little Ireland Coffee
Little Ireland Coffee is the downtown coffee-and-bakery spot a block off Route 66 — espresso, biscuits and gravy, pastries, plus open-mic and paint nights. The community gathering corner since 2017.
📍 125 N 1st St, Pacific, MO 63069

### El Agave Mexican Restaurant
El Agave is the locally owned Mexican kitchen just off old Route 66 — handmade tacos, enchiladas, fajitas, and burritos, plus catering. The dependable margarita-and-fajitas pick.
📍 180 Lamar Pkwy, Ste 109, Pacific, MO 63069

### Pacific Brew Haus
Pacific Brew Haus is the craft-beer bar and grill — sandwiches, wings, fish bites, and a solid draft list. (The name says brew; it's a craft-beer bar rather than a production brewery — either way, a good downtown hang.)
📍 220 S 1st St, Pacific, MO 63069

### Pacific Family Restaurant
For the classic plate, Pacific Family Restaurant is the made-from-scratch breakfast-and-lunch diner with daily specials. The honest, everybody's-welcome morning spot.
📍 250 Lamar Pkwy, Ste 101, Pacific, MO 63069

Pacific is a Route 66 town most people only meet through a windshield — but pull off and it's all independents: a 1963 custard drive-in, grass-fed burgers, a BBQ joint with live blues, and a coffee shop with an open mic, wrapped around sandstone bluffs and a 1934 Mother Road roadhouse. Hoffman's Drive-In — a frozen custard and burger drive-in that's been a Pacific institution since 1963.

### C&K Barbecue
The legend. Rib tips, snoots (crisp-baked pig snouts in that sauce), butter-soft pig ears, brisket and ribs. A carryout counter institution; the slogan is literally "Come Taste the Sauce." Closed Tuesdays.

A soul-food spot in Ferguson's walkable downtown, a few minutes north — comfort plates done right, a fresh pick that rounds out the Pine Lawn area honestly.

It's a young village (incorporated in 1962) in the Madison County bottoms near Horseshoe Lake, where the old Route 66 Chain of Rocks Bridge crosses the Mississippi. It blends so completely into neighboring Granite City that even Google can't always tell them apart.
We can. This guide sticks to the real, locally owned spots that are genuinely in Pontoon Beach — and we'll be honest that the town shares a ZIP and a lot of life with Granite City. Here's where to eat in Pontoon Beach.
Heads-up on geography: Pontoon Beach shares ZIP 62040 with Granite City and Mitchell, so map apps constantly mislabel which town a place is in. Everything below is confirmed Pontoon Beach. ### Uncle Linny's Restaurant
Start at the anchor. Uncle Linny's is the family-owned, home-style restaurant locals lean on — breakfast-forward, open early, hearty and unpretentious. It's grown popular enough to add a second spot ("Food & Brews") down the road, but the original on Pontoon Road is the one to know.
📍 4112 Pontoon Rd, Pontoon Beach, IL 62040

### Doit's Village Inn
For the best local-story pick, Doit's Village Inn has been a family-owned neighborhood tavern since 1986 — biker-friendly, big patio, live music several nights a week, and the two things every Metro East tavern lives or dies on: $1–$2 Taco Wednesday and a Friday fish fry .
📍 4015 Pontoon Rd, Pontoon Beach, IL 62040

### Smokey Joe's Tavern
Smokey Joe's comes with real history baked in — the building started as a family home in the early 1940s, became a beloved bar called Zamarioni's, and lived on as the local watering hole before becoming Smokey Joe's. Tavern food, outdoor seating, and a genuine sense of place.
📍 3998 Lake St, Pontoon Beach, IL 62040

### Steel City Cheesecakes
The sweet standout. Steel City Cheesecakes is owner-baker Brooke Maske's independent dessert shop with a drive-through — cheesecakes in every form, plus cinnamon rolls, gooey butter bars, and cannolis, with a soda machine pouring SKI (the regional cult soda) over nugget ice. The "Steel City" name nods to Granite City's steel-mill roots.
📍 4025 Pontoon Rd, Pontoon Beach, IL 62040

### 3 De Mayo Mexican Restaurant
3 De Mayo is the family-run authentic Mexican spot on Highway 111 — full bar, kids' menu, patio, and a loyal local following. The dependable sit-down taco-and-margarita option in town.
📍 3710 IL-111, Pontoon Beach, IL 62040

### Mike Duffy's Pub & Grill
Mike Duffy's has poured pints on Clayton Rd since 1997 — an Irish pub and grill where the toasted ravioli is the St. Louis classic done right and the burgers regularly rank among the metro's best. Open till 1 a.m. (This is the Richmond Heights original of a small local group.)
📍 6662 Clayton Rd, Richmond Heights, MO 63117

### Fozzie's Sandwich Emporium
Fozzie's is a true mom-and-pop with a working vegetable garden behind the shop that feeds its seasonal specials — and it once made Food & Wine 's list of the best sandwich shops in the country. Get "The Animal" or the cheese-stuffed Juicy Lucy, and a hand-spun shake.

### Hank's Cheesecakes
Hank's has been a St. Louis dessert mainstay since 1987 — dozens of cheesecake flavors (plus lunch sandwiches and quiche), the cake generations of locals order for birthdays and holidays. The spot for a treat.
📍 1063 S Big Bend Blvd, Richmond Heights, MO 63117

### Maggiano's Little Italy
Maggiano's anchors The Boulevard's open-air strip directly across from the Galleria — it's a national chain, not a local independent, but it's the headline restaurant of that district and currently its top-ranked. Family-style Italian-American: lasagna, chicken parm. (Labeled honestly as a chain.)

A 30-year landmark. Nachomama's has done family-owned Tex-Mex on Manchester since 1994 — the kind of margarita-and-enchilada spot that becomes a town's muscle memory. Beloved, scrappy, and still going strong.
📍 9643 Manchester Rd, Rock Hill, MO 63119

### Farotto's Pasta & Pizzeria
Here's the deep root: Farotto's has been open since 1956 — one of the oldest continuously running restaurants in the area — doing family-friendly St. Louis-style Italian and toasted ravioli. Seventy years on Manchester is its own recommendation.
📍 9525 Manchester Rd, Rock Hill, MO 63119

### A'mis Italian Restaurant & Pizzeria
A'mis has been a family-owned Italian pizzeria since 1981 , slinging New York-, Chicago-, and St. Louis-style pizza. The dependable neighborhood pizza pick, four decades deep.
📍 9824 Manchester Rd, Rock Hill, MO 63119

### Amighetti's
A St. Louis name since 1916 (born on The Hill), Amighetti's Rock Hill location carries the famous "Amighetti Special" sandwich and Italian deli tradition forward. It's a beloved local institution — a heritage-grade name rather than a one-off original, but exactly the kind of place locals are glad is close.
📍 9631 Manchester Rd, Rock Hill, MO 63119

### Huatulco Mexican Bar & Grill
The newcomer keeping the corner alive: Huatulco opened in the former Hangar Kitchen space with coastal-Oaxacan Mexican — fajitas, street tacos, and handcrafted margaritas. Fresh energy on a stretch that's seen plenty of turnover.
📍 9528 Manchester Rd, Rock Hill, MO 63119

### A historic tavern on the edge: Trainwreck Saloon
Right at the eastern edge of the corridor, Trainwreck Saloon pours burgers and beer in a building dating to 1890 — cited as the oldest continually operated tavern in St. Louis County, with a caboose out in the beer garden. (Its address sits right on the city line, so you'll see it tagged either Rock Hill or Webster Groves — either way, it's a great historic stop.) For a craft taproom proper, neighboring Webster Groves has Perennial on Lockwood.
📍 9243 Manchester Rd, Rock Hill, MO 63119

### Why this little town matters
Rock Hill is a one-stoplight kind of suburb that's lost four notable spots in the last year — and yet the Manchester corridor still holds a 1956 Italian institution, a 1994 Tex-Mex landmark, a 1916 St. Louis deli name, and the county's oldest tavern. That's resilience you'd never see on a national app, which would just show you the chains at the Market at McKnight and miss the history entirely.

What's the oldest restaurant in Rock Hill, MO?
Farotto's Pasta & Pizzeria, open since 1956 — one of the oldest continuously operating restaurants in the area. The 1890 Trainwreck Saloon building (on the eastern edge) is cited as St. Louis County's oldest continually operated tavern.
Is Katie's Pizza in Rock Hill?
Yes — the Rock Hill location on Manchester is chef Katie Collier's original flagship. It's relocating within the same shopping center in 2026, so check the current suite.
What's the Route 66 connection?
Manchester Road through Rock Hill carried the first alignment of Route 66 (1926–1932) — so the whole restaurant corridor sits on the original Mother Road.

By Lane Forman , Founder of St Louis Near Me Directory Local restaurant guides, researched and maintained · Updated June 2026 
Roxana is a tiny Riverbend village — barely 1,500 people — that exists because of oil. Shell opened the Wood River Refinery here in 1918, worker housing sprang up around it, and the town incorporated in 1921, taking its name from Shell's "Roxana Petroleum" company. Most of the village's land is still the refinery. So let's be honest: Roxana is not a restaurant town. But people here get hungry too, and there's one genuine 50-year local gem worth knowing — plus a cluster of great spots a few blocks over in the next towns.
Here's where to eat in and around Roxana.
Roxana proper has essentially one standing independent eatery (a seasonal ice cream stand), so this guide does something honest: it leads with that local gem, then points you to the genuinely good independents just over the line in South Roxana and Wood River — clearly labeled, because those are separate towns. A short drive northwest to Alton gets you the nearest craft breweries.

### Cone Barn
Start with Roxana's own. Cone Barn has been the village's walk-up ice cream and frozen-treat stand since 1975 — root beer floats, banana splits, sundaes, and cones, a genuine 50-year local institution on North Central. It's seasonal (roughly April–September), so catch it while it's open. It's ice cream, not a full meal — but it's the real, year-after-year heart of eating in Roxana.
📍 323 N Central Ave, Roxana, IL 62084

### Just next door in South Roxana: Sparky's Bar & Grill
A block over in South Roxana (a separate village), Sparky's Bar & Grill is the friendly local dive-and-grill — burgers, sloppy joes, pulled pork, fish, and daily specials, with karaoke and weekend live music. The closest sit-down meal to Roxana proper.
📍 1112 Madison Ave, South Roxana, IL 62087

### In neighboring Wood River: King Louie's Drive-In
A few blocks north in Wood River , King Louie's is the 1950s-era classic drive-in — made-to-order foil-wrapped burgers, shakes, and homemade root beer . A genuine Riverbend institution and a perfect "next town over" stop.
📍 315 S 6th St, Wood River, IL 62095

### Also in Wood River: Venecia's Pizza
For pizza, Venecia's in Wood River is the independent pizzeria locals lean on — the easy carryout pick a short drive from Roxana. (Search engines keep mis-filing it under "Roxana," but it's Wood River — and worth the hop.)
📍 1205 E Edwardsville Rd, Wood River, IL 62095

### Why this little town matters
Roxana is the kind of place a national app has no idea what to do with — a one-square-mile refinery village where most of the map is industrial. The honest truth is the table here is short: one beloved 50-year ice cream stand, and a ring of genuinely good independents in the towns next door. Telling you that plainly — and pointing you to the right spots in South Roxana and Wood River — is exactly what a hyper-local directory is for. The refinery built the town; its name comes from a Shell oil company, not (despite local legend) a Dutch queen who never existed.

Is there anywhere to eat in Roxana, IL?
Roxana proper has essentially one standing independent: Cone Barn, a seasonal walk-up ice cream stand on North Central, open since 1975. For full meals, the nearest spots are just over the line in South Roxana (Sparky's Bar & Grill) and Wood River (King Louie's Drive-In, Venecia's Pizza).
What happened to the Dee-Lux Diner in Roxana?
The Dee-Lux Diner appears to have closed — its building was razed/listed for sale — so it's no longer an operating option. Don't count on it.
What's the best burger near Roxana?
King Louie's Drive-In in neighboring Wood River — a 1950s classic with foil-wrapped burgers and homemade root beer.
Why is the town named Roxana?
It took its name from Shell's "Roxana Petroleum Company." Local legend ties it to a "Queen Roxanne" of the Netherlands, but no such queen existed — the company name is the real origin.

By Lane Forman , Founder of St Louis Near Me Directory Local restaurant guides, researched and maintained · Updated June 2026 
Let's be honest about Sauget: it's a tiny (~150-person) industrial-and-nightlife village right across the river from St. Louis, and it's short on sit-down restaurants. But what it does have is genuine and a little legendary — a no-frills worker's diner, a renovated neighborhood bar and grill, a ballpark famous for a donut-bun burger, and a 30-year, 24-hour rock nightclub. People in Sauget get hungry too — here's the real local food, minus the Soulard spots that map apps wrongly file here.
From 6 a.m. hash browns to "Baseball's Best Burger," here's where to eat in Sauget.
Sauget straddles two ZIPs (62201 and 62206), and 62206 is shared with Cahokia/Cahokia Heights — so a "Sauget" tag doesn't guarantee a spot is in the village (Camp Jackson Rd / Range Ln addresses are really Cahokia Heights). The genuine village eateries are the Monsanto Ave / Water St / Mississippi Ave cluster, below. For a full sit-down dinner, Belleville and East St. Louis are minutes away.

### The Diner
The real deal — a classic American worker's diner ranked Sauget's #1, where the hash browns get singled out again and again, alongside a Denver omelet, a Philly cheesesteak, and a cheeseburger and fries. Doors open at 6 a.m. for the industrial-shift regulars; closed Sundays.
📍 401 Monsanto Ave, Sauget, IL 62201

### Unch's Bar & Grill
The most characterful spot in the village — a recently renovated neighborhood bar and grill with a brand-new diamond pool table, Macho Nachos, buffalo wings, toasted ravioli (the St. Louis staple), and garlic cheese fries, plus open-mic night every Sunday. Sits right on the Sauget/Cahokia line on Water St.
📍 103 Water St, Sauget, IL 62206

### The famous stuff: ballpark burgers & Pop's
Two Sauget landmarks worth knowing even though neither is a normal restaurant:
- GCS Ballpark (home of the Gateway Grizzlies) is famous for "Baseball's Best Burger" — the Krispy Kreme Donut Burger , a bacon cheeseburger using a glazed donut as the bun — plus loaded nachos and frozen custard. For much of the year it's the most notable food experience in town.
- Pop's is the legendary 24-hour rock-and-concert nightclub that put Sauget on the map — a nightlife institution for 30+ years, with late-night bar food on weekends (it's a club, not a dining room).

### Why this town matters
Sauget is tiny and industrial, and we frame it honestly: short on sit-down dining, big on a donut-bun ballpark burger and a legendary all-night club, with a genuine worker's diner and a neighborhood tavern holding down the food. That mix is pure Sauget — and exactly the kind of place the chain apps mislabel. We set the record straight.

The Diner on Monsanto Ave — a classic worker's diner ranked Sauget's #1, open at 6 a.m. with hash browns reviewers love. For a beer and bar food, Unch's Bar & Grill on the Sauget/Cahokia line.
What's the famous Sauget food?
The "Krispy Kreme Donut Burger" at GCS Ballpark (home of the Gateway Grizzlies) — "Baseball's Best Burger," a bacon cheeseburger on a glazed-donut bun. Sauget is also home to Pop's, the legendary 24-hour rock nightclub (limited late-night bar food).

Yelp's "Sauget" radius wrongly pulls in Soulard and downtown St. Louis spots across the river. The genuine village eateries are the Monsanto Ave / Water St cluster; Camp Jackson Rd addresses are really Cahokia Heights. For a full dinner, head to Belleville or East St. Louis.

Shrewsbury is barely a square mile — a tidy little inner-ring suburb wedged between Webster Groves, Maplewood, and the city, with a MetroLink stop, a seminary, and not a lot of room for much else. So let's be honest about it: this isn't a town with a dozen restaurants. It's a town where, when you're here and hungry now , you want to know the closest good options — and there are a few genuinely worth knowing.
People in Shrewsbury get hungry too. Here's where to eat without leaving town — and where to head a block or two over the line when you want more.
Shrewsbury packs into about one square mile along Watson Road and Murdoch Avenue , so everything here is close. It shares its 63119 ZIP with Webster Groves, so map apps blur the two — but the spots below are in Shrewsbury proper. ### My Place (Café, Bar & Restaurant)
Start with the real standout. My Place is a genuinely independent spot opened in late 2023 by Sandeep "Sunny" Bhalla — a globe-spanning menu (burgers, Mediterranean kebabs, shawarma, Indian-influenced plates, weekend brunch) in a big, modern room with a self-serve beer wall of 50-plus taps charged by the ounce. 📍 7401 Watson Rd, Shrewsbury, MO 63119

### Pizza World
When you just want a good pie close by, Pizza World is the neighborhood pizza spot — gourmet pizzas, sandwiches, pasta, and salads, with strong local ratings. It's a family-run franchise location (so not a one-off original), but the owner's hands-on and it's a dependable Shrewsbury go-to.

### El Maguey
For the taco-and-margarita craving, El Maguey at Watson Plaza has held down its Shrewsbury corner for nearly three decades — fajitas, margaritas, and the familiar Tex-Mex comfort. It's part of a longtime St. Louis-area family Mexican group rather than a single independent, but it's a genuine local fixture and the closest sit-down Mexican in town.
📍 403 Watson Plaza, Shrewsbury, MO 63119

### Just want more options? Old Orchard is right next door
Here's the honest part: Shrewsbury's own literature admits the restaurant-and-bar scene mostly lives in the towns around it. So if My Place isn't the vibe, the Old Orchard district in Webster Groves is a five-minute drive — a walkable strip of independents (Hwy 61 Roadhouse and more) just over the line. Shrewsbury's strength is that you're minutes from a lot of good food in every direction.

By Lane Forman , Founder of St Louis Near Me Directory Local restaurant guides, researched and maintained · Updated June 2026 
Smithton is a German farm village south of Belleville with a quietly great origin story: it started as two towns — Georgetown and Smithton — facing each other across a shared Main Street, until they merged in 1850. The Turner Society here began as the Georgetown Turnverein in 1867, and for years the town recorded all its business in German. Two centuries of that heritage still hum under the surface of a town of about 4,000.
It's not a fine-dining town, and we won't pretend it is. Smithton is a Main Street of honest bar-and-grills, family pizza, and good carryout — the real food culture of a German farm village. Here's where to eat in Smithton.
Almost everything is on or just off Main Street , so it's an easy little crawl. A couple of spots close Mondays. One honest heads-up: Smithton has no standalone bakery anymore (both town bakeries have closed) and no in-town brewery — so this is a taverns-and-pizza town, and that's exactly how to enjoy it. Come for Smithton Homecoming , the long-running annual festival, if you want the whole village out at once.

### No Jacks Bar and Grill
Start at the town favorite. No Jacks is the American sports bar-and-grill locals rank #1 — known for Tuesday all-you-can-eat Alaskan snow crab , Thursday specials, and "the best fried chicken around." Under newer ownership since 2022 and still the heart of Smithton's food scene.
📍 4001 IL-159, Smithton, IL 62285

### The Roost Bar & Grill
On the Main Street corner, The Roost is the neighborhood bar-and-grill that owners Terra and Dave rebranded from a long-lived local corner bar. (If your map still calls it "Mikey's Pub" or "CJ's Pub," that's the same building — it's The Roost now.) The classic small-town gathering spot.
📍 102 N Main St, Smithton, IL 62285

### Papa Vito's Pizza
Papa Vito's is the Geoppo family's pizzeria — a locally owned Metro East operation (not a national chain) that opened its Smithton shop in 2022. Garlic cheese bread, a solid Philly cheesesteak, and dependable pies. Closed Mondays.
📍 101 N Main St, Smithton, IL 62285

### Chinese Dragon
Chinese Dragon is the family-owned Chinese carryout — friendly owners, generous portions, and a clean reputation. The reliable takeout answer on Main Street. Closed Mondays.
📍 510 S Main St, Smithton, IL 62285

### Pete's Hard Stop
Pete's Hard Stop is the local bar-and-grill billing itself "coldest beer and best food in town" — a true neighborhood tavern with a real kitchen. The unfussy stop for a beer and a plate.
📍 2 S Main St, Smithton, IL 62285

### Village Pizza To-Go
Village Pizza To-Go is the independent carryout pizza-and-deli spot — no dine-in, just good pies to take home, and a community streak (it runs charity "dine-to-donate" nights for local causes). The grab-and-go option that gives back.
📍 13 S Main St, Ste 1, Smithton, IL 62285

### Why this little town matters
Smithton is a 175-year-old German farm village that most St. Louisans have never once driven through — born as two towns sharing a street, raised on the Turnverein and the German language, and still gathering every year for Homecoming. The food matches the town: honest Main Street taverns, family pizza, good carryout, no pretense. The national apps flatten all of that history into a couple of listings and the gas-station chains. We don't.

What's the best place to eat in Smithton, IL?
No Jacks Bar and Grill — the locals' #1, known for Tuesday all-you-can-eat snow crab and "the best fried chicken around."
Is there a German restaurant or bakery in Smithton?
Not today — despite the deep German heritage, both of the town's bakeries have closed and there's no dedicated German restaurant. The heritage lives on in the Turner Hall, the church and family names, and the annual Homecoming rather than a German menu.
Where do locals get pizza in Smithton?
Two spots: Papa Vito's (the Geoppo family's locally owned pizzeria on Main Street) for dine-in/carryout, and Village Pizza To-Go for carryout only.
What's the story behind Smithton's name?
Smithton began as two villages — Georgetown and Smithton — facing each other across a shared Main Street, then merged under the Smithton name in 1850. Its Turner Society started as the Georgetown Turnverein in 1867.

By Lane Forman , Founder of St Louis Near Me Directory Local restaurant guides, researched and maintained · Updated June 2026 
Part of North County — explore the whole region in our North County restaurant guide .
St. Ann is a North County town built for working people — developer Charles Vatterott threw it up in 1948 as affordable housing for the defense-plant crews flooding into wartime St. Louis, right up against what's now Lambert Airport. The big enclosed mall came and went. The chains lined up along St. Charles Rock Road. But underneath all that, St. Ann kept something better: a layer of genuine, decades-deep mom-and-pop kitchens, several run by immigrant families who've fed this town longer than most of us have been alive.
You have to know where to look — the chains are loud and the good stuff is quiet. So here's where to look. Here's where to eat in St. Ann.
The chain strip along St. Charles Rock Road and Lindbergh is not the story — skip it. The places below are the independents tucked into that corridor and the side streets. A couple are breakfast-and-lunch only (closed by mid-afternoon) and one or two close Mondays, so check hours. If you're catching a flight out of Lambert, several of these are a five-minute detour worth making.

### Acapulco Restaurant & Lounge
Start at the landmark. Acapulco was opened in 1976 by Ernestine Zegar, who came to St. Louis from Oaxaca the year before and started with a 25-seat room — now a 40-plus-year, family-owned institution that a regional magazine flat-out calls a local landmark. Authentic Oaxacan plates, strong margaritas, and the kind of history you can taste.
📍 10114 St Charles Rock Rd, St. Ann, MO 63074

### The Sweet Spot Cafe
The Sweet Spot is a only-in-St.-Ann mashup: donuts and Mediterranean. Owner Mario Badra is a third-generation donut maker who learned the craft in his parents' 1970s shop, then folded in his family's recipes — so you can get a falafel and hummus right alongside a donut voted among the best in the country. Breakfast, lunch, and dinner, all under one delightfully odd roof.
📍 3586 Adie Rd, St. Ann, MO 63074

### Omar's Grill
Directly across Rock Road from Acapulco, Omar's Grill does Halal Mediterranean and Italian — chicken shawarma, gyros, falafel, hummus, and kebabs that have earned a loyal following. Independent, generous, and a genuine destination for the metro's halal diners.
📍 10111 St Charles Rock Rd, St. Ann, MO 63074

### Sunrise Family Restaurant
Sunrise Family Restaurant is the classic family diner — American breakfast served all day with Greek and Italian touches, homemade pies, and a recently freshened-up room. The dependable, sit-down, everybody's-welcome morning spot.
📍 3500 N Lindbergh Blvd, St. Ann, MO 63074

### Brew & Bites Cafe
The newcomer, Brew & Bites is a family-owned coffee-breakfast-and-lunch café that opened around 2024 — a small, friendly independent giving St. Ann a proper local coffee stop instead of another drive-thru chain. (Smaller hours; check before you go.)
📍 3191 Ashby Rd, Ste 2, St. Ann, MO 63074

### La Tejana Taqueria
On the St. Ann–Bridgeton line on Lindbergh, La Tejana is a triple-threat — authentic Mexican restaurant, Hispanic grocery, and a carniceria (butcher) under one roof. It's a genuine destination for tacos and street-style plates, and an experience as much as a meal. (Its address straddles the city line, so you'll see it tagged both St. Ann and Bridgeton — either way, it's worth the stop.)
📍 3149 N Lindbergh Blvd, St. Ann, MO 63074

### Why this little town matters
St. Ann was built fast and cheap for working families in 1948, and that blue-collar DNA is exactly why its food is so good and so overlooked: an Oaxacan grandmother's restaurant turning 50, a third-generation donut maker who added falafel, a halal grill, a Hispanic taqueria-and-butcher. The travel sites fly right over North County. The chain apps only show you the logos on Rock Road. The real St. Ann is in the side-street kitchens.

Acapulco Restaurant & Lounge — opened in 1976 by an Oaxacan immigrant and family-owned for over 40 years, it's been called a genuine local landmark.

St. Ann sits right by Lambert — Acapulco, Omar's Grill (Halal Mediterranean), The Sweet Spot (donuts + Mediterranean), and Sunrise Family Restaurant are all independent and minutes from the terminals.

St. Charles has the most famous Main Street in the metro — ten blocks of 19th-century brick storefronts on the Missouri River, where Lewis and Clark shoved off and where the holiday lights draw crowds every December. A few blocks north, Frenchtown is the quieter, scrappier arts district that's where a lot of the new independent energy is landing. Between the two, you can eat very, very well without a single chain.
From a steakhouse with a rooftop DJ to a firehouse brewpub, here's where to eat in St. Charles.
Two districts: cobblestoned Historic Main Street (the dense, walkable heart) and Frenchtown along North 2nd Street (calmer, newer spots) — both 63301. Parking is mostly free in lots ringing Main Street, but it fills fast during Oktoberfest and the legendary St. Charles Christmas Traditions stretch (day after Thanksgiving to Christmas Eve). A few spots close Mondays.

### Magpie's Cafe
Magpie's is the South Main fixture where the move is to walk in and check the daily quiche board — Quiche Lorraine to artichoke-parmesan, baked that morning — alongside a famous baked potato soup. Bright, casual, patio out front.
📍 903 Main St, St. Charles, MO 63301

### Tony's On Main Street
Tony's is two experiences in one building: a white-tablecloth steakhouse downstairs and “Tony's on Top,” a rooftop bar with a DJ on weekend nights. The steaks come with house steak butter so good they sell it retail. Special-occasion Main Street.
📍 132 N Main St, St. Charles, MO 63301

### Savor
Savor is the tiny, brick-walled American spot the Timme family opened in 2023 inside a 120-year-old building — about 1,000 square feet, 14 bar seats, lantern light, elevated comfort food and handcrafted cocktails. It fills up fast for a reason.
📍 221 N Main St, St. Charles, MO 63301

### Lewis & Clark's American Restaurant
Lewis & Clark's has anchored Main Street since 1985. Climb the steep stairs to the third-floor open-air patio looking out over downtown, and order the Cajun chicken sandwich or the fried catfish. The classic St. Charles view.
📍 217 S Main St, St. Charles, MO 63301

### Bella Vino Wine Bar & Tapas
Bella Vino has been locally owned since 2013 — a curated Italian wine list paired with shareable tapas, and a romantic patio with a firepit and a view down Main Street. Date-night made easy.
📍 325 S Main St, St. Charles, MO 63301

### The Midwestern on Main
The Midwestern is the casual newcomer from the Midwestern Meat & Drink team — scratch-made pub food, handcrafted drinks, open-mic nights and watch parties. The loose, fun end of Main Street.
📍 208 N Main St, St. Charles, MO 63301

### La Belle Vie — The Cafe at Frenchtown
La Belle Vie is the immaculate Frenchtown café regulars call a second home — coffee, crêpes, and breakfast like the Croque Marie and the hash-brown-nest “Lake Bake.” The calm alternative when Main Street is packed.
📍 1200 N 2nd St, St. Charles, MO 63301

### Big Mo's BBQ
Big Mo's is the family barbecue spot that opened in mid-2025 in Historic Frenchtown — slow-smoked pork steak regulars say melts in your mouth, with homemade potato salad and rib tips. New, but already a neighborhood favorite.
📍 1312 N 2nd St, St. Charles, MO 63301

### Good News Brewing Company — Frenchtown
Good News pours small-batch craft beer and wood-fired pizza out of a restored Frenchtown firehouse, with a dog-friendly back patio. It's a small local brewery (a few metro locations) — and this Frenchtown spot sometimes closes for private events, so check before you go.
📍 1121 N 2nd St, St. Charles, MO 63301

St. Charles is a genuine food destination hiding in plain sight — a cobblestoned river Main Street plus a rising Frenchtown arts district, packed with independents from a 1985 institution to a 2025 barbecue upstart. ### FAQ
What's the best restaurant in St. Charles, MO?
For a special-occasion steak, Tony's On Main Street (with a rooftop bar upstairs). For a longtime Main Street classic, Lewis & Clark's. For a hot new small room, Savor.
What's the difference between Main Street and Frenchtown?
Historic Main Street is the cobblestoned, walkable tourist heart with the densest cluster of restaurants. Frenchtown, a few blocks north on N. 2nd Street, is a quieter arts district with newer indies like La Belle Vie, Big Mo's BBQ, and Good News Brewing.
Is parking free on Main Street in St. Charles?
Mostly yes — free lots ring Main Street (a big one by the Lewis & Clark Boat House on the south end). It fills fast during Oktoberfest and Christmas Traditions, so arrive early.
Where do locals get breakfast or coffee in St. Charles?
Magpie's on South Main for the daily quiche, and La Belle Vie in Frenchtown for coffee, crêpes, and a quieter morning.
