### Choosing a yoga class

The style name tells you what the hour is like. Hatha and gentle classes move slowly; vinyasa and power flow link movement to breath and raise the heart rate; Iyengar is precise and uses props; yin holds passive poses for minutes; restorative is fully supported rest. Hot classes are heated, which changes the experience more than the sequence does.

If you are new, look for a beginner or fundamentals series rather than dropping into a flow. Ask what teacher training the studio requires, whether mats and props are provided, and tell the teacher about injuries or pregnancy before class so poses can be modified.

## How Much Does a Roof Replacement Cost in St. Louis? (2026 Numbers)
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-much-does-a-roof-replacement-cost-in-st-louis
Imagine it’s the Monday after one of those spring nights when the sirens went off and the hail came through sideways. Maybe you’re in Affton, or Florissant, or out toward St. Charles. Nothing is obviously wrong from the driveway. But there is grit in the downspout splash block that was not there last week, and a neighbor two doors down already has a yard sign for a roofing company you have never heard of.
By Wednesday you have three estimates. One says $9,400. One says $23,000. One says $6,800 and the salesman wants a signature today. All three walked the same roof.
That spread is the single most disorienting thing about buying a roof, and it is the reason most people feel like they are guessing. So here is the honest version: what a roof actually costs in the St. Louis metro right now, and — more usefully — what makes one number twice another.
### The short answer, with real numbers
Across the St. Louis market, most asphalt shingle replacements land somewhere between $8,000 and $15,000. Published market data puts the metro average around $8,155, with a typical band of roughly $5,433 to $11,032, while other cost trackers put the average closer to $12,056 once larger and more complex homes are folded in.
By roof size, installed asphalt in this market runs approximately:
1,000 sq ft of roof surface — about $4,800 to $7,600
1,500 sq ft — about $7,200 to $11,300
2,000 sq ft — about $9,600 to $15,100
A typical 1970s one-story ranch in St. Louis County — the kind with a simple gable, one chimney and an attached garage — usually sits in the $8,000 to $15,000 window depending on where it falls on the list below. Note that roof surface is not the same as house square footage. A 1,600 sq ft ranch often has closer to 2,000 sq ft of roof once pitch and overhangs are counted, which is why the estimate can look higher than you expected before anyone has tried to overcharge you.
### Why one bid is $9,400 and another is $23,000
Almost always, the two contractors are not selling the same job. These are the variables that actually move the number.
### What is being replaced, versus reused
This is the biggest hidden gap between bids. A roof is not just shingles. It is decking, underlayment, ice-and-water shield at the eaves and valleys, drip edge, flashing where the roof meets walls and chimneys, pipe boots, and ridge ventilation. A cheap bid very often reuses the flashing and the pipe boots, and skips replacing rotted decking beyond a token allowance.
Reused flashing is the most common source of a leak on a brand-new roof. Ask each bidder, in writing, which of those components is new and which is staying. The bids will start to make sense immediately.
### Tear-off versus layover
Going over an existing layer is cheaper today and more expensive later, because nobody can inspect the decking underneath and the second layer traps heat. Many St. Louis municipalities limit or prohibit a second layer outright. A full tear-off costs more and is the correct answer on most homes.
### Pitch, height and complexity
A steep roof needs staging and fall protection and takes longer. Valleys, dormers, skylights, multiple chimneys and roof-to-wall transitions all add labor and all add places for water to find. Two houses with identical square footage can differ by thousands on complexity alone.
### The shingle itself
Three-tab is the cheap end. Architectural or dimensional shingles cost more and last longer. Impact-resistant shingles cost more again — and in a hail market like this one they can lower your insurance premium, which is worth asking your carrier about before you choose.
### Who is standing on your roof
An established local company with employees, a physical address and a decade of local work prices differently from a crew that appeared after the last storm. That difference is not only profit margin. It is workers’ compensation, liability coverage, warranty service you can actually call in five years, and the likelihood that anyone answers the phone when a seam opens up.
Random, but: here’s where to eat in Berkeley.
### The 25% rule, and why your roofer keeps mentioning it
If you have been told you cannot just patch the damaged section, this is usually why. Under the International Residential Code — the model code most Missouri jurisdictions build from — when repairs exceed 25% of the total roof area within any 12-month period, the roof section has to be brought up to current code rather than simply patched. In practice that converts a repair into a replacement-level permitted job.
Two things worth knowing. First, this is a building code interpretation, not an insurance rule — it does not obligate your carrier to fund a full replacement. Second, adoption and enforcement are local. St. Louis City, St. Louis County and the individual municipalities do not all handle it identically, so the answer for Webster Groves is not automatically the answer for O’Fallon. Ask which jurisdiction is pulling the permit and what that office requires.
### What Missouri law now requires of your roofer
This changed recently and a lot of homeowners have not caught up. Since January 1, 2023, under Missouri Senate Bill 326, roofing contractors operating in the state must register with the Missouri Department of Commerce and Insurance — and registration requires proof of liability insurance of not less than $1,000,000.
There is still no single statewide roofing license, and local requirements sit on top of the state registration. Contractors working in the City of St. Louis need a Construction Industry Contractor Graduated Business License through the Office of the License Collector. Workers’ compensation is separately required under Missouri statute for construction employers with three or more employees.
So the practical ask is short. Request the state registration, the certificate of liability insurance, and the workers’ comp certificate — and ask that the insurance certificate be sent directly from the agent rather than handed to you as a photocopy. If someone is doing a $12,000 job on your house and cannot produce those in an afternoon, that is the answer to a different question you were about to ask.
### What a complete estimate itemizes
A bid you can actually compare against another bid will name:
Roof area in squares, and the pitch
Tear-off of how many existing layers, and disposal
Decking replacement — the per-sheet price and how many sheets are included before change orders start
Underlayment type, and where ice-and-water shield is going
New drip edge, new flashing, new pipe boots — each stated as new or reused
Ventilation, and whether intake and exhaust are being balanced rather than just adding ridge vent
Shingle manufacturer, line and color
Two separate warranties: the manufacturer’s on materials, and the contractor’s on workmanship, with the years stated
Permit, and who pulls it
Cleanup, including a magnet sweep for nails
The decking line is where surprise money lives. Nobody can see the decking until the old roof is off, so a good contractor includes an allowance and a stated per-sheet rate. A bid with no decking language at all is not cheaper. It is just less finished.
### Storm damage and the insurance conversation
This metro gets hail, and hail brings out-of-town crews. A few things that keep homeowners out of trouble:
Your insurer decides what it owes based on its own adjuster’s inspection. A contractor who guarantees a particular claim outcome before the adjuster has been on the roof is telling you something about themselves. Be careful with any arrangement offering to absorb or waive your deductible — that is not a discount, and in Missouri it can create real legal exposure for both parties.
Get the scope in writing before signing anything, and be cautious about contracts that bind you to whatever the insurance company eventually approves without a stated price. If a roof genuinely needs replacing, it will still need replacing next week, after you have had time to read the paperwork.
### Timing, and what it does to price
Late spring through early fall is peak season here, and peak season is peak pricing — especially in the weeks right after a significant hail event, when demand spikes and every reputable crew is booked. Late fall and winter installs are possible in St. Louis and often cheaper, with the caveat that asphalt shingles need adequate temperature to seal properly, so a good contractor will talk to you about hand-sealing in cold weather rather than pretending the season does not matter.
If your roof is not actively leaking, getting bids in the off-season and scheduling ahead is the cheapest lever most homeowners never pull.
### A reasonable way to run the decision
Three bids from established local companies. Ask each the same short list of questions: what is new versus reused, how much decking is included and at what rate, which underlayment and where, what the workmanship warranty covers and for how long, and who pulls the permit. Then compare the three bids on those answers rather than on the bottom line.
The middle bid usually wins, not because middle is a strategy, but because the low bid is normally missing components and the high bid is normally selling an upgrade you may or may not want. Once you can see which components are in each price, the right choice tends to become obvious without anyone needing to pressure you into it.

If water has already found its way in, basement waterproofing in St. Louis is the companion piece. And if you are buying rather than maintaining, what a St. Louis home inspection does and does not cover is worth ten minutes before you write the earnest money check.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is the 25% rule for roofing?
A.  Under the International Residential Code, when repairs exceed 25% of the total roof area within a 12-month period, that roof section must be brought up to current code rather than patched — effectively turning a repair into a replacement. It is a building code interpretation, not an insurance guarantee, and enforcement varies by municipality.
### Q. How much does it cost to put a shingle roof on a 2000 sq ft house?
A.  For roughly 2,000 sq ft of roof surface, expect about $9,600 to $15,100 installed for asphalt in this market. Watch your starting number: a 2,000 sq ft house usually has more than 2,000 sq ft of roof once pitch and overhangs are counted, so ask for the roof area in squares rather than assuming.
### Q. What is the cheapest time of year to get a new roof?
A.  Late fall and winter are generally cheaper than peak season, and the worst pricing follows a major hail event when demand spikes. Cold-weather installs work here, but asphalt shingles need adequate temperature to seal, so ask how the crew handles sealing in cold conditions.
### Q. How to tell if a roofer is lying?
A.  Ask for three documents and watch what happens: the Missouri Department of Commerce and Insurance registration, a certificate of liability insurance sent directly from the agent, and workers’ compensation coverage. Then ask which components are new versus reused. Anyone guaranteeing an insurance outcome before the adjuster has been on the roof, or offering to absorb your deductible, is telling you something useful about themselves.
### Q. Should a 20 year old roof replace?
A.  Not automatically. A 20-year-old architectural shingle roof in St. Louis may have life left if it was well ventilated and has no storm damage, while a 20-year-old three-tab roof on a poorly vented attic is often done. Age is a prompt to get it inspected, not a verdict on its own.
### Q. Is $30,000 too much for a roof?
A.  For a typical St. Louis asphalt replacement, yes. Most land between $8,000 and $15,000, and roughly 2,000 square feet of roof surface runs about $9,600 to $15,100 installed. Thirty thousand is a different job — slate, tile, standing-seam metal, a steep multi-level roof, or structural repair bundled in. Ask which.
### Q. Does a 20 year old roof need to be replaced?
A.  Not automatically. Architectural asphalt is generally rated 25 to 30 years and three-tab closer to 20, so at twenty years condition matters more than the number. Curling edges, granule loss collecting in the gutters, and daylight visible in the attic are the real signals. An inspection costs a fraction of a replacement.
### Q. What time of year is the cheapest to replace a roof?
A.  Late winter and early spring, when crews are least busy. Demand spikes after summer storms and stays high through fall, and that is when both scheduling and pricing tighten. If the roof is not actively leaking, booking in the slow season buys you time to collect three real bids instead of signing the first one.

## How Much Does Tree Removal Cost in St. Louis? (2026 Numbers)
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-much-does-tree-removal-cost-in-st-louis
Imagine a Saturday in Webster Groves, or Florissant, or out past Wildwood. The silver maple that shades half the back yard dropped a limb the size of a canoe during the last storm, and it missed the garage by about six feet. Nobody was hurt. But now you are standing in the yard looking up at the rest of that tree differently than you did last week.
You call three tree services. One quotes $850. One quotes $2,400. One will not give a number over the phone at all and wants to come look. That spread is normal, and it is not because two of them are trying to cheat you.
Here is what tree work actually costs in the St. Louis metro, and what makes one quote three times another on the same tree.
### The short answer
Tree removal in St. Louis averages around $1,300, with most jobs landing between $500 and $2,200 depending on height and access. Straightforward removals often run $550 to $1,000. Large or genuinely difficult jobs — a big oak leaning over a house, or anything requiring a crane — can reach $6,000.
Stumps are usually priced separately. Stump removal commonly runs $60 to $350, and grinding ranges roughly $75 to $1,000 depending on diameter, root spread and how much grinding depth you want.
That separation matters when you compare quotes. A cheap removal price that leaves a stump in your lawn is not the same job as a slightly higher price that takes the stump with it.
### What actually sets the price
### Height and trunk diameter
The single biggest driver. A 20-foot ornamental is a couple of hours with a chainsaw and a chipper. A 40-foot hardwood is a different job requiring a climber or a bucket truck, rigging, and rope-lowering the limbs in sections. A 70-foot oak with a trunk you cannot get your arms around is a different job again.
### What is underneath it
This is the variable most homeowners underestimate. A tree standing alone in an open back yard can often be felled in one piece — fast and cheap. The same tree twenty feet from a house, over a fence, beside a garage, or under power lines has to come down in pieces, each one roped and lowered. That can double or triple the labor for an identical tree.
### Access
Can the truck and chipper get to the tree, or does every limb get carried through a gate by hand? Many older St. Louis neighborhoods have deep, narrow lots with no rear alley access, and that alone moves a quote several hundred dollars.
### Condition
Counterintuitively, a dead or storm-damaged tree often costs more than a healthy one, not less. Dead wood is unpredictable to climb and unsafe to rig from, so the crew has to work from a bucket or bring in a crane. Anything already leaning toward a structure gets priced for the risk it carries.
### What happens to the debris
Chipped and hauled away, chipped and left as mulch, or cut to firewood length and stacked. Ask which one you are buying. Leaving the wood on site can reduce the price, and taking the chips as mulch is worth asking about if you have beds to fill.
Totally unrelated — but St. Ann’s restaurant lineup is worth a look.
### The ash borer problem, which is specific to here
Emerald ash borer has been positively identified in the City of St. Louis, and it has been working through the metro’s ash population for years. If you have an ash tree, this is likely the conversation you are having whether you know it or not.
Two things are worth understanding. Treatment is only viable on trees that are still reasonably healthy — once canopy loss is significant, treating is money spent on a tree that is going to come down anyway. And a dead ash gets brittle fast, which is exactly the condition that pushes removal into the higher price bracket. The cheapest version of this decision is the one made early.
On permits: the City of St. Louis Forestry Ordinance (Ordinance 68607) requires a Permit to Maintain for work on any City tree — the ones in the right-of-way, not yours. For ash trees on private property, no permit is required to treat or remove. But if a private ash dies or becomes hazardous, it is subject to a nuisance violation under the same ordinance and the city can order it removed. Surrounding municipalities set their own rules, so if your tree is anywhere near the street, confirm whose tree it actually is before anyone starts cutting.
### What a written quote should actually say
The quotes that cause arguments later are the ones that say remove tree — $1,400 and nothing else. A quote you can hold someone to names:
Which tree, described well enough that there is no ambiguity — species, rough height, and where it stands
Whether the stump is included, and if so ground to what depth
What happens to the wood and the brush — hauled, chipped and left, or cut and stacked
Whether the crew is repairing lawn damage or ruts from equipment
Proof of general liability and workers’ compensation, with policy dates that cover your job
Who is responsible for calling in utility locates before any stump grinding
That last one gets skipped constantly and it matters. Grinding a stump means putting a spinning wheel into ground that may contain gas, water, electric or fiber lines. Missouri 811 locates are free and legally expected before that kind of digging. A company that shrugs at the question is not a company you want operating that machine near your service lines.
### When removal is not the answer
Not every alarming-looking tree needs to come down, and the cheapest outcome is sometimes no removal at all.
A tree that dropped a limb in a storm may simply have had a weak union that can be pruned out, with a cable installed to support the remaining leaders. A tree with surface roots lifting a walk is often a paving problem rather than a tree problem. Deadwood in an otherwise healthy canopy is normal for mature hardwoods and gets pruned, not felled.
What genuinely does argue for removal: significant trunk decay or a cavity through the main stem, a lean that has changed recently with soil heaving on the opposite side, root damage from nearby excavation, more than about half the canopy dead, or an ash that is already past treatable. Those are structural problems that pruning does not solve.
This is the reason it is worth having a certified arborist look before you accept a removal quote from a company that only does removals. The two are not the same conversation, and the second one is more expensive by default.
### Insurance, licensing and the question people forget to ask
Tree work is genuinely dangerous, and this is the one trade where hiring the cheapest quote can create real exposure for you. Ask for two certificates: general liability and workers’ compensation, sent directly from the agent rather than handed over as a photocopy.
The reason is blunt. If an uninsured cutter is hurt in your yard, the question of who pays does not stay theoretical. Missouri requires workers’ compensation coverage for construction employers with three or more employees, and a legitimate tree company carries both policies as a cost of doing business. A crew that cannot produce them is quoting low because they are carrying less.
Ask also whether a certified arborist is involved, particularly if the question is whether the tree needs to come down at all. A company that only removes trees will tend to find that trees need removing.
### Timing, and the cheapest time of year
Late winter is generally the cheapest window in St. Louis. Demand is lowest, crews have gaps in the schedule, and with the leaves down a climber can see the structure of the tree clearly. Dormant-season work is also better for the tree if you are pruning rather than removing.
The most expensive time is the week after a major storm, when every crew in the region is booked and out-of-town outfits appear with door hangers. If your tree is not an active hazard, waiting out that surge will save you real money.
On pruning specifically: avoid heavy cuts on oaks between roughly April and July, when oak wilt transmission risk is highest in Missouri. That is a genuine horticultural constraint, not a scheduling preference.
### Getting a fair price without being difficult about it
Three written quotes, and make sure all three cover the same scope: removal, stump, debris, and cleanup. Most of the apparent price differences you will see are scope differences.
There is normally some room to negotiate, and the honest levers are these: schedule flexibility, letting the crew leave the wood, combining several trees into one visit, or booking in the off-season. What does not work — and tends to end badly — is pushing a company below its insurance costs.
If cost is the barrier, it is worth asking whether your municipality has a program. Some St. Louis-area cities run cost-share or assistance programs for hazardous trees or ash removal, and some offer help for older residents on fixed incomes. It is not universal and it is rarely advertised, so call the city forester or public works department and ask directly rather than assuming the answer is no.

And if you are trying to prevent the next one rather than clean up the last one, storm-proofing your trees is the maintenance side of the same subject.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How big of a tree to charge $1000 for removal?
A.  Roughly a medium hardwood in the 30 to 50 foot range with reasonable access and nothing valuable underneath it. The same tree standing over a house, a fence or power lines can easily double that, because it has to come down in roped sections rather than being felled in one piece.
### Q. What is the cheapest time of year for tree removal?
A.  Late winter. Demand is at its lowest, crews have schedule gaps, and with the leaves down a climber can read the structure of the tree properly. The most expensive time is the week after a major storm, when every crew in the region is booked solid.
### Q. Can seniors get free tree cutting service?
A.  Sometimes, but it is local and rarely advertised. Some St. Louis-area municipalities run cost-share or assistance programs for hazardous trees, ash removal, or older residents on fixed incomes. There is no blanket statewide program, so call your city forester or public works department and ask directly rather than assuming.
### Q. Is it cheaper to have a tree cut down or trimmed?
A.  Trimming is almost always cheaper in the moment, and it is the right answer when the tree is structurally sound and the issue is clearance or deadwood. It is the wrong answer when the trunk is compromised or the tree is dying, because you pay for the trimming now and the removal later anyway.
### Q. What months should you not trim trees?
A.  In Missouri, avoid heavy pruning on oaks from roughly April through July, when oak wilt transmission risk is highest. Dormant-season pruning in late winter is generally best for the tree. Storm damage and genuine hazards are the exception — those get handled when they happen.
### Q. What is a fair price for cutting down a tree?
A.  In St. Louis the average is around $1,300, with most removals landing between $500 and $2,200. A straightforward tree in an open yard often runs $550 to $1,000. Anything leaning over a house, or needing a crane, can reach $6,000. Stump grinding is billed separately, usually $75 to $1,000.
### Q. How much does it cost to cut down a 40 ft tree?
A.  A 40-foot tree standing clear in an open yard usually falls in the straightforward band, roughly $550 to $1,000. The number climbs fast if it leans over a house, sits near power lines, or needs a crane. St. Louis removals average around $1,300 overall, with most jobs between $500 and $2,200.
### Q. How to negotiate tree removal?
A.  Get three written quotes that itemize takedown, haul-away and stump work as separate lines, then compare the lines rather than the totals. Ask specifically whether grinding is included — it commonly runs $75 to $1,000 on its own. Bundling several trees into one visit, and booking off-season, is where real movement happens.

## How Much Does a Plumber Cost in St. Louis? (2026 Rates)
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-much-does-a-plumber-cost-in-st-louis
Imagine it’s a Sunday evening in Affton and the basement floor drain is backing up every time someone upstairs runs water. Not a flood. Just an inch of grey water and a smell that tells you this is not going to resolve itself by Monday.
You call the first number that comes up. Somebody answers, which is a relief, and says there is a service call fee and the technician can be there in ninety minutes. Nobody mentions a price for the actual work.
That gap — between the fee you agreed to and the number on the invoice — is where most plumbing bill anxiety lives. So here is what plumbers in the St. Louis metro actually charge, what the fee is buying, and how to tell a fair invoice from a padded one.
### The short answer
Plumbing labor in St. Louis generally runs $75 to $125 an hour for routine work during business hours. Master plumbers and larger companies with dispatch and warranty overhead sit higher, commonly $100 to $200 an hour.
Evenings, weekends and genuine emergencies change the math: $150 to $300 an hour is normal for after-hours dispatch.
The service call fee runs $50 to $200, and on most residential jobs that fee covers the first hour of work rather than being a pure trip charge. Ask which it is when you book. That one question resolves most of the surprise.
### Why hourly rate is the wrong thing to compare
Two companies quote you $95 and $165 an hour. The cheaper one is not automatically cheaper, because you are not buying hours — you are buying a finished repair.
A well-equipped plumber who arrives with the right parts on the truck, diagnoses in ten minutes and is gone in ninety costs less at $165 than someone at $95 who spends an hour diagnosing, leaves for parts, and comes back. This is routine, not hypothetical, and it is why hourly comparisons mislead.
Most established companies have moved to flat-rate pricing for common jobs for exactly this reason: a set price for a toilet rebuild, a disposal swap, a water heater install, regardless of how long it takes. Flat rate protects you from a slow technician and protects them from a difficult house. When a company offers both, flat rate is usually the safer choice for anything routine.
Random, but: St. John’s whole food scene is one click away.
### What common St. Louis jobs actually run
Approximate all-in ranges, parts and labor, for this market:
Clogged drain, accessible — roughly the service call plus an hour
Main line snake or auger — several hundred, more if a cleanout has to be dug
Sewer camera inspection — a few hundred, and worth every dollar before you authorize any digging
Toilet replacement — labor is modest, the fixture drives the total
Garbage disposal swap — usually about an hour plus the unit
Water heater replacement, 40 to 50 gallon gas — commonly $1,200 to $2,500 installed, with tankless conversions running well above that once gas line and venting work is included
Burst or frozen pipe repair — highly variable, because access is the cost
Old St. Louis housing stock adds its own line items. Galvanized supply lines that crumble when disturbed, cast iron drains that are original to a 1920s brick two-family, and clay lateral lines that tree roots have found are all common here and all turn a small job into a bigger one. A plumber who has worked this housing stock will tell you that before starting, not after.
### How the labor number is actually built
Homeowners often assume the hourly rate is the plumber’s wage. It is not, and understanding the difference makes the invoice easier to read.
The billed rate covers the technician’s wage and payroll taxes, the truck and its stock, general liability insurance, workers’ compensation, licensing and continuing education, drive time between calls, the person answering the phone, and the warranty on the work. On a typical residential shop the technician’s actual wage is a fraction of the billed hour.
That is not a defense of high prices — it is the reason a suspiciously cheap hourly rate is worth a second look. A rate well under market usually means something on that list is missing, and the item most often missing is insurance.
### How to tell if you are being overcharged
Rather than guessing at whether a number is fair, look at process. The signals that matter:
You got a price before the work started. On anything beyond a diagnostic hour, you should be told the cost and asked to approve it. A plumber who works first and prices afterward has removed your ability to say no.
The invoice separates parts from labor. A single lump sum with no breakdown is not something you can evaluate or dispute.
The diagnosis matches the repair. Being told the whole main line needs replacing without a camera being run down it is the single biggest red flag in residential plumbing. Insist on seeing the footage — a legitimate company will show you the screen.
Nobody is manufacturing urgency. Real emergencies exist: an active leak, no water, sewage backing up. Most other things can wait until you get a second quote, and pressure to sign tonight for a discount that expires tonight is a sales technique, not a plumbing assessment.
They are licensed and insured, and can prove it. Ask for the certificate of liability insurance direct from the agent. Licensing in this metro is handled municipally — the City of St. Louis and St. Louis County both license plumbers, and requirements differ across surrounding municipalities — so ask specifically where they are licensed and whether they pull the permit for work that requires one.
### Emergency versus tomorrow morning
The after-hours premium is real and often doubles the rate. Deciding well saves real money.
Call now for: water you cannot shut off, sewage entering the living space, no water at all in the house, a water heater leaking from the tank body, or any smell of gas — and for gas, leave and call the utility first.
It can generally wait for: a single slow drain, a running toilet, a dripping faucet, low pressure at one fixture, or a small drip you can catch in a bucket with the supply valve closed.
Knowing where your main shutoff is, before you need it, is what converts many emergencies into Monday morning appointments. In much of the older St. Louis housing stock it is in the basement near the front wall where the line enters the house. Find it on a calm day and make sure it turns.
### The St. Louis-specific problems that drive bills up
Every metro has its own plumbing failure modes, set by the age of the housing and what is under the ground. Here, four come up again and again.
Clay lateral lines and tree roots. The sewer lateral running from the house to the main is the homeowner’s responsibility, and in much of the city and inner county it is original clay tile with mortared joints. Roots find those joints. The result is a line that snakes clear, works for eight months, and backs up again. Snaking treats the symptom; a camera tells you whether you are looking at annual maintenance or a lateral that needs lining or replacing. Some municipalities run a lateral repair program funded by a small charge on the sewer bill, which is worth checking before you pay out of pocket.
Cast iron drain stacks. Original to a great many pre-war brick homes here. They rust from the inside out, so a stack can look sound and be paper-thin at the bottom. Failures tend to appear as a damp basement wall rather than an obvious leak.
Galvanized supply lines. Common in homes built before the 1960s. They corrode internally, which shows up as poor pressure at upstairs fixtures long before anything leaks. The relevant cost fact is that galvanized often cannot be disturbed without breaking — a simple faucet replacement can turn into a repipe of that run.
Freeze-thaw. St. Louis winters swing across freezing repeatedly rather than staying cold, which is harder on pipes than a steady freeze. Hose bibs, unheated crawl spaces and pipes run through exterior walls are the usual casualties, and the resulting repair cost is mostly access — opening a wall or ceiling to reach the break.
### Getting a fair price without a bidding war
For an emergency you generally take who can come. For anything planned, three quotes is right, and the way to make them comparable is to insist all three quote the same scope in writing — the fix, the parts, the permit if one is needed, and the warranty on the labor.
Ask about the warranty specifically. A year on workmanship is common and reasonable; thirty days suggests a company that expects to be argued with. Ask who pulls the permit on anything involving gas, a water heater, or a sewer line, because unpermitted work becomes your problem when you sell the house.
And ask what happens if the diagnosis changes once a wall is open. A good answer is that work stops and you are called with a revised price before anything else happens. A bad answer is silence followed by an invoice.

### Q. What is a normal call out fee for a plumber?
A.  Fifty to two hundred dollars during business hours. After-hours and weekend call-outs are higher, and a declared emergency dispatch can carry a premium on top of the hourly rate. A company that will not state the call-out fee on the phone is one to skip.
### Q. How do you calculate labor cost for plumbing?
A.  Either hourly or flat rate. Hourly in this market runs about $75 to $125 for routine work and $100 to $200 for master plumbers and larger shops, rising to $150 to $300 after hours. Flat rate prices the job rather than the clock, which is usually the safer choice for common work because a slow diagnosis stops being your problem.
### Q. How to tell if your plumber is overcharging you?
A.  Judge the process, not just the number. You should get a price before work begins, an invoice that separates parts from labor, and evidence for any big-ticket diagnosis — nobody should recommend replacing a main line without running a camera and showing you the footage. Manufactured urgency and discounts that expire tonight are sales tactics, not assessments.
### Q. What is the normal cost to replace a hot water heater?
A.  For a standard 40 to 50 gallon gas unit, commonly $1,200 to $2,500 installed in this market, depending on the unit, venting, and whether code upgrades like an expansion tank or new shutoff are needed. Tankless conversions run considerably higher once gas line sizing and venting are accounted for.
### Q. What is the labor cost to install a 50 gallon hot water heater?
A.  Labor alone typically accounts for several hundred dollars of that total — usually a two to four hour job for a straight swap. It climbs when the old unit is in a tight basement corner, when venting has to be reworked, or when the existing connections are galvanized and crumble on removal, which is common in older St. Louis homes.
### Q. What is the hourly rate for a plumber in Illinois?
A.  The Illinois side of the St. Louis metro shares the same labor market as the Missouri side, so the ranges here apply: roughly $75 to $125 an hour for routine daytime work, $100 to $200 for master plumbers and larger shops carrying dispatch and warranty overhead, and $150 to $300 after hours.
### Q. Why do plumbers charge so much to replace a water heater?
A.  The tank is the smaller half of it. A standard 40 to 50 gallon gas replacement commonly runs $1,200 to $2,500 installed here, and the spread is venting, permits, and code upgrades like an expansion tank or a new shutoff. Add haul-away of the old unit and several hours of licensed labor.
### Q. How much does Home Depot charge to replace a hot water heater?
A.  Big-box installation is subcontracted to local plumbing crews, so the number tracks your market and the crew rather than a national price list. In St. Louis a standard 40 to 50 gallon gas replacement lands at $1,200 to $2,500 installed either way. Ask what the quote excludes — permits, venting and haul-away are common carve-outs.

## How Much Does an Electrician Cost in St. Louis? (2026 Rates)
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-much-does-an-electrician-cost-in-st-louis
Imagine you have just bought a brick two-family in south St. Louis, or a 1950s ranch out in Overland. The inspection came back fine on the big things. But there is a line in the report about the electrical panel being at capacity, and a note that some of the original wiring is still in place.
Nothing is broken. The lights work. But you would like to add a circuit for the garage, and the first electrician who looked at it said the panel has to be dealt with first.
Here is what electrical work actually costs in the St. Louis metro, what makes one quote double another, and what the age of your house adds to the bill.
### The short answer
Electricians in St. Louis generally bill $35 to $105 an hour depending on experience and the shop’s overhead, with journeymen at union scale in this market earning roughly $48 to $58 an hour plus benefits — which is why a billed rate at the top of that range is not automatically padding.
The job most homeowners are actually pricing is a panel upgrade. Replacing a service panel runs $800 to $4,000, and a 200-amp upgrade typically lands at $1,300 to $3,000. Budget a full day: eight to ten hours is normal for a panel swap including the new main breaker, circuit breakers, labor and materials.
Small jobs are usually priced flat or as a minimum call. Changing an outlet or a switch is rarely billed at true hourly cost, because the trip is the expense, not the twenty minutes of work.
### Why quotes vary so much on the same panel
A panel upgrade sounds like one job and is actually several, and the difference between a $1,300 quote and a $3,500 quote is usually what else has to happen.
Is the service entrance being upgraded too? Moving from 100 amps to 200 amps often means a new meter socket, new service entrance cable, and coordination with Ameren for a disconnect and reconnect. That is a materially bigger job than swapping the panel alone.
Is the grounding system current? Older homes frequently have grounding that no longer meets code — a single ground rod where two are required, or a bond to a water line that has since been partly replaced with plastic. Bringing it current is not optional on a permitted upgrade.
How many circuits are being reused versus replaced? A quote that reconnects existing circuits to a new panel is cheaper than one replacing deteriorated cable at the panel end. Ask which you are buying.
Are AFCI and GFCI breakers included? Modern code requires arc-fault and ground-fault protection on many circuits, and those breakers cost several times what a standard breaker costs. A panel quoted with all standard breakers may simply be a panel that will not pass inspection.
Where is the panel? A panel in an open basement is straightforward. One in a finished closet, or one that has to be relocated because its current position no longer meets clearance requirements, is not.
Totally unrelated — but here’s what Swansea, IL has to eat.
### What old St. Louis wiring adds
The metro’s housing stock is old, and three wiring systems come up constantly.
Knob and tube. Common in homes built before roughly 1950 and still present in plenty of city brick homes. It has no ground conductor, its insulation embrittles with age, and it is genuinely dangerous when buried in blown-in attic insulation. Partial rewiring commonly adds $1,000 to $3,000 on top of a panel upgrade, and a whole-house rewire is a much larger number. It is also worth knowing before you call: some insurers will not write a policy on a house with active knob and tube.
Aluminum branch wiring. Used in homes built roughly 1965 to 1973. It is not inherently unsafe, but the connections at outlets and switches loosen over time and can overheat. The accepted repair is not a rewire — it is properly rated connectors at every device, which is labor-heavy but far cheaper than replacing the wiring.
Two-prong outlets with no ground. Extremely common in older St. Louis homes. Replacing them with three-prong outlets without adding a ground is both unsafe and against code. The legitimate fixes are running a proper ground, or installing GFCI protection and labeling the outlets accordingly.
None of this means an old house is a problem house. It means the quote for a job in a 1920s brick home is not comparable to the same job in a 1998 build, and a quote that ignores the difference is a quote from someone who has not looked.
### Licensing, permits and why they matter here
Missouri does not issue a statewide electrical license — it is handled municipally, and the St. Louis metro is a patchwork. The City of St. Louis, St. Louis County and individual municipalities each set their own licensing and permitting rules, so the relevant question is not whether an electrician is licensed in general but whether they are licensed where your house is and can pull the permit there.
Panel upgrades and service changes require a permit and an inspection essentially everywhere in the metro. This is not bureaucratic box-ticking. Unpermitted electrical work surfaces at resale, can complicate an insurance claim after a fire, and leaves you with no independent verification that the work was done correctly.
Ask for the license number and the certificate of liability insurance, and ask directly who pulls the permit. An electrician who suggests skipping the permit to save money is offering you their risk, not their savings.
### What a quote should itemize
Panel make, model and amperage, and whether the service entrance is included
Breaker count and type, with AFCI and GFCI called out specifically
Grounding and bonding work required to meet current code
Utility coordination for disconnect and reconnect, and who arranges it
Permit and inspection, and who pulls it
How long power will be off
Drywall and patching — whether they repair or leave openings
Warranty on workmanship, with the term stated
That drywall line surprises people. Many electricians close the wall and many do not, and a quote that leaves patching to you is not directly comparable to one that includes it.
### The jobs homeowners actually call about
Panel upgrades get the attention, but most calls are smaller. Rough expectations for this market:
Adding a circuit. A dedicated 20-amp circuit for a garage freezer, a window unit or a home office is one of the most common requests. Cost is driven almost entirely by the run — how far from the panel, and whether the path is open basement joists or finished wall. An open path is a couple of hours. A finished wall means fishing cable, cutting access holes, and someone patching afterward.
EV charger installation. Increasingly the reason people discover their panel is full. A Level 2 charger needs a dedicated 240-volt circuit at 40 to 60 amps, which many older St. Louis services simply cannot spare. That is why an EV charger quote so often arrives bundled with a panel upgrade — it is not an upsell, it is arithmetic.
Ceiling fans and fixtures. Straightforward when a box already exists and is rated for the weight. A fan going where only a light was requires a fan-rated box, which usually means attic or ceiling access.
Whole-house surge protection. A panel-mounted device, usually installed in an hour, and worth asking about in a region that gets the storms this one does.
Diagnosing a breaker that keeps tripping. Billed as troubleshooting time rather than a fixed price, because nobody knows what it is until they find it. A tripping breaker is doing its job — the fault is real and it is worth finding rather than resetting indefinitely.
### Saving money without cutting corners
The legitimate levers are mostly about batching and access. Group several small jobs into one visit so you pay one trip rather than four. Do the demolition and patching yourself if you are able, and say so up front so it is priced out. Schedule non-urgent work off-peak rather than in the week after a storm when every crew is chasing outages.
What does not save money: skipping the permit, hiring someone unlicensed for a job that requires a license, or accepting a panel quoted entirely with standard breakers when code requires arc-fault protection. Each of those defers a cost rather than removing it, and defers it to the least convenient possible moment — a failed inspection, a resale, or an insurance claim.
### When the panel is the real answer
Homeowners often arrive wanting one circuit and leave having been told they need a panel. That is sometimes an upsell and sometimes simply true, and the difference is usually visible.
Signs the panel genuinely is the constraint: no empty breaker spaces left, tandem breakers already doubled up in slots that were not designed for them, a main breaker rated 100 amps or less in a house that has since gained central air and a second kitchen appliance load, or a panel brand with a documented safety history — Federal Pacific Stab-Lok and Zinsco panels both turn up in St. Louis-area homes and both are widely considered replace-on-sight by electricians and home inspectors.
Signs it may not be: the panel has open slots, the main is already 200 amps, and the request is a single low-draw circuit. In that case adding the circuit is the whole job, and a quote that insists otherwise deserves a second opinion.
If you are unsure, a load calculation settles it with arithmetic rather than opinion. Any competent electrician can perform one, and it is worth asking for before authorizing several thousand dollars of work.

### Q. What is a fair price for an electrician?
A.  Judge the scope, not the rate. For a 200-amp panel upgrade, $1,300 to $3,000 is the normal band in St. Louis, and the spread inside it is explained by whether the service entrance, grounding, AFCI and GFCI breakers and permit are included. A quote well under that band is usually missing one of those.
### Q. How much do electricians charge to change an outlet?

A.  For planned work, get three quotes on identical written scope and compare what is included rather than the bottom line. Confirm the electrician is licensed in the municipality where your house sits, that the permit is theirs to pull, and that liability insurance can be verified with the agent. Those three checks eliminate most of the risk.
### Q. What do most electricians charge per hour?
A.  Nationally and locally the working range is similar — roughly $35 to $105 an hour for residential work, varying with licensing level, whether the company carries a warranty and dispatch overhead, and time of day. After-hours and emergency calls carry a premium, as in every trade.
### Q. How much wire for a 1500 sq ft house?
A.  A full rewire of a house that size typically consumes well over a thousand feet of cable across all circuits, but the wire is a small share of the cost — labor and drywall access dominate. That is why partial rewires targeting knob and tube or specific problem circuits are often the sensible middle path rather than doing the whole house at once.
### Q. How much should I pay my electrician per hour?
A.  In St. Louis, residential electricians generally bill $35 to $105 an hour, depending on licensing level and whether the shop carries warranty and dispatch overhead. Journeyman union scale here runs about $48 to $58 an hour plus benefits, so a billed rate near the top of that range usually reflects a licensed, insured crew.
### Q. Why are electricians so expensive?
A.  Most of the bill is not the person in your basement. Licensing, liability insurance, bonding, a stocked truck, permit fees and warranty work all sit inside the rate. That is why the $35 to $105 an hour spread exists here — the low end is often unlicensed and uninsured, which is a different product, not a better price.
### Q. What is a reasonable day rate for an electrician?
A.  Work it back from the hourly. At $35 to $105 an hour, an eight-hour day lands between roughly $280 and $840 before materials and permits. Shops quoting a flat day rate usually sit in the middle of that. If a day rate comes in well under it, ask who is actually doing the work and whether they are licensed.

## How Much Does a Concrete Driveway Cost in St. Louis? (2026 Prices)
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-much-does-a-concrete-driveway-cost-in-st-louis
Imagine the driveway at a 1960s house in Crestwood, or Ferguson, or St. Peters. It has been cracking for years and you have been ignoring it, the way everyone does. Then one winter the crack becomes a step you can catch a toe on, a corner starts to sink toward the garage apron, and it stops being cosmetic.
Three contractors come out. The quotes are $4,200, $7,900, and one that just says driveway replacement with a number and no detail at all.
Here is what concrete flatwork actually costs in the St. Louis metro, and why our particular dirt makes the base prep matter more than the concrete.
### The short answer
Concrete driveways in St. Louis generally run $7 to $12 per square foot installed for a standard broom-finish slab, with the full local range spanning roughly $6.75 to $20 depending on finish and site conditions.
For a typical two-car driveway of 400 to 600 square feet, expect about $2,700 to $7,300 installed.
If an old driveway has to come out first, demolition and haul-away adds roughly $1.40 to $6 per square foot depending on thickness, whether it is reinforced, and how far the truck has to be from the work.
Decorative finishes carry a premium: stamped patterns and exposed aggregate typically add $2 to $5 per square foot over a broom finish.
### Why the base matters more here than the concrete
This is the part that separates a driveway that lasts thirty years from one that cracks in four, and it is largely invisible once the job is done.
Much of the St. Louis region sits on expansive clay soil. Clay holds water, swells when wet, and shrinks when it dries out. Over a St. Louis year — wet spring, dry August, repeated freeze-thaw cycles rather than one steady freeze — that ground moves considerably. A slab poured directly onto undisturbed clay with no compacted base is being asked to bridge soil that will not hold still.
A proper job excavates below the slab, brings in several inches of compacted aggregate base, and compacts it in lifts rather than dumping it and driving over it once. That base is the difference between a driveway that settles evenly and one that cracks along the line where the fill was loose.
When one quote is $3,000 under another, the base is frequently where the money went missing. It is also the one part you cannot inspect afterward, which is why it is worth asking about before rather than after.
Random, but: Waterloo, IL’s dinner options are right here.
### What else moves the number
Thickness. Four inches is standard for cars. Six inches is the right answer where a truck, an RV or a dumpster will sit, and at the garage apron where turning loads concentrate. Thickness is a direct materials cost and an easy place for a low bid to hide.
Reinforcement. Wire mesh is the budget option and only works if it is actually lifted into the middle of the slab rather than left on the ground. Rebar on chairs costs more and behaves better. Fiber-reinforced mix helps with surface cracking but is not a substitute for steel.
Concrete strength. Ask what PSI mix is being poured. Exterior flatwork in a freeze-thaw climate should be a properly air-entrained mix — the tiny air bubbles give freezing water somewhere to expand, which is what prevents surface scaling. A cheaper non-air-entrained mix will look identical on day one and start flaking after a couple of winters.
Control joints. Concrete cracks; the only question is whether it cracks where someone decided or where it felt like it. Joints should be cut at sensible spacing, generally within a day of the pour, and to about a quarter of the slab depth. A quote that does not mention jointing is a quote from someone not thinking about cracking.
Drainage and slope. Water has to run away from the house and the garage. On a flat lot that can mean regrading, and on a sloped one it can mean a trench drain. Getting this wrong is expensive to fix later and is a common cause of a wet garage.
Access. If the truck can back to the forms, the pour is fast. If concrete has to be wheeled or pumped — common on narrow city lots or where the drive is behind the house — labor climbs.
### Concrete versus asphalt, honestly
Asphalt is cheaper up front, typically by a meaningful margin, and it goes in faster. It also needs sealing every few years and softens in August heat, and its usable life in this climate is generally shorter than concrete’s.
Concrete costs more initially and asks for very little afterward beyond keeping joints sealed and being sensible about de-icing salt. On a house you intend to keep, concrete usually wins on total cost over its life. On a rental or a short hold, asphalt can be the rational choice.
One genuine warning for this region: rock salt and similar chlorides are hard on concrete, especially on a slab less than a year old. Sand for traction on new concrete through its first winter.
### What a quote should itemize
Square footage, and the slab thickness being poured
Removal and disposal of the existing surface, if any
Depth of excavation and the base material, with compaction stated
Reinforcement type — mesh, rebar, or fiber — and how it will be positioned
Concrete strength and whether the mix is air-entrained
Control joint layout and when they will be cut
Finish: broom, exposed aggregate, stamped
Grading and drainage work
Permit, where the municipality requires one for a driveway or apron
Warranty, and specifically what it says about cracking
On that last point: no honest contractor warrants concrete against all cracking, because concrete cracks. What a good warranty covers is failure — settling, heaving, spalling, and cracks beyond a stated width. A contractor who promises no cracks at all is either inexperienced or telling you what you want to hear.
### Timing and how to save without cutting the base
Spring and fall are ideal for pouring here. Summer pours can be done but need care, because concrete that cures too fast in high heat is weaker at the surface. Winter pours require blankets and admixtures and are best avoided if you can wait.
The honest ways to save: keep the shape simple, since curves and multiple levels cost more than rectangles; choose broom finish over stamped; do several flatwork projects at once so one mobilization covers a drive, a walk and a patio; and schedule in the shoulder season rather than at peak.
The ways that cost you later: thinner slab, thinner base, skipping reinforcement, or a cheaper non-air-entrained mix. Every one of those is invisible at handover and obvious within three winters.
### Repair, resurface, or replace
Replacement is not always the answer, and the three options are genuinely different jobs at genuinely different prices.
Repair makes sense for isolated cracks in a slab that is otherwise flat and sound. Crack filling and sealing is inexpensive and buys years. It does not look invisible, and it does nothing for a slab that is moving.
Mudjacking or polyurethane lifting is the option people most often do not know exists. Where a slab has settled but is not broken up — a driveway panel that dropped an inch at the garage apron, a walk that tipped toward the house — the slab can be lifted back to grade by pumping material underneath it. It typically costs a fraction of replacement and takes a day. On our clay soil, settling without cracking is common, which makes this worth asking about before accepting a tear-out quote.
Resurfacing puts a thin overlay over existing concrete. It works only when the underlying slab is structurally sound and simply looks bad. Over a cracked or moving slab, the overlay will telegraph every one of those cracks within a season or two.
Replacement is the right call when the slab is broken into multiple pieces, when sections have heaved or sunk at different rates, when the surface is scaling and spalling across large areas, or when the drainage is wrong and has to be regraded anyway.
### Questions worth asking every bidder
Four questions sort most quotes quickly. How deep is the excavation and what base material goes in. What thickness and what PSI mix. What reinforcement, and how will it be held up off the ground. Where will the control joints go and when will they be cut.
A contractor who answers those crisply has done this work properly before. One who waves them off as details is telling you which parts of the job they intend to move quickly through, and those are precisely the parts that decide whether you are doing this again in six years.
### Curing, and the first year
Concrete does not dry, it cures — a chemical reaction that keeps gaining strength for weeks. What happens in the first days sets how the surface performs for decades.
You can usually walk on a new slab after a day or so and drive a car on it after about a week, though a contractor pouring in cool weather may ask for longer. Keep trucks, dumpsters and anything heavy off it for a month.
Ask how the slab will be cured. Concrete that dries too fast at the surface — hot sun, dry wind — ends up with a weaker skin that scales later. Curing compound, plastic sheeting or keeping it damp all address this, and a contractor who has a plan for it is one who has watched a summer pour go wrong before.
Through the first winter, use sand rather than salt. De-icing chlorides are hard on all concrete and hardest on concrete less than a year old, and salt damage looks exactly like poor workmanship a few years later.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How much to pour 1000 sq ft of concrete driveway?
A.  Around $7,000 to $12,000 in this market for a standard four-inch broom-finish slab with proper base. Going to six inches for truck or RV parking, or adding decorative finish, pushes it higher. Removal of an existing 1,000 square foot drive typically adds $1,400 to $6,000 on its own.
### Q. Is it cheaper to do a concrete driveway or asphalt?
A.  Asphalt is cheaper to install and faster to complete. Concrete costs more up front but needs far less maintenance and generally lasts longer in this climate. On a house you plan to keep, concrete usually wins over its lifetime; on a short hold or a rental, asphalt can be the sensible call.
### Q. What are the downsides of having a concrete driveway?
A.  Higher upfront cost, longer cure before you can drive on it, and repairs that are harder to make invisible than asphalt patching. It is also vulnerable to de-icing salt, particularly in its first winter — use sand for traction on new concrete. And it will develop hairline cracks; control joints decide where.
### Q. How much should a 20x20 concrete patio cost?
A.  Four hundred square feet at local rates works out to roughly $2,800 to $4,800 for a broom finish, more with stamping or exposed aggregate. Patios can sometimes be poured slightly thinner than driveways since they carry no vehicle load, but the base preparation matters just as much on our clay soil.
### Q. Is it cheaper to pour a concrete patio or use pavers?
A.  Poured concrete is usually cheaper to install than pavers of comparable area. Pavers cost more in labor but are easier to lift and reset if the ground settles — a real consideration on expansive clay. Concrete is lower maintenance; pavers are more repairable. Neither is wrong, they fail differently.
### Q. How much does a 200 ft concrete driveway cost?
A.  It depends whether you mean 200 square feet or 200 feet long. At St. Louis rates of roughly $7 to $12 per square foot installed, a 200 square foot slab runs about $1,400 to $2,400. A driveway 200 feet long and 10 feet wide is 2,000 square feet — closer to $14,000 to $24,000.
### Q. What is the cheapest option for driveways?
A.  Gravel, by a wide margin — it is the least expensive to install and the most expensive to maintain, since it needs regrading and topping up. Asphalt sits in the middle. Concrete costs the most up front at roughly $7 to $12 per square foot installed here, and lasts the longest with the least attention.
### Q. What is the average cost of a 12x12 concrete patio?
A.  A 12x12 slab is 144 square feet, so at St. Louis rates of roughly $7 to $12 per square foot installed you are looking at about $1,000 to $1,730 for a standard broom finish. Stamped or exposed aggregate adds $2 to $5 per square foot on top of that.

## How Much Does Car Detailing Cost in St. Louis? (2026 Prices)
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-much-does-car-detailing-cost-in-st-louis
Imagine the car after a St. Louis winter. Road salt dried in white tide lines along the rocker panels, a windshield cowl full of oak debris from last fall, and something in the back seat that has been there since a Cardinals game in September. It is not a bad car. It just looks like it has been through eleven months of this.
So you look up detailing, and the prices make no sense. One shop says $89. One says $250. One will not quote at all until they see it, and mentions paint correction in a way that suggests four figures.
They are all quoting honestly. They are just quoting different jobs. Here is what detailing actually costs in the St. Louis metro and what separates the numbers.
### The short answer
For a normal daily driver in this market:
Exterior-only detail — roughly $75 to $150. Wash, decontamination, wheels, tires, a wax or sealant.
Interior-only detail — roughly $100 to $200. Vacuum, shampoo or extract carpets and upholstery, clean and condition all surfaces, glass.
Full detail, inside and out — commonly $150 to $400, depending mostly on vehicle size and how rough it is.
Paint correction and ceramic coating — a different category entirely, running $800 to $2,000 depending on vehicle size and paint condition.
Trucks, SUVs and three-row vehicles run higher than sedans across every tier — more surface, more seats, more carpet. Condition matters as much as size: pet hair, smoke odor, spilled milk, and ground-in road salt all add labor, and reputable shops price them as add-ons rather than pretending they do not exist.
### What a full detail actually consists of
This is where the $89 and the $300 stop being comparable.
Exterior on a real detail means a proper wash, then decontamination — a clay bar or chemical treatment that pulls embedded particles the wash leaves behind — then a protective layer of wax, sealant or coating. Wheels and wheel wells get cleaned properly, tires get dressed, exterior glass is polished. Decontamination is the step budget packages skip, and it is the reason a cheap detail feels smooth for a week and then does not.
Interior on a real detail means everything out of the car, a full vacuum including under seats and in the seat tracks, carpets and cloth upholstery shampooed or hot-water extracted, leather cleaned and conditioned, all hard surfaces cleaned including vents and the crevices around the shifter, and interior glass done last.
An express package is essentially a very good car wash with a vacuum and a wipe-down. That is a legitimate product at $60 to $100 — just do not expect it to remove what a winter put into your carpets.
Totally unrelated — but Millstadt, IL eats better than you’d expect.
### Paint correction is not detailing, and it is worth knowing why
When a shop talks about paint correction, they mean machine-polishing the clear coat to remove swirl marks, light scratches and oxidation. It is skilled, slow work, and it physically removes a thin layer of clear coat — which is why it cannot be repeated indefinitely and why it should not be done casually.
A ceramic coating is a semi-permanent protective layer applied afterward. It makes the car easier to wash and holds gloss for years rather than months. It does not make paint scratch-proof, whatever the marketing says.
The reason correction and coating are quoted together is that nobody should seal swirl marks under a coating that lasts three years. The prep is most of the labor, which is why the combined price lands in the $800 to $2,000 range rather than looking like an add-on.
Whether it is worth it depends on how long you are keeping the car. On a lease with two years left, no. On a vehicle you intend to own for a decade, or a dark-colored car that shows every swirl, it can be a reasonable purchase.
### What St. Louis specifically does to a car
Two local realities drive most of the detailing demand here.
Road salt. Our winters swing repeatedly across freezing rather than staying cold, which means more salt applications across a season than a colder, steadier climate would need. Salt is corrosive and it collects in wheel wells, along rocker panels and underneath, where you cannot see it. The most valuable single thing you can do is wash the underside periodically through winter, not just the paint. A spring detail that includes a thorough underside wash is doing real preventive work rather than cosmetic work.
Tree debris and pollen. The metro is heavily wooded and spring is genuinely hard on paint. Tree sap and bird droppings are acidic and will etch clear coat if left through a hot afternoon — that is the actual mechanism behind those permanent-looking dull rings. Getting them off promptly is cheaper than correcting the etching later.
### Mobile detailing versus a shop
Mobile detailers come to your driveway or office lot, which is genuinely convenient and often priced slightly lower given the lower overhead. The trade-offs are real though: they are working in whatever weather and light exist, may need access to your water and power depending on setup, and cannot do work requiring controlled conditions.
Anything involving paint correction or ceramic coating should be done in a shop. Coatings need controlled temperature and humidity to cure properly, and correction needs consistent lighting to see what you are doing. A mobile operator who offers a ceramic coating in your driveway in August is selling you something that will not perform as promised.
For ordinary interior and exterior detailing, mobile is a perfectly good answer and the convenience is worth something.
### Tipping, since everyone wonders and nobody asks
Tipping a detailer is customary but not obligatory, and the normal range is 10 to 20 percent. On a $100 detail that is $10 to $20; on a $200 detail, $20 to $40; on a $300 detail, $30 to $60.
Two useful adjustments. If the owner did the work personally, tipping matters less — they set the price and keep it. If a technician did the work at a larger shop, the tip goes to the person who actually spent four hours on your car, and it lands differently.
And if you handed over something genuinely awful — a car that had a toddler, a dog and a spilled coffee in it — tip toward the top of the range. The person who cleaned it knows exactly what it was.
### Getting a fair price
Send photos when you ask for a quote, honestly. A detailer who sees the real condition can give you a real number, and one who is surprised on arrival will either rush the job or charge more than quoted. Both outcomes are worse than an accurate quote.
Ask what the package includes, specifically: is the clay bar step in there, is it wax or sealant, is carpet shampoo included or an add-on, is pet hair extra. Ask how long they need the car — a real full detail is four to eight hours, and a shop promising a full detail in ninety minutes is describing an express wash.
Ask about insurance too. A detailer works on a valuable asset with chemicals and machine polishers, and a legitimate operation carries coverage for damage. It rarely comes up and it matters when it does.
### How often, and what it costs over a year
Detailing is not a once-and-done purchase, and thinking about it annually makes the money easier to judge.
A common rhythm here is two full details a year — one in spring to strip the winter off, one in autumn to put protection on before the salt starts — with regular washing in between. At $150 to $400 each, that is $300 to $800 a year for a car kept genuinely clean and protected.
The spring one is the important one. Everything a Midwest winter does to a vehicle happens in the places you do not look: salt in the wheel wells, in the seams, on the underside, in the carpet where it came in on boots. A spring detail with an underside wash is the closest thing to preventive maintenance in this category.
If a ceramic coating is in the picture, the annual math changes. The coating costs more up front but reduces what routine washing has to accomplish, and most coatings want an annual inspection or top-up rather than a full re-detail.
### Before you sell the car
This is the one case where detailing pays for itself in a way you can measure. A full detail before listing a used car commonly returns more than its cost in the sale price, and it reliably shortens how long the car sits.
The reason is simple: buyers reading a clean car assume it was maintained, and buyers reading a dirty one assume the opposite — fairly or not. Photographs of a freshly detailed car also draw far more interest online, which is where the sale actually starts.
If you are selling privately, prioritize the interior. Buyers forgive a swirl in the paint far more readily than they forgive a smell.
### Questions worth asking before you book
Five questions separate a real detail from an express wash with a better name, and none of them are confrontational.
How long do you need the car? Four to eight hours for a genuine full detail. Ninety minutes is a wash.
Is decontamination included? Clay bar or chemical decon before any protection goes on. If it is not in the package, the wax is going on over embedded contaminants and will not last.
Wax, sealant or coating? Carnauba wax looks superb and lasts weeks. A synthetic sealant lasts months. A coating lasts years and costs accordingly. All three are legitimate — you just want to know which one you bought.
Is carpet shampoo included or extra? Along with pet hair and odor treatment, this is the most common add-on, and the most common source of an invoice that exceeded the quote.
Are you insured? Rarely asked, occasionally important. Machine polishers and strong chemicals near trim and glass carry real risk, and a professional operation carries coverage for it.
