### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What does a full detail consist of?
A.  Exterior: proper wash, decontamination with a clay bar or chemical treatment, then wax, sealant or coating, plus wheels, wheel wells, tires and glass. Interior: full vacuum including seat tracks, carpet and upholstery shampoo or extraction, leather cleaned and conditioned, all hard surfaces and vents, glass last. Expect four to eight hours.
### Q. How much should I tip for a $100 car detail?
A.  Ten to twenty percent is customary, so $10 to $20. Tip toward the higher end if the car was genuinely rough or if a technician rather than the owner did the work. If the owner-operator set the price and did the job personally, tipping matters less.
### Q. How much do you tip on a $300 car detail?
A.  The same 10 to 20 percent applies, so $30 to $60. At that price point you are usually buying several hours of skilled labor, and if the result genuinely exceeded what you expected, the upper end is well earned.
### Q. Is car detailing worth the money?
A.  For a car you are keeping, yes — particularly in this climate, where road salt and tree sap do real damage rather than just looking bad. A detail that includes a thorough underside wash after winter is preventive maintenance. For a car you are selling, a full detail commonly returns more than it costs in sale price and in how quickly it sells.
### Q. What’s the hardest thing to clean off a car?
A.  Pet hair woven into cloth upholstery, and smoke odor. Both take specialized tools and time, which is why they are priced as add-ons. Close behind: tree sap and bird droppings that have baked in the sun, because those etch the clear coat — at that point it is a paint correction problem rather than a cleaning problem.
### Q. How much should a full detail be?
A.  In this market a full detail, inside and out, commonly runs $150 to $400, driven mostly by vehicle size and how rough the car actually is. Exterior-only work is roughly $75 to $150 and interior-only $100 to $200. An $89 quote is almost always a wash and vacuum, not a detail.
### Q. Is a full detail worth it?
A.  Once or twice a year, usually yes — particularly after a St. Louis winter puts salt into the carpets. At $150 to $400 it is cheaper than most reconditioning and it protects resale. What is not worth it is paying full-detail money for a wash and vacuum, which is what an $89 quote generally buys.
### Q. How much to tip on a $200 car detail?
A.  Fifteen to twenty percent is the common range, so $30 to $40 on a $200 job. Tip the person who actually did the work rather than the front counter, and lean toward the top of the range for a vehicle that took real effort. On owner-operated mobile jobs, many people round the total up instead.

## Working From a Coffee Shop in St. Louis: What to Look For (2026)
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/best-coffee-shops-to-work-remotely-in-st-louis
Imagine it’s a Tuesday and the house is not working. Maybe the internet installer is coming, or there is a toddler, or you have simply been in the same room for nine days and your brain has stopped producing anything useful.
So you pack a laptop and go find a coffee shop. And forty minutes later you are sitting at a wobbling two-top with 14% battery, a wifi captive portal that will not load, and a milk steamer going off every ninety seconds directly behind your head.
The coffee was excellent. The room was simply never built for what you came to do. That mismatch is the entire problem, and it is fixable in about ten seconds of looking — if you know what to look at.
### The five things that decide whether a room works
Forget reviews for a moment. Reviews rate coffee. These rate the room.
Outlets, and where they are. Look along the walls and under the window counters. A cafe with outlets every few feet has decided it wants people to stay. A cafe with two outlets, both behind the counter, has decided the opposite — and that is a legitimate business choice on a small room with a queue.
Table size and stability. A laptop plus a mug plus a notebook needs a real surface. Tiny round bistro tables are designed for two cups and a conversation. If every table in the room is that size, the room is telling you something.
Who is already there. The single most reliable signal. Walk in and look: if three people are working quietly with laptops, you are welcome. If nobody is and it is all pairs talking, you will feel conspicuous within twenty minutes and you will be right to.
Where the espresso machine and grinder are. Grinders are loud and they run constantly. A seat directly behind the bar is a seat you will leave. Aim for the far wall or a corner away from the service line.
Whether there is a posted time limit. Some shops post one at peak hours. It is not hostility — it is arithmetic on twelve seats. Read it and respect it, or come at a different hour.
### The wifi question, asked properly
Nearly every cafe has wifi. The relevant questions are different ones.
Is it fast enough for what you are doing? Email and documents need almost nothing. A video call needs real upload bandwidth, and cafe wifi is frequently asymmetric — fine for watching, poor for being watched.
Is it stable, or does it drop every twenty minutes and make you re-accept a portal? The portal ones are the worst offenders because the drop is silent until something fails to save.
And is it available at all when you need it? Some St. Louis shops turn the wifi off on weekends by design, to keep the room circulating. That is a deliberate, published policy at several places and it catches people out.
The practical answer for anyone working seriously: bring a phone hotspot as a fallback and do not depend on the house connection for anything that matters. Battery too — assume you may not get an outlet.
Random, but: here’s where to eat in East Alton.
### Timing matters more than the shop
The same room can be perfect at 9:40am and unusable at 11:15am.
The reliable working windows are mid-morning on a weekday, roughly 9:30 to 11:30, and mid-afternoon, roughly 1:30 to 4:00. The bad windows are the 7:30 to 9:00 commuter rush, the lunch hour, and essentially all of Saturday and Sunday morning, when the room belongs to people meeting each other and you will be occupying a four-top alone while a queue forms.
Closing time is the other trap. Independent coffee shops in St. Louis close earlier than people expect — a good many are done by mid-afternoon, and planning a 4:30 session can leave you packing up at 3:00. Check the hours for the specific day rather than the general listing, and if you need somewhere later, that is a different search entirely.
### The etiquette nobody writes down
Working from cafes is normal and welcome in most of them. There is an unwritten contract and it is not demanding.
Buy something roughly every ninety minutes. That is the rent. A single drip coffee across four hours is the behavior that makes owners put up time-limit signs.
Take calls outside. All of them. A room full of people can absorb typing and quiet conversation; it cannot absorb one side of a status meeting. Headphones do not solve this, because the problem is your voice, not what you are hearing.
Size your table to your party. One person at a four-top during a rush is the specific thing that annoys everyone, staff included.
Do not rearrange the furniture to reach an outlet, and do not run a cable across a walkway. Ask instead — staff will usually solve it for you.
Tip, and tip on the whole visit. If you have occupied a seat for three hours, the tip should reflect three hours of occupancy, not one $4 drink.
Leave when the room turns. When a queue forms and every seat is taken, that is the signal. Pack up gracefully and you will be welcome next time.
### Which St. Louis neighborhoods suit it
Rather than naming rooms that change, look in the areas where the odds are good.
Midtown and the Central West End have a steady daytime population from the universities and hospitals, which means cafes there are used to people staying and generally equipped for it. Patio seating in the CWE is a genuine asset in spring and autumn.
The Delmar Loop in University City has volume and variety — if one room is full or loud, another is a two-minute walk. Student-heavy, which cuts both ways: laptop-friendly culture, but competitive for seats during term.
Maplewood is the quiet pick. Compact main street, independent shops, and parking that does not require a strategy.
Tower Grove and South Grand are good for a longer, slower session, especially outside weekend brunch hours.
Clayton and DeMun skew quieter and more conversational — better for a working meeting with one other person than for a heads-down solo stretch.
St. Charles, Kirkwood, Webster Groves and Chesterfield all have walkable independent scenes worth knowing if you are already out that way rather than driving in.
### When a coffee shop is the wrong answer
Being honest about this saves a wasted afternoon.
If you have back-to-back video calls, a cafe is the wrong room — for you and for everyone in it. If you need to spread out paper, or work with anything confidential on screen, likewise. If you need a guaranteed seat at a guaranteed time, a cafe cannot promise that.
The St. Louis alternatives are good. Public libraries across the city and county have free wifi, quiet rooms, and in many branches bookable study rooms — genuinely underused by remote workers. Coworking spaces sell day passes if you only need one reliable day. University-adjacent spaces and hotel lobbies in Midtown and downtown are usually happy to sell you a coffee and let you sit.
The best pattern for most people is a mix: cafes for the two-hour focused stretch and the change of scene, a library or day pass for the days that need a door and a guaranteed table.
### What to carry, so the room matters less
A small kit turns a mediocre cafe into a workable one and removes most of the variables you cannot control.
A phone hotspot you have actually tested. Not a theoretical one. Test it once at home so you know the speed and how to turn it on quickly, because the moment you need it is the moment a call is starting.
A power bank sized to your laptop. Modern USB-C banks will run a laptop for hours. It removes the outlet hunt entirely, which is the single biggest constraint on seat choice.
Noise-cancelling headphones. For your own concentration, not for calls. Grinders and steam wands are broadband noise and even modest cancellation flattens them.
A privacy screen if your work is at all sensitive. Cafe seating puts strangers behind you constantly, and the alternative is choosing seats by sightline instead of by comfort.
A short extension or a low-profile plug. Many cafe outlets are behind furniture or awkwardly placed. A one-metre lead solves it without you moving anyone’s table.
### A note on lists that go stale
Any article naming the ten best cafes to work from is out of date within a year. Rooms get refurbished, owners change the wifi policy, a shop adds a back room or removes the communal table, a beloved place closes.
That is why this guide is built around signals rather than names. The five checks — outlets, table size, who is already working, distance from the grinder, posted limits — will still be true in three years, and they work in a city you have never visited.
If you want current names for the coffee itself, the local guide linked above is maintained for that. For the room, trust your ten seconds of looking at the door.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Can I work remotely in a cafe?
A.  Yes, in most St. Louis coffee shops, within an unwritten contract: buy something roughly every ninety minutes, take calls outside, do not occupy a four-top alone during a rush, and pack up when a queue forms and every seat is full. Follow that and you will be welcome back. Ignore it and you are the reason time-limit signs exist.
### Q. What is a WFH cafe?
A.  Shorthand for a coffee shop that deliberately caters to work-from-home customers — plentiful outlets, larger tables, reliable wifi, and often a quieter back room. Some go further with bookable seats or a day rate. The opposite is a shop that keeps tables small and wifi limited on purpose to keep the room circulating, which is equally valid and worth recognizing on sight.
### Q. What are the best places to work remotely?
A.  In St. Louis, a mix works better than one venue. Coffee shops suit a focused two-hour stretch and a change of scene. Public libraries across the city and county offer free wifi, quiet, and bookable study rooms in many branches. Coworking spaces sell day passes when you need a guaranteed desk. Hotel lobbies downtown and in Midtown are a reliable fallback.
### Q. What is remote work anxiety?
A.  The low-grade unease that comes with working outside a structured office — uncertainty about whether you are visible enough, blurred boundaries between work and home, and isolation from working alone. Changing where you work is one of the simplest countermeasures, which is a large part of why cafes and libraries fill with remote workers on weekday mornings.
### Q. Do St. Louis coffee shops have wifi?
A.  Almost universally, but ask the right questions: is the upload speed sufficient for video, is the connection stable or does it drop and force a portal re-login, and is it available at the hour you need it. Some shops switch wifi off on weekends deliberately. Bring a phone hotspot as a fallback and do not rely on the house connection for anything critical.
### Q. Is Kaldi's only in St. Louis?
A.  Kaldi’s Coffee started here and is strongly associated with the city, though its beans reach well beyond it. For working, the roaster matters far less than the room — outlets, table height and whether the grinder runs constantly decide whether you last two hours.
### Q. What is the famous coffee brand from St. Louis?
A.  Kaldi’s is the name most locals reach for, and Chauvin has long roasted here too. Neither guarantees a good place to work though — the same brand can have one branch built for laptops and another built for turnover.
### Q. What is a must eat in St. Louis?
A.  Toasted ravioli, gooey butter cake, and a concrete from a frozen custard stand. If you are working from a coffee shop and want one thing to order, gooey butter cake is the local answer — and it survives a long sit better than anything toasted.

## How Much Does Lawn Care Cost in St. Louis? (2026 Numbers)
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-much-does-lawn-care-cost-in-st-louis
Imagine it’s a Saturday in Affton. The grass got away from you during that rainy stretch in May, the mower is making a noise it did not used to make, and the yard across the street has already been cut, edged and blown twice while you were arguing with a pull cord. So you do what everybody does. You get three quotes.
The first company says $40 a cut and can start Thursday. The second says $65, and will not take the mowing unless you also buy the six-application treatment program. The third gives you one flat monthly number for the whole season and never mentions a per-cut price at all. Same yard, same street, three completely different shapes of answer.
That same thing happens in Kirkwood, in Maryland Heights, out past O’Fallon and down in Oakville, and it is not because two of the three are trying to take you. Lawn care in this metro gets priced four different ways — per visit, per month, per application and per square foot — and until you know which one you are holding, the quotes are not comparable at all. Here is what the work actually costs around St. Louis, and what makes one number nearly double another on identical grass.
### The short answer
A standard residential mow in St. Louis averages about $69 per visit, with most homeowners paying somewhere between $40 and $118 depending on lot size and access. Plenty of local crews quote in a tighter $35 to $85 band for routine weekly work on an ordinary suburban lot.
Full-service lawn care — mowing plus a fertilization and weed program, billed monthly — commonly runs $100 to $410 a month during the growing season. A season of everything, mowing and treatments and aeration and the fall leaf mess, lands most St. Louis households somewhere around $2,000 to $3,400 a year.
Those are wide ranges on purpose. The rest of this is about which end of them you are on, and why.
### What one cut actually costs here
Mowing is priced off square footage first and obstacles second. Around the metro the per-visit tiers look roughly like this:
One-eighth acre (a typical older city lot in Dogtown or Bevo): about $34 to $46
One-quarter acre (most of Affton, Ferguson, Overland): about $46 to $63
Half acre: about $63 to $80
Three-quarter acre: about $80 to $97
Full acre (common out in Wildwood or unincorporated west county): about $97 to $114
Then the yard itself moves the number. A flat rectangle with a wide gate is the cheap version of any size. What pushes a quote up is everything that makes a crew get off the mower: a steep front bank, a retaining wall, swing sets, raised beds, a fence line with a gate too narrow for the commercial deck, trees the crew has to trim around by hand, and dogs.
Is $50 for lawn mowing good? In this market, on a quarter-acre lot with normal access, yes — that is squarely inside the fair band and probably a touch under the metro average. On an eighth-acre city lot it is a little rich. On a fenced half acre with three trees and a slope, $50 is a crew that has not walked the property yet and may revise after the first visit.
Totally unrelated — but Freeburg, IL’s whole lineup is one click away.
### Per-cut pricing versus a seasonal contract
The St. Louis mowing season runs from roughly late March into November, which pencils out to about 26 to 30 weekly visits in a normal year. That number is the whole ballgame, because it is what turns a per-cut price into an annual price.
At $55 a cut, weekly service across a full season is somewhere near $1,500 before a single bag of fertilizer. That is why so many companies would rather quote you a flat monthly figure: it hides the visit count, smooths their cash flow, and it is genuinely easier for you to budget.
It is also where people get surprised. Ask two questions before you sign anything monthly:
How many visits does that monthly number assume, and what happens to my bill in a month when you only come twice?
Is the monthly price for the mowing season only, or is it spread across twelve months including winter?
Every-other-week service looks like the obvious way to cut the bill in half. It usually is not. Skipping a week in May means the crew is removing far more than a third of the blade at once, which shocks the grass and leaves the clippings in rows that have to be bagged or raked. Most companies price biweekly at a premium per visit for exactly that reason, and some will not do it at all during the spring flush.
### How much should lawn treatment cost?
Separate from mowing entirely. Fertilization and weed control is quoted per application, and the honest national range is wide: roughly $77 to $395 per application, with big or badly neglected lawns anchoring the top. A typical residential St. Louis lawn on a bundled program is usually toward the bottom of that, in the neighborhood of $50 to $100 per round.
Bought as a program — and almost nobody sells it any other way — four to six applications a year averages about $289. For a quarter-acre property, annual fertilization commonly totals $260 to $510. Add real weed control to it and a full fertilization-plus-weed program lands most homeowners at $400 to $900 a year. Standalone weed treatments run about $49 to $200 each, and a broadcast herbicide visit is typically $50 to $150.
What you should be getting for that, on a St. Louis calendar, looks something like:
Early spring: pre-emergent for crabgrass, which has to go down before the soil warms, not after you see it
Late spring: broadleaf control for the clover, henbit and violets that clay soil grows beautifully
Early summer: a grub preventive
Midsummer: a light feed and spot treatment, not a heavy nitrogen push
Early fall: the most important feeding of the year for fescue
Late fall: the winterizer that builds root reserves
The grub timing is worth knowing, because it is the one application where being a month late means you paid for nothing. Preventive products built on imidacloprid, thiamethoxam or clothianidin reliably knock down 75 to 100 percent of grubs when they go out between June 1 and July 15 and get watered in with a half inch to an inch of irrigation right after. Chlorantraniliprole products can go down as early as April and actually perform better before June. If a company sells you grub control in September, they are selling you a rescue treatment for damage already done, which is a different and less effective product.
### Aeration and overseeding: the line item St. Louis actually needs
This is the service most homeowners skip and the one that does the most for a lawn in this region. St. Louis sits on heavy clay. Clay compacts, compaction chokes roots, and choked roots are why the thin patch by the driveway never fills in no matter how much fertilizer goes on it.
Core aeration in the St. Louis area books at an average of about $191, with most jobs falling between $130 and $250. Across St. Louis County the broader range runs roughly $99 to $300. Nationally the math works out near $15 to $18 per 1,000 square feet.
Aeration bundled with overseeding — which is how it should be bought if you have fescue — runs about $160 to $425 for 10,000 square feet, with the grass seed itself driving most of the spread. Turf-type tall fescue seed is cheaper than a premium bluegrass blend, and the difference shows up in the quote.
Two things to check before you pay for it. First, that it is core aeration pulling actual plugs, not a spike machine poking holes, because spiking compacts clay further. Second, that it is scheduled for late summer or fall rather than spring, since a spring aeration on a fescue lawn mostly opens the soil for crabgrass right when the pre-emergent barrier you already paid for gets broken.
### Fescue, zoysia, and why your neighbor pays less
St. Louis sits in the transition zone, the strip of the country where it gets too hot for northern grasses and too cold for southern ones. That is why two houses on the same block can have completely different lawn bills.
A tall fescue lawn is the common default here. It stays green longer into the shoulder seasons, which means more cuts, and it thins out every summer, which means it needs overseeding most falls. Fescue is a higher-maintenance, higher-annual-cost lawn.
A zoysia lawn is the other half of the neighborhood. It greens up late, goes tan and dormant from about mid-October until May, grows slowly enough that late-season mowing frequency drops, and it does not get overseeded. Fewer cuts, no annual seed bill. The tradeoff is a lawn that is brown for a long St. Louis winter and a lot harder to repair when something goes wrong in it.
None of that is a reason to switch. It is a reason to make sure the company quoting you knows which grass you have, because a fescue program applied to zoysia is money set on fire, and vice versa.
### The August problem
Every year, some time in late July or August, the metro gets a hot dry stretch and unirrigated fescue goes dormant. The lawn browns, growth stops, and the mowing crew has nothing to cut.
This is the single most common billing dispute in local lawn care, and you can head it off with one sentence in the first conversation: what happens to my bill when the grass stops growing? Reasonable answers are that they skip the visit and do not charge, or that they come anyway to blow the drive and trim the edges at a reduced rate. An unreasonable answer is a full mowing charge for running a deck over dormant grass, which stresses it further.
It also matters for treatments. Heavy nitrogen on drought-stressed fescue in August does damage, not good. A program that is honest about the calendar shifts that feeding to September.
### Leaves: the fall number nobody budgets for
Older St. Louis neighborhoods came with mature oaks, sycamores and sweetgums, and the bill arrives in November. Yard cleanup in St. Louis averages about $342, with most projects between $190 and $571, and fall cleanups specifically run $180 to $560 because leaf volume here is genuinely heavy.
Priced hourly, leaf work runs about $15 to $45 an hour for blowing, $25 to $50 for raking and $40 to $60 for vacuuming, usually plus $5 to $10 per bag for disposal. That per-bag line is where a cleanup quote quietly doubles under a big pin oak.
The lever you control is the number of passes. One cleanup after everything is down is cheapest. Three passes through October and November keeps the lawn from smothering but costs close to three times as much. Mulching the early drop into the turf with the mower — free, and good for the soil — and paying for one thorough pass at the end is usually the best value in the whole season.
If the leaf problem is really a tree problem, that is a different budget. Our breakdown of what tree removal costs in St. Louis covers where that number lands and what drives it.
### What a full year actually adds up to
Put the pieces together for an ordinary quarter-acre St. Louis lawn with weekly mowing:
Mowing, about 28 visits at roughly $55: near $1,540
Fertilization and weed program: $400 to $900
Fall aeration with overseeding: $190 to $425
One thorough fall cleanup: $190 to $560
That is roughly $2,300 to $3,400 for the year, which is the arithmetic behind those $100-to-$410 monthly full-service quotes. Nothing in there is exotic. It is just that the mowing is two-thirds of the total, and the mowing is the part people negotiate least.
What is the average cost of lawn care per month? For most St. Louis households paying for everything, roughly $190 to $285 a month spread across the mowing season. If you are only buying mowing, cut that to the $150 to $220 range. If you are only buying the treatment program and cutting your own grass, it drops to about $35 to $75 a month.
### Making three quotes comparable
Almost every pricing complaint traces back to comparing two numbers that were never measuring the same work. Ask all three companies the same short list:
Is this per visit or per month, and how many visits does a month include?
Does mowing include trimming, edging and blowing the hard surfaces, or are those extra?
Are clippings mulched or bagged, and is there a disposal charge for bagging?
What is the square footage you measured, and did you measure it or estimate from the street?
Is the treatment program separate, and can I buy mowing without it?
What happens in August when growth stops?
Do you carry liability insurance, and are the people on my property employees or subcontractors?
The measurement question is the sneaky one. A quote built off a satellite estimate of a lot includes the house footprint, the driveway and the patio in the square footage. A crew that walked the yard is quoting the turf you actually have.
### Where the money is genuinely negotiable
Some of this bill moves and some of it does not. The parts that move:
Prepaying the season. Discounts in the range of a free cut or two are common, because it solves a cash flow problem for a small crew.
Route density. If you and two neighbors sign together, you are worth more per stop and less drive time. This is the biggest lever most people never pull.
Bagging. Dropping bagging in favor of mulching removes labor and dump fees from every visit.
Doing the edges yourself. Trimming and blowing is a real share of the crew’s time on site.
The parts that do not move much are fuel, insurance and the applicator’s licensing. If a treatment quote is dramatically under everyone else’s, ask who is holding the license for the application, because in Missouri applying restricted products commercially on someone else’s property is a licensed activity.
If you are weighing whether to hand any of this off at all, our look at DIY lawn care versus hiring a pro in St. Louis gets into which jobs are actually worth your Saturday. And if the yard work is really a prelude to redoing the front of the house, what a concrete driveway costs in St. Louis covers the hardscape side of the same project.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How much should you pay somebody to mow your lawn?
A.  About $69 per visit is the St. Louis average, with the normal range running $40 to $118. By lot size, expect roughly $34 to $46 for an eighth of an acre, $46 to $63 for a quarter acre, $63 to $80 for a half acre and $97 to $114 for a full acre. Slopes, narrow gates, heavy tree cover and bagged clippings all push you toward the top of the band.
### Q. Is $50 for lawn mowing good?
A.  For a quarter-acre St. Louis lot with straightforward access, yes — that is a fair price and slightly under the metro average. For a small city lot it is a bit high. For anything approaching a half acre, fenced, sloped or heavily treed, $50 is low enough that you should confirm what is included, because trimming, edging and hauling clippings are often quoted as extras at that price.
### Q. How much should lawn treatment cost?
A.  Per application, the range is roughly $77 to $395, though a standard residential lawn on a bundled program usually falls around $50 to $100 per round. As a program, four to six applications a year averages about $289, a quarter-acre property typically totals $260 to $510 for fertilization, and a full fertilization-plus-weed-control program runs $400 to $900 annually.
### Q. Are lawn treatment services worth it?
A.  In St. Louis, the value is in timing more than product. Two applications genuinely pay for themselves — the early spring pre-emergent that has to go down before soil temperatures rise, and the fall feeding that builds fescue roots before winter. The grub preventive is worth it only if it goes out between June 1 and mid-July and gets watered in. If a program is selling you six visits but missing those windows, you are buying a schedule rather than results.
### Q. Is $100 an hour too much for landscape work?
A.  For one person with a mower and a trimmer, yes, that is high for routine maintenance in this market. For a two-person crew with commercial equipment, insurance and hauling, $100 an hour is normal and often a bargain compared to per-job pricing. Hourly rates make sense for cleanups, bed work and one-off projects. For recurring mowing, insist on a per-visit or per-month price instead, because hourly billing on routine work gives nobody an incentive to move quickly.
### Q. What is the 1/3 rule in lawn care?
A.  Never remove more than one third of the grass blade in a single mowing. Cutting shorter stresses the plant, weakens the roots and lets weeds in. Through a St. Louis summer that means mowing more often rather than lower, which is why routine weekly service at $40 to $118 a visit beats fixing a scalped lawn.
### Q. What is the average rate for mowing a lawn?
A.  St. Louis averages about $69 per visit, with most homeowners paying between $40 and $118 depending on lot size and access. Plenty of local crews quote a tighter $35 to $85 for routine weekly work on an ordinary suburban lot. A one-eighth acre city lot runs closer to $34 to $46.
### Q. Is mowing every 2 weeks enough?
A.  Not through a St. Louis spring. Fescue grows fast enough in April and May that a two-week gap forces you to cut off more than a third of the blade, which stresses the lawn and feeds weeds. Weekly is the right cadence in peak growth; every two weeks works in midsummer heat and late fall.

## What Hair Salon Services Cost in St. Louis (2026 Price Guide)
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-hair-salon-services-cost-in-st-louis
It is a Thursday afternoon in Kirkwood and someone is standing on the sidewalk outside a salon, reading a price list taped to the inside of the window. Cut, it says, from $55. Color, from $95. Balayage, consultation required. She wanted a number before she walked in, and what she got instead was a floor — the smallest amount anyone in that building has ever charged for that service, on the fastest head of hair, with the newest stylist on the schedule. She is standing on the sidewalk doing arithmetic she does not have enough information to do.
Across the metro in Maplewood, a guy who has had the same cut for nine years just paid a little over thirty dollars and handed his stylist a ten because she squeezed him in on a Saturday. A few miles east on the Delmar Loop, a college student is booked for a full head of highlights and has budgeted $120, which is roughly a third of what that appointment is going to ring up once the toner, the bond treatment, and the blow-dry land on the ticket. And out in Florissant, a woman who colored her hair at home two weekends ago is working down a list of salons and getting the same sentence every time: we would need to see it in person first.
Four people, one metro, four completely different relationships with the same set of numbers. Nobody in that story is being cheated. Hair pricing is genuinely confusing — deliberately vague in a few places, accidentally vague in most — and almost none of it gets explained on the website. So here is the explanation, in the order it actually costs you money.
### What a salon appointment actually costs in the St. Louis metro
Start with the honest ranges. These are what services commonly run, and the spread is wide because the spread is real: a dry trim from a newer stylist in a strip-mall suite and a full restyle from a twenty-year colorist in a boutique studio are not the same product, and they will never carry the same price.
Women’s haircut: roughly $40 to $165 across the St. Louis area depending on the salon and the stylist. Nationally the average sits closer to $69, with most cuts falling between $40 and $120.
Men’s haircut: commonly $20 to $50, with the national average around $43.
Root touch-up: about $50 to $100.
Single-process color, all over: about $60 to $150.
Foil highlights: roughly $70 to $150 for a full head, with longer or thicker hair landing at the top of that band.
Balayage: commonly $150 to $350, and it can climb past that on long or previously colored hair.
Toner or gloss: $20 to $60 on top of the color service.
Bond-building treatment: $30 to $80 added to a lightening service.
Blowout or finish styling: $30 to $70, and it is frequently not included in the color price.
Keratin or smoothing treatment: $150 to $600 or more, driven almost entirely by hair length and density.
Extensions: tape-in installs commonly start around $400, and hand-tied work often runs $800 to $1,500 before any maintenance.
That first line is where most of the frustration in this whole category lives. Why are ladies hairdressers so expensive? It is not mystique. A women’s appointment usually bundles a shampoo, a sectioned wet cut, a blow-dry, and finish styling onto longer hair that needs more of every product, and the men’s number on the same menu is often a dry clipper cut with none of that attached. Compare the same service and the gap shrinks fast.
Two other things jump out of that list. The first is that the add-ons are not small. A color appointment with a toner, a bond treatment, and a blow-dry can carry $80 to $200 of services that never appear in the headline price. The second is that the ranges overlap, which means the number on the sign tells you far less than you think it does.
### Why the same haircut has three different prices inside one salon
Most full-service salons in the region price by stylist level, not by service. A cut is a cut on the menu, but the person holding the shears is priced into it. The tiers usually look something like new talent or associate, then stylist or designer, then senior, then master or artistic director.
A new-talent stylist has a cosmetology license and has tested out on the services they are booked for — they are not practicing on you. They are simply early. Senior stylists typically have several years and a stack of continuing education behind them, and they are the ones who take on complicated color. Master stylists are usually eight years and up. The price gap from the bottom tier to the top is commonly thirty to fifty dollars on the same service, in the same room, using the same product.
This matters more than any coupon. If you want a one-length trim and a blow-dry, a lower-level stylist is not a compromise, it is correct budgeting. If you are going from box-dyed dark to lived-in blonde, booking the cheapest chair in the building is how a $180 appointment turns into a $600 repair.
Random, but: Wright City’s food scene is worth a detour.
### How to read a price list that says “from”
When a menu says cut “from $55,” that is a starting price, not an average. It is calculated on the shortest realistic version of that service, performed by the least expensive stylist, on the least demanding hair. Almost nobody pays the from-price.
Here is what silently moves the number up:
Length and density. Nearly every salon has a long-hair or thick-hair upcharge, sometimes posted, often not. More hair means more product and more time.
Stylist level. Covered above, and it is usually the single largest variable.
Bowls of color. Some salons charge per bowl or per tube once a formula exceeds the standard amount, and long, dense hair routinely needs a second bowl.
Whether styling is included. A cut price that ends at a rough dry may be twenty-five dollars cheaper than one that ends with a finished blowout. That is not a trick, it is a different service.
Add-ons offered at the bowl. Deep conditioning, scalp treatment, bond builder. These are real services with real value, and they are also where a ticket quietly grows by fifty dollars.
The fix is one sentence, delivered when you book rather than when you check out: based on my hair, what is the realistic total for everything, including styling and any add-ons you would recommend? A good front desk will answer that, or hand you to the stylist who can. A salon that will not attach any number to it before you are in the chair is telling you something worth hearing.
### Color is where the budget actually goes
Every consultation eventually arrives at the same question. How much should it cost to get your hair colored? Honestly, that depends less on the color you want than on the color you already have. Applying a single tone to virgin hair is a chemistry problem with one step. Lightening hair that has been colored before, especially with box dye, is a chemistry problem with several steps, and each one takes time and product.
Roughly in order of cost and complexity:
Root touch-up — maintenance on an existing formula, the cheapest and fastest color appointment.
Single-process — one color, all over, usually going darker or matching to a tone.
Partial highlights — foils around the face and part line only.
Full highlights — foils throughout, more time and more product.
Balayage — hand-painted and freehand, slower to place, and priced accordingly.
Color correction — a different category entirely, priced by the hour rather than by the service.
Balayage typically costs fifty to a hundred dollars more per session than traditional foils, but the maintenance math flips it. Foils generally want a touch-up every four to six weeks. Balayage grows out softly and often stretches to twelve to fourteen weeks. Over a full year the two can land in the same place, and balayage sometimes lands lower. If you are comparing prices, compare the annual cost, not the appointment.
### Why the cheapest quote for color is often the most expensive outcome
Color correction is billed by the hour, commonly starting around $100 an hour and running to $150 an hour in busier markets. Most corrections take two to three hours, which puts them in the $200 to $300 range, and difficult ones run six hours or more and pass $600. That is not a markup for the word corrective. Corrective work often requires several times the pigment of a standard session, and going from light back to dark is genuinely harder than the reverse, because bleached hair has little pigment left for the new color to hold onto.
Which is why the lowest bid on a big color change deserves a second look. If a salon quotes a full transformation on previously box-dyed hair at a price that would barely cover a single-process, one of a few things is true: they are planning fewer steps than the job needs, they have not actually seen your hair, or they intend to add to the ticket later. Any of those can end with you paying for the cheap appointment and then paying for the correction.
The stylists who quote high in that first conversation are usually the ones who have already counted the sessions. A colorist who tells you the look you brought in will take two visits eight weeks apart is not upselling you. They are describing physics.
### Smoothing, keratin, and the long-appointment services
Keratin and smoothing treatments run about $150 to $600 and up, with short hair at the bottom of the band, medium hair in the $200 to $350 range, and long or dense hair at the top. Results generally last one to six months depending on the formula, your hair, and how faithfully you use the aftercare products.
Two questions are worth asking before you book one. First, what is the actual chair time, because these are long appointments and some salons block them as a half day. Second, what does the aftercare require, because a smoothing treatment maintained with the wrong shampoo is a service you paid for twice.
### Extensions: the install is not the price
Extensions are the service where people most often budget for the wrong number. A tape-in install commonly runs $400 to $800, and hand-tied wefts often land between $800 and $1,500 once you count both the hair itself and the labor to put it in.
Then the real cost starts. Tape-ins need moving every four to eight weeks at roughly $150 to $300 a visit. Hand-tied maintenance typically runs $250 to $650 every six to eight weeks. Add replacement hair and the professional shampoo you are now committed to using, and the annual number for permanent methods commonly lands somewhere between $1,500 and $4,500.
None of that is a reason to avoid extensions. It is a reason to ask for the twelve-month number before the first appointment rather than after the third.
### The consultation is the step people skip, and it is the cheap one
Most salons will do a consultation for free, or for a small fee credited toward the service. It takes about fifteen minutes, it usually does not require a chair, and it is the single highest-value part of the entire process.
Bring photographs — several, of the same look, in different lighting, so the stylist can see what you actually mean rather than what one filtered image implies. Be honest about your hair history. Box dye, henna, a rough bleach two years ago, a keratin treatment last spring: all of it changes what is chemically possible today, and a stylist who does not know about it is formulating blind.
What you want out of a consultation is three specific things. A realistic total, in dollars, for the appointment as it will actually be performed. A count of how many sessions the look will take. And a plain description of what the maintenance costs per year. Walk out with those three numbers and you have removed almost every unpleasant surprise from the process.
It is also the moment to ask what happens if you are not happy. Many stylists will fix an issue at no charge if you come back within a set window and say so. That policy is easy to get in advance and awkward to negotiate afterward.
### Tipping at a St. Louis salon
Twenty percent is the working standard at a full-service salon. Fifteen percent reads as adequate but unremarkable. Twenty-two to twenty-five percent is for genuinely exceptional work, a stylist who stayed late, or the person who fit you in the day before a wedding.
The mechanics matter more than the percentage:
Tip on the pre-tax total, not the after-tax total.
Tip on the original price even when you used a coupon, a gift card, or a first-visit discount. The work was the same work.
If an assistant shampooed you or a second stylist did your blow-dry, tip them separately and directly. Five to ten dollars is normal.
If you are unhappy, say so before you pay. A reduced tip communicates nothing useful, and most stylists would far rather fix it.
Then the arithmetic everyone is quietly doing in the chair. How much do you tip a $50 hair stylist? Ten dollars at twenty percent, seven-fifty at fifteen. On a $200 color, twenty percent is forty dollars, and it is entirely normal to split that between the colorist and whoever else touched your hair that day.
### A quick word on licensing
Cosmetologists and barbers in Missouri are licensed through the state Board of Cosmetology and Barber Examiners, and those licenses renew every two years. You can look up a person or a business, and see whether there are disciplinary actions on record, through the state’s renewal and verification portal. It takes about a minute, and it is worth doing before a chemical service with someone new.
### Before you book: the short list
Ask for a realistic total including styling and add-ons, not the from-price.
Ask which level of stylist you are booked with, and whether that matches the difficulty of what you want.
For any color change, ask how many sessions it will take.
Ask what the annual maintenance costs, especially for highlights, balayage, and extensions.
Disclose your full hair history, including anything you did at home.
Ask about the redo policy and the window for it.
Bring several photos of the same look, and one photo of something you definitely do not want.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How much should it cost to get your hair colored?
A.  Root touch-ups generally run $50 to $100, single-process all-over color $60 to $150, full foil highlights roughly $70 to $150, and balayage $150 to $350 and up. Then budget for the extras that are usually charged separately: toner or gloss at $20 to $60, a bond-building treatment at $30 to $80, and a finish blowout at $30 to $70. Longer or denser hair sits at the top of every one of those bands.
### Q. How much do you tip a $50 hair stylist?
A.  Ten dollars is the standard twenty percent. Seven dollars and fifty cents is fifteen percent, which reads as acceptable rather than generous. Tip on the pre-tax amount, and tip on the original price even if you used a discount or a gift card. If someone else shampooed or styled you, hand them five to ten dollars separately.
### Q. Why are ladies hairdressers so expensive?
A.  Because you are usually comparing two different products. The women’s line on a salon menu typically bundles services that the men’s line does not, and it runs on longer hair, which means more chair time, more product, and often a long-hair upcharge on top. Layer in the stylist level and the add-ons that attach to color work — toner, bond treatment, finish blowout — and the totals separate quickly. Book a dry cut with no styling at a lower level and the price lands much closer to a barbershop cut.
### Q. Is it worth it to dye hair at a salon?
A.  For maintenance on a shade close to your natural color, home color is a reasonable choice and plenty of people do it well. For anything involving lightening, moving more than a couple of shades in either direction, or fixing something that already went wrong, the salon is almost always cheaper in the end. Color correction is billed hourly, commonly $100 to $150 an hour, and two to three hours is normal — which means one bad box of dye can easily cost more to undo than the professional service would have cost to do right the first time.
### Q. What is the normal price of a haircut?
A.  Nationally, men’s cuts average about $43 and generally fall between $20 and $50, while women’s cuts average about $69 and typically fall between $40 and $120. In the St. Louis metro the women’s range runs wider, roughly $40 to $165, because the market spans everything from a suite rental in North County to a senior stylist in a boutique salon. If you are being quoted well above that band, you are paying for the stylist’s level, not for the haircut itself.
### Q. Is $30 for a haircut expensive?
A.  For a men’s cut in St. Louis, no — $20 to $50 is the normal range and the national average sits near $43. For a women’s cut it is well under market, where $40 to $165 is typical. A $30 women’s cut generally means a walk-in chain rather than a booked stylist.
### Q. How much does it cost for a hairdresser to dye your hair?
A.  In this market a root touch-up runs about $50 to $100, and single-process color all over about $60 to $150. Highlights and corrective work climb well past that, which is where budgets usually get broken. Ask whether the quoted price includes the blow-dry and toner, because often it does not.
### Q. How much tip for $200 hair?
A.  Eighteen to twenty percent is standard, so roughly $36 to $40 on a $200 appointment. If more than one person worked on you — a colorist plus an assistant who shampooed — split it rather than handing it all to the stylist. Tip on the pre-discount total when a promotion applied.

## What Does an Interior Designer Cost in St. Louis? (2026 Fees)
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-does-an-interior-designer-cost-in-st-louis
A couple in Webster Groves has a living room that has never quite worked. The sofa is fine. The rug was expensive. The light fixture came from a good store. Individually every piece is defensible, and together the room reads like a furniture showroom that lost an argument. They have rearranged it four times in six years. Last spring they finally said the thing out loud at the kitchen table: maybe we should just pay somebody who does this for a living.
Then they started calling. The first designer quoted an hourly rate and asked for a retainer. The second quoted a flat fee for the whole room and would not say what her furniture markup was until they signed. The third wanted a percentage of the total project, which sounded reasonable until they realized the total project included the furniture they were going to buy anyway. A friend in Clayton told them she paid a flat fee per room and thought it was a bargain. A cousin in a century brick two-story in south city said her designer charged by the hour, ran up eleven hours before a single thing was ordered, and it was still the best money she spent—because the designer caught that the original kitchen wall the cousin wanted removed was carrying the second floor.
Three houses, three completely different bills, and all three homeowners think they got a normal deal. That is the actual problem with interior design pricing. There is no single number. There are five different pricing structures that produce five different-looking invoices for what can be nearly identical work, and until you can tell them apart you cannot compare two quotes at all. This guide breaks down each structure with real ranges, explains what the paid consultation actually buys you, and gets into the specific headaches of designing around St. Louis housing stock—plaster, radiators, brick, and kitchens that were sized for 1912.
### The short answer on what an interior designer costs
Nationally, interior designers charge roughly $100 to $500 an hour, with the residential median landing somewhere around $200 to $300. Junior designers start near $75. Flat fees per room run about $1,000 to $12,000, though most firms cluster between $1,500 and $4,900. Design-only work with no furnishing procurement attached tends to run $450 to $1,500 per room. Percentage-of-project fees run 10 to 30 percent of total project cost. Per-square-foot pricing runs about $5 to $17, with most homeowners landing between $7 and $12.
Those are national numbers, and they matter less than you think until you localize them. Designers in New York, Los Angeles, and San Francisco charge something like 40 to 60 percent above the national average. St. Louis is on the other side of that math. Our cost of doing business is lower, our design market is smaller and more relationship-driven, and the practical effect is that local quotes tend to sit in the lower and middle bands of every range above rather than the top. A St. Louis homeowner asking how much should I budget for an interior designer should anchor to the bottom half of the national spread and adjust up for a designer with a long portfolio, a big team, or a specialty in historic work.
Now here is the part nobody tells you: the fee structure changes what you are buying, not just how you pay. Read the next five sections as five different products. Whether it is worth paying for an interior designer at all depends almost entirely on which of those products you actually need, and most homeowners guess wrong on the first call.
### Fee structure one: hourly
The designer bills for time. Meetings, site visits, drawings, sourcing, emails with your contractor, the hour spent on the phone with a vendor because the fabric is backordered.
Hourly is honest and it is dangerous at the same time. It is honest because you pay for exactly what you use, and if you only need somebody for four hours to solve a paint-and-layout problem, you pay for four hours. It is dangerous because an open-ended hourly arrangement on a large project has no ceiling, and the clock runs during the parts of the job that feel like nothing is happening.
Ask for an hourly estimate in writing with a not-to-exceed number, or a cap per phase.
Ask whether travel time is billable. In a metro this spread out, that is not a small question.
Ask what the minimum billing increment is. Fifteen minutes and one hour are very different policies when the project runs on email.
Ask whether shopping and procurement time is billed hourly on top of any furniture markup. If it is billed twice, that is worth knowing before you sign.
Hourly is the right structure for small, well-defined problems: one room, a color plan, a furniture layout, a second opinion on a contractor’s proposal.
Totally unrelated — but here’s what Cabanne Place has to eat.
### Fee structure two: flat fee, per room or per project
The designer prices the whole scope up front. You know the number before work begins.
Common shapes of this in the market: a living room at roughly $2,500 to $5,000, bedrooms at roughly $1,000 to $2,000 each, and design-only packages without procurement in the $450 to $1,500 per room range. Full-service flat fees on larger rooms and whole-floor projects run higher, up toward that $12,000 per room ceiling at the luxury end.
Flat fee is the friendliest structure for a homeowner with a fixed budget, and it is the structure most likely to hide a scope fight later. The number is only meaningful if the scope document behind it is specific. A flat fee that covers two revision rounds is a different product than a flat fee that covers unlimited revisions, and the second one does not really exist at a fair price.
What to pin down before you accept a flat fee:
How many concept presentations and how many revision rounds are included.
Whether measuring, drawings, and elevations are included or billed separately.
How many site visits are in the number, and what an extra one costs.
What happens to the fee if you add a room, or cut one.
Whether install day—the day everything arrives and gets placed—is inside the fee.
### Fee structure three: cost-plus on furnishings
This is the one that confuses people the most, and it is the one most working studios prefer, so it is worth understanding properly.
Designers can buy from trade-only vendors at wholesale. Trade discounts commonly run 20 to 60 percent below retail depending on the brand. Under cost-plus, the designer shows you the trade cost of an item and adds a percentage on top when billing you. Typical markups run 15 to 35 percent, with 20 to 25 percent most common at established studios. Higher-end firms sometimes run 35 to 50 percent on premium pieces, and industry surveys have put the standard markup band as high as 30 to 50 percent above trade cost.
Here is why that is not a rip-off. If a sofa retails at $4,000 and the designer’s trade cost is $2,400, a 25 percent markup bills you $3,000. You paid a thousand dollars less than the showroom price and the designer earned $600 for sourcing it, verifying the specs, placing the order, tracking it, inspecting it on arrival, and eating the problem if it shows up with a gouge in the frame. That last part is the real service. When a designer buys under her own business account, she owns the freight claim, the reorder, and the fight with the vendor. When you buy retail, you own all of that yourself.
Cost-plus goes wrong in exactly two ways. One, the designer will not disclose the markup percentage. Two, the designer will not show you the trade cost, only the final number, which makes the markup unverifiable. A clean cost-plus arrangement shows you both numbers on every line. Ask for that in writing.
### Fee structure four: percentage of project cost
The designer charges a percentage of everything spent—construction, furnishings, fixtures, finishes. Common ranges are 10 to 30 percent of total project cost. For a significant remodel, addition, or new build, design fees regardless of structure typically land between 10 and 20 percent of construction cost.
The obvious objection is the obvious one: this structure pays the designer more when you spend more. Any honest designer will acknowledge the tension. The counterargument is that a percentage fee scales with the actual complexity and risk of the job, and a designer who talks you into a $90,000 kitchen you did not want will not get referred to your neighbor.
If you are offered a percentage fee, do two things. Ask what the percentage is calculated on—construction only, or construction plus furnishings plus your own purchases. And ask whether the percentage replaces a furniture markup or stacks on top of one. Percentage plus cost-plus markup on the same furniture is double-dipping unless it is disclosed and priced accordingly.
### Fee structure five: per square foot
Straightforward math: total square footage times a rate. Residential rates commonly run $5 to $17 per square foot, with most projects landing in the $7 to $12 band. Commercial fit-outs and luxury work run their own much higher scales.
Per-square-foot pricing is most common on new construction and gut renovations where the whole envelope is in play. It is a poor fit for a single-room refresh, because a 200-square-foot room with complicated built-ins is a lot more work than a 400-square-foot room with a rug and a sofa. If a designer quotes per square foot on a small job, ask why.
### The paid initial consultation and what you are actually buying
Most established designers charge for the first real meeting. Consultation fees commonly run $150 to $500, and initial meetings with a full site visit can run $200 to $800. Some designers credit that fee back against the project if you hire them. Many do not.
People resent this fee and they should not, because in a good consultation the designer is not selling—she is diagnosing. In ninety minutes at your house, a competent designer will walk the space, ask about how you actually live in it, identify the structural or mechanical constraints you did not know you had, and tell you whether your budget matches your ambitions. That last piece is worth the fee by itself. Being told plainly that the kitchen you described costs $70,000 and you have budgeted $28,000 saves you a year.
What a paid consultation should leave you holding:
A clear read on what is possible in the space and what is not.
Rough budget ranges for the work discussed, even if they are wide.
A sense of sequence—what has to happen before what.
Any red flags: load-bearing walls, knob-and-tube, asbestos-era flooring, plaster that will not survive the plan.
A proposal, or at least a description of how the designer would structure the fee.
If the consultation produces none of that and the designer just wants to talk about throw pillows, you have learned something useful for $200.
### Decorator, designer, or architect—which one do you need?
These words get used interchangeably and they should not be. The distinction is about what each one is trained and permitted to touch.
A decorator works with the space as it exists. Furniture, textiles, color, lighting, art, accessories, layout. No walls move. No permits are involved. If your rooms function fine and just look wrong, a decorator is very likely all you need and you will spend a fraction of what a full design engagement costs.
An interior designer works on the space itself—layouts, built-ins, cabinetry, lighting plans, finish specification, and coordination with the trades. Designers regularly work in non-structural walls, plumbing relocations, and electrical plans, and they document the work well enough for a contractor to build from.
An architect or structural engineer becomes necessary when structure is at stake: removing a bearing wall, cutting a new opening in a masonry wall, adding on, changing the roofline, or anything where the building’s load path changes. In a century brick house, that threshold arrives faster than people expect.
### What Missouri changed in 2026
Missouri has an Interior Design Council, and the title of registered interior designer is protected. To register, a person needs roughly six years of combined education and experience and must have passed the full NCIDQ examination. Missouri architects can register through a separate pathway.
The meaningful change is recent. Senate Bill 1233 passed the Missouri legislature on May 28, 2026, and Governor Mike Kehoe signed it on July 13, 2026. It extended independent practice rights so that registered interior designers can sign, stamp, and seal their own drawings within their scope of practice. Before that, a Missouri designer had to route plans through a third-party architect or engineer for approval before construction could start—a real cost that got passed to homeowners on every permitted job.
What this means for you as a homeowner: for a permitted interior project, a registered interior designer may now be able to handle the documentation that previously required an outside architect. Ask directly whether the designer is registered in Missouri and whether the drawings for your job will need an architect or engineer regardless. Structural work still needs a structural professional. And because Missouri does not license general contractors at the state level, the credential check on the builder is an entirely separate exercise—we walk through that in how to check if a contractor is licensed in Missouri.
### What a scope document should say before you sign anything
Almost every interior design dispute traces back to a vague scope. A quote is not a scope. Before money changes hands, get a document that answers all of this:
Rooms and boundaries. Exactly which spaces are included, listed by name.
Deliverables. Concept boards, floor plans, elevations, lighting plan, finish schedule, furniture specifications—name them.
Revisions. How many rounds are included and what an additional round costs.
Fee structure, stated plainly. Hourly with a cap, flat, cost-plus with the percentage written out, percentage of project with the base defined, or per square foot with the rate.
Markup disclosure. Whether you will see trade cost and markup as separate line items.
Who holds the purchase orders. Designer-purchased or client-purchased changes who owns damage claims and returns.
Payment schedule. Retainer amount, milestones, and what triggers each payment.
Freight, receiving, and storage. These are real line items on furnished projects and they surprise people.
Contractor coordination. Whether the designer manages the trades or simply hands off drawings.
Termination. What happens to money and drawings if either side walks.
A designer who will not put that on paper is telling you something. Most of the red flags when hiring a designer show up right here, in what the scope document refuses to say, long before they show up in the work itself.
### Designing around St. Louis housing stock
This is where national cost articles stop being useful. Our housing stock is old, masonry-heavy, and specific, and it changes both the design work and the price.
Century brick. A load-bearing brick wall is not a partition you knock down over a weekend. Cutting a new opening means a header, a structural professional, and often tuckpointing repair around the work. Exterior brick also means limited options for adding windows or moving them, which constrains layouts more than drywall houses do.
Plaster walls. Plaster over wood lath is harder, more brittle, and far less forgiving than drywall. Running new electrical or plumbing through it means real patching, not a quick mud-and-tape. Good designers plan runs to minimize plaster demolition, and they price the patching honestly instead of pretending it is free. If any part of your house predates 1978, paint disturbance also puts you in lead-safe territory, which we cover in our guide to interior painting in St. Louis.
Small original kitchens. Kitchens in St. Louis homes from the 1900s through the 1940s were built as work rooms, not gathering rooms. They are small, often closed off, and frequently sit next to a pantry or a back stair that is prime real estate for expansion. The best design work in these houses is usually spatial rather than decorative—borrowing from an adjacent room, reworking a doorway, changing where the sink sits relative to the window.
Radiators. Cast iron radiators are a genuine design constraint. They occupy the exact wall space you want for furniture, they cannot simply be moved without touching the piping, and they radiate heat in a way that limits what can sit against them. Options range from covers to relocating a unit to converting a zone entirely, and each has a very different price. Any designer working an older St. Louis house should raise radiators unprompted. If yours does not, ask.
Old electrical. Lighting plans die on old wiring. Knob-and-tube, ungrounded circuits, and undersized panels are common in our older neighborhoods, and a designer specifying recessed lighting and a dozen new outlets is writing an electrician a substantial bill. Get that priced early rather than late—our breakdown of what an electrician costs in St. Louis covers panel upgrades and what drives the spread.
### Putting it together in a real budget
A useful way to think about the whole number: design fee, furnishings, and construction are three separate buckets, and the design fee is usually the smallest of the three.
For a single-room refresh with no construction, a flat design fee in the low thousands plus furnishings is the realistic shape. For a kitchen or a whole first floor with walls moving, expect a design fee in the range of 10 to 20 percent of construction cost, plus furnishings handled on cost-plus, plus the construction itself. For a light-touch engagement—a paid consultation and a handful of hours—you may be out the door under a thousand dollars with a plan you execute yourself.
Whatever the structure, get at least two proposals, and make them comparable by asking every designer the same scope questions. That is the same discipline that makes any contractor bid readable; we made the same argument about hard numbers in our St. Louis concrete driveway cost guide. Two quotes are not comparable until they describe the same job.
