### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is it cheaper to refinish hardwood floors or replace them?
A.  Refinishing is cheaper in nearly every case. Refinishing runs about $3 to $8 per square foot against $10 to $16 for new solid hardwood installed, and in the St. Louis market a typical refinishing project lands between roughly $1,153 and $3,051. Replacement only wins when the boards have been sanded down to the tongue, when water damage has permanently cupped them, or when large sections are missing and cannot be matched.
### Q. Can I stay in my house while floors are refinished?
A.  You can, but most people are happier if they don’t. Sanding produces fine dust even with dust-containment equipment, and oil-based polyurethane fumes are strong for several days while the finish cures. Water-based finishes have less odor and dry faster. If you stay, plan to keep off the finished floors entirely for at least a day or two, longer before furniture goes back, and expect to live around a sealed-off work zone.
### Q. How much does a contractor charge to install LVP?
A.  Installed luxury vinyl plank runs about $4.50 to $12 per square foot including material and labor, and many St. Louis jobs land near the $6 to $8 mark for a good mid-grade product. Labor alone is the smaller share; most of the spread comes from wear layer thickness and plank rigidity. Add a vapor barrier over any basement slab and add leveling if the subfloor is not flat, because a floating floor over a wavy surface will separate at the joints.
### Q. What are the downsides of luxury vinyl plank flooring?
A.  It is a plastic product, so it can dent under heavy furniture, it can fade in a room with strong direct sun, and it will not add resale value the way real wood does. It also cannot be refinished — when the wear layer goes, the floor is replaced rather than restored. And it is unforgiving of a bad substrate: every hump and dip in an old St. Louis subfloor shows through a thin floating plank.
### Q. How do I find out if there is original hardwood under my carpet?
A.  Pull up a floor register or a heat vent cover and look at the cut edge of the opening — you will usually see the whole floor assembly in cross section. Failing that, lift a corner of carpet in a closet where the tack strip is easy to pry and nothing shows afterward. In St. Louis homes built before about 1950, narrow-strip red oak is common, and finding it changes your project from a several-thousand-dollar replacement into a refinishing job at a fraction of the price.
### Q. How much to install 2000 sq ft of laminate flooring?
A.  At roughly $6.90 to $11.80 per square foot installed, 2,000 square feet of laminate runs about $13,800 to $23,600. Most of that spread is the plank itself and whatever the subfloor needs. Carpet over the same area lands closer to $3,500 to $15,000, and luxury vinyl plank $9,000 to $24,000.
### Q. How much to install 2000 sq ft of hardwood floor?
A.  Solid hardwood runs $6 to $25 per square foot installed, with most jobs settling between $10 and $16. Across 2,000 square feet that is roughly $20,000 to $32,000 for the typical band. Engineered wood at $7 to $20 per square foot lands lower and tolerates a St. Louis basement far better.
### Q. How much does Home Depot charge to lay a floor?
A.  Big-box installation is subcontracted to local crews, so the price follows your market rather than a national rate card. In this market the installed ranges hold either way: carpet $1.75 to $7.50 per square foot, luxury vinyl plank $4.50 to $12, laminate $6.90 to $11.80. Confirm whether subfloor prep and haul-away are included.

## What Self Storage Actually Costs in St. Louis (and Why Month Four Is Different)
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-much-does-self-storage-cost-in-st-louis
A couple in Ballwin sells the house where they raised three kids and buys a condo with half the square footage. The dining set that seated ten does not fit anywhere in the new place. Neither does the workbench, or the cedar chest, and no one in the family is ready to say out loud that these things are going away.
Across the metro, someone in the Central West End has a lease that ends on the 31st and a new one that starts on the 15th. That is two weeks with an entire life in boxes and nowhere to set it down.
And in Florissant, a daughter stands in her mother’s house the week after the funeral, looking at four decades of accumulation, with a brother flying back east on Sunday and a closing date that will not move.
Three different problems. One storage unit answers all three — and depending on which of those people you are, the same answer costs anywhere from about $44 a month to well over $200. Here is what the sizes actually cost around here, what each one honestly holds, and why the number on the sign is so often not the number on your fourth invoice.
### How much is a storage unit in STL?
Average monthly rates across the St. Louis market in July 2026, for standard units without climate control:
5x5 — about $44 a month
5x10 — about $67 a month
10x10 — about $108 a month
10x15 — about $143 a month
10x20 — about $179 a month
The same sizes with climate control:
5x5 — about $47 a month
5x10 — about $75 a month
10x10 — about $120 a month
10x15 — about $161 a month
10x20 — about $218 a month
Those are metro averages, and the spread underneath them is genuinely wide. A national operator’s own St. Louis pricing page put the local 10x10 average nearer $92. A separate market tracker had the same size around $117.80 in mid-July 2026. For national context, the average street rate across the country was $133 a month in May 2026, down about 2.2 percent from a year earlier.
So the honest version of the answer is a range, not a figure. A 10x10 in this metro is roughly a hundred dollars, plus or minus thirty, before anything else lands on the bill. Everything below is about that phrase — before anything else lands on the bill.
### What each size actually holds
Renting one size too large is the most common and most expensive mistake, and it happens because square footage is abstract while a pile of furniture in a driveway is not. Translate the numbers first.
5x5 (25 square feet) — a hall closet. Seasonal decorations, a few dozen boxes of books and papers, a set of golf clubs, small tools. Not furniture.
5x10 (50 square feet, roughly 400 cubic feet) — the furniture from a studio or a light one-bedroom. A queen mattress set, a love seat, a dresser, a television, a bicycle, and a stack of boxes.
10x10 (100 square feet) — the size of a small bedroom. Commonly used for the contents of two full bedrooms or one large family room, and it is the standard recommendation for a full one-bedroom apartment.
10x15 (150 square feet, roughly 1,200 cubic feet) — the contents of a two- or three-bedroom house, including the awkward things: a sectional, an entertainment center, a dining table with its chairs, a refrigerator.
10x20 (200 square feet) — a one-car garage. A two- to three-bedroom house with the appliances, or a household plus a project car’s worth of parts.
The step from 10x10 to 10x15 costs about $35 a month here, which is $420 a year, and it is the step people take out of anxiety more than arithmetic. Should I get a 10x10 or 10x15 storage unit? Stack the boxes in the garage first and measure the footprint of the pile. If the answer is close, the 10x10 with a walkway left down the middle usually wins, because you will need to get to the back of it in February and you will not want to unload the whole unit onto the pavement to do it.
### Is a 10x10 storage unit enough for a one bedroom apartment?
For most one-bedroom apartments, yes, with room left over. The 10x10 is sized for roughly two bedrooms of furniture, so a single bedroom plus a living room plus a kitchen usually fits with a path down the center.
Where it stops fitting is not bedrooms — it is bulk. A full-size sofa sectional, a treadmill, a washer and dryer, and a dining table for six will fill a 10x10 on their own no matter how few bedrooms they came out of. Count the large rigid objects, not the rooms.
And remember the ceiling. Most units run about eight feet tall, which is where the cubic-foot figures come from, but that capacity only exists if you actually stack. Mattresses on end, boxes to shoulder height, nothing heavy on top of anything that can be crushed.
Random, but: Marthasville’s whole food scene is one click away.
### Why the advertised rate is rarely the rate you pay in month four
This is the part almost nobody explains, and it is the single most useful thing to understand before you sign anything.
The self-storage industry runs on two separate prices. The street rate is what a new customer is quoted today, and it is set low and moved constantly to fill empty units. The in-place rate is what you are already paying, and it drifts upward through what the industry openly calls existing customer rate increases.
The gap between the two is not a rumor. Street rates have been soft nationally — down a couple of percent year over year as of spring 2026 — while operators lean harder on raising rents for tenants who are already moved in. In a lot of markets, what existing customers pay now sits above what the same unit is advertised for on the website.
What that means for you, practically:
Ask, before signing, whether the quoted rate is promotional, when it expires, and what the standard rate for that unit is.
Expect a rate letter. Many tenants see their first increase somewhere in the first six to twelve months.
Check the website rate for your own unit size at your own facility every few months. If a new customer can get your unit cheaper than you are paying, call and ask for the current rate. It is a month-to-month agreement, and the facility would rather adjust you than have an empty unit.
If the answer is no, moving your things two doors down the road is a real option, and the staff know it.
None of this is dishonest on the operator’s part. It is simply how the pricing works, and the only people it costs money are the ones who never look at the bill again after move-in day.
### The extras nobody quotes you
The monthly rate is the headline. Here is the rest of the bill, in the order you will meet it:
Administrative or setup fee — a one-time charge, commonly $10 to $30, applied at move-in. This is the fee that quietly cancels out a free-month promotion on a cheap small unit.
A lock — most facilities require an approved lock and sell it at the counter, typically $10 to $30. Some accept a disc lock you bring yourself; ask before you buy one twice.
Tenant insurance — frequently required, not optional. Facility plans generally run $10 to $30 a month depending on coverage. Some facilities will waive it if you show a homeowners or renters policy that already covers off-premises property, so check your existing policy before you agree to a second one.
Late fees — commonly $10 to $50, or a percentage of the monthly rent, and they compound with the lien timeline described further down.
Add it up honestly. A $108 non-climate 10x10 with a $20 admin fee, a $20 lock, and $15 a month of required insurance is not $108. It is $163 in month one and $123 every month after — roughly fourteen percent above the advertised number, permanently.
### How to get the actual lowest price
A few things reliably move the number, and they cost nothing but attention:
Reserve online rather than at the counter. Most operators publish a lower web rate than their walk-in rate, and first-month-free offers are very often web-exclusive. Walking in and asking for the internet price does not always work; booking the internet price does.
Read what the free month actually covers. It usually applies to rent only. Admin fee, lock, and insurance are still due at move-in. Some promotions require a two- or three-month minimum stay and claw the discount back if you leave early.
Take the autopay discount if there is one. Some facilities tie the promotional rate to enrolling in automatic payment, and it also removes the late-fee risk entirely.
Move mid-month if you can. Demand concentrates at month-end when leases turn over, which is exactly when the cheap units are gone.
Take the upper floor. Inside a climate-controlled building, ground-floor units near the door are priced above upper-floor units reached by elevator. If you are storing rather than shopping the unit weekly, the elevator is a fair trade.
### Is climate-controlled storage worth the cost?
Sometimes clearly yes, sometimes clearly no, and the deciding factors are what is in the box and how long it will sit there — not how expensive the contents were.
Start with the local weather, because that is the whole argument. A St. Louis July averages a high near 89 degrees with relative humidity around 68 percent, and a metal building with a roll-up door runs considerably hotter than the air outside it. A climate-controlled space is generally held somewhere between 55 and 85 degrees, with the humidity swings flattened out.
Things that genuinely need that:
Solid wood furniture — repeated moisture cycling is what warps, splits, and loosens glued joints. The heirloom dresser is the classic loss.
Electronics — condensation on cold circuit boards, swollen batteries, and failed capacitors after a summer in a hot box.
Photographs and paper — preservation guidance puts photographs below 75 degrees with humidity held in a moderate band. Prints stick to each other and to album sleeves when they get hot and damp, and that damage is permanent.
Vinyl records — a stable 60 to 70 degrees with humidity near the middle of the range. Heat warps the discs and the sleeves grow mold.
Leather, musical instruments, artwork, wine, and anything upholstered that will sit through more than one summer.
Things that mostly do not need it:
Yard tools, bicycles, ladders, patio furniture, plastic bins of hardware.
Sealed plastic totes of clothing and linens for a short stay.
Anything already living in your garage year-round without complaint.
A move-gap stay of a few weeks in spring or fall, when the temperature swing is small.
The premium here is smaller than people assume — roughly $3 a month on a 5x5, about $12 on a 10x10, and about $39 on a 10x20. On the 10x10 that is a hundred and forty-four dollars a year to keep a bedroom set from cupping. So ask it plainly. Is climate-controlled storage worth the cost? If wood, electronics, photographs, or records are going in, and the stay will cross a Missouri summer, it is a straightforward yes. If it is lawn equipment for six weeks, it is a straightforward no.
One caution worth stating plainly: climate control is not a mold guarantee. Damp items sealed into a unit will grow mold in a conditioned building the same as anywhere else. Anything that goes in wet — a rug, a mattress, a tent, a cooler — needs to be fully dry first.
### Drive-up versus interior
Drive-up units are the ones you back a truck to and open like a garage. Interior units live inside a conditioned building down a hallway.
Pricing between the two is less consistent than you would expect and varies facility to facility. At many sites the drive-up units are simply the unconditioned concrete boxes and sit at the low end of the rate card. At others, the convenience of loading straight from the tailgate carries a small premium over an interior unit of the same size. One published comparison showed a 10x10 drive-up at $95 against $110 for the interior equivalent, with similar gaps at the smaller sizes.
Choose on how you will use it, then compare prices:
Drive-up if you are loading heavy furniture or appliances, visiting often, or moving in and out on one busy weekend.
Interior if the contents need conditioning, if security matters more than convenience, or if the unit will simply sit.
Also account for the walk. An upstairs interior unit reached by elevator adds ten or fifteen minutes to every single visit, which is invisible on move-in day and extremely visible on the ninth trip.
### The month-to-month reality, and the lien
Almost all self-storage in this market is month-to-month with no minimum term and no maximum. That flexibility is real and it is the best thing about the product.
Two details people miss:
Leaving requires notice. Facilities typically want somewhere between ten and thirty days before you vacate, and the requirement is in your lease, not in the industry. Emptying the unit and driving away does not always stop the billing.
Missing payments has a legal timeline. Under Missouri law, once an occupant has been in default for more than thirty days the operator may enforce a lien against the stored property and sell it. The operator must give at least forty-five days of notice before disposing of anything, with a second notice sent no sooner than ten days after the first, and any surplus from a sale is held for the occupant for a year.
That is not a scare story, it is a calendar. If money gets tight, the worst move is silence. Call the office early — partial payments and short extensions are common, and a sale is expensive and unpleasant for the facility too.
### The three-month rule and the two-year problem
Here is the arithmetic almost nobody runs before renting, and it is the reason people are still paying in year three.
Take a climate-controlled 10x10 at roughly $120 a month, plus $15 of required insurance, plus a $20 admin fee and a $20 lock at the start.
Three months: about $445. Against a closing delay, a renovation, or a death in the family, that is cheap. It buys time to make decisions properly instead of under pressure, and time is genuinely what you are purchasing.
One year: about $1,660, and probably more, because a rate increase has likely landed by then.
Two years: north of $3,300. At that point the question is no longer whether storage is affordable. It is whether the contents of that unit are worth $3,300 to you, because that is what you have spent to avoid deciding.
The national average tenancy is now somewhere around eighteen months, roughly double what it was a decade ago. That is not because people plan eighteen-month stays. It is because a unit is easy to open and emotionally difficult to close.
So set the exit date on the day you set the start date. Write it on the calendar, put a reminder on your phone for two weeks before, and decide then. Storage is an excellent bridge and a poor destination. If what is inside is a dining set nobody wants and a workbench nobody uses, the honest comparison is not storage versus keeping it. It is storage versus what it costs to clear it out, once.
### What items should not go in storage?
Every lease has a prohibited list, and it is broadly the same everywhere:
Flammables and pressurized containers — gasoline, propane tanks, aerosols, paint thinner, fireworks. Drain the mower and leave the grill tank behind.
Perishable food — it draws pests, and pests are a problem for the whole building, which is why leases treat it seriously.
Living things — plants and animals, without exception.
Hazardous or toxic materials, chemicals, and in most leases ammunition.
Anything you cannot afford to be without — passports, titles, medication, tax records, hard drives. Not because they are banned, but because a unit you cannot reach after hours is a bad place for them.
And to answer the question people ask but rarely say out loud: you cannot live in a storage unit, or sleep in one, day or night. It is prohibited by every lease and by building and occupancy code, the units are not habitable spaces, and getting caught means eviction from the unit. If housing is the actual problem, that is a different search and there is real help in this metro for it.
### Before you sign, ask these
Is this rate promotional, and what does it become? Get the standard rate for the unit, not just today’s number.
What is due at move-in beyond the first month? Admin fee, lock, insurance — itemized.
Is insurance required, and will you accept my existing homeowners or renters policy?
How much notice do I owe when I leave, and how do I give it?
What are your access hours, and are gate hours different from office hours?
Is this unit climate controlled or only temperature controlled? The two are marketed interchangeably and are not the same thing.
Get the answers by phone or email before move-in day, when you have leverage and time, rather than at the counter with a loaded truck idling outside. It is the same discipline that makes moving quotes comparable — ask every facility the identical questions and the prices finally line up next to each other.
Comparing units across the metro? Browse self storage facilities on St Louis Near Me Directory and ask each one the same six questions above — promotional rate, move-in total, insurance, notice period, access hours, and whether it is truly climate controlled.
Storing less is always cheaper than storing more. See what junk removal costs here, and find the rest of the metro’s help on the home services coverage map.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How much should I pay for self-storage?
A.  Pay for the size you measured, not the size that feels safe, and compare total move-in cost rather than the monthly rate. A fair total for a 10x10 in this market is around $110 to $135 a month once required insurance is included, plus a one-time admin fee and a lock. If a quote is far under that, ask what it becomes after the promotional period.
### Q. Is a 10x10 storage unit enough for a one bedroom apartment?
A.  Yes, for most one-bedroom apartments, with room to walk. A 10x10 is sized for roughly two bedrooms of furniture, so one bedroom plus a living room and kitchen generally fits. Bulk is what breaks it — a large sectional, a treadmill, and a washer and dryer will fill the space regardless of how few rooms they came from.
### Q. Should I get a 10x10 or 10x15 storage unit?
A.  Stack everything in a garage or driveway first and measure the footprint. The 10x15 costs about $35 more a month here, which is roughly $420 a year, so only step up if the pile genuinely demands it. A three-bedroom house needs the 10x15. A one- or two-bedroom household almost never does.
### Q. Is climate-controlled storage worth the cost?
A.  It is worth it when solid wood furniture, electronics, photographs, records, leather, or instruments will sit through a Missouri summer, where July averages a high near 89 degrees with humidity around 68 percent. It is not worth it for yard tools, plastic bins, or a short move-gap stay in spring or fall. The premium is about $12 a month on a 10x10, which is cheap against a warped dresser and expensive against a lawn mower.
### Q. What items should not go in storage?
A.  Flammables and pressurized containers, perishable food, plants and animals, hazardous chemicals, and in most leases ammunition. Beyond the prohibited list, keep passports, titles, medication, tax records, and hard drives with you — not because they are banned, but because a locked unit across town is the wrong place for anything you might need at ten at night.
### Q. How much can you put in a 10x10 storage unit?
A.  A 10x10 is 100 square feet, and with standard ceilings that is roughly 800 cubic feet of usable space — commonly described as the contents of a one-bedroom apartment, or two rooms of furniture with boxes stacked above. In St. Louis that size averages about $108 a month without climate control.
### Q. Can I sleep in a storage unit during the day?
A.  No. Every standard rental agreement prohibits occupancy, and fire codes bar it outright — units have no ventilation, plumbing or egress requirements built for people. Facilities monitor for it and will terminate the lease. If housing is the underlying problem, a St. Louis assistance line is the better call than a padlock.
### Q. What is the average cost of a 10x10 storage building?
A.  Worth separating two things. A 10x10 storage unit you rent averages about $108 a month in St. Louis without climate control. A 10x10 storage building you buy and put in your yard is a different purchase entirely, and often needs a permit depending on your municipality — check before you order.
The couple in Ballwin, the tenant in the Central West End, and the daughter in Florissant all need the same thing from a storage unit: a defined amount of time, at a price they can still recite in month four. Measure the pile, ask what the rate becomes, insure it the cheap way, and put the end date on the calendar before you put the first box in the truck.

## What Therapeutic Massage Costs in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-therapeutic-massage-costs-in-st-louis
Imagine it is a Tuesday morning in August and you have been running the Forest Park loop three days a week since spring. Somewhere around week nine, your right calf stopped loosening up after the first mile and started staying tight all day instead. You are not injured, exactly. You are carrying something a foam roller cannot reach, and a coworker keeps telling you to stop being stubborn and go see a massage therapist.
So you start pricing it out on your phone over lunch. A wellness studio in Kirkwood lists one number for sixty minutes. A clinic near the medical corridor in Clayton lists a higher number and calls the same hour medical massage. A franchise location out in Chesterfield Valley advertises an introductory rate that looks terrific until you notice it applies only to your first visit. A mobile therapist who would drive out to Webster Groves quotes a third number, then adds a travel fee. Four tabs open, four prices, and no honest sense of which one is fair.
That is the real problem with buying therapeutic massage around St. Louis. The service sounds simple — one person, one table, one hour — but the price can swing by more than a hundred dollars depending on the setting, the therapist’s training, the length of the session, and whether the work is aimed at general relaxation or at a specific physical complaint. This guide walks through what actually drives those numbers, so the next time you open a price list you can tell in about ten seconds whether it is reasonable.
### The short answer on therapeutic massage prices
How much does a massage typically cost in St. Louis? For a licensed therapist doing clinical or wellness work, plan on landing somewhere in the middle of the national ranges below. St. Louis is a moderate cost-of-living metro, so local pricing generally sits under coastal city rates and above small-town rates.
Here is the national picture as of 2026, which is the honest baseline to measure any local quote against:
A standard 60-minute session runs roughly $60 to $150, with hourly rates across the country generally falling between $85 and $165.
A 90-minute session runs roughly $90 to $175.
Deep tissue work costs about $80 to $130 for 60 minutes and $120 to $200 for 90 minutes.
Sports massage runs about $70 to $120, or roughly $15 to $30 above a studio’s base rate.
Prenatal massage runs about $75 to $150 for 60 minutes.
Lymphatic drainage runs about $100 to $150 for 60 minutes and $150 to $200 for 90 minutes.
Suburban markets in general tend to cluster in the $75 to $120 bracket for a 60-minute session.
If a quote in the metro sits far above the top of those bands, you should be getting something specific for the money — advanced clinical certification, a treatment room inside a medical or chiropractic practice, or a specialty modality. If a quote sits far below the bottom, ask why before you book. Legitimately low prices usually come from a student clinic, a new therapist building a book, or a promotional first-visit rate. Anything else deserves scrutiny.
### Sixty minutes or ninety minutes
Is it better to get a 60 minute or 90 minute massage? It depends entirely on what you are asking the session to accomplish, and this is the single decision that moves your bill the most.
A 60-minute session is not really sixty minutes of hands-on work. Once you subtract the intake conversation, undressing, getting settled under the sheet, and getting dressed again, you are often looking at fifty minutes or so on the table. That is enough time for a competent full-body relaxation session, or enough time for focused work on one region — neck and shoulders, or low back and hips, or that calf.
It is not enough time to do both. If you ask for a full-body Swedish session and then mention at minute forty that your hip has been bothering you, the therapist has to choose between rushing the rest of the body or shortchanging the hip.
A 90-minute session is where the math turns in your favor for therapeutic work. You are typically paying about 40 to 50 percent more for 50 percent more time, and the extra half hour is almost entirely productive time — the intake and transitions do not get longer just because the session did. For chronic tension, for anything involving more than one problem area, or for the first appointment with a new therapist who needs time to assess you, ninety minutes is usually the better value per useful minute.
Thirty-minute sessions have their place too. They are efficient for a single stubborn area and they are the cheapest way to test a therapist before committing to a longer appointment. They are a poor choice for deep tissue work, though, because deep tissue depends on warming up the surrounding tissue first, and half an hour barely covers that.
Totally unrelated — but here’s where to eat in Godfrey, IL.
### Deep tissue and sports massage premiums
Deep tissue and sports massage cost more than a standard relaxation session, and the reason is not marketing. It is labor and expertise.
Deep tissue work targets the deeper layers of muscle and the connective tissue around it. It requires the therapist to work slowly, use body weight and forearms rather than just hands, and constantly check in with you about pressure. It is physically taxing on the therapist, which limits how many of these sessions they can perform in a day, and that scarcity shows up in the price. Expect a premium of roughly $15 to $30 over a studio’s standard rate.
Sports massage is built around what your body is actually doing. A pre-event session is brisk and stimulating. A post-event or recovery session focuses on flushing and restoring range of motion. A maintenance session in the middle of a training block looks different again. Therapists who do this well have usually taken continuing education in it, and many of them work with runners on the Katy Trail crowd, cyclists, and weekend athletes who need the work timed around competition.
A few things worth knowing before you book either one:
Deep tissue should be uncomfortable at most, never sharp or breath-holding painful. Pressure is a conversation, not a test you have to pass.
You may feel sore for a day or two afterward, similar to the day after a hard workout. Drink water and do not schedule it the night before a race.
If a therapist promises to break up scar tissue or fix an alignment problem in one session, be skeptical. Good therapists talk about ranges of motion and gradual change, not miracles.
Tell the therapist about medications, recent surgeries, blood clots, and any cardiovascular condition. Some of these are genuine contraindications for deep pressure.
### Prenatal massage and specialized training
Prenatal massage is priced at or slightly above a standard session for a straightforward reason: it takes specific training and specific equipment. The therapist needs to know which positions are safe at which stage of pregnancy, which areas to avoid, and how to use side-lying bolsters or a pregnancy cushion so you are supported comfortably without lying flat on your stomach or fully on your back.
Not every licensed therapist has that training, and the ones who do have invested continuing education hours in it. That is what you are paying for when a prenatal session costs a bit more than the studio’s standard hour.
A few practical notes. Many providers prefer to start prenatal work after the first trimester, and many will ask you to confirm with your obstetrician or midwife first, particularly if your pregnancy has been flagged as high risk. That is a sign of a careful practice, not an obstacle. If a provider does not ask about your pregnancy at all before putting you on the table, that is the wrong provider.
### Clinical work: medical massage and specialty modalities
There is a real difference between an hour meant to help you unwind and an hour meant to treat a diagnosed problem, and the price reflects it.
Clinical or medical massage is generally delivered as part of a treatment plan, often inside or alongside a chiropractic office, a physical therapy practice, or a physician referral. Sessions tend to be shorter and more targeted, notes get written, and the therapist is aiming at a defined outcome such as restoring rotation in a shoulder rather than at general relaxation.
The main specialty modalities you will see on St. Louis price lists:
Myofascial release. Slow, sustained pressure into the fascia, the connective web that wraps muscle. Sessions are often quiet and unhurried and can feel strange the first time.
Trigger point therapy. Sustained pressure on specific tight knots that refer pain elsewhere — the classic example being a shoulder knot that produces a headache.
Manual lymphatic drainage. Extremely light, rhythmic strokes that move lymph fluid, commonly used after surgery or for swelling. It costs more than a standard session because it demands precise technique and specialized certification.
Neuromuscular therapy. A structured approach combining assessment with targeted pressure, usually sold as a course of sessions rather than a one-off.
Swedish and relaxation massage. The baseline. Broad, flowing strokes at moderate pressure. There is nothing lesser about it, and for stress and sleep it is often exactly right.
If you are also weighing aesthetic and skin treatments alongside bodywork, our companion piece on spa services, medical spas, and wellness retreats covers that side of the market in more detail.
### Packages, memberships, and the math people get wrong
Almost every studio in the metro will offer you a way to prepay, and the discount is usually real. Whether it is a good deal depends on one question that has nothing to do with the discount: how often will you actually go?
The common structures:
Monthly memberships. The chain model. Nationally these run roughly $60 to $80 per month and include one 60-minute session, with member pricing on any additional sessions and on upgrades. Prepaid terms are common too — six months around $360 plus an enrollment fee, or a full year around $720.
Session packages. Buy five or ten sessions up front at a per-session discount, typically 10 to 20 percent. No monthly commitment, but the money is spent.
Introductory rates. First-visit pricing designed to get you on the table. Some chains start new clients around $79 for an hour. It is a genuine discount and a genuine sales funnel at the same time.
Independent therapist packages. Often the quietest discount in the market. Solo practitioners frequently offer a modest package rate without any of the enrollment machinery.
Here is the trap. Memberships almost always accrue — miss a month and the session banks — but banked sessions often expire, and many agreements require notice in writing to cancel. If you know you will go monthly, a membership is straightforwardly cheaper than paying retail. If you are honestly a four-times-a-year person, a package or plain retail pricing will cost you less than a year of unused monthly charges.
Before you sign anything, ask three questions: do unused sessions expire, can they be shared with a spouse or partner, and what exactly is required to cancel.
### Tipping without overthinking it
What is a normal tip for a $100 massage? The standard across spas and independent therapists is 15 to 20 percent, which puts a $100 session at $15 to $20. Many people simply tip a flat $10 to $20 depending on session length and how good the work was.
The percentage does not change by modality. Swedish, deep tissue, prenatal, sports, and hot stone all sit inside the same framework — the dollar amount moves only because the price of the service moved.
Two situations change the calculus. First, if you are seeing a therapist in a clinical setting on a physician referral, tipping is often not expected the same way it is at a spa, much as you would not tip a physical therapist. When in doubt, ask the front desk quietly. Second, if you are using a discounted membership or package rate, the courteous move is to tip on the regular price of the service rather than on your discounted price, because the therapist did the same amount of work either way.
None of this is a rule with legal force. It is simply what most clients do, and knowing the norm removes the awkward moment at the front desk.
### Insurance, HSA, and FSA
This is where most of the money-saving potential hides, and most people never look.
Straight health insurance coverage for massage therapy is inconsistent. Some plans cover it when it is prescribed as part of a treatment plan for a documented condition, frequently through a physical therapy or chiropractic benefit rather than a standalone massage benefit. Many plans do not cover it at all. Medicare generally does not cover massage therapy, treating it as an alternative therapy rather than a medically necessary service, although some Medicare Advantage plans add supplemental wellness benefits that may apply. The only reliable way to know is to call the number on the back of your card and ask about your specific plan and the specific billing codes your provider uses.
Health savings accounts and flexible spending accounts are the more accessible path. Massage therapy can be paid for with HSA or FSA funds when it is medically necessary and documented in a Letter of Medical Necessity from a licensed healthcare provider that names a specific diagnosis and explains how massage treats it. Chronic back pain, injury recovery, and certain anxiety diagnoses are common examples.
The line the IRS draws is clear enough: a massage purely for relaxation or general wellness is a personal expense and does not qualify. A massage tied to a diagnosed condition, with paperwork, can. If you have a condition your physician is already treating, it is worth one conversation, because paying with pretax dollars is effectively a discount equal to your tax rate.
Keep your receipts and the letter together. Plan administrators can ask for substantiation later.
### Check the license before you check the price
Missouri licenses massage therapists at the state level through the Board of Therapeutic Massage, which operates under the Division of Professional Registration. This matters more than any price comparison in this guide, because a license is the line between a trained healthcare-adjacent professional and someone with a table.
To be licensed in Missouri, a therapist must complete at least 500 hours of supervised instruction. That coursework is structured, not vague: 300 hours of massage theory and technique, 100 hours of anatomy and physiology, 50 hours covering business practice, professional ethics, hygiene, and Missouri massage law, and 50 hours of ancillary therapies including CPR and first aid. Licenses are renewed on a set cycle, and the Board handles complaints and discipline.
Verifying a license takes about a minute:
Search the licensee database at the state MOPRO portal, mopro.mo.gov/license/s/license-search, by the therapist’s name.
Confirm the license is current and shows no disciplinary action.
If you cannot find a record, contact the Board of Therapeutic Massage directly at 573-522-6277 or by email at massagether@pr.mo.gov before you book.
In person, look for the license posted at the establishment. Licensed therapists generally display credentials without being asked.
Ask the question plainly when you call: are all of your therapists licensed by the Missouri Board of Therapeutic Massage. A professional practice answers that instantly and without any hesitation. If the answer is evasive, you have learned everything you needed to know and it cost you nothing.
### Questions worth asking before you book
Once the license checks out, a short phone call sorts out the rest of the value question faster than any amount of review reading:
Is the quoted price for hands-on time, or does it include intake and dressing time?
What training does the therapist have in the specific modality I need — prenatal, sports, lymphatic, myofascial?
Is there a separate rate for deep tissue, or is pressure included in the base price?
What do add-ons such as hot stones, aromatherapy, or cupping cost, and are they discussed before they are applied?
What is the cancellation window, and is there a fee?
Can I request a specific therapist for follow-up visits, and does that change the price?
If I have a Letter of Medical Necessity, will you provide an itemized receipt suitable for HSA or FSA reimbursement?
One more piece of advice that costs nothing. The most valuable thing you can do in a first session is talk. Say where it hurts, say what you have already tried, and say something during the session if the pressure is wrong. Therapists cannot feel what you feel, and the client who speaks up gets a better hour than the client who suffers politely.

### What all of this adds up to
Therapeutic massage is one of the few services where the cheapest option and the most expensive option can both be wrong. The cheapest hour is a poor deal if the therapist is not licensed or not trained in what you actually need. The most expensive hour is a poor deal if you are paying clinical prices for a relaxation session you could have gotten anywhere.
The way to buy it well is to decide what the hour is for before you shop. If it is stress and sleep, a standard 60-minute Swedish session at a fair market rate is the right purchase. If it is a stubborn calf that has not let go since spring, you want ninety minutes with someone trained in sports or deep tissue work, and you should expect to pay the premium and go back more than once.
Then verify the license, ask what the cancellation policy is, and find out whether your HSA or FSA can carry part of the cost. That is the whole process. It takes about fifteen minutes and it is the difference between a purchase you repeat and one you regret.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is the average cost of a deep tissue massage?
A.  Deep tissue runs about $80 to $130 for a 60-minute session and $120 to $200 for 90 minutes, which is generally $15 to $30 above a studio’s standard rate. The premium reflects real cost: the work is slower, more physically demanding on the therapist, and limits how many sessions they can do in a day. Deep tissue should feel intense but never sharply painful, and the pressure should be an ongoing conversation between you and the therapist.
### Q. Is it better to get a 60 minute or 90 minute massage?
A.  Sixty minutes works well for relaxation or for focused work on a single area, but remember that intake and dressing time comes out of that hour, leaving roughly fifty minutes on the table. Ninety minutes is usually the better value for therapeutic work because the transitions do not get longer — nearly all the added time is productive. Choose ninety if you have more than one problem area, chronic tension, or a first visit with a new therapist who needs time to assess you.
### Q. What is a normal tip for a $100 massage?
A.  Fifteen to 20 percent is standard, so $15 to $20 on a $100 session. Many clients simply tip a flat $10 to $20 depending on session length. The percentage does not change based on the type of work — only the service price moves the dollar amount. Two exceptions: tipping is often not expected in a clinical setting on a physician referral, and if you are on a membership or package rate, it is courteous to tip on the regular price rather than your discounted price.
### Q. How does medical massage differ from regular massage?
A.  Medical or clinical massage is delivered as part of a treatment plan aimed at a documented condition, frequently inside or alongside a chiropractic, physical therapy, or physician practice. Sessions are typically shorter, more targeted, and documented with treatment notes, and the therapist works toward a defined outcome such as restoring range of motion. Regular or relaxation massage aims at general stress relief and wellbeing. The distinction also matters financially, because only medically necessary massage documented in a Letter of Medical Necessity can be paid for with HSA or FSA funds.
### Q. Are prenatal massages more expensive?
A.  Prenatal sessions typically run about $75 to $150 for 60 minutes, which is at or slightly above a standard session. The difference covers specific continuing education in safe positioning by trimester and the bolsters or pregnancy cushions needed to support you comfortably. Many providers prefer to begin after the first trimester and will ask you to clear it with your obstetrician or midwife first, especially for a pregnancy flagged as high risk — that caution is a sign of a careful practice, not an obstacle.
### Q. Is $100 a lot for a massage?
A.  Not in this market. Deep tissue work runs about $80 to $130 for sixty minutes and $120 to $200 for ninety. A 90-minute standard session is roughly $90 to $175. At $100 you are mid-range for an hour of specialty work and at the low end for ninety minutes.
### Q. Is a $20 tip enough for a 90 minute massage?
A.  It is on the low side. A 90-minute session runs roughly $90 to $175 here, so $20 lands between eleven and twenty-two percent. Fifteen to twenty percent is the norm, which puts $20 at the bottom for a standard session and short for deep tissue at $120 to $200.
### Q. Is a 30-minute deep tissue massage worth it?
A.  For one specific area — a locked shoulder, a tight lower back — yes. Thirty minutes is enough to work a single region properly and nothing more. If the goal is full-body relief, it is not; deep tissue at sixty minutes runs $80 to $130 and gives the therapist room to actually finish.

## What a Will or Trust Costs in Missouri: St. Louis Estate Planning Fees
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-a-will-or-trust-costs-in-missouri
Picture a brick ranch off Gravois in Affton — detached garage, finished basement, a kitchen that has not been touched since the second grandchild was born. The owner is seventy-nine, widowed, still drives herself to the grocery store, and is fairly sure the handwritten page in the desk drawer counts as a will. Her two adult children live in Florissant and Kirkwood. Nobody in the family has ever said the word probate out loud.
One of those children finally asks the question over Sunday dinner — what actually happens to the house? — and the answer is a shrug. So the family starts calling around. The first office quotes a flat fee for a simple will. The second says what they really want is a trust, and the number is roughly four times higher. The third will not put a price on anything until after a consultation. By Wednesday there are three numbers on the refrigerator, no way to compare them, and a growing suspicion that somebody is being sold something.
That is the real problem for most St. Louis families, and it is not the law. It is the pricing. Estate planning is one of the few legal services where the fee is usually quoted up front as a flat number, which means you can comparison shop it the way you shop a roof or a furnace — if you know what the documents are, what each one normally runs in this metro, and what it costs your family if nobody does anything at all. That last number is the one nobody quotes you, and it is the reason trusts get sold. This article is the price list.
### First, the honest disclaimer
This is consumer cost information, not legal advice. It is here so you can walk into a consultation knowing roughly what things cost and what questions to ask — nothing more. It does not tell you what you should do with your own estate, because that genuinely depends on facts nobody can see from the outside: what you own, how it is titled, who your family is, and what you are worried about. Missouri law also changes, and the electronic-signing rules in particular have moved recently, so treat every figure here as a starting point and confirm the current rules with a licensed Missouri attorney before you rely on them.
### The documents you are actually buying
Nearly every estate plan sold in the St. Louis area is built from the same short list. Knowing the list is most of the battle, because it is how you tell whether two quotes are for the same thing.
A last will and testament. Instructions for who gets what, and who is in charge. It is a set of directions for the probate court, not a way to skip the probate court.
A durable power of attorney for finances. Names someone who can pay your bills and manage your accounts if you cannot. This is the document families miss most often, and its absence is what sends people to court for a guardianship or conservatorship.
A health care directive and durable power of attorney for health care. Names your medical decision-maker and records your wishes about life-sustaining treatment.
Beneficiary designations and non-probate transfers. Payable-on-death bank accounts, transfer-on-death vehicle titles, retirement accounts, life insurance, and Missouri’s beneficiary deed for real estate. These are cheap, and they move more property than most wills do.
A revocable living trust, if the plan calls for one. A container you retitle assets into so that at your death they pass by the trust’s terms instead of through probate. It normally comes packaged with a pour-over will, both powers of attorney, and a health care directive.
When one office quotes $900 and another quotes $3,200, they are almost never quoting the same package. Ask each of them to list the documents included, in writing, before you compare the numbers.
Random, but: Bridgeton’s dinner options are worth a look.
### What a simple will costs in the St. Louis area
Attorney-drafted wills in this metro are usually flat-fee work. Published pricing and regional cost guides put a straightforward individual will in the range of roughly $500 to $1,200, with the low end covering a bare-bones document and the upper end covering a will-based plan with real drafting attention. At least one St. Louis estate planning firm publishes a will-based plan at about $1,600 for an individual and about $2,500 for a married couple, which is toward the top of the range and includes considerably more than a single document.
Broader Missouri estate planning surveys put a basic plan at roughly $500 to $1,500. Both figures are consistent: a will alone is a several-hundred-dollar purchase, and a will with the supporting documents is a four-figure one.
Which raises the fair question: Do I need a lawyer for a will in Missouri? Legally, no. Missouri does not require an attorney for a will to be valid. Online services and stationery-store forms exist and people use them. What the fee buys you is drafting judgment and a correct signing ceremony — two things that are invisible until the document is challenged, at which point they are the only things that matter.
### What a full package costs — will, powers of attorney, health care directive
The package is where most families land, and it is usually the best value on the menu. A will plus a durable financial power of attorney plus health care documents typically runs from the high hundreds into the low thousands, depending on the firm and the complexity.
Some firms price the pieces separately. One published St. Louis schedule lists the powers of attorney and health care documents at about $395 per person on their own. That is a useful benchmark: if a firm quotes you a package and the difference between it and their will-only price is far more than a few hundred dollars per person, ask what else is in there.
Couples almost always pay less than two individuals would pay separately, because the documents mirror each other. The premium for a couple over an individual commonly runs around $700 to $1,100, not double.
### What a revocable living trust costs — individual versus couple
This is the number that makes people flinch, and the one that varies most between offices. It is also the point where the underlying question surfaces: Is a will or trust better in Missouri? Cost alone cannot answer that, but cost is where the comparison has to start.
Individual trust plan: Missouri firms commonly quote roughly $1,850 to $2,800 for a basic probate-avoidance trust package. One published St. Louis area schedule sits at about $2,800 for an individual.
Married couple, joint trust plan: roughly $2,950 to $4,000 is the common band, with a published St. Louis schedule around $4,000 for a couple.
Trusts with estate tax planning: roughly $4,800 to $5,000 and up. Very few St. Louis families need this — see the tax section below.
Broad national and Missouri-wide guidance puts a properly drafted revocable living trust with the pour-over will, powers of attorney, and funding help at $2,500 to $5,000 depending on complexity.
One word in that list does more damage than any other: funding. A trust does nothing until assets are actually retitled into it. Deeds have to be signed and recorded. Bank and brokerage accounts have to be changed over. If a quote does not say in writing whether funding is included, you are not comparing prices — you are comparing one price against an unfinished job. Ask directly: does this fee include preparing and recording the deed, and does it include the letters to my bank and my brokerage?
### Hourly rates, and when you will actually see one
Most consumer estate planning in St. Louis is flat-fee, so the hourly rate matters less than you would think when you are buying documents. It matters enormously afterward.
Missouri consumer legal work generally bills in the range of about $175 to $350 an hour, with a midpoint near $263, and St. Louis and Kansas City attorneys tend to sit at the higher end because of overhead. Specialist estate planning firms in the metro publish rates near $395 an hour for work outside their flat-fee packages.
You will see the hourly rate when you amend a trust years later, when you administer a trust after a death, when a probate matter gets contested, or when a family disagreement turns into litigation. That is the reason to ask, at the first meeting, what falls outside the flat fee — and to get the answer in writing.
### The number nobody quotes you: what Missouri probate costs
Families almost always arrive at this next question sideways. Do you have to go to probate if you have a will in Missouri? Frequently, yes — and understanding what that costs is the only way to judge whether a trust is worth its price.
Missouri does not leave probate fees to the market. Section 473.153 of the Revised Statutes of Missouri sets a schedule, and the personal representative and the attorney are each entitled to a fee calculated from it:
5 percent on the first $5,000
4 percent on the next $20,000
3 percent on the next $75,000
2.75 percent on the next $300,000
2.5 percent on the next $600,000
2 percent on everything over $1,000,000
Two things about that schedule matter more than the percentages themselves.
First, it is a minimum, not a cap. The statute expressly allows the court to award additional compensation where the work justifies it. Second, it runs twice — once for the attorney and once for the personal representative, who is often a family member and who may or may not waive the fee.
Run the math on a $100,000 probate estate and the statutory figure comes to $3,300 for the attorney, and the same again for the personal representative. On a $300,000 estate it is $8,800 each. That is where the trust pitch comes from, and on those numbers it is not an unreasonable pitch.
But read the base carefully, because this is where a lot of marketing gets sloppy. The percentages apply to the value of the personal property administered plus the proceeds of any real estate sold under the probate court’s order. A house that passes by beneficiary deed is not in that base. Neither is a payable-on-death account. The Affton house in the opening is only a probate number if nothing was done to move it out of probate — and moving it out is not expensive, which is the next section.
### How long Missouri probate actually takes
Cost is only half of it. Time is the other half, and the floor is set by statute, not by how motivated your family is.
Missouri gives creditors six months from the personal representative’s appointment to file claims against the estate. That window cannot be shortened, waived, or hurried. Six months is therefore the practical minimum for a supervised estate no matter how simple it is.
In practice, a straightforward estate with cooperative heirs and no disputes tends to close in six to twelve months. Add contested real estate, a serious creditor claim, or a family fight, and two years or more is entirely normal. During that stretch the house generally cannot be sold without the court’s involvement, and it still needs insurance, utilities, and a lawn service.
There are out-of-pocket costs too: the court filing deposit to open the estate, the newspaper publication of notice to creditors (in St. Louis County, publication is paid directly to the publisher rather than collected by the court), possible surety bond premiums where the will does not waive the bond, appraisal fees, and recording fees. Individually these are small next to the statutory fee. Together they are not nothing. Call the probate division — in St. Louis County it sits in Clayton — for the current filing figures rather than trusting any number you read online, including this article.
### The Missouri beneficiary deed: cheap, specific, and widely overlooked
Missouri allows something a lot of states do not, and for a family whose main asset is a house it is often the single highest-value thing on the menu. Under section 461.025, you can record a beneficiary deed that transfers your real estate to a named person at your death, without probate.
The requirements are narrow and unforgiving:
The deed must expressly state that it does not take effect until the owner’s death.
It must name the beneficiary and describe the property by legal description.
It must be signed before a notary.
It must be recorded with the recorder of deeds in the county where the property sits — before the owner dies. An unrecorded beneficiary deed is worth nothing. This is the mistake that shows up over and over.
What you keep is control. Missouri law is explicit that the beneficiary has no rights in the property while you are alive, and does not have to sign anything. You can sell the house, mortgage it, or change your mind. Under section 461.033 a beneficiary designation may be revoked or changed during the owner’s lifetime — though where there are joint owners, a change requires the agreement of all living owners.
One trap deserves its own sentence, because it undoes more plans than any other: your will does not override a beneficiary designation. Missouri law provides that a will cannot revoke or change a beneficiary designation unless the designation itself expressly says a will can. If your beneficiary deed, your payable-on-death account, or your old life insurance policy names an ex-spouse, the will you sign next week does not fix it. The designation wins.
As for price, a published St. Louis fee schedule lists a beneficiary deed at about $395 per deed, plus the county recording fee. Set that next to an $8,800 statutory probate fee and you can see why this document is worth asking about by name.
### Small estates: when Missouri lets you skip the full process
Missouri also has a short path for modest estates. Under section 473.097, when the estate is worth $40,000 or less — excluding liens, debts, and encumbrances — a distributee can generally use a small estate affidavit to collect and distribute the property without a full administration. A distributee can typically file after thirty days have passed since the death. There is also a separate procedure, a refusal of letters, that applies in certain situations involving a surviving spouse or minor children.
Two practical cautions. The $40,000 threshold is a real ceiling, and a paid-off house in Webster Groves or a retirement account blows through it instantly. And several urban Missouri counties — St. Louis City and St. Louis County among them — in practice expect an attorney to be involved even in small estate filings, so the do-it-yourself savings can be smaller than advertised.
### What makes a will valid in Missouri
Worth knowing before you pay anyone, and worth knowing before you trust the page in the desk drawer.
You must be eighteen or an emancipated minor, and of sound mind.
The will must be in writing.
It must be signed by you, or by another person at your direction and in your presence.
It must be attested by two or more competent witnesses who sign their names in your presence.
Missouri does not recognize holographic wills — a will you wrote out entirely in your own handwriting, with no witnesses, does not qualify. That handwritten page in the Affton desk drawer is, under Missouri law, most likely not a will at all.
That leads straight to the question people ask at the signing table. Does a will in Missouri need to be notarized? Not for validity. Missouri requires witnesses, not a notary. But a notary is what makes a will self-proved under section 474.337 — you, your witnesses, and a notary sign a short affidavit, and the court can then admit the will without hunting down witnesses years later to testify about a signing they barely remember. It costs almost nothing at the signing table and saves real trouble afterward, which is why most attorney-drafted Missouri wills include one.
Missouri has also modernized. The Missouri Electronic Wills and Electronic Estate Planning Documents Act, at sections 474.540 through 474.564, applies to people who die on or after August 28, 2025, and to estate planning documents signed or witnessed remotely on or after that date. Electronic signatures, remote witnessing, and online notarization are now on the table for many estate planning documents. This is exactly the sort of thing that shifts, so ask whether the firm you hire is set up for it and what they recommend.
### Taxes: the part most St. Louis families can stop worrying about
Missouri has no state estate tax and no state inheritance tax. The state takes nothing from an inheritance.
Federal estate tax applies only above the federal exemption, which is $15 million per person in 2026 — $30 million for a married couple — and is indexed for inflation going forward. The overwhelming majority of estates in this metro are nowhere near that line.
This matters commercially. If someone is selling you a complex plan on the strength of estate tax savings and your estate is a house, a 401(k), and some savings, ask them to show you the tax math. Income tax on inherited retirement accounts is a separate and much more common issue, and a different conversation.
### A word about the Illinois side
Everything above is Missouri law. If you live in Belleville, Edwardsville, O’Fallon, or anywhere else on the Metro East side, or if you own a cabin or rental property across the river, different rules apply to that property — including a state estate tax that Missouri does not have. Owning real estate in two states is one of the classic fact patterns where a trust genuinely earns its fee, because it can avoid opening a separate probate in each state. Say so out loud at the consultation.
### Questions to ask before you hire anyone
Take this list to the meeting. The answers, more than the price, will tell you what you are buying.
Is this a flat fee, and what exactly does it include? Ask for the document list in writing.
Does the fee include funding the trust — preparing and recording deeds, and the letters to banks and brokerages?
What is not covered, and what is your hourly rate when we go outside the package?
Who will actually draft my documents, and who will be at the signing?
Given what I own, would a beneficiary deed and payable-on-death designations accomplish most of this for less?
What will it cost to amend this in five years?
Will you review my existing beneficiary designations against the new plan?
Do you handle the probate or trust administration afterward, and what does that cost?
That fifth question is the one that separates a counselor from a salesperson. A good answer engages with your facts. A bad answer changes the subject.
### Where plans quietly fail
The expensive failures in estate planning are rarely bad documents. They are good documents that nobody finished.
The unfunded trust. Paid for, signed, beautifully bound, and empty, because the house was never deeded into it. The estate goes through probate anyway, and the family paid twice.
The stale beneficiary designation. An ex-spouse still named on a policy or an account. The designation controls, not the will.
The unrecorded beneficiary deed. Signed, notarized, and left in a drawer. Under Missouri law it had to be recorded before death. It was not.
The missing financial power of attorney. A parent develops dementia, no one can legally act, and the family ends up in a court proceeding that costs more than the whole plan would have.
The document nobody can find. The original will matters. Tell the person you named as executor where it is.
None of those are fixed by spending more. They are fixed by finishing.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Do I need a lawyer for a will in Missouri?
A.  No. Missouri law does not require an attorney for a will to be valid. It requires that the will be in writing, signed by you or by someone at your direction and in your presence, and attested by two or more competent witnesses who sign in your presence. What an attorney fee buys is drafting judgment and a correct signing, plus a check that your will does not conflict with the beneficiary designations already on your accounts — which is the most common way a homemade plan goes wrong.
### Q. Does a will in Missouri need to be notarized?
A.  Not to be valid. Missouri requires two witnesses, not a notary. A notary is what makes a will self-proved under section 474.337, meaning the court can admit it without calling the witnesses to testify later. It adds almost nothing to the cost at the signing and removes a real obstacle for your family afterward, which is why most attorney-drafted Missouri wills include a self-proving affidavit.
### Q. Is a will or trust better in Missouri?
A.  Neither is better in the abstract — they do different jobs, and Missouri’s inexpensive non-probate tools change the math. A will gives instructions for probate; a revocable living trust is mainly a way to avoid probate, at a higher up-front cost. In Missouri, a family whose estate is one house and a few accounts can often keep nearly everything out of probate with a recorded beneficiary deed and payable-on-death designations for a fraction of a trust’s price. Families with real estate in more than one state, a blended family, a beneficiary who cannot manage money, or a business interest are the ones who tend to get genuine value from a trust. Put your actual asset list in front of an attorney and ask.
### Q. Do you have to go to probate if you have a will in Missouri?
A.  Often, yes — a will is a set of instructions for probate, not a way around it. What determines probate is how an asset is titled. Property with a living joint owner or a valid beneficiary designation passes outside probate: payable-on-death accounts, transfer-on-death vehicle titles, a recorded beneficiary deed, life insurance, and most retirement accounts. Whatever remains in the deceased person’s sole name with no beneficiary named is what the will governs, and that is what goes through the probate division. Estates of $40,000 or less may qualify for a small estate affidavit instead.
### Q. How much can you inherit in Missouri without paying taxes?
A.  Missouri has no state inheritance tax and no state estate tax, so the state itself takes nothing from an inheritance. Federal estate tax applies only above the federal exemption, which is $15 million per person in 2026 and $30 million for a married couple, indexed for inflation going forward. That leaves the overwhelming majority of St. Louis area estates untaxed at both levels. Income tax is a separate question — an inherited traditional retirement account, for example, is generally taxable to whoever withdraws the money.
### Q. What is the downside of having a living trust?
A.  Cost and upkeep. A trust-based plan runs well above a will-based one, and it only works if you actually fund it — retitling the house, the accounts and the vehicles into the trust. An unfunded trust does nothing. A living trust also carries no income-tax benefit by itself; the payoff is avoiding probate.
### Q. What is the biggest mistake with wills?
A.  Writing one and never touching it again. Marriages, divorces, deaths, new children and property bought in another state all outdate a will quietly. The second mistake is assuming a will avoids probate — it does not. It only tells the probate court what you wanted.
### Q. What shouldn't you put in a living trust?
A.  Retirement accounts — 401(k)s, IRAs and HSAs — because retitling them can trigger tax consequences; name beneficiaries instead. Life insurance usually works better with a named beneficiary too. Vehicles are often left out for simplicity. Everything else, particularly the house, generally belongs inside or the trust does not do its job.
### Before you spend anything
Write down what you own and how each piece is titled. Pull up the beneficiary named on every account and policy. Then call two or three attorneys and ask each for a written list of documents and a flat fee. Half the time the family in Affton discovers that what they actually needed was a beneficiary deed, a financial power of attorney, and an afternoon of paperwork — and the other half of the time they learn exactly why their situation calls for more, from someone who can point to the specific fact that makes it so.
Either way, they walk in with numbers instead of a shrug.
General cost information only, not legal advice, and not a substitute for talking with a licensed Missouri attorney about your own situation. Fees vary by firm and by complexity, court costs vary by county, and Missouri law changes — the electronic wills and remote signing rules have changed recently. Confirm anything you plan to rely on.
