Extended service contracts, gap coverage, paint and fabric protection, tire and wheel plans, key replacement, prepaid maintenance — each one carries its own margin, each arrives on a menu, and every one of them is optional. Ask for the price of each item separately rather than as a change to the monthly payment.
Do not assume a federal rule is standing behind you here. The Federal Trade Commission’s CARS Rule, which would have required dealers to disclose the offering price up front and get express consent before charging for add-ons, was vacated by the Fifth Circuit on January 27, 2025 and never took effect.
Financing is the other half of that desk. Experian’s State of the Automotive Finance Market report for the first quarter of 2026 put the average new-car loan at $43,925 at 6.39%, with a $770 payment and a 69.48-month term; used loans averaged $27,070 at 11.43%. Credit unions wrote 20.09% of auto loan originations that quarter. Walk in holding a preapproval and the dealer’s rate has to beat a number you already own — our guide to a credit union versus bank auto loan in St. Louis covers how to get one.
### What does a dealership owner see that you don’t?
The car itself is close to a loss leader. The Presidio-NCM dealership benchmark published August 4, 2026, drawn from more than 4,000 franchised stores, put gross profit per new vehicle retailed at $1,840 in the second quarter of 2026, down 13.5% in a year, and used at $1,409. Finance and insurance ran the other way to a record $1,769 per unit, and fixed operations — service and parts — produced 52.8% of all dealership gross profit. Meanwhile every unit on the lot is borrowed against a floor plan line that charges interest daily until it sells, a trade-in needs tires, brakes and a detail before it can be retailed, and a slice of the factory invoice sits in holdback until the quarter closes. Aging inventory is the thing owners complain about to each other. It is also why a store wants to be found the moment someone searches this category locally, which is what a complete directory listing is for.
Related reading: how to check the car itself and what the parts will cost later.
Ready to shop the lot instead of the fine print? Browse car dealerships across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then pull your address-level tax rate and a credit union preapproval before you drive to the first one.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Do I pay taxes twice if I buy a car out of state?
A.  No. Illinois gives credit for tax properly paid to another state on that RUT-25, and a Missouri resident who buys in the Metro East pays Missouri tax once, when titling. What you do not get is the lower of the two rates.
### Q. How much is sales tax on a $30,000 car in Missouri?
A.  The state rate is 4.225%, plus your local sales tax, applied to the purchase price minus any trade-in allowance. On a $30,000 car with no trade, the state portion alone is $1,267.50, and metro local rates stack several points on top; put a $10,000 trade against it and you are taxed on $20,000 instead. The combined figure depends on your street address, not the dealership. The Missouri Department of Revenue publishes an address-level lookup, and you pay the whole amount at a license office, not at the store.
### Q. Does Illinois still cap the trade-in tax credit at $10,000?
A.  No. Public Act 102-0353 removed that cap for first-division motor vehicles effective January 1, 2022. The $10,000 limit had been created by Public Act 101-0031 and applied for two years, which is why the claim still circulates. Today an Illinois dealer sale gives you full credit for the trade-in value shown on the bill of sale, with no ceiling.
### Q. How long do I have to title a car in Missouri?
A.  Thirty days from the date of purchase. A $25 penalty applies on the 31st day and grows by another $25 every 30 days, up to $200. Your temporary permit also runs 30 days from the purchase date, costs $5 plus a $9 processing fee, and only one permit may be issued per vehicle, so a delayed title is a real problem rather than a paperwork annoyance.
### Q. Can a Missouri dealer charge any doc fee they want?
A.  No. Missouri caps the dealer administrative fee under RSMo 301.558 and raises the ceiling annually with inflation. The Department of Revenue set the 2026 maximum at $620.79, up from $604.47 in 2025. Illinois caps its documentary fee as well, and lower, at a figure Illinois dealers put at $377.63 for 2026. Check the number on your sheet against the current cap.
### Q. Do I need an emissions test to sell a car in St. Louis County?
A.  Yes, in most cases. The Gateway Vehicle Inspection Program covers St. Louis City, St. Louis County, St. Charles County and Jefferson County, and requires a test on any vehicle sale or title transfer. The fee is capped at $24. New vehicles with under 6,000 miles at first sale, plug-in hybrids and fully electric vehicles are among the exemptions.
### Q. Is Missouri a good state to buy a car?
A.  On fees, mostly yes. The 4.225% state rate beats Illinois’ 6.25%, a title costs $8.50 plus $9 instead of $165, and RSMo 144.025 keeps your trade-in credit on a private sale made within 180 days. The exception is the dealer administrative fee, capped at $620.79 for 2026 against $377.63 across the river.
### Q. Should I get preapproved before I go to the dealership?
A.  It gives you a number to beat. Experian put the average new-car loan rate at 6.39% and used at 11.43% in the first quarter of 2026, and credit unions wrote about a fifth of auto loan originations. A preapproval turns the finance office conversation from what payment works for you into whether they can beat the rate in your pocket.
### Q. Do I have to pay Missouri sales tax on a car purchased out of state?
A.  Yes. Missouri taxes the vehicle when you title and register it here, regardless of where you bought it. On a $30,000 car with a $10,000 trade-in the taxable amount is $20,000 — the state portion alone is $845, with metro local rates stacking several points on top. Buying across the river does not avoid it.

## How to Buy Furniture in St. Louis That Actually Lasts
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-buy-furniture-in-st-louis-that-lasts
Imagine it’s a Saturday in Affton and the couch finally quits. Not dramatically. One cushion just stops coming back — you sit down, sink four inches, and realize the thing you bought on sale three years ago has been dying in front of you the whole time.
So you go looking. A big showroom out by the highway. A small independent in Kirkwood with six sofas and a wall of fabric samples. An estate sale in Webster Groves where a walnut dresser costs less than flat-pack. A warehouse in Maryland Heights where every tag says 70% off, which is odd, because it said 70% off in March.
Then there’s the part nobody warns you about in a hundred-year-old brick house in Florissant: the stairwell. The turn at the landing. The doorway that measures 32 inches and gives you 29.
### How can I tell if furniture is high-quality?
On upholstery, check four things, all of them from the showroom floor: the frame, the suspension, the seat foam density, and the fabric’s abrasion rating. A sofa on a kiln-dried hardwood frame with good upholstery can run 15 to 25 years. One built on stapled softwood with cheap foam starts sagging inside two.
The frame should be kiln-dried hardwood — oak, maple, beech — joined with mortise-and-tenon joints, dowels or reinforced corner blocks. Kiln drying pulls the moisture out so the frame doesn’t warp as your house swings from January dry to August humid. Lift one front corner six inches. If the opposite leg stays planted and the frame twists, that flex is what eventually splits joints.
Underneath, eight-way hand-tied springs are the traditional gold standard, and heavy-gauge sinuous (S-shaped) springs are reliable too. Ask to see the cutaway model.
Foam is where the number matters most. Residential seat cushions run 1.5 to 2.5 pounds per cubic foot, and 1.8 is the industry average. True High Resilience foam has to hit at least 2.5 pounds per cubic foot to earn the name. So when a tag says “high density” or “high resiliency” with no number attached, assume 1.8.
Fabric durability is measured in Wyzenbeek double rubs. Roughly 15,000 is heavy-duty for household use; 30,000 and up targets commercial traffic. The Association for Contract Textiles cautions that lab results vary and that a bigger number past the guideline doesn’t reliably mean longer life. Treat 15,000 as a floor, not a scoreboard. What to avoid when buying a couch is the inverse of those four checks.
### What should you check on a dresser, table or bed frame?
Open a drawer, look at the corner joint, then find a raw edge. Interlocking dovetails signal real case-goods construction; drawers held with staples or metal clips are a reliable sign of lower-grade work. Solid wood shows consistent grain on every face. A gray or brown compressed core at an edge is particleboard or MDF.
Veneer isn’t automatically bad. Good veneer over a stable substrate resists seasonal movement better than a wide solid plank. Cheap veneer over particleboard is the problem, because once it chips there’s nothing underneath to repair.
Ask one safety question out loud about dressers. Under the STURDY Act, the Consumer Product Safety Commission adopted ASTM F2057-23 as a mandatory standard for clothing storage units manufactured after September 1, 2023. It tests stability on carpet, with drawers loaded and multiple open, and simulates a child up to 60 pounds pulling on it. Clearance stock can predate that date. Anchor it to the wall either way.
### Chain, local independent, or used — what does each get you?
National chains buy in volume, stock deep and offer financing, so you can often have it this week. You are buying a SKU. A local independent usually gets you frame and fabric choices, someone who can name the spring system without reading a tag, and the same person on the phone when there’s a problem eight weeks later.
Used and estate sources are the sleeper option here. Older case goods from a St. Charles estate sale or a Belleville consignment floor are often solid wood with dovetailed drawers at a fraction of new pricing. The trade-off is total: no warranty, no return, no delivery.
Used bedding is the one category with real rules on both sides of the river. Missouri’s RSMo 421.038 says bedding can’t be made from secondhand material unless that material has been sanitized or germicidally treated by a department-approved method, and it must carry a conspicuous label saying so. Missouri dropped bedding-company registration in 2012 but kept the labeling and sanitizing rules. Illinois runs a stricter version through its Bedding and Upholstered Furniture Act, which registers renovators and sanitizers and requires labels stating new versus secondhand content. No law tag, no sale.
### Will it fit? Measuring matters more in a St. Louis house
Measure the narrowest point of the whole path, not just the front door, and get the sofa’s diagonal depth off the spec sheet. Your tightest opening should be 2 to 3 inches wider than the sofa’s width or diagonal depth, whichever applies. Measure the clear opening, not the frame: a doorway that reads 36 inches often gives only 33 to 34 once the door and hinges are in the way.
This bites harder here than in most metros. The median year built for housing in the City of St. Louis is 1939, per 2023 American Community Survey five-year data — tied with Buffalo, Rochester and Providence for the oldest housing stock in the country. After the Great Fire of May 17, 1849 burned 430 buildings and 23 steamboats, the city required new riverfront construction to be brick or stone, and the region’s Cheltenham clay and dozens of local kilns made brick the cheap default for a century.
The consequence is masonry walls and stairs that turn. A contractor can widen a drywall opening in a Maryland Heights ranch in an afternoon. Nobody is doing that to a load-bearing brick stairwell for a sectional. Measure the landing, the handrail and the ceiling height over the stairs. Then ask whether the legs unbolt — two inches off the depth is often the whole ballgame.
Different room, different problem — flooring outlasts every sofa you buy.
### What does furniture delivery actually cost?
Three tiers, three prices. Threshold delivery, which stops at your entryway, commonly runs about $50 to $100. Room-of-choice runs roughly $100 to $200. Full white-glove — placed in the room, unpacked, legs bolted on, packaging hauled away — commonly lands between $150 and $400 locally. Distance, fragility and access difficulty move it.
Say the word “stairs” when you get the quote. Then ask three more things before you sign: who carries it up, the store’s own crew or a contracted carrier; what happens to your money if it won’t fit; and how the damage claim process works.
Inspect the piece before you sign the delivery receipt, not after the truck leaves. Signing generally acknowledges you received it in good condition, and unwinding that later is a much worse afternoon than looking behind a headboard.
### How long do special orders take in 2026?
Stock items are largely back to pre-2020 timelines. Custom is still slower: domestic custom upholstery in a manufacturer’s standard fabric generally runs 8 to 12 weeks, complex sectionals or non-standard dimensions 12 to 16, and supplying your own fabric adds 2 to 4 weeks. Imports still carry a 12 to 20-plus week window.
The 2021 and 2022 blowout came from foam and lumber shortages, plant labor gaps and ocean freight all hitting a demand spike at once. Those cleared. What replaced them is cost, not queue. Section 232 tariffs took effect at midnight on October 14, 2025 at 25% on upholstered wooden furniture, kitchen cabinets and vanities. Increases to 30% and 50% set for January 1, 2026 were postponed a full year by a proclamation signed December 31, 2025, so 25% holds through 2026 and the step-up now lands January 1, 2027. UK goods are capped at 10%, EU and Japan at 15%. Get the quoted lead time written on the sales order.
### Do mattress trials and return policies really protect you?
Less than most shoppers assume, and there is no federal three-day right to cancel a showroom purchase. The FTC’s Cooling-Off Rule at 16 CFR Part 429 covers sales of $25 or more made somewhere other than the seller’s permanent place of business — your living room, a hotel ballroom, a fairgrounds booth. Buy inside the store and the policy on your receipt is the whole of your protection.
On mattresses, 100 nights is the most common trial length, and most brands require a 30-night break-in first, leaving about 70 nights to actually decide. In-store comfort exchanges are usually one-time and rarely free: flat fees near $100 and restocking charges as high as 30% are both in the market. Custom fabric and special orders are typically final sale.
### Is that “80% off” real? What Missouri and Illinois rules say
A discount is only lawful if the “before” price was real, and both states put that in writing. Missouri’s rule 15 CSR 60-7.050 says sale terminology implying a price cut requires the reduction to come from a bona fide regular price in effect immediately before the ad, and a cut under 5% is presumed not meaningful unless disclosed. 15 CSR 60-7.060 adds that a former-price comparison must be actual and bona fide, not illusory or fictitious. 15 CSR 60-7.070 makes the seller keep records proving the basis for 12 months.
Illinois says it in its own words. Under 14 Ill. Adm. Code 470.220, comparing a current price to the seller’s own former price is deceptive unless that former price is one at which a substantial number of sales were made, or at which the item was offered openly and in good faith for a reasonably substantial period with real intent to sell.
Going-out-of-business sales get their own statute. Missouri’s RSMo 407.800 requires written notice to the attorney general at least 10 days ahead, an inventory filing, no supplementing that inventory once the sale starts, and a 60-day cap unless an extension is registered by affidavit. Illinois handles it through the Fraudulent Sales Act at 815 ILCS 350, licensed by the local clerk and also capped at 60 days. If a Belleville storefront is in month five of liquidation, something is wrong.
The move that beats all of it: ignore the percentage and price the exact model number at three stores.
### What furniture retailers wish shoppers understood
Most of that showroom isn’t owned outright. It sits on floor plan financing — a lender pays the supplier, the store pays interest while the piece sits, and curtailment clauses force principal paydowns at 30, 60 or 90 days whether anything sold or not. Every square foot is rented too, and a sofa eats 30 of them. Gross margin looks fat at 35% to 45%, but net profit typically lands near 3% to 6% once rent, freight, payroll and the delivery truck come out. Delivery is a cost center, not a profit line. Upholstery carries more margin than case goods for one reason: a dining table’s model number can be price-shopped in ten seconds and a custom sofa can’t. That’s also why special orders want a deposit and get quoted non-cancellable. Shoppers hunt furniture by neighborhood, so being listed and complete on St Louis Near Me Directory is how a store turns up in that search.
Related reading: sourcing the materials and smaller things made here.
Ready to shop frames instead of price tags? Browse furniture stores across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then call ahead with your doorway and stairwell measurements already written down.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What brand of furniture lasts the longest?
A.  Construction predicts lifespan better than the nameplate does. A kiln-dried hardwood frame with good upholstery runs 15 to 25 years; stapled softwood and 1.8-pound foam sag inside two, whatever the tag says. Ask for frame species, springs and foam density, not the brand.
### Q. What to avoid when buying a couch?
A.  A stapled softwood frame, a cushion tag claiming high density with no number attached, a fabric with no double-rub figure, and a frame that twists when you lift one front corner.
### Q. When is the best time of year to buy furniture?
A.  The industry turns its floors over twice a year, with new indoor styles landing in spring and fall, so stores discount the outgoing floor ahead of each changeover. January and February clearance and Labor Day weekend are the strongest windows for living room pieces. Presidents Day and Memorial Day are the biggest mattress events.
### Q. Are eight-way hand-tied springs worth paying more for?
A.  Sometimes. Hand-tied construction is the traditional benchmark and holds shape well over decades, but a heavy-gauge sinuous spring system performs reliably and costs less. What a seat feels like in year eight depends more on the frame under it and the foam density in the cushion.
### Q. Can I return furniture after it’s delivered in Missouri or Illinois?
A.  Only if the store’s own policy says so. The FTC Cooling-Off Rule’s three-day cancellation right applies to purchases of $25 or more made away from the seller’s permanent place of business, so it does not reach a showroom sale. Neither state grants a general right of return on in-store furniture.
### Q. Is it legal to buy a used mattress in Missouri or Illinois?
A.  Yes, with conditions. Missouri’s RSMo 421.038 requires secondhand material to be sanitized or germicidally treated by an approved method and labeled clearly. Illinois regulates it under the Bedding and Upholstered Furniture Act, which registers renovators and sanitizers and requires labels disclosing new versus secondhand content, with penalties reaching $1,000 per offense.
### Q. What size doorway does a standard sofa need?
A.  Aim for a clear opening 2 to 3 inches wider than the sofa’s width or its diagonal depth, whichever is the limiting number. Measure the actual gap with the door swung open rather than the frame — a 36-inch doorway often yields only 33 to 34 inches. In older homes, measure the stair landing and handrail too.
### Q. How do I know if a furniture sale price is real?
A.  Write down the manufacturer and model number, then price that exact piece at two other stores. Missouri’s 15 CSR 60-7.070 requires sellers to keep records substantiating a price comparison for at least 12 months, so a legitimate former price is documented somewhere. A banner that never comes down is the opposite signal.
### Q. What is the 2/3 rule furniture?
A.  Scale, not decoration. A sofa should run about two thirds the length of the wall it sits against, and a coffee table about two thirds the length of the sofa. It is why a room can feel wrong when every piece in it is individually nice — the proportions are fighting each other.
### Q. What items make your house look cheap?
A.  Usually materials failing early rather than taste. Seat foam under 1.8 pounds per cubic foot flattens within a couple of years, and true High Resilience foam has to hit 2.5 to earn the name. A kiln-dried hardwood frame with good upholstery runs 15 to 25 years; the cheap alternative announces itself by year three.

## Hiring a Property Manager in St. Louis: What to Ask Before You Sign
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/hiring-a-property-manager-in-st-louis
Imagine it’s a Tuesday in February, 10:40 at night, and your phone lights up. It’s the tenant in the little brick two-bedroom you own in Affton. No heat. You have a meeting at eight, no furnace guy, and you’re about to learn what every landlord learns eventually — the hard part of owning a rental is never the rent.
Maybe your version is the duplex in Florissant you inherited. Maybe it’s the ranch in St. Charles you couldn’t sell, so you rented it. Maybe it’s a condo in Belleville, where the landlord rules you learned on the Missouri side don’t all apply.
One rental is a hobby. Two is a second job. Somewhere in there most owners price out a property manager, and the pricing is where it gets murky.
### Should you hire a property manager for your St. Louis rental?
Hire one when the distance, the door count or the day job stops working. The practical test: if you own more than a unit or two, live more than half an hour away, or can’t leave work to meet a furnace tech, a manager usually costs less than the vacancy and the bad tenant placement you’ll absorb without one.
A manager does four jobs — price and market the unit, screen and place the tenant, collect rent and account for it, coordinate repairs and legal notices. Only the third automates easily, and it’s the one owners think they’re paying for. One house twenty minutes away with a plumber you trust is a real argument for self-managing. Three across Florissant, Affton and Belleville while working full time is not.
### What percentage do most property management companies charge?
Expect a stack, not a single number. St. Louis firms commonly advertise 8% to 12% of monthly rent, and several publish flat alternatives in the $100 to $180 range with a minimum near $100 a month. Treat that headline carefully: no public survey backs it — it’s the range operators post, not a measured average.
The leasing fee moves your return more than the percentage does, and it’s the most consistent figure in the trade — 50% to 100% of one month’s rent to place a tenant. On a house renting at $1,600, that’s $800 to $1,600, charged again every time a tenant leaves. Zillow reported on May 28, 2025 that listing views, applications and renter outreach to property managers all peak in the first week of June.
Renewal fees are where the metro splits. Some St. Louis companies charge a flat $100 to $300 when a tenant re-signs; others charge 25% to 50% of one month’s rent — $250 against $800 for one signature. For scale, the average apartment rent in St. Louis was $1,443 as of August 1, 2026, with three-bedrooms at $1,786, per RentCafe’s Yardi Matrix data.
### Which property management fees actually surprise landlords?
How much is a reasonable management fee? Not a question the headline number answers. The management percentage is rarely where contracts diverge. Start with the two-word difference that changes the whole deal: whether the fee is charged on rent collected or on rent due. On rent due, you keep paying while a tenant is delinquent or the unit sits empty.
Then price the rest. A one-time setup charge, around $300 here. A minimum monthly fee, often about $100, which quietly turns a percentage deal into a flat one on a cheap unit. A vacancy fee, billed flat or as a share of expected rent. Inspections, roughly $75 to $150 a visit, or about $149 for an annual condition report. Eviction handling, often an annual add-on near $200, or roughly $500 a case plus legal costs.
Two more need a direct question. Maintenance markup is a percentage added on top of the vendor’s invoice, and there’s no industry rate for it — some St. Louis firms advertise none at all, while elsewhere a project-management charge near 10% of project value shows up. And ask who keeps the late fee; some agreements let the manager keep a quarter to half of it.
### Does a property manager in Missouri need a real estate license?
Yes, in almost every third-party arrangement. RSMo 339.010 defines a real estate broker as anyone who, for another and for compensation, rents or leases real estate, offers to rent or lease it, or negotiates the rental or leasing of it. Managing someone else’s rental for a fee sits inside that definition.
The exemptions are narrower than owners assume. RSMo 339.010 exempts owners and lessors acting on their own property and their regular employees, licensed attorneys, and people acting as a receiver, trustee in bankruptcy, administrator, executor or guardian. It also exempts on-site personnel limited to enumerated clerical duties — showing units, delivering leases, receiving applications, deposits and rent for delivery to a broker or owner. That covers a leasing assistant, not a company running your house from across town.
The follow-on rule protects your money: under RSMo 339.105, a Missouri broker holding funds belonging to another must keep them in a separate bank account designated an escrow or trust account, with records available for Missouri Real Estate Commission inspection. Illinois runs a parallel system — under the Real Estate License Act of 2000, 225 ILCS 454, leasing residential property for someone else takes a residential leasing agent license, sponsored and employed by a sponsoring broker. Ask for the license number and look it up.
Nothing to do with leases — every building eventually needs an electrician.
### How do Missouri and Illinois security deposit rules differ?
They differ on the cap and on the clock, and the Illinois half changed recently. Missouri caps the amount: RSMo 535.300 says a landlord may not demand or receive a security deposit in excess of two months’ rent. Illinois sets no statewide dollar cap at all.
Missouri then gives you thirty days. Within thirty days after the tenancy terminates, the landlord must return the deposit or deliver an itemized list of damages, and the tenant has the right to be present at the inspection. Get it wrong and the tenant recovers twice the amount wrongfully withheld.
Illinois used to let small landlords ignore its statute. Not anymore. The Security Deposit Return Act, 765 ILCS 710, was amended by Public Act 103-224 effective January 1, 2024, and the old five-or-more-units threshold is gone — it now reaches a lessor of residential real property generally. The landlord has thirty days from the date the tenant vacated to furnish an itemized statement of damage with paid receipts, and with no statement the full deposit goes back within forty-five days. The penalty is twice the deposit plus court costs and reasonable attorney’s fees.
Interest is where the old size test survived: 765 ILCS 715 still applies only to property with twenty-five or more units in one building or contiguous complex, on deposits held more than six months. Missouri requires no interest at all.
### How much notice do you owe a tenant, and how fast is an eviction?
Missouri moves faster on unpaid rent than owners expect. Ending a month-to-month tenancy takes one month’s written notice under RSMo 441.060, terminating on a rent-paying date not less than a month after the notice is received. But for nonpayment, RSMo 535.020 says outright that the 441.060 notice is not required before filing — the landlord demands the rent and files if it isn’t paid. No statutory cure window sits at the front of it.
Illinois builds the cure window in. Nonpayment requires written notice giving the tenant not less than five days after service to pay, under 735 ILCS 5/9-209. Another lease breach takes ten days’ notice to quit under 9-210. Month-to-month takes thirty days, week-to-week seven, under 9-207. And under 735 ILCS 5/9-117, an eviction order can’t be enforced more than 120 days after entry unless the court grants an extension.
After judgment in Missouri, RSMo 535.110 controls: no trial de novo or appeal stays execution unless the tenant posts bond within ten days. Then there’s the courthouse. St. Louis City files in the 22nd Judicial Circuit and St. Louis County in the 21st — separate courts, separate sheriffs, separate dockets. Cross the river and you’re in the 20th for St. Clair County or the 3rd for Madison County. One metro, four systems.
### What does St. Louis City require before a tenant moves in?
An inspection and a certificate, before anybody gets keys. City Ordinance No. 71835 requires a Housing Conservation District inspection, and a Certificate of Inspection must be obtained before a vacant residential unit is occupied. The application fee is $120, or $200 if a resident is found occupying a dwelling with no current certificate, plus $65 for each additional unit at one address. The certificate is good for twelve months. Outside the city line it fragments — unincorporated St. Louis County runs its own occupancy permit program with an inspection at change of occupant, and municipalities inside the county set their own rules.
### What the job looks like from the management company’s side
The percentage model breaks first. Ten percent of an $800 unit is $80 a month, and one after-hours call plus a vendor dispatch spends that before the tenth — which is why minimum fees exist and cheap doors get quietly declined. Maintenance is the actual product: in Buildium’s 2026 industry report, 56% of owners named maintenance support as their main reason for hiring a manager, and it was also their top source of stress. Rent collection automated years ago; work orders didn’t, and AppFolio’s 3Q2025 update put the U.S. average near 54 rental units per employee. Turnover is the bill nobody wants: the National Apartment Association’s 2024 Income/Expense IQ data, published December 2025, shows turnover costs up 17.5% in a year and vacancy and rent loss at $1,323 per unit. Deferred maintenance and an owner who won’t approve a repair produce that bill on repeat, which is why good firms screen owners as carefully as tenants — and why one with room for another door wants a complete listing where owners already search.
### What should you ask before signing a management agreement?
Seven questions, one phone call. Ask for the license number and look it up yourself. Ask whether the monthly fee is charged on rent collected or rent due. Ask for the entire fee schedule in writing, including the leasing fee, the renewal fee and any markup added to vendor invoices.
Then the operational four. What can they spend on a repair without calling you? Who keeps late fees and pet fees? How do you end the agreement, and is there a termination fee? And how many doors does each staff member carry — that predicts how fast a work order gets answered better than anything on a website. Get the answers into the agreement, not the email thread.
Related reading: the closing side of the deal and getting a compliant sign up.
Ready to hand off the 10:40 p.m. furnace call? Browse property management companies across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then ask each one the rent-collected-or-rent-due question first.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What percentage do most property management companies charge?
A.  Eight to twelve percent of monthly rent is the range St. Louis firms advertise, alongside flat plans near $100 to $180 and minimums around $100 a month, which quietly turn a percentage deal into a flat one on a cheap unit. Ask whether that percentage is charged on rent collected or on rent due.
### Q. How much is a reasonable management fee?
A.  Judge the stack, not the headline. The leasing fee moves your return more than the monthly rate does, at 50% to 100% of one month’s rent every placement, and renewals run either a flat $100 to $300 or 25% to 50% of a month. Then price setup near $300, inspections at $75 to $150, and any markup added to vendor invoices.
### Q. Do you need a real estate license to manage rental property in Missouri?
A.  Generally yes. RSMo 339.010 defines a real estate broker to include anyone who, for another and for compensation, rents or leases real estate or negotiates a rental, so managing someone else’s property for a fee is licensed activity. Owners and their regular employees are exempt on their own property, as are attorneys and court-appointed receivers, trustees, executors and guardians.
### Q. How much can a landlord charge for a security deposit in Missouri?
A.  No more than two months’ rent, under RSMo 535.300. The same section requires the deposit back, or an itemized list of damages, within thirty days of the tenancy ending, gives the tenant the right to be present at the inspection, and lets a tenant recover twice any amount wrongfully withheld.
### Q. How long does an Illinois landlord have to return a security deposit?
A.  Thirty days to itemize, forty-five to refund. Under 765 ILCS 710 the landlord must furnish an itemized statement of damage with paid receipts within thirty days of the tenant vacating, and with no statement the full deposit is due within forty-five days. Public Act 103-224, effective January 1, 2024, removed the old five-unit threshold.
### Q. How much notice does a Missouri landlord have to give a tenant?
A.  One month in writing to end a month-to-month tenancy, terminating on a rent-paying date at least a month after the notice is received, under RSMo 441.060. Unpaid rent works differently: RSMo 535.020 states the 441.060 notice is not required before filing a rent and possession statement.
### Q. Is a property manager worth it for one rental property?
A.  Often not, if you live nearby and can take a repair call. At 8%, the monthly fee on a $1,600 house is about $128, but the leasing fee at placement runs $800 to $1,600, and one unit rarely bills enough to get prioritized. The case flips with distance or a second unit.
### Q. Can a property manager evict a tenant for you?
A.  They handle the notice, the paperwork and the coordination, and many St. Louis firms price eviction coverage as an annual add-on near $200 or bill roughly $500 a case plus legal costs. A manager isn’t your lawyer, though, so ask specifically who appears in court.
### Q. What is the 2% rule for rentals?
A.  A screening shortcut: monthly rent should be about 2% of the purchase price. It almost never holds in this market, so treat it as a filter for obviously bad deals rather than a target. Management fees come off the top of whatever it does return.
### Q. What is the 50% rule in rental property?
A.  Assume roughly half of rent goes to operating expenses before the mortgage — taxes, insurance, repairs, vacancy, management. On a $1,600 house that is $800 a month, and St. Louis firms commonly charge 8% to 12% of monthly rent on top, plus a leasing fee each turnover.

## How to Choose a Title Company in St. Louis (Missouri vs Illinois)
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-choose-a-title-company-in-st-louis
Imagine it’s a Tuesday evening in Belleville and you just went under contract on a house in Kirkwood. Your agent’s email says the title company will reach out. You read that line twice. The last house you bought was on the Illinois side, and your attorney ran all of it — the review, the objections, the table. Nobody has said the word attorney to you once.
Fifteen miles north, someone in Florissant is refinancing and just got quoted for a title policy they’re sure they already paid for in 2019. Out in St. Charles, a first-time buyer stares at four title lines on a Loan Estimate, wondering whether those numbers are fixed by law or just set by the lender.
Three confusions, one gap underneath them. The title company is the party most buyers never choose on purpose, and it’s the one deciding whether you actually own what you just wired money for. Here’s what it does, what changes when you cross the Mississippi, and how to pick your own.
### Can you pick your own title company, or are you stuck with the one you were handed?
You can almost always pick. Federal law bars a seller from requiring, as a condition of selling, that you buy title insurance from a particular company when a federally related mortgage is involved. That’s RESPA Section 9, codified at 12 U.S.C. 2608, and a seller who breaks it is liable to the buyer for “three times all charges made for such title insurance.”
Your lender adds a layer. If it lets you shop for a settlement service, it must hand you a written list of providers. Choose from that list and the charge falls under the 10% cumulative tolerance — the lender eats any overage past that. Go off-list and the protection doesn’t apply.
The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau puts it plainly: “If you shop for title insurance, you could save money.” And if your agent or lender owns a piece of the company they’re steering you toward, RESPA requires a written Affiliated Business Arrangement disclosure under 12 CFR 1024.15 before the referral — and you cannot be required to use that affiliate. A referral is a recommendation, not an assignment.
### What is the purpose of a title company?
Four jobs, in order: search the public record for everything filed against the property, examine what turns up, insure the result, and run the money. Most of it happens weeks before anyone sits at a table.
The search produces a title commitment. Schedule A says who owns the property and what’s being insured. Schedule B-I lists requirements — what must be fixed before a policy issues. Schedule B-II lists exceptions — what the policy will never cover. That second list is the one nobody reads and the one that bites later.
Then comes curative work: chasing a release for a loan paid off years ago, getting a lien satisfied, untangling an estate. The company also holds earnest money, the lender’s wire and your cash to close in escrow, disburses at closing, and records the deed and the new deed of trust or mortgage. Section 381.058 RSMo requires a Missouri insurer to issue a closing protection letter to buyer, lender and seller in every residential deal where its agent handles settlement.
### Why does an Illinois closing involve a lawyer when a Missouri one usually doesn’t?
Two courts, one on each side of the river, drew the line differently. Neither state requires an attorney at a residential closing by statute; what differs is what a non-lawyer may do once the contract is signed.
In Illinois, the state Supreme Court decided Chicago Bar Association v. Quinlan & Tyson, Inc. on January 25, 1966: a broker may fill in the blanks on a customary contract form, but drawing the deed and the other instruments used to clear and transfer title is the practice of law, and a non-lawyer cannot do it. That’s still why an Illinois deed comes off an attorney’s desk. The standard Illinois residential contract also carries an attorney-review clause, commonly five business days from acceptance, in which either side’s lawyer can approve it, propose changes or terminate.
Missouri drew it wider. In In re First Escrow, Inc., decided October 27, 1992, the Missouri Supreme Court held escrow companies may fill in the blanks of standardized forms Missouri attorneys prepared or reviewed, under supervision and as agent for a party with a direct financial interest — but may not draft documents, choose the form, or give legal advice.
So a Metro East closing usually seats your attorney, the seller’s attorney and the title company. A Missouri closing seats a closer and no lawyer at all. Illinois also taxes the transfer at 50 cents per $500 of value, counties permitted to add 25 cents per $500, declared through MyDec. Missouri charges nothing on the deed: since November 2, 2010, Article X, Section 25 of its constitution has barred the state, counties and political subdivisions from “imposing any new tax, including a sales tax, on the sale or transfer of homes or any other real estate.”
Nothing to do with closing costs — find a gym you will actually use.
### What does title insurance cover, and what does it not?
It covers what already happened before you bought, not what happens after. A standard owner’s policy insures against someone else holding an ownership interest in your land, a forged or improperly executed document in the chain of title, undisclosed liens like unpaid taxes or a prior owner’s contractor lien, undisclosed heirs with a claim, an easement nobody mentioned, and title so defective you can’t sell it.
The exclusions are short and they matter. Governmental regulation, including building and zoning rules, is not covered. Neither is eminent domain, nor any matter you created or agreed to, nor a defect you knew about and didn’t disclose in writing before the policy date, nor anything that first attaches afterward. Add every item on Schedule B of your commitment, because a listed exception is not insured. And unlike every other policy you own, you pay once, at closing.
### Lender’s policy or owner’s policy — which are you actually buying?
If you’re financing, you’re buying the lender’s policy whether you want it or not, and the owner’s policy is the optional one. The lender’s policy insures the bank for the loan amount and shrinks as you pay the balance down. The owner’s policy insures you, for the purchase price, as long as you or your heirs hold an interest.
That’s why your Loan Estimate prints “(optional)” beside the owner’s premium when the lender isn’t requiring it — a labeling rule, not a hint you don’t need it. The CFPB’s own line: “You may want to buy an owner’s title insurance policy, which can help protect your financial investment in the home.” Buy both at once and ask for the simultaneous-issue rate.
### Who pays for the title company at closing?
Custom, not law — and custom is only a default until somebody writes something different into the contract. Neither state assigns the cost. On the Missouri side the seller commonly buys the owner’s policy while the buyer covers the lender’s policy and loan-related title charges, and Illinois practice also tends to put the owner’s policy on the seller. Both patterns bend by county, price point and how hot the market runs.
So don’t assume: the contract decides it and the Closing Disclosure proves it. For the dollar side, our breakdown of what closing costs actually cost in St. Louis walks the line items.
### What does a title search turn up on a hundred-year-old St. Louis house?
Usually paperwork, not drama. Four findings stall more metro closings than anything else: a deed of trust paid off years ago but never released of record, a mechanic’s lien from a contractor who was never paid, an easement running through the yard nobody remembered, and a gap in the chain where an owner died and the estate was never properly closed.
St. Louis makes that work older than most places. The city’s land records reach into the French and Spanish colonial period — the archived grants and deeds include documents from 1766, decades before the Louisiana Purchase. A brick two-family in Affton can sit on a hundred and twenty years of recorded instruments, and every one had to be right.
The metro also isn’t one record system. A house hunt can cross the recorders of St. Louis City, St. Louis County, St. Charles and Jefferson counties in Missouri plus St. Clair, Madison and Monroe in Illinois. A company that’s fast in one county isn’t automatically fast in the next. Ask where they actually close.
### What this business looks like from the other side of the counter
The premium is a one-time charge, and most of it never reaches the underwriter — in most states the agency keeps roughly 70% to 85% and remits the balance. That retention isn’t margin. It buys the search, the examination and the curative work, which is where the hours go. Title loss ratios sit in the low single digits, around 5.1% as of December 2024, because the model is preventing a claim rather than paying one. Escrow balances don’t pay the agency interest either; they earn bank credits that offset banking fees. And the calendar is brutal in one specific way: buyers close late in the month to shave per-diem interest, so the last few business days carry a share of volume wildly out of proportion. Referrals can’t be bought — RESPA Section 8 sees to that — so agencies compete on turn time and on never blowing a date. When a buyer or agent hunts for a closer in a county you actually cover, being listed and complete is how they find you.
### What should you ask before you commit to a title company?
Five questions, asked before you agree to anything, beat any review site.
What’s the all-in number, in writing? Premium, settlement fee, search and exam, wire and recording — one page you can set beside another company’s for the same address.
Which underwriter do you write for, and will my lender accept it? Ask for the closing protection letter in the same breath.
Who is my closer, and what’s their direct number? A human name before there’s a problem, not after.
How will you send wire instructions, and what number do I call to verify? The FBI’s 2024 Internet Crime Report counted $2.77 billion in business email compromise losses across 21,442 complaints, and closings are a named target. Never take wiring instructions from an email.
In Illinois: are you coordinating with my attorney, and who drafts the deed? A vague answer is your answer.
You’re entitled to the Closing Disclosure three business days before consummation. Use them to read Schedule B of the commitment, and if a fee moved since the Loan Estimate, ask which tolerance bucket it lives in.
Related reading: who manages it afterwards and renovating what you just bought.
Want a second quote before you commit? Browse title companies across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then call two of them and ask each for the all-in number in writing on the same address.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Do I need a title company to buy a house in Missouri?
A.  If you’re getting a mortgage, effectively yes. The lender will require a lender’s title policy, and somebody has to search title, hold escrow and record the documents. Missouri lets a title or escrow company run the closing without an attorney, within the limits the Missouri Supreme Court set in In re First Escrow, Inc. in 1992. A cash buyer can technically skip it and almost never should.
### Q. Do you need a real estate attorney to buy a house in Illinois?
A.  No statute requires one, but Illinois practice effectively does. Under Chicago Bar Association v. Quinlan & Tyson, Inc., decided in 1966, drawing the deed and the instruments used to clear and transfer title is the practice of law, so a non-lawyer can’t prepare them. The standard residential contract also carries an attorney-review window, commonly five business days from acceptance. Metro East buyers should budget for a lawyer.
### Q. What should a title company not do?
A.  Give you legal advice. Missouri limits an escrow company to filling in blanks on attorney-prepared forms — no drafting, no choosing the form — and Illinois puts the deed on an attorney’s desk. Under RESPA Section 8 it also cannot pay anyone for your referral.
### Q. Who pays for the title company at closing?
A.  Custom, not law. On the Missouri side the seller commonly buys the owner’s policy while the buyer covers the lender’s policy and loan-related title charges, and Illinois practice leans the same way. The contract decides it; the Closing Disclosure proves it.
### Q. Can I get my money back from a title company?
A.  Sometimes. The closing protection letter is the underwriter’s promise to make you whole, up to the settlement funds, if the settlement agent steals them, commits fraud or ignores written closing instructions. Separately, a seller who required their own company owes you three times those title insurance charges.
### Q. Is owner’s title insurance worth it?
A.  It’s the only policy in the stack protecting your equity rather than the bank’s. The lender’s policy pays the lender and shrinks as the loan amortizes; yours covers the purchase price for as long as you hold an interest, with no renewal and no annual bill. It’s cheapest bought alongside the lender’s policy at the simultaneous-issue rate.
### Q. What is a closing protection letter?
A.  It’s the underwriter’s promise to make you whole, up to the settlement funds, if the settlement agent steals that money, commits fraud with it, or ignores written closing instructions. Missouri requires the insurer to issue one to buyer, lender and seller in residential transactions under Section 381.058 RSMo. Ask for a copy rather than assuming it exists.
### Q. Do I need new title insurance when I refinance?
A.  You need a new lender’s policy, because the old loan is paid off and the policy insuring it retires along with it. You do not buy a second owner’s policy — the one from your purchase stays in force as long as you own the home. Ask whether a reissue or refinance rate applies; many companies discount the new lender’s policy when prior coverage exists.
### Q. What is the purpose of a title company?
A.  To confirm the seller can actually convey clean title, to insure against defects that surface later, and to hold and disburse the money at closing. That last part is why they are a wire-fraud target — the FBI counted $2.77 billion in business email compromise losses in 2024. Verify wiring instructions by phone, never by email.

## How to Buy Wholesale in St. Louis: Certificates, Minimums and Terms
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-buy-wholesale-in-st-louis
Imagine it’s a Thursday morning and you’ve just signed the lease on a narrow storefront in Kirkwood. Coffee, pastries, four tables and a window seat. You have a build-out quote, a name, and a spreadsheet that finally balances. Then you go to place your first real order — cups, lids, twelve-ounce bags of beans — and the supplier’s form stops you cold at a field marked “resale certificate number.”
Maybe you’re the caterer in Florissant who has bought sheet pans at retail for two years because nobody explained the alternative. Maybe you’re opening a gift shop in St. Charles and a line sheet just told you the opening order costs more than a month’s rent. Maybe you’re a remodeler in Belleville who keeps hearing the guy across the river pays less for the same tile.
Good news. Wholesale is not a club with a secret handshake. It’s a paperwork threshold, and the paperwork is short, free, and available the same week you register your business. Here’s how the door actually opens.
### What do you need to buy wholesale in St. Louis?
Suppliers hear the same opening line all day — how do I get wholesale prices for my business — and the answer is three documents. You need a registered business, a state tax number, and a completed resale certificate — Missouri Form 149 or Illinois Form CRT-61 — that you hand to the supplier. A legitimate wholesaler will ask for that certificate before it sells you anything untaxed. If nobody asks you for one, be suspicious.
The ask is not gatekeeping. Under Missouri law the burden of proving a sale was not a retail sale falls on the seller, who must obtain and keep exemption certificates as evidence — that’s RSMo 144.210. Illinois lands in the same place from the other direction: 86 Ill. Adm. Code 130.210 says failing to present an active registration or resale number, plus a certification, creates a presumption the sale was not for resale. Your certificate is the wholesaler’s audit shield. That’s why the counter wants it before it wants your order.
### What is a resale certificate, and which form does each state use?
A resale certificate is a signed statement telling a supplier you’re buying goods to resell, so no sales tax is charged on that purchase. Missouri uses Form 149, the Sales/Use Tax Exemption Certificate. Illinois uses Form CRT-61, the Certificate of Resale. You fill it out, you sign it, the supplier keeps it. No fee, no waiting period.
On the Missouri side, check the box for purchases of tangible personal property for resale and enter your Missouri Tax I.D. Number — printed on your Missouri Retail Sales License. An out-of-state retailer can list its home state and registration instead. One wrinkle: Form 149 says a purchaser claiming resale on taxable services in Missouri must hold a Missouri retail license. Missouri’s state sales and use tax rate is 4.225 percent before local add-ons — what you stop paying on inventory.
Illinois runs it tighter. CRT-61 asks for your Illinois retailer account ID, your Illinois reseller account ID, or a certificate of resale issued to an out-of-state purchaser. The Illinois Department of Revenue tells sellers plainly that verifying the number is valid and active is their job, and MyTax Illinois has a public lookup for it. The seller must keep your certificate not less than three and a half years, and blanket certificates should be updated at least every three years. Illinois charges 6.25 percent at the state level on general merchandise, 1 percent on qualifying food, drugs and medical appliances.
An Illinois quirk: you register as a reseller only if every one of your sales is a nontaxable resale. A shop that merely buys for resale registers as a retailer and files a CRT-61 with each supplier. Both start at MyTax Illinois.
### What are the four types of wholesalers?
Four different business models, and picking the wrong one is the expensive rookie mistake. A wholesaler buys deep and resells to trade only. A distributor carries specific brands inside a defined territory. A cash-and-carry is a warehouse you shop yourself. A buying group pools your volume with other independents so you negotiate like a chain.
True wholesaler. Buys in volume, sells to trade only, usually delivers, usually extends credit terms, almost always has a minimum. The account you open once and reorder from for years.
Distributor. An authorized channel for particular brands in a set territory. You get a rep, warranty backing, often the only legitimate source for that line — plus the brand’s rules on pricing and display.
Cash-and-carry. A self-service warehouse. Show your certificate at the desk, shop the aisles, pay at the register, load your own van. No delivery, no credit account, typically no minimum. You supply the truck and the labor.
Buying group or GPO. Aggregates small buyers to negotiate contracts one independent never could. You still buy from the distributor; the group negotiates the deal. Read the membership terms and rebate structure first.
Most small operators run two or three at once. A standing distributor order for predictable volume, a cash-and-carry run for the Saturday you underestimated, a specialty wholesaler for the thing that makes you different.
Nothing to do with pallets — a good accountant pays for themselves.
### What is a minimum order, and why won’t the wholesaler budge?
Two numbers matter: the minimum opening order, what it takes to establish the account, and the ongoing minimum, what it takes to earn a delivery. They exist because picking, packing, invoicing and driving a stop costs about the same whether the order is small or large. Below a certain line, the sale loses money.
Get both numbers in writing before you fall in love with a product line. Then ask three follow-ups. Dollars or cases? Does it reset per delivery, per week, or per month? Any small-order fee underneath the threshold? Ask about case pack too — you may want a dozen when the only sellable unit is seventy-two. Splitting cases is a cash-and-carry behavior, not a distributor one.
### How does a new business get net-30 terms?
Net-30 means the supplier ships now and you pay within thirty days, which means the wholesaler is financing your inventory. Brand-new businesses rarely get it on the first order. The normal path: pay by card or COD for the first several orders, submit a credit application, supply trade references, then ask again after three to six clean months.
A credit application wants your EIN, entity paperwork, a bank reference, and two or three trade references — suppliers who confirm you pay on time. With no history, expect a request for a personal guarantee. That isn’t an insult. It’s how a stranger’s risk gets priced. Some suppliers report payment history to Dun & Bradstreet, Experian or Equifax, which is how a business credit file gets built at all. Open two or three small accounts you can pay early, and the fourth supplier answers differently.
Read the discount language. Terms written as 2/10 net 30 mean you may deduct 2 percent if you pay within ten days. On thin retail margins, that beats the extra twenty days of float more often than not.
### How is restaurant and food service supply different from general merchandise?
Food service runs on a truck route; general merchandise runs on a season. A broadline food distributor may deliver two or three fixed days a week with a hard cutoff the night before. A gift, apparel or housewares wholesaler may write orders at market twice a year and ship months later, with opening-order and per-style minimums, territory rules and minimum advertised pricing attached.
The tax treatment splits too, and Missouri has a rule worth memorizing if you feed people. Food you buy to cook and sell is inventory, so it’s a resale purchase. On top of that, RSMo 144.011(10) excludes from Missouri sales tax the purchase by eating or food service establishments of items of a nonreusable nature furnished to customers with their food or beverage — the cups, napkins, straws, wrappers and to-go containers. The mop, the dish machine, the office printer and the menus are not covered. Same invoice, different lines, different answers.
### Can I use a resale certificate for things I keep and use myself?
No, and this is the part worth being blunt about. A resale certificate covers goods you will resell. Using one to buy things you consume yourself — shop supplies, office furniture, a television for the den — is tax fraud. Missouri’s rule makes the purchaser liable for the tax when the exemption was claimed improperly or the property is later used inconsistently with the claim.
Missouri’s exemption certificate rule, 12 CSR 10-107.100, lets a seller rely on a certificate on file only in good faith — defined as “honesty of intention and freedom from knowledge of circumstances which ought to put the holder upon inquiry.” RSMo 144.210 then lets the Department of Revenue collect the proper tax, interest, additions to tax and penalty directly from the purchaser when an exemption claim proves improper. Illinois prints the warning on the form: CRT-61 has the purchaser acknowledge that misuse or misrepresentation may result in penalties, interest, and criminal prosecution.
The practical version. Buy a case of candles for the shelf, take one home, and you owe use tax on that candle — 4.225 percent at the Missouri state level. Nobody is driving out to Maryland Heights over one candle. The habit is what surfaces in an audit, and 86 Ill. Adm. Code 130.210 is explicit that resale treatment holds only to the extent goods were not first put to a use for which they were purchased. Keep a withdrawal log. Cheapest insurance in the building.
### What this looks like from the wholesaler’s side of the counter
Wholesale is a volume business with almost no cushion. In results released July 29, 2025, foodservice distributor Sysco reported fiscal 2025 sales of $81.4 billion, gross profit of $15.0 billion — an 18.4 percent gross margin — and net earnings of $1.8 billion. Roughly two cents of profit per dollar moved. Minimums aren’t attitude; a stop costs what a stop costs, and warehouse space and diesel don’t scale down. Net terms mean the warehouse is lending you inventory unsecured, and when a kitchen goes dark in month four the distributor eats the receivable. That’s why the counter checks whether you’re a real business before it checks your order — the seller carries the audit burden, and your certificate is their defense. Buyers who show up registered, papered and paying early get answers first. Operators on that side also know new accounts start with somebody searching locally, which is why a complete listing you can claim on St Louis Near Me Directory earns its keep.
Related reading: signage for the shopfront and if you lease the building.
Ready to stop buying your inventory at the register? Browse wholesalers across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then call two of them with your tax number in hand and ask the same two questions: what is your minimum opening order, and what are your terms for a new account?
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Do I need an LLC to buy wholesale?
A.  No. Neither Form 149 nor CRT-61 asks for an entity type; both ask for a state tax number, so a sole proprietor with the right registration buys wholesale exactly as an LLC does. Missouri requires a retail sales license before you make retail sales, and operating without one carries a $500 penalty for the first day plus $100 a day after, up to $10,000. Illinois issues a Certificate of Registration through MyTax Illinois or Form REG-1.
### Q. Can a regular person buy wholesale?
A.  Not as a private individual. A wholesaler sells to the trade because the seller carries the burden of proving a sale was not retail, so it needs a resale certificate on file before it sells you anything untaxed. Register the business first; a cash-and-carry asks at the desk too.
### Q. How do I get a Missouri resale certificate?
A.  Nothing to apply for. Missouri Form 149 is a free fillable PDF on dor.mo.gov that you complete and hand to your supplier; the state never sees your copy. What you need first is a Missouri Tax I.D. Number, which arrives with your Missouri Retail Sales License. Register the business, then paper the suppliers.
### Q. Can I use Missouri Form 149 at an Illinois wholesaler?
A.  No. Each state wants its own document. In Illinois, use Form CRT-61 with an Illinois retailer account ID, an Illinois reseller account ID, or a certificate of resale issued to an out-of-state purchaser. Missouri Form 149 does accept an out-of-state retailer’s home-state registration for goods, though not for claiming resale on taxable services.
### Q. How much do I need to start wholesale?
A.  It varies enormously by trade, which is exactly why you ask before you shop. Get two figures in writing: the minimum opening order, and the ongoing minimum per delivery. Then confirm whether it is counted in dollars or cases, whether it resets weekly or monthly, and whether a small-order fee applies below the line.
### Q. Is a cash-and-carry cheaper than a delivering distributor?
A.  Usually not on unit price. A cash-and-carry is self-service — no delivery, no credit terms, no minimum — and you supply the van, the fuel and the hour. That flexibility is worth real money on a surprise catering order. Once your volume clears a distributor’s minimum, the delivered price generally wins.
### Q. What happens if I buy something for resale and then use it myself?
A.  You owe the tax. Missouri’s exemption certificate rule makes the purchaser liable when property is used inconsistently with the exemption claimed, and RSMo 144.210 lets the state collect tax, interest, additions and penalty from the purchaser directly. Illinois Form CRT-61 warns that misuse may bring penalties, interest and criminal prosecution. Log withdrawals, report use tax.
### Q. How long does my supplier keep my resale certificate on file?
A.  In Illinois, the seller must keep it not less than three and a half years, and blanket certificates should be updated at least every three years. Missouri’s rule lets a seller rely on a certificate already on file for future sales unless circumstances change. Send a fresh one when your address, entity type or tax number changes.
### Q. What are the four types of wholesalers?
A.  Merchant wholesalers, who take ownership of the goods and resell them; agents and brokers, who arrange sales without holding inventory; manufacturers’ sales branches, which are the maker’s own distribution arm; and specialized wholesalers serving one trade. Which you can buy from depends on your resale certificate and your order size.

## St. Louis Food Traditions: The Dishes This City Actually Invented
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/st-louis-food-traditions-what-this-city-invented
Imagine it’s a Saturday in September and a college friend has flown in for the weekend. She wants the real thing — not the airport version, not whatever a travel list told her to eat. So you stand in your Affton kitchen with your keys in hand and realize you can’t answer a simple question: what does St. Louis eat that nowhere else does?
Maybe you start listing. Toasted ravioli, obviously. The slinger, if she’s willing to still be awake at 2 a.m. Gooey butter cake from a bakery counter in Florissant that has made it the same way since before you were born. A pork steak, because half of Kirkwood still has a grill going. Then you stall out, because you don’t know where any of it came from. You just know somebody’s grandmother made it.
Here is what most of us never learned. Some of these dishes have a paper trail. Some are folklore repeated until it hardened into fact. This is the honest answer to what foods originated in St. Louis — what this city invented, what two families are still arguing over, and why it all tastes the way it does from Belleville to St. Charles.
### What food is St. Louis famous for?
St. Louis is known for toasted ravioli, the slinger, gooey butter cake, grilled pork steaks, the St. Paul sandwich, frozen custard concretes, crispy pig snoots and Red Hot Riplets potato chips — plus its own square-cut pizza. Nearly all of it was invented in the 20th century, in working kitchens, by people trying to sell something cheap.
Two threads run through the list. One is thrift: the pork shoulder, the pig snout, the ravioli already sitting there. The other is accident. At least four of these dishes come with a story about somebody dropping the wrong thing in the wrong pot, and those stories are charming and mostly unprovable.
Pizza already has its own long argument, so it stays there: the Provel, the cracker crust and the square cut are covered in our piece on St. Louis-style pizza. Everything below is the rest of the menu.
### Who invented toasted ravioli?
Nobody can prove it, and anyone who tells you otherwise is repeating a family story. Toasted ravioli — breaded, deep-fried, dusted with Parmesan, served with red sauce for dipping — is claimed by at least three long-running restaurants on the Hill. The dispute has never been settled and the reporting on it consistently calls the origin disputed.
The competing accounts are suspiciously alike, which is part of the trouble. Two involve a cook dropping ravioli into hot oil instead of boiling water in the early 1940s. A third family says the dish came from Sicily and points to menus from the 1930s. The oldest hard evidence usually cited is a 1943 advertisement in the St. Louis Star and Times, in which one Hill restaurant offered toasted ravioli and claimed in print to have originated it.
An ad proves the dish was on sale in 1943. It does not prove who fried the first one, and nearly everyone involved died decades ago. Treat the fryer-accident tale as folklore.
### What exactly is a slinger?
A slinger is two eggs, hash browns and a hamburger patty on one plate, buried under chili and shredded cheese, usually finished with raw onion. It is a diner dish, it is enormous, and it barely exists outside this metro. Order one in another city and you will get a blank look.
The origin here is lore rather than record. The family behind a Gravois Avenue diner has long said the plate was assembled there in the 1970s, and that the name came from a cook being told to just sling it together. Other diners copied it fast, which is why there is no fixed recipe: some add a tamale, some swap in sausage, some build it on a pork steak.
The slinger is closing-time food. It turns up on late-night menus in south city, out in Maryland Heights, across in Belleville, because it does one job: it absorbs a night out. Nothing about it is delicate. That is the design.
### Is gooey butter cake really a St. Louis mistake?
Probably, but no version of the story has ever been documented. Gooey butter cake is a yeast-raised bottom crust under a dense, barely set butter-and-egg topping, and it traces to south St. Louis German-American bakeries in the 1930s. Several origin stories circulate and none has been historically verified.
Two families have gone on the record in local press. One account, from the son of a south city bakery owner, credits a different baker entirely — John Hoffman — with a mix-up between gooey butter, a sticky smear bakers used like glue, and deep butter, the batter for a coffee cake. The other comes from the daughter of a baker at California and Arsenal, and puts it in the early 1940s. Both are family memory written down decades later. Neither carries documentation.
One quieter fact is worth knowing: the cake most people bake at home is not the original. The bakery formula is yeast-raised and stabilized with corn syrup or glycerin. The cream-cheese-and-cake-mix version that spread through cookbooks is a later shortcut, and it has largely buried the real thing.
### Why do St. Louisans grill pork steaks instead of beef?
A pork steak is a half-inch slice cut across the pork shoulder — the same cut sold whole as a Boston butt. It runs with fat and connective tissue, so it needs a slow grill and a long finish: sear it, then braise it covered in beer and barbecue sauce until it goes tender.
The reason it is a St. Louis thing is actually documented, and it is a grocery story, not a restaurant one. Feast Magazine credits Schnucks Markets with popularizing the cut here in the late 1950s, when second-generation owners Don and Ed Schnuck began selling shoulder steaks as an inexpensive piece of meat that grilled well and fed a crowd. That timing lands squarely on the rise of backyard charcoal grilling, in a city already built around meatpacking.
Changing subjects completely — the Mexican food here deserves its own trip.
### What is a St. Paul sandwich?
A St. Paul sandwich is an egg foo young patty — egg with bean sprouts and onion, fried flat — served on plain white bread with mayonnaise, lettuce, tomato and dill pickle. It is a fixture of small carryout Chinese kitchens all over the St. Louis metro and almost unknown elsewhere, including in St. Paul, Minnesota.
The usual story credits a Lafayette Square chop suey parlor in the early 1940s and says the owner named the sandwich for his Minnesota hometown. That account gets repeated everywhere and it has a hole in it: the phrase St. Paul sandwich appears in American print as far back as 1904, long before the local version existed.
Food historians offer a wider frame. James Beard and Evan Jones argued that the Denver or Western sandwich came from Chinese cooks feeding railroad crews and logging camps in the 19th century, and was itself derived from egg foo young. By that reading the St. Paul is a local branch of much older Chinese-American road food. It was a metro staple by the 1970s.
### What makes frozen custard different from ice cream?
Egg yolk, and the federal government put a number on it. Under FDA rules at 21 CFR 135.110, a frozen dessert must contain at least 1.4 percent egg yolk solids by weight to be labeled frozen custard or French ice cream. Below that threshold it is legally ice cream. The yolk is why custard eats denser and smoother and melts slower.
The concrete is the St. Louis addition. It is custard blended with mix-ins until it is stiff enough to hand over the counter upside down without losing any, and it was introduced at a St. Louis custard stand in 1959 — by the shop’s own account, after a teenage regular kept asking for a thicker malt until the milk got left out. The upside-down handoff became the local test of whether it was made right.
### What are snoots, and where do they fit in St. Louis barbecue?
Snoots are pig snouts — shaved, cut away from the nasal cavity with the skin on, then smoked or fried until they shatter like a pork rind. They come sauced, sometimes on white bread, often next to rib tips. Texture is the appeal: crisp at the edge, chewy behind it, closer to bacon than rib meat.
Snoots are the clearest link between St. Louis barbecue and St. Louis history. The city ran an enormous hog-processing trade, and the parts nobody wanted were cheap and abundant. Black pitmasters in north St. Louis and across the river in East St. Louis built a tradition on those cuts from roughly 1930 on, the same decade snoot sandwiches sold in Memphis, Atlanta and Harlem.
The sauce belongs to that tradition too. St. Louis-style barbecue sauce is tomato-based, sweeter and thinner than Kansas City sauce, which is why it goes on late and why it runs down your wrist.
### Red Hot Riplets, the Hill, and the rest of the pantry
Red Hot Riplets are a ridged potato chip in a sweet-hot barbecue seasoning, made by Old Vienna, a St. Louis chip company founded in 1936. The flavor arrived in the late 1970s and now accounts for roughly 80 percent of the company’s sales, according to Feast Magazine. The seasoning was bottled on its own in 2017 and a sauce followed in 2018 — a chip that became a condiment.
The Hill is the other engine. Italians from Lombardy and Sicily started arriving in the 1880s to work the clay mines and brick works on that ridge, and by 1910 the neighborhood was roughly 90 percent Italian. It stayed dense and self-contained, with its own groceries, bakeries and butchers — which is why so much of what this metro treats as ordinary, from the salsiccia to the toasted ravioli argument itself, came out of about forty square blocks.
### What a regional specialty costs the kitchen that makes it
Here is the side diners never see. Food cost at a full-service independent typically runs 28 to 35 percent of revenue, and smaller operators under $2 million in sales sit closer to 34 percent. Labor for full-service reached a median near 36.5 percent of sales in 2025. Missouri’s minimum wage went to $15.00 an hour on January 1, 2026, with tipped staff owed at least $7.50 plus enough to reach $15.00; Illinois is at $15.00 statewide as well. What is left is a net margin around 3 to 8 percent. Regional specialties squeeze that further — toasted ravioli is labor before it is food cost, snoots take hours of smoke for a low ticket price, and a third-party delivery order can take 15 to 30 percent off the top. Which is why good operators guard their own channel: the phone, the pickup counter, and being findable when somebody searches the category.
Related reading: the pizza argument in full and how to ship it.
Ready to eat your way through the argument? Browse American food across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then pick one dish off this list and go settle it for yourself this week.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Who really invented gooey butter cake?
A.  No one knows. Two St. Louis baking families have each claimed it in local press — one crediting a baker named John Hoffman, the other a baker at California and Arsenal. Both were recorded decades after the fact and neither has documentation. The safe statement is that it came from a south city German-American bakery in the 1930s.
### Q. Is toasted ravioli actually from Italy?
A.  Not in the form St. Louis serves. Fried filled pasta exists in Italian regional cooking, and one Hill family says their version came from Sicily. But breaded, deep-fried ravioli with marinara for dipping is an American dish that spread from this city. Three Hill restaurants claim it and none can prove it; the earliest print evidence is a 1943 newspaper ad.
### Q. What goes on a slinger?
A.  Two eggs, hash browns and a hamburger patty on one plate, covered in chili and shredded cheese, with raw onion on top. There is no official recipe — diners across the metro swap the patty for sausage or a pork steak, add a tamale, or change the chili. The constant is the layering: starch, egg, meat, chili, cheese, onion.
### Q. Why are pork steaks so popular in St. Louis?
A.  Because a local grocer made them a habit. Feast Magazine credits Schnucks Markets with popularizing the cut in the late 1950s, selling half-inch steaks off the pork shoulder as cheap meat that grilled well and fed a family. That coincided with the backyard charcoal boom in a meatpacking town. The cut is still uncommon outside the Midwest.
### Q. What foods originated in St. Louis?
A.  Toasted ravioli, the slinger, gooey butter cake, the frozen custard concrete and Red Hot Riplets all started here in the 20th century, and the St. Paul sandwich took its current form here. The pork steak is the odd one out: popularized here, not invented here.
### Q. What is St. Louis food famous for?
A.  Thrift and accident. Toasted ravioli, the slinger, pork steaks, snoots, gooey butter cake, concretes and Red Hot Riplets came out of working kitchens selling cheap cuts, and several carry an origin story about somebody dropping the wrong thing in the wrong pot.
### Q. What is a must eat in St. Louis?
A.  It depends on the hour. Toasted ravioli is the standard table starter on the Hill, a pork steak is the summer backyard answer, gooey butter cake belongs to a bakery counter rather than a restaurant, and after midnight it is a slinger.
### Q. What is the difference between a concrete and a milkshake?
A.  A concrete is made with frozen custard rather than ice cream, and it is blended thick enough to hold when the cup is turned upside down. Federally, frozen custard needs at least 1.4 percent egg yolk solids under 21 CFR 135.110; ice cream has less. That yolk gives custard its density. A milkshake is thinner and made to drink through a straw.
### Q. What food is St. Louis famous for?
A.  Toasted ravioli, gooey butter cake, St. Paul sandwiches, frozen custard concretes, pork steaks off the grill, and the cracker-crust pizza with Provel that divides every visitor. Most of it came out of working neighborhoods rather than restaurant kitchens, which is why so much of it is still best at a corner place.

## Getting a Business Sign Made and Permitted in St. Louis
