Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/business-sign-permit-st-louis-metro
Imagine you signed the lease in June on an end-cap suite in a strip center, and the buildout is finally close. Floors are in. Equipment lands Thursday. Above the door sits a blank panel where the last tenant’s sign used to be, and a sign shop’s proof is in your inbox with a number on it.
Maybe the space is in Affton. Maybe it’s a brick storefront in Maplewood, a freestanding building in Florissant, or a suite in a newer center out in St. Charles. Somebody has told you the sign is the easy part — pick a font, hang it, open. Somebody else has a story about a sign that sat in a warehouse for two months.
Both are describing the same job. What separates them is whether anyone handled the permit before the aluminum got cut. Here is the order that keeps your sign off a shelf.
### Do you need a permit for a business sign in St. Louis?
Almost always, yes. The City of St. Louis Building Division handles signs and awnings as a commercial building permit category: installing or modifying a sign on your building requires a permit so the work clears local safety and zoning rules. Nearly every municipality in this metro has some version of that requirement, on both sides of the river.
Exemptions exist, but they are narrow and locally written — small window lettering, address numerals, temporary real estate signs, government signage. Those lists are not identical in Kirkwood, Belleville and unincorporated St. Louis County. Assume a permit is required and get any exemption in writing. One note for City addresses: a sign permit is not a Banner Permit, which the Board of Public Service issues only for banners on City light poles.
### Why do sign rules change from one street to the next?
Because this metro is split into an unusual number of separate governments. St. Louis County contains 88 municipalities, and the City of St. Louis sits outside it as an independent city. Add St. Charles and Jefferson counties, then St. Clair, Madison and Monroe on the Illinois side, and a fifteen-minute drive can cross four or five different sign codes.
Where it is legal to place business signs is set address by address; the sign your competitor put up two miles away tells you nothing about what you can build. Unincorporated St. Louis County works from Section 1003.168 of its zoning ordinance; the moment your address falls inside a city limit, that city’s code governs instead. Call whoever handles zoning for your exact address — Chesterfield planning at (636) 537-4733, Belleville’s planning and zoning office at (618) 233-6810, the City of St. Louis permit section at (314) 622-3313.
### What does a sign permit application require?
Plan on a scaled drawing of the sign, a site plan or elevation showing exactly where it mounts, and full specs: dimensions, materials, colors, mounting method, and whether it is illuminated. Chesterfield requires a completed application for each sign plus scaled drawings showing size, color and material.
Most jurisdictions want three more things. Written authorization from the property owner if you are a tenant. A licensed, bonded and insured installer — Missouri has no statewide contractor license, so those rules are set city by city. And a separate electrical permit for anything lit. In O’Fallon, Illinois, permanent signs go through Planning and Zoning as a Certificate of Zoning Compliance, and the permit is triggered by expanding, altering, relocating or reconstructing a sign, not just by a new one. Re-facing an old cabinet often counts.
### What does a sign permit cost?
In the City of St. Louis, permit fees run off estimated construction cost. There is a $25 application fee per application, then $44 total for work valued at $1,000 or less, $48 from $1,001 to $2,000, $55 from $2,001 to $3,000, and above $3,000 it becomes the $25 application fee plus $10 per thousand dollars of estimated construction cost. All of it is non-refundable.
Put a real number through that: a $9,000 illuminated storefront sign in the City lands around $115 in permit fees. Not the expensive part of the project. Other municipalities price differently — flat fees, per-square-foot fees, fees by sign type, plus electrical and plan review charges. Edwardsville, Illinois keeps sign rules in Chapter 94 and fees in a separate schedule. Ask for your number in writing.
Wildly off-topic — good marketing help is easier to find locally than you think.
### How are size, height and setback limits calculated?
Most codes here do not hand you a flat square-footage number. They tie your allowance to your storefront, commonly one to two square feet of sign area per linear foot of building frontage — though the exact ratio is local. That is why the 40-foot bay next door gets a bigger sign than your 22-foot bay in the same building.
Freestanding signs pick up a second layer: maximum height measured from grade, a minimum setback from the property line and right-of-way, and sight-distance rules capping height inside the visibility triangle near driveways and intersections. St. Louis County also ties setback obligations to sign height, so taller means farther back. Illumination carries its own limits — internal versus external, brightness, hours, and light spill onto residential property behind you.
### What does a historic district add?
A review step, and it happens before the building permit. In the City of St. Louis, the Cultural Resources Office reviews permit applications for exterior work on City Landmarks and buildings in City Historic Districts, applying the adopted Rehabilitation or New Construction Standards. No permit issues without CRO or Preservation Board approval.
What gets scrutinized is materials, mounting, and how the sign meets the building. Drilling into original masonry, internally lit plastic cabinets on a nineteenth-century storefront, and covering transom glass are the recurring friction points; mortar-joint anchoring, painted wood or metal, and halo-lit letters clear more easily. CRO offers a free preliminary review from photos and schematic plans, at 314-657-3865. Municipalities across the metro run their own review boards.
### Can you put up a digital or LED message board?
Sometimes, and usually with tight strings attached. Electronic message centers are the most restricted sign type in this metro. Lake Saint Louis shows the typical shape: under Section 425.550(C)(4) of its sign code, a message must hold for a minimum of thirty seconds, animation effects such as scroll, flash, twinkle, travel and melt are prohibited, and video or moving video imagery is not permitted.
Other municipalities go further — banning them outright in some districts, capping the digital portion as a share of total sign area, requiring night dimming, or allowing them only on freestanding signs. Guess wrong and it hurts, because the display is the priciest component in the sign. Get your local rule in writing before anyone orders hardware.
### Monument, pylon, wall or window — which one do you need?
Zoning and your lease usually decide this, not taste. A wall sign mounts flat to the building and is what most in-line tenants get; channel letters are individually fabricated letters, typically lit, mounted to the wall or a raceway. A window sign is vinyl or lettering on the glass, often capped at a percentage of the window area.
Freestanding signs come in two shapes. A monument sign sits low on a solid base, the form many newer commercial districts specifically require. A pylon or pole sign lifts a cabinet on poles for highway visibility, and it is the type most likely to be capped or disallowed under a modern code. In a multi-tenant center you probably are not getting your own freestanding sign at all — you get a panel on the center’s existing pylon, in a format the landlord controls.
### How much does a sign for a business cost?
Cost tracks fabrication method more than size. National sign-industry pricing guides put channel letters at roughly $75 to $150 per letter depending on size and font complexity, with complete illuminated storefront sets commonly landing between $3,000 and $8,000 installed. Installation is its own line: those guides put crane rental for a sign install at about $600 to $1,200 for the day, and high-mount channel letter work at $1,000 to $2,500.
A printed vinyl banner lives in a different universe — roughly $3 to $8 per square foot, so a 3-by-8 banner often comes in under $200. That is the right tool for a grand opening or a seasonal push, not a substitute for permanent signage, and many local codes cap how many days a year a temporary banner may stay up. Treat these as market shape, not a St. Louis price list.
### What does your lease say about signage?
Read the signage clause before you read the sign quote. Most commercial leases here require written landlord approval of design, size, materials and mounting, and many centers operate under a recorded sign criteria document dictating letter height, color, font and whether the sign may be lit at all.
Pin down three things in writing: whether the landlord approves your specific proof, who owns the sign when you leave, and who patches and repaints the facade at removal. Landlord authorization is often a permit submittal item too, so a slow landlord delays the municipal review rather than running alongside it.
### What happens if you skip the permit?
You can be ordered to take the sign down, and you pay for the removal. Missouri municipal sign codes routinely carry that language. Independence, Missouri’s ordinance shows the standard form: if the permit holder or property owner fails to comply within ten days after notice, the city may remove or alter the sign at the owner’s expense, and signs in the public right-of-way are treated as unlawful and abandoned, subject to removal without compensation.
The quieter costs land harder. An unpermitted sign can hold up an occupancy permit, surface during a sale or refinance, and hand an insurer an argument if it ever comes down. Fixing it later means paying for removal, paying for the permit anyway, and often redesigning a sign you already bought.
### What sign shops wish buyers understood
From the shop’s side, the quote you compare against an online price is not the same product. A storefront job carries hours of unbilled design time before anyone approves a proof. Then substrate and hardware — aluminum, acrylic faces, trim cap, LED modules, a raceway — priced off metal and plastic markets the shop does not control. Then installation: a bucket truck, a crew, general liability and workers’ compensation coverage, and a licensed electrician for anything lit.
And the line nobody quotes out loud — somebody drives the permit. That is a person reading a code section, redrawing a layout to fit an area allowance, and standing at a counter, often twice. An online price for a printed panel includes none of it. Whether sign making is profitable depends almost entirely on which of those costs a shop actually recovers — the ones competing head-on with an online panel price are usually giving away the install. Ask a shop to itemize permit work rather than assume it. Shops get called for these jobs by being findable, which is what a complete local listing is for.
Related reading: buying the stock behind the window and landlord approval on the lease.
Want a shop that pulls the permit, not just prints the panel? Browse sign dealers across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then call two or three with your street address in hand — the address decides the code, and the shop that asks for it first is worth a second call.
From the other side of the counter, people ask how much should I charge for a sign, and the same figures apply: roughly $75 to $150 per letter for channel letters, with installation quoted separately.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Do I need a permit to put a sign on a building I own?
A.  Owning the building does not exempt you. A sign permit is a zoning and safety approval attached to the property and the sign, not the tenancy. In the City of St. Louis, installing or modifying a sign requires a Building Division permit regardless of who holds the deed.
### Q. How long does a sign permit take in the St. Louis area?
A.  There is no single metro-wide answer, because 88 municipalities in St. Louis County plus the independent City, St. Charles County and the Illinois side each run their own review. Ask for a target date when you submit, and build in extra weeks if the building sits in a historic district or the sign needs a variance.
### Q. How much does a sign permit cost in the City of St. Louis?
A.  Fees follow estimated construction cost: a $25 application fee, then $44 total for work valued at $1,000 or less, $48 from $1,001 to $2,000, $55 from $2,001 to $3,000, and above $3,000 the $25 fee plus $10 per thousand dollars of estimated cost. Fees are non-refundable.
### Q. How much should a shop sign cost?
A.  Price a storefront sign by its parts: channel letters at roughly $75 to $150 each, complete illuminated sets commonly $3,000 to $8,000 installed, high-mount installation at $1,000 to $2,500, and crane rental around $600 to $1,200 a day. A quote far under that usually leaves something out.
### Q. How much does it cost to get a sign?
A.  Budget three lines, not one: fabrication, installation and permits. The permit is usually the small one — a $9,000 illuminated sign in the City of St. Louis runs about $115 in permit fees — but anything lit also needs a separate electrical permit, and landlord approval costs time.
### Q. Can I hang a banner while I wait on my permanent sign?
A.  Often yes, with limits. Many local codes treat temporary banners as their own category, with a maximum size, a maximum number of display days per calendar year, and sometimes a separate temporary sign permit. Ask your municipality for the day limit first.
### Q. Are digital LED message signs allowed around St. Louis?
A.  It depends on your municipality and zoning district. Restrictions are common: minimum message hold times, bans on animation and video, night-dimming rules, and caps on how much of a sign may be digital. Lake Saint Louis requires a thirty-second minimum hold and prohibits animation and video under Section 425.550(C)(4). Check your own code before ordering a display.
### Q. Is sign making profitable?
A.  It depends on what the shop recovers beyond materials. A storefront job absorbs unbilled design hours, substrate and hardware priced off metal and plastic markets, a bucket truck and crew, general liability and workers’ compensation coverage, a licensed electrician for anything lit, and somebody’s time driving the permit through a counter. Shops that itemize that work price it sustainably. Shops matching an online panel price generally are not.
### Q. Does my landlord have to approve my sign?
A.  In nearly every commercial lease in this metro, yes, and in writing before fabrication. Many multi-tenant centers also enforce a sign criteria document controlling letter height, color, font and illumination. Landlord authorization is often part of the permit application too, so chase it early or it becomes the thing holding up the project.
### Q. How much does a sign for a business cost?
A.  The sign and the permit are separate lines. Channel letters run roughly $75 to $150 per letter depending on size and font complexity, and installation adds its own cost — crane rental runs about $600 to $1,200 for the day. Permits are comparatively small: a $9,000 illuminated storefront sign in the City lands near $115.
### Q. How much should I charge for a sign?
A.  If you are quoting rather than buying, national sign-industry guides put channel letters at roughly $75 to $150 per letter depending on size and font complexity. Installation is its own line — crane rental for a sign install runs about $600 to $1,200 for the day.

## How to Get a Police Report in the St. Louis Metro
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/st-louis-police-report-guide
Imagine it’s a Tuesday morning in Affton and you walk out to the driveway with a coffee in your hand. The passenger window of your car is a pile of pebbled blue glass on the concrete. The glovebox hangs open. The bag with your work laptop in it is not in the back seat anymore.
Or maybe it’s quieter than that. A long scrape down the driver’s door after dinner in Maryland Heights, no note. A bike lifted off the porch in Florissant while you were inside boiling pasta. A credit card opened in your name by somebody in Belleville who has never met you.
All of those end in the same place: someone on a phone — an adjuster, a bank’s fraud desk, a landlord — asking for a report number. That is where people here get stuck, because the St. Louis metro has an unusual number of separate police departments and no single front door.
### How do I look up a local police report?
Ask the agency that wrote it — not the county, not the state, not 911. In the City of St. Louis that is the SLMPD Records Service Center at 1915 Olive Street. In St. Louis County it is the county’s online Sunshine request portal at recordsrequest.stlouiscountymo.gov. In Illinois it is a written FOIA request to that specific department.
The City’s Records Service Center is on the first floor at 1915 Olive, 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. weekdays, 314-444-5551. Bring a state-issued photo ID or valid passport, plus a notarized release if you are requesting for someone else who was involved. Payment is cash, money order or business check — no personal checks, no cards. A report cannot be released until it is completed and approved, which for crash reports usually takes about five days.
In person, you can get a police report in St. Louis County at the Central Police Records unit, Room B-013 at 7900 Forsyth Boulevard in Clayton, open 7:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. weekdays, at 314-615-5317.
The Illinois side has no county-wide clearinghouse. Belleville’s police department takes requests through its own records portal; Collinsville handles police FOIA at 200 West Clay Street. Give them the case number if you have it, plus the date, the exact location, and the names involved.
### Which police department do I actually call?
The one covering the city where it happened — which around here is genuinely hard to know. St. Louis County alone contains 88 municipalities plus large unincorporated stretches, boundaries change block to block, and several small cities do not run their own patrol at all. They buy it from somebody else.
Two facts trip up newcomers and lifers alike. The City of St. Louis is not part of St. Louis County; it has been an independent city since 1876, and SLMPD covers it. And St. Louis County Police patrol the unincorporated areas while also contracting service to municipalities including Jennings, Wildwood, Fenton, Green Park, Valley Park, Hanley Hills and Winchester. Dellwood moved its policing to the North County Police Cooperative in 2018.
The address decides everything. For the City, SLMPD’s locator takes a street address or an 11-digit parcel number and returns your district. St. Louis County Police publish a precinct list of the areas they patrol. If you cannot tell, call any non-emergency dispatcher and read them the address.
Watch the name collisions, too. O’Fallon, Missouri sits in St. Charles County; O’Fallon, Illinois sits in St. Clair County. Two cities, two police departments, opposite ends of the metro. St. Charles the city and St. Charles County run separate agencies as well.
### What does a police report cost around St. Louis?
In Missouri, usually under $10. The Sunshine Law caps standard paper copies at 10 cents a page and allows a charge for staff time. SLMPD charges 10 cents a page plus $15 an hour, prorated, to locate a report, and says a simple request normally comes to less than $5. In Illinois, the first 50 pages of black-and-white letter or legal copies are free, then 15 cents a page.
Crash reports run on their own schedule, and they are the ones people usually need:
Missouri State Highway Patrol: $6.00 for a basic crash report, and you wait 10 days from the crash investigation date. Check or money order only — cash gets returned. The Patrol currently notes a backlog.
Illinois State Police: $5.00 per crash report through its online E-Pay service, plus a card service fee of 2.35% with a $1.00 minimum. Allow 10 or more business days.
St. Charles County Police: $10 for an incident report at the Records Division, 101 Sheriff Dierker Court in O’Fallon, 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. weekdays. Bring a Missouri driver’s license.
O’Fallon, Missouri Police: a single accident report is free. Criminal reports run $27.00 an hour plus 10 cents a page.
Same paperwork, four prices — the arithmetic of dozens of agencies setting fees under one state law.
Nothing to do with reports — that leaning tree needs attention before spring.
### Can I file a police report online in the St. Louis area?
For a short list of non-emergency incidents, yes. St. Louis County Police launched an online citizens reporting portal in late August 2025 covering identity theft, destruction of property, stolen license plates or tabs, lost articles and general crime tips. You can file under your name or anonymously.
The limits matter. A destroyed-property report handles up to five items and two vehicles; a lost-article report handles up to five items. Lost firearms cannot go through the portal — report those in person or by phone. The forms only cover areas St. Louis County Police patrol.
Illinois State Police let you complete your own crash report online in one narrow case: a single-vehicle, property-damage-only crash with no injuries to anyone, on an Interstate or a U.S. or Illinois Route. Anything else needs an officer.
The City of St. Louis does not advertise online incident filing. SLMPD’s public FAQ sends identity theft and fraud victims to the police district where they live or where the loss occurred, with a non-emergency line at 314-231-1212. Metro East municipalities vary; several still take reports only by phone or at the counter.
### When should you call 911 instead of the non-emergency line?
SLMPD puts it plainly: 911 is for emergency situations that warrant immediate police response, such as a life-or-death situation, and the non-emergency number is for when police assistance is needed but not urgent. A break-in happening right now is 911. A break-in you discovered over breakfast is not.
Worth saving in your phone before you need them: SLMPD non-emergency, 314-231-1212. St. Louis County Police non-emergency, 636-529-8210. Collinsville, 618-344-2131. Every municipality publishes its own, and a number off a ten-year-old refrigerator magnet may no longer route anywhere useful.
### What does an insurance claim actually need from you?
A report or case number, plus proof you owned what is gone. The number is the anchor — on a theft claim, most carriers will not move without it. Everything after that is documentation you control: photos, receipts, serial numbers, purchase dates, honest values. Photograph the scene before you sweep up the glass, and write the item list the same day.
The two states split on crash paperwork. In Missouri you must file a Motor Vehicle Accident Report, Form 1140, with the Department of Revenue when an uninsured motorist was involved and the crash caused more than $500 in property damage or an injury or death, and it happened within the past year. In Illinois, motorists are no longer required to file their own crash report at all — Public Act 102-0560 removed that duty. Illinois police still submit crash reports to IDOT within 10 days of investigating, under 625 ILCS 5/11-408.
For identity theft, IdentityTheft.gov generates an Identity Theft Report that the Federal Trade Commission says is generally enough for the credit bureaus and most companies; add a local police report if you have information about a suspect or a company demands one. If a Missouri carrier stalls, the Department of Commerce and Insurance hotline is 800-726-7390.
### What if the department will not hand over the report?
Both states put a deadline in writing. Missouri’s Sunshine Law requires a response no later than the end of the third business day after the custodian of records receives your request, under Section 610.023.3. Illinois FOIA gives a public body five business days, extendable by five more for reasons the statute lists.
In Missouri you never have to say why you want a record, and fees are capped at 10 cents a page plus the time of the lowest-salaried employee capable of doing the search. Section 610.100 does let law enforcement close records when there is an “articulable concern” for the safety of a victim, witness or other person, or when an active investigation would likely be jeopardized. Basic incident information is generally open; detailed investigative material may not be. St. Charles County states outright that it cannot release reports on incidents still under investigation.
In Illinois, a request made for a commercial purpose gets 21 business days instead of five, and a denial can be appealed to the Attorney General’s Public Access Counselor within 60 calendar days of the denial letter. Either way, if the narrative is withheld, ask for the case number and the basic facts — usually all an adjuster or a bank needs to open a file.
### What a break-in looks like from behind the counter
If you run a shop, the case number is the first thing your adjuster asks for and the last thing on your mind at 6 a.m. with a sheet of plywood in your hands. Get it that morning, and price the loss at the tag — the officer has to write a dollar figure, and that figure sets the charge. Missouri makes stealing a class D felony at $750 or more under RSMo 570.030. Illinois makes retail theft a felony above $300 and a Class A misdemeanor at or under it, under 720 ILCS 5/16-25. The same cart of merchandise is charged differently in Granite City than in Kirkwood.
The loss that quietly eats margin is rarely the smashed door. It is the steady shrink nobody writes up, plus false-alarm bills. The City of St. Louis requires every commercial alarm system to be registered under Ordinance 66264 — $50 commercial, $25 residential — with the first false alarm in twelve months free, $25 for the second, $50 for the third, and police response suspended after the fourth. The Comptroller’s office reported past-due false-alarm fines of $755,989 as of June 30, 2025. County and Metro East cities run their own versions.
SLMPD offers free robbery-prevention training and a Video Surveillance Federation that links business cameras to its Real Time Crime Center; your district’s community outreach officer is the contact. And when someone three neighborhoods over needs what you sell, they search by category and city — which is why a complete, current listing earns its twenty minutes.
Related reading: if the car is gone rather than broken into and disposing of what was ruined.
Not sure whose jurisdiction you were standing in? Browse police departments across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then save the non-emergency number for the city you actually live in — not the one on your mailing address.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How long does it take to get a police report in St. Louis?
A.  Missouri’s Sunshine Law requires a response by the end of the third business day, but a response is not the same as the document. SLMPD notes a report cannot be released until it is completed and approved, which for crash reports usually takes about five days. Illinois State Police orders can take 10 or more business days.
### Q. How do I get a copy of a police report in Missouri?
A.  From the agency that wrote it, not the state. Missouri’s Sunshine Law caps standard paper copies at 10 cents a page plus staff time, and gives the custodian of records until the end of the third business day to respond to your request.
### Q. How to obtain a St. Louis city police report?
A.  Go to the SLMPD Records Service Center, first floor at 1915 Olive Street, 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. weekdays, 314-444-5551. Bring a state-issued photo ID or valid passport, plus a notarized release if the report belongs to someone else. Payment is cash, money order or business check only.
### Q. Where can I get a police report in St. Louis County?
A.  Through the county’s online Sunshine request portal at recordsrequest.stlouiscountymo.gov, or in person at Central Police Records, Room B-013, 7900 Forsyth Boulevard in Clayton, 314-615-5317. That covers incidents St. Louis County Police handled — a municipal department keeps its own records.
### Q. Do I need a police report to file an insurance claim for theft?
A.  For a theft claim, effectively yes. Carriers want the report or case number to open the file. Photograph the scene before cleaning up, write the item list the same day with serial numbers and purchase dates, and notify your insurer promptly.
### Q. Can I get a police report for somebody else?
A.  Usually only with paperwork. SLMPD requires a state-issued photo ID and a notarized release if you are requesting on behalf of an involved party. St. Charles County asks for a Missouri driver’s license and a completed request form. Illinois departments treat it as a FOIA request, and personal information may be redacted first.
### Q. What can I report to St. Louis County Police online?
A.  The county’s citizens reporting portal, launched in late August 2025, covers identity theft, destruction of property, stolen license plates or tabs, lost articles and general crime tips. Lost firearms must be reported in person or by phone, and the forms only cover areas county police patrol.
### Q. What do I do if the police report has a mistake in it?
A.  Contact the records division of the agency that wrote it rather than the officer. Agencies will not delete an officer’s observations or a witness’s statement, but factual errors — a misspelled name, a wrong plate, an item you forgot to list — can typically be corrected or added through a supplemental report. Get the corrected copy before you send anything to an adjuster.
### Q. Are police reports public record in Missouri?
A.  Incident reports are generally open under Missouri’s Sunshine Law, while records tied to an active investigation can stay closed until it concludes. Either way you request from the agency that wrote it, not the county or the state — in the City that is the SLMPD Records Service Center, 1915 Olive Street, 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. weekdays.

## Your Car Got Towed in St. Louis: What It Costs and What to Do Next
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/car-towed-in-st-louis-cost-and-what-to-do
Imagine it’s a Thursday night and you walk back to where you parked — the strip-mall lot in Affton, a side street in Kirkwood, the gravel overflow behind a bar in Belleville — and there’s a clean dry rectangle of pavement where your car should be. First thought: stolen. Four seconds later you look up and notice the small sign bolted to the light pole you parked under.
Maybe you’re in Florissant and the street sweeper came through. Maybe you ducked into a shop in St. Charles for what you swore was twenty minutes. Maybe you’re in a Maryland Heights apartment lot holding a permit you never got around to putting in the window. Different reasons, same feeling — a hot, sinking sense that the next hour will cost money you had other plans for.
This is a solvable problem with a known sequence and, mostly, a known price — including what happens if you can’t afford to get your car out of impound today. Missouri and Illinois write different rules for towing, and knowing which set covers the lot you parked in is worth real money right now.
### How do you find out who towed your car in St. Louis?
Call the police agency covering the exact spot where you parked, because whoever towed you was legally required to tell them. In the City of St. Louis, check the Towing Division’s towed car lookup or call (314) 383-7546. In St. Louis County, start with the non-emergency line, 636-529-8210.
That reporting duty is why it works. Missouri’s RSMo 304.157 requires a tow from a signed private lot to be reported to law enforcement with a crime inquiry and inspection report within two hours; other tows get twenty-four. Illinois is tighter: under 625 ILCS 5/4-203 the towing service must notify the law enforcement agency with jurisdiction within thirty minutes of finishing the tow.
In the Metro East — Belleville, Granite City, Fairview Heights, O’Fallon — call the non-emergency number for the municipality where the car was parked, not the county where you live. On the Illinois interstates, Illinois State Police Troop 8 out of Collinsville covers Madison, St. Clair, Monroe, Clinton and Bond counties.
One detail trips everyone: a private-lot tow in the City does not go to the City lot. The City impound sits at 7410 Hall Street, open weekdays 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. and Saturday 9 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. A car hooked from an apartment or restaurant lot went to that company’s own yard, and the number for it belongs on the sign.
### How much is it to release an impounded car?
If the City of St. Louis towed it, the published rates are $100 for the tow and $25 per day for storage, plus $60 for a dolly (flats, missing wheels, four-wheel drive) and $80 an hour for labor. Five days in the lot is $225 before tickets or a police hold.
A private lot is a different animal. Missouri sets no statewide dollar cap on a nonconsensual tow off private property. RSMo 304.155 gives the tower a lien for “all reasonable charges for the towing and storage,” and leaves reasonable undefined.
For contrast, look west. Kansas City’s rewritten towing ordinance took effect January 1, 2026 and caps the tow fee at $265, the drop fee at $132 and storage at $30 a day, and requires companies to hand drivers a bill of rights. St. Louis has no matching citywide cap for private tows, which is why the sign matters so much here.
### Does Missouri or Illinois cap what a private lot can charge?
In Missouri the sign is the cap. RSMo 304.157 makes a private-property tow lawful only when a sign is posted in plain view at all entrances disclosing “the maximum fee for all charges related to towing and storage.” Photograph it before you leave. If the invoice beats the posted maximum, you have an argument with teeth.
Illinois has real rate regulation, but almost certainly not where you are standing. The Illinois Commercial Relocation of Trespassing Vehicles Law lets the Illinois Commerce Commission license relocators and set rates in Cook, Will, Kane, DuPage and Winnebago counties — those five only. St. Clair, Madison and Monroe are not on the list, so the protections Chicago drivers assume — no storage charge when a car is claimed within 24 hours, credit cards accepted without a surcharge — do not follow you to Belleville.
While we are off-topic — auto body work is its own separate headache.
### What has to be on the sign before a private lot can tow you?
Both states spell it out in detail you can check with your phone camera. Missouri’s RSMo 304.157 requires a sign at every entrance no smaller than seventeen by twenty-two inches, lettering at least one inch high, warning that unauthorized vehicles will be removed at the owner’s expense, disclosing the maximum towing and storage fee, and listing a phone number for finding the car.
Illinois, under 625 ILCS 5/4-203, wants the notice within five feet of each driveway access or curb cut — or one sign every 100 feet of frontage where there are no curbs — in light-reflective letters at least two inches high, naming the towing service and its current phone number. It must have been continuously maintained for at least 24 hours before any car is towed. Ignore that and the towing service commits a Class C misdemeanor, fined not less than $100 nor more than $500.
Missouri aims a penalty at the property owner too. Under RSMo 304.158, an owner who causes a car to be removed is liable to that car’s owner for double the towing or storage charges when the signage and notice rules were not met.
### The truck is hooking up your car right now — what can you do?
In Missouri, reach the car before it leaves the lot and you pay half. RSMo 304.158 says a towing company may impose no more than one-half of the regular towing charge when the owner returns before the vehicle is removed from the private property, and that “the regular towing charge may only be imposed after the abandoned property has been removed from the property and is in transit.” That is statute, not courtesy.
Say it early and say it calmly. Photograph the truck, the sign, the car’s position, the time. Downstate Illinois has no equivalent statewide drop-fee rule, so in the Metro East your leverage is the sign, the 24-hour posting requirement, and the operator’s willingness to be reasonable. Most are.
### What do you need to bring to get the car released?
For the City of St. Louis lot: a copy of the vehicle registration, a valid driver’s license, receipts for any tickets, and a release order if police placed a hold. The City accepts Mastercard, Visa, a company or cashier’s check, and money orders. Bring a licensed driver; a car nobody present can legally drive keeps accruing storage.
Missouri also requires storage yards to take cash. RSMo 304.158 says the operator of a storage facility “shall accept cash for payment of towing and storage” from the registered owner or agent, and must keep enough on hand to make change. A yard demanding a cashier’s check at 9 p.m. Sunday is out of step with the statute.
Move fast, because storage is the part that compounds. Missouri gives the towing company five working days to mail written notice of the removal, the grounds, and the location to the registered owner and any lienholder.
### How do you dispute a tow you think was wrong?
Missouri gives you a court and a short clock. Under RSMo 304.156, the owner may petition the associate circuit court in the county where the vehicle is stored, within ten days after receiving the towing company’s notice, to decide whether the property was wrongfully taken or withheld. The petition must name the towing company as a defendant. You can post a bond equal to the towing and storage charges to get the car back while the case runs.
File a complaint alongside it. The Missouri Attorney General’s consumer protection hotline is 800-392-8222. In Illinois, the consumer fraud hotline for southern Illinois is 1-800-243-0607 (Carbondale); Springfield is 1-800-243-0618. Send the sign photo, the invoice and the time stamps.
Illinois drivers should brace for a second bill. Under 625 ILCS 5/11-208.7, an Illinois county or municipality may charge a reasonable administrative fee to release an impounded vehicle after certain offenses, on top of tow and storage, and the statute sets no maximum. It does require notice of a hearing within ten days of the impound. Ask the municipal clerk what the fee is.
### Why calling your own tow usually beats accepting whoever shows up
Three kinds of tow exist and they price completely differently. A consent tow is one you call: you pick the company, agree to the rate, choose the destination. A police-ordered tow follows a crash, an arrest or a blocked lane, and the agency picks off its own rotation. A private-property tow is ordered by a lot owner, and you were never the customer.
Only the first gives you a number before the hook goes on. Consumer cost guides put a routine local tow at roughly a $50 to $100 hook-up fee plus about $2.50 to $7 a mile, and calling two companies takes four minutes.
Check what you already pay for. Roadside plans and the towing-and-labor rider on an auto policy are cheap, and usually cover a set number of tow miles or a per-disablement dollar limit. They cover breakdowns, not impound releases — no roadside membership pays a storage bill at a private yard. Read your mileage limit now, not at midnight on Halls Ferry Road.
### What this looks like from the tow operator’s side
The equipment surprises people. A new flatbed rollback runs roughly $75,000 to $130,000, and insurance is a second payment on top — Progressive Commercial priced 2025 tow-truck policies at a median of $355 a month for new customers, averaging $606. Then the yard: fenced, lit, camera-covered land sitting on cars nobody claims, because Missouri makes a tower hold an abandoned vehicle thirty days before disposal.
The money is in volume and relationships — police rotation lists, motor clubs, body shops, fleet accounts — and holding a rotation spot means answering at 3 a.m. in an ice storm with insured trucks and a clean record. It is dangerous work: an AAA Foundation study counted 123 roadside assistance providers killed by passing vehicles between 2015 and 2021. The complaint you hear operator to operator is that a few predatory yards make the whole trade look like a shakedown, which is why the honest ones want a complete, checkable listing a stranded driver can verify before dialing.

### Frequently asked questions
### Q. How do I find out where my car was towed in St. Louis?
A.  Call the police agency covering the exact block or lot where you parked. The City of St. Louis runs a towed car lookup online plus a Towing Division line at (314) 383-7546, and St. Louis County’s non-emergency number is 636-529-8210. Towers must report the tow within two hours in Missouri from a signed private lot, thirty minutes in Illinois.
### Q. Can a tow truck take my car if I get back before it drives off?
A.  In Missouri, not at full price. RSMo 304.158 limits the charge to one-half the regular towing fee when the owner returns before the vehicle is removed from the private property, and allows the full charge only once the car is removed and in transit. Ask calmly, photograph the scene, expect to pay the half fee.
### Q. What paperwork do I need to get a towed car released?
A.  At the City of St. Louis lot: a copy of the registration, a valid driver’s license, receipts for any tickets, and a police release order if a hold was placed. The City takes Mastercard, Visa, company or cashier’s checks and money orders. Missouri law separately requires storage yards to accept cash and keep change on hand.
### Q. Is there a limit on towing and storage fees in Missouri?
A.  There is no statewide dollar cap. Missouri requires a tower’s charges to be reasonable, and requires the warning sign at a private lot to disclose the maximum fee for all towing and storage charges, which makes that sign your practical ceiling. Kansas City adopted hard caps effective January 1, 2026 ($265 tow, $132 drop fee, $30 daily storage), but only inside Kansas City.
### Q. What happens if you can’t afford to get your car out of impound?
A.  The bill keeps growing and then the car is sold. Storage accrues the whole time at $25 a day in the City lot, the Towing Division holds a vehicle thirty days before auction, and public sales run every Wednesday at 9:30 a.m. Missouri gives the towing company five working days to notify you and any lienholder in writing, so the storage clock starts well before the letter lands. The cheapest day to get the car out is the first one.
### Q. How to get impound fee waived?
A.  Not by asking — relief here is statutory. Missouri limits the charge to half the regular tow fee if you reach the car before it leaves the lot. An invoice above the maximum fee posted on the lot’s sign gives you an argument with teeth. And RSMo 304.158 makes a property owner who ignored the signage rules liable to you for double the towing or storage charges.
### Q. Who do I complain to about a predatory tow in Missouri or Illinois?
A.  In Missouri, call the Attorney General’s consumer protection hotline at 800-392-8222; RSMo 304.156 also lets you petition the associate circuit court where the car is stored within ten days of the tower’s notice. In Illinois, the Attorney General’s consumer fraud line for southern Illinois is 1-800-243-0607. Bring photos of the sign, the invoice and the location.
### Q. How much does an impound fee cost?
A.  If the City of St. Louis towed it, published rates are $100 for the tow and $25 per day for storage, plus $60 for a dolly if one was used. Five days in the lot is $225 before any tickets or a police hold are added.
### Q. Will Impounds do payment plans?
A.  Rarely — storage accrues daily, so most lots require payment in full before release, which is what makes delay expensive. Ask immediately about a hold: a car released on day two costs a fraction of one released on day ten.

## How to Check a Used Car in St. Louis Before You Hand Over the Money
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-check-a-used-car-before-buying-st-louis
Imagine it’s a Saturday morning in Florissant and the car in the driveway looks right. Straight panels, 96,000 miles, priced eight hundred under what you expected. The seller is friendly. He’s also vague about where the car came from, and he mentions twice that somebody else is coming at noon.
Maybe you drove out from Affton with an envelope of cash. Maybe you’re meeting a stranger in a Belleville parking lot on your lunch hour. Either way, the thing you’re buying isn’t the paint. It’s six or eight years of weather, water and road salt that happened to this car before you got there.
Nearly all of it is checkable in one afternoon. Most buyers skip that and find out in February, when the brake pedal goes soft on Manchester Road.
### How to properly inspect a used car before buying?
Five things, in this order. Run the VIN through the free NICB VINCheck and a federal NMVTIS report. Read the actual paper title, not a photo of it. Get under the car with a flashlight. Hunt for water lines where nobody bothers to detail. Then pay an independent mechanic you chose to put it on a lift.
The order is deliberate. The first two steps cost about ten dollars and kill a bad car before you drive across the metro. The fifth costs real money, which is why you spend it last — on the one car that survived everything else. This is a two-state market, too: a car that crossed the Mississippi passed through two titling systems, and the gaps between them are where the surprises live.
### What do Missouri and Illinois title brands actually mean?
A title brand is a permanent note that something serious happened to this car. Missouri’s core brand is salvage: under RSMo 301.010, that means repairs back to legal road condition would exceed 80 percent of what the car was worth immediately before the damage. Once repaired and examined, the new Missouri title reads prior salvage.
Missouri also prints designations for reconstructed, motor change, specially constructed and non-USA-std vehicles (RSMo 301.190). The word flood is not among them. A Missouri salvage brand tells you an insurer wrote the car off; it doesn’t tell you water did it.
Illinois names the water. Under 625 ILCS 5/3-117.1, a car submerged until water rose over the door sill into the passenger or trunk compartment is a flood vehicle, and it becomes salvage when repairs top 50 percent of fair market value. The certificate must then “indicate the word ‘flood’, and the word ‘flood’ shall be conspicuously entered on subsequent titles for the vehicle.”
Now the trap inside that same statute. An Illinois owner may keep a totaled vehicle by agreement with the insurer if it is 9 model years of age or older, or if the damage was hail only. So a hard hit on a 12-year-old car can settle, get patched, and never produce a salvage certificate. A clean title is not a clean history.
### How does title washing work, and how do you catch it?
Title washing means moving a branded car to a state that doesn’t see the brand and getting a fresh clean title issued there. The federal answer is NMVTIS, the National Motor Vehicle Title Information System, run by the U.S. Justice Department’s Bureau of Justice Assistance at vehiclehistory.gov. It keeps a brand once a brand exists.
Know its limits. About 87 percent of the U.S. vehicle population is in NMVTIS and more than half the states report into it. You buy the report from an approved provider listed there; DOJ guidance put the fees at $8 to $12.99. It shows brand history across states, reported odometer readings, insurer total-loss calls, and whether the car ever went to a salvage yard.
Both states give you a quiet checkpoint. Missouri requires an ID and odometer inspection on any vehicle previously titled out of state (12 CSR 10-23.385). Illinois goes harder on water: under 92 Ill. Adm. Code 1010.195, a car from a federally declared disaster area needs a notarized Natural Disaster Disclosure Statement, and if it doesn’t appear, Illinois brands the salvage certificate “flood” anyway.
Wildly off-topic — martial arts classes fill up faster than you expect.
### How do you spot a flood car in a two-river metro?
Look where a detailer wouldn’t. The Missouri Attorney General’s consumer alert on flood cars tells buyers to check for mud or residue in the trunk, under the carpets and floor mats, and around the pedals, and to watch for premature rust in odd places — door hinges and trunk latches especially. A musty smell counts. So does an over-perfumed one. Add the spare tire well, the seat rails and the glove box.
The risk here is local. On July 26, 2022, Lambert recorded 8.64 inches of rain in 24 hours, an all-time record breaking the 6.85 inches set on August 20, 1915, and the National Weather Service measured more than eight inches from northern Montgomery County, Missouri into St. Clair County, Illinois. Nationally, CARFAX reported on August 6, 2025 that roughly 482,000 water-damaged cars were already on U.S. roads, with as many as 45,000 more damaged that spring and summer.
Run the free NICB VINCheck, whose participating insurers covered more than 92 percent of the market as of August 2026. Understand what it is, though — a record of what insurers reported. A car that flooded and never got claimed comes back clean.
### How bad is undercarriage rust on a car that has wintered here?
Bad enough to end an otherwise healthy car. AAA estimated in February 2017 that U.S. drivers had paid about $15.4 billion over five years — roughly $3 billion annually — on rust repairs from road salt and de-icers, around $500 per occurrence. The parts that go are the ones you can’t see: brake lines, fuel tanks, exhaust, exposed electrical connectors, floorboards.
Both sides of the river salt heavily. MoDOT’s St. Louis District keeps more than 30,000 tons on hand for 6,400 lane miles, and IDOT spread over 357,500 tons statewide in fiscal 2026 through April. In June 2026, NHTSA logged a recall covering 880,514 Honda and Acura SUVs and trucks for rear subframe corrosion that can cause rear suspension failure — and it applies only in salt-belt jurisdictions, Missouri and Illinois among them.
So get low. NHTSA’s April 2015 brake-line advisory is still the clearest standard: surface film is normal, but flaking or scaling on metal brake pipes means replacing the assembly. Press a thumb into the rocker panels and rear wheel arches, then look at subframe mounts and exhaust hangers. Anything that gives under that pressure is structural.
### Why is an independent pre-purchase inspection the best $150 in the process?
Because it’s the only step where someone with a lift, a scan tool and no stake in the sale tells you the truth. A pre-purchase inspection generally runs $100 to $250 for an ordinary car, more for luxury or hybrid models. Set that against the average used-vehicle listing price, which Cox Automotive put at $27,028 in July 2026. You’re spending under one percent of the purchase to find out what you’re buying.
Pick the shop yourself. The Missouri Attorney General puts it plainly: use a technician with no connection to the seller. Ask for the car on a lift, a scan for stored and pending codes, and a written summary.
The real value isn’t the report. The clearest red flag when buying a used car is a seller who refuses an independent inspection — that refusal has already answered your biggest question. Walk away from a no.
### Do you need an emissions test before you buy a used car here?
In Missouri, a private seller has to hand you one. The Gateway Vehicle Inspection Program covers vehicles registered in St. Louis City, St. Louis County, St. Charles County and Jefferson County — Franklin County is not in it — and applies to 1996-and-newer gas vehicles and 1997-and-newer diesels at 8,500 pounds or less. Sellers must provide a current approval or waiver before the sale, and you have 60 days from the test date to use it.
Missouri also wants a safety inspection certificate no more than 60 days old, though vehicles within 10 model years and under 150,000 miles are exempt. Illinois differs: the Metro East testing area covers parts of Madison, Monroe and St. Clair counties by ZIP code, not county line; most 1996-and-newer gasoline vehicles begin testing after four model years, and the test rides on plate renewal.
Treat that certificate as information. A seller who can’t produce a passing Missouri test in those four counties is telling you about a catalytic converter, an oxygen sensor, or a light somebody cleared last week. Sales tax, doc fees and titling deadlines are covered in the guide to buying from a St. Louis dealership.
### What does “as is” really mean in Missouri versus Illinois?
Two different things, and the gap is worth real money. Illinois puts a floor under dealer sales; Missouri does not. Under 815 ILCS 505/2L, an Illinois dealer cannot disclaim the implied warranty of merchantability on the power train for 15 days or 500 miles after delivery, whichever comes first, regardless of any “as is” language in the contract.
That covers the engine block and internals, water pump, intake manifold, transmission and internals, torque converter, drive shaft, universal joints and rear axle. You pay half of a covered repair, capped at $100 per repair, for the first two. Read the exclusions, though: it doesn’t apply to vehicles over 150,000 miles, titles branded rebuilt or flood, vehicles rated 8,000 pounds or more, or antiques. Buy a flood-branded car from an Illinois dealer and you’ve given up the one protection state law hands you.
Missouri has no equivalent statute. “As is” from a Missouri dealer means as is, and neither state gives you a cooling-off period. The FTC Used Car Rule requires that Buyers Guide sticker in the window, but only from dealers — anyone selling six or more used vehicles in twelve months. Private sellers sit outside it entirely.
### What a used-car lot sees that you don’t
A small independent lot makes its money on sourcing and speed, not the sticker. Cars come from auction, where Cox Automotive’s Manheim index sat at 210 in July 2026, and every unit on the lot is borrowed money. Pre-owned floor plan lines ran 7.0 to 8.3 percent for one public dealer group at the end of 2025, so an aging car eats its own gross. That’s why a good lot turns down your trade: when reconditioning costs more than the retail spread, the car goes to wholesale. CarMax wholesaled 162,064 vehicles in the quarter ending May 31, 2026 against 230,293 retailed, at roughly half the gross per unit. The cheap end is hardest to stock — sub-$15,000 inventory fell 20 percent year over year in July 2026. And every curbstoner flipping six cars a year out of a parking lot, a class A misdemeanor under RSMo 301.570, spends credibility the licensed lot down the street has to earn back. Which is the case for being listed and easy to verify: people search this category locally.

Ready to shop with your eyes open? Browse used cars across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then ask each lot whether you can take the car to your own mechanic first.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. What is a red flag when buying a used car?
A.  A seller who will not let your mechanic put the car on a lift — that one ends the conversation. After that: a clean Illinois title on a car nine model years or older, where a total loss can settle without producing a salvage certificate; silt under the carpet or in the spare tire well; and flaking rust on metal brake lines.
### Q. How do I check if a used car has a salvage title?
A.  Run the free NICB VINCheck, then buy an NMVTIS report from an approved provider listed at vehiclehistory.gov. NMVTIS carries brand history across state lines, so a brand applied in one state stays attached after the car is retitled elsewhere. Then read the paper title — Missouri prints salvage or prior salvage on the face.
### Q. How much does a pre-purchase car inspection cost in St. Louis?
A.  Roughly $100 to $250 at an independent shop for an ordinary sedan or SUV, higher for luxury, diesel or hybrid models needing extra diagnostics. Ask for the car on a lift, a scan for stored and pending codes, and a written report. You pick the shop, and you keep the paperwork whether you buy or walk.
### Q. Does a private seller have to give me an emissions certificate in Missouri?
A.  Yes, if the vehicle is registered in St. Louis City, St. Louis County, St. Charles County or Jefferson County. Private sellers there must provide a current Gateway Vehicle Inspection Program approval or waiver before the sale, and you get 60 days from the test date to use it when you title the car.
### Q. Can I return a used car in Missouri if it breaks down?
A.  Generally no. Missouri has no cooling-off period and no statutory used-car warranty, so an “as is” sale is final once you sign. Your remaining avenue is a fraud or misrepresentation claim, and complaints against dealers go to the Missouri Attorney General’s consumer protection division.
### Q. Does “as is” hold up when an Illinois dealer sells a used car?
A.  Not fully. Illinois gives you a 15-day or 500-mile implied warranty on the power train from a dealer, and an “as is” clause can’t waive it. You cover half of a repair up to $100 for the first two. It doesn’t apply to cars over 150,000 miles, rebuilt or flood titles, vehicles rated 8,000 pounds or more, or antiques.
### Q. What is the $3000 rule for cars?
A.  It is one of several budgeting rules of thumb that circulate online, and none of them tell you whether the specific car in front of you is sound. A cheap car with a clean frame, a readable service history and no rust through the rockers can be a fine buy. A more expensive one hiding flood damage is not. Spend the inspection money first, then let the number follow the car.
### Q. What not to say to a used car salesman?
A.  Less than you think, and it matters less than you think. What actually protects you here is not wording — it is the title check, the pre-purchase inspection by a mechanic you chose, and your willingness to leave. Say plainly that the sale is contingent on an independent inspection. A seller who resists that has told you something no conversational tactic would have.
### Q. How to check if a car had flood damage?
A.  Start with the title, then the car. Illinois stamps a flood brand permanently, so an Illinois history is worth pulling. Missouri has no flood brand at all, which is exactly why a flooded car can end up wearing a clean Missouri title. On the car itself: silt in seat rails and spare-tyre wells, water lines inside lamp housings, rust on unpainted bolt heads under the carpet, and a damp or perfumed smell.
### Q. Is it worth buying a rebuilt title car?
A.  Sometimes, and only with eyes open. A rebuilt title means the car was written off and repaired, so you are buying somebody else’s repair work. It costs less, it is harder to insure for full coverage, and it resells for less again. If you go ahead, get the pre-purchase inspection from a shop you chose and ask specifically what was damaged and who repaired it.
### Q. How can I tell if a used car was in a flood?
A.  Check the trunk, under the carpets and floor mats, and around the pedals for mud or residue, then look for premature rust on door hinges and trunk latches. Musty or heavily perfumed interiors both count as evidence. Lift the spare tire and look for a silt line, then run NICB VINCheck.

## What an Eye Exam Costs in St. Louis and How to Choose an Optometrist
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/eye-exam-cost-st-louis-optometrist
Imagine it’s a Thursday night and you’re holding your phone farther from your face than you did last year. Small thing. Then the menu at a Kirkwood taco counter goes soft around the edges until you tilt it toward the light, and your kid in Florissant mentions — casually, the way kids do — that he keeps sliding up to the front row.
None of that is an emergency. All of it is a nudge. So you finally start hunting for an eye doctor somewhere between the house in Affton and the office in Maryland Heights, and you hit the wall everybody hits. Nobody will tell you the price.
One office quotes a number. Another says it depends on your plan. A third wants your insurance card first. Here is what an eye exam actually costs around here, what moves the number, and which parts of the bill are optional.
### What does an eye exam cost in St. Louis?
Getting an eye exam without vision insurance starts with one number: budget $75 to $200 for a comprehensive exam if you are paying cash. That range comes from VSP, the largest vision plan in the country, which told consumers in a July 2024 article that a full-service exam runs $75 to $200 without vision insurance and can start as low as $50. Carry a vision plan and you typically pay a copay instead, often $10 to $25, with the plan paying the practice directly.
Where is the cheapest place to get an eye exam? Nobody can tell you from a desk. No government agency publishes a St. Louis average, so anybody quoting a precise metro figure is guessing. Settle it the direct way: call two or three offices and ask one narrow question — “What is your self-pay fee for a comprehensive exam, and what costs extra?” Front desks can answer that. They cannot answer “how much is an eye exam.”
### Why two offices quote you completely different numbers
Because an eye exam is not one service. It is a bundle, and offices bundle it differently. A comprehensive exam covers the refraction — the one-or-two, better-or-worse part that produces your prescription — plus an eye health evaluation: pressure, the eye surface, the retina, the optic nerve.
The add-ons are where quotes split apart. Dilation drops. Digital retinal imaging, often offered as an alternative to dilation. And a contact lens fitting, a genuinely separate service with its own fee, because measuring how a lens sits on the curve of your cornea is not part of a glasses exam. If you wear contacts, ask for both numbers up front. That one question closes most of the gap between the quote and the bill.
### Vision insurance is not health insurance
A vision plan is a separate, limited-scope benefit most people buy on top of health coverage. It pays a set amount toward one routine exam a year and hands you an allowance toward frames, lenses, or contacts — closer to a discount program with a network than to major medical coverage. Your health plan treats your eyes like any other organ: it pays when something is medically wrong with them.
That split explains a bill that trips up a lot of people. One appointment can end up part billed to your vision plan and part billed to your health plan. Nothing shady is going on. Two different products are paying for two different things.
### When does medical insurance pay for an eye visit?
When there is a medical reason for the visit. Medicare is the clearest published example. Medicare.gov states that Original Medicare does not cover routine eye exams — sometimes called eye refractions — for eyeglasses or contact lenses. But Part B covers a diabetic retinopathy exam once a year for people with diabetes, and a glaucoma test once every 12 months for people at high risk, a group Medicare defines to include people with a family history of glaucoma, Black Americans 50 and older, and Hispanic Americans 65 and older.
Medicare also pays for one pair of eyeglasses with standard frames, or one set of contacts, after each cataract surgery that implants an intraocular lens; you owe 20% of the approved amount once the Part B deductible is met. Commercial health plans follow the same logic. Floaters, an eye injury, stubborn dry eye, or diabetes monitoring is a medical visit. Wanting a fresh pair of glasses is not.
### Optometrist, ophthalmologist, optician — who does what?
An optometrist holds a doctor of optometry degree, earned in a four-year optometry program after undergraduate study, and handles most everyday eye care: exams, glasses and contact lens prescriptions, and the diagnosis and medical management of many eye conditions. An ophthalmologist is a physician, an MD or DO, who finished medical school plus residency training in eye surgery and disease — the American Academy of Ophthalmology puts the full path at roughly 12 to 14 years. An optician does not examine eyes or write prescriptions; opticians fit, adjust, and dispense eyewear from a prescription someone else wrote.
In practice: for a routine exam, glasses, or contacts, start with an optometrist. For cataract surgery, LASIK, retinal disease, or surgical glaucoma care, you end up with an ophthalmologist — often on a referral from the optometrist who spotted it first. And the person who fixes the frames that keep sliding down your nose is your optician.
Completely unrelated — the Italian food here is worth planning around.
### You own your prescription. Two federal rules say so.
Under the Federal Trade Commission’s Eyeglass Rule, your eye doctor must give you a copy of your glasses prescription at the end of the exam — automatically, whether you ask or not, at no extra charge. They cannot require you to buy glasses first, charge for the copy, or make you sign a liability waiver. The FTC finalized an updated rule on June 26, 2024, and since September 26, 2024, prescribers must also request a signed confirmation that you received it and keep that record for three years.
The Contact Lens Rule does the same job for contacts and adds teeth. You get a copy at the end of a fitting without asking, and the prescription must be valid for at least one year unless your prescriber has a documented medical reason for a shorter term. When an online seller sends a verification request, the prescriber has eight business hours to respond; silence verifies the prescription automatically. One gap worth knowing: pupillary distance, the measurement most online retailers ask for, is not required on the prescription by federal rule, though the FTC encourages prescribers to hand it over when they have measured it. Ask before you leave.
### How often do you actually need an eye exam?
The American Academy of Ophthalmology recommends a baseline comprehensive eye evaluation at age 40 for adults with no symptoms and no risk factors, then an exam every two to four years from 40 to 54, every one to three years from 55 to 64, and every one to two years at 65 and older. Symptoms, diabetes, high blood pressure, a family history of glaucoma, or an existing prescription push you toward the short end of each window.
Children run on a different clock. The American Optometric Association’s 2017 evidence-based pediatric guideline moved to an annual comprehensive exam, up from every other year in the 2002 version, because some childhood eye conditions progress fast enough that waiting two years is a real risk. A school screening is not an exam. Screenings flag a subset of problems fast, in a hallway, with a chart on the wall.
### Missouri and Illinois do not treat eyes the same way
If your kid is starting kindergarten in Belleville, Illinois requires proof of an actual eye examination by an optometrist or a physician who performs eye examinations — not a screening — completed within the year before the first day of school and turned in by October 15. It covers kindergarteners and any student enrolling in an Illinois school for the first time. Preschool is exempt, and families who cannot obtain the exam can file a waiver.
Missouri does not require that. Missouri once mandated a comprehensive vision examination for kindergarten and first-grade enrollment under RSMo 167.194, but the legislature repealed that statute in 2018, and Missouri schools lean on vision screening instead. Same metro, same six-year-old, different paperwork depending on which side of the river you sleep on.
Driver’s licenses split as well. Both states use 20/40 as the acuity line for an unrestricted license, and glasses or contacts count toward it. In Missouri, drivers 70 and older get a three-year license instead of the standard six, and every renewal includes a vision and road-sign test. Illinois rewrote its rules with the Road Safety and Fairness Act, signed in August 2025 and effective July 1, 2026: drivers 79 through 86 renew in person with a vision test but no longer take a behind-the-wheel driving test, while drivers 87 and older still renew annually with both.
Public coverage differs too, and it is where to start if you can’t afford glasses. Under Missouri regulation 13 CSR 70-40.010, MO HealthNet allows adults one eye examination and one pair of eyeglasses every two years, with glasses covered at prescriptions of 0.75 diopters or stronger. Children, pregnant women, nursing home residents, and blind participants get one examination per year.
### What the exam looks like from behind the counter
Patients almost never see this part. In an analysis of more than 500 independent optometry practices by ABB Analyze with CareCredit, product sales — frames, lenses, contacts — made up 54% of gross revenue in 2019, while exams accounted for roughly 21% and medical services 14%. The American Optometric Association reported in August 2020 that vision plans typically paid $35 to $90 for exam services that year, below Medicare’s 2020 average of $114 and below what Medicare paid in 2005, when it averaged $90. Seven in ten optometrists said they had gone at least five years without a fee increase from their largest plan. That is why the frame board carries the practice, and why December is the crunch — vision benefits and FSA dollars expire December 31 and the schedule jams with people spending them. Filling the other eleven months is a findability problem, which is the entire case for a complete listing on St Louis Near Me Directory.
Related reading: another practitioner worth vetting and school vision screening rules.
