### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Does my health insurance cover an eye exam?
A.  It covers medically necessary eye care, not routine refractions for glasses. Medicare shows the pattern: it does not pay for routine exams, but Part B covers a yearly diabetic retinopathy exam and a glaucoma test every 12 months for high-risk patients. Show up with floaters, an injury, persistent dry eye, or diabetes monitoring and it is a medical visit billed to your health plan.
### Q. What do I do if I can’t afford glasses?
A.  Shop the prescription. The FTC’s Eyeglass Rule requires your prescriber to hand you a copy of your glasses prescription automatically at the end of the exam, free, with no purchase requirement and no waiver to sign, so you are never stuck buying frames at the counter where you were examined. Take that prescription to a big-box optical shop, an independent optician, or an online retailer and price it out. On MO HealthNet, Missouri covers one pair of eyeglasses every two years for adults.
### Q. How long is a contact lens prescription good for?
A.  At least one year under the FTC’s Contact Lens Rule, unless your prescriber documented a medical reason for a shorter term. When you order online, the seller may verify the prescription with your doctor instead of collecting a paper copy. The prescriber then has eight business hours to respond; if none comes, the prescription is verified automatically and the order ships.
### Q. Does my child need an eye exam before kindergarten in Illinois?
A.  Yes. Illinois requires an eye examination by an optometrist or a physician who performs eye examinations, done within the year before the first day of school, with proof submitted by October 15. It applies to kindergarteners and any student entering an Illinois school for the first time. Preschool is exempt, and a waiver exists for families who cannot get the exam done.
### Q. Does Missouri require a vision exam for school?
A.  Not an examination from a doctor. Missouri repealed its comprehensive vision examination requirement, RSMo 167.194, in 2018, and public schools use vision screening instead. Screening catches some problems and misses others, which is why the American Optometric Association recommends an annual comprehensive exam for school-age children regardless of what a state requires on paper.
### Q. What vision do you need to pass the driver’s license eye test?
A.  Missouri and Illinois both use 20/40 as the threshold for an unrestricted license, and glasses or contacts count. Missouri drivers 70 and older renew every three years with a vision and road-sign test each time. In Illinois, under the Road Safety and Fairness Act effective July 1, 2026, drivers 79 through 86 take a vision test but no road test; at 87 and older, both.
### Q. How much is a full eye exam at Walmart?
A.  We do not quote prices for a specific provider. Any figure we published would be out of date quickly, varies by location, and would steer you on price alone. Ask the practice directly what a comprehensive exam costs, whether the refraction is included or billed separately, and what changes if the visit turns out to be medical rather than routine. Those three questions get you a real number for your situation.
### Q. Should I see an optometrist or an ophthalmologist first?
A.  For a routine exam, glasses, contacts, or a new symptom you cannot explain, start with an optometrist. They handle most primary eye care and refer you out if you need surgery or specialist disease management. Go straight to an ophthalmologist when you already know you are facing cataract surgery, LASIK, or ongoing retinal care.
### Q. How to get a free vision exam?
A.  Community health centres, school and charity screening programmes, and some retailer promotions run free or heavily reduced exams. Screening is not the same as a comprehensive exam — budget $75 to $200 for the full version, per VSP’s published consumer guidance.
### Q. Can I wear the same glasses for 10 years?
A.  The frame may last that long; the prescription and the lens coatings usually will not. Vision shifts gradually enough that people adapt without noticing, which is the argument for an exam on schedule rather than when something feels wrong.

## How to Hire an Architect in St. Louis: When the Law Requires One
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/hiring-an-architect-in-st-louis
Imagine it’s a Saturday morning and you’re standing in a back yard with a tape measure and a rough idea. The house went up before your grandparents were born — a brick four-square in Affton, a bungalow in Florissant. Push the kitchen out twelve feet. Take down the wall by the stairs. Put a bedroom on the sun porch.
Maybe you’re in Kirkwood and the addition has to clear a setback nobody mentioned at closing. Maybe you bought a storefront in Belleville and want the back half turned into two apartments. Maybe you’re in Maryland Heights and your contractor has a guy who does plans, cheap, and you can’t tell if that’s a bargain.
Here’s the fork. Some of that work legally requires a licensed architect and some of it flatly doesn’t, and the line sits in statute in both Missouri and Illinois. Work out which side you’re on before you hand anyone a deposit. It changes who you hire, what you pay, and whether the permit counter sends you home.
### When does Missouri law actually require a licensed architect?
Missouri exempts a short list of small private buildings and requires a licensed architect for the rest. So can you draw your own house plans without an architect? Under RSMo 327.101, an unlicensed person may render architectural services for a dwelling house, a flat or apartment holding no more than two families, a farm building, or any one building serving no more than nine people, under two thousand square feet, and not part of another structure.
Read that carefully. In the version effective August 28, 2021, the conditions stack: nine people or fewer and under two thousand square feet and freestanding. A 2,400-square-foot storefront build-out fails it, however few people work inside.
A second condition gets missed entirely. The exemption only holds if the unlicensed designer states on the drawings, specifications and reports that the person is not a licensed architect. Plans with no seal and no such note are a red flag. Three- and four-family buildings get a narrower break: remodeling and repair only, where the work does not affect architectural or engineering safety features.
State law is a floor. The Missouri board’s Reference Manual for Building Officials says a municipality may use requirements more stringent than the state’s, so your permit counter is the real authority. Two provisions add teeth: RSMo 327.461 makes a contract for architectural services unenforceable by an unlicensed, non-exempt person, and RSMo 327.077 allows civil penalties up to $5,000 per offense.
### What changes on the Illinois side of the river?
Illinois exempts less. Section 3 of the Illinois Architecture Practice Act of 1989 (225 ILCS 305/3) says the Act does not apply to farm buildings outside municipal limits, detached single-family homes on a single lot, wood-framed two-family homes on a single lot no more than two stories and a basement, and interior design that does not involve life safety or structural changes.
The words wood-framed do a lot of work. A masonry two-flat in Belleville, Alton or Granite City sits outside that exemption, while the same building in south St. Louis falls inside Missouri’s, which has no construction-type test. That one word is the sharpest practical difference between the two states for a small owner.
Illinois also snaps the exemption shut when a building changes jobs. The IDFPR code enforcement manual gives the example directly: a farm building that becomes a commercial machine shop is no longer exempt. Interior alterations creating life safety or structural changes are covered too, and a local ordinance can require an architect anyway. Enforcement is not administrative-only — a first offense is a Class A misdemeanor, later offenses are Class 4 felonies, and IDFPR fines run up to $10,000 per offense.
### Architect, draftsperson or design-build contractor — which do you need?
Is there a cheaper alternative to an architect? On an exempt project, yes. A draftsperson can legally draw an exempt project in either state, and for a straightforward single-family remodel that is often the right and cheaper answer. Once a project falls outside the exemption, the drawings need a licensed architect’s seal, and experience does not substitute for the license.
Design-build muddies this. The checkable version: in Illinois, a design-build entity may not offer professional design services unless it is registered with IDFPR as a Professional Design Firm — or it independently contracts with an Illinois-licensed design professional, gives the client a written disclosure naming that professional when services are offered, keeps them in direct supervision of the design, and replaces them within 30 days if they leave. That disclosure is yours to ask for.
Missouri differs on firms. Under RSMo 327.401 a corporation offering architectural services must hold a certificate of authority from the board, and the person in charge of the architectural work must be licensed. Verify both: the individual and the entity.
Different trade entirely — concrete work decides how the whole thing sits.
### How do architects charge, and what does each method cover?
Three structures dominate: a percentage of construction cost, an hourly rate, and a fixed fee. Percentage is the common one for full-service work. Architect Bob Borson, writing at Life of an Architect, puts most percentage-based residential firms in the 8 to 15 percent range of construction cost. Iowa firm Neumann Monson publishes 9 percent on a $20 million commercial project.
One detail changes how a percentage behaves. The AIA’s B101-2017 owner-architect agreement calculates progress payments against the owner’s budget for the cost of the work rather than the final construction cost, so the fee stops sliding every time a bid comes back high.
Hourly is the honest structure for the fuzzy front end — feasibility, zoning, a historic review nobody can scope yet. Fixed fee buys predictability and gets renegotiated when scope moves. How much does an architect cost for a small project? Proportionally more. Smaller projects carry higher percentages for a reason that is not greed: a 400-square-foot addition still needs every joint and header drawn.
### What are the five phases, and which one do clients try to skip?
AIA B101-2017 splits basic services into five phases: schematic design, design development, construction documents, procurement (bidding or negotiation), and construction. That last one, construction administration, is the phase clients try hardest to cut — and the one that costs most to lose.
Schematic design sets size, shape and the relationships between rooms. Design development picks systems, structure and real materials, and pulls in the structural, mechanical and electrical consultants. Construction documents turn that into the drawings and specifications a contractor prices and a plan reviewer stamps. Procurement is bidding. Construction administration is the architect on site: visits, answers to contractor questions, submittal review, payment certification.
Firms publish their splits. Neumann Monson lists schematic design at 20 percent of the fee, design development 20 percent, contract documents 30 to 35 percent, bidding 5 percent, contract administration 25 to 30 percent. Cutting that last line looks like a quarter off the design budget. What it buys is a job site where the contractor reads the drawings alone, substitutions go unremarked, and when a change order lands nobody is there to say whether it came from a hidden field condition or the drawings themselves.
### How do you verify a Missouri or Illinois architect’s license?
Both states run a free public license search that answers in about a minute. Missouri’s Division of Professional Registration hosts a licensee search at pr.mo.gov; the board is reachable at 573-751-0047. Illinois uses the IDFPR License Look Up, where architect licenses carry the 001 prefix.
Missouri licenses renew every two years by December 31 — odd years if first issued in an odd year, even years if even (20 CSR 2030-11.010). Each cycle takes 24 continuing education units, at least 16 in health, safety and welfare. RSMo 327.411 requires the seal on all final technical submissions and makes the licensee personally responsible for what sits under it.
On an Illinois set, read the seal. It has to carry the licensee’s name, the license number and the words “Licensed Architect, State of Illinois,” with the signature, the current date and the license expiration date, on the first sheet of a bound set. A retired or inactive licensee cannot seal drawings at all.
### What do St. Louis historic districts and tax credits change?
In a City of St. Louis local historic district, exterior work is reviewed against that district’s own ordinance standards before a permit issues, which makes prior experience a real hiring criterion. The Cultural Resources Office performs more than 3,000 reviews a year, from large developments to small home repairs, and each district has its own standards written with neighborhood residents. Larger projects go to the Preservation Board. Demolition runs a separate track: in the city’s Preservation Review Districts, every demolition application is referred to that office and no permit issues without its approval. In Belleville, exterior work in the three local districts — Old Belleville, Hexenbuckel and Oakland — needs a certificate of appropriateness.
Then the money, where the states split hardest. The federal 20 percent rehabilitation credit applies only to certified historic structures in income-producing use; the National Park Service states plainly that owner-occupied residential properties do not qualify. Missouri’s state credit does cover owner-occupied homes: 25 percent of qualified rehabilitation expenditures, or 35 percent outside St. Louis City and Kansas City where no low-income housing credits are involved, with a $250,000 project cap on owner-occupied residential and a requirement that qualifying costs exceed 50 percent of the property’s basis. Illinois offers 25 percent capped at $3 million per project, income-producing use only.
All of it has to satisfy the Secretary of the Interior’s Standards for Rehabilitation. Missouri’s preservation office warns that work failing the Standards can carry financial consequences at the end of the project. Windows, porches and storefront openings are where that usually bites, and they are the calls an experienced architect makes differently on day one.
### What the fee looks like from the architect’s side
A percentage fee has to cover hours nobody bills: site visits before a contract exists, code research, two rounds of a proposal that goes to someone else. The AIA’s 2024 Firm Survey put average pre-tax, pre-bonus profit at 11.5 percent of net service revenue — 9.0 percent at firms billing under $250,000 a year against 14.1 percent at firms over $5 million. Professional liability coverage starts near $1,700 a year for a small practice and runs higher on residential work, carried whether or not the phone rings. NCARB’s 2025 data puts the average road to licensure at 12.9 years. Small jobs hold more decisions per square foot than big ones, which is why many firms set a minimum construction budget, and why construction administration — the phase clients cut first — carries the risk. People search this work by neighborhood, and a complete, current listing is how the firms that take small jobs get found.
Related reading: where the materials come from and permits are a theme here.
Not sure whether your project needs a seal? Browse architects across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then hand two firms the same one-page description of the work and compare what each includes.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is there a cheaper alternative to an architect?
A.  Yes, if the project is exempt: a draftsperson. An architect holds a state license, carries professional liability coverage, and can seal drawings a plan reviewer will accept for non-exempt buildings. A draftsperson produces drawings but cannot seal them or use the title architect — in Illinois that title without an active license is a Class A misdemeanor on a first offense. For exempt residential work a good draftsperson is usually the cheaper and sensible hire, and outside the exemption there is no legal alternative.
### Q. What is the average fee for an architect?
A.  Most percentage-based residential firms land between 8 and 15 percent of construction cost, per architect Bob Borson at Life of an Architect, with larger commercial work closer to 9 percent. Hourly is common for early feasibility and zoning work; fixed fees appear once scope settles. AIA B101-2017 bases the percentage on the owner’s construction budget, not the final cost.
### Q. Can I skip construction administration to save money?
A.  You can, and firms will tell you what you are giving up. Construction administration runs 25 to 30 percent of the fee in published firm breakdowns and covers site visits, contractor questions, submittal review and payment certification. Without it the contractor reads the drawings alone and change-order disputes have no independent voice. Many architects decline to remove it.
### Q. How do I check whether an architect is licensed in Missouri or Illinois?
A.  Missouri: use the Division of Professional Registration licensee search at pr.mo.gov, or call the board at 573-751-0047. Illinois: use the IDFPR License Look Up, where architect licenses use the 001 prefix. Check the firm too — Missouri requires a certificate of authority under RSMo 327.401, Illinois a Professional Design Firm registration.
### Q. Do I need an architect for work in a St. Louis historic district?
A.  Not automatically, but the review is real. Exterior work in a City of St. Louis local historic district is checked against that district’s ordinance standards by the Cultural Resources Office, which handles more than 3,000 reviews a year; larger projects go to the Preservation Board. Belleville requires a certificate of appropriateness in its three districts.
### Q. Does a design-build contractor count as having an architect in Illinois?
A.  Only under conditions you can verify. An Illinois design-build entity must be registered as a Professional Design Firm, or it must independently contract with an Illinois-licensed design professional, hand the client a written disclosure naming that professional, keep them supervising the design, and replace them within 30 days if they leave.
### Q. How much does an architect cost for a small project?
A.  Small residential work is usually quoted as a flat fee or hourly rather than a percentage of construction. Get the scope in writing first, and confirm they are licensed — RSMo 327.461 makes a contract for architectural services unenforceable by an unlicensed, non-exempt person.
### Q. What is the 30% rule for renovations?
A.  A budgeting rule of thumb that you should not spend more than about 30% of your home’s value on a renovation. It is a guard against over-improving for the street rather than a hard limit — and it says nothing about whether the work is worth it to you.

## Hiring a Personal Trainer in St. Louis: What to Check First
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/hiring-a-personal-trainer-in-st-louis
Imagine it’s a Tuesday evening in February and you’re sitting in a parking lot in Affton with a gym bag you haven’t opened since the second week of January. Somebody at work said what you really need is a trainer. Now your phone is full of names, every one of them with good lighting and the word certified in the bio.
Or maybe it went the other way. You came out of an appointment in Kirkwood with a number you didn’t like and advice that sounded simple — strength training, twice a week, start easy. Simple right up until you’re facing a rack of barbells with no idea which one is yours.
Here’s the part nobody mentions at the front desk in Florissant or Belleville or Maryland Heights. In Missouri and in Illinois, a person can decide tomorrow morning that they are a personal trainer, print a card, and start charging you. No state exam. No license number to look up. That puts the vetting on you, and it takes about fifteen minutes once you know what you’re looking at.
### Do personal trainers need a license in Missouri or Illinois?
No. Neither state licenses personal trainers, and neither one protects the title. Missouri has no state credential for the job at all. Illinois licenses athletic trainers through the Department of Financial & Professional Regulation — a separate health care profession with a degree requirement and a national exam — but a personal trainer there needs nothing from the state either.
That matters because the jobs sitting right next to this one are licensed, and the boundary is legal rather than stylistic. Physical therapists are licensed in both states. Dietitians are too, but differently. Missouri’s dietitian law, sections 324.200 to 324.225 RSMo, is largely title protection, and it exempts a person credentialed in nutrition who stays inside their credentialing body’s scope and out of medical nutrition therapy. Illinois is tighter — under the Dietitian Nutritionist Practice Act, 225 ILCS 30, no one may practice nutrition services for pay without a license.
General food guidance is one thing. A written plan aimed at a diagnosed medical condition is another, and a trainer in Belleville who hands you one is further out of bounds than a trainer in Affton doing the same thing. Ask who wrote it and what they’re licensed to write.
### Which personal trainer certifications actually mean anything?
Look for four letters: NCCA. The National Commission for Certifying Agencies is the accreditation arm of the Institute for Credentialing Excellence, and it audits certification programs against the 2021 NCCA Standards on a five-year renewal cycle. It doesn’t teach anybody anything — it checks whether the exam behind the credential is built and scored like a real exam.
NASM, ACE, NSCA and ACSM all hold NCCA accreditation for their personal training credentials. The ACE exam is 150 multiple-choice questions in three hours, and holders must log 2.0 CECs — 20 hours — every two years or sit it again. NASM runs the same two-year, 2.0 CEU cycle, with a current CPR/AED card counting for 0.1 of it. ACSM has announced that starting in 2027 all of its certifications will also require first aid training.
ISSA is the one to read slowly, because it sells two different things under one brand. ISSA’s own site describes the choice as “the open-book, untimed ISSA Certification Exam or the proctored NCCA Accredited Exam offered by the ISSA subsidiary the National Council for Certified Personal Trainers (NCCPT).” Both produce a certificate. Only one was proctored.
Ask two boring questions. Which certification, and is it current? Credentials expire on a schedule, and plenty of people keep using the letters after the card lapses. Ask to see it, and the CPR/AED card beside it.
### What does a personal trainer cost around St. Louis?
How much should you spend on a personal trainer? Plan on $40 to $120 for an hour of one-on-one training, with the middle of the national market near $55 to $65 in 2026 pricing surveys. St. Louis is not a premium coastal market, so local rate cards tend to land inside that band rather than above it. Semi-private with two to five people generally runs $20 to $60 a head. A ten-session package trims the single rate; it does not halve it.
One number reframes all of it. Bureau of Labor Statistics wage data for 2025 puts median pay for exercise trainers and group fitness instructors in the St. Louis, MO-IL metro at $17.55 an hour, or $36,500 a year — right on top of the Missouri statewide median of $17.52. Most of what you hand over at the desk is not going to the person holding the clipboard.
What legitimately moves the price: employee versus independent, session length, a real specialty like post-rehab, and travel if they drive to your house in St. Charles. What tends to be padding: an assessment fee stacked on the first session, an initiation fee on a package you already prepaid, and a long block discounted just enough that you overbuy.
### What should you read twice before you sign?
Read the cancellation clause and the renewal clause before you read the price. Missouri and Illinois both give you a three-business-day escape hatch on longer agreements, and both attach conditions people skate past.
In Missouri, section 407.325 RSMo defines a health spa contract as one for services rendered over a period longer than three months — so a ten-session package you will finish in six weeks is not covered by that law at all. Where it does apply, section 407.330 gives you three business days to cancel by written notice, sent certified mail with return receipt requested or hand-delivered, with the refund due inside 30 days. Death, or a permanent disability blocking use for 60 or more consecutive days, ends the contract with a prorated refund. Section 407.327 also makes selling those contracts unlawful unless the business is registered and bonded with the Missouri Attorney General. Nonprofits, member-owned clubs, martial arts schools and government facilities are excluded.
Illinois is more prescriptive. The Physical Fitness Services Act, 815 ILCS 645, covers instruction and training in exercise, caps the initial contract term at one year, and bars financing stretched past three years. You get three business days to cancel, or seven calendar days at a facility that has not opened yet. Move more than 25 miles away with no comparable location offered and you can cancel, owing a fee capped at 10 percent of the unused balance or $50, whichever is less. Automatic renewals must comply with the Illinois Automatic Contract Renewal Act, which requires written notice 30 to 60 days before the cancellation deadline on contracts of 12 months or more. Section 11 allows treble damages plus costs and attorney fees.
Do not count on a federal backstop. The Federal Trade Commission’s click-to-cancel rule was vacated in its entirety by the Eighth Circuit on July 8, 2025, and the agency only restarted that rulemaking in early 2026. What governs your cancellation today is the paragraph in front of you.
Two more clauses deserve a look: insurance and the waiver. Neither state requires a trainer to carry liability coverage, though most gyms require it of independent contractors, and fitness-specific policies bundling general and professional liability commonly run $150 to $350 a year. Ask for the certificate. On the release you sign, the Missouri Supreme Court held in Alack v. Vic Tanny International of Missouri (1996) that a health club release must use plain words like negligence or fault to cover the club’s own negligence. Illinois enforces clearly written exculpatory clauses too, but not for willful and wanton conduct, and a parent’s pre-injury waiver for a minor does not hold.
Unrelated, obviously — choosing a mortgage lender is its own kind of workout.
### What does a good first session look like?
Paperwork and questions before a single rep. A trainer working to standard opens with a health history and a readiness screen — the 2017 PAR-Q+ is the common form — and applies the ACSM preparticipation algorithm, which sorts people by current activity level, known cardiovascular, metabolic or renal disease, symptoms, and the intensity planned. If something surfaces there, you get pointed toward medical clearance before you get pointed at a squat rack.
Then a movement screen. Then your goals, out loud, with a date attached. Then a scaled-down version of the real program: light, unhurried, mostly teaching. You should leave knowing what next week looks like.
Is it worth paying for a personal trainer? That gets decided in this hour, not in the soreness afterward. A first session that leaves you easing down the stairs sideways on Thursday proves very little. It gives the trainer no baseline, and a baseline is the entire job of session one. Soreness is a sensation, not a measurement. Good trainers write down loads, reps and what to change. Ask to see the notes.
### When do you need a physical therapist instead of a trainer?
If you have pain, a recent injury, a surgery in your history, or a symptom you can’t explain, that belongs to a clinician. The certifying bodies say it themselves: a personal trainer does not diagnose, does not treat injuries, and does not rehabilitate. Recognizing that boundary and referring out is part of the credential, not an admission of weakness.
Both states let you walk into a physical therapist without a doctor’s referral, with conditions. In Missouri, section 334.506 RSMo lets a therapist holding a doctorate or five years of clinical practice evaluate and begin treatment without a prescription; with no measurable or functional improvement after ten visits or 30 days, whichever comes first, the therapist must refer you on, and continuing past that point means consulting an approved health care provider. Illinois has had direct access since 2018: the therapist must notify your treating health care professional within five business days of the first visit, and must refer you out with no measurable improvement after ten visits or 15 business days.
One caveat that costs people money: your insurance may still demand a physician referral before it pays, even where state law does not require one to treat. Call the number on the back of the card first. The two roles are not rivals — a trainer worth keeping will ask for your therapist’s restrictions in writing and program inside them.
### What this looks like from the trainer’s side of the floor
The session rate is not the paycheck. A trainer employed by a gym typically keeps 30 to 60 percent of what you pay at the desk. An independent renting floor space pays a flat monthly fee, often $250 to $1,000 depending on hours, or $20 to $50 per session off the top. Then insurance, recertification every two years with 20 hours of continuing education, then CPR. Which is why the median for this job in the St. Louis metro is $17.55 an hour while the hour sells for triple that.
Then the calendar. January fills the floor and March empties it, and the Health & Fitness Association put median member retention at 66.4 percent for 2024. That churn is why so many trainers moved toward semi-private and hybrid coaching. It is also why the ones who last treat being findable as part of the work — people search this by neighborhood, and a complete listing is how you get found without renting leads.
Related reading: the chiropractic side of the same ache and another cash-versus-insurance question.
Ready to stop scrolling and start calling? Browse trainers across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, pick three near you, and ask each one for the certification, the expiration date and the insurance certificate before you book a single paid session.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Do you need a license to be a personal trainer in Missouri?
A.  Missouri issues no credential for the job and does not restrict who may use the title. Illinois is the same, though it does license athletic trainers, a different profession entirely. Because neither state verifies anything, checking the certification, its expiration date and a current CPR/AED card falls to the person paying.
### Q. What certification should a personal trainer have?
A.  One accredited by the National Commission for Certifying Agencies. NASM, ACE, NSCA and ACSM all carry NCCA accreditation for their trainer credentials, meaning the exam was independently audited against published standards. ISSA sells both an open-book exam and a proctored NCCA-accredited exam through its NCCPT subsidiary, so the exam matters more than the brand.
### Q. Can a personal trainer give me a meal plan?
A.  General food guidance, usually. A plan built to manage a diagnosed condition, no. Illinois requires a license to provide nutrition services for pay under 225 ILCS 30. Missouri protects the dietitian title and reserves medical nutrition therapy for licensees, exempting credentialed nutrition professionals inside their own scope. Ask what license the author holds.
### Q. Can I cancel a personal training contract?
A.  Usually yes, within three business days, on both sides of the river. Missouri applies that right to agreements running longer than three months and wants written notice by certified mail or hand delivery. Illinois caps the initial term at one year and lets you cancel outright if you move 25-plus miles away with no comparable facility offered.
### Q. Is 30 minutes with a personal trainer enough?
A.  It depends entirely on the goal and how the half hour is spent. Thirty focused minutes on two or three lifts with real coaching beats an unfocused hour. For rehabilitation work, complex technique or a session that includes a movement screen and programming discussion, it is tight. Ask a prospective trainer what they would actually do with the time before you decide the length.
### Q. Is it worth paying for a personal trainer?
A.  Sometimes, and sometimes not — only you can run that calculation. It turns on what you are actually buying: technique you cannot self-correct, a program built for your history and constraints, and accountability at a point where you would otherwise stop. Weigh that against your budget, your timeline and how you have done training alone before.
### Q. Should I see a physical therapist or a personal trainer for knee pain?
A.  Pain is the dividing line, so start with a clinician. Both states allow direct access to a physical therapist without a physician referral, subject to limits on how long treatment continues without one, and your insurer may still want that referral before it pays. Once you have restrictions in writing, a trainer can build around them.
### Q. How much is a 1 hour PT session?
A.  Plan on $40 to $120 for an hour of one-on-one training, with the middle of the national market near $55 to $75. Semi-private with two to five people generally runs $20 to $60 a head, which is where most people find the value.
### Q. Is 1 month of personal training enough?
A.  Enough to learn form and build a program you can run yourself, which is a legitimate goal. Not enough to change body composition meaningfully. If budget is the constraint, a month of one-on-one followed by semi-private at $20 to $60 a head is the better structure.

## What You Can Actually Recycle in St. Louis (and Where the Hard Stuff Goes)
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-can-you-recycle-st-louis
Imagine it’s a Saturday morning in Affton and you’re standing over the bin holding a dead drill battery in one hand and a greasy pizza box in the other. Neither one feels obvious. The battery seems like something that ought to be recycled. The box is cardboard, and cardboard is supposed to be the easy one.
Or it’s a garage in Florissant: half a can of deck stain from 2019, four bald tires behind the mower, a tube television nobody has switched on in a decade. Or a condo in Belleville, where the recycling can has to be marked RECYCLE and you’re holding a bag stuffed with other bags.
Here’s the honest version. The answer depends on which side of a city line you’re standing on. Not roughly — literally. Kirkwood, unincorporated St. Louis County and the City of St. Louis run three different systems, and the Illinois side is a fourth.
### What can you actually put in the recycling bin?
Five things, in nearly every program around here: paper and flattened cardboard, plastic bottles and containers, glass bottles and jars, metal food and beverage cans, and food and beverage cartons. The City of St. Louis compresses the rest of the rule into four words — loose, clean and dry. Nothing in a bag.
Clean means rinsed, not scrubbed. Dry means the paper riding next to it still has value at the sorting line. Flatten the cardboard every time.
What are 5 things that cannot be recycled? Plastic bags and film, Styrofoam, food waste, needles and sharps, and one-time-use disposables. Styrofoam is technically recyclable somewhere in the world. There is no local processor for it, so here it is trash.
### Why do the rules change when you cross a city line?
Because curbside recycling here is set by whoever holds the contract, and that is rarely the same body twice. St. Louis County writes a minimum level of service into its waste ordinance — weekly trash, weekly recycling, twice-yearly bulky pickup for one monthly fee — but that floor covers only one- and two-family homes, and the county runs trash districts only in unincorporated areas.
Every municipality inside the county signs its own hauler contract, so Ballwin’s rules belong to Ballwin’s hauler. The City of St. Louis operates its own refuse division. Across the river, Belleville collects weekly in that marked 32-gallon can and takes glass bottles and jars, newspaper, office paper, unwaxed flattened cardboard, aluminum and tin — and no electronics of any kind.
So pull up your own city’s waste page, not a generic one. Two neighbors across a boundary street can both be right and still disagree about a yogurt cup.
### What gets a whole truckload of recycling rejected?
Bagged recyclables, tanglers and food-soaked cardboard, mostly. The local numbers are brutal. From January through May 2025, more than half of everything the City of St. Louis collected from alley recycling dumpsters was rejected at the recycling center for contamination. When the city tested collecting from roll carts and drop-off sites only in July 2025, contamination fell to 25% or less.
That is why alley recycling ended in August 2025 and those blue alley bins became trash dumpsters. Since the change, the city reports contamination down 83% and the tonnage actually recycled up 8%.
What is surprisingly not recyclable? Tanglers, the ones nobody guesses. Garden hose, extension cords, string lights, rope and plastic bags wind around the spinning screens at a sorting facility, and somebody has to climb in with a knife and cut them free. Grease and cheese wreck paper fiber: tear off the clean pizza box lid, trash the soaked bottom. Wishcycling is how a load that would have paid becomes a load somebody pays to bury.
### Is glass still worth recycling in St. Louis?
Yes. The City of St. Louis and Belleville both take glass bottles and jars at the curb. But glass has been the troubled material here for years, and the reason is mechanical rather than moral. In a single-stream truck glass breaks, the shards migrate into paper and plastic, and a bale of paper with glass in it is worth less to a mill.
So a separate channel exists. Ripple Glass — started in Kansas City in 2009 by the owners of Boulevard Brewing, bought by Strategic Materials in 2022 — expanded into St. Louis and runs free purple drop-off bins around the metro, open to anyone. Glass left there is crushed into cullet for manufacturers instead of screened out as residue.
Nothing to do with bins — lawn and garden season arrives sooner than expected.
### Where do old electronics and TVs actually go?
It depends which state you’re in, and the difference is legal rather than cultural. Illinois has banned electronics from landfill disposal since January 1, 2012 under the Electronic Products Recycling and Reuse Act, tightened by the Consumer Electronics Recycling Act in 2017. Televisions, monitors, computers, tablets and printers cannot go in an Illinois trash can at all.
Missouri has no residential landfill ban. The Missouri Department of Natural Resources says plainly that most electronics from a home can legally be thrown away, while recommending you don’t. What Missouri has instead is manufacturer takeback: under the state’s Electronics Scrap Management Rule, computer equipment bought in Missouri after July 1, 2010 carries a recovery plan, and the manufacturer has to collect and recycle it at no cost to a household.
One trap before you drive anywhere: the region’s two permanent household hazardous waste facilities list electronics, televisions and monitors among the things they will not take. E-waste is a separate errand.
### Where does household hazardous waste go in St. Louis?
Two permanent facilities, appointment only, open to residents of St. Louis City, St. Louis County and Jefferson County. The South facility sits at 291 E. Hoffmeister and runs Thursdays and Fridays plus alternating Saturdays. The North facility is at 4100 Seven Hills Drive in Florissant, Wednesdays plus alternating Saturdays. Weekday slots are 8:30 to 11:45 a.m. and 1:00 to 5:20 p.m.
Bring proof of address — a utility bill or your driver’s license. The first 50 pounds are subsidized; past that it runs $1.70 per pound, and latex paint is 50 cents per pound. Saturday dates alternate between the two sites, so book before you load the car. The scheduling line is 314-615-8958.
They accept paints, stains and varnishes, pesticides and herbicides, gasoline, motor oil and filters, antifreeze, transmission fluid, and alkaline and car batteries. They refuse explosives, ammunition, radioactive material, appliances, electronics and medical waste. Waste from a business, church, school or government office isn’t accepted here at all.
### What about paint, tires, mattresses and old appliances?
Latex paint doesn’t have to be an errand. Missouri’s DNR says to open the can, stir in kitty litter, sand, shredded newspaper or a paint hardener, leave the lid off until it dries into a hard crumble, then put it in the household trash. Oil-based paint is flammable in any state and belongs at a hazardous waste facility.
Tires have been banned whole from Missouri landfills since the 1990 law that also banned major appliances, waste oil and lead-acid batteries. The 50-cent fee on every new tire sold in Missouri funds the state cleanup program. A tire shop will take your old ones for roughly $3 to $5 each. Missouri does allow a homeowner to trash a tire cut through the tread or with the sidewalls removed.
Mattresses have no statewide recycling program in Missouri or Illinois, unlike the handful of states that fund one through a purchase fee. A recycling center that takes them charges by the piece, a hauler charges more and comes to you, and a retailer delivering a new set will usually take the old one if you arrange it at purchase.
Refrigerators, freezers and air conditioners have been banned from Missouri landfills since January 1, 1991, and the refrigerant has to be recovered by a certified technician rather than vented. If the unit still runs, Ameren Missouri pays $50 and hauls it away free through its fridge and freezer recycling program.
### Which batteries start fires in garbage trucks?
Lithium-ion. The rechargeable cell inside a laptop, a cordless drill, a phone, a hoverboard, a disposable vape. Crushed in the back of a packer truck or inside a baler, it enters thermal runaway, and that fire feeds itself and shrugs off water. Industry tracking counted 448 publicly reported fires at North American waste and recycling operations in 2025, with roughly $2.5 billion in estimated damage.
So none in the recycling cart, and none in the trash either. Tape the terminals with clear packing tape, bag it on its own, and take it to a hazardous waste facility or a retail battery drop-off. A swollen or damaged cell should go promptly rather than sit in a kitchen drawer.
Car batteries are the older, easier problem. Lead-acid has been banned from Missouri landfills since 1991, and nearly anywhere that sells one takes one back — the core charge on your receipt is the deposit that makes that happen.
### Where do motor oil, propane tanks and old pills go?
Used motor oil is banned from Missouri landfills and is simple to hand off. Most auto parts stores and quick-lube shops accept do-it-yourself oil free, commonly up to five gallons at a time, so long as it hasn’t been mixed with antifreeze, solvent or water. Once it’s mixed it stops being recyclable oil and becomes hazardous waste. Filters can be recycled too, but call ahead.
Propane tanks never go in a cart, a dumpster or a drop-off bin, because nobody downstream can be certain they’re empty. For a standard 20-pound grill tank, the exchange cage at a gas station or hardware store is the industry’s take-back loop: swap it, and the old shell becomes their problem. To be rid of one for good, ask an exchange or refill dealer to retire it. The one-pound camping cylinders are the awkward case.
Leftover medication should not be flushed. Many area police departments run permanent drop boxes, the St. Louis County Police Department keeps collection bins at several sites, and thousands of pharmacies take medication back year round. On the DEA’s April 25, 2026 take-back day, more than 30,000 pounds came in across the 323 collection sites in its St. Louis Field Division.
### What a small business owner learns the first time they price a dumpster
Commercial waste is a contract, not a service the city owes you. A shop signs for a front-load dumpster — nationally, a four-yard container on weekly pickup runs around $110 to $200 a month — and the fine print bites: a one- to three-year term, an annual escalator, and fuel and environmental surcharges outside the quoted rate. A compactor costs real money up front and pays back only above roughly one pickup a week.
Cardboard is the one stream that can pay instead of cost. Baled old corrugated has traded near $100 to $130 a short ton through 2026, under the five-year average around $140 — real money at volume, on a clean bale, with a baler you own. And a Missouri business cannot do what a household can with retired computers: businesses, schools, churches and nonprofits are barred from landfilling certain electronics, and a serialized certificate of destruction settles the customer-data question two years later. Operators who are easy to find locally get the call, and being listed and complete is the cheap half of that.
Related reading: reporting what was dumped and what to do with the old sofa.
Still holding the thing you don’t know what to do with? Browse recycling centers across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then call the closest one and read your item out loud before you load the car.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Does the City of St. Louis still pick up recycling in the alley?
A.  No. The city ended alley recycling in August 2025, after more than half the material collected from alley dumpsters between January and May 2025 was rejected for contamination. Those blue bins are trash dumpsters now. Residents without a roll cart use the city’s single-stream drop-off sites, most open around the clock.
### Q. Where can I take an old TV in the St. Louis area?
A.  Not to a household hazardous waste facility — both permanent sites list televisions and monitors among the items they refuse. In Illinois, televisions have been banned from the trash since 2012, so a certified electronics collector or a county collection event is the route. Missouri has no residential ban, but recyclers and collection events take them, often for a fee on tube sets.
### Q. How much does it cost to drop off hazardous waste in St. Louis?
A.  The first 50 pounds are subsidized for residents of St. Louis County, St. Louis City and Jefferson County. Above that it’s $1.70 per pound, and latex paint runs 50 cents per pound regardless. Appointments are required at both the South facility on E. Hoffmeister and the North facility on Seven Hills Drive, and you’ll need proof of address.
### Q. What do I do with a dead lithium-ion battery?
A.  Tape the terminals with clear packing tape, bag it on its own, and take it to a hazardous waste facility or a retail battery drop-off. Never the recycling cart, never the household trash. Crushed inside a truck or a baler, a lithium cell can go into thermal runaway; there were 448 publicly reported fires at North American waste and recycling operations during 2025.
### Q. Is glass recyclable in St. Louis?
A.  Glass bottles and jars are taken at the curb by the City of St. Louis and by Belleville, though not by every metro program, because broken glass contaminates paper and wears down sorting equipment. Free purple Ripple Glass drop-off bins sit around the region for that reason, and glass left there is crushed into cullet. Window glass, mirrors, ovenware and light bulbs are never accepted.
### Q. What are 5 things that cannot be recycled?
A.  Plastic bags and film, food-soaked cardboard, tanglers like hoses and cords and holiday lights, anything with a lithium-ion battery in it, and household hazardous waste such as paint or motor oil. None of those belong in a curbside cart anywhere in the metro. The last two are not just rejected — they start fires in trucks and at sorting facilities.
### Q. Which items cannot be recycled?
A.  Beyond the obvious five, the routine offenders here are bagged recyclables, greasy pizza boxes, polystyrene foam, disposable cups with a plastic lining, and ceramics or window glass mixed in with bottles. Bagging is the big one locally — more than half of what the City collected from alley dumpsters in early 2025 was rejected for contamination, which is why alley recycling ended that August.
### Q. Do I have to rinse containers before I recycle them?
A.  Rinse, don’t scrub. The standard across metro programs is loose, clean and dry: empty the liquid, get the food residue out, let it dry. A container with real food still in it contaminates the paper riding beside it and can get a whole load downgraded. Pizza boxes are fine if you recycle only the clean top.
### Q. What items can you not recycle?
A.  Anything that contaminates the load: greasy pizza boxes, plastic bags and film, styrofoam, ceramics, garden hose, needles. Contamination is the actual problem here — more than half of what the City collected from January through May 2025 was unusable, and it dropped to 25% or less once collection moved to roll carts and drop-off sites only.
### Q. What are 10 things you can recycle?
A.  Cardboard, paperboard, newspaper, office paper, magazines, aluminum cans, steel cans, plastic bottles and jugs, cartons, and glass bottles and jars — though glass is the one that varies most by municipality. Belleville takes it weekly in the marked 32-gallon can; check your own hauler before assuming.

## St. Louis Gifts That Are Actually From Here: A Local Buying Guide
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/st-louis-gifts-that-are-actually-from-here
Imagine it’s a Thursday night in Affton and your cousin from Denver texts that she’s flying home Sunday. She stayed four days. She ate at three places you love, saw the Arch on a clear morning, and now you want to send her back with something that actually tastes or looks like this place — not a keychain bought at the gate.
Maybe your version is different. Maybe you moved to Florissant last year and your mother in Ohio still asks what the big deal is about this city. Maybe you’re in St. Charles assembling twelve client gifts with a $40-a-head budget and a hard deadline. Maybe you’re in Belleville, on the Illinois side, and half of what you’d love to send is sitting in a freezer case across the river.
Here’s the good part. For a metro this size, St. Louis has an unusual number of things that exist nowhere else. Here’s the catch. A couple of the famous ones are harder to ship than they look, and several of the origin stories everybody repeats have never been proven.
### What makes a gift genuinely St. Louis?
A gift is genuinely from St. Louis if it was invented here, is still made here, or can’t easily be bought anywhere else. That filter leaves three categories: a regional food that started in this metro, an object made by somebody who lives here, and merchandise from an institution that belongs to the city.
The second question is logistics, and it decides more than taste does. Anything that has to stay below freezing costs more to move than to buy. Anything going out in a box of twelve has to be identical, shelf-stable and alcohol-free. Sort by recipient and distance first.
### Which St. Louis foods really started here, and which origin stories are disputed?
What is a must eat in St. Louis? The same three names come back. Gooey butter cake, toasted ravioli and Provel all began in this metro, and the first two carry origin stories told as settled fact that aren’t. The cake came out of a south city German-American bakery in the 1930s or 1940s, most accounts agreeing it was an accident with the wrong proportions in a coffee cake batter. Who did it first is unresolved: one family account credits Johnny Hoffman of St. Louis Pastries and Herman Danzer of Danzer’s Bakery, another credits John Koppe of Koppe Bakery at California and Arsenal in the early 1940s. Give the cake, then tell the argument.
Toasted ravioli is the same shape of dispute. Three legacy restaurants on The Hill claim it, and the two loudest claims describe the same accident — a cook dropping ravioli into hot oil instead of boiling water. The strongest paper trail belongs to the restaurant then called Oldani’s, now Mama’s on the Hill, which advertised toasted ravioli in the St. Louis Star and Times in 1943, four years before the restaurant now known as Charlie Gitto’s opened as Angelo’s. A third claim points to a 1930s menu with no hard evidence behind the date.
Provel is the item nobody outside this market can substitute. It’s a processed blend of cheddar, Swiss and provolone engineered to melt fast and break cleanly on St. Louis-style pizza. Hoffman Dairy filed the trademark application on June 20, 1947 and the registration came in 1950, and one company has made it ever since, the mark passing through Kraft and on to Lactalis in 2021. Sold outside the region it legally cannot use the Provel name — it goes out labeled St. Louis-style cheese. A brick of it in a cooler is a real souvenir.
### What ships well, and what really doesn’t?
Shelf-stable ships. Frozen costs more than the gift. Ted Drewes publishes its own numbers and they make the case better than any warning could: shipping averages $120 to $200 per package, UPS Overnight, orders leaving Monday through Thursday, a standard cooler holding fifteen 8-ounce concretes or eight pints, orders placed by phone at least 48 hours ahead, and no shipping within St. Louis at all. Kansas City and Chicago addresses can use ground for less. Magnificent for a homesick sister in Seattle. Odd for a coworker in Ballwin.
The categories that travel without drama: chips, coffee beans, cake mixes, sauces and spice blends, books, prints, glassware and team merchandise. If you do send something cold, know the rule — USPS Publication 52 permits dry ice in the mail only in a container that vents the carbon dioxide gas, so a sealed cooler is neither legal nor safe, and perishables move at the mailer’s risk, only if they can arrive in good condition within normal transit time.
Two local snack names carry real history and both survive a checked bag. Old Vienna started here in 1936 and its Red Hot Riplets arrived in the late 1970s; the brand is still headquartered in St. Louis, though it stopped producing at its own city plant in the 1980s. The chips now sold as The G.O.A.T. Brand began in 2002 as a side dish at a Vandeventer Avenue restaurant, proved more popular than the menu, and went full-time in 2009.
Off-topic entirely — local clothing shops solve a different gift problem.
### Can you ship Missouri wine to an Illinois address?
Yes, if the winery holds both licenses, and the two states set different ceilings. A Missouri winery needs a Missouri wine direct shipper license, which costs nothing and expires every June 30, and it may ship no more than two cases a month to any one consumer, each case nine liters or less. To reach an Illinois address that same winery also needs an Illinois winery shipper’s license and must register with the Illinois Department of Revenue; Illinois then permits up to twelve cases per adult resident per year. Your aunt in Edwardsville can receive it — but the winery has to be the shipper, not you.
It helps to know what you’re sending. Augusta, roughly 30 miles west of downtown, became the first American Viticultural Area in the United States on June 20, 1980, ahead of Napa Valley, designated in February 1981. Norton is Missouri’s official state grape, and before Prohibition Missouri was the second-largest wine-producing state in the country. A bottle of Norton with those sentences on the tag beats a pricier bottle with nothing on it.
### Which museum and institution shops are worth the stop?
Institution shops are the low-risk option because somebody already curated them and the money goes back into the place. The Arch Store sits inside the Gateway Arch Visitor Center just past the museum, operated by Jefferson National Parks Association, a nonprofit park partner, with proceeds supporting educational programs, exhibits and public events at the park. The monument is the story you’re buying: 630 feet tall, topped out October 28, 1965, redesignated Gateway Arch National Park in 2018, the newest and smallest in the system.
In Forest Park, the Missouri History Museum opened a shop in February 2024 stocked with goods from more than 100 local businesses — a shortcut when you want several makers in one trip. The Saint Louis Art Museum runs two shops carrying art glass, jewelry, books, posters and toys. City Museum sells its own particular merchandise from the old title company facade it occupies. The Missouri Botanical Garden’s shop leans toward plants, seeds and garden goods.
### When are the local maker markets?
The Best of Missouri Market at the Missouri Botanical Garden runs October 9 through 11, 2026, from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. each day, with a members-only shopping hour Saturday from 8 to 9 a.m. and more than 150 Missouri food producers and crafters selling handmade goods, baked items, native plants, wine and jewelry. For this errand it is the most efficient weekend on the calendar.
After that the metro’s holiday craft fairs, church bazaars and neighborhood markets run from early November into mid-December on both sides of the river, and their dates move every year — confirm before you drive across the county. Small Business Saturday, launched by American Express in 2010, lands on November 28 in 2026, and independent shops here build the whole weekend around it.
### What should you buy for each kind of person?
What’s a good souvenir from St. Louis? Match the gift to the distance. For a visitor flying out tomorrow, buy flat and shelf-stable: chips, a bag of beans roasted here this week, a cake mix, a print, a book about the Arch. For someone who moved away, buy what they can’t get where they live now — the frozen and refrigerated column, shipped cold or handed over at Thanksgiving. For a homesick relative, brand loyalty beats quality; nostalgia does not accept substitutions, so buy the exact one they remember.
Corporate gifting is its own puzzle. Twelve to fifty identical gifts rules out alcohol, with its licensing and age-verification problems, rules out frozen, because somebody will be out that week, and rules out anything needing a size. Shelf-stable local food in a plain box clears all three. Ask in September and a local maker will usually run the quantity.
### What the gift trade looks like from behind the counter
The math starts at keystone — buy wholesale, double it, and that 100% markup is still only a 50% margin. Independent gift shops generally run a blended 50% to 55%, with candles, cards and small impulse goods at 60% or better and home decor closer to 45%. Rent, payroll and card fees come out of that half. Then the calendar does the rest. November and December have averaged about 19% of all U.S. retail sales over the last five years (National Retail Federation), and for a gift shop the share runs far higher, which is why a slow October is frightening and why a dated ornament is worth almost nothing on December 26. Consignment with local makers, commonly 60/40 in the maker’s favor, is how a small shop carries inventory it can’t afford to buy outright. With e-commerce at 16.9% of retail sales in the first quarter of 2026 (U.S. Census Bureau), the shop that turns up in a local search is the one found after the visitor goes home — the whole job of a complete listing.

Still need something that actually came from here? Browse gift shops across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then call the closest one and ask which local makers they carry — that answer tells you everything.
### Frequently asked questions
### Q. Is St. Louis famous for anything?
A.  The Gateway Arch, and three foods this metro invented. Gooey butter cake, toasted ravioli and Provel cheese are the three with the strongest local claim, all traced to the 1930s and 1940s. Provel has the cleanest documentation, since Hoffman Dairy filed its trademark application on June 20, 1947 and registered the mark in 1950. The other two are contested between competing families and restaurants, and no single claim has ever been proven.
### Q. Can you ship Ted Drewes frozen custard?
A.  Yes, anywhere in the continental United States except within St. Louis itself. Orders go by phone at least 48 hours ahead, leave Monday through Thursday, and travel UPS Overnight at an average of $120 to $200 per package, though Kansas City and Chicago addresses can use ground for a lower rate. One standard cooler holds fifteen 8-ounce concretes or eight pints. Local buyers use pickup or grocery partners instead.
### Q. What is Provel cheese and can you buy it outside St. Louis?
A.  Provel is a processed blend of cheddar, Swiss and provolone made to melt fast and break cleanly, developed for St. Louis-style pizza in the 1940s. One company has held the trademark since 1950. You can find it in other markets, but not under that name — outside the region it must be labeled St. Louis-style cheese, which is why people haul it home in coolers.
### Q. Who invented gooey butter cake?
A.  Nobody knows, and anyone who tells you otherwise is repeating one family’s version. The dessert came from a south city German-American bakery in the 1930s or 1940s, apparently by mistake. One account names Johnny Hoffman of St. Louis Pastries with Herman Danzer of Danzer’s Bakery; another names John Koppe of Koppe Bakery at California and Arsenal in the early 1940s. Both are family recollections, not records.
### Q. Can a Missouri winery ship wine to an Illinois address?
A.  Only with an Illinois winery shipper’s license and registration with the Illinois Department of Revenue, on top of its Missouri wine direct shipper license. The limits differ by state: Missouri caps shipments at two nine-liter cases per month to one consumer, while Illinois allows up to twelve cases per adult resident per year. The winery must do the shipping, so order from the winery directly.
### Q. What are some good souvenir shops in St. Louis?
A.  Three routes work. Institution shops curate local goods year-round — the Arch Store, the two Saint Louis Art Museum shops, City Museum — and the Missouri History Museum shop opened in February 2024 carrying items from more than 100 local businesses. Markets concentrate the makers, with the Best of Missouri Market drawing more than 150 vendors to the Missouri Botanical Garden October 9 through 11, 2026. Neighborhood shops carry makers on consignment all year.
### Q. What candy is St. Louis known for?
A.  Gooey butter cake is the sweet the city actually claims, though it travels badly. For something that survives a suitcase, look to local roasters and confectioners rather than airport shelves — the gift that reads as from here is the one made here.
### Q. What is a must eat in St. Louis?
A.  Toasted ravioli, gooey butter cake, and a concrete from a frozen custard stand. Ted Drewes ships, and publishes its own shipping figures — worth checking before you try to carry frozen custard home in a bag.

## What Home Health Care Costs in St. Louis, and What Medicare Actually Pays
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/home-health-care-cost-st-louis

Imagine it’s a Thursday in February and the hip replacement went fine — the surgery, anyway. A discharge planner hands your mother a printed list of home health agencies, says somebody will call within 48 hours, and moves on to the next room. You nod like you understood. You did not understand.

By dinner there are three opinions in the family thread. Your brother in Florissant is certain Medicare covers all of it. An aunt in Belleville swears her neighbor pays somebody $30 an hour, cash, and has for two years. A friend from church in Affton says you should be touring nursing homes instead, and says it in the voice people use when they think you’re avoiding something.

None of them are wrong, exactly. They’re answering different questions. Two completely different products get called home care around here, they’re paid for in ways that have nothing to do with each other, and once you can tell them apart the money turns into arithmetic. Not cheap arithmetic. But arithmetic.

### Is home health care cheaper than a nursing home?

Usually yes, right up until the hours pile up. Medicare-covered home health costs you nothing. Paid hourly help runs a national median of $35 an hour and a semi-private nursing home room runs $315 a day, both from the CareScout Cost of Care Survey fielded July through November 2025. Divide one into the other: about nine hours a day.

That’s the crossover, and it’s the only number in this article worth writing on the fridge. Under roughly nine hours of paid help a day, home is cheaper. Over it, the facility usually wins on price, because $315 a day also buys the building, the meals, the laundry and awake staff at 3 a.m. A private room ran $355 a day in that same survey, which works out to about ten hours.

Most families never get near that line. Four hours on weekday mornings is the common shape in Kirkwood, in Maryland Heights, everywhere — roughly $3,000 a month at the national median. The trap is treating the two numbers as alternatives. They usually run at once: Medicare pays a nurse and a therapist for a few weeks after surgery, and the family pays separately for the hours in between when somebody simply needs to be there.

### What are the two types of home care?

Skilled home health, and non-medical home care. Missouri’s Department of Health and Senior Services draws the line cleanly in its own HCBS FAQ: home health is doctor-ordered care after a sudden illness or injury, short-term, paid by Medicare or private insurance. Ongoing hands-on help with bathing and dressing is a separate program with entirely different money behind it.

Skilled means a licensed clinician — a nurse, a physical or occupational therapist, a speech-language pathologist, a medical social worker. Non-medical means an aide or attendant: bathing, dressing, meals, laundry, rides, company. The second one is what most people picture when they say home care, and it’s the one Medicare will not buy for you on its own.

Illinois is stricter about naming the difference. IDPH licenses three separate things — home health agencies, home nursing agencies, and home services agencies — and its description of that third category is blunt: home services are not medical. Missouri licenses home health and hospice through the DHSS Bureau of Home Care and Rehabilitative Standards. Either way, ask a company directly which license it holds before you ask what it charges.

### Does Medicare pay for in-home care in Missouri?

Yes, for the skilled kind, and the rules are identical in Illinois because this is a federal benefit rather than a state one. You pay $0 for covered home health services. The only routine out-of-pocket piece is durable medical equipment — a walker, a hospital bed — where you pay 20% of the Medicare-approved amount after the Part B deductible, $283 in 2026.

What the benefit buys, per Medicare’s own coverage page: part-time or intermittent skilled nursing, physical and occupational therapy, speech-language pathology, medical social services, and a home health aide — but only while a skilled service is also going on. What it will not buy, in Medicare’s words: 24-hour-a-day care at home, home meal delivery, homemaker services unrelated to the care plan, and custodial help with bathing or dressing when that is the only care needed.

There’s a ceiling almost nobody hears about until week two. Part-time or intermittent generally means up to 8 hours a day combined and no more than 28 hours a week, stretching to 35 briefly if the provider documents the need. If your father needs somebody in the house all day, Medicare is not the program that solves that, and no amount of arguing with the agency changes it.

Wildly off-topic — after a week like this, somebody should order pizza.

### Who qualifies for home health care services in Missouri?

Two tests, both federal. You have to need part-time or intermittent skilled care, and you have to be homebound — leaving takes a major, taxing effort, or help from a person, cane, walker or wheelchair. Homebound is not housebound: medical appointments, religious services, a haircut and adult day care are all specifically allowed. A provider has to see the patient face-to-face and order the care, and a Medicare-certified agency has to deliver it.

Medicaid is the other door, and it runs on the opposite logic. Missouri’s Home and Community-Based Services program requires you to be 18 or older, enrolled in MO HealthNet, and assessed at home as needing a nursing facility level of care — and the state says plainly that you do not have to be homebound. HCBS exists to keep people out in the community, not parked at home.

Illinois runs its own version through the Department on Aging. The Community Care Program, created in 1979, is open at 60 and older to Illinois residents with non-exempt assets of $17,500 or less — house, car and furnishings don’t count — who screen as at risk of nursing facility placement on the Determination of Need assessment and who enroll in Medicaid. The state Senior HelpLine, 1-800-252-8966, is the front door on that side of the river.

### What happens if an elderly person can’t afford a nursing home?

Medicaid pays. That’s the real answer, and it’s the answer for a large share of the people in nursing homes right now. The sequence is what families get wrong: qualify for Medicaid first, then the long-term care benefit follows. On the in-home side Missouri adds a useful wrinkle — the state notes that people approved for Home and Community-Based Services are not required to spend down their MO HealthNet coverage.

There is a limit on the home side, and it’s honest about what it is. Missouri caps the monthly value of an HCBS care plan — the cost maximum — using the monthly cost of caring for someone in a skilled nursing facility as the guide. Past that point the arithmetic itself pushes toward the facility, which is exactly what the cap is built to do.

One more thing worth knowing before somebody quits a job. Under Missouri’s Consumer Directed Services model you select, hire, train and supervise your own attendant, and you may hire anyone except a legal spouse or guardian — so an adult child can be the paid caregiver. Under the agency model the caregiver cannot be an immediate family member. Same program, two very different family conversations. Every caregiver clears a background check either way.

### How do you check an agency before you hand somebody a key?

Start with the star rating, because it’s free and it moves. Every Medicare-certified agency carries a quality of patient care star rating on Care Compare, and the spread inside a single ZIP code is wider than people expect. In the CMS provider data released July 15, 2026, 29 certified agencies serve ZIP 63109 in south St. Louis, rated from 1.5 stars to 4.5 — fourteen at 4 or better, four below 3. Same neighborhood, same benefit, very different agencies.

Geography matters more than it should. That same file shows 30 agencies serving Florissant’s 63033 and 27 serving 63301 in St. Charles, but only 14 serving 62220 in Belleville and 14 in Edwardsville’s 62025. A Metro East family is choosing from roughly half the menu, which is worth knowing before you wave off the first agency that calls.

Then check the license and the person. Missouri publishes a directory of licensed and certified home health providers, including which counties each agency serves — and read the two lists carefully, because an agency that is licensed only, without Medicare certification, cannot bill Medicare for your mother’s visits. Missouri’s Family Care Safety Registry, running since 2001, requires elder-care and personal-care workers to register within 15 days of hire and lets an employer pull a background screening. Illinois keeps the parallel record in its Health Care Worker Registry, which shows CNA training and any administrative findings of abuse or neglect.

If that hospital discharge also left the family without a regular physician to manage the follow-up, handle that early rather than at the next crisis — our guide to finding a primary care doctor in St. Louis covers the part where you actually get an appointment.

### What this trade looks like from the other side of the counter

Owners already know the strangest part. Medicare has paid home health in 30-day periods since PDGM took effect on January 1, 2020, not per visit, so the schedule is the margin — and a period that lands under its LUPA visit threshold drops to per-visit pay. For 2026 CMS finalized a 2.4% payment update, then offset it: its own estimate has payments to home health agencies falling about 1.3%, or $220 million, against 2025. Illinois agencies also carry pre-claim review paperwork under the Review Choice Demonstration; Missouri agencies don’t. On the private-pay side the hourly rate looks generous until you subtract the wage, payroll taxes, workers’ comp, screening and the hours nobody bills: drive time, the 6 a.m. call-out, the door that doesn’t open. The phone rings on somebody else’s schedule too — a winter fall, a Friday discharge, the July visit that ends in a Monday call.

Nobody shops for this in advance, so being listed and complete where neighbors search is most of how that Monday call finds you.

Not sure who to call first? Browse home health care across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then pull each agency’s star rating on Care Compare before you agree to the first assessment. Stocking a kitchen for someone who is home all day is its own errand, and so is the other end of it — what an independent bottle shop can do that a big aisle cannot.

### Frequently asked questions

### Q. Does Medicare pay for homecare for seniors?

A.  It pays for the skilled kind — nursing, physical or occupational therapy, speech therapy, medical social work — when a provider certifies that the person is homebound and needs part-time or intermittent skilled care. It does not pay for help with bathing, dressing or meals when that is the only care needed, and it never covers 24-hour care, meal delivery or housekeeping unrelated to the care plan.

### Q. How much will Medicare pay for home health?

A.  All of it, for covered services: your share is $0, paid straight to the certified agency. There is no cap on the number of visits as long as you still qualify and a provider keeps certifying the plan. The one regular out-of-pocket cost is durable medical equipment — 20% of the Medicare-approved amount once you’ve met the 2026 Part B deductible of $283.

### Q. Who qualifies for home health care services in Missouri?

A.  Anyone on Medicare who is homebound, needs part-time or intermittent skilled care, has had a face-to-face visit with a provider who orders the care, and uses a Medicare-certified agency. Leaving home for medical treatment, church, a haircut or adult day care doesn’t disqualify anyone. Illinois applies the identical test, because the benefit is federal rather than state-run.

### Q. How to qualify for home health care in Missouri?

A.  Ask the treating provider for a home health order at the appointment or the discharge — that’s the step families skip, and no agency can start without it. The agency then does its own assessment in the home. For ongoing non-medical help the path is Medicaid instead: enroll in MO HealthNet, then request an in-home assessment through the state’s HCBS program.

### Q. Can a family member be paid to provide the care?

A.  In Missouri, yes — under the Consumer Directed Services model you hire and supervise your own attendant and may hire anyone except a legal spouse or guardian. Under the agency model the caregiver cannot be an immediate family member. Both routes run through Medicaid rather than Medicare, and every caregiver has to clear a background check.

### Q. Does a Medicare Advantage plan cover home health the same way?

A.  The benefit exists, but the plumbing differs. Networks, prior authorization and which agencies you may use are set by the plan, while Original Medicare lets you pick any certified agency serving your ZIP. Medicare’s own guidance is to check with the plan. Call the number on the card before the first visit and ask what authorization it wants.

### Q. How do I tell whether an agency is any good?

A.  Read the quality of patient care star rating on Medicare’s Care Compare, then check the state record. Missouri publishes which agencies are licensed and which are also Medicare-certified, plus the counties each serves. Illinois licenses home health, home nursing and non-medical home services agencies separately, so confirm the company holds the license that matches the help you actually want.

## How to Find a Good Bakery in St. Louis (and What to Order)
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-find-a-good-bakery-in-st-louis

Imagine it’s a Thursday in October and you volunteered, three weeks ago, to bring dessert for fourteen people to a party in Maryland Heights on Saturday. You live in Kirkwood. You have not thought about it once since. Now it’s 8 p.m., you’re scrolling a phone in your own kitchen, and every result on the screen looks exactly like every other result.

Maybe your version is different. Maybe it’s a first birthday in Florissant and one of the kids has a sesame allergy, so you need a real answer and not a shrug. Maybe you moved to St. Charles and still have not figured out where bread comes from here. Maybe you’re in Belleville, on the Illinois side, and half the places people rave about are twenty-five minutes and one river away.

Here’s the good part. For its size, this metro has an unusual number of bakeries that still mix and bake on site, on both sides of the Mississippi, plus one dessert the city genuinely invented. Here’s the catch. Plenty of what sits in a bakery case arrived frozen and got warmed up out back, and nothing on the sign says which is which. Two questions separate them.

How do I find a good bakery?
