Ask two questions before you buy anything: what did you bake here this morning, and what comes in frozen? A shop that bakes on site answers both without flinching. Then judge one plain item — a cake donut, a croissant, a loaf of white bread. Plain things have nowhere to hide, and frosting covers a multitude of sins.

### How do you judge a bakery before you spend real money?

Buy one plain thing first. A cake donut, a butter croissant, a plain loaf. If those are good, the decorated stuff usually is too, because plain items expose flour, fat, proof time and oven discipline with nothing to hide behind. A gorgeous cake with a dry crumb is a decorating shop. That is a real trade, and it is not the same trade.

The second tell is the case at closing. A shop baking small batches for same-day sale runs low late in the day and says so. A case that looks identical at 8 a.m. and 5 p.m. is usually holding long-shelf-life product. So ask about the oven, plainly: baked here, or baked off from frozen? Par-baked programs are everywhere in retail food and are not a scandal, and a good counter person answers in one sentence.

You can also check the public record before you drive anywhere. The City of St. Louis publishes food inspection reports through its online lookup for inspections issued after May 10, 2012, covering restaurants, grocers, caterers and bakeries alike (City of St. Louis Department of Health). St. Louis County posts its own reports through the Department of Public Health (St. Louis County). Illinois-side inspections run through county health departments. One violation on one visit means little; a pattern means something.

### What kinds of bakeries does the St. Louis metro actually have?

Six kinds, and picking the right kind matters more than picking the right name. People type “What is the best bakery in St. Louis?” into a phone and get a list that flattens six different businesses into one column.

Scratch retail bakeries mix, proof and bake on site and sell over a counter. Bread, morning pastry, cookies, and cakes made to order. Italian bakeries are their own tradition here, concentrated in and around The Hill, a fifty-two square block neighborhood on the near south side settled by northern Italian and Sicilian families starting in the 1880s, drawn by the clay mines and firebrick foundries (Hill 2000 Neighborhood Association). Bakers and grocers followed the families, and the neighborhood still supports bakeries, Italian grocers and a gelato shop inside a walkable grid.

Donut shops are a fry operation, not an oven operation, and they run on a clock. Raised donuts are proofed and fried in the small hours; cake donuts hold a little longer but not much. Anyone asking “Where can I find the best donuts in St. Louis?” is really asking a timing question. The best donut at 6:30 a.m. and the best one at 2 p.m. are often not the same shop.

Custom cake decorators may work from a licensed kitchen, a shared commissary, or a registered home kitchen. Wholesale bakeries supply restaurants and grocers and sometimes sell retail out a side door on short hours. In-store grocery bakeries are convenience plays — long hours, broad selection, a lot of frozen dough. All six are legitimate answers to different questions.

### What cake is famous in St. Louis, and what should you actually order?

Gooey butter cake. Ask “What dessert is St. Louis famous for?” anywhere in the metro and you get one answer, and it is the rare local claim that holds up: the cake was invented here. The common account traces it to a south city German-American bakery in the 1930s, where a baker reversed proportions in a coffee cake batter and sold the mistake by the square rather than throw it out. Which bakery, and which baker, has never been settled — several families claim it, local accounts contradict each other, and anyone who tells you the case is closed is repeating a family story rather than a documented fact.

Ordering it is where people go wrong, because two desserts share the name. The bakery version is yeast-raised: a soft dough base under a dense, barely-set butter and sugar layer, baked flat and dusted with powdered sugar. The home version, usually called ooey gooey butter cake, starts from a cake mix with a cream cheese and egg topping, and eats denser and sweeter, more like a bar. Both are good, and they are not substitutes. Say which one you want when you call.

Wildly off-topic — the metro’s coffee shops are their own rabbit hole.

### How far ahead should you order a cake?

For a standard decorated cake, plan on three to seven days at a small shop, and expect that number to double or disappear entirely around holidays. Thanksgiving, Christmas, Easter and Mother’s Day are the four walls of the retail bakery year, and most shops close custom order books days or weeks ahead of each. Wedding and graduation season stacks on from May through October. A Tuesday in February is easy. The Saturday before Easter is not.

Settle six things on the ticket rather than in someone’s memory: servings (not inches — ask how many people it feeds), flavor and filling, any allergen restriction, the pickup window, the deposit, and the cancellation terms. Deposits on custom work are usually non-refundable inside a few days, because the shop has already bought ingredients and blocked labor for you. That is fair. Just know it before you pay.

### What can a bakery tell you about allergens?

Federal labeling law recognizes nine major food allergens, and sesame became the ninth on January 1, 2023 under the FASTER Act, joining milk, eggs, fish, crustacean shellfish, tree nuts, peanuts, wheat and soybeans (U.S. Food & Drug Administration). Those rules govern packaged food labels. An unwrapped item handed to you out of a display case is not carrying that label, which is exactly why the conversation at the counter matters.

Ask two things instead of one. First, what is in it. Second, what else runs through the same mixer, sheeter, fryer and racks. Cross-contact, not the ingredient list, is what catches families out in a small kitchen where one bench does everything. A good shop will say flatly that it cannot promise a peanut-free or wheat-free product, and that honesty beats a reassuring answer. For a severe allergy, look for a dedicated facility, not a careful one.

### Missouri or Illinois: how the rules differ on your side of the river

Home bakers are regulated very differently in the two states, and the metro straddles the line. In Missouri, a cottage food operation sells baked goods — cookies, cakes, breads, pastries, pies — directly to consumers with no permit and no routine inspection, and state law says such an operation is not a food service establishment under the state food code. Labels must carry the operation’s name and address plus a statement that the food was not inspected, and internet sales require both seller and buyer to be in Missouri (Missouri Revised Statutes 196.298).

Illinois runs the other way. Under the Home-to-Market Act, effective January 1, 2022, a cottage food operator must register with the local health department where the kitchen sits, and the person preparing or packaging the food must hold an ANSI-accredited Certified Food Protection Manager certificate. Local health departments may charge a registration fee up to $50 (University of Illinois Extension). So the Belleville home baker cleared a bar the Affton home baker never had to.

Sales tax splits too. Missouri taxes qualifying food at a reduced state rate of 1.225% instead of 4.225%, and bakery items count even when still warm from the oven — though the reduced rate does not apply where more than 80% of an establishment’s gross receipts come from food prepared for immediate consumption (Missouri Department of Revenue). Illinois ended its 1% state grocery tax on January 1, 2026, and let municipalities and counties impose a local grocery tax of exactly 1% by ordinance — more than 600 filed to do so (Illinois Department of Revenue). Prepared food is taxed higher in both states.

### What bakery owners wish more customers understood

The hardest math in this trade is shrink. Bread and pastry are worth full price for one day, half price the next, and nothing after that, so every morning a baker is guessing the day’s demand and eating the difference. Custom cakes carry the margin; the case out front is often closer to a loss leader that pays for foot traffic. Four holidays and wedding season carry the year, January is the dead month, and wholesale accounts are what keep the ovens paying rent in between. The tax line matters more than customers realize: a Missouri shop that adds too many tables and sells too much coffee can cross that 80% threshold and lose the reduced food rate on everything. And every owner in the metro has watched an unlicensed kitchen undercut their price on a birthday cake. What they mostly want is to be findable when someone types a search at 8 p.m. — which is what a complete, current listing in a local business directory is for.

Need a bakery that actually bakes what it sells? Browse bakeries across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then call the two closest and ask what came out of their oven before 7 a.m. That one question sorts the list faster than any ranking will.

Related reading: if the party needs more than dessert, the region’s wineries within an easy drive are worth a look.

### Frequently asked questions

### Q. What is the best bakery in St. Louis?

A.  There isn’t one answer, because bakeries specialize. The shop with the best crusty bread rarely has the best buttercream, and neither is the best donut. Decide what you actually need — bread, morning pastry, a decorated cake, a specific baking tradition — then find the shop that treats that item as its main business rather than a sideline.

### Q. How do I find a good bakery?

A.  Ask what was baked on site this morning and what arrives frozen, then buy one plain item and taste it. A plain croissant, cake donut or white loaf shows you flour, fat and technique with nothing to hide behind. Look at the case near closing time, too. Small-batch shops run low late in the day, and that is a good sign rather than a bad one.

### Q. What cake is famous in St. Louis?

A.  Gooey butter cake, and it really did start here. The usual account puts it in a south city German-American bakery in the 1930s, where reversed proportions in a coffee cake batter produced a flat, dense, sweet layer a baker sold by the square instead of throwing away. Several families claim the invention and none has been proven, so treat the specific origin story as folklore.

### Q. What is the best butter cake in St. Louis?

A.  It depends which cake you mean, and that decides more than any ranking. The yeast-raised bakery version has a soft dough base under a barely-set butter and sugar layer. The cream cheese version, usually called ooey gooey, is denser and sweeter and eats like a bar. Buy a small piece of each from two shops before committing to a party quantity.

### Q. Is there a bakery on the Hill in Saint Louis, MO?

A.  Yes. The Hill is a fifty-two square block neighborhood on the near south side, settled from the 1880s by northern Italian and Sicilian families who came for the clay mines and firebrick foundries, and bakers followed the families in. The neighborhood still supports bakeries, Italian grocers and a gelato shop inside a walkable grid, so it is a browse-on-foot trip rather than a single-destination one.

### Q. Where can I find the best donuts in St. Louis?

A.  Whichever shop near you fries earliest and sells out fastest. Donuts are a timing product, not a shelf product: raised donuts are fried in the small hours and decline within hours, while cake donuts hold slightly longer. Go early on a weekend, and treat a shop picked over by nine as a recommendation rather than a disappointment.

### Q. What dessert is St. Louis famous for?

A.  Gooey butter cake first, frozen custard second. The cake is the one this metro invented, in the 1930s, and bakeries on both sides of the river still make it. Frozen custard — denser than ice cream thanks to egg yolk and low overrun — is the summer counterpart, and the concrete, thick enough to hold a spoon upside down, is a local serving style.

## How to Choose a Staffing Agency in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-choose-a-staffing-agency-in-st-louis

Imagine it’s a Tuesday morning and the job you held for six years ended on Friday. You’re at a kitchen table in Florissant with coffee going cold and forty browser tabs open. Two are job boards. Three are the same warehouse job posted by three companies you’ve never heard of. One wants your Social Security number before it will tell you the pay rate.

Maybe you’re on the other side of the desk. You run a small operation in Maryland Heights, you need two people who can pass a background check and clock in at six, and your last three hires off a job board lasted a combined nine days. Or you’re in Kirkwood, comfortable, and a recruiter messaged you Sunday night about a role in Earth City that pays more than you make now.

Everybody ends up in the same spot: searching for an employment agency and getting a wall of names, Affton to Belleville to St. Charles, that look identical from outside. Some will change your year. Some will take your resume, drop it in a database, and never call. Here’s how to tell them apart before you burn a month.

Is it worth it to go to an employment agency? For most people, yes — as a second channel, not the only one. An agency earns your time when it staffs the specific work you do, names the client and the pay rate before it sends you, and pays you as its own W-2 employee. It is not worth your time if it asks you for money.

### Is it worth going through an employment agency in the St. Louis metro?

It’s worth it when the agency genuinely specializes in your line of work, and mostly a waste when it doesn’t. Staffing runs on standing relationships with a fixed set of client companies. A firm that fills light-industrial roles in Earth City and Granite City cannot help a controller, and an accounting recruiter cannot get you on a forklift Monday.

The scale is bigger than most people assume. The American Staffing Association reports that nearly 2.2 million temporary and contract employees worked for U.S. staffing companies during an average week in 2024, and that staffing companies hired 12.7 million temporary and contract employees over the course of 2023. This is not part-time filler: 73% of staffing employees work full time, near the 75% figure for the workforce overall. And 64% say they took the assignment to fill a gap between jobs or to help land one (American Staffing Association).

Local pay context helps you judge an offer. The Missouri Economic Research and Information Center puts the average annual wage across all occupations in the St. Louis region at $64,828 in 2024 (MERIC). An agency pitching far under the going rate for your skill usually means the wrong desk.

### Temp, temp-to-hire and direct placement are three different products

Ask which one you’re being offered before anything else, because the three behave nothing alike. In temp work, the agency is your legal employer. It runs payroll, withholds taxes, carries workers’ compensation, and bills the client an hourly rate above what it pays you. The assignment ends when the client says it ends.

In temp-to-hire, you work a defined stretch on the agency’s payroll and the client can convert you to its own employee, usually paying a conversion fee that shrinks the longer you’ve worked. It’s the most common path into a manufacturing, distribution or clerical job here. Ask how many hours until conversion, what the conversion pay is, and how many people that client converted last year.

In direct placement, the agency recruits you and the client hires you outright from day one. You never appear on the agency’s payroll, and the employer pays a placement fee commonly quoted as a percentage of first-year base salary. If someone stays vague about which of the three you’re signing up for, the vagueness is the answer.

### Who pays the agency, and when to walk away

In legitimate staffing, the employer pays and the worker does not. That is the cleanest single test you can apply. If a firm wants money from you to see listings, to be “added to the network,” or to have your resume rewritten before it will submit you, stop and check its license before you hand over a dollar.

Illinois regulates this directly. The Illinois Department of Labor licenses and investigates private employment agencies and employment counselors under the Private Employment Agency Act, 225 ILCS 515, specifically to protect job seekers (Illinois DOL). If you’re dealing with an office in Belleville or Edwardsville and something feels wrong, there is a state agency whose job that is.

The rest of the red flags are simpler. A real agency names the client before it sends you, or explains why it can’t. It tells you the pay rate up front. It never asks for bank details in a first text message.

Unrelated, and we know it — someday you’ll need a plumber fast.

### Missouri and Illinois regulate staffing very differently

This metro straddles a real legal line, and it shows up most in temp work. Illinois runs two separate regimes; Missouri runs neither. Missouri repealed its employment agency chapter — Chapter 289, RSMo was struck by 1999 House Bill 343, effective August 28, 1999 — and staffing agencies are not licensed at the state level there today.

Illinois requires day and temporary labor service agencies to register with the state under the Day and Temporary Labor Services Act, 820 ILCS 175. Annual registration runs $3,000 per agency plus $750 for each branch office, and an unregistered agency faces $500 for each day it operates. Third-party clients carry their own duty: they must verify the agency’s registration and re-verify it on March 1 and September 1 every year (Illinois DOL).

Memorize the worker-side protections if you take Illinois assignments. Agencies must provide general safety training at no cost and pay you for that time. Before dispatch they must give written notice of any strike, lockout or labor dispute at the work site, and you may refuse that assignment without penalty. They cannot charge you for transportation to a job site or dictate where you cash your check. And a laborer assigned to the same client for more than 720 hours within a 12-month period must be paid at least the straight-time hourly rate of the lowest-paid directly hired comparator doing substantially similar work, plus equivalent benefits or their cash value (Illinois DOL FAQ).

The two states do share a wage floor: as of January 1, 2026 both sit at $15.00 an hour. Missouri’s tipped minimum is $7.50 with the employer covering the gap to $15.00 (Missouri Department of Labor); Illinois sets its tipped rate at $9.00 and allows $13.00 for workers under 18 who work fewer than 650 hours a year (Illinois Minimum Wage Law). A bare $15.00 offer is the floor in both states, not a selling point.

### Five questions that separate a real agency from a resume vacuum

Ask these in the first ten minutes.

1. What do you actually staff? You want a category and a few client industries, not “everything.” 2. Who is the client and what is the rate? An agency that won’t say either before dispatch can’t be evaluated. 3. Am I your W-2 employee or a 1099 contractor? In temp staffing the answer should be W-2. If someone wants to 1099 you for shift work under their supervision, get a second opinion. 4. How does conversion work? Get the hours threshold and the conversion pay in writing. 5. What happens if the first assignment doesn’t fit? Good desks re-place people. Weak ones stop returning calls.

Worth knowing: federal anti-discrimination law follows you into staffing. EEOC guidance holds that both the staffing firm and the client business can be responsible for EEO compliance toward the worker they share (U.S. EEOC).

### What actually happens at the first appointment

Expect an application, an ID check and a short conversation — not a job offer. Most agencies here now want the application online first, so call ahead rather than driving to an office in St. Peters hoping someone can see you.

Bring what an employer of record needs: unexpired photo ID and documents that satisfy Form I-9, direct-deposit information, and an honest list of the shifts you will genuinely work. Background and drug screening are standard for industrial, warehouse, healthcare and driving roles, and the client sets those rules, not the recruiter across from you.

The most useful thing you can do in that meeting is be specific about geography and hours. “Anything, anywhere” sounds flexible and gets you sent to a 4 a.m. start in Wentzville when you live in south county without a car. A recruiter who knows you can reliably reach Hazelwood by six calls you first.

### The free option a lot of people skip

Before paying anyone anything, use the public workforce system — free, and present on both sides of the river. In the City of St. Louis, the St. Louis Agency on Training and Employment runs a Missouri Job Center with no-cost career services, workshops and training help (SLATE), and the state’s wider Job Center network covers St. Charles, Jefferson and St. Louis counties (Missouri Job Centers). In the Metro East, the equivalent is Illinois workNet. These offices feed private agencies more than they compete: a certificate or rebuilt resume is what lets a recruiter place you at a better rate.

### What this looks like from the agency’s side of the desk

The spread between what a staffing firm pays you and what it bills the client is not profit, and owners are tired of explaining that. Out of that gap come the employer’s 7.65% share of Social Security and Medicare taxes, state unemployment insurance, workers’ compensation premiums that can be punishing on industrial accounts, the recruiter’s pay, and the float — workers get paid weekly while clients often pay on 30- to 60-day terms, so the agency finances its own payroll for a month. The seasons bite too: fourth-quarter distribution demand swallows recruiting capacity, January resets direct-hire budgets, summer goes quiet. The complaints operators trade are always the same three — the Monday no-show, the client who hires a temp directly to dodge the conversion fee, and the order that lands at 4 p.m. for six people at 6 a.m. Since people hunting work search locally first, being listed with complete, current details is part of how a desk stays full.

Not sure which agency actually staffs your line of work? Browse employment agencies across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then call two of them with the same three sentences about the shift you want and see which one names a client company first.

Care work is one of the fastest-moving staffing categories in this region, and the questions overlap almost exactly — our guide to choosing home health care in St. Louis walks the same ground from the family’s side.

### Frequently asked questions

### Q. How much do employment agencies cost?

A.  For a job seeker, the answer should be nothing — the hiring employer pays. Employers pay either an hourly markup over the worker’s pay rate on temp assignments or a one-time placement fee on direct hires, usually a percentage of first-year salary. Published percentages drift year to year and swing by role, so treat any number online as a starting point and get a written quote for your opening.

### Q. Can I just walk into an employment agency?

A.  Sometimes, but call first. Most agencies in the St. Louis metro now want an online application on file before an in-person meeting, and many run appointment-only offices. If you do get an appointment, bring unexpired photo ID and Form I-9 documentation, because a temp agency is your legal employer and has to complete that paperwork before your first shift.

### Q. Is it cheaper to hire through a temp agency?

A.  Cheaper per hour, almost never. Cheaper overall, often — the markup buys things you would otherwise pay for separately: the employer’s 7.65% payroll tax share, unemployment insurance, workers’ compensation, screening, and the ability to end an assignment without a severance conversation. Compare total cost of a filled seat over the time you need it, not hourly rate against hourly rate.

### Q. What is the average cost per hire for recruiters?

A.  The most-quoted benchmark is SHRM’s Human Capital Benchmarking Report figure of $4,129 per hire — which reflects fiscal 2015 data from a survey fielded in 2016, and that vintage is why it’s a weak input now (SHRM). Calculate your own: add internal and external recruiting costs over a period, divide by hires made, then weigh that against what an open seat costs you weekly.

### Q. What are some good staffing agencies in Saint Louis, Missouri?

A.  There is no single best one, and published lists go stale fast. Sort by fit instead: find firms that staff your exact function, check whether they name client industries, confirm you would be a W-2 employee, and ask how many temps that desk converted to permanent last year. Two focused calls beat ten applications to generalists.

### Q. What companies are currently hiring in St. Louis?

A.  Openings turn over weekly, so use sources that refresh rather than a list inside an article. The Missouri Job Center network and Illinois workNet both post live regional openings at no cost, and large employers in health care, aerospace, higher education and distribution post to their own careers pages. A recruiter who works your category often hears about openings before they reach a job board.

## How to Choose a Pharmacy in St. Louis (Without Guessing)
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-choose-a-pharmacy-in-st-louis

Imagine it’s a Tuesday evening in Affton and your mother calls, a little embarrassed. Her doctor sent a new prescription to the drugstore she has used for eleven years, and when she drove over after dinner the front of the store was bright and open and the pharmacy window was dark. Nobody told her the counter now closes at six.

Maybe your version is different. Maybe you moved from Kirkwood to St. Charles in June and the pharmacy that knows your history is now a forty-minute round trip you keep putting off. Maybe you started a job in Maryland Heights, got a new insurance card in January, and a refill that cost almost nothing in December rang up as something else. Maybe you live in Belleville and the closest “preferred” pharmacy on your plan’s list is back across the river.

Choosing a pharmacy feels like a small decision you make once and forget. It is really four stacked together: who holds your record, who your plan will pay, who is open when you can get there, and who picks up the phone when something on the label looks wrong. What follows is about how the counter works, not about what to take.

### How do I know which pharmacy to go to?

Sort it on five things, in this order: whether your plan counts the pharmacy as in-network, whether you can reach it in a normal week, whether the counter’s hours match your life, whether a pharmacist there will spend five minutes with you, and what the cash price looks like on the day your plan says no.

Network status comes first because it moves the number more than anything you can negotiate at the register. Your copay is set by your plan’s contract, not by the store manager. Any pharmacy can run a test claim on one of your prescriptions and tell you what it would cost there before you move anything.

The reachability test is the one people skip and regret. A pharmacy three miles off that you can only reach by car at 5:40 p.m. is worse than one six miles out on a bus route you already ride. Before committing, ask a pharmacist to review everything you take and flag overlaps. A counter that does that in a calm week is the one you want in a bad one.

### What is a drugstore, exactly, and who licenses the counter inside it?

Are pharmacies and drugstores the same thing? Not quite, and the gap is the license. The drugstore is the retail business — the aisles, the cooler, the greeting cards. The pharmacy is the licensed prescription department inside it, staffed by a licensed pharmacist and permitted by the state.

That same license sits inside grocery stores, big-box stores, hospital outpatient windows, clinics, independent shops and mail-order operations, which is why the two words are not interchangeable. Missouri licenses through the Board of Pharmacy under the Division of Professional Registration, and you can look up a pharmacist or a pharmacy on the state’s licensee search. Illinois runs its own License Lookup through the Department of Financial and Professional Regulation. For an online-only pharmacy, the FDA’s BeSafeRx pages explain how to spot a licensed site.

### How do you move a prescription without losing a week?

Call the pharmacy you want to move to, not the one you are leaving. Give them the drug name, the strength, and the prescription number off the bottle, and they request the transfer themselves. For ordinary maintenance medication that is a same-day errand.

Controlled substances work differently. Under a DEA final rule effective August 28, 2023, a DEA-registered retail pharmacy may transfer an electronic prescription for a schedule II–V controlled substance to another retail pharmacy at the patient’s request — one time, for the initial fill, communicated directly between two licensed pharmacists, with the prescription staying electronic. Schedule II prescriptions carry no refills, so once one is dispensed there is nothing to move and you need a new prescription.

Missouri was the last state in the country to build a statewide prescription drug monitoring program, and it went live December 13, 2023. Pharmacies here report dispensing of schedule II, III and IV drugs to the Missouri PDMP. That is not an obstacle to a transfer — it is why a pharmacist may ask a question that feels personal.

### Why are drugstores so expensive?

Why are drugstores so expensive? Because most of the price was set several steps before the box reached the shelf. In a July 2024 interim staff report, the Federal Trade Commission found the three largest pharmacy benefit managers processed nearly 80 percent of the roughly 6.6 billion prescriptions dispensed by U.S. pharmacies in 2023.

The FTC went further in a second interim report released January 14, 2025, describing the same three companies — Caremark, Express Scripts and OptumRx — marking up specialty generic drugs dispensed at their own affiliated pharmacies by hundreds and sometimes thousands of percent, generating more than $7.3 billion above estimated acquisition costs between 2017 and 2022.

Sales tax is the one piece that genuinely differs by which side of the river you shop on. Illinois taxes qualifying drugs and medical appliances at 1 percent instead of the 6.25 percent general merchandise rate, per the Illinois Department of Revenue. Missouri exempts prescription drugs outright, and its Department of Revenue notes that over-the-counter medication is exempt only when bought by an individual with a disability.

Completely unrelated — if your outlets keep tripping, here are St. Louis electricians.

### How do you find the cheaper price without guessing?

Which drugstore is cheaper, CVS or Walgreens? There is no permanent answer, and any article printing one is wrong within a quarter. Get a real answer in ten minutes: call two or three counters, ask the cash price for the exact drug, strength and quantity, then hold those numbers against your copay.

One detail is worth knowing before you hand over a discount card. When you pay a discount price instead of running the claim through your plan, that money usually does not count toward your deductible or your Medicare Part D out-of-pocket total. Saving six dollars today can cost you later in the year, so ask which way the claim is going.

Two Medicare numbers are fixed and public. Per Medicare.gov, no Part D plan may have a deductible above $615 in 2026, and once out-of-pocket spending on covered Part D drugs hits $2,100 in 2026 you move into catastrophic coverage for the rest of the year. The Medicare Prescription Payment Plan spreads those costs across the calendar year. In Illinois, the Prescription Drug Affordability Act took full effect January 1, 2026; the Illinois Department of Insurance says consumers cannot be charged more than the least costly option, and steering to PBM-owned pharmacies is banned for many plans.

### What happens if your pharmacy closes?

Your prescriptions do not vanish, but the warning you get depends on which state you are standing in. Illinois requires a closing pharmacy to notify customers at least 15 days in advance and say where their records will be kept, under Illinois Administrative Code section 1330.790. Missouri’s rule, 20 CSR 2220-2.015, requires written notice to the Board of Pharmacy within 15 days after the business ends and a secure location for records; telling patients is a recommendation, not a deadline.

This is not theoretical. Rite Aid filed its second Chapter 11 in May 2025 and closed its last locations that October, with CVS acquiring prescription files from hundreds of shuttered stores. Closer to home, St. Louis Public Radio reported that the Walgreens at 1400 N. Grand Boulevard closed in April 2024, leaving Jeff-Vander-Lou residents driving downtown or to the Central West End.

Research by GreaterHealth Pharmacy and Wellness, the City of St. Louis Health Department and Washington University School of Medicine, published in December 2025, put numbers on it: 51,781 city residents — 17.2 percent of the population — live in a pharmacy desert, defined as more than a mile from a pharmacy, or more than half a mile where at least 20 percent of households lack vehicle access. The gaps concentrate in north St. Louis. Keep a printed medication list in a drawer, and if you are coordinating refills for a parent across town, our guide to home health care in St. Louis covers that job.

### When is the counter actually open?

Store hours and pharmacy hours are two different numbers, and the second one has been shrinking as chains cut staffing and closed locations. The store can be open until midnight while the counter shut at six. Ask the specific question when you call: is the pharmacy counter open, or only the store?

Treat any published list of overnight pharmacies as out of date and verify it the same day, by phone, for the exact address you plan to drive to. Drive-thru windows often keep their own shorter hours. If it is late and you are holding a new prescription, ask the prescriber’s office or the urgent care to send it somewhere open right now instead of to your usual one.

### What this looks like from behind the counter

Pharmacy owners are not getting rich on your amoxicillin. The 2025 NCPA Digest counted 18,960 independent locations as of July 2025 and an average of 67,601 prescriptions per store in 2024, up from 59,644 the year before — more work, in a year the report calls a ten-year high in cost of goods and a ten-year low in gross profits. Eighty-four percent of those scripts are generics, and 52 percent run through Medicare Part D or Medicaid, where the reimbursement is set elsewhere. In an NCPA survey released in January 2025, 40.8 percent of independent owners said they were paid below their acquisition cost on more than 40 percent of their Part D prescriptions. The margin lives in the front of the store, the flu-shot months and the refill-sync programs, not the vial. Owners here talk to each other about the same two things: below-cost reimbursement, and neighbors who never knew they were there. Being listed and complete is how the second one gets fixed.

Not sure who should be holding your prescriptions? Browse drugstores across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then call the two closest and ask each what your regular prescription costs there without insurance. The same questions about hours, stock and who actually answers the phone apply on the animal side of the counter — see choosing a vet for routine care.

### Frequently asked questions

### Q. Are pharmacies and drugstores the same thing?

A.  A drugstore is the retail store; the pharmacy is the licensed prescription department inside it. Most drugstores hold one, though plenty of pharmacies sit inside grocery stores, big-box stores, clinics and hospitals instead. The license belongs to the counter, not the aisles, and both Missouri and Illinois publish searchable license records.

### Q. Which is better for prescriptions, CVS or Walgreens?

A.  Neither wins as a rule. The better one for you is whichever your plan treats as in-network, keeps hours you can reach, and staffs a pharmacist willing to review everything you take. Run those three checks on both, plus any independent nearby.

### Q. Which drugstore is cheaper, CVS or Walgreens?

A.  It shifts by drug, by plan and by month, so a printed answer goes stale fast. Get a current one yourself: call both, ask the cash price for the exact drug, strength and quantity, then compare that against your copay and ask whether a discount price still counts toward your deductible.

### Q. Which pharmacy is usually the cheapest?

A.  There is no permanent cheapest. Price depends on your plan’s contract, the drug, whether a generic exists, and any discount program in play. The dependable move is to price one specific prescription at two or three places, including an independent, then re-check whenever your plan or your prescription changes.

### Q. Are local pharmacies cheaper than CVS?

A.  Sometimes on cash prices, often not on insured copays, because the copay is set by your plan rather than by the store. Independents tend to be faster on transfers, compounding and actual questions. Price the exact drug at both, and ask each what it charges with no insurance at all.

### Q. Why are drugstores so expensive?

A.  Most of the price is set before the box reaches the shelf. The FTC reported in July 2024 that the three largest pharmacy benefit managers processed nearly 80 percent of the roughly 6.6 billion prescriptions dispensed in the U.S. in 2023, and its January 2025 report described steep markups at their affiliated pharmacies.

### Q. Who are the big 3 pharmacies?

A.  Most people mean the retail chains, and that trio was CVS, Walgreens and Rite Aid until Rite Aid closed its last stores in October 2025. The more consequential big three are the pharmacy benefit managers — Caremark, Express Scripts and OptumRx — which the FTC found processed nearly 80 percent of U.S. prescriptions in 2023.

### Q. What is the 5 rule in pharmacy?

A.  People usually mean the five rights of medication safety: the right medication, in the right dose, at the right time, by the right route, to the right patient. AHRQ’s patient safety primer lists them as a standard check against medication errors. It is a safety habit rather than a law.

### Q. Are there any 24 hour pharmacies in St. Louis?

A.  Overnight hours have been cut across the industry as chains trimmed staffing and closed stores, so any list you find online is likely out of date. Verify the same day: call the exact location and ask whether the pharmacy counter runs around the clock or only the store. If it is late, ask your prescriber to send it somewhere open now.

## What a Business Consultant Costs in St. Louis, and What Moves the Price
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-a-business-consultant-costs-in-st-louis

Imagine it’s a Thursday in March and you’re parked outside a job site in Maryland Heights doing the thing you do every Thursday: adding up what came in against what went out, on your phone, in a truck. Revenue is up. The checking account is not. Nobody at the shop can tell you why, and you’ve quit asking.

Maybe yours is a six-person dental office in Kirkwood where the front desk turns over twice a year. Maybe it’s a distribution outfit in Belleville, and your best estimator just left for a competitor in St. Charles. Somebody at a chamber breakfast in Florissant says the word consultant. You nod. At eleven that night you type it into your phone and get a screen full of results with no price on any of them.

That’s the actual problem. Not whether a consultant can help — some can, enormously — but that this is one of the last professional services you can buy where nobody posts a rate. So here is the arithmetic behind the number you’ll be quoted, what moves it, and how to tell inside one meeting if you’re about to spend four thousand dollars well.

### How much should I pay for a business consultant?

Most independent consultants land between $100 and $250 an hour, and most small-business work is priced as a project rather than by the clock. In the Consulting Success fee study of nearly 1,000 consultants across more than 75 countries, 39% charge $100 to $250 hourly. General management work runs from roughly $75 an hour at the inexperienced end up to $175 to $325 for consultants with 15 or more years behind them.

Hourly isn’t even the most common structure. In that same study, 30% of consultants price by project, 29% by the hour, 16% on a monthly retainer, 15% on value and 10% by the day. Project size clusters lower than owners expect: the two most common average project values are $5,000 to $15,000 and $15,000 to $50,000, with 33% of consultants sitting in that second band and only 6% averaging six figures.

Treat every printed number, including those, as a starting position rather than a quote — published rates age, and a rate is a negotiation anyway. The figure that matters is the one attached to a specific decision. What will it cost to find out why gross margin dropped four points, and what will it cost to fix it? Ask for those two prices separately. A consultant who can’t split them hasn’t scoped your job yet.

### What is the rule of 3 in consulting?

Two different things wear that name, and only one is about your invoice. The common one is the rule of thirds for setting a rate: roughly a third of the hourly number is the consultant’s actual wage, a third covers expenses, and the last third absorbs admin, unbilled hours and clients who never pay. The other version is a multiplier — charge two to three times what you earned hourly as somebody’s employee doing similar work.

Both rules exist because self-employment costs money a salary hides. The IRS sets self-employment tax at 15.3% — 12.4% for Social Security plus 2.9% for Medicare — on top of income tax, and an independent buys their own health insurance, software, liability coverage and retirement contribution out of the same rate.

Why should the buyer care about the seller’s arithmetic? Because it tells you what a low quote means. Someone offering $60 an hour is subsidizing you from other income, is brand new, or is running a practice that won’t exist in a year. The third one is the expensive kind of cheap, because you end up paying a second person to finish the first person’s work.

### Why the hour on your invoice isn’t the hour they work

Roughly a third of a consultant’s working year isn’t billable to anybody. The 2026 SPI Professional Services Maturity Benchmark, now in its 19th year, put average billable utilization at 66.4% in 2025, down from 68.9% in 2024 and the lowest reading the survey has recorded. The unbilled third is proposals, scoping calls, chasing invoices and work that never closed — the same benchmark puts bid-to-win at 48.1%.

Run it against a calendar. A 2,080-hour year at 66.4% utilization is about 1,380 billable hours. At $100 an hour that’s roughly $138,000 in billings before self-employment tax, insurance, software and the months when the phone doesn’t ring. Owners ask this in exactly these words: is $100 an hour good for consulting? Set it against the salaried alternative. The Bureau of Labor Statistics put the 2025 median wage for management analysts at $48.97 an hour, or $101,860 a year, with benefits attached and no selling to do.

So $100 an hour is a working independent rate — not a steal, not a scam. The signals worth worrying about run the other way: someone billing $300 an hour who can’t name three recent engagements resembling yours, or someone at $75 who claims forty billable hours every week, which almost nobody in this trade actually has.

Nothing to do with margins — St. Louis hair salons book out fast in December.

### How to find a good business consultant?

Start by accepting that the title guarantees nothing. Missouri’s Division of Professional Registration lists 57 regulated professions, from certified public accountants to professional wrestlers, and business consultant isn’t among them. Illinois regulates well over a hundred professions and industries through IDFPR, from acupuncturists to wholesale drug distributors, and it isn’t on that list either. Anybody on either side of the river can print the card tomorrow.

Voluntary credentials do exist. The Institute of Management Consultants USA awards the Certified Management Consultant designation, and earning it means submitting written summaries of three client engagements, supplying contact details for five or six clients, and passing an oral examination covering those engagements, core competencies and ethics. It isn’t common, and its absence isn’t a red flag — but its presence means somebody outside the relationship audited the work.

Then do yourself what that credential does. Ask for three clients from the last two years whose business looked like yours, and call them: what changed, how long did it take, what did it cost. Ask who will actually do the work, by name. Ask the consultant to describe your problem back to you before quoting anything — if the description is generic, the plan will be too. And ask what they don’t take on, because somebody who accepts every job accepts yours badly.

### What free help should you use before you pay anyone?

More than most owners realize, and it differs by which side of the Mississippi you’re on. In the Metro East, the Illinois SBDC at Southern Illinois University Edwardsville provides “confidential, no-cost advising services to entrepreneurs and existing business owners,” supported by the U.S. Small Business Administration, the Illinois Department of Commerce and Economic Opportunity and the SIUE School of Business. On the Missouri side, the Missouri SBDC network runs its own advising, funded in part through a cooperative agreement with the SBA, with an office for the St. Louis region.

SCORE covers both states on top of that: free, confidential mentoring from experienced business leaders, matched by ZIP code, which it has been doing since 1964.

None of it replaces a paid engagement. Free advising is generalist and it moves at the speed of a volunteer’s calendar, while a consultant you hire is accountable to a deliverable and a date. But two free sessions first are the cheapest way to sharpen the question you’re about to pay somebody to answer — and if those sessions answer it, you just kept the fee.

### What should the agreement say before you sign?

Five things, and you can check them in ten minutes. One: the deliverable written as an object — a pricing model, a hiring plan, a documented month-end close — never as “strategic guidance.” Two: the date it lands. Three: who performs the work, by name, and how many of that person’s hours you’re buying. Four: payment terms, and what triggers each payment. Five: the exit — how either side ends it, and what you keep when they do.

That last line matters more than the rate. Ownership of the work product should be written down rather than assumed, and so should confidentiality running both directions. If the engagement touches hiring, state plainly whether the consultant is recruiting or advising; those are different services with different economics, and the staffing decision is its own project — how to choose a staffing agency walks through that side.

Then start small on purpose. A two-week paid diagnostic that ends in a written finding tells you more about a consultant than any reference call, and it caps your exposure at a number you already agreed to. The good ones offer it before you ask.

### What this work looks like from the consultant’s side of the table

The economics are thinner than the hourly rate suggests. Billable utilization across professional services averaged 66.4% in 2025, consultants win under half of what they bid, and 56% of them work solo out of a home office. The SBA Office of Advocacy’s 2025 Missouri profile counts 64,641 small professional, scientific and technical firms in the state — 52,691 of those have no employees at all, which means the person you meet is usually the entire firm. The pipeline is personal, too: 60% of consultants got their first client through a referral from their own network, and 63% still name networking and referrals as their strongest channel, against 25% for social media. So a slow quarter is a silent one, and the free discovery call that quietly turns into a free strategy session is this trade’s loss leader. Which is the argument for being listed and easy to verify where owners look when the problem finally gets loud.

Ready to price the problem instead of guessing at it? Browse business management consultants across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then ask the first three the same two questions: what would the diagnosis cost, and what would the fix cost. Consultants who tell you to grow into new space are rarely the ones who read the lease, so pair that advice with what leasing commercial space here really involves.

### Frequently asked questions

### Q. How much should I pay for a business consultant?

A.  Most independents charge $100 to $250 an hour, and 39% of consultants surveyed by Consulting Success sit in exactly that band. For small-business work, project pricing is more common than hourly, with typical average project values of $5,000 to $15,000 or $15,000 to $50,000. Published figures age quickly, so price the decision: ask separately what the diagnosis costs and what the fix costs.

### Q. What is the rule of 3 in consulting?

A.  Usually the rule of thirds for setting a rate: about a third of the hourly figure is the consultant’s wage, a third pays expenses, and a third covers admin, unbilled time and bad debt. A related version says charge two to three times your old employee hourly rate. Neither is a law. Both explain why an independent’s number looks high next to a salary.

### Q. Is $100 an hour good for consulting?

A.  It’s a real working rate rather than a bargain. At the 66.4% billable utilization SPI Research measured for 2025, a full year is roughly 1,380 billable hours, so $100 an hour is about $138,000 in billings before 15.3% self-employment tax, insurance and software. The BLS median for salaried management analysts was $48.97 an hour in 2025, benefits included.

### Q. How to find a good business consultant?

A.  Ask for three clients from the past two years whose business resembles yours, then actually call them. Have the consultant describe your problem back to you before quoting. Confirm by name who performs the work. Then buy a small paid diagnostic rather than a six-month engagement — two weeks and a written finding tell you more than any pitch deck.

### Q. Do business consultants need a license in Missouri or Illinois?

A.  No. Missouri’s Division of Professional Registration lists 57 regulated professions, from certified public accountants to professional wrestlers, and business consultant is not one of them. Illinois regulates its professions through IDFPR and doesn’t license the title either. Voluntary certification exists — the Certified Management Consultant designation from the Institute of Management Consultants USA — but nobody is required to hold it.

### Q. What does a business consultant actually do?

A.  Diagnosis first, then a plan, and sometimes the hands to carry it out. Common small-business engagements cover pricing and margin, cash flow and forecasting, hiring and org structure, operations and process documentation, and preparing a company for sale or succession. The distinction worth holding onto is diagnosis versus doing — different amounts of work that should carry different prices.

### Q. Can I get free business advice in the St. Louis area?

A.  Yes, on both sides of the river. The Illinois SBDC for the Metro East at SIUE offers confidential, no-cost advising to entrepreneurs and existing business owners. The Missouri SBDC network runs advising funded in part through a cooperative agreement with the SBA, including an office for the St. Louis region. SCORE adds free, confidential mentoring matched by ZIP code.

## How to Rent an Apartment in St. Louis: What to Check Before You Sign
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/renting-an-apartment-in-st-louis

Imagine it’s a Tuesday in March and the renewal notice is folded under your door in Maryland Heights. Sixty days to decide, and the new number is eighty dollars higher than the one you signed last spring. You open a listing app on the couch, and by ten o’clock you have nine tabs, four saved searches and no real idea which of those buildings is worth a Saturday.

Then the search drifts, the way it always does. A two-bedroom in Affton with a garage. A rehabbed flat in Maplewood over a storefront. Something in Belleville that costs three hundred less until you price the 7:40 crawl over the Poplar Street Bridge. Your sister in St. Charles says just move out there. Your friend in Florissant says the exact opposite, and neither of them has read a lease in years.

The part nobody mentions is the part that decides it: the sequence you follow, the clauses you sign, and the fact that Missouri and Illinois answer the same deposit question in two different ways. Here’s the version worth reading before you tour anything.

### How do you find an apartment in St. Louis without losing a month to it?

Set your rent ceiling first, narrow to two or three municipalities second, and only then start touring. Reversing that order is what turns a two-week search into a two-month one. Across the metro, median gross rent was $1,113 a month in the U.S. Census Bureau’s American Community Survey five-year estimates covering 2020 through 2024.

How much do apartments cost in St. Louis? That $1,113 is the honest middle, and it is a “gross” figure — contract rent plus the utilities the tenant pays. County by county the same survey runs from $893 in Franklin County to $979 in Jefferson County, $997 in the City of St. Louis, $1,209 in St. Louis County and $1,370 in St. Charles County. On the Illinois side it lands at $1,024 in Madison County, $1,042 in Monroe County and $1,090 in St. Clair County.

Those medians cover every occupied rental, including long-held leases. Listing-site averages are asking rents on units available right now, which is why the two never match. Treat the census figure as the market’s gravity and the listing number as today’s weather. Printed numbers age fast, so verify the current ask on the specific building.

### Where in the metro are the apartments actually located?

Renters are about 30% of occupied homes across the metro, but that share swings hard by municipality, and the swing tells you where inventory is. In the City of St. Louis, 55% of occupied homes are rentals. In St. Louis County it is 31%; in St. Charles County, 19%. All from the same 2020 through 2024 Census Bureau five-year estimates.

Zoom in and the map gets useful. Maplewood is 60% renter-occupied, Richmond Heights 46%, Clayton 45%, University City 44%, Maryland Heights 43%, Belleville 40%, Brentwood 37%, Florissant 33%, Edwardsville 33%. Compare that to Kirkwood at 23% and Affton at 19%. Same metro, wildly different odds of finding three buildings worth touring on one Saturday.

The Illinois side reads cheaper on paper — Belleville’s median gross rent is $1,019 against the metro’s $1,113 — and for some households it genuinely is. Price the whole picture anyway: the bridge commute, the parking you may have to buy downtown, and the different landlord-tenant rules covered further down. A hundred dollars of rent savings evaporates quickly at 5 p.m. on Interstate 64.

### What do you need to apply, and what is the landlord checking?

Bring photo ID, two recent pay stubs or an offer letter, a bank statement, and contact details for your last two landlords. Most leasing offices underwrite to roughly three times the monthly rent in gross household income, plus a credit, criminal and eviction-record screen. That is an industry convention, not a law, and it varies building to building.

Application fees are generally non-refundable in both states, and neither Missouri nor Illinois sets a statutory cap on them. That single fact should change your behavior: apply to your first choice, not to five buildings at once. If you are turned down because of something in a credit or tenant-screening report, federal law requires an adverse action notice telling you which company supplied it, so you can get a free copy and dispute errors. The Federal Trade Commission spells out that obligation for landlords.

Screening has limits. The federal Fair Housing Act bars discrimination on race, color, national origin, religion, sex, familial status and disability, and HUD enforces it. Complaints on the Missouri side also go to the Missouri Commission on Human Rights; on the Illinois side, to the Illinois Department of Human Rights. Reasonable accommodations for a disability, including assistance animals, sit under that same law and are not a pet-policy question.

Unrelated, and we know it — your new building’s gym is probably terrible.

### What should you read in the lease before you sign it?

Five clauses do most of the damage: the auto-renewal, the notice-to-vacate window, who pays which utility, the pet and parking add-ons, and the early-termination formula. Read those five before the rent number. A lease that renews automatically unless you give sixty days’ written notice will quietly cost you a month you never planned to pay for.

Month-to-month endings differ by state. In Missouri, either side ends a month-to-month tenancy with written notice taking effect on a rent-paying date not less than one month after the other party receives it, under RSMo 441.060. In Illinois it is 30 days’ written notice under 735 ILCS 5/9-207, and a landlord chasing unpaid rent must serve a five-day notice first under 735 ILCS 5/9-209.

Two local checks are worth the ten minutes. If the unit is in the City of St. Louis, every property sits in a Housing Conservation District, and a rental unit needs a Certificate of Inspection before occupancy, with reinspection every three years or on a change of occupancy — the city building division issues it, and you can ask to see it. And if the building went up before 1978, federal law requires a lead-based paint disclosure and the EPA pamphlet before you sign, per the EPA disclosure rule.

One expectation to reset: neither state caps how much your rent can go up at renewal. Illinois goes further and forbids cities and villages from enacting rent control at all, under the Rent Control Preemption Act passed in 1997. Your leverage at renewal is the lease term you negotiate going in, not a statute.

### How much deposit can a landlord hold, and when do you get it back?

In Missouri the deposit is capped at two months’ rent, and the landlord has 30 days after the tenancy ends to return it in full or send a written itemized list of damages with the balance. You also have the right to be present at the move-out inspection. Wrongful withholding exposes the landlord to twice the amount wrongfully withheld, under RSMo 535.300.

Illinois has no statutory cap on the deposit amount, but a tighter clock on the way out. Under the Security Deposit Return Act, a landlord who intends to deduct must furnish an itemized statement with paid receipts or estimates within 30 days of the tenant vacating; without it, the full deposit is due within 45 days. Bad faith carries twice the deposit plus court costs and attorney’s fees. Public Act 103-224 deleted the old five-unit threshold effective January 1, 2024, so it now reaches a single rented condo in O’Fallon, Illinois.

Illinois adds one more wrinkle: in a building or complex of 25 or more units, a deposit held more than six months earns interest, set by the passbook savings rate at the largest commercial bank headquartered in the state, under the Security Deposit Interest Act. Either side of the river, do the same three things: photograph every room the day you move in, attend the walkthrough, and hand over a forwarding address in writing.

### What are your rights if the furnace quits and nobody calls back?

Both states give you a narrow repair-and-deduct remedy, and both are easy to blow. Missouri’s version, RSMo 441.234, requires six consecutive months of lawful residence, rent current, a condition that violates local housing or building code, and 14 days’ written notice. The deduction is capped at $300 or half a month’s rent, whichever is greater, never more than one month’s rent, and once per 12 months.

Illinois caps it lower. The Residential Tenants’ Right to Repair Act allows the lesser of $500 or one-half of the monthly rent, again after 14 days’ written notice, and the work must be done by an appropriate tradesman unrelated to you, documented with a paid bill. Owner-occupied buildings of six units or fewer are among the exceptions.

What you should not do is simply stop paying rent. That is the fastest route to an eviction filing that follows you through every screening report for years. Call the municipal inspector first, put every request in writing, and get advice before you act — the Missouri Attorney General publishes a plain-language landlord-tenant guide, and Missouri Legal Services covers the same ground for tenants who need help.

### What the leasing office is doing on the other side of the desk

Apartment margins are thinner than renters assume. The National Apartment Association’s analysis of 2022 operating statements from Freddie Mac-financed properties found that of every dollar of Missouri rent, 44 cents goes to the mortgage, 32 cents to operating costs, 9 cents to payroll, 7 cents to property taxes and 3 cents to capital reserves — leaving 6 cents of profit. In Illinois, property taxes take 14 cents instead of 7. Add the City of St. Louis inspection cycle — every three years or on a change of occupancy, with an application that starts at $120 and adds $65 for each additional unit at the same address — and the reason a leasing agent hates an empty unit in January is arithmetic: the peak leasing window is roughly May through August, and a vacancy that misses it can sit for months. The operators who fill units are the ones renters can actually find — which is why an accurate, complete listing matters as much as the sign out front.

### Frequently asked questions

### Q. Where do the wealthy live in St. Louis?

A.  Mostly in a tight cluster of small St. Louis County municipalities west of the city. In the Census Bureau’s 2020 through 2024 five-year estimates, Ladue and Huntleigh both report median household income at $250,001, the top value the survey publishes, followed by Clarkson Valley at $247,000, Westwood at $237,500, Frontenac at $233,425 and Town and Country at $232,534. For renters that matters less than it sounds, because those places are almost entirely owner-occupied.

### Q. Where is Millionaires Row, St. Louis?

A.  It is a nickname, not an address, and it points at the Central West End. The City of St. Louis traces the district to the late 1880s, when a 1,400-acre park drew the region’s wealthy elite west of downtown and the neighborhood built out Lindell Boulevard along with the private places — Westmoreland Place, Portland Place and Forest Park Terrace — in what the city calls grand and lavish style. Apartments sit a block or two away in every direction.

### Q. How much does an apartment building usually cost?

A.  There is no usable national average, because the price is set locally by land, unit count, construction type and the rent the units actually produce. A four-family in south St. Louis and a garden complex in Chesterfield are not the same asset class. Anyone shopping seriously prices it per unit against recent sales within a few miles, then verifies with an appraisal and a lender. Any published figure is stale the moment rates or insurance move.

### Q. How much is an average apartment building?

A.  Buyers do not price apartment buildings off averages. They price off net operating income divided by a capitalization rate drawn from comparable local sales, which is why two buildings with identical unit counts can trade hundreds of thousands apart. Work the math from the rent roll, actual expenses and current debt terms, and treat any headline average as a conversation starter rather than a number to bring to a closing table.

### Q. How much does it cost to build an entire apartment complex?

A.  Budget it as five stacked line items rather than one number: land, hard construction costs, soft costs such as design and permits, financing carry during construction, and an operating reserve for lease-up. Construction type moves the total more than anything else, since a wood-frame walk-up, a podium building over structured parking, and a mid-rise price on entirely different scales. Local bids and a lender’s term sheet are the only figures worth planning around.

### Q. How much does a 100 unit apartment complex cost?

A.  Unit count alone does not set the price. A 100-unit garden community on cheap suburban ground, a 100-unit rehab of an older city building and a 100-unit new-construction mid-rise with a parking deck can differ by multiples on the same unit count. Land basis, parking, construction type, labor rates and financing terms move the number, and all of those are local and change quarter to quarter.

## How to Choose a Martial Arts School in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-choose-a-martial-arts-school-st-louis

Imagine it’s a Wednesday in early September and your eight-year-old announces, with total conviction, that she is going to learn karate. Not soccer. Karate. So you do what everybody does — you type “martial arts near me” into your phone in the pickup line in Affton — and ninety seconds later you have eleven tabs open and no idea what you are looking at.

One school in Florissant teaches taekwondo and has a wall of trophies taller than your kid. A storefront in Maryland Heights advertises muay thai and Brazilian jiu-jitsu, and every photo shows adults with taped shins. A place in Kirkwood calls itself a family academy and wants you to book a free intro assessment. Across the river in Belleville, a school sells self-defense and a black belt program named like a car warranty.

Now imagine it’s you and not the kid — thirty-four, desk job, one cranky shoulder, and a sense that you should be able to defend yourself, or at least beat a treadmill in St. Charles. Same eleven tabs. This is a guide to reading them: what the disciplines are, what a trial class reveals, how to check an instructor, and what the contract in front of you is legally allowed to do — which depends on which side of the Mississippi you sign it on.

### How do I know which martial art is right for me?

Start from the outcome you want, not the name on the sign. Choose a striking art for conditioning and stand-up skill, a grappling art for control and lower-impact sparring, and an Olympic-governed art for ranked competition and formal safeguarding. Then judge the school rather than the style. The gap between two schools teaching the same art is usually wider than the gap between two arts.

Most people ask this backwards. They pick a discipline they saw in a movie, then hunt for a school that teaches it. Reverse it. Write down the one thing you want twelve months from now — my kid follows instructions and isn’t scared of other kids; I can survive three rounds — and let that pick the room.

The version people actually type into a search bar is: What is the best martial art for a beginner? There is no single answer, and a school that hands you one without asking about your body, your schedule and your goal is selling. A beginner needs classmates at their level, an instructor who corrects rather than performs, and a pace that doesn’t produce an injury in month two. Several arts supply that. Plenty of individual schools don’t.

### Karate, taekwondo, muay thai, judo, BJJ: what actually differs

Karate and taekwondo are structured striking arts built on forms, drills and rank. Muay thai is full-contact striking with knees, elbows and clinch. Judo is throwing and pinning. Brazilian jiu-jitsu is ground control and submissions. Krav Maga and the broader self-defense category borrow from all of them and skip the sport.

Rank behaves differently in each. Taekwondo, judo and karate sit inside the U.S. Olympic and Paralympic Movement, with USA Taekwondo, USA Judo and USA Karate as national governing bodies, so credentials and safeguarding rules run through a national organization. Brazilian jiu-jitsu belts are usually pegged to the International Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu Federation, whose published Graduation System sets minimum ages and time in grade for every belt. Muay thai and most self-defense curricula sit outside that structure — not worse, just unaffiliated. The certificate on the wall is only as good as the organization behind it. Ask which one.

Impact matters more than parents expect. Judo and BJJ involve constant close contact and very little getting hit. Muay thai and full-contact karate involve less grabbing and far more impact. Taekwondo sits between and is kick-heavy: hard on knees, wonderful for kids with too much energy. If a shoulder already complains, say so before you sign.

### What should a trial class actually show you?

A trial class is an audition and you are the judge. Watch four things: how much of the hour is moving versus talking, who the new person gets paired with, whether the head instructor teaches or only appears at the end, and what happens when a technique goes wrong. Correction that is specific and calm is the product. Volume is not.

Go watch a class you are not in. A Tuesday advanced session tells you more than the sales-friendly beginner hour. Look at the mats — skin infections spread on dirty ones, and a school that wipes them between classes tells you about its habits. Listen for whether kids are taught to tap and to stop instantly on command. That rule separates safe sparring from the other kind.

Ask two questions before you leave. What happens the week my kid doesn’t want to come? And can I sit and watch any class, any time? A school that welcomes parents in the room has nothing to manage.

### How do you check out a martial arts instructor in Missouri or Illinois?

Neither state licenses martial arts instructors the way it licenses barbers or nurses. Missouri’s Office of Athletics, inside the Division of Professional Registration, regulates professional boxing and wrestling, professional and amateur kickboxing and mixed martial arts, and professional full-contact karate contests. It regulates the fight, not the school your kid walks into on Tuesday.

There is one real public record worth searching. The U.S. Center for SafeSport maintains a Centralized Disciplinary Database anyone can search by name. Know its limit before you trust a clean result: the Center says its authority extends only to the U.S. Olympic and Paralympic Movement, not to non-Movement leagues or non-Olympic sports. A taekwondo or judo coach with national membership is inside that system. An independent muay thai or jiu-jitsu coach usually is not.

In Missouri, the Family Care Safety Registry screens people against seven state databases, including criminal records, the sex offender registry and child abuse findings. Registration is required for licensed child care and long-term care workers; voluntary recreational organizations are exempt, so a martial arts school generally isn’t obligated. Screening is therefore a policy choice, which makes it a fair question: who do you background check, how often, and what disqualifies someone?

Unrelated, and we know it — sore back? Try a chiropractor.

### What a martial arts contract can legally do — and how it changes at the river

This is the biggest Missouri–Illinois split in the category, and almost nobody knows it. In Illinois, a martial arts school falls under consumer contract law written for gyms. In Missouri, it is specifically carved out.

Illinois first. The Physical Fitness Services Act, 815 ILCS 645, defines physical fitness services to include “instruction, training or assistance in physical culture, bodybuilding, exercising, weight reducing, figure development, judo, karate, self-defense training, or any similar activity.” Judo and karate are named in the statute. Under it, the customer may cancel within three business days after the first business day after signing, with all monies refunded, and the initial term may not exceed one year. A second layer: under the Automatic Contract Renewal Act, 815 ILCS 601/10, a contract of 12 months or more that auto-renews for more than a month requires written notice 30 to 60 days before the cancellation deadline.

Missouri goes the other way. The health spa statute, RSMo 407.325, is what forces gyms to register with the Attorney General, post a bond and grant a three-business-day cancellation right — the Attorney General’s office sets that bond at $10,000, $20,000 or $25,000 by contract count. But the definition excludes “any organization primarily operated for the purpose of teaching a particular form of self-defense such as judo or karate.” A Missouri dojo usually sits outside it, so what protects you is the contract itself, plus the Missouri Merchandising Practices Act if something was misrepresented.

Translation: in Missouri, read before you sign, because the cooling-off period you assume exists may not. Ask for term length, renewal mechanism, the exact cancellation method — email, certified letter or in person — and whether a free trial converts automatically.

### Belt fees, testing fees and gear: where the money actually goes

Tuition is rarely the whole number. Budget five buckets: monthly or term tuition, a testing fee each time you grade, association dues if the school is affiliated, uniform and protective gear, and tournament entries. Some schools add an upgrade tier that stacks on top.

People ask flatly: Are martial arts classes expensive? It depends on format and promotion pace, and any figure printed today goes stale, so don’t shop the monthly rate. Ask instead for the twelve-month all-in total in writing, at the promotion pace the school actually uses, including every testing fee, dues payment and required piece of gear. Divide by classes you will realistically attend. That per-session number compares across schools.

Belt structure is the tell. If promotions land on a calendar rather than on demonstrated skill, and each belt costs more than the last, you are buying certificates. Compare the IBJJF model, where time in grade is published and a belt takes years. Ask how many students tested last cycle and how many did not pass. A school that never fails anyone is not testing.

### How often should you train?

Two classes a week builds a habit. Three builds skill. The federal Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans, second edition, explain why: ages 6 through 17 need 60 minutes or more of moderate-to-vigorous activity daily, including vigorous activity at least 3 days a week, plus muscle-strengthening and bone-strengthening at least 3 days a week each. Adults need 150 minutes moderate or 75 minutes vigorous weekly.

Two 45-minute kids classes a week is about 90 minutes against a weekly target of 420. A real contribution, not a plan. Three sessions clears the strengthening frequency on their own.

### What this looks like from behind the front desk

A martial arts school is a recurring-revenue business wearing a tracksuit. Mat rent is fixed, so the twelfth student in a class costs almost nothing to serve. Retention, not enrollment, is the number owners watch. Seasonality is brutal and predictable: sign-ups spike when school starts in late August and again in January, and summer is the hollow stretch camps and testing cycles exist to bridge. The free trial is the loss leader. What customers get wrong is shopping the monthly rate instead of instructor time and class size, then ghosting instead of cancelling. Good operators publish the fee schedule and call a family after two missed weeks. Parents search this locally, so being listed with complete hours, ages served and disciplines taught is how a school gets shortlisted before anyone calls.

Ready to sit in on a class instead of reading about one? Browse martial arts schools across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then call two and ask to watch a class you are not signed up for. The one that says yes without hesitating is the one to try first.

One more thing before you commit. The same test — trial lesson, instructor credentials, contract term — applies to choosing a music school in St. Louis, and comparing the two makes the tradeoffs obvious. If the fit is wrong after a few months, that is information, not failure — plenty of people move on to something like picking up golf instead.

### Frequently asked questions

### Q. What is the best martial art for a beginner?

A.  There isn’t one universal answer. Judo and Brazilian jiu-jitsu let a beginner train hard with very little getting hit. Taekwondo and karate give the most structure, which suits kids and anyone who likes a clear ladder. Muay thai builds conditioning fastest at the highest impact. Pick by what you want twelve months out, then judge the school.

### Q. Is 27 too late to start martial arts?

A.  No. Adult beginner programs exist because most people walk in during their twenties, thirties and forties. What changes with age is recovery, not capability. You want a school that scales intensity, lets you sit out a round without commentary, and has other adults at your level. Ask how many adult white belts train in the class you would join.

### Q. Are martial arts classes expensive?

A.  It depends on format, class size and how often the school promotes students, and any figure printed today goes stale. Rather than compare monthly rates, ask for a twelve-month all-in total in writing covering tuition, every testing fee at the school’s real promotion pace, dues, uniform and gear. Divide by classes you will attend. That per-session number is the fair comparison.

### Q. Is $30 for 45 minutes good for a martial arts class?
