## How to Book a Banquet Hall in St. Louis: What to Ask First
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-book-a-banquet-hall-in-st-louis

Imagine it’s a Sunday afternoon in Affton and your mother-in-law announces, over pot roast, that the family is doing something for your parents’ fiftieth. Not a restaurant. Something with a room and a head table. Somebody says the word hall. Everyone looks at you.

Or it’s a graduation party in Belleville with eighty people and rain in the forecast. A quinceañera in south city. A retirement dinner in Granite City. A funeral luncheon that has to be Thursday because half the family flies home Friday. Same problem every time: a rough head count, a date that will not move, and no idea what it should cost.

Most people book a hall once or twice in a lifetime and are still expected to be good at it. The contracts have their own vocabulary — guarantee, service charge, flip, load-out — and nobody hands you the glossary.

### Where can I rent a hall in St. Louis?

Halls here come in roughly eight types, and the type sets your rules more than the address does: dedicated banquet centers, veterans’ and fraternal posts, parish and church halls, union halls, hotel ballrooms, country club and golf course rooms, municipal and park district community buildings, and event rooms attached to breweries, wineries and restaurants. Each carries its own catering and alcohol policy.

Sort that policy first, because it decides everything downstream. A dedicated banquet center usually runs its own kitchen and bar, so you buy a package. A parish hall or veterans’ post more often rents a bare room and lets you bring food — cheaper, and every logistical problem is now yours. A hotel ballroom bundles the most and flexes the least.

Geography matters less than people expect, since families will drive for a party. The state line matters more. Kirkwood, Florissant and St. Charles run on Missouri rules; Belleville, Edwardsville and Collinsville sit under a different alcohol regime and health department.

### What defines a banquet hall?

A banquet hall is a room built and permitted for assembly use: a large open floor with no fixed seating, restrooms sized for a crowd, marked exits and egress capacity, parking, and either a commercial kitchen or a staging area a caterer can legally work from. That kitchen question is the real dividing line, and the one people forget to ask.

Two things get called halls and are not. A restaurant’s private dining room is a restaurant — their menu, their bar, out when the next seating needs the space. A blank-box venue, a loft or warehouse with no kitchen or furniture, is a shell you rent and then fill.

### What are banquet halls used for?

Weddings are the loudest use, not the most frequent. Across a year a working hall runs reception dinners, quinceañeras and sweet sixteens, milestone birthdays and golden anniversaries, graduation parties, baby and bridal showers, first communion lunches, funeral luncheons, corporate holiday parties, sales meetings and trainings, union meetings and retirement dinners, church banquets and fundraisers.

Those uses pull on different parts of the calendar. Graduation parties stack into May and early June. Corporate holiday dates are largely spoken for by late summer. Funeral luncheons book on two or three days’ notice, which is why many halls keep weekday daytime open — a room that looks impossible on Saturday can be wide open Tuesday at noon. Say what your event actually is on the first call, not just the head count.

### How far ahead should you book a banquet hall?

For a Saturday evening between May and October, treat a year out as normal and eighteen months as safe. For a Friday, Sunday, weekday, or anything from January through March, three to six months is usually plenty. The mechanism is simple: a hall has a fixed number of prime Saturdays, and a sold one cannot be resold.

That scarcity is your leverage too. The same room on a Friday night is the same room, and off-peak dates are where halls can move on minimums and rental fees. If your date is flexible and your budget is not, say so out loud. May collides with prom, first communions and Mother’s Day, so it books hard.

Wildly off-topic — someday you’ll want an estate planning attorney too.

### What does a per-head quote actually include?

A per-head price almost always covers the food, the staff who serve it, and the china, glassware, flatware and house linen it is served on. It usually does not cover room rental, the bar, the service charge or sales tax. Those four turn a comfortable number into an uncomfortable one.

Ask for the list of things added later: cake cutting, chair covers and upgraded linen, a projector or microphone, security, ceremony setup, vendor meals for your DJ and photographer, coat check, valet, overtime, a cleaning fee. None of those are scams. You want them itemized before you sign.

Understand the service charge, the most misread line in the industry. A mandatory service charge is revenue to the house that helps cover labor and overhead. It is not by itself a tip to the people working your party, and it is typically applied to food and beverage and then taxed. Ask whether any of it reaches the staff.

For scale only: The Knot Worldwide’s 2026 Real Weddings Study, released February 18, 2026 from 10,474 U.S. couples married in 2025, put the average American wedding at $34,000 with 117 guests and $292 spent per guest — a national figure covering every vendor, not a hall rate. More useful: ask for a sample banquet event order, the sheet the kitchen and floor staff actually run a party from. It lists timing, counts, courses, bar hours, setup and every fee.

### In-house catering or your own caterer?

Three models, and they are not close substitutes. Some halls cook everything in house and sell you a package. Some keep an approved vendor list you must hire from. Some rent the room and let you bring anyone, usually with a kitchen access fee. Know which you are buying before you tour.

In-house catering is the least work and the least flexible. One contract covers everything, which matters when something goes wrong at 6:40 on a Saturday. The trade is menu: you eat what that kitchen does well, and cultural menus — Bosnian, Vietnamese, Indian, Mexican, soul food — are often the whole reason families hunt for an outside-catering hall. An approved vendor list sits in the middle, kept because those caterers know the kitchen and carry the right insurance.

If food is coming from outside a licensed catering operation — a family cooking, a church group, a friend with a smoker — check the health rules first. St. Louis County’s Department of Public Health issues temporary food establishment permits, application due at least ten calendar days before the event, $35 fee; the City of St. Louis runs its own temporary food permit process through Environmental Health, and Illinois events fall under the county health department on that side.

### What are the rules on alcohol, corkage and BYOB?

Alcohol is the most regulated part of your event. In Missouri, a caterer or other holder of a by-the-drink retail license can serve at your location under a temporary caterer’s permit. Under Missouri Revised Statutes section 311.485 that permit runs no more than 168 consecutive hours and costs ten dollars per calendar day, or fraction of one, paid to the director of revenue.

Inside the City of St. Louis there is a second layer. The Excise Division issues its own caterer’s permit at $15 per catered area per day alongside the state permit, and advises roughly ten days to process it. Nonprofits take a different path: a $25 picnic liquor license per booth, plus a state picnic license. The city also requires any event with alcohol to have security from a City-licensed provider — a budget line that catches people late.

On the Illinois side, licensing is municipal and training is statewide. Each city or village has its own local liquor commissioner, and the Illinois Liquor Control Commission requires BASSET certification for sellers and servers at on-premise establishments, banquet halls included, renewed every three years, under a state law effective July 1, 2015. That is why an Illinois hall often insists its own certified staff pour even when you supply the bottles.

Which brings you to corkage. Many halls forbid outside alcohol entirely, and the reason is not greed — their license and their dram shop liability ride on who poured. Where it is allowed, expect a corkage or setup fee, trained bartenders pouring it, and a hard cut-off time in the contract.

### What does capacity really mean once you add a dance floor?

Capacity is usually quoted as a maximum occupant load, not a comfortable seated dinner. Under International Building Code Table 1004.5, the occupant load factor for assembly without fixed seats is 15 square feet net per person for unconcentrated use — tables and chairs — against 7 for chairs only and 5 for standing room. A room advertised for 300 standing seats far fewer for dinner.

Then start subtracting. A dance floor, a DJ or band footprint, a buffet line with room to queue on both sides, a head table, a cake table, a gift table, a bar with a line in front of it and aisles wide enough for staff carrying trays all come out of the same net floor area the code just counted.

Table math is the fastest sanity check. Most rental inventories here are built around 60-inch rounds, which seat eight comfortably and ten tightly, and 72-inch rounds, which seat ten to twelve. Ask for a to-scale floor plan drawn with your actual table count, dance floor and buffet in place. Any hall that runs real events can produce one.

### What is in the contract, from deposit to teardown?

Read for six things: the deposit and whether any part is refundable, the payment schedule with dates, the cancellation and postponement terms, the guaranteed guest count deadline, the setup and teardown windows, and the insurance requirement. Those six decide almost every dispute between signing and the day itself.

The guarantee is what costs people money. Halls require a final guaranteed count some days ahead — often three to seven business days — and you pay for that number whether those people show up or not. Counts can usually rise after the deadline and cannot fall. Ask about postponement separately from cancellation; since 2020 most contracts treat them differently.

Setup and teardown are where good planning quietly falls apart. Find out when vendors can load in, whether another party uses the room earlier that day, how long staff needs to flip it, when the music must stop, and when everything you brought has to be out. If tables, chairs or a tent come from an outside supplier, coordinate those windows in writing — our guide to renting tools and equipment in St. Louis covers how rental periods get counted. Many halls also require event liability insurance naming the venue.

### What does the business look like from the hall’s side?

A banquet hall sells perishable inventory. Saturday, October 10 exists once, and an unsold peak Saturday cannot be recovered in February. That is why minimums exist, why prime dates carry premiums, and why deposits are usually non-refundable — the moment they hold your date they stop selling it. The room fee is rarely where the money is. Beverage carries the fattest gross margin in the building, food is thinner than guests assume once labor and waste are counted, and the mortgage, insurance, heat and core staff run whether anyone is in the room or not. Weekday daytime work — luncheons, trainings, union meetings, funeral lunches — turns a decent year into a good one. And the thing operators say to each other: the guest count always drops after the guarantee, never rises. Families hunting a hall start on a phone, which is the argument for a complete, current listing.

Got a date and a head count and nowhere to put them? Browse banquet halls across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then tour two rooms the same day and ask each for a sample banquet event order before you talk price.

### Frequently asked questions

### Q. How much does a banquet typically cost?

A.  There is no single metro number, and any figure quoted before someone knows your date, head count, menu and bar is guesswork. Five things move it: day of week and season, head count, open bar or cash bar, the room rental and minimum, and what service charge and tax add.

### Q. How many banquet tables for 50 guests?

A.  Most metro rental inventories are built around 60-inch rounds, which seat eight comfortably and ten tightly, so fifty guests is five to seven of them. Six tables of eight leaves breathing room and a seat for a late yes. Budget floor space for the tables nobody sits at: gifts, cake, buffet, DJ.

### Q. What permits are needed for a venue?

A.  The venue carries its own building occupancy and food service permits. What falls on you is event-specific. In Missouri, alcohol service off a licensed premises runs on a temporary caterer’s permit under RSMo 311.485, and the City of St. Louis adds an Excise Division permit plus licensed security. Food from an unlicensed kitchen may need a temporary food permit.

### Q. What caterers are available in St. Louis?

A.  Start with the hall, because the answer may already be decided. Ask whether it caters in house, keeps an approved vendor list, or allows open catering with a kitchen fee. If the list is open, favor caterers who have worked that specific room — they know the kitchen and the load-in.

### Q. What are some cheap banquet halls in St. Louis that cost under $500?

A.  A full-service hall on a peak Saturday evening is unlikely to land there once minimums, staffing and the bar are counted. A small budget goes furthest on a weekday or Sunday daytime rental of a parish hall, veterans’ post, union hall or park district community room, where you handle food and cleanup yourself.

### Q. What are some cheap and fun venues for small parties in Saint Louis?

A.  For twenty to forty people a banquet hall is often the wrong tool. Restaurant private rooms, brewery and winery back rooms, park pavilions, library and community center meeting rooms, and bowling or arcade party rooms handle small groups with less overhead. Check the alcohol rule first; many ban outside drinks.

### Q. How to get an event space for free?

A.  Free usually means membership rather than luck. Parishes, veterans’ posts, fraternal lodges and union halls often let members use the room at no charge or for a cleaning fee. Library branches and some community centers offer free meeting rooms to residents, generally with no alcohol and set hours. Ask about a damage deposit anyway.

### Q. What are the advantages of a banquet?

A.  One room, one timeline, one bill. A banquet keeps a large group together instead of split across three tables in a noisy restaurant, gives you a stage for toasts and a slideshow, and hands cooking, serving and cleanup to professionals. It also gives you a fixed per-person number to budget against.

### Q. Do banquet halls make good money?

A.  They can, and the economics are lumpier than they look. Revenue concentrates into a small number of prime Saturdays, beverage carries the strongest gross margin, and food is thinner than guests assume once labor and waste are in. Fixed costs run whether the hall is booked or empty, so weekday bookings often decide the year.

## How to Get Health Insurance in Missouri Right Now
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-get-health-insurance-in-missouri

Imagine it’s a Thursday afternoon in Affton and the HR email lands: your position is being eliminated, and your health plan ends the last day of the month. Or maybe you turned 26 last week and the coverage you had through a parent quietly stopped. Or you’ve been driving for a delivery app out of Maryland Heights for two years and have simply never had a card in your wallet.

Whatever put you here, the feeling is the same. You’re fine until you’re not, and the not is one bad step on an icy Kirkwood driveway. A single overnight stay in a hospital can cost more than a used car.

Here’s what most people miss: Missouri has more doors into coverage than it did five years ago, several cost little or nothing, and people around St. Louis are paid to sit down and fill out the application with you for free.

### Where do you actually get health insurance in Missouri?

Five realistic routes exist: a job (yours or a spouse’s), the ACA Marketplace at healthcare.gov, MO HealthNet — Missouri’s Medicaid program, which now covers many working adults — CHIP for children, and COBRA or state continuation from the plan you just lost. Nearly every uninsured person in the metro fits one of those five.

Order matters. Check MO HealthNet eligibility first, because if your household qualifies for Medicaid you generally can’t get the Marketplace premium tax credit, and paying full freight for a Marketplace plan you didn’t need is a costly mistake. Then check whether any job in the household offers coverage — employer plans usually beat what you can buy alone. Then the Marketplace. COBRA is worth pricing, but it’s rarely the cheapest answer.

Employer coverage. A new job, a spouse’s job, or a part-time job that offers benefits. Ask HR for the Summary of Benefits and Coverage, not the brochure.

The ACA Marketplace. Missouri uses the federal exchange at healthcare.gov. Income-based premium tax credits are applied there and nowhere else.

MO HealthNet. Missouri’s Medicaid program, expanded by a constitutional amendment voters approved in August 2020; adult coverage began in 2021 after a Missouri Supreme Court ruling.

MO HealthNet for Kids and CHIP. Children qualify at household incomes well above the adult cutoff.

COBRA or Missouri state continuation. Keeps the exact plan you had, at the full price nobody showed you before.

### What is a Special Enrollment Period, and do you have one?

A Special Enrollment Period is a window — generally 60 days — when you can buy a Marketplace plan outside the annual open enrollment because your life changed. Losing job-based coverage, moving, marrying, divorcing, having or adopting a baby, aging off a parent’s plan, and certain income changes all count. Miss the window and you may wait months.

Two details save people. First, losing coverage usually opens the window both before and after the loss, so you can line up a new plan before the old one ends instead of gambling on a gap. Second, you will likely have to prove the event — a termination letter, a lease, a birth certificate — so save the document the day you get it.

MO HealthNet and CHIP have no enrollment window at all. If you qualify, you apply the day you need it, in January or in July, and coverage can begin quickly. That’s why you check Medicaid eligibility first instead of assuming you missed your shot for the year. Exact open enrollment dates change, so confirm the current window at healthcare.gov before you plan around it.

### How does the Marketplace at healthcare.gov work for Missourians?

Missouri never built a state exchange, so Missouri residents enroll through healthcare.gov. You enter your household size and your estimated income for the coverage year, the site calculates a premium tax credit, and plans are sorted into bronze, silver and gold tiers by how much of the cost the plan carries versus how much you carry.

One rule catches almost everyone: the extra help with deductibles and copays — the cost-sharing reductions — only attaches to silver plans. A household that qualifies for that help and buys bronze to shave the monthly premium walks away from real money. Compare the silver plan even when the sticker looks higher.

Your income estimate gets settled at tax time: guess low and you may repay part of the credit, guess high and you get money back. Update healthcare.gov mid-year if your hours change. And before you click enroll, open the plan’s provider directory and drug list and confirm your doctor, your hospital and your prescriptions are in it. Networks in the St. Louis metro are narrower than they look, and a plan that excludes the hospital ten minutes from your house is a bad plan at any price.

Unrelated, and we know it — every old house eventually needs an electrician.

### Who qualifies for MO HealthNet, Missouri’s Medicaid program?

MO HealthNet now covers adults ages 19 to 64 whose household income falls under a limit set as a percentage of the federal poverty level, plus children, pregnant women, people with disabilities and seniors under separate rules. Missouri voters wrote that adult expansion into the state constitution in August 2020. You apply at mydss.mo.gov.

The income figures move every year and the family-size math is not obvious, so don’t decide you’re over the line from memory. A single person working part time at a St. Charles warehouse, a self-employed contractor in Florissant having a slow year, a parent between jobs — plenty of them talk themselves out of applying and are wrong. Check the current numbers at mydss.mo.gov.

Two things belong on your radar. Federal Medicaid rules are tightening over the next couple of years, including more frequent eligibility checks and work-related requirements for some adults, so confirm what applies to you now rather than what applied last year. And if you apply at healthcare.gov and the system thinks you may qualify for Medicaid, it routes your application to Missouri instead of selling you a plan — that hand-off is normal, not a rejection.

### What about coverage for your kids?

Children qualify at household incomes well above the adult cutoff through MO HealthNet for Kids, which includes Missouri’s CHIP program. Families above a certain income pay a modest monthly premium set on a published state chart; below that line there’s no premium at all. Coverage runs to doctor visits, immunizations, prescriptions, dental and vision.

The practical takeaway: a household can sit too high for adult MO HealthNet and still have kids who qualify. Parents on a Marketplace plan with children on MO HealthNet for Kids is ordinary and allowed, not a loophole. One application at mydss.mo.gov screens the whole house at once.

### Is COBRA worth it after you lose a job?

Sometimes, but price it against the Marketplace before you sign anything. COBRA lets you keep the exact plan you had, usually for up to 18 months, if your employer had 20 or more employees. You get 60 days to elect it, and coverage is retroactive to the day the old plan ended. The catch is the price: you pay the entire premium, including the share your employer used to pay, plus an administrative charge.

That is why COBRA quotes shock people. The plan didn’t get more expensive — you’re just seeing the whole cost for the first time. A subsidized Marketplace plan often costs a fraction of it for someone whose income just dropped, because a job loss lowers the income estimate the subsidy is built on.

Missouri also has a state continuation law for smaller employers — fewer than 20 employees — that runs up to nine months, and its election deadline is far tighter than COBRA’s. Ask HR in writing on your last day. One more trap worth knowing: exhausting COBRA opens a Special Enrollment Period, but voluntarily dropping it partway through generally does not.

### Where do you find free help enrolling in the St. Louis area?

Two kinds of people will help you at no charge. Navigators and certified application counselors are federally trained, funded by grants rather than commissions, and are not allowed to steer you toward one insurer. Licensed brokers and agents also cost you nothing, because carriers pay them, but they only sell the carriers they’re appointed with.

Both are worth using. An assister is the better call when the situation is messy — mixed eligibility inside one household, immigration questions, income that swings month to month, a stalled Medicaid application. A broker is faster once you know you want a Marketplace or Medicare plan and want help comparing networks.

To find an assister near you, use the Find Local Help tool on healthcare.gov, which lists trained organizations by ZIP code. Federally qualified health centers and area agencies on aging around the metro also keep certified counselors on staff. Bring your paperwork to the appointment and you can often finish in one sitting.

### What if you live in the Metro East on the Illinois side?

Illinois residents no longer use healthcare.gov. Get Covered Illinois became a full state-based marketplace for 2026 coverage, and existing healthcare.gov accounts moved over at the end of 2025. If you live in Belleville, Edwardsville, O’Fallon or Granite City, you enroll at getcovered.illinois.gov, and Illinois runs its own certified navigator network.

Illinois Medicaid is a separate system too. Applications run through the state benefits portal at abe.illinois.gov, and children’s coverage there is called All Kids. The eligibility rules, the premiums and the renewal paperwork are Illinois rules, not Missouri rules, even when your doctor sits five minutes across the Poplar Street Bridge.

Then there’s the thing Metro East families get wrong most often: living in Illinois and working in Missouri. Your plan follows where you live, but the network decides whether the St. Louis hospital you actually use is covered. Check the network map before enrolling, not after. Big medical bills are one of the most common paths into filing bankruptcy in Missouri, and a network mismatch is one of the quiet ways people get there.

### What this trade looks like from the agent’s side of the desk

If you run a health insurance agency here, the client never pays you. Carriers do, and on individual ACA business that is typically a flat per-member-per-month commission that keeps paying only while the member stays enrolled — so a client who lapses in March erases most of that case’s year. Group benefits pay a percentage of premium or a per-employee-per-month fee, usually level at renewal. The calendar is unforgiving: the fall and early-winter enrollment windows compress most of a year’s new business into a few weeks, and then spring and summer are unpaid service work — denied claims, replacement ID cards, terminations, a member who moved and broke their network. The complaint agents trade with each other is a carrier cutting commissions mid-year. The good ones still answer the phone in July, because retention is the whole business. Being easy to find locally is part of that — people search for help by their own ZIP code, so agencies keep a complete, current listing on St Louis Near Me Directory.

### Frequently asked questions

### Q. Do you really need health insurance?

A.  For most people, yes — not because of a penalty, but because of arithmetic. One appendectomy, one broken leg, one week in an ICU can run into five or six figures at list price. Insurance is mainly protection against the bill you can’t pay, and the annual out-of-pocket maximum on an ACA-compliant plan is the number that caps your worst year.

### Q. What is the best way to pick a health insurance plan?

A.  Start with your doctors and your prescriptions, not the premium. Open each plan’s provider directory and drug list, confirm the people and pills you already use are covered, then weigh the deductible, the out-of-pocket maximum and the premium together as one number. The lowest monthly payment is often the most expensive plan for someone who actually uses care.

### Q. Should I choose HMO or PPO?

A.  An HMO usually costs less each month, keeps you inside a defined network, and often routes specialist visits through a primary care doctor. A PPO costs more and gives you wider choice plus some out-of-network benefit. In the St. Louis metro the real question is which hospital system and specialists sit inside the network — check that first, then pick the plan type.

### Q. What does health insurance not cover?

A.  Plans differ, but common exclusions include most cosmetic procedures, routine adult dental and vision, long-term custodial care, and anything the plan judges not medically necessary. Out-of-network care may be covered poorly or not at all. Every plan publishes a Summary of Benefits and Coverage with an exclusions list — read it before you enroll, not after a claim gets denied.

### Q. Does the US penalize you for not having health insurance?

A.  The federal penalty for going uninsured was reduced to zero starting with the 2019 tax year, so there’s no federal fine now. A handful of states impose their own mandate; neither Missouri nor Illinois does. The real cost of going without isn’t a tax penalty — it’s the full retail bill, negotiated down by nobody, if something goes wrong.

### Q. How long do I need to have health insurance before I can use it?

A.  You can use it the day coverage takes effect. ACA-compliant plans can’t make you wait out a pre-existing condition. Job-based plans may impose a waiting period before coverage starts, which federal rules cap at 90 days, and Marketplace coverage generally begins the first of a month after you enroll and pay the first premium.

### Q. Is it actually cheaper to not have health insurance?

A.  It’s cheaper right up until it isn’t. Going without works out only if you never have a serious accident, a cancer diagnosis or a pregnancy, and hospitals bill uninsured patients at rates nobody negotiated down for you. Before you decide the premium is the problem, check whether you qualify for MO HealthNet or a subsidized Marketplace plan.

### Q. Can I get covered in Missouri if I missed open enrollment?

A.  Possibly. A qualifying life event — losing job-based coverage, moving, marrying, divorcing, having a baby, aging off a parent’s plan — generally opens a 60-day Special Enrollment Period at healthcare.gov. MO HealthNet and CHIP have no enrollment window at all, so you can apply any day of the year at mydss.mo.gov and coverage can start quickly if you qualify.

### Q. What documents do I need before I apply?

A.  Social Security or document numbers for everyone applying, birth dates, your best estimate of this year’s household income, recent pay stubs or self-employment records, policy numbers for any current coverage, and details of any job-based plan you were offered. The income estimate stalls more applications than anything else, so work it out before you sit down. Long-term care costs follow separate rules, covered in how to pay for a retirement home in St. Louis.

Want someone local to sit down and walk you through it? Browse health insurance agents & brokers across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then bring your pay stubs and your list of prescriptions to the first appointment — that’s the visit where most people finally get covered.

## What an Event Photographer Actually Covers in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-an-event-photographer-actually-covers-in-st-louis

Imagine it’s a Tuesday night and you’ve been handed the one job nobody at the planning meeting wanted: find the photographer. The party is in Kirkwood, eleven weeks out, and three quotes are already sitting in your inbox. One says four hours. One says half-day coverage. One just says coverage, which could mean almost anything.

Maybe you’ve been on the wrong end of this before. A cousin’s wedding in St. Charles where the photographer packed the bags before the toasts. A company anniversary in Maryland Heights where the gallery landed four months later with 60 images and not one shot of the whole team together. Nobody argued about the price on those jobs. They argued about what the price bought.

That gap is the whole story. An event photography booking isn’t a picture — it’s a contract with five moving parts: a block of hours, a count of people holding cameras, a delivery format, a delivery date, and a license telling you what you may legally do with the files. Read those five lines and you know almost everything that matters. Here’s what each one means around here, from Florissant to Belleville.

### What is included in event photography?

Event photography is sold as a block of time, not as a set of pictures. A standard booking includes a named window of coverage hours, a stated number of photographers on site, a set of edited digital images delivered through an online gallery, and a license describing how you may use them. Nearly everything else is a separate line item.

The separate lines are where the surprises live: a second shooter, an album, prints, raw files, drone footage, travel past a set radius, rush delivery, and overtime. None of those are hidden fees when they’re written down. They only become hidden when the quote said coverage and you assumed it meant everything.

One more thing to watch. Image counts are usually written as estimates, not guarantees. A contract that promises “approximately 400 edited images” is promising a range, because a four-hour cocktail reception and a four-hour graduation produce very different numbers of usable frames. If a specific shot matters — the full staff, the grandparents, the sponsor banner — put it on a shot list and attach it to the contract instead of hoping the number covers it.

### How many hours of coverage do you actually need?

Count backward from the moments you can’t lose, then add a buffer at both ends. For a wedding, that’s usually the last hour of getting ready through the first twenty or thirty minutes of dancing. For a corporate event, it’s registration and clean room shots before doors open, then the keynote, then whatever awards or headshots happen afterward.

The buffer matters more than people expect, because events run late and contracts don’t. If coverage starts at 4:00 p.m. and the ceremony that was supposed to start at 4:30 actually starts at 5:10, you just spent 70 minutes of paid coverage on an empty room. Ask the photographer when their clock starts — at the contracted time, or when they begin shooting.

Then read the overtime clause before you sign, because it is the line people never look at. Three questions answer it: is overtime available at all, what is the rate, and what is the billing increment? Some photographers bill in half-hour blocks, some in full hours, and some have a hard out because the venue exit or a booking the next morning won’t bend. A photographer who tells you no in advance is doing you a favor.

### Is a second shooter included, or is that a separate line?

Assume a second shooter is a separate line unless the contract names two photographers and the hours each one works. This is not a luxury upgrade. It is a coverage question, because one person cannot photograph two rooms at the same time and plenty of events run two rooms at the same time on purpose.

The obvious case is a conference with concurrent breakout sessions. The less obvious case is a wedding where one side is getting ready at a hotel in Clayton and the other side is at a house in Affton, twenty minutes apart in Saturday traffic. A single photographer solves that by cutting one location short. Two photographers solve it by being in both places.

If a second shooter is included, ask three follow-ups. Who edits their images, the lead or the second? Do those frames land in the same gallery as everything else? And does the second shooter work under the lead photographer’s contract and insurance, or their own? The answers are usually reasonable. You just want them in writing before the day rather than discovered afterward, when a set of images you assumed you owned turns out to belong to someone you never met.

### What do you actually get back, and when?

In almost every current booking you get edited, color-corrected JPEG files in an online gallery you can download, plus a print release. Four numbers turn that vague sentence into something enforceable: how many images, at what resolution, how long the gallery stays live, and the delivery deadline stated in business days or weeks.

There is no industry-wide standard turnaround. That is the honest answer, and it is exactly why the number has to be in your contract instead of in your head. Some photographers deliver a corporate event in a week because the client needs images for a Monday newsletter. Some deliver a wedding in eight to ten weeks because a full gallery is a genuinely long edit. Both are normal. A contract that says the gallery will arrive in a timely manner is not.

Ask about the sneak peek too — a handful of images sent within a day or two, which is what you post while the full set is still being edited. And ask what happens if the deadline slips. A contract with a stated remedy is a contract someone has thought about.

Gallery expiration is the quiet one. Online galleries are hosted, hosting costs money, and most of them come down eventually. Find out whether yours lives for 90 days, a year, or forever, then download the full-resolution set to two places the week it arrives. If your event runs indoors and you are also weighing a controlled portrait session on the side, the tradeoffs are different again, and we walk through those in renting a photo studio in St. Louis.

### Who owns the photos — you or the photographer?

The photographer owns the copyright by default, and you get a license. The U.S. Copyright Office states the general rule directly: the author and initial copyright owner of a photograph is the person who takes the photo. Paying for a session does not transfer that ownership on its own, and most event contracts do not try to.

There is one exception, and it is narrower than people assume. A commissioned photograph becomes a work made for hire only when there is an express written agreement between the photographer and the commissioning party and the work serves a purpose the statute specifically identifies, according to the Copyright Office guidance written for photographers. A work-for-hire line dropped into a party invoice often does not meet that bar. If your organization genuinely needs to own the images outright — a hospital system, a school district, an agency shooting for its own client — that gets negotiated on purpose, in writing, and it usually costs more.

What you should actually read is the usage language. Personal-use licenses cover printing, sharing and posting. Corporate clients often need more: paid social, recruiting materials, a billboard, a press release. Those uses are frequently excluded from a standard license and priced separately, so tell the photographer where the images are going before the quote, not after the campaign is built.

Raw files are the other flashpoint. Most contracts exclude them, and the reason is craft rather than stinginess: a raw file is an unfinished negative that looks flat and wrong without the photographer’s edit, and handing it over puts unfinished work into the world under their name. If the underlying worry is that you only got 300 frames out of 2,000, ask for a larger edited set or one specific extra edit instead. That request usually gets a yes.

Wildly off-topic — the metro’s bakeries deserve a Saturday morning.

### What do travel, parking and venue access actually cover?

Most metro bookings include travel inside a stated radius, with mileage, parking and sometimes lodging billed beyond it. Ask where the radius is measured from and whether downtown parking and valet are included, because those are small numbers that turn into awkward conversations. The bigger variable is not distance. It is permission at the location.

Rules differ sharply from one St. Louis landmark to the next. At Gateway Arch National Park, the National Park Service says permits and fees are not required for filming or still photography involving eight or fewer individuals, in areas open to the public, using hand-carried equipment only, and without exclusive use of a site. That national policy took effect January 4, 2025 under the EXPLORE Act, Public Law 118-234, and it treats commercial, personal and news shooting the same. Larger crews need a permit and the park charges location and cost-recovery fees. The park also notes that no separate photography permit is required when the shooting is tied to an activity already authorized in writing, such as a permitted wedding.

The Missouri Botanical Garden runs the other way. Formal photography — weddings, family sessions, prom, quinceañera portraits — requires a permit, reservations are asked for at least 24 hours ahead, sessions are limited to outdoor public areas of the Garden, and Garden policy prohibits lighting equipment and reflectors while capping props at one per person, no larger than two feet square. Sessions have to be finished and the group departed by closing. A photographer who has worked there knows all of that. One who has not may show up with a light stand and no permit.

Tower Grove Park is the easy one: its FAQ states that photography permits are not needed in the park. Across the river, the Illinois Department of Natural Resources requires an Activity Permit for groups of 20 or more at IDNR-owned, managed or leased sites, plus a separate Filming Questionnaire for any filming used for commercial, publication or advertisement purposes. Visitors shooting for personal use sit outside that rule.

Drone coverage adds a federal layer. The FAA is explicit that a small drone under 55 pounds flown for work or business must be operated under Part 107, which means a certificated remote pilot and a registered aircraft. Around here that is geographic as much as legal, because controlled airspace surrounds St. Louis Lambert International, Spirit of St. Louis Airport in Chesterfield, St. Louis Downtown Airport in Cahokia Heights and MidAmerica St. Louis Airport in Mascoutah. A drone shot inside that airspace needs an authorization, not just a good camera. Ask to see the certificate.

One last access item. Many venues require vendors to carry liability insurance and to send a certificate naming the venue as an additional insured, often weeks ahead of the date. The venue sets the limit, so get the requirement from the venue and hand it to your photographer early instead of the week of.

### What shows up on the invoice in Missouri versus Illinois?

In Missouri, sales tax on photography turns on whether you receive something physical. The Missouri Department of Revenue Photographers Tax Matrix — issued November 28, 2022 and revised March 28, 2025 — lists downloaded photos, and photography services that do not include tangible personal property, as exempt. Photography services delivered with a CD, DVD, USB device, photo album, frames or canvas images are taxable, and a portrait sitting fee bundled into a sale of physical goods is taxable as well.

Practically, that means a digital-only gallery and a package with a leather album can be taxed differently in Missouri even when the shooting is identical. The album is not only a nicer keepsake. It changes the tax character of the sale.

Illinois handles the same money through a different mechanism. Under 86 Ill. Adm. Code 130.2000, the Illinois Department of Revenue says that when photoprocessing is the only service provided, tax is collected on 100 percent of the selling price, and that when a professional photographer separately states a photoprocessing charge alongside other services, tax is collected on 10 percent of that separately stated amount. So an itemized invoice for a Belleville or Edwardsville event can be built quite differently from one for the same night in Webster Groves.

Neither of us is your accountant, and any specific situation turns on its own facts. What you can do is simple: ask whether the quoted figure includes tax, and ask which line items are taxable. A photographer who answers that quickly has been doing this a while.

### What event photographers wish clients understood

The event is the short part of the job. A long reception produces thousands of frames that get culled, corrected and retouched one at a time at a desk, which is why turnaround is measured in weeks and why a rush fee is real work rather than a penalty. The calendar is brutally uneven too. October is the single biggest wedding month at 17 percent of 2024 weddings, according to The Knot 2025 Real Weddings Study of 16,956 couples, November and December fill with corporate holiday parties, and January is when the phone stops. Federal wage data explains the rest: the Bureau of Labor Statistics put the median photographer wage at $42,520 a year in May 2024, with 66 percent of the 151,200 photographers self-employed. The person quoting you is usually the whole company — sales, shooting, editing, invoicing, and the sales tax on their own cameras and computers. Being findable is the other half of that job, which is why a complete, current listing on St Louis Near Me Directory matters to the people who work these rooms.

### Frequently asked questions

### Q. What is included in event photography?

A.  A standard event photography booking includes a set number of coverage hours, a stated number of photographers, edited digital images delivered in an online gallery, and a license describing how you may use them. Second shooters, albums, prints, raw files, drone work, travel beyond a set radius, rush delivery and overtime are usually separate line items rather than inclusions.

### Q. What is the purpose of event photography?

A.  Event photography documents something that happens once, in real time, without stopping it. The photographer works around a live schedule instead of directing it, capturing people, the room, the speakers and the details as they occur. For businesses and nonprofits the output doubles as reusable material for recaps, sponsor reporting, recruiting and next year’s promotion.

### Q. What are some examples of event photography?

A.  Weddings and receptions, corporate conferences and keynotes, galas and fundraisers, award banquets, grand openings, retirement parties, graduations, quinceañeras, bar and bat mitzvahs, sporting events, trade shows, and school or church events. Headshot stations running alongside a conference are common too, though those are usually quoted as a separate service with their own hourly block and delivery timeline.

### Q. Where are some good locations for a photoshoot in St. Louis?

A.  Choose by permit rules as much as by scenery. Tower Grove Park states that photography permits are not needed there. The Missouri Botanical Garden requires a permit for formal sessions, limits you to outdoor public areas, and prohibits lighting equipment and reflectors. Gateway Arch National Park needs no permit for eight or fewer people using hand-carried gear in public areas. Illinois DNR sites require an activity permit for groups of 20 or more.

### Q. What is the 20 60 20 rule in photography?

A.  There is no single accepted definition, and it is not a standard taught by any recognized photography body. Online sources use the phrase in at least three conflicting ways: a split of the frame into foreground, subject and background; a claim that 20 percent of your shots are strong, 60 percent average and 20 percent unusable; and a split of practice time. Do not let it drive a booking decision.

### Q. How much should an event photographer charge?

A.  There is no single right number, because the price is assembled from coverage hours, how many photographers work the room, editing time, delivery format and deadline, license terms, travel, and whether physical goods make the sale taxable. Ask for one total plus the itemized list behind it. For local ranges, see what a photographer costs in St. Louis.

### Q. Is $100 an hour good for a photographer?

A.  It depends entirely on what the hour includes. A quoted hourly rate for event coverage also has to fund editing hours you never see, gear, insurance, self-employment taxes and unbilled travel, so $100 an hour of shooting is nothing like $100 an hour of take-home pay. For scale, the Bureau of Labor Statistics put the median photographer wage at $20.44 an hour in May 2024. Judge the whole package, not the divided rate.

### Q. How much to charge for a 4 hour event photography?

A.  Four hours is a block of time, not a package, so the number depends on what sits on either side of it: one photographer or two, how many edited images get delivered, how fast, what license comes with them, travel, and whether an album or USB drive makes the sale taxable. Price the whole scope as one total, then confirm the overtime rate and billing increment before signing.

### Q. Is $4000 a lot for a wedding photographer?

A.  It depends on what the figure covers. Ten hours with two photographers and an album is a completely different product from four hours of digital-only coverage, even at the same price. For context, The Knot 2025 Real Weddings Study of 16,956 couples married in 2024 put the national average total wedding cost at $33,000, photography being one line among many. Compare hours, shooters and deliverables rather than headline numbers.

### Q. How many photographers are making over $300,000 a year?

A.  Very few, and the Bureau of Labor Statistics does not publish a count at that level. What it does publish for May 2024: a median photographer wage of $42,520 a year, or $20.44 an hour, with the top 10 percent earning more than $45.56 an hour, across 151,200 jobs of which 66 percent were self-employed. Photographers clearing $300,000 are outliers, usually running a studio with staff.

## Gelato vs. Ice Cream, and Where to Get Both in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/gelato-vs-ice-cream-and-where-to-get-both-in-st-louis

Imagine it’s the first Thursday all year that stays warm after sundown. Dinner in Kirkwood is done, or the ballgame let out early, and somebody in the back seat says the word out loud. Ice cream. Ten minutes later you’re standing at a lit-up window reading a board that lists gelato in one column and ice cream in the other, at different prices, in different sized cups.

You pick one. It’s good. But somewhere between the first spoonful and the bottom of the cup the question shows up anyway: what is actually different about these two things, and did the smaller cup just cost more for no reason? Meanwhile a stand three miles away in Affton sells neither, because it only makes frozen custard — and a fair number of people in this metro would tell you that settles the whole argument.

There is a real answer, and it comes down to three things you can measure: how much butterfat is in it, how much air got whipped into it, and how cold it is when it reaches your spoon. Price, texture, and how loud the flavor tastes all fall out of those three. Here’s how it works, and where St. Louis’ own frozen dessert fits into the comparison.

### Is gelato basically just ice cream?

No. Gelato is a different formula served a different way — less butterfat, far less whipped-in air, and a warmer serving temperature. Federal law sets a floor for anything sold as ice cream: under the FDA standard of identity at 21 CFR 135.110, ice cream must contain at least 10 percent milkfat and at least 20 percent total milk solids. Traditional gelato is built below that line, commonly in the 4 to 9 percent range.

That same rule also caps how much air a maker can sell you. Ice cream must weigh at least 4.5 pounds per gallon and carry at least 1.6 pounds of total food solids per gallon. Without that weight floor, a manufacturer could keep churning air into the mix until a gallon container held almost nothing.

The word for that whipped-in air is overrun, and it is the single biggest difference between the two products. Robert Roberts, head of Penn State’s food science department, explained the range in an April 2015 university piece: low-overrun ice creams run roughly 20 to 40 percent, meaning the air boosted the volume of the starting mix by that much, while high-overrun products reach up to 100 percent — double the original volume, light and fluffy. Gelato sits at the bottom of that scale, with very little air whipped in.

One more wrinkle that surprises people: there is no federal standard of identity for gelato at all. The International Dairy Foods Association said so plainly when it opposed a proposed California gelato standard in October 2013, noting that gelato has no federal definition and that each maker’s product carries different levels of dairy solids, fat, egg yolk solids, and flavoring. Ice cream and frozen custard are legally defined terms in this country. Gelato is a tradition, not a regulation.

### What is so special about gelato ice cream?

Density and temperature. Because gelato carries so little air, a scoop of it weighs noticeably more than the same-size scoop of airy ice cream, and it lands on the tongue as dense and elastic rather than fluffy. It is also served warmer — commonly cited in the low teens Fahrenheit, against the 0 to 10 degree range Penn State says it serves its own hard-pack ice cream at.

Those two facts do the work. Fat coats your tongue and mutes aroma, so a lower-fat base lets fruit and nut flavors read sharper. Cold numbs your palate, so a few degrees warmer means you taste more of what’s there. That is why a lemon gelato can taste almost aggressive next to a lemon ice cream made from the same fruit, and why gelato pistachio tastes like pistachio instead of like sweet cream with a green tint.

The trade-off is that gelato is fragile. Warmer serving temperature and low fat mean it melts fast and goes grainy if it warms and refreezes. A gelato case is a fussier piece of equipment than a dipping cabinet, and a shop that runs both is running two different temperature zones on purpose.

### Which is healthier, gelato or regular ice cream?

Gelato usually has less fat per bite, but that does not automatically make it the lighter dessert. Gelato bases typically run 4 to 9 percent butterfat against the 10 percent minimum U.S. law requires of ice cream, and many premium ice creams run considerably higher. So gram for gram, gelato is often the lower-fat choice.

The catch is the air. Since gelato is denser, an identical-looking scoop contains more actual dessert — more sugar and more milk solids — than a scoop of high-overrun ice cream. Gelato also tends to lean on sugar to keep the texture soft at that warmer serving temperature. Lower fat, more mass, often more sugar. Those partly cancel out.

The honest version: neither is health food, and the portion in front of you matters more than the category on the sign. If you want the lighter option, order the smaller size, or order a sorbetto, which is fruit and sugar with no dairy at all. Anyone managing blood sugar, cholesterol, or a dairy allergy should be reading the shop’s posted nutrition information rather than trusting the word gelato to do the work.

### Is gelato ice cream expensive?

Gelato usually costs more per cup than a comparable scoop of ice cream, and there are real reasons rather than pure markup. Low overrun means the shop is selling you dessert instead of air, so a gallon of mix yields fewer servings. Gelato is also made in small batches, turns over faster, and sits in equipment that costs more to buy and run than a standard dipping cabinet.

For a baseline on the grocery side of the comparison, CNN reported on July 19, 2026 that the average price of a half gallon of packaged ice cream tracked by the Bureau of Labor Statistics slipped back below $6 in June 2026, after running near $6.26 for the prior two years and hitting roughly $6.49 in June 2025 — the drop credited to falling butter prices. Shop prices in the St. Louis metro are a different market entirely, and they move with rent, labor, and the weather, so ask at the window rather than trusting a number you read online.

Worth knowing before you compare receipts: a scoop shop is selling a made-on-site product with a person behind the counter, and a half gallon from the freezer aisle is selling you volume. Those are not the same purchase, and price per ounce is a poor way to judge either one.

Wildly off-topic — that drip under the sink needs a St. Louis plumber.

### Where does frozen custard fit, and why does St. Louis care so much?

Frozen custard is ice cream with egg yolk in it, and unlike gelato, it is legally defined. The same FDA rule, 21 CFR 135.110, covers both products: it is called ice cream when it contains less than 1.4 percent egg yolk solids by weight, and frozen custard when it contains at least 1.4 percent. That yolk is why custard eats silkier and richer than either of the other two, and why it holds a spoon standing up.

This metro treats custard as its own food group, and that is not marketing. Ted Drewes has been selling frozen custard here since 1929 by the company’s own count — the Missouri Encyclopedia dates the first stand to 1930 on Natural Bridge Road — and the Chippewa Street stand opened in 1941 on an alignment of Route 66, where it still is. The concrete, the malt so thick it gets handed to you upside down, dates to 1959. The Chippewa stand opened its 97th season in 2026.

Custard also explains a habit visitors find strange. Around here the default summer stop is a walk-up window with a line in the parking lot, not a sit-down shop, and the line is part of the deal. It’s where teams end up after a game, which is roughly the same reason a Saturday morning in this town so often runs from a gym to a custard stand — if that is your household, our guide on signing your kid up for gymnastics in St. Louis covers the part that happens before the ice cream.

### How can you tell real gelato from ice cream sold as gelato?

Look at the case before you look at the menu. Because there is no legal definition of gelato in the United States, the word on the sign guarantees nothing — the product in the pan does. Four tells are worth more than any label:

Color. Real pistachio is a dull khaki-brown, not fluorescent green. Banana is grayish, not yellow. Mint is off-white unless something was added to make it green. Bright, uniform, candy-store colors mean coloring, and coloring usually travels with the rest of the shortcuts.

How it’s held. Traditional Italian shops keep gelato in covered metal tins, called pozzetti, sunk into a cold well — you can’t see the product at all. Open display cases are common and fine, but towering whipped mountains with decorations stuck in them are a display technique, and holding a mound that tall generally takes more air and more stabilizer.

The flavor list. A short list that changes is a good sign, because it usually means small batches. Forty flavors available every day of the year usually means a mix shipped in rather than made on site. Neither is a crime, but they are different products.

The spade. Gelato is served with a flat paddle, not a round scoop, because it’s soft enough to spread and fold. If it comes out in hard spheres straight from the freezer, you are being handed something colder and harder than gelato is supposed to be.

### Does Missouri or Illinois define what gelato is?

Neither state defines gelato, and both lean on the federal rules for the products that are defined. What each side of the river does regulate is the plant. In Missouri, a frozen dessert license must be obtained from the Department of Health and Senior Services by any food establishment, processing plant, or broker manufacturing or distributing ice cream, mellorine, or frozen dessert products in the state, under 19 CSR 20-1.025.

In Illinois, frozen desserts are handled as manufactured dairy products under Title 77 of the Illinois Administrative Code, Part 785, with supplemental requirements for plants that manufacture and package frozen desserts at Sections 785.900 through 785.990 — covering pasteurization of the mix, cooling, storage, lab testing, and labeling. Those rules also require dairy products to meet the federal standards of identity in Title 21 of the Code of Federal Regulations, under the Illinois Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act at 410 ILCS 620.

The practical upshot for a customer in Belleville or Edwardsville is the same as for one in Florissant or St. Charles: a shop calling something ice cream or frozen custard has a federal composition standard to meet on both sides of the river, and a shop calling something gelato does not. Judge the gelato with your eyes and your spoon.

### Where is the best place to get gelato?

The best gelato near you is almost always the shop making it on the premises in small batches, and you can usually confirm that by asking one question at the counter: do you make it here? A shop that does will tell you within about four seconds, and will often tell you what got made that morning. That answer is a better signal than any award sticker on the door.

In this metro, the search is worth doing by neighborhood rather than by ranking. Italian bakeries and cafes, coffee shops that added a case, and dedicated gelaterias all sell it, and the mix of them differs a lot between The Hill, Kirkwood, St. Charles, Maryland Heights, and the Metro East. Go for the small list, the muted colors, and the paddle. Ranked lists go stale; those three tells do not.

### What ice cream and gelato shop owners deal with that customers never see

Ask anyone who runs a scoop shop and the same two complaints come up. First, the calendar does the hiring and firing. Ice cream production nationally peaks March through September, according to the International Dairy Foods Association, and a walk-up stand’s year is decided by maybe fourteen good weather weekends. A cold, wet June is not a slow month — it is a hole that November cannot fill. Ted Drewes historically closed for winter and sold Christmas trees to bridge the gap, which is the oldest answer in this market to a problem every operator still has.

Second, the mix is rarely what hurts. Labor, rent, and equipment do the damage, and running gelato alongside hard-pack means holding two temperature zones and eating more waste, because gelato that warms and refreezes is finished. The operators who make it work usually shrink the flavor list and turn batches faster instead of expanding the case. People search for this category locally and by neighborhood, so having a complete, accurate listing with real hours matters most in exactly the weeks that decide the year — which is the argument for getting listed on St Louis Near Me Directory before the season, not during it.

Ready to settle the gelato question with your own spoon? Browse ice cream and gelato shops across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then pick two near you — one gelateria, one custard stand — and taste them a week apart so the comparison is honest.

### Frequently asked questions

### Q. Why do people prefer gelato over ice cream?

A.  Texture and flavor intensity, mostly. Less air makes gelato dense and elastic instead of fluffy, and less butterfat plus a warmer serving temperature lets fruit, nut, and chocolate flavors come through sharper. Plenty of people prefer ice cream for the opposite reasons — it is colder, richer, and holds up better in a cone on a hot night.

### Q. Is gelato healthier than ice cream?

A.  Usually lower in fat, not necessarily lighter overall. Gelato typically runs 4 to 9 percent butterfat versus the 10 percent floor U.S. law sets for ice cream. But gelato is denser, so an identical-looking scoop holds more dessert, and many recipes carry more sugar to stay soft. Portion size decides more than the category does.

### Q. Is Talenti actually gelato?

A.  It is sold and labeled as gelato, and no U.S. rule stops that — the International Dairy Foods Association confirmed in 2013 that gelato has no federal standard of identity. Talenti started as a Dallas gelateria in 2003 and was bought by Unilever in 2014. Packaged pints stored near 0 degrees eat colder and firmer than gelato scooped fresh from a shop case.

### Q. Is gelato more expensive than ice cream?

A.  Usually, per serving. Low overrun means a shop gets fewer portions out of a gallon of mix, because it is selling dessert rather than whipped-in air. Small batches, faster turnover, and dedicated equipment add cost on top. Grocery-aisle ice cream stays cheapest per ounce, but that is a different product than a scoop made on site.

### Q. How much is one serving of gelato?

A.  On a packaged label, one serving of a frozen dessert is two-thirds of a cup. The FDA raised the reference amount for ice cream from half a cup to two-thirds of a cup in its Nutrition Facts label final rule, effective July 26, 2016. Shop portions ignore that number entirely, and a small cup often holds two servings or more.

### Q. Does gelato go in the freezer or refrigerator?

A.  The freezer, always. Refrigerator temperatures melt it and ruin the texture permanently. Home freezers are meant to sit at 0 degrees Fahrenheit or below, which is colder than a gelato case, so leftover gelato turns hard as a brick. Set it on the counter five to ten minutes before serving and it comes back to something close to right.

### Q. Is gelato stronger than ice cream?

A.  In flavor, generally yes. Two things drive it: less butterfat means less fat coating your tongue and dulling aroma, and a warmer serving temperature means your palate is less numbed. That is why fruit and nut flavors read sharper in gelato. It is not stronger in calories or sugar, and it contains no alcohol or caffeine unless a flavor adds them.

### Q. What is the most famous custard in St. Louis?

A.  Ted Drewes, and it isn’t close. The family has sold frozen custard here since 1929 by its own count, and the Chippewa Street stand opened in 1941 on a Route 66 alignment, where it opened its 97th season in 2026. Its concrete — handed to you upside down to prove how thick it is — dates to 1959. Plenty of other custard stands operate across the metro.

### Q. What is a signature St. Louis dessert?

A.  Gooey butter cake and the frozen custard concrete are the two. Gooey butter cake came out of a south St. Louis German-American bakery in the 1930s, reportedly by accident when a baker got the proportions wrong; the Danzer, Koppe, and St. Louis Pastries families have all been credited, and the origin is still argued about locally.

### Q. Which president loved ice cream the most?

A.  Ronald Reagan is the one who put it in writing. He signed Proclamation 5219 on July 9, 1984, naming that July National Ice Cream Month and July 15, 1984 National Ice Cream Day, and the proclamation called ice cream a nutritious and wholesome food enjoyed by over ninety percent of Americans. National Ice Cream Day has been marked on the third Sunday in July ever since.

## What to Know Before Signing Your Kid Up for Gymnastics in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-to-know-before-signing-your-kid-up-for-gymnastics-in-st-louis

Imagine it’s a Saturday morning in Affton and your five-year-old has spent four months turning the living room into a landing mat. The coffee table has been moved twice. Something got cartwheeled into. A friend swears by her daughter’s gym in Kirkwood, a coworker in St. Charles says the one near her is better, and now you’re holding a phone with eleven tabs open and no idea which question to ask first.

Here’s what nobody says out loud at the start. Signing your kid up for gymnastics is two completely different decisions wearing the same word. One is a 45-minute class that ends the week your kid gets bored. The other is a multi-year, several-nights-a-week commitment with meet entry fees, out-of-town weekends, and a national governing body with a real rulebook and real minimum ages. Gyms from Florissant to Belleville run both tracks, frequently in the same building, and the hand-off between them arrives sooner than most parents expect.

So this is a decision guide, not a ranking of gyms. What the sport actually requires at each age, what the levels commit you to in hours and dollars, what a first class looks like from the bleachers, the credential questions worth asking before you hand over a card, and how the answer shifts depending on which side of the river you land on.

### At what age should you start gymnastics?

Whenever your kid can walk, if you just want a rec class — but the sport’s own rulebook says competition starts at four. The 2026-2027 USA Gymnastics Women’s Rules & Policies sets the minimum age for Development Program Level 1 at the 4th birthday, Level 2 at the 5th, Level 3 at the 6th, and Levels 4 through 7 at the 7th. Nothing before that is competitive.

That matters because of what it tells you about the years before four. Parent-and-tot classes, walking-age tumbling and preschool classes are motor-skill work with music and stamps on hands. They are genuinely good for balance, body awareness and taking turns, and they are not a competitive on-ramp in any formal sense. A three-year-old in a Tuesday morning class in Webster Groves is not behind anyone. There is nothing yet to be behind in.

The Xcel track, the alternative competitive program USA Gymnastics runs alongside the Development Program, opens earlier at the bottom and stays open longer. Its published minimums are the 5th birthday for Bronze, the 6th for Silver, the 7th for Gold, the 8th for Platinum, the 9th for Diamond and the 12th for Sapphire. Bronze, Silver and Gold carry no prerequisite scores at all, which is exactly why a kid who starts at eight still has somewhere real to go.

### What does a first gymnastics class actually look like?

Forty-five minutes to an hour, a small group per coach, and far more rolling, hanging and jumping than anything you’d recognize from television. Preschool classes run as a station circuit. School-age rec classes usually rotate through vault, bars, beam and floor, spend roughly ten minutes at each, and finish with a stretch.

Go watch one before you pay for a session. Most gyms across the metro will let you observe or take a trial class, and one hour in the viewing area answers questions no brochure will. Count the kids per coach. Watch whether coaches are physically spotting on beam and bars or standing back and talking. Notice whether the youngest group is being taught or babysat — the difference is visible within about four minutes.

Bring the practical stuff too: leotard or fitted athletic clothes, hair tied back and off the face, no jewelry, bare feet. Long hair loose on beam is a real problem, not a style note. If your kid is nervous, the first class is almost always the hardest one and gyms know it, so ask whether you can sit where your kid can see you for the first few weeks.

### What is the difference between recreational and competitive gymnastics?

Rec is one class a week with no meets, no national membership dues and no season. Competitive means your child is a registered USA Gymnastics athlete on a team, training multiple days a week across a fall-to-spring season, traveling to sanctioned meets, and climbing a defined ladder with published age minimums and score requirements.

The step between them usually gets called pre-team or developmental, and it is where most families get surprised. Pre-team typically means two practices a week instead of one, a longer practice, and a coach who starts talking about the fall. It is the last low-commitment stop on the road. Once a kid is invited to team, the hours, the fees and the family calendar all change together rather than one at a time.

Neither track is the serious one and neither is the fun one. Plenty of kids do rec gymnastics for six years, never compete, and come out with better body awareness than anyone else on the middle-school volleyball roster. If you’re still sampling activities generally, our roundup of the best kids music, art and dance classes in St. Louis covers the other lanes worth trying before you hand a whole calendar to one sport.

### What do the USA Gymnastics levels and Xcel divisions commit you to?

Two separate ladders, and the one your gym puts your kid on shapes the next several years. The Development Program runs Levels 1 through 10 with score-based mobility between them. Xcel runs Bronze, Silver, Gold, Platinum, Diamond and Sapphire with flexible routines, fewer required hours by design, and no prerequisite scores below Platinum.

Inside the Development Program, Levels 1 to 3 are the developmental segment and can be run non-competitively within a gym’s pre-team. Levels 4 and 5 are compulsory, meaning every gymnast in the country performs the same routine. Levels 6 through 10 are optional, meaning routines are built around the individual athlete. Moving up is not a coach’s opinion: USA Gymnastics requires a mobility score at a sanctioned meet — 34.00 all-around at Level 4 to reach Level 5, 32.00 at Level 5 to reach Level 6, 32.00 at Level 7, then 34.00 at Level 8 and again at Level 9. Athletes may not skip levels except under the published exceptions.

Xcel is the track more St. Louis families should be asking about by name, because it is built for exactly the kid this article is about. A gymnast with no previous competitive experience can enter Xcel at Bronze, Silver or Gold at her coach’s discretion. Divisions are assigned by current skill rather than a fixed climb. Ask any gym you’re considering whether it fields an Xcel team, how many hours a week each division trains, and roughly what share of its competitive athletes sit on that track versus the Development Program. The answer tells you what kind of gym it is.

The hours question is the one that reshapes a household. Rec is one hour. Pre-team is commonly two short practices. A Development Program team schedule climbs steadily from there and, at the upper optional levels, becomes the dominant fixed object in a family’s week — several evenings plus meet Saturdays through the winter and spring. Ask for the actual practice schedule for each level in writing before you say yes to team. Not the range. The schedule.

Unrelated, and we know it — that ceiling stain means you need a roofer.

### What does gymnastics cost in St. Louis?

Tuition is the smallest line on a competitive season sheet, and no honest article can quote you a metro-wide rec class price, because gyms bill by the session, by the month and by the punch card and none of it is standardized. What can be quoted are the fixed national fees, and those are the ones parents never see coming.

USA Gymnastics athlete membership for the 2026-2027 season is $75, or $27 for a first-time athlete, covering August 1, 2026 through July 31, 2027. That fee is per athlete, per year, and it is entirely separate from whatever your gym charges. On the Illinois side there is one more small one: Region 5 collects $2.00 per athlete at any USA Gymnastics sanctioned event held in Illinois, Indiana, Kentucky, Michigan or Ohio.

The honest cost ladder runs bottom to top like this. A weekly rec class is monthly tuition and nothing else. Pre-team adds a second practice, so roughly a second tuition. Entry-level team adds the $75 USA Gymnastics athlete membership, a competition leotard, warm-ups, a team fee, and a per-meet entry fee for every meet on the schedule. Upper-level team adds travel — hotel nights, gas, meals, and a coach travel share that gyms commonly split across the athletes attending each meet. Nobody hands you that whole stack at once. Ask for it at once.

Three questions get you most of the way to a real number before you sign anything. What is the total of the season fees, listed line by line, for the level we’re joining? How many meets are on the schedule and what is the entry fee for each one? And what happens if we withdraw mid-season — is the season fee refundable, prorated, or gone? Get all three answers in writing, from the gym, before the season opens.

### What safety and coach credentials should you ask about?

Ask whether every coach on the floor holds a current USA Gymnastics professional membership, and ask to see it. For the 2026-2027 season a USA Gymnastics Competitive Coach membership costs $99 and requires a background check renewed every two years, the U110 U.S. Center for SafeSport core course, USA Gymnastics Safety Certification renewed every four years, the U100 fundamental instruction course, the U112 course on tough coaching and emotional abuse, and a concussion education acknowledgment.

Those are requirements, not suggestions, and a gym that has done the work will answer in one sentence without getting defensive. Worth knowing too: under the Protecting Young Victims from Sexual Abuse and Safe Sport Authorization Act of 2017, signed into law in February 2018, an adult authorized to interact with a minor amateur athlete must report a reasonable suspicion of child abuse within 24 hours. That is federal law and it applies to your kid’s gym.

You can also check names yourself, for free, before the first class. The U.S. Center for SafeSport maintains a public Centralized Disciplinary Database at cdd.uscenterforsafesport.org, searchable by name, city, state and sport affiliation. USA Gymnastics separately publishes a list of suspended, restricted and permanently ineligible participants. Five minutes with both is an ordinary thing for a parent to do and nothing to feel awkward about.

Then look at the floor itself. Where is the AED and who on shift is trained to use it? Is there a written concussion protocol, and who has authority to sit a kid down? How often is equipment inspected and pit foam replaced? Is anyone spotting new skills, or are kids attempting them alone at the end of a rotation? A gym that has thought about injuries answers fast. And if an injury does show up and keeps showing up, that is a physician’s call, not a coach’s — our guide on when to see an orthopedist in St. Louis covers what actually warrants the appointment.

### Does it matter which side of the river your gym is on?

Yes, in two concrete ways. Competitively, Missouri and Illinois sit in different USA Gymnastics regions, so two St. Louis gyms twenty minutes apart send their teams to different state and regional championships. Legally, Illinois carries an AED requirement for fitness facilities that Missouri does not.

Take the competitive side first. In women’s gymnastics, Missouri sits in Region 4 alongside Iowa, Minnesota, Nebraska, North Dakota and South Dakota. Illinois sits in Region 5 with Indiana, Kentucky, Michigan and Ohio. A team out of Chesterfield or Florissant qualifies through Missouri state and then heads north and west for regionals. A team out of Belleville or Edwardsville qualifies through Illinois state and travels east. If your family already crosses the river for work, ask a prospective gym where its meets physically are before assuming the travel is equivalent.

On safety law, Illinois requires a physical fitness facility to keep at least one AED on the premises and to have a trained AED user on staff during staffed business hours, under the Physical Fitness Facility Medical Emergency Preparedness Act (210 ILCS 74).
