Missouri’s state plan requires districts to keep a full continuum available: general education classes, special classes, special schools, home instruction, and instruction in hospitals and institutions, plus supplementary services such as a resource room or itinerant instruction alongside a general class placement. Then it adds the line every parent should know: a student does not have to fail in the less restrictive options before being placed in the setting that is appropriate for that student. Nobody has to earn support by falling apart first.

ISBE frames it from the other direction: placement is not an either-or decision, and services are meant to follow the child rather than the child following the services. In practice a St. Louis-area IEP is usually a mix — general education for most of the day, pull-out for a specific skill, a related service such as speech or occupational therapy on a set schedule.

### What happens before kindergarten, and what changes at age three?

Under age three, this is not your school district’s job. It is the state’s early intervention system under Part C of IDEA, and the two states run it through different agencies with different front doors.

In Missouri the program is First Steps, for infants and toddlers from birth to age three with delayed development or a diagnosed condition associated with developmental disability. DESE is the lead agency, and referrals run through the regional System Point of Entry. In Illinois the program is Early Intervention, and referrals go to one of 25 regional Child and Family Connections offices; anyone can refer a child, and the screening is free. Illinois eligibility rests on a 30 percent developmental delay in at least one domain, a condition known to cause delay, substantial risk of delay, or a substantiated case of abuse or neglect.

A change worth knowing on the Illinois side: as of July 1, 2026, Illinois Early Intervention is no longer run by the Department of Human Services. The new Illinois Department of Early Childhood became the lead agency for Early Intervention, child care licensing, home visiting and several other programs that day. Same services, new name on the letterhead.

At three, it changes hands again. Missouri’s Regulation IV requires FAPE no later than the third birthday, with an IEP in effect by that date; for a summer birthday, the IEP team sets the start date. Illinois requires services to begin on the third birthday for children already in early intervention or referred 60 school days before it, and for a summer birthday, no later than the first day of the school year. Illinois starts the transition process at two years, six months, which is early on purpose.

On cost: federal rule 34 CFR 303.521 bars charging families for child find, evaluation and assessment, service coordination, and developing the IFSP. Ongoing early intervention services can carry an income-based family fee, and both states have adjusted their fee systems recently, so ask your System Point of Entry or Child and Family Connections office what applies this year rather than trusting a figure you read anywhere, including here. If your first conversation about any of this is with a pediatrician, and you are still looking for one, our guide to choosing a pediatrician in St. Louis covers that separately.

### What can you do if you disagree with the school?

Four things, in rough order of escalation: ask for an IEP meeting, request mediation, file a state complaint, or file for a due process hearing. You can call an IEP meeting at any time in either state, and a surprising share of disagreements end there. The other three are formal, and the two states route them differently.

Mediation is voluntary, free, and confidential, and both sides have to agree to it. Nothing said in mediation can be used later as evidence, and a signed mediation agreement is legally binding and enforceable in court. In Missouri, both parties request it from DESE’s Office of Special Education; once a mediator is assigned it must be scheduled within 15 days and completed within 30. In Illinois, either side contacts the ISBE mediation coordinator, and if mediation fails you have 10 days afterward to file for due process if you want to keep stay-put running.

The state complaint is the low-cost route, and it is underused. Missouri calls it a child complaint. You file a signed written complaint with DESE, the violation must have happened within the past year, and DESE has 60 calendar days to investigate and issue a decision letter with findings and corrective orders. Illinois works the same way through ISBE: filed with the state, a one-year window, 60 calendar days to a letter of finding. In both states a complaint can cover more than one child and can allege a systemic problem, and you do not need an attorney to file one.

Due process is the formal hearing, and the states diverge sharply on where you file. In Missouri it goes to DESE’s Office of Special Education, which forwards it to the Administrative Hearing Commission within two business days; a resolution meeting is due within 15 calendar days, and the written decision within 45 days after the 30-day resolution period ends. In Illinois, ISBE’s own comparison table shows due process is filed with the local school district, on a 75-calendar-day timeline when the full resolution period runs. Both states use a two-year window, against one year for a state complaint. Due process is also where stay-put applies — your child’s placement holds while the case runs — and it is the only route where attorneys’ fees can be awarded.

### What if your child is in a private or parochial school?

This is the most misunderstood piece of the whole system, so read it slowly. If you enroll your child in a private or parochial school yourself, your child does not have an individual right to FAPE. Missouri’s Regulation IV lists parentally placed private school students as an explicit exception to the FAPE obligation. The ISBE guide says the same from the other direction: students with disabilities in private schools are not entitled to an IEP.

What survives is still worth using. Child Find still applies — 34 CFR 300.111 covers children attending private schools, and ISBE states that a district cannot refuse to evaluate or reevaluate a student because that student attends a private school. The responsible district is the one where the private school sits, not the one where you live, which trips up families who cross a district line for a parochial school. If your child is designated to receive services, the document is a services plan in Missouri and an Individual Service Plan, or ISP, in Illinois — both far thinner than an IEP. Funding comes from a proportionate share of federal Part B dollars, and ISBE warns bluntly that when that money runs out mid-year a district may end services for the rest of the year.

A completely different situation: when the IEP team places a child in a private program because the district cannot deliver FAPE itself, that placement is at public expense and the child keeps full IDEA rights. Missouri’s Regulation XIV is explicit that such a student is served under an IEP at no cost to parents, and that public agencies may contract only with private agencies the State Board of Education has approved.

One Missouri-only wrinkle. The MOScholars program run by the Missouri State Treasurer allows a qualified student with a current IEP to receive up to 175 percent of the State Adequacy Target, per the January 2026 parent handbook for school year 2026-27. Illinois has no equivalent since the Invest in Kids tax credit scholarship sunset on December 31, 2023. Before you take the Missouri money, understand the trade: enrolling privately makes your child a parentally placed private school student, with the thinner rights above. If you are weighing districts, magnet, charter and private options in general, that is a separate decision, and our family guide to choosing a school in St. Louis handles it.

### Where do Missouri and Illinois parents get free help?

Both states have a federally funded Parent Training and Information Center, both are free to families, and both will sit with you over an IEP draft. This is the resource most parents find two years later than they should have.

In Missouri it is MPACT, the Missouri Parents Act, a nonprofit that has been the state’s federally funded Parent Training and Information Center since 1988, offering free trainings, resources and one-on-one support. In Illinois it is Family Matters Parent Training and Information Center. As of October 1, 2025, Family Matters expanded to cover the entire state and describes itself as the only federally funded PTIC in Illinois, funded by the U.S. Office of Special Education Programs; its line is 1-866-436-7842.

On the agency side, Missouri families deal with the DESE Office of Special Education at 573-751-5739, and Illinois families with the ISBE Special Education Department. Both states require the district to give you a written procedural safeguards notice. Read it once when nothing is wrong, so you are not reading it for the first time during a bad week.

### What this looks like from the other side of the desk

The economics of a special education school do not work like a private school’s. Much of the enrollment at approved programs arrives by district placement rather than admissions, and the rate is often not set by the market. In Missouri, a public agency may contract only with private agencies the State Board of Education has approved, and Part B funds cannot pay an unapproved provider. In Illinois, ISBE staff apply the Illinois Purchased Care Review Board’s rate-setting rules to determine allowable costs for roughly 330 nonpublic education facilities serving Illinois children with disabilities. That shapes the year: census moves when one district changes one placement, the calendar runs on IEP meetings and cost reports rather than open houses, and the fixed cost that hurts is credentialed staff you cannot replace in February. What operators say to each other is that families arrive believing they apply and pay, when often the team decides and the district pays. Parents still search this locally long before any team meets, which is why a complete listing is worth keeping current.

Ready to see what is actually near you? Browse special education schools across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then send your evaluation request to your district in writing the same day — the clock does not start until you do.

### Frequently asked questions

### Q. How to determine if a child needs special education?

A.  A school evaluation determines it — not a parent, and not a doctor alone. The team looks for three things together: a disability in a federal IDEA category, an adverse effect on educational performance, and a need for specially designed instruction. A medical diagnosis supports the case. It does not decide it.

### Q. How do I know if my child has special educational needs?

A.  Often you do not know, and you are not required to. Persistent gaps in reading, speech, attention, motor skills or social communication that do not close with ordinary classroom help are reason enough to ask. Under Child Find at 34 CFR 300.111, a district must evaluate a child it suspects has a disability. Put the request in writing.

### Q. Do kids with ADHD get an IEP or 504?

A.  Either one, depending on what the child needs. Nothing in federal law requires ADHD to be handled under Section 504. Federal regulation 34 CFR 300.8(c)(9) names ADHD in the other health impairment definition, so an IEP is available when the child needs specially designed instruction. A 504 plan delivers accommodations without it.

### Q. Are special ED and autism the same thing?

A.  No. Autism is one disability category under IDEA; special education is the service system a qualifying child receives. Most children in special education are not autistic, and an autism diagnosis by itself does not make a child eligible. The team still has to find an adverse educational effect and a need for instruction.

### Q. Why would my child be put in a special education class?

A.  Only if the IEP team decides the general classroom, with supplementary aids and services, cannot work for that part of the day. Federal law at 34 CFR 300.114 requires the least restrictive environment, and Missouri’s state plan says outright that a student does not have to fail in less restrictive settings first.

### Q. How long can special ED kids stay in high school?

A.  It differs across the river. Missouri ends the FAPE obligation when a youth with a disability reaches age 21. Illinois runs through the day before the 22nd birthday, and if that birthday falls mid-year, through the end of that school year. In both states a regular diploma ends eligibility.

### Q. Do parents get money for special ED students?

A.  Not from IDEA. Those funds flow to states and districts and buy your child services, not a payment to you. Missouri does run MOScholars, where a qualified student with a current IEP may receive up to 175 percent of the State Adequacy Target. Illinois has no equivalent since Invest in Kids sunset on December 31, 2023.

### Q. What can autistic children get for free?

A.  Under IDEA, the evaluation, the IEP, and every service written into it cost the family nothing. Before age three, Missouri First Steps and Illinois Early Intervention provide free evaluation, assessment and service coordination, though ongoing services can carry an income-based family fee. MPACT and Family Matters support is free too.

### Q. What are some good special education schools in St. Louis?

A.  There is no ranking worth trusting, and for many children the school is not chosen by the family at all. When an IEP team places a child privately, the district pays and the state must have approved the program. Ask your district for its approved-provider list, and observe any program before you agree.

## What a PR Firm Actually Does for a St. Louis Business
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-a-pr-firm-actually-does-for-a-st-louis-business

Imagine it’s a Thursday morning and you’re behind the counter of your shop in Maplewood with a cold email open on your phone. A public relations firm wants twenty minutes. The note mentions storytelling and earned media, and the attached deck carries logos of outlets you actually recognize. You have no idea whether this is the thing that finally gets people talking about you, or a $4,000-a-month habit you’ll feel stupid about by March.

Maybe you’ve had the other version of that morning. A shift lead in Overland posted something ugly from the company account. A customer in Fairview Heights filmed ninety seconds in your parking lot. An inspector wrote you up in Clayton and a reporter has already called twice. Your phone is doing something it has never done before, and you’re searching “crisis PR St. Louis” with one thumb.

Both owners are asking the same question in very different tones of voice: what does a PR firm actually do, and is this something I need or something somebody sells? Here’s the even-handed version, including the parts a firm pitching you has no reason to volunteer.

### What exactly does public relations do?

Public relations manages what other people say about your business. The Public Relations Society of America defines it as “a strategic communication process that builds mutually beneficial relationships between organizations and their publics.” In practice that means media relations, reputation management, crisis response, community and government relations, and employee communication — earning attention instead of buying it.

Strip the vocabulary away and a PR firm does five recognizable jobs:

Media relations. Deciding what about you is genuinely newsworthy versus what is only news to you, then pitching the specific reporters who cover it.

Message and spokesperson work. Writing the two sentences you say every time, then drilling whoever has to say them on camera without wandering.

Reputation management. Shaping what fills page one when a stranger searches your business name, and what an AI assistant repeats when someone asks about you.

Crisis communication. The holding statement, the order you tell people in, and the decision about what you do not say yet.

Community, government and public affairs. The neighborhood meeting, the zoning hearing, the chamber, the school district, the alderman.

PRSA describes the underlying work as analyzing public opinion, advising leadership on policy and communication decisions, protecting reputation, and researching and evaluating programs. Notice what is missing from that list: selling anything directly. A firm that opens by promising you leads is describing a different service.

### Is public relations necessary?

For most small local businesses in the St. Louis metro, not yet. If customers find you by searching for what you do, your next dollar works harder on being findable and reviewable than on a media campaign. PR becomes necessary when your reputation is under threat, or when someone who will never buy from you — a lender, a zoning board, a reporter — has to trust you first.

That is not a knock on the profession. It is a sequencing argument. PR is an amplifier, and an amplifier attached to nothing is expensive silence. Here is the honest split.

PR is probably worth real money if:

Trust is your product and strangers decide — healthcare, financial services, childcare, senior care, anything licensed or regulated.

You need a yes from a body rather than a buyer: a zoning variance in Kirkwood, a development incentive in Maryland Heights, a contract with a school district.

You’re raising money, selling the company, or recruiting people who will search your name before they answer.

You have a story a reporter would run without being asked twice — a genuine first, a milestone with a real number attached, a person worth meeting.

You’re already in the news, and it is going badly.

PR can wait if:

Your hours are wrong somewhere online, your listings are thin, or you have eleven reviews.

You need revenue this quarter. PR is slow and indirect by design; paid search and ads are the fast levers.

Nothing about the business survives a reporter’s first question, which is always some version of “so what?”

Nobody at your company can call a reporter back inside two hours. Media relations dies on deadline, and the deadline is not yours.

### How is PR different from advertising, marketing and SEO?

You control advertising and you pay for the space. You cannot control PR, and you pay for the effort rather than the result. Marketing is the umbrella over both, plus pricing, product and distribution. SEO is the slice of marketing aimed at what search engines and AI assistants surface. Clean test: an ad runs because you bought it, a story runs because a reporter put their byline on it.

The line blurs the moment money or free product moves toward the person doing the talking — and at that point it stops being a style question and becomes a legal one. The Federal Trade Commission finalized updated Endorsement Guides (16 CFR Part 255) on June 29, 2023. Any material connection between an endorser and a brand — payment, free product, an employment relationship, a family tie — has to be disclosed clearly enough for an ordinary reader to notice it. A sponsored post dressed up as a review is advertising with a compliance problem.

Practical version for an owner with one budget: SEO and listings decide whether you get found by someone already looking. Advertising decides how many strangers see your offer this month. PR decides what those strangers think when they run into your name somewhere you didn’t pay to be. Most small businesses need the first two working before the third earns its retainer.

### How much do PR people charge per hour?

Most PR is not sold by the hour at all — it is sold as a monthly retainer. BuzzStream’s 2025 digital PR pricing survey of roughly 70 agency leaders and freelance consultants found an average monthly contract of $5,458, with 52.5% of contracts under $5,000 a month and contracts above $10,000 described as rare. Agencies in that sample averaged $6,357 a month; freelancers averaged $4,200.

Read that survey as a shape, not a quote for your business. It covers digital PR specifically, the sample was small, and 54% of respondents were in the UK against 23% in the US — though the US respondents came in higher, averaging $6,154 a month. Nothing in it is a St. Louis number.

Here is the honest gap: there is no neutral, published survey of US public relations hourly rates that I could find. The figures that circulate online, usually $150 to $500 an hour, come from agency marketing pages rather than research, so treat them as a rumor with a dollar sign in front. What you can anchor on is labor cost. The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics put the median annual wage for public relations specialists at $69,780 in May 2024, with the bottom 10% under $40,750 and the top 10% above $129,480. A firm has to cover that salary plus payroll taxes, benefits, rent, software, and every unbilled hour spent pitching stories that never ran. That arithmetic is why a $1,200-a-month retainer cannot hold much senior time, whatever the proposal implies.

### What does a retainer actually buy?

A retainer buys a block of senior attention each month — hours spread across strategy, writing, pitching, monitoring and reporting — not a number of stories. Agencies price this way because media relations compounds: month three of a relationship with a reporter outperforms month one, and nobody can predict which pitch lands. Around 90% of agencies in BuzzStream’s 2025 survey worked on monthly retainers.

A retainer with no hours written into it is a subscription to hope. Before you sign, get five things on paper: how many hours are included and what happens to unused ones, the names of the people doing the work rather than the ones in the pitch meeting, the fixed monthly deliverables, the reporting cadence, and who owns the media list and the written materials when the relationship ends. That last one surprises people every single time.

Project pricing fits more often than agencies admit. A single opening, a funding announcement, a relocation, a media training day, one crisis — those have an end date. Professional services around here price in three shapes, hourly, retainer or commission, and the same tradeoff repeats across trades; you can see it play out in what a real estate consultant does and what it costs. Ask for the project number first. If a firm will only quote twelve months of retainer for a one-week job, that tells you who the retainer is for.

Wildly off-topic — but your hands: St. Louis nail salons.

### Why can nobody guarantee you a story in the Post-Dispatch?

Because the decision belongs to a newsroom, not to a vendor. An editor at the St. Louis Post-Dispatch, the Belleville News-Democrat or KSDK decides what runs, and the moment money changes hands for editorial coverage it stops being earned media. PRSA’s Board of Ethics and Professional Standards calls that pay-for-play and treats undisclosed payment for coverage as a conflict with its Code of Ethics.

The other reason is arithmetic. Northwestern’s Medill State of Local News report, published October 20, 2025, found that close to 3,500 newspapers have stopped printing since 2005 and more than 270,000 newspaper jobs have disappeared — north of 75% of that workforce. St. Louis got its own version in May 2024, when the Riverfront Times, a 46-year-old alt-weekly, was sold and its entire editorial staff was laid off, as St. Louis Public Radio reported. Fewer reporters cover the same metro, and every one of them gets more pitches than they did five years ago.

That contraction is the strongest argument for hiring a good firm, oddly enough. The value is no longer the press release. It is knowing which three or four people still cover restaurants, or health care, or Metro East development, knowing which side of the river they file for, and not wasting their afternoon. Ask any firm to name the reporters they would approach for you and why. A firm that answers with outlet logos instead of names is guessing.

If someone does guarantee placement, ask one question: is it paid? Guaranteed placement is paid media wearing a press release, and paid content that looks editorial carries FTC disclosure obligations. It is not automatically a scam. It is just not the thing you thought you were buying.

### When does a small business urgently need crisis communications?

The moment someone else can publish your story before you can explain it. A lawsuit, a data breach, a failed inspection, an injured customer, a video with your sign in the frame. Crisis communication is the one PR service a small local business can genuinely need on a specific Tuesday afternoon, and the one that costs the most when you go shopping for it afterward.

A data breach is the cleanest example of why the state line matters. Under Missouri law (Mo. Rev. Stat. § 407.1500) you notify affected consumers without unreasonable delay, and if you are notifying more than 1,000 consumers at one time you must also notify the Attorney General’s office and the nationwide consumer reporting agencies. Illinois sets the bar lower. Under the Personal Information Protection Act (815 ILCS 530/10), a business that has to notify more than 500 Illinois residents from a single breach must also notify the Illinois Attorney General, no later than when it notifies those consumers. A Metro East business serving both sides of the river can trip the Illinois requirement at half the head count.

Legal notice is the floor, not the message. It tells you what you have to mail and says nothing about what your regulars, your staff and the reporter who just called are going to hear. That gap is the actual product a crisis communicator sells, and it is why the good ones bill in days rather than months.

Resist the two instincts that make everything worse. Do not bury reviews, and do not have staff or relatives post replacements. The FTC’s Trade Regulation Rule on the Use of Consumer Reviews and Testimonials, announced August 14, 2024 and effective October 21, 2024, specifically bans fake reviews, undisclosed insider reviews and the suppression of negative ones, and it carries civil penalties per violation. A cover-up is now a second story, and a more expensive one.

What to do in the first two hours, whether or not you hire anyone: pick one spokesperson and route everything through that person. Write down what you actually know versus what you assume, and say only the first part out loud. Tell your own staff before they read it somewhere else. Call the reporter back inside their deadline even if all you can give them is what you can confirm right now — “no comment” reads as guilt, and silence lets other people write your sentences for you.

### How do you tell whether PR actually worked?

Not by counting clippings. Watch the numbers that move when people hear about you and never click anything: branded search volume for your business name, direct traffic, inbound calls that mention where they heard you, referral traffic from the outlet itself, and what fills page one when a stranger searches you. PR attribution is genuinely hard, and any firm claiming otherwise is overselling.

Three habits make the fuzziness manageable. Capture the baseline before the work starts — branded searches, direct sessions, monthly inbound calls — because a number nobody recorded in month zero cannot be improved in month six. Agree on the same three metrics, reported the same way, every month. And give it a fair window: earned media compounds, and three to six months is where a program either shows a pulse or does not.

One number to reject outright is advertising value equivalency, where a firm multiplies your coverage by what the equivalent ad space would have cost. The industry’s own measurement body, AMEC, has spent years telling practitioners it is not a valid measure of communication value. When it shows up in a monthly report, it is usually there to make a slow month look busy.

Then apply the plain test the numbers cannot capture: did a door open that was closed? A call back from someone who never returned yours, an invitation onto the panel, a banker who already knew the name. That is what earned media buys, and it is why the honest answer to “what is my ROI” is a range with a shrug in it.

### What should you ask a PR firm before you sign?

Interview three firms, and ask each one who does the work day to day rather than who runs the pitch. Then ask what they would do in month one, what they would tell you not to spend money on, and for two references at roughly your size instead of their biggest logo. Vetting a firm is the same discipline as any five-figure purchase — you wouldn’t buy a commercial truck without looking under the hood.

Two checkable credibility signals exist, and neither is required by law. The APR — Accredited in Public Relations — is administered by the Universal Accreditation Board, an association of nine public relations organizations; roughly 5% of practitioners in the US and Canada hold one of its credentials, candidates are advised to have at least five years of full-time experience, and it renews every three years. The second is local: PRSA’s Mid-America Chapter serves the St. Louis metro along with Mid-Missouri and Southern Illinois communities including Edwardsville and Carbondale. Neither guarantees good work. Both mean somebody has an ethics code to answer to.

Walk away from four things: a guarantee of placements, a media list they will not describe, per-release pricing with no strategy behind it, and any refusal to write hours into the scope. Ask for a 30- or 60-day exit in the first contract. A firm confident about month three will not fight you on it.

### What this looks like from the other side of the desk

If you run a small firm here, none of this is news to you. You sell hours, not outcomes, and the whole business is utilization — salary is your cost of goods, and BLS put the median public relations specialist at $69,780 a year in May 2024, before benefits, rent, software and every hour spent on pitches that never ran. The seasonality is budget cycles rather than weather: new fiscal years and Q1 fill the pipeline, August and late December go quiet, and crisis work arrives unbudgeted at nine at night. The loss leader is the pitch itself, a spec strategy deck written free against three other shops. And the complaint traded between owners is always the same one — the client who goes dark for six weeks, judges you on a placement nobody controls, then cancels in month three, right as the relationships start paying. The operators who last write hours into the scope and report the same three numbers every month. Plenty of owners still start by searching locally, so being listed and complete where people look — including on St Louis Near Me Directory — is part of being findable at all.

Ready to talk to somebody local instead of a cold email? Browse public relations firms across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then ask the first two for a project quote and the names of the reporters they’d approach for you.

### Frequently asked questions

### Q. What exactly does public relations do?

A.  Public relations manages what other people say about your business. PRSA defines it as a strategic communication process that builds mutually beneficial relationships between organizations and their publics. Day to day that means pitching reporters, writing statements, preparing spokespeople, handling crises, running community and government relations, and communicating with employees. It earns attention rather than buying it.

### Q. What does a public relations department do?

A.  An in-house PR department does what an agency does, except it sits on payroll and knows the business cold. Typical duties: fielding media inquiries, writing press materials, executive and employee communication, community partnerships, and crisis response. Most small St. Louis businesses never need one. The owner is the spokesperson until a full-time salary costs less than the retainer it would replace.

### Q. Why is public relations important?

A.  Because most decisions about your business get made by people you never spoke to. Coverage, community presence and a clean first page of results give strangers a reason to trust you before they call. For a small local business that effect usually arrives faster through reviews and referrals. PR is the version that scales past people who already know you.

### Q. Is public relations free?

A.  No. Earned media is unpaid only in the sense that you do not buy the placement itself. You still pay for the strategy, the writing, the relationships and the hours behind them. Anything sold to you as guaranteed placement is paid media, and the FTC requires paid or incentivized content that looks editorial to disclose that connection plainly.

### Q. How much do PR people charge per hour?

A.  Most PR is billed monthly rather than hourly. BuzzStream’s 2025 survey of about 70 digital PR agency leaders and freelancers found an average monthly contract of $5,458, with 52.5% under $5,000. There is no neutral published survey of US hourly PR rates, so ask any firm directly for its blended hourly rate and how many hours your retainer includes.

### Q. How to choose the right PR agency?

A.  Interview three and ask who does the work day to day. Get hours written into the scope, the same three metrics reported monthly, two references at your size, and a 30- or 60-day exit clause. Check whether anyone on the team holds the APR credential. Walk away from guaranteed placements, which are paid media wearing a press release.

### Q. What are the 7 types of public relations?

A.  There is no official list, but the seven usually taught are media relations, community relations, crisis communication, internal or employee communication, public affairs and government relations, investor relations, and influencer or marketing communication. A small St. Louis business realistically touches three of them: media relations, community relations and crisis. The rest belong to much larger organizations.

### Q. What are the five main functions of public relations?

A.  Most versions reduce to research, strategy, communication, relationship management and evaluation. PRSA describes the work as analyzing public opinion, advising leadership on policy and communication, protecting reputation, researching and evaluating programs, and managing content and staff. If a proposal has no research at the front and no evaluation at the back, it is publicity rather than public relations.

### Q. What are the big 4 PR agencies?

A.  There is no fixed big four. The largest firms sit inside global holding companies such as Omnicom, WPP and Publicis, alongside the independent Edelman. Worth knowing locally: FleishmanHillard was founded in St. Louis in 1946 and is still headquartered here, part of Omnicom since 1997. A neighborhood business will almost never hire at that tier, and does not need to.

### Q. Is PR being replaced by AI?

A.  Reshaped rather than replaced. AI drafts releases, builds media lists and monitors coverage far faster than a junior staffer did, which should compress the hours a retainer covers. What it cannot do is take responsibility, work a Metro East reporter, or stand in front of a camera. Ask a firm which tasks it automates and whether your fee reflects it.

## Home Window Tinting in St. Louis: What Film Actually Does
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-to-know-about-home-window-tinting-in-st-louis

Imagine it’s the third week of July and there’s a room in your house you have quietly stopped using. West-facing, big windows, lovely at ten in the morning and unusable from four o’clock on. The blinds have been down since Memorial Day. The thermostat insists it’s 74 in there. That room disagrees.

Maybe you’re in Valley Park and it’s the back bedroom. Spanish Lake, and it’s the whole west wall of the great room. A brick two-story in Glendale where the original glass goes warm against the back of your hand by mid-afternoon. A newer build out past Weldon Spring with a wall of double-pane that still bakes. Somebody in Waterloo is having the same argument with a sunroom that was a wonderful idea in October and a mistake by June.

So you start reading about window film. Within ten minutes you have run into car tint laws that have nothing to do with your house, a company promising to cut your cooling bill in half, and a nagging sense that gluing something to the inside of an expensive window might not be free. All three of those instincts are worth following. Here is what residential film actually does, what it can cost you besides money, and the one mistake that turns a comfort upgrade into a glass bill.

### What are the benefits of home window tinting?

Four things, roughly in order of how reliably film delivers them: it kills glare, it blocks ultraviolet light, it rejects some solar heat, and it adds daytime privacy. Security is a fifth thing people expect from tint and it is a separate product entirely. Energy savings are real in some houses and close to nothing in others.

Glare is the one nobody argues about. You feel it the afternoon it goes on, on the television, on a monitor, on the kitchen island at 5 p.m. It is also the reason a lot of St. Louis homeowners end up satisfied with a job that saved them no measurable money at all.

Ultraviolet blocking is the most consistent technical claim in the trade. A 2012 final report submitted to the U.S. Department of Energy by CPFilms under project DE-EE0004013 describes modern architectural films as protected by UV-absorbing layers that “usually block 99% or more of the UV rays.” That matters for hardwood, rugs, upholstery and anything you have hung on a sunny wall. It is not the whole fading story, though — visible light and heat fade fabrics and pigments too, so film slows fading rather than stopping it. If what you are protecting is art or photographs, the glazing in the frame does at least as much work as the film on the window, and that decision is covered in what custom framing costs in St. Louis.

Privacy from film is daylight privacy. Reflective and mirrored films work because the outside is brighter than the inside. After dark, with the lamps on, the effect reverses and the room is more visible from the street, not less. Anyone selling you nighttime privacy from a solar film is selling you physics that does not exist. Frosted and decorative films are the honest answer for a bathroom or a sidelight, because they diffuse in both directions.

### Dyed, metalized, ceramic, low-e: what the price gap actually buys

The price spread across film types is not padding, and it maps to genuinely different technology. There are four broad families, and the difference between the cheapest and the most expensive is measured in how much heat they stop per unit of light they give up, and in how long they stay looking like glass.

Dyed film is the entry product. Dye in an adhesive layer absorbs light across the spectrum, which darkens the room and cuts glare well, but it is the weakest performer on heat and the dye is what fades. A purple-brown cast on an old dyed film is the classic tell.

Metalized film puts microscopically thin metal layers on a polyester substrate to reflect solar energy back outside before the glass can absorb it. The DOE report above describes the standard construction as roughly a 0.001-inch polyester film carrying a micro-thin transparent metal coating. Metalized films are durable and reject heat well. The trade-off is real and worth asking about: a conductive metal layer across a window can attenuate radio signal, which shows up as weaker cell service or a fussy garage remote in the affected room.

Ceramic film uses non-conductive ceramic particles instead of metal. It gets you high infrared rejection while keeping the window looking close to clear, with no signal interference and no dye to fade. It is also the most expensive film per square foot, which is the entire reason the category exists.

Low-e film is the odd one out, because it targets winter as well as summer. The same DOE report is blunt about the distinction: most window films “produce savings only during the cooling season,” while low-e films lower the emissivity of the glass surface so that room heat radiating toward a cold window gets reflected back inside. If your problem is a drafty, cold-feeling window in January rather than a hot one in July, low-e is the only family that speaks to it.

On price, be careful what you accept as a number. The most defensible published figure is from Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory’s November 2014 report for the U.S. General Services Administration, which put installed costs of applied films at “between $6.40/ft2 for simple tinted films to $10/ft2 for spectrally selective reflective films.” That is commercial work, more than a decade old, and it is not a quote for your house. Treat it as proof that the gap between cheap film and good film is roughly a factor of one and a half, not as a price. Anyone quoting you a St. Louis residential rate should put it in writing, itemized, with the film brand and product number on it.

One more finding from that same lab report is worth carrying into a showroom: a reflective spectrally selective film outperformed the absorbing film in every case the researchers modeled. Absorbing films soak the heat up. Reflective films send it back out. If two products cost the same, that difference is not cosmetic.

### Does tinting home windows void the warranty?

Often, yes, and the major window makers say so in plain language rather than fine print. This is the single biggest trap in residential window film, and almost nobody checks it before the installer arrives. Three examples, pulled from the manufacturers’ own current warranty documents.

Andersen’s limited warranty, in the section headed what is not covered, lists “product modifications or glass shading devices (e.g., glass tinting, security systems, improper painting or staining, insulated coverings, etc.).” The Pella Vista Window & Patio Door Limited Warranty, which applies to products purchased on or after January 1, 2026, excludes damage due to “After-market products not manufactured by Pella, including security systems, accessories, window films or other treatments to glass surfaces.” The Marvin Limited Warranty effective February 26, 2024 excludes failure caused by “misuse, abuse, modification, alteration, accident, negligence, or application or use of third party products (films, tinting, security systems, etc.).”

Read the grammar of those exclusions closely, because it is the part that decides your outcome. All three are written around causation — the manufacturer has no obligation for failure due to the modification. In practice that means a seal failure or a cracked pane on a filmed window turns into an argument about what caused it, and you are having that argument after the glass has already failed, on a claim you were counting on.

Two things protect you here, and both happen before installation. First, call or email the window manufacturer with your product line and ask in writing whether film is permitted and under what conditions. Some lines allow specific films; the answer is not uniform across a brand. Second, ask the installer for the film manufacturer’s written warranty and read who and what it covers. The stronger residential film warranties cover glass breakage and seal failure on filmed windows precisely because the window maker’s coverage steps aside. If your installer cannot produce that document, that is your answer.

### Thermal stress, low-e glass, and why the installer has to identify your glass first

Film can crack glass. Not usually, and not randomly — through thermal stress, when a film raises how much solar energy the pane absorbs and the middle of the glass gets much hotter than the shaded edge held in the frame. The International Window Film Association states it directly: “Glass breaks when stressed. Thermal stress, from absorption of solar radiation, is the one which film may affect. The window film manufacturers have recommended film-to-glass tables for use by factory-trained dealer installers.”

Those tables exist because the risk is not the same on every pane. Industry guidance on film-to-glass compatibility holds that tempered glass will never see excess thermal stress in normal architectural use, that heat-strengthened glass is highly unlikely to, and that ordinary annealed float glass “is subject to thermal stress breakage” and should always be assessed before film goes on. Most of the glass in a house is annealed, except in the spots where building codes require safety glazing, such as doors, glass beside a door and glass around a tub or shower. So the assessment is not a formality on a residential job. It is the job.

Low-e glass adds a second question. The IWFA’s position is that whether film should go on a low-e window “depends on three factors: Type of Low E surface used on glass, location of Low E surface in the window system, the desired amount of heat gain reduction, heat loss reduction, or other film benefits.” Translated: a filmed low-e insulated unit already has a coating doing part of this work, the two can fight, and the answer depends on which surface the factory coating sits on. That is a question for the dealer with the compatibility chart, not for a forum thread.

How hot does it actually get behind the film? When Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory instrumented a St. Louis office building for GSA, it measured interior glass surface temperatures of 120 to 140 degrees Fahrenheit on windows with an absorbing film applied to the inside of double-pane glass. That is the mechanism, in numbers, on this side of the river.

Local geography matters more than people expect here, because the metro is not one housing stock. In the 2024 American Community Survey, 98,061 of the 174,694 housing units in the city of St. Louis — 56.1 percent — were built in 1939 or earlier, and about 87 percent went up before 1980. St. Louis County is a mid-century place instead: 9.2 percent predates 1940, but 17.5 percent went up in the 1950s and 17.9 percent in the 1960s. Across the river in St. Clair County, Illinois, 12.0 percent predates 1940 and roughly 54 percent was built before 1980. Translation for a film job: a Tower Grove or Dutchtown house is likely to have single-pane annealed glass, which is where film has the most room to work and where the compatibility check matters most; a 1990s subdivision in Chesterfield or O’Fallon probably has low-e double-pane, where film has less left to do.

Nothing to do with glass — the metro handyman list lives here.

### How effective is house window tinting?

For comfort and glare, very. For your energy bill, it depends almost entirely on the glass you already have, and the best local evidence says be skeptical of big savings numbers. That evidence happens to come from a test run right here.

In November 2014, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory published a Green Proving Ground report for the U.S. General Services Administration on a solar control window film retrofit. The demonstration building was the GSA’s Goodfellow Federal Center in St. Louis, Missouri, monitored from February to August 2013. The researchers were explicit about why: “The St. Louis climate was also selected to provide a mixture of heating and cooling load conditions, to evaluate the claims of both heating and cooling energy savings.”

Applied to the inside of the existing double-pane bronze-tinted windows, the film produced cooling savings of 8 percent or less in some zones and none in others, while total heating-plus-cooling energy consumption rose by 10 percent or more. Applied to the outside of the same windows, measured cooling savings averaged about 30 percent — and total energy use still went up 3 to 7 percent, because the passive solar heat given up in winter outweighed the summer gain. The report’s verdict on the vendor’s marketing was one sentence: the manufacturer’s claim of heating and cooling savings of 20 to 40 percent “was not supported by the measured data or simulation results.”

Be fair to the film, though. That was one absorbing product, on double-pane bronze commercial glass, in an office building — and the same report says that on other buildings with other base windows in other climates the researchers would expect useful savings. Their modeling for the St. Louis climate makes the pattern clear. On single clear glass, simple payback ran 7.3 to 11.4 years depending on the film. On single bronze glass, 12.7 to 22.5 years. On double bronze glass, most cases ran past 20 years unless a reflective film was used or the film went on the outside.

So the honest summary for a St. Louis homeowner: window film is a comfort, glare and fade-control product that sometimes pays for itself, and the sometimes is spelled single-pane, west or south-facing, unshaded. If you have newer low-e double-pane windows, buy film for the room you cannot sit in at 5 p.m., not for the utility bill. And do not count on help with the cost. Ameren Missouri’s current residential efficiency programs run to things like Pay As You Save, HVAC PAYS and CommunitySavers assessments, and neither those nor Ameren Illinois’s weatherization measures list window film. The federal Energy Efficient Home Improvement Credit covers exterior windows and skylights meeting ENERGY STAR Most Efficient criteria, capped at $600, and per the IRS it applied to qualifying property placed in service before December 31, 2025 — film was never on that list, and that door has closed for work done now.

If the actual problem is a west room that overheats between four and seven, film is one of three fixes, and it is not automatically the cheapest. Exterior shade, a solar screen and interior treatments all compete for the same job; the price side of the interior option is laid out in what window blinds and shades cost in St. Louis.

### Security film is a different product, and none of it is bulletproof

Safety and security film is thicker, is chosen for tear strength rather than heat rejection, and is designed to hold broken glass together instead of letting it fall as shards. Solar film does not do this job, and the two are frequently confused in the same sales conversation. The International Window Film Association lists forced entry, accidental impact, earthquake, blast, windstorm, graffiti and spontaneous tempered glass failure as the events these films address.

The detail that separates a real installation from a decorative one is attachment. The IWFA’s language repeats the same three conditions every time: film that is properly specified, installed and attached. Film bonded only to the face of the glass can hold the pane together and still let the whole glazed panel come out of the frame. An attachment system anchors the filmed glass to the frame itself. If a quote for security film says nothing about attachment, it is a quote for a different product than the one you think you are buying.

And one flat correction, in the association’s own words: “To this date, the IWFA is unaware of any films that have Ballistic properties.” A security film buys delay — seconds and minutes for an alarm to matter. It does not buy bullet resistance, and any local pitch that suggests otherwise should end the conversation.

### Should you install window film yourself?

On a small, flat, ordinary window with clear single-pane glass, DIY film is a reasonable Saturday. On anything else, the odds turn hard against you, and the failure modes are specific. Contamination is permanent: one speck of dust under the film is a bump you will see for the life of the install, and household air is full of dust. Cutting to the glass line without scoring the gasket takes practice on glass you do not care about.

The bigger issue is what DIY skips rather than what it botches. A homeowner with a kit does no film-to-glass compatibility check, and that check is the only thing standing between an absorbing film and an annealed pane that cracks in August. A retail roll carries a materials warranty. It does not carry a labor warranty and it does not carry a glass breakage warranty, so a thermal fracture is entirely yours — on top of a window manufacturer’s coverage that already excluded the film.

If you hire out, one question sorts the field fast: which accreditation does the installer hold? The IWFA runs separate testing tracks for Automotive Film Specialists, Safety & Security Film Specialists, Solar Control Specialists and Advanced Solar Control Specialists, and its exam requires at least 80 percent correct to pass. A shop that does beautiful car tint has not necessarily been tested on architectural glass, and those are different tracks for a reason. The association also suggests asking for references from recent residential customers, whether the company belongs to any trade associations, and simply: are my windows suitable for window film installation?

### What a window film shop is really selling you

The film is a small share of a residential invoice. What you are buying is prep, measurement and glass identification — unpaid work, because the shop must know your glass type before it can quote, and the compatibility chart decides whether the job is allowed at all. The risk sits on the shop too: if the installer specs off that chart and the pane cracks in August, that is the film maker’s and the dealer’s glass warranty, not yours. Residential film is also often sold with a lifetime warranty: a one-time sale with an open-ended service tail — edge lift and bubbling return years later on a job nobody is paid for anymore. Meanwhile the phone rings the first week it hits 95 and goes quiet in November — backwards from when low-e film is easiest to justify. Owners who fix that swing stay findable in the off months, which is what a complete listing on St Louis Near Me Directory is for.

### Frequently asked questions

### Q. What are the cons of window tinting?

A.  Four worth weighing. It is not easily reversible — removing old film means adhesive residue and hours of labor. Reflective film gives you daylight privacy only, and reverses after dark. Solar film cuts winter solar heat gain along with summer gain, so a cold room can get colder. And dyed films fade to a purple-brown cast over years, which is the version most people picture when they picture bad tint.

### Q. What are the downsides of tinting house windows?

A.  The house-specific ones are warranty and glass. Andersen, Pella and Marvin all exclude film in their current limited warranties, so a later seal failure or crack becomes an argument about cause. Ordinary annealed glass can fracture from thermal stress when an absorbing film raises how much solar energy it soaks up. Add appearance rules if you are in a historic district or under an HOA, since some restrict exterior reflectivity.

### Q. How to choose the right house window tint?

A.  Start with the problem, not the product. Glare on a screen, heat in one room, fading furniture and winter chill each point to a different film family: dyed for cheap glare control, metalized or ceramic for heat, low-e for cold glass. Then let your glass narrow it — single-pane, double-pane, low-e or tempered changes what is safe. Ask which films the dealer’s compatibility chart allows on your specific windows.

### Q. What is the average cost to tint a house window?

A.  There is no verified current St. Louis residential average, and any single number you see quoted online is usually a marketing estimate rather than measured data. The most defensible published figure is from Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory’s 2014 report for GSA, which put installed applied-film costs at $6.40 to $10 per square foot — commercial work, over a decade old. Get two or three itemized written quotes instead.

### Q. How much should home window tinting cost?

A.  Rather than chase an average, look at what moves your quote. Film family is the biggest lever, since ceramic and low-e cost multiples of dyed. After that: total square footage, the number of separate panes, since ten small windows cost more labor than one big one, shape and access, whether old film has to be stripped first, and whether your glass type forces a higher-spec product. Ask for the film brand and product number in writing.

### Q. Is residential window tinting worth it?

A.  It turns mostly on the glass you already have. On original single-pane windows — common across the city of St. Louis, where 56.1 percent of housing units predate 1940 per the 2024 American Community Survey — film has real room to work, and LBNL’s St. Louis modeling put simple payback on single clear glass at roughly 7 to 11 years. On newer low-e double-pane, most of the solar work is already done and the payback stretches past 20 years.

### Q. Is tinting your home windows a good idea?

A.  It is a good idea when you can name the specific problem it solves. A room you cannot use at 5 p.m., glare that ruins a television, a hardwood floor bleaching by the patio door, a bathroom that needs daytime privacy — film handles all of those well. It is a poor idea if you are buying it purely to cut a utility bill, or if you have not first confirmed your window warranty and glass type.

### Q. What are the window tint rules in Missouri?

A.  Missouri’s tint law is a motor vehicle law, not a building rule. Section 307.173 RSMo sits in the Motor Vehicles title and sets 35 percent light transmission, plus or minus 3 percent, for front side windows. Illinois does the same thing in its Vehicle Code at 625 ILCS 5/12-503, allowing 50 percent on front sides under stated conditions. Neither state limits how dark you tint your house — your HOA or historic district might.

### Q. Where can I get my home windows tinted in St. Louis?

A.  Look for architectural rather than automotive specialists, since the IWFA tests those as separate accreditation tracks. Search a local directory for home window tinting across both Missouri and Illinois sides of the metro, then shortlist on three things: they ask what glass you have before quoting, they hand you the film manufacturer’s written glass breakage and seal failure warranty, and they put the film brand and product number on the estimate.

## How Much Should You Expect to Pay for Framing in St. Louis?
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-custom-framing-costs-in-st-louis

Imagine it’s a Saturday morning and you’re standing at a framing counter in Ladue with a rolled-up print under your arm. Or you’re in Bridgeton holding a signed jersey that has lived folded in a closet since 2011. Maybe it’s a photograph of your grandmother that came out of a box in Hanley Hills after the estate sale, curled at the corners, the only copy anyone has.

You already know how this goes. The framer measures, asks a few questions, starts pulling corner samples off the wall, and somewhere in the next ten minutes a number arrives that is three or four times what you had in your head. Then you do what almost everybody does. You smile, say you’ll think about it, and drive home with the piece still in the tube.

Here’s the useful part. That number isn’t arbitrary, and it isn’t really one number — it’s four or five separate decisions stacked on top of each other, and you control most of them. Once you can see which decisions are the expensive ones, and which ones are actually worth paying for, the quote stops being a shock and starts being a menu.

### How much should I expect to pay for framing?

Expect the quote to scale with three things: the size of the finished package, the grade of the glazing, and the grade of the mat. It does not scale with what the picture is worth to you. The same 16x20 print can be framed three legitimate ways with a wide spread between the cheapest version and the most protective one, and the shop is not padding the difference — the materials genuinely cost that much more.

You will notice this article doesn’t print a dollar range. That’s deliberate. Custom framing is priced per shop, per moulding, per project, and moulding costs move with import pricing and freight, so a published range is stale by next quarter and wrong across the river anyway. What you can learn instead is the arithmetic happening behind the counter, so you can read your own quote and see which line item is driving it.

One number in this whole category is published and dated, and it’s worth knowing as a floor: Michaels announced a 10-minute custom framing service on November 18, 2025 — a digital photo printed, framed, and gift boxed for $29, in an 8x8 or 8x10, with four frame finishes and an optional mat. That is a packaged product, not a custom quote. It tells you what the cheap end of a gift photo looks like. It tells you nothing about your grandmother’s portrait.

### What are you actually paying for?

A framing quote is built from four buckets: moulding measured by the foot, mat and backing measured in united inches, glazing measured by area, and labor. Understanding the four is what lets you negotiate. You can’t argue a shop down on glass, but you can absolutely redesign the mat.

Moulding by the foot. Frame shops buy moulding in lengths from distributors and price it per foot. Here’s the part customers never expect: the footage you need is not the perimeter of your picture. Because all four corners are mitered, the trade formula adds eight times the moulding width to the perimeter. A 16x20 opening has a 72-inch perimeter, but in a 2-inch-wide moulding it consumes 32 + 40 + 16 = 88 inches, or about 7 feet 4 inches. So a wider frame costs you twice: more dollars per foot, and more feet.

United inches. This is the industry’s shorthand for size — one long side plus one short side. A 16x20 is 36 united inches. Mats, backing, fitting and a lot of the labor line are priced off that single figure, which is why shops can quote so fast once they know your dimensions.

Glazing by area. Glass and acrylic are priced from sheets, so glazing cost tracks square inches, not united inches. This is the reason big pieces jump in price faster than they look like they should.

Labor and fitting. Cutting the mat opening with a beveled edge, joining and clamping the corners, mounting or hinging the artwork, cleaning the glazing, fitting everything into the rabbet, sealing the back with a dust cover, and attaching hardware. Hobby Lobby’s own custom framing page describes the package the same way: the moulding, the matting, protective glass, an acid-free dust cover on the back, and the hangers needed to mount it.

### How much does it cost to frame a 24x36 picture?

There’s no honest single number, but there is a very clear reason a 24x36 quote lands so much higher than a 16x20 one: it is a step change, not a proportional increase. Run the arithmetic and you can see exactly where the money goes.

A 16x20 is 36 united inches and 320 square inches of glass. A 24x36 is 60 united inches and 864 square inches. So the size figure the mat and labor are priced from rises about 67 percent, while the glazing area rises about 170 percent. That alone explains a lot of the gap.

Now add a 3-inch mat all the way around, which is a normal design choice at that scale. Your outside dimension becomes 30x42 — 72 united inches and 1,260 square inches, nearly four times the glazing area of that 16x20. In a 2-inch moulding, the footage goes from about 7 feet 4 inches to 13 feet 4 inches.

And there’s a hard break you should know about. A standard full sheet of mat board is 32x40 inches. A 30x42 outside dimension does not fit on one, so the shop has to move to jumbo board, commonly 40x60. That is a genuine material step, not a markup. If your budget is tight on a large piece, the single most effective thing you can do is design the mat so the outside dimension stays inside 32x40 — a 2-inch mat instead of a 3-inch mat on a 24x36 keeps you at 28x40 and on a standard sheet.

At that size the glazing conversation changes too. A sheet of glass over 1,200 square inches is heavy and genuinely dangerous if it lets go on the stairs, so many shops steer large work to acrylic, which weighs roughly half as much as glass and won’t break into shards.

### Which choices actually move the number?

Glazing and mat grade move it most, and both are real value rather than upsell. Everything else — a fancier moulding, a second mat, a v-groove, a fabric wrap — is taste, and taste is where you cut if you have to.

Glazing tiers. The spread here is enormous and the labels are slippery, so ask for the actual specification. Tru Vue, the dominant glazing manufacturer in the trade, lists its non-conservation Premium Clear glass at 45 percent UV protection. Its Conservation Clear line blocks up to 99 percent of UV, with more than 89 percent light transmission and about 8 percent reflection. Its Museum Glass blocks up to 99 percent of UV and adds the anti-reflective coating — less than 1 percent reflection and more than 97 percent light transmission. The manufacturer states its conservation-grade products meet ISO 18902 and pass ISO 18916, the photographic activity test. If a shop says only “UV glass,” that could mean 45 percent or it could mean 99. Make them say which.

Mat grade. A decorative paper-faced mat, a conservation mat made of purified alpha-cellulose, and a museum mat of 100 percent cotton rag are three different products at three different prices. Cotton is naturally acid-free and needs the least chemical processing, which is why museums default to it. Alpha-cellulose conservation board is the sensible middle, and it is what most people should buy for anything they care about.

Float mounting. Floating a piece so the deckled or torn edges show, instead of covering them with a mat window, means the artwork sits on top of the board rather than under it. That requires spacers to hold the glazing off the surface, which adds depth and a step of labor. It looks fantastic on hand-torn paper and it costs more.

Mounting method. Dry mounting bonds the piece to a board with heat and adhesive. It is flat, it is cheap, and it is permanent. Hinging with Japanese paper and wheat starch paste is the conservation alternative, and the paste releases with moisture, which is the entire point. For a poster, dry mount it. For anything signed, numbered, original, or irreplaceable, do not.

Oversize. Past 32x40 you are in jumbo materials, and past that you are into shipping considerations and acrylic. Ask where the price breaks are before you fall in love with a mat width.

Nothing to do with frames — lawn and garden help.

### What does archival or conservation framing actually mean?

It means every material touching your piece is chemically stable, and every step taken today can be undone tomorrow without damaging the artwork. Reversibility is the real test, not the word on the sticker. “Acid-free” only describes the pH of a board at the moment it was made; it says nothing about what that board does in twenty years inside a sealed frame.

The Northeast Document Conservation Center’s preservation leaflet on matting and framing works on paper describes the standard: a window and backboard of 4-ply 100 percent ragboard or lignin-free archival board, with the object attached to the backboard using hinges of Japanese paper and wheat starch paste, or with corner supports and edge strips that put no adhesive on the object at all. Wheat starch paste can be removed with moisture. That is why conservators use it.

The second half of conservation framing is the air gap. Nothing should press against the glazing. A mat creates that gap automatically; a float mount needs spacers to do the same job. This matters more here than in a dry climate, because a St. Louis August moves a lot of moisture through a house, and a photographic emulsion held tight against glass through enough humid summers can bond to it. Separating them again is a conservation job, not a framing job.

Buffering is the last wrinkle. Buffered board carries an alkaline reserve that absorbs acidic gases from inside the frame, including from wood mouldings, which are themselves acidic. Some photographic processes do better on unbuffered board. If you are framing photographs, say the word “photographs” out loud and let the framer pick.

One honest limit: UV glazing filters ultraviolet light, not visible light, and visible light fades things too. Conservation glass buys years, not immunity. Nothing you care about should hang where afternoon sun lands on it, which is why the cheapest preservation upgrade in most houses isn’t glass at all — it’s a blind or a shade on the window, or a UV-blocking film on the glass itself.

### Where is the cheapest place to get custom framing?

The cheapest framing is the framing you don’t buy custom. If your piece is already a standard size — 5x7, 8x10, 11x14, 16x20, 18x24, 24x36 — a ready-made frame and a pre-cut mat will beat any custom quote by a wide margin, and for a reproduction poster that is the correct answer, not a compromise.

Four more ways to move the number down without wrecking the result:

Let the mat do the fitting. If your piece is an odd size but close to a standard, buy a ready-made frame at the nearest standard size and pay only for a custom-cut mat. That is often the single biggest saving available.

Print to a standard size. If you are having a photo printed anyway, size the file to a standard frame before you print it, not after.

Bring your own frame. Most shops will fit new mat, glazing and backing into a frame you already own. Ask. If a moulding you love turns up at an estate sale in Webster Groves, it may be worth more to you than the sample corner on the wall.

Spend the savings on glazing. If you have to choose, a plain moulding with conservation glass protects your piece. An ornate moulding with 45 percent UV glass does not.

And read the discount carefully. Hobby Lobby’s custom framing page states that custom frames are 50 percent off the marked price and that the discount applies to frames only. That is a real saving on one of the four buckets. It is not 50 percent off your ticket, and two quotes carrying the same headline percentage can still land far apart.

### Is Hobby Lobby or Michaels cheaper for picture frames?

Nobody can answer that honestly as a blanket yes or no, and this article isn’t going to pretend otherwise. Both chains price custom work per project, both run promotional structures that change what a shelf number means, and neither publishes a comparable price list you could hold side by side. Anyone declaring a winner is guessing or selling something.

What can be verified is what each says about its own service. Hobby Lobby’s custom framing page says there is a framing expert in every store, that custom frames are 50 percent off the marked price for frames only, that the package includes moulding, matting, protective glass, an acid-free dust cover and hangers, and that UV-protective glass is standard with museum glass and cotton rag mats available. Michaels announced its 10-minute service for printed photos on November 18, 2025, at $29, in more than 500 stores at launch with a chainwide rollout by February 2026.

Rather than chasing a winner, compare the seven things that actually differ between any two framing counters, chain or independent:

Who cuts the mat, and where. Cut on site, or ordered from a central production facility? This drives turnaround more than anything else.

Does your piece leave the building? For a replaceable poster, who cares. For the only photograph of your grandmother, that is the whole question.

Which glazing lines are stocked. Ask for the UV percentage, not the adjective.

What mounting is the default. Is hinging offered, or is dry mounting simply what happens?

Will they refit a frame you already own? Some will, some won’t.

Can they handle the unusual piece? A jersey needs sewing, not adhesive. A shadow box needs depth. A diploma with a raised seal needs a spacer.

Turnaround, in writing. Especially in May and December.

Broadly, the independent shop’s advantage is the design conversation and the odd job; the chain’s advantage is convenience and visible discounting. Which of those is worth more depends entirely on what is in your hands. Get an itemized quote from both on identical specifications and the comparison answers itself.

### Does the Missouri or the Illinois side change what you pay?

Barely, and probably not enough to drive for. A finished framed piece is tangible goods, taxed at the shop’s address. Missouri’s state sales tax rate is 4.225 percent; Illinois charges 6.25 percent on general merchandise. Local add-ons close most of that gap: the Tax Foundation’s 2026 figures put the average combined state and local rate near 8.44 percent in Missouri and about 8.75 percent in Illinois.

On a $600 framing job, roughly three tenths of a percentage point is under two dollars. Meanwhile a single address in the city of St. Louis can sit well above the Missouri average, and a Belleville or Edwardsville shop can come in under the Illinois average. The rate that matters is the one at the counter you are standing at, and both states publish address-level lookup tools — the Missouri Department of Revenue rate map and the Illinois Tax Rate Finder.

The differences worth caring about are practical, not fiscal. Turnaround, in-house work and whether anyone there will touch a jersey vary far more between two shops in the same county than between the two states.

### What the person on the other side of the counter is watching

A frame shop is a custom manufacturer with a retail front, and the arithmetic is unforgiving. Moulding is bought by the foot, and miter waste is real — that 16x20 in a 2-inch profile eats 88 inches of stick, not the 72 the perimeter suggests, and the drop usually can’t be sold to anybody. Output is capped by one bench, one mat cutter and one pair of hands, so a shop can only finish so many pieces in a day no matter how hard the phone rings. The year is lumpy too: graduation season in May and the holiday run in the fall carry months that are much quieter. And the thing framers say to each other is that percentage-off signage down the road resets what a fair price sounds like before they have opened their mouth. The good ones answer it by showing the work — naming the board, naming the UV number, saying out loud whether the mounting can be undone. Which is also why being findable matters: people search this trade the week they need it, and a complete listing is how a shop gets into that search at all.

### How do you get a quote you can actually compare?

Bring the piece, not the measurements — a framer needs to see the paper, the edges and the condition. Then ask for the quote itemized, and take the same list to a second shop. Nine questions do the whole job:

What is the moulding footage, and the price per foot?

What is the mat made of — decorative paper, alpha-cellulose conservation, or 100 percent cotton rag?

What percentage of UV does the glazing block, and what is the product name?

Is the mounting reversible, and what adhesive is used?

Does the outside dimension cross 32x40, and what does that change?

Glass or acrylic, and why for this piece?

Who does the work, in which building, and what is the turnaround?

What happens if the piece is damaged while it is with you?

Does anyone here hold a Certified Picture Framer credential?

That last one is a real thing, not a nicety. The Professional Picture Framers Association has run the Certified Picture Framer exam since 1986, developed with Educational Testing Service — a three-and-a-half-hour written test covering preservation, mounting, mechanics and framing math, with a Master credential above it that requires five years in the trade. Plenty of excellent framers never sat it. But if someone has, they will tell you, and the conversation that follows will be a better one.

Still carrying it around in a cardboard tube? Browse framing shops across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then take the same nine questions to two of them and compare the itemized quotes line by line.

### Frequently asked questions

### Q. Where can I find custom picture framing in St. Louis?

A.  Four kinds of places do it: independent frame shops, galleries and art-supply stores with a framing counter, craft chains with an in-store framing department, and photo labs that sell framed prints. Shortlist two or three, then call and describe your piece — size, condition, and what it actually is — before you drive anywhere.

### Q. Where can I find custom framing services in Saint Louis, Missouri?

A.  Both sides of the river have them, and for an Illinois-side reader a shop in Belleville or Edwardsville is often a shorter trip than crossing into the city. Rather than sorting by distance, call ahead and ask three things: is the mat cut on site, does my piece leave the building, and which glazing lines do you stock?

### Q. Does Hobby Lobby still do framing?

A.  Yes. Hobby Lobby’s custom framing page says there is a framing expert in every store, and describes a package that includes the moulding, matting, protective glass, an acid-free dust cover on the back, and the hangers needed to mount it. The same page lists museum glass and cotton rag mats as options.

### Q. Does Hobby Lobby charge for framing?

A.  Yes — custom framing is a paid service. The advertised 50 percent off applies to the frame, and Hobby Lobby’s own page states the discount is for frames only. Matting, glazing, mounting and fitting labor are priced separately, which is exactly why two quotes carrying the same headline discount can land far apart.

### Q. Why is framing necessary?

A.  For a poster you would happily replace, it isn’t. For anything you can’t replace, it is. A frame holds the piece flat, keeps hands and dust off the surface, and with conservation glazing filters up to 99 percent of the ultraviolet light that fades ink and paper. For an original photograph or a signed item, that protection is the entire purchase.

### Q. Do paintings sell better, framed or unframed?

A.  Nobody publishes a reliable number on this, so treat any confident answer as sales talk. What is verifiable: juried shows publish presentation rules in the artist prospectus, and works on paper generally have to be matted or framed to hang. The Art Fair at Queeny Park, run each spring and fall by the Greater St. Louis Artists Organization, juries more than 120 artists. Read the rules before you spend.

### Q. What are the trends in picture framing for 2026?

A.  The clearest documented shift is speed.
