### Frequently asked questions

### Q. What is the 30% rule in AI?

A.  Two different rules share that number and neither has a traceable origin. One says AI should handle about 70% of a repetitive task while a human keeps the 30% requiring judgment. The other, from education, says no more than about 30% of submitted work should be AI-generated. Turnitin does not set a 30% threshold, and a BGR explainer dated June 9, 2026 could only say the idea may have started in schools.

### Q. What are the four stages of AI adoption?

A.  It depends whose four you mean, because there is no canonical model. Innovate UK Business Connect publishes an Adoption Stages Framework of Strategy, Data, Build and Implement. Other organizations publish four stages running from resistant through exploring and implementing to optimized, and others publish five. The phrase cannot be traced to a single originator, so treat any four-stage list as one firm’s map rather than a measurement.

### Q. What are the three rules of AI?

A.  People usually mean Isaac Asimov’s Three Laws of Robotics, which appeared in full in his short story Runaround in the March 1942 issue of Astounding Science Fiction. They are fiction. No statute contains them, no AI product implements them, and Asimov wrote most of his robot stories about the ways three tidy rules come apart when a real situation gets complicated.

### Q. What are the 3 AI laws?

A.  The same three, in Asimov’s wording: a robot may not injure a human or through inaction allow a human to come to harm; a robot must obey human orders except where that conflicts with the first law; a robot must protect its own existence except where that conflicts with the first two. Asimov credited editor John W. Campbell Jr. with helping formulate them in a December 1940 conversation. They are a storytelling device, not regulation.

### Q. What is AI not allowed to do?

A.  In the United States there is no comprehensive federal AI statute, so it depends on your state. Illinois bars AI from delivering therapy or making mental health treatment decisions under a law announced August 4, 2025, and from January 1, 2026 bars AI with a discriminatory effect in employment decisions. Missouri has no AI-specific statute; more than a dozen bills died in the 2026 session.

### Q. What was Stephen Hawking’s warning about AI?

A.  In a BBC interview published December 2, 2014, Hawking told correspondent Rory Cellan-Jones that the development of full artificial intelligence could spell the end of the human race, because such a system would redesign itself faster than slow biological evolution lets humans keep up. He was describing hypothetical self-improving general AI, not the business tools sold today, and he was using assistive technology at the time.

### Q. What jobs will be gone by 2030 due to AI?

A.  Nobody knows, and any list presented as settled is a guess in list form. The closest official source is the US Bureau of Labor Statistics Employment Projections for 2024 to 2034, released August 28, 2025, which extrapolates occupational trends rather than forecasting AI effects and names no occupation as eliminated by AI. The 2030 date itself comes from headlines, not from a study.

### Q. Which 5 jobs will survive AI?

A.  There is no authoritative list of five, and the ones circulating rarely name a source because there usually is not one. Work that requires showing up in person, holding a license, and being legally liable for the result is hardest to hand to software — but that is reasoning from how the work is structured, not a research finding, and it should be labeled that way.

### Q. What 5 jobs will remain after 2030?

A.  No credible source counts jobs that way. Occupations are bundles of tasks, and AI reaches different tasks inside the same job unevenly, so a whole occupation rarely vanishes on a date. Government projections exist — the BLS Employment Projections released August 28, 2025 run through 2034 — but they are trend extrapolations, not AI forecasts, and they publish no five-item survivor list.

## What AI Won’t Replace in a Local Service Business
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-ai-wont-replace-in-a-local-service-business

Picture a Tuesday in February. You are on your back under a house in Fenton with about eight inches of clearance, phone light in your teeth, working out why a supply line that was fine in November is weeping at a joint somebody soldered before you were born. Your phone has four texts on it. Two are from a customer in Spanish Lake who wants to know, politely, whether she really needs the whole run replaced or whether you are padding it.

You get out from under the house. You sit in the truck with a gas station sandwich, and the phone hands you a video: a man in a rented office explaining that artificial intelligence is about to make your trade obsolete, and also that you can clear $1,000 a day with it, and also that his course is $997 until midnight. You scroll. The next one says the same thing in a different room.

This is for the person who has to give a real answer to that — a plumber in Fenton, a stylist in Spanish Lake, a veterinarian or a general contractor bidding a job over in Troy in Madison County. Not a comforting answer. An accurate one. There is a real displacement happening inside a local service business, and there is also an industry selling you a story about it, and those two things are not the same size.

### Which business can AI not replace?

A business whose product requires a licensed human to be physically present and legally accountable. That is not a claim about how capable the software is. It is a claim about who signs the permit, who carries the liability policy, and who a state board can discipline afterward. Software holds none of those three, so the work stays with a person.

It is worth being precise, because “AI can’t replace the trades” gets repeated as a comfort blanket and it is only about two-thirds true. Run your own work through three questions.

Does somebody have to be there? Not on a screen. In the crawlspace, on the roof, hands on the animal, scissors in someone’s hair.

Does the state issue a credential to a human being for this? A license, a registration, a certificate with a person’s name on it.

Is somebody answerable a year later? When the joint fails, when the color goes green, when the dog is worse instead of better.

Work that answers yes to all three is structurally protected, and the protection has very little to do with the technology being bad at it. Work that answers no to all three — writing the estimate, answering the same question for the fortieth time, chasing a schedule — is exposed right now, today, in your business. Almost every local service company is a mix of the two, and the mix is the whole story.

### Why is licensed work a legal problem before it is a technology problem?

A license is issued to a human being, not to a process. That single fact does more work than any argument about what models can and cannot do. In Illinois you cannot legally perform plumbing work of any kind without a license from the Illinois Department of Public Health, and the route to it runs years of documented apprentice hours under a licensed plumber before you sit the state exam.

Cross the river and the rule changes shape rather than disappearing. Missouri has no statewide plumbing license at all — plumbing is licensed by cities and counties, so a card issued in one jurisdiction does not travel to the next one. That is its own moat, incidentally. A licensing regime stitched together out of municipalities is a local-knowledge business by construction.

Roofing splits along the same river, and it is worth knowing which side you are standing on. Illinois licenses roofing contractors statewide under the Illinois Roofing Industry Licensing Act; 225 ILCS 335/9 makes it unlawful to hold yourself out as a roofing contractor without a license from the Illinois Department of Financial and Professional Regulation, and the license requires an examination, liability insurance, workers’ compensation and a surety bond — $10,000 for a limited license, $25,000 for an unlimited one. Missouri does it by registration instead. Since January 1, 2023, a roofing contractor working in Missouri must hold a certificate of registration from the state, and to get one you file proof of liability insurance, a current workers’ compensation policy and motor vehicle insurance.

Personal-service trades are no softer. A cosmetology license requires 1,500 hours of approved training in Missouri and 1,500 hours in Illinois before you are permitted to sit for the exam. Fifteen hundred hours, attached to a named person, verified by a school.

Veterinary medicine puts the whole point into one sentence of statute. Missouri’s definition of a veterinarian-client-patient relationship, at RSMo 340.200, requires that the veterinarian has recently seen the animal or made medically appropriate and timely visits to the premises where it is kept, and has assumed responsibility for the medical judgments. Assumed responsibility. That is a person accepting consequences, written into law, as the precondition for the practice existing at all.

Read those four together and the pattern is not “AI is bad at pipes.” The pattern is that the statute names a person, requires that person to have been present, and holds that person answerable. Even in a version of events where a model diagnoses better than you do, a licensed human still has to own the output, because owning the output is what the license is. Changing that is not a software release. It is fifty state legislatures and the insurance industry behind them.

### Somebody has to be accountable when it goes wrong

Your customer is buying two things and only one of them is the work. The other is recourse. If the water heater floods a finished basement in March, there is a name on the permit, a policy number, sometimes a bond, and a state board that will take a written complaint. That entire apparatus assumes a specific human being can be found and held to it.

Notice how much of licensing is really insurance wearing a different hat. Missouri’s roofing registration requires proof of liability coverage, a current workers’ compensation policy and motor vehicle insurance before the certificate issues. Illinois stacks a surety bond on top of the insurance. An underwriter prices a risk it can attach to a person with a loss history and an address. No carrier writes a general liability policy on a language model, and no licensing board has the authority to suspend one.

Which is also why “the software told me to” will not function as a defense in a complaint hearing or a claim. If you run an estimate, a diagnosis or a treatment plan through a tool and hand the result to a customer, you have adopted it. The liability did not move. It cannot move, because there is nowhere for it to go. That asymmetry is permanent in a way that no capability benchmark is: you can be sued and the tool cannot.

The broader question of where these tools fit in a local business at all is covered in AI for St. Louis: how local businesses can actually use it. This page is about the narrower thing sitting underneath it — who the law can actually hold responsible, and why that is the line that does not move.

### Where is AI genuinely taking work in a service business?

The exposed work in a local service business is the paperwork around the work, and there is far more of it than most owners like to say out loud. An owner who insists nothing is exposed is making the same error as the one who panics, just in a more flattering direction.

Drafting. Estimates and proposals built from scrappy notes, job descriptions, letters to an insurer, the follow-up email you have been avoiding since Thursday.

Summarizing. A forty-minute call, a warranty document, six months of maintenance history before you walk into the building.

First-pass customer support. Hours, service area, do you work on that brand, do you take that insurance, are you licensed in Illinois too.

Scheduling and dispatch admin. Confirmations, reminders, the reshuffle when a morning job runs three hours long.

Marketing copy. Service page text, review responses, the seasonal post you have not written since spring.

If a person on your payroll does mostly those five things, that role is changing already. Say so honestly to yourself, then decide what you want that person doing instead, because the good version of this is usually redeployment rather than a headcount cut — the constraint in most service shops is billable hours, not admin hours.

The most-cited academic look at task exposure is by Tyna Eloundou, Sam Manning, Pamela Mishkin and Daniel Rock, first posted in March 2023 and published in Science in 2024. Worth stating plainly: several of the authors were at OpenAI, so read it as interested research rather than neutral measurement. Its headline estimate is that around 80% of the US workforce could have at least 10% of their work tasks affected by large language models, and roughly 19% could see at least half their tasks affected. The more useful detail sits at the other end of the distribution — the occupations that scored at the absolute floor, with no measured exposure, were the physically embodied ones: roofers, construction laborers, grounds maintenance workers.

Adoption is a separate question from capability, and the adoption numbers run well below the noise. The Census Bureau’s Business Trends and Outlook Survey, published May 26, 2026 and covering December 14, 2025 through May 3, 2026, put AI use at under 20% among firms with four or fewer employees, 32% among firms with 100 to 249 employees, and 37% among firms with 250 or more. A Federal Reserve note dated April 3, 2026 put it at about 18% of firms as of the end of 2025.

One warning about any trend line you are shown on this. In November 2025 the Census changed its question from whether a firm uses AI to produce goods or services to whether it uses AI in any business function, and reported rates rose between 47% and 159% depending on the industry. Any chart crossing that date is measuring a rewritten question as much as a change in behavior. Under the older wording, firms under 250 employees came in at 8.8% in August 2025, up from 6.3% six months before. The full mess of those numbers is unpacked in what percent of small businesses actually use AI.

And there is a figure that appears in no survey: what your own staff are already doing with these tools on their own initiative, on their own phones, without mentioning it. That one is worth knowing about before a customer finds out for you, and it is the subject of your staff is already using AI.

Wildly off-topic — those storm limbs hanging over the driveway: tree services.

### What about the “make $1,000 a day with AI” videos?

They are selling the course. That is the answer, and it is not cynicism — it is the business model. The revenue comes from people buying the method, not from people running it, which is why the pitch is always urgent and the price always expires at midnight.

The Federal Trade Commission has been working this in public. On September 25, 2024 it announced Operation AI Comply, five enforcement actions against companies making deceptive AI claims; three of the five were business-opportunity schemes promising AI-powered income. The most instructive case came after. On March 18, 2025 the FTC sued the operators of Click Profit, alleging they charged consumers a management fee of at least $45,000 — plus thousands more for inventory — to run “AI-powered” storefronts on Amazon, Walmart and TikTok, and claimed supplier partnerships with companies including Nike and Disney that they did not have. The FTC put consumer losses at at least $14 million. In August 2025 the operators settled and were permanently banned from the industry, with a $13.6 million judgment against one group of defendants.

These persist for three unglamorous reasons. The claim is unfalsifiable to somebody who has never tried it. The product is information, so the margin on the ten thousandth sale is identical to the first. And when it does not work, the buyer’s most natural explanation is that he failed to follow it properly — so he does not complain, and a meaningful share of buyers purchase the next one.

There is something concrete you can do with this. The FTC’s Business Opportunity Rule, at 16 CFR Part 437, requires a seller of a business opportunity to hand you a one-page disclosure document at least seven calendar days before you sign anything or pay anything. If the seller has stated or implied what you can earn, they must also give you a separate Earnings Claim Statement showing the start and end dates of those earnings and the number and percentage of buyers who actually earned at least that much. Ask for both, in writing. A legitimate seller has them ready. One caveat worth knowing: a plain online course often does not meet the Rule’s definition of a business opportunity, which is part of the reason so much of this is packaged as a course.

None of that makes learning the tools a scam. The distinction is whether you are being sold a skill or a rented outcome. A skill you keep, and you can test it on a Tuesday against work you already understand. That is the whole idea behind the AI workshops — sit down with the tools, on your own jobs, and find out where they help and where they quietly get things wrong.

### The judgment nobody sells a course on

The hardest parts of a trade to automate are also the parts nobody talks about, because they are the parts that were never written down. There are four, and every experienced operator will recognize all of them.

Diagnosing an unfamiliar problem in an old house. Much of this metro is century-old brick with three additions and four generations of plumbing stacked in one wall. The skill is not knowing the code; the code is a lookup. The skill is holding six plausible explanations at once and picking the one that is true in this house, from a smell, a stain pattern, the age of the fittings, the direction the floor slopes, and one sentence the homeowner said about last winter. It is also knowing when the honest answer is that you have to open the wall to find out, and saying that out loud instead of guessing confidently. A model is built to produce a confident answer from whatever it was given. You are allowed to say you do not know yet.

Reading a person. A customer goes quiet, and the silence means they do not understand and are embarrassed to say so. Another says “do whatever you think” and means “I cannot afford this and I am hoping you will notice.” A pet owner asks a question about cost that is actually a question about whether the animal is going to die. You have the room, the face and the pause. A tool has the transcript.

Deciding what not to sell. This is the least discussed and the most valuable. Telling somebody the $400 repair will hold four more years, when you could have written $6,000 of replacement that same afternoon, is a deliberate reduction in this month’s revenue in exchange for a referral base you cannot see on a spreadsheet. Every recommendation system ever built optimizes the transaction in front of it, because the transaction in front of it is the only thing it can observe. An operator with twenty years in one set of zip codes is optimizing something else entirely.

Improvising when the plan meets reality. The joist is in the wrong place. The part is discontinued and the supply house is closed. The chair in front of you has a home color job on it that nothing in the training covered. Every trade is really a long sequence of small recoveries, and the recovery is where the expertise lives. None of it is documented anywhere for a model to have read.

### What this looks like from your side of the counter

Most owners in the service trades know the economics better than they say out loud. The trip or diagnostic fee is close to a loss leader — it exists to get the truck to the door, and the money is made on planned work, the labor rate and parts margin, not on the 11pm emergency. Two weeks of weather can make a quarter: the first hard freeze, the first run of 95-degree days. February and October are the months you stare at a thin schedule. One callback eats a job’s profit and the second one eats the next job too. And the complaint owners actually make to each other is never about the work — it is the six-quote price shopper, the no-show, and the ninety-minute estimate that went to a guy working out of a trunk with no insurance.

The one thing AI genuinely changes in that picture is how people find you. They ask an assistant, in plain sentences, for somebody nearby who does this — a shift explained in Google AI Mode, explained for a local business owner. Being listed, complete and consistent is how you turn up in that answer instead of the guy with the trunk. If you are not on St Louis Near Me Directory yet, you can add your business.

Want the version where you learn the tools instead of buying an outcome? Take a look at the AI workshops for business owners across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then pick the one job in your week you would hand over first — the estimates, the phone, or the follow-up nobody has time for.

### Frequently asked questions

### Q. What jobs will be gone by 2030?

A.  Nobody can tell you honestly, and a source that names a year and a percentage is usually selling something. What is measurable now is task exposure, not job elimination. In the 2024 Science paper by Eloundou and colleagues, the occupations scoring zero exposure to large language models were the physically embodied ones — roofers, construction laborers, grounds maintenance workers. That is a description of today’s task mix, not a forecast.

### Q. What 5 jobs will survive AI?

A.  The framing is off, though the instinct behind it is sound. Instead of five job titles, use three tests: does somebody have to be physically present, does a state issue a license to a named human for the work, and is that human answerable a year later. Licensed trades, veterinary medicine, cosmetology, nursing and skilled construction pass all three. Office work built on drafting and summarizing passes none of them.

### Q. What are 10 jobs that AI can’t replace?

A.  Lists like this circulate constantly and most are guesswork. A defensible version is any occupation where the law requires a licensed person on site: plumbers, electricians, HVAC technicians, roofers, veterinarians, dentists, nurses, cosmetologists and barbers, home inspectors, and heavy equipment operators. The common thread is not difficulty. It is that a statute names a person who must be present, carry insurance, and can be disciplined.

### Q. What jobs will still be around in 10 years?

A.  That is a prediction, and this page will not make one. The structural answer is more useful anyway. Work stays with humans where the law requires a licensed individual, where the task is physical, and where somebody has to carry insurance and answer for the result afterward. Those requirements sit in state statute and insurance underwriting, and they move at the speed of legislatures, not software.

### Q. What will be AI after 10 years?

A.  Unknowable, and worth being suspicious of anyone who claims otherwise, particularly if a course is attached to the claim. What is checkable is current adoption. The Census Bureau’s Business Trends and Outlook Survey, published May 26, 2026, put AI use under 20% among firms with four or fewer employees and at 37% among firms with 250 or more. Plan against measured numbers.

### Q. What job is most safe from AI?

A.  By the task-exposure research, the most insulated work is the most physically embodied. In the 2024 Science study by Eloundou and colleagues, the occupations that scored at the absolute floor for exposure to large language models were manual ones such as roofers, construction laborers and grounds maintenance workers. Add a state license and personal legal liability on top of physical presence and you have the most protected combination available.

### Q. Which jobs will AI replace in 5 years?

A.  No credible source can name them with a date attached, and the ones that try are usually vendor marketing rather than research. The honest version of the question is which tasks are exposed today: drafting, summarizing, first-pass customer support, scheduling admin and marketing copy. If a role in your business is mostly those five, it is changing already. If it requires a person in a crawlspace, it is not.

### Q. Which jobs will not survive AI?

A.  Nobody can list them responsibly, and the dated versions people quote are modeling exercises reported as findings. What can be said is narrower. Roles built almost entirely on producing routine text, summarizing documents and answering repetitive first-line questions are exposed to tools that exist right now. Roles requiring physical presence, a state license and personal liability are not exposed in the same way.

### Q. What job is most at risk from AI?

A.  Judged by measured task overlap rather than headlines, the most exposed roles are text-heavy office ones. The 2024 Science paper by Eloundou and colleagues scored medical transcriptionists, customer service representatives, general office clerks and accountants among the highest-exposure occupations. Higher-paid, cognitive, screen-based work came out more exposed than manual work, which reverses the assumption most people start with.

## How Much Does It Cost to Use AI for a Business?
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-ai-actually-costs-a-small-business

Imagine it’s a Thursday night in Sunset Hills and you’re still at the kitchen table with the laptop open, because somebody at a chamber breakfast said you were behind on AI. Six tabs are running. One says $20. One says $200. One insists the whole thing is free. Not one of them tells you what it would cost you.

Maybe you’re running a two-truck operation out of Berkeley and the question is blunter than that. Is this another charge that lands on the card every month forever, like the website plugin nobody has opened since 2023? Or maybe you’re in Wood River, on the Illinois side, where payroll is tight enough that $25 a month per person is a real conversation and not a rounding error.

Here’s what nobody selling a course says out loud. The subscription is the cheapest part of this, and it is also the only part anybody quotes. What follows is every current price, checked against the provider’s own page on August 22, 2026 — plus the two costs that never show up on a pricing table.

### How much does it cost to use AI for a business?

Between $0 and about $25 per person per month for the tools a small business actually uses. Every major AI assistant runs a real free tier. Paid consumer plans cluster at $20 a month, and business plans with admin controls run $20 to $25 per user per month. All figures checked August 22, 2026.

That range looks wide because it spans two different products. A $20 consumer seat is one person with a login. A $20 business seat buys the same assistant plus centralized billing, an admin console, single sign-on, and a default setting that keeps your company’s content out of model training. The jump from $100 a month upward is a research-and-coding tier built for people who run the tool all day. A four-person plumbing outfit does not need it.

The honest headline, though, is the one further down: software is the smallest line on this bill. Our broader overview of how St. Louis businesses can actually use AI makes the same point in a paragraph. This post is the version with receipts, dates, and arithmetic you can run against your own week.

### What do the major AI tools charge per person right now?

Every figure below came off the provider’s own pricing page on August 22, 2026. AI pricing changes often enough that you should click through and re-check before you enter a card — one of these prices sits on a promotion that expires in five weeks, which is exactly why a dated list beats a remembered one.

ChatGPT (chatgpt.com/pricing). Free: $0. Go: $8 a month, and the page notes this plan may include ads. Plus: $20 a month. Pro: from $100 a month. ChatGPT Business: $20 per user per month billed annually, or $25 per user per month billed monthly, with a two-user minimum. Enterprise is custom-priced.

Claude (claude.com/pricing). Free: $0. Pro: $17 per month on an annual subscription billed at $200 up front, or $20 if billed monthly. Max: from $100 per month. Claude Team: a standard seat is $20 per seat per month billed annually, or $25 billed monthly, for teams of 2 to 150. A premium seat is $100 per seat per month annually, $125 monthly.

Google Gemini (gemini.google/about and one.google.com). The Gemini app is $0 a month with a Google Account. Google AI Plus is $4.99 a month, Google AI Pro is $19.99 a month, and Google AI Ultra starts at $99.99 a month. That $4.99 tier is the cheapest paid step on this whole list, which matters if all you want is the limits lifted a little.

Google Workspace (workspace.google.com/pricing.html). Business Starter is $7 per user per month, Standard is $14, and Plus is $22, on a one-year commitment billed monthly. New customers are shown 50% off for three months. The Gemini assistant is folded into these plans rather than sold separately — Gmail on Starter, and Gmail, Docs and Meet on Standard. If you already pay for Workspace, you are already paying for some AI.

Microsoft 365 Copilot (microsoft.com/microsoft-365-copilot/business). The Copilot Business add-on normally starts at $21.00 per user per month paid yearly. It is discounted to $18.00 between July 1, 2026 and September 30, 2026, first year only, annual commitment required, and the add-on is sold only to existing Microsoft 365 customers on an eligible Business plan. Bundled instead: Microsoft 365 Business Standard with Copilot is $23.50 per user per month paid yearly, and Business Premium with Copilot is $32.00.

Canva (canva.com/pricing). Free: US$0. Pro: US$180 a year for one person. Business: US$250 a year per person. Canva earns a place on this list because for a lot of local operators the AI they actually touch every week is the one sitting inside a design or scheduling tool they already bought, not a chat window they opened on purpose.

One thing this list deliberately leaves out is usage-based API pricing, where you pay by the token instead of by the seat. That is a developer product. If a vendor is quoting you token pricing for a five-person service business, you have wandered into the wrong aisle.

### Which AI is 100% free?

Every one of the big ones, at the entry tier. ChatGPT Free is $0. Claude Free is $0. The Gemini app is $0 a month with a Google Account. Microsoft 365 Copilot Chat carries no additional cost for users already on an eligible Microsoft 365 subscription. Canva Free is US$0. Checked August 22, 2026.

“Free” is doing honest work in that sentence, not marketing work. On ChatGPT’s own comparison table the Free plan lists unlimited everyday text chats, with the caps landing on the heavy stuff: limited messages with uploads, limited and slower image generation, limited voice chats, limited deep research, limited memory and context. Which is to say the ceiling sits above where most small business use actually lives.

Think about what an owner really asks an assistant to do. Rewrite a rambling estimate into something a customer can read. Turn six bullet points into a Facebook post. Draft a reply to a two-star review without sounding defensive. Summarize a 14-page insurance letter. Those are short text jobs. They do not come near the caps.

So here is the advice from a directory that runs paid AI workshops for local business owners and would happily sell you a seat: run free for thirty days first. Use it on real work, not on test prompts. If you hit a wall you can name out loud — you keep running out of file uploads, or you want the tool inside your email instead of in a separate tab — then upgrade, and you will know exactly what you are buying. If you never hit a wall, your AI spend is zero and you should keep it there.

Two caveats on free that are worth more than the money saved. First, consumer free tiers and business tiers handle your data differently, and the business tiers exist partly for that reason — ChatGPT Business, for one, states no training on your business data by default. Second, free tools need no purchase order, which means your staff can already be using them without telling you. That gap is its own subject, covered in what happens when your staff is already using AI.

### What are the costs nobody puts on the price list?

Two, and together they dwarf the subscription. The first is the time to learn the tool well enough that it stops producing generic mush. The second is the review step — somebody has to read the output before it reaches a customer, every single time. An owner budgeting only for seats is budgeting the smallest line on the page.

Start with learning. The first month is the expensive one, because you are paying the subscription and have not yet earned the hours back. Nobody gets good output on day one. They get output that sounds like a press release wrote it. Getting past that takes a few sessions of feeding the tool your actual specifics: your service area, your pricing structure, the four questions every customer asks, the way you talk. That is unpaid time and it is real. It is also the part a decent workshop compresses, which is the whole argument for training over trial and error.

Then the review. This is the cost that quietly decides whether AI is worth anything to you. AI output is confidently wrong sometimes — wrong hours, a service you dropped two years ago, a warranty you never offered, a price that is not your price. If that reaches a customer you have not saved time, you have manufactured a callback. So somebody reads it first. If that somebody is you, at the end of a ten-hour day, price it honestly.

Wildly off-topic — veterinarians across the metro, for the other kind of emergency.

Here is the test that sorts the good tasks from the bad ones. Compare the time to review a draft against the time to write it from scratch. Reviewing a 90-word review reply takes about twenty seconds and writing one takes four minutes, so that task wins easily. Reviewing a technical quote where every line item has to be checked against your cost sheet can take longer than typing it yourself. Same tool, same $20, opposite result.

A few smaller ones people trip over. Annual commitments: Claude Pro at $17 a month means $200 charged up front, and the Microsoft Copilot add-on requires an annual commitment with the promotional rate applying to the first year only. Seat sprawl: three people quietly expensing three different $20 subscriptions that do roughly the same job is $720 a year for redundancy. And the cost of not deciding — which is real, has no dollar figure, and anyone who hands you one for it is guessing.

### What actually moves the price, and what is padding?

Three things move it: how many people genuinely need a login, whether you commit annually, and whether you are buying an assistant you already own inside another subscription. Everything else being sold around AI right now — strategy retainers, prompt packs, certificates — moves your bill without moving your capability.

Seat count is the big one, because per-user pricing is brutally linear. Ten seats at $25 is ten times one seat at $25. The lever is not negotiating the rate, it is being honest about who actually opens the thing. In a lot of small offices two people use it daily, one uses it monthly, and four never log in after week two. Buy for the two, revisit in ninety days.

Annual commitment is the second lever, and the discount is real. As of August 22, 2026, Claude Pro drops from $20 monthly to $17 on an annual plan, ChatGPT Business drops from $25 per user monthly to $20 billed annually, and the Microsoft Copilot Business add-on requires an annual commitment outright. Call it fifteen to twenty percent for locking in twelve months. Take that deal only after the thirty-day free trial has told you the answer, not before — a discount on a tool you abandon in March is not a discount.

The third is duplication, and it is the one that gets people. If you pay for Google Workspace Standard at $14 per user per month, a Gemini assistant is already in your Gmail, Docs and Meet. If you pay for Microsoft 365, Copilot Chat is already there at no additional cost. Adding a separate $20 consumer subscription on top buys you a second front door to a room you were already standing in. Sometimes that is the right call, because the standalone tools do more. Often it is just two invoices.

As for padding: be careful with anything priced as a setup fee for work that takes an afternoon, any package built around secret prompts, any guarantee of a specific result, and any certificate that no customer of yours will ever ask to see. The tidy rules-of-thumb quoted to justify these packages deserve the same scrutiny; a number that cannot be traced to a named source and a date is a sales line, not a finding. Training itself is not padding; a half day that gets you past the generic-mush stage is often cheaper than three months of paying for a subscription you use badly. The test is whether you leave with your own work improved, or with a folder of somebody else’s templates.

### How do you tell whether it is worth it for your business?

Tie it to one task you already do every week, not to a productivity claim. Pick the task, time it honestly for two weeks, price your hour, and compare. A $20-a-month seat has to save you roughly 80 minutes a month at a $15 hourly replacement cost just to break even. That is arithmetic, not a promise.

Where the $15 comes from: Missouri’s minimum wage is $15.00 an hour for 2026, in effect January 1 through December 31, 2026, per the Missouri Department of Labor. Illinois guarantees $15.00 an hour for workers 18 and older, per the Illinois Department of Labor. Both sides of the river landed on the same floor, which makes the math unusually simple for a metro that straddles a state line. Treat it as a floor and nothing more — if the task is one you would hand to a $28-an-hour office manager, run the numbers at $28.

The sequence, in order. One: name the weekly task. Social posts, review replies, quote write-ups, after-hours inquiries, the monthly email nobody wants to write. Two: time it for two weeks, on paper, because your estimate of how long it takes is wrong in both directions. Three: run it for thirty days on the free tier. Four: measure the same task again and subtract the review time — the number that matters is time saved after somebody checks the output. Five: multiply by your real hourly cost and hold it against $20, or $25, or $18.

If the answer comes out close, do not buy. Close means the gain sits inside your own measurement error, and a marginal subscription is exactly the kind that renews for three years while nobody opens it. If the answer is not close — if you got back two hours a week on quote write-ups — you already know, and you did not need a vendor case study to tell you.

Worth saying plainly: most small firms have not made this call yet. Census Bureau data published May 26, 2026, covering December 14, 2025 through May 3, 2026, put AI use at under 20% of firms with four or fewer employees, against 32% of firms with 100 to 249 employees and 37% of those with 250 or more. You are not late. Those figures, and the reason they are so easy to misquote, get broken down in what percent of small businesses actually use AI.

One free thing costs nothing to check before any of this: what AI already says about your business in search results. Google’s AI answers carry no fee and no paid placement, and how that surface behaves is walked through in Google AI Mode explained for a local business owner. Before you spend $20 a month generating content, spend twenty minutes finding out what the free answer engines are already telling people about you.

### What this math looks like from the owner’s side of the counter

If you run a small local service business, your margin does not live in the price you quote. It lives in labor utilization — how many of the hours you pay for turn into billable hours. Revenue gets booked in the field, and everything that keeps the business alive happens after the trucks are back: quotes, invoices, the review reply you have been avoiding, the third voicemail from someone who wants a number over the phone and will never book. That is the unpaid shift, and it is where a $20 subscription either earns out or does not. Add the seasonality — the two or three weeks that carry the year, and the dead month where you are paying people to look busy — and a tool that drafts fast is worth most exactly when you have the least time to use it. What the good operators do differently is boring: they answer first. Speed of response wins more local jobs than price does. Being findable is that same problem wearing a different hat, which is why a complete, accurate listing — yours on St Louis Near Me Directory — is worth an hour of the same evening.

### Frequently asked questions

### Q. How much does AI cost for a small business?

A.  Checked August 22, 2026: $0 to about $25 per person per month for the tools most small businesses use. Free tiers at ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Canva cost nothing at all. Paid consumer plans sit at $20 a month. Business plans with admin controls and single sign-on run $20 per user per month billed annually, or $25 billed monthly. Learning time and review time are separate costs, and larger ones.

### Q. Is it worth paying for AI?

A.  Only after you have hit a wall on the free tier that you can name out loud. Run free for thirty days on one weekly task you already do, time the task before and after, and subtract the minutes somebody spends reviewing the output. At a $15 hourly replacement cost, a $20 seat needs to give back roughly 80 minutes a month to break even. If it comes out close, do not buy.

### Q. Is it worth to pay $20 for ChatGPT?

A.  ChatGPT Plus was $20 a month as of August 22, 2026, and there is now an $8 Go tier sitting between Free and Plus, so the choice is no longer all-or-nothing. Plus earns its price if you keep hitting upload limits, want the reasoning models, or need projects and scheduled tasks. If you mainly write short text — review replies, post drafts, tidied-up estimates — the free tier covers it and $8 covers most of the rest.

### Q. Is ChatGPT Pro $200 worth it?

A.  Check the current price before answering that. On August 22, 2026 the ChatGPT pricing page listed Pro as starting from $100 a month, not $200. Either way it is built for research and coding at volume: five to twenty times the usage, maximum deep research, the largest context window. For a local service business drafting a few dozen messages a week it is the wrong product, and Plus or Business is the honest fit.

### Q. Does ChatGPT offer a free business plan?

A.  No. ChatGPT Free is an individual plan, and OpenAI’s pricing page states plainly that Free, Go and Plus are designed for individuals while Business and Enterprise are for businesses. ChatGPT Business was $20 per user per month billed annually, or $25 billed monthly, on August 22, 2026. Nonprofits are the exception — OpenAI advertises up to a 75% discount on Business or Enterprise through OpenAI for Nonprofits.

### Q. How many users are allowed on a ChatGPT business plan?

A.  ChatGPT Business starts at two users, per OpenAI’s pricing FAQ as of August 22, 2026, and no upper limit is published — larger organizations get pointed toward Enterprise. For comparison, Claude Team is sold for teams of 2 to 150 seats. If you are a sole operator, neither business plan applies to you and the individual tiers are what you actually want.

### Q. Which AI tool is best for small business?

A.  Usually the one already inside software you pay for. If you run Google Workspace, the Gemini assistant is bundled into Business Starter at $7 per user per month and Standard at $14. If you run Microsoft 365, Copilot Chat carries no additional cost on an eligible subscription. Buying a separate assistant makes sense once you have outgrown what is already sitting on your desk, and not before.

### Q. What is the best AI for pricing?

A.  None of the general assistants, and be skeptical of anything sold to you that way. ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini do not know your labor rates, your material costs, your drive times or what the shop down the road charges, so any number they hand you is a guess dressed up in confident prose. They are genuinely useful for explaining a quote clearly to a customer. Setting the number stays your job, off your own cost sheet.

### Q. What is the best pricing software for small businesses?

A.  That depends entirely on your trade, and it is usually a feature of the estimating, booking or point-of-sale system you already run rather than a standalone purchase. Judge it on whether it pulls your real costs, handles sales tax correctly for your side of the river, and exports cleanly to your accounting software. An AI label on the box is not a reason to switch, and no software knows your margin better than you do.

## Where to Buy Craft Supplies in St. Louis Without Overpaying
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/where-to-buy-craft-supplies-in-st-louis

Imagine it’s 8:40 on a Tuesday night in Ballwin and the poster board is still blank. The project is due Thursday. It needs foam sheets, a glue stick that is not welded shut, and something, anything, that can pass for a river. You have one open store and about forty dollars of patience.

Or picture the version where you live in Florissant and the ask is bigger. A whole classroom set. Thirty of something. You do the arithmetic standing in the aisle, put half of it back, and drive home wondering how a craft that costs a dollar to imagine costs sixty to actually make.

Then there is the version in Maplewood or south city, where somebody just cleaned out a grandmother’s sewing room and now four bins of buttons, yarn and half-used ribbon are riding around in the trunk with nowhere to go. Those two problems are the same problem. The St. Louis metro has an entire category of store built to solve both at once, and most people have never heard of it.

### What is a creative reuse center, and how is it different from a craft store?

A creative reuse center takes in donated surplus materials and resells them cheaply, usually by weight or by the container rather than by the piece. Fabric, yarn, paper, beads, frames, buttons, wood scraps, classroom leftovers. Part thrift shop, part supply closet, and most of the time it is the honest answer to the cheapest-supplies question.

The stock arrives from places that generate leftovers as a byproduct of doing business. Estate cleanouts. Retiring teachers. Print shops with end rolls. Framers with cut-offs. Upholsterers, sign makers, theater companies, a graphic designer clearing out a studio. Nobody manufactures this inventory, which is exactly why it costs so little and exactly why it is unpredictable.

Two St. Louis names come up when people go looking for this. Perennial is a local non-profit built around teaching creative reuse. The STL Teachers’ Trading Post, which also operates as the Upcycle Treasure Box, is a creative reuse center that sells materials by the pound. Check each organization’s own site before you drive out, because reuse operations run on volunteer hours and donation flow, and both of those move.

The pricing works because the math underneath is different. A conventional craft store buys wholesale and marks up. A reuse center receives its inventory at no cost and prices to cover sorting, storage and keeping the lights on. That is the whole trick. The EPA’s own waste management hierarchy ranks reuse above recycling for a related reason: the cheapest material in the world is one that already exists.

### How do you shop a store that sells by the pound?

You shop it backwards from a big-box craft aisle. Walk in with a material in mind rather than a finished product, because the shelf decides what is possible that day. Bring your own bags or bins, bring a list of properties instead of brand names, and give yourself an hour. Rushing a reuse center is how you leave empty-handed.

Weight is the entire pricing model, so learn which categories win. Paper, fabric scraps, felt, ribbon, trim, yarn and thread weigh almost nothing and land absurdly cheap by the pound. Glass, ceramic, hardware, books and solid wood are heavy and price accordingly. If you are outfitting a classroom, a scout troop or a vacation week of rainy afternoons, the light categories are where a budget stretches furthest.

Substitution is the skill that separates people who love these places from people who bounce off them after one visit. You wanted twelve matching blue felt squares. There are nine, plus teal. Either the project bends or the trip failed. Crafters who shop reuse well decide the palette after the trip, not before, and they treat the bin as a prompt rather than a catalog.

Here is the trap nobody warns you about. Cheap per pound is still money if it sits in a closet. The failure mode at a reuse center is not overpaying, it is over-acquiring, and then storing five pounds of somebody else’s good intentions in your basement for six years. Buy for a project you have already started. The same discipline applies to vintage, thrift and antique shops around the metro, where the temptation is identical and the storage problem is bigger.

### Is Hobby Lobby or Walmart cheaper for craft supplies?

Neither one wins across the board, and any page that tells you otherwise is guessing. The answer flips by category and by whether you happen to be buying during a sale. General-merchandise retail tends to hold the line on commodity basics. A dedicated craft chain usually wins on specialty stock nobody else bothers to carry. Compare unit price, not shelf price.

Unit price is the only comparison that survives contact with a craft aisle, because package sizes are deliberately hard to line up. Price it per yard, per sheet, per ounce, per foot, per skein. Do it on your phone while you stand there. A larger package at a higher shelf price is frequently the cheaper one, and a small package on sale frequently is not.

Do not build a trip around a coupon you have not confirmed today. Craft retail promotions change, apps replace paper, and category sales rotate on a schedule the store does not publish anywhere. Check the retailer’s own site or app the morning you go. Store-brand basics deserve a look too, since glue, poster board, construction paper and acrylic craft paint are close to commodities.

Then price the drive, which almost nobody does. Two stores twenty-five minutes apart, one trip each, to save four dollars is a losing trade once you count fuel and an evening you do not get back. The households that spend least on crafts are rarely the ones chasing the lowest sticker. They are the ones consolidating trips and buying against a written project list.

### Which craft supplies should you always buy new?

Three categories, and it is the same three every time. Anything with chemistry in it, anything that touches skin or food, and anything that has to match across a large surface. Adhesives, sealants, resins, safety gear and food-contact materials belong on a fresh receipt. Almost everything else is fair game secondhand, and cheerfully so.

Glue is the one people learn the hard way. Adhesives, mediums, sealants, spray finishes and two-part resins keep curing in the container whether anyone opens them or not. A donated bottle that looks perfectly fine can be stringy, separated, or simply dead. Acrylic paint goes rubbery. Elastic loses its snap. You cannot see any of that through the packaging, and you tend to find out at the exact moment you have no time left.

Then there is the safety tier, and it is not negotiable. If a material will touch skin, touch food, or end up in front of a small child, buy it new and buy it labeled. Jewelry findings for pierced ears. Glazes on anything that will hold food. Soap and candle fragrance oils. Respirators, cut-resistant gloves, eye protection. Craft materials intended for kids under three. Certification lives on the packaging, and packaging is the first thing a donation bin strips away. An unlabeled bag of beads is a lovely mystery until a toddler is involved.

Last, the matching problem. Yarn from one dye lot and yarn from another look identical under store light and obviously different in a finished blanket. If your project needs consistent color across a big surface, buy the full quantity new, in one purchase, and buy one extra. Blades get the same treatment. Rotary cutters, craft knife blades, machine needles and drill bits are cheap, and a dull one quietly ruins expensive material while you stand there blaming your own technique.

### Where to donate craft supplies in St. Louis?

Start with a creative reuse center, because it is the only kind of place purpose-built for the awkward stuff. Half-used skeins. Mismatched buttons. One-sided paper. Fabric remnants, partial bead strands, somebody’s inherited box of embroidery floss. A general thrift store will decline most of that on sight. A reuse center exists precisely for it.

After that, the list runs longer than people expect. Art teachers and classroom teachers take paper, markers, yarn and containers. Libraries running maker programs take kits and consumables. Senior centers and memory care programs want large-print, large-piece, easy-grip materials. Scout troops burn through felt, glue and cardboard at a rate that has to be seen. Community theater and school costume shops will take fabric, trim, notions and anything that fastens. Animal shelters take clean towels and fleece scraps, which is not crafting, but it does empty a bin.

Prep matters more than volume. Check the posted wanted list before you load the car, because a rejected carload rides home with you. Sort by material instead of by which drawer it came from, bag like with like, and label the outside so a volunteer does not have to open everything. Keep out anything dried, rusted, mildewed or leaking, plus open solvents and elderly aerosols. Those belong in a household hazardous waste stream rather than a donation bin, and your county or municipal solid waste program is the right place to ask about them.

Timing is the part nobody plans for. Estate cleanouts and downsizing moves produce the biggest donations on the tightest deadlines, which is the worst possible combination for a small non-profit running on volunteer hours and finite shelf space. So call first. Ask what they actually need this month, ask when the drop-off window is, and ask whether they can absorb four bins today or would rather take two now and two in the fall. A donation that fits is worth more than a donation that is merely large.

### Is there a Hobby Lobby near Florissant, MO?

Almost certainly within a reasonable drive, but confirm it through the retailer’s own store locator rather than a third-party page, this one included. Chain craft stores open, close and relocate, and the pages listing them go stale quietly. North county sits close enough to the metro’s major retail corridors that this is a question of minutes, not counties.

The real failure mode is not the store, though. It is the shelf. A locator tells you a building exists. It does not tell you whether the thing you need is inside it. Online availability counts are estimates drawn from a system of record, and a system of record has no idea that the last four packs walked out at lunchtime or are sitting in a cart somebody abandoned in aisle nine.

So call, and ask for something specific. Not “do you have foam sheets,” which gets you a yes from a person who has not moved. Ask whether somebody can walk over and physically check for the color, size and quantity you need, then ask them to hold it at the register under a name. Two minutes on the phone beats a forty-minute round trip. Most craft retail staff will do it if you ask politely and you are not calling at 5:45 on a Saturday.

North county has options past the chain, too. General-merchandise and discount stores carry the commodity basics: glue, poster board, construction paper, tape, basic acrylics. Thrift stores along the same corridors turn up frames, yarn, fabric and cardboard worth cutting up. And if the project has any flexibility in it, one reuse-center run per season beats four emergency trips at full price. The households that spend least on crafts are simply the ones that stopped shopping in emergencies.

### What are some artsy things to do in St. Louis?

More than the budget suggests, and a good share of it is free. Forest Park anchors that end of the list, since the art museum there offers free general admission and the surrounding institutions run family programming and outdoor work you can walk past for nothing. Beyond the park sits a deep bench of galleries, studios, classes and neighborhood fairs.

Galleries are the cheapest ticket in town, which is to say usually no ticket at all. University and college galleries rotate student and visiting shows through the academic year. Community and co-op galleries across the metro hang local work, and the people minding the desk are generally delighted that you asked. Evening openings are free, sociable and low-commitment. Warm-weather neighborhood art fairs add a few dozen more, free to walk, and both are where you find out which artists also teach.

Then the hands-on side, where craft supplies and artsy things stop being separate subjects. Library systems run maker programs and craft nights. Parks and recreation departments run seasonal classes. Reuse centers teach workshops built around whatever material happened to come through the door that month, which is a genuinely different experience from a kit. Paint-your-own pottery and studio-night formats cover people who want a finished object and no cleanup. For kids, the metro’s music, art and dance classes run on a session calendar that fills earlier than parents expect.

Confirm current admission, hours and schedules on each venue’s own site, or start from galleries and arts listings across the metro. Free days rotate, exhibitions close, class sessions fill, and a page that was accurate last season is a memory rather than a plan.

### What this looks like from the other side of the counter

Independent craft retail and reuse non-profits both run on margins that would alarm a normal retailer, and they fight different battles. A reuse center cannot forecast inventory, because inventory is whatever showed up Tuesday. An independent shop cannot beat a chain on price, so it competes on stock nobody else carries, on staff who actually know the technique, and on classes that turn a browser into a regular.

Which explains the two things shoppers find maddening. Hours shift, because volunteer hours shift. And the perfect thing you saw last visit is gone forever, because there was exactly one of it. Neither is disorganization. It is the business model doing precisely what the business model does.

If you make things and sell them — at markets, from a booth, out of a spare bedroom — the same visibility problem lands on you at a smaller scale. People search for what you make by neighborhood and by material, not by your business name, and the half-finished listing is usually the thing deciding whether they ever find you. ### Frequently asked questions

### Q. Where is the cheapest place to get craft supplies?

A.  Usually a creative reuse center, where donated surplus materials sell by weight or by the container instead of by the piece. Light categories such as fabric scraps, paper, felt, ribbon and yarn stretch a budget furthest. Thrift stores, estate sales and rummage sales come next, with big-box basics after that.

### Q. What do creative reuse centers usually not accept?

A.  Anything dried out, rusted, mildewed, moldy or leaking, plus open solvents, old aerosols and most electronics. Soiled fabric and broken furniture are common declines as well. Wanted lists vary by organization and change with available shelf space, so read the current list on the group’s own site before you load the car.

### Q. Can you sell things you make from reuse-center materials?

A.  Generally yes, and plenty of metro makers do exactly that. Ask the organization about its own policy first, since a few limit bulk resale of unaltered donated goods. Two practical cautions: reuse stock rarely repeats, so a hit product may be unrepeatable, and anything touching skin, food or small children still needs new, labeled materials.

### Q. Is it cheaper to make a craft than to buy one?

A.  Only when you already own the tools and the materials come cheap. A single handmade item bought new, from scratch, usually costs more than a mass-produced equivalent once you count adhesives and the trip. Quantity flips it. Thirty of something, made from by-the-pound materials, beats thirty retail every time.

### Q. Do you need to bring anything to a by-the-pound craft store?

A.  Bring your own bags or bins, a tape measure, a phone for unit-price math, and a written list of material properties rather than brand names. Wear clothes you can dig in. Leave an hour, since sorted bins reward patience, and skip the shopping-list mindset that expects an exact match to be sitting there.

### Q. Where do teachers find free or cheap classroom craft supplies in St. Louis?

A.  Creative reuse centers are built for exactly this, and some operate a teacher program specifically — the STL Teachers’ Trading Post grew out of that idea. Terms differ by organization and by school district, and they change as donated stock moves, so check the current program on the organization’s own site rather than assuming last year’s arrangement still holds.

### Q. Is Hobby Lobby or Walmart cheaper for craft supplies?

A.  Neither wins outright, and treating either as the cheap option is how budgets go. Big-box general merchandise tends to beat a craft chain on commodity basics, while the craft chain carries depth the general store does not. Compare unit price on the specific item, and check a creative reuse center first for anything you can buy by weight.

### Q. Where to donate craft supplies in St. Louis?

A.  Start with a creative reuse center, which will take categories a thrift store turns away. After that: school art teachers, libraries with maker programs, senior centers, scout troops, and theater or costume shops. Read the current wanted list first, sort by material, and keep out anything dried, rusted, mildewed or leaking.

### Q. Is there a Hobby Lobby near Florissant, MO?

A.  North county shoppers generally have chain craft and general-merchandise retail along the larger commercial corridors, with more options toward mid county and St. Charles County. Use the retailer’s own store locator rather than any published address, then call and ask someone to physically check the shelf before you drive.

### Q. What are some artsy things to do in St. Louis?

A.  More than most residents ever use, and much of it free — a major art museum in Forest Park with free general admission, university and community galleries, neighborhood art fairs through the warm months, library maker programs, and hands-on classes at reuse centers and parks departments. Confirm current admission and schedules on each venue’s own site.

## What to Know Before Buying a Used Boat in Missouri
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-to-know-before-buying-a-used-boat-in-missouri

Imagine it’s the first warm Saturday in May and you’re standing in a driveway in Lake St. Louis, looking at a bowrider on a trailer. The seller is friendly. The upholstery looks better than the photos did. He runs it on a hose, it sounds fine, and he mentions that the title is “around here somewhere.” You have cash in the truck.

Or the afternoon goes another way. You drive to Alton to look at a pontoon, or you take the long trip to Osage Beach because the selection at the lake is deeper, and now you’re doing arithmetic in a parking lot with a St. Charles address in your head and no clear idea what the state is going to want from you on Monday.

Here is the part almost nobody tells a first-time buyer in Missouri. The boat is not one purchase. It is usually three separate pieces of titled property, taxed and registered under rules that do not work the way your car does. Get that wrong on a Saturday and you can spend the next month unwinding it.

### Do boats need titles in Missouri?

Yes, and usually more than one. Missouri titles the boat itself, and it titles an outboard motor separately, with its own paperwork and its own serial number. Put a trailer under all that and you are looking at a third titled item. One handshake in a driveway, three transactions at the license office.

That catches out almost everyone who has only ever bought a car. With a car, one title covers the whole machine, engine included. Missouri does not treat a boat that way. The hull carries its own title and its own identifying number, and an outboard motor carries its own title and its own serial number, because motors get sold, swapped, stolen and re-hung on different boats constantly. Inboard and sterndrive setups behave differently, since the engine is built into the boat rather than bolted onto the transom, so ask the license office which rule applies to the exact rig in front of you.

So the first question for a private seller is not about engine hours or maintenance. It is this: do you have the title for the boat, the title for the motor, and the title for the trailer, all in your name, all in your hand, today? If the answer to any one of those is a shrug, you have not found a bargain. You have found a paperwork project with a boat attached.

Then match the paper to the metal. Every boat built for sale in the United States carries a hull identification number, a twelve-character string stamped or plated on the starboard side of the transom, up near the top corner. Read it out loud against the title. A digit that does not match is not a typo you sort out later, it is the whole deal. Do the same with the motor’s serial number and, if the trailer has one, the plate on the trailer tongue.

One exception is worth knowing about. A vessel documented with the U.S. Coast Guard runs on a different track than a state title, and that shows up on larger cruisers more often than on a runabout. If a seller hands you a federal certificate of documentation instead of a state title, stop and call the Missouri Department of Revenue before any money changes hands.

### Can I buy a used boat without a title?

You can hand somebody money for almost anything. Whether you can then put that boat legally in the water under your own name is a very different question, and the honest answer is that a missing title is the most expensive problem in a used boat deal. Not the motor. The paperwork.

The clean fix costs the seller a modest fee and costs you nothing. The seller applies for a duplicate title in their own name, waits for it to arrive, and then signs it over to you at closing. A seller who resists that is telling you something useful. Maybe the boat is not theirs to sell. Maybe a lien is still open on it. Maybe they bought it the same way you are about to, on a handshake, and the problem is already three owners old.

That is exactly how these things compound. Every buyer who accepts a bill of sale instead of a title passes a slightly bigger mess to the next buyer, and whoever is holding it when the music stops has to prove ownership to the state. In our experience watching listings across the metro, the “no title, priced to move” boat is not underpriced at all. It is priced correctly for what it actually is.

Recovery paths do exist for a boat with a broken paper trail, and the Department of Revenue will tell you which one fits your situation. They generally involve a serial number verification, sworn statements about how you came to own the thing, and patience. If you decide to buy a paperwork project with your eyes open, fine. Just do not discover it on Monday.

### Do you pay sales tax on a used boat in Missouri?

Yes. Missouri collects state and local sales tax on a used boat purchase, including a private sale between two neighbors, and it is collected when you title the boat rather than at the moment of the handshake. The outboard motor is taxed too. This is the bill that ambushes first-time buyers.

The rate is not one flat number. Missouri layers a state rate together with local rates, and for titled property the local portion generally follows where the buyer lives rather than where the seller lives or where the boat happened to be sitting. A buyer in St. Charles and a buyer in Jefferson County can owe different totals on the identical boat. Look up the current rate for your own address using the sales tax rate tool on the Department of Revenue site before you agree to a price, not after.

The tax is figured on what you actually paid, documented by the bill of sale. Which brings up the thing people mutter about in driveways. Writing a lower number on the bill of sale to shrink the tax is fraud, it is obvious to the people who process these transactions all day, and it is a genuinely bad trade. You save a few hundred dollars once, and you carry a false purchase record on a titled asset you may want to insure, finance or resell later.

Nothing to do with boats, and far cheaper — metro farmers markets, town by town.

Missouri does allow certain credits against that tax in defined situations, such as when you sold or traded a comparable titled item close to the same date. The rules are specific and time-limited, so the move is to ask the license office what applies to your situation instead of assuming, and to keep every scrap of paperwork from the sale you made. Bring it with you. Nobody is going to go looking for a credit on your behalf.

### How much is personal property tax on a boat in Missouri?

There is no single statewide figure, because personal property tax is assessed and levied county by county. Missouri counties treat a boat as taxable personal property, the same broad category as your car. Your assessor puts a value on it, your county’s levies get applied, and a bill arrives later in the year. Then it repeats, every year you own it.

The mechanics matter more than the number. You declare what you own to your county assessor early in the year, the assessment reflects the value of the boat, the motor and the trailer as of the first of January, and the collector bills you in the fall with payment due before the year closes. Own the boat on January 1 and it lands on your list for that year, even if you sell it in February.

This is also the tax that comes back around at renewal time, because Missouri ties registration renewal to proof that you paid it. No paid receipt, no renewal. So when you buy in August, the smart move is a short call to your county collector and assessor asking exactly how and when the boat lands on your account, and what you will need to show next time.

Here is the part that ought to change how a buyer thinks about a bargain. The purchase price is a one-time number. Personal property tax, insurance, registration, slip or storage fees, winterization and shrink wrap are the recurring number, and on a used boat the recurring number is usually what decides whether you still own the thing in three years. Price the year, not the boat.

### Can you register a boat in Missouri with just a bill of sale?

Generally, no. A bill of sale documents what you paid, and you will need it for the sales tax calculation, but it is not proof of ownership. Missouri wants the title, properly signed over by the person actually named on it, before the boat gets titled, numbered and registered in your name.

Think of them as two documents doing two different jobs. The title says who owns it. The bill of sale says what changed hands and for how much. Show up with only the second one and you have told the state about a transaction without proving there was anything there to transact.

A useful bill of sale names both parties with addresses, describes the boat, the motor and the trailer with their identifying numbers, states a price for each of those items separately, gives the date, and carries both signatures. Splitting the price of the hull from the motor and the trailer is not busywork. Those are three titled items and the state handles them as three titled items.

The place where a bill of sale genuinely carries weight is on a small, unpowered, unregistered craft, and even there the rules turn on how the thing is powered and used rather than on what it looks like. Buying a jon boat with an electric trolling motor for the back of a farm pond? Ask first. Do not assume you have wandered outside the system just because the boat is small.

### What the Highway Patrol has to do with your boat purchase

The Missouri State Highway Patrol runs serial number verification for boats and outboard motors, and there are situations where a license office simply will not process your title without one. Out-of-state purchases are the common trigger for buyers in this metro, which matters a great deal here, because a good share of the listings sit on the Illinois side.

A verification is not an insult, and it is not a check on whether the boat runs. A trooper reads the hull identification number and the motor’s serial number, compares them against your paperwork and against stolen property records, and certifies that the numbers on the metal are the numbers on the page. It exists because boats and motors are unusually easy to steal, move across a state line, and quietly renumber.

Call the troop headquarters that covers your county before you drive out, since hours and appointment rules vary by location, and bring everything: the boat, the motor, the trailer, the title or out-of-state paperwork, and your own identification. The other thing worth knowing is that a number ground off, painted over, or covered by a plate that does not sit quite right gets discovered here. Far better there than in your driveway two seasons from now.

### Buying across the river, and other metro wrinkles

Cross-river shopping is normal around here, and it is not a problem so much as extra steps. If you live in Missouri, you title and register the boat in Missouri and you pay Missouri tax on it, whether you bought it in Alton, in Grafton, or out of a driveway in Godfrey. Do not assume an Illinois seller’s paperwork does your Missouri work for you.

The Lake of the Ozarks pull is the other one. Plenty of metro buyers end up shopping in Osage Beach because the inventory runs deeper and the boats have been used the way most people plan to use them. That is a real advantage. The tradeoff is that a lake boat has typically seen more hours, more sun and rougher water than a river-and-trailer boat that lived in a St. Charles garage, and the asking price should reflect that difference.

One pattern shows up in local listings every single spring: the boat that has been parked on a side yard since 2021 and “just needs a battery.” Sometimes that is true. More often the fuel has gone bad, the impeller has taken a set, the seals have dried out, and the bill to make it safe eats a real fraction of the asking price. A boat that has been run regularly and maintained beats a low-hour boat that has been sitting, nearly every time.

### What should you check on the boat itself?

Paperwork is the part that costs you money you did not plan on. Condition is the part that costs you weekends. On a used boat the expensive failures are structural and mechanical, and most of them will announce themselves to anybody willing to spend twenty unglamorous minutes before writing a check.

### The walkaround

Step on the transom and across the deck and feel for softness or flex, because wet, rotting core is the repair that turns a good deal into a bad one. Look into the bilge for standing water, an oil sheen, or fresh paint hiding a repair. Check the steering for slop, the wiring for household-grade splices, and the trailer for cracked leaf springs, dry-rotted tires with the date code actually read, and bearings that feel gritty when you spin a wheel by hand.

Then the motor. Ask for hours, ask for service records, and treat a compression test as normal rather than nosy. Pull the cowling and look for corrosion, chalky powder around the powerhead, and a lower unit that has clearly never had its gear oil changed. On a sterndrive, look hard at the bellows and the outdrive. Marine mechanics across this metro are booked deep into the season, and a repair you find in June is a boat you do not use in July.

### The water test

Never buy a powerboat you have not run on water. A hose test proves the engine starts. It does not prove the boat gets on plane, holds pressure at speed, shifts cleanly, charges the battery or tracks straight. Meet at a ramp, run it up to speed, let it idle long enough to surface a cooling problem, then shut it down and restart it hot. If a seller will not put it in the water, you already have your answer.

The same habit of mind that protects you on a used car protects you here, only with fewer independent inspectors and pricier surprises. Our walkthrough of how to check a used car before you hand over the money covers that discipline in detail. And if you are buying the boat mostly to fish out of, the best free public water around St. Louis is worth reading before you decide how much boat you actually need.

### What this looks like from the dealer’s side of the counter

Marine shops in this metro live and die on a season that is genuinely short. The phone starts ringing in April, the service bay fills by May, and by the time the water is warm the calendar is spoken for. That is why a used boat bought in August sometimes cannot be repaired until October, and why a good shop will tell you the truth about a rig instead of selling you the wrong one in a hurry.

It also explains why comparing shops matters before you need one. A dealer who knows the model, a mechanic who works on your engine brand, a trailer shop, an upholstery place, a marina with winter storage: that is four or five relationships, and the week to build them is the week before you buy, not the morning something breaks. St Louis Near Me Directory is where a lot of metro buyers compare local marine dealers and services side by side. If you run one of those shops, keeping your listing complete and current is how neighbors find you when the season turns.
