### Frequently asked questions

### Q. How much should it cost to install a car stereo?

A.  For a single head unit, labor typically falls around one hundred to two hundred and fifty dollars, with roughly fifty to two hundred and fifty more in required parts: dash kit, wiring harness, antenna adapter and, on newer vehicles, a steering-wheel or data interface module. Older, simpler vehicles sit near the bottom of that. Late-model cars with a factory amplifier, camera and wheel controls sit at the top. Speakers, amplifiers and subwoofers are priced as separate labor on top of that.

### Q. Is it cheaper to install a car radio yourself?

A.  On paper, yes, by the labor charge, commonly a hundred to two hundred and fifty dollars. You still have to buy the same dash kit, harness, antenna adapter and any interface module, because those are the car’s requirements and not the shop’s markup. Where the math flips is a broken trim panel, a snapped clip set, a lost backup camera or a cut harness that a later buyer spots. On an older, simple vehicle it usually pays. On a modern one it often does not.

### Q. Is installing a car radio hard?

A.  It depends almost entirely on the car, not on you. An older vehicle with a plain double-DIN opening and a radio that only plays music is genuinely a beginner job with hand tools and an adapter harness. A modern vehicle where the radio also handles climate display, chimes, parking sensors and the camera is not, because keeping those features means adding and configuring an interface module. Anything involving dash or steering column wiring also puts you near airbag circuits, which deserves real caution.

### Q. Can I replace my car stereo myself?

A.  Often yes, if you buy the vehicle-specific dash kit and harness adapter rather than cutting factory wires, disconnect the battery before you start, and stay away from yellow airbag connectors. Take your time with trim panels and expect to replace a few clips. The honest limit is features: if your car routes the camera, chimes or steering-wheel buttons through the radio, you need the right interface module, and buying the wrong one is the most common way this project stalls.

### Q. What are common radio install mistakes?

A.  Cutting the factory harness instead of using an adapter, which permanently marks the car. Skipping the antenna adapter and getting no reception. Buying a dash kit that fits the model but not the trim. Forgetting the interface module and quietly losing the backup camera, the chimes or the wheel controls. Breaking trim clips so panels rattle over rough pavement. And leaving wire unsecured behind the dash, where it eventually buzzes against something that moves.

### Q. How long does it take to install a stereo in a car?

A.  A basic head unit swap on a cooperative vehicle typically takes one to two hours. Add an interface module to retain the steering-wheel controls, the camera and the chimes and it commonly runs three to five. A full system with front and rear speakers, an amplifier and a subwoofer is usually a full day and sometimes two. The bigger delay is often parts: if the dash kit and interface are not in stock, the appointment waits on the order.

### Q. What all do I need to install an aftermarket radio?

A.  The receiver, a vehicle-specific dash kit, a wiring harness adapter, and an antenna adapter, at minimum. Many vehicles also need a steering-wheel control interface and, on newer ones, a data or amplifier interface module so the chimes, camera and factory amp keep working. Tools are modest: trim removal tools, a socket set, wire strippers and either crimp connectors or a soldering iron. Spare trim clips for your model are cheap insurance and almost always worth having on hand.

### Q. What are common car stereo problems?

A.  Screens that freeze or reboot, especially on cold mornings. Bluetooth that drops or refuses to pair after a phone update. A unit that cuts out over bumps, which usually means a loose connector or a bad ground rather than a dead radio. Speakers that sound fuzzy because the foam surrounds have dried and cracked after enough summer heat and winter cold. Rattling door panels from broken clips. And a backup camera or set of chimes lost during a previous install.

## What Cosmetology School Costs in Missouri
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-cosmetology-school-costs-in-missouri

Imagine it’s a Thursday night in St. Ann. The kids are finally down, the dishwasher is running, and there’s a cosmetology school folder open on the kitchen table next to a calculator and last week’s pay stub. You have wanted to do hair since you were fifteen. What is stopping you is not the wanting. It is the number on the brochure, and the year of reduced earning sitting quietly behind it.

That kitchen table looks about the same in Imperial, in O’Fallon, in Jennings. Somebody is thirty-four, working full time, doing color for friends in the living room on Saturdays, and trying to figure out whether the math works. Not whether she can cut hair. She already can. Whether she can stop earning enough, for long enough, to get a license that lets her charge for it legally.

Nobody hands you that math. So here it is. What Missouri actually requires, what a program of that length generally costs once you add the kit and the fees nobody quotes you, how long 1,500 hours takes on a full-time schedule versus nights, and the one thing that blows up more beauty school budgets than tuition ever does. It is not the price. It is the calendar.

### How much does it cost to go to cosmetology school in Missouri?

A full 1,500-hour cosmetology program in Missouri commonly runs somewhere in the ten to twenty thousand dollar range at a private school, with public career and technical programs often meaningfully less. Shorter licenses cost far less: a 400-hour manicuring program is a fraction of that. Confirm current tuition with the school.

Those are the ranges this kind of training generally runs, not a quote from any particular campus, and they move for real reasons. Price in a clock-hour trade is driven mostly by two things: how many hours the license requires, and what the school puts in your kit. That is the honest structural point, and it is the one that makes brochure-shopping so confusing. A 400-hour nail program and a 1,500-hour cosmetology program are not the same purchase compared badly. They are different purchases entirely.

Which is why the per-hour view is more useful than the sticker. Divide any program’s total by its required hours and you get a number you can actually compare across schools, and across license types. It also stops you from reading a shorter, cheaper program as a bargain when it simply leads to a narrower license. Cheaper is not the same as less expensive per hour, and neither one tells you what the credential is worth in a chair.

Public career and technical education programs, the ones attached to school districts and community colleges, are usually the lower end of the range in Missouri. Private academies sit higher and often justify it with smaller cohorts, brand-partnered product education, or a busier student salon floor. Both routes lead to the same state license. Verify current tuition directly with the school, because these numbers change every catalog year and no blog post is a price quote.

### What does the full cost of attendance actually include?

Tuition is roughly three quarters of the story. The full cost of attendance is tuition plus the kit, plus books and any digital course access, plus the state exam fees and the initial license fee at the end. The kit is the line people forget, and on a full cosmetology program it is a real number, not a rounding error.

A cosmetology kit is shears, a razor, combs and brushes, clips, a blow dryer, irons, a mannequin head or several, color bowls and brushes, a cape, chemical supplies, and a rolling case to carry the whole thing. Some schools bundle it into tuition. Some bill it separately, and a few let you use tools you already own if they meet the standard. Ask which arrangement you are signing, because a low tuition figure next to a separately billed kit is not the deal it appears to be.

The fees at the end are smaller but they are not zero, and they arrive right when your savings are thinnest. You pay to sit the licensing examination, written and practical, and you pay again for the license itself once you pass. Budget for both plus a retake you hopefully will not need. Then there is the quiet category: gas, parking, scrubs or uniform, and childcare for the hours you are on the floor instead of at home.

One thing worth knowing before you buy anything on your own. Schools set kit standards for a reason, and a bargain shear from a big-box shelf can genuinely make your practical exam harder. If you are pricing tools out of curiosity, what to buy at beauty supply stores around St. Louis is a fair orientation to what professional tools cost and why some of them are worth the money.

### How many hours does Missouri require for each license?

Missouri sets its training hours by license type through the Missouri Board of Cosmetology and Barber Examiners. A cosmetologist license requires 1,500 clock hours at a Board-approved school. A public vocational-technical school path is recognized at a lower minimum of 1,220 hours. An apprenticeship route exists at 3,000 hours.

The specialty licenses are shorter and correspondingly cheaper. Esthetics, the skin care license, is 750 hours in school or 1,500 as an apprentice. Manicuring, the nail technician license, is 400 hours in school or 800 as an apprentice. Those numbers explain the whole price spread you see when you start calling around. You are not comparing schools so much as comparing lengths of road.

Barbering is the one that trips people up. In Missouri it is a separate license with its own program of roughly 1,000 hours, not a specialty inside cosmetology. If your plan is a barbershop chair, a men’s grooming clientele and a straight razor, look hard at whether the barbering license is the correct door rather than assuming cosmetology covers it. The two licenses overlap in the public’s imagination far more than they overlap in the statute.

The entry requirements are modest and worth stating plainly, because they surprise people who assume beauty school needs a diploma. Missouri’s minimum age is 17, and applicants need at least a 10th grade education. Licensing itself runs through the Missouri Division of Professional Registration, and the examination has both a written and a practical component. Confirm every one of these numbers with the Board at pr.mo.gov and with the school before you enroll, because requirements change and the Board is the only authority that counts.

### How long will cosmetology school take?

Full time, a 1,500-hour cosmetology program generally takes somewhere around ten to thirteen months. On a part-time or evening schedule, plan on roughly eighteen months to two years. Part time does not reduce the requirement at all. It spreads the same 1,500 hours across more calendar, which is the trade you are actually making.

The arithmetic is simple enough to do yourself, and you should. At about 35 hours a week you are looking at roughly 43 weeks of attendance before you add holidays and breaks. At 25 hours a week it is around 60 weeks. At 20 hours a week, which is what a realistic evening schedule looks like when you are already working days, it is about 75 weeks. Run your own number against the schedule the school offers and see whether it survives contact with your life.

This is where the career-change decision gets honest. The full-time route gets you earning sooner but requires you to survive on less for most of a year. The evening route protects your income and stretches the strain across two. Neither is wrong. The mistake is choosing the full-time calendar because it looks faster on paper and then dropping to part time in month four, having already lost the income you were counting on. If you are weighing this against other training paths, trade schools and apprenticeships around St. Louis lays out how the earn-while-you-learn options compare.

### Why do missed days cost you money?

Because clock hours are attendance, not coursework. You do not pass 1,500 hours. You are present for them. Every sick kid, every dead battery on Telegraph Road, every shift your manager will not let you swap comes straight off your progress and pushes your finish date, and the finish date is what your budget was built on.

This is the single biggest gap between what people budget and what they spend, and it has almost nothing to do with tuition. Somebody plans for eleven months of tight living, misses a scattered five weeks over the year for entirely reasonable reasons, and now needs thirteen months of tight living instead. Two extra months of childcare, gas and reduced income is a serious number, and nobody wrote it on the brochure because nobody could have.

There is a contract dimension too. Enrollment agreements commonly set a scheduled completion date, and going past it can carry additional charges for the extra time. Terms vary a great deal from school to school, so ask directly what happens if you fall behind, what the attendance policy allows, and whether hours can be made up on other days. Ask it before you sign, in the same conversation where you ask about tuition. It is a cost question, not a policy question.

Tuition is one big number you plan for. A pest problem is one you don’t.

### Can you get financial aid for cosmetology school?

Sometimes, and this is the question to ask before you apply rather than after you enroll. Some cosmetology programs are accredited and participate in federal Title IV aid, meaning the FAFSA and Pell grants are on the table. Others are not, and at those schools your options are cash, a payment plan, or private financing.

The difference between those two situations can be most of your budget, so make it the second question you ask on the phone. Say it plainly: is this program Title IV eligible, and what is the accreditation. A school that participates will answer immediately and hand you to a financial aid office. A school that does not should still tell you straight, and then you know you are pricing a payment plan instead of a grant.

Workforce funding is the piece most career-changers never look at. Missouri Job Centers administer federally funded training assistance for eligible adults and dislocated workers, and cosmetology programs sometimes appear on the approved training list. Eligibility rules are real and not everyone qualifies, but a conversation at a Job Center costs you an afternoon. Scholarships from industry associations and product companies exist as well, generally small, generally worth the application anyway. For the broader version of this decision, how to choose a college or trade school in St. Louis covers what to verify about any program before you commit money to it.

### Why aren’t students paid for the salon floor?

Because the student salon is the training, not a job. Once you have the fundamentals, you work on paying clients at a reduced rate under instructor supervision, and those hours count toward your 1,500. The client pays the school. You are the one paying for the education, which is exactly why no wage flows the other direction.

Understanding that arrangement matters, because it is where most of your real learning happens. A mannequin head does not have opinions, a schedule, or hair that behaves badly. A live client in the chair on a Tuesday afternoon has all three. The busier a school’s student salon, the more of that you get, and the more prepared you are the week after you pass your exam. A quiet floor is a training problem dressed up as a calm environment.

Tip policies vary and are worth asking about, since some schools allow students to keep tips and others do not. What does not vary is that the student floor is priced well below a licensed salon, which is the whole reason the appointment book fills. If you want a feel for the gap between student pricing and the professional market you will be entering, what hair salon services cost in St. Louis is a useful benchmark for what your work is eventually worth.

### What happens to your license if you move?

Licenses are issued state by state, and moving means applying in the new state rather than carrying yours across the line. Most states have a reciprocity or endorsement process for someone already licensed elsewhere, but the receiving board decides, and the usual sticking point is whether your training hours meet its own minimum.

That is a live concern here, because the metro straddles a state line. A Missouri license is a Missouri license, and working a chair in Illinois is a separate application with its own requirements. If you already know a move is possible within a few years, look up the destination state’s hour minimum before you choose a program, not after. Training beyond your own state’s minimum sometimes makes a later transfer far simpler.

Keep your paperwork like it matters, because one day it will. Your official transcript, your hour records, your exam results and your original license are the documents another state’s board will ask for, sometimes years later, and schools do close. Scan everything the week you graduate and store it somewhere that is not just your phone. It costs nothing now and saves a genuine headache later.

### How do you choose which schools to interview?

Shortlist two or three programs worth interviewing, then go see them. Tour the building, sit in the student salon for twenty minutes and watch, and state plainly what you want: a finish date you can actually hit, a kit you will still use after graduation, real exam preparation, and help getting placed. Then compare that against what each school is prepared to deliver.

The gap is the signal, not the price. One school hears “I work days, I have two kids, I need to be licensed by next fall” and walks you through a schedule that does it, with an honest note about where it gets tight. Another says it can be done and stays vague. A third tells you the timeline is unrealistic and here is what would have to change. That third answer is the most valuable one in the room, and it is the one that gets mistaken for a bad sales pitch.

### What to watch for while you are sitting there

Is the student floor busy, or is it four students and two clients on a weekday afternoon? Is an instructor actually on the floor, hands in the work, or in an office? Do clients seem to be regulars? Are the students at different levels helping each other, or is everybody stranded? Twenty minutes of watching tells you more about the training than an hour of admissions conversation, and it costs you nothing but the drive.

Ask about outcomes in specific terms and listen for specifics back. How do recent graduates do on the licensing exam. What happens if someone does not pass the first time. Where did last year’s class end up working, and does the school have relationships with salons that hire from it. A program proud of its results will answer with details and names of the kind of shops, not adjectives. Vagueness about outcomes is information too.

Start with the schedule you can actually keep, not the tuition. Compare what each one says it can do against what you need, and confirm current hour requirements with the Missouri Board of Cosmetology and Barber Examiners at pr.mo.gov before you sign anything.

### Frequently asked questions

### Q. Do cosmetology students get paid?

A.  No. The student salon is part of your training, not employment. Once you have the fundamentals, you work on paying clients at a reduced rate under instructor supervision, and those hours count toward your required total. The client pays the school, not you, because you are the one paying for the education. Tip policies vary, so ask whether students keep tips. Plenty of students hold an outside job, which is the main reason evening and part-time schedules exist at all.

### Q. Is cosmetology hard to pass?

A.  Missouri’s licensing examination has a written portion and a practical portion, and most people who attend consistently and prepare pass it. The practical is the part that rattles candidates, because it is timed, procedural, and judged on sanitation and safety as much as on the finished look. Steady attendance is the best predictor of passing, since skills are built by repetition. Ask any school you tour how it prepares students for the exam and what happens if someone needs a retake.

### Q. Is there a lot of math in cosmetology school?

A.  Not the kind that scares people. It is arithmetic with a purpose: mixing ratios for color and developer, measuring product, calculating percentages for chemical services, and timing processing. Later, if you rent a booth or run your own chair, the business math matters just as much, which is pricing, commissions, taxes and supply costs. Nobody is asking you to do algebra. They are asking you to measure accurately and time things carefully, every single day, without shortcuts.

### Q. What is the first thing you learn in cosmetology school?

A.  Sanitation and safety, almost universally, and it is not filler. Disinfection, tool handling, state rules and infection control come before anybody touches a client, because that is what the Board regulates most tightly and what the practical exam scores hardest. Alongside it come the basics: how to hold shears, sectioning, shampoo and scalp technique, and long stretches on a mannequin head. The glamorous parts arrive later, built on top of habits formed in those first weeks.

### Q. Are cosmetology schools worth it?

A.  The license is not optional, so the real question is which program and which schedule, not whether to go. In Missouri you cannot legally charge for cosmetology services without one. Worth it depends on your plan afterward: a stylist building a book behind the chair, a booth renter running a small business, and someone who leaves the trade in two years all get very different returns. Price the program per required hour and be honest about the calendar you can actually keep.

### Q. What field of cosmetology pays the most?

A.  Generally the specialized and business-owning ends rather than a general chair. Chemical work like color and corrective color, salon ownership or booth rental with a full book, advanced esthetics, and educator or platform work with product companies tend to sit at the higher end. The common thread is not the service, it is repeat clients and control over your own pricing. Earnings vary widely by location, clientele and hustle, so treat any single figure you see online with caution.

### Q. Is it hard to get accepted into cosmetology school?

A.  Admission is generally not the hard part. Missouri’s baseline is a minimum age of 17 and at least a 10th grade education, and schools typically add an application, an interview or tour, and enrollment paperwork. The real gates are financial and logistical: whether the program is Title IV eligible, whether you can fund the kit and fees, and whether the schedule fits your life. Confirm current requirements with the Missouri Board of Cosmetology and Barber Examiners at pr.mo.gov.

### Q. What is the hardest part of cosmetology?

A.  Attendance, honestly, and then the client conversation. The hours are clock hours, so missed days push your finish date and your budget with it, and that undoes more students than any technique does. After school, the hardest skill is the consultation: understanding what someone actually wants, saying honestly what their hair will and will not do, and managing the disappointment when those two things do not match. Both are stamina problems more than talent problems.

## Buying Fabric by the Yard in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/buying-fabric-by-the-yard-in-st-louis

The window is measured. Ninety-six inches from the top of the rod down to the floor, forty-eight inches across, and a photo on your phone of the exact print you have been thinking about since spring. Then you drive to the store where you bought fabric for twenty years, and the lot is empty and the sign is gone off the front of the building.

That happened to a lot of people in 2025. Joann filed for bankruptcy and closed all of its stores, which pulled the default chain fabric counter out of most of the country, St. Louis included. For a home sewer in Godfrey or Herculaneum or O’Fallon, the question stopped being which print and became something more basic. Where do I buy fabric now, and how much of it do I actually need?

So here is the sequence, with the math worked out. What a yard generally costs at three different weights, why bolt width makes the same yard a very different amount of cloth, how to calculate curtains without guessing, what a pattern repeat quietly does to your total, and the honest answer on whether sewing your own saves money. Usually it does not. Sometimes it absolutely does.

### How much should 1 yard of fabric cost?

For basic quilting cotton, expect roughly eight to fifteen dollars a yard. Mid-weight home decor fabric commonly runs about fifteen to forty. Heavyweight upholstery typically starts near thirty and climbs past eighty. Those are typical ranges, and bolt width changes what a yard is actually worth.

Start at the bottom of the ladder. Utility cloth like muslin, broadcloth and plain cotton lining is the cheapest thing on any wall, commonly a few dollars to around eight a yard, and it is what you should be buying for a first attempt at a pattern you have never sewn. Basic quilting cotton sits above it. Licensed prints and designer quilting cotton from a named collection push higher again, and it is normal to see the same weight of cloth priced twice as high because of whose name is on the selvage.

The middle tier is where most curtain and cushion projects live. Home decor fabric is heavier than quilting cotton, comes on a wider bolt, and is built to hang or to take a seat cushion without going limp. Printed decorator cotton, cotton duck, linen blends and drapery weaves generally land in that fifteen to forty range. Lining is a separate line item most first-timers forget, and it usually runs at the cheap end while adding real weight and light control.

Upholstery is its own world. Chenille, jacquard, heavy woven texture, performance weaves rated for scrubs and faux leather all cost more per yard because there is simply more fiber in them, and the premium end of that market runs well past a hundred dollars a yard. Some of it is “to the trade,” meaning you order it through a designer or a workroom rather than off a retail wall, which is one of the quieter things an interior designer in St. Louis is actually being paid for. Treat every number here as a broad typical range, not a quote.

### Why does bolt width change what a yard is worth?

Because a yard is a length, not an area. Quilting cotton is commonly 44 inches wide. Home decor and upholstery fabric is commonly 54 to 60 inches. A yard off a 54-inch bolt gives you about twenty-three percent more cloth than a yard off a 44-inch bolt, at the same stated price per yard.

This single fact explains most of the price gaps that look unfair on a shelf. Two bolts marked eighteen dollars a yard are not the same purchase if one is 44 inches and the other is 60. Before you compare anything, look at the end of the bolt where the width is printed, and do the comparison on width-adjusted cloth rather than on the shelf tag. It takes ten seconds and it changes which bolt is the better buy surprisingly often.

Usable width is smaller than stated width, too. The selvage edges on both sides are woven differently, sometimes printed with the manufacturer name and color dots, and they behave badly in a seam. On a 44-inch quilting cotton, plan on roughly 42 inches you can really use. On a 54-inch decorator fabric, plan on 52. At the far end, quilt backing and sheeting come in extra-wide bolts around 108 inches specifically so a quilt back or a wide panel can be cut without a seam down the middle. If a project is close to a width boundary, going wide is often cheaper than going long.

### How do you figure the fabric for a pair of curtains?

Five steps in order. Add hem and header allowances to the finished length to get your cut length. Multiply window width by a fullness factor of 2 to 2.5. Divide that by usable bolt width to get the number of widths you need. Multiply widths by cut length. Divide by 36 for yards.

The allowances are where beginners lose the most fabric. A drapery bottom hem is usually doubled, four inches turned twice, which eats eight inches. The top gets a doubled header or a rod pocket with a small ruffle above it, call that another eight. Add two inches for squaring the cut and for the shrinkage you did not plan on. So a panel that finishes at a given length needs roughly eighteen more inches of cloth than the number on your tape measure, before you have considered anything else.

Fullness is the step people skip, and it is why homemade curtains sometimes look thin. A curtain that is exactly as wide as the window hangs flat like a bedsheet. To read as a proper gathered drape it wants two to two and a half times the window width across the pair, more for sheers, less for a panel that is purely decorative and never actually closes. Decide that number before you shop, because it doubles or triples everything downstream.

### A worked example on a 96-inch curtain

Take a 48-inch-wide window with a 96-inch finished drop, which is a common combination in a foursquare in Rock Hill or a newer build out in Wright City. Cut length is 96 plus 8 for the bottom hem plus 8 for the header plus 2 for squaring, so 114 inches. That is 3.17 yards for one cut. At 2x fullness you need 96 inches of gathered width across the pair, and on a 54-inch decorator fabric with 52 usable, that is two widths, one per panel.

Two widths at 114 inches each is 228 inches, or about 6.4 yards. Round up to 7. If the same window took a 44-inch quilting cotton instead, 96 inches of fullness needs three widths rather than two, and your total jumps to roughly 9.5 yards for a fabric that is also lighter than the job wants. Now widen the window to 72 inches and go to 2.5x fullness. That is 180 inches of gathered width, four widths of 54-inch fabric, two per panel, and about 12.7 yards before lining. This is why a quote for a pair of custom drapes can look startling. The cloth alone is a serious number.

### Does a pattern repeat really add that much yardage?

Yes, and it is the biggest budget surprise in the whole project. A printed or woven design repeats itself at a fixed interval down the bolt, often 12 to 27 inches on decorator fabric. Every cut has to start at the same point in that design so the panels match, which means rounding every cut length up to the next full repeat.

Run it through the example above. A 114-inch cut length on a plain fabric stays 114 inches. On a fabric with a 24-inch vertical repeat, 114 rounds up to 120, because 24 does not divide evenly into 114 and you cannot start a panel halfway through a motif. That is six wasted inches on every single cut, plus usually one extra repeat at the top of the order so the first cut can be placed correctly. Across four widths it can add most of a yard, and on a large repeat it adds considerably more.

The repeat size is printed on the bolt end or the sample tag, usually as a vertical repeat and a horizontal one. Ask for it if you cannot find it. The same rule applies to a slipcover, to cushions that sit side by side on a bench, and to a headboard, because the eye catches a mismatched pattern across two adjacent pieces instantly. If the budget is tight and the window is large, a texture or a small all-over print with no meaningful repeat is the honest way to save money without the result looking cheap.

### Is it actually cheaper to make your own curtains?

For a standard window at a standard length, usually not. Ready-made panels are cut by the thousand on wide machinery, and a pair often costs less than the fabric alone for the example above. Sewing your own wins on odd sizes, extra-long drops, specific cloth, and quality you cannot buy off a rack.

Be honest with yourself about which situation you are in. If the window takes an ordinary rod at an ordinary height and a common stock length works, buying is faster and cheaper, and there is no shame in it. Where the arithmetic flips is a 108 or 120-inch drop, a window that is unusually wide or narrow, a bay that needs three panels in graduated widths, an old house with a nine-foot ceiling, a blackout requirement in a bedroom, or a print you have found and cannot get any other way. In those cases ready-made either does not exist or has to be altered anyway.

There is also a quality argument that is real. A ready-made panel usually has a single-turn hem, no weight in the corners, and no lining, so it hangs like what it costs. A lined panel with a doubled hem and drapery weights hangs straight and blocks light, and it is a different object in the room. Budget it the way you would budget any other permanent surface, alongside the paint and what new flooring costs in St. Louis, rather than as a small craft purchase you make on a Saturday.

### Where do you buy fabric now that Joann is gone?

No single chain has taken that slot. The closing of Joann in 2025 removed the default cutting counter, and what replaced it is a mix rather than a successor: independent fabric shops, quilt shops, upholstery and drapery suppliers, big-box craft stores carrying a narrower selection, and online sellers who cut yardage to order.

Each one is good at a different thing. A quilt shop carries deep quilting cotton at 44 inches, notions, thread to match, and staff who will actually work through your block math with you. An upholstery or drapery supplier carries the 54-inch goods and the heavy weaves, along with foam, welt cord, webbing and lining, and some of them sell retail while others work only through a workroom or a designer. A general craft store will have thread, cutting tools, interfacing and a limited fabric wall, which is fine for pillows and school projects, and where to buy craft supplies in St. Louis covers that end in more detail. Estate sales, thrift stores and remnant bins are genuinely worth a look for anything small.

Online cut yardage fills the gap for selection, with one hard rule: order a swatch first. Screens lie about color, and they say nothing at all about hand, drape or weight, which are the three things that decide whether a fabric works. Pay the few dollars, hold the swatch against the wall at the time of day you will actually be in the room, and wait. That patience matters even more on garment and formal sewing, where the fabric decision drives everything else, in the same way the wedding dress shopping timeline in St. Louis is really a story about lead time.

### What should you check before they cut?

Four things, every time. Buy a little more than your number says, take it all off one bolt, know whether the finished item will be washed, and check the print direction. A cutter cannot un-cut a bolt, and a second trip for matching fabric usually ends in a different dye lot.

Add roughly ten percent, or at least a half yard, to whatever you calculated. That covers a crooked cut off the bolt, a cutting mistake at home, straightening the grain, and the small piece you will want later for a tie-back, a pillow or a repair. Fabric is dyed in lots, and two bolts of the same print from the same shop can be visibly different under a window. Cut everything you need at once, from one bolt, in one transaction.

Prewash only if the finished item will be washed. Cotton commonly shrinks a couple of percent, sometimes more, and a curtain that shrinks after it is hemmed is scrap. So a slipcover, a duvet, an apron or a garment gets washed and dried before you cut, the same way you plan to launder it later. Drapery and upholstery that will be dry cleaned or vacuumed should not be prewashed, because washing strips the finishes that make it behave. Last, check whether the print is directional or a one-way design, because a one-way print means every piece is cut in the same orientation and your yardage goes up again.

Fabric piles up fast. Storing the overflow has its own price.

### How do you pick a shop or a workroom worth the drive?

Shortlist two or three worth interviewing, then walk in with your measurements written down. The window size, the finished length you want, the fullness, the weight you have in mind and the budget. Let each one show you what it would do with that. You are comparing what you want against what each is prepared to deliver.

The gap is the signal, not the price. One shop hears “forty-eight inch window, ninety-six inch drop, lined, and I want it to actually close” and immediately talks about bolt width, repeat and lining weight. Another says any of the wall will work and does not ask what the window does. A third tells you plainly that the fabric you are pointing at is too light for that drop and will look tired in a year. That third answer is the one worth driving back for, even when it is not what you hoped to hear.

Bring a picture and a piece of what is already in the room. A cushion, a paint chip, a photo of the floor. Ten seconds of holding something against a bolt beats twenty minutes of describing a color. If you are handing the sewing to a workroom rather than doing it yourself, the same interview applies: say what you want, hear what they would build, and pay attention to whether anyone asks about the room, the light and how often the panels get pulled. Those questions are how you tell who has done this before.

### Where do you find fabric stores near you?

Go in with the measurements, not just the idea. You can browse fabric stores across the metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then visit two or three with your window size, your finished length and your fullness number in hand. Quilt shops, decorator suppliers and general fabric counters all cut yardage, and they are good at different jobs, so ask which one yours is before you drive across the county.

### Frequently asked questions

### Q. Is 2 yards a lot of fabric?

A.  It is a moderate amount, and what it makes depends entirely on bolt width. Two yards of 44-inch quilting cotton is 72 by 44 inches, roughly twenty-two square feet, enough for about three envelope-back eighteen-inch pillow covers or a simple top. Two yards of 54-inch decorator fabric is closer to twenty-seven square feet. Neither is enough for a single floor-length curtain panel, which needs over three yards by itself.

### Q. How to calculate how much material is needed for curtains?

A.  Work in five steps. Add hem and header allowances to the finished length, roughly eighteen inches for a doubled four-inch bottom hem, a doubled header and squaring, to get your cut length. Multiply the window width by a fullness factor of 2 to 2.5. Divide that by the usable bolt width to find how many widths you need. Multiply widths by cut length, then divide by 36 for yards. Round up.

### Q. How many yards of fabric do I need for my curtains?

A.  For an average window with a floor-length drop on 54-inch decorator fabric, plan on roughly six to eight yards for a lined pair, plus a similar amount of lining. A wide window at 2.5 times fullness can reach twelve or thirteen yards. Short cafe curtains or a sink window may need only two to three. A pattern repeat adds on top of all of those numbers.

### Q. How many yards of fabric do I need for 96 inch curtains?

A.  A 96-inch finished panel needs a cut length near 114 inches once you add a doubled hem, a header and squaring, which is about 3.2 yards per width. A 48-inch window at 2x fullness takes two widths of 54-inch fabric, so roughly 6.4 yards, and most people buy 7. On 44-inch quilting cotton the same window takes three widths and roughly 9.5 yards.

### Q. Is it cheaper to make own curtains?

A.  For a standard window at a stock length, usually no. Ready-made panels are mass cut, and a pair often costs less than the fabric alone for a lined homemade version. Sewing your own wins on extra-long drops of 108 or 120 inches, unusual widths, bay windows, blackout requirements and fabric you cannot buy ready-made. It also wins on quality, since ready-mades rarely have lining, doubled hems or weights.

### Q. What is the best fabric to use for curtains?

A.  Mid-weight home decor fabric on a 54-inch bolt is the workhorse: cotton duck, printed decorator cotton, linen blends and drapery weaves all hang properly and take a hem well. Add a separate lining for light control, insulation and to protect the face fabric from sun. Sheers and voile suit a room that wants privacy without darkness. Quilting cotton is generally too light for a floor-length drop and will look limp.

### Q. What company is replacing Joann fabrics?

A.  No single chain has replaced it. Joann filed for bankruptcy and closed all of its stores in 2025, and the practical replacement is a mix: independent fabric shops, quilt shops, upholstery and drapery suppliers, big-box craft stores carrying a narrower fabric wall, and online sellers who cut yardage to order. Different needs go to different places now, so it is worth calling ahead to ask what a shop actually stocks.

### Q. Does Walmart still carry fabric by the yard?

A.  It varies by store, and most locations no longer staff a cutting counter. What you typically find on a shelf is precut packages, fat quarters, remnants and craft felt rather than cut-to-order yardage. Cut yardage is generally a website purchase, often shipped by third-party sellers, which means no touching the cloth first. Call your nearest store before driving over, and order a swatch if you buy online.

## What Video Production Costs in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-video-production-costs-in-st-louis

Two quotes land in the same inbox on a Thursday afternoon. Same brief, same ten minute runtime, same delivery date in November. One of them says nine thousand dollars. The other says forty one thousand. The marketing lead at a Maryland Heights manufacturer reads both of them twice, then forwards them to her boss with a subject line that is just a question mark.

She is not being naive, and neither quote is a scam. They are almost certainly both honest. They are simply descriptions of two completely different films that happen to run the same number of minutes. One is a producer, a camera, a microphone and three afternoons of interviews. The other is a scripted shoot with hired actors, three locations, a lighting package, animated product cutaways and four rounds of client changes.

Nobody explains this to a first-time buyer. Video is the one marketing purchase where the deliverable everyone pictures, the shoot day, is often the smallest part of the invoice. So here is what this work actually costs around St. Louis, in broad ranges, why runtime tells you almost nothing about price, and how to read two wildly different numbers without guessing.

### How much does it cost to produce a 10 minute video?

There is no honest single number, because runtime barely predicts cost. A ten minute single camera interview edit commonly lands somewhere in the low thousands. A ten minute scripted piece with actors, multiple locations and animation can run twenty five thousand and up. Crew, shoot days and post drive it.

That is not a dodge. Runtime is close to useless as a price predictor, and any company that quotes you off minutes alone is guessing. A ten minute recorded panel discussion with two cameras is a long afternoon and a straightforward edit. A ten minute brand film can be a small production company’s entire month.

What actually moves the number is a short list. How many shooting days. How many people are on the crew each of those days. How many locations, and whether any of them charge for access. Whether there is a script, and whether somebody has to write it. Whether there is paid on camera talent. Whether the edit needs motion graphics or animation. And how many rounds of revisions you get before changes start billing separately.

In rough terms, and these are typical ranges that move hard with the specifics: a single camera interview or testimonial piece, shot in a few hours and cut simply, commonly lands somewhere in the one to five thousand dollar range. A branded piece with a small crew, a real lighting setup, b-roll across a couple of locations and a polished edit generally runs something like five to twenty thousand. A scripted commercial with cast, multiple shoot days, a full crew and animation starts around twenty five thousand and climbs from there without much of a ceiling.

Those are the numbers this kind of work generally runs, not any particular company’s rate card, and the overlap between the tiers is real. A ten minute video can sit comfortably in any of the three.

### Where does the money actually go on a video project?

Three buckets: pre-production, the production day itself, and post. Most first-time buyers picture only the middle one, which is frequently the smallest of the three. The work that decides whether the video is any good mostly happens before anyone rolls a camera and after everyone has gone home.

Pre-production is scripting, storyboarding, casting, location scouting, permits where a location needs them, scheduling, shot lists and the call sheet. On a simple interview piece that might be two hours of a producer’s time. On a scripted spot it can be weeks, and it is where a project quietly succeeds or fails. A shoot day that starts without a shot list burns money in real time, at the rate of everybody standing in the room.

The production day is the visible part: crew, camera package, lenses, lighting, grip gear, audio, and whatever you are paying for the space. It is normally billed by the day or the half day, and it is the least flexible bucket, because a day is a day whether you use nine hours of it or four.

Post is the bucket that surprises people. Ingesting and organizing footage, a first assembly, the edit itself, color correction, sound mix, music, titles, motion graphics, subtitles, and then every revision round and every alternate version. On a documentary style piece, post is routinely the largest line on the project. The working rule inside the industry is that one hour of finished screen time represents many, many hours at the edit bay, and the ratio gets worse the more footage you shot.

This is why “can you just shoot it and send me the files” is a different product at a different price, and why the answer is sometimes yes. If you have a capable in-house editor, buying only pre-production and a shoot day is a legitimate way to spend less. Just be honest with yourself about whether that editor actually exists and actually has the hours.

### Why do two quotes for the same video differ by five figures?

Because “the same video” describes the runtime, not the work. The gap between a nine thousand dollar quote and a forty one thousand dollar quote is almost always crew size, shoot days and post hours, in that order. Two companies read one brief and pictured two entirely different productions.

The cheaper quote is usually assuming fewer people, one location, one day, existing footage wherever possible, library music and two revision rounds. The expensive one is usually assuming a written script, a casting session, two or three shoot days, a lighting and grip package, custom graphics and a longer approval cycle with a client who will want changes. Neither company is wrong. They answered different questions, because they were asked a vague one.

The fix is not to squeeze the high quote. It is to say out loud what you actually want, then let both companies price against the same picture. Nine times out of ten the numbers move toward each other, and the gap that remains tells you something real about how each shop works.

It helps to know what the neighboring services cost, because video sits in the same budget conversation as stills and gear. If a controlled space is part of the plan, renting a photo studio in St. Louis covers what those rooms charge and what comes with them. If the video is being made at an event, what it costs to rent AV gear for a St. Louis event is the other half of the same line item.

### How big does the crew need to be?

Crew size is the single biggest lever on a video budget, bigger than camera choice and far bigger than runtime. Every additional person on set is a day rate, and day rates for experienced specialists commonly run several hundred dollars to well over a thousand apiece. Two extra people across a multi-day shoot can move a quote by five figures.

At the bottom is the one-person band: a single videographer who directs, shoots, records sound, lights the room and then edits the whole thing. This is a real and often correct choice for interviews, social content, and anything where the subject matters more than the polish. What you give up is attention. One human cannot watch the frame, the audio levels and the person talking at the same time, and something gets less of them.

A small crew usually means a producer or director, a shooter, a sound recordist, and sometimes a gaffer or a general assistant. This is the sweet spot for most business video. The producer keeps the day on schedule and manages your people so you can go back to work, the shooter gets to actually look at the image, and the sound is being handled by somebody whose only job is sound.

A full commercial crew adds a director of photography separate from the camera operator, a first assistant camera pulling focus, a gaffer with an electrician, grips, hair and makeup, an art department, a production assistant or three, and a producer who has already been working for weeks before the day. That is what a national-looking spot costs, and the price is not padding. Each of those people exists because a specific thing goes wrong without them.

### What does the sound person actually buy you?

Sound is the line people cut first and regret most. Audiences forgive a soft image and will not forgive a hollow, echoing room or an air handler humming underneath the CEO’s best answer. Bad audio cannot be repaired later in any meaningful way, and it is the most common reason a finished corporate video feels cheap without the viewer being able to say why. If the budget forces a choice between a second camera and a dedicated sound recordist, take the sound.

### What should the agreement say about revisions and deliverables?

Two things, in writing, before the shoot: how many rounds of revisions are included, and exactly which files you receive at the end. Those two lines are where video budgets actually break. Not on the camera, not on the crew. On “just one more small change” and “we also need a vertical cut.”

A revision round means one consolidated set of notes from your side, applied once. Most agreements include two or three. What blows that up is feedback arriving in pieces, from four people, over ten days, each batch triggering another pass through the timeline. Collect every note from every stakeholder into one document, send it once, and you will use fewer rounds than you were given. A company that bills hourly past the included rounds is not being difficult. It is being accurate.

Deliverables are the other trap, and the more expensive one. A finished ninety second video is one file. The same project delivered as a hero cut, a sixty, a thirty, a fifteen, a square version, a vertical version, six social clips, a captioned version and a version with no music under it is ten separate exports, each one its own timeline and its own export. Decide up front where this video is going to run and put those versions in the original scope. Adding them after the edit is locked costs considerably more than including them from the start.

Settle the subtitle question early too. Captions are cheap when they are planned and irritating when they are an afterthought, and if the video is going anywhere near a public website, you want them.

A camera shows everything. Including the carpet you meant to clean.

### Who owns the footage, the music, and the people on screen?

Three separate questions, and the answers are often not what a first-time buyer assumes. In most agreements you are buying a license to use the finished video for a defined purpose. Not the raw footage, not the music, and not unlimited rights to the faces in it. All three are negotiable, and all three cost money to widen.

Music is the one that catches people. Library and stock music is inexpensive, often tens of dollars per track, and it is what the large majority of business video uses. A recognizable commercial song is a different universe, involving two separate sets of rights, and the answer is usually four or five figures at minimum for a limited term in a limited territory. If someone tells you they can put a hit song under your video for a few hundred dollars, something in that conversation is wrong.

Stock footage and licensed graphics behave the same way. So does paid on camera talent. An actor’s rate is tied to usage: where the video runs, for how long, and in which media. A piece shot for your website that later becomes a paid ad campaign may owe additional usage money, and that is a real bill rather than a technicality. Say up front where the video will run, including the honest possibility that it runs somewhere else later.

The raw footage question is worth settling before the shoot rather than after. Some companies hand over everything, some archive it and will pull clips on request, some charge for the drive and the transfer time. There is no universal right answer here, but there is a wrong outcome, and it is discovering two years later that the only copy of your founder’s interview lives on a hard drive at a company that has since closed its doors.

### What drives the price of a wedding or event videographer?

Coverage hours and edit hours, in that order, with nearly everything else downstream of those two. A videographer pricing a full wedding day is pricing ten or twelve hours on their feet plus somewhere between twenty and sixty hours of editing afterward. Typical packages around the metro commonly run in the low thousands, with a wide spread in both directions.

Coverage is the first question to answer. Getting-ready through the reception exit costs more than ceremony and toasts, and it costs more again with a second shooter, which is the only way to have a camera on the aisle and a camera on the faces at the same moment. Couples who regret their wedding video almost always regret the coverage window, not the color grade.

The edit is the invisible half. A five minute highlight film is built out of hours of ceremony audio, drone shots if the venue allows them, toasts, dancing and two or three synced camera angles. Choosing between a short highlight, a longer feature edit, and full documentary cuts of the ceremony and the speeches changes the price more than any equipment decision anybody makes. A vineyard ceremony out toward Ste. Genevieve with a long drive and a sunset window is a different day than a downtown reception hall with everything in one building.

Ask about raw footage delivery, because it is genuinely valuable and often cheap to add. Twenty years from now the polished four minute film will be lovely, and the unedited twelve minutes of your grandmother talking at the reception will be the thing you cannot replace. Some videographers include the raws, some charge a modest fee, some do not offer them at all. Worth knowing which before you sign anything.

The same logic that governs a photographer’s day governs a videographer’s, and pricing them together makes both conversations easier. What a photographer costs in St. Louis and what an event photographer actually covers in St. Louis both break coverage hours down the same way, and the two vendors are going to be standing three feet apart all day anyway.

### How should you choose a video production company?

Shortlist two or three companies worth interviewing, then watch their actual work before you speak to any of them. Not the sizzle reel. Full pieces, start to finish, ideally made for a client that looks something like you. A reel hides whether a company can hold a viewer’s attention for ninety straight seconds.

Then interview them, and state plainly what you want. What the video is supposed to accomplish, where it will run, who has to approve it, how many revision rounds you expect, which versions you need at the end, and who owns the footage. Say all of it out loud in the first conversation rather than discovering it in month three. Then compare that list against what each company is prepared to deliver.

The gap is the signal, not the price. One company hears your list and tells you which parts are realistic at your number and which are not. Another agrees to everything and stays vague about how. A third tells you straight out that the budget will not carry the scripted version and proposes a smaller idea that will actually work. That third answer is usually the most valuable one in the room, because it is the only one that has been checked against a real production schedule.

Pay attention to what they ask you. A company that wants to know what the video is for before it asks your budget is thinking about the right problem. There is a version of almost every video that fits almost every budget, but only when somebody is willing to change the idea instead of just shaving the shoot day.

One local note worth having. St. Louis carries a deeper production community than people outside it assume, with experienced crew, camera and grip rental houses, and studio space scattered from downtown out to Earth City and over the river toward O’Fallon, Illinois. Missouri also runs a state-level film production incentive program, which matters far more to larger productions than to a corporate video shoot. The practical benefit for a business buyer is simpler than the headline: you can usually hire a good local sound recordist on a week’s notice, and that is not true everywhere.

### Where do you find video production near you?

Bring the goal, not the runtime. You can browse film and video production companies across the metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then interview two or three with the real details: what the video has to do, where it will run, how many revision rounds you expect, and which files you need at the end. Compare what you asked for against what each one is prepared to deliver.

### Frequently asked questions

### Q. How much for a videographer for 2 hours?

A.  Most videographers do not sell two hours, because setup, teardown, travel and file handling surround the shoot no matter how short it is. The usual smallest unit is a half day, and a half day of a solo videographer commonly runs somewhere in the several hundred to low four figures range in this market. Editing is normally quoted on top of that, not inside it. If somebody does quote you two hours, ask whether the number includes an edit or only the recording.

### Q. What is a video production company?

A.  A company that handles a video from idea to finished file, rather than only operating a camera. That means pre-production such as scripting, casting, location scouting and scheduling, the production day with crew and gear, and post-production including editing, color, sound mix, graphics and the various delivery versions. Some are full-service shops with staff producers and editors, some are a small core team that hires specialist crew per project. Both models are legitimate and the second one is very common in St. Louis.

### Q. Is it worth hiring a videographer for a wedding?

A.  It depends entirely on whether sound and motion matter to you, because that is the whole difference from photography. Video is the only thing that keeps the vows, the toast, the laugh and the music. Couples who skip it most often say later that they wish they had heard the ceremony again. Couples who regret paying for it usually bought a short highlight film and never watched it twice. If you book one, buy coverage hours first and polish second.

### Q. What is a good budget for a wedding videographer?

A.  Around this metro, packages commonly land in the low thousands for meaningful full-day coverage with an edited film, with plenty of options above and below that. The spread comes from coverage hours, whether a second shooter is included, and how much editing the deliverables require. A ceremony-and-toasts package with a short highlight sits at the bottom. Full day coverage, two shooters, a feature edit plus documentary cuts of the ceremony and speeches sits well above it. Decide coverage first, then price it.

### Q. How much do video producers get paid?

A.  It varies widely by whether they are staff or freelance. Freelance producers commonly work on a day rate that runs from several hundred dollars into four figures depending on experience and the size of the production. Staff producers at agencies, in-house marketing teams or broadcast typically earn a salary somewhere in the range of other mid-level marketing and media roles, moving with market and seniority. Anyone quoting you one national number for this job is flattening an enormous range.

### Q. What does the 80/20 rule mean in video editing?

A.  It is a rule of thumb rather than a standard, and editors use it two ways. First, roughly eighty percent of your usable material comes from about twenty percent of the footage, which is why organizing and logging clips before cutting saves so much time. Second, the last twenty percent of polish consumes about eighty percent of the hours. That second version is the one that matters to your budget, because it explains why revision rounds cost real money.

### Q. What is the hardest job on a film set?

A.  Ask ten crew members and you will get three answers. By pressure and responsibility, most people name the first assistant director, who owns the schedule and has to keep dozens of people moving without losing the day. By physical demand, grips and electricians, who are hauling and rigging heavy gear before anyone else arrives and after everyone else leaves. By concentration, the first assistant camera pulling focus. On a small corporate crew, all of that lands on two or three people at once.

### Q. How far ahead should a St. Louis business book a video shoot?

A.  For a straightforward interview or testimonial piece, two to four weeks is usually comfortable, mostly to line up the people you need on camera. Anything scripted, cast or shot across multiple locations wants six to ten weeks, because pre-production is real work. Build in edit time as well, since a first cut plus two revision rounds commonly takes another two to four weeks. If the video has a hard date attached to it, count backward from that date and add slack.

## What Flight Lessons Cost in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-flight-lessons-cost-in-st-louis

Imagine a guy in St. Charles who has been driving out to the airport on Saturday mornings for a month without booking anything. He parks at the fence, watches a small trainer come around the pattern twice, tells himself he will walk in and ask next weekend, then drives home. What stops him is not nerve. It is that he cannot find out what the whole thing costs, and he refuses to start something he might have to quit halfway through.

Imagine that same month playing out elsewhere in the metro. A nurse in Maryland Heights who wants a certificate before she turns forty. A high school senior in Godfrey whose counselor mentioned that regional airlines are hiring. A machinist in Washington MO who has wanted this since he was eleven and finally has the money. Somebody in Sauget who drives past runway lights every evening on the way home. Different lives, one identical question underneath all of them.

So let us answer it plainly. What does flight training actually cost, what drives that number up or down, how long does it take, and what would disqualify you before you spent a dollar? None of it is secret. It is just scattered across a dozen places and buried under sales pitches.

### How much does it cost to get a private pilot’s license in the US?

Nobody can quote you one honest number. Training is priced in three parts: the aircraft by the flight hour, the instructor by the hour, and then ground school, books, testing fees and the medical exam. The FAA minimum hour requirement is a floor almost nobody finishes at, so how often you fly decides your total.

That is the whole structure, and once you can see it, the sticker shock gets easier to reason about. You are not buying a course with a price on it. You are renting an airplane by the hour, hiring an instructor by the hour, and paying a handful of fixed fees along the way. Two of those three lines are open-ended, and they stay open until you pass your checkride.

Here is the part that catches people. Regulations set a minimum number of logged flight hours for a private pilot certificate, and every school will tell you that number if you ask. Almost nobody finishes there. The minimum assumes an ideal student flying on an ideal schedule with ideal weather, and none of those three describe a real person learning to fly in Missouri weather around a full-time job.

So when you budget, budget against a realistic hour count instead of the legal floor. Ask each school what their students actually average, not what the regulation says. And gather local rates yourself from two or three schools in the metro rather than trusting a figure printed in an article, including this one. Rental rates and instructor rates are set field by field, and they move.

### Why does the same license cost one person twice what it costs another?

Because the biggest cost driver is not the hourly rate. It is consistency. Two people can train at the same school in the same airplane with the same instructor and finish hundreds of miles apart in total spend, because one flew twice a week and the other flew twice a month.

### Flying often is cheaper than flying rarely

Flying is a physical skill, and physical skills decay between sessions. If you fly twice a week, each lesson starts roughly where the last one ended. If three weeks pass, you spend a chunk of every lesson re-learning what you already paid to learn, and you pay for that airplane and that instructor while you do it.

This is why the cheapest-looking rate is not always the cheapest license. A school with a slightly higher hourly rate but real availability, meaning aircraft you can actually book and an instructor who is not stacked six students deep, will usually cost you less by the end. Availability is a price, it is just not printed anywhere.

### The aircraft you train in

Older, simpler training aircraft rent for less per hour than newer ones with glass panels. Neither choice is wrong. A basic trainer with analog gauges teaches the same fundamentals, and plenty of very good pilots learned that way. Newer equipment costs more per hour and may line up better with what you will fly later if this is a career move.

What matters more than the panel is whether the airplane flies. An aircraft that is down for maintenance half the month is not a cheap airplane, it is a schedule problem wearing a low price tag. Ask how many trainers the school has and how often they are grounded.

### The fees that are not flying

Beyond the hourly lines, there is a short list of one-time costs, and they are worth knowing about before they surprise you. A medical certificate from an aviation medical examiner. Books and study materials. Ground school, whether it is in person, online or one-on-one with your instructor. The written knowledge test. And the checkride itself, which means paying an examiner.

None of these individually will break your budget. Together they are real money, and they tend to land in clumps at the beginning and the end. Ask each school to walk you through them in order so you know roughly when each one hits.

### How long does it take to become a pilot?

For a private pilot certificate, most people are thinking in months rather than years, and the honest answer depends almost entirely on how often you fly. Someone flying two or three times a week finishes in a fraction of the time it takes someone squeezing in one lesson when the weather and the schedule happen to agree.

The sequence itself is fixed. You start flying with an instructor, you work toward solo, you build cross-country experience, you pass a written knowledge test, and then you take a practical exam with an examiner, the checkride, which includes both an oral portion and a flight. Along the way you need a valid medical certificate. That order does not change from school to school.

What changes is the calendar. Missouri weather will take weeks away from you, especially in winter and in the thick of summer storm season. Aircraft go into maintenance. Instructors move on. If somebody promises you a finish date without asking a single question about your availability, treat that as a sales number rather than a plan.

### If you are aiming at an aviation career

The private certificate is the first rung, not the destination. After it comes an instrument rating, then a commercial certificate, and most people then become flight instructors themselves in order to build experience while getting paid rather than paying. That instructing stretch is the long part of the career timeline, and it is where a lot of people underestimate the years involved.

Plan it as a multi-year path with a job in the middle of it. Anyone telling you otherwise is selling something.

### Is flight training actually hard?

It is demanding, but not in the way most people fear. The flying itself is a coordination skill that almost everybody can learn with repetition. The hard parts are the volume of ground knowledge, the discipline of studying between lessons, and the sheer persistence it takes to keep showing up for months.

Ask any instructor what makes students stall out and you will rarely hear “they could not fly the airplane.” You will hear that life got busy, that the money got tight, that they took a two-month break and never came back. Attrition in flight training is mostly a scheduling and stamina story, not a talent story.

### The ground knowledge is the real workload

You will study weather, airspace, regulations, aircraft systems, aerodynamics, navigation and how to compute weight and balance. It is a lot, and it is unfamiliar. But it is memorizable, structured material with published sources, and thousands of ordinary people get through it every year. Treat it like a real class with a real study schedule and it stops being frightening.

### The checkride

The practical exam is a genuine test, and it is meant to be. Your instructor is not supposed to sign you off until you are ready, which is the actual safeguard here. If a school seems eager to push students toward the examiner before they are prepared, that tells you something about the school. People do fail checkrides, they retrain on the deficient areas, and they go back. It is a setback, not an ending.

### What disqualifies you from becoming a pilot?

Far less than people assume. The main gate is the medical certificate, which is issued by an aviation medical examiner and covers things like vision, hearing, cardiac and neurological history, certain medications, and a history of substance issues. Most conditions people worry about are manageable, and some require extra paperwork rather than a flat no.

If you have any concern at all about your medical history, go get the medical certificate figured out before you spend money on lessons. That is the single most useful piece of sequencing advice in this whole article. Talk to an aviation medical examiner first, ask directly about your situation, and let a qualified professional tell you where you stand. This is general information, not medical or legal advice.

Corrected vision is not a barrier for most people. Age is not a barrier. Not being a math person is not a barrier. There are also non-medical requirements, including English language proficiency and identity and citizenship documentation at the start of training, and any school will walk you through those on day one.

Grounded for a week? Fabric by the yard in St. Louis fills a hangar afternoon.

### How do you choose a flight school in the St. Louis metro?

Shortlist two or three that are worth interviewing, then go interview them in person. Not a phone quote. Walk in, look at the airplanes, meet an instructor, and pay attention to how they answer you. You are hiring a school for the better part of a year, and you cannot evaluate that from a rate sheet.

### Say plainly what you want

Before you go, decide what you are asking for and say it out loud when you get there. Something like: I want to fly Tuesday evenings and Saturday mornings. I want to be ready for a checkride by a specific month. I want to train in this aircraft. And I want an instructor who is still going to be here in six months.

Then stop talking and listen to what each school says it can actually provide. One will tell you the Saturday slots are booked through spring. One will be honest that their instructors are building hours and turn over regularly. One will say yes to all four things without hesitating, which is either excellent or a warning, and the follow-up questions will tell you which.

### The gap is the signal, not the price

Compare what you asked for against what each place is prepared to deliver. That gap is your real decision. A school that says “we can do three of those four, and here is why not the fourth” is being straight with you, and straight is worth paying for. A school that agrees to everything and then cannot book you for three weeks has already cost you money you have not spent yet.

A few other things worth asking while you are standing there. How many students does the average instructor carry? How far ahead do students book? What happens when weather cancels, do you get rescheduled that week or pushed out? Who is your instructor if yours leaves? Those answers predict your total cost better than any hourly rate will.

### Instructor turnover is normal, plan for it

Many instructors are building experience toward the next step in their own careers, so some turnover is built into the system and is not a scandal. What matters is whether the school has a handoff process. Ask what happens to your training records and your syllabus position if your instructor moves on mid-training. A school with a real answer has done this before.

Most people starting this search do not begin with a school name. They begin with a location and a question about cost, and whoever shows up in that search gets the first conversation. If you are an instructor or a school in the metro, being listed where those searchers already look is how the walk-in at the fence becomes a booked discovery flight.

### Frequently asked questions

### Q. How difficult is it to get a private pilot license?

A.  It is demanding but achievable for most ordinary people. The flying is a coordination skill that comes with repetition. The heavier lift is the ground knowledge, covering weather, airspace, regulations, systems and navigation, plus the discipline of studying between lessons. The most common reason people do not finish is not ability. It is a long break in training that they never come back from.

### Q. How many years does it take to become a pilot?

A.  A private pilot certificate is usually measured in months, and how often you fly decides the number. A professional path is different. After the private certificate you add an instrument rating and a commercial certificate, and most people then instruct in order to build experience while earning. Plan that career route as a multi-year commitment with a working job in the middle of it.

### Q. Is it hard to pass flight school?

A.  The checkride is a real exam with an oral portion and a flight portion, and it is meant to be rigorous. Your instructor is not supposed to sign you off until you can meet the standards, which is the safeguard that matters. People do fail, retrain on the specific deficient areas and go back. Consistency in training is the best predictor of a smooth checkride.

### Q. Is 35 too old to become a pilot?

A.  No. Age is not a barrier to earning a private pilot certificate, and plenty of people start later than that. Your medical certificate matters far more than your birth year, so if you have any health history you are unsure about, see an aviation medical examiner before you spend money on lessons. Career timelines are worth researching separately, since those involve mandatory retirement rules.

### Q. What disqualifies you as a pilot?

A.  The main gate is the medical certificate issued by an aviation medical examiner, which looks at vision, hearing, cardiac and neurological history, certain medications, and substance-related history. Many conditions are manageable or require additional paperwork rather than a flat denial. There are also English proficiency and identity documentation requirements. Sort the medical out first. This is general information, not medical or legal advice.

### Q. Can I be a pilot if I’m bad at math?

A.  Yes. The math in private pilot training is arithmetic, ratios and simple formulas: fuel burn, time and distance, weight and balance. It is procedural rather than abstract, you learn the specific calculations you need, and you use tools and charts to do them. If you can follow a recipe and keep your units straight, you can handle this part.

### Q. Do pilots make good money?

A.  It varies enormously by segment and by seniority, and the early years look nothing like the later ones. Instructing while you build experience typically pays modestly. Pay at airlines and in corporate flying is published and negotiated, so look up current pay scales for the specific operators you would target rather than trusting a general figure. Weigh that against your training cost honestly.

### Q. Is there still a pilot shortage in 2026?

A.  Hiring in aviation moves in cycles, and headlines lag the actual market by a long way. Rather than plan a career around a shortage narrative, check what the operators you would want to work for are actually doing right now, and ask working instructors in the metro what they are seeing. Train because you want the certificate, and treat hiring conditions as a variable.

## What Laser Hair Removal Costs in St. Louis
