## What Massage School Costs in Missouri
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-massage-school-costs-in-missouri

Picture a woman in Arnold coming off her third twelve-hour shift of the week at a long-term care home. She has spent the day turning, lifting and steadying people, and her hands are the only part of the job she still loves. A resident told her last month that she has good hands. There is a tab open on her phone about massage school, and it has been open for six weeks, because every page she finds talks about her future and not one of them tells her what the thing actually costs.

She is not the only person in the metro running that math. A man in Florissant whose warehouse shift got cut is comparing trade programs and trying to work out which one pays him back fastest. A personal trainer in O’Fallon wants to add bodywork so her clients stop leaving her for somebody else. A bartender in Washington who has stood on concrete for eleven years wants a job that does not end at three in the morning. A nurse in Edwardsville is done with hospital staffing and wants to work on one person at a time.

All of them want the same three answers. What does the schooling cost, how long am I out of the workforce, and is there real work waiting on the other side? This guide covers the hours Missouri requires and what those hours contain, every line item that lands on a student’s bill including the ones no tuition page lists, how long a program takes on days versus evenings, what the licensing path looks like after graduation, what the working life is genuinely like, and how to tell a school worth your money from one that is only worth its brochure.

### How much does it typically cost to become a massage therapist?

Nobody can quote you one honest number, because Missouri sets the hours and each school sets the price. The state requires at least 500 clock hours from an approved program. Take a school’s per-hour tuition rate, multiply by its total hours, then add books, a kit, the exam, a background check and license fees.

The reason an article cannot hand you a figure is that two of the three variables belong to the school rather than the state. Missouri sets a floor of hours. Each program decides how far above that floor it runs, what it charges per hour or per term, and what it folds into that price. Two approved schools can sit a long way apart on all three, and both can be perfectly legitimate.

### The line items nobody puts on the tuition page

Tuition is the headline, usually quoted either per clock hour or as one program total. Underneath it sit the costs that arrive later: books and anatomy materials, a table or a linens and lotion kit if the school requires one, the national exam fee, fingerprinting and a background check, the state license application fee, and liability insurance once you start putting hands on people.

Treat the per-hour rate multiplied by the program hours as the floor, not the total. That one sentence is the whole difference between the number a student writes in a notebook in March and the number that comes off their card in October. Some schools include books and a kit. Some do not. The word you want from an admissions office is included, and you want it said about each item by name.

### How to build your own number

Ask every school on your shortlist for the total program cost in writing, and ask directly whether books and the kit are in or out of that figure. Then go around the school for the rest of it. The exam fee comes from the Federation of State Massage Therapy Boards, which administers the MBLEx. The license application fee and the background check requirements come from the Missouri Board of Therapeutic Massage, part of the Missouri Division of Professional Registration.

Both bodies publish current figures, and both revise them from time to time. That is exactly why you should not trust a dollar amount printed in any article, including this one. Ten minutes on the phone with the Board and the FSMTB gets you numbers that are true this month rather than numbers that were true when somebody wrote a blog post.

Then add the cost nobody writes down: the income you give up while you sit in class. A student on a day cohort is usually cutting shifts somewhere else, and a student on evenings is giving up overtime, side work or childcare-free hours. It never appears on an invoice, and it is one of the largest lines in the real budget.

### What do Missouri’s 500 hours actually cover?

Missouri requires a minimum of 500 clock hours of supervised massage therapy instruction from an approved program before you can apply for a license, and the Missouri Board of Therapeutic Massage sets that standard. Confirm the current requirement with the Board directly before you enroll anywhere. Five hundred is a floor, and plenty of programs run well past it.

### The classroom half

Expect anatomy, physiology, kinesiology and pathology, plus ethics, boundaries, sanitation, documentation and the basics of running a practice. Anatomy is the piece that surprises career changers. You are not learning the names of a few muscles. You are learning origins, insertions, actions and the tissue underneath your hands, well enough to tell a client something accurate about why their shoulder hurts.

Pathology matters more than students expect too. A large part of your training is learning when not to work on somebody: which conditions are contraindications, which need a physician’s clearance, and which need you to change what you were planning to do. That judgment is the difference between a technician and a therapist.

### The table half

The rest is hands-on. Technique, draping, positioning, communication, pressure, and body mechanics drilled until they are automatic. Then comes student clinic, where you work on members of the public under supervision, at a reduced rate, in the school’s own treatment space.

Student clinic is the part that turns a program into a job, and it is the part to ask about hardest. The classroom content is broadly similar from school to school because the state requirements shape it. The number of supervised hours you spend on real bodies, with real complaints, varies far more, and it is what makes you employable on the day you graduate.

### How long does massage school take, days versus evenings?

A full-time day cohort can move through a 500-plus hour program in a matter of months. The same hours spread across evenings and weekends commonly take roughly twice as long. The hours do not change. The calendar does, because an evening cohort meets three or four nights a week instead of five full days.

Evening programs stretch for ordinary reasons. Fewer contact hours per week, holiday breaks, and student clinic shifts that are often scheduled separately from class nights. A program advertised as a year can land closer to eighteen months once all of that lands on a real calendar with a real job attached to it.

So ask for the cohort calendar, not the marketing length. A school should hand you a start date, an end date, the class nights, and where clinic hours sit in the schedule. If clinic is on top of class rather than inside it, that is additional time out of your week, and people underestimate it almost every time.

Changing careers with kids at home? Start with choosing a preschool in St. Louis.

### How hard is the coursework, really?

People ask whether massage school is difficult, and the honest answer splits into two halves. The academic load is heavy but ordinary, mostly memorization rather than hard reasoning. The physical load is the part that catches career changers off guard, because you are learning a trade your own body has to survive for twenty years.

### The memorization

Muscles, origins, insertions, actions, bones, joints, nerve pathways, systems, pathologies and contraindications. Flashcards become a lifestyle. Most programs test with written exams and hands-on practicals, so you have to know the material and then perform it on a table while an instructor watches. If you have not studied in fifteen years, the first month is a shock and the third month is fine.

### The physical part

You will be sore. Students practice on each other for hours, and beginners tend to work from their thumbs and shoulders because that is what feels natural. A good program spends the whole term correcting that, teaching you to work from your legs and your body weight so the load goes through your frame instead of your joints.

Take that seriously, because it is a career-length issue rather than a school-length one. Therapists who never learn clean body mechanics are the ones who leave the field with wrist, thumb or lower back injuries a few years in. The students who ask their instructors to watch their posture are not being fussy. They are protecting their income.

### What happens after graduation, and how do you get licensed?

Graduating is not the same as being licensed. Missouri graduates typically sit a national licensing exam, the MBLEx, which is administered by the Federation of State Massage Therapy Boards, and then apply to the Missouri Board of Therapeutic Massage for a license. Fingerprinting and a background check are part of that path, and each step carries its own fee.

Build your timeline backwards from the date you need to be earning. There is study time between graduation and the exam, scheduling time for the exam itself, and processing time on the license application. None of that is dramatic, but it is weeks, and weeks matter when you have already stopped working extra shifts to attend class.

Ask your school how their graduates usually sequence those steps and how their students perform on the exam. A program that prepares you for the MBLEx as part of the curriculum, rather than waving at it on the last day, is worth something real. So is a school that helps with the application paperwork.

One more line for the budget: liability insurance. You carry it once you start working on the public, whether you are employed by a clinic or working for yourself, and it is an annual cost rather than a one-time fee. Professional membership organizations frequently bundle it with membership, which is a large part of why new therapists join one.

### What is the working life actually like?

The honest headline is that your day is capped by your body, not by the schedule. A therapist can be booked back to back on paper all day long. Very few can deliver genuinely good deep work at that pace, five days a week, year after year, without their hands and back sending the bill.

Most working therapists settle on a number of sessions per day they can repeat sustainably and then defend it. That is the whole economics of the profession in a sentence. You are paid for hands-on time, hands-on time is finite, and learning to decline the extra late booking is a professional skill rather than a character flaw.

The rest of the working life is quieter than people picture. You are alone in a room with one person. You talk less than you would think. Clients bring things into the room that have nothing to do with their shoulder, and holding that steadily takes something out of you. Plenty of therapists say it is the best part of the job. Others find it draining. It is worth knowing which one you are before you enroll.

Schedules skew toward evenings and weekends, because that is when clients are free. If you are leaving a job specifically to get your nights back, look hard at that. If you are leaving a job to stop lifting and standing for twelve hours, this trade genuinely delivers on that part.

### Which settings and specialties change what you can earn?

Setting shapes your income more than technique does, because setting decides who finds you, who books you and who keeps the fee. A spa or high-volume clinic hands you a filled schedule and takes a share. A chiropractic or physical therapy office sends you a steady stream of referred clients. Working for yourself gives you the whole fee and the whole job of filling the table.

### The common settings around the metro

Day spas and resorts, high-volume membership clinics, chiropractic and physical therapy offices, sports and athletic settings, medical and hospital-adjacent work, and independent practice out of a rented room or a home studio. Each one trades stability against control. The high-volume end gives you steady bookings and less say over your schedule. Independence gives you control and hands you the marketing, the booking, the taxes and the empty Tuesday.

Most therapists in the metro do not pick one forever. A common path is two or three years somewhere with a full schedule, building stamina and a client base, then a move toward a clinical setting or a room of their own once the phone rings on its own.

### What type of massage pays the most

The specialties that command the highest rates are the ones with the fewest qualified practitioners and the most specific demand. Clinical and medical work, sports and rehabilitation, prenatal, oncology massage, and post-surgical lymphatic drainage all sit in that category. Every one of them requires continuing education beyond your initial license, and some require supervised experience on top.

The pattern is the same here as anywhere. General relaxation work is the most available and the most competitive. Specialized work is harder to get into, harder to replace you in, and easier to charge properly for. That is the trade, and it is why most therapists keep adding certifications for years rather than stopping at 500 hours and calling it done.

### How do you choose a massage school worth the money?

Shortlist two or three schools worth interviewing, then go and stand in each of them. You are not shopping for the cheapest program. You are looking for the school whose plan for your training matches what you actually want out of the career, and there is no way to learn that from a web page.

Say plainly what you want. Tell them you intend to work clinically, or in a spa, or for yourself out of a rented room in St. Charles County. Tell them evenings are the only thing that works with your kids. Tell them you want as many supervised clinic hours as you can possibly get. Then listen to what comes back, and notice the distance between what you asked for and what the school is prepared to deliver. That gap is the signal, not the price.

### What to ask while you are standing there

Ask to sit in on a class if they allow it. Ask how many students are in a cohort and how many instructors are on the floor during hands-on time. Ask how many supervised clinic hours you get with actual members of the public. Ask what happens if you have to pause for a term. Ask what graduates are doing a year out, and whether they can put you in touch with two of them.

Watch the room more than the pitch. Are students working on each other with an instructor moving between tables correcting posture, or is one person circling twenty pairs? Does the clinic space look like somewhere a paying client would come back to? A school that is happy to let you stand in the room has already told you a great deal.

### Approval, transfer and the honest questions

Confirm with the Missouri Board of Therapeutic Massage that the program is approved for licensure before you pay a deposit. Ask what happens to your hours if you leave the state, since requirements differ elsewhere and hours do not always transfer cleanly. If there is any chance of a move in the next few years, raise it on the first visit rather than the last.

It is also fair to compare this path against the others in the same bracket. If you are weighing it against another hands-on trade, the same interview approach works for trade schools and apprenticeships in St. Louis, and the questions that matter barely change.

### For massage schools and therapists in the metro

If you are on the other side of this, notice that every person described above starts with a search rather than a school name. They type what they want to become and where they live, then contact whoever turns up with enough detail to sound honest. Being visible where those searches land is how a small program keeps cohorts full without buying ads.

Spell out the concrete things on your own page. Total program hours, day and evening cohort options, how many supervised clinic hours a student gets, and whether books and a kit are included or extra. Those four items are already written in every prospective student’s notebook. The school that answers them plainly, before anyone has to ask, gets the phone call.

Interview two or three schools before you sign anything. You can browse massage schools across the metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then visit the ones that fit your schedule and say out loud what you want from the career. Ask for the total program cost in writing, ask what is included, and get the current exam and license fees from the FSMTB and the Missouri Board yourself.

### Frequently asked questions

### Q. How long would it take to become a massage therapist?

A.  Missouri requires at least 500 clock hours of supervised instruction from an approved program, and many programs run longer than that. A full-time day cohort can finish in a matter of months. Evenings and weekends commonly take roughly twice as long, because you meet three or four nights a week instead of five full days. After graduation, add time to study for and sit the MBLEx and to have your license application processed.

### Q. Is massage school difficult?

A.  It is demanding in two separate ways. The academic side is heavy memorization: muscles, origins and insertions, bones, nerve pathways, pathologies and contraindications, plus ethics and documentation. That is manageable with steady work even if you have not studied in years. The physical side surprises more people. You practice for hours at a time, and you spend the whole program retraining your body mechanics so your thumbs, wrists and lower back survive the career.

### Q. What type of massage pays the most?

A.  The specialties that command the highest rates are the ones with the fewest qualified practitioners and the most specific demand: clinical and medical work, sports and rehabilitation, prenatal, oncology massage, and post-surgical lymphatic drainage. Each requires continuing education beyond your initial license. Setting matters as much as technique, since a spa, a chiropractic office and independent practice split the fee in completely different ways.

### Q. What is the downside of being a massage therapist?

A.  Your earnings are capped by your body. You are paid for hands-on time, that time is finite, and pushing past what your hands and back can repeat is how therapists end careers early. Beyond the physical ceiling: evening and weekend hours, because that is when clients are free, the emotional weight people bring into the room, and the unpaid work of filling your own schedule if you go independent.

### Q. Is massage therapy a good career in 2026?

A.  It suits people who want hands-on work with one client at a time and a short training path compared with most health-adjacent careers. Demand across the St. Louis metro spans spas, membership clinics, chiropractic and physical therapy offices, sports settings and private practice. The honest caveat is that it rewards planning. Therapists who add specialties, protect their bodies and build a repeat client base last. Those who do not tend to burn out.

### Q. How many massages can a therapist do in a day?

A.  Fewer than a schedule allows, and that is exactly the point. A therapist can be booked back to back on paper, but very few can deliver good deep work at that pace five days a week for years without injury. Most settle on a sustainable number of sessions per day and then protect it. Newer therapists usually start lower while they build stamina and clean body mechanics.

## How to Get Into Nursing School in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-get-into-nursing-school-in-st-louis

Danielle works the opening shift at a coffee counter in Arnold and has wanted to be a nurse since she was nineteen. She is twenty-six now. Last spring she finally sat down, filled out an application to a nursing program, hit submit, and felt like she had done the big scary thing. Six weeks later a polite email arrived explaining that her file could not be scored, because she had not completed the prerequisite science sequence. Nobody had ever told her the application was the last step rather than the first one. She had spent seven years waiting to be brave about the wrong task.

She is not alone, and the people around her in the metro are standing at slightly different doors. A CNA in Florissant has three years on a busy floor and wants the license to match the work she already does. A thirty-eight-year-old in O’Fallon has a marketing degree collecting dust and just learned there is such a thing as an accelerated second-degree BSN. A senior at a high school in Union is trying to decide whether to start at a community college or head straight into a four-year program. A mother of two in Belleville is going back at forty-four and quietly wondering whether she is too old and too rusty at chemistry to pull this off.

All four of them want an answer to the same question: what actually decides whether I get a seat? This guide walks through it in order. The real first step, how to choose between an ADN, a BSN, and an accelerated route, the prerequisite list and why one C is worth more attention than your essay, the entrance exam and how people under-prepare for it, the points formula programs use to rank applicants, the paperwork that quietly knocks people out late, an honest conversation about the science and the math, and what to do if the first cycle does not go your way.

### What is the first step to get into nursing school?

The first step is not the application. It is choosing your route, ADN or BSN, and starting prerequisites at a school whose credits transfer where you plan to apply. Prerequisite grades are the long pole and the main thing that ranks you. Most applicants begin those courses a year later than they should.

Here is why the timing matters so much. Anatomy and physiology I and II are usually taken in sequence, one semester after the other, so you need two terms minimum before you hold both. Microbiology frequently wants chemistry finished first. Stack those dependencies end to end and you are looking at three or four semesters of prerequisite work before your file is even scoreable, and that assumes nothing fills up, nothing gets dropped, and no semester goes sideways on you.

So the honest first step is one unglamorous afternoon at the kitchen table. Pick two or three programs you would genuinely attend. Open each program’s nursing admissions page. Write down the exact prerequisite list, the exact entrance exam they require, and the exact application deadline. Then find the overlap. The courses that appear on all three lists are the ones you register for first, at a school whose credits you have already confirmed will transfer.

Confirm that transfer question out loud, by course number, before you pay tuition on anything. “If I take this anatomy course at this college, does it satisfy your prerequisite?” A four-minute phone call has rescued more nursing careers than any admissions essay ever written. If you are still weighing schools in general, our guide on how to choose a college or trade school in St. Louis covers the accreditation and transfer questions worth asking before you enroll anywhere.

### ADN, BSN, or accelerated: which route fits the life you actually have?

There is no best route, only the one that matches your money, your calendar, and your starting point. An ADN is an associate degree, roughly two years of nursing coursework at a community college. A BSN is a bachelor of science in nursing, roughly four years. Graduates of both sit for the same NCLEX-RN licensure exam.

That last sentence surprises people, so sit with it a second. Missouri RNs are licensed by the Missouri State Board of Nursing, part of the Missouri Division of Professional Registration, and graduates must pass the NCLEX-RN to be licensed. The route in front of the license changes. The exam at the end does not.

The ADN route tends to fit people who need to be earning as an RN sooner, who have a household depending on that timeline, and who want community college pacing and cost while they work. Plenty of nurses finish an ADN, get hired, and complete an RN-to-BSN bridge later, often with employer support, while drawing a nursing paycheck the whole time. That is a completely normal way to arrive.

The BSN route fits the high schooler in Union who can go full-time for four years, and anyone aiming at units or career tracks where a bachelor’s is preferred or required. You get more coursework in leadership, research, community health, and public health along the way.

The accelerated or second-degree BSN exists for people who already hold a bachelor’s degree in something else, like our marketing graduate in O’Fallon. It is compressed and intense, and it is genuinely hard to hold a full-time job through one. And the CNA in Florissant has her own on-ramp: LPN programs and LPN-to-RN bridges are built for people already working in care who want to climb without starting from zero.

Whatever route you pick, every one of them puts you in clinical rotations, in real facilities, with real patients who are having a bad week.

Soon you’ll be the one in scrubs, not the patient choosing a specialist.

### What are the requirements to enter the school of nursing?

Requirements vary by program, but the shape is remarkably consistent across the metro. You will need a prerequisite course block, an entrance exam score, a criminal background check, a drug screening, and current immunization and CPR certification records. Some programs add an essay or an interview on top of that.

The prerequisite block typically includes anatomy and physiology I and II, microbiology, chemistry, statistics, a psychology or human development course, and English composition. Some programs also want nutrition, a lifespan development course, or a general education spread on top. Write the list down per program. Do not assume the school across the river wants the identical set, because it often does not.

The entrance exam is usually the TEAS or the HESI A2. The background check and drug screen are non-negotiable, because clinical sites require them before they will let a student on the floor. Immunizations and CPR certification are the same story. These are not admissions preferences. They are the conditions your clinical partners impose, and the program cannot waive them for you.

Now the part almost nobody does, and the part that changes outcomes most. Shortlist two or three programs and go interview them. Attend the information session. Sit down with an advisor. Say plainly what you want out of the program and what your actual situation is: I work thirty hours a week, I have a seven-year-old, I have a C in chemistry from 2019, I need evening clinicals. Then listen to what that program is prepared to provide. The gap between what you need and what they can offer is the signal. It tells you where to apply, and it tells you what to fix first.

### Why is retaking a C often the highest-leverage move you can make?

Because prerequisite grades usually carry the heaviest weight in the ranking formula, and a single science C can quietly cost you more points than anything else in your file. You cannot rewrite your essay into an acceptance. You can retake anatomy. One course, one semester, and your score moves.

Most applicants resist this. Retaking a class you already passed feels like going backward, like admitting something. It is not. It is the cheapest, most controllable point gain available to you, and the people who get in have usually done it without advertising it.

Before you register, ask the program two specific questions. First, do you replace the original grade or average the attempts? Second, is there a limit on how many times a science prerequisite can be repeated? Those two answers decide whether the retake helps you or hurts you, and they differ by program. Ask them by name, in writing if you can, and keep the reply.

### How do people under-prepare for the entrance exam?

They treat it like a formality. The TEAS and the HESI A2 are not pass or fail hurdles in most admissions formulas. They are scored inputs, and your number becomes points that get compared directly against every other applicant in the pool. A rushed sitting is a permanently weaker file.

The second mistake is scheduling the exam for a week you are already drowning, right at the end of a term, on top of finals. The third is skipping the sections outside your comfort zone. Nursing entrance exams sample reading, math, science, and English usage. People who love the science content lose points on grammar and reading comprehension they never studied, because they assumed those parts would take care of themselves.

Ask the program how many attempts they allow, how long they make you wait between sittings, and which score they use if you test twice, the highest or the most recent. Then build backward from the application deadline so you have room for a second attempt if the first one lands soft. Give it real study weeks, not a weekend.

### What does the points formula actually reward?

Nursing programs generally admit by a points or ranking formula rather than a single cutoff. Prerequisite grades, entrance exam score, and sometimes an essay or interview each convert into points, the pool gets sorted, and seats go down the list. You are not being measured against a bar. You are being measured against everyone else who applied that cycle.

This is why the published minimum misleads so many people. A minimum is the floor to be considered, not the profile of who actually got in. The competitive average in a given cycle typically sits well above the published minimum, and it moves year to year with the applicant pool. There is no statewide number, and anyone who quotes you one is guessing.

So get the real figure from the only place it exists. Call or email the nursing admissions office and ask, in these words: what was the score range or admitted-student profile for your most recent cycle? Many programs will tell you. That number tells you whether you are a strong applicant, a borderline one, or someone who needs another semester of work before applying. Guessing costs you a whole year. Asking costs you an email.

What you control is short and worth taping to the fridge: which prerequisites you take and where, the grade in each one, how hard you prepare for the entrance exam, and whether you apply to more than one program in the same cycle.

### What paperwork quietly disqualifies people at the last minute?

The boring documents, every time. Background checks, drug screening, immunization records, CPR certification, and deadlines. These do not reject applicants for being unqualified. They reject applicants for being late, and that is the most painful way to lose a seat you had already earned on the merits.

Immunization records are the classic. People need childhood shot records they have not seen in twenty years, or a titer drawn to prove immunity, and they start looking for the clinic in the same week the file is due. Some vaccination series take weeks to complete. Start that folder the month you start prerequisites, not the month you apply.

Criminal history deserves a straight answer rather than a rumor. Licensure through the Missouri State Board of Nursing includes a criminal history review, and certain convictions can affect eligibility. Those situations are decided case by case by the Board, not by an internet forum and not by your cousin who heard something. If you have something on your record, ask early, ask the Board and ask the program, and get the answer before you spend two years and real money on prerequisites. Knowing sooner is always better than hoping longer.

### Is the science and the math really as hard as people say?

It is hard in a specific, survivable way. Nursing science is heavy on volume and memorization rather than abstraction, and nursing math is arithmetic under an accuracy standard rather than higher mathematics. People are asking “is it really hard to get into nursing school” when the honest strain is the sustained pace, not the ceiling of the material.

Anatomy and physiology is a vocabulary marathon. Microbiology is detail work. Chemistry is the one that scares returning students most, and it is usually the one that responds best to a tutor, a study group, and a lighter course load in that particular semester. Nobody is expecting you to enjoy all of it. They are expecting you to get through it while paying attention.

The math is dosage calculation, unit conversion, ratios, and drip rates, plus a statistics course as a prerequisite in most programs. What makes it feel heavy is not the difficulty. It is that a decimal in the wrong place is a patient safety problem, so programs hold you to a precision standard that ordinary math classes never did. That standard is learnable. Repetition builds it.

If you are forty-four in Belleville and your last chemistry class was in another century, take one prerequisite alone in your first semester back. Prove to yourself that you can still do this, get a strong grade, and then add load. Starting with four science courses at once is how confident people talk themselves out of the whole plan by October.

### What should you do if you are not admitted the first cycle?

Apply again, but not with the identical file. Programs rank applicants against a pool that changes every cycle, so resubmitting the same numbers is a coin flip with the same coin. Change something measurable first, then reapply. Most people who get in on a second attempt did exactly that.

Start by asking the program where your file fell short. Some will tell you your score, your rank band, or the component that dragged you down. That single conversation replaces a year of speculation. Then pick the fixable item: retake the science course with the weakest grade, sit the entrance exam again with real preparation, finish an outstanding prerequisite, or apply to more programs in the same cycle instead of just one.

Meanwhile, get closer to the work. Becoming a CNA, taking a patient care tech role, or working in a clinic puts income in your pocket, tells you whether you actually like bedside care before you borrow money for it, and gives you something real to talk about in an interview. If you are mapping out earning options while you wait, our St. Louis career roadmap is a reasonable place to look.

And give yourself the honest reframe. A denied application is not a verdict on whether you will be a good nurse. It is a ranking outcome in one competitive pool in one particular spring.

Start with the prerequisite list, not the application form. Pick two or three programs, get their exact course requirements and deadlines side by side, and register for the overlap this term. You can browse nursing schools across the metro on St Louis Near Me Directory to build that shortlist, then call each admissions office and ask for the admitted-student profile before you commit a single semester.

### For nursing programs and healthcare employers in the metro

If you run a nursing program or hire clinical staff, the applicants above are your pipeline, and most of them are losing a year to information they could not find. The programs that publish a plain prerequisite list, an admitted-student score range, a retake policy, and a real deadline calendar get stronger applicants, not fewer.

The same goes for employers. Candidates who know that tuition assistance, RN-to-BSN support, or a CNA-to-nursing pathway exists will apply for the entry role today. Say it in the job posting. A clear listing that spells out the pathway does more recruiting than a career fair table, especially in North County, Jefferson County, and the Metro East where people are weighing commute against schedule.

### Frequently asked questions

### Q. Is it really hard to get into nursing school?

A.  Yes, admission is competitive, but it is competitive in a way you can plan around. Programs rank applicants by a points formula built on prerequisite grades and entrance exam scores, then fill seats from the top down. That means the difficulty is comparative, not fixed. Strong prerequisite grades and a well-prepared exam score move you up the list more than anything else in your file.

### Q. Does it take 2 years to be a nurse?

A.  Roughly, for the nursing coursework in an ADN, but that number leaves out the prerequisites. Most people spend two to four semesters finishing anatomy and physiology, microbiology, chemistry, and the rest before nursing courses even begin. A BSN runs about four years. Accelerated second-degree BSN options are shorter for people who already hold a bachelor’s degree. Then you still have to pass the NCLEX-RN.

### Q. What disqualifies you from nursing school?

A.  Incomplete prerequisites and missed deadlines knock out more applicants than anything else. Beyond that, programs require a criminal background check, drug screening, and current immunization and CPR records, because clinical sites demand them. Licensure through the Missouri State Board of Nursing also includes a criminal history review, and certain convictions can affect eligibility. Those cases are decided individually by the Board, so ask early rather than assuming.

### Q. What is the lowest GPA to be a nurse?

A.  There is no single statewide answer, and be suspicious of anyone who gives you one. Each program publishes its own minimum, and the competitive average of admitted students usually sits well above that published floor. The only reliable source is the nursing admissions office at the program you want. Ask them directly for the minimum and for the most recent admitted-student profile.

### Q. Is math for nursing hard?

A.  It is more demanding than difficult. The math is dosage calculation, unit conversion, ratios, and IV drip rates, plus a statistics course as a common prerequisite. None of that is advanced mathematics. What makes it feel hard is the accuracy standard, since a misplaced decimal is a safety issue, so programs test precision far more strictly than a general math class ever did.

### Q. Can I be a nurse if I don't like science?

A.  Plenty of excellent nurses were never the science kid in high school. You cannot skip it, though. Anatomy and physiology, microbiology, chemistry, and later pharmacology are all part of the path. Many people find they disliked how science was taught rather than science itself, and applied clinical context changes that. Try one prerequisite before you decide the whole field is not for you.

## What Outdoor Gear You Actually Need in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-outdoor-gear-you-actually-need-in-st-louis

On a Thursday night in Arnold, a mom and dad are standing in the garage staring at a pile on the concrete floor. There is a tent somebody handed down to them, a cooler left over from a graduation party, four beach towels, and a flashlight with corroded batteries rattling around in it. Their first campsite is booked for Friday afternoon. They have one evening to figure out what is missing, and the honest problem is that they don’t know what missing looks like. Every checklist they found had forty items on it, and half of those items sounded like things you buy after your tenth trip, not before your first one.

That garage scene repeats itself all over the metro this time of year. A dad in Florissant is taking two kids out for one single night and wondering whether he needs a stove at all. A couple in Edwardsville inherited a full tent kit from an uncle and has no idea whether any of it still seals. A scout parent in O’Fallon got a packing list with the words “personal gear” on it and nothing else. Somebody in Washington wants to try exactly one night before committing a single weekend of shopping to the idea. Different people, same question underneath.

All of them want the same thing: to sleep warm, stay dry, see what they’re doing after dark, and come home without a garage full of stuff they never touch again. So here is the whole argument up front. Three things are worth real money for a Missouri car camper, and they are the sleep system, rain and layering that works in humidity, and light. Nearly everything else can be borrowed, bought used, pulled out of your own kitchen, or skipped for the first few trips. This guide walks the buy list, the borrow list, the used-gear route, a realistic first-night kit, the Missouri-specific extras, and an honest list of what to skip.

### What camping gear is good for beginners?

Good beginner gear is the stuff that decides whether you sleep. That is the whole test. A sleeping pad, a bag rated colder than the forecast, a headlamp for every person in the group, and rain protection you actually trust: those four categories carry a first trip. The tent matters less than people assume, because almost every campground within an hour or two of St. Louis is drive-in car camping. You are not carrying anything on your back. Weight and pack size, the two things gear marketing obsesses over, barely apply to you.

That changes the math in your favor. A heavy, roomy, unfashionable tent from a garage sale works fine when it rides in a trunk for twenty minutes. A cast iron skillet works fine. A wool blanket from a closet works fine. What does not work fine is a thin foam mat on packed Ozark clay, or one flashlight shared by five people, or a cotton hoodie as your only warm layer when the temperature slides after sunset.

So spend where the misery lives. Sleep, dry, light. Borrow the rest and find out what you actually miss. After one night you will have opinions about your own trip that no checklist could have given you, and those opinions are worth more than anything you could have bought on Thursday night in a panic.

### Why does the sleep system come first?

Because cold comes up from the ground, not sideways through the tent. This is the single most common beginner mistake in Missouri and southern Illinois, and it ruins more first trips than rain does. People buy a warm bag, lay it directly on the tent floor, and then lie awake at three in the morning wondering why their back is freezing while their shoulders are sweating. The bag is doing its job. The ground is winning anyway.

### The pad before the bag

A sleeping pad is rated by R-value, which is just a measure of how well it stops heat from leaving your body and sinking into the dirt. Higher number, more insulation. A pool float or a thin air mattress has almost no R-value at all, which is why an air mattress can feel colder than a foam pad half its thickness. For three-season use around here, a mid-range insulated pad handles spring and fall nights and does not complain. Closed-cell foam is bulkier and less comfortable, but it never punctures, and it costs less than anything inflatable.

Then the bag. Buy for a colder night than the forecast promises, because the Ozark foothills drop harder after dark than a warm afternoon suggests. A humid ninety-degree Saturday can still hand you a genuinely chilly Sunday morning, especially down in a valley near water. Synthetic fill is the sane choice for this region: it holds some warmth when it gets damp, and around here things get damp. Down is lighter and packs smaller, which matters to backpackers and not much to you.

One more small thing that punches way above its weight. Bring a real pillow from your bed. Not a stuff sack full of jackets. The pillow costs nothing, takes up trunk space you already have, and it is the difference between sleeping and lying there.

### What rain and layering gear actually works in Missouri humidity?

Rain gear here has a harder job than rain gear in dry climates. A pop-up thunderstorm can build in forty minutes on a summer afternoon, dump hard, and leave the air heavier than it was before. If your jacket is fully waterproof and completely unbreathable, you get soaked from the inside instead of the outside. You just trade whose water it is.

So look for a shell that vents. Pit zips, a mesh liner, anything that lets steam out while shedding rain. A cheap non-breathable poncho is still better than nothing, and for a kid standing under a picnic shelter it is genuinely fine. For an adult hauling firewood in a downpour, breathability earns its keep. Rain pants are optional on a first trip; a change of dry pants sealed in a plastic bag is not.

The layering rule is short: no cotton next to your skin once the weather turns. Cotton holds water, stops insulating, and stays cold for hours. A synthetic or wool base layer, a fleece or puffy in the middle, and a shell on top will cover the whole spring and fall range around here. Pack the warm layer even in July, because that is the layer people leave home and regret.

Dry socks deserve their own sentence. Bring more pairs than seems reasonable. Wet feet are how a fun weekend turns into a quiet, miserable drive home.

### Why is light the third thing worth real money?

Because everything after sunset takes twice as long in the dark, and campsites get dark in a way suburban yards never do. There are no streetlights, no porch light two houses over, no glow off a parking lot. When you are setting up late after a Friday drive out of the city, one shared flashlight held in somebody’s teeth is not a system.

Headlamps beat lanterns for anything involving your hands: pitching a tent, cooking, finding the bathhouse, digging through a bin. A lantern beats a headlamp for sitting around a table, because a headlamp pointed at a face is rude and blinding. The honest answer is that you want one headlamp per person and one soft light for the table, and the per-person part is what people skimp on. Kids especially. A kid with their own headlamp is a calmer, braver, more useful kid at nine at night.

Whatever you buy, bring spare batteries and check them at home. A dead light is the same as no light, and there is no store around the corner from a campsite.

### What should you borrow or rent before you buy?

Almost everything else. The tent is the big one, and it is the item beginners most want to buy first. Borrow it instead. Ask around at work, at church, at the scout troop, on your street. Tents sit in basements across this metro doing nothing eleven months a year, and most owners are happy to hand one over to somebody who will actually use it.

Camp chairs, a cooler, a two-burner stove, a folding table, a hatchet: all of it borrows well. Some outfitters around the metro rent packages for a weekend, which is a clean way to test a category before committing. Renting a stove for one trip teaches you whether you want a two-burner propane setup for family cooking or a single canister burner for boiling water and nothing else. That is a real question with a real answer, and the answer depends on whether you plan to cook eggs for four people or just make coffee.

Your kitchen already owns half a camp kitchen. A pot, a skillet, a spatula, mismatched forks, a dish tub, an old towel. Put those in a plastic bin and you are done. Nobody at a campsite has ever been judged for cooking in a saucepan from home.

### What is safe to buy used, and what is not?

Used gear is the best value route in outdoor equipment, and the metro has an active resale scene through swaps, yard sales, consignment racks, and online groups. The trick is knowing which categories forgive age and which ones hide failures you cannot see until you are already out there in the dark.

### Buy used without much worry

Tents, camp chairs, coolers, tables, lanterns, cast iron, dry bags, trekking poles, and hard-sided storage bins. Set a used tent up in the yard before you trust it. You are checking for missing poles, torn mesh, a rain fly that no longer matches, and a floor coating that has gone sticky or flaky. Zippers are the usual killer. Run every zipper twice.

### Be careful, or buy new

Sleeping bags lose loft with hard use and bad storage, so a bag crushed in a stuff sack for a decade may not be worth what it says on the tag. Inflatable pads can hold slow leaks that only reveal themselves at two in the morning; inflate one and leave it overnight before you buy, if the seller will let you. Anything that burns fuel, a stove, a heater, a lantern with a fuel tank, deserves a hard look for cracked hoses, corroded fittings, and missing regulators. Helmets and climbing hardware are not used-gear categories at all. And skip anything soft and secondhand that you cannot wash, because ticks and mildew both travel.

### What goes in a realistic first-night kit?

One night, one car, one family. Here is the whole thing, and it fits in two bins and a duffel.

Sleeping pad and bag for each person, plus a pillow from the house

Borrowed tent, with a ground tarp or footprint cut to fit under it

A headlamp per person and one soft light for the table, with spare batteries

Rain shell, a warm mid layer, and one full change of dry clothes in a sealed bag

Extra socks, closed-toe shoes, and a hat

Cooler with drinks, ice, and food that needs almost no cooking on night one

Kitchen bin: pot, skillet, spatula, knife, cutting board, plates, utensils, dish tub, towel, trash bags

Water jug, because not every site has a spigot right there

Bug spray, sunscreen, a small first aid kit, and tweezers for ticks

A second tarp, some paracord, a lighter, and a roll of duct tape

That is close to the classic ten must-haves for camping, minus the specialty items that get added by people selling specialty items. If you want the other half of the job, picking a site and getting the reservation, our guide on how to book a campsite near St. Louis covers reservations and timing so this one can stay on gear.

Nothing beats the first hot breakfast after a night in a tent.

### What does Missouri weather add to the list?

Four things that people from drier states never think about. Bug protection, a spare tarp, a way to dry out, and a warm layer you were sure you would not need.

### Bugs, ticks, and chiggers

Ticks and chiggers are a constant here, not a rare event, and they do not care that it is a nice campground. Treat clothing, tuck pants into socks on trails, and do a full tick check every single night with a light. Tweezers belong in the first aid kit, not the junk drawer at home. For chiggers, the misery usually starts where clothing is tight, so change out of hiking clothes and shower when you get back. A screen shelter over the picnic table is a luxury on a July evening and a sanity-saver on a still, humid one.

### Tarps and drying out

One tarp goes under the tent, sized slightly smaller than the floor so rain does not pool between the two. A second tarp goes overhead with a length of cord, and that one is the difference between waiting out a thunderstorm in the car and waiting it out in a chair with a snack. When you get home, everything comes out of the bins and hangs up. Humid weather plus a sealed tote equals mildew, and mildew is how good gear dies in a basement.

### The cold night after a hot day

Pack the fleece in August. Down in the river bottoms and the Ozark foothills, a warm afternoon can hand back a morning cold enough to see your breath, and the person who left the warm layer at home spends that morning sitting in a running car.

### What changes when you bring kids?

Kids do not need smaller versions of adult gear. They need warmth, light, and something of their own. A child who is cold at night is done with camping forever, so the pad matters even more for them than for you; small bodies lose heat faster and they cannot tell you why they feel bad, only that they want to go home.

Give each kid a headlamp and let them own it. Give them a job, hauling water, staking corners, feeding the fire from a safe distance. Bring more snacks than the plan requires and a couple of quiet things for the tent, because bedtime comes early when the sun goes down and nobody is tired yet. Then keep the first trip short and close. One night at a site forty minutes from the house beats three nights four hours away, every time, for the same reason a first sleepover is at grandma’s.

And if the kids are still deciding whether they like the outdoors at all, start with a daytime win. A morning on one of the easy family-friendly hiking trails around St. Louis tells you a lot about who is ready for a night in a tent.

### How do you test the setup in the backyard first?

Pitch the tent in the yard on a weeknight, in the dark, with the same headlamps you plan to bring. That one exercise finds more problems than any amount of research. Missing stakes. A pole section that will not seat. A rain fly that goes on backwards. A zipper that has to be coaxed. Better to learn that in Hazelwood at eight at night with the kitchen twenty feet away than at a site in Franklin County with a storm building.

Then sleep in it. Actually sleep. Lay out the pad and bag, turn off the porch light, and see whether the pad holds air until morning and whether you are warm enough. Run the stove once too, in the driveway, so you find out at home that the fuel fitting is wrong. A backyard night is a free dress rehearsal, and for people asking how to start camping as a beginner, it is the single best first step there is.

### What should you skip for now?

This is the part nobody writes, so here it is plainly: these are the categories people buy first and use least.

A plug-in electric cooler or camp fridge. A good cooler with block ice handles a weekend. Solve the weekend before you solve the week.

A big multi-room tent. Heavy, slow to pitch, and worse in wind than a simple dome. Rooms sound great in the aisle and matter very little at midnight.

A dedicated camp kitchen set. Your kitchen already owns it. Buy the set later, once you know what you actually reach for.

Freeze-dried backpacking meals. You have a trunk. Bring real food.

A hatchet or a big fixed-blade knife. Most sites sell or supply firewood, and a saw does more work with less risk.

Ultralight anything. You are car camping. Paying a premium to save ounces you never carry is the most common money leak in beginner gear.

Solar panels and power stations. A charged power bank covers one or two nights fine.

Matching everything. Mismatched hand-me-down gear works exactly as well and tells a better story.

Spend the skipped money on the sleep system instead. That is the trade that pays every trip.

### For outdoor gear shops and outfitters in the metro

If you own or run a shop, the beginners walking in are not asking for a product. They are asking whether the trip is going to go badly. The staff who win them are the ones who ask about the trip first: where are you going, how many nights, who is sleeping outside with you, what do you already own in the garage.

For shoppers, that same behavior is the buying signal. Walk into two or three places worth talking to. Tell the person plainly what trip you are taking and what you already have, then compare that against what they steer you toward. Somebody who asks about your trip before pointing at a shelf, and who tells you to borrow a tent this time, has just earned every future purchase you make.

Buy the three things that matter, and ask questions about the rest. Rentals, gear swaps, and staff who camp locally are worth more than any online review, and you can find outdoor gear shops across the metro on St Louis Near Me Directory before your first trip, from St. Charles County out to the Metro East.

### Frequently asked questions

### Q. What are the 10 must-haves for camping?

A.  Most versions of the list land in the same place: shelter, a sleeping pad, a sleeping bag, light, water, food and a way to cook it, a knife or multi-tool, fire or a lighter, weather-appropriate clothing, and a first aid kit. For car camping around St. Louis, add bug protection and a tarp and you have covered nearly every problem a first trip can hand you.

### Q. What is the 3-3-3 rule for camping?

A.  It is common road-trip guidance, not a regulation. Drive no more than three hundred miles in a day, arrive by three in the afternoon, and stay at least three nights. The point is to stop rushing: arriving with daylight left means you pitch camp calmly, and staying multiple nights means you unpack once instead of living out of the trunk.

### Q. What is the 4-4-4 rule for camping?

A.  Same idea, slightly longer legs. Drive no more than four hundred miles, arrive by four in the afternoon, and stay four nights before moving on. Some people use it as an alternative for longer trips where three hundred miles feels too short. Either version is a habit for pacing travel days, and neither one is enforced by anybody.

### Q. What are the 7 C's of camping?

A.  The list grew out of the survival “C” categories, and versions differ. The core five are a cutting tool, a combustion source, cover, a container, and cordage. The extra two are usually candling, meaning a light source, and cotton cloth such as a bandana. It is a memory device for carrying redundant basics, and it maps neatly onto a car camping bin.

### Q. What is the 200 rule for camping?

A.  Stay two hundred feet, roughly seventy adult steps, away from water, trails, and other campsites when you are washing dishes, going to the bathroom, or setting up in an undeveloped area. It is standard low-impact guidance meant to protect creeks and keep sites pleasant. At developed campgrounds with bathhouses and marked pads, the facilities already handle it for you.

### Q. How to start camping as a beginner?

A.  Pick one night at a drive-in site close to home in spring or fall. Borrow a tent, buy or borrow a real sleeping pad, and give everyone a headlamp. Test the whole setup in your backyard first, including sleeping on the pad. Bring easy food for the first night. Then adjust based on what you actually missed, not what a list told you.

## What Real Estate School Costs in Missouri
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-real-estate-school-costs-in-missouri

Picture a woman in Arnold sitting in the elementary school pickup line with her phone propped against the steering wheel and a real estate school’s enrollment page open on it. She has been half-thinking about this for two years. Every page she finds says the same thing, 72 hours, as if that were the whole answer. What she actually wants to know is what those hours cost, what arrives in the mail after them, and whether her household can survive the stretch between passing an exam and getting paid for anything.

The same month, other people around the metro are reading the same page with the same expression. A man in Florissant who has given fifteen years to a warehouse job that keeps getting reorganized around him. A parent in Wentzville whose youngest just started kindergarten, who wants work that bends around a school calendar. Somebody in Washington who flipped one house with a brother-in-law, enjoyed every part of it, and quietly wondered whether the agent was the one having the better week. A retiree in Granite City who wants a few closings a year, not a second career.

They all want the same three answers. What does this cost in total, how long until money actually comes in, and is it worth doing at all. Here is what the 72 hours contain, how the Missouri exam is built and why so many people stumble on the state half, the bills that start the day after you pass, and the brokerage decision that will shape your first year far more than anything you learn in a classroom.

### How much does it cost to get your realtor license in Missouri?

Missouri requires 72 hours of pre-license education, then an exam, fingerprinting and a criminal background check, and a license application. Those are the one-time bills, and they are the ones everybody counts. The larger column starts after you pass: brokerage fees, insurance, dues, MLS access, marketing, a car, and the self-employment taxes of a 1099 worker.

Nobody can hand you a real total, and you should be a little suspicious of any page that tries. Course prices change. State fees get revised. Brokerages differ from one another far more than schools do, and the brokerage line is the big one. What you can do instead is build your own number in an afternoon, which is more useful anyway, because the number you build belongs to your situation rather than to an average of strangers.

### The two columns nobody puts side by side

Draw two columns on a sheet of paper. The left one is getting licensed: the 48-hour Missouri Real Estate Practice course, the 24-hour Missouri Real Estate Principles course, exam prep if you decide to use it, the exam fee, fingerprinting and the background check, and the license application. That column has a bottom. You will reach it, pay it, and be done with it.

The right column is staying in business, and it has no bottom. Brokerage desk or monthly fees. Transaction or franchise fees taken off each closing. Errors-and-omissions insurance. Local, state and national association dues if you join. MLS access. Lockbox or key access. Marketing and signage. Mileage and a vehicle. Self-employment tax and health insurance. Most people fill in the left column carefully and leave the right one blank, which is exactly backward.

### How to build your own number this week

Three conversations and one website. Get current fees straight from the Missouri Real Estate Commission, which sits inside the Missouri Division of Professional Registration and sets and administers the licensing requirements. Get the course total in writing from the school, including whether books, exam prep and any retake sit inside that price or outside it. Then ask two or three brokerages for their full fee schedule before you sign a thing.

That last one is the step people skip, and it is the one that matters most. Not the split. The whole schedule, written down: what you pay monthly whether or not you close anything, what comes off the top of a closing, what technology or franchise fees ride along, and what insurance and dues you are required to carry. In our experience that single document changes people’s plans more than any course price ever does.

### What do the 72 hours of Missouri pre-license education actually cover?

Missouri’s 72 hours arrive in two pieces: a 48-hour Missouri Real Estate Practice course and a 24-hour Missouri Real Estate Principles course. You complete both before sitting the salesperson exam, and the Missouri Real Estate Commission sets the requirement. The split between the two courses tells you something honest about the job you are signing up for.

Principles is the law-and-vocabulary half. Ownership, agency, contracts, disclosure, fair housing, and the rules that govern how a licensee is allowed to behave. Practice is closer to the daily work: how a transaction moves from showing to contract to closing, what each piece of paperwork does, and what you owe a client at every step. Neither course teaches you how to find your first client. That surprises almost everybody.

### Online self-paced, or a classroom?

Both formats satisfy the same requirement, so the real difference is not quality. It is accountability. Self-paced online costs you less time, fits around a shift or a nap schedule, and lets you move at whatever speed your week allows. A classroom, live or virtual, puts you on somebody else’s calendar and gives you an instructor you can interrupt with a question the moment it forms.

### Who each format actually suits

Self-paced suits people who have finished a self-directed course before and know from experience that they will finish this one. Shift workers. Parents of small kids. Anyone whose week refuses to look the same twice. The failure mode is quiet rather than dramatic: you enroll, you do two sessions in the first week, and then the login sits untouched until the enrollment window closes.

A classroom suits people who want the calendar to supply the discipline, people who learn by asking things out loud, and career-changers who get value from sitting next to others in the same position. Ask any school two questions before you pay: how long do I have to finish, and what happens if I do not. Both answers are perfectly fair to ask, and the way they are answered tells you plenty.

### Why do so many people fail the state portion of the exam?

The Missouri salesperson exam has two parts, a national portion and a Missouri state portion, and people fail them for different reasons. The national portion rewards general real estate vocabulary and math, which courses drill heavily. The state portion covers Missouri’s own rules, and that is where under-prepared candidates most often come unstuck.

The reason is not mysterious. General material is everywhere, in every practice app and every video, so people over-study it and feel confident. State material is narrow, dry, and easy to skim on a tired Tuesday night. If you are budgeting study time, weight it toward the part that has the fewest study aids, not the part that has the most. That is the opposite of what most people do naturally.

There is more than an exam standing between you and a license, too. You complete fingerprinting and a criminal background check as part of the process. And once you pass, your license has to be held by a licensed broker. A new salesperson cannot practice independently in Missouri, which means choosing a brokerage is not a decision for later. It is part of becoming licensed at all.

One more piece nobody mentions in the enrollment brochure. New licensees complete required post-license education within their first licensing period, and continuing education after that. Get the current requirement from the Missouri Real Estate Commission rather than from a forum thread, because rules like this get revised and a stale answer costs you either money or a scramble at renewal.

### Is a Missouri license the same thing as being a Realtor?

No, and this is precisely where the after-the-exam bills begin. A license comes from the state and is what legally lets you practice. “Realtor” is a trademarked membership term for members of the National Association of Realtors, a private association you choose to join and pay to stay in. Holding a Missouri license does not make you one.

In practice the two get tangled, because membership usually arrives as a bundle. Local association dues, state dues and national dues, often billed together, frequently with MLS access sitting alongside them. Plenty of brokerages expect or require membership as a condition of hanging your license there, which means the choice may effectively be made for you the moment you pick an office.

So ask it early, and ask it in this exact shape: if I join you, what am I required to join, what does each piece cost per year, and when is it billed. Annual dues that land in January are a very different problem for somebody who got licensed in November than for somebody who got licensed in February.

### Which bills start the day after you pass?

The recurring column decides whether your first year works, and it starts immediately. Brokerage fees come first, usually as some mix of a monthly desk fee and a cut of each closing. Then errors-and-omissions insurance, association and MLS dues, lockbox or key access, marketing and signage, a vehicle, and the self-employment tax that nobody withholds for you.

Take them one at a time. Desk or monthly fees are charged whether you close anything or not, which is exactly why they sting in month three. Transaction or franchise fees come off each closing before your share is calculated. Errors-and-omissions insurance, often abbreviated E&O, protects against claims arising from your work, and how it is billed varies: some brokerages charge it monthly, some per transaction, some fold it into another line.

Then the working costs. Lockbox or key access is its own fee in most markets. Signs, photography, mailers and whatever you spend to be visible all come out of your pocket, not the brokerage’s. And the car: you are about to put serious miles on a vehicle, driving from Jefferson County to St. Charles County and back for a showing that lasts eleven minutes. Fuel, wear and insurance are business costs now.

Finally, the two that ambush every new 1099 worker. Self-employment tax, because nobody is withholding anything on your behalf and the bill arrives whether you set money aside or not. And health insurance, if you are leaving a job that provided it. That second one has quietly ended more real estate careers around this metro than any exam ever has.

Buyers ask about the furnace. Here is how HVAC estimates work.

### How do you choose a brokerage without guessing?

This is the single biggest financial decision of your first year, and it is not close. Brokerages differ on splits, caps, desk fees, training, mentorship, lead access and floor time, and those things trade against each other constantly. Shortlist two or three worth interviewing, then compare what you need against what each one is actually prepared to provide.

Start by saying plainly what you want. Do you need structured training, or have you sold something before and just need a place to hang a license? Do you want a mentor on your first three contracts? Are you hoping for leads, or bringing your own? Are you full-time, or working evenings while a W-2 job pays the mortgage? And how many months of runway do you have. Say that number out loud.

Here is the tension nobody at a recruiting lunch will name for you. The most generous split in the metro is worth nothing to an agent who is getting no training. A large share of zero closings is still zero. A smaller share of a year in which somebody sat beside you through your first four contracts is a real number, and it compounds, because you come out of that year knowing how to do the job.

### What to ask, and what to listen for

Six questions, asked the same way at each office. What do I pay whether or not I close anything? What comes off each closing, and in what order? Is there a cap, and what happens after I hit it? What training happens in my first ninety days, and who runs it? Is there a mentor, and what does the mentor take from my transactions? Do you provide leads, and what do those cost me?

Then listen to the gaps rather than the numbers. One office describes a training calendar with names attached to it. Another says training is available and changes the subject to the split. A third says you will learn by doing and offers you a desk. Those three answers are not variations on a theme. They are three different first years, and the gap between what you asked for and what came back is the signal.

### How long is the runway before your first commission lands?

Longer than the course calendar makes it look. People ask how long it takes to get a real estate license in Missouri, which is the wrong question. A license is not income. The gap between activating a license and depositing a first check is the stretch that decides who is still doing this a year from now.

Walk the whole sequence. You enroll and complete the 72 hours at whatever pace your life permits. You schedule and sit the exam. You complete fingerprinting and the background check. You submit the application. You find a broker willing to hold your license and you activate it. Then onboarding and training. Only after all of that do you begin, from zero, with no clients, no listings and nobody in the metro aware that you do this now.

And a closing is not fast. You find a client, then wait for the right property or the right offer, then go under contract, then wait out inspection, appraisal and financing before anyone signs anything. Commission is paid at closing, not at contract. Add those weeks to everything above and the honest planning horizon is measured in months of household expenses, not weeks.

Which is why plenty of people around the metro start this part-time and keep a paycheck coming while the pipeline fills. It is slower, and some brokerages are better set up for it than others. Ask about that directly during your interviews, because a brokerage built around full-time floor time will treat an evenings-and-weekends agent very differently than one that expects it.

### How much money does a real estate agent make in Missouri?

There is no salary to quote, and that is the truthful answer rather than a dodge. Missouri agents are almost always independent contractors paid per closing, so income is a function of how many transactions you close, what you keep from each, and what your overhead costs. Two agents in the same office can have completely different years.

If you want a reference point, look at published labor statistics for real estate sales agents rather than a figure from a recruiting video, and read it knowing what it contains. Any average blends full-time veterans with a long tail of licensees who closed almost nothing, and it rarely subtracts the overhead column above. The median in that kind of data is describing two very different populations at once.

### Who this actually works for

People with a financial runway, a network they are genuinely willing to talk to, real tolerance for irregular income, and enough self-direction to make calls nobody asked them to make. It rewards consistency more than charisma. The agents who last are usually the ones who did unglamorous follow-up in month four, when nothing was happening and nobody would have noticed if they stopped.

### Who it does not work for

Anyone who needs a predictable amount of money next month. Anyone who dislikes prospecting enough to avoid it, since prospecting is most of the job for the first two years. And anyone hoping for something part-time and easy, which is the version sold on social media and almost nobody’s actual experience. If the runway math does not work, the same comparison habits apply to any training path, and how to choose a college or trade school in St. Louis walks through that. Going in clear-eyed is not pessimism. It is the difference between a plan and a wish.

### For real estate schools and brokerages in the metro

If you are on the other side of this, notice that every person described above starts with a search and a fear, not with a school name. They are trying to work out the total, and the pages that answer them plainly are the ones they call. Being findable when somebody in Franklin County types the question at ten at night is most of the work.

Publish the specifics. Which courses you offer, the format, how long the enrollment lasts, what is included, and what a retake involves. Brokerages, the same instruction applies to your fee schedule: the offices willing to put the whole thing in front of a new licensee before signing day earn a reputation for it quickly, and new agents talk to each other constantly.

Interview two or three before you commit to either decision. You can compare real estate schools across the metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then do the same with brokerages: say plainly what training, mentorship and lead support you need and how many months of runway you have, and ask for the full fee schedule in writing. The gap between what you asked for and what came back is the signal, not the split.

### Frequently asked questions

### Q. How long does it take to get a real estate license in Missouri?

A.  It depends mostly on how fast you complete the 72 hours, since self-paced students set their own pace and classroom sections run on a fixed calendar. After the coursework you schedule and sit the exam, complete fingerprinting and a criminal background check, submit your application, and find a licensed broker to hold your license. Motivated full-time students move through it briskly. People studying around a job should plan in months rather than weeks.

### Q. How hard is it to become a realtor in Missouri?

A.  The coursework is manageable for most adults and the exam is passable with honest preparation, though the Missouri state portion trips up people who over-study the national material. The genuinely hard part comes after you pass. You are building a business from nothing while overhead runs from day one, and no one hands you clients. Getting licensed is a hurdle. Staying in business through the first year is the real test.

### Q. Is it hard starting out as a realtor?

A.  Yes, and the difficulty is financial and emotional more than technical. There is no salary, no withholding and no guaranteed first closing, while desk fees, insurance, dues and mileage start immediately. You are prospecting people who did not ask to hear from you, often for months before anything closes. Training and a real mentor make an enormous difference here, which is why the brokerage you choose matters more than the school you attend.

### Q. Is being a real estate agent still worth it in 2026?

A.  That depends entirely on your runway and your fit for the work, and anybody promising a universal answer is selling something. The honest test is arithmetic plus temperament. Can you cover household expenses for months without commission income, and will you keep prospecting when nothing is happening? If both answers are yes, the licensing path is straightforward and worth exploring. If either is no, fix that first rather than enrolling and hoping.

### Q. Is 30 too late to become a real estate agent?

A.  Not remotely. Career-changers are extremely common in this field, and thirty is early by the standards of most offices around this metro. An adult who has already worked somewhere else brings a network, a track record of showing up, and judgment about people that a twenty-two-year-old is still developing. What matters is your runway and your willingness to prospect, not your birth year. Plenty of people start considerably later than thirty.

### Q. How much would a real estate agent make on a $300,000 house?

A.  Less than the headline suggests, and there is no standard rate to quote. Commission is negotiable on every transaction. Whatever total is agreed is typically divided between the brokerages involved, then divided again between the agent and their broker under the split in your agreement, then reduced by transaction or franchise fees, then taxed as self-employment income. What a new agent actually keeps is a fraction of a fraction. Ask any brokerage to walk that chain with you before you sign.
