## What Happens at a First Oncologist Appointment
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-happens-at-a-first-oncologist-appointment-st-louis

The call came on a Tuesday afternoon and the appointment was the following Monday, and the days in between felt longer than the month that produced them. Dana had gone into her primary care office in Creve Coeur about something she assumed was nothing. Then there was a scan, then a biopsy, and then a phone number for an oncology practice she had never heard of, and a scheduler asking whether mornings or afternoons worked better. Mornings, she said, because it was the only question all week she knew the answer to.

She is not alone in that week. A retired bus mechanic in Bellefontaine Neighbors is going in with his daughter, who has already started a note on her phone and keeps adding to it at red lights. A woman is driving up from Waterloo with a folder of paperwork on the passenger seat, unsure whether any of it is the paperwork they actually want. None of them are hunting survival statistics at midnight. They want something smaller and far more useful: what the appointment itself is going to be like, and how to walk in ready.

That is what this guide is. Not medicine, and not reassurance nobody asked for. Just process: how a referral gets made, what usually gets gathered before you arrive, what happens in the room, why a first visit runs longer than the ones that follow, why staging is often still in progress when you sit down, and what to ask before you leave. Anything clinical belongs to your own care team. The rest of it, the part that is really just logistics wearing a heavy coat, you can prepare for.

### Why would you need to see an oncologist?

Because someone found something that needs a specialist’s read, and that is a wider category than most people assume. A referral usually starts with a primary care visit, a screening result, a scan ordered for some other reason, or a symptom that did not settle down. A biopsy or a lab result goes to a pathologist, and the report that comes back is what sends you down the hall.

Not every referral means a diagnosis is settled. Some people are sent because a finding is unclear and needs someone who looks at findings like it every day. Some are sent because a blood count has been off across two draws. Some arrive with a confirmed diagnosis and a pathology report already in hand. Those are three very different appointments, and it is worth knowing which one you are walking into. If you are not sure, the person who made the referral can usually tell you in one sentence.

It also helps to know that oncology is not one job. Medical oncologists manage systemic treatment and are often the doctor coordinating everything else. Surgical oncologists operate. Radiation oncologists plan and deliver radiation. Hematologists work with blood and bone marrow, which covers blood cancers and also a long list of conditions that are not cancer at all. Many patients end up seeing more than one of these, sometimes in the same building on the same morning, and a first appointment is frequently with a medical oncologist who will sort out who else needs to be involved.

### What will an oncologist do on a first visit?

Expect a long conversation, not a treatment start. An oncologist typically takes a full history, examines you, reviews your pathology and imaging, explains what is known and what is still being worked out, and orders whatever tests are still missing. Staging may not be complete yet, so the plan often comes later.

The history is more thorough than you may be used to. Expect questions about when symptoms started and how they have changed, previous illnesses and surgeries, every medication and supplement you take, allergies, alcohol and tobacco, what you do for work, and who is at home with you. Family history matters, so if you can, ask relatives ahead of time about cancers on both sides and roughly what age. That one piece of homework is often the thing patients wish they had done.

Then comes an examination, usually focused on the area in question plus a general look at lymph nodes, and often vitals and labs alongside it. Somewhere in there, before or after you sit back down, the oncologist walks through the pathology report and the imaging. This is the part worth slowing down for. Ask what the report says in plain language. Then ask what it does not say yet.

Because that gap is the honest center of a first visit. It is common to arrive expecting a complete answer and to be told that staging is still in progress, or that a marker is pending, or that another scan is needed before anyone commits to a direction. That is not a delay in your care. It is the care. A plan built on incomplete information is the thing everybody is trying to avoid, and the tests ordered at the end of a first visit are usually the shortest route to a real recommendation.

You will likely also meet people who are not the doctor. An oncology nurse or a nurse practitioner, a scheduler, sometimes a social worker or a financial counselor. Practices vary in who is involved and when, so ask what the rest of the team looks like and who your first call should go to.

### At what stage do you see an oncologist?

Earlier than most people expect, and often before anyone can tell you a stage at all. Staging is a description of how far a cancer has spread, and it is built from pathology, imaging and sometimes surgery. Plenty of first appointments happen while that work is still underway, which is a large part of why the visit exists.

The order of events surprises people. You do not wait until everything is known and then meet the specialist. The specialist is frequently the person who decides which remaining tests are worth doing and in what order, because those choices depend on the specific diagnosis and on what a possible treatment path would need to know. Sending every patient for every test first would be slower, not faster.

Some people are also referred before any cancer is confirmed. A suspicious finding, an unexplained lab pattern, a mass that needs a biopsy a specialist should plan. If that is your situation, say so when you call to schedule, because it changes what the office should gather beforehand and sometimes how much time they set aside.

And some people are referred years after treatment ended, for surveillance visits that check whether anything has changed. Same specialty, an entirely different appointment. It is completely fine to ask the scheduler which kind of visit yours is, and it is a better question than most people think to ask.

### How long is a first oncology appointment?

Longer than the follow-ups, and longer than the time slot on your calendar suggests. A first visit has to cover a full history, an examination, a review of records that may have arrived from several different places, and a conversation nobody should rush. The exact length varies by practice, so ask when you schedule rather than guessing.

Plan for the whole block, not the appointment. There is check-in and registration paperwork, often lab work before you are seen, and sometimes imaging on the same trip. Then there is waiting, which in oncology is not usually a sign of disorganization. The patient ahead of you got a conversation that ran long, and one day that patient will be you. Bring something to read and do not schedule anything tight afterward.

A practical move is to ask the scheduler three things: how early to arrive, whether labs or scans are part of the same visit, and roughly how much of the day to set aside. Then add an hour to whatever they tell you. If someone is driving you in from a distance, that extra hour is the difference between a stressful afternoon and an ordinary one.

### What should you bring, and who should come with you?

Bring a person and bring paper. In our experience those two things change a first appointment more than anything else a patient can control. A companion hears what you miss, and a written list keeps the conversation from drifting away from the things you actually needed to know.

Ask ahead of time what the office already has. Records, pathology slides, imaging discs and outside lab results often move between offices ahead of you, but not always, and not always completely. Call a few days out and ask plainly whether everything they need has arrived. If something is missing, they will tell you who to chase, and that phone call is far easier on a Wednesday than in a waiting room on Monday.

What to have with you: a photo ID and your insurance card, a complete medication list including doses, over the counter items and supplements, a list of allergies, the names and phone numbers of your other doctors, any records or discs you were handed, and your written questions. A notebook beats a phone for most people, because you can hand it across and let your companion write while you listen.

Companion, not audience. Decide in the parking lot who is taking notes and who is asking. Some people also want to record the conversation, which some practices allow and some do not, so ask permission first rather than assuming. The daughter from Bellefontaine Neighbors already knows her job. That is why the note on her phone keeps growing.

### What questions are worth writing down before you go?

The ones you will forget the second the conversation starts. Nearly everyone walks out of a first appointment having remembered a question in the elevator. A written list, in priority order, with the two or three that matter most sitting at the top, is the cheapest thing you can do to make an appointment work harder.

Ask what the diagnosis is called, exactly, and how to spell it. Ask what is known so far and what is still pending. Ask what tests come next and when results are expected. Ask how results get delivered, whether that is a phone call, a portal message or a visit, and how long it usually takes. Ask who to call between visits, what number to use after hours, and what would count as a reason to call rather than wait.

Then ask the structural questions. What is the next decision point, and when does it happen? Who is coordinating my care if more than one specialist is involved? Is my case reviewed by a group of specialists together, and if so, when? Is there a nurse navigator or a social worker I can talk to? What should I be doing between now and the next appointment, and what should I not worry about doing?

Second opinions belong on the list too. Asking for one is normal, expected, and not an insult to anybody. Ask how to arrange it, what records would need to travel, and whether waiting for it would change any timing. A doctor who is comfortable with that question is telling you something useful about the practice.

Between appointments, life keeps its own calendar, including a first horseback riding lesson.

### How does a treatment plan actually get made?

In stages, and usually not in the room on day one. What typically follows a first visit is a short list of remaining tests, then a recommendation, then a conversation about that recommendation, and then scheduling. How long that takes depends on the tests, the practice and your insurance, which is why nobody can hand you a calendar on the first afternoon.

Many cases are reviewed by a group of specialists together, a conference where surgery, medical oncology, radiation and pathology all look at the same case. If that applies to you, ask when it happens and how you will hear the outcome. Knowing there is a date on the far side of the silence makes the waiting much easier to carry.

Insurance authorization is a real step and worth understanding early. Some treatments and some scans need approval before they can be scheduled, and that process runs on its own clock. Ask who in the office handles it, whether anything is needed from you, and who to call if a week goes by with no news. Many practices have financial counselors for exactly this, and asking early is not premature.

Whatever the recommendation turns out to be, it belongs to you and your care team, not to an article on the internet. What you can do here is make sure you understand what is being proposed, why it is being proposed, what the alternatives are, and what happens next if the first approach does not go the way everyone hopes.

### How do you choose an oncology practice when you have a choice?

Sometimes you do not, and that is fine. A referral, an insurance network and a drive time often settle it before you get a vote. When you do have a real choice, treat it the way you would treat any other consequential decision: shortlist two or three practices worth interviewing, say plainly what you want and expect, and compare that against what each one is actually prepared to provide.

Say it out loud. I want to know who my point of contact is. I want results explained by a person, not only posted to a portal. I want to know whether my case is reviewed by a group. I want to know how far ahead appointments get scheduled and how flexible you are if I have a bad week. I want to know what happens after hours and on a Saturday.

Then listen to what comes back. One office answers every bit of it in five minutes. Another cannot tell you who your nurse would be. That gap is the signal, and it predicts the next year of your life better than anything printed on a website.

The practical things belong in the comparison as well. Whether the practice is in your insurance network, how far it is and what parking looks like on a bad day, whether labs and imaging sit in the same building, and whether they coordinate cleanly with a surgeon or a radiation team you may also need. The woman driving up from Waterloo is not being fussy about distance. She is being realistic about repetition.

Not sure where to start the shortlist? You can browse oncologists across the metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, pick two or three that are realistic for your insurance and your driving, and call each one with the same short list of questions. What comes back, and how quickly it comes back, tells you a great deal.

### For oncology practices and cancer centers in the metro

Look again at who is in the opening of this article. Nobody was comparing outcomes data at midnight. They were trying to find out what Monday morning is going to be like, and whether they will be able to find the right entrance, the right parking garage and the right paperwork. Almost all of that is publishable, and most practices do not publish it.

Put the practical things where a frightened person can find them in one visit to your website. What a first appointment involves and roughly how much of the day to set aside. What to bring. Whether labs happen the same day. Which records you want sent ahead and who should send them. Where to park and which door to use. Whether a companion can come back into the room. Who answers the phone after hours.

Name your subspecialties plainly and say who does what. A new patient does not know the difference between medical, surgical and radiation oncology, and four clear sentences explaining it does more good than a paragraph about a “commitment to excellence.” Say how results are delivered and how long they usually take, because the silence between a test and a result is where people suffer most.

And say plainly that second opinions are welcome, along with how to arrange one. Patients who are afraid to ask will simply leave and never tell you why. The practices that answer the question before anyone has to ask it are the ones that get the call.

### Frequently asked questions

### Q. Do oncologists do anything other than cancer?

A.  Yes. Many oncologists are trained in hematology as well, and hematology covers a long list of blood and bone marrow conditions that are not cancer. Anemias that will not resolve, clotting and bleeding disorders, low platelet counts, iron overload and abnormal blood counts found on routine labs all commonly land in the same clinic. So a referral to an oncologist does not automatically mean anyone believes you have cancer. If you are unsure why you were sent, ask the referring office to tell you in one plain sentence.

### Q. What type of cancer does an oncologist treat?

A.  It depends on the doctor. Some oncologists treat a broad range of cancers, and others concentrate on a specific area such as breast, lung, gastrointestinal, urologic, gynecologic or blood cancers. The specialty also splits by what the doctor does rather than what they treat: medical oncology handles systemic therapy, surgical oncology operates, radiation oncology plans and delivers radiation. When you call to schedule, it is reasonable to ask what this particular physician focuses on and whether your diagnosis is in that focus.

### Q. How long do oncology appointments last?

A.  It varies by practice and by the type of visit, so ask the scheduler rather than assuming. A first consultation is generally the longest one you will have, because it includes a full history, an examination and a detailed review of records. Follow-up visits are usually shorter. What tends to stretch the day is everything around the appointment: registration, labs beforehand, imaging in the same trip, and waiting. Ask how early to arrive, whether labs are same day, and how much of the day to set aside.

### Q. What are the best questions to ask an oncologist?

A.  The ones that pin down facts and timing rather than predictions. What exactly is the diagnosis, and how is it spelled? What is known so far, and what is still pending? What tests come next, and when will results be back? What is the next decision point, and when does it happen? Who is coordinating my care? How do results reach me, and how long does that usually take? Write them down in priority order, because the first two are the ones that always get asked.

### Q. What are some important questions I should ask my oncologist?

A.  Beyond the diagnosis itself, ask the questions that govern the weeks between visits. Who do I call with a problem, and what number after hours? What symptoms are worth a phone call rather than waiting? Is there a nurse navigator, a social worker or a financial counselor I can talk to? Is my case reviewed by a group of specialists, and when? How do I arrange a second opinion, and what records would need to travel? What should I be doing between now and the next appointment?

### Q. How soon does chemo start after seeing an oncologist?

A.  There is no standard interval, and anyone offering one is guessing about your situation. Timing depends on what the plan turns out to be, whether remaining tests or procedures are still needed, whether insurance authorization is required, and how the practice schedules. Some plans do not involve chemotherapy at all. The useful question at a first visit is not how soon, but what has to happen before anything can be scheduled, who is responsible for each of those steps, and when you should call if you have not heard back.

### Q. Should you bring someone with you to a first oncology appointment?

A.  If you can, yes. A first visit covers a great deal of information at a moment when most people are not absorbing much of it, and a second set of ears catches what you miss. Give your companion a defined job: taking notes while you do the listening and the asking. Decide who does what before you walk in. If you want to record the conversation instead, ask the practice first, because policies differ and some offices do not permit it.

### Q. Is asking for a second opinion going to offend your oncologist?

A.  It should not, and in oncology second opinions are common enough to be routine. Practices are generally used to arranging them, sending records and slides, and coordinating with another physician. Ask directly how to set one up, what would need to be sent, and whether waiting for it would affect any timing that matters. The response itself is informative. A team that handles the request calmly and helps you organize it is showing you how it will handle harder conversations later.

## What to Buy at a Pet Store for a New Puppy
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-to-buy-at-a-pet-store-for-a-new-puppy

In Maplewood, the crate was still in its box at nine o’clock on a Friday night, and the puppy was due at ten the next morning. Two adults sat on the kitchen floor with a screwdriver and a folded diagram, disagreeing politely about which panel was the door. They had spent a good deal of money that week. They had not bought a single bowl.

Across the river in Fairview Heights, another household did the opposite and bought almost nothing. The plan was to see what the puppy actually needed and then go get it, which is a perfectly reasonable plan right up until eleven at night, when a nine-week-old is loose in a living room and there is no crate, no gate and nothing safe to chew. Down in Imperial, a family bought carefully and then bought everything twice, because the harness that fit in July did not fit the same dog in September.

None of them were careless. Puppy shopping is confusing because the aisle is enormous, the dog is small, and the dog is going to change size in about six weeks. So here is the honest version: what genuinely earns its place on day one, what can wait a week or a month, what tends to sit unused in a closet, where the puppy should sleep that first night, how long to let it cry, and how to pick a shop that will help you rather than just ring you up.

One boundary first. Nothing here is medical advice. Vaccination timing, deworming, how much food goes in the bowl and anything that looks like a health question belongs to your own veterinarian, and a visit in the first few days is standard practice.

### What to buy for a first day puppy?

A short list covers the first day: a crate sized for now with a divider, washable bedding, two bowls, a flat collar with an ID tag, a leash, the same food the breeder or shelter was feeding, an enzymatic cleaner, and a couple of safe chews. Everything else can wait.

The crate deserves the most thought, and the mistake almost everybody makes is buying for the adult dog and stopping there. A crate sized for a seventy-pound dog gives a nine-week-old a bathroom at one end and a bed at the other, which teaches exactly the wrong lesson. Buy the crate the dog will grow into, then use the divider panel to fence off a space just big enough to stand, turn around and lie down flat. Move the panel back as the puppy grows. That one piece of wire does more house-training work than anything else you will carry out of the store.

Bedding should be washable and cheap enough that you are not upset when it gets destroyed, because it probably will be. Two bowls, one for food and one for water, in something heavy or stainless that a puppy cannot flip or chew apart. Light plastic gets gnawed, and a bowl that slides across the floor becomes a toy within a day.

A flat collar with an ID tag goes on before the puppy comes into the house, not after. Tags get engraved in store or ordered and mailed, and the gap between those two options is exactly the window when a frightened puppy slips out of a door somebody left open. A plain six-foot leash is enough. You do not need a retractable one, and for a puppy learning not to pull, you actively do not want it.

Buy the same food the breeder or shelter has been feeding, in the same formula, even if you intend to switch later. A puppy arriving in a new house is already handling new floors, new smells, new people and no littermates. Changing the food on the same day adds a digestive problem to an emotional one. Ask what they feed, write it down, buy that, and talk to your vet about how and when to transition. Buy an enzymatic cleaner at the same time, the kind sold specifically for pet messes, because ordinary household cleaner lifts the stain and leaves behind the scent marker that tells the puppy this is the spot.

Finish with two or three safe chews and a puppy-appropriate toy or two. Not a bin, not a haul. Puppies teethe, and when there is nothing legal to chew, the legal thing becomes a chair leg or your shoe. Pick chews sized for the dog you have right now, check them for pieces that come off, and rotate a small number instead of dumping fifteen toys on the floor at once.

A surprising amount of the rest you already own. Old towels, a laundry basket of rags, a baby gate from a cousin, a phone charger coiled up out of reach. The store is for the things that have to be right, not for the things that simply have to exist.

### What can wait a week, and what usually goes unused?

Most of it can wait, and the reason is size. A puppy at nine weeks is not the animal you will have at five months, so anything fitted to the body is worth delaying until the body slows down. A week of patience saves you from buying the same item twice, which is the single most common way people overspend on a new dog.

A harness is the clearest example. Fit matters, puppies grow in odd bursts, and a harness bought before the dog arrives is a coin flip. Wait until you can measure the actual chest, then fit it with the dog present if the shop allows it. The same logic applies to a proper bed, which is worth having and worth buying late, once the chewing phase settles and you know how your dog likes to sleep. Grooming tools can wait a couple of weeks, although the nail trimming conversation should start early with your vet or a groomer. Training treats in bulk can wait too, at least until you learn what this particular puppy will work for, which may not be what your last dog worked for.

Then there is the drawer. Every household with a dog has one, and the contents are remarkably consistent: the plush toy destroyed in an afternoon, the second bed nobody uses, the pen bought a size too small, the scented training spray, the elaborate slow feeder for a dog who does not bolt food, the coat for a dog who does not mind the cold. None of it was a scam. It was bought for an imagined dog, before anybody met the real one.

Puppy pads deserve their own paragraph, because they are genuinely useful in some households and quietly counterproductive in others. If you are on an upper floor with no fast route outside, they help. If you have a door and a yard and your goal is a dog that never goes indoors, pads teach the puppy that indoors is sometimes acceptable, and you will have to unteach it later. Decide which house you live in before you buy a case of them.

So what do people wish they had bought sooner? Gates. Not for the whole house, just one or two, so the puppy has a small approved area rather than the run of a floor. A confined puppy is a supervised puppy, and a supervised puppy learns faster than one you keep fishing out from under the dining table.

### What is the 7 7 7 rule for puppies?

It is a socialization checklist, not a shopping list, and it comes from breeders rather than from veterinary medicine. The idea, sometimes called the Rule of Sevens, is that before a puppy leaves for its new home it should have met seven of a great many things: seven different surfaces underfoot, seven objects to play with, seven locations, seven people, seven small challenges, and so on down the list.

The exact categories vary between breeders, which tells you something useful about its status. A common version runs through surfaces such as carpet, tile, grass, gravel, wood and metal; objects of different shapes and textures; locations inside and outside the house; people of different ages and appearances; small challenges like a step, a tunnel or a box to climb into; and eating from seven different containers in seven different places. It is a memorable way to organize early exposure, and it is widely used because it works as a prompt, not because it is a veterinary standard.

For a buyer, the value is in the asking. When you talk to a breeder or a rescue, ask what this puppy has already been exposed to. A puppy that has walked on gravel, heard a vacuum, ridden in a car and been handled by strangers arrives at your house with a real head start. One that has spent nine weeks in a single quiet room does not, and you will be doing that work yourself, later, when the window is narrower.

Which is why it is not a reason to buy seven of anything. The exposure work is free. It is a cardboard box, a baking tray to walk across, the noise of the dishwasher, a friend who turns up in a hat. Nothing on that list has a barcode, and confusing it with a shopping list is how people end up with a garage full of enrichment products and a dog who has never met a bicycle.

### Where should a puppy sleep first night in a new home?

In a crate, next to your bed, for the first several nights at least. That is where most experienced owners and most trainers land, and it solves two problems at once. The puppy is not alone in the dark in a strange building, and you are close enough to hear the difference between a puppy settling and a puppy that genuinely needs to go outside.

The instinct to put the crate in the kitchen or a laundry room is understandable, because nobody wants to be woken up. It usually backfires. A puppy that has lost its littermates, its mother and every familiar smell in a single afternoon does not experience a closed door down the hall as independence. It experiences it as abandonment, and the crying goes on longer and gets louder. Sleeping close for a week or two costs you a few nights and buys you a dog who thinks the crate is a safe place rather than the place where everyone disappears.

Set it up so the crate is worth being in. Something soft and washable, an item that smells like the litter if the breeder or shelter sends one home, and the space kept small with the divider. Some puppies settle better with a cover over part of the crate, which cuts the light and the visual noise. Others hate it and tell you so. You will know within two nights.

Once the puppy is sleeping through and the crate reads as a bed rather than a cage, you can move it, a few feet at a time, toward wherever it will live permanently. Doing it gradually is the entire trick. Move it across the house in one jump and you will hear about it, loudly, at two in the morning.

### What do you do when the crying starts?

Not long, and the real question is what kind of crying you are hearing. A young puppy has a small bladder and a genuine need to go out overnight, so the first job is deciding whether this is a complaint or a request. A few minutes of grumbling that fades out is a puppy settling. Escalating, sustained crying at two in the morning usually means the yard.

A common rule of thumb puts a puppy’s holding capacity at roughly one hour per month of age, and not more than a few hours even at the top of that range. Treat it as a guideline rather than a law, because puppies vary and a stressed puppy on its first night varies more. At eight or nine weeks, plan on at least one trip outside during the night, and quite possibly two.

Make that trip boring on purpose. Carry the puppy out, stand in the yard, wait, praise quietly when something happens, and carry it straight back to the crate. No lights, no play, no conversation. You want a puppy that learns nighttime is dull and the crate is where sleeping happens. The moment the overnight trip becomes fun, it will be requested nightly, and you will not be the one who decided that.

The uncomfortable middle ground is the puppy that has just been out, is dry, is safe and is still shouting. In our experience that one settles fastest if you are present but boring: a hand resting near the crate, no talking, no lifting out. Letting a puppy scream for an hour on night one is not training. Getting it out every time it makes a noise is not training either. The line you are drawing is between needs, which you meet immediately, and opinions, which you can outlast.

Once the puppy finally sleeps through, feeding yourself properly becomes the next overdue project.

### How do you choose a pet store worth walking into?

Shortlist two or three and interview them, the same way you would a groomer or a trainer. You are not shopping for the biggest aisle. You are looking for a shop that will size a collar on your actual dog, tell you plainly what they do not carry, and still be useful to you in six months when the questions get harder.

Say what you want out loud. You have a puppy arriving on a date, this is roughly how big it should get, this is what the breeder or shelter has been feeding, and you need a crate with a divider, bowls, a collar and tag, a leash and a couple of chews. Then listen. Do they carry that food, or something close, and will they sell you a small bag instead of the largest one on the shelf? Can they engrave a tag while you wait? Will they let you bring the dog in to fit a collar and later a harness? Will they take back a crate that turns out to be the wrong size, and in what condition?

The gap between what you asked for and what they are prepared to provide is the signal. A shop in Ellisville that says we do not stock that food, but here is who does, has told you something useful about the next two years. A shop that answers every question with yes and then cannot produce a divider panel has told you something as well.

Pay attention to whether they ask you anything. The good ones do. How old is the puppy, how big will it get, is this your first, where is it sleeping. A staff member who asks the puppy’s age before recommending a chew is doing the job properly. One who walks you straight to the most expensive bed in the store without asking a thing is doing a different job.

Not sure where to start the shopping? You can browse pet stores across the metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, pick two or three near you, and call each one with your arrival date, the food your puppy is already eating and the crate size you think you need. What comes back, and how quickly, tells you which one to drive to.

### For independent pet shops across the metro

Read the opening of this article again. Nobody was hunting the cheapest crate in the metro. They were trying to work out what they actually needed before a deadline they could not move, and every one of them would gladly have paid a little more to be told the right answer by a person standing in front of them.

That is the whole opportunity, and most of it is publishing. Put a first-day checklist on your website with the categories and sizes you stock, so somebody can read it at eleven at night and drive to you at ten the next morning. Say which crate sizes you keep on the floor and whether the divider panel comes with them, because that single detail sends more people to a delivery box than price ever does. List the food lines you carry so a new owner can check before getting in the car, and say whether you will break a case or sell a small transition bag.

Then publish the services wrapped around the product. Tag engraving while you wait. Collar and harness fitting with the dog present. Your return window on a crate or a collar that turned out to be wrong. Whether you host a trainer, a nail-trim clinic or a vaccination clinic, and on which days. Those are the things a first-time owner cannot get from a cardboard box on the porch, and they are the only durable reason to drive.

Say what you do not do, too. A shop that says we are not the place for that diet, try these two, keeps the customer for the other forty things. And keep your hours accurate, because the puppy is arriving on Saturday whether the sign on the door is current or not.

### Frequently asked questions

### Q. What are the best things to buy for a new puppy?

A.  The ones you will use in the first week. A crate with a divider so the space grows with the dog, washable bedding, two heavy bowls, a flat collar with an engraved ID tag, a plain leash, the same food the breeder or shelter was feeding, an enzymatic cleaner for accidents, and a few safe chews. Add one or two gates if your house has open rooms. Everything after that, the harness, the proper bed, grooming tools, bulk training treats, is better bought a week or a month in, once you know the dog’s real size and habits.

### Q. Should puppies sleep in a crate?

A.  Most do well in one, and it is the arrangement most experienced owners and trainers recommend for the first months. A correctly sized crate gives the puppy a den it will not want to soil, keeps it safe overnight when nobody is watching, and makes house-training considerably faster. The crate has to be small enough to be a bed rather than a bedroom, which is exactly what the divider is for. It also has to be a good place instead of a punishment: meals inside it, chews inside it, door open during the day. If your puppy panics rather than settles, talk to your vet or a trainer.

### Q. Should puppies sleep in the dark at night?

A.  Dim and quiet helps most puppies settle, and it reinforces the difference between night and day. That does not mean total blackout. Plenty of puppies do better with a partly covered crate and a low light in the hall, because the goal is a calm room rather than a dark one. Watch your own dog. If covering the crate settles it within a couple of nights, keep going. If the puppy is more agitated with the cover on, take it off. Consistency matters more than the light level: same place, same routine, every night.

### Q. Do dogs like to sleep with blankets?

A.  Most do, and puppies especially, because they are used to sleeping in a pile of littermates and a blanket is the nearest substitute available. Something soft, washable and inexpensive is the right call, since early bedding gets chewed and soiled. Watch for a puppy that shreds and swallows fabric rather than nesting in it, because that is a hazard and a good reason to switch to a flat mat until the chewing phase passes. If the breeder or shelter sends home something that smells like the litter, put it in the crate on night one. It does more than anything you can buy.

### Q. How long to let puppy cry in crate first night home?

A.  Only as long as it takes to work out what the crying means. A few minutes of grumbling that gets quieter is a puppy settling, and interrupting that teaches the puppy that noise opens the door. Crying that escalates and keeps going usually signals a real need, and at eight or nine weeks that is almost always a trip outside. Take the puppy out with no lights and no play, then straight back to the crate. Keeping the crate beside your bed cuts the crying down enormously, because most first-night distress is about being alone rather than about being crated.

### Q. Can I leave a 7 week old puppy alone for 4 hours?

A.  No, and it is kinder to be direct about that. A common rule of thumb gives a puppy roughly one hour of bladder control per month of age, and not more than a few hours even at the top end, which puts a seven-week-old well short of four. Beyond the physical limit, a puppy that age is still learning that people come back, and long stretches alone in the first week build anxiety you will spend months undoing. If your schedule has a four-hour hole in it, arrange a person: a partner on a different shift, a neighbor, a family member, a paid sitter.

### Q. How big should a puppy’s first crate be?

A.  Big enough to stand up, turn around and lie down flat, and no bigger. That is the standard guideline, and it is why the divider panel matters more than the crate itself. Extra room does not feel generous to a puppy. It creates a bathroom corner, which is the opposite of what you are trying to teach. Buy the crate that suits the adult dog you expect, then squeeze the usable space down with the divider and move it back in stages as the puppy grows. One purchase, four or five sizes, no second trip.

### Q. Do you need puppy pads?

A.  It depends on your house rather than on your puppy. If you are up a flight of stairs with no quick route outside, pads are a practical bridge for a few weeks. If you have a door and a yard and the goal is a dog that never relieves itself indoors, pads teach a habit you will later have to untrain. Whichever way you go, buy an enzymatic cleaner at the same time, because ordinary cleaners lift the stain and leave the scent marker that tells the puppy to use that exact spot again.

## What to Look For When Buying Vinyl Records
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-to-look-for-when-buying-vinyl-records

On a Saturday in Tower Grove, Renata has been parked at the same bin divider for eleven minutes, which is not a long time by crate standards. She pulls a sleeve, tips the record halfway out, angles it toward the window, slides it back. Two people have squeezed past her already. She is not being precious. She is looking for the one thing the price sticker never tells you, which is whether the record inside sounds anything like the record on the cover.

Three aisles over, Dell is doing the arithmetic every returning collector does. He sold his LPs in 1994 for gas money and he is buying them back one at a time, and he cannot work out why the same album sits in an unsorted bin near the door and also behind the counter at a price that made him blink. His daughter, who started all of this by finding his old turntable, has an armful of reissues and a quiet worry that reissues are somehow cheating.

None of them need a lecture about warm analog sound. They need to know what to look at, what to feel for, what the letters on the sticker mean, and what separates a record worth carrying home from a frisbee with nice artwork. So: how grading works, how to inspect a disc in ninety seconds under bad store lighting, what actually sets the price, how to tell an original from a later pressing, what really destroys records, and how to pick a shop worth your Saturday.

### What should I look for when buying vinyl records?

Look at the disc and the sleeve as two separate purchases, because that is how shops grade them. Tilt the record toward a light and read the surface for scuffs, deep scratches, groove wear and warps. Then read the grade on the sticker, the label copy, and the etching in the run-out area. Condition, pressing and demand set the price.

The most useful habit you can build is handling. Take a record out by the edges, fingers on the rim and thumb on the label, never flat across the playing surface. Skin oil holds dust, and dust is what you hear three years later. Slide the inner sleeve out with the disc still inside it, then tip the disc into your palm. Shop staff notice. So does the record.

After that it is a sequence, and it gets quick once you have done it fifty times. Sleeve first, since a beaten jacket often means a beaten record. Disc next, under the best light in the room. Label and run-out last, because those tell you what you are actually holding, which is not always what the front cover implies. If anything in that sequence stops you, put it back. There is usually another copy.

One thing worth saying early. Perfect is not the goal for most buyers. A clean Very Good Plus copy of an album you will genuinely play beats a sealed one you are afraid to open, and it costs a fraction. The question is never whether a record has flaws. The question is whether the flaws you can see will show up in the part you listen for.

### What do Mint, Near Mint and Very Good Plus actually mean?

Most American shops grade with some version of the Goldmine standard, a scale that runs from Mint down through Near Mint, Very Good Plus, Very Good, Good, Fair and Poor. It is a visual scale, applied by eye, by a person, usually in a hurry. Two honest shops can grade the same record half a step apart, and both are acting in good faith.

Mint means untouched, and careful shops use it sparingly. Many will not use it at all on a played record, reserving it for sealed stock. Near Mint is the realistic ceiling for anything that has been on a turntable. It looks close to new, the jacket has no creases or ring wear worth mentioning, and the disc shows nothing under a raking light except perhaps the faintest sleeve scuffs.

Very Good Plus is where most good used records live and where most of the smart money goes. Expect light marks, a little jacket wear, maybe a corner that has been bumped, and surface noise that is present but sits under the music rather than over it. Very Good drops another step: visible scratches, noise you notice between tracks and sometimes during them, a sleeve that has clearly been lived with. Good means it plays through without skipping, and that is roughly the whole promise.

The detail newer buyers miss is that the sleeve and the disc are graded separately, and you will often see two grades written side by side. A record listed as Near Mint disc over Very Good sleeve is telling you the vinyl is lovely and the jacket has been through something. Which of those you care about depends on whether you are a listener or a collector, and it is worth deciding which one you are before you reach the counter.

### How do you inspect a record in the store?

Find the light and use it. Angle the disc so light rakes across the grooves rather than hitting them head on, then rotate it slowly through a full turn. Flaws vanish when light comes at them square and jump out when it skims. Ninety seconds of that catches nearly everything that would have annoyed you at home.

Learn the difference between a scuff and a scratch, because it decides most purchases. Scuffs are shallow surface marks, often from a paper inner sleeve, and they usually look far worse than they sound. A scratch crosses the grooves, and the test is your fingernail: run it gently across the mark, and if you feel it catch, you will probably hear it. Feel it catch in more than one place around the disc and you are looking at a tick every single revolution.

Groove wear is subtler and worse. It shows as a grey or slightly frosted cast in the playing area, usually heaviest on the loud passages, and it means a worn stylus has already been through there. No cleaning fixes it. Spindle marks are the halo of fine scratches around the center hole, left by dropping the record carelessly onto the platter. They are cosmetic in themselves, but they tell you how this copy was treated. For warps, hold the disc at eye level and sight along the edge. A gentle dish often plays fine. A ripple near the rim or a kink you can see from across the room usually does not.

Then the jacket. Ring wear is the circular impression the disc wears into the cardboard from the inside, and on a common title it costs a grade. Seam splits run along the bottom or the open edge and grow every time the record goes back in. Water damage is the one to walk away from: wavy board, a stiff or rippled feel, a tide line, a musty smell. Water gets into the paper inner too, and a mildewed inner keeps passing that smell back to the disc.

### How much should a vinyl record cost?

There is no fixed answer, and anyone quoting you one number is selling something. The price of a used record comes out of four things stacked together: condition, which pressing it is, how many people currently want it, and how many copies survive in that condition. Move any one of those and the number moves with it, sometimes enormously.

Condition is the biggest lever and the only one you can see with your own eyes. The same title in Near Mint and in Very Good is not the same product and should not carry the same price. Common records in rough shape are close to worthless. The same common record in exceptional shape can be worth real money precisely because almost every surviving copy was played to death.

Pressing comes next. An original first pressing, from the original run, with the original label design and matrix numbers, generally commands more than a later repress of the same album. That gap widens on records that mattered to people, and it can vanish entirely on records that were pressed by the million. A hugely successful album from the seventies exists in staggering quantity, and no amount of originality makes such a copy scarce.

So, practically. Before you pay a serious price for anything, check what comparable copies in comparable condition have actually sold for recently, not what sellers are asking. Asking prices are hope. Sold prices are the market. And for the cheap bins, honestly, do not overthink it. The cost of a mistake down there is the price of a sandwich, and the flyer is most of the fun.

### How do you tell an original pressing from a reissue?

You read the record, not the cover, because covers get reproduced faithfully and the disc rarely lies. Three places carry the evidence: the label, the run-out area, and the jacket printing. None of them is conclusive on its own. Taken together they usually settle the question in a minute or two.

Start with the label. Record companies changed label designs, logos, colors and addresses regularly, and collectors have mapped those changes carefully for most catalogs worth caring about. A label design that did not exist yet in the year printed on the cover means a later pressing. So can a barcode, a rights society mark, or a catalog prefix from a later era. Mono or stereo matters too, and on certain records the mono is the one people chase.

Then the run-out, the smooth deadwax between the last groove and the label. Look for stamped or hand etched letters and numbers. Those are matrix numbers, and they identify the lacquer and the stampers used to press that copy. Hand etched markings often point to earlier cuts, and some engineers signed their work with initials or a small symbol. Which specific markings mean what varies hugely by label and by era, so treat any rule you read as a starting point and check it against a discography for that catalog.

A word in defense of reissues, since Dell’s daughter is still worrying about it. A reissue is not automatically worse. Some are cut from the original tapes by careful engineers and pressed on quiet, well made vinyl at a better plant than the original ever saw. Others are cut from a digital file of a CD master and pressed thin. The variable is care, not age. If you are buying to listen, a good modern reissue frequently beats a tired original that spent fifty years on bad gear.

Crate digging wrecks your lower back. Three Pilates sessions a week might undo it.

### What destroys vinyl records?

Heat, dust, sun, moisture and a bad stylus, roughly in that order, and all of them are preventable. Nothing on that list is exotic. The records that arrive at shops unplayable were almost always stored somewhere hot, stacked flat under weight, or played with a needle that should have been replaced years earlier.

Heat warps, and faster than people expect. A car trunk in a Missouri August, an attic, an uninsulated garage, a shelf beside a radiator or a sunny window: any of those can put a permanent dish or a ripple in a record in a single afternoon. Sunlight also fades jacket spines, which is why the row nearest the window always looks worse than the row in the corner. If a room is uncomfortable for you, it is bad for the records.

Humidity works slower and is just as final. Damp basements grow mildew on cardboard and on paper inner sleeves, and once a jacket carries that smell it rarely lets go. Dust is the everyday enemy. It settles into the grooves, the stylus grinds it in, and it becomes the crackle people mistakenly call character. A record left uncovered on a turntable for a week collects more grief than a record played weekly and sleeved every time.

Then there is what happens during play. A worn stylus with a chipped or flattened tip carves at the groove walls, and that damage is permanent. Tracking force set too light lets the tip chatter in the groove, which is often worse than a touch too heavy. Poor alignment drags the tip through the groove at the wrong angle. And handling the playing surface with bare fingers leaves oil that grabs dust and holds onto it.

### Is it better to store vinyl records flat or upright?

Upright, snug, and not leaning. Records stored vertically and supported on both sides carry their own weight through the edge, which is what the edge is built for. Stacked flat, every record in the pile carries everything above it, and over a few months the bottom of that stack takes on a bow that does not come out.

Snug is the word doing the work there. Too loose and records lean, and a leaning record slowly warps in the direction it leans. Too tight and you cannot pull a sleeve without scraping it, so you start yanking, and yanking is how seams split. A shelf you can slide a record out of with two fingers is about right. Dividers every so often keep whole sections from slumping sideways.

The rest is unglamorous. Buy a shelf that will hold the weight, because records are far heavier than they look and a sagging particle board shelf is a common and expensive lesson. Keep them off a concrete floor and out of direct sun. Anti static inner sleeves beat the original paper ones, and you can tuck the originals into the jacket behind the record if completeness matters to you. Outer plastic sleeves stop ring wear before it starts, which counts for far more on a jacket you cannot replace than on one you can.

### How do you pick a record shop worth your Saturday?

Shortlist two or three and treat the first visit as an interview. The metro carries very different kinds of shops: high turnover used bins, curated stores that price carefully by genre, general secondhand places where records are one department among many, and shops weighted heavily toward new releases. None of those is better than the others. They are aimed at different people with different Saturdays.

Say plainly what you collect and what condition you expect. Tell them you want early soul on original pressings in Very Good Plus or better, or that you want listening copies of anything decent and cheap, or that you are rebuilding a collection you sold thirty years ago. Then compare that against what the shop is actually set up to provide. Do they grade to a published standard? Do they grade sleeve and disc separately? Will they let you play something first? Do they hold things back for regulars who tell them what they hunt?

The gap between what you asked for and what the shop is prepared to deliver is the signal. Not the price. A store in University City that grades strictly and prices high is a better deal than one that grades loosely and prices low, if you are buying records to keep. If you are digging for the sport of it, the reverse can be true, and an unsorted wall of ungraded bins in Alton is exactly the right afternoon.

Not sure where to start digging? You can browse record stores across the metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, shortlist two or three near you, and walk in with one sentence about what you collect and the condition you expect. How each shop answers that, and whether the bins back it up, tells you most of what you need to know.

### For independent record shops in the metro

Look again at who is in the opening of this article. Not one of them was hunting the cheapest bin in the region. They were trying to work out whether what was written on the sticker matched what was inside the sleeve. Trust in your grade is the entire product. Everything else is inventory.

Publish your grading standard. Say on your site, and on a sign in the store, that you grade to the Goldmine scale, that you grade sleeve and disc separately, and roughly where you sit on the strict to generous spectrum. Buyers forgive a strict shop instantly and come back for it. They do not come back to a shop where Near Mint turned out to mean playable.

Publish what you actually carry, by genre and era, in plain words. “All genres” reads as nobody’s shop. “Deep soul and jazz on originals, a wall of ungraded rock, new reissues to order” tells a collector in fifteen seconds whether the drive across town is worth it. Say whether you have a listening station, whether you buy collections and how you like them presented, and how you price: from a guide, from recent sold comparables, or from what moves in your own bins.

And write the flaws on the sticker. Light seam split, bottom edge. Faint groove wear, side one, plays through. A shop that names the defect and prices for it earns the sale twice, once now and once when that buyer brings somebody. Say what you do not stock, too. Sending a customer across town for something you do not carry costs you nothing and earns you the next visit.

### Frequently asked questions

### Q. Can you still purchase vinyl records?

A.  Yes, easily, and in more places than at almost any point in the last thirty years. New titles are pressed and sold through independent record stores, chain retailers, artists at shows, and online. Used records turn up in dedicated shops, general secondhand stores, estate sales, flea markets, church basements and online marketplaces. Availability is not the problem. Condition and price are, and both vary wildly between a graded shop copy and an ungraded box at a yard sale. Buying used rewards patience and a working grasp of grading far more than it rewards spending.

### Q. Are vinyls worth it in 2026?

A.  That depends entirely on what you want from music. Records are worth it if you like the ritual: choosing a side, sitting with it, reading the jacket, getting up to flip it halfway through. They are worth it if you collect, since a well kept record holds value in a way a download never will. They are not worth it if you mainly want convenience or the cheapest possible listening, because a decent turntable, cartridge and amplifier all cost money before the first record does. Plenty of people run both, streaming to discover and records to sit with.

### Q. What is the lifespan of a vinyl record?

A.  Records do not really have a fixed lifespan, which is why the play count numbers floating around online are better treated as folklore. A record kept clean, sleeved, stored upright in a stable room and played on a properly set up turntable can be played for decades without meaningful degradation. The same record played weekly with a worn stylus and left out to gather dust can be audibly damaged within a couple of years. Care and stylus condition matter far more than the number of spins. Pressings from the fifties still sound excellent when somebody looked after them.

### Q. Do cheap vinyl players ruin vinyls?

A.  The very cheap all in one suitcase players can, and the mechanism is not mysterious. Most use a heavy ceramic cartridge with a stiff stylus tracking at a force well above what a decent magnetic cartridge needs, mounted on a plastic tonearm with no adjustment at all. That combination bears down on the groove walls and wears them. The damage is gradual, cumulative and permanent, and it eventually shows as that frosted look in the loud passages. Not every inexpensive turntable is a problem, though. A modest belt drive deck with an adjustable arm and a replaceable stylus is a different animal.

### Q. What does the number 33 mean on vinyl records?

A.  It is the playback speed: 33 1/3 revolutions per minute, the standard for full length albums since the late nineteen forties. The other speeds you will meet are 45 rpm, used for singles and for some audiophile albums cut across extra discs, and 78 rpm, used on older shellac records that need a different stylus entirely. The speed is normally printed on the label. Playing a record at the wrong speed will not hurt it, but a 45 rpm album accidentally played at 33 has convinced more than one new buyer that the pressing was faulty.

### Q. What is the hardest vinyl record to find?

A.  There is no single answer, and anybody naming one is really naming a favorite. The genuinely scarce items tend to fall into a few groups: test pressings and acetates made in tiny numbers before a commercial run, releases withdrawn or recalled shortly after issue, private pressings a band paid for themselves in runs of a few hundred, and regional records that never got distribution beyond one city. Rarity alone does not create value, though. A record has to be both scarce and wanted. Plenty of extremely rare records are rare because nobody bought them.

### Q. What is ring wear, and should it stop you buying a record?

A.  Ring wear is the circular impression a record wears into its jacket from the inside, usually visible as a faded or scuffed halo on the front or the back. It comes from the disc pressing outward over years of storage, and it is one of the most common reasons a sleeve grades below the disc. Whether it should stop you depends on you. If you are buying to listen, it is cosmetic and often worth a discount. If you are buying a scarce title to keep, sleeve condition drives a large share of the value, and heavy ring wear costs a grade.

### Q. How should you clean a used record you just brought home?

A.  Start with a dry pass. A carbon fiber brush held lightly against the spinning record lifts loose dust before the stylus can grind it in. For anything that came out of a basement or a garage, go further with a wet clean, using a solution made for records rather than household cleaners, a microfiber applicator, and a rinse if the product calls for one. Let it dry fully before sleeving. Then replace the old paper inner with an anti static sleeve, because putting a freshly cleaned record back into a dusty inner undoes the work.
