## When a St. Louis Business Owner Needs an Investment Bank
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/when-a-st-louis-business-owner-needs-an-investment-bank

The call came in on a Thursday afternoon, right as second shift was starting. Dave has run a machine shop in Brentwood for twenty-two years, forty-one people on the floor, and the voice on the phone said he represented a buyer who admired the business and had a number in mind. Then he said the number. Dave wrote it on the back of a job traveler and looked at it on and off for the rest of the day. He had no idea whether it was generous or insulting.

Other owners around the metro are holding their own version of that piece of paper. A woman in Ladue who built a specialty contracting firm is sixty-three, would like to be out inside three years, and has no child who wants it. Two brothers who own a distributor in Maryland Heights got an unsolicited letter of intent in the mail and cannot agree on whether to answer it. A regional services company in Frontenac is profitable and growing and needs real money to buy out a founding partner who wants his cash now. Four different situations, one shared question: who is actually sitting on my side of the table?

Here is what this covers. What an investment bank does for the owner of a closely held company, how that differs from a business broker, the signs that a sale is getting close, what a sell-side process looks like from the inside, how advisors get paid and why the structure matters more than the headline, and how to interview two or three of them without wasting anyone’s time. One thing up front: none of this is legal, tax or financial advice. Your deal will turn on facts that only your own CPA, your attorney and an advisor reading your actual numbers can weigh.

### What is the role of an investment bank?

An investment bank runs the sale or the financing of a company on behalf of its owner. It prepares the financials, sets a defensible value range, builds a confidential buyer list, runs a competitive process, manages diligence and negotiates terms. The job is creating options, so the owner is not negotiating alone against a professional buyer.

Strip the language away and the mechanism is competition. One buyer talking to one seller sets a price. Several credible buyers, working from the same information on the same timeline, discover one. That difference is not a rhetorical trick. It is the reason the same company can trade at meaningfully different values depending only on how it went to market, and it is most of what an owner is paying for.

The second half of the job is quieter. The person who cold-called Dave does acquisitions for a living and has done dozens. Dave will do one, ever. That asymmetry shows up in small places: what gets included in the definition of working capital, how an earnout is measured, which representations survive closing and for how long. Those clauses are worth real money and they are settled by whoever understands them better.

There is also a buffering role nobody advertises. An advisor can push, stall, ask an insulting question and say no, all without poisoning the relationship the owner may still need after closing, through a transition period or an earnout year. You can be the reasonable one in the room precisely because somebody else is being difficult on your behalf.

A word on terms. Investment bank, M&A advisor, middle-market advisor and sell-side advisor all get used for roughly the same work at this size. The label on the door tells you less than the answer to a plain question: do you routinely sell companies that look like mine, to the kind of buyer likely to want mine?

### What do investment bankers actually do all day?

Far less phone-slamming than the movies suggest. Most of a sell-side engagement is preparation, research and document work, punctuated by a few weeks of genuinely intense negotiation. Owners are often surprised by how much of it happens before a single buyer hears the company’s name.

### Getting the numbers ready to survive a stranger

Your books were built to satisfy a bank line and a tax return. A buyer will read them looking for reasons to pay less. So the first stretch of work is rebuilding the financial story: normalizing earnings, separating the owner’s personal expenses from the business, explaining the year revenue dipped, showing gross margin by product line or by job. This is unglamorous and it is where a lot of value is either protected or quietly lost.

### Building the buyer list

Then comes research. Strategic buyers already in your industry, adjacent companies that want your capability or your customers, private equity groups with a platform in your space, sometimes a management team or a family member with financing behind them. A good list is longer and stranger than an owner expects, because the buyer who pays the most is often one you have never heard of and would never have called.

### Running the process and the negotiation

After that it is outreach under a confidentiality agreement, management meetings, indications of interest, a letter of intent, then diligence. During diligence the advisor becomes a project manager, chasing documents, keeping the buyer’s list from expanding forever, and keeping the owner focused on running the company. That last part matters more than it sounds. Deals fall apart when the business misses its numbers during diligence because the owner spent the quarter in a data room.

### When is your company big enough for an investment bank instead of a business broker?

The honest answer is that the line is not a revenue number, and anyone who gives you one is guessing. What actually decides it is who the likely buyer is. If the probable buyer is an individual borrowing against the business to buy himself a job, that is broker territory. If the probable buyer is another company or a financial sponsor with a diligence team, you want an M&A advisor.

### What a business broker does well

Brokers move owner-operated businesses efficiently: the restaurant, the small route, the neighborhood service company, the shop that runs on one person and a phone. They typically list, market to a pool of individual buyers, and help with a comparatively simple transaction. For the right business that is exactly the right tool, and paying investment banking fees on it would be waste.

### What an investment bank does differently

An M&A advisor does not list your business. It runs a confidential, targeted, competitive process aimed at a specific set of buyers, with real diligence support and real negotiation over structure. Structure is the point. On a deal of any size, how you get paid, in cash, in a note, in rolled equity, held in escrow, tied to an earnout, matters as much as the number on page one.

### The awkward middle

Plenty of companies sit between the two, and the tell is complexity rather than size. Multiple locations, meaningful customer concentration, licensing, real estate held in a separate entity, a management team that could run it without you, intellectual property, licensed trades, regulated work: any of these push you toward an advisor. So does a business that has already attracted unsolicited interest, because interest means somebody strategic has noticed you.

### What are the signs that it’s time to sell my business?

Rarely one dramatic moment. It is usually a set of smaller signals that have been accumulating for a year or two while the owner told himself he would think about it after the busy season. Naming them out loud is often the useful part.

Repeat unsolicited interest is the loudest one. A single cold call is noise. Three approaches in eighteen months, from different directions, means your industry is consolidating and buyers have a thesis about companies like yours. That is a market signal about timing, and it has nothing to do with how you feel.

The next set is personal. You have stopped reinvesting. You are turning down growth that would require debt or a new building because you cannot see yourself paying it off. A partner wants out, or a health issue changed the math, or the next generation has made it clear, kindly, that they are not coming back. When the owner’s horizon gets shorter than the company’s, the business starts drifting whether or not anyone says so.

Then there are structural signals. The company needs capital it cannot fund from cash flow. One customer has grown into a share of revenue that keeps you up at night. Everything still runs through you personally, which is exactly the thing a buyer will discount. Notice that most of these are fixable, and that fixing them takes years, not weeks. Which is why the best time to talk to an advisor is well before you intend to do anything.

The worst timing is forced timing. Illness, a partner dispute, a lost anchor customer, a lender getting nervous. Buyers can smell urgency, and it comes out of the price.

### What does a sell-side process actually look like?

Longer than you want and shorter than you fear. A full process is measured in months rather than weeks, and it moves in distinct phases with different demands on your time. Knowing the shape of it ahead of time is most of what keeps an owner sane through the middle of it.

### Preparation

Financial cleanup, normalized earnings, a value range you and your advisor both believe, and the written materials: a short blind teaser with no identifying details, and a confidential information memorandum for buyers who have signed an NDA. This is also when the ugly items get found on purpose. Every business has two or three. Finding yours now, with a plan, is far better than a buyer finding them in week nine of diligence.

### Going to market

Outreach goes out quietly. Interested parties sign confidentiality agreements, receive the memorandum, ask questions, and the serious ones request management meetings. Then indications of interest arrive, and this is the moment competition does its work. Several parties, on the same deadline, form their own view of value without knowing what the others said.

### Letter of intent and diligence

You pick one, sign a letter of intent, and usually grant exclusivity for a defined window. Then diligence begins and it is thorough: financial, tax, legal, insurance, customer contracts, employment records, environmental if there is a building involved, quality of earnings work by an outside accounting firm. Meanwhile you have to run the company well. That is the part owners underestimate.

### Documents and closing

Purchase agreement, disclosure schedules, escrow terms, non-compete, a transition or employment arrangement if you are staying. Your attorney and your CPA do the heavy lifting here and the advisor keeps everyone moving. Closing is anticlimactic. Most owners describe it as a quiet afternoon that does not feel like twenty years ending.

Closed the deal? Take the family somewhere loud: plan an amusement park day.

### How do investment banks charge, and what should you look at?

The structure is consistent across the industry even though the numbers are not. An owner pays a retainer, monthly or upfront, and then a success fee at closing. The success fee is by far the larger piece, which is the design: the advisor is paid mainly for getting a deal done on good terms, not for the work of trying.

Percentages vary with deal size and complexity and they are negotiated, so treat any number you read online as somebody else’s deal. What deserves your attention is not the rate anyway. It is the definitions around it, and those live in the engagement letter.

Read that letter with your attorney and ask, in plain words, about four things. What exactly counts as transaction value, since cash at closing, assumed debt, rolled equity and a future earnout are very different animals. Whether the retainer is credited against the success fee. What the exclusivity period is and how you exit if the relationship is not working. And what the tail provision says, meaning how long after the engagement ends you still owe a fee if a buyer they introduced comes back around. Tail clauses are normal and reasonable. Being surprised by one is not.

Ask about expenses too, and about who on the team actually does the work. Sometimes the person who wins the engagement is not the person you will speak to in month four.

### How do you choose between two or three advisors?

Interview them the way you would interview a surgeon. Shortlist two or three worth an hour, then tell each of them the same plain story: here is my company, here is roughly what it earns, here is why I am thinking about this, and here is what I want to happen. Then stop talking and listen to what comes back.

You are not collecting quotes. No serious advisor is going to hand you a written estimate for a deal that does not exist yet, and asking for one mostly signals that you have not done this before. What you are comparing is the distance between what you asked for and what each of them is prepared to deliver. The gap is the signal, not the fee.

Useful questions to bring. Have you sold companies in my industry, and what happened. Who is my day-to-day contact and how many engagements are they carrying right now. How do you build the buyer list, and roughly how many parties would you approach for a business like mine. What do you think my weaknesses look like to a buyer. How do you protect confidentiality when the buyer is a competitor. How many of your engagements in the past two years actually closed.

That last one is the question people are embarrassed to ask. Ask it. An advisor who takes every engagement that walks in and closes a fraction of them is running a different business than one who is selective and finishes what it starts. And pay attention to whether anyone is willing to tell you no. An advisor who says your company is not ready, or that a broker is the better fit, has just given you something more valuable than a pitch.

Got a number written on the back of a job traveler and no idea what to do with it? You can browse investment banks on St Louis Near Me Directory, pick two or three worth interviewing, and tell each the same short story: what you do, roughly what it earns, and what you want to happen. What they ask you in return, and what they refuse to promise, will tell you a great deal before you sign anything.

### For investment banks and M&A advisors across the metro

Think about Dave in Brentwood again, or the brothers in Maryland Heights with an unsolicited letter of intent on the kitchen table. They are trying to answer one question before they pick up the phone: is my company even the kind of company this firm works with, or am I about to embarrass myself?

So answer it on the page, in language an owner uses. Say what size and type of company you actually take on, and say it without a coy range. Name the industries you have real depth in. Explain how you are engaged, retainer plus success fee, in structure, since owners have no idea that is even how it works and the mystery is what keeps them from calling.

Then answer the practical fears. Is the first conversation confidential and does it cost anything. What documents should an owner bring. How do you keep a process quiet when the natural buyer is a competitor down the road, and what happens to employees who find out. Roughly how long does a process take. Do you also do buy-side work, financing, or valuations for estate and partner-buyout purposes, because a lot of owners in Frontenac and Ladue need that years before they need a sale.

The firms that publish those things get calls from owners who have already decided. The ones that publish a page of vague language about maximizing enterprise value get calls from nobody, and then wonder why the deal flow comes only from referrals.

### Frequently asked questions

### Q. At what point should you sell your business?

A.  Ideally while the business is performing well and you still have the energy to be useful through a transition. Buyers pay for momentum, and a company with growing earnings, a stable customer base and a management team that functions without the owner is a far easier story to tell. The point to avoid is a forced sale after illness, a partner dispute or a lost anchor customer. Since preparing properly takes years rather than months, most owners are better off starting the conversation long before they intend to act.

### Q. Should I sell my business to a private equity firm?

A.  It depends on what you want afterward. A financial buyer often wants the owner or the management team to stay involved and to roll some equity into the new company, which can mean a second payout later if things go well, and a real loss if they do not. A strategic buyer in your industry may want full ownership and may fold the operation in. Neither is better in the abstract. Compare them on structure, on what happens to your people, and on how much of your money stays at risk.

### Q. How much is a business worth with $1,000,000 in sales?

A.  Nobody can answer that, and revenue is the wrong input. Buyers price on earnings, usually seller’s discretionary earnings for smaller owner-operated companies and EBITDA for larger ones, then apply a multiple. That multiple moves with industry, margin, growth, customer concentration, recurring versus one-time revenue, the quality of the books, and how dependent the business is on the owner personally. Two companies with identical sales can be worth very different amounts. A real answer requires an advisor or a valuation professional reading your actual financials.

### Q. How do I calculate capital gains on the sale of my business?

A.  Broadly, gain is what you receive less your basis, but for a business that calculation is more complicated than it sounds. The structure drives everything. An asset sale allocates the price across categories of assets, and some of that can be taxed as ordinary income rather than capital gain, including depreciation recapture on equipment. A stock or membership interest sale is treated differently. Installment sales spread proceeds over years. The actual numbers depend entirely on your entity, your basis and your deal terms, so this belongs to your CPA and a tax attorney reading the real documents.

### Q. How do I avoid capital gains tax on selling my business?

A.  Reframe it as managing the tax rather than avoiding it, because the honest planning levers are about structure and timing. Deal structure matters, since buyers usually prefer an asset purchase and sellers often prefer a stock sale, and that tension is negotiated. Installment sales change when proceeds are recognized. Certain stock and trust and charitable structures carry strict statutory requirements and typically must be put in place years ahead. None of that can be evaluated from an article. Bring your CPA and a tax attorney in before you sign a letter of intent, not after.

### Q. Will investment bankers be replaced by AI?

A.  Parts of the work are already getting faster. Research, buyer list building, first drafts of marketing materials and document review inside diligence are all tasks software handles well. What does not transfer is the rest of it: reading a buyer’s real motivation in a management meeting, knowing which term to concede and which to hold, calming an owner at two in the morning, and having the relationships that get a phone call returned. For a closely held company, the job is judgment and negotiation under pressure. Expect the tools to change and the role to stay.

## What to Expect at a St. Louis Lounge
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-to-expect-at-a-st-louis-lounge

The invitation said lounge, nine o’clock, and nothing else. Nadia spent most of an hour in front of a closet in Lafayette Square trying to work out whether that word meant a dress, or whether it meant she could get away with clean white sneakers. She went with the sneakers. A friend intercepted her on the sidewalk and sent her back upstairs to change, which felt like an overreaction right up until they reached the door and watched two people ahead of them get turned away for exactly that.

Other people around the metro are working out the same thing tonight. Six friends in Soulard booked a birthday table and learned at the table that the minimum was a spend, not a cover, and nobody had explained the difference before they sat down. A man on The Hill reached for the tongs at a hookah lounge to move a coal himself and got a very patient look from the server. In The Grove, a couple walked into a hotel lounge in shorts at four in the afternoon and were seated without comment, came back at ten, and were not. Same room, different rules, and no sign on the wall explaining either.

Here is what this covers. What a lounge dress code actually asks of you and what the words on the website mean, when the code tightens, whether you need a reservation or can walk in, what bottle service includes and how the minimum works, how tipping is usually handled on that check, when bottle service earns its money and when it is money set on fire, what changes at a hookah lounge, how to go as a group without a mess, and the short phone call that answers all of it in ninety seconds. One note up front: policies are set venue by venue and change by the night. Nothing here beats asking the room you are actually going to.

### What is the dress code for a lounge?

Most lounges expect smart casual at minimum: a collared shirt or a nice top, dark denim or trousers, and real shoes. Athletic wear, gym shoes, tank tops, hats and anything oversized are the usual refusals. Dress codes tighten after nine and on weekends, so call the venue and ask.

That is the floor, not the ceiling, and the floor is where most people get caught. Nobody gets turned away for being slightly overdressed. People get turned away for one item, almost always shoes, and the rest of the outfit never gets a vote. If you are unsure and out of time, the safe build is dark trousers or dark denim with no rips, a plain top with sleeves or a collar, and leather or leather-look shoes. That passes at the overwhelming majority of rooms in this metro.

### What the words on the website actually mean

Venues use a small vocabulary and assume you speak it. “Smart casual” means clean, fitted, no athletic gear, and denim is usually fine if it is dark and intact. “Business casual” borrows from the office: collared shirt, trousers or a dress, closed shoes. “Upscale casual” or “dressy casual” pushes it one step further, so a blazer, a dress, or a shirt you would not wear to mow the lawn. “Cocktail attire” is a real instruction and means what it sounds like. And “no athletic wear, no sportswear” is not a style note, it is a list of things the door will refuse.

### What actually gets people turned away

Shoes lead by a mile. Gym shoes, slides, work boots and anything that looks built for a job site or a treadmill are the most common refusals, even when the rest of the outfit is fine. After that: athletic shorts and track pants, sleeveless tops on men, hats of any kind indoors, hoods up, oversized or excessively baggy fits, and clothing with large graphics or team branding. Some rooms add rules about bags. None of this is a judgment about you. It is a door trying to keep a room feeling like one thing rather than four.

### When the code gets stricter

Time of day does more work than the calendar. A hotel lounge at four in the afternoon is a lobby with drinks and will seat almost anyone. The same room at ten on a Saturday has a host, a list and an opinion about your shoes. Weekends, holidays, nights with a DJ or live music, and anything described as a special event all tighten the code. If you are going after nine on a Friday or Saturday, assume the strictest reading of whatever the website says.

### What does lounge dress code mean?

This phrase carries two meanings, and which one you are hearing depends entirely on who said it. Most of the time it means a venue’s door policy: the list of things a particular lounge will and will not let through, enforced by a person standing at the entrance. That is the sense used everywhere else in this article.

The older meaning is formal-wear vocabulary. A lounge suit is a matched jacket and trousers, the ordinary business suit, and on an invitation “lounge suit” historically meant a suit and tie rather than a tuxedo. You still see it on wedding and event invitations, mostly from British or international hosts. So if a venue says lounge dress code, they mean their door rules. If an invitation says lounge suit, somebody is telling you to wear a suit. Two different sentences that happen to share a word.

### Do you need a reservation, or can you walk in?

Both are normal, and the answer changes with the hour. Small cocktail lounges often hold most of the room for walk-ins and take a handful of bookings. Hotel lounges usually take walk-ins all day. Rooms with table service, a list at the door, or anything approaching a nightlife crowd on a weekend will want a reservation, and some take nothing else after a certain hour.

Two things are worth knowing before you show up hopeful. First, table turns are real: a reserved table often carries a time window, and a walk-in table may come with a polite “we need this back by eight thirty.” Ask when you sit down rather than being surprised later. Second, a booked table at a busy room can carry a minimum spend, which is not a cover charge and not a deposit you get back in cash. It is a floor on what your table will buy over the night.

If you want the room without the negotiation, go early. The hour after opening is the same bartenders, the same list and the same seats, with none of the door, none of the wait and usually none of the minimum. Plenty of people who say they cannot get into a place have only ever tried at ten thirty on a Saturday.

### What is bottle service, and what do you actually get?

You are buying a table, and a bottle is how the table gets billed. That is the cleanest way to think about it. You reserve a specific table for the night, a server is assigned to it, and full bottles of spirits come to you instead of individual drinks. Mixers, ice, glassware, garnishes and the pour are handled at the table.

So yes, alcohol is included, in the sense that the bottles are the thing you are paying for. What is not automatically included is everything around it: mixers are sometimes bundled and sometimes billed, and tax, service charges and any door fee are separate lines. The bottle price on the list is not the price of the night. Ask what comes with the bottle before you agree to anything, because that answer differs from venue to venue in the same three blocks.

### How the minimum works

The number people quote as the cost of bottle service is usually a minimum spend, set per table, by the venue, for that specific night. A table near the middle of a busy room on a Saturday carries a higher minimum than a corner table on a Tuesday. Holidays and event nights carry higher ones again. Anything you order goes toward the minimum, but if the table spends less than the floor, you pay the difference anyway.

There is no published metro-wide number for this, and any article that hands you one is guessing. The only reliable way to know what a table costs is to call the venue, name your night, your party size and roughly where you want to sit, and let them quote you. Get it in a text or an email if they will send one.

### How does tipping work on a bottle service check?

Read the check before you add anything. Bottle service almost always carries an automatic gratuity or a service charge that has already been applied, often alongside a separate administrative or table fee, and it is easy to tip a second time by accident on a check that already includes one. Look for the line, and look at whether it is labeled gratuity or service charge, because those are not always the same thing and the second does not always reach your server.

If a gratuity is already on there, anything further is genuinely optional and is usually about the service you got: a server who kept the table stocked, moved fast on a busy night, or sorted something out for you. People quote all sorts of ranges for what to add on top, and those numbers vary by city, by venue and by who is doing the quoting, so treat any single figure you read as opinion rather than rule. If the check confuses you, ask the server or the host to walk you through the lines. Nobody minds that question, and it is a far better outcome than a table of six arguing over a phone calculator.

One practical note for groups: decide who is holding the card before the bottle arrives, not after. Many venues will not split a bottle service check across six cards, and the person who volunteers at midnight is the person who spends the next month chasing everybody.

### Is bottle service ever worth it?

Sometimes, and the deciding factor is almost never the alcohol. Work out what you are actually buying: guaranteed seating for a group on a night the room is full, a server who comes to you instead of a twenty-minute wait at the bar, a defined place for people to find each other, and a fixed cost you agreed to in advance. For an eight-person birthday on a Saturday, that can be the difference between an event and two hours of standing in a hallway.

It is money set on fire in a few predictable situations. Two people almost never come out ahead. A quiet weeknight where the room is half empty and you could have walked in and sat down is the clearest waste. Buying a table to impress people who did not ask you to is another. And a group that says yes to a minimum nobody did the division on, at eleven at night, with the music loud, is a group that will have a bad conversation at the end.

Do the arithmetic before you go, out loud, with the people who are paying. Divide the minimum by the number of people who have actually committed, not the number in the group text, and compare that to what everyone would have spent anyway. If the per-person number is close, the table is probably worth it. If it is double, you are buying a table, and you should decide whether you want one.

### What is different about a hookah lounge?

Almost everything about the pacing, and one or two things about the manners. A hookah is ordered per hookah, not per person, and a session runs long, so a table of four might buy one or two and stay for two hours. The lounge is selling you time and a seat as much as anything else, so nobody is going to rush you, and nobody is going to be impressed if you rush yourself.

### The etiquette that is easy to get wrong

Leave the coals to the staff. There is a person whose job is managing heat, and moving a coal yourself with the tongs is the single most common first-timer mistake. When you pass the hose, set it down on the table for the next person or hand it over with the mouthpiece pointed away from them rather than putting it directly into their hand. Ask for fresh disposable tips if they are not already on the table, and use one each. Do not blow back into the hose. Keep the hose off the floor. And if the session is fading, ask for a coal change instead of pulling harder.

### What to wear and what to expect afterward

Hookah lounges are generally the most relaxed rooms in this whole article, and many run closer to smart casual than to anything stricter, though the ones attached to a nightlife crowd on a weekend still keep a door policy. The real consideration is smoke. Everything you wear will smell like it, and hair holds it longer than fabric does, so wear something you can wash and skip anything dry-clean only. Layers help, since these rooms swing warm.

### The rules nobody can answer for you

Indoor smoking rules in this metro are set at the municipal level, and the exemptions that let tobacco venues operate indoors vary from one place to the next on both the Missouri and Illinois sides. That is why one lounge has an indoor room, one has a patio only, and one down the road does something else entirely. Do not take a rule from an article, this one included. Call the venue and ask what their room actually is. Expect to be carded at the door, and expect the answer on private events or bringing your own anything to be no unless they tell you otherwise.

### What changes when you go as a group?

Six is the hinge. Below it most lounges will find you something. At six and above you are a logistics problem, and a room with thirty seats has to decide whether to give you a fifth of the floor. Call ahead for anything at six or more, and call earlier in the week than you think you need to.

Arrive together, or at least send four of the six in first. Almost every venue holds a table only for the party that is present, and a host watching two people sit at a six-top for forty minutes on a busy night is a host who is about to have a conversation with you. Put one name on the reservation and let that person do the talking at the door. Sort the money before you leave the house. And ask, when you book, whether the table has a time limit and whether it carries a minimum, because both of those are ordinary and neither is a surprise if you asked.

### How should you call ahead, and what should you listen for?

Say plainly what you want, then compare it against what the venue tells you it can actually do. That gap is the whole signal. You are not interrogating anybody and you are not asking for a quote in writing. You are describing a night out loud so somebody who works there can tell you where it does not fit.

It sounds like this. “Six of us, Saturday around nine, it’s a birthday, we’d like a table where we can hear each other. What’s your dress code, do you have a minimum on a table that size, and how long do we get it for?” That is under thirty seconds and it settles the door, the money and the clock in one call.

Then listen to the shape of the answer. A venue that says “nine is our loudest hour, but if you came at seven thirty I could put you in the back corner with no minimum” has just told you something worth more than the reservation. A venue that cannot tell you its own dress code, or gets vague about what the minimum covers, has also told you something. Neither answer is a verdict on the room. Both are information you did not have when you dialed.

Home a mess before guests arrive? Here is what a home organizer costs.

### What does a good first visit actually look like?

Boring, mostly, which is the point. You arrive dressed a notch above what you guessed, a little earlier than the reservation, with the whole party or most of it. You wait to be seated instead of picking a table. You ask the server what the room is known for rather than ordering defensively, because a lounge bartender given a hint about what you like will nearly always beat you at choosing.

A few small things carry more weight than people expect. Keep your voice at the level of the room rather than the level of your table. Take calls outside. Do not move furniture between tables without asking, since that seating plan is somebody’s night. If the room is full and you have finished, giving the table back earns you a genuinely warmer welcome next time. And tip the person who is doing the work, which at a hookah lounge means the attendant managing your coals as much as the server bringing drinks.

Invited somewhere and not sure what kind of room it is? You can browse lounges on St Louis Near Me Directory, pick two or three that look like your night, and call each with the same short summary: how many of you, what time, what the occasion is, and what you want the table to be like. What they tell you they can do, and what they tell you they cannot, sorts the list faster than any review will.

### For lounge owners across the metro

Think about Nadia standing on that sidewalk in Lafayette Square, and the six friends in Soulard finding out about a minimum after they sat down. Neither of them was trying to break a rule. They could not find the rule. Every one of those people is a reservation you either got or quietly lost, and the loss never shows up anywhere you can measure it.

So publish four things, in plain words, where a phone can find them in ten seconds. Your dress code, written as items rather than adjectives, since “upscale” means nine different outfits and “no gym shoes, no athletic wear, no hats” means one. The hours or nights when that code tightens, because a hotel lounge at four and the same room at ten are two different policies and only one of them is on your website. Whether you take reservations, at what party size, and whether a table carries a time limit or a minimum, stated as a minimum spend so nobody arrives thinking it is a cover.

Fourth, if you run hookah or cigar service, say clearly what your room is: indoor, patio, or both, and what the age policy at the door is. Readers cannot work that out from the outside and they will not call to find out. They will pick the venue that already answered. First-timers are nervous, not difficult, and the rooms that write the rules down get the group of eight that would otherwise have stood in a hallway somewhere else.

### Frequently asked questions

### Q. What is the proper etiquette at a hookah bar?

A.  Let the staff handle the coals, always. Order per hookah rather than per person, and expect the session to run long, since the lounge is selling you time as much as tobacco. Pass the hose by setting it down or offering it mouthpiece-away, use a fresh disposable tip each, and never blow back into the hose. Keep the hose off the floor, ask for a coal change instead of pulling harder, and tip the attendant who is managing your heat all night.

### Q. What to wear at a hookah lounge?

A.  Smart casual covers most of them, and hookah lounges tend to run more relaxed than cocktail rooms, though any lounge attached to a weekend nightlife crowd still keeps a door policy on shoes and athletic wear. The bigger consideration is smoke. Everything you wear will smell like it afterward, so choose something washable and skip anything dry-clean only. Hair holds the smell longer than fabric does. Layers help, because these rooms usually run warm.

### Q. What is the etiquette for bottle service?

A.  Confirm the minimum and what comes with the bottle before you agree to the table, not after the ice arrives. Decide who is holding the card in advance, since many venues will not split that check six ways. Stay at your table, let your server pour rather than reaching across, and do not pull chairs from tables around you. Read the check for an existing gratuity or service charge before adding anything. And give the table back when you are done on a full night.

### Q. How much do you tip for bottle service?

A.  Check the bill first, because bottle service usually carries an automatic gratuity or service charge that is already applied, sometimes alongside a separate table or administrative fee. Look at how the line is labeled, since a service charge and a gratuity are not always the same thing. If one is already there, anything extra is optional and reflects the service you actually got. People quote wildly different ranges for what to add, so treat any single figure as opinion. Ask the server to explain the lines if the check is unclear.

### Q. Does bottle service include alcohol?

A.  Yes, the bottles are the thing you are buying, and the price normally covers the spirit plus ice, glassware, garnishes and a server assigned to your table. What varies is everything around it. Mixers are bundled at some venues and billed separately at others, and tax, service charges and any door fee are their own lines. The quoted number is also usually a minimum spend rather than a flat fee. Ask exactly what comes with the bottle before you commit.

### Q. Why is it called a lounge?

A.  Because the verb came first. To lounge is to recline or linger, and by the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries a lounge was a room built for exactly that: comfortable seating where people waited, talked and stayed put. Hotels, theaters, clubs and later airports all borrowed it for their sitting rooms. The drinking sense grew out of the same idea, a room with seats and service rather than a bar rail. That is also where the lounge suit gets its name, the comfortable day suit rather than formal evening wear.

## What a Wedding Officiant Costs in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-a-wedding-officiant-costs-in-st-louis

The venue in Wildwood was booked eleven months out. Claire and Ben had the caterer, the photographer, the rentals, a shuttle for the parents, and a spreadsheet with a line for all of it. Then Ben’s mother asked, on a Sunday afternoon, who exactly was going to be standing up front marrying them. Nobody had booked anybody. The line was there in the spreadsheet, blank, and neither of them had the faintest idea what number belonged in it.

Other couples around the metro are staring at the same blank line. A pair getting married out in wine country near Hermann want somebody who will make the drive, stay for the rehearsal the night before, and not charge a fortune for the mileage. A couple in Shaw want something short, warm and not religious, and cannot work out whether that should cost more than a traditional ceremony or less. A family in Town and Country assumed their congregation would simply handle it, and have just learned there is a fee, or a donation, or something in between that nobody quite wants to name out loud. All of them are trying to price a person, and a person is harder to price than a tent.

Here is what this covers. What an officiant fee usually includes and what quietly sits outside it, the things that actually move the number up or down, who traditionally pays and when the money changes hands, what a courthouse or civil ceremony changes, what a friend ordained online really costs you in effort, the difference between a house fee at a place of worship and an independent professional’s quoted price, and the Missouri paperwork that is the one part of the day with legal consequences attached. One thing up front: fees, county requirements and license rules vary and they change, so treat everything here as the start of a conversation rather than a quote.

### How much do you normally pay an officiant for a wedding?

Most couples pay one flat fee covering the ceremony plus everything around it: the planning call, a custom-written script, travel, and signing and returning the license. Commonly quoted national ranges run from a modest civil ceremony fee to over a thousand dollars for a fully custom ceremony with rehearsal. Interview two or three and compare what each includes.

Those ranges are worth reading carefully. They are the figures that circulate in national wedding surveys and vendor guides, not measured St. Louis prices, and the metro has officiants sitting comfortably at both ends of them. A number pulled off the internet will not tell you what the person you are about to call charges. It will only tell you whether you are in the right neighborhood before you pick up the phone.

The more useful question is not what the number is but what the number buys. Two officiants can quote within a hundred dollars of each other and be selling completely different things. One spends an hour on the phone with you, writes your ceremony from scratch, runs the rehearsal and handles the license. The other reads a polished standard script, arrives thirty minutes early, and is gone after the recessional. Neither of them is wrong. They are simply not the same purchase, and comparing the two on price alone tells you nothing.

So the reliable move is to shortlist two or three officiants worth interviewing and ask each what their fee includes. Not a line-item breakdown. Just a plain answer to four things: is the rehearsal in there, is the script written for us, do you sign and return the license, and is travel to our venue covered. The differences that come back will sort your shortlist far faster than the prices will.

### What actually drives an officiant’s fee?

Half a dozen things, and none of them is the length of the ceremony. Officiants price the work around the twenty minutes you actually see, not the twenty minutes themselves. Once you know what sits on that list, you can look at two quotes and understand why one is higher, which beats guessing.

### Travel and the date

Distance is real money. An officiant based near the city who is asked to be out in wine country near Hermann for a Saturday afternoon is giving up the entire day, not an hour, and many build a travel charge past a set radius. The date does similar work. Peak Saturdays in late spring and early fall book out first, holiday weekends carry a premium across nearly every wedding category, and a Friday evening or a Sunday morning is usually easier to book and easier on the budget.

### The rehearsal

Attending the rehearsal is a whole extra evening, and it often gets priced that way. Plenty of officiants include it. Plenty charge for it. A few will tell you honestly that a simple processional does not need them there at all. If you have a large wedding party, children walking, or an awkward space, having the person who runs the ceremony also run the rehearsal is usually worth the extra. Ask rather than assume. An officiant who does not appear until the day is not a lesser officiant, they just quoted a different job.

### A custom ceremony or a standard one

This is the single biggest driver. A standard ceremony is a script the officiant already owns, adjusted with your names and a reading you chose. A custom ceremony is an interview, a draft, your edits, a rewrite and a rehearsed read. That is hours of writing before anyone puts on a suit. If you want your story told from the front of the room, you are paying for writing as much as for officiating, and that is the honest way to think about the gap between two quotes.

### Premarital meetings

Some officiants include one or more conversations before the wedding, sometimes structured, sometimes just a long coffee that doubles as research for the script. Some places of worship require a full course of premarital counseling before they will marry you at all, which is less a fee than a calendar commitment. Either way it is time, and time shows up somewhere, in the price or in your schedule.

### The license and the paperwork after it

Collecting the license, completing it correctly and returning it to the issuing county on time is part of the job for most professional officiants. It sounds like a small thing. It is the only part of your wedding day with legal consequences, and somebody who does it every weekend is quietly worth paying for. Ask directly whether they handle it and how they handle it.

### Experience and how full their calendar is

An officiant with years of ceremonies behind them and a booked spring prices like anybody else whose Saturdays are finite. Newer officiants often charge less and many are excellent. What you tend to buy at the higher end is composure: somebody who has already handled a dead microphone, a wedding party twenty minutes late, a grandmother who needed a chair brought up front, and a downpour that moved everything indoors with no warning.

### Who pays the officiant, and when does the money change hands?

Traditionally the groom’s side covered the officiant, and the fee was handed over in an envelope by the best man right before or right after the ceremony. Etiquette guides still describe it that way. In practice, most couples now pay it themselves out of the wedding budget along with everything else, and families contribute wherever they are contributing.

Timing matters more than tradition here. Most officiants take a retainer to hold your date, with the balance due before the wedding, sometimes at the rehearsal and sometimes a week or two out. Ask when the balance is due and how they want it, because nobody wants to be hunting for a checkbook an hour before the ceremony. If a place of worship is involved, the money may go to the institution rather than to the person, and there may be separate amounts for the building, the musician and the officiant.

Tipping an independent officiant who quoted you a flat fee is optional and not expected the way it is in some other categories. Many couples give something anyway when the person clearly did more than they were paid for. Where clergy performed the ceremony and a donation stood in for a fee, a separate personal gift is a common and gracious touch.

### What changes if you have a courthouse or civil ceremony?

Almost everything except the legal effect. A civil ceremony is short, scheduled and performed by an authorized official rather than by someone you hired to write about you. The marriage is exactly as valid as any other. What you give up is the custom script, the rehearsal, the choice of hour and usually the choice of place.

The cost side is simpler but it is not free, and the numbers are set locally. You still need a marriage license from a county Recorder of Deeds, and there may be a separate charge for the ceremony itself depending on who performs it and where. Fees and requirements vary by county and they change, so confirm the current amounts with the Recorder of Deeds in the county where you plan to apply rather than trusting a figure you read somewhere, this page included.

Plenty of couples across the metro quietly do both. A small civil ceremony on a weekday, then a celebration months later with an officiant or a friend leading a ceremony that carries no paperwork at all in front of everyone they love. It solves the budget, the family logistics and the legal side in one move. If that is your plan, say so when you call an officiant, because a ceremony with no license to sign is a different script and sometimes a different fee.

Different fight entirely: what to do when an insurance claim is denied.

### Is having a friend ordained online actually free?

Not really, and the cost is not in dollars. Online ordination is common, widely used, and usually cheap or free to obtain. What it does not come with is any of the work: the writing, the timing, the microphone, the nerves, and the paperwork afterward. Somebody is doing all of that, and if it is not a professional, it is your friend.

Think honestly about what you are asking. Write and rehearse a ten to twenty minute piece of public speaking about two people they love, deliver it in front of everyone those two people know, and hold the emotional temperature of the room steady while a mother starts crying in the second row. Some friends are built for it and it becomes the best part of the whole day. Others spend three months dreading it and read a folded printout in a shaky voice.

Then there is the license, and that is where the real risk sits. Who may legally solemnize a marriage is set by state law, not by the website that ordained your friend in four minutes. Online ordination is common and widely used, but if you are relying on it, confirm acceptance with the Recorder of Deeds in the county issuing your license before the day. The exposure is not that your ceremony gets stopped in front of your guests. It is that the completed license is rejected afterward and you are left with a paperwork problem instead of a marriage certificate.

If you do go this route, help them. Give them a script, or pay somebody to write one and let your friend deliver it. Walk the rehearsal properly. Put one sober, organized person in charge of the license, the pen and the return envelope, and tell them that is their entire job. In our experience that last part is where friend-officiated weddings actually go wrong, not the speaking.

### What is the difference between a house fee and an independent officiant’s price?

One is usually a donation to an institution and the other is a quoted price for a defined service. That distinction explains most of the confusion couples run into when they try to compare the two, because they are not the same kind of transaction and they do not carry the same expectations.

At a place of worship, what you pay might be called a donation, an honorarium, a building or custodial fee, or some combination of all three. There may be separate amounts for the sanctuary, the musician and the officiant. There may be membership expectations, a required premarital course, or limits on dates, readings and music. None of that is hidden, exactly, but a good deal of it is unwritten, and the only way to learn it is to ask the office directly what the total looks like and what will be asked of you.

An independent professional officiant works the other way around. They quote a fee for a defined job, they will tell you what is inside it, and they are generally flexible on venue, hour, script and tone. You are hiring a vendor with a calendar. The trade is that you do not get the building, the community or the tradition that comes attached to a congregation.

A lot of couples land somewhere in the middle: clergy willing to travel to a venue, or an independent officiant perfectly comfortable including religious elements. Both exist across the metro. Say what you want out loud and early, because “somewhere between religious and secular” means five different things to five different officiants.

### How does the Missouri marriage license work, and who signs it?

The license comes from a county Recorder of Deeds, and your officiant signs it and returns it. That is the whole chain, and it is the one piece of the wedding with legal consequences attached. Nearly everything else can go sideways and you are still married at the end of the night. This part cannot.

You apply at a Recorder of Deeds office. The identification required, the fee, whether both of you must appear in person, how soon the license can be used and how long it stays valid are all set locally and all subject to change, so confirm the current details with the Recorder of Deeds in the county where you intend to apply. Do not rely on a friend’s memory from four years ago, and do not rely on this page. Call the county or read the county’s own instructions.

On the day, the officiant completes and signs the license, witnesses sign it if the county requires them, and the officiant returns it to the issuing county inside the window that county sets. After that you request certified copies, which are the documents you will actually hand over for a name change, a bank, a lease or a benefits form. The souvenir certificate somebody hands you at the ceremony is not that.

Who may legally solemnize a marriage is set by state law. Online ordination is common and widely used, and a great many weddings across the metro are performed by ordained friends with no trouble whatsoever. Even so, if that is your plan, confirm acceptance with the issuing Recorder of Deeds ahead of time. The risk sits with the license being rejected, not with the ceremony.

One habit worth stealing from officiants who do this every weekend: get the license into their hands before the ceremony, not after. A license sitting in a car, a hotel room, or the bottom of a maid of honor’s bag is the most common near-disaster in this whole part of the day.

### How do you interview two or three officiants?

Get on a call and say what you want out loud. This is not a bidding process, and treating it like one gets you a cheap ceremony that sounds like it was written about somebody else. Shortlist two or three officiants worth talking to, then have the same conversation with each of them.

Tell them four things. What you want the ceremony to feel like, in plain words: short and warm, formal and traditional, funny, tearful, over in ten minutes. How long it should run. Whether you want it religious, secular or somewhere in between, and if in between, which parts specifically. And whether you want them at the rehearsal.

Then stop talking and listen. Some will ask questions back, about how you met, what your families are like, what you are nervous about. Some will describe what they usually do and leave it there. Some will gently tell you the thing you did not want to hear about the reading you picked. Compare what you asked for against what each one is actually prepared to deliver, and notice how quickly and how clearly they answer.

The gap between your ask and their answer is the signal. Not the fee. An officiant who costs two hundred dollars more and comes back the same afternoon with a thought about the two of you is a better buy than one who is cheaper and vague, and you can usually tell which is which inside a single phone call.

Ask one more question before you book. What happens if you are sick that weekend? A professional will have an answer ready, a colleague they trust or a stated policy. It takes ten seconds and it tells you a great deal about how seriously they take the date.

Still staring at a blank line in the budget? You can browse wedding officiants on St Louis Near Me Directory, pick two or three worth interviewing, and call each with the same short summary: your date, your venue, how long you want the ceremony to run, and whether you want it religious, secular or somewhere between. What they ask you back, and how fast they answer, will tell you more than any price list.

Go back to Claire and Ben in Wildwood, looking at an empty cell in a spreadsheet. They are not hunting for the cheapest officiant in the metro. They are trying to work out what an officiant costs at all and what they get for it, and until somebody answers that, they will keep putting the decision off. ### Frequently asked questions

### Q. Who traditionally pays for the officiant?

A.  Traditionally the groom’s side covered it, and the fee was handed to the officiant by the best man just before or just after the ceremony. Etiquette guides still describe it that way. In practice most couples now pay it out of the wedding budget, with families contributing wherever they are contributing. What matters more than the tradition is the timing. Most officiants take a retainer to hold the date, with the balance due at the rehearsal or shortly before the wedding, so ask when they want it and how.

### Q. What are common officiant mistakes?

A.  The license first, and worst: not collecting it before the ceremony, filling it in incorrectly, or failing to return it to the issuing county on time. After that come the recoverable ones. Mispronouncing a name, running long when the couple asked for short, forgetting to invite everyone to be seated, speaking away from the microphone, or reading a script that was clearly written about somebody else. A careful officiant confirms names phonetically, rehearses the read out loud, and treats the paperwork as the real job.

### Q. What is the 30-5 minute rule for weddings?

A.  It is planning shorthand rather than a rule anybody enforces, and people use it to mean slightly different things, so be careful repeating it as a definition. What actually matters underneath it is ceremony length and arrival buffer. Most non-religious ceremonies run roughly twenty to thirty minutes and religious ones often longer, while guests are typically asked to arrive around half an hour before the stated start. Build in a buffer for late arrivals, then confirm one real start time with your officiant, your venue and your photographer so all three are working from the same schedule.

### Q. How to make your officiant stand out?

A.  By being specific in public. Say what your ceremonies actually sound like, publish a starting fee and what it covers, state clearly whether you write custom scripts, name the styles you are comfortable with from fully religious to entirely secular, and say how far you travel. Post a short video or audio clip so couples can hear your voice instead of guessing at it. Then answer inquiries fast. In a category where couples are anxious and usually behind schedule, the officiant who replies clearly within a day very often wins the booking.

### Q. What color should an officiant wear to a wedding?

A.  Something that disappears into the background of every photograph. Dark neutrals are the safe default: navy, charcoal, black, deep gray. Avoid white, ivory and champagne, avoid matching the wedding party unless the couple asked for it, and avoid loud patterns that pull the eye in close-ups. Clergy wear what their tradition calls for. The rule that never fails is simply asking the couple, since some weddings have a color story and some have a strict dress code, and the officiant stands in very nearly every photograph of the ceremony.

### Q. What is the typical wedding budget for 2026?

A.  There is no honest single number. Published averages vary enormously by survey, by region and by who happened to be asked, so treat any figure you see as one sample rather than a benchmark. Guest count drives the budget more than anything else, because catering, bar, rentals, invitations and the size of venue you need all scale with it. After that come the date, the venue type, whether furniture and tenting have to be brought in, and how much photography and video you want. Set the guest list first, then build everything else around it.
