## St. Louis Talent Agencies: How to Get Signed
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/st-louis-talent-agencies-how-to-get-signed

The message landed at 11:40 on a Tuesday night. “We love your look.” Dana had posted four photos from a friend’s wedding in Soulard, nothing staged and nothing professional, and by breakfast an account with an agency-sounding name wanted her height, her measurements and a phone number. She sent all three. The next reply asked for a registration fee and a headshot session with a photographer they named. Dana is thirty-one, works the front desk at a dental office, and had never once thought of herself as talent. She almost paid it.

That same week, a mother in Bethalto got stopped at a mall kiosk because a stranger with a lanyard thought her seven-year-old had “the look,” and she left with a card and an appointment she could not quite explain to her husband later. A guitarist in The Grove who has played bars for a decade wants commercial voice work and cannot tell an agency from a casting website that bills him monthly. Nobody here did anything foolish. They walked into a business where the money is supposed to move in one specific direction, and nobody ever told them which one.

Here is what this covers. How a legitimate talent agent gets paid, and why that single fact sorts out almost everything else. The difference between an agent, a manager, a casting director and a paid casting website. What a submission actually contains, and what a headshot has to do. Whether you can get signed with no experience at all. How to check that an agency is what it says it is, including the licensing question you are allowed to ask out loud. What the actors’ unions change, and why a first paid job is usually non-union. How long a response really takes. Where auditions get posted around the metro. And at the end, a note to the agencies themselves about what they ought to be publishing.

### Does it cost money to join a talent agency?

Signing with a legitimate talent agency should not require an up-front fee. An agent earns a commission out of work they book for you, paid after you get paid. Money moving the other way, registration fees, a mandatory paid headshot session with their photographer, required classes you must buy before representation, is the oldest warning sign in the business.

Turn it around and it gets even clearer. An agent takes a percentage of what they earn you, so if you never book, they never earn. That structure is the entire reason an agent has any motivation to submit you at all. An operation that collects at the door has already been paid, whether you work or not, and it does not need you to book anything.

This does not mean the work is free. Real costs exist and honest people say so out loud. Headshots cost money. A demo reel costs money. Classes cost money, and good ones are worth it. The distinction is not whether you ever spend a dollar. It is whether an agency requires you to spend it with them, or with one named vendor they steer you to, as the condition of being represented. That is the line, and it is a bright one.

So if a fee comes up before any job has been booked, stop and ask two plain questions in writing. What exactly is this payment for? And is representation conditional on my paying it? Those are easy questions for a working agency to answer in a sentence. Watch what comes back. An answer that arrives as urgency, a deadline, a slot that will be given away tonight, has told you everything.

### How do talent agents get paid?

Out of commission on the jobs they book for you, deducted after the client or production pays out. The work comes first, the payment comes second, the commission comes out of that payment. Percentages vary by market, by the category of work, and by whether the job is union or not, and the number that applies to you belongs in your written agreement.

You will find percentages quoted all over the internet, and we would rather you did not carry one into a meeting as a fact. Rates differ across print, commercial, film, theatrical and voice work, and union agreements limit commissions in ways non-union work does not. Ask the agency what they take, on which categories of work, and then read it on the page before you sign it. A number said out loud is not a term.

Then read the rest of the agreement, because it matters more than the pitch did. How long is the term? Is it exclusive, and exclusive in which categories, so you can still take a theater job or a local voice gig on your own? How is commission calculated, and when does it get paid over to you? How does either side end this? If you are signing on behalf of a child, that is a conversation worth having with somebody who reads contracts for a living before anyone signs anything.

### What is the difference between an agent, a manager, a casting director and a casting website?

Four different jobs, and people confuse them constantly. An agent submits you for work and takes a commission on what you book. A manager advises your career for a separate cut. A casting director works for the production and never works for you. A paid casting website is a subscription listing service, not representation at all.

### The agent

Agents have relationships with the people who hire. They get the breakdown, decide who on their roster fits, submit you, negotiate the rate, and collect commission when you are paid. A small market like ours means a smaller roster and a lot more generalists: the same agency may handle commercial, print, industrial and voice work rather than specializing the way a coastal shop does.

### The manager

A manager takes a longer view. They shape what you go out for, who you study with, how you present. Managers take their own percentage on top of the agent’s, which is not a scam by itself, it is simply a second cut of the same job. Most people starting out in this metro do not need one, and paying two percentages before you have booked anything is a hard way to start.

### The casting director

A casting director is hired by the production to find people. They do not represent you, they do not owe you feedback, and they are not the person to pester. They are, however, worth being good to, because the room remembers who was easy to work with. A casting director who charges you to audition is not casting anything.

### The paid casting website

Subscription sites list open calls and let you submit yourself. Some are genuinely useful, particularly for background and non-union work. None of them is an agency. Paying a monthly fee to see listings is a service you chose to buy, which is a completely different transaction from paying somebody for the privilege of being represented. Keep the two categories separate in your head and most of the confusion goes away.

### How do I get signed to a talent agency?

You submit, properly, to agencies that are actually open to new talent, and you make it easy to say yes. That means a current headshot, an honest resume, real measurements and sizes, and a short note that says what you are and what you want. Then you wait, and you keep working while you wait.

### What a submission contains

Keep it boring and complete. One headshot, taken recently enough to look like you today. A one-page resume listing training, any credits, and special skills that are genuinely skills, not hobbies. Your height, sizes, hair and eye color. A phone number that you answer. If you have footage, a link, kept under two minutes. And an email that says in three sentences who you are, what categories you want to be submitted for, and that you are seeking representation.

### Headshots that do the job

A headshot has exactly one job: to look like the person who walks through the door. Overworked lighting, heavy retouching and a haircut you no longer have all work against you, because the room feels misled the second you arrive. You do not need the most expensive photographer in the metro. You do need current, well lit, and recognizably you. And you never need the specific photographer an agency insists you use.

### The unions, and why a first job is usually non-union

The actors’ unions set minimum rates and working conditions on covered productions, and joining changes what you can accept afterward. Most people in this metro start on non-union work: industrials, local commercial spots, corporate video, background. That is normal and it is not a lesser path. Understand the eligibility rules before you make a decision you cannot reverse, and do not let anyone tell you a union card is something they can sell you.

### Can I get an acting agent with no experience?

Yes, and it happens more often in a market this size than in a large one. Agencies here regularly sign people with no credits, particularly for commercial, print and industrial work, where the client wants a believable pharmacist or a plausible dad rather than a trained lead. What they will not sign is somebody unprepared.

No experience is not the same as no preparation. Take a class. Do a student film or two. Get on stage with a community theater company for a season. Read a commercial script out loud into your phone until you stop sounding like you are reading. Every one of those gives an agent something to put on a page, and more importantly it means you will not fall apart the first time somebody puts a camera on you.

Also be honest about availability, because it is the thing that quietly ends most beginner careers here. Auditions come with a day of notice and shoots happen on weekdays. If you cannot leave your job at two in the afternoon on a Wednesday, say so up front rather than turning down the first three things you are offered. An agent stops submitting somebody who cannot go.

### How to tell if a talent agent is legit?

Follow the money first, then check the paperwork. A legitimate agency is paid out of your bookings, has a real office and a real phone, will tell you which categories it works in, and will let you take an agreement away and read it. An agency that needs money from you today is answering the question for you.

In both Missouri and Illinois, talent agencies are regulated at the state level, and the requirements differ on each side of the river. We are not going to quote you a statute number here, because the wrong specific is worse than none at all. What you can do is ask directly: how are you licensed to operate as a talent agency in this state, and how are you paid? A working agency answers both in a sentence and does not act insulted that you asked.

Then run the ordinary checks. Does the agency have an address you can find, and does anyone answer the phone during business hours? Are the people they represent findable, working, and willing to talk to you? Does the written agreement match what was said in the room? Did anyone promise you work, which nobody honest ever does, because an agent can promise submissions and nothing more?

And trust the pressure signal above all of it. Legitimate representation moves slowly and unglamorously. Somebody who found you in a mall or in your direct messages, told you that you have the look, and then produced a payment link within two exchanges is running a different business entirely.

Between gigs and watching every dollar? See how St. Louis corner store prices compare.

### How long do talent agents take to respond?

Longer than feels reasonable, and often not at all. Weeks is normal for a cold submission, and silence is the most common outcome anyone gets. Small agencies read submissions between the actual job of servicing clients, so your email lands in a pile that gets opened when the booking calendar allows it, not the day you sent it.

One polite follow-up after a few weeks is fine. Two is pushing it. Three is a decision they will make about you rather than about your work. Keep the follow-up short, attach the headshot again so nobody has to go looking, and say plainly that you are still seeking representation and still available. Then let it go and submit somewhere else.

Here is the part people take too personally. No response is very rarely a verdict on you. Rosters fill by type, and an agency that already has four women in your age range and coloring cannot use a fifth, no matter how good you are. That is a math problem, not a talent problem. Six months later the roster looks different and the same submission gets read differently.

### Where can I find auditions in St. Louis?

In four places, and most people only ever look at one. Community and professional theater companies post their own open calls. Universities post student film notices. State and regional film offices publish production notices when a shoot comes through. And the largest category, agency submissions, you never see at all, because they go to represented talent.

Theater is the easiest door to walk through without representation, and it is where a lot of people around the metro build their first page of credits. Companies publish audition dates, what to prepare, and whether the roles are paid. Student and independent film pays little or nothing but gives you footage, which is currency later. Background work on anything shooting in the region is worth doing once, if only to learn how a set behaves.

Paid casting sites fill the gap for self-submitted commercial and background work. Use them with your eyes open: you are buying access to a listing feed, and the ratio of listings to bookings is not flattering. What none of these replace is an agent, because the commercial and industrial work that actually pays in this market mostly moves through agency submissions that are never posted publicly anywhere.

### How do you pick which agencies to approach?

Shortlist two or three worth interviewing, then say plainly what you are and what you want. A thirty-one-year-old with no credits looking for commercial and print work, available weekdays with a day of notice. Then compare that against what each agency says it can actually do with you. The gap between your ask and their answer is the signal.

Ask concrete things and write down what you hear. Are you open to new talent right now? Which categories do you submit for most: commercial, print, industrial, voice, film? How are you paid, and on which categories? Is the agreement exclusive, and for how long? Roughly how many people do you represent in my range? What happens at a first meeting, and does it cost anything?

Then listen for fit rather than for flattery. An agency that says “we do mostly industrial and corporate work, and you would go out for that” is more useful to you than one telling you how special you are. Praise is free. A specific description of the work they would send you on is not, and it is the closest thing to a forecast anybody in this business can honestly give.

One more question, and it is the one that ends the conversation fastest when it needs ending. Ask what you will be expected to pay for, and when. If the answer involves any money before a single booking, you have your comparison already.

Not sure who to approach first? You can browse talent agencies on St Louis Near Me Directory, pick two or three worth contacting, and send each one the same short note: what you are, which categories you want, your availability, and that you are seeking representation. What comes back, how fast, and whether anybody mentions a fee will tell you plenty before you sign a thing.

### For talent agencies across the metro

Think about Dana at 11:40 on a Tuesday night, and the mother in Bethalto holding a card from a mall kiosk. Both of them wanted the same handful of facts before they replied to anybody. Neither could find those facts on a single website in this market, which is exactly why the people charging registration fees got to them first.

So publish them. State how you are paid, in one plain sentence, and that there is no fee to be represented. Say whether you are open to new talent right now, and update that when it changes. List exactly what a submission needs: headshot, resume, sizes, contact, and where to send it. Give a response window, even an unflattering one, because “we read submissions monthly and only contact people we want to meet” stops a hundred follow-up emails.

Then add the line almost nobody publishes: what happens at a first meeting. Who will be in the room, how long it takes, whether anything is signed that day, whether a parent stays for a minor, and that it costs nothing. Say which categories you actually book so people stop submitting for work you do not handle. Agencies that put those things in writing get better submissions and fewer phone calls, and they make it considerably harder for the fee operations to keep working this metro.

### Frequently asked questions

### Q. Is it hard to get signed by a talent agency?

A.  It is competitive but not mysterious, and a smaller market helps. Most rejections are about roster fit, not ability: an agency with four people in your age range and look cannot use a fifth. A current headshot, an honest resume, real availability and a submission that follows instructions puts you ahead of most of the pile. Silence is normal. Keep submitting.

### Q. How do I get picked up by talent agencies?

A.  Submit properly to agencies open to new talent, and give them nothing to fix. Current headshot, one-page resume, sizes and measurements, a phone number you answer, and three sentences saying what categories you want. Build a little something to point at first: a class, a student film, a season with a community theater company. Then follow up once, politely, and move on to the next name.

### Q. How do talent agents get paid?

A.  By commission on work they book for you, taken out after the client or production pays. No booking means no commission, which is the whole reason the incentive works. Rates differ by category and by whether the job is union, and the figure that applies to you should be written into your agreement. An agency asking for money before any booking is not working on commission.

### Q. What percentage do talent agents take?

A.  It varies by category and by whether the job falls under a union agreement, and we are not going to hand you a number to treat as local fact. Commercial, print, industrial, voice and theatrical work are often commissioned differently. Ask the agency what they take on each category, then confirm it appears in the written agreement before you sign. Verbal figures are not terms.

### Q. What is the average fee for a talent agent?

A.  There should not be a fee to you at all. A talent agent is compensated through commission on bookings, not through payments you make to join, register, be listed, or get photographed. Any “fee” presented before you have earned anything deserves two written questions: what is this for, and is representation conditional on paying it? Real costs like headshots and classes should never be tied to one required vendor.

### Q. How long do talent agents take to respond?

A.  Weeks is normal for a cold submission, and no reply at all is the most common result. Small agencies read submissions around the work of servicing existing clients. Send one polite follow-up after a few weeks with the headshot attached again, then let it go. Rosters change, so a submission that goes nowhere in March can land differently in September.

### Q. How to get noticed by a talent agent?

A.  Be findable, be current, and be easy to book. A headshot that looks like you today, a resume that adds up, sizes that are accurate, and availability that survives a weekday afternoon call. Do the small work that creates credits: classes, student films, community theater, local industrial shoots. Referrals from people already working carry more weight here than any social media following does.

### Q. Where can I find auditions in St. Louis?

A.  Theater companies post their own open calls with dates and what to prepare. Universities list student film notices. State and regional film offices publish production notices when a shoot comes through the region. Paid casting sites carry self-submit commercial and background listings. The biggest pool, agency-only submissions, is never posted publicly, which is the practical argument for getting represented.

## St. Louis Moving Truck Rental: Costs and Sizes
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/st-louis-moving-truck-rental-costs-and-sizes

The number on the screen was one thing. The number at the counter was another. Marisol had booked a truck three weeks ahead for a Saturday move out of Lafayette Square, screenshotted the quote, and told her brother-in-law what the whole day would cost. When she signed the paperwork that morning, the total had grown by mileage, by a coverage waiver she had never thought about, by an environmental fee she could not explain, and by a hold on her card that would not clear for a week. Nothing was hidden, exactly. It was all written down somewhere. She simply had not been reading the part of the page that decides the price.

That morning repeats all over the metro. A couple in Weldon Spring take the smaller truck to save money, make three round trips, and spend more on miles and gas than the bigger truck would have cost outright. A man in High Ridge clips a low canopy at a drive-through he has driven a car under a hundred times. A family leaving Mascoutah books a one-way and discovers the pricing works nothing like the local rate they had been comparing it against. Nobody here was careless. They priced the sticker instead of the trip.

Here is what this covers. How truck rental is actually priced, and why the advertised day rate is almost never the total. The two pricing models, per-mile and flat-window, and how to work out which one wins on your route. Who rents trucks besides the obvious name. The real fee categories, none of which are secret. How to size a truck to a bedroom count and to whether you own a refrigerator. One-way rentals and why they behave differently. Driving a box truck without hitting anything. Loading order. Whether your own auto policy follows you into a rental truck, which is the question people get wrong most often. And at the end, a note to the local rental and moving outfits about what they ought to be publishing.

### How much is it to rent a moving truck per day?

There is no single day rate. Most rentals price as a low advertised base day rate plus a charge for every mile, with fuel returned full, damage coverage, an environmental fee, and possible after-hours or one-way surcharges on top. Price your actual route, because the advertised rate is almost never the total.

Do not take a dollar figure off an article, this one included. Rates move by company, by location, by truck size, by day of the week and by season, and the last weekend of the month is the busiest window in the business. What you can rely on is the shape of the bill. Base rate, miles, fuel, coverage, fees, taxes, deposit. Build your budget from those seven lines and confirm each one with the company you are actually renting from.

### Do all moving truck rentals charge per mile?

No. Two models dominate. The first is a low advertised day rate plus a charge for every mile you drive, which is what most consumer truck rental counters run. The second is a flat-rate short-window rental, often sold in hours or quarter-days with local miles included, which is common at retail and at some local yards.

Which one is cheaper depends entirely on your mileage, so price your actual route on both before you book. A move from one side of Shrewsbury to the other is a short, dense, many-trips job where a flat window can be excellent value. A move from the Metro East out to St. Charles County is a long-haul day where per-mile charges stack quickly and a bigger truck with fewer trips usually wins.

The arithmetic takes five minutes and it is worth doing on paper. Map the one-way distance between the two addresses. Multiply by two for a round trip, then by the number of trips you honestly expect, and add the run to the lot and back at each end. People forget the lot. A truck rented in Spanish Lake for a move within north county can rack up twenty miles before a single box is loaded, and on a per-mile contract those miles are not free.

### Who rents moving trucks besides U-Haul?

Plenty of places. The well-known national options include Penske, Budget and Enterprise alongside U-Haul, and large home improvement retailers rent trucks by the hour or by a short flat window. Beyond those, independent rental yards, some self-storage facilities and a handful of local moving companies keep trucks available to the public.

### The national counters

These are the ones with the widest fleet, the most size options and, importantly, the ability to do a genuine one-way rental between cities. They are also the ones whose advertised rate is most likely to be a base plus miles. Rates, mileage charges and terms differ by company and change over time, so confirm the current numbers with the company itself rather than with any article.

### Retail, storage and local yards

A home improvement store truck is built for a different job: a short, local, round-trip haul that comes back to the same parking lot, usually in a flat-rate block of time. That is a genuinely good fit for a one-load apartment move or a mattress and a dresser. It is a poor fit for a full house across the metro, because the clock runs whether you are driving or carrying.

Storage facilities and small local outfits are the ones people overlook. Some keep a box truck for tenants, sometimes bundled with a rental agreement, sometimes hourly. Availability is thin and it is first come, so call early in the week for a weekend. A local yard in Caseyville or a storage office in south county may have exactly one truck, and the answer is either yes or no.

### What are common U-Haul hidden fees?

None of them are truly hidden, and the categories are the same across the major companies. Expect lines for mileage, fuel, damage coverage, an environmental fee, dolly and pad rental, after-hours drop-off, late return, cleaning, a one-way surcharge where it applies, taxes, and a security hold placed against your card.

Mileage and fuel are the two that move the total most, and they are the two people underestimate. Damage coverage is the next largest and the one most likely to be declined at the counter by someone who assumes their own policy has it handled. The environmental fee is a small flat charge that surprises people purely because they have never seen it before.

The smaller lines are behavioral. Return the truck after the lot closes and you may pay an after-hours drop-off charge. Return it late and the clock restarts in whatever increment the contract uses. Return it with the cargo floor full of packing peanuts and you can be charged for cleaning. Take the dolly and the furniture pads that were sitting in the cargo box and you have rented them, whether you meant to or not.

The security hold is not a fee, but it behaves like one in your bank account. It is an authorization against your card that sits there until the rental closes out and the bank releases it, which can take several business days. If your moving week is tight on cash, that hold matters more than the environmental fee ever will.

The counter is the place to settle all of it. Ask them to walk the estimate line by line, then ask two questions: which of these lines changes if I bring it back late, and which changes if I bring it back short on fuel. A clear answer takes ninety seconds. If it does not come easily, you have learned something useful about the location before you hand over a card.

### Should I get a 15 or 20 ft U-Haul?

Size to your bedroom count and to whether appliances are coming. As a working rule, a studio or small one-bedroom fits a small van or a ten to twelve foot box, a full one to two bedroom fits the mid-size fifteen foot class, and a three bedroom house wants twenty feet or more. When in doubt, go up one size.

### Sizing by what you actually own

Bedroom count is a proxy, not a measurement, and it fails in both directions. A one-bedroom belonging to someone who has lived there nine years, with a garage, a workshop bench and a treadmill, is not a one-bedroom load. A three-bedroom house where two of the bedrooms hold a bed and nothing else is smaller than the chart says. Walk the rooms and count the large items rather than the doors.

### Appliances and the awkward pieces

Appliances change the answer immediately. A refrigerator, a washer and a dryer eat floor space, they must stand upright, and they need to go in early against the cab where the weight belongs. A sectional sofa, a large dining table, a piano or a full-size mattress set all behave the same way: they set the minimum size before a single box is considered. Measure the widest piece you own and confirm it clears the truck’s door opening, not just the box length.

### Why one bigger truck usually beats two trips

This is the mistake that costs the most money in the metro. Renting down a size to save on the base rate looks smart until you have made a second round trip. On a per-mile contract you have now paid for every one of those extra miles, plus the fuel, plus three or four hours of a Saturday you were not planning to spend, plus whatever the friends who agreed to help think about the second load. One oversized truck almost always wins. A half-empty cargo box is cheap. A second trip is not.

### Can you rent a truck for a one-way trip?

Yes, from the national companies, and that is the main reason people use them. A one-way rental lets you pick the truck up at one location and drop it at a different one, typically an assigned destination location rather than any lot you choose. Local yards and retail programs generally require the truck back at the same lot.

One-way pricing usually behaves differently from local pricing. Rather than a small day rate plus every mile, a one-way is commonly quoted as a single rate that bundles a set number of days and a set number of miles for your specific route, with charges if you exceed either. That is why a one-way quote and a local quote cannot be compared line for line, and why the family from Mascoutah felt blindsided. They were reading two different products.

Availability drives one-way rates as much as distance does. These companies have to keep trucks pointed where demand is, so the same route can price differently in different weeks and in different directions. Book as far ahead as you can, especially at the end of a month, and confirm three things in writing: the pickup location, the assigned drop-off location, and the day and hour the truck is due.

Replacing what did not survive the move? Start with our St. Louis department stores guide.

### What are some tips for driving a moving truck?

Drive it like the tall, heavy, slow-stopping vehicle it is. Know your height and read every clearance sign. Take turns wider and later than feels right. Leave far more braking distance than you would in a car. Never reverse without a spotter on the ground. Then slow everything down by about a third.

### Height and clearance

Find the clearance height, which is usually posted in the cab or on the door frame, and say it out loud before you pull away. Then write it on a sticky note on the dash. The things that catch people are not highway bridges; they are drive-throughs, bank canopies, parking garages, fast food overhangs, gas station awnings and low tree limbs over a residential street. A car’s worth of experience with a route tells you nothing about a truck’s roof.

### Turns, lanes and stopping

A box truck needs a wider arc and a later turn-in, because the rear wheels track well inside the front ones and will climb a curb or clip a pole you thought you had cleared. Stay out of the fast lane, use the mirrors constantly since there is no rear window, and check them before every lane change rather than relying on a glance. Braking distance is the big one. A loaded truck carries momentum a car does not, so double your following gap on the highway and start slowing far earlier at lights and ramps.

### Reverse, parking and the ramp

Do not reverse alone. Put someone on the ground where you can see them in the mirror, agree on hand signals before you start, and stop the moment you lose sight of them. Think about the exit before you park: pulling into a tight driveway in Lafayette Square is easy, and backing out of it around parked cars at dusk is not. When you set the ramp, make sure the truck is in park with the brake set and the ramp is fully seated before anyone walks a dolly up it.

### Does my car insurance cover renting a U-Haul?

Often it does not, and this is the assumption that costs people the most. Many personal auto policies limit coverage to passenger vehicles and small trucks, and large rental box trucks commonly fall outside that. Credit card rental benefits frequently exclude them too. Check your own policy and the counter’s coverage rather than assuming either one has you covered.

Make the call before moving day, not at the counter with a line behind you. Ring your agent, tell them the size and class of truck you are renting and the dates, and ask plainly whether your liability, collision and comprehensive extend to it. Ask the same about a towed trailer or a car dolly if you are pulling one, because that is very often a separate answer.

Then ask the rental counter what their coverage products actually cover: damage to the truck itself, damage to your loaded belongings, liability to other people and property, and what the deductible is on each. Those are usually different products, and cargo is the one people assume is included when it is not. Declining coverage is a reasonable decision if you have confirmed you are covered elsewhere. Declining it because you assume you are is a gamble against the cost of a truck roof.

### What to pack first in a moving truck?

Heaviest first, loaded tight against the cab wall. Appliances, the washer, dryer and refrigerator, plus dressers, bookcases, filing cabinets and the heaviest boxes go in that front section. Weight belongs over and just behind the front axle, because a truck loaded tail-heavy handles badly and stops worse.

Build in vertical tiers from the front of the box toward the door. Heavy and square at the bottom, mattresses and sofa cushions upright along the walls, mirrors and table tops standing on edge between padded pieces rather than lying flat where something will be set on them. Fill every gap. Air is what lets a load shift, and a load that shifts on the first hard stop will keep shifting the rest of the way.

Use the tie rails. Run ratchet straps across the face of each tier every few feet as you build it, rather than throwing one strap over everything at the end. Furniture pads go between anything that can rub, and pads are cheap insurance on a dining table. Load the things you need first at the new place last, so they come off first: tools, a box of cleaning supplies, the bedding, the coffee maker, and whatever keeps small children occupied for an hour.

### How do you pick a local truck rental or moving outfit?

Shortlist two or three worth calling, then say plainly what you have and what you expect. Two-bedroom apartment, second floor, no elevator, one refrigerator, moving eleven miles on the last Saturday of the month, need the truck from eight until four. Then compare that against what each one is prepared to deliver. The gap is the signal.

Ask concrete questions and write the answers down. What size do you actually have available that day? Is it priced per mile or as a flat window? Is fuel expected back full? What does your coverage include and what is the deductible? Is a dolly and are pads included or rented separately? What time do you close, and is there a charge for an after-hours return? How much is the hold on my card and when does it release?

Not sure who has the right truck on your date? You can browse truck rental on St Louis Near Me Directory, pick two or three worth calling, and give each one the same short summary: the size of the load, the distance, the date and the hours you need it. What they quote back, and how clearly they explain the miles and the fuel, tells you plenty before you put a card down.

### For truck rental and moving outfits across the metro

Think about Marisol at that counter with a screenshot that no longer matched the paperwork, and the couple in Weldon Spring making a third round trip because they rented down a size. Both of them wanted the same small set of facts before they booked. Neither could find them anywhere in writing.

So publish them. Put up two or three all-in pricing examples for real, ordinary jobs, an apartment move across town and a house move across the metro, showing the base, the miles, the fuel expectation and the fees as separate lines. Say whether you price per mile or by a flat window. Say whether you do one-way at all, because that single sentence saves everybody a phone call. State plainly what your coverage covers, what it does not, and what the deductible is.

Then add the operational details nobody publishes and everybody needs. Whether a dolly and furniture pads are included or rented. Your cutoff time for same-day pickup and your closing time for returns. Whether after-hours drop-off is available and whether it costs anything. What size hold goes on a card and how long it takes to release. What documents a renter has to bring. List the truck sizes you stock with the door opening dimensions, not just the box length, because that is what decides whether a sofa goes in. The outfits that put these in writing get customers who arrive already decided, and far fewer arguments at the counter on a Saturday morning.

### Frequently asked questions

### Q. Is renting a moving truck worth it?

A.  For most local moves, yes, if you have the labor. Renting is nearly always cheaper than full-service movers, and the trade is your weekend and your back. It stops being worth it when the load needs multiple trips, when nobody can lift a refrigerator down a staircase, or when the drive is long enough that per-mile charges close the gap with hiring help.

### Q. How much does it cost to hire someone to drive a moving truck?

A.  It varies too much to quote, and it is usually sold as labor rather than as a driver alone. Some moving companies offer a driver plus crew on a truck you rent; some labor-only services load and unload but will not drive a rental. Rates are commonly hourly with a minimum, and insurance requirements differ by company, so ask who carries the coverage while your rental is being driven.

### Q. Is it cheaper to rent a U-Haul or a truck from Home Depot?

A.  It depends entirely on your mileage and your hours. The two common models are a low advertised day rate plus per-mile charges, and a flat-rate short-window local rental. Flat windows tend to win on very short, quick, round-trip hauls; per-mile day rentals tend to win when you need the truck all day. Price your actual route on both and confirm current rates with each company.

### Q. How does U-Haul charge for one way?

A.  One-way rentals are generally quoted as a single route-based rate that includes a set number of days and a set number of miles, with additional charges if you exceed either. That is a different product from a local rental priced by day plus mile, which is why the two quotes never compare cleanly. Confirm the current rate, the included days and miles, and the assigned drop-off location with the company.

### Q. Should I get a 15 or 20 ft U-Haul?

A.  Go by load, not by label. The mid-size fifteen foot class generally suits a one to two bedroom home; twenty feet and up suits a three bedroom or anything with a garage, a workshop or a full appliance set. If you are genuinely on the line between them, take the larger truck. A half-empty cargo box costs far less than a second round trip across the metro.

### Q. Does my car insurance cover renting a U-Haul?

A.  Do not assume it does. Personal auto policies commonly cover passenger vehicles and small trucks, and a large rental box truck often falls outside that; credit card rental benefits frequently exclude them as well. Call your agent with the truck size and dates, ask specifically about liability, collision and any trailer, then ask the rental counter what their coverage covers and what the deductible is.

### Q. Do I need a special license to drive a rental moving truck?

A.  Consumer moving trucks are built to be driven on an ordinary license, which is exactly why they are rented to the public. Companies set their own minimum age and documentation rules, so confirm those when you book. What you do need is caution: the truck is taller, wider and much slower to stop than anything you drive daily, and no license requirement prepares you for that.

### Q. What size truck do I need for a studio or one-bedroom?

A.  A cargo van or a small ten to twelve foot box usually handles a studio, and a small one-bedroom often fits the same range. Step up to the mid-size class if you own a full-size mattress set, a sofa that is not a loveseat, a treadmill, or a garage and basement worth of stored boxes. Count the large items rather than the bedrooms.

## What Vegan Food Actually Means in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-vegan-food-actually-means-in-st-louis

The green beans were the problem. Gene had the whole meal worked out: a lentil loaf, a big salad, roasted potatoes, and a pot of beans on the back burner. His daughter had gone vegan in March and this was the first dinner in Glendale since. She ate everything and left the beans, and only when he pushed did she say why. He had finished them the way he always had, a spoon of butter and the last of Sunday’s chicken stock. Four hours of cooking, and he missed it on the one dish he never thought about.

Same week, different version, in a Southampton dining room. Ruthie ordered “the veggie option” because it was the only thing on the menu without an animal in the name. It was good. She said so. Then the server mentioned, cheerfully, that the risotto gets a knob of butter stirred in at the end. She was not upset either. She just wished she had known to ask, and she genuinely did not know what she was supposed to ask.

Here is what this covers. What vegan actually means, and how it differs from vegetarian and from “plant-based.” The foods that make up most of an ordinary vegan week. The ingredients that quietly are not vegan, which is where nearly every accident happens: butter and cream finishing a vegetable dish, chicken or beef stock in soup and beans, eggs in pasta and batter, honey, gelatin, whey and casein, anchovy in Worcestershire and Caesar dressing, parmesan in pesto, lard in some refried beans and pastry, and the shared fryer. What to ask a kitchen, and why the shape of the question matters more than how politely you ask it. Whether eating this way is actually cheaper. What the honest downsides are. And at the end, a note to restaurants and food shops around the metro about what they ought to be publishing.

### What is vegan food exactly?

Vegan food contains no animal products at all. That means no meat, poultry or fish, and also no dairy, eggs or honey. Vegetarian food excludes meat but often still uses butter, milk, cheese and eggs. The difference shows up in the small stuff: stock, batter, dressing and the finish on a dish.

Vegetarian is the older and much looser word. A vegetarian menu section can be full of cheese, cream, eggs and butter, and usually is, because those are the easiest ways to make a plate of vegetables taste rich. So a dish being vegetarian tells a vegan diner almost nothing. Most of the time it is a starting point, not an answer.

### Where “plant-based” fits in

“Plant-based” is not a regulated term, and people use it two different ways. Some mean strictly vegan. Others mean mostly plants, with a little dairy or honey still in play. On a menu it usually signals intent rather than a guarantee. Treat it as a friendly sign that the kitchen has thought about it, then confirm the specifics anyway.

### Why the line is drawn where it is

People land on vegan eating for different reasons: animals, environment, health, religion, an allergy in the house, or simply a doctor’s suggestion to eat more plants. Those reasons change how strict somebody is about trace amounts. A guest avoiding dairy for a milk allergy needs a different answer about a shared pan than a guest avoiding it on principle. It costs nothing to ask which situation you are cooking for.

### What foods do vegans eat?

Ordinary food, mostly. Beans, lentils and chickpeas. Rice, oats, pasta, bread, potatoes and tortillas. Every vegetable and every fruit. Nuts, seeds, peanut butter, tofu and tempeh. Olive oil, vinegar, herbs, spices, chili crisp and hot sauce. Coffee, tea and most of what is already in a normal St. Louis pantry.

### The everyday base

A vegan week is built on the cheapest aisles in the store. Dried or canned beans, lentils, rice, oats, pasta, frozen vegetables, onions, garlic, potatoes, cabbage, carrots and whatever produce is in season. Add tofu, canned tomatoes, coconut milk and a decent spice shelf and you can cook chili, curry, stew, stir fry, pasta, tacos, soup and fried rice without ever visiting a specialty aisle.

### What stands in for dairy and eggs

Oat, soy, almond and cashew milks handle coffee, cereal and most baking. Olive oil, tahini, hummus, avocado and cashew cream do the job butter and cream were doing. Nutritional yeast gives a savory, cheesy note for a fraction of what vegan cheese costs. Eggs are the fiddly one: mashed banana or ground flax works in baking, and seasoned crumbled tofu covers breakfast. Boxed egg replacers exist and are convenient, and they are also the expensive route.

### Which ingredients are quietly not vegan?

The ones nobody lists on the menu. Butter and cream finishing a vegetable dish. Chicken or beef stock in soup, rice and beans. Eggs in fresh pasta, batter and mayonnaise. Honey. Gelatin in marshmallows and gummy candy. Whey and casein in things that look dairy-free. Anchovy in Worcestershire and Caesar dressing. Parmesan in pesto. Lard in some refried beans and pastry.

### Butter, cream and stock

This is the big one, and it is where Gene and Ruthie both got caught. Butter is a finishing move, not an ingredient anybody thinks to mention: it goes into risotto, mashed potatoes, sauteed vegetables, grits, pasta sauce and the pan the bread is toasted in. Stock is the same story on the savory side. Rice, greens, beans, gravy and soup are all commonly built on chicken or beef broth even when nothing in the bowl looks like meat.

### Eggs, honey and gelatin

Fresh pasta is usually made with egg. So is most batter on fried vegetables, most mayonnaise, and a lot of baked goods that get an egg wash on top. Honey turns up in salad dressings, marinades, cornbread, granola and plenty of drinks. Gelatin, which comes from animal collagen, sits in marshmallows, many gummy candies, some marshmallow-topped desserts, and a few yogurt-style products. None of the three announce themselves.

### The ones hiding on the label

Whey and casein are milk proteins, and they show up in bread, crackers, chips, protein bars, seasoning blends and some products marketed as non-dairy. “Non-dairy” on a package is a marketing phrase, not a promise. A few other names worth knowing: lactose, ghee, carmine or cochineal for red coloring, isinglass in some drinks, and lard or tallow in pastry, tamales and refried beans. Reading a label gets fast quickly, but the first few weeks are slow.

### Anchovy, parmesan and the shared fryer

Worcestershire sauce usually contains anchovy, which pulls in anything it seasons. Classic Caesar dressing has anchovy too. Pesto is typically finished with parmesan, and traditional parmesan is made with animal rennet, so even a vegetarian is on shaky ground with it. Then there is the fryer. If the fries share oil with breaded chicken or fish, they are not vegan, no matter how the potato started out. Same idea for a shared grill surface or one busy saute pan.

### What should you ask a St. Louis kitchen?

Ask “can this be made vegan?” instead of “is this vegan?” The first question sends a server to the kitchen with a task. The second invites a guess, and the guess is usually optimistic, because most people hear “vegan” and mentally check only for meat.

Then get specific about the three things that go wrong most. Is there butter or cream in it, including at the finish? Is the stock vegetable, or chicken or beef? Is the fryer shared with anything breaded? Those three questions catch the overwhelming majority of accidents. Add a fourth if there is bread, pasta or dessert involved: does it have egg?

Timing helps more than people expect. Ask when you order, not after the plate lands, and if you are going somewhere new, call in the mid-afternoon lull rather than at seven on a Friday. A cook with five minutes to think will tell you honestly which two dishes work and what changes on each one. A cook in the middle of a rush will tell you what gets you off the phone.

### How to shortlist a place before you go

Pick two or three spots worth calling and give each one the same short summary. One vegan in the party, no dairy or eggs, and here is when we want to come in. Then compare the answers. One kitchen says “we can do the pasta with oil and no cheese, and the beans are made with vegetable stock.” Another says “we have a salad.” A third says “everything is fine, we have vegetarian options.” That third answer is the one to be careful with, because it is answering a different question.

You are not asking anyone to itemize their recipes or prove anything. You are asking what the kitchen can do on a normal Tuesday, and listening for whether the person on the phone knows the difference between vegetarian and vegan. That single detail predicts how the night goes better than the size of the menu does.

### Is it cheaper to eat a vegan diet?

It depends entirely on which cart you fill. Beans, lentils, rice, oats, potatoes, frozen vegetables, seasonal produce and tofu are among the cheapest calories in any grocery store. Meat substitutes, specialty cheeses, boxed egg replacers and frozen convenience meals are not. Same diet on paper, wildly different receipts.

That is the whole honest answer, and it is the part most articles skip. A pot of lentil soup and a pan of rice and beans will beat almost any meat-based meal on cost. A cart built around vegan burger patties, cashew cheese, oat milk creamer and frozen entrees will cost more than the meat version of the same week. Nobody is wrong for buying the second cart. It just should not be a surprise.

Restaurants follow the same rule. A vegetable-forward plate at a neighborhood spot in Shaw or on The Hill is often the cheapest thing on the menu. A specialty vegan version of a comfort dish, built on substitutes, usually is not. Prices move constantly and vary by block, so do not take a figure off an article, this one included.

### What is the cheapest way to eat vegan?

Cook dry beans and lentils, buy rice and oats in the big bag, use frozen vegetables without apology, and let the seasonal produce decide the menu instead of the recipe deciding it. Skip the substitutes almost entirely. That single choice is the difference between the cheap version of this and the expensive one.

A few habits do most of the work. Cook once and eat twice, because a pot of chili or curry costs barely more than a single portion. Keep a short list of meals you can make without a recipe: beans and rice, lentil soup, pasta with garlic and olive oil, chickpea curry, fried rice with whatever is in the drawer, oatmeal, baked potatoes with beans and hot sauce, tofu tacos. Buy spices from the bulk bins or the international aisle, where the same jar of cumin often costs a fraction of the branded version.

Shop the sales and the seasons. Cabbage, carrots, onions, potatoes and sweet potatoes hold for weeks and cost very little. Frozen spinach, corn, peas and mixed vegetables are picked ripe and never go bad in the crisper drawer, which quietly saves more money than most coupon strategies do. Farmers markets around the metro get cheap late in the day and late in the season, and produce stands from Jefferson County to St. Charles County price by the box in high summer.

One more thing worth saying plainly. Treat the substitutes as a treat rather than a staple. A package of vegan sausage on a Friday is fine. Building every dinner around one is what makes people say vegan eating is expensive, and they are right when that is the cart.

Grocery budget stretched thin? The St. Louis Diaper Bank helps families cover essentials.

### Is going vegan actually healthier?

A diet built on whole plants, beans, vegetables, fruit, whole grains, nuts and seeds, is generally associated with good health outcomes. But “vegan” describes what is absent, not what is present. Fries, soda and packaged snacks are all vegan. The pattern matters far more than the label on it.

This article is not medical advice, and you should talk to a doctor or a registered dietitian about your own situation, especially if you are pregnant, nursing, feeding a child, managing a chronic condition or taking medication. What can be said generally is that a well-planned vegan diet works for a lot of people, and a poorly planned one causes problems that are entirely avoidable with a little attention.

### The nutrients worth planning for

Vitamin B12 is the one that genuinely requires attention. It is not reliably available from plant foods, so it comes from fortified foods or a supplement, and that is not optional over the long run. Iron, calcium, omega-3 fats, iodine and vitamin D are the others worth planning for rather than assuming. Protein is usually fine when beans, lentils, tofu, nuts and whole grains show up regularly, though it does take a little more thought than most people expect at the start.

### What’s the downside of being vegan?

Social friction, label reading, thin restaurant options in some neighborhoods, nutrient planning that does not manage itself, and the real cost of convenience products. None of that is fatal, and pretending the downsides do not exist is how people quit in month three feeling like they failed at something.

The social part is the one nobody warns you about. Family dinners get complicated. Work lunches get complicated. Somebody cooks for you with real affection and gets the green beans wrong, and now you are managing their feelings while hungry. In our experience the households that handle it well do one simple thing: the vegan brings a dish big enough to share, every time, without being asked. It removes the whole negotiation.

The practical part is label reading, which is genuinely tedious for a few weeks and then becomes automatic. Restaurant availability varies a lot across the metro. A neighborhood full of independent kitchens gives you more to work with than a stretch of highway exits in Wright City or a quick stop in Dupo, so a road trip takes a little planning. And convenience is where the money goes. The cheapest vegan week and the most expensive one differ only in how much cooking happens.

Not sure where to eat this weekend? You can browse vegan food on St Louis Near Me Directory, pick two or three places worth calling, and give each one the same short summary: one vegan in the party, no dairy or eggs, and here is when we want to come in. What comes back, and how confidently, tells you plenty before you spend an evening on it.

### For St. Louis restaurants and food shops

Think about Ruthie in that Southampton dining room, happily eating a risotto she would not have ordered if she had known. She was not looking for a special menu. She was looking for one sentence that nobody had written down.

So write it down. Mark dishes vegan, not just vegetarian, because the two words are doing completely different jobs and only one of them answers the question. Say whether your stock is vegetable or chicken. Say what the fryer is shared with, plainly, even when the answer is “everything.” Note which dishes can be made vegan on request and what actually changes: no butter finish, no cheese, oil instead of cream. That last line is the one diners screenshot and send to their friends.

Then put it on the online menu, not in the server’s head. Menus in a diner’s hand at 6pm are the ones that get read, and a server on a busy Friday cannot be the single point of truth for an ingredient question. Shops can do the same with a short page on which sections carry plant milks, tofu, tempeh, nutritional yeast and vegan baking staples, and whether the deli or bakery counter has anything without dairy or egg. A little of this in writing turns a maybe into a table, and it costs nothing but an afternoon.

### Frequently asked questions

### Q. Can vegans eat fish?

A.  No. Fish and shellfish are animals, so they are not vegan, and neither are fish sauce, oyster sauce or the anchovy in Worcestershire and classic Caesar dressing. People who eat fish but no other meat are usually described as pescatarian, which is a different thing entirely. This matters at a restaurant, because a “seafood only” dish is sometimes offered as the vegetarian substitute when it is neither.

### Q. Do vegans eat potatoes?

A.  Yes. Potatoes are a plant, and they are one of the cheapest and most useful staples in a vegan kitchen: baked, roasted, mashed, in soup, in curry, in tacos. The catch is what happens to them. Mashed potatoes are usually made with butter and milk, restaurant fries often share a fryer with breaded meat, and some potato salads are bound with egg-based mayonnaise.

### Q. Can vegans eat ice cream?

A.  Not dairy ice cream, which is made from milk and cream and often eggs. Vegan versions do exist and are widely sold, usually built on oat, coconut, almond, soy or cashew bases, and plenty of sorbets are dairy-free by nature. Check the label rather than the front of the package, since “non-dairy” is a marketing phrase and some products still contain whey or casein.

### Q. Are bananas vegan?

A.  Yes. Bananas are fruit, so they are vegan, and they double as a useful egg replacement in baking when you mash about half a banana per egg. The question comes up because a few producers have used a coating to slow ripening, and some coatings are not animal-free. For everyday purposes a banana is a banana, and it is not a thing most vegans think twice about.

### Q. What are some cheap vegan meals?

A.  Rice and beans with hot sauce. Lentil soup. Pasta with garlic, olive oil and whatever green is in the crisper. Chickpea curry with frozen spinach. Fried rice with frozen mixed vegetables and tofu. Baked potatoes topped with beans. Oatmeal with peanut butter and banana. Chili made from two cans of beans and one of tomatoes. All of them scale up cheaply and reheat well.

### Q. What is the average cost of a vegan diet?

A.  There is no honest average to hand you, because the range is enormous and prices move constantly. A cart of dried beans, lentils, rice, oats, potatoes and frozen vegetables is among the cheapest ways anyone eats. A cart of meat substitutes, specialty cheeses and frozen entrees costs more than the meat version of the same week. Track your own receipts for a month; that number is the only one that applies to you.

### Q. Is a vegetarian dish automatically vegan?

A.  No, and this is the single most common mix-up. Vegetarian only rules out meat, so a vegetarian dish can still contain butter, cream, cheese, milk, eggs or honey, and it very often does. Menus label things vegetarian far more often than vegan. Treat the vegetarian section as the shortlist to ask about, not as the answer.

### Q. How do you ask whether a dish can be made vegan?

A.  Ask “can this be made vegan?” rather than “is this vegan?” The first sends someone to the kitchen; the second invites a guess. Then name the three usual culprits: butter or cream, including at the finish, chicken or beef stock, and a shared fryer. Ask at ordering rather than afterward, and call ahead in the mid-afternoon lull if the place is new to you.
